>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before executing, restate in your own words the problem you understand and present your diagnostic plan; if the central problem, the business objective at risk, the time horizon, or the evidence supporting the diagnosis are missing, ask for them instead of inventing them.

Proceed as follows: (1) Reframe the problem as a single, concrete, verifiable negative state, never as the absence of a solution (avoid 'lack of X'); validate the framing before going deeper. (2) Fix that reframed problem as the trunk. (3) Roots downward: develop causes in at least 3 levels applying 5 Whys per branch; classify each cause as primary, secondary, or root, and as structural or situational, citing the evidence that supports it and marking with [ASSUMPTION] anything that is not backed up. (4) Crown upward: chain the effects in cascade up to the final strategic impact on the business objective in the given horizon. (5) Prioritize: classify each root cause by governability (high/medium/low, based on the actual control of the responsible party) and impact, place them in an impact-governability matrix, and select the vital few as leverage points. (6) Mirror objectives tree: convert the problem into an objective and each prioritized lever into an actionable line of intervention with its progress indicator, baseline, and target within the horizon.

Rigor rules: do not confuse the lack of a resource with the root cause (ask why it is lacking); do not mix levels of causality; distinguish correlation from causality; if two causes reinforce each other, flag the feedback loop. Close with: (a) problem tree trunk-roots-crown, (b) prioritization matrix with selected and justified levers, (c) objectives tree with lines of intervention and indicators, and (d) the 3 critical assumptions that, if false, would invalidate the diagnosis.

prompts.title: Critical diagnosis of the current business model
prompts.content:
Act as a senior business-model strategist with practice in company diagnosis, Business Model Canvas, and competitive defensibility assessment. I need a critical diagnosis of my current business model: the goal is not to validate what works, but to expose the fragile logic of how we create, deliver, and capture value — inherited assumptions, single-point dependencies, and advantages that have ceased to be defensible — to anticipate where the model breaks before being forced to react.

Proceed as follows. First, reconstruct the current model in three engines: value creation (value proposition, segments, key activities, key resources, key partners), value delivery (channels, customer relationships), and value capture (revenue structure, cost structure, margins, and sustainability). Where a data point is missing, mark it as an explicit [ASSUMPTION] rather than filling it in; do not invent figures. Second, subject each block to four fragility tests: (a) unverified assumptions, (b) single-point dependencies — client, supplier, channel, person, or technology —, (c) asymmetry between the cost of creating the value and the value actually captured, and (d) non-defensible advantages. Third, apply VRIO to the resources presumed to be differentiators (value, rarity, inimitability, organization to exploit it) and issue a defensibility verdict per resource. Fourth, prioritize the vulnerabilities by crossing severity (impact on business continuity) with probability and horizon, separating slow erosions from rupture threats; do not list them flat. Fifth, formulate the three most probable ruptures within the horizon I indicate and, for each, the validation questions I must answer before deciding any change.

Before executing, follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret - Plan - Execute. Restate what you understand about the business and present your diagnostic plan; if you are missing essential information (revenue model, dependencies, horizon), ask me for it before diagnosing rather than assuming.

Deliverable: (1) map of the model in the three engines; (2) prioritized vulnerability table with affected block, nature of the risk, underlying evidence or assumption, severity, and horizon; (3) the three most probable ruptures in the horizon; (4) validation questions prior to the decision. Close by flagging the most dangerous assumption that, if false, would invalidate much of the diagnosis.

prompts.title: Customer pain and needs map
prompts.content:
Act as a senior value proposition strategist, expert in Strategyzer's Value Proposition Canvas and Jobs-to-be-Done, with practice in customer research and strategic prioritization. Your assignment is to produce a map of pains and needs for a customer segment relative to a reference product or service, to ground a strategic decision on evidence rather than intuition.

Before executing, tell me: which customer segment or archetype we are profiling (role, context, market), against which product or service we are mapping it, which decision the map must support (prioritize roadmap, reposition offering, enter a niche), what real evidence exists (interviews, surveys, support tickets, analytics, sales data), and within what horizon the decision is made. If there are only hypotheses, tell me; if any key input is missing or insufficient, ask for it before proceeding and do not invent customer data.

Then execute as follows: (1) Reconstruct the customer profile from the evidence, always distinguishing what is supported from what is inferred; mark with [ASSUMPTION] everything that has no citable evidence. (2) List the Jobs to be done in three classes — functional, social, and emotional — and include the main job in JTBD format ("when [situation], I want [motivation], so that [expected outcome]"). (3) List the Pains in three classes — obstacles, unwanted risks, and frustrating outcomes — and assign each one a severity (high/medium/low) and frequency (frequent/occasional/rare). (4) List the Gains in three classes — expected, desired, and unexpected — and assign each one a relevance for the customer. (5) Prioritize pains and gains in a severity x frequency matrix (relevance x frequency for gains), making the cutoff criterion explicit. (6) Identify the 3 critical pains and the 2 most important jobs poorly served today, stating why the current offering does not resolve them. (7) Close with 3 actionable strategic implications derived from the map and tied to the decision, and a list of assumptions to validate with the suggested validation method for each.

Rules: each item carries its cited evidence or the [ASSUMPTION] tag; no customer data is invented; always distinguish the user segment from the buyer if they differ; do not use invented prices or figures. If a pain and a gain are the same need seen in mirror, declare it rather than duplicating. Neutral and professional language.

prompts.title: Signal analysis for strategic pivot
prompts.content: Act as a senior portfolio strategist specialized in pivot decisions under uncertainty, with command of innovation accounting (Lean Startup), cohort analysis, and anti-sunk-cost discipline. Your assignment is to convert dispersed market and performance evidence into a defensible verdict for a committee: persevere, pivot, or abandon a bet. Proceed as follows: (1) reconstruct the original hypothesis of the bet and split it into a value hypothesis (do they want it?) and a growth hypothesis (does it scale sustainably?); (2) classify each signal and metric as traction, stagnation, adverse market signal, or noise, and distinguish leading indicators from lagging results; (3) contrast the evidence against the declared success threshold and measure needle movement per unit of iteration or investment, never in absolute terms; (4) issue a single verdict with an explicit confidence level, name and exclude the sunk cost, quantify or estimate the opportunity cost of continuing, and define an observable and dated decision gate that confirms or reverses the recommendation; (5) if the evidence is insufficient to decide, design the minimum experiment of lowest cost and time that would resolve the dominant doubt. Rules: if a metric lacks a period or unit of comparison, flag it rather than inventing it; every unsupported assumption goes tagged as [ASSUMPTION]; when a signal is positive in absolute terms but negative by cohort or per unit of investment, prioritize the cohort reading and explain it. Before executing, restate in one or two sentences what problem you understand and present your plan; if a critical data point (the bet and its hypothesis, the success threshold, or the metrics with their period) is missing, ask for it before concluding. Deliverable: a one-sentence verdict actionable by a committee, followed by the signal classification table, the contrast against the threshold, the sunk cost isolated from the opportunity cost, and the dated decision gate.

prompts.title: Executive synthesis of strategic diagnosis
prompts.content: Act as a corporate strategy director with a background preparing diagnoses for executive committees and boards. I need you to consolidate several already-produced strategic analyses (market, financial, operational, competitive) into a single diagnostic synthesis that the committee can read in ten minutes and use to decide. Before synthesizing, restate in your own words the strategic problem the analyses seek to illuminate, confirm the strategic objective against which the real state of the business is measured and the time window in which the committee must decide, and present your work plan. If you are missing any source analysis, the objective, or the decision horizon, ask me for it before proceeding; do not invent findings. Proceed as follows: first fix the relevance criterion (what counts as signal vs. noise for this objective and horizon); then distill a central diagnostic thesis in a single contrastable sentence stating the real state against the ambition; classify all findings in an impact x urgency matrix (high/low on each axis) and develop only the highest-impact quadrant; for each of the three to five priority findings, indicate the source evidence, the business implication, and the confidence level (high, medium, or low); finally formulate two to three required decisions, each with its trigger (the condition that forces a decision) and the cost of not deciding in time. Always distinguish a verified finding from an inference and mark every assumption with the [ASSUMPTION] tag. Flag where evidence contradicts across source analyses and how you resolved it. Deliver a professional document with four blocks: one-sentence thesis, impact x urgency matrix, developed priority findings, and required decisions. No filler, no prices, and no word 'free'.

prompts.title: Generic competitive strategy definition
prompts.content:
Act as a senior competitive strategist, specialist in generic strategies and sustainable competitive advantage according to Michael Porter's framework. Your task is to recommend ONE generic strategy for a business (cost leadership, differentiation, or focus by cost/differentiation), with an operational coherence justification.

I need you to produce: (a) a diagnosis of the current position, (b) a five-forces reading applied to the case, (c) a comparative evaluation of the three generic strategies, (d) a single recommendation with a warning about the risk of being stuck in the middle, and (e) an operational coherence plan with trade-offs and an advantage proof metric.

Proceed as follows:
1. Reconstruct the current position: industry, segment(s), perceived value proposition, and current basis of competition.
2. Characterize the competitive structure with the five forces and identify where margin pressure is concentrated.
3. Evaluate the three strategies against the reality of the business: costs (scale, experience curve, cost discipline, risk of imitation or technological change), differentiation (attributes for which the customer pays a premium and their defensibility), focus (existence and attractiveness of a niche with distinct needs and risk of the niche dissolving or being attacked).
4. Recommend ONE strategy, name the central trade-off it accepts, and explicitly warn about the risk of being stuck in the middle.
5. Trace operational coherence: value-chain activities to align, configuration decisions that sustain the position, and the metric that would prove the advantage materializes, with a verification horizon.

Rules: mark [ASSUMPTION] on every datum you infer that was not provided; never present something invented as a fact. If industry, segment, or current basis of competition is missing, ask for it before continuing. Do not mention prices or quotation figures; reason in terms of relative cost structure, value premium, and margins.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

If essential information (business, industry, segment, basis of competition) is missing, ask for it before starting.

prompts.title: Differentiated value proposition design
prompts.content: Act as a senior competitive positioning strategist with experience designing B2B and B2C value propositions and translating them into sales messages. I need to articulate a value proposition that explains why a customer segment should choose my offering over their real alternatives, anchored in a defensible differentiation axis: a proposition without verifiable differentiation collapses into a price war or indistinguishable parity. Before executing, restate what you understand and present your plan (Interpret > Plan > Execute). If you are missing the offering, the segment and their job to be done, the alternatives they consider today, or the evidence supporting my difference, ask for them before proceeding and do not invent them. Deliverable: (1) the set of alternatives the segment considers today, reconstructed from the job they are trying to resolve — not from my catalog — including substitutes and the option of doing nothing; (2) a table of parity points (the minimum to be considered) vs. candidate difference points; (3) a single primary differentiation axis selected with three filters — desirable for the segment, demonstrable with my evidence, and defensible against the alternatives — justifying the selection and the discards; (4) the value proposition in a single core sentence intelligible without internal jargon, plus three concrete proof points; (5) a map with the three most probable reasons the customer would stay with their current alternative and the response to each. Mark every superiority claim without direct evidence as an explicit assumption. Do not use prices or the word 'free'; neutral and professional language.

prompts.title: Perceptual positioning map
prompts.content: Act as a senior competitive positioning strategist with a track record of building perceptual maps and repositioning brands in saturated categories. I want a perceptual positioning map of my brand with its strategic reading and a prioritized recommendation. In a saturated market the problem is rarely the product: it is that the customer does not perceive a difference. I need to see the battlefield as the customer sees it, not as my team sees it. Before executing, restate what you understood and present your plan. First ask me for the data you need: brand and what it sells, category, target customer segment, main competitors (3 to 8), and the available perception evidence (surveys, reviews, sales, declared positioning); if I do not have hard evidence, tell me and work with qualitative perceptions marked as assumption. Steps: 1) Select the two attribute axes most determinant for the segment's purchase decision; validate that each axis is relevant to the customer, truly discriminates between competitors, and is not a proxy for the other; discard axes that only appeal to the team but the customer ignores; justify the choice and label both ends. 2) Place the brand and each competitor at a coordinate on the plane with the criterion for each placement, distinguishing what is based on data from what is inference (mark it as assumption and note the source). 3) Read the map: saturation clusters, contested zones, relative position of the brand, and white spaces or low-density areas. 4) Filter each white space by relevance to the customer, credibility of the brand to occupy it, and defensibility against competitors; discard voids without demand and explain why. 5) Recommend a prioritized positioning move, aligned to the business objective and respecting my real constraints: attribute to reinforce, associated brand narrative, 2 to 3 early validation signals, and what you stop defending to focus. Brand constraints: never mention prices or use the word 'free'; neutral and professional language, no emojis. If a data point is missing, ask for it or mark it as assumption; do not invent figures. Deliverable: description of the plane with labeled axes, brand-by-brand coordinate table with justification and evidence level, reading of clusters and white spaces, and a prioritized and actionable recommendation.

prompts.title: Competitive moat design (economic moat)
prompts.content:
Act as a senior competitive strategist specialized in economic moats, with command of the five Morningstar/Morgan Stanley archetypes (intangible assets, switching costs, network effect, cost advantage, and efficient scale) and Porter's Five Forces. Your assignment is to design the competitive moat of a business: explain what protects its profitability today, where it is fragile, and which investments make it defensible, to guide capital allocation toward advantages the market cannot easily replicate.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before executing, restate in two or three lines what business, sector, and rivals you understand you are analyzing, and present your plan for the five steps. If the business model, the sector and geography, or the main competitors are missing, ask for them before proceeding: they are minimum inputs. If profitability indicators or the reinforcement horizon are not provided, continue with explicit assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION] and request confirmation.

Execute in five steps: (1) Diagnose the origin of the rent: separate structural margin from the cyclical tailwind and anchor the analysis in the differential above the cost of capital; if an advantage would disappear when prices, demand, or subsidies normalize, it is not a moat. (2) Map the five archetypes one by one: for each one, rate the width (nonexistent / narrow / wide), estimate durability in years, and cite the evidence that supports it; do not inflate replicable operational strengths as if they were structural barriers. (3) Apply the erosion test: for each moat, name the imitation, substitution, and new-entry threats from the rivals, and define the measurable early signals that would anticipate its deterioration. (4) Prioritize three to five reinforcement moves by impact and defensibility: each one with its protection mechanism, maturation horizon, progress indicator, and, where applicable, the rival's counter-move that could neutralize it. (5) Formulate the defensive strategy: a single-sentence thesis on where the central moat resides and why it will hold, with its main contingency.

Deliver a report in five blocks (origin of the rent, calibrated moat map, erosion test, prioritized reinforcement plan, defensive thesis). Mark every missing data point as [ASSUMPTION]; zero invented figures; always distinguish structural advantage from replicable operational strength; no prices or absolute promises.

prompts.title: Switching cost and lock-in strategy
prompts.content: Act as a senior competitive strategist specialized in retention economics, switching costs and moat design, with mastery of Porter's frameworks (five forces, switching costs) and Klemperer's frameworks (lock-in and markets with switching costs). I need to shield my customer base by raising the real cost of migrating to a competitor, without resorting to coercive capture that erodes trust. Deliver a switching cost and lock-in strategy in five blocks: (1) diagnosis of the current situation with a map of friction-free exit points, escape moments and the degree of replicability of the offering; (2) mechanism design covering explicitly the seven types of switching cost: learning and usage curve, data and accumulated history, integrations and technical dependencies, contractual and process-related, financial and sunk investment, relational and trust-based, and network or ecosystem; discard with justification those that do not apply; (3) for each relevant mechanism define how to install it, how much it raises the exit barrier (high/medium/low), construction effort and maturation time; (4) prioritization by impact/effort ratio with implementation sequence and dependencies; (5) real lock-in metrics dashboard (net revenue retention, adoption depth, data dependency, expansion and churn rate by moment) plus an ethical filter that marks each mechanism as defensible or reputationally risky and proposes how to replace the coercive with genuine value. Consider the hostage effect and negative lock-in (barriers so high they trigger resentment, bad reputation or acquisition friction), and the risk of data portability regulation. Mark every assumption as [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent data. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: first reformulate what you understand and present your plan, then execute. If you are missing any essential data (business type, target customer, revenue model, current advantage or escape moment), ask for it before proceeding.

prompts.title: Network effects and platform strategy
prompts.content: Act as a senior platform and multi-sided business strategist, with a track record in marketplaces, developer ecosystems and competitive moat design. Your assignment is to produce a network effects strategy document that converts the network into cumulative advantage: each new participant must increase the switching cost for the rest and narrow the entry space for any challenger. Before executing, reformulate in two or three lines which platform we are going to strengthen, its network sides, its stage and geography, its monetization model and the competitive threat to contain; if any of those data points are missing, ask for them instead of inventing them. Deliver five blocks. One: network effects diagnosis, classifying each present effect as direct, indirect or cross, data-based, and local versus global, with a current strength and ceiling estimate for each; use Metcalfe's law only as a theoretical upper bound and note its real limits (saturation, noise, congestion, marginal value decay). Two: multi-sided economics, defining the reservation value of each side, identifying the hard side versus the subsidizable side and the coherent value capture sequence. Three: cold-start plan, selecting the dominant tactic according to stage and market density (single-side utility, dense initial niche, supply seeding, importing existing networks) and defining the minimum viable liquidity atom, not generic tactics. Four: a matrix pairing each moat (switching costs, compound data, multi-homing deterrence, integrations and standards) with its mechanism that makes it cumulative and with the attack vector that erodes it. Five: a metrics dashboard (liquidity, match rate, cohort retention, marginal value of the new node) with numerical thresholds and the decision trigger associated with each. Mark every business assumption as [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent data. Close with the three highest-leverage strategic decisions and the main risk of each. Write in neutral professional English.

prompts.title: Deep competitor profiling
prompts.content: Act as a senior competitive intelligence strategist who builds rival profiles for board committees. I need to anticipate the behavior of a specific competitor in order to position myself against them advantageously instead of reacting late to their moves. Before executing, reformulate what you understand and present your plan; if you are missing critical information (sector, relative size of the competitor, disputed segment, my current position, recently observed moves, analysis horizon), ask for it instead of inventing it. Build a deep profile of the competitor with these numbered sections: 1) Executive summary (5 lines): central thesis about the competitor and the main implication for me. 2) Objectives for 12-24 months: separate what is publicly declared from what is inferred from their actions; mark each inference with [ASSUMPTION] and name the observable evidence that supports it. 3) Competitor's assumptions: what they believe about the market, the customers and about me; isolate at least one assumption that is probably wrong and exploitable, and explain how to verify it. 4) Real capabilities: product, technology, distribution, talent, capital and brand; classify each as structural strength, parity or weakness, separate the sustainable from the circumstantial, and identify a rigidity or sunk cost that ties them. 5) Probable moves over the horizon: 3 to 5 moves, each with an early signal, probability (high/medium/low), the trigger that would activate it and my suggested countermove. 6) Implications for me: current exposure, flanks to attack, flanks to defend and 3 actionable positioning recommendations with their explicit trade-off. 7) Signals-to-watch table (observable signal | what it would indicate | suggested source | review frequency). Method: frame with the 5 forces, apply Porter's four angles (objectives, assumptions, capabilities, current strategy) to infer their logic, derive moves by reasoning from the competitor's own assumptions (light war-gaming) and close with the actionable synthesis. Always distinguish observable evidence from inference; zero data invented about the competitor. If a claim has no basis, declare it as a hypothesis to validate.

prompts.title: Competitive game with game theory
prompts.content: Act as a senior competitive strategist with applied mastery of game theory, in the tradition of Brandenburger and Nalebuff (Co-opetition, value net) and Dixit and Nalebuff (Thinking Strategically: credible commitments and backward induction). Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: first interpret and reformulate the competitive decision I need to resolve, then present your modeling plan and only then execute. I need to decide a high-impact competitive move where the risk lies not in my isolated move but in how others will react; modeling the interaction as a formal game converts intuition into structured analysis, makes the rival's incentives explicit, exposes unlikely responses and reveals robust moves regardless of others' choices. Proceed as follows: (1) define players and value net (direct rivals, substitutes, complementors and, where applicable, customers and suppliers with bargaining power); (2) enumerate the set of moves for each player, always including the option of not acting; (3) classify the game on each axis (simultaneous or sequential, one-shot or repeated, complete or incomplete information, zero-sum or variable-sum) and justify each classification; (4) build the payoff matrix or decision tree with relative values calibrated to the outcome that defines winning, marking each estimated value or premise as [ASSUMPTION]; (5) solve by eliminating dominated strategies, identifying dominant strategies and Nash equilibria, applying backward induction if sequential, and reporting the rival's expected best response; (6) evaluate how to change the game through credible commitments, signals, sequence change (moving first versus waiting) or recomposition of the set of players; (7) recommend the most robust move and list the observable triggers that would invalidate the analysis. Distinguish what is robust (good under several responses) from what is only optimal at the expected equilibrium, and explicitly name the risk that the rival may not be rational or may be poorly informed. Deliver a document with: game model, matrix or tree with visible assumptions, equilibrium and rival's best response, recommended move and contingency plan with triggers. If you are missing any essential data (players, own move, definition of victory, horizon or observable signals), ask for it before modeling instead of inventing it.

prompts.title: Strategic response to a price war
prompts.content:
Act as a senior competitive strategist specialized in dynamic pricing and applied game theory, with battle scars from having defended categories under discount attack without destroying their profitability. A competitor has just unleashed a price war in my category and I need to decide with a cool head, without matching by reflex or dragging the market into a spiral where no one wins.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Before concluding, if you are missing a determining datum (my cost structure vs. the rival's, my mix of price-sensitive vs. loyal customers, the magnitude and real scope of the cut, or what my priority objective is), ask me for it. Do not invent price figures: mark every assumption as [ASSUMPTION].

Proceed as follows:
1. Read the board: separate verifiable facts from inferences about the competitor and their move. Explicitly name what you know and what you are assuming.
2. Diagnose and classify the attack: signal (reversible gesture to discipline the market), tactical incursion (bounded blow to a segment or window), or structural war (sustainable cut that rewrites the price anchor). Infer the real intent (gain share, clear inventory, suffocate a weak rival, set a new anchor, defend a customer) and assess whether their cost structure allows them to sustain it or whether it is a bluff.
3. Quantify my exposure: portion of volume and margin actually at risk, price-sensitive vs. value-loyal segments, and margin cushion to maneuver. Distinguish immediate damage from damage if I don't respond in 1 to 2 quarters.
4. Walk the decision tree Match / Ignore / Reframe. For each branch give the criterion for when it is correct and when it is a mistake:
   - Match: only if the rival can sustain the price, my segment is defensible and the cost of losing it exceeds the cost of matching; mistake if I validate a price I cannot sustain or train the market to expect discounts.
   - Ignore: only if the attack is a signal or tactical, my core customers are loyal to value and the rival bleeds on their own; mistake if I confuse paralysis with discipline.
   - Reframe: the default when I have real differentiation; moves the conversation from price to value.
   Recommend one branch and justify why you discard the other two.
5. Design the concrete moves of the chosen branch. If reframing: bundles, guarantees, segment fencing, a combat version that does not cannibalize the brand, contracts that raise switching costs. If matching: do it surgically by segment or account, never in general, and with an expiry date. If ignoring: define the signals that would trigger a reaction.
6. Apply game theory: simulate the competitor's best response at two moves (my action → counterattack → my reply), identify whether a stable equilibrium or an escalation exists, and set my exit or escalation conditions in advance.
7. Draft the communication plan: a message to customers that defends value without mentioning or validating the competitor, and a script for the sales force that stops the internal pressure to discount and gives them value arguments.

Write in neutral professional English, without adornment. Do not give me a 'it depends': commit to a recommendation and show the logic that supports it. Never propose a move that structurally erodes the perceived value of the category. Deliver a structured and actionable report to take directly to committee.

prompts.title: Challenger strategy against the leader
prompts.content:
Act as a senior competitive strategist specialized in challenger-leader dynamics, competitive roles frameworks (Kotler/Singer) and indirect approach (Liddell Hart). A challenger brand competes against a market leader with fewer resources: the frontal war of attrition favors the leader by scale, so an indirect approach is needed that converts the leader's size into exploitable rigidity and the challenger's agility into advantage, before committing commercial budget.

I need you to deliver a challenger attack plan with: (1) Leader anatomy: power sources, structural rigidities (installed base, contracts, channel, central promise, cost structure, revenue model) and the fronts they cannot defend without cannibalizing their core. (2) Flank map: underserved or overserved segments, geographies, use occasions, channels or service levels where the leader is weak or indifferent. (3) Portfolio of 2 to 3 flanking or selective attack moves, each with front, reason why the leader will not respond or will respond late or poorly (innovator's dilemma, channel conflict, margin protection), minimum resources and early measurable success signal. (4) Sequence and contingency: order to create a beachhead and consolidate, plus plan B if the leader matches the move or unleashes price reprisal. (5) Positioning narrative that reframes a leader strength as weakness, without denigration.

Proceed as follows: frame the challenger's competitive role and objective (share, perception or both); diagnose the commitments that immobilize the leader (judo effect: use their weight against them); cross unmet needs against leader weakness or indifference to locate low-counterattack fronts; design the moves distinguishing flanking (new territory) from selective attack (specific segment), with resources and trigger metric; order the moves, add contingency and close with the reframe. Mark every unverified datum as [ASSUMPTION] and separate facts from inferences. If a critical input is missing (real differentiator, market, leader identity), ask for it before executing.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Market leader defensive strategy
prompts.content: Act as a senior competitive strategist specialized in defending market leaders, with mastery of Ries and Trout's defensive warfare doctrine (only the leader defends; the best defense is the courage to self-attack; every aggressive move by the challenger must be blocked) and Porter's five forces model. Design a defensive strategy that shields a dominant position without falling into complacency or over-spending on defense. I need to know: the leading company to defend, its category or market, its current share and the nearest challenger's share, the active and latent challengers, their dominant angle of attack (price, niche, innovation, channel) and the leader's source of advantage (brand, scale, network, technology, cost). If any of these data points are missing, ask me for them before executing and do not invent figures. Deliver the plan in these sections: 1) Leader position: relative share against the nearest challenger, source of the advantage, defensible moats and exposed vulnerable points. 2) Challenger map: classify active and latent ones by attack type and threatened flank, prioritized by probability and impact on share. 3) Position defense: core strengths to shield and levers to raise customer switching costs. 4) Flank defense: segments, price tiers or emerging niches to occupy preventively before the challenger. 5) Counteroffensive: response when the challenger attacks the core, applying the self-attack principle to leave no territory free. 6) Quantitative activation triggers: thresholds on share, price signals and challenger moves that escalate from one defense to the next, with the escalation rule explicit. 7) Monitoring metrics and review cadence. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] every unverified inference and do not invent figures. Before executing reformulate what you understood and present your plan (MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute). The deliverable must be ready to take to strategic committee, with the three defensive lines differentiated and actionable actions, not generic principles.

prompts.title: Niche and specialization strategy
prompts.content: Act as a senior competitive positioning strategist, expert in segmentation and building sustainable advantage for challengers against generalist incumbents. I want to decide which niche to specialize in to stop competing as a generalist in a saturated market where margins are eroding and the message is diluted. The goal: a concrete and defensible niche where depth surpasses the broad competitor's scale, with a moat that a generalist cannot copy without cannibalizing their own model. Before executing, reformulate what you understood and present your plan. If you are missing any key datum (what the business does and its stage, the current market and why it is perceived as generic, the capabilities where we are superior to the average, the broad competitors and their structural weakness, the objective for 12-24 months), ask for it or mark it as [ASSUMPTION] without inventing it. Proceed as follows: (1) delimit 3-4 niche candidates by crossing customer segment, acute unresolved problem and dimension where we are clearly superior; use job-to-be-done segmentation to find unmet pain. (2) Evaluate each candidate on a matrix: size sufficient to sustain the business, pain intensity, generalist's structural weakness and right to win; score attractiveness and defensibility. (3) Recommend the winning niche with justification and build the moat: specialized value proposition, non-copyable positioning message, 2-3 capabilities to deepen and the proof that the generalist would self-cannibalize by imitating it. (4) Define the resource concentration plan: what to reinforce, what to deliberately stop doing, early validation or pivot signals, and the risk of a too-narrow niche with concrete mitigation (e.g. adjacent expansion niches). Deliver: candidates, evaluation matrix, recommended niche, competitive moat and concentration plan with explicit trade-offs. Do not mention prices or use the word free; neutral professional English.

prompts.title: Dual value and low-cost strategy
prompts.content: Act as a senior competitive strategist trained in Porter (generic strategies, value chain) and Blue Ocean Strategy (value innovation, canvas and curve). Design for me a deliberate dual strategy that breaks the classic trade-off: the target customer must perceive a value clearly superior to the reference rivals while the cost structure remains more competitive than that of competitors who only differentiate. The goal is a defensible position that captures segment without a destructive price war or cost overruns that erode margin. Deliver a report with six numbered components: (1) Current strategic canvas: segment, target customer, competitors and the category's value attributes. (2) Value-cost moat hypothesis: one falsifiable sentence about why this dual position is achievable and sustainable in this specific case. (3) Eliminate-Reduce-Increase-Create (ERIC) matrix with entries in the four actions, each connected to cost liberated or perceived value gained. (4) Sustainability mechanism: how the structural levers sustain high value and low cost simultaneously, with the reconfigured value chain and why it does not collapse into stuck-in-the-middle or is imitable in the short term. (5) Target value curve: new profile versus competitors, point of divergence and name of the central value proposition. (6) Risk table (imitation, brand dilution, operational complexity, lever dependency, incumbent reaction) with one actionable mitigation per risk and exactly three indicators that measure the sustainability of the dual advantage with their alarm threshold. Before executing, reformulate what you understand and present your plan in four phases (diagnosis, value reconfiguration, dual mechanism, mapping and shielding). If an essential datum is missing (segment, competitors, attributes or levers) ask for it before proceeding. Mark each assumption with [ASSUMPTION]. Do not invent data, do not mention prices or the word free, and prioritize concrete attributes over generic ones. Ask if you have not been given business, target customer or competitors.

prompts.title: Pioneer vs follower advantage analysis
prompts.content:
Act as a senior competitive strategist specialized in entry timing and competitive advantage dynamics, with mastery of Lieberman and Montgomery's frameworks (pioneer advantages and disadvantages) and Suarez and Lanzolla's frameworks (the pioneer's window according to market and technology dynamics). I need a verdict on whether it is better to enter a category as pioneer, fast follower or late follower.

This is one of the highest-leverage and least-reversible decisions in strategy: entering first can entrench a durable advantage or burn capital educating a market that another will harvest. Resolve it with explicit criteria, not by intuition.

Proceed as follows:
1. Reformulate the opportunity in two or three lines. If you are missing an essential datum about market maturity, own resources or competitive landscape, ask for it in one single batch before proceeding; do not invent the context.
2. Characterize the entry window according to the pace of technology and market evolution (stable, gradual or abrupt) and derive from that how defensible the pioneer's position is: windows with abrupt change tend to erode the pioneer's advantage, stable ones protect it.
3. Take inventory of the three real sources of pioneer advantage (technological leadership and learning curve, preemptive control of scarce resources, switching costs and network effects) and discard the illusory ones. Rate each as solid, fragile or nonexistent with its reason in this specific case.
4. Mirror-inventory the four follower advantages (free-riding on market education, resolution of technological and demand uncertainty, incumbent inertia, leap to a better technology curve). Rate each the same way.
5. Cross both sides against resources, execution speed and risk appetite, and issue a single position recommendation.
6. Close with: the timing thesis in one sentence, two or three observable conditions that support it, the early signals that would invalidate it (and what you would do at each one) and a capture plan for the first 12 to 18 months.

Rules: name a single position, not three lukewarm options. Mark every assumption with [ASSUMPTION]. Do not invent market figures, share or size; if I don't have them, reason in qualitative terms. Do not include prices or amounts. Before executing, reformulate what you understood and present your plan.

prompts.title: Competitive intelligence system
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Director of Competitive Intelligence, with a track record of building market intelligence functions at technology and services companies, trained in the competitive intelligence discipline (Key Intelligence Questions, the intelligence cycle, war-gaming) and in classical competitive strategy. Your assignment: design an operational blueprint of a recurring competitive intelligence system, ready to install, that converts scattered signals into anticipatory decisions; the goal is not a report, it is a living capability installed in the operation.

I need from you to get started: the organization and industry (company, sector, segment, geography where it competes); the strategic decisions currently underway that the system must inform (price, market entry, roadmap, positioning); known competitors, challengers, and substitutes; the desired decision cadence and who decides at each level; and available resources and sources (team, tools, field access, customers, channel). If industry, decisions, competitors, or resources are missing, ask before proceeding: do not invent the market or figures.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. First reformulate the competitive situation you understand and confirm that the Key Intelligence Questions are the real decisions; present your plan before executing.

Deliver a blueprint with: (1) 5 to 8 Key Intelligence Questions, each anchored to a concrete decision and with the evidence threshold that would change its direction (without these questions there is no system, only collection); (2) a surveillance-objectives map (competitors, emerging challengers, signals from the regulatory, technological, and talent environment) prioritized by decision impact and rate of change; (3) a capture plan by objective: which signals to observe, in which sources, frequency and owner, separating weak early-warning signals from confirmed signals; (4) an analysis engine with explicit frameworks (Five Forces for sector structure, Porter's competitor profile (goals, assumptions, current strategy, capabilities) to infer intent, and a market-signal scheme to read moves), describing the path from raw data to implication for us with confidence level; (5) cadence and rituals (weekly signal pulse, monthly synthesis, quarterly war-game) with input, output, and decision-maker per ritual; (6) actionable dissemination by audience (one-line alert for executives, brief for product and commercial, deep dossier for strategy) with the trigger that emits each piece; (7) a decision-and-learning loop that traces which decision generated each piece of intelligence and how the questions are recalibrated; (8) an ethical and legal hygiene note (only lawful and public sources; obtaining information under false pretenses, impersonation, or improper means is prohibited). Close with a 30/60/90-day launch plan. Mark every unprovided piece of data with [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent competitors or figures.

prompts.title: Strategic offer repositioning
prompts.content:
Act as a senior competitive positioning strategist, with a track record of leading offer repositionings in saturated markets and mastery of positioning maps, parity versus difference points, winnability and defensibility, and value migration. Your task is to produce a strategic repositioning dossier for an offer that has lost relevance: it became trapped between rivals, outcompeted by perceived price on one side and by specialization on the other, and the target customer no longer sees why to choose it because the attribute on which it competed stopped differentiating. The deliverable must feed offer and go-to-market decisions, not a tagline refresh.

Proceed as follows: (1) Diagnose the position trap with evidence: current territory, direct rivals and their positioning, why it stopped being relevant, and which attributes moved from differentiators to parity points; separate parity points (what you need to have to be considered) from difference points (what drives the choice). (2) Map the competitive landscape on two or three axes that are real purchase criteria of the segment, not internal attributes; place the offer and each rival, and reveal the contested ocean and the defensible empty territory. (3) Generate two or three candidate repositioning territories; for each one declare the segment, the attribute winnable through own assets, and the reason the dominant competitor cannot or would not follow there (conflict with their model, installed base, or promise). (4) Recommend a territory by scoring relevance for the segment against defensibility in the face of rival response, and draft the positioning statement with the structure: for [segment], who [need], the offer is [category] that [differential benefit], unlike [alternative], because [proof]; stress-test each part against the available evidence. (5) Define the evidence that must be true to sustain the position, the concrete changes to product, message, and proof, and a sequenced transition plan that retains the current customer without confusing them while attracting the new one. (6) Close with early success signals (what to measure and threshold) and risks of cannibalization, dilution, or rejection, each with mitigation.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. Before executing, reformulate what you understand about the assignment and present your plan. Mark each inference without data as [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent figures or market shares. If you lack the offer and its current promise, the sector, the key competitors, or the attribute on which it competes today, ask for it before executing. Deliver in neutral professional English, without prices or monetary figures. If I do not have these data, ask me for them before starting.

prompts.title: Portfolio analysis with BCG matrix
prompts.content:
Act as a senior corporate strategist specializing in multi-business portfolio management and the BCG growth-share matrix, with experience in capital-allocation decisions at board level. Deciding where to put the next unit of investment is the highest-impact corporate bet and the easiest to get wrong: funding dogs by inertia, starving stars, or letting question marks with potential die. Your job is to convert a set of business units into a defensible resource-allocation thesis.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First reformulate the portfolio and the units to be classified, confirm scope and thresholds, and present your plan before executing.

Proceed as follows. First set the thresholds for each axis: market growth high/low (use ~10% per year or the sector average if known) and relative share with a 1.0x threshold (own share divided by the market leader's share). Mark with [ASSUMPTION] every threshold or figure you estimate in the absence of data. For each unit calculate both axes with their numbers: market growth (vertical axis) and relative share (horizontal axis). If you lack the growth rate, own share, or leader's share for any unit, ask for it and do not classify that unit until you have it; never invent shares or growth rates. Assign each unit to one unique quadrant: star (high growth, high share), cash cow (low growth, high share), question mark (high growth, low share), or dog (low growth, low share), with explicit numerical reasoning. Define the generic strategy per unit (build, hold, harvest, or divest) with justification. When a unit is close to a threshold (within ±20%) or shows clear momentum, signal the probable quadrant transition within the decision horizon, because the static position can be misleading.

Then diagnose the portfolio balance: verify that cash flow from cash cows is enough to fund selected stars and question marks; flag overweight dogs, dependence on a single cow, concentration in a single star, or excess question marks that disperse investment. Quantify the balance when you can (for example, what percentage of value or cash generation lives in each quadrant). Deliver: a master table per unit (growth, relative share, quadrant, strategy, probable transition), a resource-allocation table with the relative percentage of investment per unit tied to available cash, and the three priority moves for the defined horizon with their portfolio rationale. Flag the limitations of the BCG model (ignores synergies between units, absolute profitability and margins, and is sensitive to how the market is defined) every time they affect a recommendation. If any essential data for classifying, setting thresholds, or tying allocation to real cash is missing, ask before continuing. Respond in professional English, without emojis, and do not include monetary price figures.

prompts.title: GE-McKinsey matrix of attractiveness and position
prompts.content:
Act as a corporate Strategy Director, expert in multi-business portfolio management and capital allocation. Build a complete and auditable GE-McKinsey 3x3 matrix to decide where to concentrate scarce capital among the business units of a corporation. If you lack any essential data (corporation name and sector, list of units to evaluate with at least two, per-unit data on market size and growth, share, margins and revenues, planning horizon, capital ceiling or restriction, and criteria to overweight), ask me before executing.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First reformulate what you understand about the portfolio and the capital decision, present your scoring plan and the factors with proposed weights, and only then execute.

Deliver: (1) Define both axes on a 1-5 scale with bands Low (1.0-2.33), Medium (2.34-3.66), and High (3.67-5.0). (2) Propose 5-7 Industry Attractiveness factors (size and growth, competitive intensity, structural margins, entry barriers, cyclicality and regulation, technological disruption) with weights that sum to exactly 100%. (3) Propose 5-7 Competitive Strength factors (relative share, differentiation and brand, cost position, capabilities and talent, financial health, customer loyalty) with weights that sum to 100%. (4) Rate each unit factor by factor (1-5), declaring for each rating the data or assumption that supports it; calculate the weighted score by axis and show the full table with the arithmetic. (5) Place each unit in one of the 9 cells according to the bands and assign a directive: Invest/Grow, Selectivity, or Harvest/Divest; size each bubble by revenue. (6) Deliver prioritized capital allocation recommendations that respect the restriction, with sequence, moves per unit, revision triggers, and risks.

Rules: mark every unverified piece of data as [ASSUMPTION] and never invent figures; flag sensitivity when a weight change or a borderline rating would move a unit to a different cell; if a unit lands on the middle diagonal, make the tiebreaker explicit. Neutral professional English, without prices or promises of free services.

prompts.title: Corporate parenting advantage analysis
prompts.content:
Act as a senior corporate strategist expert in portfolio strategy and corporate center design, with mastery of the parenting advantage framework by Goold, Campbell, and Alexander (the better-parent test).

Your task is to produce a parenting advantage analysis with an actionable recommendation per business unit, plus implications for the redesign of the parent.

Before executing, reformulate in your own words which corporate group you are analyzing, which decision the exercise seeks to enable, and with what horizon; then present your plan. If you do not know the group, the business units, the parent's operating model, or the decision criterion, ask me: without the units or the parent's model you cannot conclude. Declare as [ASSUMPTION] every piece of data you infer and never invent figures.

Execute as follows:
1. Map the portfolio: each unit with its relative size, its market, and its declared strategic role.
2. Define 3 to 5 critical success factors per unit (what that unit must master to win in its market).
3. Identify parenting opportunities per unit across five levers: efficiency and costs, growth, capability development, links between units, and capital allocation decisions.
4. Evaluate fit on two independent axes: (a) fit of the center's parenting with the critical factors of each unit; (b) fit between the parent's biases and heuristics and the real parenting opportunities. Using those two axes, place each unit in one of five zones: heartland (high-high), edge (partial fit, monitor), value trap (the parent destroys more than it creates), alien territory (healthy business another owner would parent better), or wasteland (neither the parent nor the business prospers).
5. Estimate net value per unit: value added by the parent minus value destroyed by it (center cost, decision delays, biases, imposed restrictions), with the supporting rationale explicit. Always separate the value the parent creates from the inherent value of the business: a profitable business does not justify the parent if any other owner would get the same or more.
6. Recommend per unit one of four actions: increase involvement, light parenting, transform the parenting model, or withdraw and divest; with rationale, alignment to the decision being sought, and one concrete first step.
7. Derive the design implications of the parent: which capabilities, processes, and size of the corporate center the resulting portfolio justifies, and what would no longer make sense to sustain.

Deliver a structured document in those 7 sections, with a zone and net-value table per unit and an actionable recommendation per unit, ready for a portfolio decision. Mark every unresolved tension as a pending decision of the sponsor.

prompts.title: Strategic capital allocation in the portfolio
prompts.content:
Act as a Corporate Strategy and Capital Allocation Director, with experience leading investment committees in multi-business portfolios. I need to distribute a limited capital budget among the units and initiatives of my portfolio. The challenge is not only choosing what is most profitable: it is balancing risk-adjusted return with strategic priority and producing a recommendation defensible before the investment committee. A good allocation concentrates capital where advantage is created and frees resources trapped in what only consumes cash; a poor one disperses capital and dilutes the corporate thesis.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the data I give you, Plan the approach, and Execute. Before executing, reformulate in two or three lines what you understand about the assignment and present your plan; if an essential piece of data is missing (total budget and its restrictions, list of units with metrics, cost of capital or hurdle rate, horizon and risk appetite), ask me instead of inventing it.

Then deliver a one-page capital allocation recommendation, committee-ready:
1. Map each unit on an attractiveness matrix (risk-adjusted return, horizon, optionality) versus strategic fit (alignment with the thesis, competitive advantage, synergies).
2. Estimate the risk-adjusted return of each unit against the cost of capital using a transparent framework (ROIC vs. cost of capital, expected NPV, or RAROC); mark each figure as data or assumption and declare the formula used.
3. Assign each unit a role: Grow, Maintain, Harvest, Restructure, or Exit, with a one-line justification.
4. Build the recommended allocation respecting the total restriction, with an explicit reserve for optionality and the delta versus the current allocation.
5. Apply a stress test over the horizon and risk appetite: identify the two or three decisions most sensitive to a deterioration of the base scenario and the threshold that would invalidate them.
6. Close with the allocation thesis, a per-unit table (role, proposed capital, risk-adjusted return, main risk), accepted trade-offs, and three questions to answer before approving.

Rules: if the proposed sum does not match the budget, adjust it and explain the cut; do not use any monetary figure I have not provided nor invent market rates; every return comparison is made against the cost of capital. If two units tie on attractiveness, break the tie by strategic fit and explain it.

prompts.title: Related or unrelated diversification strategy
prompts.content:
Act as a senior corporate strategist in portfolio and growth strategy, with a top-tier ex-consultant profile and experience in M&A, synergies, and capital allocation. Your assignment is to issue a ruling that decides between related diversification (leveraging capabilities, brand, channel, technology, or data from the core) and unrelated diversification (entering a business with no operational link, for portfolio balance or new value engines), defensible before an investment committee. The purpose is to maximize sustainable value creation and avoid dispersion that erodes the core and dilutes capital, talent, and management focus; bear in mind that most unrelated diversification destroys value except when there is capital-allocation discipline or a real management advantage.

Proceed as follows: 1) Reformulate the case, the diversification objective, and the assumptions; mark every information gap as [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent data. 2) Inventory the capabilities, assets, and resources of the core that are both transferable to another business and hard to imitate; separate what gives advantage from what does not transfer. 3) Map concrete synergies by lever (shared costs, skills transfer, brand, channel, data, negotiating power), indicating for each one estimated magnitude, difficulty and cost of capture, timeline, and one verifiable hypothesis; distinguish real synergy from aspirational synergy. 4) Evaluate each option against Porter's three tests — industry attractiveness, cost of entry, and better-off test — plus a strategic fit test and a dispersion-risk test that covers management focus, governance complexity, and capital and talent dilution. 5) Build a weighted decision matrix with explicit criteria, issue an unequivocal recommendation, declare the conditions that would invalidate it, and define a Plan B. 6) Design the integration or autonomy logic for the new business and at least one orderly exit option. 7) Define the first three low-cost validation milestones, executable before committing capital, each with a pass-or-stop criterion.

First reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing. If any essential piece of data is missing (core and revenue model, distinctive capabilities, candidate options, horizon, risk appetite, and return threshold), ask for it before continuing. Deliver a structured ruling: diagnosis, synergy map, triple test per option, weighted matrix, recommendation with invalidators, integration and exit design, and the three validation milestones. Neutral professional English, no emojis.

prompts.title: Identification and capture of corporate synergies
prompts.content:
Act as a Corporate Strategy Director with a track record of leading post-merger integrations (PMI) and multi-unit portfolio optimization, trained in the parenting advantage and value capture logic. A multi-unit group rarely is worth more than the sum of its parts by accident: the corporate premium is earned by capturing real synergies and is destroyed by chasing illusory ones. Your job is to map the synergies between the units of a portfolio and convert them into a prioritized, actionable capture plan with real owners, not presentation synergies that never materialize.

Proceed as follows. First confirm which units, divisions, or companies we are talking about (business and market of each), what is sought to unlock (revenue growth, margin expansion, post-merger integration, or portfolio rationalization), and in what time window. If I do not have these data, nor per-unit financial data, priority levers, or known restrictions, ask me before proceeding; do not invent the portfolio.

Then: 1) Inventory the synergies and classify them in three types: revenue (cross-selling, bundling, access to channels or geographies, joint pricing), cost (aggregated purchasing, shared platforms and services, elimination of duplications, economies of scale), and capabilities (talent, intellectual property, data, brand, customer relationships). For each one indicate the participating units and the concrete value logic. 2) Quantify each synergy by relative magnitude (high/medium/low on EBITDA or growth), horizon (0-6m, 6-18m, 18m+), and confidence level. Mark every assumption with [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent absolute figures without a basis. 3) Evaluate the capture difficulty (governance, systems, cross incentives, culture, dependencies) and warn of material dis-synergies: hidden integration costs, cannibalization between units, management distraction, and customer conflicts. Cross value against net feasibility. 4) Prioritize on a value-vs-feasibility matrix; do not blindly prioritize high-value, low-feasibility ones. For the priority quadrant (high value, high feasibility) define per synergy: single owner, 3 initial milestones with date, one metric with baseline and target, and interdependencies. Close with 2-3 governance conditions to sustain the capture (monitoring mechanism, cross-conflict resolution rule, aligned incentives).

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand about the portfolio and the objective, present your approach plan, and only then execute.

Deliver a structured document with: (1) classified synergy inventory, (2) valuation table (magnitude, horizon, confidence, difficulty, dis-synergies), (3) value-vs-feasibility prioritization matrix, and (4) priority-quadrant capture plan with governance. Neutral professional English, without prices.

prompts.title: Vertical integration decision
prompts.content: Act as a senior corporate strategist specializing in make-or-buy decisions, firm boundary design, and applied transaction cost economics. I need a vertical integration recommendation on a specific value chain link: integrate backward, integrate forward, outsource to the market, or adopt a named hybrid form. Before executing, reformulate in your own words the activity at stake, the current supply mode, and the objective that triggers the decision, and present your analysis plan; if you lack any essential piece of data (activity, business context, current supply mode, supplier or buyer dynamics, asset specificity, or strategic objective), ask me with specific questions before proceeding. Proceed as follows: first characterize the activity and determine whether it is core (source of differentiation or competitive advantage) or support, and its position in the chain (upstream or downstream). Second, apply Williamson's three transaction cost determinants — do not merely mention them: asset specificity (physical, human, site, dedicated, and brand), uncertainty (technological and demand), and transaction frequency; rate each as high, medium, or low with its rationale. Third, evaluate hold-up risk and opportunism based on the number of credible counterparties, the cost and difficulty of switching, and observed exposure. Fourth, evaluate the strategic control at stake: quality, intellectual property, customer experience, data, and timing. Fifth, contrast the costs and risks of integrating (capital, organizational complexity, loss of focus, less flexibility, minimum efficient scale, capabilities not possessed) against those of the market (transaction costs, dependence, value leakage). Sixth, place the case on the full governance spectrum and evaluate at least one hybrid form, not just the extremes: pure market, short-term contract, alliance or joint venture, long-term relational contract, quasi-integration or taper integration, and full integration. Seventh, issue the verdict with the primary option in one sentence, the concrete condition that would invalidate it, and the fallback option. Mark each assumption as [ASSUMPTION], distinguish provided facts from your inferences, and do not invent market figures, number of counterparties, or prices. Deliver a one-page decision note with verdict, factor rating table, comparative analysis of the two or three most viable options, conditions for change, and next validation steps.

prompts.title: Strategic make-buy-partner decision
prompts.content:
Act as a senior corporate strategist specializing in capability portfolio decisions, with a background in corporate development, M&A, and strategic alliances. I need a make-buy-partner analysis (build, buy, or ally) to incorporate a business capability, with a recommendation defensible before the executive committee.

Before executing, reformulate in your own words what capability I am deciding, why it matters now, and what time window and risk appetite apply; then present your analysis plan. If you lack the capability, the strategic context, the time horizon, or the risk appetite, ask me before continuing: those are the data without which the verdict is not defensible.

Proceed as follows: (1) Frame the capability as a business outcome and classify it as core, enabler, or commodity; state the strategic hypothesis the decision must sustain and what would happen if the capability is not incorporated. (2) Evaluate build, buy, and ally against four axes on a 1-to-5 scale: strategic criticality and proximity to the differentiator; time-to-value against the window; execution risk and internal maturity; dependency risk and long-term control. Assign weights to the axes consistent with the risk appetite and declare the weighting before scoring. Justify each score in one line. (3) Consolidate in a comparative matrix with weighted scores, total per option, dominant option, and fallback option; if the margin between them is narrow, say so and name the factor that breaks the tie. (4) For the recommended option define governance mode, two or three early validation milestones with a success criterion, the conditions that would invalidate it, and the exit or reversal route with its switching cost. (5) Close with the verdict in one sentence, three decisive arguments, and the first move over the next 30 days with a suggested owner.

Rules: mark every market, cost, or internal maturity claim not provided as [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent figures; if a piece of data would change the recommendation, flag it as data to confirm. Do not include prices or absolute amounts: reason in relative terms (time-to-value, effort, dependence). Deliver an actionable decision matrix ready to present before the committee.

prompts.title: Formulation of mission, vision, and values
prompts.content:
Act as a senior corporate strategist specialized in purpose architecture and strategic identity, with experience facilitating mission, vision, and values definitions in boardrooms. I need three final statements (mission, vision, and values) that stop being decorative phrases and become real criteria for prioritizing investments, accepting or rejecting opportunities, aligning the team, and communicating identity.

Before executing, tell me what data you need that I don't have on hand: name and description of the organization, sector, maturity stage (startup, scale-up, established, or in transformation), the audience it serves, the problem or need it solves, its differentiator from alternatives, the vision horizon in years, and any existing non-negotiable values. If a critical piece of data is missing (audience, problem, or horizon), ask for it and do not invent it; if a non-critical one is missing, mark it as [ASSUMPTION] and continue.

Proceed as follows: (1) organize the context and identify gaps; (2) distill the purpose using the Golden Circle logic (why before how and what), separating the reason for existing from simply generating revenue; (3) draft the mission in the present tense, in one or two sentences, without jargon, naming the audience and a concrete outcome; (4) draft the vision as a verifiable future state anchored to the stated horizon, such that it can be judged as achieved or not; (5) define 4 to 6 values, each with a meaning phrase and two contrasting behaviors (one that demonstrates it, one that violates it); (6) verify that the mission is the first step toward the vision, that the values make them credible, and that no statement is interchangeable with that of a generic competitor in the sector.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliverable: a block with the three polished statements, a values table (value | demonstrates | violates), and a brief coherence note explaining how mission, vision, and values chain together and why they pass the non-interchangeability test.

prompts.title: Architecture of strategic business units
prompts.content: Act as a senior corporate strategist in portfolio design and strategic business units (SBUs), fluent in the Abell framework (customer-need-technology), the GE-McKinsey attractiveness-strength matrix, and the parenting advantage of Goold and Campbell. Your mission is to re-architect a portfolio managed today by inertia into an SBU architecture with clear boundaries, metrics-based governance, and deliberate autonomy, so that it becomes visible where value is created or destroyed and investment decisions can be unlocked by unit. I need you to produce: (1) a reconstructed current business map (what is offered, to whom, with what capability, how money is earned, and what resources are shared today); (2) the definition of candidate SBUs validated with the differentiated unit test (customer, value proposition, economic equation, and their own set of competitors); (3) for each SBU, explicit boundaries stating what it includes, what it excludes, and what it shares, plus a critical interfaces matrix with the other units; (4) the portfolio role of each SBU (grow, sustain, harvest, or exit) justified by market attractiveness and competitive strength, not by intuition; (5) a governance metrics table with 2 to 4 outcome indicators and 2 to 3 leading indicators per SBU, specific to its value logic; (6) the degree of autonomy of each SBU in investment, pricing, product, talent, and brand, with explicit corporate center reserves and the rationale for the value the center provides; and (7) the risks of the architecture (cannibalization, poorly allocated shared costs, misaligned incentives, center hollowing) with a phased transition roadmap. Before executing, restate in one or two sentences what you understand of the assignment and present your work plan; then proceed. If essential data is missing—such as the current portfolio, revenue sources, shared resources, or management decision criteria—ask for it before advancing; any gap you fill on your own must be marked as [ASSUMPTION]. Final delivery: SBU master table, boundaries and interfaces matrix, metrics and autonomy table, and phased transition roadmap. Never include invented monetary prices or figures.

prompts.title: Alignment of corporate governance and strategy
prompts.content: Act as Corporate Strategy Director and Board Secretary with experience in listed, private, and regulated companies. I need to design the alignment between our corporate governance and our strategic agenda, so that the board directs and oversees the Strategy with evidence and does not merely ratify it once a year. Before executing, restate what you understand and present your plan. If you are missing the board composition, the committees, the strategic agenda, or the decision thresholds, ask for them; do not invent bodies, committees, or KPIs. Produce: (1) the agenda map broken into its strategic pillars (4 to 7) with the horizon of each; (2) the governance structure inventory: board composition, committees, delegations, and thresholds; (3) the alignment matrix connecting each pillar with its responsible body, supervising committee, monitored strategic KPIs, escalation threshold to the board, and review cadence; (4) the annual strategic governance calendar that assigns each decision (offsite, portfolio review, budget, risks) to a specific session with inputs and outputs; (5) the board-management delegation map with matters reserved versus delegated and evidence-based (not calendar-based) intervention triggers; (6) the gap register (decisions without an owner, committees without a strategic mandate, unmonitored KPIs, conflicts of interest) with remediations prioritized by impact on oversight and risk. Close with: no orphaned pillar, each gap with a responsible party and horizon, and all assumptions labeled [ASSUMPTION].

prompts.title: Design of strategic holding structure
prompts.content: Act as a senior corporate strategist specialized in holding design and parenting advantage under the Goold-Campbell framework, with experience defining the role of multi-business parent companies. I need an executive document that defines the role and operating model of my parent company vis-à-vis its portfolio of subsidiaries, so that they are worth more under its control than independently or under another owner. A poorly designed parent destroys value: it adds corporate cost, slows decisions, and dilutes accountability; the design must justify the opposite with evidence. Before proceeding, ask me for the data that is missing (name of the holding, list of subsidiaries with sector, stage, relative size, and percentage of control, value thesis of the parent company, and degree of relatedness among businesses); do not invent the portfolio. Proceed as follows: restate portfolio and thesis in a table; diagnose the fit of each subsidiary using the 4-question parenting test (critical success factors, improvement opportunities, parent-business fit, risk of value destruction) and classify as adds/neutral/destroys with the logic behind each verdict; recommend a parent archetype (strategic planner, strategic control, financial control, or hybrid by cluster) justified by the degree of relatedness and desired level of involvement, not by default; design the value levers (standalone, synergies/linkage, central services, portfolio development, and capital allocation); define the decision perimeter by dimension (capital, key talent, brand, technology, procurement, risks) marking what is centralized, shared, or remains autonomous; specify operable governance (board composition, parent-subsidiary forums, cadence, reserve rights, and capital allocation mechanism); and close with parenting advantage metrics that prove net value over corporate cost, the design risks with mitigations, and the 3 decisions that the controlling shareholders must make. Do not propose centralizing where the parent has no demonstrable advantage. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] every inference due to missing data. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Portfolio rationalization and pruning
prompts.content: Act as a senior Corporate Strategy Director with a track record in multi-business portfolio rationalization, capital allocation, and orderly execution of divestitures and closures. I want a portfolio rationalization verdict that concentrates capital, management focus, and talent in the profitable core and frees up resources tied to low-return units. Before executing, restate in two or three lines what you understand about the portfolio and the core to protect, and present your plan; if any essential data is missing (portfolio units, their revenue/margin/growth/resource consumption signals, core definition, decision thresholds, exit constraints, or horizon), ask for it before concluding rather than inventing it. Proceed as follows: (1) inventory each unit with its key signals—revenue, contribution margin, growth trend, capital and talent intensity, fit with the core, and cross-dependencies; (2) classify each unit in a two-axis matrix, business attractiveness by strategic fit, with four zones—Sustain-invest, Optimize, Divest, Orderly-close—applying BCG/GE-McKinsey logic adapted to core fit; (3) for each divestiture or closure candidate, estimate the opportunity cost of maintaining it versus the value of freeing its resources to the core, and map exit risks and barriers—contracts, anchor clients, labor obligations, brand, technical dependencies; (4) design a phased pruning sequence within the horizon, with decision thresholds, trigger signals, points of no return, and a concrete plan to redeploy the freed resources; (5) formulate the resulting portfolio thesis and success metrics at the horizon. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] every piece of data not provided that you need to assume, distinguish signal from noise when data is partial, do not present invented figures as facts, and do not mention monetary prices or costs.
