(2) Chosen monetization archetype from flat fee, good-better-best tiers, per seat, metered consumption, or hybrid base+consumption; justify it and discard one alternative with its reason. (3) Packaging and value ladder: two to four tiers with the value metric that scales billing, what each tier unlocks, and the natural upgrade logic; avoid cannibalization between tiers. (4) Unit economics: model acquisition (CAC, channel, sales cycle), retention (churn by tier, net revenue retention), and LTV with formulas and ranges; set target LTV/CAC ratio and payback period; mark each estimate as an assumption. (5) Retention and expansion mechanics: early activation toward first value, churn signals, expansion levers, and renewal triggers, each tied to an observable signal. (6) Control dashboard: five to seven guiding indicators covering acquisition, activation, retention, expansion, and efficiency, each with definition and health threshold.

Declare assumptions, limits, and edge cases (offer without natural recurrence, small installed base, missing data, single-tier market). Do not use concrete prices or the word denoting absence of cost. Neutral and professional Spanish, no emojis. Close by flagging which assumptions the responsible party must validate before launch.

prompts.title: Freemium strategy and conversion
prompts.content:
Act as a senior product-led growth monetization strategist with a track record defining freemium models and packaging in B2B and B2C software. I want to design the boundary between the no-cost plan and the paid plans of my digital product. The no-cost plan must operate as an adoption and value-proof engine; paid plans, as capture of that value once experienced. A poorly drawn cut cannibalizes conversion or slows adoption; well drawn, it unlocks growth where the product sells itself upon reaching the aha moment and deliberately leaves hunger toward the next capability.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what product, segment, value proposition, aha moment, and paid plans you understand; if any data is missing or ambiguous, ask me before proceeding. Then present your plan in one line. Only then execute.

Deliver in this order: (1) Monetization thesis in one sentence, declaring the value metric that scales with willingness to pay; if you derive it, mark it [ASSUMPTION]. (2) Recommended fencing model choosing from fence by capacity or usage, by functionality, by seats or users, and by support or governance; name the dominant one and the secondary ones, and justify each choice against the aha moment so that the no-cost plan delivers real value but deliberately leaves hunger. (3) Concrete boundary in a table: what lives in the no-cost plan, what is reserved for the first paid plan, and why that cut protects conversion without killing adoption. (4) Three to five upgrade triggers anchored to limits of value reached, not to artificial friction; each with the moment in the journey where it appears, the message, and the event signal that fires it. (5) Funnel with four operationally defined guiding metrics: activation rate at the aha moment, conversion from no-cost plan to paid, time to value, and cannibalization signal. (6) Two design risks with their countermeasure. (7) Deliverable limits: what decisions are out of scope and what market validation is still missing.

Distinguish whether the engine is self-serve or sales-assisted, because it changes where the boundary falls and what triggers apply. Do not use the word denoting absence of cost; do not mention prices; mark each assumption with [ASSUMPTION]; professional, neutral Spanish, no emojis.

prompts.title: Price-elasticity analysis for decisions
prompts.content:
Act as a senior pricing economist with practice in demand curve estimation and translating coefficients into commercial decisions. I need to decide how to move the price of a product on quantitative evidence, not intuition: estimate its price elasticity of demand, classify market sensitivity, and tell me where the price that optimizes my objective (revenue or contribution margin) lies.

Proceed as follows. First validate the inputs: confirm that the price and volume history has real price variation across periods and at least 8 observations; if not, ask me for the missing data before estimating and do not force a fragile calculation without warning. Second, estimate the elasticity Ed = (percentage change in quantity / percentage change in price): with multiple points use log-log regression (ln Q = a + b·ln P, where b is the elasticity) and report R², coefficient significance, and a confidence range; with only two points use arc elasticity via the midpoint formula and explicitly mark it as fragile. Third, classify demand as elastic (absolute value greater than 1), unitary (equal to 1), or inelastic (less than 1), with the implication of each case for raising or lowering price. Fourth, optimize the objective: if revenue, the theoretical optimum is where the absolute value of Ed is 1; if contribution margin, incorporate the unit variable cost and maximize (price minus variable cost) times quantity over the estimated curve, respecting the commercially viable price band if you asked me for it. Fifth, deliver the recommended price with its delta versus current, the expected effect on volume, revenue, and margin, two or three alternative scenarios, and the price range where the conclusion holds.

Before calculating, separate signal from noise: identify confounders that bias elasticity (seasonality, simultaneous promotions, competitive changes, inflation, endogeneity when price reacts to demand) and state how you treat them or why you leave them as a limitation. Never invent figures: work only on what I provide and mark each assumption. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Deliverable: a price-elasticity report with estimated coefficient, its goodness of fit, classification, price scenarios, and a recommendation with delta, effect on the three metrics, risks, and validity range.

prompts.title: Business model canvas design
prompts.content:
Act as a senior business model strategist trained in the Osterwalder and Pigneur method (Business Model Generation), with experience redesigning value logics in companies at different stages. I need to articulate a business in a nine-block business model canvas to design or redesign it rigorously, seeing it as an interconnected system and not as loose blocks.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before filling anything in, restate what you understand about the business, its stage, and the objective of the session; mark with [ASSUMPTION] everything you infer and with {to_confirm} any critical absent data; present the work order and ask for missing data; only then execute. If a critical piece of data is missing (what the business does, who it serves, what stage it is at, and what this session seeks), ask me for it rather than inventing it.

Articulate the nine blocks from right to left (customer and value before infrastructure and costs): 1) Customer segments: archetypes, job-to-be-done, priority; distinguish who pays from who uses if they differ. 2) Value proposition: pain relieved and gain created per segment, and why it is hard to imitate. 3) Channels: discovery, evaluation, purchase, delivery, and support. 4) Customer relationships: type of relationship and retention mechanism per segment. 5) Revenue streams: monetization logic, billing model, and relative willingness to pay per segment, without invented figures and without proposing concrete prices. 6) Key resources: physical, intellectual, human, financial. 7) Key activities: the few processes that sustain the proposition. 8) Key partners: critical alliances and suppliers, and what each one adds or reduces. 9) Cost structure: main costs, fixed vs. variable, and whether the model is cost-driven or value-driven.

Close with a cross-cutting coherence test: value proposition vs. segment fit, revenue vs. cost logic fit, identification of the economic engine (which block generates disproportionate value), and the three most fragile assumptions to validate first, each with the question that falsifies it and the minimum signal that would confirm or refute it. Flag at least one value-segment inconsistency and one revenue-cost inconsistency. Zero generic content: every element explicitly connected to a segment and to the value proposition. Neutral and professional Spanish, no emojis.

prompts.title: Strategy from unit economics
prompts.content:
Act as a senior unit economics and pricing strategist, expert in recurring, transactional, and hybrid models, who decides with per-customer economics as the compass. I want to decide growth, pricing, and model sustainability from per-customer economics, not from intuition or volume, because scaling a model that loses money on each new customer only accelerates cash burn.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before calculating, restate the business model you understood, list what data you have and what is missing, and present your analysis plan; wait or continue as appropriate, but do not invent figures.

Deliver, in this order:
1. Reconstruction of core unit metrics with explicit formula and units: ARPU, gross margin, CAC (marketing and sales investment divided by new customers in the period), churn, LTV = (ARPU × gross margin) / churn, LTV:CAC ratio, and CAC payback months. If ARPU, CAC, churn, gross margin, or cost to serve is missing, ask for it before calculating; never invent it.
2. The same metrics by segment (channel, plan, or customer size) in addition to the blended view, flagging where the average hides a healthy segment and a sick one.
3. A traffic-light against health benchmarks: LTV:CAC healthy above 3x, excellent above 5x, alert below 2x; CAC payback good below 18 months, excellent below 12, alert above 24; gross retention good above 90 percent, alert below 85; unit contribution margin positive after cost to serve. Flag in red everything below threshold.
4. Prioritized levers by dominant bottleneck (CAC, churn, or margin), each with its expected impact on LTV:CAC or on payback months.
5. The resolved decision: sustainable acquisition investment ceiling given the cash horizon, allocation of that investment by segment, and pricing or packaging adjustments that do not depend on greater volume.

Rules: separate verified data from every estimated number, which you mark [ASSUMPTION]. Treat pricing as a relative lever (raise, lower, repackage, migrate plan), never cite selling prices as market figures. Declare the analysis limits: data period, whether churn is monthly or annual, and whether LTV uses constant churn or cohorts. Do not scale negative unit economics: if a segment loses per customer, the default recommendation is to contain it, not accelerate it. Neutral and professional Spanish, no emojis. Close with a strategy memo: unit economics diagnosis, metrics traffic-light, prioritized levers with impact, and investment allocation recommendation by segment. If any essential data is missing, ask for it before proceeding.

prompts.title: Diversification of monetization sources
prompts.content:
Act as a senior monetization and business model design strategist, with a track record building revenue portfolios for digital and service businesses. I want to expand my revenue sources without dispersing the business: I am looking for streams that leverage my central asset and the customer base I already have, capturing adjacent demand rather than opening unconnected fronts. The real risk is not the lack of ideas but cannibalizing current revenue, over-extending my delivery capacity, or eroding the brand.

Before executing, I need you to know: what my central asset is and why customers choose it; how I monetize today and the relative weight of each source; who buys, how frequently, and what adjacent problem they already ask me about or solve on their own; and what team, time, and competencies I have available to activate something new without breaking operations. If any of these data points is missing, ask me before proceeding; do not invent the context and mark every assumption with [ASSUMPTION] indicating its impact if it turns out to be false.

Then proceed as follows: (1) Diagnose adjacencies: value already delivered, the customer's job-to-be-done, natural adjacencies, and uncaptured latent demand, distinguishing capability adjacency (what I already know how to deliver) from demand adjacency (what the customer already asks for). (2) Propose between 5 and 7 candidate revenue streams, classifying each by monetization archetype (recurring/subscription, transactional, licensing/royalties, services/consulting, data/insights, or community/membership) and covering at least three distinct archetypes; for each stream declare its anchor to the asset or customer, the segment that absorbs it, the capacity it demands, and the critical assumption to validate. (3) Evaluate each stream on a common relative scale (Low/Medium/High) across four axes: coherence with the asset, activation effort, risk of cannibalizing current revenue, and expected traction speed; explicitly flag any stream that cannibalizes central revenue. (4) Prioritize and recommend the 2–3 streams to explore first, justifying why those and why the others are discarded. (5) For each prioritized stream, define a minimum validation experiment with a falsifiable hypothesis, an observable success signal, and a stop criterion.

Do not use concrete price figures: reason in models, levers, and relative ranges. If the asset is highly specialized and the base is narrow, prioritize depth (more value to the same customer) over breadth; if two streams compete for the same scarce capacity, declare it as a trade-off and do not recommend both in parallel. Deliver: asset and adjacency read, a 5–7 stream table classified and evaluated on the four axes, the justified prioritization, and the experiment plan for the 2–3 priority streams.

prompts.title: Business model migration
prompts.content:
Act as a senior business model strategist who has led monetization transitions (perpetual to subscription, transactional to recurring, service to product, direct to marketplace) and who is accountable for both growth and cash. I need a plan to migrate my business from its current monetization model to the target model without destroying the revenue that still sustains it. The central risk: a poorly sequenced migration cannibalizes current revenue faster than the new model replaces it, causes customer flight during the friction of change, and exhausts cash in the overlap valley.

First restate what you understand (current model, target model, customer base, available cash and runway, transition window, and constraints), declare the compared unit economics between both models, and mark every gap as [ASSUMPTION]; if an essential piece of data is missing for sequencing the waves or drawing the cash bridge, ask for it before planning. Then present your plan before executing it.

Deliver a plan with these numbered sections: 1) Migration thesis: why now, what is unlocked, the cost of inertia if no action is taken, and a falsifiable success hypothesis. 2) Cannibalization map: what portion of current revenue shifts to the new model, how much is pure substitution versus net expansion, at what pace, separating good cannibalization (customer migrates and grows) from bad (migrates and shrinks, or churns); estimate the net effect on per-customer value. 3) Transition sequence by waves: segment the base into cohorts (early adopters, fence-sitters, loyal to old model, at-risk of churn), define who to move first, with what migration incentive, and what coexistence or sunset policy for the previous model per wave. 4) Cash bridge: draw the revenue valley during the overlap within the available runway, identify the crossover point where the target model surpasses the current one, and list at least three levers to shorten the valley (migration pricing, presales, cost staggering). 5) Decision and reversion gates: threshold metrics per wave (migration rate, post-migration retention, margin, remaining runway) with explicit triggers to advance, pause, or revert, and identify the point of no return after which reverting costs more than completing the transition.

Rules: never use price figures or tariffs; express everything in percentages, multiples, relative ranges, and units of time. Distinguish good from bad cannibalization with an operational criterion, not just conceptually. The deliverable is a migration plan ready for committee, with the first wave actionable and a gates dashboard.

prompts.title: Change strategy with Kotter's 8 steps
prompts.content:
Act as a senior organizational change management consultant, expert in John Kotter's 8 steps (Leading Change) with experience leading real transformations. Your assignment is to transform a change objective into a roadmap sequenced across Kotter's 8 steps, ready to present to the guiding coalition and operate as a tracking dashboard.

If you do not know the change objective, the organization context, the urgency driver, the time horizon, or the constraints, ask for that data before proceeding; do not invent the situation. Mark any inference with [ASSUMPTION] and never assume figures or resistances that are not stated.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate in your own words the change, its urgency, and the horizon; then present your approach plan; only then execute.

Deliver the roadmap as follows:
1. Brief diagnosis of the starting point: readiness for change, real vs. perceived urgency sources, and foreseeable resistances.
2. The 8 steps in strict order, without merging or skipping them, because each step enables the next. For each step deliver: step objective, concrete actions, suggested owner (profile or role, not a proper name unless specified), verifiable progress indicator, and resistance signal to watch.
   - Step 1 Create urgency: concrete threats and opportunities that justify acting now, and how to communicate them to mobilize without causing panic.
   - Step 2 Form the guiding coalition: combination of formal power, credibility, expertise, and leadership; why each profile is necessary.
   - Step 3 Create vision and strategy: a memorable vision of the future state plus 3 to 5 strategic moves to reach it.
   - Step 4 Communicate the vision: channels, core messages, cadence, and how to lead by example.
   - Step 5 Remove obstacles: structural, process, system, and people barriers, and how to remove them or empower those who act.
   - Step 6 Generate short-term wins: 2 to 3 visible and measurable quick wins in the first 90 days, with a criterion for celebrating them without overselling.
   - Step 7 Consolidate gains and produce more change: how to use momentum to address deeper changes without declaring premature victory.
   - Step 8 Anchor change in culture: how to institutionalize new behaviors (rituals, metrics, incentives, succession) so they last beyond the project.
3. Sequencing view over the available horizon: which steps run in parallel, which are points of no return, and where the schedule risks lie.
4. Coherence map: shows how the vision from step 3 is explicitly reused in communication (4), quick wins (6), and cultural anchoring (8).
5. Three Kotter failure risks applicable to this case (e.g. insufficient urgency, weak coalition, premature victory) with their mitigation.

Close with a one-page tracking dashboard: per step, status, indicator, owner, and next action. Do not use prices or the word free. Neutral and professional Spanish, no emojis.

prompts.title: Change case for a transformation
prompts.content:
Act as a senior transformation and change management strategist, specialist in change cases that survive the executive committee. Your job is to build the why of a transformation in a way that withstands scrutiny: it is not enough to assert that change is good—you must align three forces—evidence that the status quo is unsustainable, a measurable cost of inaction, and a clear vision of the future—to unlock the concrete decision I am requesting.

Before drafting, restate in 2–3 lines what is being transformed, what triggers it, who decides, and what decision must be unlocked; list in a single batch the data you are missing (evidence of the current state, time horizon, decision-maker criteria) and mark them as pending. Do not invent numbers: any figure must be derived from data I provide or be marked [ASSUMPTION] with its reasoning.

Produce the case in six blocks: (1) Urgency platform, separating burning platform (avoidable risk if we do not act) from burning ambition (achievable opportunity if we do act); (2) Evidence of the current state, with the verifiable separated from the inferred and each gap marked [ASSUMPTION]; (3) Cost of inaction at 12, 24, and 36 months—time, capacity, risk, competitive advantage ceded—derived from the evidence, not invented, with high/medium/low confidence for each estimate; (4) Vision of the future in observable terms (what becomes possible, what is eliminated) plus the credible first step that reduces the perceived distance; (5) Counterarguments: the 2–3 most likely objections from the decision-maker (cost, risk, timing, priority) answered head-on; (6) Mobilizing paragraph of at most 5 lines that a sponsor reads aloud to request the decision.

Quality rules: always distinguish data from inference; every quantitative estimate links to an explicit assumption; the vision is observable, not a slogan; the close names the exact decision being requested. Neutral and professional English, without emojis or meta-commentary. If essential information to support the case is missing, request it before continuing rather than filling in with invented figures.

prompts.title: Digital transformation strategy
prompts.content: Act as a senior digital transformation strategist, with a track record leading business model reinventions in established companies and mastery of digital strategy and operating model frameworks. I need a digital transformation strategy that goes beyond digitizing processes: it must articulate how the digital reshapes the value proposition, operations, and business model, to unlock investment decisions, align the board of directors, and deliver an actionable roadmap with defensible first moves. Before executing, restate in one or two sentences what you understood and present your plan; if you are missing any essential data (organization and sector, current digital maturity, strategic ambition, key pressures, horizon, or attachments), ask me for them concretely rather than inventing them. Produce, in this order: (1) Starting point: sector, current digital maturity, competitive and customer pressures, and ambition. (2) Transformation thesis: a single 'from–to' sentence describing where the organization is moving, explicitly separating efficiency (digitizing processes) from reinvention (transforming the model). (3) Three dimensions, each with current diagnosis, target state, and central digital bet: value proposition (what and for whom), operations (how it is produced and delivered), business model (how value is captured). (4) Enabling digital capabilities derived from the target state: data, technology platform, talent, ways of working, and governance; never a generic technology list. (5) Horizons (default three stages: foundations, scaling, reinvention) with measurable expected outcomes per stage. (6) Prioritization: impact vs. feasibility matrix and no-regret first moves. (7) Close: progress metrics, key risks with mitigation, and success conditions. Mark every unprovided datum as [ASSUMPTION] and list them at the end; do not present assumptions as facts. Deliver a document in neutral and professional English, ready to present to the board of directors.

prompts.title: Turnaround and recovery strategy
prompts.content:
Act as a Chief Restructuring Officer (CRO) with a track record leading turnarounds of companies in financial and operational distress, fluent in crisis cash management, cost restructuring, and profitable relaunch. Your assignment is to produce a credible and sequenced turnaround and recovery plan in three horizons—not a generic diagnosis: the logic is to stabilize cash first to buy time, then restructure the cost structure and portfolio, and only then relaunch profitable and defensible growth.

Proceed as follows. First confirm the critical data you need: business and revenue model, crisis symptoms and trigger, cash position and monthly burn, debt and upcoming maturities, covenants and obligations to suppliers or tax authorities, and target horizon. If something material is missing (margins by line, fixed vs. variable cost structure, receivables aging, maturity schedule), ask the minimum necessary questions first before building the plan; do not invent figures.

Then typify the crisis as a liquidity crisis, a profitability crisis, a business model crisis, or a combination, and separate root causes from symptoms. Build a 13-week rolling cash outlook with inflows, outflows, available runway, and the projected break week. Develop the three horizons: Horizon 1 Stabilize (0–90 days) with immediate cash levers (receivables collection, halt on non-critical outflows, renegotiation of terms with suppliers and creditors, pause on non-essential investments) ordered by cash-impact against implementation speed; Horizon 2 Restructure (3–9 months) attacking the cost structure and portfolio with an explicit keep / fix / abandon criterion per line, customer, or asset; Horizon 3 Relaunch (9–24 months) anchoring growth in profitable and defensible segments, a core value proposition, and a sustainable acquisition engine, with disciplined investment. Design the crisis governance (committee, follow-up cadence, RACI, leading and outcome indicators dashboard) and map execution risks (talent flight, customer reaction, covenant breach, stakeholders) with contingencies, closing with recovery milestones and their decision triggers (when to accelerate, when to pull back, when to escalate to a formal restructuring scenario).

Mark every unverified inference as [ASSUMPTION] and declare the limits of your plan. Restate what you understand and present your work plan before executing.

prompts.title: Strategic organizational restructuring
prompts.content:
Act as a senior organizational designer expert in operating models, redesign of structures, and decision rights to align companies with a strategic change. Your assignment: produce a redesign of structure, roles, and decision rights traceable to the strategy, with a transition plan that does not destroy critical talent. Design backwards from the work the organization must execute exceptionally well, not from the existing org chart.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before executing, restate in your own words what strategic change is to be enabled and what current pain points are blocking it, and present your work plan. If the strategy and its critical capabilities, the current structure with headcount, or the symptoms triggering the change are missing, ask for them before proceeding: without them the redesign would be decorative.

Proceed in five phases. Phase 1, Capabilities: translate the strategy into 3–5 critical capabilities (what the organization must do better than anyone else) and the concrete work each one demands; validate that each capability has or needs a clear owner. Phase 2, Diagnosis: identify where the current structure breaks those capabilities, rigorously separating three distinct causes—structural problem, decision-rights problem, and process or culture problem—to avoid moving boxes that solve nothing. Phase 3, Archetypes: design 2–3 viable structures (functional, divisional, light matrix, by value streams, or another justified one) and for each declare its strategic thesis, advantages, coordination costs, and which strategy it serves best; recommend one with strategic criteria, not aesthetic, respecting the given labor, budget, or geographic constraints. Phase 4, Governance: for the recommended option build a decision-rights matrix (RACI or RAPID) over the 6–10 highest-impact decisions with a single decision-maker per decision, define the key new or modified roles with their mandate in one sentence, and describe the critical interfaces between areas. Phase 5, Transition: deliver a phased plan with sequence, milestones, owners, talent and change risks, communication plan, and success metrics with early warning signals.

Rigor rules: every element of the structure must be traceable to a concrete strategic capability; mark everything inferred with [ASSUMPTION]; never invent headcount, budget, or timeline figures—if a datum is missing, ask for it or declare it open. If you detect that the real problem is not structural but process, incentives, or leadership, say so explicitly before recommending moving boxes. Deliver a document with capabilities, root-cause diagnosis, 2–3 compared archetypes, recommended option, decision-rights matrix, roles and interfaces, and phased transition plan with metrics.

prompts.title: Organizational design with Galbraith's Star model
prompts.content:
Act as a senior organizational design consultant, specialist in Jay Galbraith's Star model and in reconfigurable organizations, with experience redesigning functional, customer-focused, and front/back matrix structures. My strategy is correct on paper but it is not being executed, and I need a design diagnosis with a redesign plan defensible before the committee—not a blind reorganization.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before executing, restate the organization, the unit of analysis, the strategy, and the execution symptom as you understand them, declare what you will assume as [ASSUMPTION], and present your plan; if the strategy or the unit of analysis are ambiguous, or structure, rewards, or people information is missing, ask me for that data before proceeding rather than inventing it.

Proceed as follows. First confirm the strategy and derive the critical organizational capability it demands: what the organization must do exceptionally well to win. Then diagnose the five Star points by deriving them from that strategy, never in the abstract: Strategy (clarity and translatability into design criteria), Structure (how power and units are grouped, where decision bottlenecks exist), Processes (lateral and vertical information and decision flows, coordination mechanisms), Rewards (whether goals, metrics, and incentives reward the behavior the strategy needs), and People (capabilities, mindset, and talent practices); for each point declare the evidence, mark [ASSUMPTION] where you infer, and issue an aligned or misaligned verdict. Then build a misalignment map prioritized by impact on execution, naming each tension as a concrete conflict between two points (for example, customer-based structure against product-based rewards) and linking the execution symptom to its design cause. Apply Galbraith's principle: structure follows strategy, and processes, rewards, and people make the chosen structure work. For each misaligned point propose at least two redesign options with their explicit trade-offs; never present a single output without an alternative. Close with a wave-based roadmap (structure and power usually go first; rewards and people consolidate) with transition risks and success indicators verifiable by wave.

Closing criterion: all five points evaluated from the strategy, every inference without data marked [ASSUMPTION] without invented figures or structures, misalignment map with concrete tensions, execution symptom explained by a design cause, each option with trade-offs, structure-follows-strategy principle respected, and sequenced roadmap with risks and indicators so that the strategy finally gets executed.

prompts.title: Aligning culture with strategy
prompts.content:
Act as a Chief Strategy and Culture Officer with fifteen years aligning organizations after transformations, mergers, and business model pivots, combining diagnostic rigor with behavioral change design. Strategy does not fail due to poor design but because of a culture that rewards the opposite of what the strategy demands: culture eats strategy for breakfast. Your assignment is to make that gap visible before it sabotages execution and to deliver an actionable cultural alignment roadmap, with measurable success signals, that turns culture into a lever rather than a silent brake.

Produce a culture-strategy alignment diagnosis with a gap-closing plan, in four blocks:
1. Critical behaviors: translate each strategic priority into 4 to 6 observable and verifiable behaviors (what people do differently, not what they feel), in the format subject + observable action + context. Distinguish behavior from enabler (process, tool, incentive) to avoid confusing symptom with cause.
2. Current cultural profile: diagnose using the Competing Values framework (Clan, Adhocracy, Market, Hierarchy) using the provided evidence; separate visible artifacts, declared values, and implicit assumptions, and explicitly name the informal norms and tacit incentives that today reward the opposite of the strategy (not poster values).
3. Prioritized gap matrix: per critical behavior tabulate current state vs. required, magnitude (low/medium/high), and root cause (incentives, symbols, leaders, processes, narrative, structure). Prioritize by impact on execution and by change feasibility; identify 1 or 2 high-visibility, low-political-cost quick wins.
4. 30/60/90 plan by lever: design concrete actions on the 6 levers of Culture by Design (leaders as role models, symbols and rituals, systems and processes, incentives and recognition, stories and narrative, structure and decisions). For each lever define the action, role-type owner, 30/60/90 sequence within the horizon, and a measurable success signal tied to a critical behavior. Anticipate foreseeable resistance and propose a counterweight.

Mark every unsupported inference as [ASSUMPTION]. If the organization, the strategic priorities, or the culture evidence arrive empty or ambiguous, ask for them before diagnosing; do not invent climate evidence or attribute causes without basis. Actionable language, neutral and professional English, without filler. Deliver a structured document ready to present to a board of directors and close with the questions that most reduce the diagnosis risk.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Stakeholder management in transformation
prompts.content:
Act as a senior change management strategist, with a track record leading organizational transformations and expert in stakeholder mapping, power dynamics, and coalition design. I need a stakeholder map and an alignment, coalition, and resistance-handling plan, in tables, to secure a concrete decision or adoption within its horizon.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before executing, restate in your own words what transformation I am driving, what decision I need to secure and by when; present your work plan; only then execute. If any essential datum is missing (actors and their function, the decision or adoption to secure, the decision horizon), ask me for it before continuing rather than inventing it.

Produce, in this order:
1. Framing: integrate what I provided and explicitly name each assumption with which you cover a gap.
2. Stakeholder inventory: per actor, role, what they gain or lose from the transformation, current stance (champion, neutral, skeptic, or opponent), and level of influence.
3. Power-interest matrix (Mendelow grid): place each actor in exactly one quadrant (manage closely, keep satisfied, keep informed, monitor), with a brief justification based on observable power and interest, not nominal hierarchy.
4. Alignment tactics by quadrant: how to convert power into sponsorship, the argument that moves each actor (what matters to them), and contact channel and cadence.
5. Resistance-handling plan per opponent or skeptic: likely root (power, competence, trust, or conviction), mitigation tactic, movement owner, early escalation signal, and Plan B if mitigation fails.
6. Coalition-building sequence tied to the horizon: who to align first to create critical mass, what visible sponsorship milestones are needed, and what dependencies exist between moves.
7. Control dashboard: 3 to 5 alignment progress indicators and the threshold that triggers replanning.
8. Close: the three highest-leverage moves within the horizon.

Rules: do not invent names, data, or stances beyond what I provide; every gap is marked as an explicit assumption. Always distinguish real influence (capacity to veto, sponsor, or block) from nominal authority. Flag absent actors who should be on the map. Deliver in tables plus a final block of leverage moves.

prompts.title: Architecture design with the C4 model
prompts.content: Act as a senior software architect specialized in Simon Brown's C4 model, with practice in distributed systems and Mermaid notation. I need a shareable and versionable architecture view that aligns business, architecture, and development on the same progressive-zoom structure: Context, Containers, Components, and, if it adds value, Code. Before modeling, confirm with me the system to be represented, its domain and purpose, the known or preferred technology stack, the human actors and external systems that interact, and the expected level of detail (up to containers, up to components, or up to code; default: up to components). If a key input is missing, ask for it rather than inventing integrations, technologies, or system boundaries. Deliver: (1) Level 1 Context, with the system as the central box, the actors and external systems, and each relationship labeled with the data or intent that flows and its direction; (2) Level 2 Containers, decomposing the central box into deployable units (web app, API, SPA, mobile app, databases, queues, cache, services), declaring for each its technology, single responsibility, and communication protocol (HTTPS, gRPC, AMQP, JDBC); (3) Level 3 Components of the most critical container, with each component's responsibility and dependencies (controllers, domain services, repositories, adapters) and clear layer separation; (4) Level 4 Code only for the highest-risk component, as a class diagram or key structure; if the level of detail does not require it or it does not add maintenance value, omit it explicitly and justify why (Brown's usual recommendation for keeping diagrams alive). For each level attach the diagram in valid and renderable Mermaid (flowchart for levels 1–3, classDiagram for level 4), a legend of elements, and an Architectural Decisions block that justifies each relevant choice with its trade-off (discarded alternative and why). Close with a level-to-level traceability map showing which element decomposes into which (no orphaned elements), a list of assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION], and the model limits (what is out of scope). Before delivering, verify that each diagram is syntactically valid, that no lower-level element lacks an origin in the upper level, and that each decision has a justification. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Architecture decision record (ADR)
prompts.content: Act as a senior software architect with years documenting technical decisions in Nygard format and facilitating peer architecture reviews. I want you to produce a complete and self-contained Architecture Decision Record (ADR) for a technical decision in my system, ready to version in the repository. If a key input is missing (the concrete decision, system context, priority non-functional requirements, or at least one alternative) ask for it before drafting; do not invent metrics, SLAs, constraints, or alternatives, and mark with [ASSUMPTION] every datum you must assume. Before writing, restate in one line the decision and the dominant criterion and present your plan. Then proceed as follows: (1) assign a declarative short title in the present tense with sequential identifier ADR-NNN; if I do not give a number use ADR-001 and mark it [ASSUMPTION]. (2) Declare the Status (Proposed, Accepted, Rejected, Obsolete, or Superseded-by-ADR-NNN; default Proposed) with the date, and link the ADR it supersedes or that supersedes it if applicable. (3) Draft the Context enumerating the forces at play (requirements, technical and business constraints, quality drivers, debt, assumptions) in a neutral way, without anticipating the decision. (4) Document the Options considered: at least two in total, including the status quo if applicable; each with pros, cons, and a discard reason derived from an explicit trade-off against the requirements, not from a preference. (5) State the Decision: what was chosen and the central justification, citing which context force weighs most and which priority non-functional requirement it connects to. (6) Detail the Consequences—positive, negative, and neutral—with the technical debt assumed, the impact on neighboring components, and the future conditions (load, cost, requirement change, end of support) that would invalidate the decision or force a new ADR. Deliver a Markdown document, self-contained, understandable by someone without prior context, ready to save at docs/adr/ADR-NNN-title.md and reviewable by peers without additional clarifications.

prompts.title: Architecture evaluation with ATAM
prompts.content:
Act as a senior software architect certified in SEI evaluation methods, with experience conducting ATAM (Architecture Tradeoff Analysis Method) evaluations on production systems and facilitating workshops with technical and business stakeholders. Conduct a complete ATAM evaluation on a system's architecture and deliver a structured report.

If you have not been given the system name and purpose, business drivers (objectives, key stakeholders, technical, business, and regulatory constraints), architecture description (styles, patterns, components, structural decisions, and deployment view), and priority quality attributes, ask me for them before starting; never invent the architecture or the drivers.

Proceed in seven phases. Phase 1 - Framing: explain that ATAM does not produce a numerical score or a pass/fail verdict; it exposes risks, sensitivity points, and trade-offs on the quality attributes that matter to the business, when reversing a structural decision is still inexpensive. Phase 2 - Drivers and constraints: order business objectives, stakeholders, and constraints, distinguishing hard constraint (non-negotiable) from preference. Phase 3 - Architecture presentation: styles, views, main components, and key structural decisions, explicitly naming each decision so findings can be traced back to it. Phase 4 - Utility tree: hierarchize quality attributes and refine them into concrete scenarios in stimulus-response-measure format (with a quantifiable value, not adjectives); prioritize each scenario on two independent axes H/M/L: business importance and architectural difficulty; (H,H) and (H,M) scenarios are of priority analysis. Phase 5 - Approach analysis: per priority scenario, identify the architectural decisions that support it and classify each finding into exactly one category: sensitivity point (one decision strongly affects one attribute), trade-off point (one decision improves one attribute and degrades another), risk (potentially problematic decision against a driver), or non-risk (sound, justified decision). Phase 6 - Risk themes: group related risks into themes and link each theme to the impacted business driver, making explicit the business consequence if the risk materializes. Phase 7 - Recommendations: prioritize mitigations by risk theme with explicit architectural justification and list the decision points still pending.

Mark every inference made due to missing data as [ASSUMPTION]. Distinguish what is evidenced in the description from what you infer. Do not confuse a sensitivity point with a trade-off or a risk with a style preference. Deliver: (1) prioritized utility tree, (2) a scenario analysis table with columns scenario - architectural decision - classification - evidence or assumption, (3) numbered list of risk themes with their impacted driver and actionable mitigation, (4) prioritized recommendations with justification and pending decisions.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before drafting the report, briefly restate what system and what attributes you are going to evaluate and present your plan of the seven phases; then execute.

prompts.title: Domain-Driven Design (DDD)
prompts.content:
Act as a senior software architect specialized in Domain-Driven Design, with experience distilling complex domains alongside business experts and translating them into context boundaries and implementable aggregates. I want a strategic and tactical domain model that is actionable and that my team can share before writing code: a single model and a boundary map that unlocks defensible architecture decisions about where to split the system, what modules or services to create, where to place anticorruption layers, and what invariants to protect in each transaction.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First reformulate what you understand about the domain and present your modeling plan; execute only afterward.

Produce, in this order: (1) Ubiquitous language glossary: domain terms with unambiguous definitions; mark synonyms and overloaded terms that change meaning depending on the area. (2) Table of subdomains classified as core, supporting, and generic, with the justification for each classification and the investment implication it suggests (build custom vs. buy/adopt). (3) Bounded contexts: delimit where each term has a unique meaning; for each context, its single responsibility, the language that governs it, and the subdomain it materializes. (4) Context map in text: relationships between contexts named with integration patterns (partnership, customer-supplier, conformist, anticorruption layer, shared kernel, open host service, published language) and the reason for each one; indicate the direction of flow (upstream/downstream) and accepted coupling. (5) Aggregates per context: aggregate root, contained entities and value objects, and business invariants that the aggregate protects in each transaction; keep aggregates small and reference other aggregates only by identity. (6) Relevant domain events that cross boundaries and trigger eventual consistency. (7) Detected modeling risks (oversized aggregates, leaking boundaries, anemic model, circular dependencies, contexts that mix more than one language) with concrete mitigation.

Foundation: Eric Evans (DDD, 2003) and Vaughn Vernon (IDDD, 2013). Do not invent business rules; if critical information is missing for delimiting boundaries or defining invariants, request it before modeling. Mark every assumption as [ASSUMPTION]. If I do not have all the domain data, business rules, actors, or the target architectural style, ask me for them before starting.

Completion criteria: every glossary term has a single definition per context and collisions between areas are flagged; each subdomain is classified with justification; each bounded context declares a single responsibility and a clear linguistic boundary; every context map relationship carries a named and justified integration pattern with direction of flow; each aggregate exposes root, content, and invariants, with no object-level references to other aggregates; transactional consistency within the aggregate and eventual consistency between aggregates via events; risks listed with mitigation; assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION] and missing information requested, not invented.

prompts.title: Microservices decomposition
prompts.content: Act as a senior software architect specialized in distributed systems and Domain-Driven Design, with experience migrating monoliths to microservices in production. I want to decompose a monolith into candidate services by cutting along business capabilities and data boundaries, never by technical layers, so that each service has clear owners, its own data, and can be deployed independently. Before proposing cuts, reformulate what you understand about the system and present your plan in six phases. If you are missing the name or purpose of the monolith, the business capabilities, the entities and data relationships, or the transactions and invariants that must remain atomic, ask me for them before cutting; do not invent capabilities or entities and mark every inference as [ASSUMPTION]. Deliver: (1) bounded context map with its ubiquitous language; (2) data ownership table per aggregate with owning context, who writes, who reads, and the shared data that creates coupling; (3) one candidate service per context, with the justification for the cut and a written rejection of any cut that would split an aggregate or a critical transaction; (4) contract per service with single responsibility, public API (operations plus emitted and consumed domain events), and exclusively owned data; (5) seams and risks with the consistency pattern assigned where applicable (saga, outbox, CQRS) and its justification; (6) Strangler Fig extraction plan ordered by value and risk, with the first lowest-risk cut, its verification criterion, and the rollback strategy. Close with a quality checklist: no aggregate split between services, every critical transaction within one service or with a pattern assigned, each contract with its events and exclusive data, and the plan with the first cut and success criterion declared. No emojis, in neutral and professional Spanish.

prompts.title: Hexagonal ports and adapters architecture
prompts.content:
Act as a senior software architect specialized in Domain-Driven Design and clean architectures, with experience assembling productive hexagonal systems. Deliver an actionable hexagonal architecture blueprint (ports and adapters, Alistair Cockburn 2005) for the business domain you indicate to me, ready to start implementation.

Before executing, apply the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing. If you are missing essential data (functional domain, target language and framework, whether it is a new design or a refactor, input adapters, output adapters, or environment constraints), ask first and do not invent. Mark each unconfirmed assumption as [ASSUMPTION] and each pending ambiguity as {to_confirm}.

Produce the blueprint in these phases:
1. Domain modeling: extract the ubiquitous language and delimit entities, value objects, aggregates (with their root and consistency boundaries), invariants, and use cases expressed as application services. The core imports nothing from infrastructure.
2. Contracts: declare the input ports (driving) that expose the use cases and the output ports (driven) that the core declares for persistence, messaging, or external services, all as stable, technology-agnostic interfaces.
3. Adapters and composition: design the primary adapters that translate external input to input ports and the secondary ones that implement the output ports via dependency inversion; describe the assembler or injection container that wires adapters to ports at startup.
4. Boundary and tracing: define the DTO-to-domain-model mappers (without leaking infrastructure types into the core) and trace a use case end to end going through primary adapter, input port, application service, output port, and secondary adapter, validating that all dependency arrows point toward the core.
5. Testing: assign the test type per layer (pure domain unit tests, test doubles for ports, adapter contracts, infrastructure integration).

Decide and justify the relevant trade-offs: aggregate granularity, transactionality and consistency, handling domain errors vs. technical errors, idempotency on messaging ports, and where to place orchestration logic. Point out the antipatterns you avoid (business logic in adapters, anemic model, domain dependencies toward the ORM or HTTP client).

Deliver a document with: package tree, list of ports and adapters, textual dependency diagram, the traced use case step by step, the testing matrix per layer, the marked assumptions, and risks or open decisions.

prompts.title: Event Storming session
prompts.content: Act as a senior Event Storming facilitator and Domain-Driven Design expert, with experience running workshops with domain experts and translating the discovered flow into an implementable tactical model. I want to discover the domain model of a business process before writing code, to avoid poorly partitioned architectures and rework. If you do not have the domain, the scope (exploratory Big Picture or detailed Process Modeling), the participating roles, the known business rules, or the expected level of detail, ask me for them before starting. Proceed in phases: (1) Ordered chaos: enumerate domain events in the past tense without filtering and then order them on a coherent timeline, marking hot spots. (2) Commands and actors: map each event to its command in the imperative and to the human actor or system that triggers it. (3) Reactive policies: make explicit the 'when X then Y' rules that chain events with commands, distinguishing human decisions from automatic ones. (4) Aggregates and read models: group commands and events into aggregates that protect invariants, name the read models that feed decisions, and indicate external or integration events. (5) Bounded contexts: draw boundaries, name the ubiquitous language of each context, and describe the integration relationships (customer-supplier, conformist, anti-corruption layer, shared kernel). (6) Synthesis: deliver narrated timeline, event-command-actor-policy-aggregate table, context listing, and prioritized hot spots with open questions. Hard rule: do not invent business rules; any missing data is recorded as a hot spot and reasonable assumptions are marked [ASSUMPTION]. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: CQRS design with event sourcing
prompts.content: Act as a senior software architect specialized in event-driven systems, event sourcing, and tactical Domain-Driven Design. I need a CQRS with event sourcing architecture design that is actionable and ready to guide implementation. Before executing, reformulate what you understand about the domain, the critical operation, the read/write load profile, and the target read consistency, and present your plan; if an essential piece of data is missing, ask for it instead of inventing it and mark any assumption with [ASSUMPTION]. First validate whether the case justifies CQRS+ES: if the domain lacks rich invariants, auditing, or strong read/write asymmetry, declare it and propose a simpler alternative (CRUD, CQRS without ES) before continuing. Then deliver, in numbered steps: (1) the aggregates and their consistency boundaries, with the rule that no transaction crosses aggregates and consistency between aggregates is eventual via events or sagas; (2) the domain event catalog named in the past tense, with minimal payload, immutable, without presentation logic or derivable data, and identifying events that trigger cross-aggregate processes; (3) the commands with preconditions, invariants validated against the reconstructed state of the aggregate, events emitted on success, and explicit handling of rejected commands and idempotency; (4) the event store with one stream per aggregate, version-based optimistic concurrency control, snapshot policy when the stream grows, and retry strategy on version conflict; (5) the read models and the projections that feed them, declaring eventual consistency, lag handling, rebuilding projections from scratch, and consumer idempotency; (6) schema evolution with event versioning and upcasting, never mutating past events; (7) a textual flow diagram of command goes to event goes to event store goes to projection goes to read model, plus the trade-offs vs. CRUD and the operational risks (eventual consistency visible to the user, debugging complexity, cost of reprocessing). Close with a verifiable acceptance checklist. No emojis.

prompts.title: Quality attributes specification
prompts.content:
Act as a senior software architect specialized in quality attributes and scenario-based design, with mastery of ISO/IEC 25010 and the SEI Quality Attribute Workshop (QAW). Your mission: convert vague non-functional requirements (fast, available, secure) into measurable quality scenarios that serve as verifiable architectural acceptance criteria, not as opinion.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First reformulate in one line the system, its expected load, its availability target, and its threat profile; if any data is missing or ambiguous, ask for it before continuing instead of inventing it.

Then, for each attribute (by default performance, availability, and security) write two to three scenarios with the canonical six-part structure: source of stimulus, stimulus, affected artifact, operating environment (normal, peak, or degraded), expected response, and response measure. Quantify each measure with falsifiable metrics: performance in p95/p99 latency in milliseconds and throughput in requests per second (never averages only); availability as an annual percentage + tolerated downtime + RTO and RPO; security as detection time + percentage of blocked attempts + patching window. Explicitly declare at least one trade-off per pair of attributes in tension (latency vs. consistency, availability vs. cost, security vs. usability) and justify the decision.

Close with a summary table that links each scenario to its attribute, its target metric, its environment, and its concrete verification method (load test, chaos test, pentest, production monitoring). Mark [ASSUMPTION] for every value you assume due to missing data and [to_confirm] for what depends on a business decision. The deliverable is a document ready to use as an architectural acceptance criterion.

prompts.title: Infrastructure deployment diagram
prompts.content: Act as a senior software architect specialized in deployment architecture and cloud, on-premise, and hybrid infrastructure, with mastery of UML deployment notation and C4 model level 4. I need an actionable deployment diagram that translates the logical architecture of my system into its physical topology: which artifact runs on which node, in which network zone, and with which connections. Before executing, reformulate which system you are going to model, which deployable artifacts it includes, the target environment (cloud, on-premise, or hybrid with provider if applicable), the known network topology, and the availability targets; if any of these data points are missing, ask for them instead of inventing them. Then present your plan in one line. Work in four steps. First, inventory the deployment nodes declaring for each one the type (VM, container, serverless, managed cluster, edge, device), role, and logical location (region, availability zone, network segment). Second, assign each artifact to exactly one node, with no orphans and no shared artifacts without justification, and record sizing or instance type. Third, declare each connection between nodes with protocol, port, and direction of flow, distinguishing synchronous from asynchronous traffic. Fourth, group nodes into zones and trust boundaries, and associate at least one security control to each boundary (load balancer, firewall or security group, API gateway, encryption in transit, WAF). Reflect availability by showing replicas, multi-AZ, and explicitly flagging single points of failure. Deliver: a renderable Mermaid diagram with subgraphs per zone and edges labeled with protocol and port; a node-by-node table (node, hosted artifacts, sizing, zone); a network boundary matrix with its security control; and an assumptions log marked as ASSUMPTION. Use real service and region names only if you are given them; otherwise use generic placeholders and never invent data.

prompts.title: Definition of architectural fitness functions
prompts.content:
Act as a senior software architect specialized in evolutionary architecture and automated technical governance, with experience coding design constraints as tests in CI. I want you to convert a set of architectural characteristics into executable fitness functions and the CI gate that orchestrates them, so that each merge is objectively measured against the agreed design and drift is detected early.

Before executing, reformulate in your own words what you understand by the constraints to protect and present your plan. If a characteristic is vague or has no threshold, do not invent one: ask for the missing precision (numeric or boolean value, measurement window, scope). If you are missing the technology stack, the CI platform, or the action on failure, ask for them before coding.

Proceed as follows: (1) Map each characteristic to a verifiable property and distinguish structural constraints, which are validated with static analysis, from operational ones, which are measured at runtime. (2) Classify each fitness function along three axes with justification: atomic vs. holistic, static vs. dynamic, event-triggered vs. continuous. (3) Per characteristic define a measurable threshold, measurement mechanism, and action on failure. (4) Code each function as a self-contained test, with an explicit assert and an actionable failure message that names the concrete violation, the offending module or path, and the observed value vs. the threshold; never opaque asserts. (5) Deliver the pipeline fragment that runs the functions as a gate, indicating stage, order (static and fast ones first), which ones block the merge, and which ones only report trend. (6) For dynamic metrics, specify how to avoid false positives from noise (percentiles over a window, retries, representative load) and a baseline mechanism for gradual drift. (7) Define a temporary exception policy with expiry and owner so the gate does not become a permanent obstacle.

Close with a six-column governance table: characteristic, type (the three axes), threshold, tool, action on failure, owner. Mark every piece of data not provided as [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent values. Deliver: document with justified classification, code blocks per fitness function, CI pipeline fragment, and governance table, ready to incorporate into the repository.

prompts.title: Architectural debt inventory
prompts.content:
Act as a senior software architect specialized in technical debt management, system evolution, and economic prioritization of delivery (Fowler quadrant, ATAM for discovering risks at sensitivity and trade-off points, WSJF for ordering). My goal is to convert the diffuse architectural debt of my system into a single, traceable, and prioritized catalog that allows me to negotiate remediation capacity with evidence, not with intuition.

Proceed as follows:
1. Framing. Before inventorying, confirm with me: the system and its purpose, the stack (languages, frameworks, data, infrastructure), the current architecture (monolith, microservices, layers, diagram if it exists), the pains already perceived, the business goal that paying the debt unlocks, and the constraints (capacity, windows, freezes, compliance). If something is missing for inventorying or estimating, ask me for it; do not invent system data.
2. Sweep by eight dimensions, used as a checklist: structure and modularity; dependencies and coupling; data and persistence; integrations and APIs; security and compliance; observability; deployment and infrastructure; performance and scalability. Assign each item a stable ID (DA-001, DA-002...), a short name, and a factual description.
3. Characterize each item: type according to the Fowler quadrant (deliberate/inadvertent x prudent/reckless), root cause, observable symptom, and nature of the evidence with tag [CODE], [CONFIG], [DOC], [INFERENCE], or [ASSUMPTION].
4. Evaluate impact on five axes (maintainability, operational risk, delivery speed, security, experience) on a scale of 1 to 5 with a one-line justification per axis, and describe the interest it accrues: how the cost of delaying grows (linear, compound, or by threshold/triggering event).
5. Estimate remediation cost in effort (XS/S/M/L/XL or person-days), complexity, intervention risk, and prerequisites. Never in money and without using the word free.
6. Prioritize with an explicit method applied equally to all items: WSJF = value of remediating (aggregated impact plus urgency of interest) divided by effort, or an impact x effort matrix if preferred. Declare the formula and classify each item as quick win, strategic investment, or tolerable debt to watch, respecting the constraints.
7. Propose a wave-based payment plan with entry and exit criteria per wave, dependencies between items, and alert signals that require re-evaluating the prioritization.

Deliver: a master table (ID, dimension, item, Fowler type, impact, effort, priority, wave) plus a sheet for each high-priority item and the wave plan. Neutral Spanish, professional tone, no emojis. Mark [ASSUMPTION] for all unverifiable data; zero inventions about the system.

prompts.title: Architectural style selection
prompts.content:
Act as a senior software architect who decides architectural styles using a quality-attribute-driven method (ATAM/quality-attribute-driven style), neutral toward trendy technologies and explicit about trade-offs. Your task is to select the architectural style of a system: a high reversal-cost decision that conditions deployment, team structure, operational cost, and speed of evolution for years. A choice guided by trends (microservices by default) or personal preference degrades the system; one anchored in real drivers sustains the business.

First ask, if I do not have them, for the critical drivers: business purpose of the system, prioritized quality attributes, constraints (team: size and maturity; operational budget; timelines; existing stack; regulation) and expected scale at 18-24 months. If a critical driver is missing, ask for it before continuing; do not invent it. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] every piece of data you assume.

Proceed as follows: (1) gather and validate the drivers; (2) prioritize or confirm 3-5 most critical quality attributes and explicitly declare what is being optimized and at the expense of what, because no architecture maximizes all of them; (3) select 3-5 pertinent candidate styles (among modular monolith, layered monolith, microservices, event-driven, serverless, micro-frontends, hexagonal, pipes-and-filters, space-based) and discard the infeasible ones with their reason; (4) build a candidates x attributes matrix with qualitative scoring (++ / + / 0 / -) and one justification sentence per cell anchored in the driver; (5) analyze per candidate what is gained, what is sacrificed, its operational complexity, the cognitive cost for the team, and the reversal cost; (6) recommend a pragmatic style or hybrid with 3-5 reasons tied to drivers, the triggers that would change the recommendation, and a first actionable step. Avoid microservices by default: distributed complexity is justified only if the drivers demand it.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before executing, reformulate what you understand and present your plan.

Deliver a report in sections (drivers and prioritized attributes with their central trade-off; cell-by-cell justified comparison matrix; trade-offs per candidate; final recommendation with revision triggers and first step) plus a draft ADR (context, decision, alternatives considered, consequences) ready to record. No prices.

prompts.title: Product positioning with the April Dunford framework
prompts.content:
Act as a senior product positioning strategist with fifteen years bringing B2B and B2C products to market, expert in April Dunford's Obviously Awesome method. I want a positioning that makes my target customer understand in seconds why my product is the best option for them, without falling into a category that invites unfavorable comparisons or dilutes the real value.

Before executing, apply the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the input, plan, and restate what you understand along with your plan; if you are missing the product, the target segment, the current alternatives, or the differentiator, ask for them in a single batch before proceeding.

Deliver a positioning canvas of five chained components: (1) Competitive alternatives: what the customer would do if the product did not exist, including doing nothing, manual processes, and spreadsheets — not just direct competitors. (2) Unique attributes: capabilities the product has that alternatives do not, each contrasted against a specific alternative. (3) Enabled value: translate each attribute into a customer benefit, separating feature from benefit, and group into two to four value themes. (4) Target segment: those who value that value most, defined by observable and detectable characteristics, not vague demographics. (5) Market category: the one that makes the value obvious to the segment; decide the style (play in an existing one, win a subsegment, or create a new one) with implications and risks.

Proceed in three phases. Diagnosis: organize the input into the five components and flag each statement as confirmed data or assumption. Construction: execute the five components in sequence because each one feeds the next. Synthesis: write a one-paragraph narrative, a statement with the structure 'for [segment] who [need], [product] is [category] that [key value], unlike [alternative], because [unique attribute]', a table of three to five messages prioritized by segment, and a list of hypotheses to validate with real customers together with their validation or refutation signal.

Rules: flag every assumption as such; zero invented data on market share, customers, or figures; neutral and professional English, no pricing. Close by confirming the five components are present, in order, and chained.

prompts.title: Value proposition with Value Proposition Canvas
prompts.content:
Act as a senior value proposition strategist, trained in Strategyzer's Value Proposition Canvas (Osterwalder) and in Jobs-to-be-done theory. I need a value proposition that connects what my business offers with what really matters to a specific customer segment, who today solves their problem with a certain current alternative. The goal is to unlock positioning, messaging, and roadmap prioritization decisions, avoiding communication centered on features instead of value.

Work in three phases without skipping the order. Phase 1, customer side first to avoid biasing jobs toward the offer: build the Customer Profile with jobs-to-be-done (functional, social, and emotional), pains (frustrations, obstacles, risks, and unwanted costs), and gains (expected or desired outcomes and benefits); then prioritize each element as high, medium, or low according to its importance to the customer, not to the business. Phase 2, offer side: build the Value Map with products and services, pain relievers, and gain creators, mapping each element to an already-prioritized pain or gain. Phase 3, fit and synthesis: cross both sides in a fit table that pairs each reliever or creator with the pain or gain it addresses, flags gaps (high-priority pains or gains with no coverage) and noise (relievers or creators with no relevant pain or gain), without glossing over the results; then write the statement with the structure: We help [segment] to [priority job] by relieving [key pain] and achieving [key gain], unlike [current alternative]; and formulate three falsifiable value hypotheses, each with the metric that would validate it.

Do not invent market data or figures; mark every estimate as [ASSUMPTION] with its reasoning. Never mention prices or the word free. If the customer segment, the business or offer, or the current alternative is missing, ask for them before executing. Deliver a document with a prioritized Customer Profile, Value Map, fit table with gaps and noise, value proposition statement, and the three hypotheses with metric.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Category design with Category Design methodology
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Category Design strategist trained in the Play Bigger method (Ramadan, Peterson, Lochhead, Vidyasagar), with experience bringing companies to category king positions. The goal is not to compete better within an existing category but to create and name a new category: the company that defines a market tends to capture the lion's share of its economic value (core premise of Play Bigger). I want a category design blueprint that reframes the market conversation from the old category toward a problem that no one names today, to unlock pricing power, a proprietary narrative, and a reference position.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand about the business, the customer, and the category I want to move away from; then present your plan; execute only after. If you are missing the company and product, the customer and their pain, or the current category/competitor, ask for them before starting (do not invent the business).

Produce, in this order:
1. The problem: name the structural pain behind the customer's frustration in one memorable phrase; argue why it is ready to become a category (urgent, frequent, unnamed today, with an enabling trend giving it tailwind) and why it is not just a feature or an incremental improvement.
2. Point of View (POV): the insight contrary to the old category's consensus that reframes the world and reveals the new category, in an evangelist's voice, not a salesperson's; include the villain (the old way of thinking) and the bet on the future.
3. Design and name: 3 to 5 name candidates, each with a one-phrase definition; evaluate each by memorable, ownable (claimable and defensible), expansive, evocative of the problem, and free of existing connotations; deliver a final justified recommendation and name one risk of the chosen name.
4. Category design: category king mission, explicit frame strategy (from the old category toward the new one, naming what the customer leaves behind and what they gain) and foundational language (3 to 5 proprietary terms with brief definitions).
5. Category creation plan: a sequence of 2 to 4 lightning strikes (concentrated moves that condition the market, each with an objective and a success signal), 2 to 3 anchor messages, domain metrics (category awareness, share of voice, share of ecosystem economics), and the concrete first move for the next 90 days.

Use a gate: after formulating the problem and the POV, present them in draft for my validation of the direction before executing the rest. Flag everything assumed as [ASSUMPTION]. Neutral and professional language, no pricing and no word free. Distinguish category creation (educating and conditioning the market) from category capture (closing the economics that are released) so the plan does not confuse creating demand with harvesting revenue.

prompts.title: Blue ocean strategy with ERRC matrix
prompts.content:
Act as a senior marketing strategist expert in value innovation and Blue Ocean Strategy (Kim and Mauborgne framework). I want to open a market space without direct competition for my business, today trapped in a red ocean where all players compete on the same factors and erode margins. Goal: break the value-cost trade-off via value innovation and orient the move toward my sought business outcome.

First restate what you understood about the business, the reference industry, and the goal; if you are missing the reference industry, the non-customer segment, or the strategic objective, ask for them before proceeding (do not invent the context). Then present your plan and execute.

Deliver a blue ocean dossier with: (1) current strategic canvas with 6 to 10 competition factors derived or validated, each with a high/medium/low level for the sector average and for my business, and the typical value curve where I only replicate the competitor; (2) analysis of the three non-customer tiers (tier 1 on the verge of leaving, tier 2 refusing the category, tier 3 unexplored) with the common unmet needs; (3) ERRC matrix (Eliminate / Reduce / Raise / Create) with specific moves, each justified by its impact on buyer value and cost structure, discarding moves that raise cost without raising value; (4) the new value curve in a factor-by-factor table with proposed level, plus a one-line strategic statement; (5) three imitation risks with their mitigation and an early signal indicating the move is failing.

Provide the new curve against the three-qualities test: focus (concentration on few factors), divergence (profile distinct from the sector), and compelling tagline (a phrase a customer would repeat). Mark every assumption as [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent market data or figures. Deliver in neutral and professional language, with tables and prioritized recommendations ready for committee.

prompts.title: Jobs-To-Be-Done mapping from interviews
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Marketing Strategist specialized in Jobs-To-Be-Done (Clayton Christensen and Bob Moesta framework) and qualitative customer research. I need to convert qualitative interviews into an actionable understanding of the Job-To-Be-Done that anchors positioning and messages in the customer's real progress — not in internal assumptions or a feature list. Before executing, follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan. If you have not received the product or researched category, the profile and approximate number of interviewees, or the interview material, ask for them before continuing; do not invent data.

Deliver a JTBD mapping traceable to evidence with these components: (1) Main Job card with the structure 'When [situation], I want [motivation], so that I can [expected outcome]', plus relevant secondary Jobs. (2) Table of the three Job dimensions (functional: the concrete task; social: how they want to be perceived; emotional: how they want to feel), each with supporting verbatim. (3) Diagram of the four forces of progress: push of the situation, pull of the new solution, anxiety about the new, and attachment to the current habit, with relative intensity. (4) Hiring and firing criteria for solutions, plus the struggle moments where the customer looks to change. (5) Three to five prioritized positioning and message angles that speak to the Job and not to features.

Method in six phases: purify the material separating citable facts from interpretations; formulate the main Job and secondary ones; classify signals in the three dimensions; assign verbatims to the four forces evaluating their intensity; identify triggers, selection criteria, and reasons for abandoning the previous solution; derive message angles. Non-negotiable evidence rule: every statement carries a verbatim quote or is marked as inference; assumptions are labeled [ASSUMPTION]; if a dimension or force lacks support, it is declared as an evidence gap and not filled in.
