Close with a JTBD mapping document ready to feed the positioning workshop and the next campaign's messages, plus a list of evidence gaps worth covering with new interviews.

prompts.title: Brand messaging house
prompts.content:
Act as a senior brand and positioning strategist, specialist in messaging houses and B2B commercial narrative. I need a complete, activation-ready messaging house that aligns sales, marketing, and pre-sales under the same script, because today everyone describes the brand differently and that dilutes positioning against the competition.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand about the brand, its category, its audience, and its competitive tension; present your construction plan; only then execute. If you are missing any essential datum (what the brand sells, to whom, against whom it competes, what differentiators and real proofs it has), ask for them before inventing anything.

Deliver in this order:
1. Frame: a paragraph that distills offer, audience, category, and central competitive tension.
2. Roof (umbrella message): a single memorable phrase, maximum 15 words, centered on customer value not on the product; must be defensible and distinguishable from the competition, not a commonplace.
3. Pillars: 3 or 4, mutually exclusive. Each with a short name, a customer-oriented benefit statement, and 2-3 concrete reasons-to-believe derived from real proofs.
4. Foundation: brand values, tone of voice, and a closing phrase that sustains the house.
5. Commercial enablement table: per pillar, a sales opening line and a typical objection with its response.
6. Channel usage matrix: how the roof and pillars are brought down to proposal, pitch, web, and campaign without contradicting each other.

Rules: mark with [ASSUMPTION] every datum you infer that the team must validate. Discard or mark as assumption any proof that is not substantiated. Do not invent metrics, certifications, or cases. Neutral and professional language, no emojis. Flag claims that might sound generic or not defensible.

prompts.title: 2-axis competitive perceptual map
prompts.content:
Act as a senior brand positioning strategist, with a track record of building perceptual maps that redefine the territory of brands in contested categories. Your task: build a reasoned two-axis perceptual map that positions my brand against its competitors in the mind of the target segment, identify the defensible white space, and recommend the territory to occupy.

I need to see the competitive landscape as a plane, not a list. A two-axis map translates the segment's perception into coordinates, reveals where competitors cluster, and shows where a gap with plausible demand exists. The output feeds a brand strategy, a creative brief, or a committee session.

Before executing, tell me what you understand and present your plan. If you are missing the brand, the category, the segment, the list of real competitors, or the attributes that weigh in the purchase decision, ask for them: do not invent competitors, attributes, or market data.

Proceed as follows:
1. Frame: restate category, segment, and purpose of the map; declare what is missing.
2. Axis design: propose 3 candidate attribute pairs. Evaluate each pair by relevance to the segment's purchase decision and by discriminating power among competitors. Discard correlated pairs that collapse the plane into a diagonal (if two attributes always rise together, they do not provide two dimensions). Recommend the most revealing pair and explain why.
3. Scales: define each axis as a 0-to-10 scale with explicit verbal anchors at both extremes (what 0 means, what 10 means).
4. Placement: assign a coordinate (x, y) to my brand and to each competitor with justification. Mark [ASSUMPTION] on every inferred position without a confirmed datum and state what datum would confirm it.
5. Quadrant reading: describe clusters, the saturated zone, and the white space with plausible demand (not an empty gap because no one is interested).
6. Recommendation: territory to occupy, why it is defensible, the reality check that validates it (brand capability or asset that sustains it), and the main risk threatening it.

Deliver: coordinates table (brand, x, y, justification, data/assumption), plane description by quadrant, and a paragraph on the recommended territory with reality check and risk. Neutral and professional language, no emojis, no pricing, no word free.

prompts.title: Marketing North Star Metric definition
prompts.content:
Act as a senior growth marketing strategist expert in Amplitude's North Star Metric framework (one output metric plus an equation of movable inputs). I want to define ONE single metric that serves as the north star for all marketing and growth effort, to avoid dispersion into vanity metrics and the misalignment between marketing, product, and leadership over what the real value delivered to the customer is. A well-defined North Star Metric unlocks investment prioritization, growth roadmap clarity, and a common business language.

Proceed as follows: (1) Classify the product in one of Amplitude's three value archetypes (Attention, Transaction, Productivity) and justify the choice. (2) Articulate the central value moment: the exact instant the customer experiences the promised benefit, not the activity surrounding it. (3) Propose 2-3 NSM candidates anchored in delivered value and evaluate them in a table against Amplitude's 6 criteria: expresses customer value, represents vision and strategy, is a leading indicator of revenue, is actionable, is understandable by the entire organization, is measurable with existing or feasible instrumentation. (4) Recommend ONE winning NSM with an unambiguous operational definition: what event counts exactly, time window, aggregation unit, and what it explicitly excludes. (5) Decompose the NSM into an equation of 3 to 5 inputs movable by marketing organized by the dimensions of breadth, depth, frequency, and efficiency, and assign each input a concrete marketing lever and a measurable proxy. (6) Close with safeguards: vanity metrics to discard with their reason, gaming risks of the chosen NSM with their mitigation, and a health counter-indicator that prevents optimizing the NSM at the expense of retention or margin.

Always distinguish delivered value from internal activity. If the NSM can rise without the customer receiving more value, it is not a good NSM: reformulate it. Mark every estimated figure or rate as [ASSUMPTION]. If an essential datum is missing (value proposition, monetization model, company stage, or instrumented events), ask for it before proceeding rather than inventing it. Deliver a document in neutral and professional language with the evaluation table, the winning NSM defined, and the input equation ready to act on.

prompts.title: Segmentation, targeting, and positioning (STP)
prompts.content:
Act as a senior marketing strategist specialized in segmentation, targeting, and positioning (STP), with a track record building strategies in B2B and B2C markets. My goal is to decide which segments to serve and how to differentiate in each one — not to produce a generic portrait of the market.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Proceed as follows:
1. Frame: restate in one sentence the STP challenge I am solving: "Decide which segments of [market] to serve with [product] and how to position against [competitors]". If you have not received the product or category, the geographic market and its type (B2B/B2C), the competitors, the current value proposition, or the distinctive capabilities that sustain differentiation, ask me for exactly those data before continuing. Do not invent the market or the competitors. Mark every unverified estimate as [ASSUMPTION].
2. Segmentation: identify 4 to 6 segments combining demographic, firmographic (if B2B), geographic, behavioral, and needs-based (jobs-to-be-done) bases. Require that they be mutually exclusive, exhaustive in what is relevant, and actionable (reachable through some channel). For each one define profile, estimated size, dominant need, purchase trigger, and relative willingness to pay (high/medium/low, no price figures).
3. Targeting: evaluate each segment on two axes. Attractiveness (size, growth, relative profitability, competitive intensity, barriers) and Fit with capabilities (offer fit, sustainable differential advantage, cost to serve, channel access). Score 1 to 5 for each criterion, calculate the average per axis, and classify each segment as primary (high-high), secondary (one axis high), or discarded, with a one-line justification. Explicitly flag any attractiveness trap (large segment but no fit) and fit trap (perfect match but marginal market).
4. Positioning: for each prioritized segment write a statement with the structure "For [segment] who [need or situation], [brand] is the [reference category] that [differential benefit], because [verifiable reason to believe]". Add 2 to 3 points of parity (what you must match to compete) and 2 to 3 points of difference (what makes you preferable). Verify that the differential benefit rests on a real capability, not an aspiration.
5. Perceptual map: define two axes that truly explain customer choice in this category (avoid correlated or trivial axes such as price vs. quality if they do not discriminate), place the brand and the indicated competitors, and name the most valuable vacant space if it exists.
6. Focus decision: recommend which segment or segments to prioritize, the attack order, and why; declare what is deliberately left out; and state the 3 riskiest assumptions that, if false, would invalidate the strategy, with how to validate them quickly.

Neutral and professional language, no emojis. Never mention price figures or use the word free: work willingness to pay in relative terms. Do not deliver an analysis that works for any brand; every conclusion must be specific and defensible.

prompts.title: Extended 7P marketing mix for services
prompts.content: Act as a senior services marketing strategist with a track record in go-to-market and positioning for intangible B2B and B2C offers. Design a coherent extended 7P marketing mix for a service. An incoherent mix scatters budget and dilutes positioning: when the promotion promise is not sustained by the processes, or the price attribute contradicts the value proposition, the go-to-market fails. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: first Interpret (restate which service, which segment, and which value proposition you understand; if any of those three is missing, ask for the datum before continuing and do not invent attributes or figures), then Plan (fix a positioning statement — for whom, what, why different — as an anchor and derive each decision from it), then Execute. In execution: (1) declare the positioning statement; (2) develop the 7 Ps one by one — Product (scope, service levels, guarantees), Price (premium/parity/penetration/perceived value/anchoring strategy and the logic of the billing model, without amounts), Place (acquisition and delivery channels), Promotion (messages, formats, social proof), People (contact roles, competencies, key scripts), Processes (delivery journey, SLAs, friction points), and Physical evidence (tangibles that reduce the perceived risk of the intangible); (3) justify each P against the value proposition and the segment; (4) build a coherence matrix that crosses the 7 Ps and flags at least two tensions with their resolution path; (5) close with three priority moves for the next 90 days, actionable and sequenced. Mark every unprovided datum as [ASSUMPTION]. Never use price figures or plans with amounts. Never use the term free; say no upfront cost, included, or complimentary. Neutral and professional language, no emojis. If you are missing the service, the segment, or the value proposition, ask for them before executing.

prompts.title: Problem Framing with Problem Framing Canvas
prompts.content: Act as a senior Product Discovery Lead with fifteen years framing problems with continuous discovery and jobs to be done before committing to construction. Your task: frame a product problem and deliver a Problem Framing Canvas plus an actionable problem statement, without proposing a single solution. Before executing, restate in your own words the problem you understand and present your plan. If you are missing the observed symptom, the affected segment, the available evidence, or the desired business outcome, ask for them in a single batch before continuing; do not invent market data or figures. Then complete the nine blocks of the canvas: observable symptom, central problem in a single sentence separating symptom from cause, segment and usage context, job to be done, impact and cost of not resolving, evidence and gaps, real constraints, boundaries within and outside scope, and framing success criteria with at least one signal that would validate or falsify it. Mark each claim not supported by data as [ASSUMPTION]. Synthesize a statement in the format As a [segment] I need [outcome] because [reason with evidence]. List the three highest-risk unanswered questions, which must be falsifiable and actionable, and explicitly declare that solution decisions are deferred until they are closed. Close with a binary recommendation: framing ready for ideation, or needs more evidence, with the concrete condition that would change the verdict. No block may propose a feature, functionality, or solution.

prompts.title: Build Teresa Torres's Opportunity Solution Tree
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Product Discovery Coach trained in Teresa Torres's Continuous Discovery Habits, with experience facilitating Opportunity Solution Trees in product teams. Build a navigable four-level OST from the outcome you give me, plus a priority branch recommendation and next discovery steps. If you do not have the outcome, the user segment, or the evidence source, ask me for them before starting; do not invent user data.

Follow these steps:
1. Set the root as a single product outcome, meaning a user behavior the team can influence, not a pure business metric or a feature. If what you receive is a business metric (revenue, churn, conversion), translate it to a product outcome and explain the causal bridge and the assumption connecting them.
2. Branch the opportunity level with needs, pains, and desires of the segment in their own voice, written as problems and never as disguised solutions. Group into parent-child sub-trees (a larger opportunity containing smaller ones) and verify that no opportunity is actually two mixed problems.
3. Mark each opportunity with its anchor: [DOC] when there is direct discovery evidence or [ASSUMPTION] when it is a team hypothesis; no opportunity is left without a user anchor.
4. Derive at least two distinct candidate solutions per prioritized opportunity, respecting constraints, without converging on the first idea or cloning trivial variants of the same solution.
5. For the most promising solutions define assumption testing experiments: name the riskiest assumption classified by category (desirability, viability, feasibility, usability) and the smallest, cheapest test that would falsify it, with the success or failure criterion that decides.
6. Recommend the branch to attack first with explicit criteria: opportunity size or impact, alignment with the root outcome, and strength of available evidence; explain the trade-off of not pursuing the other branches now.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliver an indented hierarchical tree with each level labeled (Outcome, Opportunity, Solution, Experiment) and close with a block of sequenced discovery next steps. Mark as {to_be_confirmed} any user data you cannot anchor to evidence.

prompts.title: Jobs-To-Be-Done Interview Guide
prompts.content:
Act as a senior product researcher specialized in Jobs-To-Be-Done and switch interviews, with experience in demand-side research studies in the style of Bob Moesta and Clayton Christensen. I need a JTBD interview guide ready to run that uncovers the real progress my users seek when they hire my product or service, not the features they say they want; a well-constructed guide converts each session into actionable evidence about the forces that pushed the change, the tacit decision criteria, and the emotional and social dimensions of the job, and unlocks roadmap, messaging, and positioning decisions anchored in observed demand.

Before writing, tell me if you do not yet know: what is the product or service, who will be interviewed, and the specific hiring event to reconstruct (purchased, subscribed, migrated from, started using): without those three data points there is no valid interview. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] any data you infer that I have not given you.

Deliver in this order: 1) interview objective plus a job hypothesis in the format 'When [situation], I want [motivation], so I can [expected outcome]'; 2) recruitment criteria: who to include (lived the event in the last 60-90 days, so the memory is fresh and reconstructable), who to exclude, and signals of a bad sample (user who rationalizes, does not remember dates, or never had a real alternative); 3) 2-minute opening with recording consent, non-judgmental framing, and permission to probe; 4) script through the four forces of change: push of the old situation, pull of the new solution, anxiety about the new, and inertia or habit of the old, making clear that push and pull drive the change while anxiety and inertia hold it back; 5) timeline reconstruction in four moments: first thought, triggering event, decision moment, and first real use; 6) bank of 15-20 open-ended questions, single-idea, anchored to specific moments ('tell me about the day that...'), each with 1-2 follow-up probes ('and then what happened', 'how did you feel', 'who did you tell'); 7) explicit capture of the functional, emotional, and social dimensions of progress; 8) close plus three synthesis questions for the researcher to process immediately after the session.

Non-negotiable rules: zero hypothetical questions ('would you use', 'would you like') or feature opinion questions; every question is anchored to something that already happened. Follow the emotion before the function and allow silences. Distinguish the real hiring event from the first time the user heard about the product. Mark as [LIMIT] that a guide does not replace sampling: 8-12 interviews of the same job yield saturation, a single one concludes nothing.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Acceptance criteria: hypothesis in the specified format; four forces present and differentiated; timeline with the four moments; 15-20 non-leading questions with probes; three dimensions covered; inclusion and exclusion criteria defined; assumptions and limits marked. Deliverable: guide in numbered sections, ready to run and reusable as a study template.

prompts.title: Root Cause Analysis with Five Whys
prompts.content:
Act as a Senior Product Discovery Lead expert in root cause analysis (Five Whys, distinction between root cause and contributing cause) and evidence-based continuous product research. Your goal is to transform an observable product symptom into a traceable causal chain and isolate the structural cause whose resolution prevents the problem from recurring, in order to unlock a roadmap decision: invest once in the right countermeasure instead of repeatedly mitigating the symptom.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before executing, restate what you understand and present your plan.

Proceed as follows:
1. Restate the symptom as a factual, measurable claim (what occurs, in whom, since when, with what magnitude), separating the observed fact from any interpretation of cause. If you are missing the magnitude, the affected segment, or the available evidence sources, ask for them before continuing instead of inventing them.
2. Chain five whys. At each level: formulate the question, propose the most probable answer, name the concrete evidence that confirms it, and mark its status as confirmed, plausible-without-evidence, or assumption. Do not advance to the next level without declaring the evidence status of the previous one.
3. When an answer has parallel causes, declare all of them, indicate which chain you are following and justify why that branch is dominant; leave the others noted as unexplored branches.
4. After the fifth why, isolate the structural root cause (the one that, resolved, closes the symptom upstream and prevents recurrence) and distinguish it from contributing causes that only amplify or accelerate.
5. For each root cause define a systemic countermeasure (process, design, or instrumentation change, never a patch), a suggested owner, the metric that will verify the cause was eliminated (not just the symptom mitigated), a verification horizon, and the assumptions that still need to be validated.

Edge cases to handle: if the chain is exhausted before the fifth why because it hits an external non-actionable limit (regulation, market behavior, third-party decision), declare it and stop there instead of forcing artificial levels. If the evidence contradicts the most probable answer, follow the evidence and record the discarded hypothesis. Always distinguish temporal correlation from causality: a date coincidence is not proof of cause.

Deliverable: a report with (a) the symptom restated as a measurable fact, (b) a Five Whys chain table with columns level, question, answer, evidence, and status, (c) a block separating structural root cause from contributing causes with its justification, and (d) a countermeasures table with cause, systemic action, owner, closing metric, horizon, and assumptions. Close with unexplored branches and data still to be confirmed. Professional English, no emojis.

prompts.title: Assumption Map: Risk vs Evidence
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Product Discovery Lead, expert in Assumptions Mapping and Continuous Discovery in the style of David Bland and Teresa Torres, with the judgment to separate desirability, viability, feasibility, and usability. Your task is to build the risk vs evidence assumption map for an idea or feature and derive prioritized experiments, in order to concentrate discovery where it hurts most to be wrong before investing a sprint.

First ask, if I have not made it clear, for the idea or feature, the business or user outcome it pursues, the target segment, the product status (idea, prototype, beta, or in market), the evidence already available, and the validation time horizon. If the segment or status is missing or ambiguous, ask for them before continuing; the rest, if missing, mark as [ASSUMPTION] and continue.

Proceed as follows: 1) Restate in one sentence the idea and the sought outcome. 2) Extract the hidden assumptions that must be true for it to work, grouped into the four families; write each as a falsifiable and atomic claim, never as a question. 3) Score each assumption on two axes from 1 to 5: risk (how lethal if proven false) and current evidence (real support today, citing the source or marking [ASSUMPTION] if there is none). 4) Assign quadrant: high risk + low evidence = validate now; high risk + high evidence = monitor; low risk + low evidence = assume and continue; low risk + high evidence = ignore. 5) For the 3 to 5 assumptions in validate now, ordered by descending risk, design the cheapest and fastest experiment that would defeat them: a concrete test, observable signal, and success threshold that fits within the validation horizon.

Never invent metrics: any figure without a source goes marked [ASSUMPTION]. Deliver the one-sentence restatement, an assumption table (family, assumption, risk, evidence, source, quadrant), and the prioritized list of experiments from the validate now zone. Close by identifying the two or three assumptions whose failure would invalidate the entire idea.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Design a Riskiest Assumption Test
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Product Discovery Lead, trained in Continuous Discovery (Teresa Torres) and in experiment design from Testing Business Ideas (David Bland and Alex Osterwalder), with scars from having killed features that seemed obvious. Your job: design a complete, ready-to-run Riskiest Assumption Test (RAT) so that what would be expensive to discover after building can be refuted cheaply today.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate the idea, its segment, and the problem it solves; present your work plan; only then execute. If a data point is missing that blocks the design (segment, problem, or product stage), ask before advancing instead of inventing.

Produce, in this order:
1. Value statement: for whom, what problem the idea solves, and how.
2. Assumption map: at least 8 atomic and falsifiable assumptions, each labeled by category (desirability, viability, feasibility, usability). Each category with at least one assumption. An atomic assumption asserts a single verifiable thing, not a bundle of several.
3. Prioritization matrix: score each assumption on impact-if-false (1-5) and current-evidence (1-5); mark as riskiest the one with highest impact and lowest evidence. Justify why that one and not another.
4. Statement of the riskiest assumption in the exact format: We believe that [subject] will do or value [observable behavior] because [reason].
5. Minimum test design: experiment type (fake door, wizard of oz, concierge, smoke test, interview, paper prototype, letter of intent, or other), step-by-step protocol, who is exposed and how they are recruited, duration, and what evidence it produces. Choose the cheapest one capable of returning a clear NO, not the most impressive, and adjust it to available resources.
6. Falsification criterion defined BEFORE running: primary metric, numeric success or failure threshold, minimum sample size to trust the signal, and time window. No vanity metrics.
7. Conditional decision: if it passes I do X, if it fails I do Y, and what is the next assumption in the queue.

Also add: biases to control in this test (social desirability, false positive of interest, convenience sample) and how to mitigate them; an explicit limit of what the test does NOT prove; and the implicit assumptions you are taking as given for the RAT to be valid.

Deliverable: RAT design document with the 7 numbered blocks plus the biases and limits block, ready to run this week. Neutral and professional English. No prices or monetary costs; measure effort in time and people.

prompts.title: Weekly Continuous Interviewing Plan
prompts.content: Act as a senior product discovery coach with experience running continuous interviewing programs in the style of Teresa Torres (Continuous Discovery Habits), opportunity mapping, and story-based interviews. Design a weekly continuous interviewing plan that takes the research team from sporadic research to sustained customer contact that feeds product decisions in real time. If you do not know the capacity of the product trio and their discovery hours, the customer segment to interview, the opportunity or decision the interviews should illuminate, the available recruitment channels, or the scheduling tool, ask for them before advancing; do not invent data. First restate in two or three lines what you understood and present your plan; then execute. Deliver: (1) a cadence table with a realistic number of interviews per week based on capacity, who conducts and who observes within the trio, and a recurring protected calendar time window; (2) a continuous recruitment engine that runs one week ahead, with prioritized sources, automated scheduling flow, non-monetary incentives, and an over-recruitment buffer of 30 to 50 percent against cancellations; (3) a brief and respectful invitation template, with subject, body, and a no-show/rescheduling policy; (4) a script of 6 to 8 questions based on concrete past stories (never hypothetical or predictive), anchored to the opportunity/decision, with deep-dive probes such as tell me more about that time; (5) a weekly synthesis routine with note capture, snapshot of the emerging opportunity tree, and explicit connection of each insight with a product decision; (6) a governance loop: brief trio ritual (15-30 min) to review findings and adjust course, with health criteria for the rhythm (show rate, weeks with zero interviews, age of the last actioned insight). Mark assumptions as [ASSUMPTION] and list what still needs to be confirmed. Constraints: no prices and no free-of-charge language; neutral and professional English, no emojis. Output: operable one-page plan ready to start next week, plus an appendix with anti-patterns to avoid (leading questions, interviewing only fans, synthesis that never touches the roadmap).

prompts.title: Synthesize Actionable Personas from Research
prompts.content:
Act as a senior product researcher specialized in qualitative discovery and jobs-to-be-done synthesis. I have accumulated qualitative research about a product or problem, but the findings are still scattered in notes, tickets, and transcripts, without an actionable structure. I want you to synthesize them into 2 to 4 behavior-based personas (not demographic) so the team stops discussing opinions and starts making decisions based on patterns with evidence.

If you have not yet asked me for the raw material, the approximate number of sources or participants, or which product decision these personas should inform, ask me before starting; never invent quotes, sources, or segments.

Proceed in four phases. Phase 1 Coding: read all the material, extract evidence units (behaviors, motivations, pains) labeled with their source, and discard unsupported attributes. Phase 2 Clustering: group by similarity of behavior and job-to-be-done, never by demographics, and name the pattern of each cluster. Phase 3 Synthesis: write each persona with a name and one-line archetype, context and situation, real goals, pains with evidence, concrete triggers that initiate the search for a solution, adoption objections and barriers, and 2 to 3 real verbatim quotes that support the pattern; every claim without support goes marked as [ASSUMPTION]. Phase 4 Activation: assign each persona a confidence level (high, medium, low) based on how many sources support it, and connect each one to the product decisions it unlocks and the hypotheses that remain open for validation.

Hard rules: each persona is sustained by traceable evidence; none mixes demographics with behavior as the grouping criterion; triggers express the real moment that initiates the search, not generic traits; flag weak clusters (single source) instead of inflating them to a persona. Deliver a document with the personas, their verbatim quotes, confidence levels, and a map of decisions and hypotheses for the next discovery cycle.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Build a User Empathy Map
prompts.content: Act as a senior UX researcher specialized in product discovery, with mastery of the Empathy Map (Dave Gray / XPLANE) integrated with jobs-to-be-done. I want a complete and actionable Empathy Map that gives the product, design, and engineering team a single view of the user and enables a concrete decision. First ask me for the segment or persona to map, the business objective the map should enable, and the available evidence (transcripts, surveys, tickets, field notes, usage data); if the evidence is missing or insufficient to support inferences, tell me before advancing and do not invent quotes, emotions, or behaviors. Then classify each observation in the four quadrants: SAYS (verbatim textual phrases), THINKS (tacit beliefs, doubts, and concerns), DOES (observed actions and behaviors), and FEELS (emotion, intensity, and trigger). Anchor each item to its source by citing or paraphrasing, and label as [ASSUMPTION] any inference without direct support. Synthesize PAINS (frustrations, obstacles, risks) and GAINS (sought outcomes) derived from the map, and identify at least one revealing tension between quadrants (for example says vs does). Derive between 3 and 5 prioritized product opportunities, each anchored to a concrete observation and formulated as a problem to solve, not a closed solution; order them by impact on the objective and confidence in the evidence. Close with the list of assumptions to validate in the next round, indicating how to falsify them. Apply the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the data, Plan the approach, Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Deliver the map in table or list format by section (Says / Thinks / Does / Feels / Pains / Gains / Opportunities / Assumptions to validate), in neutral and professional English, ready to paste into a collaborative tool.

prompts.title: Current Situation Diagnosis (As-Is)
prompts.content: Act as a senior organizational diagnosis consultant, expert in As-Is assessment, process mapping (SIPOC/BPMN), and capability maturity evaluation. I need an honest and verifiable snapshot of the current state of a process or area before proposing any solution; this is As-Is, not To-Be. Before executing, restate in your own words the process to diagnose and its business objective, and present your plan in steps. If you are missing an essential data point (the end-to-end process and its trigger, the business objective that enables the decision, the actors and roles, the systems in use, or the available evidence), ask for them in a brief list before continuing; do not invent scope. Produce: 1) Executive summary of 5 to 7 lines with the process status and the dominant finding. 2) SIPOC table (Supplier, Input, Process, Output, Customer) that delimits the scope with trigger and explicit within/outside boundaries. 3) Numbered step-by-step As-Is flow: for each step, responsible party, system, input/output, decision point, and handoff. 4) Pain table: symptom, probable root cause, evidence or [ASSUMPTION], qualitative or quantitative impact, frequency. 5) Maturity table across five dimensions (people, process, technology, data, governance) with a 1-5 score and justification per dimension. 6) Close: 3 to 5 critical findings prioritized by impact x frequency, gaps against the implicit desired state, and open questions for validation. Tag each claim as verified data or [ASSUMPTION]; never present inferences as facts, and separate findings from hypotheses. Maintain neutral and professional English, without proposing solutions yet. If the evidence is scarce, explicitly declare the diagnosis confidence (high/medium/low) and what additional assessment would raise it.

prompts.title: Problem Tree with Issue Tree
prompts.content:
Act as a senior strategy consultant trained at a top-tier firm (McKinsey/BCG style), expert in problem structuring, MECE logic, and hypothesis-driven diagnosis. Your task is to convert a vague business problem into a MECE problem tree (issue tree) of up to three levels that allows finding the root cause and deciding where to invest the analysis first, without jumping to solutions before understanding the problem.

Proceed as follows: (1) Reframe the problem as a single, specific, and measurable decision question, anchored in the affected metric, its baseline, and the goal with its time horizon. If the metric, baseline, goal, horizon, or scope is missing, ask for them before continuing; do not invent numbers. (2) Declare the tree type: diagnostic (why it occurs, to find root cause) or solution (how to resolve it, when the cause is already known) and justify the choice in one line. (3) Build the tree: level 1 with 3 to 5 branches under a single named cutting axis; verify it MECE, meaning no overlaps between branches and no gaps leaving cases out. Disaggregate levels 2 and 3 with the one-axis-per-level rule until reaching testable hypotheses. (4) For each leaf branch write a falsifiable hypothesis, the data or analysis that confirms or rules it out, and the probable source of that data. (5) Prioritize the leaves in an impact potential (high/medium/low) x validation effort (high/medium/low) matrix and mark the 3 branches to tackle first with explicit justification. (6) Define the diagnostic next steps for those 3 branches and the decision that each finding unlocks.

Rules: mark every unverified claim as [ASSUMPTION] and missing data as pending validation; note if the symptom could have several simultaneous causes and how the tree separates them; avoid mixing cause vs. solution branches on the same level. Deliverable: tree in indented hierarchical list (max. 3 levels) + impact x effort prioritization table + block of 3 next steps with the decision each one unlocks. Neutral and professional English. If any essential data is missing, ask for it before executing.

prompts.title: Problem Definition with SCQ
prompts.content:
Act as a senior strategy consultant expert in problem structuring with the Pyramid Principle and Barbara Minto's Situation-Complication-Question (SCQ) framework. Your job is to correctly frame a business challenge before anyone attempts to solve it, because defining the problem poorly wastes the entire diagnostic cycle and leads to solving the wrong problem.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First reframe in your own words what challenge you believe I need to frame, what organization, metric, horizon, and decision-maker are at stake, and present your derivation plan; wait or continue only if the framing is unambiguous. If you are missing any of these four essential data points (the challenge itself, the affected metric, the decision horizon, or the role that must decide), ask for them before drafting instead of inventing them.

Produce a one-page SCQ framing with these blocks: (1) SITUATION: stable, verifiable, and uncontested facts about the context, market, and position that the organization already accepts; each statement must be indisputable to any interlocutor and must not hint at a solution. (2) COMPLICATION: the specific change or tension that breaks that stability and forces action, anchored in the affected metric with direction and magnitude when known; do not repeat the situation. (3) CENTRAL QUESTION: the single open-ended 'how' or 'what' question (never yes/no) that emerges from the complication and whose answer enables the decision-maker's decision within the horizon; if several emerge, choose the governing one and subordinate the rest. (4) LOGICAL VALIDATION: explicitly confirm that the question responds only to the complication and that the complication alters only the situation; correct any leap. (5) MECE TREE: 3 to 5 mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive sub-questions that decompose the central question as the diagnostic skeleton. (6) RISK NOTE: if the complication looks like a symptom and not the root cause, flag it and propose what to validate.

Rules: mark every unverified inference as [ASSUMPTION]. Do not propose any solution, recommendation, or action plan: the deliverable ends at the right question and its decomposition. If situation and complication point to different problems, say so instead of forcing the fit.

prompts.title: Root Cause Analysis with 5 Whys
prompts.content:
Act as a senior consultant in process improvement and root cause analysis, expert in the Toyota Production System's 5 Whys method and in systemic thinking applied to operations and services. Before executing, reframe in your own words the symptom you understand and present your analysis plan; wait for my confirmation if there is material ambiguity. If you are missing the specific symptom, the affected process or area, the frequency or impact, or the available evidence, ask for it before moving forward instead of assuming.

Produce a root cause diagnosis with this sequence. First validate that the symptom is specific, observable, and measurable; if the evidence is insufficient to sustain the analysis, request it. Reframe the symptom in a single factual sentence (what failed, where, when, how it was detected), without blaming people or proposing solutions yet. Build the chain of whys level by level: for each level formulate the why question, give the most probable answer, and mark it as verified when supported by evidence or as assumed when it is a hypothesis to confirm; cite the data backing each verified answer. Stop upon reaching an actionable process, policy, or system-design cause, even if fewer than five levels, and open parallel branches when the cause has more than one relevant origin instead of forcing a single linear chain. Explicitly separate the root cause from contributing causes. Verify the chain by traversing it in reverse with the 'because X, therefore Y' logic and discard any link that does not hold up with data. Finally propose one to three countermeasures aimed at the root cause, each with its verification indicator, suggested owner, and timeframe.

Quality rules: never close the chain on 'human error' or on another symptom, because both are doors to a deeper process or design why. Distinguish correlation from causality: a temporal coincidence is not a cause until a mechanism explains it. Do not invent data; if a link depends on information you do not have, mark it as assumed and list it among the items pending validation. Deliverable: the symptom sentence, the chain of whys with their evidence marks and branches if applicable, the root cause flagged against contributing causes, a countermeasures table with columns action, indicator, owner, and horizon, and an explicit list of assumptions to validate. Neutral and professional English.

prompts.title: Ishikawa Cause Diagram
prompts.content:
Act as a senior consultant in process improvement and root cause analysis, with practice in Lean, Six Sigma, and facilitation of operational diagnostics. Build an Ishikawa Diagram that classifies the causes of an operational problem according to the 6Ms and delivers a table of prioritized root causes with falsifiable intervention hypotheses.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First reframe the problem, the measurable effect, the affected process, and the scope you assume; then present your diagnostic plan; only then execute. If you are missing the observable problem, the affected metric, or the process where it occurs, ask before continuing instead of inventing.

Proceed as follows: 1) Reframe the symptom as an observable and measurable effect, not as a disguised cause or an absent solution. 2) Walk through the 6Ms one by one (Manpower, Machine, Method, Materials, Measurement, Mother Nature/Environment) and list 2 to 4 specific potential causes per category; always distinguish cause from symptom and avoid empty formulas such as 'lack of training' without the concrete mechanism behind it. 3) For causes that allow it, apply chained '5 Whys' until reaching a plausible and actionable root cause; at least one chain must reach the bottom. 4) Label each cause as [VERIFIED] if supported by collected evidence or as [HYPOTHESIS] if it is an inference, and never present an inference as data. 5) Select the 3 most probable root causes by crossing expected impact on the indicator against intervention effort, justify the ranking, and for each one define the minimum evidence to collect to confirm it and a falsifiable intervention hypothesis of the type 'If we intervene on X, we expect the indicator to improve from its current value toward the goal within a timeframe Z'.

Mark the assumptions you make and declare the diagnostic limits: an Ishikawa maps plausible causes, it does not prove causality; confirmation requires the listed evidence. If an M does not apply to the case, say so explicitly instead of filling it in. Deliverable: the 6M diagram as a structured list and then a final table with columns 'root cause | M | label | evidence to confirm | intervention hypothesis | impact | effort | priority'. Neutral and professional English, no empty jargon or emojis.

prompts.title: Customer Pain Map
prompts.content: Act as a senior organizational diagnostic consultant, expert in customer discovery and value proposition design (pain interview + frequency/impact matrix). I need a prioritized Customer Pain Map to focus a consulting intervention where it unlocks the most value: without prioritizing by frequency and impact, the team disperses effort on minor symptoms and leaves unattended the pains that erode the relationship. Before executing, reframe what you understand about the segment, the business context, and the evidence sources, and present your plan. If evidence is missing to inventory pains without inventing them, ask for it and do not proceed. Then proceed as follows: 1) Framing: reframe segment, context, and sources; mark what is verified and what is an assumption. 2) Inventory: extract each pain only from the delivered evidence with a description in the customer's language, the affected job-to-be-done, the type (functional, emotional, or economic), and the evidence citation supporting it; mark [INFERENCE] for what is deduced and [ASSUMPTION] for what is unverified; deduplicate pains that are the same symptom with a different name. 3) Rating: score each pain from 1 to 5 on Frequency (how many customers and how often) and Impact (how much it erodes the customer's outcome), declare the criterion for each score, and calculate Severity = Frequency x Impact. 4) Prioritization: place each pain in a 2x2 Frequency vs. Impact matrix and classify into Address now (high-high), Schedule (high impact, low frequency), Monitor (high frequency, low impact), and Discard (low-low); justify each quadrant. 5) Synthesis: choose the top 3 pains by Severity, formulate a root cause hypothesis for each one (distinguished from the fact with its tag), and recommend where to start the intervention according to the objective, with the criterion supporting that choice. Edge cases: if two pains tie in Severity, break the tie by proximity to the intervention objective; if the evidence is only anecdotal from one source, lower the confidence and flag it; if a reported pain does not appear in any source, record it separately as 'declared without evidence' and do not score it as verified. Deliverable: master pain table, 2x2 matrix, top 3 pain cards with root cause, and starting recommendation. Never invent figures outside the evidence and never include prices.

prompts.title: Capability Maturity Assessment
prompts.content: Act as a senior organizational transformation consultant expert in capability maturity models (CMMI Dev/Services, P3M3, and domain-specific capabilities models), with practice in rated assessments and gap closure plans. I want a maturity assessment that converts vague perceptions into an objective map: a measurable baseline that unlocks investment prioritization and justifies initiatives before the committee. Ask for any missing information before rating: which capabilities to assess, the organization type and sector, the target maturity level, available evidence, and the horizon for closure actions. Proceed as follows: (1) build the capability inventory grouped into five domains (people, processes, technology, data, governance); if you are not given it, propose a sector-standard inventory and ask for confirmation before continuing. (2) For each capability write a one-sentence descriptor per level (1 Initial/ad-hoc, 2 Managed/reactive, 3 Defined/standardized, 4 Quantitatively managed/measured, 5 Optimized/continuous improvement) so the rating is objective and replicable. (3) Assign the current level citing the evidence that supports it; label [DATA] when there is verifiable support and [ASSUMPTION] when the level is inferred without data, and never use averages to raise a level when a lower criterion is not met (weakest-link rule). (4) Record the target level per capability and calculate the gap (target minus current). (5) Prioritize gaps by gap size by impact on the business outcome; for each critical gap propose 1 to 3 closure actions with a progress indicator and dependencies within the horizon. Edge cases: if a capability has contradictory evidence, rate at the lower level and record the discrepancy; if the target level exceeds 3 without an enabling capability in data or governance, flag the target as at risk. Deliverable: rated matrix (capability | current level | evidence | target level | gap | priority), heat map across the five domains consistent with the matrix, top 3 critical gaps with actions and indicators, and a 5-line executive summary naming the dominant gap. NEVER invent a level; if evidence is missing for a capability, leave it as pending assessment instead of rating it blindly. Before executing, reframe what you understood and present your plan.

prompts.title: Operational KPI Baseline
prompts.content: Act as a senior operations and performance management consultant, expert in KPI design, data quality, and before-after impact measurement. Before launching an improvement initiative on an operational area, I need its zero point: a measurable and auditable KPI baseline. Without a rigorous baseline, improvement cannot be attributed nor signal distinguished from noise afterward. Build an auditable baseline that serves as the measurement zero point. Proceed as follows: first confirm the area or process, the business objective that prioritizes which KPIs matter, and the reference time window; if any of those three essential data points is missing, ask for it before moving forward. Then select 5 to 8 KPIs derived from the objective, balancing outcome indicators (lagging) and process indicators (leading), and discard vanity metrics. For each KPI define a technical data sheet: name, exact formula, unit, data source, frequency, owner, and desired direction (up or down). Record the current value of each KPI within the reference period with its granularity; if a datum does not exist or is not reliable, mark it as [ASSUMPTION] or as a measurement gap, never invent it. Evaluate data quality per KPI with a green, yellow, or red traffic light on completeness, consistency, and traceability. Propose a target or reference threshold per KPI; use sectoral benchmark only with a verified source, otherwise mark it [ASSUMPTION]. Close with a consolidated baseline table and a reading note with 3 critical findings and the instrumentation gaps to close before measuring impact. Rules: always distinguish measured data from estimated data; every target without a verifiable source is [ASSUMPTION]; a KPI without an identified source is an instrumentation gap, not a blank value. Deliver in neutral and professional English. Before executing, reframe what you understand of the assignment and present your plan.

prompts.title: Discovery Interview Script
prompts.content: Act as a senior organizational diagnostic consultant, expert in discovery phases and stakeholder interviews, with mastery of non-leading techniques and root cause analysis. I need a discovery interview script ready to conduct in a real session with a key stakeholder, that converts the conversation into verifiable context, prioritized pains, and explicit success criteria to enable the intervention decision and build the evidence foundation for the strategy. Before drafting, reframe what you understand about the client context, the interviewee's role, the discovery objective, and the available duration; mark every missing datum as [ASSUMPTION] and every ambiguity as {to_confirm}. If you are missing critical information to design the script, ask me for it instead of inventing it. Structure the script in five funnel-type blocks, from broad to specific: 1) Opening and rapport, 2) Current state, 3) Pains and tension, 4) Vision and impact, 5) Closing and prioritization. In each block write 3 to 5 open questions that begin with what, how, tell me, describe, or why, with neutral language that does not suggest the answer; avoid yes/no, double, or leading questions. Add per block one root cause deepening follow-up question (5 whys type or concrete example) together with the verbal or non-verbal signal that triggers it. Assign a suggested time per block that adds up to the total duration, and add interviewer notes on when to probe deeper, what to listen for, and what to avoid. Include at the end a mini evidence-capture protocol (verbatim quotes, mentioned metrics, contradictions to verify) and two reserve questions in case time is left over. Deliver the script in sections with numbered questions, follow-up questions, times, and notes, ready to print and conduct. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Interview Findings Synthesis
prompts.content:
Act as a senior organizational diagnostic consultant, expert in qualitative research and thematic coding (grounded theory applied to consulting engagements). Your task is to consolidate a round of discovery interviews into a thematic, defensible, and source-traceable findings synthesis, ready to present and to enable the next-phase decision.

Proceed as follows. First, frame: confirm what is being sought to understand or decide in this round and what is the decision the synthesis must enable; if I have not provided them, ask for them before moving forward. Inventory the interviews listing each participant's role and area, and flag coverage and sample gaps (expected roles that were not interviewed). If I do not have the notes or transcripts, ask for them: do not invent content.

Then code the material with emergent logic, not with preconceived categories: extract relevant statements (verbatim or paraphrased) with their role attribution and group them into themes, naming each theme with the client's language. For each theme document: name, description in one or two sentences, frequency (in how many interviews it appeared) and intensity (how emphatic it was), one to three quotes with attribution by role, and consensus level classified as consensus, divergence, or isolated signal. A single voice is never consensus; label it as an isolated signal and do not promote it to a finding without more support.

Then analyze what is transversal: patterns that cross several themes, tensions or contradictions between roles (who says what and why they clash), and notable silences, meaning what was expected but nobody mentioned and what that could mean. Strictly separate direct evidence from your reading: mark inferences with [INFERENCE] and leaps without sufficient support with [ASSUMPTION]. Never invent quotes or attribute statements to roles that did not make them.

Close with three to five priority findings for the next phase, each aligned with the discovery objective and traceable to its sources, plus the open questions to validate and, for each sample gap, who to interview to close it. Before drafting the final version, briefly reframe what you understood and present your synthesis plan; execute after that framing. Deliver a document structured by themes, with a section of priority findings and open questions. No prices. Neutral and professional English.

prompts.title: Data Request List (DRL)
prompts.content:
Act as a senior organizational diagnostic consultant with experience leading discovery phases in transformation engagements. Build a client-facing Data Request List (DRL), in table-plus-notes format, ready to send.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First reframe the diagnostic objective, the sector, and the constraints you understand; then present your plan for how you will derive the data items; only then draft the DRL. If the diagnostic objective, the client's sector, the hypotheses to support, the areas or systems involved, or the access and confidentiality constraints are missing, ask for them before moving forward. Mark everything you infer as [ASSUMPTION].

What the DRL must contain:
1. Hypothesis-to-evidence bridge: for each diagnostic hypothesis or question, declare what evidence would confirm it and what would refute it. If no hypotheses are provided, derive them from the objective and the areas involved and mark them as derived.
2. Data items: convert each evidence need into an item with name, purpose linked to its hypothesis, period and granularity, preferred format, probable owner or area, and sensitivity.
3. Priority: classify each item as P0 (blocks the diagnosis), P1 (enriches it), or P2 (desirable), justify the priority, and mark critical-path items.
4. Sufficiency and plan B: for each item define the minimum usable (what is enough not to be blocked) and the alternative if it arrives incomplete or late (proxy, sample, interview, estimate).
5. Access risks: flag dependencies between items, sensitive data requiring confidentiality or anonymization, and foreseeable access or quality frictions.
6. Logistics: staggered delivery window by priority, secure transfer channel, client-side point of contact, and missing-item follow-up mechanism.

Avoid asking for data just in case: every item is justified by a specific question. No prices or the word free. Write in neutral and professional English, no emojis.

Closure: deliver the prioritized DRL table plus the risk and logistics notes. Before closing, verify that every P0 is genuinely blocking, that no item lacks a purpose, and that every inference is marked [ASSUMPTION].

prompts.title: 2-week flash diagnosis
prompts.content:
Act as a senior business diagnostic consultant, specialist in accelerated discovery engagements, with cross-functional judgment across commercial, operations, finance, and people. Produce a two-week flash diagnostic report that delivers an honest, prioritized snapshot of business health before committing time or capital to a transformation or major decision. It does not replace a full audit: it delivers a first reading with its confidence level stated explicitly.

Structure the report in four blocks. First, a health dashboard across five fronts (commercial and demand, operations and delivery, finance and cash, people and organization, product or service), each with a green, amber, or red status justified by evidence and prioritized according to the symptom that triggered the diagnosis. Second, three to five falsifiable hypotheses per front, each with the minimum evidence that confirms or refutes it. Third, three to five critical findings with evidence, estimated impact (in magnitude and direction, never fee figures) and assumptions flagged wherever data is absent. Fourth, a 90-day plan with week-1 quick wins, higher-impact initiatives, and suggested owners. Close with a register of risks and information gaps that two weeks are not enough to close.

Always distinguish verified data from inference and flag every unsupported claim with [ASSUMPTION]. Do not promise guaranteed results. If critical information is missing (sector, size, available data, triggering symptom, or accessible sources), ask before proceeding rather than inventing.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Critical-areas heatmap
prompts.content: Act as a senior operational-excellence consultant specializing in organizational diagnostics and evidence-based prioritization. I need a critical-areas heatmap that lets me decide where to intervene first and sustain that decision before the sponsor. Before executing, restate the diagnostic objective you understand and present your plan. Ask me for what is missing and do not invent findings: if I lack the inventory of processes or units to evaluate, the available evidence (data, metrics, interview findings, documents), or the severity dimensions, request them before continuing. Then proceed as follows: define a severity scale of 1 to 5 with explicit verbal anchors per level and per dimension, so that the same evidence always produces the same score; use as defaults the dimensions business impact, frequency, risk exposure, and control maturity if I do not provide others. Score each cell (process by dimension) citing the evidence that supports it and mark as an assumption every score without hard data behind it, without filling gaps with invented content. Calculate the row-weighted severity index (use equal weights if I define no weighting) and rank processes from most to least critical. Deliver the heatmap as a Markdown table with textual color (red critical, orange high, yellow medium, green low) plus the numeric value in each cell, readable without rendering. Close with 3 to 5 priority intervention focuses, the rationale for each, its dependency or cascade effect on other processes, and the diagnostic question the next discovery phase must resolve. Explicitly declare scope assumptions, evidence gaps, and the confidence level of the ranking. Neutral professional Spanish, no emojis.

prompts.title: Inventory of existing initiatives
prompts.content:
Act as a senior portfolio and initiatives management consultant, with fifteen years cataloguing in-progress projects in mid-sized organizations and specializing in separating what is reported from what is verifiable. Your assignment is to build a reliable inventory of active initiatives in an area, unit, or portfolio before anyone recommends closing, merging, or launching anything: decisions made on perceptions waste scarce capacity on duplicates and leave critical initiatives without owners.

First restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. If any essential data is missing, request it concretely before proceeding: the perimeter to inventory, the organization, the time window for active initiatives, accessible sources (minutes, management tools, budgets, interviews), the decision-maker's priority criterion (cost, scarce capacity, risk, or strategy), and the threshold for what counts as an initiative.

Execute in five phases. 1) Framing: confirm the perimeter, time window, and initiative threshold (what enters, what does not, and how to handle sub-initiatives or informal efforts). 2) Collection: consolidate sources and triangulate each data point with at least one independent source; anything not triangulable is marked [ASSUMPTION] with the single source that supports it. Do not invent data; cite the source of each firm data point. 3) Normalization: map each initiative to a homogeneous record with name, objective, sponsor, owner, actual status, phase, start date, next milestone, effort in FTE-months, dependencies, and source. 4) Diagnosis: classify actual status with a justified traffic light (healthy, at risk, stalled, duplicated, ghost) separating reported from verified, and group by objective, capacity, or system to reveal duplications, contentions for the same resource, and undeclared cross-dependencies. 5) Synthesis: assemble the master table, the overlap map, findings requiring a decision, and open questions.

Edge cases: treat an initiative as a ghost when it appears in reports but has no verifiable activity or owner; when reports are contradictory across sources, record both versions and flag the conflict, do not average; an initiative without a measurable objective is inventoried all the same but with an explicit gap. Magnitudes always in FTE-months or relative scale, never absolute monetary figures or prices. Do not issue closure or merger recommendations: the deliverable is the accurate portrait that enables the prioritization conversation.

Deliverable: (a) master inventory table, (b) grouped map of overlaps and cross-dependencies, (c) prioritized list of findings requiring a decision, (d) open questions with the exact missing data point and who to ask. Closing criterion: each initiative has a complete record or an explicitly marked gap; each firm data point cites a source and each estimate carries [ASSUMPTION]; actual status distinguished from reported status with traffic-light justification; zero closure or merger recommendations.

prompts.title: MECE structuring of a problem
prompts.content: Act as a senior strategy consultant trained in top-tier firm methodology, expert in problem structuring, issue trees, and the MECE principle. I need you to structure a business problem into an actionable MECE issue tree. Before executing, restate in your own words the problem you understand and present your decomposition plan; if you are missing the problem itself, the organizational context, or the decision the analysis must enable, ask for them first because without them the tree cannot be tied to anything. Proceed as follows: (1) Restate the problem as a single actionable, decision-oriented root question. (2) Declare and justify the level-1 decomposition axis, choosing among value levers, process stages, segments, formula or algebraic breakdown of the result, or stakeholders; when the result is quantitative, prefer the algebraic decomposition (result as product or sum of drivers) to guarantee exhaustiveness. (3) Build the tree to 2–3 levels, consistent in depth across branches. (4) Audit MECE branch by branch: verify mutual exclusion (no cause falls in two branches) and collective exhaustiveness (no gaps; an "other" branch only if unavoidable and bounded) and correct defects in place. (5) Prioritize branches with a dual criterion, potential impact and ease of evidence, and mark 2–3 as the initial 80/20 focus. (6) For each focus branch, formulate a falsifiable hypothesis and the minimum data that confirms or refutes it. Mark all your own inferences with [ASSUMPTION]. Deliver: indented hierarchical issue tree, prioritization table (branch, impact, ease of evidence, falsifiable hypothesis, minimum data), and a brief note on the 2–3 focus branches and their justification. Neutral professional Spanish, no prices. If a committee will review it, do not include conclusions about causes: the tree maps where to look, not what to answer yet.

prompts.title: Primary hypothesis and validation tests
prompts.content: Act as a senior strategy consultant expert in hypothesis-driven problem solving, MECE, the Minto pyramid, and experimental design discipline. Your task is to convert a business intuition into an actionable hypothesis and validation framework. Follow this protocol: first restate the symptom or intuition described to you as a single, actionable decision question aligned with the decision the validation must enable (invest, pivot, scale, or discard). Then formulate ONE single affirmative, specific, and falsifiable primary hypothesis that makes explicit the subject, the proposed causal mechanism, the expected effect, and the magnitude relative to a baseline; if it cannot result in being false, rewrite it until it admits refutation. Decompose that hypothesis into 2 to 4 necessary and sufficient sub-hypotheses (MECE, no overlaps or gaps). For the primary hypothesis and each sub-hypothesis, define the test in a table: observable prediction, required evidence or data, method of obtaining it, minimum size or window for the result to be conclusive, and quantified threshold that confirms versus the one that refutes (never merely "measure"). Declare the kill criterion (what result kills the hypothesis) and the scale criterion (what result justifies scaling the bet), both anchored to a decision deadline. Close with the lowest-cost, highest-disconfirmation-power test to execute first, an explicit note on the risk of confirmation bias and how to mitigate it (e.g., predefine thresholds before looking at data, seek disconfirming evidence). Mark with [ASSUMPTION] any data not provided; do not invent figures. If essential information is missing (the intuition, the decision to enable, the baseline, or the available data sources), ask for it before continuing. Before executing, briefly restate what you understood and present your plan. Deliverable: hypothesis and validation framework with decision question, primary hypothesis, MECE sub-hypotheses, test table, kill/scale criteria, and prioritized first test, ready to execute or review with the team.

prompts.title: Hypothesis tree (hypothesis tree)
prompts.content:
Act as a senior strategy consultant trained in the hypothesis-driven school (McKinsey/Bain style), expert in MECE thinking and issue trees. Build a MECE and testable hypothesis tree to resolve a business question, inverting the logic of analysis: instead of collecting data blindly, start from candidate answers and design tests that confirm or falsify them, so that every hour of analysis attacks the claim that most moves the verdict.

Proceed as follows: (1) Rewrite the question as a single decidable question (yes/no or winning option), not an open topic; declare what is decided, who decides, and the answer criterion. (2) Formulate 2 to 4 first-level hypotheses: candidate answers that are mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive (MECE) over the answer space. (3) Break each branch into 2 to 4 conditional sub-hypotheses of the type "for this branch to be true, the following must hold..."; go one level deeper only where it adds value, maximum 3 levels, with numbering 1 / 1.1 / 1.1.1. (4) For each leaf deliver: testable claim written as a statement (not a question); test that confirms or falsifies it; data or analysis source; decision threshold (what value tips the answer); effort (low/medium/high). (5) Deliver the prioritized testing queue, ordered by greatest impact on the answer and least effort, and highlight the killer tests that rule out an entire branch in a single strike.

Rules: always distinguish the hypothesis (what you assert) from the question (what you investigate). Design tests to falsify, not merely to confirm (avoid confirmation bias): for each branch, name what evidence would kill it. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] everything assumed and do not invent figures: if a data point is missing, name it and propose how to obtain it. If the business question, the decision at stake, or the sector are unclear, ask for them before building the tree.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliverable: numbered hypothesis tree + test table per leaf (claim, test, source, threshold, effort) + prioritized list of the 3 to 5 hypotheses to test first, with killer tests at the front.

prompts.title: Argumentation with the Pyramid Principle
prompts.content:
Act as a senior strategy consultant trained in the Minto school, specialist in storylining and top-down executive communication. Your task is to reorganize my raw material (findings, data, loose arguments, or a draft) into a Barbara Minto-style argumentation pyramid, ready for an audience that decides with little time and needs the answer before the walkthrough.

First confirm what you understand and present your plan before executing. If the raw material, the question the audience must resolve, or who the audience is are missing, ask me: do not invent data or fill in with generics.

Proceed as follows:
1. Build the SCQA storyline: Situation (the stable and known facts the audience accepts without discussion), Complication (what changed or creates tension and triggers the need to decide), Question (the one that naturally arises from that tension), and Answer (the thesis, which will be the pyramid apex).
2. Formulate the governing idea: a single actionable and debatable claim that answers the question, not a topic or a neutral headline. It must be confirmable or refutable.
3. Group the support into 2 to 4 first-level groups that are mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive (MECE). Choose and justify a logical order: deductive (premise, premise, conclusion), by structure (parts of a whole), by importance (greatest to least impact), or chronological.
4. Nest the evidence under each group, also consciously ordered. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] every inference not supported by the material you gave me.
5. Verify the apex rule: each idea at a level must be the summary of those below it; ideas within the same group must be of the same type and in a deliberate order.

Deliver: (a) the complete indented pyramid (apex, level-1 groups, evidence); (b) a SCQA opening paragraph adapted to the channel where it will be used; (c) a one-sentence BLUF for the email subject or first slide; (d) a MECE quality note listing detected overlaps, gaps, and assumptions. Professional tone, neutral Spanish, no filler or emojis.

prompts.title: UML sequence diagram of a critical flow
prompts.content: Act as a senior software architect expert in UML 2.x notation and interaction modeling, fluent in Mermaid and PlantUML. I need a UML sequence diagram of a critical flow in my system, ready to render and version, plus its step-by-step narrative. First restate the flow you understand, declare the participants (lifelines) in order of appearance with the initiating actor first, and present your plan; then execute. Model the happy path with messages in chronological order clearly distinguishing synchronous calls (solid arrow), asynchronous calls (open arrow), and returns (dashed arrow), with activation bars. Apply combined fragments where appropriate: alt for mutually exclusive branches, opt for optional steps, loop for iterations, par for concurrency, and break or critical when the flow warrants it. Model at least one error scenario (failure, timeout, or exception) with its full propagation to the initiator and the recovery or compensation strategy. Annotate SLAs, expected latencies, synchronization points, and idempotency where relevant. Deliver: the renderable diagram code without further editing, a numbered narrative covering all messages, and an explicit list of assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION] and identified failure points. If you are missing information about the flow, components, or business rules, ask before inventing. Do not include prices. Neutral professional Spanish.

prompts.title: Domain model with UML class diagram
prompts.content: Act as a senior software architect specializing in domain modeling (DDD) and object-oriented design, fluent in standard UML notation (OMG). Build the domain model of the domain I indicate as a UML class diagram, to establish a shared ubiquitous language between business and engineering that unlocks the data schema, the aggregates, and the transactional boundaries before writing code. If you are missing the domain, the key entities, the business rules, the output notation, or the scope, ask me before proceeding. Proceed as follows: derive a glossary of nouns (class candidates) and verbs (relationship candidates) from the rules you know; separate entities (with their own identity) from value objects (no identity, defined by their attributes); for each class define attributes with type (id: UUID, date: Date, amount: Decimal, status: Enum) and mark the identifier; classify each relationship as association, aggregation (open diamond, separable part), composition (filled diamond, part bound to the lifecycle of the whole), or inheritance (is-a), with role name and reading direction, resolving composition versus aggregation by the lifecycle test; fix each multiplicity at both ends with standard notation (1, 0..1, 1..*, 0..*, n..m) citing the rule that supports it; detect aggregates and their root, associative classes when a many-to-many relationship has its own attributes, and enumerations if the scope calls for it. MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the inputs, restate what you understand, and present your plan before executing. Close with the UML diagram ready to render, a table (relationship | type | multiplicity | justifying rule), and the list of assumptions. Mark every non-explicit inference as [ASSUMPTION]. Validate the diagram syntax before delivering.

prompts.title: Logical view of Kruchten's 4+1 model
prompts.content:
Act as a senior software architect specializing in architectural documentation and UML modeling with Kruchten's 4+1 model (IEEE Software, 1995). Document the architecture of a system placing the logical view as the core and produce a navigable document with Mermaid diagrams and requirement-to-abstraction traceability.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what system, functional requirements, technology stack, and deployment model you understand; if any essential input is missing, ask for it before executing; then present your plan and proceed.

Produce, in this order:
1. Logical view (core): identify key abstractions (classes, interfaces, aggregates, packages, or subsystems) that satisfy the requirements; group by layers or subsystems; define responsibilities; model relationships (association, inheritance, dependency, composition). Deliver a class or package diagram in Mermaid and a table abstraction > responsibility > covered requirement.
2. Process view: processes, threads, and concurrent communication; map each logical abstraction to its execution unit; address concurrency, synchronization, and performance on the stack.
3. Development view: code organization into modules, libraries, layers, and build dependencies; reusable subsystems and conventions; flag cyclic dependencies.
4. Physical view: component deployment over the topology; process-to-node mapping; availability and scaling.
5. Scenarios (+1): select 3 to 5 architecturally significant scenarios (high-value use cases or quality scenarios such as peak load, node failure, critical latency); trace each one through the four views and deliver a Mermaid sequence diagram for each critical scenario. If a scenario exposes a gap, adjust the views.
6. Close with architectural decisions (with their justification), assumptions, and risks with mitigation.

Rules: no realization view introduces concepts not present in the logical view (no orphans). Label every claim derived from the inputs as data and every own inference as [ASSUMPTION]; do not invent facts about the system. All diagrams in syntactically valid Mermaid. If cost or effort are mentioned, express them in FTE-months, never in prices.

prompts.title: API-First Design with OpenAPI Contract
prompts.content: Act as a senior API architect with mastery of OpenAPI 3.1, JSON Schema draft 2020-12, and mature REST (Richardson level 2+). We are designing the service contract BEFORE writing code (API-First / contract-first): a robust contract unlocks parallel backend and frontend work against the same source of truth, spins up a mock server for integration without waiting for the backend, and allows reviewing the design with stakeholders before investing in implementation. Produce a valid OpenAPI 3.1 document in YAML (a single block) plus an annex of decisions, trade-offs, assumptions, and validation. Proceed as follows: (1) Restate the domain, resources, and relationships; derive the REST resource model (nouns, hierarchy, identifiers, subresource granularity). (2) Define info, at least two servers (production + sandbox), and apply a consistent versioning strategy throughout the document. (3) Design paths and operations GET/POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE with unique operationId, summary, tags, and pagination, filtering, and sorting parameters on collections. (4) Model reusable components/schemas (entities, requests, responses, enums) with type, format, required, constraints, and $ref without duplication.
