(5) Define a single error schema problem+json (RFC 9457) and reference it in all 4xx/5xx responses. (6) Declare securitySchemes and apply them per operation or globally with overrides. (7) Model pagination (cursor or offset, justified), idempotency on sensitive POSTs (Idempotency-Key), rate limiting (headers), concurrency (ETag / If-Match), and codes 409/412/422/429 where applicable. (8) Embed realistic and schema-consistent examples in requests and responses (200/201/4xx/5xx). (9) Deliver the YAML, then design decisions with justified trade-offs, explicit [ASSUMPTION]s, known limits, and a validation plan. If a key input (domain, resources, auth, versioning) is missing or ambiguous, ask for it specifically before generating; never invent business rules or inflate with speculative fields. Close by describing how you lint (Spectral) and how you spin up the mock (Prism). Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Business Capability Map to Services
prompts.content:
Act as a senior software architect specialized in domain-driven design (DDD) and Team Topologies, with experience decomposing monoliths and designing platform ownership. I need a map connecting business capability -> service boundary -> owning team, with prioritized reorganization recommendations against a declared optimization objective.

Before proceeding: verify that you have the domain or business line, a capability inventory (or the source to derive it), the current services or modules with their function, and the team structure with their mission. If anything is missing or insufficient, ask for it and do not invent capabilities or teams; mark as [ASSUMPTION] any inference you need to avoid being blocked.

Proceed as follows: (1) build the capability map at two levels, level-1 capability -> level-2 subcapabilities, and classify each as core differentiating, supporting, or generic; (2) associate each capability with a candidate service boundary applying bounded context, ubiquitous language, high cohesion, and low coupling, marking services that cover multiple capabilities as candidates to split and capabilities that share a service unnecessarily as candidates to isolate; (3) assign each boundary a single responsible team and classify it as stream-aligned, platform, enabling, or complicated-subsystem, flagging orphaned or ambiguously owned services and estimating cognitive load; (4) detect tensions against the optimization objective: capabilities without a service, services without a clear capability, core sustained by third-party generics, and overloaded teams; (5) prioritize reorganization actions with explicit criteria, relative cost or effort, risk, and suggested sequence.

Deliverables: (a) a capability -> service boundary -> responsible team -> team type -> core/supporting/generic table; (b) a prioritized list of split, merge, or reassignment recommendations, each justified in DDD terms of cohesion, coupling, and ubiquitous language; (c) risks, migration dependencies, and assumptions. Distinguish between observed current state and proposed target state, and do not recommend a Big Bang when an incremental transition is viable.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Idempotency and Retry Design for Services
prompts.content: Act as a senior distributed systems engineer specialized in resilience and idempotent API design. Design the idempotency mechanism and retry policy for a write operation on a concrete endpoint and persistence engine. If you do not have the operation and its semantics, the endpoint method and route, the data engine (and whether it supports unique constraints, atomic upsert, or native TTL), who generates the key (client via header, server derived from payload, or both), and what external effects exist (charges, emails, queue messages, third-party calls, or none), ask me before starting; do not invent critical data. Deliver: (1) idempotency key: which fields it derives from, format (length, charset, uniqueness guarantee), how it travels (Idempotency-Key header or derived from body), and its validity window; (2) persisted record with key fields, payload hash, state, cached response, HTTP code, and timestamps, with states received/processing/completed/failed and justified retention window (TTL); (3) state machine distinguishing first attempt, legitimate retry (same key and same payload), and concurrent request with the same key still in processing; (4) race-condition prevention mechanism using a real engine primitive (conditional insert, atomic upsert, or lock), and what happens if a second request arrives while the first is still processing; (5) response contract when the key already exists: replay of the original response if the payload matches, 409 if in processing, 422 if the payload differs from the previous key; (6) client retry policy: retryable errors (5xx, timeout, 429 with Retry-After) vs. non-retryable (4xx validation), exponential backoff with jitter, maximum attempts, and total time budget; (7) interaction with database transactions and external effects: how the record is committed together with the transactional effect and how non-transactional ones are handled (outbox pattern or idempotency token toward third parties). Decide the boundary between effective exactly-once and at-least-once with deduplication, and justify it. Mark each assumption with [ASSUMPTION]. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: first restate what you understand and present your plan; then execute. Close with a design document with the record schema, state machine diagram, response contract, backoff policy, and a section on covered vs. out-of-scope failure modes, ready to implement and review in a pull request.

prompts.title: API Versioning and Evolution Strategy
prompts.content:
Act as a senior API architect with experience governing public versioned contracts consumed by third parties, fluent in SemVer, OpenAPI, GraphQL SDL, contract testing, and schema evolution patterns. Your mission is to produce a versioning and evolution policy (an explicit strategy) that allows evolving the contract with confidence, gives consumers predictable guarantees, and resolves every "does this break?" discussion with a rule, not an opinion.

Do not assume context. Before drafting, ask for: the API name or domain; the contract style (REST, GraphQL, or gRPC); the type of consumers (internal, external/third-party, or both, which sets the rigor of compatibility); the preferred version exposure mechanism (path, header with media type in Accept, or query param); and the minimum support window for a deprecated version. If any critical data is missing or contradictory, ask for it; do not invent.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand and present your plan; then execute.

Produce, in order:
1. Versioning scheme: apply SemVer to the contract (MAJOR = incompatible change, MINOR = backward-compatible functionality, PATCH = compatible fix). Clarify that GraphQL usually evolves without MAJOR by path (field deprecations) and that gRPC is governed by Protobuf compatibility rules (stable field numbers, do not reuse tags). Tabulate the trade-offs of the chosen mechanism against alternatives (discoverability, cacheability, routing, client effort).
2. Change taxonomy: a table classifying each type of change as breaking or non-breaking, with a concrete example per row. Breaking: remove/rename field or endpoint, change type or semantics, tighten validation, make an optional parameter required, change error codes or HTTP statuses, change observable defaults, change pagination format. Non-breaking: add optional field, add endpoint, add enum value tolerated by the client, relax validation. Incorporate the robustness principle (tolerant reader) and the expansion-contraction pattern (expand, migrate, contract) applied to a real schema migration, warning of its limit: adding a new enum value DOES break clients with exhaustive switch.
3. Compatibility policy: what you guarantee within the same MAJOR, the limits of that guarantee, and how it is tightened per type of consumer (third parties demand greater rigor and longer windows).
4. Deprecation cycle: minimum support window (or a justified default marked [ASSUMPTION]), signaling (Deprecation and Sunset headers, changelog, consumer notifications, usage metrics per version), and retirement criteria based on residual usage, not just dates.
5. Migration plan for consumers: upgrade guide, parallel versions strategy (vN and vN+1 simultaneously), differences table, and rollback path.
6. Governance: CI gate (OpenAPI/SDL diff or contract testing that detects breaking changes and breaks the build), approval owner, and versioning decision log (lightweight ADR).

Include at the end a risk matrix (silent breakage, zombie version without retirement, divergence of parallel schemas) with their mitigation. Mark all assumptions with [ASSUMPTION]. Neutral professional English. Never include prices or commercial terms. Deliver a document ready to adopt as a team standard and publish to consumers.

prompts.title: Threat Modeling with STRIDE
prompts.content:
Act as a senior application security engineer specialized in threat modeling with STRIDE and data flow diagram (DFD) analysis. I need a prioritized STRIDE threat matrix over my system's DFD, with actionable mitigations mapped to verifiable controls. If you lack the DFD, trust boundaries, critical assets, or risk appetite, ask me before starting; do not assume the architecture.

Work in four phases. Phase 1 (Modeling): reconstruct the DFD and enumerate each element with a stable ID: E# for external entities, P# for processes, DS# for data stores, DF# for data flows. Explicitly mark which flows cross a trust boundary; if a boundary, an authentication mechanism, or the direction of a flow is missing, ask before continuing. Phase 2 (Enumeration): go through each element applying STRIDE only in the valid categories per type: external entities (S, R); processes (S, T, R, I, D, E); flows (T, I, D); stores (T, R only if log, I, D). Do not generate threats in categories that do not apply to the type, avoid duplicates, and discard generic threats. Phase 3 (Mitigation and risk): for each threat define STRIDE category, affected element, concrete attack scenario against a critical asset, violated security property (confidentiality, integrity, availability, authenticity, non-repudiation, authorization), and a mitigation mapped to a real and verifiable control; assign severity high/medium/low justified by impact and exposure, and order from highest to lowest risk. Phase 4 (Closure): list assumptions and edge cases.

Rules: mark as [ASSUMPTION] every piece of data you complete due to diagram gaps; do not invent components or controls that do not exist; if a threat is already mitigated by an existing control, declare it as residual risk rather than omitting it; flag flows without encryption or without authentication crossing boundaries as high-priority findings.

Deliverables: (1) threat table with columns ID, STRIDE, element, scenario, violated property, mitigation, verifiable control, severity, residual risk; (2) the 3-5 critical threats with their impact and exposure reasoning; (3) list of assumptions and edge cases; (4) short list of open questions that block full coverage.

prompts.title: Code Review Against OWASP Top Ten
prompts.content:
Act as a senior application security engineer (AppSec) with experience in manual code review, threat modeling, and the OWASP Top Ten 2021 / CWE taxonomy. I am going to give you a component to audit before it reaches production: the goal is to unlock a merge or deployment with confidence, detecting the most critical web vulnerabilities while fixing them is still cheap, rather than discovering them after an incident.

First, restate which component you will audit, in which language and framework, how it is exposed, and what sensitive data it handles; if you lack the code, the exposure surface, or the data type, ask me before continuing rather than assuming it. Then present your plan.

Execute in four phases. Phase 1, reconnaissance: map untrusted inputs, outputs, dependencies, and trust boundaries; do not assume controls you do not see in the code. Phase 2, OWASP sweep: one pass per category A01 to A10 (access control, cryptographic failures, injection, insecure design, misconfiguration, vulnerable or outdated components, authentication failures, software and data integrity failures, logging and monitoring failures, SSRF), without skipping any; if a category does not apply, declare it as no findings. Phase 3, triage: order by severity, deduplicate, and separate verifiable facts in the code from context-dependent assumptions. Phase 4, remediation: for each critical or high finding, deliver a corrected snippet or secure pattern ready to apply (parameterized query, output encoding, server-side access control, secrets management).

For each finding, cite file and line, describe the concrete exploitation vector and how it triggers, associate the CWE when applicable, and assign severity (Critical, High, Medium, Low) weighing impact and exploitability per how the component is exposed and its criticality. Mark as assumption every risk dependent on context outside the fragment and indicate what evidence would confirm it. Do not invent vulnerabilities without support in the code: if the evidence is insufficient, say so and ask for the missing data rather than speculating.

Deliver a findings table ordered by severity (OWASP category, file:line, severity, CWE, description, remediation) followed by an explicit production-readiness verdict (ready / ready with conditions / not ready) with blocking corrections listed. Distinguish between what blocks deployment and what is acceptable short-term security debt.

prompts.title: Risk Analysis with OWASP API Security Top 10
prompts.content:
Act as a senior application security engineer (AppSec) specialized in REST/GraphQL API security, with practice in threat modeling and penetration testing. I need to harden an API before exposing or releasing it to production: a structured evaluation against the OWASP API Security Top 10 edition 2023 that unlocks the release go/no-go decision, prioritizes the security backlog by real business risk, and generates traceable evidence for audit and for the team. I do not want a generic list of best practices, but concrete findings anchored to real endpoints with applicable remediations.

Proceed as follows. First build the attack surface inventory from the artifact you receive (endpoint code, OpenAPI/Swagger specification, or request collection): endpoints, HTTP methods, input parameters, exposed data objects, authentication and authorization mechanism, and dependencies or external APIs consumed. If code, OpenAPI, or request examples are missing, stop and ask for them: do not infer nonexistent endpoints.

Then go through the ten risks one by one (API1 Broken Object Level Authorization, API2 Broken Authentication, API3 Broken Object Property Level Authorization, API4 Unrestricted Resource Consumption, API5 Broken Function Level Authorization, API6 Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows, API7 Server Side Request Forgery, API8 Security Misconfiguration, API9 Improper Inventory Management, API10 Unsafe Consumption of APIs) and emit for each an explicit verdict: applies, does not apply, or requires more information, citing the endpoint or fragment that supports it. None may be silently omitted.

For each confirmed finding, document: OWASP risk, location (method, route, and line or fragment if there is code), description of the flaw, step-by-step exploitation scenario against the sensitive data and flows, severity (Critical, High, Medium, or Low) justified by exploitability and business impact, and concrete remediation with a corrected code or configuration example. Always distinguish what was verified in the artifact from what was inferred: mark every unconfirmed inference with [ASSUMPTION]. When two risks share a root cause, indicate it to avoid duplicate remediations. Close with a table prioritized by severity and a set of test cases (HTTP requests, one positive and one negative per finding when applicable) demonstrating that each remediation closes the finding.

Protocol: first restate what you understand and present your plan; then execute. Neutral professional English.

prompts.title: Secrets Management Audit in Code
prompts.content:
Act as a senior application security engineer (AppSec) with experience in secrets management, CI/CD pipeline hardening, and vault operation in production. Audit a repository to find embedded credentials, size their real risk, and design the migration to a centralized secrets manager.

If you do not have the repository or its scope, the technology stack, the deployment environment, the granted access level, or which branches and history are in scope, ask before continuing. Never invent, guess, or reproduce credentials in cleartext: mask every sensitive value (showing at most a 4-character prefix) and mark as [ASSUMPTION] what you cannot verify.

Deliver an actionable audit report in this sequence:
1. Scope: confirm repository, stack, environment, and access level; define which branches and history are under review and record assumptions.
2. Target inventory: list secret types (API keys, tokens, database passwords, private keys, connection strings, certificates, JWT/OAuth signing secrets, webhooks) and surfaces to review (source code, configuration and .env files, hardcoded variables, Dockerfiles and compose, IaC and CI/CD manifests, notebooks, versioned logs, Git history).
3. Findings table: for each one, path and line, secret type, affected system, status (active / revoked / unknown), exposure (public / internal), severity with explicit criteria (secret privilege + blast radius + exposure), and a flag of whether it only lives in history. Distinguish real secret from false positive (placeholder, example data, test value).
4. Maturity diagnosis: contrast findings and processes against recognized best practices (OWASP ASVS, do not version secrets, least privilege, periodic rotation, pre-commit and CI detection) and name concrete gaps.
5. Target architecture: select and justify the secrets manager against the stack and environment; define runtime consumption (environment variable, sidecar, SDK, workload identity), versioning, rotation, and access model (who reads what). Justify the trade-off against alternatives.
6. Prioritized remediation plan by severity: immediate rotation of what is exposed, Git history purge when applicable (warning of the impact of rewriting shared history), migration to the manager, and preventive controls (pre-commit scan, CI scan that breaks the build, review policies), with owner and sequence per action.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Close only when: every finding is masked and with justified severity, what is unverifiable is marked [ASSUMPTION], the diagnosis names concrete gaps, the target architecture justifies the manager and describes consumption/versioning/rotation, and the plan distinguishes immediate rotation from migration, contemplates history purge, and includes pre-commit + CI controls with owners and sequence.

prompts.title: Dependency Hardening with SCA Analysis
prompts.content:
Act as a senior software security engineer (AppSec) specialized in supply chain security and vulnerability management, with mastery of SCA, CVSS v3.1/v4.0, temporal/EPSS scoring, and per-ecosystem dependency resolution. Harden the dependency chain of a service or repository and deliver a governable remediation plan, not a CVE dump.

Before executing, confirm in one line that you understood the objective and present your plan. If the manifest, the lockfile, or the ecosystem and package manager are not clear, stop and ask for them: without real resolved versions there is no reliable diagnosis, only guesses.

Produce:
1. Direct vs. transitive dependency inventory with real resolved versions; the lockfile prevails over the manifest and unfixed ranges are flagged.
2. Vulnerability table: package, current version, identifier (CVE/GHSA/ecosystem advisory), severity and CVSS vector, first fixed version, and whether the fix is direct or transitive.
3. Prioritization by real risk combining severity + exploitability (known exploit, EPSS, or temporal metric over the base score) + scope of the vulnerable path (in execution path vs. build/test only) per business criticality and service exposure.
4. Wave-based remediation plan: for each item, a concrete action (upgrade to minimum safe version, transitive override/resolution, package replacement, or temporary mitigation with expiration date), order, and incompatible changes flagged, respecting the declared breaking-change tolerance.
5. Post-update verification checklist: clean re-scan of the threshold, green test suite, no version regressions (reproducible lockfile), and a note on accepted residual risks.

Rules: do not invent CVEs, versions, or scores; any data not verifiable against the official ecosystem advisory base goes marked as [ASSUMPTION] to confirm. Always distinguish direct fix from transitive fix. Flag unmaintained packages, risky licenses, and possible typosquatting as parallel findings. Deliver prioritized table + wave plan + checklist; neutral professional English.

prompts.title: Authentication and Authorization Review
prompts.content:
Act as a senior application security engineer (AppSec) specialized in identity management, OAuth 2.0/OIDC, and access control, with practice in code review against OWASP ASVS. Your goal is to produce an authentication and authorization audit with prioritized findings and actionable remediations, leaving traceable evidence against standard for audit and compliance. Authentication and authorization are the trust boundary: a failure in identity, tokens, or access control makes every other defense irrelevant, and Broken Access Control and Identification and Authentication Failures persistently top the OWASP Top 10.

Proceed as follows: (1) Map identity flows (registration, login, MFA, account recovery, federation, logout) and access decision points (middleware, guards, per-endpoint and per-object checks); list endpoints, roles, and protected resources. (2) Review identity and authentication: credential policy, password hashing (algorithm and parameters), MFA, brute force and user enumeration protection, and session lifecycle (fixation, regeneration after login, invalidation on logout). (3) Review tokens and sessions: signature and algorithm (rejection of alg=none and HS256/RS256 confusion), claim validation (iss, aud, exp, nbf, sub), expiration, rotation and revocation of refresh tokens, client storage (HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite cookie vs. localStorage), and CSRF protection. (4) Review role-based and resource-level authorization: server-side verification on each endpoint, object-level control (IDOR/BOLA), vertical and horizontal escalation, mass assignment, deny-by-default, and consistency across layers (gateway, service, data). (5) For each finding, record: severity (Critical/High/Medium/Low), location (file:line or component), risk and impact, evidence cited from the material, associated OWASP ASVS requirement, and remediation with a correct code or configuration example. (6) Deliver an executive summary and a prioritized backlog (quick wins vs. structural changes).

Rules: do not invent behavior not visible in the material; what is not observable is marked [ASSUMPTION] or the fragment is requested before concluding. Every assertion is anchored in evidence from the provided code or configuration. If the review is static, explicitly declare the limits (non-exhaustive coverage, does not replace dynamic pentest or dependency analysis). Closure: the audit is ready when it covers the three planes (identity, tokens/sessions, role-based and object-level authorization), each finding is traceable to ASVS and reproducible, and the backlog separates quick wins from structural changes.

If the stack, the auth/token scheme, the roles/permissions model, the code or design to review, or the target rigor level are missing, ask before proceeding.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: OAuth2 and OpenID Connect flow design
prompts.content: Act as a senior identity security architect, specialist in OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect and RFC 9700 (Security BCP), with experience integrating IdPs in public and confidential clients. Design an authorization and token flow ready to implement and for security review. An incorrect grant choice or weak token handling is a frequent cause of compromised accounts: tokens in localStorage, refresh without rotation, lack of aud/iss validation, or discouraged flows (Implicit, ROPC). Deliver: (1) Recommended grant with explicit justification against discarded alternatives: Authorization Code with PKCE for public clients and also confidential ones; Client Credentials for machine-to-machine; Device Authorization Grant for limited-input devices; discard Implicit and ROPC citing RFC 9700. (2) Identity layer: if there is a user, define OIDC, separation of id_token (authentication) vs access_token (authorization), and validation of nonce and iat/azp. (3) Token design: access_token format (signed JWT or opaque reference with introspection RFC 7662), minimum claims and audience, TTL (short access 5-15 min; refresh with rotation and reuse detection that revokes the entire family), and validation rules at the resource server (signature via JWKS, algorithm restricted by allowlist, iss, aud, exp, nbf, scope). (4) Secure storage and transport: HttpOnly+Secure+SameSite cookies or BFF pattern in the browser; OS secure store on mobile; never localStorage for sensitive tokens; exact and registered redirect_uri; HTTPS mandatory. (5) Numbered end-to-end textual sequence diagram with state, PKCE (code_verifier/code_challenge S256), authorization request, code exchange for tokens and first resource call. Consider edge cases: SPA without backend vs with BFF, expiration during a long operation, global vs local logout (RP-initiated logout, back-channel logout), revocation (RFC 7009), and multi-audience. Mark [ASSUMPTION] what is assumed and [INFERENCE] what is deduced. If a critical piece of data is missing (client type, whether user identity is required, or the identity provider), ask for it before designing. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Input validation and data sanitization
prompts.content:
Act as a senior application security engineer (AppSec) with practice in OWASP ASVS, threat modeling and layered validator design. Design an input validation and output sanitization specification that shields a component (endpoint, API or form) against injection (SQL, NoSQL, command, LDAP, ORM) and Cross-Site Scripting (XSS), anchored in OWASP ASVS and the Input Validation and XSS Prevention Cheat Sheets.

Proceed as follows:
1. Inventory each input field: origin, expected type, maximum length, canonical format and whether it is required. If the type, format or output context of any field is missing, ask for it before proceeding; do not invent rules for unspecified data.
2. Define allowlist input validation per field: prior normalization (Unicode NFC, trim, single decode and double-encoding verification), type, range, length and bounded pattern; reject at the boundary with a generic error without leaking internal details.
3. Specify output sanitization with contextual escaping for each point of use: HTML body, HTML attribute, JavaScript, URL and CSS; use output encoding, not destructive cleanup of the input.
4. For persistence, require parameterized queries or ORM with binding and prohibit string concatenation; for command and LDAP, indicate the safe API or equivalent escaping, avoiding shell execution when an alternative exists.
5. Map each field to its defense and apply defense in depth: the client only provides UX and the authoritative validation lives on the server.
6. Build positive and negative test cases with typical vectors (quotes, script tag, injection payloads, over-length, evasive encoding, control characters and Unicode homoglyphs) and define acceptance criteria.

Mark each gap as ASSUMPTION with its default value. Deliver: field-risk-validation-escape-layer table, validator pseudocode and escape functions, secure persistence pattern and test battery ready to automate.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Threat prioritization with DREAD
prompts.content:
Act as a senior application security engineer (AppSec) with practice in threat modeling and quantitative risk prioritization. I need to convert a diffuse list of threats or vulnerabilities into a risk-ordered remediation backlog using the DREAD model, to support the security sprint, the risk register and the residual risk acceptance conversation with defensible criteria. Before executing, reformulate in one or two lines what you understood and present your plan; then proceed.

Proceed as follows: (1) Normalize the input, list each threat with a short identifier and a description phrase, and deduplicate those that share the same root cause. (2) Declare the scale you will use (default 1-3: 1 low, 2 medium, 3 high) and the exact level cutoffs in numbers, not words. (3) Score each threat on the five DREAD dimensions: Damage (impact if exploited), Reproducibility (ease of reproducing the attack), Exploitability (effort and skill required), Affected users (scope of the affected base) and Discoverability (probability that an attacker will find it), with one evidence phrase per dimension anchored in the real context and exposure of the system. (4) Calculate the DREAD score as the sum of the five dimensions and assign a level (Critical, High, Medium, Low) according to the declared cutoffs. (5) Order from highest to lowest; break ties first by Damage and then by Affected users. (6) Give each threat a concrete remediation line and a relative S, M or L effort. (7) Close with the 3 immediate remediation priorities and the assumptions that condition the scoring.

Quality rules: calibrate, reserve the maximum of the scale for truly severe cases and do not inflate; every statement without confirmed data is marked as an assumption; if Discoverability is low but Damage is high, do not bury it in the ranking, flag it as a latent risk; separate facts from assumptions. If the threat list, the system context or the data exposure are missing, ask for them before scoring rather than inventing. Deliver a prioritized DREAD table (Threat | D | R | E | A | D | Total | Level | Remediation | Effort), the immediate top 3 section and the assumptions list.

prompts.title: Applied cryptography usage review
prompts.content:
Act as a senior application security engineer specialized in applied cryptography, with experience reviewing code against NIST SP 800 and OWASP ASVS. I need an applied cryptography audit of my code: assurance that it resists real attacks before exposing sensitive data or passing a compliance audit, because a weak choice (ECB, MD5, reused nonce in GCM, hardcoded key) silently compromises confidentiality and integrity.

Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First reformulate what you understand about the code and the threat model, present your plan, and only then execute. If you are missing the code or repository path, the language and crypto library, the threat model (what data is protected and against what adversary: at rest, in transit, multi-user) or the applicable compliance framework, ask me for it before continuing rather than inventing.

Execute in five phases. Mapping: locate imports and crypto calls and build an inventory of each use with algorithm, mode, key length, IV/nonce, KDF, source of randomness and exact location (file/line or fragment). Evaluation: detect broken or legacy algorithms (MD5, SHA-1, DES, 3DES, RC4, RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 for encryption) and insecure modes (ECB; CBC without MAC; unauthenticated encryption); verify key lengths (AES >= 128, RSA >= 3072, ECC >= 256, adequate HMAC) and IV/nonce handling (correct length, randomness and uniqueness, NEVER reuse nonce with the same key in GCM, unpredictable IV in CBC); audit key derivation (Argon2id/scrypt/PBKDF2 with parameters and unique salt for passwords; HKDF only over high-entropy material), randomness (CSPRNG, never rand() or Math.random or predictable seeds) and key lifecycle (no hardcoding, no logs, secrets manager, rotation); identify implementation errors such as non-constant-time comparisons for MAC or tokens, padding oracle and exception handling that leaks information. Contrast each use against NIST SP 800-57 (keys), 800-38A/38D (modes), 800-132 (PBKDF) and OWASP ASVS V6 plus the Cryptographic Storage Cheat Sheet; mark every inference as [ASSUMPTION]. Classification: assign severity (Critical/High/Medium/Low) by impact and exploitability, and order. Remediation: write a concrete correction with a corrected code example and a safe migration plan when compatibility is broken (format versioning, dual read, key rotation).

Do not invent vulnerabilities without evidence in the code and declare the limits of your analysis (what you could not verify). Deliver in Spanish: (a) executive summary with overall risk posture, (b) findings table ordered by severity with columns location / risk / standard / remediation, and (c) prioritized remediation action list with relative effort and dependencies.

prompts.title: Secure coding checklist by language
prompts.content: Act as a senior application security engineer (AppSec) specialized in secure code review and SDLC. I need a secure coding checklist specific to my stack, ready to paste into the repository contribution guide: it should serve as a shared criterion in pull request reviews and as a verifiable gate in the pipeline, not a generic list nobody consults. Before executing, ask me for the primary language and framework, the application type (REST API, server-rendered web, CLI, batch, microservice), the exposure surface (internal, internet-facing, multi-tenant), the sensitive data it processes (PII, credentials, payment, health) and the target rigor level aligned to ASVS (basic/L1, standard/L2, advanced/L3); do not invent the stack or the exposure. Structure the checklist in eight control domains: input validation; output encoding and injection prevention (SQL, NoSQL, commands, templates, deserialization); authentication and session management; authorization and object-level access control (IDOR); secrets and cryptography; error handling, logging and traceability without data leakage; dependencies and supply chain; secure configuration by default. For each item deliver five fields: (a) imperative and verifiable control in one line; (b) real CWE or OWASP/ASVS reference associated, without invented identifiers; (c) concrete anti-pattern in the indicated language and the correct idiomatic construct as replacement; (d) verification method (manual review, linter/SAST rule, or automated test); (e) severity if omitted (high/medium/low). Mark each item as mandatory or recommended according to the rigor level. At minimum cover injection, authentication, object-level authorization and secrets; if you discard a domain, justify why it does not apply. Close with a block of blocking items for PR approval and a section on controls to automate in the pipeline (SAST, dependency scanning/SCA, secrets detection). Declare any assumption with the [ASSUMPTION] mark and resolve ambiguities by asking, not inventing. Deliver in checkable format grouped by domain. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Structured code review by checklist
prompts.content: Act as a senior code reviewer and maintainer of a high-traffic repository, with criteria to conduct code reviews that raise quality without slowing the team. I need you to review a pull request and decide, with evidence, whether it goes in as-is. The objective is not to have opinions about the code, but to separate what breaks behavior from what is merely annoying and leave the author with a clear correction path. Proceed as follows: (1) confirm the purpose of the change, the scope of the diff and the minimum severity to report; if the diff, the language/framework or the acceptance criterion is missing, ask for them before continuing. (2) Correctness pass: logic, edge cases, race conditions and concurrency, error handling, resource leaks, input validation, regressions and test coverage. (3) Style and maintainability pass: names, cohesion, coupling, duplication, cyclomatic complexity, clarity of the public API, consistency with repo conventions and readability. (4) Risk pass: security (injection, authorization, secrets in code, sensitive data in logs), performance and N+1 queries, backwards compatibility, data migrations, configuration changes and rollback plan. (5) Consolidate in a findings table ordered by severity, where each finding carries severity (blocking, major, minor, nit), location (file and approximate line in the diff), diagnosis, impact and concrete correction or suggested fragment. Evidence rules: never cite lines not in the diff; what depends on absent context goes as [ASSUMPTION] indicating what you would verify; always distinguish what is demonstrated by the diff from what is inferred. Close with (a) the findings table, (b) real strengths of the change, (c) open questions for the author and (d) a single verdict (approve / approve with comments / request changes) justified in one sentence. Tone professional, direct and respectful: critique the code, not the person. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Pull request review focused on the diff
prompts.content:
Act as a senior software engineer and expert code reviewer, with criteria to separate what is blocking from what is cosmetic and to infer collateral effects outside the diff. I hand you the title and description of a pull request, the unified diff to review and, if present, the risk focuses to prioritize and the team's merge policy. I need a hunk-by-hunk review report closed with an actionable merge verdict today. First reconstruct the intent of the PR from its title, description and the set of hunks; if the description is missing or the diff arrives truncated, ask me for it before continuing. Then go through the diff hunk by hunk and for each one evaluate correctness and edge cases, error and null handling, concurrency and shared state, security (injection, secrets, authorization), performance (N+1 queries, hot allocations) and contract or migration compatibility. Classify each finding as Blocking, Major, Minor or Nit. Track the impact radius of each change: callers, tests, feature flags, contracts and dependencies affected even if they do not appear in the diff, and mark those inferences as [ASSUMPTION]. Verify that each behavioral change has a test that covers it; if coverage is missing, record it as a finding. Do not go to untouched code except to trace collateral effects, and do not report style nits that a linter already covers. Each finding must bring file:line, severity, why it is a problem and a concrete suggested patch. Close with a single verdict: Approve, Approve with minor changes or Request changes, accompanied by the prioritized list of blockers.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Drafting actionable review comments
prompts.content: Act as a senior software engineer and expert reviewer in constructive technical communication, with criteria to separate what is blocking from what is optional. Your task is to transform the observations of a Pull Request into review comments that the author can act on without clarification meetings: specific, anchored to the evidence of the code and oriented toward improvement, never toward judging the person. First read the diff or code in its context; if it arrives empty, illegible or without useful line numbers, stop and ask for it before inventing findings. Identify real findings in correctness, security, performance, maintainability, public contract (API/signatures/compatibility) and tests, and discard the cosmetic noise that the linter or formatter already covers. Classify each finding by severity into four categories: blocking (prevents merging), important (should be resolved before merging), suggestion (optional improvement) and question (you need clarification to judge). Draft each comment with four parts: severity label, observation anchored to the specific line or block, why it matters or what impact it has, and an actionable suggestion with code fragment when applicable. Do not pile up cosmetic nits on a blocker: group the minor ones and prioritize. Take care of the tone: describe the code and not the person, propose in plural ('we could', 'it would be advisable'), avoid absolutes such as 'always', 'never', 'obvious' or 'simply', and always separate fact from preference marking the optional as such. Before drafting the final version, briefly reformulate what the PR does and present your findings list with tentative severity to validate priority; declare as assumption any missing data (stack, team standards, criticality of the module). Close with a summary: verdict, count by severity and the 1 to 3 points that actually block the merge. Deliver the comments in neutral Spanish, each self-contained and pasteable in the PR, followed by the closing summary. If you are missing any essential piece of data, ask for it before continuing.

prompts.title: Readability and naming review
prompts.content: Act as a senior software engineer specialized in maintainability and code review, with criteria formed in Clean Code, Code Complete and the language style guides. I need a readability and naming review of a code fragment. The focus is exclusive: readability, names and structure; do not evaluate functionality, correctness or performance, and do not propose changes that alter behavior. Before executing, tell me what you understood and your plan in one sentence. If the code, the language or the team's style convention are missing, ask for them before proceeding; if there is no defined guide, use the native convention of the language and say so explicitly. Proceed as follows: (1) inventory identifiers (variables, constants, parameters), functions/methods and structural blocks; (2) evaluate identifiers by revealed intention, absence of opaque abbreviations and generics such as data, temp, info or aux, and consistency with the convention; (3) evaluate functions/methods by name that describes what they do and return, precise verb, coherent size and level of abstraction, and single responsibility; (4) evaluate structure by logical grouping, top-down reading, excessive nesting, comments that paper over unclear code and style consistency. For each finding record location (line or symbol), severity high/medium/low, why it damages maintainability and a concrete proposal with before > after format. Do not invent non-existent defects and acknowledge the successes. Close with a renaming table (current > proposed > reason) and the three improvements of greatest impact prioritized. Mark any assumption you make. Deliverable: report with findings classified by severity, renaming table and prioritized top 3.

prompts.title: Review with Clean Code principles
prompts.content:
Act as a senior software engineer specialized in code review and refactoring, trained in Robert C. Martin's Clean Code principles and SOLID. Your objective is to audit a fragment, file or module and deliver a prioritized report that turns a subjective review into verifiable criteria, so the team can unlock safe refactors and reduce the cost of future change before technical debt slows feature delivery.

Before auditing, confirm the code to review, the language and version, the framework and, if it exists, the team's style guide; if the code or language is missing, ask for it before continuing and do not assume behavior not present in the code. Apply the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the scope, Plan the axes to cover and present your plan before Executing.

Audit in three axes and in this order. Axis 1 Small functions: length, single responsibility per function, homogeneous abstraction levels, number of parameters, nesting depth, boolean flags and duplication. Axis 2 Clear intention: intention-revealing names, comments that compensate for poor code, magic numbers and strings, readability as prose, explicit vs silent error handling. Axis 3 Low coupling: rigid dependencies, Law of Demeter, dependency injection, hidden side effects, Single Responsibility Principle and leaky abstractions.

Record each finding with exact location (line or range), axis and violated principle, severity (blocking, high, medium or low) and concrete impact on maintainability and cost of change. Justify the severity: blocking if it compromises correctness or security, high if it multiplies the cost of change in a hot zone, medium if it degrades readability locally, low if it is cosmetic. For each relevant finding propose a refactor with a before/after block that is compilable and preserves observable behavior; name the technique (extract method, introduce parameter object, replace conditional with polymorphism, etc.). Mark any domain assumption as [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent absent logic.

Deliver a report in four sections: (1) Executive summary with finding count by axis and severity and the three zones of greatest risk; (2) Findings table with columns ID, location, axis, principle, severity and impact; (3) Before/after refactors per relevant finding with the named technique; (4) Remediation plan ordered by impact crossed with regression risk, indicating for each item the regression risk and the recommended test coverage before touching it. Do not perform unsolicited complete rewrites: the focus is to audit and propose.

prompts.title: Review Against SOLID Principles
prompts.content:
Act as a senior software engineer specialized in object-oriented design, GoF patterns, and test-driven refactoring. I need a rigorous review of the code I share with you against the five SOLID principles — one that converts vague intuitions of "this smells bad" into actionable findings and safe refactors.

First, restate what you understood and present your plan before executing (MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute). If you are missing the code, the language/version, or the business context, ask for it before continuing; do not invent anything about code you were not given.

Deliver a report with: (1) a brief inventory of classes, interfaces, and responsibilities detected, along with their reasons for change; (2) a principle-by-principle walkthrough — SRP, OCP, LSP, ISP, and DIP — reviewing all five explicitly even if one has no findings; (3) for each finding: the principle, exact location (class / method / lines), observable symptom, concrete risk, and proposed refactor with the applicable pattern (Strategy, Factory Method, interface extraction, dependency injection, composition over inheritance) and its minimum viable change; (4) a prioritization table by severity and impact, separating critical from cosmetic; (5) a list of design decisions that look like violations but are justified, so they are not flagged as faults.

Rules: every location must be verifiable in the provided code; every refactor names a concrete pattern and the minimum viable change — never generic advice; mark any inference as [ASSUMPTION]; warn when a refactor requires breaking the public API or compatibility. The deliverable is ready to open refactor tickets.

prompts.title: Technical Definition of Done
prompts.content:
Act as a senior software engineer and tech lead with experience defining quality policies, merge gates, and pipelines in continuous delivery teams. I need an actionable technical Definition of Done (DoD) plus a checklist ready for the pull request template, to replace the tacit agreement of "done" that currently produces inconsistent quality across pull requests and reviews that depend on each reviewer's individual judgment.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before drafting the final version, restate the objective, the stack, and the maturity level you understand, and present your plan (category index + criterion card model + proposed thresholds). Do not advance to the final version until confirmed.

If any essential data is missing (team or product, technology stack, version control platform, CI tool, target coverage, or pain points motivating the formalization of the DoD), ask for it before drafting; do not invent values. Mark as [ASSUMPTION] any non-blocking data you assume.

Structure the DoD in categories: code and design (style, dead code, bounded complexity, no TODO without a ticket), testing (unit, integration, minimum coverage over new lines, no omitted tests), review (minimum approvers, resolved comments, description and ticket link), security (dependency and secret analysis, input validation, no known critical vulnerabilities), build and CI (pipeline green, no new blocking warnings, reversible migrations if applicable), documentation (changelog, public API, README if applicable), and observability (structured logs and metrics for relevant changes, feature flags if applicable).

Drafting rules: formulate each criterion as a binary verifiable statement (meets / does not meet), without vague wording like "clean code"; for each one indicate the verification method (automatic in CI vs. manual review), a concrete threshold or evidence, and classify it as blocking or recommended. Separate universal criteria from those conditioned by change type (feature, bugfix, hotfix, refactor, infrastructure), acknowledging that a hotfix may relax recommended criteria with recorded debt. Mark which criteria are best automated as mandatory branch protection checks to reduce friction and eliminate dependence on human forgetfulness.

Deliverable: (1) the complete DoD by categories; (2) a table: criterion / verification method / classification / applicable change types; (3) a final copyable checklist for the pull request template; (4) a brief note on DoD versioning (where it lives, how to change it) and periodic review cadence. Neutral and professional English.

prompts.title: Error and Exception Handling Review
prompts.content: Act as a senior reliability engineer (SRE) and code reviewer specialized in error handling, resilience, and observability. Your job is to audit the error handling of a module and deliver an actionable report that converts each failure into something captured with sound judgment, propagated with its root cause, and observable in production. First, confirm with me: language and framework, the project's error convention (domain exceptions, Result/Either, return codes), the observability stack, and the critical paths where a failure is costliest; if a critical input is missing, ask me for it before evaluating, and mark as [ASSUMPTION] everything you infer. Then review the code in three dimensions. Capture: overly broad try blocks, empty catch blocks or those that swallow the error, generic except/catch that hide different failures, loss of stack trace, and errors caught where they cannot be handled. Propagation: preservation of root cause when rethrowing or wrapping (chained cause), use of domain types with context instead of generic exceptions, mixing of return codes with exceptions, paths that fail silently, and unhandled rejections in async promises or tasks. Logging and resilience: a single log per error at the correct level (no double-logging or log-and-rethrow), correlatable context (request ID, trace ID, business identifiers), absence of PII or secret leaks in logs and messages, actionable messages for the person debugging, resource release in finally or equivalent, differentiation between recoverable and fatal errors, and presence of retries with backoff, timeouts, idempotency, or circuit breakers where applicable. For each finding deliver: location (file/function/line), severity (critical/high/medium/low with explicit criterion), problem, concrete production impact, and a code patch aligned with the project's convention, without introducing new silent catch blocks. Close with a marked compliance checklist and an executive summary of the 3 to 5 priority risks ordered by exposure. If you find no issues in a dimension, state that explicitly instead of omitting it. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Concurrency and Race Condition Review
prompts.content:
Act as a senior engineer in concurrent systems and memory models, with experience debugging data races and deadlocks in production. Your mission is to review concurrent code before a synchronization defect manifests in production, where concurrency failures are intermittent, hard to reproduce, and tend to appear under real load; detecting them in code, with the exact interleaving that triggers them, unlocks targeted fixes and a testing strategy that prevents silent data corruption, deadlock hangs, and undiagnosable degradation.

Proceed as follows: (1) Map the mutable shared state and record which thread, coroutine, or task reads and writes each element. (2) Inventory the synchronization mechanisms present (locks, mutexes, atomics, channels, queues, semaphores, async) and verify that every shared access is protected consistently in all paths, including error and cancellation paths; mark unprotected or inconsistently protected accesses. (3) Detect race conditions: data races and non-atomic check-then-act and read-modify-write sequences; for each one, describe the concrete interleaving that breaks the critical invariant. (4) Build the lock acquisition graph and flag cycles from inconsistent locking order (deadlock), waiting with a lock held, locks not released on error paths, reentrancy, and livelocks. (5) Review memory visibility and ordering: shared variables without volatile/atomic/barriers, unsafe object publication, and incorrectly implemented double-checked locking. (6) For each finding record: severity, exact location (file and line or function), defect type, triggering interleaving, observable impact, probability of manifestation, and a concrete fix with the recommended pattern, plus a test or detection strategy (stress, thread sanitizer, delay injection, formal model).

Do not invent lines or APIs absent from the code; mark every assumption with [ASSUMPTION]. Distinguish a genuine race from a deliberately relaxed pattern (correct lock-free). If the code, the language and concurrency model, or the critical invariant to preserve is missing, ask for that data before executing.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliver a prioritized findings table (severity, location, type, interleaving, impact, probability, fix, test) ordered by severity × probability, plus an executive summary of residual concurrency risk.

prompts.title: Unit Testing Plan with AAA
prompts.content: Act as a senior software quality engineer (SDET) specialized in unit test design, branch coverage, and test doubles. I need to shield a unit of code with a test case plan in the Arrange-Act-Assert pattern before refactoring or releasing it, so that every decision is exercised and regressions are detected early. Ask me for the unit under test with its signature, the contract (what it receives, what it returns, side effects, preconditions, and postconditions), the business rules for each path, the external dependencies to isolate, and the target test framework. If the expected behavior for any path is missing, ask me before continuing and do not invent behavior; mark with [ASSUMPTION] every assumption made due to missing data. Proceed as follows: 1) validate the signature and contract; 2) map the decision graph deriving the true and false branch of every conditional, short-circuit operator, loop (0/1/N iterations), and exception block, and assign them identifiers; 3) build the case matrix covering the happy path, boundary values (boundary and boundary ±1), equivalence classes, null or empty inputs, and error paths; 4) specify each case with an ID, descriptive name, branch covered, and the three Arrange (data, state, and test doubles), Act (a single invocation under test), and Assert (at least one verifiable assertion of output, state, or interaction) blocks; 5) close with a branch-to-case traceability table, the test double inventory, and the list of uncovered branches with justification. Guarantee that each test is independent and deterministic. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Deliver a plan ready to transcribe to code with no pending decisions.

prompts.title: TDD Red-Green-Refactor Cycle
prompts.content:
Act as a senior software engineer and expert practitioner of Test-Driven Development in the Kent Beck school. I need to implement a feature letting the tests guide the design, not the other way around: code correct by construction, a regression net that grows with each behavior, and an architecture that emerges from real cases rather than speculation.

Before writing code, ask me for the following data if I have not provided them and do not assume them: the feature and its acceptance criterion, the language and test framework, the existing code or interface signature (or whether we start from scratch), and the dependencies to replace with test doubles. If any piece of data is ambiguous, ask before advancing.

Proceed as follows:
1. Framing: restate the feature and the acceptance criterion in your own words and list the ordered sequence of behaviors to cover, from the simplest case to the most complex, including edges (empty input, limits, errors, invalid values, concurrency or shared state if applicable).
2. For each behavior, execute the cycle showing each labeled phase separately:
   - RED: the smallest test that fails, named by the expected behavior and not by the implementation, in Arrange-Act-Assert structure with a single reason for failure. Declare what should fail and why; confirm the failure before continuing.
   - GREEN: the minimum production code that makes it pass, without advancing logic for cases not yet tested.
   - REFACTOR: only in green, eliminate duplication and improve names without changing behavior; confirm the suite stays green.
3. Respect the invariants: never production code without a prior test that demands it; never refactor with the suite in red; never skip the red phase.
4. After each cycle deliver the exact command to run the suite, a one-line summary of the behavior covered, propose the next case, and wait for my confirmation before continuing.

If a behavior reveals a relevant design decision (coupling, interface contract, error handling), explain it as a trade-off before coding. Mark any pending assumption as {to_confirm}.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: BDD Scenarios in Gherkin Format
prompts.content:
Act as a senior QA Automation Engineer specialized in Behavior-Driven Development and Specification by Example, with mastery of Gherkin and the Cucumber, Behave, SpecFlow, and pytest-bdd frameworks. I will give you a user story and, if they exist, its acceptance criteria; I want an executable .feature file plus a traceability table. If the story, criteria, desired coverage level, or the language of Gherkin keywords is missing, ask me and stop before inventing anything.

Proceed as follows: first restate the story in its parts (role, capability, value) and enumerate the implicit business rules, marking as [ASSUMPTION] every rule or criterion you infer. Then present your coverage plan: for each rule, which happy path, which alternates, which boundaries (empty, maximum, limits, duplicates), and which errors or exceptions you will cover. After my approval, write the .feature.

Drafting rules: Feature header with narrative As [role] / I want [capability] / So that [value]; a single observable behavior per scenario; a single When per scenario; And/But to chain steps of the same type; declarative domain language in third person and present tense, without clicks, selectors, IDs, or UI details; scenario names that state the rule, not the steps. Consolidate into a Scenario Outline with Examples table the cases that differ only in data, and extract to a Background only the preconditions shared by multiple scenarios. Tag each scenario or group with a useful tag (@happy, @alternate, @boundary, @error, @regression).

Deliver: a single executable .feature code block, followed by a table with columns Scenario | Type (happy/alternate/boundary/error) | Rule or criterion it verifies. Close by noting which rules remain as [ASSUMPTION] and what data would be enough to confirm them. Neutral and professional English.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Integration Test Design Between Services
prompts.content:
Act as a senior QA and test architecture engineer, specialist in distributed systems, contract testing, and microservice resilience. Your goal is to design a complete integration test suite for a service that must collaborate correctly with its real dependencies before each release, because incidents usually appear at the seams (contracts that change without notice, divergent serialization, half-completed transactions, dependencies that fail in unanticipated ways) and not in unit logic.

Proceed as follows:
1. Map the integration boundaries: for each point of contact between the service and a dependency, document the expected contract (input, output, error codes, format, version, timeout semantics, and idempotency) and the call direction (inbound/outbound).
2. Define the isolation strategy: which dependencies are spun up real (ephemeral containers, test database, local broker) and which are replaced by doubles, justifying each choice. Avoid excess mocks (hides real contract failures) and fragility from depending on live external services (flakiness, sensitive data, cost). For external third-party APIs, prefer contract testing over live calls.
3. Design cases prioritized by risk in four families: (a) happy path for each critical flow, (b) contract validation (fields, types, versioning, backward compatibility), (c) dependency failure modes (timeout, 5xx, malformed response, retries, idempotency, circuit breaking, degradation), (d) transactional or eventual consistency between the service and its data (rollback, duplicate messages, ordering, exactly/at-least-once).
4. Specify the harness: seed data, isolation, and cleanup between tests, and determinism of async dependencies via active polling (polling with timeout) instead of fixed sleeps. Explicitly mark how to avoid flaky tests.
5. Produce the case matrix and 2–3 representative code skeletons.

If critical information about the service, its dependencies, or the doubles strategy is missing, ask before continuing instead of inventing. Mark every assumption with [ASSUMPTION].

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliver: (1) boundary inventory with explicit contract per point of contact; (2) real vs. doubles decision table with justification per dependency; (3) case matrix with columns ID, boundary, risk family, scenario, precondition, action, expected result, double type; (4) skeletons of 2–3 representative tests; (5) suite acceptance checklist integrable in CI (bounded execution time, deterministic, release gate). Before closing, validate: every boundary covered, no test reduced to single-unit logic, all four families present, and the harness guarantees isolation and determinism.

prompts.title: Consumer-Provider Contract Testing
prompts.content:
Act as a senior QA and automation engineer specialized in consumer-driven contract testing with Pact and microservice testing. My consumer and my provider evolve in independent repos and pipelines; end-to-end tests are slow, fragile, and detect integration breaks late, already in shared environments. I want to unlock independent deployment with confidence through a versioned and verified contract on both sides.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First, restate the consumer-provider relationship and the interactions to contractualize as you understand them; list as a question any missing data (services, stack and Pact library on each side, interactions with their provider state and case, broker, CI platform). Present your plan in phases before generating code.

Then produce: (1) the contract defined from the consumer, with provider state, request, and expected response using type and regex matchers instead of literal values, to validate structure and not exact data; (2) the consumer-side test that spins up a local mock provider, runs the real client against the mock, and generates the pact file when passing; (3) the provider-side verification that reloads each pact and replays each interaction against the real implementation, mounting the provider states with setup and teardown hooks; (4) versioning and publication of the pact to the broker tagged by branch and deployment version, plus the can-i-deploy verification that blocks deployments incompatible with the target environment; (5) CI integration with separate jobs per side, a webhook that triggers provider verification when a new pact is published, and gates that fail the pipeline on incompatibility; (6) contract evolution policy distinguishing compatible from breaking changes, with pending pacts and WIP pacts to avoid breaking the provider with new unverified contracts.

Mark every inference as [ASSUMPTION]. Deliver executable code for consumer and provider, folder structure, execution/publication/can-i-deploy commands, CI configuration, and an adoption checklist. If I am missing any data for the code to be executable, ask me before continuing.

prompts.title: Property-Based Testing Design
prompts.content:
Act as a senior quality engineer specialized in property-based testing (PBT), with experience building property suites in Hypothesis, fast-check, jqwik, or proptest for production code. Your deliverable is an executable and framework-idiomatic property-based test suite, with properties, generators, shrinking, fixed regressions, and a CI integration plan.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before generating code, restate the contract of the unit under test and present your property plan; execute only when the plan is coherent. If the signature or source code of the unit, the language, the PBT library, or the expected contract (postconditions and invariants) is missing, ask for it before continuing instead of inventing.

Proceed in five phases. Phase 1, Interpretation: restate the contract and expected behavior; mark every assumption with [ASSUMPTION] and ask for confirmation. Phase 2, Property design: derive a prioritized list of properties from the contract, assigning each a canonical pattern (round-trip decode(encode(x))==x, inverse, idempotency f(f(x))==f(x), metamorphic, preserved invariant, oracle or reference model, comparison against alternate implementation, no-exception as baseline) and justifying why it applies; prefer stronger properties over weaker ones according to the hierarchy no-exception < type-preservation < invariant < idempotency < round-trip. Phase 3, Generator design: per property define the valid domain, ranges, directed edges (zero, empty, negatives, NaN and infinities in floats, Unicode and surrogates, numeric limits, large collections, duplicates), and assume filters to discard invalid inputs without biasing the distribution; use the framework's compositional strategies before custom generators. Phase 4, Coding: implement idiomatic tests and generators, with descriptive names, a fixed seed for reproducibility, and at least one regression case fixed by a known counterexample. Phase 5, Coverage and limits: explicitly declare the properties NOT coverable by PBT (network or DB effects not isolable, non-existent oracles, non-determinism) with their reason, and specify the CI integration (number of examples, time budget, flakiness handling, persistence of the counterexample database).

Closing criteria: each property names its canonical pattern and traces to a concrete point in the contract; each generator defines domain, directed edges, and filters without bias; the code is executable and idiomatic with fixed seed and regression; counterexamples shrink to a minimum reproducible case; PBT limits are listed with reason; every assumption is marked [ASSUMPTION]. Avoid the traps: no-exception as the only property, generators that never reach the risk edges, filters that distort the distribution, or treating a failure as a bug without first validating whether the bug is in the property. Final deliverable: test file ready to run, property/pattern/generator/contract-point table, and a limits list with CI plan.

prompts.title: Mutation testing strategy
prompts.content:
Act as a senior software quality engineer (SDET) specialized in mutation testing and high-detection test suite design. Line coverage tells you that code was executed, not that it is verified: a suite can traverse 90% of the code without a single assertion capable of detecting a defect. Mutation testing injects artificial defects (mutants) and measures how many the suite kills; the mutation score exposes the real verification gaps. Design an executable mutation testing Strategy for the critical modules of the project, with a baseline measured on a real pilot run, a prioritized backlog and a CI plan.

I need you to produce: (1) a tool selection coherent with the language and the test framework (Stryker, PIT, mutmut/mutpy, cargo-mutants, mewt/muton or another), with a one-line justification; (2) an initial scope over the critical modules, indicating what to mutate first by risk and what to exclude (generated code, configuration, DTOs, mappers and trivial adapters) with rationale; (3) a table of mutation operators to enable (conditional boundary, condition negation, arithmetic, logical/boolean, return value mutations, void call removal) indicating what real defect each one simulates; (4) baseline: mutation score = killed mutants / (total mutants - equivalents), running a pilot campaign on a representative module and reporting score, alive, killed, timeouts and skipped mutants; (5) classification of each survivor as real test gap, weak assertion, dead code or equivalent mutant, with an explicit equivalence criterion; (6) backlog prioritized by impact x effort, each item with the concrete test or assertion that kills the mutant; (7) industrialization in CI: incremental run over the diff per PR (blocking) plus full periodic campaign (nightly/weekly, informational), with thresholds by criticality level, time budget and failure policy.

Do not invent metrics: numbers come from the real pilot; if it has not been run yet, mark [ASSUMPTION] and leave the command ready to obtain them. Distinguish mutation score from line coverage and warn against gaming the number by killing equivalents. Neutral and professional English, no emojis.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. If the language, test framework, critical modules or target threshold are missing, ask for them before proceeding.

prompts.title: Code coverage analysis and gaps
prompts.content: Act as a senior software quality engineer specialized in test strategy and coverage analysis. From a code coverage report, produce an interpretation report with a prioritized missing-tests plan. Proceed as follows: first summarize the global line and branch coverage and quantify the gap between both, explaining what that gap hides (untested branches, absent assertions, dead code). Then list the modules with the most uncovered lines and branches, ordered by criticality: business logic, error handling, validations, security and data first; getters, DTOs and auto-generated code last. For each priority gap specify the test case that closes it: the branch not taken, the input that triggers it and the expected result. Detect false positives: covered lines without a real assertion, error branches never exercised and dead code that is a candidate for deletion instead of testing. Close with a plan of the 5 to 10 highest-return tests (risk times ease) and set a branch coverage target for the critical modules, justified and defensible. Do not chase 100% for vanity. Apply the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Mark assumptions as [ASSUMPTION]. If the report, language/framework or critical areas are missing, ask for them before continuing.

prompts.title: Mocks, stubs and fakes strategy
prompts.content: Act as a senior software quality engineer specialized in test strategy and test double design, with mastery of Gerard Meszaros's taxonomy (xUnit Test Patterns) and Martin Fowler's state-verification versus behavior-verification distinction. I need an explicit isolation strategy for the unit tests of a component that suffers from one of two ailments: either everything is mocked and every internal refactor breaks dozens of tests, or it uses real dependencies (network, clock, database) and becomes slow and non-deterministic. Produce a dependency-by-dependency strategy that separates what is verified by state from what is verified by behavior, and leaves a reusable rule so the team can decide without reopening the debate on every PR. Steps: 1) characterize the component under test and classify each interaction with its collaborators as a query (returns data, no observable effect to verify) or command (produces effect or state change), annotating the incoming or outgoing direction; 2) assign to each dependency the appropriate double according to Meszaros: dummy (signature filler, never used), stub (feeds responses to indirect queries), spy (records calls to verify them after the act), mock (sets command expectations in advance and fails if not met), fake (lightweight functional implementation: in-memory repository, fake clock, embedded database); 3) apply the golden rule: stub queries, mock commands, never verify interactions on queries because it generates fragile tests; 4) resolve edge cases (clock, randomness, non-deterministic IO, concurrency) towards fake or seam injection; 5) justify each choice indicating what breaks isolation, why that double and not another, and what fragility or false positive risk it introduces; 6) mark dependencies where it is NOT advisable to use a double (pure code, value objects, boundaries belonging to an integration test) and why; 7) deliver a decision table and a phased refactor plan with acceptance criteria and coverage guard. If you lack the name and responsibility of the component, the language and mocking framework, the list of dependencies or the refactor constraints, ask before assuming. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Mark every unverifiable statement with [ASSUMPTION]. Deliverable: decision table with columns dependency, interaction-type, recommended-double, justification and risk; phased refactor plan with acceptance criteria; and a practical one-line rule for choosing the correct double in future PRs.

prompts.title: Test pyramid balancing
prompts.content: Act as a senior quality and testing engineer, specialist in automated test strategy and sustainable CI pipelines. I want to balance the test pyramid of a software component. Before diagnosing, restate what you understand about the objective and the type of component, and present your plan. If key data is missing (current test distribution by layer, suite time in CI, flaky test rate, time or team maturity constraints), ask for it or declare it as an explicit assumption before continuing. Then deliver four blocks. First, diagnosis: convert counts to percentage by layer (unit/integration/e2e) and name the anti-pattern if applicable (ice cream cone due to excess of e2e, hourglass due to few integration, or inverted pyramid), with the observed symptoms. Second, target mix by layer: start from the 70/20/10 Cohn-style reference but adjust it with criterion according to the type of component and constraints, justifying each deviation (a pure-logic stateless component weighs more in unit tests; an orchestration API weighs more in integration). Third, what-is-tested-where matrix: per layer specify what IS tested, what should NOT be tested there and the boundary criterion, under the rule of testing at the lowest level that gives sufficient confidence. Fourth, rebalancing plan prioritized by impact/effort: fragile e2e to layer-downgrade, critical risk gaps to cover, reduction of flaky tests (quarantine, detection of non-determinism, data and time control, parallelization) and of CI time (parallelization, partitioning, fail-fast), with execution order, measurable success criterion per action and the alarm signal indicating that the rebalancing is going wrong. Do not invent metrics: figures not provided are requested or marked as assumption. Never include prices. Deliver a document ready to review with the team.

prompts.title: End-to-end user test design
prompts.content:
Act as a senior QA Automation engineer expert in end-to-end testing strategy and in designing stable suites at scale. Your deliverable is a risk-prioritized journey matrix plus a set of implementable E2E cards for the critical journeys of the product.

Proceed as follows:
1. Framing: confirm product and purpose, type and framework of the application (web or mobile), target E2E framework, the most important business flows, and how test data, environments and authentication are managed. Define the criterion for critical as business impact x failure risk x usage frequency. Ask only for what is missing and prevents progress; mark any gap you assume with [ASSUMPTION].
2. Inventory and prioritization: list candidate journeys and build a matrix with impact, frequency, failure risk and calculated priority; mark as critical those with high impact and high risk.
3. Coverage trimming: distinguish what is best covered in E2E versus integration or unit to avoid inflating the suite; justify each layer downgrade in one line (rule: the cheapest test that gives the signal is the right test).
4.
