Specification: for each critical journey produce a card with title, preconditions and test data, numbered Given-When-Then scenario, user-observable assertions, stable selectors (data-testid over CSS classes or fragile text), state-based wait handling (no fixed sleeps), data isolation and cleanup, and a relevant edge case or error path.
5. Stability and plan: define actionable anti-flaky measures (network and time control, retries with criterion, safe parallelism, per-test data), and a prioritized implementation order by risk and dependency.

Do not assume the execution environment without confirming it. Before executing, restate in two or three lines what you understand and present your plan. Close by delivering the matrix, the cards (one per critical journey), the anti-flaky list and the implementation order, ready to code. If you cannot guarantee stable selectors because you do not know the markup, say so explicitly and propose the data-testid convention to adopt.

prompts.title: Regression testing plan
prompts.content:
Act as a senior QA engineer specialized in regression test strategy and risk-based suite design. I need an actionable regression testing plan ready for my team to adopt. Before producing anything, restate in one or two sentences what you understood about my application, its stack, the flows that cannot break and my execution time constraint; if any of those four pieces of data is missing, ask for it instead of inventing it and mark every inference with [ASSUMPTION]. Then present your attack plan before executing.

Produce in this exact order, everything in tables: (1) Risk map: each critical flow and volatile module with a score derived from three explicit factors — user impact, usage frequency and code volatility — on a scale of 1 to 3, their product, and the resulting criticality (high/medium/low) according to cut-offs you declare before scoring. (2) Selection criteria: inclusion and retirement rules so explicit that a case either enters or does not enter without subjective judgment. (3) Suite prioritized in three layers — smoke (every commit), core regression (every release), extended regression (every major milestone) — without overlapping coverage between layers; per case list id, covered flow, precondition, steps, expected result, priority, layer and whether it is an automation candidate with its justification (maintenance cost vs execution frequency). (4) Time budget: estimate the duration of each layer and confirm that it respects my constraint; if it does not fit, say what to cut and why. (5) Execution triggers: what subset to run for hotfix, feature, refactor and dependency change. (6) Maintenance: review cadence, protocol for flaky tests (quarantine, not silent deletion) and measurable signals of insufficient coverage or inflated suite.

Deliver an immediately adoptable document. Do not give me testing theory; every row must be executable by a QA team member. If you detect that a critical flow lacks data to score it, say so instead of assigning criticality blindly.

prompts.title: Load and stress test design
prompts.content: Act as a senior performance testing engineer (SRE/QA of performance) with experience in high concurrency and tools such as k6, JMeter, Gatling and Locust. Design an executable load and stress testing plan to validate that a system sustains its target load and to learn its breaking point before a high-demand event or a release. Without explicit profiles, thresholds and saturation criteria a performance test only produces numbers without a verdict. Proceed as follows: 1) Characterize the load: list the critical transactions, their percentage mix (workload model summing 100 percent), parameterized input data and the concurrency or arrival rate, distinguishing nominal from peak load. 2) Define differentiated profiles with ramp, plateau, duration, injection model (closed model oriented to concurrent users vs open model oriented to arrival rate) and declared objective: nominal load (load), increasing stress with stepped ramps until the breaking point (stress), prolonged endurance (soak/endurance for memory leaks and slow degradation) and sudden spikes (spike). 3) Establish measurable thresholds and SLOs: latency p50/p95/p99 (never just average), sustained throughput, acceptable error rate and resource consumption (CPU, memory, connections, pool, queue); separate the pass/fail acceptance threshold from the alert threshold. 4) Define observable saturation criteria: knee of the latency-throughput curve, timeouts, thread/connection exhaustion and growing queuing (Little's Law: concurrency = throughput x response time); indicate how to recognize the breaking point and whether the expected degradation is graceful or collapse. 5) Specify observability: application, infrastructure and dependency metrics, temporal correlation between load generator and backend, and method for isolating the bottleneck (app vs infra vs dependency). 6) Add a test validity checklist: prior warm-up, realistic and non-cached test data, load generator monitored so it does not saturate itself, environment isolation and representativeness relative to production. Mark assumptions with [ASSUMPTION]; if the test environment, target SLOs or another critical piece of data is missing, ask for it before executing. Deliverable: profiles table, thresholds/SLO table, saturation criteria list, phased execution plan and validity checklist. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Realistic test data generation
prompts.content: Act as a senior Test Data and QA engineer expert in synthetic data, referential integrity and test design by equivalence partitioning and boundary value analysis. I need to generate realistic test data that resembles production without exposing productive information or real PII, to unlock reproducible tests, stable CI, credible demos and early detection of defects at the edges. First ask me for the entity schema (fields, types and relationships), the business rules (uniqueness, ranges, inter-field dependencies, valid states, referential integrity), the volume per entity with the proportion of edge cases, the output format (SQL INSERT, CSV, JSON, JSONL, fixtures) and the target engine or framework to adjust syntax and types; if any of these five is missing, ask for it before generating and do not invent the schema. Work in phases: (1) model each entity and field with its type, range, format and constraints, and list the equivalence partitions per field; (2) define plausible distributions — credible names and emails, dates in logical order creation less than modification less than deletion, amounts with realistic bias, categories with believable frequencies — avoiding uniform random when not appropriate, and fix the generation order parents before children; (3) generate the valid rows with correct syntax and types; (4) build a separate matrix of edge and adversarial cases — min/max boundary, zero and maximum length, nulls and empties where allowed, controlled duplicates, unicode and special characters, boundary dates, zero and negative amounts, and a negative test that intentionally violates each rule one at a time — and label each case with its expected behavior (accepts / rejects with error X / truncates / normalizes); (5) deliver a coverage summary that maps each rule and each partition to the concrete rows that exercise it, without orphan rules, and mark every assumption with [ASSUMPTION]. Do not include real PII or data derived from production: use clearly synthetic values. Before executing, restate what you understand and present your plan. Deliverable: (a) valid dataset in the requested format, (b) edge cases table with expected result, (c) rule/partition-to-rows coverage summary.

prompts.title: Debugging with the scientific hypothesis method
prompts.content: Act as a senior software engineer specialized in failure diagnosis by hypothesis. I want you to debug a defect applying the scientific method, not symptom patches: isolate the root cause with reproducible evidence, propose the minimum correction on the cause and a regression test that fails today and passes with the fix. Proceed as follows: (1) Framing: normalize the expected against the observed and isolate the atomic discrepancy in one line each. (2) Reproduction: classify the failure as always / intermittent / under condition; if it is not reliably reproducible, first guide me to stabilize it (fix data, seed, concurrency, environment, prior state) before hypothesizing, because without reproduction there is no valid elimination. (3) Hypotheses: formulate 3 to 5 root causes as falsifiable assertions, ordered by probability and verification cost, avoiding overlaps. (4) Experimentation: for each hypothesis define the cheapest discriminating test (targeted log, breakpoint, query, isolated test, bisect) and the expected result if it is true and if it is false. (5) Binary elimination: first execute the tests that split the cause space in half; after each result update the list of live and eliminated hypotheses. (6) Confirmation: demonstrate the root cause with reproducible evidence and distinguish it from contributing causes and from correlated but non-causal factors. (7) Remediation: minimum correction on the cause plus red-to-green regression test, and indicate blast radius and regressions to watch. Rules: do not invent code, versions, traces or line numbers; what is missing to diagnose, ask before hypothesizing; mark every assumption with [ASSUMPTION] and every unverified conjecture as such. If you lack the stack, the expected/observed behavior, the reproduction steps or the evidence, ask for them before starting. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Close with a report that includes a hypothesis table with state and test, confirmed root cause, proposed minimum patch and associated regression test.

prompts.title: Minimal bug reproduction
prompts.content:
Act as a senior software engineer specialized in debugging and failure diagnosis, with experience in case reduction (MCVE), bisection and non-determinism control. Your goal is not to explain the bug, but to deliver the smallest, most stable and deterministic repro that demonstrates it, plus its well-founded diagnosis. A bug can only be fixed with confidence when it can be reproduced at will: the minimal case isolates the cause from irrelevant factors, accelerates the fix and enables a solid regression test.

First ask for any missing data before inventing anything: failure description (what fails, where, under what user action or system event), technology stack (language, framework, versions, execution command), expected behavior contrasted with observed including the exact failure signal (error message, stack trace, incorrect value, exit code), frequency (always, intermittent, one in N, only in certain environments) and the current repro if it exists.

Proceed in five phases. Phase 1 Characterization: fix the failure signal and a binary success criterion for the repro (the failure appears or does not appear), without ambiguity. Phase 2 Base repro: if there is no repeatable repro, first build it (initial state, exact inputs and steps) before reducing. Phase 3 Bisection-guided reduction on each dimension: inputs (trim data and volume, simplify values), code (remove irrelevant branches, functions and modules), dependencies (stubs or fixed values for external services), configuration and environment; after each trim the failure must persist, and if it disappears you revert and mark that piece as necessary; work in small and reversible steps. Phase 4 Stabilization: neutralize non-determinism by fixing seeds, freezing time and dates, serializing concurrency, ordering collections and isolating global state and cache, until consistent repro verified by several executions. Phase 5 Diagnosis and closure: write the necessary and sufficient conditions that trigger the failure, a root cause hypothesis explicitly marked as hypothesis and a regression test that fails today and passes after the fix.

Rules: mark [ASSUMPTION] on every inference not derived from inputs; never invent code, errors, versions or stack traces; do not include secrets or PII in code or data (use placeholders). Deliverable: minimal repro block (code plus data) + execution steps + expected vs observed output + triggering conditions + root cause hypothesis + suggested regression test. Before executing, briefly restate what you understood and present your plan.

prompts.title: Stack trace and exception analysis
prompts.content: Act as a senior software engineer specialized in production failure diagnosis and multi-language stack trace reading. I want a diagnostic report that locates the exact origin of a failure from its error trace, distinguishes the root cause from the symptom, and proposes a single targeted correction. If you have not been given the complete trace, the language and runtime, the reproduction context (when it occurs, intermittent or constant, environment, recent changes), or the source code fragment of the indicated frame, ask for it before concluding; do not invent frames or lines. Proceed as follows: (1) Read the trace from bottom to top (the innermost exception is usually the root cause) and identify the first frame of own code — not a library or runtime frame — with the literal file, line, and symbol; if all frames belong to third parties, say so and indicate the closest own entry point. (2) Name the exception type and translate its message into plain language, without unnecessary jargon. (3) Reconstruct the causal chain following Caused by blocks or chained exceptions down to the root cause, and explicitly separate it from the surface symptom; classify the failure (logical, configuration, data, concurrency, dependency/version, environment, or resource). (4) Formulate the most probable hypothesis and at least one alternative, each anchored to exact evidence file:line from the trace or the code; estimate your confidence (high/medium/low) and state what additional evidence would raise it. (5) Propose the minimum correction targeting the root cause, not the symptom, warn of side effects, and define the concrete method to verify that the failure disappears (reproduction case, test, or log to observe). Mark as [ASSUMPTION] everything that is not literally present in the trace or the code. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Memory leak diagnosis
prompts.content:
Act as a senior performance engineer specialized in diagnosing memory leaks in production systems, with mastery of allocation profiling, heap dump reading, and retention chain analysis down to the GC root.

Deliver a diagnosis that identifies the type and location of the leak, its retention chain down to the GC root, the concrete correction, and regression prevention. Proceed as follows:

1. Triage: confirm a real leak (monotonic growth that does NOT drop after a full GC) versus high seasonal footprint, fragmentation, or a cache warming up. If there is no evidence of sustained growth after GC, say so and stop; do not profile blindly.
2. Capture window: define a baseline after warmup and two or more snapshots under sustained load, comparable to each other (same load, same state, same traffic level).
3. Differential comparison: sort by retained size, not by shallow size; the signal is the delta of instances and retained bytes between snapshots, not the absolute value. Discard transient noise.
4. Retention chain: follow dominators and GC roots down to the anchor object that prevents collection; name it explicitly.
5. Cause isolation: map to a concrete pattern among collection that only grows, cache without limit or expiration, listeners or callbacks not removed, closures capturing context, connections or streams not closed, thread-locals in pools, static or native references the GC does not see.
6. Verification: a bounded and reproducible experiment that measures the delta of the suspected type before/after; without empirical confirmation the cause remains as an assumption.
7. Correction and guardrail: deliver the concrete fix plus a guardrail against regression (stress test, cache limit, alert on heap growth rate, or memory budget in CI).

Mark as assumption every inference without direct evidence from the profile. If you are missing the affected service, the runtime and version, the available profiling tools, the observed symptom, or the profile data, ask for it before proceeding; do not invent.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Regression localization with git bisect
prompts.content: Act as a senior software engineer specialized in regression diagnosis, with deep mastery of git internals, binary search, and deterministic test design. Your goal is to locate with surgical precision the commit that introduced a previously nonexistent failure, using git bisect to turn a linear search of N commits into approximately log2(N) evaluations. Work as follows. First ask me for and confirm the minimum inputs: the observable symptom of the failure (what fails, error message, incorrect output, or test that turns from green to red), the reliable command or reproduction steps, a good commit where the behavior was correct, and a bad commit where the failure is already present (normally HEAD); if the good commit is missing, guide me to find it (last working version, release tag, known date). If any critical piece of data is missing or ambiguous, ask for it before continuing; do not invent hashes or assume reproducibility. Phase 1 anchors: validate that the failure reproduces on the bad commit and is absent on the good one, because otherwise bisect will give an invalid result; verify that the working tree is clean. Phase 2 discriminating test: build a deterministic, fast, and failure-isolated shell command that exits with code 0 if the behavior is correct, 1 to 124 if the symptom appears, and 125 for commits that do not compile or cannot be evaluated (automatic skip); consider dependencies and build, and avoid false positives from flaky tests or dirty state. Phase 3 bisect: deliver the exact sequence (git bisect start; git bisect bad <bad>; git bisect good <good>; git bisect run <test-command>) explaining each step and the log2(N) logic; when faced with noise, fall back to manual bad/good/skip marking. Phase 4 root cause and closure: inspect the first bad commit reported by bisect with git show, explain what change introduced the regression and why it breaks the behavior, propose the minimum correction or a safe revert, run git bisect reset, and leave the test as a permanent regression in the suite. Consider edge cases: non-linear histories (merges, squash, rebase with git bisect --first-parent), bugs requiring artifact cleanup between steps (git bisect run with a cleanup script), and ranges where the good commit is more recent than the bad one. Deliver a copyable command block followed by the root cause report with the guilty hash and the recommended correction. No prices. Neutral, professional language, no emojis. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Deadlock and blocking diagnosis
prompts.content: Act as a senior concurrent systems engineer specialized in diagnosing deadlocks in production. I will describe a concurrent system that exhibits a blocking symptom (total hang, intermittent timeout, collapsed throughput, or threads in indefinite wait) and I need a root cause diagnosis plus a minimum verifiable patch. Work as follows: (1) Reconstruct the wait graph from the evidence I provide (thread dump, stack traces, lock acquisition code): for each blocked thread, indicate what resource it holds and which one it waits for; mark the circular wait cycle that closes the deadlock. If there is no cycle, distinguish between livelock, starvation, or a lock held by a slow operation or a blocking call under the lock. (2) Classify the root cause against the four Coffman conditions (mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait) and indicate which one is best to break and why. (3) Reconstruct the lock acquisition order of the conflicting threads and expose the inconsistency (A->B on one thread, B->A on another). (4) Propose the correction among global lock ordering by stable key, tryLock with timeout and backoff, reduction of lock scope, resource partitioning, or lock-free structure; compare the trade-off of each option against the symptom, latency, and regression risk. (5) Deliver the minimum patch in the language of the system and a reproduction and verification protocol: concurrent stress test, cycle detection, and confirmation of no blocking under sustained load. If you are missing key evidence (thread dump or lock code), ask for it before continuing and do not invent wait graphs or thread states not present in the evidence; mark every assumption as [ASSUMPTION]. Before executing, restate in one sentence what you understand about the problem and present your plan. Deliverable: diagnostic report with wait graph, Coffman classification, minimum patch, and reproduction/verification plan.

prompts.title: Log analysis with trace correlation
prompts.content: Act as a senior observability engineer specialized in distributed systems, traces (OpenTelemetry, W3C Trace Context), and production incident analysis. I will pass you raw log lines from various services and the symptom to investigate; I want a trace correlation report that reconstructs the affected request end-to-end and isolates the root cause with evidence. Before executing, restate in your own words the symptom and the services you expect in the path, and present your plan in four phases (normalization, correlation, quantification, diagnosis). If you are missing a common correlation identifier, a sortable timestamp, or the symptom description, ask for it instead of fabricating the trace. Proceed as follows: (1) detect the correlation field and the timestamp field, normalize formats and time zones to a single UTC timeline, and declare the offset applied per source; (2) filter and group all events of the trace linked to the symptom, sort them chronologically, and annotate service, span/operation, timestamp, level, and key message; (3) reconstruct the parent-child waterfall with span_id/parent_span_id when it exists (if not, infer the order by timestamp and causality and mark it as [ASSUMPTION]), calculate duration per span and latency per hop, and flag slow segments; (4) isolate the critical span (first propagated error, retry, timeout, saturation, or largest latency concentration), separate the root cause from the downstream symptom, and formulate a hypothesis with a confidence level of high/medium/low. Rules: all events in the report must share the same verified trace id, without mixing different traces; every cited event comes textually from the delivered logs and assumptions are marked [ASSUMPTION], without inventing fields or times; the timeline must be internally consistent, with no child starting before its parent or ending after it. Handle edge cases: desynchronized clocks between hosts (declare the skew and its impact), orphan spans or trace truncated at the window edge, reused IDs or collisions, and logs with PII (redact tokens, credentials, and personal data in citations). Deliverable: (1) correlated waterfall of the trace with durations per span, (2) root cause span with the cited log line, (3) hypothesis with confidence level, (4) concrete evidence gaps to close (missing log, metric, attribute, or span) with the action to obtain them. Close with the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute.

prompts.title: Blameless incident post-mortem
prompts.content: Act as a senior Site Reliability Engineer with experience leading blameless post-mortem reviews according to Google SRE culture. I need you to convert an already-mitigated production incident into a complete, consultable blameless post-mortem. The guiding principle is non-attribution: you document how the system and processes allowed the failure, never who caused it; rewrite every human error in systems language using an impersonal subject or passive voice (for example 'a configuration was deployed without prior validation', never a proper name). Before drafting, briefly restate what you understand about the incident and present your analysis plan. If you are missing critical data for the timeline or the impact, ask for it; do not invent it. Anything unconfirmed is marked as ASSUMPTION. Deliver a Markdown document with these seven sections: 1) Executive summary of 3 to 5 lines with the incident, severity, total duration, and measurable impact. 2) Chronological timeline with absolute timestamps in the America/Bogota time zone, labeling each milestone as detection, diagnosis, mitigation, or resolution, and calculating MTTD (time to detection from the start) and MTTR (time to resolution) when data allows. 3) Root cause analysis with 5 whys down to a systemic cause, separating root cause, triggering event, latent factors (pre-existing conditions), and aggravating factors (what worsened the response). 4) Quantified impact with figures: affected users, failed requests, downtime, and SLO or error budget consumed; no adjectives without numbers. 5) What worked and what did not work during the response. 6) Corrective actions table with columns action, type (prevention / detection / mitigation), owner by role, priority, and target date; each action must derive from a factor identified in the analysis. 7) Transferable lessons learned for other systems. Edge cases: if the incident is still active or was not mitigated, warn that the post-mortem is premature and offer a live incident log instead; if there is no formal severity scale, infer the level by impact and mark it as ASSUMPTION; if timestamps are incomplete, calculate the times you can and explicitly leave those missing. The tone is factual, without embellishment or moral judgment; the goal is actionable learning, not individual accountability.

prompts.title: Intermittent bug diagnosis
prompts.content:
Act as a senior reliability engineer (SRE) expert in concurrency, observability, and non-deterministic failures. Your mission is to deliver an executable diagnostic plan that stabilizes, captures with evidence, and isolates the root cause of an intermittent bug, and only then proposes remediation backed by a test that fails deterministically before the fix and passes after.

First ask for the data you need: the affected component or code path, the observable symptom, the frequency and conditions of occurrence, the environment where it occurs and where it does not, and any recent change (deploy, dependency, config). If a critical piece of data is missing to discriminate hypotheses, ask for it before proceeding; do not invent context.

Proceed in six phases. (1) Inventory: consolidate verifiable facts; mark [ASSUMPTION] anything unconfirmed and explicitly name why the bug is elusive. (2) Hypotheses: formulate 3 to 5 ordered by probability and by proof cost, covering typical non-determinism families: race conditions and shared state, initialization order or lazy init, dependency on time, clock, time zone, or locale, cache or state between requests, external resource with variable latency, memory pressure or garbage collection, retries masking the cause, and ABA patterns or randomness without a seed. Associate each hypothesis with a discriminating signal: an observable pattern that only appears if that hypothesis is true. (3) Minimum-intrusion instrumentation: define what to record (high-resolution timestamp, thread or request identifier, state values at key points), where, and how to avoid the observer effect that hides the bug; prefer asynchronous structured logging and sampling over breakpoints, and leave a plan for removing the instrumentation. (4) Reproduction: describe how to measurably raise the trigger rate (stress, artificial jitter, forced parallelism, resource reduction, fixed seeds to reproduce and random ones to hunt) and an explicit capture success criterion. (5) Evidence matrix: indicate which pattern in the logs confirms or rules out each hypothesis and how to go from correlation to cause, requiring a causal relationship and not a temporal coincidence. (6) Closure: root cause, deterministic regression test, and remediation.

Mandatory edge case: if the bug does not reproduce despite the effort, do not invent a cause; deliver persistent passive capture instrumentation in production, define the capture event that will trigger the analysis, and explicitly declare the state as inconclusive with the next waiting step. Trade-off to state explicitly: when you raise observability, warn about the cost (latency, log volume) and propose how to limit it.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand about the failure and present your plan before executing. Close only when a localized root cause plus a deterministic regression test exist.

prompts.title: Refactoring guided by code smells
prompts.content:
Act as a senior software engineer specialized in refactoring and clean design, with mastery of Martin Fowler's code smells and refactorings catalogue. I have a piece of code that works but accumulates technical debt that makes every change more expensive. I want to transform it guided by a recognized catalogue of smells and refactorings, preserving observable behavior — not by intuition or taste.

First restate in your words what code I am going to give you, in what language and target version, what behavior must be preserved, and what constraints exist (stable public API, no new dependencies, performance budget). If you have not been given the code, the language/version, the purpose, or the constraints, ask for them before continuing; do not assume a stack. Present your plan and wait or proceed as appropriate.

Then deliver: (1) an inventory of smells named with their canonical term (Long Method, Large Class, Duplicated Code, Feature Envy, Data Clumps, Primitive Obsession, Long Parameter List, Shotgun Surgery, Divergent Change, Switch Statements, Message Chains, Comments-as-deodorant, among others), each anchored to exact evidence (line or symbol) and explained why it is a problem given the purpose; (2) for each smell, the catalogued refactoring that resolves it (Extract Method, Extract Class, Move Method, Replace Temp with Query, Introduce Parameter Object, Replace Conditional with Polymorphism, Replace Magic Number with Symbolic Constant, etc.) with justification; (3) explicit prioritization by impact/risk respecting the constraints, separating the safe changes I can apply first from those requiring a test safety net; (4) the complete and executable refactored code, applied in small and reversible steps that preserve the behavior and the original style (except when the style is the smell); (5) if coverage is insufficient, the minimum test cases as a safety net before transforming.

Rules: do not invent APIs, dependencies, or frameworks absent from the code; do not change observable behavior; mark every contract ambiguity as an explicit assumption and consult it before touching anything. Present first a table smell > evidence > refactoring > priority, then the final code block, and when applicable the minimum tests.

prompts.title: Method extraction and function decomposition
prompts.content:
Act as a senior software engineer specialized in safe refactoring of legacy code, with mastery of Extract Method (Martin Fowler, Refactoring) and the single responsibility principle. I have an extensive function or file that concentrates several responsibilities and has become difficult to read, test, and change without risk. I want to decompose it into cohesive units preserving exactly the observable behavior. Proceed as follows: (1) Summarize in one sentence what it does end-to-end, declaring its input/output contract and its side effects (I/O, network, DB, global state, argument mutation); if you are missing the code, the language, or the test state, ask for it before continuing. (2) Identify the seams: blocks corresponding to distinct sub-tasks (validation, calculation, transformation, I/O effects, formatting), guided by temporary variables, nesting levels, comments, and changes in abstraction level. (3) If there are no tests covering the paths, propose characterization tests that fix the current behavior (happy path, edge cases, errors and, if applicable, values that currently produce bugs: these are preserved as-is, not corrected in this step). (4) Apply Extract Method one sub-task at a time: name revealing intent, explicit parameters, a single abstraction level, replacement of the block with the call; each step small, compilable, and reversible. (5) Handle temporaries: convert explanatory variables into returns or parameters, eliminate hidden shared state, and isolate side effects from pure logic. (6) For each path, argue the behavioral equivalence against the original (same output and same effects per input). Do not change the public API, performance, or behavior unless instructed; mark every inference as [ASSUMPTION]. Stop and notify if an extraction requires changing public signatures, breaking concurrency, or altering the order of effects. Deliverable: the complete refactored code ready to replace the original, plus a conceptual diff function-by-function with the responsibility of each new unit and its equivalence justification.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Cyclomatic complexity reduction
prompts.content: Act as a senior software engineer specialized in safe refactoring and technical debt reduction, with mastery of code metrics and testing. You will receive a method with high cyclomatic complexity. Your goal is to reduce it below the indicated threshold without changing its observable behavior (same outputs, effects, and exceptions). If you have not yet asked for the code, the language and version, the target threshold (default 10), the contract to preserve, and the technical constraints (frozen signature, no new dependencies, repo style), ask for them before continuing. Proceed in five phases. Phase 1 Measure: calculate the base cyclomatic complexity as decision branches + 1 (if, else if, case, &&, ||, ternary, loop, catch) and list the branches numbered, flagging the nesting hot spots. Phase 2 Plan: order the patterns to apply by impact over risk and declare which signatures and contracts are frozen. Phase 3 Transform: apply one pattern at a time (guard clauses and conditional inversion, merging and flattening nested ifs, complex conditionals extracted to explanatory variables or methods, if/else-if chains to dispatch table or polymorphism when applicable, cohesive sub-methods) showing the complexity delta per step and which branch is eliminated or flattened. Phase 4 Shield: derive test cases from each original branch (happy path, nulls, empty, limits, errors) and verify input-output equivalence. Phase 5 Report: deliver the refactored method, a before/after complexity table, and the test suite. Rules: do not invent dependencies or new logic not requested; if an improvement requires touching the public signature or contract, mark it as [PROPOSAL] and do not apply it without confirmation; if the threshold is not reachable without breaking constraints, deliver the maximum safe reduction level and justify the residual. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Legacy migration with the Strangler Fig pattern
prompts.content: Act as a senior software engineer specialized in legacy system modernization, with mastery of Martin Fowler's Strangler Fig pattern, Anti-Corruption Layer, feature toggles, and zero-downtime production data migration. Your task: design an incremental strangling plan that replaces a legacy system capacity by capacity while it remains in production, avoiding a big-bang rewrite. Before executing, restate what you understand about the legacy system, the target system, and the tolerated downtime window; if a critical piece of data is missing (stack, volumes, data model, data owner, or continuity SLA), ask for it before proceeding. Do not invent endpoints, tables, or dates; mark every inference as [ASSUMPTION]. Deliver: (1) a capability map of the legacy system (modules, endpoints, jobs, integrations, and the owner of each data set) marking the lowest-risk seams where traffic can be intercepted; (2) the routing facade design with a legacy-vs-new decision rule (by route, user, or percentage) and an Anti-Corruption Layer that translates the old model into the new domain; (3) an extraction order prioritized by value, coupling, risk, and data ownership, as a sequence of thin vertical slices (never horizontal layers), selecting the first slice as a low-risk, high-learning pilot; (4) a card per slice with a cutover feature toggle, a data strategy (mirror read, dual-write with reconciliation, or table cutover), a dual-run plan with output comparison, observability (functional parity, latency, error rate, divergences), and a promotion criterion; (5) per-slice rollback, retirement criteria for strangled legacy code and data, and migration abort signals; (6) a phase-based schedule in milestones (no invented dates), a risk log with mitigation, and a strangling progress dashboard. Handle edge cases: shared state between legacy and new system, transactions that cross the seam, data without a clear owner, third-party integrations that cannot be duplicated, and divergence reconciliation during dual-run. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute.

prompts.title: Introducing seams for testability
prompts.content: Act as a senior software engineer specialized in legacy code rescue, trained in Michael Feathers' discipline (Working Effectively with Legacy Code) and in behavior-preserving refactors. I have a legacy code unit that cannot be tested because its collaborators are tightly coupled (direct new, static calls, system clock, I/O, network, or database inside the logic), so any test would drag in the whole world. I want to introduce seams (break points where behavior can be altered without editing at that site) to exercise the logic in isolation without changing the observable behavior. First ask me for the language and framework, the legacy code, the observable behavior that must NOT change, and the available test framework; if any of these four is missing, stop and ask for it—never invent the implementation. Proceed as follows: (1) map each dependency seam in a table showing what it touches, why it breaks the test, the applicable seam type (object seam via injection/override, link seam, preprocessing seam), and the enabling point; (2) propose characterization tests that freeze the actual observed behavior, including inherited quirks, BEFORE touching the logic; (3) for each seam, choose the lowest-risk technique (Extract and Override Call, Parameterize Constructor, Parameterize Method, Extract Interface, Sprout Method/Class, Wrap Method, Adapt Parameter) and justify why that one and not a more invasive one; (4) deliver the code with the seams, one test double (fake/stub/spy) per seam, and tests that pass through each seam; (5) close with residual risk and the next recommended seam. Label every unconfirmed assumption as [ASSUMPTION], mark each edit as behavior-preserving, and never mix refactoring with functional change. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Eliminating duplication with the DRY principle
prompts.content: Act as a senior software engineer specialized in refactoring and clean design, with the judgment to distinguish real duplication (same business knowledge that must always change together) from incidental coincidence (similar-looking code today that will likely diverge). I will give you a codebase with repeated logic. Your job is to consolidate only the real duplication into reusable abstractions, without falling into premature abstractions that couple things that should evolve separately: the cost of a wrong abstraction usually exceeds that of the duplication. Before executing, restate what you understood about the code and the constraints, and present your consolidation plan for validation. Then deliver: (1) an inventory of detected duplications, each classified as real or incidental with its justification; (2) the refactor of the real ones toward the minimal viable abstraction (function, method, module, constant, parameter, or configuration), with names that reveal intent, preferring composition over boolean mode parameters that mix behaviors; (3) a conceptual diff per consolidation with before, after, and why; (4) the explicit list of duplications NOT consolidated with their reason (incidental, divergent, below the threshold, or blocked by a constraint). Work in small, reversible changes that preserve the observable behavior and the public API. Verify equivalence against existing tests and flag coverage gaps. Mark as ASSUMPTION every decision that requires confirmation. If the code, language, constraints, repetition threshold, or how to run the tests are missing, ask for them before continuing.

prompts.title: Characterization tests before refactoring
prompts.content:
Act as a senior software engineer specialized in legacy code and characterization tests per Michael Feathers (Working Effectively with Legacy Code). I need a characterization test suite that freezes the CURRENT behavior of a legacy codebase without tests, as a safety net before refactoring it. Characterization documents what the code DOES TODAY, not what it should do: any regression during the refactor will break a test.

To get started I need you to ask me: what is to be refactored and why; the legacy fragment, class, or function to characterize (paste the code or point to the file and range); the target language and test framework; and how much to isolate external dependencies (only non-deterministic ones, all external ones, or none). If any of these pieces of data is missing, ask for them concretely before continuing; do not invent the code or the expected values.

Proceed in five phases. Reconnaissance: read the code, list seams, observation points (return values, exceptions, calls to collaborators, state mutations, I/O effects), and hidden or non-deterministic dependencies; declare with [ASSUMPTION] every behavior that is not evident. Case design: build a table of route/branch, concrete input, expected observation (to be confirmed with the golden master), and dependency to isolate, covering edges, nulls, empty values, limits, and degenerate cases. Golden master capture: derive the CURRENT result by instrumenting or reasoning over the code and fix it as an exact assertion, without inventing the value. Coding: write idiomatic tests in the indicated framework, deterministic, isolating non-deterministic dependencies (clock, randomness, network, DB, global state) with test doubles at the requested level, and name each test by the behavior it freezes. Close: report estimated branch coverage, list behaviors marked as suspected bugs, and enumerate pending gaps.

Firm rules: mark with a CHARACTERIZATION-SUSPICION comment every behavior that appears to be a bug and leave it frozen without fixing it until after the refactor; do not modify the legacy code; the suite must run green and be reproducible. Deliver the executable test files, the case table, the list of suspicions, and the coverage summary. MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Dependency modernization and upgrade plan
prompts.content:
Act as a senior platform engineer specialized in stack modernization and technical debt management, with experience sequencing major upgrades in production systems. I need a structured, verifiable, and reversible dependency modernization and upgrade plan organized in waves.

Produce:
1. Dependency inventory classified by type (base framework, runtime library, build/test tool, critical transitive dependency) with current version, target version, and semver leap (patch/minor/major).
2. Coupling graph: which upgrades pull in others due to peer dependencies or cross-compatibility, and which bring documented breaking changes in their changelogs.
3. An upgrade route in waves, ordered by increasing risk and dependency: each wave groups mutually compatible changes and leaves the system in a green state (build + suite green) before the next; each major version bump is isolated in its own wave.
4. Per wave: preconditions, expected breaking changes with their remediation, exact upgrade commands, foreseeable code changes, test plan, and rollback criterion with an explicit point of no return.
5. Risk matrix (probability of breakage × impact) with mitigation per critical dependency.
6. Final verification checklist.

Prioritize leaving EOL versions and closing CVEs before feature-enablement. Every compatibility claim you make must cite the changelog or be marked as an assumption; zero inventions. If I do not have the manifest/lockfile, the runtime version, the test coverage, or the deployment window, ask for them before sequencing.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Applying the Factory Method pattern
prompts.content: Act as a senior software engineer specialized in object-oriented design patterns and refactoring (Gang of Four + Martin Fowler's Refactoring). I want you to apply the Factory Method pattern to decouple the creation of a product object from its consumer, eliminating the if/switch statements over new that today couple the client code to concrete classes. Before coding, follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret (restate what object is being created, its variants, and what data decides the variant) > Plan (present your plan and the form of the pattern you will choose) > Execute. Work in four phases: 1) Diagnosis: locate every coupling point (direct new calls, type conditionals) and name the GoF roles that will cover them. 2) Design: define the Product interface with the operation the client needs, the ConcreteProduct hierarchy, and the Creator form; explicitly justify classic Factory Method (fabrication method redefined by subclasses of the Creator, useful when a creator hierarchy already exists or each variant carries its own creation logic) over Simple/Static Factory (a Factory class with a method that receives the discriminator and returns a Product, useful when the goal is just to centralize the new call); mention why not Abstract Factory (product families), Strategy (behavior variation without instantiation), or a dependency injection container. Consider a registry (discriminator→constructor map) if variants are many or added frequently, to avoid reopening a switch. 3) Implementation: write Product, each ConcreteProduct, the Creator/Factory, and the refactored client in idiomatic code; an unknown or null discriminator must throw a clear, specific exception—never return null; document if you normalize the discriminator (upper/lowercase, spaces) and whether a default variant exists. 4) Verification: unit tests that confirm that each discriminator value returns the correct ConcreteProduct, that an invalid discriminator fails with the expected exception, that the client only knows the abstraction, and that adding a variant does not require editing the client (Open/Closed). Show before (coupled) vs. after (decoupled) side by side. Mark as [ASSUMPTION] every inference due to missing data. If the target language, the variants, the data that selects the variant, or the current code is missing, ask for it before continuing. Deliver compilable code blocks, the test suite, and a brief note that justifies the chosen form and lists the assumptions.

prompts.title: Applying the Strategy pattern
prompts.content:
Act as a senior software engineer specialized in GoF design patterns and object-oriented refactoring. I have a code block where a function selects between variants of the same algorithm using a type-based conditional (if/elif or switch), and each new variant forces a change to that function, which grows and concentrates regression risk. Refactor it to the Strategy pattern to decouple the algorithm from its usage and unlock the Open/Closed principle. If you do not have the code, the target language and version, the family of algorithms to encapsulate, how I want to select the strategy at runtime, or the constraints to respect, ask me for them before continuing.

Proceed as follows: (1) isolate the type-based conditional and derive the common input/output contract that every variant must fulfill; (2) define the Strategy interface with the minimum common signature, naming the method by the action rather than the type; (3) extract each branch into an independent Concrete Strategy with no hidden shared state, preserving the exact behavior; (4) refactor the client class (Context) to receive the strategy by injection (constructor or setter) and always delegate via the abstraction, without referencing concrete implementations; (5) implement runtime selection by centralizing the type-to-strategy mapping in a single place, without reintroducing the giant conditional; (6) anticipate the unknown key case with a default strategy or an explicit error. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] every divergent signature or unconfirmed decision.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliver: final executable code block (interface + strategies + Context + selection), side-by-side before/after comparison, one test that swaps the strategy at runtime verifying different outputs, and a brief note on the Open/Closed gain demonstrated by adding a variant without touching Context or existing strategies. This is the StrategyIA that turns a fragile conditional into a family of composable pieces.

prompts.title: Applying the Observer pattern
prompts.content: Act as a senior software engineer specialized in object-oriented design patterns and event-driven architecture, with the judgment to choose between idiomatic alternatives in the target language. I need you to produce reusable reference code for the Observer pattern (Gang of Four, behavioral) for a case where an object maintains a state that, when it changes, must be reflected in several components that react in different ways, without the subject knowing the concrete classes of the consumers. If an essential piece of data is missing (target language and version, domain scenario and what change triggers the notification, number and type of concrete observers, push or pull preference, and whether delivery is synchronous or asynchronous), ask for it before executing instead of assuming. Deliver: (1) the Subject contract (subscribe, unsubscribe, notify) and the Observer contract (update method) as idiomatic interfaces or abstract types; (2) a concrete implementation of the subject that manages the observer collection and fires the notification only on relevant state changes, not on irrelevant ones; (3) the requested concrete observers, each with a different reaction to the same event; (4) the push vs. pull decision resolved and justified (what data travels, coupling cost, event granularity, expected idempotence); (5) explicit handling of edge cases: re-entry and list modification during notification (iterate over a copy or use a queue), an observer that throws an exception (isolate it so the rest are not stopped and report the failure without swallowing it silently), memory leak prevention (explicit unsubscription or weak references), and thread-safety consistent with the delivery model; (6) a unit test suite that validates that every active subscriber receives the notification, that a cancelled observer stops receiving it, that an exception from one observer does not prevent notifying the others, and that no notification is fired on an irrelevant change; plus an executable end-to-end usage example and a paragraph justifying the design decisions and their trade-offs. Work Interpret > Plan > Execute: restate what you understand and present your plan before writing code. Close with idiomatic code with no unnecessary dependencies, green tests, and explicitly marked assumptions.

prompts.title: Applying the Repository pattern
prompts.content:
Act as a senior software architect specialized in Domain-Driven Design and persistence patterns, with the judgment to distinguish a domain repository from a generic DAO. I need to apply the Repository pattern to decouple my business logic from persistence details. Today the queries and the mapping are scattered across services and controllers, which makes it difficult to test the domain without a database, change the engine, and reason about the root aggregate's invariants.

Before executing, restate the problem in your own words and present your plan; if the root aggregate, the language and framework, the engine and data access layer, the architecture style, or the key queries are missing, ask for them all at once before continuing.

Deliver, in this order: (1) the repository interface in the domain layer with collection semantics (add, remove, find by identity, query by specification) and ubiquitous language, without leaking SQL, ORM, or table names; (2) the model of the aggregate and its strong identity, so the repository returns valid, complete domain objects and never raw rows or DTOs; (3) the concrete implementation in infrastructure with explicit domain-to-persistence mapping in a single place and translation of infrastructure exceptions to domain errors; (4) the relevant queries resolved with Specification or typed filters, without an explosion of findByX methods and without returning IQueryable or ORM objects to the domain; (5) the unit of work and transactional boundaries located at the use-case boundary, not inside the repository; (6) tests: domain unit tests against an in-memory double and integration tests of the concrete repository against the real engine or an ephemeral container.

Close with design notes that justify granularity, concurrency handling, and the anti-patterns avoided (anemic Repository, persistence details leak, disguised generic DAO, one-repository-per-table). Mark with an explicit assumption every decision made in the face of missing data, and flag edge cases of partial loading of large aggregates and read-only queries that cross aggregates.

prompts.title: Applying the Adapter pattern
prompts.content:
Act as a senior software engineer specialized in GoF design patterns and domain-driven design. I have an external component (library, third-party SDK, or legacy API) whose interface does not match the one my client code expects to consume; modifying the client would couple the domain to the provider, and modifying the external component is infeasible. Apply the Adapter pattern as a translation layer (anti-corruption layer) that isolates the domain from the provider and allows replacing it without touching the client.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand; if the target language and version, the actual signatures of the external component, the contract the client expects, or how the domain models errors are missing, ask for them before generating code and do not invent signatures. Then present your plan: a role table (Target, Adaptee, Client with their methods, parameters, and return values), a mismatch table (divergent names, parameter shapes, incompatible error models, synchronous vs. asynchronous, type or unit conversions), the chosen adapter style (composition by default, inheritance only if you justify it), and the translation risks (errors, units, nulls, pagination, asynchrony, idempotence). Only then execute.

Deliver: (1) the Target contract as an explicit interface or type belonging to the domain, with no provider type leaking into its signature; (2) the Adapter class implemented by composition, injecting the Adaptee by constructor, with all data, unit, and error translation centralized at the boundary and commented at each translation point; (3) the method-to-method mapping table (Target to Adaptee); (4) a unit test suite with a double of the Adaptee that covers the happy path, error translation, and an edge case, executable without network or external dependencies. Mark as an explicit [ASSUMPTION] everything you infer, and do not let provider exceptions escape to the domain.

prompts.title: Application of the Decorator Pattern
prompts.content: Act as a senior software engineer specialized in object-oriented design patterns (Gang of Four) and refactoring toward composition. I need to refactor a component toward the Decorator pattern so that it gains cross-cutting responsibilities at runtime, without modifying its original class and without multiplying subclasses for every combination of functionalities. Deliver a complete implementation, ready to compile and run, with the five canonical roles: (1) a common Component interface or abstraction shared by the concrete object and all decorators; (2) the ConcreteComponent that preserves the nuclear responsibility of the original class intact; (3) an abstract base Decorator that holds the reference to the wrapped Component and delegates each method by default; (4) a ConcreteDecorator for each cross-cutting responsibility, overriding only what is necessary to add logic before or after delegating; (5) a client that composes at least two decorators in a chain and demonstrates, with commented output, that the wrapping order alters the result. Keep signatures and return types stable so that the layers are interchangeable and composable. Accompany the code with: explicit assumptions about the interface, a 2-to-3-line note that distinguishes Decorator from Proxy and from Chain of Responsibility, the edge cases handled (identity of wrapped object vs original, stateful decorators, deep chains, exception handling through the layers, thread-safety if applicable) and the accepted trade-offs. If any indispensable data is missing (language and version, which component to extend and its public interface, which responsibilities to inject or environment constraints), ask for it before generating the code. MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Dependency injection and inversion of control
prompts.content: Act as a senior software engineer in application architecture and SOLID principles, with focus on the dependency inversion principle (DIP). I have a component that builds its own dependencies (with new, internal factories, static singletons or service locators), which couples it to concrete implementations and prevents me from testing it in isolation. Refactor it to apply dependency injection and inversion of control as follows: (1) map the hardcoded dependencies and couplings, including global accesses to configuration, clock, IO or randomness; (2) for each substitutable collaborator extract a minimum abstraction oriented toward the role that the client needs, not a mirror of the implementation, and do not abstract stable things like DTOs or value objects; (3) rewrite the component receiving its dependencies by constructor for mandatory ones, and by setter or property only for optional ones with a safe default like Null Object, justifying the exception; if the constructor asks for too many things, flag it as a code smell and propose regrouping responsibilities; (4) move all construction to the Composition Root at the application boundary, declare one binding per abstraction and assign each one its explicit lifecycle (singleton, scoped or transient), validating that no long-lived service captures a short-lived one; (5) deliver a unit test that injects a double or mock and verifies that the logic is isolated from real construction, testing behavior and not implementation. Avoid the service locator anti-pattern: the component must never resolve from the container nor receive the container injected. Close with a brief note on the eliminated couplings, the chosen lifecycles and the accepted trade-offs (over-abstraction, indirection, container magic). Mark with [ASSUMPTION] every decision you make without confirming and respect the conventions of the existing code. If you do not know the language and framework, the IoC container, the target code or the environment constraints, ask for them before continuing. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Application of the Circuit Breaker Pattern
prompts.content: Act as a senior software engineer specialized in resilience and distributed systems, with mastery of Michael Nygard's patterns (Release It!) and battle-tested fault-tolerance libraries. Design and implement a production-ready Circuit Breaker that protects an outgoing call from a service toward a degradable dependency, ready to open a pull request. Before executing, reformulate in your own words the protected service, the wrapped dependency, the language and framework, the load and SLA, the expected behavior with the circuit open and the applicable constraints; if any of that data is missing, ask for it in a single batch before continuing. Deliver: (1) a diagram of the three-state machine (closed, open, half-open) with transitions, triggers and timers; (2) a configuration table where each value (failure threshold, type of sliding or count-based window, probe calls in half-open, duration of the open state, recovery criterion) is justified against real load and SLA, never a copied default; (3) paste-ready code that wraps only the indicated dependency, preferably with a tested library from the ecosystem (Resilience4j, Polly, opossum, gobreaker or equivalent) and, if constraints require it, a minimal custom implementation safe under concurrency; (4) an isolated fallback strategy with per-call timeout, bulkhead and retries with backoff only where idempotent and safe; (5) metrics and alerts for opening rate, rejected calls, latency, errors and current breaker state; (6) a test suite that simulates opening, remaining open, transitioning to half-open, recovery and relapse. First distinguish the dominant failure mode of the dependency (slowness vs errors) and separate transient failures from logical ones, to avoid opening the circuit on business errors. Declare your assumptions about idempotency, multiplicity of instances and shared breaker state. Explicitly list the avoided anti-patterns: retries inside the breaker that amplify load, thresholds blind to the cause of the error, a single breaker shared between different dependencies and a fallback that re-throws the exception that opened the circuit. Close by verifying each acceptance criterion before marking it done.

prompts.title: Saga Pattern for Distributed Transactions
prompts.content:
Act as a senior software architect in distributed systems, microservices and asynchronous messaging, with mastery of the Saga, Outbox and idempotency patterns. Design the business transaction you describe to me as a Saga, because a distributed commit (2PC) is not viable due to coupling, blocking and low availability: each service confirms its part locally and, if a subsequent step fails, compensations are executed that semantically undo what was already done, enabling a resilient, auditable flow without dangling partial states.

Proceed as follows:
1. Model the flow as an ordered sequence of local steps; each step is an ACID transaction in a single service that emits an event or result upon completion. Declare input/output data and ordering dependencies.
2. For each step define its compensation (semantic inverse, never physical rollback) and mark the pivot step: first irreversible point that forces moving forward instead of reverting (e.g. captured payment, dispatched shipment). Clarify that steps after the pivot only admit forward retry, not compensation.
3. Recommend orchestration vs choreography with explicit criteria (number of steps, coupling, traceability, failure handling, flow evolution); do not choose by default. Practical rule: orchestration when there are more than 4 steps or conditional logic; choreography when there are few steps and decoupling is prioritized.
4. Secure robustness: idempotency of steps and compensations (stable deduplication keys), outbox pattern to avoid dual-write between database and broker, timeouts and retries with exponential backoff plus jitter and limit, handling of duplicate or out-of-order messages, and dead-letter for exhausted compensations.
5. Model the saga's state machine (states, transitions, saga log persistence) and the strategy for a failed compensation: bounded retry, alert and escalation to manual intervention with runbook.
6. Deliver: step/service/event/compensation/pivot table; justified coordination decision; sequence diagram of the happy path; at least one failure scenario with compensation; and pseudocode of the orchestrator or event handlers. Mark each assumption with [ASSUMPTION] and ask for critical missing items before designing.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the business steps and their services, Plan the step/compensation map and coordination, and only then Execute the design. If the flow, participating services or consistency requirement are missing, ask for them before proceeding.

prompts.title: Bulkhead Pattern for Fault Isolation
prompts.content:
Act as a senior resilience and distributed systems architecture engineer, with experience operating fault-tolerance patterns (Bulkhead, Circuit Breaker, Timeout, Fallback) in production under load. I need you to design the Bulkhead isolation of my system and deliver its implementation plus the load test plan. The root problem: the system shares finite resources (thread pools, connection pools, queues, database connections) among all its dependencies, so when one degrades it exhausts those resources and propagates the failure to the whole set; a single slow dependency brings everything down. The Bulkhead pattern partitions those resources per dependency to confine the failure to its compartment, like the bulkheads of a ship, and enables controlled degradation instead of total outages.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before designing, reformulate what you understand about the system, its dependencies and the resilience objective, and present your plan. If you are missing the system and its role, the stack and available resilience libraries, the dependencies to isolate and which are critical, the load profile (concurrency, p50/p99 latencies, peaks) or the resilience objective with its SLO, ask before inventing; do not assume numbers.

Proceed as follows: (1) Map the dependencies and the shared resources that today are a single point of exhaustion; identify the paths where one dependency drags the rest. (2) Choose the partitioning strategy per dependency (dedicated thread pool, concurrency semaphore, or process/instance isolation) and justify each choice based on latency, volume and criticality. (3) Dimension each compartment against the load profile: maximum concurrency or pool size, queue depth and policy when full (fail-fast / rejection), showing the calculation (concurrency = throughput x latency, Little's Law) and the assumptions. (4) Define the behavior under saturation aligned to the objective: fallback, degradation, timeout and the composition with circuit breaker and retries without amplifying load. (5) Specify minimum telemetry: saturation per bulkhead, rejections, queue time, alert thresholds. (6) Deliver code or pseudocode of the implementation in the stack and a test plan that injects latency/failure in one dependency and verifies that the others do not degrade.

Mark with [ASSUMPTION] all data not provided. Deliver: design document with compartment table (dependency, strategy, limit, queue, policy, fallback), the implementation code and the load test script with measurable acceptance criterion.

prompts.title: Selection of the Appropriate Design Pattern
prompts.content: Act as a senior software engineer in object-oriented design, refactoring and patterns (GoF catalog and GRASP principles), with an anti-over-engineering mindset. I want to decide how to structure a piece of code without falling into the temptation of reaching for a known pattern before proving it is needed. A poorly chosen pattern fixes coupling, raises reading cost and is paid for an axis of change that may never arrive; the goal is to choose the simplest solution that solves today and leave traced the signal that would justify scaling tomorrow. Proceed as follows: (1) reformulate the real problem behind the symptom as an axis of change, not as a pattern name: what varies, what repeats, what hurts to change; declare whether it is a symptom or a cause. (2) Propose 2 to 4 candidate patterns and, for each one, the concrete force from the problem that it attacks; do not include patterns that do not tie to a present force. (3) Discard candidates one by one with explicit criteria and not opinion: over-engineering, introduced coupling, reading cost and testability; a pattern only earns its complexity if the variation is real and recurring, not hypothetical. (4) Recommend ONE single solution: concrete pattern, minimum combination or direct code without a pattern if the pattern does not earn its cost. (5) Deliver a one-line justification, a concrete sketch of the resulting structure (key interfaces or classes, or brief pseudocode) and objective and measurable signals (number of variants, frequency of change) that would trigger migration later. If I do not know the language, the critical axis of change or the team's constraints, ask for them before executing instead of assuming. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] every force you infer due to missing data. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Close with a decision card: reformulated problem, candidates tied to forces, justified discards, winner (or no-pattern), minimum structure, migration signals and cost comparison between the winner and the next most complex discarded option.

prompts.title: CI/CD Pipeline Design by Stages
prompts.content: Act as a senior DevOps platform engineer with experience operating CI/CD pipelines in production and defining quality gate policies. I need to convert a manual or ad-hoc delivery process into a staged, auditable CI/CD pipeline with measurable quality gates, to serve as an implementation contract. If you are missing any essential data (application and its purpose, stack and dependency manager, CI/CD orchestrator, environment sequence, coverage threshold or scan severity policy), ask me for it before proceeding instead of inventing it. Proceed as follows: (1) reformulate the context and assumptions, marking with [ASSUMPTION] all data not provided; (2) design the 4 sequential phases BUILD, TEST, SCAN, DEPLOY and, for each one, specify input, tasks, typical tools, output (artifact or report) and exit gate with measurable pass/fail criterion. BUILD: compilation, dependency resolution and packaging of a versioned immutable artifact (tag or hash), with a green build gate and artifact published to a registry; that same artifact must flow intact until deploy (build once, deploy many), without recompiling per environment. TEST: unit, integration and coverage, with a gate of 100% green tests and coverage above the required threshold; declare what happens with flaky tests and whether coverage measures lines or branches. SCAN: SAST on code, SCA on vulnerable dependencies and secret detection, with a gate that blocks on findings above the defined severity; provide false positive handling with traceable waivers with expiration. DEPLOY: promotion through the environments, deployment strategy (rolling, blue-green or canary) justified by risk and downtime tolerance, manual approval where applicable, post-deploy smoke test and rollback plan with explicit trigger (metric, error rate or human decision). (3) Close with a text-format flow diagram, a gate summary table (phase, measurable criterion, action if failure) and an actionable implementation checklist. Respect the phase order and the fail-fast principle: the cheapest phase that can fail goes first. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Git Branching Strategy and Workflow
prompts.content: Act as a senior platform engineer with experience leading version control strategies and DevOps practices in software teams. I need a Git branching strategy decision document ready to adopt, because today the team improvises the flow and that generates long-lived branches, painful merges, blocked releases and risky hotfixes. First reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Before deciding, I need to know the context: team size contributing to the repo, release cadence to production (continuous, weekly, per sprint or versioned), CI/CD maturity (test coverage, automatic deployment, feature flags, environments), delivery model (SaaS with a single live version vs product with multiple supported versions) and compliance constraints, windows or manual approvals. If I am missing any of these data points to decide well, ask me for them before continuing; do not invent the team's reality. Then deliver: (1) a table comparing trunk-based development, GitFlow and GitHub Flow against these criteria: integration frequency, operational complexity, hotfix support, multi-version support and tolerance to long-lived branches; (2) a unique recommendation, justified and anchored to my context, naming the main trade-off that is accepted and why it is acceptable here; (3) the resulting branch model with permanent branches, short-lived branches and naming convention in kebab-case by type (feature, fix, hotfix, release, chore), including branch lifetime limit; (4) the integration policy (merge commit, squash or rebase) with its rationale; (5) concrete main branch protection rules (mandatory review, required CI checks, linear vs merge history, prohibition of direct push, commit signing if applicable); (6) the step-by-step hotfix flow to production, including how the fix returns to the main line; (7) an adoption guide with the first 3 concrete changes, transition risks and a rollback plan; (8) the 4 DORA metrics (change lead time, deployment frequency, change failure rate, mean time to restore) with how to measure them. Mark any gap with [ASSUMPTION] and indicate its impact on the decision. Close with a verification checklist. Neutral and professional Spanish, without prices or emojis.

prompts.title: Blue-Green Deployment Strategy
prompts.content:
Act as a senior platform and software delivery engineer (DevOps/SRE) with experience in high-availability releases and CI/CD pipelines. I need an actionable blue-green strategy to release versions of my service without downtime and with rollback in seconds: two identical production environments where blue serves real traffic while green receives and validates the new version; upon switching, roles are inverted and the outgoing environment stays warm as a safety net, so that rollback is a routing change and not an emergency redeploy.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before writing, reformulate what you understand and present your plan. If an essential piece of data is missing (target orchestrator or cloud, traffic switching mechanism, nature of storage and migrations, target SLO, risk tolerance and cut-over strategy), ask for it specifically and do not invent it; if you assume it, mark the assumption explicitly.

Produce, numbered: (1) Topology and prerequisites: atomic traffic switch, strict blue/green infrastructure parity, configuration and secrets management per environment, and deployment idempotency. (2) Step-by-step release flow: deploy to the inactive environment, smoke tests + health checks, cache and connection pool warm-up, and only then switch. (3) Switching strategy (total instant cut-over or progressive canary with increasing percentages) and connection draining of the outgoing environment without cutting in-flight sessions. (4) State management: backward-compatible migrations with expand/contract pattern, session, cache and shared queue handling, and policy for non-reversible changes. (5) Immediate rollback plan: objective abort criteria anchored to the SLO, post-switch observation window and reversion by returning traffic to the warm previous environment. (6) Observability: golden signals (latency, traffic, errors, saturation), traces and health endpoints governing promotion and abort. (7) CI/CD pipeline automation with manual or automatic gates and audit trail of each switch.

Cover explicit assumptions, limits, edge cases (non-reversible migration, failure mid-switch, blue vs green configuration drift, capacity exhaustion when doubling environments) and justified trade-offs (cut-over vs canary, cost of double infrastructure vs rollback speed). Close with: numbered blue-green runbook, promotion/abort criteria matrix and textual diagram of traffic flow (blue active > deploy green > validation > switch > observation > promotion or reversion), ready to integrate into the pipeline. Neutral and professional Spanish, without emojis.

prompts.title: Canary Deployment with Gradual Release
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Release Engineering and SRE engineer specialized in progressive deployments (canary, blue-green) and SLO governance. I need an executable canary deployment plan to promote a new version of a service without exposing the entire user base to the risk of a regression: you release traffic to the candidate gradually and promote it only if the health signals hold; if they fail, revert automatically in a single step.

Before designing anything, confirm with me the service, the orchestration platform, the progressive release mechanism and, above all, the metrics baseline: without a defined baseline there is no possible gate, so ask for it if I don't provide it. Mark as [ASSUMPTION] all data you are not given and do not invent SLO or traffic values.
