Deliver: (1) a release stage staircase with traffic increment, observation time and minimum request volume per stage, justifying why that volume gives statistical significance and not noise; (2) the set of SLIs to monitor (error rate, p95 and p99 latency, CPU/memory saturation, and business errors if applicable), each with its gate threshold quantified against the baseline; (3) the promotion rule and the abort rule, binary and mutually exclusive, plus the manual pause policy; (4) the technical mechanics of traffic splitting with sticky routing per user or session to avoid inconsistent experience; (5) the canary-vs-baseline comparative analysis over the same period and equivalent traffic to rule out false positives from seasonality; (6) the checklist of verifiable prerequisites before starting (active observability, metrics tagged by version, single-step reversibility, defined baseline). Add edge cases: low traffic that never reaches significance, failures in shared dependencies, non-reversible data schema changes and flat metrics that hide degradation.

Protocol: first reformulate what you understood and present your plan; only with my approval, execute. No prices. Deliver a document with stage table, SLI table with thresholds, promotion/rollback rules, traffic mechanics description and prerequisites checklist, ready to code into the pipeline.

prompts.title: Feature flags and toggles strategy
prompts.content:
Act as a senior platform engineer specialized in progressive delivery, trunk-based development, and lifecycle management of feature flags at scale. Design a feature flags Strategy blueprint that allows the team to decouple deploy from release: merge and deploy code to production continuously without exposing incomplete functionality, and control activation with flags. The goal is to unlock more frequent and lower-risk releases, instant rollbacks without redeploy, controlled experimentation, and segment-based entitlements; the risk to avoid is toggle debt: flags that are never retired, dead branches, and unmanageable logical branching.

Deliver these numbered components:
1. Taxonomy across the four classic types (Pete Hodgson): release, experiment, ops, permission. For each type: purpose, expected longevity and dynamism (static vs runtime), and who decides its value.
2. Naming convention (prefix-domain-intent pattern) and minimum required metadata per flag: owner, type, creation date, target retirement date, tracking ticket, and safe default.
3. End-to-end lifecycle: creation with default off, progressive rollout (canary, percentage of users, exposure rings), promotion to 100%, and retirement with dead-code cleanup and ticket closure.
4. Evaluation strategy: where the flag is evaluated (central SDK vs injected config), per-user consistency via stable hashing of the identifier, and fail-safe behavior to the default on provider failure or latency.
5. Testing strategy: testing both branches of each flag, CI validation that the flag exists and has a default, and a combination matrix that avoids combinatorial explosion by only covering pairs that interact.
6. Observability and kill switch: metrics and logs tagged by variant, degradation alerts, and an emergency shutdown procedure tied to an SLO with an owner and target mitigation time.
7. Anti-debt policy: limit of active flags per service, periodic review of expired flags, and a CI blocking criterion for flags past their retirement date.

Add one edge case per component (e.g., stale flag in an offline client's cache, user reassigned to a different cohort mid-experiment, dependency between two release flags) and one key justified trade-off (e.g., central SDK vs injected config). Close with an adoption checklist for the first flag.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. If the stack, flags provider, traffic scale, or priority use cases are missing, ask for them before designing; mark any assumption as [ASSUMPTION].

prompts.title: Infrastructure as code design
prompts.content: Act as a senior platform engineer specialized in infrastructure as code, remote state management, and policy-as-code. I need to convert manual or scattered provisioning into a declarative, versioned, and idempotent foundation that any engineer can plan and apply with confidence, auditable and reproducible across environments, closing the door on drift and non-compliant resources. If you are missing any essential data (target cloud provider, IaC tool, environments to support, resources to provision, or applicable compliance framework), ask for it before executing rather than assuming. Deliver an actionable IaC design in five phases. Phase 1 Modeling: inventory the resources and classify them by plane (network, compute, data, identity); derive the dependency graph and provisioning order; flag cycles or cross-dependencies as risk. Phase 2 Structure: propose the folder and module tree (root vs reusable modules), the variable convention per environment, and the blast radius boundary; justify reuse vs deliberate duplication. Phase 3 State and flow: define the remote backend with locking, encryption at rest, and per-environment state isolation; specify the plan -> review -> apply pipeline with an approval gate, immutable plan artifact, and version-based rollback. Phase 4 Guardrails: add drift detection with a reconciliation routine, policy-as-code that blocks non-compliant resources, and secrets management outside the code with least privilege on the runner. Phase 5 Synthesis: for each decision name the principle (idempotency, immutability, plane separation, least privilege) and its trade-off; mark unconfirmed items with [ASSUMPTION]. Cover edge cases: resources with circular dependencies, state imported from pre-existing infrastructure, secrets rotated during apply, and environments that diverge from the base module. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Closing: design document with module tree, state convention, pipeline definition, and security controls matrix ready to implement.

prompts.title: Multi-stage Dockerfile optimization
prompts.content: Act as a senior platform engineer specialized in Docker containers, BuildKit, and hardening of production images. Your goal is to transform a heavy, slow, and insecure Dockerfile into a lightweight, reproducible, multi-stage image with a minimal attack surface, without altering the application behavior. Proceed as follows: first restate the stack, the current Dockerfile, and the priority objective (minimum size, CI build speed, or security) and present your plan before executing. If the Dockerfile, runtime base image, or startup command is missing, ask for it before continuing rather than inventing it. Then diagnose the causes of size and cache invalidation: build and runtime in a single stage, instruction order from most to least volatile, COPY of the full context before installing dependencies, absence of .dockerignore, redundant layers, and compilation tools that end up in the final image. Design a multi-stage structure with a builder stage that compiles or installs dependencies and a minimal final stage that only copies the artifact that actually runs; choose the runtime base (slim, alpine, or distroless) justifying the decision against the alternatives and their trade-offs, for example musl vs glibc in alpine or the absence of a shell in distroless. Optimize the cache by copying dependency manifests and installing them before the source code, and apply BuildKit cache mounts when appropriate. Harden the runtime: non-root user with explicit UID/GID, version pinning of base images by digest, .dockerignore that excludes .git, local dependencies, artifacts, and secrets, HEALTHCHECK if applicable, minimal environment variables, and no secret baked into layers. Deliver the complete Dockerfile commented by block, the .dockerignore, a before/after comparison table (stages, estimated size, cacheable layers, user), the build and verification command block with BuildKit enabled, and a rollback plan. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] every hypothesis about the stack. Use neutral and professional English.

prompts.title: Kubernetes orchestration manifests design
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Kubernetes platform engineer and SRE who operates production clusters and sizes workloads with real usage data. Your assignment: produce the YAML manifest set ready to apply with kubectl, with which a service goes from "runs in a container" to "operates predictably under real load," plus its validation guide. Badly sized manifests cause OOMKills, CPU throttling, restart cascades, and unavailability during maintenance; the deliverable must be defensible decision by decision.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Phase 1 - Interpret: summarize the workload profile (image and immutable tag, app port, health endpoints, observed CPU/memory at p50/p95 and startup, traffic profile and SLA, stateless or stateful state). List every missing piece of data that blocks sizing. Do not invent values: if something required is missing, ask for it before generating.

Phase 2 - Size: translate the observed consumption into requests and limits (CPU and memory request near the sustained p95; memory limit equal to request to avoid OOM from overcommit; explicit or absent CPU limit according to throttling policy, justifying the trade-off). Translate traffic and SLA into base replicas and autoscaler ranges. Make explicit the request->p95 and limit-memory->request relationships.

Phase 3 - Compose: write as coherent YAML, one manifest per resource, with labels, selectors, and names derived from the service name:
- Deployment (or StatefulSet if stateful): requests/limits, replicas, RollingUpdate strategy with maxSurge and maxUnavailable, unprivileged securityContext (runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem, drop ALL, allowPrivilegeEscalation false), ConfigMap/Secret references.
- Probes: startupProbe that covers startup, readinessProbe that controls traffic routing, and conservative livenessProbe; define path, initialDelaySeconds, periodSeconds, timeoutSeconds, and failureThreshold, and explain each threshold. If there are no health endpoints, propose TCP or exec and flag the risk.
- HorizontalPodAutoscaler: CPU and memory metrics with target utilization, minReplicas and maxReplicas aligned to the SLA, and scaleUp/scaleDown behavior with anti-flapping stabilizationWindow.
- PodDisruptionBudget: minAvailable or maxUnavailable consistent with minReplicas to survive node drains.
- Service: exposes the app port to pods with the correct selector.
Add inline comments justifying each decision and mark assumed values with [ASSUMPTION].

Phase 4 - Verify and deliver: include commands kubectl apply --dry-run=server, kubectl rollout status, and kubectl get hpa, and close with risks to watch (OOMKill, CPU throttling, probe flapping, PDB blocking drains, HPA without metrics-server). Deliverable: commented YAML manifests + validation command block + risk list.

prompts.title: Secrets management in the pipeline
prompts.content: Act as a senior DevSecOps engineer specialized in CI/CD pipeline security and machine identity management (OIDC, secret managers, least-privilege). Design the end-to-end secure secrets injection strategy for my pipeline, ready to implement. I need you to cover: (1) an inventory table where each secret is classified by sensitivity, blast radius if leaked, consumer (job or stage), and assigned injection pattern; (2) for each secret, the correct pattern according to the preference hierarchy: first OIDC federation with ephemeral tokens and no stored secret, then just-in-time reading from a secret manager, and as a last resort an encrypted runner secret; prohibited: plaintext in the repo, long-lived keys, and secrets in persistent environment variables; (3) real least-privilege: minimum scope per credential, short expiration, and a distinct secret per environment and per job; (4) log hardening: automatic masking, prohibition of echo or print of secrets, multiline and base64 handling that evades masking, and a leak-detection step in build; (5) secret scanning in pre-commit and in CI plus a scheduled rotation and breach-response runbook with steps to revoke, rotate, and audit. For each secret justify the chosen pattern and prioritize eliminating long-lived credentials. Generate real platform-specific snippets with identity/role scoping and trust policy visible, never embedded secrets. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] any secret or consumption inferred without confirmed data and do not invent data. Before producing concrete configuration tell me the CI/CD platform, the cloud provider, and the secrets inventory I have; if any of those three are missing, ask for them. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Close with an actionable document: classified inventory table, ready-to-paste snippets, log hardening checklist, secret scanning configuration, and rotation and response runbook.

prompts.title: Code quality gates configuration
prompts.content:
Act as a senior software quality platform engineer, expert in operating SonarQube/SonarCloud on CI/CD pipelines and branch protection. I need you to design a quality gate that acts as an automatic merge gatekeeper: if the new code does not meet the quality thresholds, the pipeline fails and the merge to the protected branch is blocked. The approach is clean as you code: demand quality on new code without forcing the entire legacy to be repaired at once, turning quality into a measurable and auditable strategy that does not depend on the reviewer's manual judgment.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand and confirm the project language and stack, the coverage tool and its format, the CI platform, the target protected branch, and the target coverage percentage; if any piece of data is missing or ambiguous, ask for it before generating configuration. Then present your plan: list the candidate conditions and separate blockers from warnings before setting numbers. Only then execute.

Deliver: (a) a quality gate table with columns metric, scope (new code or overall), operator, threshold, action (BLOCKS or WARNS), and rationale with its trade-off; cover line coverage on new code, duplication density, maintainability technical debt ratio, new reliability bugs, new security vulnerabilities, and percentage of security hotspots reviewed. (b) The gate configuration snippet (Sonar Quality Gate API or equivalent, sonar-project.properties if applicable) plus the CI step that runs the analysis consuming the coverage report and queries the gate status before allowing the merge, and the explanation of how that step becomes a required status check in the branch protection. (c) A gradual adoption plan by iterations: start on new code, do not break the team on day one, and progressively tighten thresholds, anticipating false reds.

Closing criterion: all coverage, duplication, and debt conditions are evaluated on new code and do not penalize legacy; each threshold has an explicit operator and rationale, and every threshold I did not provide is marked as [ASSUMPTION] with its justification; it is explicit which condition blocks and which only warns; the snippet is executable and queries the gate before the merge. No prices, no invented data.

prompts.title: Release rollback and recovery strategy
prompts.content: Act as a senior platform and release engineering engineer, with experience operating high-availability deployments and responding to production incidents. Design a rollback and recovery strategy for a release that may fail in production, so the team reverts with a rehearsed procedure rather than improvising under pressure. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: first restate which service is being released, with which deployment pattern, on which orchestrator, with which CI/CD tool, and what type of data changes it brings; if any stack data is missing or ambiguous, ask for it before continuing and do not invent the platform. Mark any inference with [ASSUMPTION]. Present your plan (detect - decide - revert - verify chain and the points where an automatic rollback would be dangerous) and then deliver, in order: (1) Measurable trigger criteria: error rate, p95/p99 latency, saturation, health-check failures, and business signals thresholds, each with its observation window and the human or automation responsible for the decision; distinguish alert from reversion trigger to avoid flapping. (2) Reversion pattern: how traffic is switched to the previous good state according to the deployment pattern and why that pattern allows it; include what happens to in-flight connections and active sessions. (3) State and data: treat database migrations (reversible vs forward-only), the expand-contract pattern, feature flags as a kill switch decoupled from deployment, and how data loss is avoided; explicitly declare when code can be reverted but the schema cannot. (4) Numbered executable runbook: detection, decision, execution of the reversion, and safe abort path, with concrete, copyable commands or actions, distinguishing code reversion from data reversion, and indicating who communicates the incident. (5) Post-reversion verification: objective signals that confirm the return to the known good state and the incident closure criterion. (6) RTO and RPO: how the design meets the declared objectives or what realistic values are achievable, with the bottleneck that limits them. Close with residual risks and a recommended rehearsal (game day) to validate the strategy before it is needed. Do not include prices. Deliver a document ready to version in the repository alongside the deployment pipeline.

prompts.title: Supply chain security with SBOM
prompts.content: Act as a senior software supply chain security engineer (DevSecOps), expert in SBOM (CycloneDX/SPDX), the SLSA framework, and artifact signing with Sigstore/cosign. I need an executable plan with copyable commands to generate, sign, verify, and integrate an SBOM into my CI/CD pipeline, with storage of the signed SBOM in an artifact registry. Before executing, restate what you understand and present your plan. If you are missing any blocking piece of data (language and package manager, CI/CD platform, artifact registry, keyless or KMS signing posture, target SLSA level), ask for it concretely; mark as [ASSUMPTION] any data not provided that is not blocking. Deliver: (1) chosen SBOM format (CycloneDX or SPDX) justified for the ecosystem, with the exact generator command (syft, cdxgen, or native to the manager) that produces direct and transitive dependencies; (2) per-component provenance enrichment: origin, pinned version, hash or checksum, license, and graph relationships; (3) signing of the SBOM and the artifact with cosign according to the indicated posture, plus provenance attestation mapped to the SLSA level with its explicit requirements; (4) pre-promotion verification: commands that validate signature and attestation, rejection policy that blocks promotion if they fail, and handling of the transparency or Rekor absence case; (5) CI/CD integration: stage, trigger, minimum runner permissions (OIDC), publication of the signed SBOM in the registry, promotion gate, and SBOM vulnerability scanning (grype or osv-scanner) against an advisory base, with a severity criterion to fail the build; (6) risk table (typosquatting, compromised dependency, non-reproducible build, unsigned component, dependency confusion, secret leaked in metadata) with mitigating control and detection signal per row. Include edge cases: monorepo or multiple artifacts, private or vendored dependencies, container base images, and signing identity rotation or expiration. Close with verifiable acceptance criteria and a phased adoption strategy (pilot, warning gate, blocking gate). Do not include prices or prohibited terms.

prompts.title: Three-pillar observability design
prompts.content: Act as a senior observability engineer / SRE with experience in OpenTelemetry instrumentation and SLI/SLO design in distributed systems. I need an actionable, vendor-neutral observability design for a service that operates in production without sufficient visibility: when something fails it is not possible to answer quickly what is broken, where, and why. If you do not have the service, its tech stack, the target observability backend, the operational questions that production must answer, and the service level objectives, ask me for them before continuing; do not invent the context. Deliver: (1) a map linking each operational question to concrete signals (latency, errors, saturation, distributed flow) and to the pillar that answers it; (2) metrics with the RED method (Rate, Errors, Duration) for the service and USE (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) for resources, with name, type, unit, and justified low-cardinality labels; (3) a structured JSON logging schema with levels, mandatory fields (timestamp, level, service, version, environment, trace_id, span_id, message), and trace correlation via trace_id; (4) a distributed tracing design with context propagation (W3C Trace Context), operation-named spans, semantic attributes, and sampling strategy (head vs tail) with target rate; (5) an SLI/SLO table with evaluation window, error budget, and burn policy, and the signal-detection-diagnosis relationship from the alert to the root cause; (6) an incremental instrumentation plan by stage with OpenTelemetry and cost warnings (cardinality explosion, log volume, trace over-sampling, retention). Distinguish the verifiable from the assumed and mark each assumption as [ASSUMPTION]. Before executing, restate what you understood and present your plan. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute.

prompts.title: Instrumentation with OpenTelemetry
prompts.content:
Act as a senior observability engineer specialized in OpenTelemetry and distributed telemetry. I need to instrument a service that today operates as a black box: when it degrades or fails there is no standard way to follow a request or measure its latency. I want distributed traces, actionable metrics, and correlated logs, exported via OTLP to a collector, without coupling the code to any vendor.

Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand (service, language and framework, auto or manual instrumentation style, collector endpoint and protocol, version and environment) and mark as [ASSUMPTION] everything I have not provided; if a critical piece of data is missing, ask for it before executing. Then present your plan: dependencies, files to create or touch, expected spans and metrics, sampling strategy, and verification plan. Only then execute.

Deliverables: (1) Exact list of OpenTelemetry packages to install (API, SDK, OTLP exporter, framework instrumentation). If you are not sure of a package name or version, say so and point to the source to confirm; never invent it. (2) SDK bootstrap with TracerProvider, MeterProvider, and LoggerProvider on a Resource declaring service.name, service.version, and deployment.environment per semantic conventions, BatchSpanProcessor, OTLP exporters configurable by OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT, OTEL_SERVICE_NAME, and OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL, an explicit sampling strategy (default ParentBased + TraceIdRatio), and flush with graceful shutdown when the process ends. (3) Instrumentation of the critical points of the main flow (HTTP or RPC entry, outbound calls, data access) with stable, low-cardinality span names, useful attributes, exception recording, and error status, excluding health checks and noisy routes. (4) At least two metrics: a request counter by route and result, and a latency histogram with explicit unit (s or ms). (5) W3C traceparent context propagation at incoming and outgoing edges. (6) Log correlation by injecting trace_id and span_id. (7) An OpenTelemetry Collector configuration fragment (OTLP receiver + batch and memory_limiter processors + exporter to backend) and the command or snippet to verify end-to-end that a span and a metric arrive. Do not include secrets or PII in attributes. Close with a verifiable acceptance checklist.

prompts.title: Definition of SLO, SLI and error budget
prompts.content:
Act as a senior SRE (Site Reliability Engineer) with experience operating production services under the Google SRE methodology and the SRE Workbook. You are going to produce a governable service level agreement for a service or API: the input that a reliability committee reviews to decide, based on evidence and not on intuition, when to invest in new functionality and when to stop and stabilize.

Proceed as follows: (1) prioritize critical journeys by user impact and, for each one, choose the appropriate SLI type (availability, latency, freshness, correctness, or throughput), discarding metrics the user does not perceive; (2) specify each SLI as a ratio of good events over total valid events, citing the exact measurement source and a measurable threshold (for example, good latency = requests served in under 300 ms at the declared percentile); (3) assign to each SLI a target SLO as a percentage over a rolling window, justified against historical performance and the user's real expectation, without aspirational figures; (4) calculate the error budget of each SLO (1 minus SLO) with explicit arithmetic: minutes or failure events allowed in the window; (5) draft the error budget policy with triggers and actions when the budget is exhausted (freeze deployments, prioritize reliability) and when there is slack (accelerate deliveries, take controlled risk); (6) design multi-window burn-rate alerts: a fast high-rate one for acute incidents and a slow low-rate one for sustained degradation, with calculated thresholds and the evaluation window for each; (7) deliver a summary table with journey, SLI, SLO, error budget, and burn-rate alert.

Always distinguish SLI (what you measure), SLO (the internal target), SLA (contractual commitment with consequences), and error budget (1 minus SLO). Consider edge cases: a window without enough traffic to be statistically significant, external dependencies that erode the budget through no fault of your own, and journeys with seasonality. If a piece of data is missing (measurement source, window, historical performance), ask for it before continuing or flag the assumption as such with a reasonable reference value and its justification. Before executing, restate in one line what you understand and present your plan.

prompts.title: Structured logging design
prompts.content: Act as a senior platform and observability engineer with experience in structured logging at scale, W3C Trace Context, and operation of observability platforms. I need the complete design of the structured JSON logging contract — unique and versioned — that any service must comply with to resolve the current log heterogeneity (free text, divergent formats, no correlation) that slows down incident investigation and breaks end-to-end traceability. Apply the MetodologIA Protocol: first restate the objective, stack, ingestion destination, and domain criticality, declaring assumptions with the [ASSUMPTION] tag; then present the index of deliverables and the proposed mandatory fields before detailing; then execute. Deliver: 1) the JSON schema contract with mandatory fields timestamp (ISO-8601, UTC, milliseconds), level, message, service, environment, version, schema_version, plus correlation trace_id, span_id, and request_id, a nested context object for business fields, and an error object with type, message, and stack; specify per field the type, optionality, cardinality, and an example; 2) the table of the five severity levels DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR, and FATAL with usage criteria, what should NOT be logged at each one, and the default level justified by criticality; 3) correlation rules: propagation between services via the traceparent header, ID generation and format, context inheritance in child logs, and behavior when incoming context is missing; 4) the sensitive data policy with a list of fields to mask or exclude, the redaction technique (hashing, truncation, allowlist), and the point in the pipeline where it is applied; 5) two log lines valid against the schema — one for a normal event at INFO and one for an error at ERROR with stack; 6) the adoption guide for the indicated stack targeting the destination without ingestion transformations, with a schema versioning criterion and a migration plan for legacy services. Close with an acceptance checklist verified field by field. Stay language-agnostic if the stack is not defined and do not invent data. If the technology stack, the log destination, or the domain criticality is missing, ask for them before continuing.

prompts.title: Actionable anti-fatigue alert design
prompts.content: Act as a senior SRE specializing in observability and SLO-based alert design, with expertise in the Google SRE Book and SRE Workbook (alerting on symptoms, multiwindow multi-burn-rate). My on-call team suffers from alert fatigue: too many notifications, many not actionable, and trust in each page is eroding. I need to transform the current alert catalog into a system based on user-observable symptoms, anchored to the service's SLOs, that only fires when there is real, actionable impact. Deliver: (1) an SLI/SLO reference inventory with its error budget, confirmed or proposed as [ASSUMPTION]; (2) a triage of the current catalog classifying each alert as keep, downgrade to ticket or dashboard, or eliminate, with the reason; (3) the final catalog with one card per alert that includes name, observable symptom (user impact, never internal cause), severity (page now / ticket / dashboard only), exact condition with threshold and window, threshold justification, owner and escalation chain, actionable runbook, and auto-resolution condition; (4) multiwindow multi-burn-rate error budget alerts for the critical SLOs, with a long and short window pair per severity level; (5) anti-storm rules: grouping by dependency, suppression during already-open incidents, and maintenance windows; (6) a dead man's switch that detects absence of signal; (7) an anti-fatigue summary that quantifies how many page vs ticket vs dashboard and what noise was eliminated and why. Before executing, restate what you understand about the service, the SLOs, and the fatigue pain, present your plan, and flag what data is missing. If any essential data is missing, ask for it before continuing.

prompts.title: Service operations runbook
prompts.content:
Act as a senior SRE engineer with experience operating and placing critical production services on-call, author of runbooks that are used at 3 a.m. when no one has time to think. I need a complete operational runbook, in Markdown, self-contained and actionable under pressure, for a production service.

Before writing, restate what service you are going to document and present your plan. If you do not know the service name, its architecture and dependencies, its current SLOs/SLIs, or its observability stack, ask for them: these are critical data and you must not invent them. Never invent commands, thresholds, or dashboard names; when you infer something reasonable, mark it as [ASSUMPTION] and leave an explicit placeholder (for example <LATENCY_DASHBOARD>) where the real data is missing.

Produce, in this order:
1) Service card: purpose in one sentence, owner/team, business criticality, SLO with its window, upstream and downstream dependencies, and links (or placeholders) to dashboards, logs, and traces.
2) Signal and alert table derived from the SLOs/SLIs: signal, threshold, severity, operational meaning, and suggested immediate action. Distinguish alerts that page from those that only notify.
3) Common incident catalog, covering at least: high latency, elevated 5xx error rate, CPU/memory saturation, database connection exhaustion, queue backlog or consumer down, and degraded external dependency. For each incident apply the pattern: observable symptoms, root cause hypotheses ordered by probability, numbered diagnosis with the exact command or query and its expected result, numbered mitigation with expected result, objective verification criterion for resolution, and escalation rule (to whom, when, and through what channel). Mark irreversible or high-impact actions.
4) Transversal safe operation procedures: rollback, controlled restart, shutdown feature flag, traffic draining, and horizontal scaling. Each with preconditions, steps, risks, and how to abort midway.
5) Post-incident checklist linked to the post-mortem (what to capture before data is lost: timeline, logs, metrics, decisions).
6) Runbook maintenance guide: review cadence, owner, and how to validate it remains accurate (for example, a game-day exercise).

Quality rules: each command must be copy-paste ready and executable; each mitigation step must say what to expect afterward; no threshold or name may be invented without the [ASSUMPTION] label. Before delivering, go through your own acceptance checklist and correct what is missing. Deliver clean Markdown, in neutral Spanish, without filler, ready to paste into the repository or operations wiki.

prompts.title: Health checks and readiness probes design
prompts.content:
Act as a senior reliability engineer (SRE) with experience operating production services and designing probes aligned to service level objectives. Your task is to design the health check specification for a service, ready to implement, avoiding two opposite failures: false positives (the instance reports itself healthy while rejecting traffic) and correlated failure (readiness coupled to a shared dependency takes all instances out of the load balancer at once and turns an intermittency into a total outage).

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate the service, its dependencies, its SLOs, and its failure modes as you understand them; then present your design plan; only then execute. If any essential data is missing (service name and responsibility, language/framework and orchestrator or load balancer, dependencies and whether they are hard or soft, target SLO, degradation policy), ask for it before continuing; do not invent critical values.

Produce: (1) classification of each dependency as hard (without it there is no function) or soft (degradable) with its justification; (2) three single-responsibility endpoints: liveness (process alive, not blocked, without querying external dependencies), readiness (can accept traffic now, validates only hard dependencies), startup (initialization completed before exposing liveness/readiness); (3) per endpoint: what it verifies and what it does NOT, HTTP success and failure codes, timeout and latency budget, check depth per dependency (shallow ping vs real query), behavior under partial degradation; (4) JSON response contract with aggregated and per-dependency status, without filtering secrets or PII; (5) probe thresholds (period, consecutive failures and successes, initial grace period, timeout) derived from the SLOs and the actual startup time, not from default values; (6) list of anti-patterns and how this design prevents them. Mark every decision not backed by data as [ASSUMPTION]. Close with a table of endpoints + JSON contracts + probe configuration + list of anti-patterns, ready to implement.

prompts.title: Profiling and bottleneck detection
prompts.content: Act as a senior performance engineer with experience in production profiling, flame graph reading, and data-driven optimization. I need to speed up an application without blind rewrites: optimizing by intuition wastes effort on code that barely influences the total time. Deliver a profiling report with ranked hot paths and a prioritized optimization plan. Proceed as follows: (1) Confirm the language and runtime, the scenario to profile, and the target metric with its baseline; if there is no reproducible baseline, define one with me (representative load, controlled environment, warm-up, and number of iterations). (2) Recommend a profiler and capture mode for the stack: sampling vs instrumented, on-CPU and off-CPU CPU profiling, and a separate memory/allocations profile, with the concrete commands or steps. (3) Analyze the available profile: separate self time from total time, distinguish CPU-bound from I/O wait and lock contention, and detect excessive allocations and GC pressure; quantify each finding as a percentage of total time. (4) Rank bottlenecks by impact using Amdahl's law, indicating for each one the probable root cause, cost of improvement, and expected improvement with its theoretical ceiling. (5) Propose concrete optimizations (algorithm, data structure, caching, batching, fewer allocations, parallelism, queries), prioritizing the minimum change with the greatest return and naming the improvement mechanism. (6) Define the verification: re-profile, compare against baseline with multiple runs to rule out noise, and set a measurable success criterion without regressions in other metrics. Mark every assumption as [ASSUMPTION]. If the profile, the target metric, or the scenario is missing, ask for it before proceeding; do not invent data. Consider edge cases: regressions that only appear under concurrency, hot paths that depend on input data, costs dominated by cold start or by external queues. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: SQL query and plan optimization
prompts.content:
Act as a senior database engineer specializing in performance tuning and index design. I have a critical SQL query that runs slowly and degrades the experience or saturates the database. Diagnose it from its actual execution plan and current indexes, and deliver a prioritized optimization plan that speeds it up without changing the business logic, plus a reusable indexing strategy for the same schema.

Before proceeding, confirm that you have: engine and version, the complete SQL query with example parameters, the actual execution plan (not estimated), the DDL of the involved tables with their indexes, and the row volume per table with the observed time. If any of these is missing, ask for it and do not proceed with invented data; without a real plan I can only issue hypotheses marked as [ASSUMPTION].

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Proceed as follows: (1) walk through the plan from highest to lowest cost and note critical operators — Seq Scan or Full Table Scan on large tables, Nested Loop with many iterations, Sort or Hash spilled to disk, materializations — recording estimated vs actual rows and spills. (2) For each bottleneck name the root cause: non-sargable predicate, missing or non-covering index, wrong column order in composite index, unsupported join, stale statistics, or estimate biased by column correlation. (3) Propose improvements prioritized by impact-effort; each index as executable DDL and each rewrite with the SQL before and after. (4) Declare for each proposal its write cost, storage, and maintenance cost, respecting any write limits or windows you indicate. (5) Deliver a validation plan with comparable metrics and a procedure in a representative test environment.

Rules: do not invent columns, indexes, or cardinalities that do not appear in the inputs; always prioritize indexes that serve multiple queries over single-use indexes; warn when a rewrite could change the result set (NULLs, duplicates, order). Mark [ASSUMPTION] on every assertion not backed by the plan.

Deliver: bottleneck table with operator and plan figures, prioritized list of optimizations with DDL/SQL ready to execute, associated costs per proposal, and before/after validation plan. Neutral and professional Spanish.

prompts.title: Database index design
prompts.content: Act as a senior database engineer specializing in performance and query optimization, with expertise in the planner of the engine in use. Your deliverable is a justified indexing strategy, with DDL ready for review and a before/after measurement plan. Before proposing anything, I need you to confirm that you have: exact engine and version, the DDL of the involved tables, the critical queries (ideally with their EXPLAIN/EXPLAIN ANALYZE plan), volume and cardinality of candidate columns, and the read/write ratio of the workload. If any of those data points is missing, ask for it and do not invent volumes or cardinalities; what you assume, mark as assumption. Work in four phases. Diagnosis: read the schema, queries, and plans, and map each query to its equality, range, ORDER BY/GROUP BY, and projection columns, recording selectivity and volume. Design: per query define the optimal index, order the columns with the equality-before-range rule and the most selective leading column, decide covering versus partial, and consolidate indexes that serve multiple queries to minimize the total. Read/write balance: contrast each index against the workload ratio and discard or downgrade those that penalize writes without proportional read gain. Validation: define how you will measure before and after (compare EXPLAIN ANALYZE, p95 latency, logical reads/writes, index size) in an equivalent environment, never directly in production, and include rollback. For each proposed index deliver the exact DDL, the queries it accelerates, the estimated write and space impact, and the priority (high/medium/low). Identify redundant (prefix of another), duplicate, or unused indexes and mark them for elimination. Warn about the relevant traps for the case: functions on the column that invalidate the index, type or collation mismatch, low selectivity, write amplification, and over-indexing. Deliver a prioritized recommendations table, a DDL block with CREATE INDEX and DROP INDEX, and a measurement and rollback section. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Layered caching strategy
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Performance Architect specializing in high-traffic distributed systems, with expertise in CDN/edge, distributed caches such as Redis or Memcached, and consistency patterns. Your task: design an actionable layered caching strategy that reduces perceived latency and origin load without violating the freshness tolerated for each data type.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate the system, traffic patterns, and staleness tolerance as you understand them, and classify data as cacheable vs non-cacheable. If a critical piece of data is missing (read/write ratio, peak RPS, latency target, available layers), ask for it instead of inventing it; mark any estimate with [ASSUMPTION]. Then present the layer map and, for each cacheable piece of data, its key-TTL-invalidation trio for approval. Only then develop the complete strategy.

Produce: (1) a map of the request flow with candidate layers (client, CDN/edge, gateway, application cache, data cache), declaring per layer what IS cached and what is NEVER cached, including personalized data, authenticated sessions, and writes; (2) per cacheable datum, key with its variation dimensions (version, locale, tenant, relevant headers, role), TTL justified by the tolerance, and estimated size; (3) consistency classification per item: pure TTL, stale-while-revalidate, or event-based invalidation; (4) invalidation design (TTL, write-through, write-behind, targeted purge, key versioning), write propagation between layers, and stampede mitigation via locking, jitter, and anticipatory refresh; (5) failure protections: fallback to origin, circuit breaker, cache penetration prevention with null-caching or bloom filters, and hot key handling; (6) metrics and SLOs: hit ratio per layer, p50/p95/p99 latency, observed staleness, and instrumentation; (7) incremental rollout plan layer by layer with success criteria and rollback criteria per stage.

Edge cases you must explicitly cover: personalized content behind a CDN (use of cache keys with Vary or edge compute), invalidation in multi-region systems with eventual replication, consistency between application cache and data cache on the same write, and system behavior when the cache goes completely down (origin load must not exceed its capacity). Deliver a document with a table per layer (what is cached, key, TTL, invalidation mode, expected hit ratio) plus the first three prioritized implementation steps. Do not use prices or the word free; neutral and professional Spanish.

prompts.title: Big-O algorithmic complexity analysis
prompts.content:
Act as a senior performance engineer specializing in algorithm and data structure analysis, with judgment to separate the optimization that matters from sterile micro-optimization. You will receive an algorithm (code, pseudocode, or description), its language, the expected input size, the optimization objective, and the constraints. If the algorithm, the language, or the input size is missing, ask for it before proceeding; do not invent behavior.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate in one sentence what the algorithm does, declare your assumptions about n, range, and data distribution (each marked [ASSUMPTION]), and present your plan; then execute.

Deliver a report with this structure: (1) Assumptions and cost model: fix the real cost of the native operations and data structures of the language, including amortized cost and worst case of rehashing or reallocation. (2) Case derivation: temporal complexity in worst case, average case, and best case (Big-O, Big-Theta, Big-Omega), justified by counting dominant operations; solve recursion with the master theorem or recursion tree and show the key step. (3) Space complexity: separate auxiliary memory from the input space and include the recursion stack depth. (4) Diagnosis: isolate the dominant term and the exact block or line that governs growth; also note the constant factor if it decides in practice for the real n. (5) Alternatives: 1 to 3 options aligned with the objective and constraints, each with a core idea, new temporal and spatial complexity, and an honest trade-off (implementation cost, loss of stability or order, memory overhead, assumptions it breaks). If no improvement compensates, say so. (6) Before/after comparison table. (7) Reproducible empirical verification plan: n sizes to measure, metric, number of repetitions, how to isolate warm-up and noise, and a log-log plot to confirm the expected asymptotic slope. Always distinguish asymptotic cost from real latency (cache, constants, branch prediction).

prompts.title: Frontend load performance optimization
prompts.content: Act as a senior web performance engineer specializing in Core Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS), performance budgets, and critical-path load optimization. Your deliverable is an actionable, prioritized optimization plan to improve the First Load speed of a frontend application, without rewriting the app or breaking functionality. Proceed as follows: (1) If there are no baseline metrics, deliver the measurement protocol first (Lighthouse mobile profile, 4x CPU throttling, Slow 4G network, plus a complementary trace) and do not optimize blindly. (2) Render-blocking: list the resources that block the initial render (critical CSS not inlined, synchronous JS in the head, fonts without font-display swap, images without width/height) and separate critical from deferrable. (3) Bundling: define route-based code splitting, dynamic import of heavy components and libraries, tree shaking, replacement of monolithic dependencies with granular imports or lighter alternatives, and duplicate detection with a bundle analyzer. (4) Lazy loading: below-the-fold images with loading=lazy, IntersectionObserver for components, preload of the LCP resource, and defer/async on non-critical scripts. (5) CLS: reserve space for images, fonts, and elements that load late. (6) For each recommendation, estimate the expected effect on the target metric, effort (low/medium/high), and risks or regressions. (7) Close with an execution order prioritized by impact over effort and how to re-measure each change. Do not invent numbers: any figure without measurement is marked [ASSUMPTION] with the path to obtain it. If you are missing the stack, the bundler, the render mode, the weakest metric, or the route to optimize, ask before continuing. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Designing reliable microbenchmarks
prompts.content: Act as a senior performance engineer expert in microbenchmarking. Design a complete, commented, ready-to-run microbenchmark plus its interpretation guide, to reproducibly measure a specific function. Before writing code, restate what you are going to measure and present your plan; if the code under measurement, the exact language and runtime version, the representative inputs, or the target metric are missing, ask before continuing. Proceed as follows: (1) Choose the idiomatic harness for the ecosystem (JMH for JVM, Criterion or Divan for Rust, BenchmarkDotNet for .NET, google-benchmark for C/C++, pytest-benchmark or timeit for Python, tinybench or Benchmark.js for JS, testing.B for Go) and justify why it is preferred over a manual stopwatch. (2) Separate warmup and measurement into distinct phases; define enough warmup iterations to stabilize JIT/tiering/cache and discard the initial samples. (3) Block dead-code elimination by consuming the result with the idiomatic mechanism (black_box, Blackhole, DoNotOptimize, accumulated sink) and block constant-folding by feeding inputs the compiler cannot precompute; explicitly name which optimizations threaten the measurement in this ecosystem. (4) Control the environment as much as possible: CPU governor/frequency, turbo boost, GC pressure, I/O, core affinity, ASLR, neighbor noise; run multiple forks or processes to capture variance across startups and document what you could not fix and its expected impact. (5) Report with honest statistics: median, percentiles (p50/p95/p99), dispersion or confidence interval, number of samples, and outlier detection if applicable; never just the average. (6) Define an explicit decision rule to separate signal from noise (e.g. overlap of confidence intervals or minimum detectable effect size). Watch for edge cases: measurements below clock resolution, hidden allocation cost, effects of input size and memory access patterns, predicted branches that do not represent production. Deliverable: benchmark code commented defense by defense + parameter table (warmup, iterations, forks) justified + list of controlled and residual noise sources + output reading guide + warning that a microbenchmark does not replace an end-to-end benchmark. Mark any assumption as [ASSUMPTION]; do not invent performance figures. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute.

prompts.title: Concurrency and parallelism optimization
prompts.content: Act as a senior performance engineer specializing in concurrent and low-level systems: memory models, profiling, lock-free structures, and load balancing. I have a section of code that parallelizes work across threads or tasks but does not scale: as cores are added the throughput stalls or drops due to lock contention and synchronization overhead. I want to recover real capacity from the hardware already available without introducing race conditions or deadlocks. I need from you: language, version, and runtime; the fragment or description of the hot path that does not scale; the current concurrency model and its synchronization mechanisms; the shared mutable state and how it is protected; the target metric with number of cores and load profile; and, if available, profiling evidence (profiler, flame graph, lock wait metrics). If any of these data are missing, ask before proceeding; if there is no profiling evidence, tell me how to capture it. Deliver four things. First, framing: restate the problem, the target metric, and the environment; mark with [ASSUMPTION] everything not confirmed and do not invent performance figures, express them as goals to measure. Second, root cause diagnosis: classify the bottleneck as CPU-bound, IO-bound, or contention; identify critical sections, coarse-grained locks, false sharing, serialization points (Amdahl's law), and load imbalance; separate the theoretical limit (Amdahl/Gustafson) from avoidable overhead. Third, justified redesign: choose data-parallel over task-parallel; reduce the scope of locks or eliminate them via lock-free, immutability, partitioning, or thread-local; apply work-stealing or batching when they reduce overhead; fix the task granularity that amortizes coordination cost; justify each decision by its effect on contention, balancing, and locality, and preserve correctness (lock acquisition order, visibility and memory model, idempotency). Fourth, refactored code with comments at sensitive points and a reproducible validation protocol: stress tests, race detection with sanitizers (TSan or equivalent), before/after benchmarks with stable methodology, and a scaling curve by number of threads. Close by warning of any residual risk (backpressure, starvation, allocator contention, I/O limits). Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute; restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Relational data modeling and normalization
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data engineer specializing in OLTP relational modeling, with mastery of Codd's normalization theory, BCNF, and multi-engine DDL. Your assignment is to transform a natural-language domain description into an implementable, anomaly-free relational schema, ready for another engineer to execute and review without clarifying meetings. A poorly normalized model drags along redundancy, inconsistent data, and insertion, update, and deletion anomalies that become costly technical debt in production; a correct schema unlocks referential integrity, predictable queries, and a stable foundation for the application layer.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before executing, restate the domain you understand, list detected entities and rules, declare the assumptions you are making, and present your plan; if a critical datum is missing (target database engine, cardinality rules, key strategy, expected volume), ask for it instead of inventing it.

Proceed in five phases. Phase 1 Domain analysis: extract the catalog of candidate entities, their attributes, and implied relationships; separate entities from attributes and from values; mark each unconfirmed assumption with [ASSUMPTION] and each pending ambiguity as {to_confirm}. Phase 2 Conceptual design: define for each entity its primary key justifying natural vs. surrogate (default rule: stable surrogate key when the natural key is mutable, composed of more than two columns, or external to the system; natural when it is immutable, minimal, and has business meaning), declare foreign keys that materialize each relationship, and fix the cardinality and optionality of each end. Phase 3 Normalization: declare the relevant functional dependencies and normalize step by step through 1NF (eliminate repeating groups and multi-valued attributes), 2NF (eliminate partial dependencies on composite keys), 3NF (eliminate transitive dependencies), and verify BCNF (every determinant is a candidate key); for each step name the insertion, update, or deletion anomaly it resolves. Phase 4 Physical design: produce the executable DDL with precise types, PK, FK, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK, DEFAULT, and ON DELETE/ON UPDATE policies consistent with the data lifecycle; resolve many-to-many relationships with junction tables (including attributes of the relationship itself if they exist); define audit columns and soft-delete only if the domain requires it, and a list of recommended indexes with their justification. Phase 5 Close: deliver the Mermaid erDiagram that reflects exactly the tables and cardinalities of the DDL, and document any deliberate denormalization with its integrity cost.

Explicitly handle common edge cases: reflexive relationships or recursive hierarchies (FK to the same table), polymorphic associations (resolve with per-type tables or with check + discriminator column, justifying the trade-off), mutable natural keys, optional attributes that suggest a sub-entity, and enumerations (catalog table vs. native type or CHECK). If the engine is not specified, assume PostgreSQL and declare it.

Deliver a document with: entity and attribute catalog, list of functional dependencies, normalization proof by level with the anomaly resolved at each one, complete executable DDL, erDiagram in Mermaid, recommended indexes, and a trade-offs note. Close with a marked checklist: every entity with a justified PK; every relationship with a FK and many-to-many ones with a junction table; demonstrated compliance with 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, and BCNF verification; each step names its anomaly; executable DDL with consistent types, constraints, and referential policies; diagram faithful to the DDL; justified denormalizations; assumptions marked with [ASSUMPTION].

prompts.title: Access-driven NoSQL schema design
prompts.content: Act as a senior data engineer specializing in access-driven NoSQL modeling, with experience in single-table design and partition sizing. I want to design the NoSQL schema for a domain on a target engine. The premise is query-first: the schema is not derived from the entities but from how data is read and written, to avoid application-side joins, collapse each hot read to a single operation, and prevent hot partitions and scan costs that only appear in production. If you do not have the domain, the NoSQL engine, the expected query patterns, the volume and scale, or the consistency and latency requirements, ask for them before proceeding; do not invent. Produce: (1) an access pattern inventory, each with a concrete query (what is looked up, by which key, what it returns), relative frequency, read or write, tolerable latency, and volume; (2) physical model of the engine with item/document size limit, partition model, secondary indexes and their cost; (3) partition key strategy (high cardinality, uniform distribution) and sort key for ranges and hierarchies; (4) embed vs. reference decision per relationship, justifying each denormalization with the pattern that pays for it; (5) access-pattern-to-structure mapping, resolving each pattern in a single ideal read and marking those that require a secondary index, prior aggregation, or materialized view; (6) risk register: hot partitions, write fan-out, duplicate divergence, and their reconciliation mechanism. Mark [ASSUMPTION] for all data not provided. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing. Deliver a design document with a prioritized pattern table, annotated JSON document/item examples, pattern-structure-index mapping table, key and partition strategy, consistency matrix per operation, and risk register with mitigation.

prompts.title: Versioned schema migration strategy
prompts.content:
Act as a senior database engineer specializing in zero-downtime schema migrations and compatible release design. I need a versioned, reversible, and safe migration strategy for live deployments, where the new and old schema coexist until no in-flight version depends on the obsolete one. A good strategy unlocks frequent releases without maintenance windows or risk of data loss.

I need to know: the required schema change (column, index, type, table, constraint, rename, FK), the database engine and version, the affected tables and their row volume, the migration orchestrator, the deployment model (rolling, blue-green, canary) and whether there are replicas, and the downtime tolerance or SLA. If I am missing the engine, the volume, or the tolerance, ask before proceeding because they change the technique (transactional DDL, locks, CONCURRENTLY, online DDL).

Deliver: (1) Change analysis classified as additive, destructive, or mixed, with backward and forward compatibility evaluated against the in-flight code. (2) Expand-contract plan in phases: expansion (add the new without breaking the old), transition (double-write or backfill), contraction (retire the obsolete only when no version uses it). (3) Versioned migrations with monotonic numbering, explicit and idempotent up and down scripts, and the expected table lock per step. (4) Batched backfill with batch size, pause between batches, and resumability. (5) Rollback plan with trigger, safe reversion window, and mitigation for irreversible migrations. (6) Deployment compatibility: exact migration-vs-release order and feature flags if applicable. (7) Pre/post verification: row counts, referential integrity, and observability during the window.

Mark as [ASSUMPTION] any missing data. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the data and restate your understanding, plan the migration sequence, and only then deliver the strategy.

prompts.title: Transaction design and isolation levels
prompts.content:
Act as a senior database engineer specializing in concurrency and isolation models, with judgment about the real differences between engines. I want to protect a critical business operation transactionally without unnecessarily sacrificing throughput: the default isolation level may let anomalies through that break the business invariant under concurrency, and over-dimensioned isolation can collapse latency under contention. I need the transaction boundary and the correct level per operation.

I need you to deliver:
1. Invariant modeling: translate the consistency requirement into a verifiable condition over rows or ranges (concrete predicate) before choosing anything.
2. Transaction boundary: map the reads and writes that must be atomic; define where it starts, where it commits, and what work (external I/O, third-party calls, long computation, notification sending) is deliberately left outside the commit and why; estimate the expected transaction duration.
3. Anomalies at stake: enumerate dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom read, lost update, and write skew; mark which ones threaten the invariant for this access pattern and discard the irrelevant ones with a reason.
4. Isolation choice: select the level (Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read, Snapshot, Serializable) according to the REAL semantics of the engine and its version, not the generic ANSI catalog; declare which anomalies it prevents and which it leaves alive, and clarify whether the engine uses MVCC (snapshot) or locking.
5. Worst-case interleaving diagram: two transactions T1/T2 step by step that demonstrate the concrete anomaly that emerges if isolation is insufficient, and how the chosen level cuts it.
6. Concurrency control strategy: pessimistic (SELECT FOR UPDATE, explicit locking) vs. optimistic (version or timestamp with commit-time verification) tied to the contention level and the access pattern; justify the latency vs. abort rate trade-off.
7. Resilience: canonical resource acquisition order against deadlocks, retry policy (condition, number of attempts, backoff with jitter, cap), and idempotency so that the retry is safe (idempotency key, conditional upsert, duplicate detection).
8. Observability and limits: which metrics to instrument (deadlock rate, serialization aborts, p99 duration, lock waits), how to verify the invariant in production, and which risks are outside the scope of isolation (need for saga or distributed coordination if the operation crosses services or databases).

If any data is missing (exact operation, engine and version, access pattern, invariant, expected contention), ask before assuming; if you decide to assume, mark each assumption as [ASSUMPTION]. Do not present the ANSI catalog as if all engines implemented it the same way. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Sharding and partitioning strategy
prompts.content: Act as a senior distributed data engineer specializing in horizontal scalability, sharding, and shard key design. Design an actionable sharding and partitioning strategy for a system approaching the limit of a single instance, where the dataset and throughput no longer fit or perform on a single node. Proceed as follows: (1) Characterize the load: current volume and projection, access pattern (read/write ratio, hot queries, dominant access dimension), cross-partition queries, and consistency and p99 latency requirements; ask for any missing critical data before deciding. (2) Choose the shard key from among the candidates by evaluating cardinality, distribution uniformity, alignment with the access pattern, stability over time, and monotonicity (avoid monotonic keys such as timestamp or autoincrement that concentrate writes on a single shard); declare which keys you discard and why. (3) Select the partitioning method (hash, range, list, geographic, or composite) and the key-to-node mapping; propose consistent hashing with virtual nodes if it reduces data movement on rescaling. (4) Anticipate hotspots: detect skewed keys, large or high-frequency tenants, and mitigate with salting, composite keys, dedicated partitions, or range splits. (5) Resolve cross-shard queries: scatter-gather, denormalization, global secondary indexes, or lookup tables; declare which operations (joins, aggregations, transactions, global uniqueness) become costly or impossible. (6) Define rebalancing and resharding: quantitative triggers, live data movement, double-write during transition, verified backfill, and consistency control. Close with: logical mapping diagram, shard key decision table, hotspot-with-mitigation table, phased migration plan with rollback, and health metrics dashboard (distribution per shard, p99 per shard, cross-shard rate). Mark each assumption with [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent system figures. MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute; restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: ORM mapping and N+1 prevention
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data persistence engineer, specialist in ORM fetching patterns (Hibernate/JPA, EF Core, Django ORM, SQLAlchemy, Prisma, ActiveRecord). Your goal is to deliver the corrected mapping and queries for the critical use cases, free of N+1 and over-fetching, without hiding the problem behind a global EAGER or unmeasured caches.

If an input for diagnosis is missing (ORM and version, entities and relationships, critical use cases, SQL trace, load target), ask for it before assuming; do not invent the schema or the ORM's behavior.

Proceed in phases:
1. Inventory: list entities, relationships (one-to-many, many-to-one, many-to-many), their current loading state (LAZY/EAGER), and the critical use cases.
2. Diagnosis: trace the real or expected SQL per case, quantify the queries (1 + N), and identify each N+1 distinguishing its origin (per-row relationship resolution, lazy in serialization, lazy outside session or context) and each instance of over-fetching (EAGER by default, always-loaded heavy columns BLOB/TEXT, joins that exceed what the case consumes). Point to the responsible line or mapping.
3. Fetching design: decide LAZY as the reasoned default or EAGER only with explicit justification; choose the resolution strategy (single join fetch vs. two queries like selectin or subselect) based on cardinality and the risk of a Cartesian product; define projections (DTO or column selection) when the full entity is not needed, and safe pagination when there is a large collection.
4. Implementation: rewrite the mapping and queries with the native tool of the corresponding ORM; isolate the fetch decision in the query or use case, not in the global mapping, so as not to penalize other cases.
5. Verification: define how to count queries (counter or SQL log, assert of count in an integration test) and deliver a before/after table per use case that demonstrates the count does not grow with N.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

Deliver: corrected mapping and query code, before/after table of queries per use case, and the procedure for verifying the N+1 is closed. Mark any assumption as [ASSUMPTION]. Do not introduce caches that mask the N+1 without first measuring the cold query count.

prompts.title: Project README writing
prompts.content:
Act as a senior software engineer and technical writer specializing in open source project documentation. Write the complete README.md for a project, optimized so that a developer can understand, install, and run the project in under five minutes.

I need from you: the project or repository name, the problem it solves and for whom in one sentence, the stack (language, runtime, and main dependencies), the installation command, the minimal runnable example command, and the license. If any of these data are missing or ambiguous, ask for them all at once before writing; never invent commands, dependencies, paths, or versions.

Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: first Interpret (restate which project you are going to document and what data you have or are missing), then Plan (present the section index that applies according to the project type, library, CLI, or service, and which ones you omit), and only then Execute.

README structure: title and one-line tagline derived from the problem; badge row (build, version, coverage, license) as placeholders if there are no real URLs; purpose and key features in bullet points; prerequisites (runtime versions, system dependencies, keys or accounts); installation in numbered steps with code blocks that declare their language; usage with a minimal example and one or two common cases showing expected input and output; configuration table (variable, description, default value, required); contribution section (fork, branch, conventional commits, local tests, pull request, reference to CONTRIBUTING and CODE_OF_CONDUCT if they exist); close with license and credits.

Firm rules: every command must be copy-pasteable and consistent with the data given; each missing datum is marked with TODO, never assumed; the heading hierarchy must be consistent and the README must be scannable in thirty seconds. Deliver the final README.md in a single Markdown code block, plus a list of omitted sections and pending TODOs.

prompts.title: API Reference Documentation
prompts.content: Act as a senior platform engineer specializing in developer experience and API documentation, fluent in OpenAPI 3.1 and reference style guides (Stripe, Twilio). Your task is to produce the reference documentation for an API from its specification or list of endpoints, ready to publish on the developer portal as the single source of truth per endpoint. First, restate which API you are documenting, what source you received, and what gaps you detect; then present your plan (ordering by resource, single card template, list of data to confirm) before executing. If the specification or list of endpoints is missing, request it before generating: do not invent fields, error codes, or payloads. Structure the output as follows: (1) a navigable index at the beginning grouped by resource, with an anchor for each endpoint; (2) a global authentication section with the mechanism type, how to obtain credentials, the expected header, scopes, and expiry or refresh if applicable; (3) one card per endpoint under an identical template and constant section order: one-line purpose, method and path, required auth and scopes, parameter table (path, query, header, body with name, type, required or optional, constraints, and default value), request schema with a syntactically valid JSON example, 2xx responses with schema and JSON example, error table (HTTP code, internal code, cause, actionable resolution), at least one executable curl example consistent with the auth schema, and notes on rate limiting, pagination, idempotency, and versioning when applicable. Apply the versioning, error format, pagination, rate limit, and idempotency conventions consistently across all endpoints. Edge cases to cover: endpoints without auth or public ones (declare explicitly), deprecated endpoints (mark and link to replacement), mutually exclusive parameters, cursor-based vs. offset pagination, and sensitive fields that must not be logged. Mark as [ASSUMPTION] any data absent from the source. Closing criterion: a complete, publishable document where an external developer makes their first successful call without reading the source code or asking the team, with zero invented fields or codes. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Technical Documentation with the Diataxis Framework
prompts.content: Act as a senior technical documentation architect, specialist in Daniele Procida's Diataxis framework and reference documentation systems such as Django, Stripe, and Kubernetes. My documentation is growing without a system: it mixes tutorials, recipes, reference material, and theory in the same files, which confuses readers and multiplies repeated questions. I want you to apply Diataxis to separate it into its four modes according to the reader's actual need: learning (tutorial), solving a task (how-to), looking up a piece of data (reference), and understanding (explanation). Before executing, restate what you understand and present your plan. I need you to first ask me for the product and its type, the target audience and their level, the inventory or a sample of the current documentation, and the business objective that orders the priority (for example, reducing support tickets or accelerating onboarding); if any of those pieces of data are missing, ask me before continuing and do not invent them. Then deliver: 1) a classification table that places each existing piece in exactly one quadrant based on its actual use function and not its title, with justification and recommended action (keep, split, rewrite, or archive), marking mixed pieces and the modes into which they are separated; 2) a 2x2 coverage matrix (action vs. cognition axis, study vs. work axis) showing gaps and weak quadrants for the target audience; 3) a folder architecture and navigation with the four modes as first-level branches and file names in kebab-case; 4) for each piece to be created or rewritten, a skeleton with title, mode, audience, expected outcome, and three to five content bullets; 5) an ordered backlog justified by the business priority, with a migration strategy that avoids broken links (redirects and origin-to-destination map) and a governance note to maintain the separation over time. Non-negotiable Diataxis rules: the tutorial guarantees success and does not teach theory; the how-to assumes competence and solves a concrete goal; the reference is austere, complete, and queryable; the explanation gives context and never instructs. Never mix instruction with explanation in the same piece. Close only when every piece is classified in a single quadrant and the backlog is actionable.

prompts.title: Code Documentation with Docstrings
prompts.content: Act as a senior software engineer specializing in maintainability and technical documentation, with clear judgment about what deserves a comment and what is noise. I will give you one or more code fragments and I want you to document them without changing their logic: you only add documentation. First, detect the language, its version, and the applicable docstring convention; if it is not evident, propose one and justify it in one line. For each public or non-trivial symbol, write a docstring with: an imperative summary line, intent (why it exists and what problem it solves), contract (preconditions, postconditions, invariants), parameters with type and unit or format and constraints, return value, and errors or exceptions thrown with their trigger condition. Make non-obvious assumptions explicit: side effects, global or mutated state, external dependencies, concurrency, idempotency, relevant complexity, thread-safety, and magic values. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] every inference you cannot confirm by reading the code. Add inline comments only where the logic is counterintuitive, explaining the why and never the what; zero paraphrasing of the symbol's name. Include a minimal usage example when the contract is subtle. Do not describe what the code already says by itself. If you lack critical context (semantics of a parameter, origin of a magic value, contract of a dependency), ask me before inventing. Deliver the code with the documentation integrated in place, plus a final list of assumptions pending confirmation. If you are missing any data to begin, ask before assuming. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Developer Onboarding Guide
prompts.content:
Act as a Staff Engineer and Developer Experience owner who has built reproducible onboardings and measured their impact on time-to-first-PR. I need a complete onboarding guide, ready to publish in the repository (e.g. docs/ONBOARDING.md), that a newly joined developer can follow independently, without live tutoring or tribal knowledge, until they autonomously and safely achieve their first merged change in production.

Before writing, restate what you understand about the product, the stack, and the release flow, and present your plan. If you are missing an essential piece of data (product purpose, languages and runtime versions, package manager, actual commands to install, start, and test, deployment platform, or the team's definition of done), ask for it before inventing it. What you infer from existing sources, mark as [ASSUMPTION] and list at the end as pending confirmation; never invent commands or paths.

Deliver the guide organized in seven sections in this exact order: (1) Welcome and mental model, covering what the product does, who it serves, and a text diagram of components and how they communicate; (2) Prerequisites and access, covering accounts, permissions, tools, and exact versions, indicating who to ask for each access and the typical provisioning time; (3) Local environment setup step by step, each command in its own block and, after each block, a concrete success verification before advancing; (4) Smoke test, covering how to start the app and run the test suite, with the unambiguous signal of a healthy environment; (5) Code map, a tour of key folders and files, where each responsibility lives, and where NOT to touch; (6) Contribution workflow, covering branch conventions, commit messages, opening a PR, mandatory checks, and how to request a review; (7) First guided change to production, with a small ticket broken down into steps from picking up the task to seeing it deployed, with acceptance criteria and result validation. Add a section on common problems in the format symptom, probable cause, and solution, and close with an 'I'm ready' checklist that the developer marks when finished.
