Close with a three-row summary table, a sequence plan indicating the anchor piece to produce first per stage, and a block of three bottleneck diagnostic signals — one per stage — each with its actionable interpretation. Mark every inference without data as [ASSUMPTION]. If you are missing the offer, the audience, the buying cycle, the channels, or the main objective, ask me before executing. Do not mention prices. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Editorial and writing style guide
prompts.content:
Act as an editor-in-chief and senior brand linguist, with a track record defining editorial style manuals for media and brands in neutral Spanish. Your assignment is to build an editorial and writing style guide ready to adopt as the official reference document and to feed a writing AI, so that writers, designers, and AI produce consistent texts without piece-by-piece review.

Proceed as follows. First, distill the brand's voice attributes into three to five principles, each with its operational definition (what to do in practice, not an adjective) and a correct-versus-incorrect example pair; if I have reference texts, extract the actual patterns from them rather than inventing them. Second, codify grammar and mechanics: person and tense, active voice, sentence and paragraph length, commas in enumerations, capitalization in headings, and format for numbers, dates, times, percentages, and currencies. Third, define format and structure: heading hierarchy, when to use bullets versus prose, use of bold, link style, and call-to-action format. Fourth, build a preferred terminology table (approved term versus term to avoid), with the exact capitalization of product names and the handling of acronyms and anglicisms, calibrated to my audience and channels. Fifth, draft ten to fifteen Do and Don't rules in correct/incorrect pairs. Sixth, list the inviolable brand restrictions in a Compliance section. Seventh, close with a publication checklist that an editor runs through before publishing.

Each rule must be verifiable, not aspirational, and accompanied by an example where applicable. Mark as [ASSUMPTION] every inference that does not derive from data I have provided; do not invent brand data. If I am missing an essential data point (brand, voice attributes, target audience, channels, or reference texts), ask for it specifically before executing.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliver in neutral professional Spanish, without emojis, without mentioning prices or cost figures, and without using the word free or promotional synonyms. Document in second-level headings, with tables and correct/incorrect pairs. The wordplay EstrategIA is permitted at most once.

prompts.title: Paid search campaign structure by intent
prompts.content:
Act as a senior paid search (PPC) strategist with experience managing high-budget accounts on Google Ads and Microsoft Ads, specialized in intent-based account architecture. I need to convert a scattered keyword list into a governable account architecture where each campaign and ad group maps a distinct search intent: a structure organized by intent and match type is what unlocks relevance between keyword, ad, and landing page, spend control by funnel stage, and a sustainable Quality Score. Without it, campaigns cannibalize each other, search terms spill over, and budget leaks toward irrelevant traffic.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. First, restate what product or offer I am promoting, in what market, language, and audience, what the measurable objective and the conversion that counts are, and what my value proposition is. If the product, market, or objective is missing, ask for it before continuing; do not invent the offer. Then present me with the intent map and the proposed campaign and group tree for validation before detailing keywords.

Once validated, deliver the complete blueprint:
1. Intent map: classify demand into brand, high-intent generic (transactional), category or research (informational-commercial), and competitors; indicate which to target first and why, based on proximity to conversion and cost of entry.
2. Campaigns: one campaign per intent or stage, with its funnel role, canonical name, and budget separation logic (what each campaign isolates and why they do or do not share budget).
3. Ad groups by theme: within each campaign, group keywords by a single meaning; per group deliver name, 5 to 12 keywords with their match type (exact, phrase, or broad) and the match type justification based on volume and intent (broad only with Smart Bidding and sufficient conversions; exact for high-intent terms with low irrelevance risk).
4. Negatives: negative terms per group (anti-cannibalization between groups and anti-irrelevance), plus a layer of negatives at campaign and account level that seals leaks between intents (brand vs. generic, generic vs. competitors).
5. Ad angle: per group, the message angle that responds to that intent to align keyword, ad, and landing page, plus the landing page implication if the current page does not match.
6. Governance: consistent naming convention, SKAG vs. STAG vs. thematic recommendation justified by volume, and minimum measurement plan (conversion that counts, search term report review cadence, and observable signal for when to restructure).

Mark every volume or performance estimate as [ASSUMPTION] and flag any pending data; do not invent figures. Deliver the blueprint as a tree or table ready to build the account.

prompts.title: Meta Ads campaign structure with CBO
prompts.content:
Act as a senior paid media strategist specialized in Meta Ads (Facebook and Instagram), with experience managing campaign-level budget with Advantage Campaign Budget (CBO) in performance accounts, and mastery of the learning phase, attribution, and audience overlap. Your task is to design the complete, buildable structure of a CBO campaign, where a single budget lives at the campaign level and the algorithm distributes it in real time toward the audience-and-creative combinations that perform best. A poorly assembled hierarchy (too many ad sets, overlapping audiences, budget that does not feed learning, unnecessary spend limits) fragments signals, traps ad sets in learning, and drives up cost per result.

Proceed as follows: (1) define the correct campaign objective and optimization event for the desired business outcome, justifying the choice against the funnel; (2) determine the number of ad sets and the segmentation logic for each, avoiding overlap that would cannibalize delivery and keeping them bounded to avoid fragmenting budget (start from a few broad ad sets and consolidate rather than multiply); (3) recommend campaign-level budget using the 50x rule, where the optimization event should be able to reach approximately 50 conversions per week per active ad set to exit the learning phase; if volume does not allow it, propose optimizing a higher-funnel event (e.g., initiate checkout or add to cart instead of purchase); (4) indicate whether minimum or maximum spend limits per ad set are advisable and why, with the default criterion of not using them because they restrict the algorithm; (5) define 3 to 5 ads per ad set with distinct creative angles (not cosmetic variations) and a consistent naming convention campaign | ad set | creative; (6) deliver a table with the final structure ready for Ads Manager with campaign, ad sets, placements, attribution window, and creatives; (7) specify reading rules: duration and care of the learning phase without edits that restart it, the metric that defines the winner, when to consolidate budget, and when to turn off. Close with a two-week EstrategIA iteration plan: what to watch, what not to touch, and what to adjust.

Mark with [ASSUMPTION] everything you assume. Do not invent benchmark figures or cost-per-result figures; express volumes as ranges or relative terms. If you are missing a critical piece of data (especially the conversion event and whether pixel or CAPI is installed), ask before designing. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Respond in professional English, no emojis, and without mentioning investment amounts.

prompts.title: Responsive search ad copy (RSA)
prompts.content: Act as a senior SEM specialist and direct-response copywriter with proven experience in Google Ads RSA. Your objective is to produce a responsive search ad ready to upload that maximizes relevance (Quality Score) and CTR without breaking character limits or policies. Before writing, restate what you understand about the product, the main keyword, the value proposition, the audience, and the desired action, and present your intent and variation group plan. If any of those five key data points is missing, ask for them before continuing. Then deliver: 15 headlines of up to 30 characters each with their visible count, distributed across four intents (keyword insertion with {KeyWord:fallback} syntax whose fallback text fits within 30 characters, benefit, proof or differentiator, and call to action); 4 descriptions of up to 90 characters each with count and intent; an explicit pin recommendation for positions 1 and 2 of the must-have headlines leaving the rest in rotation; assignment of each element to a variation group to avoid message cannibalization; and 2 display URL paths of up to 15 characters each with a relevance note connecting keyword, headline, and landing page. Respect these rules: never include prices, never use the word meaning without cost, no emojis, neutral professional English; mark every data point without a source as [DATA TO CONFIRM]. Deliver a table with columns element, text, count, intent, group, and pin, plus the paths block and the relevance note, ready to paste into Google Ads. MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute.

prompts.title: Paid social creative matrix by angle
prompts.content:
Act as a senior paid social strategist specialized in performance creative, with practice in Meta Ads, TikTok Ads, and LinkedIn Ads and in angle-testing frameworks. I want to move from producing scattered creatives by intuition to a system where each piece validates an isolated hypothesis: a matrix that crosses message angles x formats x hooks to cover the message space with discipline and reinvest the learning in the next batch.

To produce the matrix I need you to know the product or offer and its central value proposition, the audience (profile, main pain point, context), the primary paid social platform, the campaign objective, how many variants I want in the first test batch, and any brand restrictions (prohibited claims, tone, limits). If any of these critical data points is missing, ask for it before continuing; do not invent the value proposition or the audience.

MetodologIA Protocol: first restate in your own words what you understood about the product, the audience, and the objective; second present your work plan; third execute only after presenting the plan.

Deliver in this order:
1. Angles: 4 to 6 message angles with real contrast among them (not variations of the same message). Cover levers such as pain/agitation, functional benefit, social proof, objection/counter-objection, identity/aspiration, and comparative, as applicable. Write the central proposition of each angle in one sentence and name the audience insight it activates.
2. Formats: define the formats to produce that are coherent with the platform and objective (short hook video, educational carousel, static with strong copy, UGC testimonial, before/after, or others), justifying each choice by its fit with the funnel stage and the platform algorithm.
3. Hooks: 2 to 3 opening hooks per angle (first 3 seconds or first line), each with its explicit psychological lever and the objection or curiosity it triggers.
4. Matrix: table with one row per variant with ID, angle, format, hook, main copy, CTA, and the falsifiable hypothesis it validates (format 'if... then... measured by...').
5. Prioritization: mark the first batch with the number of variants I requested, flag the high-contrast bets to isolate learnings, and declare what variables are kept constant across pieces so as not to confuse the learning.
6. Reading plan: decision metric per stage (hook: hook rate / 3s retention; persuasion: CTR, CVR, or equivalent), minimum impression threshold per variant before judging, loser cut rule, and second-batch iteration rule (what to keep, what to discard, what new hypothesis opens).

Rules: do not invent prices or investment figures; do not use the word free; declare any assumptions you make and mark as pending any data that is missing; neutral professional English, no emojis. Close only when the first-batch matrix is complete and the reading plan is actionable for a media buyer with no additional context.

prompts.title: Cold, warm, and hot audience structure
prompts.content: Act as a senior paid media strategist with more than ten years in Meta Ads, TikTok Ads, and LinkedIn Ads and full-funnel B2C and B2B acquisition funnels. Design a cold, warm, and hot audience structure ready to set up in Ads Manager. Most paid social budget is wasted showing the same ad and the same offer to people at opposing decision moments: the stranger who has just discovered the category receives the same thing as the customer ready to convert. Your job is to assign to each funnel level the message, offer, creative, and metric that correspond to it. Before executing, restate in your own words the business, the audience, the platforms, the conversion objective, and the available data assets; ask for any missing data instead of inventing it, and mark as [ASSUMPTION] everything you infer. Deliver: (1) definition of the three temperatures with mutually exclusive membership criteria and concrete audience source per platform; cold is new audiences with no contact (interests, lookalikes, broad segments, advantage+), warm is engagement without conversion (web visitors, video views from 25 percent, profile engagement, cart or form abandonment), hot is high intent or customer (buyers, leads, own list, checkout retargeting); (2) per temperature, the message angle derived from the prospect's awareness level according to Eugene Schwartz's five levels, the type of offer, and the recommended creative format; (3) retargeting map connecting the three levels, naming the trigger event and the time window at each jump from cold to warm and from warm to hot, avoiding overlap through audience exclusions; (4) primary and secondary metric per temperature coherent with its function (reach, CPM, and CTR for cold; cost per interaction, video depth, and frequency for warm; CPA and ROAS for hot); (5) suggested budget distribution across levels expressed in percentages, with the logic behind it; (6) one-page summary table with columns temperature, source, awareness level, message, offer, creative, and metric; (7) three prioritized A/B tests for the first two weeks, each with hypothesis, isolated variable, and success criterion. If traffic volume or the own list is insufficient for reliable custom audiences or lookalikes, flag it and propose an alternate route. Do not include prices or the word suggesting absence of cost; write in neutral professional English, no emojis.

prompts.title: Bid strategy by campaign objective
prompts.content:
Act as a senior paid media strategist (Google Ads and Meta) expert in Smart Bidding and acquisition unit economics. I am going to configure or audit the bid strategy for a campaign and I need to align the bid model to the real business KPI, not to the platform default: a correct choice lets the algorithm optimize toward the result (CPA, ROAS, or volume); an incorrect one burns investment in poorly calibrated learning.

Deliver a bid model recommendation with an implementation plan. First, restate what you understand about the objective and present your plan before executing; if you are missing a critical piece of data (primary KPI, platform and campaign type, conversion history, budget), ask for it before recommending instead of assuming it.

Then proceed as follows: 1) Map the KPI to the correct model: volume with no efficiency ceiling and budget to spend goes to Maximize conversions; controlled CPA goes to tCPA; profitability or ROAS with variable conversion values goes to tROAS; maximum value with fixed budget goes to Maximize value; awareness or consideration phases go to CPM/CPV or Maximize clicks as a bridge. 2) Audit prerequisites against historical data: sufficient recent volume (indicative reference of approximately 30 conversions in 30 days for tCPA and approximately 50 for tROAS; mark as assumption any unconfirmed data) and correctly instrumented conversion and value tracking. 3) Set the initial target from the real data (real CPA for tCPA, real ROAS for tROAS) with a progressive ramp, never aggressive targets on day one. 4) Define the expected learning period and the rule of not moving target or budget by more than 20% while it lasts. 5) Define guardrails tied to budget, alert signals, and adjustment triggers.

Consider edge cases: new account without historical data (start with volume bidding and define the threshold to migrate to target bidding), seasonality or promotions that distort history, conversion values not instrumented that invalidate tROAS, budget too low to exit learning, and mixing funnel stages in the same campaign. Flag trade-offs when they exist (efficiency vs. volume, control vs. learning speed).

Deliverable: bid strategy card with (a) recommended model and one-sentence justification, (b) initial target and its calculation basis, (c) prerequisites checklist with status, (d) transition and learning plan, (e) guardrails and triggers table. No prices or gratuitous promises; neutral professional English.

prompts.title: Retargeting sequence by intent level
prompts.content:
Act as a senior paid media strategist specialized in performance retargeting and audience architecture. Your assignment: design a stepped retargeting sequence by intent level, ready for a team to configure on their advertising platforms. Before executing, apply the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before producing the deliverable.

First ask for the data you need if I do not have it on hand: the offer and who it targets, the typical purchase cycle duration and the relative weight of the ticket, the available advertising platforms, the behavioral events that are actually tracked today, and the final action that counts as a conversion. Do not invent events or figures: if an event is not tracked, do not use it as an audience and say so.

Then execute in five phases. Phase 1 - Framing: restate offer, cycle, and available events; mark with [ASSUMPTION] every window or frequency you estimate. Phase 2 - Intent ladder: order the tracked events from lowest to highest intent (e.g., shallow visit, interest, consideration, high intent, hot abandonment) and justify the cutoff for each retention window based on the purchase cycle. Phase 3 - Design per step: for each level define the seven elements: audience (exact behavioral condition plus retention window in days), message angle and promise based on awareness level, format and piece, call to action, frequency window plus impression cap per person, exclusion logic, and exit criterion. Phase 4 - Exclusion architecture: trace the inclusion/exclusion matrix that guarantees mutual exclusivity between steps and excludes converters from all levels. Phase 5 - Flow and control: draw the complete journey between steps (what moves the person to the next level, what makes them expire, what removes them by conversion or saturation) and assign three control metrics per step, at least one of cost, one of relevance, and one of advancement.

Deliver a document with the intent ladder, one card per step, the exclusion matrix, the flow map, and the control metrics. Flag as an edge case what to do when an audience is too small to serve (step merger or window extension, marked [ASSUMPTION]) and how to handle overlap between platforms. Use neutral professional English, no prices, no the word free, and without promising guaranteed results.

prompts.title: Creative testing plan with iterative method
prompts.content:
Act as a senior creative testing strategist in paid media, with experience managing acquisition budgets and designing experiments with statistical rigor. Design an iterative creative testing plan that turns advertising into a learning machine: each round isolates a variable, tests a falsifiable hypothesis, and promotes only winners with statistical backing, so that the cost of acquisition drops sustainably instead of depending on a lucky break.

First restate what you understand about the business objective, the advertising platform, the primary decision metric, and the available conversion volume; present your plan before executing. If any of those four data points or the budget in investment units is missing, ask for it before continuing: without them the sample cannot be sized.

Deliver: (1) prioritized variable table (hook, format, message angle, offer, CTA) by expected impact vs. effort, with the one-variable-per-round rule; (2) a falsifiable hypothesis per variant with the structure if I change X then I expect Y in the primary metric because W; (3) winner criterion set BEFORE launching: primary metric, minimum relevant improvement (MDE), confidence level, power target, and sample size derived from available volume; (4) at least one guardrail metric per test to discard false winners (e.g., CTR rises but CPA spikes, or initial conversion rises but retention or LTV drops); (5) cadence by rounds with an explicit rule for promoting the winner to control and archiving the loser with its learning; (6) accumulated learnings log template; (7) an early stopping protocol to halt clearly losing variants without waiting for the full sample.

Size the minimum sample and learning window from conversion volume. If volume does not reach significance, do not force the calculation: warn about the risk of inconclusive tests and propose alternatives (sequential reading with correction, early signals such as CTR or playback rate, consolidate budget into fewer variants, or raise the MDE so the test is decidable). Respect the platform algorithm's learning phase and avoid reading results during it. Do not invent benchmarks or historical figures: mark every assumption as [ASSUMPTION]. Neutral professional English, no prices.

prompts.title: Target ROAS and break-even calculation
prompts.content:
Act as a senior performance marketing analyst specialized in unit economics and paid media profitability for e-commerce and direct acquisition. I need to know whether my advertising investment is profitable and at what efficiency level I should operate, because without a clear break-even ROAS I scale or pause campaigns blindly and confuse a high panel ROAS with real margin.

Before calculating, confirm that you have the average ticket or average order value, the variable costs per order (in value and/or as a percentage of the sale), and the operating margin goal I want to preserve after advertising. If any of those three data points is missing or inconsistent, ask for it; do not invent figures. If you receive costs in both value and percentage, warn about the double-counting risk and clarify what component each covers before adding them.

Then calculate, with visible arithmetic at each step: (1) contribution margin per order = ticket minus variable costs in value minus (ticket times the variable cost percentage), expressed in value and as a percentage of the ticket; (2) break-even ROAS = 1 divided by the contribution margin in decimal, which is the minimum ROAS without operating loss per order; (3) target ROAS = 1 divided by (contribution margin in decimal minus target margin in decimal), which reserves profit after advertising; validate that (margin minus goal) is positive, because if the goal equals or exceeds the margin the target ROAS tends to infinity and you must flag it as an unachievable goal with that economics. Define the maximum allowed CPA: equal to the contribution margin in value for break-even, and equal to margin minus goal in value for the target.

Build a table of three scenarios (break-even, conservative target, aggressive target) with ROAS, equivalent ACOS (1 divided by ROAS, as a percentage), and CPA cap in each. Close with actionable reading: what panel ROAS I must exceed, how to read the gap between the ROAS reported by the platform and the real margin ROAS, bid and budget recommendations, and a sensitivity analysis showing how break-even and CPA cap move with +/- 10% variations in ticket and variable costs.

Clarify these limits: the calculation is per order and first purchase, it does not incorporate LTV or repurchase unless I indicate so; panel ROAS is usually inflated by attribution and must be contrasted against real sales or margin; taxes and returns are not modeled unless included in variable costs. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the data, Plan the calculation, and only then Execute. Mark every estimate as [ASSUMPTION] and do not assume market prices. Deliver a brief memo in neutral professional English, no emojis.

prompts.title: Performance Max campaign configuration by asset groups
prompts.content:
I need you to configure the complete structure of a Google Ads Performance Max campaign, organized by asset groups, ready to upload to the platform. Act as a senior Google Ads specialist certified in search and display, focused on Performance Max and asset strategy for acquisition. Context: PMax consolidates Search, Display, YouTube, Discover, Gmail, and Maps in a single campaign governed by the conversion signal; its performance depends less on manual bids and more on how asset groups are structured, because each group feeds the algorithm with coherent creatives, search themes, and audience signals. A poorly defined group mixes incompatible audiences and dilutes learning.

Before writing, apply the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret what you understand about the offer, the conversion objective, the audience, and the market; Plan the groups you are going to create and why; then Execute. If you are missing a critical piece of data (conversion objective, audience segments, or market), ask for it before producing.

Deliver: 1) 2 to 4 asset groups, each representing a coherent audience or line; name each group and declare who it represents and what funnel stage it operates in. 2) Per group, 5 to 10 search themes that express the prospect's intent (not standalone product names). 3) Per group, the audience signals: own segments (customers, visitors, converters), custom segments by interest or intent, and demographic data, with one line justifying why each signal accelerates learning. 4) Per group, the asset inventory with exact counts and limits: 3 to 5 short headlines (up to 30 characters), 5 long headlines (up to 90), 5 descriptions (up to 90, one up to 60), business name, up to 5 logos, up to 20 images (landscape, square, portrait), up to 5 videos, and final URL; write real headlines and descriptions, not templates. 5) Per group, the message angle and value proposition based on the differentiators. 6) A funnel coverage map (prospecting vs. recurring) and 3 early signals to read learning in the first two weeks without touching budget in that period.

Restrictions: zero mention of prices, discounts, or the word indicating the service is given away; neutral professional English, no emojis; each group unique and coherent, no catch-all buckets; message, search theme, and signal of each group point to the same intent. Verify counts and character limits before closing. If no video is provided, indicate how to substitute with images and note that PMax can auto-generate video. Deliverable: document structured by asset groups ready to upload.

prompts.title: Paid media plan and budget allocation by channel
prompts.content:
Act as a senior paid media strategist who has managed multichannel budgets and reasons by marginal CAC and saturation curves, not by equal distribution or inertia. I need to allocate a paid media budget across several channels to convert a campaign objective, a target CAC and historical performance into a defensible allocation: how much goes to each channel, why, with what saturation ceiling and under what rule it is reallocated.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First reframe the objective, budget, channels, target CAC, time horizon and level of available history; mark as [ASSUMPTION] any data I have not provided and present your plan before executing. If a critical piece of data is missing (dominant objective, budget and its periodicity, list of channels, CAC or acceptable cap, time horizon), ask before assuming.

Then deliver: (1) classification of each channel by the funnel stage it best serves (cold prospecting, consideration, direct conversion, retargeting) and by its role relative to the objective; (2) estimated efficiency per channel with a declared evidence hierarchy (CAC observed in my historical data > industry benchmark marked [ASSUMPTION] > proxy by CPM/CTR/CVR), naming the source of each figure; (3) saturation ceiling per channel, locating the point where marginal CAC rises due to exhausting quality audience; (4) base mix as a percentage of the budget, stress-tested against the target CAC and without over-concentrating in a single channel without justification; (5) a test pool of 10 to 20 percent for channels or creatives without history, with hypothesis and success criterion; (6) per allocation, KPI, reallocation threshold, pause threshold and reading window within the time horizon.

Edge cases: if there is no history, base the entire mix on benchmarks marked [ASSUMPTION] and raise the test pool to the upper limit. If the target CAC does not appear achievable with the given channels, say so and propose adjusting the target, expanding channels or reviewing the offer. If I depend on a single channel, flag the concentration risk and reserve an alternative.

Output format: channel-by-channel table (funnel role, CAC source, expected CAC, mix weight, saturation ceiling, KPI, cut threshold) + summary of the allocation reasoning + list of [ASSUMPTION] items + test plan with scaling and pause criteria. Reason in percentages and CAC multiples, never in invented monetary figures. Neutral, professional Spanish, no emojis.

prompts.title: Creative fatigue diagnosis and rotation plan
prompts.content:
Act as a senior paid media strategist specializing in performance and creative management at scale, with the judgment to separate real fatigue from measurement noise. I need a creative fatigue diagnosis and a rotation plan with a calendar for my campaigns. Before diagnosing, briefly reframe what you understand and present your plan. If any critical data is missing (platform, campaign objective, temporal window of the data, primary cost or result metric, per-ad data on impressions, frequency, reach, CTR, CPM and spend), ask me for it before continuing instead of inventing it.

Proceed as follows. First, consolidate the data per ad for the period: impressions, frequency, reach, CTR, CPM, the primary metric and spend; validate coverage and quality and list missing fields. Second, trace the performance curve of each creative over time and locate the inflection point where frequency rises while CTR falls and the primary metric deteriorates. Third, classify each piece as healthy, on alert or fatigued with explicit and reproducible thresholds: frequency limit, relative CTR drop compared to its best week and deviation of the primary metric from the period average; declare each threshold. Fourth, discriminate real fatigue (sustained degradation from overexposure, at least two weeks) from noise (seasonality, bid or budget changes, exhausted audience, supply or tracking problem, insufficient volume for significance); contrast each borderline case against these explanations before concluding. Fifth, issue a verdict per creative: keep, watch, refresh variant or retire, each with its numerical evidence. Sixth, define the refresh cadence (how often to rotate, how many variants per cycle, what angles or hooks to test) and a staggered replacement sequence that does not restart the algorithm's learning phase. Seventh, deliver a 4-to-6-week rotation calendar with monitoring routine and early rotation triggers.

Rules: back every verdict with numbers, not intuition; mark every estimate as [ASSUMPTION]; flag with [VERIFY] anything that depends on data I don't have; if the volume is insufficient to distinguish signal from noise, say so instead of forcing a diagnosis; do not promise guaranteed results and do not include prices. Deliverable: per-creative diagnosis table with verdict, rotation plan with cadence and 4-to-6-week calendar with monitoring routine.

prompts.title: Welcome and onboarding email sequence
prompts.content: Act as a senior email lifecycle and CRM strategist specializing in activation and early retention flows. Design a complete welcome and onboarding email sequence ready to automate. I need you to first ask me for, if I don't provide them, the following data: what I offer and who subscribes, the event that triggers entry into the flow, the specific action that defines an activated user, the brand voice, the sending tool and, optionally, how many emails I want. Before drafting: (1) declare the single objective of the flow and the activation metric derived from the target action; discard secondary objectives that dilute; (2) map the subscriber's state at each step (just entered, exploring the value, resolving doubts or objections, ready to act) and name the friction that each email removes; (3) define the structure: number of emails (recommend between 4 and 6 with justification if you are not told), behavioral or time-based trigger and unique purpose of each send, plus an exit rule when the contact has already activated so as not to over-send. Then draft each email with: objective, two or three subject line options (one direct, one curiosity-driven), a preheader that complements without repeating the subject, a complete body ready to paste, a single call to action and a personalization or segmentation note. Close with a reactivation email for those who did not open or execute the action and a flow summary table (email, trigger, objective, CTA, metric). Add deliverability risks to watch (first send, frequency, fatigue) and an expected numerical success criterion per email where you can estimate one; mark any missing data as [ASSUMPTION] instead of inventing it. MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; reframe what you understand and present the plan before executing. Write in neutral, professional Spanish, no emojis, no prices and without the word free.

prompts.title: Abandoned cart recovery flow
prompts.content:
Act as a senior email marketing and ecommerce lifecycle automation specialist, with experience measuring recovery rates and deliverability. I need an abandoned cart recovery flow ready to configure. A high fraction of purchase intent is lost in the cart: the visitor showed explicit desire but did not complete, and that revenue evaporates if we don't recover it through relevance and timing instead of price. I want a strategy that converts without eroding margin or training the customer to wait for discounts, and without burning sender reputation.

Before drafting, ask me for any missing data: what is sold and its key feature, the cart ticket range, the automation platform, the brand voice, and the non-monetary value courtesy we will reserve for the last email. If I don't have that incentive yet, propose two or three options coherent with the product.

Deliver in four steps. First, reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing. Second, design the cadence: define the entry trigger and the initial wait window before the first email, then a sequence of 3 to 4 emails with send times relative to the abandonment (for example 1h, 24h, 48-72h), each with a different objective and angle that escalates from useful reminder to objection handling to trust reinforcement, without cannibalization between emails. Third, draft for each email a subject line, preheader, brief body and a single CTA that returns to the cart; reserve the value courtesy only for the last email, named by its benefit and never as a discount. Fourth, specify the exit conditions from the flow: completed purchase, opt-out or unsubscribe, and sequence exhausted.

Brand and delivery rules: no prices, no the word free, no false urgency or invented countdown timers; a single CTA per email; brevity; consistent tone throughout the sequence; respect suppressions and consent. Close with the cadence table, the copy block per email and the list of exit conditions.

prompts.title: Email list segmentation with RFM model
prompts.content:
Act as a senior CRM and email marketing specialist with mastery of RFM analytics and customer lifecycle stages. I need to convert a flat contact list into actionable segments to personalize my email campaigns; today I treat everyone the same and that burns the list, lowers engagement and leaves value on the table. With the RFM model (Recency, Frequency, Monetary value) I will be able to know whom to retain, whom to reactivate and whom to let cool down, and unlock a messaging strategy differentiated by the real value of each relationship.

I want you to deliver an RFM segmentation map with a personalization plan per segment. Before executing, reframe in your own words what you understood and present your plan; if you are missing any critical data (the contact list with its three key fields, the reference date, the analysis window or the business objective), ask me for it instead of inventing it.

Proceed as follows: 1) Validate the data: confirm that each contact has the last purchase or interaction date, number of events and accumulated monetary value; mark non-critical gaps as [ASSUMPTION] and halt the flow only for critical gaps. 2) Compute R, F and M per contact with a 1-to-5 score by quintiles and document the cutoff for each quintile; if the sample is too small for stable quintiles, say so and propose terciles or justified fixed thresholds. 3) Assign each contact to exactly one named segment: Champions, Loyal, Potential to Retain, New, Promising, Need Attention, At Risk, About to Sleep, Hibernating, Can't Lose Them. 4) Build the master table with, per segment: size, percentage, profile, message angle, offer or hook, channel and cadence, and success metric. 5) Recommend the 3 segments to activate first, prioritized by impact against effort and justified relative to the objective.

Edge cases to resolve: contacts with no purchases go into a separate group (prospects), do not force RFM on them; value outliers must not distort the cutoffs, comment on them; in case of quintile ties, use recency as the tiebreaker. Close with: RFM segmentation table plus personalization plan per segment plus top-3 activation list. Zero invented figures, assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION], neutral and professional Spanish, no prices, no freeness promises, no emojis.

prompts.title: Nurturing campaign with educational drip sequence
prompts.content:
Act as a senior email marketing and lifecycle strategist, specializing in B2B nurturing, with over a decade building drip sequences that move leads from subscription to conversion. I want an educational nurturing sequence that matures a lead stage by stage: they submitted their email but are not yet ready to speak with sales, and pushing them toward conversion now burns them. The purpose is to build trust with real utility before asking for anything, so as to achieve an orderly transition from subscriber to qualified opportunity.

If I have not given you the lead profile, the problem the offer solves and the result it enables, the educational assets available (guide, webinar, case study, template), the number of emails (I recommend 5 to 7) and the behavioral signal or lead score that marks the mature lead, ask for it before drafting; do not invent any of these data points.

Proceed as follows. First, map the five stages of buyer awareness (unaware of the problem, problem-aware, solution-aware, product-aware, most aware) and align them with the decision phases (discovery, consideration, evaluation, decision). Assign each email exactly one stage, so the sequence escalates without jumps or backtracking and each email builds on the idea of the previous one. For each email draft eight fields: number and purpose in one line; awareness stage; send day relative to entry (D+0, D+2, ...) with cadence that opens up as the sequence advances; two contrasting subject line options (one curiosity-driven, one concrete-benefit); opening hook; central educational idea, a single useful concept that adds value on its own and is not a disguised sales pitch; call to action proportional to the stage, escalating from reading to responding to scheduling without asking for the conversion before its time; behavioral signal that enables progression. Then define the branching logic for three minimum routes: opens without clicking, clicks without responding, and the milestone that declares the lead mature and hands them off to sales. Include an exit path for the lead who does not interact after two or three emails (frequency reduction or pause) and a handover note to sales with the context the representative needs.

Firm rules: never mention prices or the word free (value is communicated through the utility of the content); neutral and professional Spanish, no emojis; do not invent performance metrics and mark every assumption as [ASSUMPTION]. Before drafting, reframe what you understand about the assignment and present the stage-phase map with the email-stage assignment and cadence for my confirmation; only then draft the complete emails and the branching tree, ready to load into an automation tool.

prompts.title: Subject line generation and A/B testing
prompts.content: Act as a senior email marketing copywriter and lifecycle experimentation specialist, expert in subject line writing and A/B open-rate test design. Your deliverable is a table of eight subject line variants plus an A/B experiment card ready to load into the sending platform. Before drafting, confirm with me: target audience, product or topic, campaign objective, historical reference open rate and list size. If any of these five data points is missing, ask me for it; do not invent values because the experimental design depends on them. Generate eight subject lines covering six psychological angles: information-gap curiosity, genuine urgency or scarcity, concrete benefit, social proof, segmentation-based personalization and before-after contrast. Do not duplicate an angle unless you justify it. For each subject line deliver text of maximum fifty characters, a complementary preheader that does not repeat the subject line's keywords, the angle and the cognitive trigger in one line. Then define the experiment: falsifiable hypothesis, primary metric of unique open rate, guardrails for spam complaints and unsubscribes, audience split, minimum sample size per arm based on the baseline rate and the minimum detectable effect, measurement window and decision rule with numerical threshold. If the list is too small to detect the desired effect, say so and propose reducing variants or increasing the minimum detectable effect. Distinguish a two-arm champion-versus-challenger test from a multivariate test; recommend whichever the sample size supports. Flag validity risks: short window biased by time zone, novelty effect, cross-arm contamination. Do not use prices, do not use the word free, do not use emojis; neutral professional Spanish. Close with the variants table and the experiment card, plus a note on what to measure in the next iteration. MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. Reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Win-back reactivation campaign for inactive contacts
prompts.content:
Act as a senior CRM and email lifecycle strategist with experience in deliverability and sender reputation management. I need a complete win-back reactivation flow for a dormant cohort on my list, because inactive contacts drag down the deliverability of the entire base and increase the spam risk; the objective is not to send more, but to re-engage those who can still come back and gracefully unsubscribe those who no longer will.

Before drafting, tell me what data you are missing (segment size, brand and voice, sending platform, operational definition of inactive, best re-engagement value proposition). If any piece of data does not arrive, declare an explicit assumption marked as [ASSUMPTION] and continue; do not invent business figures.

Deliver: (1) operational inactivity criterion and segmentation into three cohorts (recent, deep, zombies) with the default action and estimated size of each, assigning effort intensity inversely to depth; (2) a sequence of 4 to 5 emails with tone escalation up to an explicit final unsubscribe notice, each email with objective, subject line, preheader, body angle, a single call to action, wait window until the next touch and early exit criterion if the subscriber reacts; (3) technical hygiene rules that protect reputation: send only from a warmed IP/domain, gradual send pace, verified SPF/DKIM/DMARC authentication and complaint monitoring; (4) a sunset plan that defines who is suppressed, who gets reduced cadence, how a reactivated subscriber is marked and how they are reintegrated into the regular flow; (5) success metrics with decision threshold (re-open, click, reactivation, spam complaints, unsubscribes, post-cleanup deliverability improvement) and an operable send calendar.

Edge cases to cover: what to do if the zombie cohort exceeds the safe complaint threshold, how to handle subscribers with unverifiable consent, and how to avoid reactivating contacts who only open to unsubscribe.

Restrictions: no prices, no the word free, neutral and professional Spanish, no emojis. Maximum one brand wink. Close with the consolidated deliverable: cohort table, sequence ready to load, sunset plan and KPI dashboard with calendar.

prompts.title: Email marketing map by customer lifecycle
prompts.content:
Act as a senior email marketing and lifecycle automation strategist with over 10 years designing behavior-triggered flows. I want to convert a scattered contact list into a lifecycle-orchestrated email system, where each contact receives the right message according to their stage, from cold lead to loyal customer and promoter. Before executing, reframe what you understand and present your plan; if you are missing any essential data (business and industry, model and purchase cycle duration, available email/lifecycle platform, segments or personas to differentiate, priority objective of the map), ask me for it in a single batch before proceeding and mark any assumption with [ASSUMPTION].

Deliverable: a lifecycle email marketing map, ready to configure. First define the lifecycle stages (minimum: subscriber/lead, nurtured lead, opportunity/trial, new customer in onboarding, active customer, at-risk customer, loyal customer/promoter), adjusting or renaming according to the purchase model; declare the membership criterion for each stage so it is mutually exclusive and a contact never falls into two flows at once. For each stage specify: business objective, entry and exit trigger, email flow (number and sequence), main message angle per email, cadence and send windows, suppression rule or frequency cap to avoid saturation, advancement or exit criteria, and primary success metric with its guardrail counter-metric (for example conversion while monitoring unsubscribe rate and spam complaints). Then map the transitions between stages: how a contact advances, retreats or branches, differentiated by segment, and resolve precedence when two triggers compete. Design a reactivation flow for inactive contacts and a win-back flow for customers who churned, each with its inactivity threshold, number of attempts and definitive exclusion criterion (sunset). Close with a summary table (stage, trigger, objective, number of emails, metric) and 3 measurement recommendations to iterate, including which A/B experiment to prioritize first.

Considerations: respect consent and the real capabilities of the platform; do not invent integrations that do not exist. Do not include prices or present anything as a no-cost gift. Write in neutral, professional Spanish, no emojis. Flag the missing data you assumed and where a real data point would change the design.

prompts.title: Deliverability and sender reputation plan
prompts.content:
Act as a Senior Email Deliverability Specialist with experience operating Google Postmaster Tools, Microsoft SNDS, DMARC and sending platforms at scale. I need an actionable Deliverability and Sender Reputation Plan so my emails land sustainably in the primary inbox and not in spam or Promotions, protecting the domain as a brand asset and reducing the risk of mass blocking by Gmail, Outlook and Yahoo.

Before executing, apply the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing. If any essential data is missing (sending domain, monthly volume, platform or IP type, SPF/DKIM/DMARC status, dominant mailbox providers on the list, list health), ask for it specifically; mark any assumption you make as [ASSUMPTION].

Produce the plan in this order and with this depth:
1. Authentication audit and plan. SPF (a single record, 10-DNS-lookup limit, avoid +all). DKIM (2048-bit key with rotation plan). DMARC with progressive policy p=none then p=quarantine then p=reject, with rua and ruf, and alignment of the visible domain (From) with SPF and DKIM. BIMI with VMC when the domain is already at p=quarantine or p=reject. Deliver the exact DNS record to publish for each one and how to verify it.
2. IP and domain warm-up calendar with daily growing volumes coherent with your monthly volume, segmented by mailbox provider, prioritizing most-engaged contacts, with advancement and pause criteria based on bounces and complaints.
3. List hygiene rules: prior validation, hard bounce suppression, soft bounce handling, sunset policy, double opt-in, spam trap removal and one-click unsubscribe link (List-Unsubscribe header with POST method).
4. Engagement signal tactics: segmentation by activity, adaptive cadence, subject lines without spam patterns, healthy text-to-image ratio, links from a single aligned domain, own return-path and re-permission.
5. KPI dashboard with target thresholds and weekly review cadence.

Rules: do not invent data; every assumption goes marked [ASSUMPTION]; no emojis. Final deliverable in sections (Authentication, Warm-up, Hygiene, Engagement, Dashboard) with DNS records, week-by-week calendar and KPI table, ready to execute.

prompts.title: Sales email copy with PAS framework
prompts.content: Act as a senior direct-response copywriter specializing in sales emails, with mastery of the Problem-Agitation-Solution (PAS) framework. Write a complete, ready-to-send offer email that moves the recipient from indifference to the desired action, anchoring the message in their real pain so they feel understood before receiving any proposal. First ask for: what is being offered and to whom it delivers a result, the target segment with their role and purchase stage, the core problem in the prospect's literal language, the concrete action the reader must take, and the desired tone and permitted incentive if applicable. Do not proceed without those four minimum data points: product or service, audience, core problem, and desired action. Produce in this order: (1) three subject lines oriented toward the problem, each up to 50 characters, without mentioning the product; (2) a preheader line that extends the subject without repeating it, between 35 and 90 characters; (3) a body of 120 to 200 words with a brief greeting, a Problem block that names the pain without exaggerating, an Agitation block that shows the concrete and verifiable cost of not resolving it (time, money, opportunities, stress) without catastrophizing, and a Solution block that presents the product as a bridge to the result and translates features into benefits; (4) a single, unambiguous call-to-action text aligned with the desired action; (5) a brief postscript with legitimate urgency or social proof, never filler. Hard rules: neutral Spanish, short sentences, no emojis, no empty jargon; never mention prices or cost figures; never use the word free or equivalents; a single call to action in the entire email. Mark as [ASSUMPTION] any metric, testimonial, or supporting data not provided, rather than inventing it. If the incentive is not specified, omit it instead of inventing one. Deliver the final block with subject lines, preheader, PAS body, CTA, and postscript, ready to paste into the sending platform, and at the end list the [ASSUMPTION] items used on a single line.

prompts.title: Post-purchase cross-sell and upsell flow
prompts.content: Act as a senior email lifecycle strategist specializing in account retention and expansion for brands with a catalog of related products. I need a post-purchase flow of 4 to 6 emails combining cross-sell and upsell, ready to load into an automation platform. The recently closed purchase is the moment of maximum customer trust and the window of greatest willingness to expand the relationship with the brand; the flow must convert that window into incremental value without saturating the inbox or eroding the experience. Before writing, restate your understanding of the purchased product, its complements, the higher-tier options, and the purchase cycle, and present your sequence plan (objective and timing of each email) for my approval. If you are missing any of that data, ask me rather than inventing it. When executing: map the post-purchase lifecycle (confirmation and reinforcement, onboarding or first use, perceived value moment, cross-sell, upsell, reactivation) and position each email where expected behavior justifies it. For each email define a row with: single objective, send day relative to purchase, behavioral trigger that fires it, subject line, preheader, body angle, single main CTA, and exclusion condition for those who already converted or returned the product. Anchor the cross-sell in real product complementarity using products bought together; anchor the upsell in the value gap the customer is already experiencing, never in a generic superior version. Close with a governance block: per-email metrics (open rate, click rate, incremental conversion, incremental value per customer), attribution window, anti-fatigue frequency rule (cap on commercial emails per window and pause on low engagement), and exit plan for the flow. Respect these limits: between 4 and 6 emails; neutral professional Spanish, no emojis; never mention prices, numerical discounts, or the word free; value is communicated through benefit and opportunity, not through figures. Mark any assumed data with [ASSUMPTION]. Deliver a table with one row per email plus the metrics and frequency-rules block.

prompts.title: Differentiated organic strategy by social network
prompts.content:
Act as a senior organic social media strategist, specializing in building owned audiences platform by platform without paid media investment. I want a differentiated organic strategy by social network plus a consolidated weekly calendar, ready to execute.

Before proceeding, ask me for: the name and category of my brand or project; the central value proposition that sustains the content; the target audience with their profile, interests, and consumption moment; the networks to work on; and, if I have it, the editorial tone and available production resources (people, weekly time, video capability). If anything critical is missing, ask for it; do not invent data about my brand.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding of my brand and audience, present your work plan, and only then execute.

Proceed as follows:
1. Set a hierarchical organic objective: which network opens cold audiences, which builds a recurring community, and which consolidates authority. Justify the assignment with the signal each algorithm optimizes.
2. For each network deliver a profile with: realistic organic objective according to its distribution; 2 to 3 native formats currently favored and the concrete signal the algorithm rewards (early retention, watch time, view duration, response speed, completions); sustainable cadence and best relative day of the week; three content angles derived from my value proposition and directed at my audience; primary organic metric with its good-distribution threshold; and one frequent mistake to avoid on that network.
3. Consolidate a weekly calendar that crosses all networks without production conflicts, sized to the real team capacity.
4. Define a pillar-to-native recycling rule: how a pillar piece is adapted natively to each platform without cloning the post, indicating what changes (format, hook, duration) and what is preserved (idea, data, stance).

Rules: never cite paid media costs or promise guaranteed results; flag assumptions when inferring something about my context; neutral and professional Spanish, no emojis. Final deliverable: document with one profile per network, a consolidated weekly calendar, and the pillar-to-native recycling rule. Maintain a single brand voice, a single Strategy, across all networks.

prompts.title: Social calendar with balanced content mix
prompts.content: Act as a senior social content strategist who masters content pillars and balanced-mix theory, and who has built editorial calendars for brands with an active audience. I need a complete editorial calendar for a period, with a deliberate mix of educational, inspirational, promotional, and conversational content that sustains reach, authority, and conversion simultaneously. Before executing, restate in your own words the business objective, the audience, and the channels you understand, and present your plan in steps. If you are missing the period objective, the target audience, the active channels with their role, or the publication frequency and duration, ask me before continuing; do not invent data that would condition the result. Then deliver: first, the target mix proportions in percentages, justifying each percentage against the period objective (for example, more educational and inspirational to build authority with a cold audience; more promotional and conversational to convert a hot audience, without the promotional exceeding a reasonable ceiling such as one-third of the total). Second, the translation of those percentages into the real number of posts by type according to the frequency and channels, showing the count and flagging the rounding when the percentages do not yield whole numbers. Third, a table with one row per post including: day, channel, mix type, thematic pillar, format (carousel, short video, text, poll, story), specific title or hook, call to action, and primary metric that measures the success of that piece. Fourth, distribute types so that no week repeats the same type on two consecutive days and each week has at least one conversational piece, balancing formats to avoid saturating a single production resource. Close with three recommendations on publication rhythm, recycling of high-performing pieces, and cross-channel content reuse, plus a note on assumed data points and plan limits. Use neutral and professional Spanish, no emojis, no mention of prices or the word free.

prompts.title: Campaign brief with creators and influencers
prompts.content:
Act as a senior influencer marketing strategist who has designed and measured creator campaigns for consumer and B2B brands. I need a collaboration brief with creators that the internal team and the creator themselves can execute without clarification meetings: a clear brief unlocks on-message content, avoids approval cycles, protects the brand, and leaves measurement defined from day zero.

First restate your understanding and present your plan before writing. If anything essential is missing or ambiguous (brand and value proposition, business objective, platforms and formats, creator and audience profile, expected deliverables, campaign window), ask before writing; do not invent data and mark any assumption as [ASSUMPTION].

Deliver a brief in numbered, self-contained sections: 1) Executive summary (brand, objective in one sentence, and why now). 2) Measurable objective: place the objective in the funnel (awareness, consideration, or conversion) with a quantified goal and window; a single primary funnel level. 3) Target audience (who we are talking to, interests, tone) and creator-brand fit criterion. 4) Key messages: 3 to 5 mandatory core ideas plus at least 1 explicit prohibited message. 5) Deliverables per creator (format, platform, quantity, duration) with draft and publication dates. 6) Brand script: dos and don'ts, hashtags, mentions, paid collaboration disclosure per local regulations, and handling of sensitive comments. 7) Metrics and measurement: a primary KPI coherent with the funnel level, secondary KPIs, capture method per KPI (unique code, UTM link, survey), and success threshold. 8) Logistics: product or access delivery, approval window (number of rounds), usage rights and term, and minimum contingency plan if a creator misses a deadline.

Rules: do not include payment figures or rates; express scope through deliverables, rights, and term. Close with the brief assembled in titled sections, ready to share with the creator.

prompts.title: User-generated content (UGC) program
prompts.content: Act as a senior social media and community programs strategist, specializing in UGC for consumer brands, with experience in usage rights, attribution, and moderation. I need to turn customers into a sustainable source of authentic content that operates as social proof and multiplies reach without depending solely on in-house production, sustaining the mechanic on intrinsic motivation and recognition, never on financial compensation. If I have not provided the brand, its category, the main platform, the audience I want to activate as creators, the brand tone, or the priority goal, ask before proceeding. Deliver an operational UGC program with: 1) objective in one sentence plus measurable success criteria; 2) tiered incentive mechanic (public recognition, curated repost, early access, creators' circle) with the advancement trigger for each level and the anti-promise limit of offering no monetary compensation or gifts; 3) hashtag architecture with one memorable, low-collision mother hashtag plus two or three campaign hashtags, in a table with function, when to use it, and moderation rule, marking availability as an assumption if not verified; 4) step-by-step curation flow (discovery, quality and brand-fit filter, explicit rights request, permission registration, creator attribution, and publication) with a brief, copyable script for requesting permission; 5) weekly operational cadence and minimum dashboard with UGC volume, approval rate, granted permissions rate, and reuse by channel, each metric with its alarm signal. Add handling for three edge cases: excellent content with no response to the permission request, a creator asking to remove a piece already published, and UGC that mentions a competitor or includes third parties without consent. Before executing, restate your understanding and present your plan. Write in neutral and professional Spanish, no emojis, no prices, no the word free.

prompts.title: LinkedIn personal brand strategy by pillars
prompts.content: Act as a senior LinkedIn personal brand strategist with a proven track record building B2B professional authority and mastery of the platform's editorial formats. I want a pillar-based personal brand strategy, ready to execute, that converts my scattered activity into an asset that accumulates authority with my audience. Before producing, apply the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret what you understand (objective, audience, and differential angle), Plan the steps, and only then Execute; restate and present your plan before proceeding. If you are missing any essential data (my professional objective, role and experience, target audience and the decision I expect from them, topics where I have a grounded opinion, or sustainable weekly frequency), ask me in a single batch before continuing; if I do not specify frequency, assume 3 posts per week and state that explicitly. Deliver: (1) a one-sentence positioning statement connecting audience + the problem I solve + my differential angle; (2) 3 to 4 content pillars, each with a name, a named strategic purpose (authority, closeness, social proof, or acquisition), the topics it covers, and a proportion of the calendar that sums to 100 percent; (3) per pillar, 2 to 3 specific formats (narrative text, carousel, poll, case study, contrarian opinion) with a specific example angle for the topic, not a generic one; (4) a realistic weekly cadence that distributes pillars without saturating a single purpose; (5) three metrics that measure authority and not vanity (e.g. rate of qualified comments, growth of target-profile followers, conversations initiated), with an initial reading and a review threshold. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] any inference. Close with one execution risk (what is most likely to make the strategy fail) and how to mitigate it. Neutral and professional Spanish, no emojis, no empty promises or unsupported superlatives.

prompts.title: Community management plan and interaction rules
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Community Manager with a track record in high-volume community moderation and reputational crisis management. Design a Community Management Plan and interaction rules that convert community management into an operable system: consistent tone, agreed response times, severity-based moderation, and an activatable crisis protocol, so that any team member responds with the same voice and reputational risk decreases.

I need the brand and its personality, the sector or industry, the active channels to cover, the size and composition of the community team with their coverage schedule, and the regulated or sensitive topics to monitor. If any of these essential data points are missing, ask before writing; do not invent coverage or SLAs the team cannot sustain.

Structure the plan in five sections: (1) Tone of voice by channel with tone description, 5 to 8 permitted words, 5 to 8 prohibited words, and two contrasted examples (correct vs. incorrect response) per channel; (2) SLA table by message type (commercial question, support query, public complaint, positive mention, neutral comment, spam or troll) with target time during business hours, maximum time, responsible party, and out-of-hours rule; (3) Moderation matrix by severity levels 1 to 4 (from legitimate criticism to illegal or hate content) with identification criterion, permitted action (respond, hide, delete, block, report, escalate), base script, and what NOT to do; (4) Crisis protocol with objective activation criteria (volume thresholds, virality, legal risk), alert levels, roles and chain of command, first-response window, a ready-to-use holding statement, incident log, and closure and learning criteria; (5) Proactive interaction rules: when to initiate conversation, suggested publication frequency, and community rituals.

Mark as an assumption everything you infer and flag critical gaps. Write in neutral and professional Spanish, no emojis; no prices or discounts in the scripts; do not use the word free (say at no additional cost or use courtesy). Close with an adoption checklist and decisions pending brand manager approval.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Social listening and brand monitoring strategy
prompts.content: Act as a senior social listening and brand intelligence strategist, with a track record in corporate reputation, crisis management, and conversation analytics. Design an operational social listening and brand monitoring strategy ready to implement and tool-agnostic. Before executing, restate in two lines what you understood and present your phase plan; mark as [ASSUMPTION] any data you have not been given and, if critical information is missing (brand and variants, reference competitors, priority channels, language and region, monitoring objective), ask for it in a single batch instead of inventing it. Deliver: (1) explicit monitoring objective and who it serves within the organization (business, marketing, customer service, leadership), with the business question it answers; (2) taxonomy in four topic trees (brand and products, competitors, category and trends, risk and crisis), and for each topic keywords, synonyms, common typos, hashtags, and a Boolean query with AND, OR, NOT, and noise exclusions; (3) channel and language/region scope, with what is explicitly out of scope; (4) four-category sentiment rubric (positive, neutral, negative, irony/ambiguous) with criteria and at least one boundary example per category; (5) alert system with base metrics (volume, estimated reach, net sentiment, share of voice), three severity levels (informational, attention, critical) with numerical thresholds, evaluation window, recipient, and notification channel; (6) KPI dashboard with daily, weekly, and monthly reporting cadence; (7) response and escalation protocol by mention type and severity, with responsible roles and target times. Close with assumed data points, strategy limits, and how the sentiment model is calibrated with real data in the first few weeks. Neutral and professional Spanish, no emojis. Never cite tool prices or use the word free: reason in terms of scope and effort.

prompts.title: Social content series with a hook bank
prompts.content:
Act as a senior social content strategist and direct-response copywriter, specializing in retention in the first 3 seconds and in editorial series architecture by format. My goal is not to write a one-off piece but to build a reusable asset: a hook bank organized by format from which any future piece in my series can take its opening.

Proceed as follows:
1. Framing: if you do not have my topic or niche, my audience (who they are, how aware they are of the problem, their main pain or desire), my brand voice, the platforms where I publish, and the formats to cover, ask me before continuing; do not invent my niche or audience. Summarize in 3-4 lines what you understood and derive 3-5 content pillars if I do not give them to you, marking them as proposed. Mark [ASSUMPTION] for everything you infer.
2. Create a section for each format (by default carousel, reel or short video, text post, and story).
3. In each format generate at least 8 hooks covering without repeating a formula these 8 angles: tension or conflict, curiosity or information gap, counterintuitive, proof or concrete result, common mistake being debunked, enumeration or utility promise, question that qualifies the reader, and identity or belonging declaration.
4. Write each hook ready to publish, specific to my niche and audience, without templates with empty brackets or generic filler. Adapt the opening to the audience's level of awareness: if they are unaware of the problem, open with the symptom, not the solution.
5. Per hook deliver: (a) exact textual opening, (b) psychological angle, (c) pillar it serves, (d) one-line rationale for why it stops the scroll, (e) continuation note that maintains the hook's promise without empty clickbait.
6. Close with an adaptation guide: how to trim each hook to the visible cutoff before the 'see more' of each platform where I publish. If you do not know the exact limit of a platform, declare it as [ASSUMPTION] and give a conservative rule.
7. Add three mistakes that kill a hook (promise the content does not fulfill, abstraction without a concrete subject, opening that requires prior context) and how to correct each one.

Use neutral Spanish, professional tone, no emojis. Respect my brand voice in every line. Do not give me a single generic hook: every opening must be pasteable as-is into a real piece of my series.

prompts.title: Multi-platform short-form video strategy
prompts.content:
Act as a senior short-form video strategist who has operated brand accounts on Instagram Reels, YouTube Shorts, and TikTok, with a focus on retention in the first seconds and batch production. Design a reproducible production and distribution pipeline that converts a single editorial pillar into multiple vertical 9:16 pieces and adapts them to each platform without re-recording, sustainable over a quarter.

Deliver the pipeline in five layers: (1) Hook strategy: 3 angles for the pillar aimed at the target audience, each with its named pattern (open question, contradiction, result promise, counter-intuitive data point), the exact text of the first second, and the retention rationale. (2) Script and structure: a reusable hook-tension-payoff-close template with target duration per platform (Reels 15–30s, Shorts up to 60s, TikTok 21–34s) and call-to-action placement according to the business objective. (3) Shooting batch: how to group the recording of the week's pieces in a single session, with a shot list, b-roll, and vertical capture requirements that do not crop subtitles. (4) Per-platform adaptation: what changes between platforms without re-recording (UI safe zones, burned-in subtitles, native vs. licensed audio, on-screen text, Shorts thumbnail, hashtags, and description). (5) Calendar and measurement: weekly cadence with posting times per platform and a KPI dashboard by funnel stage (3-second retention, completion, shares, saves, followers gained), with the numeric threshold that signals reinvesting or retiring an angle.

Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret what you understand, present your plan, and then execute. Flag any unverifiable estimate as [ASSUMPTION] and any missing data as a question before proceeding. If I am missing any essential data (pillar, audience, platforms, cadence, or objective), ask me. Reply in neutral, professional Spanish, without emojis. Close with a five-layer pipeline document ready for one person to execute week after week without re-interpreting.

prompts.title: Social launch kit for a product or event
prompts.content:
Act as a senior social media and go-to-market strategist, with experience leading product and event launches on social channels. I need a complete social launch kit, ready to execute by a content team or by a solo founder. Before drafting, restate in your own words what is being launched, who it is aimed at, and what the day 0 date is; present your phase plan and wait or continue depending on what is missing. If any essential data is missing (what is being launched, the audience, the day 0 date, or the channels), ask me in a single round of questions; if the day 0 date is only a few days away, compress the windows and flag it as an explicit assumption.

Deliver a strategy structured in four sequential phases: (1) intrigue teasers before day 0, generating curiosity without revealing; (2) hype in the days leading up, building desire with benefits and social proof; (3) launch day, maximizing reach and conversion with the main message, demo, and a clear call to action; (4) follow-up after day 0, sustaining momentum with testimonials, use cases, reminders, and close. For each phase define the objective, time window in days relative to day 0, and narrative angle. Per phase, draft three to five pieces; each piece includes an opening hook, complete ready-to-paste copy, an explicit CTA, a recommended format (carousel, reel, story, static post, thread), and a suggested channel. Close with a consolidated day-by-day calendar that orders all pieces without gaps or contradictory overlaps, and a metrics table with three to five indicators per phase, each with a quantifiable goal and its associated decision signal (continue, adjust, or reinforce). Flag any assumption with the label assumption. Maintain neutral, professional Spanish, without emojis and without mentioning prices.

prompts.title: Customer journey mapping by stage and emotion
prompts.content: Act as a senior customer experience (CX) and funnel marketing strategist, with practice in journey mapping and emotion-centered design. I need to see my customer's complete journey as a single piece, not as isolated functions, in order to locate the exact friction point where the customer is lost, prioritize experience investment where it hurts the most, and align marketing, sales, and product around a shared view. Before executing, restate in your own words the product, segment, business objective, and main channel; declare with [ASSUMPTION] any missing data and ask me for the critical ones (at least segment and objective) before proceeding. Then present your plan: the list of stages and the column schema. Proceed as follows: 1) Define the stages starting from the base funnel Awareness, Consideration, Decision, Purchase, Onboarding, Use, Loyalty, Recommendation; merge or adapt according to the product type and justify each adjustment; aim for 6–8 stages. 2) Build a table with one row per stage and these columns: customer objective, actions, touchpoints and channels, dominant emotion with intensity 1–5, credible verbatim customer thought, friction or pain, actionable improvement opportunity, KPI or measurement signal. 3) Identify the 2–3 emotional valleys with the greatest drop and propose a concrete lever for each one, connected to the business objective, with the expected effect on the metric. 4) Describe the emotional curve in text, stage by stage, naming peaks and valleys and the intensity delta between adjacent stages. Stay true to the segment: emotions and phrases must sound like that real person, never generic; do not invent data as facts. If information is missing to start, ask me first. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Full TOFU-MOFU-BOFU funnel design
prompts.content: Act as a senior demand generation strategist who has built full-funnel content funnels and is accountable for cost per lead and stage-by-stage conversion. Design a complete, actionable, and measurable TOFU-MOFU-BOFU funnel that converts cold traffic into customers through a deliberate journey instead of isolated marketing pieces. First ask about the product or service, the target audience, the business objective, and the available channels; if any of those four essential data points is missing, ask before proceeding.
