Then deliver: (1) an ideal customer profile with the central problem, conscious vs. latent pain, an awareness map from latent to decided, and 3 purchase criteria; (2) three tables, one per level, with stage objective, anchor piece, prospect intent, 3 to 5 content formats, channels drawn from the available ones, exact CTA, capture or advancement mechanism, and 1 to 2 KPIs with their definition and formula; (3) a transition map that connects the three levels with the behavioral signal that moves the prospect and the bridge piece that triggers the jump; (4) a minimum measurement plan with the funnel's north metric and review cadence. Respect stage boundaries: TOFU educates on the problem and never mentions the product; MOFU nurtures and captures the lead with the anchor offer; BOFU resolves objections with at least one proof piece (case, demo, or comparison) and pushes toward the commercial action. Do not invent performance figures: flag every benchmark or assumption as [ASSUMPTION] and declare assumptions at the start. Use neutral, professional Spanish, without absolute promises. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Landing page conversion optimization
prompts.content:
Act as a senior conversion rate optimization (CRO) strategist who has redesigned dozens of acquisition landing pages and masters direct-response copy, visual hierarchy, and experiment design. I need you to audit a landing that receives traffic but does not convert as it should, and deliver ready-to-implement corrections, not generic recommendations.

Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: first Interpret (restate the conversion objective, the audience, and the offer you understand, and declare assumptions), then Plan (present your audit plan before executing), and only then Execute. If you are missing the current content or structure of the landing, ask for it before auditing: do not invent sections.

Produce three deliverables. First, an audit across five axes: value proposition above the fold, clarity of the main benefit, cognitive friction and load, placement of social proof at the point of doubt in the journey, and CTA architecture in its four dimensions (text, contrast, hierarchy, and repetition). For each finding indicate what is wrong, why it costs conversions by naming the persuasion or cognitive load principle it violates, and the concrete correction already rewritten. Second, ready-to-paste copy: hero headline in 2 or 3 variants, subheadline, and main CTA text in verb-plus-value format. Third, a test hypothesis backlog ordered by expected impact against effort, where each hypothesis declares its success metric and how it would be measured.

Edge cases: if no social proof is available, propose which signal to build first and why; if the landing pursues multiple actions, prioritize one primary conversion and demote the rest to secondary. Do not use the word free, do not include prices, write in neutral, professional Spanish, without emojis.

prompts.title: Lead magnet and capture offer design
prompts.content: Act as a senior demand and conversion strategist, specialist in lead magnets that qualify leads without discounts or giving away value without building commitment. I want a complete lead magnet and capture offer design package for the entry of my funnel. If you are missing any key data — the ideal lead profile and their problem awareness level, the most urgent problem they face today, the funnel stage where the offer appears, the next step it should lead to, or my actual production capacity — ask me before proceeding; do not invent the context. Deliver six blocks: 1) Problem map: reconstruct the central problem, the lead's awareness level (unaware, problem-aware, solution-aware, product-aware), and the concrete transformation the asset must unlock in fewer than fifteen minutes of consumption. 2) Three lead magnet candidate concepts, each with a suggested format, a transformation promise in one sentence, consumption effort for the lead, fit with the urgent problem, and a risk or limitation of the concept. 3) Recommendation of the winning concept with explicit justification in terms of perceived value against production cost, plus a discard criterion for the other two. 4) Complete copy for the capture offer: outcome-oriented headline, subheadline, three to five concrete benefit bullets, one proof or credibility element, and the form's call to action. 5) Minimum form fields that balance low friction and useful qualification, indicating for each field what it decides or segments. 6) Three-message delivery sequence that delivers the asset, confirms value, and opens the next step naturally. Before executing, restate what you understood and present your plan. Close with a verification checklist: the asset resolves a concrete portion of the problem and not a generic topic; the transformation is consumable in fewer than fifteen minutes and demonstrable; the winner is justified by value against cost, not preference; the headline promises an outcome and does not describe a format; the fields minimize friction and still qualify; the sequence leads naturally to the next step. Use neutral, professional Spanish, without emojis, without mentioning prices, and without using the word that refers to giving away value without commitment.

prompts.title: Value ladder design
prompts.content:
Act as a senior direct-response marketing strategist specialized in offer architecture and value ladders. Design for my business a value ladder of 4 to 5 rungs in strictly ascending order of commitment: from a low-friction entry rung to the summit offer that materializes the customer's final transformation.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand about the business, the ideal customer, the final transformation, and the summit offer, and present your plan before executing. If any of those four data points is unclear, ask me before proceeding; do not invent the business, customer, transformation, or summit offer.

Design backwards from the destination: fix the final transformation and the summit offer first, then place the intermediate rungs so that none demands a confidence jump that the previous one has not prepared. For each rung define: offer name, concrete promise, value it unlocks, commitment level it requires (measured in friction, time, and exposure, never in price), role in the journey (entry access, bridge offer, main offer, summit offer, or continuity), and the outcome that enables the next step. For each transition between rungs define: evidence of value the customer has already received, ascension trigger, and main objection to resolve. Close with an overview showing the complete ascending flow and pointing to the rung where to concentrate effort (likely bottleneck).

Rules: the entry rung is named by its function (low-friction access, diagnosis, entry resource), never as a gift or with the word free. Do not mention price figures on any rung; the reasoning is about friction, commitment, and perceived value. If the business only supports 3 real rungs, say so and justify rather than artificially inflating to 4–5. Neutral, professional Spanish, without emojis. Deliverable: rung table, transition table, and overview, ready to implement.

prompts.title: Tripwire entry offer design
prompts.content:
Act as a senior conversion funnel and offer architecture strategist, specialized in entry offers and value ladders. I need to convert cold prospects into first-time buyers: the obstacle is not the product but the psychological barrier of the first yes. Design a tripwire entry offer (relatively low price, very high perceived value) that breaks that barrier and, through the commitment consistency principle, predisposes the buyer to advance through the value ladder toward the core offer. The purpose of the tripwire is not margin — it is to transform the relationship from prospect to customer and build a base of qualified buyers to scale on.

Deliverable: a complete tripwire offer in one page, ready to take to a landing page. Proceed as follows: (1) define the target buyer and the specific, immediate pain the offer resolves in fewer than one week; (2) isolate a single, concrete, near-instant quick win that demonstrates capability without resolving the full problem, which is reserved for the core offer; (3) package that quick win as a concrete deliverable asset — template, mini-audit, diagnostic session, or actionable kit — with its format and scope; (4) build irresistibility on four levers: perceived value greater than the price, zero risk for the buyer, specificity of the result, and a credible reason for the accessible entry price; (5) anchor the price in relative terms against the value of the core offer, expressed as a low psychological barrier, without specific figures; (6) define the transition — the bump or immediate offer after accepting the tripwire — that starts the ladder toward the core offer; (7) draft the copy angle: headline, central promise, price justification, and call to action.

If you are missing the business, the audience, the core offer, or the quick win, ask me before proceeding. Flag with [ASSUMPTION] any inference. Do not invent price figures and do not use the word that suggests total absence of cost. Neutral, professional Spanish.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Closing criterion: the tripwire delivers a single quick win (does not resolve the full problem) deliverable in fewer than one week; the four levers are explicit and justified; the price is a relative barrier against the core offer without figures; there is a defined transition toward the core offer; the copy includes headline, promise, price justification, and call to action.

prompts.title: Lead scoring model by fit and interest
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Head of Revenue Operations with experience in B2B demand generation and operating scoring models in CRM and marketing automation platforms. Design an implementable two-axis lead scoring model (fit and interest) that converts the lead flow into a prioritized queue, defines when a lead becomes an MQL and SQL, and triggers the handoff to sales with a clear SLA.

Before executing, restate what you understand about the business, its offer, and its ideal customer, and present your plan. If you are missing the value proposition, the ideal customer profile, the actions already tracked, the current MQL/SQL definition, or the destination platform, ask for it pointedly or declare it as an explicit assumption before continuing.

Deliver: (1) FIT axis with 5 to 8 firmographic-demographic attributes, each with a relative weight on a scale you declare (e.g., 0 to 100), an explicit scoring rule per possible value, and at least two disqualifiers that subtract points or veto the lead. (2) INTEREST axis with 6 to 10 actions separated into high intent (demo, pricing, commercial contact) versus exploration (blog reading, educational download), with a score per action, a cap per repeated action, and a temporal decay rule with its half-life. (3) A 2×2 prioritization matrix (high/low fit by high/low interest) with a concrete and distinct action per quadrant: immediate handoff, commercial acceleration, educational nurturing, and discard or recycle. (4) Numeric MQL and SQL thresholds per axis, aligned to the current definition, with a first-contact SLA per quadrant. (5) A calibration plan: historical data to review, model validation against real conversion per quadrant, a falsifiable success or failure criterion, and a recalibration cadence.

Cover these edge cases: leads with high fit but zero interest (not MQL yet), high interest without sufficient firmographic data (enrichment before scoring), insufficient volume to validate per quadrant (minimum sample threshold), and leads that reactivate after decaying (score recalculation). Justify each weight with business logic, mark assumptions as [ASSUMPTION], and do not invent conversion figures. Avoid vanity scoring: every point must correlate with a closing hypothesis, not with activity for its own sake. Without prices. Close with an implementable document of tables.

prompts.title: Checkout friction reduction
prompts.content:
Act as a senior conversion rate optimization (CRO) and funnel strategy specialist, with experience in e-commerce, payment UX, and A/B experimentation. The checkout is the final stretch of the funnel: every step, field, and unresolved question is a revenue leak from a gain already made. Your mission is to diagnose the real checkout friction and deliver a prioritized friction dashboard plus an actionable elimination plan, without weakening trust or losing critical business data.

Proceed in four phases. Phase 1 – Mapping: reconstruct the complete flow from cart to confirmation, listing each screen, form field, and decision asked of the buyer; flag as [ASSUMPTION] any data you do not have confirmed. Phase 2 – Diagnosis: classify each element as essential, deferrable, or removable, label the type of friction (cognitive effort, manual effort, surprise cost, security doubt, lack of trust, technical friction), and cross-reference with doubts and objections per step (shipping, returns, payment security, additional costs, delivery times, payment methods), indicating where they are resolved and where they remain open. Phase 3 – Prioritization: place each friction in an impact-by-effort matrix (high/medium/low), estimating the effect on completion rate and ordering by expected return. Phase 4 – Intervention: for the highest-impact points, define the concrete intervention (reduce or group fields, autocomplete, guest checkout, show costs upfront, trust signals, progress bar, inline error handling), the behavioral rationale, and an A/B test hypothesis with primary metric, counter-intuitive guard metric, and decision criterion.

Draw on recognized frameworks: cognitive load reduction, Hick's law, cost transparency, social proof, trust signals, and the minimum effort principle. Always distinguish mobile from desktop because friction differs. Consider edge cases: returning user vs. first purchase, single-item vs. multi-item cart, discount codes, payment failure, and retry. Do not invent conversion or abandonment figures; every estimate goes as [ASSUMPTION] with its reasoning. Distinguish the verifiable (what is seen in the described flow) from the inferred. If critical information for the diagnosis is missing (current flow, platform, known abandonment point), ask for it before continuing.

Deliver: (1) prioritized friction dashboard in a table with step, element, classification, friction type, associated objection, impact, and effort; (2) actionable elimination plan with 3 to 5 experiments ordered by expected return, each with intervention, behavioral rationale, hypothesis, primary metric, guard metric, and success criterion; (3) list of assumptions and missing data. Neutral, professional Spanish, without emojis.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Evergreen webinar funnel design
prompts.content: Act as a senior evergreen webinar funnel strategist, with proven experience in marketing automation, conversion copywriting and sequence architecture. Design an end-to-end evergreen webinar funnel: automated, measurable by stage and replicable, that captures qualified prospects, brings them to attend, presents the offer with a structured pitch and recovers those who did not attend or did not decide. Before drafting pieces, derive the angle and the central promise from the topic, the offer and the audience's awareness level; explicitly declare which awareness level you assume. Deliver six blocks: (1) Funnel map with its stages (ad, registration, confirmation, reminders, attendance, pitch, follow-up, reactivation), the main metric for each one (CTR, registration rate, show-up rate, retention to pitch, offer rate, conversion, non-attendee recovery) and a reference target value per stage marked as assumption. (2) Registration page: headline and subheadline oriented toward the transformation, 3 to 5 value-promise bullets, social proof, minimum field form and CTA; declare the central angle. (3) Confirmation and reminder sequence: immediate confirmation, 24h reminder, 1h reminder and live reminder, each with objective, suggested subject line and key message to raise the show-up rate. (4) Webinar structure and pitch adjusted to the indicated duration: hook, promise, real-value teaching, transition to pitch, offer presentation, handling of the 3 to 5 most probable objections, call to action and close with legitimate urgency (based on seats, cohorts or expiring bonuses, never on fictitious scarcity). (5) Post-webinar follow-up segmented into at least 3 audiences: attendees who did not buy, non-attendees with replay and hot prospects who saw the offer, each with cadence, objective and sending trigger. (6) Automation triggers and conditions: which event moves the prospect between stages (registration, attendance, pitch minute reached, CTA click, non-open) and how to avoid duplicate sends or conflicts between sequences. Close with verifiable acceptance criteria and the assumptions you made. Brand restrictions: never mention prices or monetary figures; never use the word free or equivalents; argue the value of the offer; neutral and professional Spanish, no emojis. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] any data you assume. If the topic, the offer, the prospect profile, the automation platform or the webinar duration is missing, ask for that data before executing. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Funnel micro and macro conversion map
prompts.content: Act as a senior growth marketing analyst specialized in funnel instrumentation and measurement. The business measures its funnel only by the final sale, so when conversion drops it does not know at which stage it broke or how far in advance. Your job is to build a micro and macro conversion map that allows measuring progress stage by stage, detecting leaks before they impact revenue and prioritizing where to optimize. Before executing, restate what you understand and present your plan. If you are missing the product or service, the closing action that counts as a sale or the main traffic channel, ask before continuing; do not invent the business. Proceed as follows: (1) Reconstruct the funnel by stages choosing the AARRR or TOFU-MOFU-BOFU framework according to which fits best, and justify the choice in one line; describe the prospect's mental state at each stage. (2) Per stage define exactly ONE macro conversion, the closing event that confirms advancement to the next stage, and between 2 and 4 micro conversions, intermediate events that predict it. (3) For each event specify technical name, trigger definition or exact action that activates it, why it is an intent signal and the capture tool. (4) Mark which micro conversions are lead indicators of the macro of their stage and propose a step-through rate to monitor between each consecutive pair of events. (5) Deliver a table per stage with stage, mental state, macro, micro, trigger, tool and step-through rate, plus a diagnosis of the 3 points where a declining micro conversion would reveal a leak before the sale drops, with its corrective action. Rules: micro conversions must be observable and predictive, never vanity metrics; always distinguish lead indicators (predict, anticipate) from lag indicators (confirm, arrive late); do not invent figures from the account and mark any external benchmark as an explained assumption; deliver a single coherent measurement strategy end to end. If a required tool is not available, mark it as a recommended assumption instead of omitting the event.

prompts.title: Funnel leak diagnosis by stage
prompts.content:
Act as a senior growth and conversion analyst (CRO) with a track record of optimizing B2B and B2C funnels and financial reading of impact. I want a quantitative diagnosis of my funnel's leaks, stage by stage, that tells me with evidence which transition to fix first before spending on campaigns, content or automation.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand about my funnel and present your plan; only execute afterward.

I need you to ask me, if I do not have them at hand: the funnel stages in order from top to bottom with their volume; the time window the data covers; the nature of the business or type of funnel; the value or average revenue per customer (optional, to estimate economic impact); and the conversion reference ranges of my own or the industry (optional). If a critical piece of data is missing, ask me for it before calculating and never invent figures.

Proceed as follows: (1) validate that the stages come in descending order and that each one does not exceed the previous one; note any inconsistency and, if there is suspicion of double counting or stage overlap, mark it. (2) Build a table with step-by-step conversion, drop rate (1 minus conversion) and cumulative conversion from the top; round to one decimal and preserve absolutes. (3) Identify the critical leak by triple lens: greatest percentage drop, greatest absolute volume lost and, if I have an average ticket, greatest economic value drained; when the lenses point to different stages, explain the conflict and recommend with criteria. (4) Contrast each rate against my benchmarks; if I do not have them, use references appropriate to the funnel type marked as [ASSUMPTION] with their criterion and range, not a single point. (5) Order the stages to intervene with an impact-versus-effort scheme and deliver a numbered ranking with justification. (6) For the two priority stages, formulate root-cause hypotheses (message, offer, friction, segmentation, timing, traffic source quality) and propose one experiment per hypothesis with success metric, decision threshold and indicative sample size or minimum duration.

Close with: conversion table, critical leak justified by at least two lenses, prioritized intervention ranking and experiment plan per hypothesis. Mark any ambiguity or missing data explicitly instead of filling it in. Neutral and professional Spanish, no emojis.

prompts.title: Data-based buyer persona construction
prompts.content: Act as a senior marketing and customer research strategist with fifteen years building evidence-based buyer personas (voice of customer, jobs-to-be-done, objection analysis) that translate into campaigns and offers, not decorative profiles. I need an actionable buyer persona for my product or service, built from real evidence and not from intuition, to decide with data what to say, in which channel and with which offer. Before executing: restate in your own words the segment, the business objective and the purchase decision in focus; inventory the available evidence and name the gaps; tell me which blocks are backed and which depend on assumptions to validate, and ask me for the missing data before inventing. If you have not been given product, segment, objective, data sources or purchase decision, ask me first; do not assume a market. Then deliver, in order: 1) evidence inventory that each source contributes and what gaps it leaves, separating observed fact from interpretation and marking what is not backed as [ASSUMPTION] to validate; 2) identity and demographics relevant to the decision, without filler; 3) context and situation: role, environment, constraints, time budget and purchase moment; 4) job-to-be-done with its functional, emotional and social progress; 5) motivations and triggers that initiate the search; 6) pains and frustrations prioritized by intensity and frequency; 7) objections and barriers, each with the message response that neutralizes it; 8) decision criteria, alternatives evaluated and includes the option of doing nothing; 9) channels, information sources and trusted voices; 10) voice of customer with verbatim phrases attributable to a source for each block; 11) activation map with three anchor messages, two priority channels and one measurable metric to validate the persona in the field. Close with three persona risks (sample bias, critical unvalidated assumptions, segment too broad) and the minimum experiment to confirm it. Neutral and professional Spanish, no prices, no the word free, no emojis. Mark as [ASSUMPTION] everything not backed; zero invented data.

prompts.title: Target customer empathy map
prompts.content:
Act as a senior brand strategist and customer researcher, expert in empathy maps (XPLANE/Strategyzer model) and in Jobs to be Done. I need to deeply understand a target customer before deciding on message and positioning, converting scattered intuitions into a shared view and separating evidence from assumption.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. First restate the segment and the objective of the map, list the evidence I gave you and signal gaps; if an essential piece of data is missing to avoid inventing, ask for it before continuing.

Then deliver an actionable empathy map:
1. Define the segment as a named archetype with a concrete situation (role, context, decision stage, trigger). Reject "everyone" and declare who you exclude.
2. Complete the six quadrants in the first person of the customer, without marketing jargon inside the quotes: Thinks, Feels, Sees, Hears, Says and Does. Include at least one explicit contradiction between discourse and behavior.
3. Derive Pains (fears, frustrations, obstacles, perceived risks) and Gains (desires, success metrics, functional and emotional benefits), prioritized by impact x frequency; do not literally repeat the quadrants.
4. Mark each statement as evidence or assumption according to its origin; do not invent figures, testimonials or sources.
5. Close with three positioning and message implications and two validation questions for real customers.

If you have no evidence, work everything as explicit hypothesis. Deliver in neutral and professional Spanish, no emojis, in sections: Segment, Six quadrants, Pains, Gains, Implications, Validation. If you are missing the business, the segment, the objective or the available evidence, ask me for them.

prompts.title: Brand archetype definition
prompts.content:
Act as a senior brand strategist specialized in Jung's archetypes and in the Mark and Pearson model (The Hero and the Outlaw). I am going to define the dominant archetype of a brand and translate it into an operable personality that guides copy, identity and campaigns without reopening the identity debate with every deliverable.

Before executing, restate in your own words which brand you are going to profile, in which category it competes, who it serves and why it is different; if any of that data is missing, ask me for it in a single batch and do not advance until you have it. Mark as [ASSUMPTION] any inference you make without confirmed data.

Then deliver, in this order: (1) Brand synthesis in 4 lines: what it sells, who it serves, what transformation it promises and how it competes. (2) Mapping of the 12 archetypes (Innocent, Sage, Explorer, Outlaw, Magician, Hero, Lover, Jester, Everyman, Caregiver, Ruler, Creator) scored 1 to 5, each score supported by concrete business evidence, never by generic opinion; use the triad central desire / fear / promise to evaluate. (3) Decision: declare the dominant archetype and the secondary one that modulates it, explain why the dominant beats the second strongest archetype (explicit contrast, not just assertion) and name the shadow to avoid (the excess of the archetype that would degrade the brand) with the concrete behavior that triggers it. (4) Activation derived from the dominant: 5 to 7 personality traits, tone of voice (2-3 axes like close/expert), 3 to 5 words the brand uses and 3 it avoids, and 3 test messages written in the voice of the brand for 3 different contexts (launch, objection, community). (5) Brand manifesto of 60 to 90 words in the voice of the chosen archetype.

Close with a traceability block: which decisions were by evidence and which by [ASSUMPTION] pending validation. Neutral and professional Spanish, no emojis and without mentioning prices.

prompts.title: Brand tone and voice definition
prompts.content: Act as a senior Brand Voice Strategist with more than a decade designing verbal voice systems and style guides for brands across multiple sectors. I need an operative tone and voice guide, ready for any team member to write on-brand without depending on expert review and to accelerate the onboarding of writers and agencies. Before executing, ask me for the essential missing data: name of the brand, desired personality (sought traits), target audience, priority channels where the voice will apply and tone references I like or dislike. If you infer something, mark it [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent data. Then deliver: (1) 4 to 5 voice attributes, each with a one-line definition and its explicit opposite, what the voice is NOT; (2) positioning on four spectrum axes (formal to close, serious to playful, respectful to irreverent, factual to enthusiastic), with a point from 1 to 5 per axis and justification; (3) concrete do and don't rules per attribute, covering lexicon, syntax, sentence length, grammatical person and use of punctuation marks, each rule traceable to the attribute that originates it; (4) a calibrated matrix of the same base message rewritten per channel and per three emotional situations: celebratory announcement, response to complaint and communication of incident or bad news; (5) a checklist of 6 to 8 actionable points to audit pieces before publishing. If the references contradict each other, signal the conflict and propose a resolution; if there is only one channel, deepen variations by situation; if the sector is regulated, note the compliance limits that constrain the voice. Neutral, professional Spanish, no emojis. Restate what you understood and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Unique selling proposition (USP) definition
prompts.content:
Act as a senior brand and positioning strategist, specialized in defensible unique selling propositions (USP), that is, anchored in structural advantage that a rival cannot copy in less than twelve months: network effects, proprietary data, own process or asset, integrations, or customer switching cost. Your goal is not a pretty slogan but a differentiator that shifts the conversation from how much does it cost to why only you, and that serves as the axis for home page, sales pitch and positioning narrative.

I need you to define the USP of my offer. If you have not been given the offer, the target segment, the problem it solves, the competitors or real alternatives (including the option of doing nothing) and the evidence backing my advantage, ask me for them before advancing; do not invent data.

Proceed as follows. First reconstruct the offer: what is sold, to whom and what specific problem it solves, and mark with [ASSUMPTION] any gap. Second, map the competitive terrain: tabulate each competitor or alternative and what it promises, including the inertia of not acting, to isolate the space that nobody occupies credibly. Third, evaluate my declared advantage against the structural defense sources and classify each element as defensible (with verifiable evidence today) or empty claim (discarded), estimating how long it would take a rival to match it. Fourth, formulate three candidates with the structure: for [segment], we are the only ones who [differential benefit] because [defensible proof], unlike [dominant alternative]. Fifth, score each candidate 1 to 5 on four filters (relevance for the segment, verifiable today, copying difficulty greater than twelve months, memorability in one phrase) and recommend one with explicit justification.

Rules: the recommended USP fits in a single memorable phrase and names segment, differential benefit and proof; the support is structural and demonstrable today, not an aspiration or an attribute that any rival can match in weeks; if all candidates rely on non-defensible advantages, say so directly and propose a path to build real defense instead of forcing a weak USP; every claim without backing goes as [ASSUMPTION] and never invent metrics or capabilities. Before executing, restate in one or two lines what you understood and present your plan. Respond in neutral, professional Spanish, no emojis.

Deliver: recommended USP in one line, extended version of one paragraph, defensible support with its evidence and estimated copying timeline, the two discarded candidates with their reason, and the list of missing data if any.

prompts.title: Brand tagline and slogan generation
prompts.content:
Act as a senior creative director of branding, expert in naming, positioning and high-density copywriting. Your objective is to produce a tagline and slogan system that condenses the central promise of a brand, distinguishes it from the competition and withstands the word-of-mouth test. Before proposing anything, ask me for this data if I have not given it to you: the brand name and its sector; who it talks to (segment, moment, pain); what it sells or what central problem it solves; the differential attribute it can claim honestly and almost nobody else; the personality of the phrase (close, technical, challenger, aspirational); and where it will live (logo signature, campaign, web, social media, packaging). Do not invent data: what is not confirmed mark it as [ASSUMPTION] and make visible how the recommendation would change if the assumption were false.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate in your own words the promise you understand and the territory you are going to exploit; then present your plan of routes; only then execute.

Proceed in four phases. Phase 1, Distillation: extract the central promise and the differential; define a single power idea, the emotional territory and the functional benefit the phrase must convey. Phase 2, Divergence: work separately through three distinct creative routes to avoid premature convergence: (a) direct benefit, (b) metaphor or territory, (c) tension twist or wordplay. Each route delivers five taglines of maximum seven words, plus its short logo-signature version when applicable. Each phrase must arise from a real insight, not from an empty commonplace (leader, quality, solutions, innovation, passion) unless the twist resignifies it. For each option note: angle, insight that sustains it and a risk (ambiguity, fragility of translation to another language of the market, unsustainable claim, collision with a known brand). Phase 3, Evaluation: score each option 1 to 5 on memorability, distinctiveness, clarity of promise and apparent legal ownership; discard those that depend on an unsubstantiated claim or that in regulated sectors (health, finance, legal) promise guaranteed results. Phase 4, Recommendation: select the three best, justify the trade-off of the winner and apply a read-aloud test (rhythm, ease of repetition, absence of unwanted double meaning).

Handle these edge cases: if the brand is a single evocative word, prioritize slogans that explain it without redundancy; if the market is bilingual or international, verify that the phrase does not generate negative meaning in the other language; if the differential does not withstand scrutiny, say so and propose a defensible alternative territory. Closing criterion: the recommendation is ready for legal and brand validation, it is not a definitive registration ruling.

Deliver a document with: power idea (emotional territory + explicit functional benefit), the three routes with their fifteen annotated options, the top 3 evaluated with its scoring table, and the recommended phrase with its logo-signature version and the read-aloud test.

prompts.title: Brand platform with brand key model
prompts.content: Act as a senior brand strategist specialized in the Unilever Brand Key model, with a track record of aligning teams around a distilled platform that serves as the single source of truth for product, communication and commercial. I want the complete platform of my brand with the nine components of the Brand Key, in this order and without overlapping: 1) Competitive roots: legacy and category that give authority. 2) Competitive environment: position versus competitors and the disputed space. 3) Target: who it serves, described by motivations, not just demographics. 4) Insight: the real human tension it resolves, written in the first person of the customer. 5) Benefits: functional (what it does) with its emotional pair (how it makes you feel). 6) Values and personality: 3 to 5 guiding values and a set of traits. 7) Reason to believe: real proofs that make the promise credible. 8) Discriminator: the only own, hard-to-copy reason for choice. 9) Essence: a single core phrase, permanent, that distills everything. Before drafting, restate what you understand and present your plan. If you are missing the brand name, the category, the target or the available proofs, ask me before continuing; do not invent evidence. Anchor the reason to believe only in real proofs and mark [ASSUMPTION] every inference. Verify at the end that essence, discriminator and reason to believe do not contradict each other and that the insight connects with the emotional benefit. Without prices, without the word that denotes absence of cost, neutral Spanish, no emojis. Deliver the nine labeled blocks plus a final coherence test paragraph ready to validate with stakeholders.

prompts.title: Brand positioning statement
prompts.content: Act as a senior brand strategist specializing in competitive positioning: your job is to distill a single defensible idea and discard generic promises. I want to fix how my brand is positioned in the mind of its ideal customer before writing any message, page, or campaign, so that sales, product, and communications speak with a single differentiating voice. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. First, restate in your own words who the brand serves, in what reference category it competes, against what real alternative it differentiates itself (competitor or status quo), and with what reason-to-believe it sustains the promise; if any of those four blocks is missing or arrives ambiguous, ask about it one thing at a time before moving forward. Then propose the single differentiating idea that will govern the statement and confirm it with me. Only then deliver: (1) the canonical statement in a chained paragraph with the form 'For [audience], [brand] is [category plus benefit], unlike [alternative], because [reason-to-believe]'; (2) three variants that shift only the angle of the differentiator while keeping the same audience and category, each with a note on when to use it; (3) the one-word or one-idea attribute the brand wants to own in the customer's mind, with a sentence justifying why it is ownable and not yet saturated; (4) a three-line message test (headline, subheadline, one anticipated objection with its response) derived from the statement; (5) a completed checklist that validates specificity, credibility, relevance, and distinctiveness. Do not invent figures, awards, or clients; mark every unverifiable claim [ASSUMPTION] to validate. Each block must be a single idea, free of empty adjectives, in neutral and professional Spanish, without prices or promises of free anything.

prompts.title: Brand perception and health audit
prompts.content:
Act as a senior brand strategist with experience in brand tracking, brand equity, and multi-category perception studies. I want a brand perception and health audit that separates perceived image from desired positioning, locates where the brand funnel breaks down against competitors for the target audience, and unlocks a prioritized investment plan based on evidence, not intuition. Proceed as follows: (1) Map the brand health funnel and define metrics and measurement questions for the four dimensions: awareness (aided and spontaneous), associations (attributes and imagery), consideration (purchase intent vs. competitors), and loyalty (NPS, repurchase, advocacy). (2) Declare the model applied at each step (brand funnel, Keller CBBE, or Brand Asset Valuator) and the proposed weighting for the four dimensions, justifying each weight according to the business objective. (3) Diagnose the current state of each dimension using the available data sources; normalize each dimension to a 0–100 scale, documenting the normalization rule. If a critical data point is missing, ask for it before continuing and mark every estimate as [ASSUMPTION] with its impact on index confidence. (4) Calculate an aggregated and reproducible brand health index, contrast it against the category benchmark, and indicate the confidence level of the result (high/medium/low) based on data coverage. (5) Identify the three most critical perception gaps (perceived image vs. desired positioning) and prioritize them with an impact/effort matrix. (6) Deliver a gap-closure plan with actionable initiatives, tracking metrics, suggested owners, and a re-measurement cadence; consolidate a one-page executive dashboard (index, traffic-light by dimension, three priorities). Edge cases: if only qualitative data is available, declare the index as directional, not statistical; if a dimension has no data at all, mark it as non-measurable instead of inventing a value; if the desired positioning is not defined, ask for it before deriving gaps. Limits: do not invent data or market figures; do not recommend investments without support from available evidence. Closure: the report is considered complete only if all four dimensions are measured or explicitly marked as non-measurable, the index is reproducible, and the gap-closure plan is actionable. Neutral and professional English, without emojis. If any essential data is missing (brand, category, competitors, audience, desired positioning, or sources), ask for it before executing.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Product or brand naming process
prompts.content: Act as a senior naming and brand strategy strategist with experience leading product and brand namings in Spanish-speaking markets. I need a complete naming funnel that ends in a recommended and defensible finalist trio. First, restate the briefing I am going to give you (what is being named and its category, audience, core promise, competitive territory, tone, and preferred name architecture) and, if any critical data is missing, ask for it before generating; do not invent the business — mark every inference with [ASSUMPTION]. Then generate at least 24 candidates grouped in 4 creative routes (semantic roots, territory metaphors, neologisms and fusions, heritage words and language twists), with each route's idea summarized in one line; prioritize volume and variety without self-censorship. Then filter in cascade through three sieves, explicitly and justifiably discarding what does not pass: 1) meaning (evocation of the promise, absence of negative connotations in neutral Spanish and relevant dialects, frictionless pronunciation and spelling), 2) availability — ALWAYS declared as pending verification and never as fact (domain .com and local, trademark registration by Nice class, social media handles, phonetic or visual clash with competitors), and 3) resonance (distinctiveness, memorability, tone fit, capacity to extend to a product family). Deliver the finalist trio with meaning rationale, phonetic reading, risks, availability checklist to verify, and a tagline per name. Close with a prioritized recommendation and explicit tiebreaker criterion. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Competitive differentiation with the 3C model
prompts.content:
Act as a senior brand and positioning strategist, expert in Kenichi Ohmae's 3C model (strategic triangle Customer-Company-Competition) and applied competitive analysis. Your objective is to find the offering's own defensible competitive space: the point where a real strength coincides with an important customer need that the competition does not cover well, and convert it into an actionable differentiation angle and positioning statement.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First, restate what you understand about the offering, the segment, the strengths, and the competitors; then present your analysis plan; only then execute. If the offering, the target segment, the real strengths, or at least two competitors are missing, ask for that data before continuing rather than inventing it.

Proceed in three phases. Phase 1: build the three vertices of the triangle independently and with evidence: (a) Customer: functional and emotional needs, decision criteria, and the unresolved pain, ranked by relevance; (b) Company: real strengths, distinctive capabilities, assets, and honest limitations; (c) Competition: for each competitor, their value proposition, their strengths, and the gaps they leave open. Do not assert any advantage without support; mark every inference without data as [ASSUMPTION]. Phase 2: overlay the three vertices, discard the spaces where the competition is already strong or the customer does not value, and keep only the defensible intersection where own strength + relevant need + competitive gap coincide. If no clean intersection exists, say so explicitly and propose the strength to build in order to open it. Phase 3: derive a single prioritized differentiation angle, draft a one-sentence positioning statement (for [segment] who [need], [offering] is the [category] that [unique differentiator] because [proof]), specific and verifiable, not a generic slogan; list exactly 3 risks that could erode that differentiation (imitation, change in customer need, competitive move), and for each one an early-warning signal.

Deliverable: table of the three vertices, own space justified by the cross, prioritized differentiation angle, positioning statement, the 3 risks with their early-warning signal, and 2–3 next positioning validation steps. Neutral and professional English, without emojis. Do not mention prices.

prompts.title: Campaign creative brief
prompts.content:
Act as a senior agency creative director, trained in the discipline of the single-idea brief, with experience in brand strategic planning and multichannel activation. I need a creative brief that serves as a contract between brand, creativity, and media before investing in production: a diffuse brief multiplies revision rounds and scatters budget; one with a tensioned insight and a single message unlocks consistent and defensible creativity.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. First, restate what you understand about the product, the audience, and the objective, and present your brief plan before drafting it. If you are missing the product or service, who we are talking to, the business objective with its goal, the channels, or the differentiator, ask for it before writing; mark every inference of yours with [ASSUMPTION].

Deliver the brief in seven sections in order, each derived from the previous:
1. Business challenge and campaign objective: SMART objective with success metric, baseline if it exists, and time horizon; distinguish business objective from communication objective.
2. Target audience: a vivid profile with context, consumption moment, current tension, and the concrete barrier that today prevents the desired action.
3. Consumer insight: one tensioned human truth with the structure 'I [audience], when [situation], feel [tension], because [belief]'. Not a demographic data point nor a product benefit.
4. Single campaign message (single-minded proposition): one single memorable idea the consumer must remember and believe, with its reason-to-believe anchored in the differentiator.
5. Brand tone and personality: three guiding adjectives, one sentence that embodies the tone, and one sentence that violates it to fix the boundary.
6. Deliverables by channel: one table per channel with format, adapted message, call to action, and success criterion per piece; preserve the single idea across all.
7. Restrictions and mandatories: what must always be included, what it must never do, and legal or brand limits.

Close by verifying vertical coherence: each section derives from the previous one (objective, audience, insight, message, activation). Neutral and professional English, without prices, without the word free, without emojis. The deliverable is a single-idea brief ready to be converted into concepts without additional clarifications.

prompts.title: Big idea and campaign concept development
prompts.content:
Act as a senior creative director and brand strategist with fifteen years leading integrated multichannel campaigns, trained in advertising planning and campaign platform building. Your task is to develop the big idea and creative concept that function as the backbone of a campaign: a single thought from which all executions hang, across all channels, throughout the entire campaign. Campaigns fail when each piece says something different and they compete instead of adding up; what is missing is not more creativity but a single, defensible idea born from a real human insight.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

I need from you to start: the brand and its differential value proposition, the campaign's business objective, the target audience, the brand's tone and personality, and the planned channels and duration. If any of these five is missing, stop and ask for it before moving forward; without them the concept would be decorative. Mark every market or audience inference as [ASSUMPTION].

Proceed in five phases. Diagnosis: extract brand, objective, audience, tone, and channels from what I provided. Insight: formulate a genuine human tension between what the audience lives and what it desires (truth about the person, not a demographic data point or a cliché) and validate it. Conceptual leap: derive the big idea from the insight, not from the product; verify that it is unifying and not a tactic, and clearly distinguish the three levels (insight / big idea / concept). Expression: draft the concept, manifesto, and claims in the brand's tone. Elasticity and defense: test the idea across different channels and build the criteria to sustain it with the client.

Deliver, in this order: 1) Human insight. 2) Big idea in a single memorable sentence plus a campaign platform name. 3) Creative concept with the narrative territory, the tone, and the explicit central metaphor or mechanism. 4) Manifesto of six to ten lines with the voice of the campaign. 5) Main claim with two to three alternatives. 6) Channel executions in at least three channels without repeating the execution. 7) Elasticity test with three different executions that demonstrate the idea holds. 8) Defense criteria with the client. Close by confirming that each execution traces back to the big idea and that you have not included loose tactics or a media calendar: the focus is the unifying thought.

prompts.title: Go-to-market launch plan by phases
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Product Marketing Director with experience leading go-to-market launches in competitive markets. Design me a fully executable phased launch plan from start to finish for the product I am going to describe.

Before drafting, restate in two lines what you understand about the product, its category, its priority segment, its differentiator, and the available channels; if any of those five data points or the day-zero date are missing, ask me instead of inventing them. Mark as [ASSUMPTION] every data point you infer and make explicit that it must be validated with the owner.

Structure the plan in three sequential phases and, within each one, resolve in this order: measurable objective, audience and message, recommended channels, calendar in weeks relative to day zero (format W-4, W0, W+2), assets to produce, and suggested owner.

1. Pre-launch: positioning and value proposition, priority segment and core message, expectation building, interested-party list capture, and assets that must be ready before day zero.
2. Launch: moment of release, announcement sequence by channel, coordinated activation, and entry offer (without mentioning prices).
3. Post-launch: converting interested parties into active users, early activation and retention, testimonial and social proof collection, and iteration based on data.

Keep the core message coherent from pre to post. Close with: (a) metrics dashboard with one main indicator per phase plus two alert signals per phase and the threshold that triggers them; (b) the three most likely risks with probability, impact, and concrete mitigation; (c) a no-launch criterion (what must be in place to move day zero). Professional tone in neutral English, without prices or absolute promises. Deliver a document ready to review with the team and execute.

prompts.title: 360 integrated multichannel campaign plan
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Integrated Marketing Director, with experience orchestrating 360 campaigns in BFSI and technology, expert in the IMC model and the See-Think-Do-Care funnel. I need an executable 360 integrated multichannel campaign plan, with a single governing narrative deployed coherently and sequentially across all channels, ready for the team to execute without reinterpreting the message in each piece.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First, restate what you understand and mark with [ASSUMPTION] everything you infer; if you are missing the product, the business objective, the audience, the channels, the duration, or any brand restriction, ask me before moving forward. First fix the governing message and verify that every channel and every phase derives from it: no asset can contradict the big idea. Then present your plan before executing.

Deliver these sections in order, with a single recognizable narrative thread from end to end:
1. Core strategy: SMART objective, primary and secondary audience with their emotional insight, differential value proposition, and the creative big idea (governing message in one sentence) from which all assets derive.
2. Channel matrix: for each channel, role in the See-Think-Do-Care funnel, asset format, adaptation of the governing message, call to action, and success signal per channel.
3. Phase sequence: expectation, launch, sustain, and close, with narrative, deliverable, and criterion to advance to the next phase.
4. Editorial calendar: week-by-week table with piece, channel, owner, and dependency.
5. KPI table by funnel stage: metric, goal, measurement source, and review cadence.
6. Measurement plan and risk flags: two or three early signals that would require adjusting message, channel mix, or rhythm.

Rules: do not invent media prices or investment amounts; express any budget allocation as relative percentages and ask for it as data if needed. Professional tone, neutral English, without emojis. Mark assumptions with [ASSUMPTION].

prompts.title: Seasonal and key-dates campaign plan
prompts.content: Act as a senior seasonal marketing strategist with fifteen years designing campaign calendars that connect commercial seasons and observances with real demand moments by category and region. I need an actionable seasonal campaign plan for my brand or product, targeting my audience, in my market or region, during the time horizon I am going to plan. If any of this data is missing (brand and what it offers, audience, market, horizon with start date, commercial objective, available channels, or mandatory internal dates), ask me for it before continuing; do not invent the offering or the regional calendar. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. First, restate in one line what you understood and present your plan; then execute. Work in five phases. Inventory: list seasonal, commercial, observance, and mandatory date candidates, each with their exact date in the indicated market. Prioritization: score each candidate from 1 to 5 on relevance to the audience, fit with the offering, inverse competition (the less saturated, the better), and production feasibility; rank, cut the forced ones, and classify into anchor moments, support moments, and moments to ignore. Concept: for each selected date define a specific (not generic) message angle, a value hook without prices and the word free prohibited, content assets, channels, and cadence. Timeline: for each campaign, calculate backwards from the key date three milestones (production start, teaser window, and main publication) and detect collisions between nearby dates. Consolidation: build a master calendar in table format, a one-page mini-brief for each anchor moment, dependencies, saturation risks, and a success metric per campaign aligned with the commercial objective. Declare assumptions when context is missing and mark with what must be confirmed. Deliver the master calendar plus the mini-briefs, ready to assign to production. Neutral, professional English, without emojis, without prices, and without the word free.

prompts.title: Pre-launch sequence and hype generation
prompts.content:
Act as a senior product launch strategist, specializing in pre-launch campaigns and early demand building (waitlist, teaser cadence, and ethical scarcity). Your objective is to accumulate qualified demand and sustained attention before the product goes public, so that launch day starts with a base of already-convinced prospects instead of a cold audience. I need a complete and ready-to-execute pre-launch sequence.

Deliver these components in order:
1. Sequence objective and success metrics: main metric (qualified subscribers on the waitlist and expected conversion on launch day) plus 2 or 3 guide metrics (teaser open rate, confirmation rate, cost per subscriber if applicable). Define what counts as a qualified subscriber.
2. Waitlist mechanics supported by the differential benefit: value proposition for subscribing, entry hook, fields to capture (minimum viable, justify each field), confirmation sequence (double opt-in and welcome email), and a membership benefit that rewards being inside before the general public.
3. List segmentation: how to distinguish the hottest from the warm ones (brief survey, micro-commitment, behavior) and how to treat each segment differently at close.
4. Teaser calendar in countdown by channel: number of teasers, angle of each one (problem, partial glimpse, social proof, objection handling, date reveal), the central copy piece of each teaser, and a suggested asset (visual or text format).
5. Legitimate scarcity and urgency mechanisms: limited spots, early access window for the list, visible countdown and registration close, each with a real and verifiable basis. Distinguish genuine scarcity from invented urgency.
6. Day-by-day schedule from start to launch day: what piece goes out each day, through what channel, with what call to action, and what metric is reviewed.
7. Contingency plan: what to do if registrations are below expectations at the midpoint of the campaign (correction levers without resorting to false urgency).
8. Pre-launch-day verification checklist.

Work method: Interpret the data I give you, plan the sequence, and only then execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before drafting the detail. If the product, launch date, target audience, differential benefit, or channels are missing, ask before drafting; do not invent data. Mark every assumption with [ASSUMPTION].

Output rules: without prices and without the word free; neutral and professional English, without emojis. Every scarcity mechanism must have a verifiable basis; zero invented urgency. Each teaser with a different angle, without repeating the message, with a coherent countdown. The schedule covers every day until launch day with piece, channel, call to action, and metric.

Deliverable: ready-to-execute pre-launch sequence (waitlist + segmentation + teaser calendar + scarcity plan + day-by-day schedule + contingency plan + checklist).

prompts.title: Account-based marketing (ABM) campaign plan
prompts.content:
Act as a senior B2B account-based marketing strategist with experience orchestrating one-to-one and one-to-few campaigns between marketing and sales in complex cycles. I need to concentrate marketing and sales effort on a limited set of high-value accounts, rather than generating scattered demand, in order to unlock higher-quality pipeline, shorten the cycle on strategic accounts, and align both teams around the same accounts and buying groups. The plan must be executable by a small team and measurable from the first week.

Before designing, restate what you understand and present your plan; ask for any missing data (target segment, number of accounts, value proposition, relative average ticket, sales cycle, and available intent signals) in a single batch before proceeding. Mark each missing or assumed datum as [ASSUMPTION].

Deliver an ABM plan with six numbered sections: 1) ICP and scoring: firmographic, technographic, and intent-signal criteria, with a weighted and replicable scoring model (weights by dimension, cutoff threshold, and tiebreaker) that prioritizes the short list. 2) Buying group: map of the five roles (economic decision-maker, champion, user, technical influencer, blocker) with a specific pain, probable objection, and distinct central message per role. 3) Tiering: one-to-one / one-to-few / one-to-many classification by account value, with personalization level, coverage, and promotion or demotion criteria between tiers. 4) Orchestration: week-by-week matrix by journey stage (awareness, engagement, conversion, expansion) crossing channels (LinkedIn, email, content, events, direct sales), triggers, and sequence, scaled to the sales cycle. 5) Content and alignment: personalized assets by account or cluster plus the marketing-sales model (handoff SLA, definition of an engaged account, joint review cadence). 6) Measurement: dashboard with metrics by stage, account engagement, influenced pipeline, attribution schema, and one early success signal per tier in the first two weeks.

Add explicit assumptions, plan limits, and edge cases (very short or very long list, missing intent signals, incomplete buying group). Keep everything in relative intensity and effort: never invent investment figures or tool costs, do not include prices or the word free.

prompts.title: Campaign message structure using the AIDA model
prompts.content: Act as a senior direct-response advertising copywriting strategist, with mastery of persuasion psychology and campaign strategy. I need a campaign message that not only informs but also guides the prospect step by step to a single action, using the AIDA model in its four successive mental states: Attention, Interest, Desire, and Action. Before writing, restate in your own words what product I am promoting, to what audience, what tension drives them, what is my differential value proposition, on what channel the message runs, and what the exact and single action I am seeking is; if you are missing any of those data points, ask for them rather than inventing them. Then build: (1) Attention, a hook that interrupts scrolling, names the audience or their tension, and promises relevance in the first line; (2) Interest, data, context, or a reframe of the problem that sustains reading and connects with the tension; (3) Desire, translates the value proposition into desirable outcomes, adds proof or a demonstration, and neutralizes the main objection; (4) Action, closes with a single clear instruction toward the target action, with low perceived risk and a legitimate reason to act now. Deliver the message labeled by the four AIDA blocks, a running version ready to publish calibrated to the channel, and two alternative variants of the Attention hook. Rules: a single call to action; no prices; no word free; neutral and professional language, no emojis; every claim about the product must be defensible and anything unconfirmed is marked as an assumption. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, and Execute; present your interpretation and your plan before writing.

prompts.title: Co-marketing and partner campaign plan
prompts.content: Act as a senior partner marketing strategist with experience in co-branded B2B campaigns and shared demand-gen models. Design an actionable co-marketing plan to jointly and fairly activate the audiences of two complementary brands. If I do not provide the partner and their fit, the business objective, the audiences of each party, the assets and channels each contributes, or the target period, ask before continuing. If the partner is a direct competitor or the audience fit does not justify the alliance, say so explicitly before proceeding. Deliver the plan in numbered sections: 1) Joint value proposition (what problem they solve together that neither solves alone, shared audience, co-branded angle, and proof that supports the narrative). 2) Fit and objectives (audience overlap and complementarity, SMART objective, a single north metric, and two or three guardrail metrics such as unsubscribe rate or spam complaints). 3) Audience sharing (segment each party contributes, legal basis for data processing and consent, who sends to whom, and how to avoid overlap or excessive cross-contact). 4) Shared assets (co-branded inventory: joint landing page, webinar or event, downloadable content, email sequence, social kit, press release; owner of each piece and usage rules for both logos and names). 5) Responsibility sharing (RACI matrix of who produces, approves, and distributes each asset, with no ambiguous owner, and which channels each party contributes with their estimated reach). 6) Calendar (pre-launch, launch, and sustain phases with milestones and dates relative to the target period, including legal and brand approval window). 7) Measurement and results sharing (definition of shared lead, agreed attribution model, lead sharing and handoff rules with follow-up SLA, KPI dashboard, and joint review cadence). 8) Agreements and risks (minimum terms to document: brand use, exclusivity, data, term, and exit; risk register with probability, impact, and mitigation; success condition and abort condition for the campaign). Mark all estimates as [ASSUMPTION] and separate confirmed from inferred. Do not include prices or promises of free offerings; use relative effort and in-kind contributions if you need to discuss investment. Neutral and professional language. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Campaign post-mortem and learnings
prompts.content: Act as a senior Head of Growth specializing in campaign closure and learning, with mastery of objective-vs-actual gap analysis, attribution by channel and by funnel stage, and blameless retrospectives. Your assignment: convert the close of a recently finished campaign into reusable knowledge and deliver an actionable post-mortem. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the campaign data (name, period, purpose, measurable objectives, actual results, budget and resources, audience, and channels); Plan by restating what you understand and presenting your plan before executing; Execute only after that framing. If any critical datum is missing or ambiguous, ask for it before proceeding and do not invent figures. Proceed as follows: (1) reconstruct the case with the available data; (2) quantify the gap by metric, with fulfillment in percentage and absolute value, and classify each as above-target, on-target, or below-target using an explicit threshold (by default, on-target = between 95 and 105 percent of the goal); (3) attribute causes by channel and by funnel stage (reach, consideration, conversion, retention), separating root cause from symptom and marking each unverifiable assumption with [ASSUMPTION]; (4) distill learnings using the Keep / Adjust / Drop framework, coherent with the diagnosis; (5) prioritize by impact and effort and deliver three to five actions, each with a suggested owner, measurable success signal, and time horizon. When data do not allow clean causal attribution (no control group, overlapping measurement windows, external changes), declare the uncertainty rather than forcing a cause. Maintain a professional and blameless tone: analyze decisions and mechanisms, never people. Deliver: compliance table by metric, cause map by channel and stage, Keep/Adjust/Drop block, and prioritized action list. Neutral and professional language, no prices or amounts unless provided as input, no emojis.

prompts.title: Multitouch attribution model design
prompts.content:
Act as a senior marketing analytics analyst, specialist in multitouch attribution and media mix, with the judgment to distinguish correlation from causality. Your assignment is to design an actionable and auditable multitouch attribution model that distributes the credit of a target metric across a set of channels, to underpin a concrete investment decision. Before executing, restate the decision that motivates the model, the active channels and touchpoints, the conversion and lookback window, the metric to be attributed, and the available tracking data; if any of those elements is missing, ask for it and do not assume. Mark as [ASSUMPTION] every figure or datum not provided by the user.

Deliver, in this order: (1) Typical customer journey: frequent order of touchpoints, role of each in the funnel (discovery, consideration, decision), overlaps, and fit with the conversion window. (2) Data maturity diagnosis: evaluate cross-device, user identifiers, costs by channel, and conversion volume; determine whether a data-driven model is viable (typically requires a sufficient monthly conversion volume for stable estimation; declare the threshold you assume) or whether a rules-based one is preferable, and list critical missing data. (3) Comparative table of candidate models: last-touch, first-touch, linear, time decay, positional U (40-20-40), and data-driven (Shapley or Markov), with their bias, implicit assumption, required data, and when each is appropriate. (4) Recommended model and explicit justification against the business decision, sales cycle, and data maturity; never by default, and state the accepted trade-off. (5) Unambiguous sharing rules: percentage by touchpoint, treatment of repeated channels, direct and branded traffic, lookback window, and de-duplication. (6) Numerical example applied to a concrete journey, with a table showing the distribution of the metric by channel summing to 100% of credit and reflecting the model's logic. (7) Validation plan with an incremental experiment (geo-test or holdout): hypothesis, design, incrementality metric, minimum duration, and decision criterion, to confirm causality rather than merely correlation.

Edge cases to cover: single-touchpoint journeys, conversions without a click (view-through), channels that cannot be tracked, and what to do if volume is insufficient for data-driven. Close with the model's limitations and a periodic review criterion. Do not use prices or the word free; neutral and professional language.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Marketing KPI dashboard design
prompts.content: Act as a senior marketing analytics analyst with experience building decision dashboards in Looker Studio, Power BI, and Tableau, and in funnel modeling. Design the complete blueprint of a marketing KPI dashboard aimed at driving decisions, not accumulating vanity metrics. Before executing, restate the business objective, the audience that reads and decides, and the applicable funnel model, and explain how they condition metric selection; if you are missing a critical datum (objective, audience, funnel, channels, comparison base, BI tool, available data granularity), ask for it rather than inventing it and mark every assumption as [ASSUMPTION]. Deliver: (1) a metric-objective tree that connects each metric to the business decision and filters out what does not move it; (2) a catalog of 5 to 9 primary KPIs mapped to funnel stages (acquisition, activation, conversion, retention, revenue), each with exact formula, unit, source, update frequency, data owner, and justification for why it moves the objective, discarding vanity with the actionable-relevant-comparable criterion; (3) a segment and dimension map (campaign, audience, geography, device, period) plus global filters; (4) a three-layer layout (executive: 3 to 5 north KPIs plus trend; tactical: breakdown by channel and campaign; diagnostic: funnel plus cohorts), indicating for each metric the correct visualization type by its analytical intent (trend, comparison, composition, distribution, detail) and justifying it; (5) an alert matrix with targets and green/amber/red thresholds by KPI and the comparison base; (6) a governance contract with a source table, a single definition per metric, a review cadence, and a criterion for retiring or replacing a KPI. Consider edge cases: incomplete data or source latency, ambiguous multi-touch attribution, KPIs that contradict each other across stages, and mixed audiences in a single view (resolve by separating layers). Explicitly declare assumptions, data limits, and trade-offs (e.g. executive simplicity vs. diagnostic depth). Close with the deliverable ready to implement in any BI tool. MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the request, Plan the blueprint, and only then Execute.

prompts.title: CAC, LTV, and LTV:CAC ratio calculation
prompts.content: Act as a senior unit economics and growth marketing analyst with experience in subscription and recurring-revenue models. I need a diagnosis of the unit economics of my acquisition engine to decide whether to scale, sustain, or correct growth investment. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: first restate what you understood and present your plan; only then execute. Proceed as follows: (1) Normalize all figures to the same period and a single currency; list missing data and ask for it if critical before calculating. (2) Calculate CAC by dividing total acquisition spend (advertising, salaries of the marketing and sales team, agencies, and tools) by new customers in the same period; show the formula with the actual numbers. (3) Calculate LTV using the margin method: average revenue per customer multiplied by gross margin, divided by the churn rate for the period; if there is no churn, use LTV = average revenue multiplied by gross margin multiplied by average life in months, and mark which method you used. (4) Calculate the LTV:CAC ratio and CAC payback period = CAC divided by (average revenue multiplied by gross margin). (5) Validate that the time units for churn, revenue, and payback coincide. (6) Interpret each result against benchmarks (ratio below 1 destroys value; between 1 and 3 tight; around 3 healthy; well above 3 possible underinvestment; payback under 12 months comfortable) and issue a one-sentence health verdict. (7) Propose three prioritized levers to move the ratio: lower CAC, raise gross margin, reduce churn, or increase revenue per customer. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] any estimated value and never invent figures: if a datum is missing and cannot be provided, say so explicitly. Deliver a table (metric | formula | result | reading), the one-sentence verdict, three prioritized recommendations, and the highest-leverage question about which datum is worth refining.

prompts.title: Cohort analysis and retention curves
prompts.content:
Act as a senior retention and growth analyst, expert in product analytics and reading cohort matrices for marketing and product teams. I need to understand the real health of my product's retention by separating the noise from growth: grouping users by entry date and comparing their curves over time makes it possible to distinguish whether the product improves cohort by cohort, where value is lost, and whether product or acquisition changes moved the needle. This feeds investment decisions in onboarding, channels, and retention, and produces LTV projections more honest than a global churn rate.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before executing, restate the objective, confirm the definitions of active user, cohort unit, and retention type, list missing data, and present your plan.

Produce a cohort and retention curve report with these steps: (1) Precisely define the cohort unit (weekly or monthly), the event that counts as active, and the retention type (N-day, unbounded, or rolling); declare each assumption as [ASSUMPTION]. (2) Build the cohort matrix: rows = cohort by entry date, columns = periods 0..N since entry, cells = percentage retention over the size of each cohort; exclude or flag cells of recent cohorts that have not yet matured the period to avoid survivorship bias, and report the size (n) of each cohort to avoid reading noise in small cohorts. (3) Trace the superimposed curves; identify the retention floor (plateau), the period at which it stabilizes, the magnitude of early churn (drop from period 0 to 1), and the slope of the subsequent decay. (4) Compare cohorts against the available segment or channel and against time: flag which ones improve or worsen, distinguish real improvement from mix effect, and correlate breaks with known launches, campaigns, or channel changes, without asserting causality. (5) Close with 3 to 5 recommendations prioritized by expected impact on the curve, distinguishing early-churn interventions from sustained-decay ones, each with the lever and the metric it would move.

Constraints: zero invented figures; every quantitative assertion supported by data or marked as an assumption; do not infer causality from a temporal correlation. If any input data is missing (product, granularity, active event, retention type, horizon, or segment), ask for it before building the matrix. Deliver in neutral and professional language.

prompts.title: Measurement plan with KPI tree
prompts.content: Act as a senior Head of Marketing Analytics with experience building measurement plans and KPI trees (north-star metric, driver trees, input-output models) in digital businesses. I need a measurement plan that connects my business objective to actionable metrics and traces an auditable causal chain from instrumentable activity to business value, not a board of vanity figures. Before executing, restate what you understand and present your plan. Deliver: (1) North-star: 1 north metric aligned to the objective, its formula, why it measures value delivered to the customer and not just activity, and 1-2 health counter-metrics to prevent gaming. (2) KPI tree: decompose the north-star into level-1 KPIs with an explicit equation (sum, product, or funnel) and each KPI into actionable level-2 drivers with an owner; present it as an indented hierarchy showing the mathematical relationship between levels. (3) Metric cards: for each north-star, KPI, and driver provide name, one-sentence definition, exact formula, unit, time granularity, cut dimensions, data source, owner, and goal/threshold with baseline.
