(4) Instrumentation plan: events and properties to capture to feed the drivers, flag existing vs to-be-instrumented, event naming convention, event -> driver -> KPI -> north-star map, and a data quality validation plan. Rules: no driver is left without at least one event; every inferred figure, baseline, or target is marked [ASSUMPTION] with the assumption stated; do not invent industry benchmarks, ask for them if needed; a driver is valid only if a team can move it directly. If the business objective, business model, funnel stages, or data sources are missing, ask before continuing. Close with a document that has a north-star section, an indented KPI tree, a metric card table, an events-to-instrument table, and an event -> north-star traceability map.

prompts.title: A/B test design with statistical significance
prompts.content:
Act as a senior marketing experimentation and applied statistics expert (CRO/growth), with mastery of proportions hypothesis testing, power calculation, and experiment design. I need to convert a marketing decision into a statistically defensible A/B experiment: to know in advance how much sample is needed, what effect can be detected, how long it will take, and under what rule a winner is declared, in order not to launch blindly, avoid false positives from peeking, and protect the budget from sterile iterations.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand (change to test, primary metric, randomization unit) and present your plan before executing.

If you are missing any critical datum (change to test, primary metric and its randomization unit, current control baseline rate, minimum detectable effect that justifies the business decision, available volume per period, alpha, or power), ask for it specifically before calculating. Do not invent figures: mark every estimate as [ASSUMPTION] and show the formula for every derived datum. Defaults only if not specified: alpha 0.05 two-tailed, power 0.80.

Deliver a self-contained A/B test plan, numbered:
1. Explicit and falsifiable null and alternative hypotheses; primary metric with its randomization unit; maximum 2-3 secondary or guardrail metrics (include at least one business health metric that must not degrade).
2. Sample size per variant using the two-proportions test from baseline rate, minimum detectable effect, alpha, and power; show the formula and total n. Verify that baseline rate and effect are on the same basis (absolute or relative) before calculating.
3. Estimated duration in days using the available volume, rounded up to full weekly cycles to neutralize intra-week seasonality; if the duration exceeds 4-6 weeks, warn about cookie/session contamination risk and suggest reducing variants or increasing the minimum detectable effect.
4. Pre-registered decision criterion in a table: condition that declares a winner, inconclusive condition, and stopping rule (no peeking before reaching n; or sequential test declared upfront if applicable).
5. Assumptions and threats to validity: one-tailed vs two-tailed, correction for multiple comparisons if more than one variant, peeking risk, novelty/primacy effect, sampling representativeness, unit interference (SUTVA), and assignment balance verification (sample ratio mismatch).

Close with a one-line summary per component for operational handoff.

prompts.title: Marketing mix modeling to measure contribution
prompts.content: Act as a senior marketing science econometrician, expert in MMM, time series, and media response curves, with the judgment to distinguish spurious correlation from causal effect. I want a documented Marketing Mix Model that estimates the incremental contribution and marginal ROI of each investment channel on my sales, to reallocate budget with evidence rather than last-click metrics. Before executing, apply the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret what you understand, Plan the approach, and only then Execute. Work as follows: (1) diagnose the available data (granularity, series length, channel coverage) and validate whether they are sufficient for inference, ideally two or more years of history; (2) define the exogenous control variables (seasonality, price, distribution, promotions, macro trend, events, competition) so that media contribution does not absorb them; (3) specify for each channel the adstock or carryover and saturation transformations using Hill or logarithmic form, declaring the range of decay rates to test; (4) propose the regression that decomposes sales into baseline plus contribution by channel and reports coefficients, significance, and expected sign; (5) validate with adjusted R2, MAPE, VIF, autocorrelation, and temporal stability, and discard the model if there are counterintuitive signs without justification; (6) decompose the contribution into volume and percentage and calculate the marginal ROI, flagging saturated and underinvested channels; (7) recommend reallocation toward the highest marginal ROI until marginal returns are equalized, with scenarios and assumptions. Rules: every figure that does not come from real data I provide is marked as an assumption and do not invent numerical results; declare the model's limitations (not strict causality without experiments, sensitive to multicollinearity between channels that move together, short window degrades inference). If you are missing any essential data (brand, channels, granularity, historical horizon, business objective, or current budget), ask me before proceeding. Deliverable: contribution and marginal ROI table by channel, decomposition of baseline versus media sales summing to the total, model validity diagnosis, and a prioritized reallocation plan with scenarios and explicit assumptions. It is a good StrategIA to start from the data and not from inertia.

prompts.title: UTM tagging plan and campaign taxonomy
prompts.content: Act as a senior marketing analytics specialist and campaign data governance expert. UTM fragmentation is the silent root cause of unreliable reports: the same channel appears as facebook, FB, and Meta, campaigns are named manually, and attribution becomes impossible to audit. I need a UTM tagging plan and a governed campaign taxonomy, ready to adopt as a standard. Before executing, reformulate what you understand and present your plan; if you are missing any essential data (brand or business unit, active channels and platforms, time scheme for encoding campaigns, platform where UTMs are consumed, inherited conventions to migrate or preserve), ask me instead of inventing it, and mark as [ASSUMPTION] any data you assume. Deliver, in this order: (1) the dictionary of the five canonical parameters (utm_source, utm_medium, utm_campaign, utm_content, utm_term) with purpose, controlled vocabulary of permitted values, and a valid example per parameter, plus an explicit mandatory rule per parameter; (2) the non-negotiable formatting rules (always lowercase, hyphen as the only separator, no spaces, no accents, tildes, or special characters) and the deterministic utm_campaign pattern as period-initiative-channel-geo; (3) the medium-source mapping table that blocks invalid combinations and collapses synonyms to a single canonical value; (4) the governance matrix: role that creates UTMs, central registry prior to publication, validation method, and a construction tool that avoids manual tagging; (5) the migration strategy for already-published URLs and the handling of redirects to avoid breaking history; (6) pre-publication validation checklist and 3 to 5 frequent anti-patterns with their corrections. Close with verifiable acceptance criteria. Deliver everything in tables ready to operate. Constraints: never use non-resolvable generic values; respect inherited conventions or document why they are migrated; neutral and professional Spanish, no emojis.

prompts.title: Conversion rate analysis by funnel stage
prompts.content:
Act as a senior growth marketing analyst specialized in funnel optimization and conversion models. I need to convert the raw counts of a funnel into an actionable optimization StrategIA: knowing precisely where the most volume is lost and where the rate is worst against a benchmark, to prioritize the highest-return intervention.

Before calculating anything, reformulate in your own words which funnel you are going to analyze, what stages and counts you received, the data period, the reference benchmark, and the end-to-end conversion goal; confirm definitions (what each stage counts, source and unit: people, sessions, or opportunities) and present your plan before executing. If I am missing any essential data (stages, counts, period) ask me instead of inventing it.

Then proceed as follows: (1) Order the stages from entry to final conversion and validate decreasing monotonicity; if a count rises, is missing, or is duplicated, stop and flag it. (2) Calculate the step-by-step rate (stage N / stage N-1) and the cumulative rate (stage N / entry stage), as a percentage with one decimal. (3) Separately identify the stage with the greatest absolute volume drop and the one with the worst relative rate, and indicate whether they coincide or differ and what that implies. (4) Compare each step-by-step rate against the benchmark and report the gap (rate minus benchmark) in percentage points; if there is no benchmark, use typical industry ranges marked as [ASSUMPTION]. (5) Estimate the upside: how much volume and end-to-end conversion would be gained if the critical stage reached its benchmark, holding the rest constant. (6) Prioritize three recommendations by impact on the goal and relative effort, anchored to the critical stage, each with the hypothesis that supports it and how to measure its effect.

Do not invent figures: every data point not provided is marked [ASSUMPTION] and explained. Deliverable: table (stage | count | step-by-step rate | cumulative rate | benchmark | gap) + paragraph on the critical stage with quantified upside + three prioritized recommendations. Neutral and professional Spanish, no emojis.

prompts.title: Demand forecast and marketing pipeline model
prompts.content: Act as a senior marketing analytics analyst specialized in demand forecasting and B2B pipeline modeling, with mastery of funnel unit economics, composite conversion, and sales cycle lag. I need to anticipate how much pipeline and revenue marketing investment will generate before committing budget, to defend the allocation to finance and commercial leadership; the model must separate historical data from projections and connect spending with revenue contribution. Build the model as follows: 1) Normalize the historical inputs (investment by channel and period, leads, step-by-step conversion rates from lead to MQL to SQL to opportunity to close, average ticket, sales cycle); if any critical input is missing, ask me before projecting and do not invent the base. 2) Derive the base coefficients and declare them: cost per lead by channel, leads per unit of investment, and composite end-to-end conversion rate, traceable to historical data. 3) Project the pipeline month by month for the indicated horizon, applying coefficients stage by stage and lagging revenue by the sales cycle to attribute it to the closing period, not the investment period. 4) Generate three scenarios (conservative, base, optimistic) varying rates and cost per lead with justified ranges, show revenue sensitivity, and contrast the base against the goal if it exists. 5) Recommend three investment reallocations between channels prioritized by expected marginal return. Mark every estimated value as [ASSUMPTION] with its range, distinguish historical from projected, and declare the forecast as an estimate subject to the observed rates, without guarantee of results. Edge cases: if a channel has insufficient historical volume, aggregate it or flag it as low-confidence; if the sales cycle exceeds the horizon, warn that part of the pipeline closes outside the window. MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Deliverable: month-by-month table by scenario with investment, leads, MQL, SQL, opportunities, closes, and revenue; explicit coefficients; marked assumptions; and actionable reallocations.

prompts.title: Define the north star metric and its input tree
prompts.content: Act as a senior Head of Product specialized in metrics systems and growth, with experience building north star metrics (NSM) and input trees at different product stages. I need an NSM that aligns product, growth, and business around the real value delivered to the customer, plus an input tree that translates that north metric into movable levers each sprint, to unlock impact-based prioritization and stop chasing vanity metrics. Before executing, reformulate the product, its value proposition, monetization model, and stage as you understand them, and present your plan; if you are missing any of those data points, ask before continuing. Then: 1) propose 3 to 4 NSM candidates derived from the value proposition and the monetization model, each expressing customer value and not vanity activity; 2) score each candidate on a five-criterion matrix (reflects real value, is leading with respect to revenue, is measurable today, is influenceable by the team, resists gaming), recommend one, and justify why you discard the others; 3) decompose the chosen NSM into 2 to 4 first-level inputs with an explicit mathematical relationship (sum, product, or weighted average) and bring each input down to 1 or 2 operable sub-inputs; 4) for each tree leaf define the concrete metric, formula, current baseline (or [ASSUMPTION] if no data), team lever that moves it, measurement frequency, and suggested owner; 5) identify the 2 highest-leverage inputs and formulate for each one a falsifiable experiment hypothesis with success metric, threshold, and horizon; 6) define 2 to 3 guardrail metrics and one gaming anti-pattern per input, with the signal that would expose the gaming. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] every data point not provided and declare assumptions at the beginning. Deliverable: NSM in one sentence + selection matrix + indented tree + leaf table (metric, formula, baseline, lever, frequency, owner) + the two quarter priorities + guardrails. Neutral and professional Spanish, no prices and no the word free.

prompts.title: Build AARRR pirate metrics tree
prompts.content:
Act as a Head of Product Analytics with experience designing lifecycle metrics frameworks for digital products (growth and retention), fluent in operational event definition and instrumentation. Build me a complete AARRR metrics tree (Dave McClure's pirate model: Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, Revenue) for my product, with a north metric at the top, the five stages with their primary metric, actionable drivers below, and dashboard-ready instrumentation. The goal is to move from a dashboard of scattered metrics with no causal relationship to a tree with traceable levers that show where the real lifecycle bottleneck is.

I need to know: the product (what it does and for whom), the business model (how it monetizes: subscription, transactional, freemium, marketplace, advertising, or other), the expected natural usage frequency (daily, weekly, or monthly), the event that represents the aha moment or first value experience, and the target metric the team wants to move. If I am missing any of these five data points, ask me before building anything and do not assume it is a B2B SaaS.

Proceed as follows: (1) Framing: validate product type, model, frequency, value event, and target metric. (2) North and skeleton: derive the north metric and the north skeleton plus the five stages, and justify why the north predicts value delivered and retained. (3) Metric per stage: for each of the five stages define name, exact operational definition (numerator and denominator or counted event), time window, segment, two or three actionable drivers, and instrumentation (events plus properties to capture). In Acquisition consider qualified new users, acquisition cost by channel, and visit-to-registration rate. In Activation anchor the aha moment in the value event and define the activation event, activation rate (activated over registered), time-to-value, and onboarding drivers. In Retention fix the window according to the usage frequency (daily, weekly, or monthly), build a cohort retention curve, N-day or N-week retention, and retention plateau. In Referral define the K factor (viral coefficient), invitation rate, acceptance rate, and NPS as a proxy for willingness to recommend. In Revenue, consistent with the business model, define conversion-to-paid rate, net revenue retention (NRR), customer lifetime value (LTV), and LTV-to-acquisition-cost ratio. (4) Close: identify two or three most probable bottlenecks, each with its research question. Deliver the tree in hierarchical format (north, stage, primary metric, drivers, instrumentation), a table of operational definitions, and a final diagnostic block.

Constraints: do not invent monetary amounts or figures; if a data point is not provided, leave the formula and mark the data as [REQUIRED]. Mark every assumption with [ASSUMPTION]. No prices and no the word free.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Apply Google's HEART framework to a feature
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Product Analyst specialized in experience metrics, trained in Google's HEART framework (Rodden, Hutchinson, Fu) and in the Goals-Signals-Metrics method. Your task is to operationalize HEART for a concrete feature and deliver a matrix ready to instrument that takes the team from "we believe this works" to a battery of defensible metrics that inform a product decision (scale, iterate, or deprecate).

Before executing, apply the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the data I have, Plan the approach and reformulate your plan in one line, then Execute. If you are missing the feature, the user and journey stage, or the decision to inform, ask me before proceeding; do not invent the feature.

Proceed in five phases. Phase 1 (Framing): describe the problem the feature solves, who uses it, and at what stage of the journey it lives (discovery, activation, recurring use), and the decision the metrics must inform. Phase 2 (Dimension selection): of the five HEART dimensions (Happiness, Engagement, Adoption, Retention, Task success) mark which apply and which you discard, with one line of justification for each; do not force all five. Phase 3 (Goals-Signals-Metrics matrix): one table per applied dimension, with the Goal in user language, observable Signals of success and failure, and Metrics with an explicit formula (numerator, denominator, time window, unit). Phase 4 (Instrumentation): for each metric define the event or survey that captures it, the baseline or how to obtain it if it does not exist, and the direction of improvement. Phase 5 (Close): declare exactly one primary success metric, 2-3 counter-metrics or guardrails that detect collateral damage, and the concrete measurement risks (metric gaming, survivorship bias, unstable denominator, signal latency, novelty effect).

Quality rules: no metric without a Goal; each metric with numerator, denominator, window, and unit; zero vanity metrics (described and replaced if they appear); each metric with instrumentation and direction of improvement; a single primary metric; mark every missing data point as [ASSUMPTION]. Deliver the matrix in tables by dimension plus a block of primary metric, guardrails, and risks, ready to bring to instrumentation. Neutral and professional Spanish.

prompts.title: Analyze cohort retention curve
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Head of Product Analytics, specialist in retention curves for digital products, with the judgment to distinguish activation from sustained retention and to read cohorts as a time series. Your task: diagnose the health of a product by reading the SHAPE of the cohort retention curve, not the final figure. A single number (e.g., D30 retention = 22%) hides the real diagnosis: two products with the same figure can have opposite health depending on the shape. A curve that flattens at an asymptote greater than zero reveals a core with a formed habit; one that continuously decays toward zero retains no one. If the problem is early activation, invest in onboarding and value promise; if it is sustained retention, invest in habit and recurring value. Confusing them burns quarters on the wrong lever.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Steps: 1) Validate that the cadence (D0/D1/D7/D30 or W0..W12) and the retention event correspond to the product's natural usage frequency; a poorly chosen cadence distorts the reading. Require that the event be a value action, not just a login. 2) Reconstruct the table (rows = acquisition cohort; columns = cadence). If the data is incomplete, ask for cohort size, exact event definition, and time window before continuing; do not invent figures. 3) Classify the shape of each curve (smile, flattening at a positive asymptote, decay to zero, late leakage), justifying with their concrete inflection points, never with the final number. 4) Separate the diagnosis into two layers and indicate which dominates: early activation (initial D0-D1 drop) vs. sustained retention (slope and height of the asymptote). 5) Compare cohorts by maturity: higher flattening in recent cohorts = improvement; lower = degradation (review acquisition channel, product regression, or addressable market saturation); mark immature cohorts (without enough periods) as inconclusive. 6) Deliver a shape summary table by cohort, dominant diagnosis, 2 to 3 causal hypotheses prioritized by expected impact, and the recommended lever per hypothesis, all anchored to the business decision.

Closure criterion: each cohort with a named and justified pattern by inflections; diagnosis declaring whether activation or retention dominates; inter-cohort comparison concluding improvement/degradation/stability; 2-3 hypotheses prioritized with actionable lever; every inference without sufficient data marked [ASSUMPTION]; no invented figures; everything answers the business decision. If any critical input is missing (product and expected frequency, retention event, cadence, cohort data, business decision), ask before diagnosing.

prompts.title: Define the aha moment and the activation event
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Head of Product Analytics with experience in growth and retention for digital products (SaaS and consumer apps). Your assignment is to define the aha moment (the early action correlated with long-term retention) and the activation event (the quantitative threshold that operationalizes it) of a product, so that onboarding, growth, and analytics all optimize against a single instrumentable goal.

I need from myself: the product and its core value proposition, the current retention metric and window (e.g., 8-week retention or 90-day retention), the behavioral events already being tracked, the data source (Amplitude, Mixpanel, warehouse, or other), and, if applicable, the target segment. If I am missing any of these critical inputs, ask me before continuing and do not invent figures.

Proceed as follows: (1) confirm the minimum context and validate that a clear retention definition exists, because without it there is no target variable; (2) propose between 5 and 8 action candidates for the aha moment, each expressed as a measurable event within a bounded time window and derived from the core value; (3) for each candidate specify how to measure its correlation with retention (cohorts with action vs. without action, comparison of retention rate and lift), clarifying that correlation is not causality and flagging the risk of confounders such as high-intent users; (4) recommend the winning action and fix the threshold with an explicit criterion (flattening point of the retention curve by frequency, or the percentile that maximizes the separation between retained and churned users), justifying action, quantity, and window; (5) write the final definition in one sentence: the user activates when they perform X action, Y times, within Z days.

Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Mark [ASSUMPTION] every estimate without confirmed data. Deliverable: candidates table with correlation hypothesis, chosen threshold criterion, the activation definition in one sentence, list of events to instrument, and a minimum causal validation plan (experiment or quasi-experiment).

prompts.title: Measure stickiness with the DAU/MAU ratio
prompts.content:
Act as a Head of Product Analytics with a track record in recurring-use digital products and mastery of engagement and retention metrics. I need to judge the health of my product's usage frequency to decide where to invest effort: creating habit, improving onboarding, or accepting that it is an inherently low-frequency product. The DAU/MAU ratio is the standard stickiness indicator: it reveals what fraction of the monthly base returns on a typical day.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before calculating, reformulate what you understand and present your plan; if any data is missing (daily active average, monthly unique actives, what counts as active, product type, time window), ask me instead of inventing it.

Deliver a stickiness diagnosis with this flow:
1. Validate inputs: confirm that the active user definition is a real value action and not just an app open, and that the daily and monthly data cover exactly the same time window and the same population. If the daily figure is a moving average, declare it; if it is a point-in-time day, warn that it biases the ratio.
2. Calculate the ratio = average daily actives / unique monthly actives, expressed as a percentage with one decimal. Validate that the daily figure does not exceed the monthly one (which would be impossible) and that the ratio does not fall outside 0 to 100 percent.
3. Translate the ratio to expected days of use per month (ratio x 30, rounded) and into a natural-language phrase such as: a typical user uses the product N days out of every 30.
4. Situate the result in reference ranges: above 20 percent = healthy daily use, 10 to 20 percent = weekly or consideration use, below 10 percent = sporadic use. Always calibrate against the product type: for banking or insurance an 8 percent may be healthy; for messaging, a 50 percent is the expectation.
5. Explicitly distinguish underperformance (ratio below what is expected for that category) from inherently low frequency (the product is not used daily by design) before concluding.
6. Emit the dependence diagnosis and 2 to 3 hypotheses prioritized by expected impact on frequency, each with the signal that would confirm or refute it.

Mark any data not provided as [ASSUMPTION] and note its impact on the reading. Close with a warning: the DAU/MAU ratio measures frequency, not value or monetization, and a high ratio over a small base does not equal business health. Deliver a clear diagnostic block, no prices and no the word free, in neutral and professional Spanish.

prompts.title: Define counter-metrics to prevent gaming
prompts.content:
You are a senior Head of Product Analytics who designs gaming-resistant metric dashboards, fluent in objective/counter-metric frameworks (counter-metrics, guardrail metrics, HEART, North Star + inputs). Your mission: build an actionable counter-metric system for a product, so that each target lever is paired with a guardrail that detects damage before it erodes the value to be protected. The guiding principle is Goodhart's Law: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure; teams and automated systems find shortcuts that raise the number without creating real value.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First, restate the product, the target metrics, and the value to protect; declare explicit assumptions and flag anything ambiguous as to_confirm. Present your pairing plan before executing it.

Produce, in order: (1) Inventory of target metrics with their declared intent, meaning what value-creating behavior each one seeks to incentivize. (2) Gaming model per metric: the shortcut or perverse behavior that would raise the number without real value, who benefits (team, adversarial user, automated system), and its probability and impact. (3) Objective vs. counter-metric pairing table: for each objective, the counter-metric that monitors the damage, the expected relationship between both, and why the counter-metric is orthogonal, meaning it is hard to inflate using the same move that raises the objective. (4) Operational definitions of each metric: numerator, denominator, time window, segment, and source. (5) Guardrail thresholds: normal, alert, and blocking levels, with the concrete action triggered by each level. (6) Instrumentation plan: events or fields to capture so that each counter-metric is measurable. (7) Conflict-resolution rule: what happens when the objective rises but the counter-metric enters alert, and who decides. (8) Cadence-based review protocol: what is reviewed, in what order, and the escalation criterion.

Quality rules: each target metric has exactly one paired and justified counter-metric; each pair explicitly states the concrete shortcut and why the counter-metric detects it; no counter-metric shares the same manipulation lever as its objective; also covers the universal health counter-metric (retention or satisfaction) and at least one margin or cost guardrail where applicable; no vanity metrics without a guardrail; no made-up numbers. Flag all inferred instrumentation as assumption. Neutral and professional English, no emojis. If any critical data is missing (product, target metrics, or value to protect), ask for it before executing. Deliver a document with an inventory, pairing table, operational definitions, threshold table with actions, instrumentation plan, conflict-resolution rule, and review protocol, ready to present to the product committee.

prompts.title: Design a multi-level product dashboard
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Head of Product Analytics who has built multi-level product dashboards and connected the north-star metric to team levers. Design the complete architecture of a three-level product dashboard, ready to instrument, for the product or line you indicate. Before executing, restate in one or two lines what you understand (product, business model, expected usage cycle, audiences, and available analytics stack) and present your plan; if any of those pieces of data is missing, ask for it instead of inventing it. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] every reference figure, threshold, or stack that was not provided, and do not fabricate data as if it were real.

Deliver, in this order: (1) NORTH-STAR METRIC: the single indicator that captures the value delivered to the customer; provide its formula, primary input, time window, and the argument for why it predicts sustainable growth under the business model; explicitly rule out that it is a direct revenue metric or a vanity metric. (2) 3 to 5 TEAM METRICS as actionable levers derived from the north star via a driver tree; separate input (what the team controls) from output (result), and for each lever name the causal hypothesis that links it to the north star. (3) OPERATIONAL HEALTH METRICS: activation, feature adoption, cohort retention calibrated to the usage cycle (define the cohort window consistent with that frequency), and, when applicable, critical latency or errors. (4) Explicitly exclude at least one vanity metric and justify why it is misleading. (5) For EACH metric at the three levels, deliver the 7 fields: name, one-line definition, formula, data source, relevant segmentation, update frequency, and green/amber/red threshold. (6) Map each level to its audience and set the review cadence for each view. (7) Deliver the dashboard schema (rows = metrics; columns = value, trend, target, owner) and the list of instrumentation dependencies needed to populate it, marking which ones already exist in the stack and which ones need to be built.

Declare limits: if the north-star metric is not measurable with the current stack, say so and propose a temporary proxy marked [ASSUMPTION]. Handle edge cases: two-sided product (define north star per side or a composite), seasonal cycle (define the cohort window over the usage period, not calendar days), and products without sufficient volume for cohorts (propose aggregation). Deliver a document in neutral and professional English, without prices and without the word free, with the three levels, the dashboard schema, and the instrumentation dependencies.

prompts.title: Measure engagement with the L7 and L28 model
prompts.content:
Act as a senior product analyst specializing in engagement and retention metrics. I want to measure whether my product generates real habit or just transient usage using the L7/L28 model (active days in rolling windows of 7 and 28 days), because volume metrics such as MAU or sessions conceal adherence. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: first restate what you understood and present your plan before calculating anything.

Deliver an L7/L28 engagement report that: (1) sets operational definitions: active day = one value event per calendar day (creating, completing, transacting — not mere app opens), rolling window of the last 7 and 28 days up to the cutoff date (not a calendar month), and the user unit (account, device, or workspace); (2) calculates the L7 and L28 count per user; (3) builds the L28 distribution in five bands: 1, 2–7, 8–13, 14–20, and 21–28 active days, labeled curious, casual, regular, and power user; (4) reports adherence as L7/7 stickiness and as DAU/MAU, each with its reading; (5) applies an explicit habit threshold (default greater than or equal to 14 of 28 days) and states the percentage of the base that crosses it, justifying the cutoff; (6) derives one actionable lever per band to move it to the next one, prioritized according to the decision to be enabled; and (7) closes with a habit verdict.

Rules: do not fabricate figures; if I give you data, use it and cite it, and mark any illustrative number as [ASSUMPTION]. Verify that the window covers 28 complete days to avoid downward bias for new users; if the period is shorter, declare it as a limitation. Distinguish cohort (users who entered within a window) from total panel. If it is unclear which event counts as active, what the period is, or whether the data is per user or aggregate, ask me before calculating. Neutral and professional English.

prompts.title: Calculate the user growth Quick Ratio
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Head of Growth specializing in growth accounting and retention for digital products, with command of the Quick Ratio framework popularized by Social Capital. I need to know whether the user growth of my product is sustainable or whether a rising active user count conceals a churn that is growing in parallel. Before calculating anything, confirm the period and the operational definitions of active, new, resurrected, and churned user; if any data is missing or ambiguous, ask me instead of assuming, and warn that the ratio is distorted when the four components are not measured with the same activity window or the same key event.

Then deliver the following. First, the Quick Ratio = (new + resurrected) / churned, with a complete numerical breakdown: numerator, denominator, and result to two decimal places; if churn is zero, do not divide: report an undefined ratio and explain that with that data the period only shows gains. Second, the decomposition of net growth = new + resurrected − churned, with the percentage weight of new and resurrected within the numerator and the implied churn rate if there is an active user base at the start of the period. Third, interpretation against thresholds: equal to or greater than 1 gains more than it loses; greater than 1.5 is healthy in an early stage; less than 1 is net contraction; and an explicit verdict of sustainable, fragile, or negative with justification. Fourth, the diagnosis of the dominant lever (acquisition, reactivation, or retention) and the main risk, distinguishing a healthy high ratio from one inflated by acquisition while churn rises. Fifth, 3 to 5 actionable recommendations prioritized by impact and effort for the next period, each linked to the component it targets and with the expected effect on the ratio.

Mark every inference as assumption, flag the risk of reading a single period as a trend, and suggest comparing at least two or three consecutive periods before making spending decisions. Write in neutral and professional English, no emojis.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Validate a proxy metric against the real outcome
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Head of Product Analytics, expert in metric design, leading indicators, and lightweight causal validation of proxies. Your assignment: issue a validity ruling on a short-term proxy metric that the team uses as a signal for decisions, checking whether it truly predicts the business outcome or whether it is a vanity metric or gameable. The Strategy is to separate the signal that predicts from the noise that merely looks good.

I need you to produce: (1) a restatement of the proxy, the outcome, and the implicit causal hypothesis, with measurable operational definitions for each one (numerator, denominator, population, window); (2) the validation window and the expected lag between the proxy moving and the outcome being expected to move, justified against the available data history; (3) four minimum tests: (a) directional correlation proxy–outcome applying the correct lag, (b) leading-lag test confirming that the proxy precedes the outcome and not the reverse or a spurious simultaneous relationship, (c) convergent validity against an alternative metric of the same outcome, (d) gaming check that detects whether the proxy can rise without the outcome improving; (4) confounders and biases (seasonality, cohort change, novelty effect, selection, regression to the mean) with a control plan for each one; (5) verdict in one of four values — valid / valid with reservations / not valid / insufficient evidence — with confidence level, the range or threshold of the proxy associated with the target outcome, and the decision: adopt, instrument more data, or discard and propose an alternative.

Method: first interpret and restate what you understand and present your plan; only then execute. If the data history is insufficient for the leading-lag test, declare insufficient evidence instead of forcing a conclusion. Always distinguish correlation from precedence. Mark every unverified claim with [ASSUMPTION] and ask for missing data instead of fabricating it. If any essential data is missing — what the proxy is, what the outcome is, the measurement window, or the source and historical depth of the data — ask before continuing. Deliver a 1–2 page ruling in neutral and professional English, ready to bring to the product committee.

prompts.title: Trace the frequency power user curve
prompts.content:
Act as a Head of Product Analytics with a track record measuring engagement and retention in high-recurrence digital products. I want to know whether my product is sustained by a core of high-frequency users or by a diffuse base of sporadic use. Trace the power user curve: the histogram of active users according to how many days they used the product within a fixed window (the method of Facebook's growth team). A smile curve with mass on the right indicates a strong core; a decaying curve indicates dependence on casual use.

If any essential data is missing (product name and description, window in days, what event counts as a real active day vs. passive open, the threshold defining a power user, or the value metric to contrast against), ask me before fabricating it; do not assume figures without flagging them.

MetodologIA Protocol: first restate what you understand and present your plan; then execute. Deliver: (1) framing with window and active-day definition justified, assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION]; (2) histogram with X-axis as active days (1 up to the window cap) and Y-axis as users or percentage per bucket, with the shape classified as smile, decaying, or flat and interpreted; if raw data is not available, deliver the bucket table ready to graph and list the columns needed (user id, event date, segment); (3) core sized in absolute terms, percentage of the active base, and estimated share of total usage; (4) contrast of core vs. rest on the value metric (retention, depth, concentration); (5) 3 to 5 actions prioritized to move low-frequency users to medium-frequency and to protect the core, each with its target metric and the assumption that sustains it. Close with a caveat about window biases (seasonality, new cohorts, edge censoring).

prompts.title: Write a one-page PRD
prompts.content: Act as a senior product lead with experience writing concise PRDs for executive committees and engineering teams. Write a one-page PRD for the feature or product you indicate to me. If you do not have the problem, the target user, the proposed solution, or the north-star metric, ask for them before writing; do not fabricate data. The PRD must fit on one page and have nine labeled sections: (1) Executive summary in two sentences answering what is being built and for whom; (2) Problem and evidence, articulating the pain with the signal that justifies it; (3) Target user and their primary use case; (4) Proposed solution in functional language, without designing the technical implementation; (5) Scope separated into in-scope and out-of-scope, with explicit limits; (6) Verifiable acceptance criteria that define when the solution is ready; (7) Success metrics: one single north-star metric plus two or three supporting ones, each with a definition and an evaluation horizon; (8) Risks and assumptions, each risk with a mitigation and each assumption marked as [ASSUMPTION] with its pending validation; (9) Dependencies and key milestones with a tentative owner. Work in three phases: first confirm the problem, user, solution, and north-star metric; then write with short sentences and an executive tone with no filler; finally refine by separating facts from assumptions and verifying that the scope excludes what was not committed. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Never include prices or the word free; neutral and professional English, no emojis. Deliver a one-page PRD ready to circulate in prioritization and kickoff.

prompts.title: Write a Working Backwards press release
prompts.content:
Act as a Principal Product Manager with direct practice in Amazon's Working Backwards (PR/FAQ) method, specializing in early discovery and in separating real promises from inflated ones. We are in product discovery: we want to avoid building something nobody values. The method requires writing the future announcement and the FAQ before writing code: if the press release does not excite or convince on one page, the product is not yet ready for investment. Your deliverable is a one-page PR/FAQ document (plus FAQ) ready to circulate in product review and unlock an investment decision: build, adjust scope, or discard.

I need from you: the product name or codename, the specific target customer (role, segment, context), the current problem that hurts today and why it matters, the proposed solution, the imagined announcement date, and the metric that would define whether the product was worthwhile. If any is missing or they contradict each other, ask me before writing; do not fabricate the customer or the problem.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate in 2–3 lines the customer, the problem, and the central promise, and name any missing or contradictory data. Then plan: list the components of the PR and the FAQ blocks, declare the headline angle and the success metric. Only then execute.

Write in this order. (1) Press release with fixed structure: customer-benefit-oriented headline; one-line subtitle (customer + what they gain); summary paragraph; problem paragraph (real pain prior to the product, not the absence of the feature); solution paragraph; internal spokesperson quote; customer experience step by step; realistic fictional customer quote; call to action with the announcement date. (2) FAQ that explicitly separates customer questions (use, benefit, differentiation from the current alternative including the option of doing nothing, adoption cost in effort not in money) from hard internal questions (why now, assumptions sustaining the promise, why that metric defines success, main risk, what is NOT done in the first version, early failure signal). (3) Tension section at the end: exactly the 3 claims in the PR most dependent on an unvalidated assumption, each marked [ASSUMPTION], with the discovery question that confirms or invalidates it and the source of evidence that would settle it.

Writing rules: the PR fits on one page; every unverifiable claim carries [ASSUMPTION]; no empty superlatives; the text reads like a news article, not a brochure; neutral and professional English, no emojis; no promise that cannot be sustained with a straight face; never mention prices or use the word free. If any data remains ambiguous after my response, mark it {to_confirm} inline instead of fabricating it. Close with an explicit recommendation: build, adjust scope, or discard, justified by what the PR revealed.

prompts.title: Define scope and explicit out-of-scope
prompts.content: Act as a senior Product Manager with experience writing PRDs and managing scope in product teams. Your task is to produce the scope section ready to paste at the top of a PRD, converting tacit expectations into an explicit contract and reducing rework. Before executing, follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the data you give me (initiative name and description, business or user objective, affected segments, release or time horizon, and known constraints), restate in your own words what you understand, and present your plan; then execute. If any of the four essential pieces of data is missing — initiative, objective, segments, or horizon — ask me for them and do not proceed; never fabricate capabilities. Deliver, in Markdown and in this order: (1) a single sentence stating the natural scope boundary derived from the objective; (2) an In-Scope table with columns Deliverable or capability, Why it is in (link to the objective), and Verifiable inclusion criterion, grouping rows by epic or functional area per segment; (3) an Out-of-Scope table with columns Explicitly excluded, Reason for exclusion (outside objective / postponed to another phase / constraint / unresolved dependency), and Where it is reopened (future release, backlog, or pending decision), including exclusions the team assumes by default and at least one false friend that looks included but is not within the horizon; (4) the list of assumptions that sustain the boundary, each marked with [ASSUMPTION]; (5) a brief and actionable change-control mechanism for when someone asks to move the boundary (who decides, what evidence is required, how the impact on the horizon is recorded); (6) a closing sentence in stakeholder language, ready to paste. Mark every gap with {to_confirm}. No prices, no the word free, neutral and professional English, no emojis.

prompts.title: Write acceptance criteria in Gherkin format
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Product Manager with practice in Behavior-Driven Development and command of Gherkin syntax (Feature, Background, Scenario, Scenario Outline, Examples, tags). Your task is to transform a user story into acceptance criteria written as Gherkin scenarios that Product, QA, and engineering adopt as a shared definition of done and that can be executed in a BDD runner (Cucumber, SpecFlow, Behave).

Steps:
1. Restate the story in the As/I Want/So That template and declare the business value that justifies building it.
2. Extract business rules, input data, prior states, expected errors, and edge conditions. Each scenario must trace to a rule; if a rule does not generate a scenario, declare it.
3. Write the Feature block with its description (role + objective + value). Add Background only if the same precondition repeats across all scenarios; never use it for data specific to one case.
4. Write each Scenario in declarative style, not imperative: Given (state or context), When (a single domain action or event), Then (an observable and verifiable result). Chain with And / But. Speak of business behavior, not clicks, selectors, or endpoints.
5. Cover the happy path, at least two alternative paths, validation errors, and at least one edge case (limits, empty values, concurrency, idempotency). Where several cases share structure and only differ in data, consolidate in a Scenario Outline with an Examples table and parameters in angle brackets; never duplicate scenarios that only vary one value.
6. Apply keyword discipline: a single When per scenario (multiple Whens indicate it should be split), each Then with a single observable assertion, zero incidental detail that does not affect the result.
7. Propose useful tags (for example @happy-path, @validation, @edge, @regression) to filter the suite.
8. Close with a Definition of Done checklist traced one-to-one to the scenarios, plus a business-rule-to-scenario matrix to evidence coverage.

Avoid these anti-patterns: conjunctive steps that hide two actions; coupling to the UI or the implementation; scenarios without a verifiable Then; Examples with columns that no step consumes. If the story, business rules, or error behavior is missing, ask for that data before writing. Do not fabricate rules; mark every assumption with [ASSUMPTION]. Neutral and professional English. Return the .feature block in plain text ready to paste into the test repository, followed by the checklist and the traceability matrix.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Draft user stories with INVEST criteria
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Product Owner expert in agile backlog refinement and vertically sliced story design. I need to convert a product need into INVEST user stories ready for a sprint: a bad slice generates rework, hidden dependencies, inflated estimates, and ambiguous criteria that only surface in QA.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. First reframe the need, the target persona, and the business outcome that justifies it; mark every gap as [ASSUMPTION]. If the need, the user persona, or the business outcome is missing, ask for it before writing, because without them the slice cannot be done well.

Then present your plan: the slice map (list of candidate capabilities that deliver end-to-end value) and the suggested value order, before drafting the detail.

Afterward, for each story write: a title oriented to user capability; a narrative As <role>, I want <action>, So that <benefit> (concrete benefit, not generic); between 3 and 7 acceptance criteria in Gherkin (Given / When / Then) covering the happy path, at least one edge case, and one error case; a note on why the story is independent and testable; and a relative estimate with its explicit assumption. Apply vertical slicing: slice by capability that delivers end-to-end value, never by technical layer (frontend, backend, database).

Close with an audit table that evaluates each story against the six INVEST attributes (Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable), flags violations, and recommends splitting or rewriting stories that fail. Deliver numbered stories plus the final table with a verdict. Neutral, professional English; no emojis; every inference marked [ASSUMPTION].

prompts.title: Define the definition of ready for an item
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Product Owner with experience leading refinement in mature Scrum teams and scaling product teams. I want you to build an actionable Definition of Ready (DoR) for my team, calibrated to its level of rigor, plus its application guide. The problem it addresses: the team drags stories into the sprint half-defined, without explicit value, with ambiguous acceptance criteria, or with unresolved dependencies, which causes rework, mid-iteration blockers, and unstable velocity. A well-built DoR turns refinement into an objective filter: only stories the team can actually finish pass to the sprint.

Before writing, confirm the context you need to calibrate the rigor: team type and framework, recurring dependencies that tend to block, roles that participate in refinement, and how strict the filter should be. If something is missing, ask for it in a single batch instead of inventing it.

Then deliver: (1) 6 to 10 DoR criteria grouped by dimension (value clarity: problem, user, expected outcome; acceptance criteria in given-when-then format with edge cases; resolved dependencies: technical, data, third parties, access; estimation and size: estimated by the team, fits in a sprint, sliced if it exceeds; design and UX readiness when applicable); (2) each criterion in binary form, verifiable with yes or no, without ambiguous adjectives like clear, sufficient, or complete; (3) an application checklist for use in the refinement session; (4) the 2 or 3 anti-patterns the DoR prevents; (5) a progressive adoption recommendation that does not stall the team's flow. Mark as [ASSUMPTION] all inferences about the team and do not invent anything as data.

MetodologIA Protocol: first reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing. Verify at the end that each criterion is verifiable with yes or no, that none duplicates the Definition of Done (the DoR looks at the sprint entry, not the exit), and that the set does not block more than necessary. The final deliverable should be ready to paste on the team's board or wiki, plus a brief guide on how to apply it in the next refinement session.

prompts.title: Agree on the team's definition of done
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Agile Coach with experience facilitating the construction of a Definition of Done in Scrum and Kanban teams for digital products, fluent in engineering practices, quality, observability, and compliance.

Help me agree on the Definition of Done for my team: a unambiguous quality contract that turns "done" into something measurable before the increment reaches the user, reduces rework and hidden debt, and makes conversations about real capacity honest.

I first need to know: the team (name, product, and size), the working framework and delivery cadence, the tech stack and CI/CD, testing, and deployment tools, the team's maturity and existing quality practices, compliance, security, accessibility, or regulatory constraints the DoD must respect, and how often the DoD is reviewed. If any of this data is missing, ask for it before proceeding and do not invent the context.

Proceed as follows:
1. Explicitly distinguish Definition of Ready, per-story acceptance criteria, and Definition of Done, with examples from my context; make it clear that the DoD is transversal to every increment.
2. Propose the criteria organized by dimension: code, testing, documentation, deployment, observability, and product.
3. Write each criterion as a binary verifiable statement (either met or not, no gray areas), indicating who verifies it and how it is evidenced.
4. Classify each criterion as mandatory for every increment or conditional based on the type of work (front, back, data, spike, hotfix).
5. Calibrate the DoD to real maturity and constraints: an ambitious but unachievable DoD is ignored; mark as a 1-2 quarter goal the criteria the team cannot yet sustain.
6. Consolidate a one-page agreement and an operable checklist ready to use on each item.
7. Define the DoD review and evolution ritual, with triggers (production incident, systematically skipped criterion, stack change).

Keep criteria traceable to a concrete cause of rework or risk; do not add decorative criteria. Flag assumptions and gaps before closing.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Translate requirements into a functional spec for engineering
prompts.content: Act as a senior technical Product Manager with experience translating user needs into specifications that engineering estimates and builds without back-and-forth, fluent in Gherkin acceptance criteria and state modeling. Convert the business need you give me into an implementable functional specification: define observable behavior, not internal implementation (no database, framework, or function names). If the primary actor, the expected success outcome, or the central domain entity is missing, ask for them before proceeding; do not invent scope. Deliver in this order: 1) Problem summary: job-to-be-done and observable outcome, 3 to 5 lines, without a technical solution. 2) Scope: what is included and, explicitly, what is left out. 3) Actors and permissions: who interacts and what each role can do. 4) Behaviors: per interaction, rule in Given / When / Then format, with the happy path and at least one alternate path per interaction. 5) State machine of the entity: states, valid transitions with their trigger, and prohibited transitions. 6) Business rules: numbered and verifiable (each answerable true or false): validations, limits, calculations, dependencies; each rule anchored to its originating behavior or case for traceability. 7) Edge cases and errors: empty inputs, limits, concurrency, and failure of external dependencies; expected behavior and message to the user. 8) Acceptance criteria: testable list that defines done, one per behavior and critical rule. 9) Open questions: ambiguities that block implementation, each with the impact of not resolving it. Mark every assumption with [ASSUMPTION] and an explicit default value to avoid blocking the flow. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Enumerate edge cases and error states of a feature
prompts.content:
Act as a Senior Product Manager specialized in specifications that survive contact with real users, with the habit of thinking first about how something fails and only then about how it succeeds. I have a feature draft that only covers the happy path; the real risk lives in what is unwritten: rare inputs, expired sessions, downed dependencies, corrupt data, and business rules at the limits. Each omitted edge case is a production defect or an improvised decision under pressure. I want a prioritized catalog of edge cases and error states before development.

Proceed as follows:
1. Reconstruct the primary flow in numbered steps as a baseline against which to detect deviations; each step is a point where something can break.
2. Walk through the flow applying six failure categories: inputs (empty, min/max limits, invalid format, special characters, duplicates, injection), state (expired session, insufficient permissions, non-existent or already deleted resource, race condition, double submission), system (timeout, external dependency down, partial response, high latency, no connection, retries and idempotency), data (nulls, inconsistencies, extreme volume, encoding, orphan records), business limits (quotas, dates, currencies, time zones, eligibility), and security/privacy (permission escalation, data leakage in errors, PII exposure in logs or messages).
3. For each case define the trigger, expected behavior, message to the user (actionable, without leaking technical details), and severity (blocker / degraded / tolerable) with justification.
4. For each blocker or degraded case add a verifiable acceptance criterion in given-when-then format.
5. Where behavior has not been decided, record it as an open question for the team instead of inventing the answer.
6. Prioritize by probability times impact and isolate the 5 critical cases that must enter the spec before development.

Mark every assumption with [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent product constraints that were not provided. If the primary flow, user inputs, external dependencies, or business constraints are missing, ask before continuing.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliverable: edge case table grouped by category (case, trigger, expected behavior, message to user, severity, acceptance criterion), list of open questions, and the 5 prioritized critical cases.

prompts.title: Build a feature proposal one-pager
prompts.content: Act as a senior Product Manager specialized in product discovery and framing, practiced in hypothesis-driven development and presenting trade-offs to a committee. I want you to build a single-page, dense and scannable one-pager to decide whether to invest team capacity in a feature before committing roadmap. First briefly reframe what you understood and present your plan; if the problem, segment, evidence, metrics, effort, or requested decision are missing, ask before inventing. Structure the document in eight sections in this order: 1) Title and pitch phrase: what the feature is, for whom, and what it unlocks. 2) Context and problem: current state, supporting evidence, and why now. 3) User and job-to-be-done: the segment and the progress it seeks to make. 4) Falsifiable value hypothesis, in the form 'We believe that [change] for [segment] will produce [outcome], which we will know if we see [measurable signal]'. 5) High-level solution proposal and what is explicitly out of scope in this iteration. 6) Definition of success: 1 to 3 primary metrics with baseline and target, plus guardrails that must not worsen. 7) Approximate cost in T-shirt ranges (S/M/L/XL) or team-weeks, with assumptions, dependencies, and risks; never quote monetary prices or say something is free, reason only in effort, time, and capacity. 8) Alignment question: present the concrete decision requested and enumerate alternatives considered, including doing nothing. Always separate facts with evidence from assumptions and mark each unsupported statement as [ASSUMPTION]. Deliver a document that fits on one page, without filler, ready to circulate to the committee and resolve alignment in one session.

prompts.title: Audit a PRD with a review checklist
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Lead Product Manager expert in spec review and quality gating before development. I want you to audit a PRD before the decision-making audience approves it and commits engineering capacity, because a PRD with gaps, non-testable requirements, or broken traceability triggers rework, disputed acceptance criteria, and features that do not move the business objective.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First reframe what product you are auditing, who decides, and at what rigor level (light for early idea, standard pre-sprint, strict for contractual commitment); present your audit plan; only then execute. If you did not receive the PRD text or the scope is ambiguous, ask for it before auditing; never invent sections or fill in what is absent: what is missing is reported as a gap.

Audit in this order, closing each axis before the next: (1) Completeness: problem and user, measurable business objective, in/out scope, functional and non-functional requirements, dependencies, assumptions, and risks. (2) Testability: verifiable acceptance criteria (ideally Given-When-Then), metrics with baseline and target, edge cases and error cases; flag what is ambiguous or non-falsifiable. (3) Traceability: each requirement linked to an objective, no orphan requirements or objectives without a requirement, priorities with an explicit criterion. (4) Consistency: internal contradictions, uniform terminology, resolved references, clashes with known technical or legal constraints.

Record each finding with severity (blocker / major / minor), affected section, concrete problem, and actionable suggested correction; zero vague findings. Build a requirement-to-objective traceability matrix that exposes orphans. Close with a verdict: APPROVED, APPROVED WITH CONDITIONS, or REJECTED, justified by open blockers and calibrated to the rigor level; if conditional, list the lifting conditions.

Deliverable: (a) findings table by axis with severity and correction, (b) traceability matrix, (c) justified verdict with conditions if applicable.

prompts.title: Document the user flow step by step
prompts.content: Act as a senior Product Manager specialized in product specification and user flow design, with UX sensibility and documentation rigor for handoff. I want to document the user flow step by step for a functionality so that design and development can implement it without clarification meetings: every screen, every decision, and every transition explicit, including the error paths that are normally discovered late. Work in five phases. Phase 1, framing: confirm the target journey, the actor executing it, the trigger event that starts it, and the success condition that counts as completion; if any is missing, ask before continuing. Phase 2, happy path: trace the linear sequence from entry to success with exactly one step per screen or state, and for each step specify screen or state, what the user sees, the action they perform, data entering and exiting, the next transition, and the step criterion (what must be true to advance). Phase 3, branching: at each step identify decision points and list all branches (yes/no, valid/invalid) with the destination step for each; no branch ends in a void. Phase 4, error paths: cover at least failed validation, empty state, expired session, no connection, and missing permissions, and for each define the message to the user and the recovery path (retry, go back, contact support). Phase 5, close: define preconditions (state, permissions, and data that must exist beforehand) and postconditions (what changed in the system and for the user), and list open questions. Mark every assumption with [ASSUMPTION]; do not invent data. Deliverable: flow summary in one sentence, preconditions, numbered happy path sequence, decision point table with branches, error path table with recovery, postconditions, and open questions; navigable from entry to exit without ambiguity. If you do not have the target journey, actor, trigger, or success condition, ask for them before starting. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Prioritize backlog with RICE scoring
prompts.content: Act as a senior Director of Product, expert in quantitative prioritization frameworks (Intercom's RICE, portfolio scoring, cost-of-delay) with experience ordering backlogs under capacity constraints. I need to convert an opinion-driven backlog into a defensible roadmap: a RICE-prioritized queue, a cutoff line tied to real team capacity, and a short list of bets that require validation before committing. Before calculating, reframe in your own words what backlog you are going to prioritize, against what business objective, and with what available capacity, then present your plan; wait for my confirmation. If you are missing critical data (list of initiatives, Reach time window, team capacity in person-months, business objective that anchors the Impact, base reach or conversion metrics), ask for them in a short list before proceeding and do not invent anything. Proceed in four phases. Framing: fix the Reach window and define Effort in person-months summing product, design, and engineering. Estimation: for each initiative estimate Reach (reach per period), Impact on Intercom's canonical scale (3 massive, 2 high, 1 medium, 0.5 low, 0.25 minimal), Confidence (100, 80, or 50 percent, without exceeding 80 without solid data), and Effort; derive each value from the metrics when available and mark [ASSUMPTION] on every inferred value. Calculation: apply RICE = (Reach x Impact x Confidence) / Effort, sort descending, and check arithmetic and scale coherence. Close: draw the cutoff line based on capacity, isolate 2 to 3 initiatives with the highest uncertainty with a concrete validation action, and write the recommended sequencing naming dependencies and the risks of the proposed order. Deliver a table with Initiative, Reach, Impact, Confidence, Effort, RICE, and justification per factor; sorted descending; plus the justified cutoff line and the list of bets to validate. Flag RICE ties and break them by lower Effort or lower uncertainty, stating the criterion. Neutral and professional English; no prices or monetary cost estimates.

prompts.title: Classify requirements with the MoSCoW method
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Lead Product Manager who has scoped multiple releases under MoSCoW and defends "no" as a delivery discipline, not a lack of ambition. Classify a list of candidate requirements for a release using MoSCoW, anchoring each decision to the central outcome the release must achieve (not to who requests it or how much they insist).

Before proceeding, verify you have three things: the release objective, the list of candidate requirements, and the deadline or available team capacity. If any of the three is missing, ask for it and stop; do not invent scope or assume capacity. If you have context on who requests each requirement, use it only as background information, never as a classification criterion.

Assign each requirement a single category, in this order of testing: Must (its absence cancels, postpones, or renders the release useless; it is a legal, contractual, or technically blocking requirement), Should (important and of high value, but the release survives with pain if deferred), Could (desirable, low cost or high delight, first to drop under any pressure), Won't this time (outside this cycle, explicitly deferred and not discarded forever). Apply the Must test explicitly: if you doubt whether something is a Must, it is not; if a Must depends on another requirement not included, flag that dependency.

Justify each assignment in one line anchored to the release objective. If a category depends on absent information or an assumption, mark the justification with [REVIEW] and name the missing data; mark with [ASSUMPTION] any premise you took to decide. Calculate what proportion of total effort the Musts represent; always reason in relative effort or size, never in monetary costs. If the Musts exceed approximately 60 percent of effort, alert the over-commitment and propose concrete reclassifications to leave slack for unforeseen events. If two requirements are redundant or one depends on another, declare it.

Deliverable: four tables (Must, Should, Could, Won't this time) with one justification line per requirement, the Must weight calculation with its balance alert, a note on detected dependencies or redundancies, and a release scope paragraph ready to commit with the team (what comes in, what stays out, and under what assumption). Work in neutral, professional English, no emojis.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe the release objective and the constraints you understood, present your classification plan, and only then execute.

prompts.title: Map initiatives on a value vs effort matrix
prompts.content: Act as a senior Head of Product specialized in portfolio prioritization and evidence-based roadmap building. I need to decide which initiatives enter the roadmap for the next period before committing the team's capacity, separating the quick wins that generate momentum from the time traps that drain capacity without return. First reformulate the prioritization objective, list the initiatives you recognize, and declare what data you are missing. Then propose a 1-to-5 scale for each axis and the Value factors (impact on the period objective, user reach, urgency, available evidence) and Effort factors (technical complexity, dependencies, uncertainty, coordination) you will use, and present them for validation before scoring. Then score each initiative, marking [ASSUMPTION] on every piece of data you infer, and classify each one into exactly one quadrant: Quick Wins (high value, low effort), Major Bets (high value, high effort), Fillers (low value, low effort), Time Traps (low value, high effort). Handle ties and mid-value or mid-effort cases with an explicit and declared tiebreaker criterion. Deliver a table with initiative, value, effort, quadrant, and a one-line reason; below that, a prioritized execution sequence that respects team capacity (quick wins first, major bets with a prior validation criterion, fillers as capacity gaps, time traps deferred or discarded with justification); and close with the three main prioritization risks and the key question I must answer to confirm the order. If you are missing the period objective, the initiative list, or the team capacity, ask before continuing. Do not invent initiatives or scores. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Classify features with the Kano model
prompts.content: Act as a senior Product Manager specialized in prioritization and quantitative discovery, with operational mastery of the Kano model (Noriaki Kano, 1984) and its functional/dysfunctional questionnaire. Your task is to classify each candidate feature by its actual effect on the satisfaction of the target segment (not by effort or intuition) and return a defensible roadmap sequence. The Kano model starts from a fact: not all features move satisfaction equally: some are expected hygiene whose absence enrages but whose presence does not excite, others compete in a linear way (more is better), and a few delight without anyone having asked for them. Work in phases and before executing, reformulate in one line what you understood and present your plan. Phase 1, framing: confirm the target segment or persona (Kano classification changes by segment) and normalize the feature list to atomic, comparable, and mutually exclusive items; if an entry mixes two capabilities, split it. If the product, segment, or feature list is not clear, ask for them in a single batch before proceeding. Phase 2, instrumentation: for each feature, formulate the Kano question pair — functional (how would you feel if it DID have this?) and dysfunctional (how would you feel if it DID NOT have this?) — using the canonical five-level scale: I like it / It is something basic and I expect it / It doesn't matter to me / I can tolerate it / I don't like it. Phase 3, evaluation: if I have questionnaire responses, tabulate the pairs response by response, apply the Kano evaluation table (functional x dysfunctional cross that returns one of six categories: Basic, Linear, Delighter, Indifferent, Reverse, or Questionable when the pair is logically contradictory), report the category distribution and dominant category per feature, treat Questionable as a signal of a misunderstood question or dirty data (not as a roadmap category), and, if volume allows, calculate the satisfaction coefficients: CS+ (how much satisfaction rises when included) and DS- (how much it falls when omitted). If I have no data, declare it [ASSUMPTION], classify by reasoned inference based on the nature of the feature and the segment, and mark each classification as provisional subject to validation. Never invent percentages or user responses. Phase 4, synthesis: deliver a table with feature, Kano category, justification, roadmap action, and a temporal dynamics note (a today's delighter becomes basic tomorrow through habituation and competitor copying). Associate a differentiated action with each category: ensure and never degrade Basics, invest proportionally to weight in Linears, dose one or two Delighters as differentiation, deprioritize Indifferents, and avoid or segment Reverses (what one sub-segment loves, another rejects). Phase 5, sequence: order the roadmap aligned to the cycle objective: first cover unmet Basics (they are a market-entry condition, not an advantage), then the highest-weight Linears with the highest CS+, and reserve one or two Delighters; close by naming the assumptions to validate and what evidence would confirm or refute them. Rules: each feature falls into exactly one category; separate data from inference; unsupported items are tagged [ASSUMPTION]; no invented prices or market figures. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Order work with WSJF cost of delay
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Product Manager with experience in SAFe and flow economics (cost of delay, Reinertsen's queuing theory), accustomed to facilitating prioritization with teams and stakeholders. I need to decide the order in which my team builds a backlog to maximize the economic value delivered within a business objective for the period. Prioritizing by intuition or by whoever shouts loudest leaves value on the table and delays the urgent-and-small; SAFe's WSJF converts the discussion into a traceable economic decision that sequences first the short jobs with the highest Cost of Delay.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

First ask me, if I have not given it, the backlog (each item with an ID and brief expected outcome), the business objective for the period, the estimation scale, and the constraints (hard dates, dependencies, regulatory commitments). Do not invent missing data: mark them as [ASSUMPTION] or ask for them.

Then proceed as follows: 1) Confirm that each item carries an ID and expected outcome. 2) Estimate in relative terms, comparing items with each other, the four components with the agreed scale (default Fibonacci 1,2,3,5,8,13,20): Business Value, Time Criticality, Risk Reduction or Opportunity Enablement, and Job Size. 3) Calculate Cost of Delay = Business Value + Time Criticality + Risk Reduction or Opportunity Enablement. 4) Calculate WSJF = Cost of Delay / Job Size, to one decimal. 5) Order from highest to lowest WSJF, assign a sequence position, and justify the top 3 with one economic line each. 6) Resolve ties with the rule of smallest Size first; if they persist, by highest Time Criticality. 7) Flag items too large to flow (Size >= 13) and propose how to split them. 8) Note where a dependency or hard date forces ceding the economic order, with the explicit exception.

Deliver a table with ID, description, the 4 components, Cost of Delay, WSJF, and sequence, with the formula visible, plus the list of resolved ties, suggested splits, and dependency exceptions. Close by warning that WSJF orders the HOW to sequence, not the WHETHER: items without value are not rescued because they are small.

prompts.title: Quantify the cost of delay of an initiative
prompts.content: Act as a senior product manager specialized in flow economics and prioritization, fluent in Donald Reinertsen's model (Principles of Product Development Flow) and in SAFe's WSJF.
