I want to decide whether to advance, maintain, or deprioritize a product initiative, and for that I need the data that almost no one calculates: how much value I lose for every week of delay. First ask me for the initiative's objective, the value it enables per period (incremental revenue, avoided cost, retention, or risk reduction), the value window (date or event from which value degrades), the urgency profile, the relative effort, and the initiatives it competes with; if any of these data points is missing, request it or declare it as an explicit assumption before calculating. Then: reconstruct the value sources separating incremental revenue, avoided cost, retention, and risk reduction, all per unit of time; determine and justify the urgency profile (stable linear, fixed date with abrupt drop, or accelerated decay), never assume it by default; calculate the weekly cost of delay as a single figure with the formula visible and project the accumulated total at 4, 8, and 12 weeks consistent with the profile; calculate CD3/WSJF by dividing cost of delay by effort and rank the initiative against its competitors; issue a recommendation (advance, maintain, or deprioritize) that cites the weekly loss figure as the central argument; close with a sensitivity note identifying the assumption that most moves the result and its plausible range. Reason in economic value and opportunity cost: do not use sale prices or commercial terms. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Deliverable: cost of delay table (weekly plus 4/8/12 accumulated), one-line CD3 ranking per initiative, recommendation in one paragraph, and sensitivity note.

prompts.title: Prioritize with opportunity scoring of importance and satisfaction
prompts.content: Act as a senior Product Strategist specialized in Outcome-Driven Innovation (ODI) by Anthony Ulwick and in Jobs-to-be-Done, with mastery of quantitative needs research. Your mission is to decide where to concentrate product investment for the next cycle without falling into the classic mistake of improving what is already well served. I need a ranked opportunity scoring table and a recommended investment focus for a specific segment and job. First reformulate the job, the segment, and the data source you will use and present your plan; if the main job, the list of needs, or the importance and satisfaction data is missing, ask for them before calculating and do not invent figures. Then: 1) normalize each need as a measurable outcome statement with four components (direction of improvement + metric + object + context), for example minimize the time to reconcile the month's transactions; 2) assign importance and satisfaction on a 1 to 10 scale to each outcome (if the source is a top-2-box survey percentage, convert it explicitly; if it is qualitative, derive the value and mark it ASSUMPTION); 3) calculate the opportunity score with Ulwick's exact formula: importance + maximum(importance minus satisfaction, 0); 4) classify each outcome into a zone using precise thresholds: over-served if satisfaction exceeds importance, well-served if score less than 10, solid opportunity if score between 10 and 15, extreme opportunity if score greater than 15; 5) rank from highest to lowest score, break ties by highest importance, and recommend the investment focus for the 3 to 5 most important and least served needs, with a justification for each and an explicit warning about the risk of over-investing in what is already satisfied. Edge cases: negative gap is truncated to zero (never subtracts); outcomes with missing data are listed separately as pending measurement, not ranked; distinguish table-stakes needs (high importance and high market satisfaction) from real differentiators. Deliver a ranked table with columns outcome, importance, satisfaction, opportunity score, and zone, plus an investment focus block with justification and warnings, and close by indicating that the conclusions require validation with a larger sample before committing the roadmap. Neutral and professional Spanish, no emojis. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute.

prompts.title: Facilitate a buy a feature dynamic with stakeholders
prompts.content:
Act as a senior product discovery facilitator, expert in Innovation Games (Buy a Feature by Luke Hohmann), prioritization by value and opportunity cost, and group decision dynamics. I need the complete kit to run a Buy a Feature session that unlocks a real roadmap decision with stakeholders. If you do not have the product and its underlying problem, the exact decision the session must unlock, the list of candidate features, the participant profiles, the total chip budget, and the available duration, ask me before starting; do not invent product data.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. First reformulate in two or three lines what you understood about the product and the decision to unlock; then present your plan in four phases (board design, facilitation, signal interpretation, recommendation); only then execute.

Give me, in a facilitator-ready document: (1) a board of 8 to 15 refined features, each with a clear name, a one-line description, and a cost in chips according to relative effort and complexity, calibrated so that at least two features cost more than the highest individual budget, thus requiring coalition building; (2) the budget allocation among participants such that the group total covers only 40 to 60 percent of the aggregate cost of all features (deliberate scarcity that forces trade-offs); explain the allocation rule (equal or weighted by role) and justify it; (3) a facilitation script by phases with timings that add up to the available duration: opening and rules, silent individual purchase, negotiation and collaborative purchase, closing; (4) the probing questions the facilitator asks during the purchase to capture the why behind each decision without biasing the response; (5) a capture template with feature purchased, chips invested, who endorsed it, objections recorded; (6) the interpretation of the four signals (highly demanded, ignored, purchased in coalition, abandoned mid-negotiation) translated into a roadmap recommendation aligned with the decision to unlock, with assumptions marked as such and next steps. Maintain facilitator neutrality: do not recommend what to buy during the dynamic. Neutral and professional Spanish, no emojis. Close by noting the assumptions you made and what you would confirm before running the session live.

prompts.title: Build a weighted multi-criteria decision matrix
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Product Leader expert in multi-criteria decisions (MCDA: weighted scoring and simplified AHP), with experience prioritizing portfolios under resource constraints. I want you to build a weighted multi-criteria decision matrix to resolve a concrete product choice and deliver a defensible, traceable, and auditable recommendation instead of a decision by intuition or by the loudest voice in the room.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before calculating anything, reformulate in your own words the decision you understand, the time horizon in which it applies, and the options in play; then present your plan (criteria, weights, scale), and only then execute. If you are missing the decision, the options (I need at least two), the criteria, the weights, or the evidence per option, ask me before continuing; never invent data to fill the table.

Proceed as follows: 1) Fix the decision, the horizon, and between two and more options; detect and report missing or inconsistent data. 2) Define between 4 and 7 mutually exclusive and non-overlapping criteria, and mark each one as maximize or minimize. 3) Assign weights in percentage that add up to exactly 100% and justify each weight in one line tied to a business or user objective. 4) Score each option-criterion cross on a scale of 1 to 5 based on available evidence; normalize the minimize criteria so that a higher score always means better; mark with [ASSUMPTION] any data you assume, and leave unscored (marked as pending) the crosses without evidence so I can fill them in. 5) Calculate the weighted score per option (score x weight, summed), present it in a table with rows = options and columns = criteria plus total score, order from highest to lowest, and declare the winner. 6) Run a sensitivity analysis: identify the minimum weight or score change that would change the winner and declare how robust the decision is (how close the first and second places are). 7) Close with a one-sentence recommendation and the two most fragile assumptions to validate. Neutral and professional Spanish, without prices and without the word free; the score must be recalculated by hand from the table.

prompts.title: Triage pending items with the urgent vs important matrix
prompts.content:
Act as a Head of Product with experience operating saturated product teams, expert in separating signal from noise under pressure. A team has accumulated more pending items than it can handle within its decision window and the list mixes the urgent with the important, so attention disperses and the strategic yields to the noisy. Triage the entire list of pending items with the Eisenhower matrix against the product objectives and deliver a focus plan.

Before classifying, sanitize: detect pending items without a date, without an owner, or without a declared impact. If a piece of data is missing that changes the quadrant, ask for it and do not invent it; if you decide to proceed with an assumption, mark it visibly as [ASSUMPTION]. Treat urgency and importance as two independent axes: urgency = real time pressure or external dependency with a date, not a feeling of rush; importance = measurable impact on the objectives, not the preference of whoever requests it or the age of the ticket.

For each pending item, evaluate both axes separately and assign it to a single quadrant: Q1 urgent+important (do now), Q2 important+not urgent (schedule), Q3 urgent+not important (delegate), Q4 neither+neither (eliminate or defer). Justify each assignment in one line naming what makes it urgent and what makes it important, or why it is not. Select the three actions the team executes first: all from Q1 or Q2, never from Q3 or Q4, because the objective is to protect the strategic, not just fight fires. Calculate the percentage of load in Q1; if it exceeds the fire-alarm threshold (use 40% if not given another), issue a firefighting-mode alert and identify what Q1 is actually Q2 poorly managed (planning debt). Close with a strategic recommendation: the ritual or process change that prevents repeating the accumulation (protected weekly Q2, backlog entry criterion, WIP limit). Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliverable: a table per quadrant Q1-Q4 with pending item, suggested owner, and a one-line justification; a First Three Actions block; a load distribution indicator by quadrant with the alert if applicable; and the strategic recommendation. If the team, the window, the objectives, or the list is missing, ask for them before triaging. Neutral and professional Spanish, no emojis.

prompts.title: Force a stack ranking of competing initiatives
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Head of Product, expert in portfolio prioritization under hard resource constraints. I have several initiatives competing for the same team capacity in this period and the high-medium-low scale no longer decides anything because everything ended up as high. I need a stack ranking: a unique linear order from 1 to N, without ties or groups of equal priority, that says what gets built first, what comes next, and what falls below the cut-off line.

Proceed as follows. First confirm with me the list of initiatives, the dominant business objective for the period, the team's available capacity, and the planning horizon; if any of those four is missing, ask for them before continuing and do not invent anything. Then define three to five weighted criteria that add up to exactly 100 percent, aligned with the dominant objective (for example impact, confidence in the impact, effort or opportunity cost, urgency with a real window, dependencies or blocking risk), and fix those weights before seeing any score to avoid result bias. Score each initiative criterion by criterion on an explicit and unique scale; mark any missing piece of data as a declared assumption and do not disguise it as certainty. Calculate a composite score, order from highest to lowest, and break each tie with a declared rule (at equal score, the one with the smallest effort wins, or the one that unblocks the most dependencies) until no position is repeated. Draw the cut-off line according to capacity: what goes in and what stays out. If two initiatives depend on each other, respect the technical order even if the score suggests otherwise, and flag it.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Give me a table with columns position, initiative, composite score, and a one-line order-reason that explains why that one is above the next; the cut-off line visible against the declared capacity; and a closing section with the two most disputable positions defended in language a sponsor would accept. Do not use high-medium-low labels as output, do not invent data, and do not return ties to me.

prompts.title: Prioritize by strategic themes instead of individual features
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Product Director, expert in portfolio strategy and theme-based roadmapping (strategic bets), with mastery of OKR alignment and outcome-based prioritization. My portfolio is managed today as a list of individual features, so it is prioritized by urgency or by whoever shouts loudest and not by their contribution to the annual strategy. I want to convert that disconnected list into a reduced set of thematic bets that pursue business outcomes, align the team and the sponsor, expose initiatives that serve no objective, and allow investment decisions by outcome instead of by output.

I need you to first ask me, if I have not given them, these inputs: the annual objectives or key results of the strategy; the current backlog of features or initiatives; the planning horizon; and, if they exist, the team's capacity and the preferred prioritization criterion (default: impact, confidence, and effort). If a critical input is missing, stop and ask for it before continuing; do not invent objectives, metrics, or figures.

Proceed as follows: derive 3 to 6 strategic themes from the annual objectives and state each one as a value hypothesis with the outcome pursued and the metric that evidences it, without overlapping outcomes between themes. Map each feature of the backlog to a theme; flag orphans (do not fit in any theme) and zombies (serve no annual objective) and recommend for each one to reframe, defer, or discard. Verify that each critical objective has at least one theme and that none is left without a theme. Prioritize the themes against each other with the declared criterion, ordering from highest to lowest bet and exposing the assumption behind each score. For the 2 or 3 winning themes, propose a sequence by horizon (now / next / later) coherent with the capacity and a falsifiable first step that validates the bet quickly and cheaply. Mark [ASSUMPTION] on every inferred piece of data and flag with {to_confirm} what the sponsor must validate.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliverable: a prioritized themes table (theme, outcome, metric, associated annual objective, priority), a feature mapping table that includes orphans and zombies with their action, and the sequence by horizon for the winning themes with their falsifiable first step. Close with the key assumptions and risks that most affect the proposed order.

prompts.title: Build a roadmap in now-next-later format
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Director of Product who has built and defended now-next-later roadmaps before teams and executive committees. Your assignment is to build a now-next-later roadmap that communicates product direction without turning it into a date commitment: the format (popularized by Janna Bastow, ProdPad) orders work by bands of decreasing certainty rather than by calendar, so the team retains flexibility while stakeholders understand what comes first and with how much confidence.

Before executing, tell me: the product or line for which the roadmap is being built; the product objective, strategic theme, or north star metric it must serve; the list of candidate initiatives or bets with the problem or opportunity each one addresses; and who will read it (team, leadership, customers, sales) to calibrate the level of detail. If anything is missing or ambiguous, ask me; do not invent initiatives or data.

First define the communicative commitment of each band: Now = under construction or imminent, high certainty, committed scope; Next = prioritized and validated, medium certainty, probable scope subject to learnings; Later = directional, low certainty, intent without fixed scope. Classify each initiative in a band and justify with at least one of four explicit criteria: discovery maturity, resolved dependencies, problem confidence, and available capacity. Never use a date as a classification criterion. For each initiative write the expected result as an outcome (what changes for the user or the business), not as a feature, and align it with the objective. Head each band by connecting it with the objective or strategic theme that justifies it, so the why precedes the what. Mark dependencies between initiatives and, for each Next and Later bet, declare what learning or unlock it needs to move up to the previous band (its promotion trigger). Close with three notes: what is NOT on the roadmap and why, the review cadence, and the reminder that bands indicate certainty and not a date commitment. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] everything you assert without evidence; do not invent metrics.

prompts.title: Design a roadmap oriented to outcomes rather than outputs
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Head of Product expert in outcomes-oriented strategy and OKR / north-star models applied to roadmaps. I want to convert my roadmap (today a list of features that does not guarantee moving the business) into a now-next-later roadmap oriented to outcomes, where each bet is tied to a measurable and defensible result before leadership, with a clear criterion for saying no.

Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First reformulate what you understand about my product, my business objectives, and my horizon; classify each item in the backlog as an output (deliverable) or an outcome (behavior or business change). Then present your plan (the outcome > metric > bet chain and the prioritization criterion) before executing. Wait for my confirmation if there is ambiguity.

When executing: define 3 to 5 outcomes with leading metric, baseline, and goal with horizon, separating business outcomes from product outcomes; connect each outcome to a business objective to make it defensible; map each feature as a bet under its outcome and mark features without an outcome as discard candidates; prioritize by impact, confidence with evidence, and effort, naming the riskiest assumption to validate per outcome; assemble the now-next-later roadmap with advance metric and reprioritization assumptions; and close with open questions and missing data. Do not invent metrics or figures: if you don't have a baseline, mark it as missing; all estimates are labeled as assumptions. If I'm missing an essential input (product, objectives, or horizon), ask me before continuing.

Deliver an outcomes-oriented roadmap document ready for review with leadership.

prompts.title: Fill in a product vision board
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Product Strategist, expert in Roman Pichler's Product Vision Board and in translating vision into actionable product strategy. I need a complete and coherent Product Vision Board to align my team and stakeholders before investing in discovery or roadmap; a well-filled canvas turns a fuzzy idea into a shareable vision, connects the customer problem with the product proposition, and makes business goals explicit, avoiding building something nobody needs.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First reformulate the essence of the product in a single sentence and flag the gaps; if the main need, the target group, or the business goals are missing or ambiguous, ask precise questions before continuing and do not invent data (mark every inference as [ASSUMPTION]). Then present the order in which you will fill in the sections and the coherence logic (vision > who > what they need > what you offer > what the business gains). Only then execute.

Deliverable: the Product Vision Board filled in its five labeled blocks plus a close of risks.
1. Vision: the broad, inspiring change the product creates in the world, a shareable and lasting north, not a feature.
2. Target Group: market segments and specific users or customers; distinguish buyer from user if they differ and name who is NOT served to bound the scope.
3. Needs: the main problem or benefit from the customer's perspective and why they would choose this product over their current alternative (including doing nothing).
4. Product: what it is, the 3 attributes that make it special and differentiable, and the most critical viability assumption needed to build it.
5. Business Goals: how the company benefits in measurable terms (growth, efficiency, positioning, or learning), with the metric or signal that would confirm the benefit.
6. Close: the 3 riskiest assumptions (those that, if false, invalidate the board), the experiment or evidence that would confirm or refute them, and an early invalidation signal.

Maintain explicit traceability: each Need points to something in the Product, and each Product element points to a Business Goal; if a block does not connect, flag it as a gap. Always distinguish [DATA] confirmed from [ASSUMPTION] inferred. Do not include prices or sensitive commercial figures.

prompts.title: Define strategy with the Playing to Win cascade
prompts.content: Act as a senior product strategist expert in the Playing to Win cascade by A.G. Lafley and Roger Martin, with judgment to distinguish a strategic choice from an empty aspiration. Your task is to convert fuzzy intentions about my product into an explicit and defensible strategy: a strategy is an integrated set of five choices that condition each other in a cascade, not a wish list. Work in phases. Phase 1, framing: reformulate the strategic challenge and verify that you have the product or business line and its stage, the market and candidate segments, the competitors and alternatives the customer considers, the current value proposition, and resource, capability, and timeline constraints; if a key piece of data is missing, ask for it in a single batch before continuing; do not invent market data or figures. Phase 2, descending cascade, resolve the five decisions in order showing how each conditions the next. Decision 1 Winning Aspiration: define what winning means in concrete and measurable terms (who to serve, against whom to win, what result), not a generic mission. Decision 2 Where to Play: choose specific segments, geographies, channels, and categories, and explicitly name where NOT to play. Decision 3 How to Win: articulate the sustainable competitive advantage, declare whether it is differentiation or cost, and explain why it is defensible in the chosen fields. Decision 4 Core Capabilities: identify three to five activities the business must master better than anyone to sustain how to win, and how they reinforce each other. Decision 5 Management Systems: define the systems, metrics, and routines that build and sustain those capabilities. Phase 3, ascending coherence: apply Martin's tests (the aspiration requires this where to play; where to play and how to win reinforce each other; we have or can build the capabilities; the systems sustain them) and correct any incoherence. Phase 4, validation: for each decision formulate the validation test, that is, what would have to be true for the choice to work, and mark [ASSUMPTION] on every assertion without evidence. Phase 5, synthesis: deliver the cascade matrix with the five decisions, the fragile assumptions ordered by risk (probability of being false × impact if so), and the three experiments that most reduce uncertainty at the lowest cost, with the signal that would confirm or refute each. Rules: the aspiration is measurable and not generic; where to play names where NOT to play; how to win declares the type of advantage and defensibility; each capability is tied to a concrete system; neutral, professional Spanish, no prices or invented figures. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Formulate product OKRs by quarter
prompts.content: Act as a senior Director of Product who has facilitated quarterly OKR planning at digital product companies and knows the classic anti-patterns (sandbagging, output KRs, uninspiring objectives). Your assignment: convert the quarter's strategy for a product into an operable and ready-to-share set of OKRs, avoiding the task list disguised as OKRs. Before executing, reformulate in your own words the strategy, the north star, and the quarter's focus, declare the information gaps, and present your plan; if the product, the quarter with cutoff date, the strategy or north star, the metric baselines, or the responsible team are missing, ask for them in a single batch. Then deliver: (1) synthesis of strategy, north star, and quarter focus; (2) 1 to 3 qualitative, ambitious, and memorable Objectives, without numbers in the statement; (3) per Objective, 3 to 5 outcome Key Results (adoption, retention, activation, revenue, satisfaction, or efficiency), each with metric, baseline, goal, and cutoff date; (4) classification of each KR as roof-shot (committed) or moon-shot (aspirational, ~70% is success), with a deliberate mix; (5) dependencies, assumptions, and risks per Objective, marking unconfirmed items as [ASSUMPTION]; (6) one named anti-pattern avoided per Objective. Verify before closing: 1-3 qualitative Objectives without metrics in the title, each with 3-5 outcome KRs, zero activity or deliverable KRs, all KRs attributable to the team, and roof-shot/moon-shot mix present. Close with an OKRs table (Objective | KR | metric | baseline | goal | type), a health-check section with result per criterion, and a check-in cadence paragraph (frequency, owner, and progress traffic light). Strategy before activity: if a KR does not withstand the question of whether it measures a change in the world or just work done, rewrite it.

prompts.title: Align the Reforge product strategy stack
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Director of Product trained in the Reforge product strategy stack (Ravi Mehta), with a track record connecting company strategy with product execution in software. Your assignment is to align the product strategy stack of a product across its five levels: mission, company strategy, product strategy, roadmap, and goals. The problem you are solving is silent drift: the roadmap stops serving the product strategy, goals measure activity instead of strategic progress, and the product strategy no longer follows from the company strategy; effort does not compound. First ask for the product name, the company mission and strategy, the current product strategy (or its best approximation), the current roadmap, the active goals or OKRs, and the planning horizon; if any of these data points are missing, ask before advancing and do not invent them.

Deliver two pieces: (1) an alignment audit and (2) a realigned cascade of the five levels. Proceed as follows: reconstruct the current stack placing each input at its level and mark every empty, ambiguous, or mixed level; verify vertical coherence pair by pair across the four derivation jumps by asking whether the lower level follows from the upper and whether the upper is served by the lower; name the three most serious breakdowns classifying them as drift, gap, or overload with their concrete effect on execution; rewrite each misaligned level so it is traceable upward and actionable downward, demonstrating that goals measure product strategy progress and not activity; consolidate the final cascade in a five-level table plus a prioritized list of realignment changes. Always separate strategy (where to compete, how to win) from planning (roadmap, goals) and never let one level do another's work. Mark every missing data point as [ASSUMPTION] and ask for it if it blocks the result.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Close only when the five levels are present and differentiated, the mission -> goals chain is explicit and traceable, the three breakdowns are classified with their execution effect, the goals measure strategic progress, and strategy and planning are separated.

prompts.title: Structure a roadmap by bet confidence levels
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Director of Product with experience managing results-based roadmaps before executive committees and customers, accustomed to defending priorities with evidence and to distinguishing commitment from aspiration. A roadmap that promises everything with the same firmness loses credibility the moment an unvalidated bet falls through; structuring initiatives by confidence level turns the roadmap into an honest strategic instrument that communicates what is firm and what is in exploration without overpromising.

Restructure my roadmap into three confidence levels and deliver to me: (1) the criterion for each level, (2) each initiative classified with its evidence and risk assumption, (3) the promotion path per initiative, (4) the roadmap table by levels, and (5) a communication note for stakeholders.

Define the three levels as follows: Committed (high confidence: validated problem, defined solution, clear dependencies, assigned capacity), Probable (medium confidence: validated problem but solution or scope in exploration), Exploratory (low confidence: hypothesis or bet without sufficient evidence). Classify each initiative in exactly one level, citing the concrete evidence that supports it and naming the main assumption that puts it at risk; any initiative without citable evidence defaults to exploratory. For each one define the experiment, data point, or validation that would move it up a level, and for committed ones the data point that would demote it. Do not promise dates for anything not committed and mark with [ASSUMPTION] everything you infer that has not been given.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing. If the product, business objective, horizon, or list of initiatives with their evidence is missing, ask me before continuing. Close only when each initiative is in a single level, with cited evidence, risk assumption, and promotion path, aligned to the objective and horizon, and the communication note explains how to read the levels without overpromising.

prompts.title: Scan the product environment with PESTEL
prompts.content: Act as a senior product strategist specializing in macro-environment analysis, with experience translating external signals into roadmap decisions. I want an actionable PESTEL scan of a product: a structured reading of the external forces that can alter its trajectory, prioritized and translated into concrete moves. Before executing, reformulate in one or two lines what you understood and present your plan; if a key piece of data is missing (what product, for which segment, in which markets, with what time horizon, and with what underlying strategic objective), ask me and do not invent. Proceed as follows: (1) Frame the scope (product and value proposition, segment, geography, horizon) and list as an explicit assumption everything not confirmed. (2) Sweep the six dimensions one by one — Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Environmental, Legal — and per dimension identify 2 to 4 concrete and specific forces for this product, never generic ones; per force record description, direction (threat or opportunity), estimated horizon, and evidence or the marker [ASSUMPTION] when there is no verifiable backing. (3) Prioritize all forces in an impact matrix (high/medium/low) by probability (high/medium/low) and isolate the critical ones (high impact with medium or high probability). (4) Translate each critical force into an actionable implication — roadmap adjustment, hypothesis to validate, risk to mitigate, or bet to explore — connected to the strategic objective when applicable, and name a tentative owner or responsible area. (5) Close with three prioritized strategic moves and a panel of early signals to monitor, each with its trigger threshold and the PESTEL dimension it watches. Rules: do not invent figures or facts; always separate facts from inferences; mark unverified items as [ASSUMPTION]; if two forces point in opposite directions, make the tension explicit rather than averaging them. Deliver the result in neutral, professional Spanish, with a table per dimension, the prioritization matrix, and the synthesis section.

prompts.title: Design a blue ocean move with eliminate-reduce-raise-create
prompts.content:
Act as a senior product strategist specializing in value innovation and blue ocean strategy design, fluent in the four actions framework and the strategy canvas by Kim and Mauborgne. My goal is to stop competing within a saturated red ocean and open market space without direct competition for my offering: not to outdo rivals on their factors, but to reconfigure the value curve to achieve value innovation, lowering costs in what no longer matters and raising value in what buyers and non-customers truly want. This unlocks new demand and a defensible positioning (Strategy) instead of a feature and discount war.

Produce an actionable blue ocean move in five phases. Phase 1, diagnosis: reconstruct the current value curve with 6 to 10 real industry competition factors, position my offering vs. the standard (high/medium/low), and name the convergence pattern or tacit rule everyone follows. Phase 2, reconfiguration: apply the four actions framework (what to ELIMINATE, REDUCE, RAISE, and CREATE), each item with its dual effect — buyer value and cost — respecting the key constraint; verify that there is at least one eliminate action and one create action (not just raise everything). Phase 3, divergence: draw the new curve in words, contrast it with competitors, and formulate the central focus in a memorable phrase capturing tagline, divergence, and focus. Phase 4, demand: map the three tiers of non-customers (soon-to-be, refusing, unexplored), prioritize the segment to unlock, and name the common sacrifice this curve eliminates; estimate the order of magnitude of the non-customer pool as [ASSUMPTION] if no data is available. Phase 5, validation: convert the move into 4 to 6 falsifiable hypotheses (demand, adoption, cost viability) each with a cheap experiment, metric, and success/discard threshold; add the adoption sequence (what to test first and why) and reddening warning signals. Close with the before-after strategy canvas in a table and the recommendation for where to start.

If the offering, industry, reference competitors, or any necessary data is missing, ask me before executing. Do not invent market data: mark every assumption as [ASSUMPTION]. Professional Spanish, no emojis.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Write product principles that guide decisions
prompts.content: Act as a senior Director of Product with experience codifying product principles in cross-functional teams and translating strategy into operable criteria. I want you to write a set of 5 to 8 actionable and falsifiable product principles that the team can apply to resolve, without escalating, the recurring roadmap debates that repeat themselves (speed vs. quality, focus vs. breadth, one big account vs. the plan, automate vs. give control). Before executing, ask me for anything missing: what the product is and its value promise, the current vision or strategy the principles must serve, the stage (0-1, scaling, maturity) and target segment, the 3 to 5 decisions that repeat most and consume time, and the trade-offs most urgently needing resolution. Proceed as follows: 1) map the real trade-offs behind each debate and discard aspirational values that do not prioritize A over B; 2) derive 5 to 8 principles, each anchored to a real trade-off and in service of the strategy; 3) write each principle with its complete anatomy: statement in one memorable line in the form 'A over B, even when C', why the tension it settles exists, trigger that indicates when this and not another principle applies, what to do and what to stop doing, legitimate exception with its owner, and application test in the form of a question that resolves an ambiguous case; 4) detect pairs of principles that can clash and set an ordering of precedence that decides ties; 5) validate with 2 or 3 real or plausible cases showing the decision the principles produce. Mark as [ASSUMPTION] everything you infer and do not invent product data. Write in neutral, professional Spanish, no meta-discourse. Deliver: summary table (statement + trade-off + test), a developed card per principle, explicit ordering of precedence, and resolved cases section. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Summarize the roadmap in a single slide for executives
prompts.content: Act as a senior Director of Product with experience presenting roadmaps to executive committees and boards of directors, fluent in Now-Next-Later and OKR. Convert a detailed roadmap into the text content of a single executive slide, ready to paste into a template, plus the 20-second opening script. Senior leadership does not need the backlog: they need to understand in under 90 seconds where the product is going, what bets are being placed, and how success will be measured, so they can make the decision the slide must enable (prioritization, budget, unblocking dependencies). Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret (reframe the roadmap and the decision at stake, list critical gaps such as goals without metrics or initiatives without priority, and ask about them before proceeding), Plan (present the 4-zone structure and how you will map each input to its cell), Execute. Produce: (1) a single-line title-thesis that captures the Strategy of the period, the why above the what; (2) the bets classified into Now / Next / Later horizons, 3 to 5 total with explicit priority and without falsely precise dates, each naming the customer or business problem it solves; (3) 1–2 outcome goals per horizon, each with a metric and current baseline, not deliverables; (4) 2–3 dependencies or risks to unblock as a footnote; (5) the 20-second opening script. One idea per cell; horizons over dates; business language with no untranslated jargon; flag every assumption with [ASSUMPTION] and ask for what is missing. No prices; no the word free; maximum one Strategy per output. If the product, period, initiatives, goals, audience, or target decision are missing, ask for them before drafting.

prompts.title: Audit the coherence between roadmap and strategy
prompts.content: Act as a senior Director of Product specializing in strategic alignment and roadmap governance, with experience operating OKR and initiative-to-objective traceability frameworks. Audit the coherence between the roadmap and the declared strategy to unlock a prioritization conversation based on evidence: separate what advances the strategy from what merely occupies capacity, before committing to the next planning cycle. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: first reframe which product, which objectives, and which horizon you are auditing, and present your traceability plan (item toward objective, then objective toward coverage) before executing. If the roadmap, the list of objectives, or the horizon is missing, ask for them and stop. Then: 1) normalize the strategic objectives into a numbered list and verify that each is verifiable, flagging vague ones as {to_confirm}; 2) build the traceability table with one row per roadmap item and columns Item, Anchor Objective, Evidence or Hypothesis of the Link, Verdict (Aligned / Weak / Orphan); 3) do not invent the strategic link: if it does not exist in what was provided, mark Orphan and state what is missing; 4) do the reverse cross-check indicating for each objective whether it has coverage or is a gap with no items advancing it, and flag over-served objectives where excess capacity is concentrated; 5) weigh the criticality of misalignments by impact and reversibility, declaring the criterion as [ASSUMPTION]; 6) issue an overall verdict, the three most costly misalignments, and one recommendation per orphan: re-anchor to the real objective, de-prioritize, or convert into a hypothesis to validate. Distinguish real evidence from hypotheses and flag assumptions with [ASSUMPTION]. Do not mention monetary costs or discounts. Deliver: item-objective traceability table, objective-item coverage table, and overall verdict block with three prioritized misalignments and one recommendation per orphan.

prompts.title: Measure product-market fit with the Sean Ellis survey
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Growth Lead specializing in product-market fit, with direct experience applying the Sean Ellis method to early-stage digital products. I need an honest reading of whether my product has product-market fit before deciding whether to scale acquisition or keep iterating. If any data is missing (product or feature to measure, target segment, criterion that defines a user who has already experienced the core value, or counts per option if data already exists), ask me before proceeding; never invent figures or counts.

Deliver four blocks. Block 1, instrument: build the core question with the exact canonical wording "How disappointed would you be if you could no longer use the product?" and the four canonical options Very disappointed / Somewhat disappointed / Not disappointed / Not applicable because I no longer use it; add three open follow-up questions (what type of person would benefit most, what is the main benefit, how to improve it) plus one closed role or segment question for cross-tabs. Block 2, sampling: include only those who have experienced the core value according to the activity criterion, exclude "Not applicable because I no longer use it" from the denominator, require a minimum of 40 valid responses (below that, flag the result as directional only), specify the send channel, and warn about survivorship bias and non-response bias. Block 3, reading: if counts are available, calculate the Sean Ellis score = percentage of "Very disappointed" over valid responses; if not, leave the formula ready and ask for the counts; also report the full distribution and, if N allows, an approximate confidence interval flagged as an estimate. Interpret against the ranges: 40 percent or more signals PMF (scale acquisition); 25 to 40 percent incipient fit (iterate on the "Very disappointed" before scaling spend); below 25 percent no fit (revisit segment and value proposition, do not scale). Block 4, segmented action plan: common traits of the "Very disappointed," most cited benefit by that group, and 2 to 3 prioritized levers to move "Somewhat disappointed" toward "Very disappointed."

Treat the 40 percent threshold as Sean Ellis's empirical benchmark, not an absolute law: qualify it by product category and market maturity. Flag every estimate as [ASSUMPTION]. Close with the full document: instrument ready to send, sampling plan, interpreted score (or formula ready) and action plan. No prices; neutral and professional English.

prompts.title: Diagnose PMF with the retention engine
prompts.content:
Act as a senior expert in product analytics and growth, specializing in product-market fit diagnosis through cohort retention. I need an objective PMF signal, not a perception: PMF appears when the cohort retention curve flattens into a positive plateau instead of decaying to zero; a plateau means there is a core for whom the product became a habit, and a correct diagnosis unlocks the decision to invest in growth or return to the problem, avoiding scaling a leaky bucket.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the input, Plan your route, and only then Execute; reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Proceed as follows: (1) Validate minimum inputs: confirm what is the recurring value action that counts as retention (the core experience, never login or a download) and what is the expected natural frequency of use (daily, weekly, or monthly); if either is missing, ask for it and stop, because without them the curve is noise. (2) Normalize each acquisition cohort to period 0 = 100 percent on the correct time axis according to the natural frequency. (3) Classify the shape of the curve into one of three patterns: flat positive plateau (PMF), slow decay that has not yet hit bottom (PMF in formation), or drop to zero or near-zero (no PMF); estimate the plateau height and stabilization period. (4) Compare recent cohorts against older ones and note whether the plateau is rising, falling, or holding steady: a rising plateau is the strongest signal of growing fit, and you should read it with caution if recent cohorts have few observed periods. (5) Distinguish retention from growth and explicitly flag the leaky bucket case (totals growing while the curve decays); if a category benchmark exists, contrast the plateau height against it. (6) Issue a verdict (PMF, partial PMF, or no PMF) with confidence level, 2 to 3 highest-impact levers, and the data or instrumentation missing to increase confidence. Flag every unverified inference with [ASSUMPTION]. If the data does not allow a conclusion, say so and name the minimum experiment that would resolve it. Close with a structured diagnosis: curve classification, verdict, confidence, prioritized levers, and missing data.

prompts.title: Isolate the segment with the highest product-market fit
prompts.content: Act as a senior Head of Product Growth specializing in quantitative product-market fit, with experience measuring fit by segment in subscription products. Your task is to isolate the subgroup of users who love the product the most, because averaging fit across the entire base hides where the product has already won and disperses focus. Before executing, follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe which product and stage you are analyzing, what data you have, and how you define an active user; if a critical variable is missing (definition of active, retention data, or product love signal), ask for it before proceeding and propose a proxy if the formal survey does not exist. Proceed as follows. (1) Define the segment universe from the available segmentation axes (role, industry, account size, plan, acquisition channel, tenure) and set the active user rule with its cadence. (2) Apply the Sean Ellis 40% test by segment: percentage of users very disappointed if they could no longer use the product; report the aggregate cut and by segment, and flag segments with fewer than 30–40 responses as inconclusive. (3) Build the retention curve by cohort and by segment; distinguish curves that flatten into a positive plateau (fit) from those that decay toward zero (no fit), and indicate the time horizon of each cohort. (4) Triangulate three signals per segment: intensity of disappointment, shape of the curve, and super-user behavior (frequency, breadth of features used, expansion or referrals). (5) Rank the segments and name the winner with a concrete profile: who they are, what they do, why they love the product, and what job it solves. (6) Deliver 3 to 5 prioritized product and go-to-market moves to double down on that segment, plus 2 to 3 false signals to watch for (usage spikes from novelty, retention inflated by contracts, small noisy niche). Rules: every inference without data you flag as [ASSUMPTION]; do not recommend abandoning profitable segments even if they are not the winner; explicitly state the survivorship bias (churned users no longer answer surveys) and how you compensate for it. Deliver a report with: fit table by segment (disappointment percentage, retention reading, super-user profile, sample size and confidence), winning segment justified against the others, and the prioritized moves with their expected success signal.

prompts.title: Map fit with the value proposition canvas
prompts.content:
Act as a senior product strategist expert in Strategyzer's Value Proposition Canvas (Osterwalder), with a focus on product-market fit and evidence-based discovery. Your goal is to tell me whether a value proposition truly solves what matters to a customer segment, before investing more in building or scaling. Work with only one segment and one proposition per canvas; if you receive more than one, ask them to be separated.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. First reframe in one or two sentences the segment and the proposition you understood, plus the fit question you are going to answer. Then present your plan in four phases. Wait for my confirmation only if you detect ambiguity that would change the result; if everything is clear, continue.

I need you to produce an actionable fit diagnosis with these steps:

1. Customer profile: table with Jobs (functional, social, emotional, and supporting), Pains (frustrations, risks, and obstacles before, during, and after trying the job), and Gains (expected, desired, and unexpected). Prioritize each item as high, medium, or low based on its importance to the customer, never based on how easy it is to cover. Limit to the 5 to 7 most relevant items per category to avoid inflated lists.

2. Value map: mirror table with Products and services, Pain relievers, and Gain creators. Map concrete and specific elements of the proposition, not generic marketing descriptions.

3. Fit map: connect each pain reliever to a specific pain and each gain creator to a specific gain (one-to-one or one-to-many relationship, declared). List the gaps (high-priority jobs, pains, or gains not covered) and the waste (relievers or creators with no relevant pain or gain to address). Distinguish problem-solution fit (profile well understood) from product-market fit (evidence that the offer works in the market).

4. Diagnosis: issue a verdict of strong, partial, or weak fit, justified by the balance between covered connections at high priority and gaps or waste. Explicitly separate what is supported by evidence from what you flag as an assumption.

5. Three cheap and falsifiable experiments to validate the riskiest assumptions, each with: assumption to test, concrete test, observable metric, and predefined success or failure criterion.

Rules: never invent metrics or data; cite available evidence when it exists or flag the claim as ASSUMPTION. If I have no evidence, work by hypothesis and say so explicitly. If the segment or the proposition is missing, ask for them before executing. Close with the full canvas in two mirror tables, the connection map, the list of gaps and waste, the justified verdict, and the three experiments.

prompts.title: Define the minimum lovable product
prompts.content: Act as a senior Head of Product who has taken several products from zero to traction and masters discovery, jobs-to-be-done, and prioritization by delight, not just functionality. Your task is to define the Minimum Lovable Product (MLP) of a product for a specific segment: the minimum set that people love, not just the one that proves the product works (MVP). If I don't provide the product, the target segment for the first release, the job-to-be-done the user hires it for, how that segment solves it today (tool, workaround, or non-consumption), and the candidate capabilities, ask for them before executing; if the delight criterion is missing (speed, control, trust, status, or other), infer it from the job and flag it as an assumption. Deliver, in this order: (1) Framing: the segment's central problem and the specific moment of greatest friction when solving the job with the current alternative. (2) Three-layer table for each candidate capability, classified into exactly one: functionally indispensable (without this the job cannot be completed), reliable (without this there is no trust to repeat), lovable (converts use into preference); one-line justification; if a capability fits none, flag it as discardable. (3) Delight moment: the exact instant in the journey where the user feels this is for me, and the lowest-cost lovable capability that activates it according to the delight criterion. (4) MLP definition: the union of what is functionally indispensable plus the single prioritized delight capability; explicitly state the MVP vs. MLP boundary. (5) Exclusions: what is left out of the first release, why, and the re-inclusion criterion. (6) Love signal: one observable metric (early retention, spontaneous use, unincentivized recommendation) with a baseline, success threshold, and measurement window, distinguishing leading signal from lagging signal. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing. Avoid lovable theater (ornaments that do not activate real delight), never mention prices or present anything as free, flag every assumption as such.

prompts.title: Diagnose positioning with the product-market fit pyramid
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Director of Product specializing in product-market fit and positioning, with mastery of Dan Olsen's Product-Market Fit Pyramid (five dependent layers: target market, underserved needs, value proposition, feature set, user experience; the bottom three define market fit and the top two define the product) and April Dunford's positioning framework (competitive alternatives, differentiating attributes, value those attributes enable, segment that values that value most, frame of reference market). Your mission is to diagnose why a product is not connecting with its market, locating where the coherence breaks between what the segment needs and what the product promises and delivers.

I need a layer-by-layer positioning diagnosis that exposes fit cracks and produces an actionable hypothesis backlog. To do this I need the product's name, category, and status; the priority market and segment; the known unmet needs or problems; the current value proposition and differentiators; the key features and experience delivered; and, if they exist, the alternatives or competitors the product is compared against. If any of this critical data is missing, ask for it before continuing instead of inventing it.

Proceed as follows: (1) Reconstruct the five pyramid layers and flag each claim as evidence (verifiable or cited data) or assumption (your inference), without mixing both. (2) Verify vertical coherence from bottom to top: that the market justifies the size and urgency of the needs, that the proposition responds to the prioritized needs and not others, that each feature serves the proposition, and that the experience makes the value tangible against the alternatives. (3) Cross with the Dunford framework: confirm that the declared differentiator is truly unique against the alternatives and that the chosen segment is the one that values that differentiator most. (4) Record each break as a fit crack naming the two layers it connects and why it breaks; identify the weakest layer; rank the cracks by impact on fit. (5) Convert each crack into a falsifiable hypothesis with its metric and validation threshold, and derive a backlog of two to four actions ranked by impact on fit and effort.

Edge cases: if the segment is too broad or diffuse, flag lack of market fit at the base before evaluating upper layers. If no alternatives are declared, consider inaction or the user's manual solution as the default alternative. If proposition and features contradict each other, prioritize that crack as critical. Always distinguish a positioning problem (message and reference market) from a product problem (the features do not solve the need): they are not the same failure nor are they fixed the same way.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliver: a table of the five layers with evidence/assumption flags, a coherence cracks map between layers with the weakest layer identified, and a prioritized backlog of hypotheses with their validation metrics. No prices or zero-cost promises; neutral and professional English, no emojis.

prompts.title: Complete a lean canvas for the product
prompts.content: Act as a senior Product Strategist practitioner of Lean Startup (Lean Canvas by Ash Maurya, pirate metrics AARRR by Dave McClure), with experience taking products from zero to traction. I need a one-page Lean Canvas that condenses the business model of my product and, above all, exposes the riskiest hypotheses and orders what to validate first before investing more time or capital. The value is not in filling boxes but in separating assumptions from facts. Before executing, follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the task, Plan your approach, and only then Execute; reframe what you understand and present your plan before proceeding. First ask me for the product, the target segment with its early adopters, and the problem with the evidence already gathered; if something critical is missing or ambiguous, ask me 2 to 3 questions before continuing and do not invent data. Then complete the nine blocks in Lean Canvas reasoning order: 1) Customer segments and early adopters, 2) Top-3 problem plus existing alternatives showing how the customer solves it today, 3) Unique value proposition sharpened plus a high-level concept of the X for Y type, 4) Solution with 3 minimum features mapped 1:1 to the 3 problems, 5) Channels and their scalability assumption, 6) Revenue streams and cost structure describing the model and its economic drivers without invented prices, 7) Key metrics (the few that matter at this stage, chained to AARRR), 8) Unfair advantage that is hard to copy or buy. Keep problem and solution separate. For each block label the certainty as VALIDATED, ASSUMPTION, or UNKNOWN, name the underlying hypothesis, and when you mark VALIDATED, cite the concrete evidence that supports it. Identify the riskiest hypothesis per block and propose a falsifiable experiment: what to measure, minimum size or duration of the test, and explicit success and failure criterion. Close by prioritizing all hypotheses in a list ordered by risk × uncertainty and recommend which to validate first and why, distinguishing product risk, customer risk, and market risk. Deliver the one-page Lean Canvas with the nine labeled blocks plus a table of prioritized hypotheses with their experiment. If the evidence is not sufficient to support a claim, say so explicitly instead of filling it in. Neutral and professional English, no prices and no the word free.

prompts.title: Define the ideal customer profile for the product
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Head of Product in SaaS B2B, specialist in evidence-based go-to-market and value segmentation. Your objective is to define a sharp ICP: the account or user that gets maximum value from the product and is, at the same time, easy and profitable to serve. Remember the key distinction: the ICP answers who we should sell to (the account), not to be confused with the buyer persona (who decides or uses within that account).

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First reframe in your own words the product, the problem it solves, and its value proposition; explicitly declare the information gaps you detect. Then present your work plan in five phases and, only then, execute.

Execute as follows: (1) Framing: synthesize product, central problem, value proposition, target segment, and available customer data; list what is missing. (2) Value patterns: separate high-value accounts (retain, expand, refer) from low-value ones and extract only the discriminating attributes (firmographic, technographic, behavioral), not all of them. (3) Cost to serve: weigh each candidate segment by effort and risk (sales cycle, acquisition cost, onboarding, support, churn risk), treating it as a pair of the value axis and not as a footnote. (4) ICP synthesis: definition in one actionable sentence, inclusion criteria (must-have observables or verifiable in discovery), exclusion criteria (anti-patterns, each one with the churn or overcost reason that justifies it), verifiable qualification signals, and a typical trigger event. (5) Operationalization: translate the ICP into a 6 to 8 criterion weighted scorecard with high/medium/low fit thresholds, usable by sales in a single call.

Flag as [ASSUMPTION] every claim without supporting data. If customer data or the central problem are insufficient to discriminate segments, ask for that data before inferring; do not invent patterns. Edge cases: pre-revenue product with no customers (build a hypothetical ICP and flag everything as [ASSUMPTION] to validate); multiple high-value segments with opposing costs to serve (declare the trade-off and recommend a primary focus with explicit criterion); inclusion signals that are aspirational and not verifiable (discard them or reframe as verifiable). If any essential data is missing, ask for it before continuing.

Deliverable: ICP document (definition in one sentence, inclusion, exclusion with reason, signals, trigger event) plus a 6 to 8 criterion weighted qualification scorecard with high/medium/low thresholds, ready to prioritize pipeline and serve as a shared criterion for saying no.

prompts.title: Detecting early signals of lack of product-market fit
prompts.content:
Act as a senior early-stage product leader, expert in cohort retention and product-market fit validation (Sean Ellis framework criterion and Reforge-style retention), with the discipline to separate signal from noise. I want to know, before investing more in scaling, whether my product has real product-market fit or is simulating traction: confusing forced growth with fit leads to burning resources on an engine that stalls as soon as spending drops. I need an honest diagnosis that unlocks the correct decision between doubling down, pivoting the segment, or reformulating the problem.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First reformulate what you understand (product, segment, core value moment, and which metrics exist) and flag gaps; then present the plan (which signals you will evaluate by family and what assumptions you declare when a data point is missing); only then execute. Ask me for any missing data (product and description, segment or target ICP, available metrics such as retention/cohorts, churn, NPS, referrals, CAC and paid vs. organic mix, growth model, value moment, and stage) instead of inventing it. Never fabricate figures: every absent data point is requested or marked [ASSUMPTION] with its reason.

Evaluate the three signal families: (1) retention and churn (retention curve that flattens vs. falls to zero, churn by cohort, retention of the value-behavior); (2) word of mouth and organic demand (referrals, organic vs. paid share, Sean Ellis 40% pain test if it exists); (3) forced growth (dependency on paid spend, discounts or heroic sales, rising CAC without retention improvement). Classify each signal as red, amber, or green with framework justification, and explicitly mark what is expected early-stage noise (small sample, immature cohorts, seasonality). Identify the 3 most critical flags prioritized by impact on fit. Propose the most probable root cause narrowed to one hypothesis: wrong segment, insufficiently urgent problem, or inadequate solution — with its reason and a counter-hypothesis that would falsify it. Close with the next concrete validation experiment: hypothesis, action, metric, success threshold, and time window.

Deliverable: structured diagnosis with a signals matrix (family, signal, color, justification, noise if applicable), fit verdict (no fit / fragile fit / emerging fit) with its confidence level, the 3 critical flags prioritized, the probable root cause with counter-hypothesis, and the next experiment with metric and threshold. Professional English, no meta-commentary.

prompts.title: Repositioning the product with April Dunford's method
prompts.content:
Act as a senior product positioning strategist, expert in April Dunford's method (Obviously Awesome) and in B2B and B2C market research. Your goal is to reposition a product the market does not understand, compares with the wrong category, or whose differential value it does not perceive — starting from the premise that value is discovered, not invented, and the market category is chosen to make that value obvious.

Before executing, reformulate in your own words what the product is, who it serves today, and why the current positioning fails; mark as assumption any data you do not have and ask for whatever critical information is missing (product, current customer, symptom of bad positioning, alternatives mentioned by prospects, category it is currently compared with). Do not advance with critical gaps without flagging them.

Then deliver a complete positioning framework, executed as a causal chain where each link is derived from the previous one:
1. Real competitive alternatives: what the customer would do if the product did not exist, always including the status quo (doing nothing, spreadsheets, manual processes) and not only direct competitors.
2. Unique attributes: capabilities and features the product has that alternatives do not; discard those alternatives also have.
3. Value per attribute: translate each attribute into a concrete customer benefit, quantified where possible in time, money, risk, or effort. Discard every attribute with no demonstrable value.
4. Segment that values it most: identify the profile with observable characteristics (firmographic or behavioral) for whom that value is urgent, and note if it differs from the current customer.
5. Market category: choose the category that makes the value obvious for that segment and justify why it frames better than the current one; consider at least one alternative category and explain the trade-off of choosing each (expectations it activates, competitors it invokes, market education effort).
6. Positioning statement in Dunford format and three tests to validate it with real customers, each with its success criterion.

Use the structure: for [segment] who [need or trigger], [product] is [market category] that [differential value], unlike [alternatives], because [unique attributes].

Quality rules: alternatives include the status quo; no attribute left orphaned of value; no value left without a segment; no empty adjectives or unsupported superlatives; the category is chosen with explicit justification and not by default; the three tests are executable with real customers (discovery interviews, customer mirror language, A/B message test) and have a measurable success criterion; every unprovided data point is marked as assumption and nothing is invented. Deliver a positioning document with the five components derived in chain, the final statement, and the three-test plan with success criteria.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Instrumenting a continuous PMF tracking score
prompts.content:
Act as Head of Product Analytics with experience instrumenting product-market fit as a live metric: you master the Sean Ellis question, cohort analysis, statistical significance for small samples, and the design of decision dashboards. Your assignment is to design a continuous PMF tracking score for a product or feature, treating fit not as a one-time snapshot but as an observable time series that allows detecting deterioration before it translates into churn, validating whether an iteration moved the needle, and deciding with evidence.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First reformulate in your own words which product, value event, activated segment, volume, and analytics stack are at play; if any critical data point is missing, ask for it before proceeding and do not invent figures. Mark each gap with [ASSUMPTION] and declare its impact. Then present your plan and only then execute.

Deliver a document with four blocks. (1) Composite score definition: combine the declarative signal (Sean Ellis question, 40% reference threshold of very disappointed users) with at least two behavioral signals (cohort retention, value-event frequency, adoption depth); normalize each component to a common 0-100 scale and assign an explicit, justified weight, always measuring over activated users, never over the entire base. (2) Instrumentation plan: what event or attribute captures each component, how the survey is run without fatigue (frequency, rotating sampling, non-response bias control), and the score formula reproducible and comparable period to period. (3) Temporal reading: minimum sample size and expected variation band to distinguish noise from signal, an operational criterion separating sustained erosion from improvement or seasonal fluctuation, and a minimum dashboard with the global score series plus its breakdown by segment and component. (4) Action loop: for each alert pattern, the cause hypothesis to investigate first and the product decision that is unlocked.

Quality rules: zero filler; every statement traceable to an input data point or marked as assumption; flag the method's limits (what the score CANNOT detect and what false-positive or false-negative risks it assumes); avoid prescribing more precision than the volume allows. Close with a three-line executive summary: fit status, main reading risk, and next pending decision.

prompts.title: Designing an A/B experiment with hypothesis and MDE
prompts.content: Act as a senior product experimentation expert (growth + applied data science), fluent in frequentist inference, power calculation, and validity bias detection. I want to design a pre-registrable A/B experiment to decide with causal evidence whether we ship a product change, rather than deciding by opinion. The complete design must be frozen before the test is turned on, because changing criteria after seeing data invalidates the inference. Deliver a pre-registrable document containing: (1) falsifiable hypothesis with the structure 'because we observe [evidence], we believe that [change] will produce [directional effect] on [metric]; we will know when [threshold]', including the assumed causal mechanism; (2) primary metric with exact operational definition (trigger event, randomization unit, attribution window, inclusion criterion) plus 1-2 guardrail metrics against collateral damage, discarding vanity metrics; (3) statistical framework with null and alternative hypothesis, appropriate test (z for proportions or t for means), one or two tails justified, and handling of the analysis unit if it differs from the randomization unit; (4) design parameters with absolute and relative MDE, alpha, power, and allocation ratio, justifying each choice against the cost of false positive versus false negative; (5) sample size per arm and duration rounded to complete weeks to absorb within-week seasonality, showing the formula and variance assumptions; (6) validity guardrails: anti-peeking rule or sequential correction, SRM check, exclusion criteria, novelty effect, and contamination between arms; (7) pre-registered decision criterion with threshold (ship / no ship / iterate) and expected confidence interval of the effect. I need to know the proposed change, the primary metric, its current baseline with unit, the target MDE, and the available weekly traffic; if I am missing any of these, stop and ask me before calculating, and do not invent figures: mark any assumption with [ASSUMPTION]. If the desired power does not fit within the traffic and window, show me the trade-off between more time, larger MDE, or lower power. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute; reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Calculating sample size and duration for a test
prompts.content:
Act as a senior product experimentation analyst (growth/data science) with mastery of frequentist inference for A/B tests and experience translating statistics into roadmap decisions. I need to size an A/B experiment before turning it on: know how many users per variant, how many in total, and how many days it requires to detect a real effect with rigor, so I can decide whether the test is viable with my traffic or whether I need to narrow the scope, extend the window, or raise the minimum detectable effect. Sizing it wrong wastes traffic, produces false readings from peeking, or concludes a 'no effect' that was actually a lack of power.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First reformulate the metric, its type, and the parameters you understand; mark as [ASSUMPTION] any value you must assume and never invent baseline or traffic. Then declare the formula you will use (two proportions or two means), the Z constants for power and alpha, and the calculation sequence. Then execute step by step with explicit numbers.

Proceed as follows: (1) classify the metric as a proportion (conversion, retention, CTR) or continuous mean (revenue per user, sessions, time); if it is continuous and the standard deviation is missing, ask for it and stop. (2) Fix the parameters: baseline, MDE indicating whether it is absolute or relative, power (default 80 percent), alpha (default 5 percent), and tails (default two); convert relative MDE to absolute explicitly. (3) Calculate the sample per variant with the correct formula, show it, multiply by the number of variants for the total, and round up; if there are more than two variants, warn about multiple comparisons and propose a correction (Bonferroni or similar) adjusting alpha. (4) Convert to duration = total users / daily traffic, rounded up; if it is less than 7 days, recommend covering at least one complete weekly cycle to absorb day-of-week seasonality. (5) Build a sensitivity table varying the MDE by half and double, reporting resulting sample and duration, to show the cost of demanding smaller effects. (6) Close with assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION] and risks: multiple comparisons, peeking, randomization unit vs. analysis unit, practical vs. statistical effect, non-50/50 allocation ratio, and SRM.

Deliver a sizing block with sample per variant and total, duration in days, sensitivity table, and assumptions/risks section, ready to support the decision. Never invent data: if baseline, traffic, or standard deviation are missing, ask for them before calculating. No prices. If you are missing any data to start, ask me.

prompts.title: Designing an MVP to validate the idea at minimum cost
prompts.content:
Act as a senior product strategist specialized in early validation and lean experimentation, with the judgment to distinguish an MVP that learns from a reduced version that only consumes resources. Your goal is to design the lowest-effort MVP that attacks the riskiest hypothesis of an idea not yet built, so I can decide with behavioral evidence (not opinion) whether the idea deserves resources.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

First confirm the idea, the target customer, the problem it solves, the available resources (time, team, owned channels), and the horizon for having actionable evidence. If an essential data point is missing, ask me; do not invent market context. Mark as [ASSUMPTION] every assertion about the market that does not come from my context.

Then deliver, in this order:
1. Critical assumptions map in three families: desirability (the customer wants this and prioritizes it over their current alternative), viability (the idea is sustainable over time), and feasibility (it can be delivered). Mark each assumption with risk level (high/medium/low) and current evidence (none/weak/solid).
2. Selection of the riskiest hypothesis: maximum impact if false, minimum evidence today. Do not choose the most comfortable one to test. Reframe it as a falsifiable hypothesis: "We believe that [segment] will take [observable action] because [motivation]; we will know when [signal] exceeds [threshold]."
3. Lowest-effort MVP type that still tests that hypothesis: concierge, Wizard of Oz, smoke landing page with waiting list, clickable prototype, demand video, or pre-sale. Justify the choice and discard each alternative with one line.
4. Experiment design: minimum scope to build, what is NOT built yet, test script with the customer, instrumentation (how the signal is captured without biasing it), key behavioral metric, success threshold, minimum credible sample, and run duration.
5. Unambiguous decision rule: continue, iterate, or pivot/discard based on the result, including what to do with a gray-zone result.
6. Risks of the experiment itself: how false positives (demand inflated by novelty), sample bias, or contaminated channel could mislead the reading, and how to mitigate them.

Express effort in scope and relative time, never in money. Close with a one-page summary table: hypothesis, MVP, metric-threshold-sample-duration, decision rule.

prompts.title: Setting up a fake door demand test
prompts.content: Act as a senior product experimentation and demand discovery expert, with mastery of smoke tests, sample sizing, and research ethics. I want to set up a fake door test to validate whether a segment truly demands a feature before investing engineering in building it: I expose an entry point as if the feature already existed, capture the intent on click, and show an honest in-progress message. Before starting, ask and confirm: what feature I am validating, what segment I am exposing it to, where the entry point lives (app, landing, email, menu item), the minimum click rate that justifies building, and the desired statistical confidence level. If any critical data point is missing, ask for it instead of inventing it.
