Then deliver: (1) falsifiable hypothesis in the format 'if we expose the feature to the segment, we expect a click rate of at least X', with primary metric CTR on the door and guardrails (bounce, complaints, unsubscriptions, NPS of those exposed); (2) the control version and the exposure condition, plus the criterion to distinguish genuine interest from accidental click or curiosity; (3) exact exposure point, trigger copy, and honest post-click capture screen copy with no inducement to deception, with an optional one-question micro-survey to capture the why; (4) sample sizing and duration with the proportions method, visible formula, and baseline rate assumption, covering at least one usage cycle of the segment; (5) binary decision threshold around the target rate (build / iterate the value proposition / discard) and how to read a gray zone close to the threshold; (6) instrumentation plan with triggered event, recorded attributes, and per-user deduplication; (7) communication script for those who left their email, closing the loop with dignity and without creating empty waiting lists; (8) ethical and reputational risks of the fake door and their mitigation, including exposure limit per user and a plan if the test goes viral. Mark every estimate as [ASSUMPTION]. No prices or the word free; neutral, professional English. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Designing a Wizard of Oz experiment
prompts.content: Act as a senior Product Discovery Lead, expert in hypothesis validation and low-cost experiments before writing code. Design a ready-to-execute Wizard of Oz experiment, where the user perceives an automated system while a person manually executes the backend. First reformulate the feature to validate and the target segment, and declare the value hypothesis as a falsifiable statement (we believe the segment values a certain outcome enough to take an observable action), with the exact condition that would refute it. Then deliver: 1) the facade, precisely separating what the user sees and does versus what the wizard executes behind the scenes (intake, manual processing, output delivery with credible latency); 2) the wizard's operational script, with numbered steps, target response times, tone, output templates, and rules for unanticipated cases, executable by a third party without context; 3) the instrumentation: activation event, primary decision metric with quantitative threshold, secondary metrics, and qualitative signals; 4) minimum sample, duration, and stopping criteria for success, failure, and ethical or operational risk; 5) method risks (wizard bias, non-scalability, user expectations, handling of real data) with mitigation; 6) the build/iterate/discard decision rule and the next experiment. Explicitly address the ethical handling of the simulation and of real data: the user must not be deceived in a way that harms them, and sensitive data must be treated with the same diligence as in production. Mark each assumption with [ASSUMPTION]. If the feature, segment, or success metric are missing, ask for them before executing. MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute; reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Deliver an immediately actionable one-to-two-page dossier for the product team.

prompts.title: Running a manual service concierge MVP
prompts.content:
Act as a senior product lead in discovery and lean experimentation, with experience operating concierge and Wizard of Oz MVPs. Design a concierge MVP operable this week: deliver a value proposition by hand to a specific, reachable segment, without building anything scalable yet, to convert assumptions into observed evidence before investing in product or automation.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First reformulate what service, what segment, and what tangible outcome you understand; if the problem, segment, or verifiable outcome is missing, ask before proceeding. Do not invent metrics or demand; mark everything unconfirmed as [ASSUMPTION].

Deliver the plan in five numbered blocks:
1. Hypothesis and focus: a single falsifiable sentence stating the belief, exact segment, and expected outcome, plus the criterion that would declare it refuted.
2. Manual service script: recruiting the first users, explicit promise, request intake channel, manual production of the outcome, delivery, committed response times, and verbatim contact script.
3. Learning instrumentation: research questions, signals to observe (real requests, repetition, perceived quality, friction, intent to continue), and a recording method that does not contaminate the user or induce the response.
4. Experiment design: bounded sample and window, and numeric or verifiable thresholds separating advance, pivot, and discard, with what to do with an ambiguous result.
5. Transition: what is done manually now, what is a candidate for automation later, and the observable signal that triggers exiting manual mode.

Include at the end an explicit assumptions block, experiment limits, and one anticipated edge case (e.g., zero demand, or demand exceeding manual capacity). Close with the self-assessed quality checklist.

Brand rules: never mention prices; never use the word free; neutral, professional English, no emojis. The service must be deliverable 100% manually: no piece can require building a product to start.

prompts.title: Launching a landing smoke test to measure conversion
prompts.content:
Act as a Senior Growth Product Manager specialized in early validation and painted door experiments, with statistical judgment to separate signal from noise. I want to design a landing smoke test (a single-CTA page with no product behind it) to buy cheap demand evidence before committing months of development. I need to know: who the test targets, what value proposition it puts to the test, which channels will drive traffic, what conversion signal defines success, what threshold we will use to decide, and for how long we will collect data. If I am missing any of those data points, ask before proceeding; do not invent figures and mark every assumption as [ASSUMPTION].

Deliver a ready-to-launch design document with these parts: (1) falsifiable hypothesis naming the segment, assumed problem, proposition, metric, threshold, and window; (2) metrics system with one north metric (conversion rate = conversions / unique visitors) and two guardrail metrics with their formula, plus a minimum sample size so the result is conclusive and not chance; (3) landing copy in blocks (proposition headline, pain subheadline, three benefit proofs, single CTA, and an honest thank-you screen that clarifies the solution is under exploration, collects email for notification, and does not promise dates); (4) instrumentation with events to fire, UTM parameters by channel, and a conversion-to-source attribution rule; (5) a decision tree that translates the observed number into continue, pivot, or discard, with the explicit rule to distinguish signal from noise (confidence interval or margin). Cover edge cases: insufficient traffic at the close of the window, high conversion with poor sample, and a channel that distorts the average.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First reformulate what you understood and present your plan; then execute. No prices, no the word free, in neutral professional English, no emojis. Close only when the document allows launching the test without additional steps.

prompts.title: Define the overall evaluation criterion for the experiment
prompts.content: Act as a senior product experimentation leader with a track record designing OEC (Overall Evaluation Criterion) and guardrails for A/B testing programs at scale. Your task is to deliver a one-page OEC card that decides whether a variant wins or loses, avoiding the optimization of a short-term proxy that is easy to inflate (clicks, sessions) and that improves in the test but degrades long-term value. Before executing, restate in one line the hypothesis and the long-term north star, and present your plan. Work in phases. Phase 1, interpret: if the hypothesis and the concrete change, the population or test surface, the long-term goal, the metrics already being monitored, the estimated duration, and the randomization unit (user, session, account) are not clear, ask for them in a single batch before proceeding; do not invent context. Phase 2, design: translate the long-term goal into a measurable construct and propose a primary OEC metric with exact formula, unit, measurement window, and aggregation level; if a composite OEC is appropriate, declare the components and justified weights, and warn that poor weighting can hide regressions. Phase 3, audit: run the OEC through four properties and flag the risk of each. Sensitive: it moves within the chosen duration and unit with the available sample size; if not, declare it insensitive and propose a surface proxy correlated with the goal. Directional: going up is always better for the business. Causal and non-gameable: name at least one concrete scenario of how the variant could inflate the metric while degrading the experience, and how a guardrail prevents it. Attributable: the movement is caused by the tested change and not by seasonality or network effects. Phase 4, decide: define 2 to 4 guardrails that must NOT worsen (latency, churn, error rate, revenue per user, satisfaction), each with a non-regression threshold anchored in current metrics; set the decision rule (which combination of OEC plus guardrails triggers launch, iterate, or discard) and the minimum practically relevant effect size that justifies launch, distinguishing it from mere statistical significance. Close with the card ready to review with the team. Rules: tie the OEC explicitly to the long-term goal, not to a vanity proxy; flag everything not supported by data as [ASSUMPTION]; do not recommend launching if the OEC is insensitive or if a critical guardrail lacks a threshold. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Interpret the results of a test and its significance
prompts.content: Act as a Staff Product Analyst specialized in online experimentation and A/B test design. An A/B test has ended and the numbers must be converted into an investment decision: ship the change, kill it, or iterate. The risk is reading the p-value as a traffic light and shipping noise, or killing a real improvement by confusing 'not significant' with 'no effect'. I need a justified SHIP / KILL / ITERATE verdict. Proceed as follows: (1) Summarize the experiment in one line: primary metric with its desired direction, control vs. treatment, and hypothesis tested. (2) Read the p-value against the declared alpha; if there is no alpha, assume 0.05 and flag it as an assumption. State whether the null hypothesis is rejected and clarify explicitly that the p-value is NOT the probability that the variant is better. (3) Interpret the confidence interval: report the full range, note whether it crosses zero (or 1 in ratios) — in which case it is inconclusive — and translate both extremes (pessimistic and optimistic) into business impact. (4) Compare the effect size against the minimum effect that makes the change worthwhile: a significant result but below that threshold does not justify shipping. (5) Audit validity: statistical power, peeking or early stopping, achieved vs. planned sample, novelty effect, contamination between variants (SRM/sample ratio mismatch), seasonality, and multiple comparisons. (6) Deliver the verdict with justification, risks assumed, and a concrete next step. Label each claim as [DATA], [ASSUMPTION], or [INFERENCE]. If the p-value, confidence interval, sample size, profitability threshold, or metric direction is missing, ask for it before concluding; do not invent figures. MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Deliver a one-page decision with a summary of the experiment, reading of the three statistics, validity audit, and final recommendation with its next step.

prompts.title: Prevent peeking and early stopping errors
prompts.content:
Act as a senior growth and experimentation data scientist, proficient in classical frequentist inference (power, sample size) and in sequential methods (alpha spending, group sequential, always-valid inference with e-values). Your assignment: shield an A/B test against peeking and early stopping, two practices that inflate the false-positive rate far above the nominal alpha because each additional look is an extra opportunity to cross the threshold by chance.

Produce a documented stopping protocol, ready to attach to the experiment ticket and audit, with these steps:
1. Restate in one line the hypothesis on the primary metric and name the concrete peeking risk in this case.
2. Confirm the framing: single primary metric, hypothesis direction, randomization unit, and whether the metric is binary (proportion) or continuous (mean), because it changes the sample size formula.
3. Choose and justify the stopping regime: (a) fixed sample with a single analysis at the end, or (b) sequential design with planned interim reviews. Spell out the trade-off: speed of decision vs. error control. Recommend fixed sample when the horizon is short and the discipline of not looking is viable; sequential when the business will demand looking or cutting early.
4. If fixed sample: calculate the sample size per variant from the baseline rate, minimum detectable effect, and alpha/power; translate it into duration according to daily traffic, and set ONE single read date.
5. If there will be interim reviews: choose the method that controls the accumulated Type I error (O'Brien-Fleming boundary, Pocock via alpha spending, or sequential testing with e-values/always-valid p-values); declare the number of looks and deliver the table of look-corrected thresholds. O'Brien-Fleming is conservative at the start; Pocock spends evenly; e-values allow unlimited and optional looks.
6. Define the decision rule per look (stop for efficacy / stop for futility / continue) and draft a one-page governance script that prohibits stopping the test without crossing the pre-registered threshold: what is decided, when, with what threshold, who approves.

Edge cases to cover: metric with unstabilized or highly skewed variance (consider transformation or CUPED to reduce variance), novelty/primacy effects that distort early looks, multiple variants requiring multiple-comparisons correction, and guardrail metrics that can trigger stopping for harm even when the primary does not cross.

If any data is missing (metric, minimum detectable effect, baseline rate, alpha, power, number of looks, traffic), ask for it BEFORE calculating. Flag every value you assume as [ASSUMPTION] and isolate it so the user can correct it; never invent a missing value.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Close when the document contains: framing, justified regime, calculation or threshold table, decision rule per look, and a one-page governance pre-registration, with every assumption traced.

prompts.title: Build a prioritized experiment backlog
prompts.content: Act as a senior Head of Product Discovery with experience ordering experimentation backlogs by assumption risk and learning velocity in digital products. I want a prioritized experiment backlog for a product, feature, or initiative, in service of a business outcome for the period and focused on a user segment. The underlying problem: the team carries more hypotheses than validation capacity, so without an evidence-based order, discovery spends effort on what is comfortable rather than what is risky. Before proceeding, restate what you understand and present your plan. If essential context is missing (product, business objective, segment, list of hypotheses, resources, or timeline) or something is ambiguous, ask for it in a single batch before executing; do not invent figures or evidence. Proceed as follows: (1) Frame the objective, segment, and belief inventory, and mark each starting claim as fact or assumption. (2) Rewrite each belief as a falsifiable hypothesis using the template: We believe that [action] will achieve [measurable outcome] for [segment] because [reason]; we will know it is true if [measurable signal and threshold]. (3) Classify each hypothesis by risk type: desirability, viability, feasibility, or fit (business/legal/ethics). (4) Score two axes on a scale of 1 to 5: assumption risk (impact if the hypothesis is false, weighted by weakness of current evidence) and learning velocity (speed and low effort to obtain a reliable signal; faster and cheaper = higher score), justifying each score. (5) Calculate priority = assumption risk x learning velocity, sort from highest to lowest, resolve ties by lowest learning cost, and adjust the order to available capacity and timeline. (6) For the top items define the test method (interview, fake door, prototype, smoke test, concierge, analytics), the metric with success and failure thresholds, the sample or duration, the underlying assumption being validated, and the decision it unlocks (persevere, pivot, or discard). (7) Close with the prioritized table and a kickoff note for the three experiments to run first, their justification, and the confirmation bias they avoid. Flag limits: what cannot be concluded, dependencies between experiments, and measurement risks (insufficient sample, novelty effect, contamination between variants). Keep one experiment per critical assumption to avoid confounding signals. Neutral and professional English, without emojis.

prompts.title: Design a self-reinforcing growth loop
prompts.content: Act as a senior Head of Growth specialized in product loops and experimentation, with the judgment to distinguish a real self-reinforcing loop from a disguised linear funnel. I want the complete design of the growth loop for my product in four artifacts: textual diagram of the loop, equation with variables, bottleneck table with levers, and falsifiable experiment card. Proceed as follows. First, restate what my product does, for whom, and what its current growth engine is; if you do not know the core action where the user gets value, how users arrive today, or what growth metric to maximize, ask for it and stop without inventing figures. Second, map the loop in 4 to 6 chained nodes starting from the value action: observable output produced by the user, channel or surface through which that output reaches non-users, moment and conversion trigger of the non-user, and the step that returns the new user to the start of the cycle; explicitly verify that the last node feeds back into the first. Apply the loop-vs-funnel test: if sustaining the flow requires re-injecting external spending or effort on each turn, it is a funnel, not a loop, and you must declare it. Third, classify the loop type (invitation viral, indexable user-generated content, data that improves the product and raises retention, or direct network effect) and justify why it applies according to how users arrive today; do not assign a type by default. Fourth, formulate the loop equation with three components: amplification factor per cycle (how many new users each user generates per turn), cycle time (how long a complete turn takes), and conversion rate at each step; label each estimated value as an assumption and indicate how to instrument it in production (event, property, cohort). Interpret the result: if the factor is greater than or equal to 1 the loop is self-sustaining; if between 0 and 1 it amplifies acquisition but cannot sustain itself alone, and name the threshold that changes the regime. Fifth, identify the bottleneck as the step with the lowest pass-through rate and propose three levers, each with the metric it moves, its expected effect on the amplification factor, and the cost or risk of implementing it, all aligned to the target metric and within the given constraints. Sixth, design a falsifiable experiment with hypothesis, variant, primary metric, numerical success criterion, approximate sample size, duration, and the condition that would invalidate it. Consider and name two risks: channel saturation (the loop is exhausted when the reachable non-users run out) and leaks or counter-loops (churn, fatigue, decreasing output quality). Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Do not invent figures, respect all constraints, no meta-commentary. Deliver: textual diagram of the loop, equation with variables, bottleneck table with three levers, and experiment card.

prompts.title: Map experiments against north star metric inputs
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Growth Product Lead expert in north star metrics, input metric trees, and ICE/RICE prioritization of experiments. Your objective is to build the map that connects each experiment in the backlog with the input of the north star metric it intends to move, so that each test justifies its place by causal chain toward the north star and not by trend.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First, restate the north star metric, its definition, and the input tree as you understand them; if the input equation is unclear or the backlog has no hypotheses, ask for them before inferring, because a poorly derived tree contaminates the entire map. Then present your mapping and scoring plan. Only then execute.

Proceed as follows: (1) Break down the north star metric into its input tree: first-level levers and second-level actionable sub-levers, derived from the provided equation, never invented. (2) For each experiment in the backlog identify the exact input it targets, the explicit causal chain that would move it, and the critical falsifiable assumption that must be true for it to work. (3) Mark as orphan every experiment that does not map to any input and issue a decision: discard or re-justify. (4) Score each experiment with ICE (Impact on the input, Confidence according to evidence, Effort) using only available evidence; label [ASSUMPTION] every estimate without backing and lower its confidence. (5) Build the coverage map: inputs saturated with too many experiments versus orphan inputs with no tests. (6) Explicitly flag the popular experiments that do not move anything that matters. (7) Recommend 3 to 5 bets to run first within the defined horizon, each with its causal justification.

Closing criterion: deliver a master table (experiment, input, lever, critical assumption, ICE, decision run/de-prioritize/discard) plus the input coverage map plus the top 3 to 5 justified bets. Always distinguish verified data from [ASSUMPTION]. If evidence is missing to estimate, say so instead of inventing a number. Close by unlocking an experimentation strategy where each test has a causal reason. Neutral and professional English, without emojis.

prompts.title: Design a research plan with questions and method
prompts.content:
Act as a Lead UX Researcher with more than ten years designing discovery and evaluation studies for product teams, fluent in qualitative, quantitative, and mixed methods. Design an actionable user research plan ready to take to the field this very week, that unlocks a concrete product decision with evidence rather than opinion.

Before writing, restate the decision the study must unlock, the product and its maturity stage, the target user segment, and the available timeline and resources. If the decision, the segment, or the stage is missing, ask for it before proceeding: without a topic, without a segment, or without a decision the plan cannot be anchored. If you assume something to avoid blocking, mark it explicitly as an assumption.

Derive the plan in this strict order and do not invert it: first the decision, from the decision the learning objectives, from the objectives the research questions, and only then choose the method that best answers those questions. Always distinguish the type of question (generative or evaluative, attitudinal or behavioral) and let that, together with the product stage, govern the method and sample size. Never choose the method out of preference or convenience.

Deliver a plan with nine numbered sections: 1) product decision and why the research unlocks it; 2) learning objectives (two to four), each tied to a concrete decision and the action that will be taken according to the result; 3) research questions, separating what you want to learn (research questions, internal) from what will be asked of the user (discussion guide), without leading questions; 4) hypotheses or assumptions to falsify where applicable, written as testable statements with their confirmation or refutation signal; 5) recommended method (exploratory qualitative, evaluative, quantitative, or mixed) justified against the question and the stage, with one discarded alternative and why; 6) recruitment: target profile, inclusion and exclusion criteria, sample size reasoned by study type, and recruitment channels; 7) discussion guide or session protocol with opening, thematic blocks or tasks, and closing, plus estimated duration; 8) analysis plan and success or decision criteria defined before data collection; 9) risks, biases to mitigate, and ethical and consent considerations.

Quality rules: sample size is reasoned by study type (for example, 5 to 8 participants per segment in evaluative qualitative; larger n when the objective is to measure or compare); the discussion guide does not contain leading, double-barreled, or hypothetical questions the user cannot answer with real behavior; decision criteria are set before the field, not after. Flag the design decisions you made and their trade-offs. Before delivering, restate your understanding and present the proposed plan. Write in neutral and professional English, without emojis.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Choose the research method according to the question
prompts.content:
Act as a Senior UX Research Lead who has built mixed research programs (quali + quanti) in product teams and masters the Christian Rohrer / NN/g methods landscape framework (attitudinal-behavioral and qualitative-quantitative axes, plus product usage context). Your objective is to decide the correct research method BEFORE investing effort, starting from what the team needs to learn, so that the product decision at stake is unlocked with adequate evidence rather than opinions, and to avoid recruiting users for questions that already available data answers.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First, restate what you understand about the question and the decision that depends on it; then present your classification and selection plan; only then execute the recommendation. If any critical data is missing (what needs to be learned, what decision it unlocks, what stage the product is in, what prior data exists, or what time and user access constraints exist), ask for it in a single round of questions before continuing; do not invent the context.

Produce a one-page method recommendation that: (1) reformulates the question in a single falsifiable sentence tied to the decision, separating the dominant question from any others if they come mixed (the others go to a named backlog); (2) classifies the question on two axes (attitudinal vs. behavioral: what they say vs. what they do; qualitative vs. quantitative: the why vs. the how much) justifying each axis according to the product stage; (3) recommends exactly 1 primary method and 1 triangulation secondary method choosing from: interviews, moderated or unmoderated usability tests, surveys, card sorting, tree testing, product analytics, A/B testing, diary studies, intercept surveys, and support ticket analysis, where the secondary covers the opposite axis from the primary; (4) designs the primary method with sample and recruitment criterion, location on both axes, evidence it produces, and how it is analyzed, all adjusted to the constraints; (5) lists 2 biases or validity threats of the chosen method (social desirability, self-selection, recall bias, moderator effect, unrepresentative sample, novelty, survivorship) with concrete mitigation; and (6) resolves a no-research gate: if existing data already answers the question, state it with an explicit flag and propose analyzing what exists before launching a new study. Close with a research-new yes/no verdict. Flag any assumption you had to make. Neutral and professional English, without emojis.

prompts.title: Write an open exploratory interview guide
prompts.content:
Act as a senior product researcher specialized in qualitative discovery, trained in the discipline of The Mom Test (talk about the past and about concrete facts, never about the future or hypothetical opinions) and in non-directed ethnographic interviewing. You will write a ready-to-conduct open exploratory interview guide from start to finish.

Before writing, restate in one sentence the behavior or problem we will explore, the profile of the person to be interviewed, and the product decision the research must unlock; present a brief outline of the guide and then execute. If you are missing any of those three pieces of data, ask for them: without a topic, without a segment, or without a decision the guide cannot be anchored.

Produce, in this order: (1) Learning objective in one sentence, naming the decision to unlock and the assumption we currently hold without evidence. (2) 3 to 5 hypotheses or assumptions to falsify, each written in a verifiable way during the conversation and mapped to the central block question that tests it. (3) Opening and consent: framing, permission to record, and the phrase there are no right answers. (4) Warm-up: 2 context questions about role and routine. (5) Central block: 8 to 12 open questions, ordered from general to specific in a funnel, each anchored to the last time the behavior occurred, with 1 or 2 follow-up probes in parentheses that deepen motivation, context, and consequence. (6) Closing: 2 questions, what you did not ask and a referral request. (7) List of prohibited formulations with, for each one, the anti-pattern and its equivalent open rewrite.

Non-negotiable quality rules: each central block question is open and contains a single idea; at least 70 percent of the questions are anchored to a specific past episode and not to future intentions; zero hypothetical questions of the type would you use, would you pay, or would you like; zero mention of any solution before having explored the problem; each hypothesis is falsifiable and maps to at least one question; eliminate double-barreled, leading, yes/no, and adjective-loaded questions. Missing data is asked for or flagged [ASSUMPTION]; do not invent context. Deliver in neutral, professional English, without internal jargon, and reusable for future rounds with the same segment.

prompts.title: Design a task-based usability test
prompts.content:
Act as a senior UX Researcher specialized in task-based usability testing, with mastery of usability metrics (task success, time on task, error rate, number of assists, SEQ, SUS, or UMUX-Lite) and of sampling for qualitative and comparative studies.

I need a complete usability test plan, ready to recruit and run, that any team facilitator can conduct consistently and that converts diffuse opinions into observable evidence before committing engineering and budget. First restate what you understand and present your plan; then execute.

If you do not have the interface to evaluate, the product decision the test must inform, the user profile and segments, the critical flows to cover, or the modality and number of participants, ask for them before proceeding rather than inventing them.

Deliver these numbered sections:
1. Research objectives: 3 to 5 questions the test must answer, each explicitly linked to the product decision, with the falsifiable hypothesis and the decision criterion (what result triggers proceed, adjust, or halt).
2. Participants: target profile, screener of 4 to 6 filter questions with disqualifying answers marked, recommended number per segment justified by modality, and a note on incentives and recruitment logistics.
3. Tasks and scenarios: 4 to 6 tasks covering the critical flows; for each task, a scenario narrated in user language (context plus goal, without naming buttons or revealing the path), initial state, required test data, and an observable and unambiguous success criterion. Define the order and whether to counterbalance to mitigate the learning effect.
4. Metrics per task: which apply among task success (binary or by levels), time on task, error rate, number of assists, and SEQ from 1 to 7, with a target threshold per metric and how each is recorded.
5. Facilitator script: introduction, consent and recording, think-aloud instruction, no-help and hint escalation rules, post-task and post-test questions, and a global satisfaction instrument (SUS or UMUX-Lite) if applicable.
6. Analysis plan: master table to tabulate by participant and by task, severity scale (1 cosmetic, 2 minor, 3 major, 4 critical), prioritization rule (severity by frequency), and findings report format.
7. Study risks and mitigations: biases (moderator, order, sample), validity of the chosen modality, and pilot plan with 1 participant before the full group.

Mark with [ASSUMPTION] every data point you assume. Do not include prices. Write in neutral and professional English, without emojis.

prompts.title: Write a participant recruitment screener
prompts.content:
Act as a senior UX research specialist in participant recruitment and screener design, with experience running panels, quotas, and anti-fraud controls for qualitative and quantitative studies. Your assignment is to produce the entry filter for a study: the screener that decides who gets in and who stays out. A weak screener contaminates the entire research effort: if participants who do not represent the target — or who lie to access the incentive — get through, the conclusions are expensive noise and the product EstrategIA that depends on those data starts off skewed.

Before drafting anything, I need to know: the research question or decision the study must inform; the target profile described by real behavior, context, and experience — not just demographics; sample size and method (interviews, usability test, survey); quotas by segment if any; exclusion criteria (industry, market research, recent participation, conflicts of interest); and modality and logistics (remote/in-person, duration, type of planned incentive, without amounts). If any of these data are missing, ask me before continuing rather than inventing them; mark every inferred criterion with [ASSUMPTION] and leave [to_confirm] for anything you cannot resolve.

Proceed as follows. First, reframe the objective and translate the profile into observable and verifiable criteria: demographic quotas, behavior (frequency of use, context, tools), experience level, and tenure as a user; each criterion must be measured by behavioral evidence, not by abstract self-declared attitudes. Second, convert each criterion into one or two closed-choice questions with an explicit decision rule per option (QUALIFIES / DISQUALIFIES / QUOTA per cell). Third, insert at least three quality controls: a plausibility trap (a non-existent but credible option within a list of tools or brands that disqualifies anyone who selects it), a conflict-of-interest filter based on the exclusion criteria (working in the industry, in market research, media, or a competitor; participation in recent studies), and an internal consistency check (two questions that must align — e.g., stated frequency vs. last time the product was used) so you are not relying on honesty without cross-checking. Fourth, order the flow from lowest to highest friction: fast disqualifiers first, quota questions next, fine profiling and sensitive data at the close, to avoid burning incentive or time on those who will be screened out. Fifth, translate the quotas into concrete cells that sum to the sample size, and include an over-recruitment buffer for no-shows (suggest the percentage based on modality and justify the assumption). Sixth, draft a neutral, non-leading introduction that does not reveal the target profile or the desired answer, and a close that captures contact details, availability, and consent in line with the modality.

Deliver three artifacts: the numbered screener ready to load into a survey tool; a qualification-logic table with columns question | option | action (QUALIFIES/DISQUALIFIES/QUOTA); and a quota matrix with cells, target per cell, total, and buffer. Before drafting the final screener, briefly restate your understanding of the objective and profile, and present your criteria-and-controls plan for validation. Avoid leading language in every question, do not reveal which option qualifies, and do not include incentive amounts: refer to it as the planned incentive.

prompts.title: Design an unbiased quantitative survey
prompts.content: Act as a senior product researcher (quantitative UX researcher) grounded in psychometrics and questionnaire design. Design a quantitative survey whose sole purpose is to enable a concrete product decision with reliable data — not to collect scattered opinions. Remember that the central risk of any survey is bias: loaded questions, unbalanced scales, and carry-over order produce numbers that look valid but point to the wrong decision, costing weeks of rework and credibility with stakeholders. Before drafting anything, ask me for the bare minimum if you do not have it: the decision the survey must enable, the central research question, and who answers (segment, role, relationship with the product). Do not invent those data. When you have them, deliver: (1) a construct map that translates the decision into measurable variables, each with its operational definition, discarding what cannot be measured; (2) a block of numbered questions where each item declares its type (single, multiple, scale, ranking, open-ended), its options, and its associated scale, measuring one single concept per question, in neutral language, without double negatives or loaded terms; (3) balanced scales with a justified number of points, symmetric labels at both ends, an explicit neutral point or its absence justified, and an exit option (Not applicable / Prefer not to answer) where appropriate; (4) a recommended order: general before specific, sensitive items at the end, grouping by construct, with a note on why that sequence reduces carry-over effects and fatigue, and randomization of options where applicable; (5) a register of biases avoided (acquiescence, social desirability, leading framing, double-barreled questions, order anchoring) with the technique used against each; and (6) a pre-field analysis plan indicating, per construct, how each result will be read to make the decision, preventing the definition of success from being redefined after seeing the data. Flag every assumption you make as [ASSUMPTION] and warn when a small sample size cannot support cuts by segment. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing. Close only when every construct is traceable to the decision and every item passes the bias checklist.

prompts.title: Synthesize findings with affinity mapping
prompts.content:
Act as a senior UX researcher specializing in qualitative synthesis and affinity mapping, with sharp judgment for separating signal from noise. I have raw research observations (notes, verbatim quotes, behaviors, and complaints) that I need to convert into prioritized emerging themes with traceable evidence, so I can make defensible roadmap decisions rather than deciding by anecdote. Before executing, restate the research objective in your own words and present your work plan; if any essential data are missing (the research objective, the observation material, the number of distinct participants, the product dimension to prioritize, or the desired level of detail), ask me for them rather than assuming.

Proceed as follows once you have what you need: (1) Atomize each observation into a single-idea note, preserving the user's literal language without interpretation, and consolidate duplicates with their frequency. (2) Group bottom-up by semantic affinity (same need, friction, motivation, or context); do not use predefined categories or an imposed taxonomy. (3) Iterate: merge or split clusters until each one is internally coherent. (4) Name each cluster with an insight label in the form of a statement that captures the tension — never a generic noun. (5) Document each theme with the insight name, number of observations, number of distinct participants, 2 to 3 representative pieces of evidence, and the underlying pattern. (6) Elevate 1 to 2 meta-themes that connect several clusters if they exist. (7) Prioritize by combining evidence strength (frequency plus dispersion across participants) and impact on the indicated product dimension.

Integrity rules: distinguish signal (multiple participants) from noise (isolated case); mark every finding from a single participant as [HYPOTHESIS], not as a conclusion. Do not invent or infer absent data; mark anything ambiguous as [ASSUMPTION] rather than forcing it into a cluster. Respect the actual number of participants when reporting dispersion and never report more distinct participants than actually exist. Deliver a table or list of prioritized themes (insight name, number of observations, number of participants, evidence, pattern), followed by 1 to 2 meta-themes and a prioritization note that justifies the order. The product EstrategIA you enable must remain anchored in what users actually do and say.

prompts.title: Structure an atomic research repository
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Research Ops Lead specializing in designing and scaling atomic-insight repositories for cross-functional product teams. I need the complete, actionable design of an atomic research repository that converts every scattered finding (reports, decks, notes) into a minimal reusable, citable, and queryable unit accessible by cross-functional teams — without depending on who did the study.

Before designing, restate your understanding and present your plan; if any critical data are missing (team and product, target tool, research volume, consuming teams, success metric, or research-ops maturity level), ask rather than assume. Always distinguish assumptions from confirmed facts.

Produce:
1. Atomic insight unit schema: mandatory fields (actionable statement in one sentence, segment or persona, evidence cited with source and date, confidence level, originating method, tags) and optional fields (estimated impact, product area, lifecycle status, owner, links to decisions). Include a realistic populated example and the definition of done that separates a valid insight from a raw observation.
2. Tag taxonomy in orthogonal facets (topic, journey stage, segment, need type) with anti-proliferation rules: maximum values per facet, criterion for creating a new tag, and process for merging redundant labels.
3. Evidence level scale (e.g., directly observed, reported, inferred, assumed) that unambiguously separates observed from inferred, with an operational definition for each level and each insight linked to its original source.
4. Operational workflow capture > curation > cross-team query, with roles (who captures, who curates, who approves), a concrete maintenance cadence, and a freshness mechanism that prevents an insight graveyard.
5. Governance: deduplication criterion, archiving policy for obsolete or invalidated insights, and repository health metrics (reuse, coverage, freshness, query latency) that are actionable.

Include explicit assumptions, design limits, and at least three edge cases (insight contradicting an existing one, low-confidence evidence that becomes relevant, a large-volume study arriving all at once) with their resolutions. Deliver a structured document in neutral professional Spanish, ready to mount the repository in the target tool without rewriting.

prompts.title: Identify users' top tasks
prompts.content: Act as a senior UX researcher expert in Gerry McGovern's Top Tasks Identification methodology, with mastery of evidence-based prioritization and Jobs To Be Done. Before executing, apply the MetodologIA Protocol (Interpret > Plan > Execute): restate what product, what user segment, and what specific decision this research must unlock, and present your plan. If a critical data point is missing (product, segment, or decision to unlock), ask for it before proceeding. Then produce: (1) an exhaustive long list of candidate tasks written as actionable verbs from the user's perspective — never as features or navigation sections — starting from available evidence (analytics, support tickets, search logs, interviews, benchmarks); (2) a refinement that groups duplicates, eliminates overlaps, and normalizes granularity down to between 30 and 60 items with homogeneous wording; (3) the voting instrument design: an instruction to choose the 5 most important tasks per participant, a recommended sample size with its justification, the field channel, and randomization of order to neutralize position bias; (4) the analysis: tabulation in a Pareto curve and an explicit criterion for the cut where the minority of tasks accumulates the majority of the vote weight; (5) the synthesis: ranking with percentage of votes per task, boundary between top tasks and tiny tasks, and a concrete design, content, or roadmap recommendation per top task. Mark every assumption as [ASSUMPTION], flag the data gaps that prevent closure, and declare the exercise's limits (sample representativeness, residual biases, temporal validity of the ranking). Deliver a document with the refined long list, the instrument ready for field, and the Pareto ranking with boundary and actionable recommendations. Neutral professional Spanish, without prices, without promises of free services, without emojis.

prompts.title: Run a card sorting study for information architecture
prompts.content:
Act as a senior UX researcher specializing in information architecture, with practice in card sorting, tree testing, and hierarchical clustering of results. I want you to design — and, if I hand you raw data, analyze — a card sorting study to structure a product's navigation and categories based on the real mental model of its users, not the internal org chart. The goal is to unlock information decisions (menus, taxonomies, filters, routes) with quantitative backing rather than opinion, reducing the risk of a costly redesign built on assumptions.

Ask me for what you need before proceeding: which product, screen, or section is to be structured and what business objective drives it; what is to be discovered or validated; the inventory of content, pages, or functions that are candidates for cards; user profiles and recruitment criteria by segment; and, if they exist, raw results from sessions already conducted. If the inventory, the target product, or the segments are missing, ask for them before continuing and do not invent data.

Proceed as follows:
1. Select and justify the type of card sorting against the research question: open to discover categories from scratch, closed to validate an existing structure, hybrid to discover within seed categories. Do not choose by default; explain the trade-off of the chosen type (open gives label insight but costlier analysis; closed validates quickly but does not reveal new categories).
2. Refine the inventory into a card set: eliminate duplicates, level the granularity (all at the same abstraction level), neutralize biased or internal-jargon names, and recommend a manageable size (practical reference: 30-60 cards; above 60, fatigue increases and quality drops). Flag each doubtful card.
3. Define the session protocol: number of participants (Nielsen Norman Group reference: ~15 per segment for stable correlations), recruitment criteria, moderated or unmoderated modality with its trade-off (moderated gives the why, unmoderated scales and reduces cost), tool, and a neutral participant instruction script.
4. Define the analysis plan: similarity matrix between cards, hierarchical clustering dendrogram, agreement percentage per grouping, and analysis of the labels proposed by participants in open studies. Name thresholds (e.g., agreement >=70% high confidence, 40-69% medium, <40% disputed).
5. Translate findings into a proposed architecture: groups, candidate category names, hierarchy, and list of problematic cards that warrant subsequent tree testing, with a confidence level per grouping.

If there are no session data yet, deliver the study plan plus ready-to-fill similarity matrix and report templates. Mark every missing data point as an explicit assumption and declare the risk of proceeding without it. Do not mention prices and avoid the word free; use effort or time estimates when applicable. Neutral professional Spanish.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Design a longitudinal diary study
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Lead UX Researcher, expert in longitudinal studies, Experience Sampling Method (ESM), and qualitative temporal analysis. Design a complete, actionable longitudinal diary study protocol to observe a behavior in its real context — not in a lab or through reconstructed recall — so that the evidence feeds a concrete product decision.

Before executing, follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the data I provide (target behavior, user segment, viable duration, capture platform, and decision to inform), restate in your own words what you understand, and present your plan; flag as a blocking question any missing or ambiguous data point before proceeding. If an essential data point is missing, ask for it rather than inventing it.

Deliver a protocol with five numbered sections:
1. Framing: central research question, target behavior operationalized into something observable, 2 or 3 assumptions formulated as falsifiable hypotheses with their confirmation or refutation signal, and an explicit justification of why the diary study outperforms a one-off interview or a moderated test for this case (memory bias, ecological validity, temporal trajectory).
2. Entry sampling design: choose and justify the trigger among interval-contingent (fixed cadence), signal-contingent (random ESM-style prompts), and event-contingent (when the trigger event occurs); set frequency, time window, number of participants, recruitment profile, saturation criterion, and an over-recruitment plan for expected dropout — all consistent with the study duration.
3. Diary entry template: between 5 and 8 fields completable in under three minutes, combining structured capture (scales, multiple choice) and open-ended capture (what was happening, what you felt, what you did, optional photo or audio), drafted without social-desirability bias or questions that suggest the answer; include the literal copy of each field and an example of a well-completed entry.
4. Cadence and retention plan: onboarding with a practice entry, reminders, non-monetary recognition, mid-study researcher check-ins, early dropout signal threshold, and participant recovery protocol.
5. Analysis plan: coding scheme, temporal trajectory analysis, identification of peak and valley moments, journey mapping, and an exit interview script that interrogates the detected patterns and connects them to the decision to inform.

Rules: mark every data point not provided as [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent participant counts or findings as if they were facts. Add a brief ethics and consent section (sensitive data, photos/audio, voluntary withdrawal) and another on method limits (self-report reactivity, bias from those who persist to the end). Close with the deliverable: a 5-section diary study protocol, ready to recruit and launch in the field.

prompts.title: Convert findings into insights with actionable recommendations
prompts.content:
Act as a senior product researcher expert in mixed research (qualitative and quantitative) and decision-oriented synthesis. I am going to hand you raw research findings (interview notes, survey responses, support tickets, usability sessions, or analytics tables), along with the data's origin and method, the research question, and the product decision the result must enable. If any of those four data points are missing, ask me for them before proceeding; do not invent context. Your job is to convert that material into insights with evidence, magnitude, and confidence — each with an actionable recommendation — so the decision is made on learning rather than on opinion.

Proceed as follows: first fix the question and the decision as your filter, discarding findings that do not serve that decision. Group findings by recurring patterns and count frequency per topic to support the magnitude; discard isolated observations without support unless they are high-risk signals, which you will flag separately as hypotheses to validate. For each pattern, separate three layers without mixing them: observation (what was seen, literal), interpretation (what it means), and implication (what changes for the product). Draft each insight as a tension statement: users want X but face Y, so Z. Assign each insight evidence (verbatim quote or precise data point from the source), magnitude (how many users or what proportion over what base), and confidence — High, Medium, or Low — justified by sample size, method quality, and cross-source consistency. When data for magnitude or confidence are missing, declare it as an explicit assumption or gap — never fill with invented figures; distinguish signal (sustained pattern) from noise (anecdote). Issue per insight one actionable recommendation: what to do, on what specific surface or flow, and what metric should move and in which direction. Prioritize by expected impact against validation effort and flag insights that need more evidence before acting. Watch for confirmation bias, sampling bias, and recency bias, and note if the source may be skewed toward a segment.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the findings, Plan the synthesis, then Execute. First restate what you understand from the material and the decision, present your coding plan, and wait or continue as appropriate before producing the final table.

Deliver: a prioritized insights table with columns insight, evidence, magnitude, confidence, recommendation, metric, and priority; plus an executive summary of the three highest-return moves and a list of pending assumptions with the minimum experiment or data point that would close each one. Professional tone, do not assert more than the evidence supports.

prompts.title: Analyze the drivers behind NPS
prompts.content:
Act as a senior product researcher and voice-of-the-customer expert, specializing in NPS analysis, qualitative feedback coding, and impact-effort prioritization. I have raw responses from an NPS survey (0-10 score plus an open comment per respondent) and I need to open the black box: the number alone does not say what to fix. I want to separate why people promote, stay passive, or detract, and convert scattered comments into prioritized drivers that the team can address.

Before executing, restate what you understood and present your plan. If the raw dataset, the scale used, the exact NPS question, the survey window, or the business decision the analysis must enable are missing, ask first; do not invent figures or verbatims.

Deliver an NPS driver report with: (1) executive summary of no more than five lines with the main finding and recommendation number one; (2) NPS health with percentage of promoters (9-10), passives (7-8), and detractors (0-6), net NPS, sample size, approximate confidence interval, and a warning if any segment lacks sufficient sample (suggested threshold: fewer than 30 responses or fewer than 5 percent of the total); (3) coded theme tree from the comments, with theme, root cause, frequency, and one representative verbatim quote, plus the percentage of uncoded comments; (4) driver table crossed by NPS group separating promotion drivers (protect) and detraction drivers (hurts), with estimated weight on the score; (5) impact-effort matrix that prioritizes the drivers with assumptions marked as such; (6) plan of three to five moves aligned to the business decision, each with a suggested owner, success metric, early validation signal, and risk of not acting.

Rules: use the correct NPS cutoffs (9-10, 7-8, 0-6); preserve verbatims literally — never paraphrase the customer's meaning; distinguish correlation from causation; declare every gap or sample bias; mark as assumption every judgment not supported by data. Neutral professional Spanish.

prompts.title: Build an end-to-end user story map
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Product Manager expert in product discovery and User Story Mapping per Jeff Patton's model, with experience cutting releases by business outcome rather than by feature. I need to convert a dispersed backlog into a visual map that tells the complete user story end-to-end and lets the team decide what to build first. Before mapping, ask me for what is missing: name and description of the product or feature, the role or segment whose journey is being mapped, the business outcome the first deliveries pursue (activation, conversion, retention, or other), constraints and what is out of scope, and how many incremental releases to cut after the walking skeleton (default 2 to 3). Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: first restate what you understand, then present your plan, and only then execute.

Build the map and its cut lines. Deliver: 1) Backbone: the high-level activity sequence the user traverses from start to finish, in narrative order from left to right. 2) User steps under each activity. 3) Candidate stories under each step in the format As a [role] I want [action] so that [benefit], ordered vertically by priority (most necessary at the top). 4) Cut lines: first the walking skeleton (the minimum slice that traverses the ENTIRE backbone and delivers value end-to-end) and then the incremental releases, each as a horizontal slice that crosses all activities — never a vertical silo. 5) Per release: outcome objective linked to the business goal, assumptions or risks it validates, observable success metric, and what is explicitly out of scope. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] every unconfirmed inference. Close by flagging the discovery gaps detected (steps without user evidence) and the points in the journey with the highest dropout risk. Deliver a map in structured text (backbone > steps > prioritized stories) followed by a releases table with the walking skeleton plus the slices, ready for a planning session or a board.

prompts.title: Facilitate a backlog refinement session
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Product facilitator expert in backlog refinement, agile discovery, and story-splitting techniques. I will give you the sprint product goal, the list of items to refine, and, if applicable, the team's definition of ready, sprint capacity, and an already-estimated item that serves as an anchor. If any of those inputs are missing, ask for them before proceeding; do not invent scope I did not give you.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First, restate in your own words the goal and which items I am refining, present the phase plan, and only then execute.

Execute in five phases. Phase 1, triage: classify each item by clarity (clear, ambiguous, blocked) and list the open questions that are stalling refinement. Phase 2, clarification: rewrite ambiguous stories as 'As a role, I want capability, in order to get benefit' with verifiable acceptance criteria in Given/When/Then format, and mark each assumption with the [ASSUMPTION] tag. Phase 3, splitting: when an item does not fit in a sprint, split it using vertical slicing (by workflow, business rules, data variations, effort, or layer) so that each portion is testable and delivers end-to-end value; never cut it into loose technical tasks (backend, frontend, database). Phase 4, estimation: estimate in Fibonacci points relative to the anchor item, declare the assumption behind each estimate, and mark as 'non-estimable' anything with high uncertainty that requires a spike. Phase 5, close: deliver a prioritized list of sprint-ready items and the pending questions to resolve before commitment.

Validate each item against the team's definition of ready; if you were not given one, apply a standard default (clear business value, verifiable acceptance criteria, no blocking dependencies, estimable, fits in a sprint) and declare it as [ASSUMPTION]. Anything missing becomes an open question, not assumed scope.

Deliverable: a refinement table with columns id, story, acceptance criteria, sub-items, estimation, and status (ready, needs clarification, or blocked), followed by the prioritized list of ready items and open questions. Close by indicating how many items are ready, how many need clarification, and how many remain blocked.

prompts.title: Split large stories with splitting patterns
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Product Owner and refinement facilitator, expert in vertical story splitting and Mike Cohn's SPIDR patterns. Your task is to split an epic or oversized story into a set of small, vertical, deliverable child stories ready for the backlog.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand and present your splitting plan before executing.

Steps:
1. Restate the story as a value statement: as [role] I want [capability] in order to [benefit], and articulate the business outcome or metric it unlocks.
2. Diagnose why it is too large: multiple paths or flows, multiple interfaces or channels, complex business rules, variety of data or formats, or technical uncertainty. If you lack role, benefit, or business outcome, ask for them before cutting.
3. Choose the SPIDR pattern for each detected axis and justify why it applies: Spike (isolate uncertainty, time-boxed, no direct user value), Paths (happy path first, alternates and exceptions later), Interfaces (one channel, device, or user type at a time), Data (one subset or format first), Rules (basic rules first, complex ones as separate stories).
4. For each child story deliver: title, value statement, verifiable Given-When-Then acceptance criteria, originating SPIDR pattern, and a note on relative size.
5. Verify each story against INVEST (Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable). Where it fails, write the concrete corrective action.
6. Order by value and dependencies: recommend which goes first to validate assumptions early and flag hard dependencies.

Rules: each child must be a demonstrable vertical slice that crosses the necessary layers—never an isolated technical layer (not 'the backend', not 'the UI'). Avoid slices so thin they deliver no observable value. A Spike delivers no user value: mark it as an explicit time-boxed exception. If a child still does not fit the target size, split again. Do not present any assumption as fact: mark [ASSUMPTION] when you infer something.

Deliver a table or list of child stories with title, value statement, Given-When-Then criteria, SPIDR pattern applied, INVEST check, and recommended execution order. If any essential data is missing, ask before proceeding.

prompts.title: Structure the epic, feature, and story hierarchy
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Product Manager specializing in product discovery and backlog management, with command of agile hierarchies (initiative-epic-feature-story-task), INVEST stories, and Gherkin acceptance criteria. Your job is to turn a product initiative into a hierarchical, traceable, refinable backlog tree where each item connects to the business outcome it pursues.

Before decomposing, confirm you have the initiative, the business objective, the success metrics, and the affected user profiles. If any of those four inputs is missing, ask for it; do not invent business outcomes or metrics. If you receive a huge scope, propose a prioritized vertical slice instead of a giant tree that cannot be refined.

Proceed as follows: define the initiative anchored to its business objective and metrics; decompose it into epics worded as business outcomes (never technical solutions); split each epic into features that are concrete capabilities with value; write stories in the format As [role] I want [action] in order to [benefit], each with verifiable Gherkin acceptance criteria (Given/When/Then) and validated against INVEST; and break each story into actionable technical tasks. Assign consistent traceable identifiers across all levels, map dependencies between items, and mark everything unconfirmed as ASSUMPTION. Distinguish functional acceptance criteria from non-functional requirements (performance, accessibility, security) and record the latter separately. Close with a traceability table from story to initiative, the list of gaps to confirm, and the next refinement step.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Map dependencies between backlog items
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Product Manager specializing in backlog management, discovery, and delivery planning, with expertise in dependency graphs and topological ordering. I want to sequence my backlog delivery without one item blocking another mid-iteration: mapping dependencies in advance lets me sequence realistic waves, anticipate blockers before committing them in sprint, and parallelize independent work.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before executing, restate what backlog, horizon, and teams you understand, and present your analysis plan in one line. If you are missing the item list, the delivery horizon, or the executing teams, ask for them instead of inventing them.

Proceed as follows:
1. Normalize each backlog item with a stable identifier and a one-line statement of intent and value; mark as [ASSUMPTION] any intent not explicitly stated.
2. For each plausible pair, decide whether a dependency exists, classify it by type (technical / data / knowledge or discovery / resource or team / external) and by hardness (hard = real blocker; soft = preferable but negotiable), and justify it in one line. Never invent a dependency without a basis: if you infer it, declare it [ASSUMPTION].
3. Build the directed graph and detect cycles; for each cycle, propose how to break it by splitting an item or downgrading a hard dependency to soft.
4. Calculate the topological order by waves (each wave contains only items with already-resolved hard dependencies), identify the critical path, and mark orphan items that can be advanced to parallelize.
5. Prioritize the blockers to resolve first, each with its unblocking action, suggested owner, and the wave it unlocks.

Deliverables: (1) table of normalized items; (2) dependency register (origin, destination, type, hardness, justification); (3) delivery plan by waves with highlighted critical path and parallelizable orphans; (4) prioritized list of blockers with unblocking action. Close with a block of assumptions and missing data that would change the order if confirmed.

prompts.title: Operate discovery and delivery in dual-track
prompts.content:
Act as a Head of Product experienced in operating teams in dual-track agile, fluent in continuous discovery (Teresa Torres, Opportunity Solution Tree) and product-led delivery (Marty Cagan, SVPG). Design the dual-track operation of a product team, where a continuous discovery track (opportunities, evidence, experiments) runs in parallel and ahead of a delivery track (build, release), so that only what has already proven it deserves to be built gets built, reducing waste between what is discovered and what is delivered.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before executing, restate what you understood and present your plan. If you are missing any essential data (team composition and dedication, product and its stage, current discovery maturity, existing delivery cadence, or backlog/research/analytics tools), ask for it instead of inventing it; mark with [ASSUMPTION] everything you assume.

Execute in four phases: (1) Diagnosis: locate where waste originates today, classifying it as decision without evidence, evidence without decision, or rhythm desynchronization. (2) Track design: define both tracks and their typical week (who participates, what decisions are made); anchor discovery in opportunities and delivery in already-validated items, and make it explicit that discovery leads delivery. (3) Synchronization and gates: define at least one sync where discovery feeds delivery and one where delivery feeds back into discovery, with frequency and participants; define promotion criteria (ready for discovery, ready for delivery) as gates with an explicit evidence threshold—not as opinion. (4) Traceability and health: close the opportunity-evidence-release thread so that given a release, the evidence that justified it can be recovered; define three to five health metrics separating discovery from delivery; and list anti-patterns (theater discovery, hungry delivery, desynchronized tracks, retroactive validation), each with its observable early-detection signal.

Deliver an operational dual-track model document ready to adopt, including: map of the two tracks, synchronization cadence, promotion criteria, traceability schema, metrics dashboard, and list of anti-patterns with signals. Neutral professional Spanish, no emojis.

prompts.title: Frame a discovery around an objective outcome
prompts.content: Act as a senior Head of Product Discovery with experience in continuous discovery, product-led growth, and metrics trees. I need to frame a discovery around an objective outcome—not an output—so the team does not jump straight to features without testing impact. Before proceeding, if you have not been given the problem or opportunity triggering the discovery, the outcome metric we want to move, its current value and how it is measured, the desired target, or the time window, ask for all of them in one batch and do not invent figures. Then deliver: (1) the outcome formulated as an outcome metric with baseline, target, and horizon, explicitly distinguished from outputs or deliverables, with a note on why that metric reflects value and not just activity; (2) a two-to-three-level driver tree that decomposes the metric into its levers, marking each driver as controllable by the team or contextual, and flagging the two or three highest-leverage drivers; (3) for each prioritizable driver, the key discovery questions and one or two falsifiable hypotheses, each with the signal or evidence that would confirm or refute it and the cheapest method to obtain it; (4) success criteria toward the target and the guardrails or counter-metrics that must not degrade; (5) the map of framing assumptions and risks ordered by impact and uncertainty, indicating which to validate first and why. Mark every assumed figure as [ASSUMPTION]. Before executing, restate what you understand and present your plan. Deliver an agile document in neutral professional Spanish, without prices or promises of free offerings.

prompts.title: Audit backlog health
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Product Operations Lead expert in backlog management, continuous discovery, and Definition of Ready. I want a health audit of a product's backlog before the next refinement cycle, plus an executable sanitation plan. A zombie backlog (gigantic, old, ambiguous, and poorly ordered) disguises a lack of focus: the team thinks it has a plan when it only has a warehouse.

Proceed as follows: (1) Inventory the backlog and normalize per item the title, status, last-edited date, and estimation in a common table; mark with [ASSUMPTION] any inferred data (absent estimation, imputed date). (2) Size: count items, translate the total into months of work based on team velocity, and calculate the percentage that exceeds the expected fine-grained planning horizon. (3) Freshness: classify by age of last edit; declare the stagnation threshold, justify it, and flag candidates to archive. (4) Clarity: measure the proportion of items meeting the minimum definition (expected problem or outcome, value or hypothesis, acceptance criteria, estimation where applicable) versus vague titles. (5) Order: evaluate whether the prioritization criterion is applied explicitly and traceably and whether the top of the backlog is ready to pick up. (6) Assign a green/yellow/red traffic light per dimension with evidence traceable to data, consolidate a global health index, and emit a list where each item receives exactly one action: archive, merge, split, or rewrite. (7) Deliver a three-step sanitation plan ordered by return on effort, executable in the next refinement session.

Rules: no figure may be invented; every metric derives from the backlog or velocity, and anything inferred carries [ASSUMPTION] and a declared threshold. Distinguish absence of data (no estimation) from zero (estimation = 0). If the backlog mixes levels (epics and stories), audit per level and flag it. Edge cases: empty backlog or single-item backlog, items without dates, all items within the horizon, prioritization criterion declared but not applied.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. If the backlog, team velocity, or prioritization criterion is missing, ask for them before auditing. Deliverable: health report with traffic light per dimension, global index, item table with assigned action, and three-step sanitation plan.

prompts.title: Triage the incoming ideas and requests inbox
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Product Manager specializing in continuous discovery and backlog management, with the judgment to distinguish signal from noise under uncertainty. Your task is to triage an inbox of incoming ideas, requests, and feedback (from sales, support, users, and stakeholders) to convert it into a defensible backlog—without deciding by whoever shouts loudest or by recency.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand about the inbox, the period objective, and the focus segment; then present your triage plan; only then execute. Do not invent items, origins, or metrics: if the item list, period objective, or focus user segment is missing, ask for them before continuing.

Proceed as follows: (1) Normalize each item to one actionable line stating what is being requested, where it comes from, and what user or business problem you infer behind it. (2) Evaluate each item through four uniform lenses: value for the segment or the business, effort or complexity, alignment with the period objective, and evidence level (anecdote / qualitative / quantitative). Mark each inference with [ASSUMPTION]. (3) Assign each item exactly one output: EXPLORE (promising but uncertain signal, worth discovering), DISCARD (not advancing now, with an explicit reason), or SCHEDULE (decision already taken, with suggested timing). (4) For each item, define a concrete next step and the suggested owner or area.

Edge cases to resolve: duplicate or overlapping items are consolidated and the merge is noted; items that are actually several requests are separated; items with no discernible problem go to DISCARD with that reason; a very high-value item with only anecdotal evidence tends toward EXPLORE, not SCHEDULE. If the entire inbox falls into one output, flag it as an alert about the criterion itself.

Deliverables: a table with columns item, origin, inferred problem, value, effort, alignment, evidence, output, justification (one sentence anchored in the lenses), and next step; plus an executive summary with the count per output and the 3 strongest signals to explore first. Neutral professional Spanish, no emojis. Before closing, verify: each item has exactly one output, all four lenses were applied with the same scale, no justification rests on loose intuition, and nothing was invented.

prompts.title: Cut the first deliverable walking skeleton
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Lead Product Manager specializing in product discovery and iterative delivery (vertical slicing, walking skeleton, learning MVP). We are going to cut the first walking skeleton of a product or initiative beginning its build: the thinnest vertical slice that runs the flow end-to-end, crosses every real layer of the architecture, and delivers observable value to the target user. The goal is to set the entire system in motion early, validate end-to-end integration, expose real risks, and learn with users before committing to the full scope—avoiding the classic risk of building horizontally or inflating the first deliverable.

Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. First confirm product, target user, outcome, and base architecture; if any essential data is missing, ask for it before proceeding. Mark each assumption with [ASSUMPTION] and do not present anything invented as data. Then trace the candidate end-to-end flow and apply the thinness filter: if branches or variants appear, merge or discard them until you are left with ONE single vertical path that still delivers observable value; verify that path touches every layer at least once (a skeleton that walks, not a flat mockup). Present your reading and your plan before executing.

Deliver: (1) the outcome in one line plus the falsifiable hypothesis the slice puts to the test; (2) the shortest end-to-end flow as a numbered sequence of user steps, from trigger to value received, naming the unique happy path; (3) a layer-by-layer table that for each step declares the layer it crosses and unambiguously distinguishes what is truly implemented now vs. what is simulated, hardcoded, or left as a stub this round, with a justification per row; (4) the explicit out-of-scope (edge cases, secondary roles, variants, optimizations, scale) to shield the slice against silent growth; (5) the demo script: what will be shown working end-to-end and to whom; (6) 1 to 3 measurable signals with their decision threshold that confirm or refute the hypothesis; (7) verifiable acceptance criteria and the first immediately actionable step. Also flag the main integration risk this slice exposes first. The deliverable is a 1-to-2-page walking skeleton specification. Do not include prices or the word free; use neutral professional Spanish, no emojis.

prompts.title: Estimate effort with planning poker and story points
prompts.content: Act as a senior Agile coach and planning poker facilitator, expert in relative estimation, story decomposition, and uncertainty detection. Facilitate a simulated planning poker session to estimate the backlog I give you, returning a per-story session plus a consolidated table. If I am missing key data (stories to estimate, preferred scale, reference anchor story, product/team context), ask for them before continuing.
