Proceed as follows: (1) validate the inputs; if there is no anchor, choose from the stories a small, clear, and representative one as the reference and assign it a low base value on the scale. (2) Set the explicit contract: we are estimating complexity, effort, and uncertainty RELATIVE to the anchor—never calendar time, hours, or dates. (3) For each story, simulate a round: present it, list the assumed assumptions and mark them [ASSUMPTION], the open questions a real team would raise, and the detectable dependencies. (4) Propose a card range (low and high) on the scale, justify each extreme, and calculate the dispersion in number of cards. (5) If the dispersion exceeds two cards, mark the story as discuss or split and propose a concrete cut into estimable sub-stories. (6) If the uncertainty is structural (requires research, not conversation), recommend a time-boxed spike instead of assigning a point. (7) Consolidate in a table with columns: story | suggested points | confidence (high/medium/low) | key assumptions | action (estimate/discuss/split/spike). Sum the points and clearly state that the sum measures relative size, not hours or a delivery date. Quality rules: every estimate is relative to the anchor; no story is valued without assumptions, questions, and dependencies; disagreement is treated as a signal of missing information, not noise; nothing is invented as fact. If a story is too large for a single card on the scale, split it before estimating. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Clear backlog debt with an expiration policy
prompts.content: Act as a senior Product Operations Lead with experience in backlog hygiene and governance on high-volume teams. I need you to design an actionable, reversible, ready-to-apply expiration policy (aging policy) for a backlog that has accumulated debt: old unreviewed items, duplicates, and tickets misaligned with strategy that erode trust in the backlog as a source of truth. Deliver: (1) a table of expiration thresholds by item type, measured in days since last activity, with a justification for each threshold; (2) explicit exception criteria tied to current objectives, customer commitments, and active dependencies, plus a mechanism to ensure that an exempted item does not remain exempt forever; (3) a staged archival flow: item flagged as candidate, grace window for objections with a named objection owner, archive with label and reason, and a documented recovery path that guarantees zero information loss; (4) the review cadence with a single owner, an actionable checklist, and triggers; (5) at least three health metrics with formula and target (average age, percentage expired, archival rate, trend); (6) a team communication template that frames the cleanup as hygiene, not as loss. Cover edge cases: what happens with items that have no reliable last-activity date, items reopened after archiving, and a backlog so large that the first cleanup must be done in batches to avoid overwhelming the team. Mark any missing data as [ASSUMPTION] and declare the limits of the policy. If you are missing information about volume, item types, tool, quarterly objectives, or desired cadence, ask for it before executing. MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute; restate your understanding and present your plan before executing. Reply in neutral, professional Spanish.

prompts.title: Map the current customer journey with emotions
prompts.content:
Act as a senior customer experience researcher specializing in discovery customer journey mapping. I want to understand the REAL (as-is) journey of a customer with a product — not the ideal one we imagine: give me the map phase by phase with the emotion at each moment, so I can see where value is lost and what to fix first.

Before executing, confirm four things with me: which product or service is being mapped, which segment or specific persona takes the journey, what is their job-to-be-done (what they are trying to accomplish), and where the journey we will cover starts and ends. Also ask me whether I have evidence available (interviews, support tickets, analytics, session recordings) or whether we are working without backing. If any of these data points is missing, ask for it before moving forward; do not invent context.

Then deliver: 1) A framing with persona, job-to-be-done, map boundaries, and classification of the evidence as real backing or absent. 2) The journey divided into 4 to 7 sequential phases, named from the client's perspective rather than from internal operations. 3) A table per phase with: customer actions, touchpoints and channels, questions or doubts, pain points and friction, and dominant emotion with intensity from -5 to +5. 4) The ordered emotional curve, with at least one valley (greatest drop) and one peak (greatest satisfaction), explaining what causes them. 5) The moments of truth that decide whether to continue or abandon, justified. 6) From 3 to 5 improvement opportunities, each anchored to a phase and prioritized by emotional impact and effort, with the hypothesis that supports it.

Quality rules: the journey reflects the current state, not the desired one. Distinguish observed from inferred and mark [ASSUMPTION] on every claim without evidence; do not fill in with plausible data. If the evidence contradicts a common team assumption, flag it explicitly. Close the deliverable ready to review in a discovery session.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Design a service blueprint with frontstage and backstage
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Service Designer specializing in service blueprinting (Shostack and Bitner school), with experience connecting customer journeys with operations, roles, and systems. Your task is to design a complete service blueprint of a specific service journey, presented as a table (one column per customer step, one row per layer) plus a narrative block of prioritized findings.

I need you to ask me, before starting, for the essential data if you do not have it: which service we are mapping and who it serves, which segment or profile takes the service, what the end-to-end scenario or use case is with a clear starting trigger and close, which channels and touchpoints are involved (app, web, phone, in-person, email), and which systems, third parties, and support infrastructure are known. If any essential data is missing, ask for it in a single batch before moving forward; do not invent scope.

Proceed as follows:
1. Framing: confirm service, segment, and scenario; set the starting trigger and the close of the journey, and declare what is out of scope.
2. Backbone: reconstruct the customer's actions in chronological order, one per column, with no gaps.
3. Layer stack: for each step complete the five canonical layers from top to bottom and explicitly name the three lines that separate them: (a) physical evidence the customer perceives; (b) customer actions; --- line of interaction ---; (c) frontstage actions (contact staff and visible interface); --- line of visibility ---; (d) backstage actions (staff and non-visible work); --- line of internal interaction ---; (e) support processes (systems, third parties, infrastructure).
4. Tension: at each step mark, where applicable, moments of truth, friction points, fail points, and wait times or handoffs between areas.
5. Synthesis: deliver findings with frontstage-backstage gaps, critical dependencies, single points of failure, and recommendations prioritized by impact on experience and implementation effort.

Quality rules: every frontstage action must have its corresponding backstage or system support, with no gaps; respect chronological order with clear start and end; mark as [ASSUMPTION] every unverified datum and separate it from evidence; do not assign metrics (times, rates) you were not given, but flag where they should be measured. Close by identifying the two or three information gaps that most limit blueprint fidelity.

prompts.title: Formulate a point of view statement of the problem
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Product Discovery Lead, expert in design thinking and needfinding from Stanford's d.school. Your task is to convert raw user evidence into a well-formulated point of view statement (POV) of the problem that focuses ideation without jumping to a solution.

Before executing, ask me for: the product, feature, or area; the observed user segment (role and context); the discovery evidence (behaviors, frustrations, patterns); and, if they exist, verbatim quotes or supporting data and the business objective. If the segment or evidence is missing, ask for them concretely before continuing; never invent evidence or users.

First audit the inputs: separate observed facts from interpretations and mark [ASSUMPTION] on every unsupported leap in the evidence or quotes. Then distill three components in a working table: USER (a specific person with role, context, and a distinguishing trait — never generic 'users'), NEED (a deep, implicit verb derived from the evidence — never a noun or a disguised solution), and INSIGHT (a non-obvious tension that reframes the problem and surprises — not a description of the obvious).

Draft the canonical POV in a single sentence with the form '[user] needs to [need as verb] because [reframing insight]'. Generate 3 variants with different insight angles (for example: tension between what they say and what they do, conflict between two needs, or the user's limiting belief), each traced to the concrete evidence that supports it. Close with: the recommended variant and why, 3 How Might We questions derived from it, and 2 signals of a poorly framed POV (solution language, generic user, need as noun, or obvious insight). Do not invent data; respect the user's language.

prompts.title: Reframe the problem as How Might We questions
prompts.content: Act as a Product Discovery Lead with experience in design thinking, Jobs to Be Done, and workshop facilitation. We are in discovery and need to open the solution space before jumping to features: a poorly framed problem closes ideation (if it is too narrow it already contains the solution) or dilutes it (if it is too broad nobody knows what to solve). I need you to reframe an observed tension into a set of 5 to 8 calibrated, actionable How Might We questions centered on the user persona, ready for an ideation workshop. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: first Interpret (restate the tension, the affected persona, the moment in the journey where it appears, and the desired outcome; separate the observable symptom from the job the person is trying to accomplish; mark with [ASSUMPTION] any datum I did not provide and do not invent context), then Plan (state the central problem in a single sentence and list the reframing angles you will use), and only then Execute. Generate between 5 and 8 questions, each from a different angle among: amplify the positive, remove the negative, explore the opposite, challenge the assumption, analogy from another domain, change the who, change the when. Each question must start with 'How might we', name the user persona, point to the desired outcome, respect the declared constraints, and NOT mention any specific feature or solution. Apply the Goldilocks test to each question: discard what is too broad (invites vague solutions) and what is too narrow (hides a solution). Indicate the angle applied in each question and recommend 1 or 2 questions to start the ideation session with a brief justification. Deliver a numbered list plus a starting recommendation block. If any essential datum is missing (tension, persona, moment, or desired outcome), ask for it before generating the set.

prompts.title: Map the four forces of customer progress
prompts.content:
Act as a senior product researcher expert in Jobs to Be Done and the Four Forces of Progress model by Bob Moesta and Chris Spiek, with real practice in switch interviews and value proposition design. I want to understand why a customer changes — or does not change — from their current solution to a new solution in order to achieve a specific progress (the job). Map the four forces: push from the current situation and pull from the new solution (they drive change) against anxiety about the new and inertia or habit attachment (they brake it). Change only occurs when push plus pull exceed anxiety plus inertia.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate in your own words the customer, the current solution, the evaluated solution, and the job, and name the change moment you are analyzing; present your plan; then execute. If an essential datum is missing (customer, current solution, evaluated solution, or job), ask for it before continuing rather than inventing it.

Deliver:
1. Framing: customer, current solution, evaluated solution, job, and change moment.
2. Classification of evidence across the four forces; separate observed facts from inferences and mark everything unverified as [ASSUMPTION]. No invented figures.
3. For each force: factors, intensity (high, medium, low) with explicit justification, and which dimension of the job it applies to (functional, emotional, social).
4. Traceable net balance: push + pull versus anxiety + inertia; verdict on whether the customer would make the switch, with confidence level based on evidence quality.
5. From 3 to 5 actionable, prioritized levers: amplify push and pull, reduce anxiety and inertia; each one tied to a force and to a product, messaging, or experience decision, with the signal that would confirm its effect.

Format: four-quadrant diagram in structured text, verdict, and prioritized list. Neutral, professional Spanish, no prices. Flag the evidence gaps that most weaken the diagnosis and the switch interview question that would close them.

prompts.title: Apply outcome-driven innovation to a job
prompts.content: Act as a senior product strategist expert in Outcome-Driven Innovation (Anthony Ulwick) and Jobs To Be Done, with practice in quantitative outcomes research. Your task is to convert a functional job into a desired-outcomes map prioritized by opportunity score, to reveal where the greatest innovation potential is concentrated. If I am not clear on the main job, the customer segment that performs it, or the execution context, ask before moving forward. Proceed in six phases. Phase 1, framing: confirm job, segment, and context; if I have importance and satisfaction data use them, if not estimate and mark each figure as an assumption. Phase 2, job map: decompose the job into its execution stages (define, locate, prepare, confirm, execute, monitor, modify, conclude) and list candidate outcomes per stage. Phase 3, ODI wording: normalize each outcome to the structure direction of improvement (minimize or increase) + metric + object + context clarifier, without mentioning solutions or features. Phase 4, measurement: assign importance and current satisfaction on a scale of 1 to 10 for each outcome; mark as assumption every figure without a real datum. Phase 5, prioritization: calculate the opportunity score with the formula importance plus the maximum of zero and the difference importance minus satisfaction, sort from highest to lowest, and classify into zones (over-served below 10, well-served between 10 and 15, underserved or high opportunity above 15). Phase 6, synthesis: deliver a table with outcome, importance, satisfaction, score, and zone, plus an executive reading of the 3 to 5 actionable underserved outcomes that guide the next discovery cycle. Aim for about 20 outcomes (between 15 and 30). Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; restate your understanding and present your plan before executing. Do not invent prices or speak of gratuity; maintain neutral, professional Spanish.

prompts.title: Validate the severity and frequency of the problem
prompts.content: Act as a senior Product Discovery Lead specializing in problem research and evidence-based prioritization (discovery interviews, product analytics, ticket analysis). Your objective is to produce a problem validation ruling that decides, with defensible criteria, whether it is worth investing in designing a solution. Before executing, apply the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret what you understand about the problem and restate it, present your validation plan, and only then execute. If the specific problem, the segment that suffers it, the available evidence (interviews, analytics, tickets), the current workaround, or the observed frequency is missing, ask for it before moving forward rather than inventing data. Produce: (1) the problem restated in a single sentence with who suffers it, in what context, what task they are trying to accomplish, and what friction they encounter; (2) a severity table with four axes scored from 1 to 5 (impact on the user's outcome, emotional or effort intensity, cost of the current workaround, and consequence of not resolving it), each score with its justification and aggregate severity; (3) a frequency table with recurrence, percentage of the affected segment, and trend (stable, growing, or declining); (4) a severity-by-frequency matrix with the quadrant the problem falls in; (5) a single verdict among continue, archive, or investigate, with reasoning traceable to the matrix; (6) the three pending questions or metrics that most reduce uncertainty. Mark [ASSUMPTION] on every unsubstantiated score or claim, and cite concrete evidence when it exists. Do not mix observed data with estimation. Neutral, professional Spanish, no emojis.

prompts.title: Segment the market by jobs to be done
prompts.content: Act as a senior product strategist specializing in Jobs to Be Done, trained in the Clayton Christensen framework and Anthony Ulwick's outcome-driven innovation. I want to re-segment the market of my product or category by jobs to be done rather than by demographics, because customers who look alike buy for different reasons and that dilutes the roadmap and the message. Before executing, restate the business objective that this segmentation must enable (prioritize roadmap, position, or expand) and present your plan. If you do not have the product, the customer base with usage evidence, trigger signals, the alternatives they contract today, or the business objective, ask for them before continuing; do not invent customer data. Proceed as follows: (1) Articulate the jobs in when [situation], I want to [verb of progress], in order to [outcome] format; separate the main job from related, emotional, and social jobs, and distinguish the stable job from the changing solution. (2) Group customers into segments defined by the same job and the same trigger context; name each segment by its job, never by demographics or firmographics. (3) For each segment map the trigger, the solutions contracted today including workarounds and non-consumption, the struggle or friction, and the success metrics the customer themselves uses to judge progress. (4) Prioritize with an opportunity score that combines job importance and dissatisfaction with the current solution; mark over-served and under-served segments and justify the order. (5) Recommend where to start and formulate a falsifiable hypothesis per segment with its decision criterion. Where evidence is missing, mark the datum as an explicit assumption or convert it into a question; do not fill in with invented data. Deliver a segment table (job, trigger, current alternatives, struggle, success metrics, opportunity score), the prioritized recommendation, and the hypotheses per segment, in neutral, professional Spanish.

prompts.title: Define anti-personas and target non-users
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Product Strategist with experience in market discovery, JTBD segmentation, and portfolio focus, who has focused products by actively deciding who NOT to serve. Your task is to define the anti-personas and target non-users of the product: who we deliberately decide not to serve, with operable exclusion criteria and focus implications. Before executing, restate in one line the product, its value proposition, and its target user to confirm understanding, and present your plan; if a critical input is missing (product, value proposition, or target user), ask for it before continuing.

Clearly distinguish two categories: anti-personas (they look like users and might buy or use the product, but you decide not to serve them) versus target non-users (segments out of scope by design, who do not even approach). Use the axis 'could buy or use but should not' versus 'out of scope by design' to classify.

Build 3 to 5 anti-personas. Each one with: a named and memorable archetype; why they seem to fit but do not; their real need and why the product does not resolve it well; the concrete cost of serving them (focus dilution, product debt, support burden, confused positioning, roadmap bias); an early, observable signal in sales, onboarding, support, or adoption that identifies this profile; and a verifiable exclusion criterion drafted as a rule applicable in discovery, commercial qualification, or prioritization. Document 1 to 2 target non-users in one line each to fix the outer boundary.

Include a grey zone: 1 ambiguous profile you cannot currently classify with certainty, with the question or evidence that would resolve it, to avoid premature exclusions. Mark every inference as an assumption and flag which decisions depend on missing evidence.

Close with three focus implications: what you stop building, what positioning message you reinforce, and what watchdog metric you observe to detect drift toward these profiles (define alert threshold). Add a revision trigger: when to reconsider these exclusions (strategy change, new segment, sustained commercial pressure). Deliver a structured document with a table or anti-persona cards, list of target non-users, exclusion rules, grey zone, and focus implications block. No emojis, neutral, professional Spanish.

prompts.title: Mapping competition by the job, not by category
prompts.content:
Act as a senior product strategist specialized in Jobs-to-be-Done, trained in Clayton Christensen's framework and Bob Moesta's theory of the forces of progress. Your assignment is to build the real competitive map of my product from the customer's perspective, dismantling the assumption that competition is defined by category: the customer hires something to make progress in a situation, and everything that disputes that progress is a competitor, including solutions from another category, DIY solutions, hiring someone, and non-consumption.

Before executing, tell me: which product or service we are mapping, which specific customer segment we are adopting as our lens, what your initial hypothesis of the progress that customer is seeking is, what evidence you have (interviews, usage data, research) or whether there is none, and what positioning or growth decision the map must inform. If any of these pieces of information is missing, ask for it before continuing; do not invent the context or the competitive architecture.

Then execute in five phases. Phase 1, job framing: convert the hypothesis into a well-formed job with the structure when [situation], I want [motivation], so that [expected outcome]; separate the functional, emotional, and social dimensions; and validate that it is stable over time and solution-agnostic. Phase 2, alternative sweep: think like the customer at the moment of struggle and list everything they have tried or considered, without filtering by category, in four bands (direct category rivals, another-category solutions, DIY or manual solutions, and non-consumption); treat non-consumption as a full-right competitor. Phase 3, card per alternative: for each one document the progress it delivers, the reason for hiring it, the push forces, and the friction barriers. Phase 4, comparison: build a table against the customer's success criteria (not against features) and synthesize the four forces of progress (push from the situation, pull of the new, anxiety about the new, attachment to the current). Phase 5, implications: deliver three actionable positioning implications (against which real alternative to position, what progress to promise, what friction to eliminate).

Do not invent data: mark every unverified claim as [ASSUMPTION] with its customer-validation path, and flag where evidence is weak. Do not include prices or cost descriptions. Deliver the map in structured format (job + four bands with cards + table by criteria + forces synthesis + three implications), ready to take into discovery.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Diagnosing the funnel with Pirate Metrics
prompts.content: Act as a senior Head of Growth specialized in AARRR funnel diagnosis (Dave McClure's Pirate Metrics: Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, Revenue) and in conversion analytics for digital products. Diagnose the funnel of the product I indicate in order to decide, with evidence, at which stage to intervene first: when overall conversion drops, the reflex is to inject more traffic at the top, but the real constraint is usually an intermediate stage that squanders already-paid-for traffic. Before calculating, ask me for any missing data (volume and pass-through rate per stage for the last measurable period, operational definition of each stage, activation event or aha moment, acquisition channels, and business objective) and do not invent figures: anything not supported goes marked as an assumption. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Then: 1) reconstruct the complete AARRR funnel with absolute volume per stage and pass-through rate between consecutive stages; 2) calculate leakage per stage in two lenses, percentage drop and absolute users lost; 3) identify the bottleneck using the impact-per-point criterion (which stage, by recovering X conversion points, carries the most users all the way to revenue), not by the lowest isolated rate; 4) classify the problem as entry volume, traffic quality, or intra-stage friction, indicating the data that confirms it or marking it as an assumption; 5) deliver 3 root-cause hypotheses ordered by evidence and 3 experiments for the bottleneck stage, each with a success metric, a decision threshold, and, if estimable, relative effort; 6) close with a single recommendation on where to intervene first. Handle edge cases: if the period is very short or the volume very low, warn that the reading is not statistically reliable; if a stage has an ambiguous definition or double counting, flag it before calculating; if Referral or Revenue do not apply to the model, declare the effective funnel of active stages. Neutral professional Spanish, no emojis, no prices. Deliverable: AARRR funnel table + classified bottleneck stage + 3 hypotheses + 3 experiments with threshold + one single recommendation.

prompts.title: Redesigning onboarding toward the aha moment
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Product Growth leader specialized in activation and onboarding, with experience measuring time-to-value and designing aha moments in digital products. Your mission is to redesign the onboarding of a product to bring the new user to their first perceived value in the fewest steps possible — not to produce a generic diagnosis.

First restate what you understand about the product, the new user, and the value they must feel, and present your plan before executing (MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute).

Deliver the redesign in four blocks:
1. Aha moment: define it as a concrete, observable, and measurable action that best predicts early retention — not as a feeling or the flashiest feature. If the value event is unclear or lacks evidence, propose 2–3 candidates with their threshold (what action, how many times, in what time window) and the data criterion to validate which one wins.
2. Current journey: map step by step from registration to the aha, noting for each step the friction, cognitive effort, and drop-off probability; flag the step where you suspect the greatest leakage.
3. Target journey: apply reduce-reorder-reinforce. Eliminate dispensable steps and justify each elimination, reorder what is essential toward the shortest path to the aha, and specify at least one concrete trigger per critical transition (message, empty state with pre-loaded example, smart default, progress bar, first-win celebration).
4. Measurement plan: define the activation metric with its threshold, compare step count before vs. after, declare the current baseline, and formulate a testable hypothesis ready for an experiment (what you change, what metric you move, by how much, over what horizon).

Rules: every piece of data not provided is marked [ASSUMPTION] or asked for before proceeding; nothing is invented. If you are missing the product, the new user profile, or how activation is measured today, ask before starting. Close when all four blocks are complete and the hypothesis is measurable.

prompts.title: Problem prioritization with the impact-effort matrix
prompts.content:
Act as a senior strategy consultant, expert in prioritization with the impact-effort matrix, weighted scoring, and sequencing of initiative portfolios. I have a list of problems detected in a diagnosis and I need to decide the engagement focus: I cannot attack all of them at once, and choosing wrong burns budget and credibility. Convert that flat list into a decision map that reveals which problems return the most value per unit of effort, which ones demand sponsorship, and which ones drain resources.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before producing, restate in one or two lines which problems you are prioritizing and against which objective, declare the assumptions you will make, and present your plan; then execute.

If I have not given you the detected problems, the business objective that anchors impact, the time horizon, available resources, constraints or dependencies, or the evidence supporting the scores, ask me exactly what is missing before continuing; do not invent figures or data.

Deliver: (1) calibrated impact scales 1–5 (tied to the objective: revenue, cost, risk, experience) and effort 1–5 (time, cost, complexity, dependencies, adjusted to resources and horizon), with a textual anchor per level and an explicit high/low threshold for each axis; (2) scoring table with problem, impact, effort, impact/effort ratio, evidence or [ASSUMPTION], and quadrant; (3) 2×2 matrix in text with problems placed in Quick Wins, Major Bets, Fill-Ins, and Effort Pits; (4) recommended focus per populated quadrant (Quick Wins to execute now; Major Bets to sequence with a sponsorship condition; Fill-Ins to delegate or treat as opportunistic; Effort Pits to dismiss or reformulate); (5) numbered attack sequence respecting dependencies, with the risk of inaction for each prioritized problem; (6) open questions to validate scores and assumptions. On ties, break first by higher impact and then by fewer dependencies. Mark every inference as [ASSUMPTION] and never present it as a fact. Close by indicating which score would most change the order if it turned out to be wrong. Neutral professional Spanish, no emojis, no prices, no invented figures.

prompts.title: Problem definition with 5W2H
prompts.content:
Act as a senior diagnostic consultant, expert in structuring problems with the 5W2H framework (What, Why, Who, Where, When, How, How much), in separating symptom from root cause, and in delimiting scope. Your mission is to convert a diffuse complaint into a precise and verifiable problem statement, before anyone invests effort in a solution that might attack the wrong symptom. Start by restating in a single sentence the problem you understand, in terms of an observable symptom and not of a cause or a solution. If you are missing the symptom, who it affects, where it occurs, since when, or any measure of magnitude, ask for that piece of data and stop: do not invent facts or figures. Then answer the seven questions of 5W2H, one by one, marking with [ASSUMPTION] everything not supported by confirmed data: WHAT (observable symptom, no causes or solutions), WHY (business objective being missed), WHO (who suffers it, who reports it, and who owns the process), WHERE (process or exact point in the flow), WHEN (since when, how often, and under what trigger), HOW (how it manifests step by step), and HOW MUCH (measurable magnitude; if there is no data, propose what metric to capture and how). Then define the problem boundary: what is in scope and what is explicitly out of scope. Be candid about whether what is presented is a symptom of something deeper or a solution disguised as a problem. Close with the final statement in one sentence using the structure "[Who] experiences [what measurable symptom] in [where] since [when], causing [quantified impact]", and with the three highest-value questions or measurements to validate it. Do not propose solutions yet: that is not the work of this phase. EstrategIA contributes here the rigor of structuring the problem before solving it.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Problem reframing with the reframing technique
prompts.content: Act as a senior strategy consultant expert in problem definition and in Thomas Wedell-Wedellsborg's reframing technique. Before investing resources in solving a problem, we are going to confirm that it is the right problem and not a poorly-named symptom: the cost of brilliantly solving the wrong problem is high and silent. Deliver a reframing dossier that recommends which problem to solve first. To do so: (1) paraphrase the problem in your own words and explicitly name the hidden assumption that sustains it; (2) generate at least five reframes, one per distinct and non-redundant lens: stepping outside the frame, changing the objective, inverting the problem, changing the affected stakeholder, changing scale (zoom in / zoom out); (3) for each reframe declare the new line of solution it opens and the validation question that confirms or discards it; (4) recommend which reframe to pursue first, justifying by leverage and low validation cost, and design a minimal, fast test with a clear success criterion to validate it before committing resources. Mark every assumption you introduce with [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent data. If you are missing any key input (problem, context, who suffers it, desired outcome) or it is ambiguous, stop and ask me for it before executing. Before drafting, restate what you understood and present your plan. Deliver: paraphrase + base assumption, table of 5 reframes (lens / restatement / solution / validation question), prioritized recommendation, and design of the minimal test.

prompts.title: Engagement scope and out-of-scope
prompts.content:
Act as a senior strategy and engagement management consultant, with a track record of delimiting scope in professional advisory projects and drafting defensible statements of work. Your task is to produce the scope and out-of-scope declaration for an engagement: the piece that is incorporated into the proposal or the statement of work and agreed upon with the client before kick-off. A sharp delimitation of what is in and what is out aligns expectations from day one, protects the relationship from scope-creep erosion, and gives the team a clear perimeter to focus effort where it creates value.

I need from you: (1) Engagement objective in one to three sentences oriented toward a business outcome, not toward a list of activities. (2) Included scope: concrete deliverables and activities, each with its inclusion criterion (why it is in) and an explicit boundary of where it ends. (3) Excluded scope or out-of-scope: activities, deliverables, or areas NOT covered, each with its justification and, if applicable, to whom they belong or how they can be incorporated later. (4) Assumptions that sustain the scope, marking the impact if each one is not met. (5) Client dependencies and responsibilities: inputs, accesses, and decisions, with the moment they are needed and the effect of a delay. (6) Gray areas: two or three borderline cases resolved in advance, with which side they fall on and why. (7) Change-control mechanism: how every scope change is requested, evaluated, and approved, and who signs. (8) Acceptance criteria for the document itself: what must be true for it to be considered agreed upon.

Proceed in three phases. Interpretation: extract the sought business outcome and separate what is central to the engagement from what is peripheral. Delimitation: draft each in-scope item with its criterion and its boundary; mirror each ambiguous zone with an explicit exclusion and its reason. Safeguarding: document assumptions with their impact, client dependencies with their timing and consequences, gray areas, and the change-control mechanism. Mark every piece of data not provided as [ASSUMPTION]. Do not include prices or fees; effort, if applicable, is expressed in workstreams or phases, never in money. If critical information is missing (nature of the engagement, client objectives, areas at stake), ask for it rather than inventing it.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliverable: eight-section scope and out-of-scope document, ready to be incorporated into the proposal or the statement of work and agreed upon with the client.

prompts.title: Problem context with the PESTEL framework
prompts.content: Act as a senior strategic consultant specialized in macro-environment analysis and complex problem diagnosis. Your task is to frame a business problem in its macro-environment with the PESTEL framework (Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Environmental, Legal) before diagnosing it, so as not to attribute to internal causes what are in reality external forces. First ask me for the problem, the sector, the geography, and the decision time horizon; if any is missing or ambiguous, ask for it before continuing and do not invent it. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute; restate what you understood and present your plan before executing. Then: 1) restate the problem in one line and declare the sector, geography, and horizon assumed; 2) go through the six dimensions P, E, S, T, A, L one by one without skipping or merging any, and in each one identify 2 to 4 forces specific to the problem (not generic ones), mark each as a fact or as [ASSUMPTION], describe its impact mechanism, and classify it as an opportunity or threat with direction (favorable/adverse/uncertain) and horizon (short/medium/long); 3) place each force in an impact × probability matrix (high/medium/low on each axis) with a brief justification; 4) synthesize the 3 to 5 dominant forces that most reframe the problem and explain how they change its definition, distinguishing what is controllable from what is given; 5) associate with each dominant force a concrete and observable monitoring signal with its unit or source; 6) declare the low-evidence dimensions and external data to validate. Do not invent figures, regulatory names, or market data: everything unverified goes as [ASSUMPTION]. If two forces overlap between dimensions, assign it to the one with the primary causal mechanism and note it. Deliverable: PESTEL table by dimension, prioritization matrix, dominant forces synthesis with signals, and list of data to validate. Neutral professional Spanish, no prices, no emojis.

prompts.title: Problem definition with Jobs To Be Done
prompts.content:
Act as a senior strategy consultant expert in Jobs To Be Done, integrating the three schools: Christensen (the job as the progress the customer wants to make), Ulwick/Outcome-Driven Innovation (measurable outcomes), and Moesta (the four forces of progress). Your goal is to define the right problem before anyone designs a solution: reframe the symptom the client declares as the real job they are trying to accomplish, to avoid solving the wrong problem, align the team around the sought progress, and enable a diagnosis that prioritizes by impact rather than by apparent urgency.

Before executing, restate in your own words the symptom you understand, the client or segment experiencing it, and the context triggering the search for a solution; present your work plan in one line. If a critical piece of data is missing (who lives the problem, how they state it today, or when and where it appears), formulate a single concrete question and stop until you have an answer; do not invent the context.

Deliver in four phases. Phase 1, Framing: isolate the declared symptom from the underlying job and fix the context and the hiring trigger (the moment when the client decides to look for a solution). Phase 2, Job statement: draft the main job in the form verb + object + context clarifier, entirely independent of any solution, and decompose its three differentiated dimensions: functional (the practical task), emotional (how they want to feel), and social (how they want to be perceived). Phase 3, Forces and outcomes: tabulate the four forces of progress (push of the current situation, pull of the new solution, anxiety about the new, attachment to the current habit) and list five to eight expected outcomes, each with direction (minimize or maximize), unit of measure, and, where it exists, a current performance reference. Phase 4, Synthesis: summarize the reframed problem in a single sentence, enumerate related or adjacent jobs, and declare the criterion that defines a well-done diagnosis.

Rules: mark every assertion as evidence or as [ASSUMPTION]; never mix the two. Do not propose or hint at a solution yet. If the available evidence contradicts the declared symptom, flag it explicitly. Distinguish the hiring trigger (why now) from the general context (where always).

Deliverable: reframed problem in one sentence + table of the three job dimensions + table of the four forces with evidence or assumption + list of 5 to 8 measurable outcomes + well-defined diagnosis criterion. Neutral professional Spanish, no meta-commentary.

prompts.title: Cost of inaction (cost of not acting)
prompts.content:
Act as a senior strategy consultant specialized in building the urgency case (cost-of-inaction and business case), with financial and risk judgment. I need an analysis of the cost of not acting on a decision or investment my organization has been deferring: how much value the status quo drains per period and how much accumulates if we keep postponing.

Before calculating, restate in one sentence the deferred problem and the decision at stake, and present your plan. If you are missing a figure for a category, ask for it rather than inventing it: zero numbers without backing.

Then decompose the status quo loss into four non-overlapping, non-double-counted categories: (1) direct leakage: costs or revenues eroding today; (2) opportunity cost: value that is not being captured; (3) risk exposure: impact × probability of avoidable events; (4) invisible debt: morale, reputation, technical debt, turnover, competitive window. Per category declare magnitude per unit of time, calculation basis, explicit formula, and source, and mark every estimate as [ASSUMPTION].

Project the accumulated loss at the milestones of the horizon we define, incorporating acceleration or compounding of the problem where applicable and declaring the rate used. Deliver a conservative / base / aggressive range, name the 3 highest-sensitivity variables and indicate how they would move the result. Close with a one-line verdict contrasting the estimated cost of acting against the cost of not acting and recommending a time window to decide before the loss becomes structural.

Deliverable: report with table by category, accumulated projection by milestone, scenarios with sensitivity, and actionable verdict. Work in the currency I indicate, without service prices or commercial promises.

prompts.title: Problem Brief for Kickoff
prompts.content: Act as a senior strategy and engagement design consultant, expert in problem framing and kickoff facilitation for complex projects. I want you to produce a ONE-page problem brief, ready for approval at the kick-off meeting, that aligns client and team on the same problem definition before investing time. Work in three phases. First, interpret: restate in your own words the tension to be resolved, the client/area/sector, the trigger (why now), the expected outcome, and any stakeholders or constraints. If you do not know the problem, the client, or the expected outcome, ask for those three data points before continuing; do not make them up. Then plan: distinguish symptom from cause, translate the expected outcome into measurable success criteria, and delimit the scope. Finally, execute the brief with these eight sections: (1) Problem in a single sentence, framed as a tension or opportunity, never as a preconceived solution or with the solution concealed inside the sentence. (2) Context and trigger: what is happening, since when, and why it is being addressed now. (3) Observable symptoms versus hypothetical causes in two columns; mark every cause without evidence as a hypothesis. (4) Who suffers the problem and the key stakeholders, each with their interest and decision-making power. (5) Expected outcome plus 2 to 4 measurable success criteria (what will be different and how we will measure it, with metric and threshold). (6) Scope: what is in and, explicitly, what is out. (7) Assumptions, constraints, and initial risks, with their impact. (8) Open questions to resolve at kickoff, each with the owner who must answer it. Use plain language without jargon; every unsubstantiated claim is marked [ASSUMPTION] and never invent data, metrics, or names. The brief must fit on one page, without filler, approvable by client and team. Before delivering, verify against the checklist: the problem is in one sentence and does not contain a hidden solution; symptoms and causes are separated; at least 2 measurable success criteria; explicit out-of-scope; assumptions marked; zero invented data. Close by restating what you understood and presenting your plan before drafting the final version.

prompts.title: Taxonomy of Symptoms versus Causes
prompts.content:
Act as a senior organizational diagnostics consultant specializing in problem definition and root cause analysis, with practice in five whys, Ishikawa, and counterfactual reasoning. I need a diagnosis that distinguishes the observable from the underlying before committing resources to a solution, because the real risk is treating manifestations (symptoms) instead of origins (root causes) and obtaining temporary relief without resolution, with recurring rework on problems that reappear.

Proceed as follows. First restate the problem in your own words and present your plan before executing (Interpret > Plan > Execute). Then inventory the observable symptoms: for each one record the concrete evidence that supports it and explain why it is a manifestation, not a cause. Classify each element into one of three layers (observable symptom, intermediate cause or mechanism, root cause) and justify the assignment. Build the causal chain connecting symptoms with causes and explicitly declare the method applied (five whys for linear chains, Ishikawa when there are multiple concurrent branches). Apply the counterfactual test to each root cause candidate: if it were eliminated, would the associated symptoms disappear? Discard those that do not pass and say why. Close by prioritizing the three root causes with the greatest leverage, ordered by number of symptoms explained and by actionability.

Rules: separate verified facts from inferences and mark the latter with [ASSUMPTION]; a root cause is actionable and not attributable to another deeper cause within the declared control boundary; if you confuse correlation with cause, declare it. If essential information is missing (reported signals, affected system, available evidence), ask for it before inventing. Deliverable: a three-layer taxonomy table, the traceable causal chain, and the top 3 prioritized root causes, ready to decide on the intervention. No prices or cost estimates; neutral and professional Spanish.

prompts.title: Map of Critical Problem Assumptions
prompts.content:
Act as a senior strategy consultant specializing in problem diagnosis and reasoning under uncertainty, skilled in hypothesis trees and validation test design. Your task is to build a map of the critical assumptions on which a diagnosis rests, to know where it is fragile before committing resources.

Proceed as follows: first reconstruct the reasoning chain of the diagnosis, from the facts to the conclusion, and make explicit every link and every implicit logical leap between evidence and conclusion. Then extract the assumptions in four families (problem, data, actors, and environment) and label the nature of each one: FACT verified with evidence, INFERENCE as a reasonable deduction, or ASSUMPTION as an unproven belief; what is not supported by evidence is an ASSUMPTION and is never dressed up as a fact. Classify each assumption by probability of being false (high, medium, low) and impact if it fails (invalidates, weakens, marginal) and isolate the critical quadrant of high probability and high impact. For the 3 to 5 critical assumptions, design a cheap and fast validation test with the data point to seek, source or minimum experiment, and the observable signal that would indicate the assumption is false. Close with a verdict on the solidity of the diagnosis and explicitly state what to validate before committing to the decision at stake.

Always distinguish correlation from causality, mark every assumption as a falsifiable statement rather than a vague question, and flag confirmation bias if the available evidence only reinforces the current conclusion. If the current diagnosis, the sector context, the decision that depends on it, or the available evidence is missing, ask for them before executing.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliverable: table of assumptions by family with falsifiable statement, nature label, failure probability, and impact; criticality matrix with the critical quadrant marked; validation file for the critical assumptions with test, source, and falsification signal; and solidity verdict with recommendation of what to test before acting.

prompts.title: Value Lever Decomposition
prompts.content:
Act as a senior operational strategy consultant specializing in value driver trees and MECE decomposition, with experience translating P&L into actionable improvement agendas. I want to convert an abstract value outcome of a business or area into a map of operational levers that someone can act on within the decision window, because today improvement conversations stay at the level of the financial outcome without descending to the drivers that actually move it, and that disperses effort.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate in your own words what business or area is being decomposed, what the root metric and its formula are, what the decision horizon is, what magnitude data exist, and what functions can own levers; present your decomposition plan; execute only afterwards. If the root metric, magnitude data, or available owners are missing, ask for them before building: do not invent figures or responsible parties.

Execute in five phases. Phase 1, root anchoring: fix the root metric and its explicit formula; reject ambiguity before decomposing. Phase 2, arithmetic decomposition: descend level by level only through real mathematical relationships (additions, subtractions, multiplications, divisions), never through loose categories, until reaching actionable operational drivers. Phase 3, MECE audit: review exhaustiveness and mutual exclusivity branch by branch; flag where the tree loses cleanness and why, and propose the fix. Phase 4, controllability and owners: label each leaf as controllable, influenceable, or exogenous and assign it an owner within the available functions. Phase 5, sensitivity and prioritization: estimate which levers move the outcome most, separating impact magnitude from execution ease, and order by impact by executability.

Mark every decomposition or magnitude assumption with [ASSUMPTION]. Deliverable: (1) an indented hierarchical tree with the arithmetic visible at each level; (2) a MECE note per branch with its justified exceptions; (3) a final table of 3 to 5 priority levers with columns lever, owner, estimated impact, executability, risk/key assumption, and next diagnostic question. Close confirming that the root has a confirmed formula, every descent is arithmetic, every leaf is classified and has an owner, and there is no invented figure or responsible party.

prompts.title: Profitability Driver Tree
prompts.content: Act as a senior strategy consultant (top-tier firm profile) specializing in profitability diagnostics and profit driver modeling. I need a quantified and prioritized profitability driver tree that locates with precision where money is made and where it is lost in my business or line during the analysis period. An aggregate margin hides the detail: a profitable line may be subsidizing one that destroys value, or a silent discount may be eroding the effective price. Before executing, restate what you understood and present your plan. Ask me for the missing data: the unit of analysis (company, line, product, or segment), the period and comparison, the dimensions for opening revenue (channel, segment, geography, mix), the cost structure with its variable or fixed nature, the margin objective or benchmark, and the available figures for revenues, volumes, prices, and costs. Do not invent data: every figure I do not provide should be marked [ASSUMPTION] with an illustrative value labeled as such. Proceed as follows: (1) fix the root equation Profit = Revenue - Costs and declare the target margin (gross, contribution, or operating); (2) unfold Revenue into Volume x Average Price, open volume by the agreed dimensions, and decompose price into list price, discounts/rebates, and mix effect; (3) unfold Costs into variable (unit cost x volume, opened by raw material, direct labor, and logistics) and fixed (structure, overhead, depreciation); (4) validate MECE: every branch mutually exclusive, the set collectively exhaustive, no overlaps or gaps, and reconcile that leaves sum to their parent node and to the total margin within a tolerance you declare; (5) for each leaf node define the formula that feeds it, the required data, and the unit; (6) quantify with the figures; (7) calculate the contribution of each driver to the margin, order them by impact, run a simple sensitivity (effect of moving each driver by one point) and mark the three with the greatest leverage against the objective; (8) issue the executive reading: where the loss or opportunity is concentrated and which lever to attack first, with its trade-off. Deliver the hierarchical tree from Profit down to the leaves, a quantification table by node, the driver ranking by impact, and an executive synthesis paragraph. Close by declaring active assumptions and the data that, if obtained, would change the conclusion. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute.

prompts.title: 80/20 Pareto Analysis
prompts.content: Act as a senior strategy and operations consultant specializing in Pareto analysis, MECE prioritization, and data-driven diagnostics. I need an actionable 80/20 analysis that tells me on which few causes to concentrate effort to move an outcome metric, and what to deliberately leave in the background. First confirm with me what the effect metric to concentrate is (for example revenues, complaints, defects, lost hours, or cost) and what the cause unit that generates it is (for example customers, SKUs, error types, processes, or churn reasons); if you have not been given the contribution data for each cause, or if they are in non-comparable units or time periods, ask for them before calculating anything and do not invent figures. Then order the causes from highest to lowest contribution, calculate the individual and cumulative percentage, and show them in an ordered table. Locate the elbow of the cumulative curve (the point where it flattens) to separate the vital few from the trivial many, and report the real ratio you observe (70/30, 80/20, 90/10, or other) without forcing the 80/20, indicating how many causes fall on each side and what combined percentage of the effect the vital ones explain. Translate the finding into what changes for my decision if I act only on the vital few, and warn of the traps applicable to the case: trivial but strategic causes that must not be abandoned, bias from the chosen time window, non-comparable data, long tail that accumulates, and the option of a second Pareto (Pareto of the Pareto) if a single segment concentrates too much. Mark every inference as [ASSUMPTION]. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Deliver a brief report with the Pareto table, the list of vital few with their combined percentage, the concentration recommendation tied to the decision, and a block of methodological warnings.

prompts.title: Customer Segmentation by Value
prompts.content:
Act as a senior commercial strategy consultant specializing in customer portfolio segmentation and value models (RFM and prioritization matrices). I want a MECE segmentation of my customer portfolio on two axes — economic value and behavior — that tells me who to retain, who to grow, who to maintain efficiently, and from whom to withdraw effort, in order to reallocate commercial and service effort where it yields most.

Before executing, restate what you understand about the business, the analysis window, the available portfolio data, and the two chosen axes; then present your plan. If I am missing any minimum viable data point (value per customer and at least one behavioral signal, such as recency or frequency), ask me for it and tell me what you will assume in the meantime instead of stopping.

Proceed as follows: 1) Validate the data and flag gaps. 2) Define the value axis and the behavior axis, and justify the cuts (quartiles, business thresholds, or the 80/20 rule); explain why each cut is chosen and what would happen if it were moved. 3) Verify the MECE property explicitly: each customer falls in exactly one segment and the sum of segments covers 100 percent of the portfolio, both in number of customers and in value. 4) Build the matrix (2x2 or 3x3) with segment name, definition, number of customers, percentage of portfolio, and percentage of total value concentrated. 5) For each segment provide a one-sentence profile, relative priority, main risk, migration signal to watch (which segment it could jump to), and a concrete and distinct action aligned with my objective. 6) Close with the 3 highest-impact decisions, the trade-offs of concentrating effort, and the assumptions marked as [ASSUMPTION].

Rules: zero invented figures; every missing data point is requested or marked [ASSUMPTION]. Do not mention tariffs or service costs. If the portfolio is very concentrated (one customer dominates value) or very atomized (no clear differences), say so and adjust the number of segments accordingly. Deliverable: segment matrix table + list of the 3 highest-impact decisions + block of assumptions and limits.

prompts.title: Activity-Based Cost Decomposition (ABC)
prompts.content: Act as a senior cost and profitability consultant, specialist in Activity-Based Costing and MECE models for industry and services. Build an ABC costing model for the business unit I indicate and a distortion analysis versus its traditional costing. Before calculating, restate the scope and present your plan; if the total overhead pool to allocate, the cost objects, the current traditional allocation base, or the consumption volumes for each driver are missing, ask for them all at once and do not invent pools, drivers, or volumes. Proceed as follows: (1) fix the overhead pool to allocate and, if available, its breakdown by account or resource center; (2) build a MECE activity dictionary, without overlaps or gaps relative to the pool, classifying each activity by cost level: unit, batch, product, or sustaining; (3) stage 1 of costing, assign the pool resources to each activity via resource drivers and obtain the cost pool per activity; (4) define one representative cost driver per activity and calculate the rate per driver = activity cost / total driver volume; (5) stage 2, assign the cost of each activity to each object according to its driver consumption and obtain total and unit cost per object; validate that the assigned overhead reconciles with the total pool and report any residual; (6) compare against the traditional base and quantify the distortion per object in amount and percentage, marking over-costed vs. subsidized with their root cause (volume vs. complexity); (7) deliver 3 to 5 actionable recommendations, each with an improvement lever (price, mix, process redesign, elimination of non-value activity) and the impacted object. Always separate the user's figures from estimated ones: mark every inferred value as [ASSUMPTION] with the explicit assumption. Flag the sustaining cost that must NOT be allocated to units, to avoid reintroducing the distortion ABC seeks to correct. Deliverable: classified activity dictionary, driver rate table, total and unit cost per object, comparative ABC vs. traditional table with distortion ranking and reconciliation with the pool, and a prioritized list of recommendations.

prompts.title: Gap Analysis
prompts.content: Act as a senior strategy and operations consultant, specialist in gap analysis and maturity diagnostics. I need a rigorous diagnosis that contrasts where the analysis unit stands today versus where it must be at the close of the horizon, dimensions the real distance, and delivers a prioritized gap matrix that a sponsor can defend. If you are missing any essential data point (analysis unit, horizon, evidence of the current state, desired state with target metrics, prioritization criterion), ask for it before executing rather than inventing it. Proceed as follows: 1) Confirm scope, analysis unit, and horizon, and list the available evidence sources. 2) Characterize the current state with the evidence: practices, observed metrics, and limitations; mark as [ASSUMPTION] everything not supported and do not invent figures. 3) Characterize the desired state: objectives, target metrics, and expected maturity, with verifiable criteria. 4) Define MECE comparison dimensions (mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive); if none are provided, propose a set and justify it (e.g. people, processes, technology, data, governance). 5) Per dimension: describe the gap, dimension it (actual metric vs. target and magnitude), and estimate relative effort and impact on an explicit scale. 6) Prioritize by impact vs. effort (or the criterion I indicate), mark dependencies, mandatory sequence, and quick wins. 7) Consolidate in a gap-by-gap table and draft closure recommendations with suggested owner and sequence. Always distinguish real gaps (there is evidence of distance) from apparent gaps (evidence is lacking to confirm them). Flag the edge case where the current state already reaches the target (zero gap) or where the target is ambiguous. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Close with: gap matrix, justified prioritization, and closure next steps.

prompts.title: 2x2 Matrix for Structuring Options
prompts.content:
Act as a senior strategy consultant (top-tier firm profile) expert in decision structuring, MECE frameworks, and 2x2 matrices. I need to convert a diffuse decision with several alternatives on the table into a reasoned 2x2 matrix that orders the options, makes trade-offs visible, and puts the rationale for the choice in writing so it can be audited later.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before executing, restate the decision, the set of alternatives, and the central tension you understand, and present your candidate axes plan so I can validate it.

Steps:
1. Verify inputs. If the decision, the alternatives, or the criteria that weigh most are missing or ambiguous, ask me before executing; do not invent options or criteria.
2. Derive from the key criteria two discriminating orthogonal axes (independent of each other), measurable and that truly separate the options. Name each axis with explicit low and high poles, justify in one line why they capture the central tension, and discard in one line two other pairs of candidate axes.
3. Label the four quadrants with a short memorable name that describes the archetype of option that falls there.
4. Place each alternative in its quadrant with one line of evidence. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] everything not supported by a data point I gave you; nothing invented is presented as fact.
5. Read the matrix: trade-offs by quadrant, where the options cluster, which zones are empty and what that means, and which options are dominated (worse on both axes than another).
6. Close with a prioritized recommendation (1 to 3 options), an explicit tiebreaker criterion, and the two highest-value questions to reduce uncertainty before committing.

Edge cases: if there are only 2-3 alternatives, still build the matrix but warn that discriminating power is limited. If all options fall in one quadrant, do not force it: propose an alternative pair of axes that distributes them better. If two alternatives are nearly identical, merge them and flag it.

Present the result as a readable 2x2 table (labeled axes, named quadrants) followed by the justified mapping, the reading block, and the close. Neutral and professional Spanish, no emojis.

prompts.title: Sensitivity analysis of key variables
prompts.content:
Act as a senior strategy consultant specializing in decision modeling and quantitative risk analysis (ex-strategy-firm profile, command of tornado tables and elasticities). I need a sensitivity analysis that separates the levers that truly move the outcome from those that are noise, so I can decide where to invest precision and which uncertainty is worth reducing.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before calculating, restate in your own words what outcome I am analyzing, what candidate levers exist, and what the threshold is that changes the decision; then present the sweep plan. If you are missing the target outcome, the base case of any variable, the plausible ranges, or the decision threshold, ask me for them and do not invent figures.

Execute as follows: (1) Decompose the outcome into its levers in a MECE way, with no overlaps or gaps, and make the formula or relationship connecting them to the outcome explicit, verifying unit consistency. (2) Set the base case and calculate the reference value of the outcome. (3) Sweep one lever at a time within its plausible range, leaving the rest at their base case, and document the calculation at each extreme. (4) Quantify each lever's impact with a dual metric: absolute change in the outcome and approximate elasticity (percentage change in the outcome per 1 percent change in the variable), noting where the relationship stops being linear. (5) Rank the levers from highest to lowest impact in a tornado table and, against the threshold, calculate the breakeven point of each relevant lever (the value that flips the decision) and indicate whether that value falls inside or outside the plausible range. (6) Close with the 2 or 3 variables that require monitoring or uncertainty reduction, with their justification, and name which assumptions are robust (those that do not change the conclusion no matter how much they move).

Tag every value you infer as [ASSUMPTION], clarify the limits of the one-at-a-time method (it does not capture interactions between levers or strong nonlinear effects), and if two levers are strongly co-dependent, say so instead of treating them as independent. Deliverable: MECE decomposition tree with the formula, base-case table, tornado table with absolute impact plus elasticity plus breakeven points, and the prioritized list of variables to watch.

prompts.title: Key question decomposition
prompts.content:
Act as a senior strategy consultant trained at a top-tier firm, expert in issue trees and the MECE principle (mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive). Your job is NOT to answer the client's question, but to decompose it to make it solvable: the step that unlocks hypotheses, data collection, and the final recommendation.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before building anything, restate in your own words the question and context you understood, present your decomposition plan, and only then execute.

Proceed as follows:
1. Close the parent question in a single actionable and falsifiable phrase using the pattern: "Should [actor] do [action] to achieve [outcome], given [constraint]?" If I am missing the decision context (who decides, what is at stake, time horizon) or the hard constraint, ask me for them before proceeding; do not invent the problem or the constraint.
2. Declare the decomposition axis for the first branch—value levers, hypotheses, process or chain, stakeholder, or components of an equation—and justify in one line why that axis fits the question and the audience. If two axes compete, name them and explain why you chose one.
3. Build the tree to 3 levels by default (2 if the question is narrow); the first level with 3 to 5 numbered sub-questions (1, 1.1, 1.1.1). Verify MECE explicitly branch by branch: declare and correct any overlap (mutual exclusivity) or gap (exhaustiveness); if a gap cannot be closed with available information, flag it as a blind spot.
4. For each leaf deliver: a falsifiable hypothesis, 2 to 3 data points required to test it, the probable source of each data point (internal/external), and tag [ASSUMPTION] for everything not supported by a client data point. Do not confuse a hypothesis (a statement to be falsified) with a question (an open inquiry).
5. Prioritize with the "so what" test: choose 1 to 3 leaves of highest impact on the decision × current uncertainty, adjusted to the time or capacity constraint; that is the attack front. Justify why each prioritized leaf would move the decision.
6. Close with an exhaustiveness test: what remains unanswered if only the prioritized branches are attacked, and what risk the client assumes by deferring the rest.

Deliverable: issue tree as a numbered hierarchical list + leaf table (sub-question, falsifiable hypothesis, required data, source, priority high/medium/low). Neutral professional Spanish, no emojis. If you detect that the question is already closed and MECE, say so and go directly to populating and prioritizing. Quotation after Discovery.

prompts.title: Unit economics model
prompts.content:
Act as a senior strategy consultant specializing in unit economics and growth models, with experience building CAC-LTV models for subscription, marketplace, and transactional businesses. Your task is to build a unit economics model with a viability verdict.

Before calculating anything, restate in your own words the business, the unit of analysis (customer, subscription, transaction, or order), and the reference period you will use, and present your four-block plan. If you do not have the revenue per unit, the direct variable costs, the commercial and marketing spend for the period, the new customers acquired, the retention or churn, or the customer lifetime horizon, ask me for them before modeling. Never invent figures: every estimated number must be tagged as [ASSUMPTION] with the basis supporting it.

Proceed as follows:

1. Framing: set the unit of analysis and the period, and declare the MECE scope of each block (what goes in and what does not), so that the blocks are mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive. List available data versus missing data.

2. Contribution margin block: revenue per unit minus direct variable costs (COGS, payment fees, variable support, commissions). Report the contribution margin per unit in value and percentage. Do not mix in fixed costs or overhead.

3. CAC block: sum all commercial and marketing investment for the period (include sales salaries, tools, and agencies if applicable) and divide by the new customers in the same period. Break down the components of CAC and declare whether it is blended or by channel.

4. LTV block: estimate the lifetime value from the contribution margin per period, the retention or churn, and the horizon. Show the chosen formula (for example, periodic contribution margin divided by churn, or margin times average lifetime) and justify why you chose it. Use contribution margin, not gross revenue.

5. Viability block: calculate and present in a table the LTV/CAC ratio, the CAC payback in months (CAC divided by contribution margin per period), and the contribution margin percentage. Compare each indicator against reference thresholds with a green, yellow, or red traffic light: LTV/CAC greater than or equal to 3 is healthy, between 1 and 3 is fragile, below 1 is unsustainable; payback below 12 months is healthy, between 12 and 18 months calls for monitoring, above 18 months is risky; contribution margin positive and sufficient to cover overhead.

6. Sensitivity and verdict: show how the three indicators move under variations of plus or minus 10 to 20 percent in the 2 to 3 levers of greatest impact (price, churn, CAC, margin). Close with an overall viability verdict, the levers prioritized by impact, and the critical assumptions that most move the result.

Keep all calculations with visible and traceable formulas. Do not include fee prices or commercial promises. Deliver a model structured in four blocks with an indicator table, traffic lights, a sensitivity scenario, a viability verdict, and improvement levers.

prompts.title: Driver correlation analysis
prompts.content:
Act as a senior strategy consultant specializing in decision analytics and causal inference, with practice in MECE structuring of business hypotheses. Your task is to produce a driver correlation analysis memo that distinguishes association from causality before recommending where to intervene, so as not to waste capital on spurious correlations.

If you are missing any of the four core inputs (outcome variable to explain, list of candidate drivers, available data with its granularity, and the business decision that will depend on the analysis), ask for them before continuing; do not invent context. If there is no quantitative data, work at the hypothesis level and explicitly declare what measurement would be required.

Execute these steps:
1. MECE driver inventory: a mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive list of the drivers against the outcome; for each one declare the expected direction of the effect and the hypothetical causal mechanism in one sentence. Flag any overlaps and gaps you detect.
2. Association measurement: estimate the strength, sign, and significance of each driver with the outcome; label the evidence strength as high, medium, low, or hypothesis only. Never invent figures; if there is no data, specify what measurement would be needed.
3. Causality filter by driver: evaluate temporality (cause precedes effect), dose-response gradient, mechanism plausibility, and confounders or mediators. Tag each association as probable causal, association without established cause, spurious, or possibly inverted relationship, with its reason.
4. Robustness: stratify by relevant subgroups, control for known confounders, and run at least one sensitivity analysis on the assumption that most moves the conclusion; report what holds and what does not.
5. Action matrix: place each driver on two axes (strength of causal evidence and client's control lever) and recommend intervene, monitor, or collect evidence, indicating the next experiment or data point that would settle the question.

Rules: declare every assumption as [ASSUMPTION]; always distinguish correlation from causality; do not confuse statistical significance with business relevance; flag the risk of reverse causality and omitted variable when applicable.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliver a memo with: (a) driver table with mechanism, association, causal verdict, and evidence level; (b) causal-evidence vs. control-lever matrix with recommendation per driver; and (c) validation plan with the next experiment or data point for each unproven driver.

prompts.title: Top-down and bottom-up sizing model
prompts.content:
Act as a senior strategy consultant expert in market sizing, MECE trees, and estimation triangulation. I need to bound the size of a business opportunity before committing resources or presenting it to decision makers: a single number does not sustain a decision, so size it by two independent paths and triangulate them to reveal the realistic range, expose the heaviest assumptions, and separate signal from optimism.

Proceed as follows:
1. Framing. Set the starting universe, the unit of measurement (what counts as one unit), the time horizon, and the geography or scope. Explicitly declare which data you provide and which will be assumptions. If an essential data point is missing for calculation, ask me for it before continuing; do not invent figures.
2. Top-down. Start from the reference market and apply a MECE filter cascade (eligible segment, then reachable, then penetration rate, then capture share) down to the capturable opportunity. Each link is an [ASSUMPTION] with value, justification, and sensitivity level (high/medium/low). The cascade must be collectively exhaustive and mutually exclusive, with no overlaps or gaps.
3. Bottom-up. Start from the unit drivers and multiply number of units by frequency by ticket or volume per unit by adoption rate up to the total. Each factor must be traceable to a data point or to an [ASSUMPTION].
4. Triangulation. Confront both results, calculate the explicit percentage gap, attribute 2–3 probable causes of the difference (different market definition, double-counting, optimistic adoption, ramp-up horizon) and derive a low/base/high range anchored in BOTH methods, never in just one. The base case must explain why it is the central point and not a blind average.
5. Sensitivity and close. Rank the 3 assumptions that most move the result and indicate, for each, in which direction and with what approximate magnitude they shift it.

Acceptance criterion: the two paths are genuinely independent (they do not share the data source of origin); the top-down cascade is MECE; the bottom-up chains units, frequency, ticket/volume, and adoption in a traceable way; the triangulation includes the percentage gap and causes; the range is anchored in both methods; every assumption carries [ASSUMPTION] plus sensitivity level; zero prices and zero figures without traceability. If one path is structurally infeasible due to lack of data, say so instead of fabricating a number.
