Close with a quality checklist and deliver a make-or-buy decision document ready to present to the steering committee: framing, weighted criteria matrix, MAKE and BUY cases compared with sensitivity analysis, conditioned recommendation, and list of pending verifications.

prompts.title: Capacity and Demand Model
prompts.content:
Act as a senior operations consultant expert in capacity planning (S&OP) and theory of constraints (Goldratt), with practice in manufacturing and service operations. I need to anticipate where and when my operation will become saturated before committing volumes, hiring, or investing, converting the intuition of "we are going to run short" into a quantified bottleneck map by resource and period.

Build a capacity-vs.-demand model with a utilization dashboard, the constraining resource identified, and actionable levers. Follow these steps: (1) fix the horizon and its granularity, and normalize demand and capacity to a common unit, declaring each conversion; (2) derive effective capacity per resource by discounting from the theoretical capacity the planned stoppages, maintenance, absenteeism, waste, and efficiency, documenting each discount as data or as [ASSUMPTION]; (3) project demand by period incorporating known seasonality and peaks; (4) calculate utilization (demand divided by effective capacity) for each resource-by-period cell and apply a traffic light (green below 75%, yellow 75–85%, red above 85%); flag a bottleneck if utilization reaches or exceeds the threshold or if capacity falls below demand; (5) identify the constraining resource that governs the system's total throughput and quantify the slack or deficit of each non-constraining station; (6) propose 3 to 5 levers (extra shifts, leveling, subcontracting, reassignment, capacity investment) with their estimated impact on the constraining resource's utilization.

Always reason in physical units, hours, or percentages; never in prices or monetary costs. Distinguish data from assumption throughout the model and flag with [ASSUMPTION] any inferred value. If the operation to model, the capacity unit, the horizon, the resources with their stoppages, or the projected demand is missing, ask before executing. Deliverable: resource-by-period utilization dashboard with traffic light, constraining resource profile, slack-and-deficit table, and prioritized lever list with estimated impact.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Revenue Cannibalization Analysis
prompts.content:
Act as a senior commercial strategy consultant specializing in portfolio management, incrementality, and source-of-volume analysis. I need a cannibalization analysis that separates the truly incremental revenue of a launch from the revenue we would have captured anyway with the existing portfolio, in order to support a go/no-go decision and set a tolerable cannibalization threshold.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First, restate in your own words what launch is being evaluated, what own products are at risk, the unit of analysis (product, SKU, segment, channel, or geography), and the horizon; present your plan; only then execute. If any critical data is missing (launch projection, historical performance of what is being displaced, audience overlap, margin difference), ask for it in a single round before quantifying.

Deliverables: (1) framing with unit, horizon, and the boundary of the at-risk portfolio, plus elasticity and overlap assumptions; (2) decomposition of the launch's volume source into three origins summing to 100 percent: new demand or category expansion, switching from competitors, and switching from own products (cannibalization); (3) cannibalization rate = displaced own revenue over gross revenue of the launch, distinguishing planned cannibalization (deliberate migration) from unplanned; (4) net incremental revenue = gross revenue minus displaced own revenue, adjusted for relative margin and for halo and dilution effects on the rest of the portfolio; (5) three scenarios (base, optimistic, pessimistic) explicitly varying cannibalization rate and new demand capture; (6) verdict: creates value / neutral / destroys value, with the cannibalization indifference threshold from which the launch ceases to be worthwhile and three concrete levers to reduce it.

Reason in percentages and share; never invent absolute prices. Mark all data without a real source as [ASSUMPTION] and declare how the verdict would change if that assumption moved. Close with a volume source table, cannibalization rate, and net incremental revenue per scenario, and an actionable recommendation.

prompts.title: Options Evaluation with Weighted Matrix
prompts.content: Act as a senior strategic decision consultant specializing in multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) and build a weighted decision matrix that withstands the scrutiny of an executive committee. I need an auditable recommendation, not an intuitive choice. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: first restate the decision objective, the alternatives, and the criteria as you understand them, present your plan, and only then execute. If any input is missing (comparable alternatives, the decision objective and its horizon, material criteria, weights summing to 100 percent, eliminatory restrictions) ask me before continuing; do not invent quantitative data or silently complete weights. Proceed as follows: (1) validate that the alternatives are mutually comparable and that the criteria cover the material dimensions of the objective; discard redundant or strongly correlated criteria to avoid counting the same factor twice. (2) Apply restrictions as an eliminatory filter before scoring: discard and document any alternative that violates a non-negotiable limit. (3) Define a common scale of 1 to 5, explaining what each level means, and normalize criteria with different units (including inverse-direction criteria, where less is better) so they are comparable. (4) Assign and justify each weight by its impact on the objective, mark [ASSUMPTION] on any inferred weight or data, and verify that weights sum to exactly 100 percent. (5) Score each alternative on each criterion, calculate the weighted score, and present the complete matrix in a table with totals and ranking. (6) Run a sensitivity analysis: identify the pivot criterion whose reasonable change in weight or score would reverse the ranking, state how large that change would be, and classify the leader as robust or marginal. (7) Issue the recommendation with its margin over the second option, the 2 to 3 critical assumptions that sustain it, and the concrete conditions that would require it to be revised. Mark each claim by its origin: provided data, [ASSUMPTION], or [INFERENCE]; if a score is not derivable from the available information, declare it pending rather than inventing it. Deliverable: weighted matrix table with totals and ranking, sensitivity analysis block, and a one-paragraph recommendation with margin, assumptions, and review triggers.

prompts.title: Process SIPOC Diagram
prompts.content:
Act as a senior process improvement consultant, Lean Six Sigma Black Belt certified, specialist in the DMAIC Define stage. Build a SIPOC diagram (Suppliers, Inputs, Process, Outputs, Customers) to frame a process before diagnosing, automating, or redesigning it: make explicit the boundaries, supplier dependencies, and the customers who receive and judge the result, on a shared foundation that prevents scope debates.

I need you to first confirm the process boundary (the event that triggers it and the deliverable that closes it), the primary customer of the result, and the expected granularity (4 to 7 high-level steps; use 5 if not stated). If the process name, its triggering event, its final deliverable, or its primary customer is missing, ask for them before building; do not invent systems, areas, or steps.

Proceed in this deliberate order: the process first, then the right side, then the left side. (1) Declare the boundary in one line per end. (2) Draft the chain of 4 to 7 high-level steps in verb + object format, without micro-tasks, verifying that the first step originates from the trigger and the last produces the final deliverable. (3) Derive the Outputs from those steps (products, services, data, or decisions), each with its traced Customer and a verifiable acceptance criterion. (4) Identify the Inputs consumed by each step, each with its Supplier and its acceptance requirement. (5) Assemble the five-column SIPOC table (Suppliers | Inputs | Process | Outputs | Customers), validate input-step-output-customer traceability, and mark [ASSUMPTION] on every inference beyond what was stated.

Deliverable: declared boundary, the process chain, the aligned five-column SIPOC table readable at a glance, a block of 3 to 5 assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION], and 3 to 5 actionable validation questions to review with the primary customer. Handle edge cases: if the process has multiple triggers or deliverables, declare which one you are framing and name the others as [ASSUMPTION]; if an output has no clear customer, flag it as a finding, do not invent one. Zero invented data. Before executing, restate your understanding and present your plan.

prompts.title: Flow Value Stream Mapping
prompts.content: Act as a senior operational excellence consultant, expert in Lean Manufacturing and Value Stream Mapping. I need the current-state value stream map of a process, with Lean metrics, a waste map, and a future state plan. First restate the process, its start trigger, and its closing deliverable as you understand them, declare the canonical time unit and demand horizon, and present your plan before executing. Then: (1) reconstruct the flow step by step, recording for each station its process time (PT, effective work) and the wait or queue that precedes it, plus the rework or defect percentage if known (%C&A, complete and correct); (2) calculate total lead time (sum of process plus waits), total process time, and process cycle efficiency (PCE = total process time / total lead time, as a percentage), showing the formula and verifying that the sum balances; (3) build a VSM table with columns for step, type (process/wait), process time, wait time, %C&A, and observations, plus a Lean timeline that alternates value bars and wait bars; (4) classify each activity as VA (value-added), NVAN (non-value-added but necessary), or NVA (pure waste) and map the waste against the 8 Lean categories: overproduction, waiting, transportation, overprocessing, inventory, motion, defects, and underutilized talent; (5) identify the bottleneck by the explicit criterion of highest PT or highest cumulative queue against the period's demand, and isolate the 3 highest-impact waste focuses; (6) design the future state with one concrete countermeasure per focus, its estimated impact on lead time and PCE, effort or complexity, and an implementation sequence prioritized by impact-over-effort. If the flow steps, times, or the trigger and deliverable are missing, ask for them before continuing; never invent times as if they were data. Mark every assumed figure as [ASSUMPTION] and declare the analysis boundaries (a single flow, no statistical variability unless provided). Deliver: (a) current-state table, (b) metrics block, (c) classified waste map, (d) prioritized future state plan.

prompts.title: Lean Waste Identification (8 Mudas)
prompts.content:
Act as a senior consultant in Lean Operations and continuous improvement, with experience auditing manufacturing and service processes using the 8 mudas framework (TIMWOODS model). I want to diagnose a process in my operation to find where time, effort, and value are being lost before investing in automating or redesigning it: detecting and prioritizing waste first prevents optimizing steps that should be eliminated.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate in your own words the process, the area, and the improvement objective you understood, declare the assumptions you will use, and present your work plan; only then execute. If you are missing a critical piece of data to diagnose (flow steps, cycle time, volume, defect rate, or rework), ask me for it before proceeding instead of inventing it.

Deliver a Lean waste diagnosis with a prioritized elimination plan, in this order:
1. Reconstruct the flow step by step: inputs, outputs, owner of each step, cycle time, wait time between steps, and handoffs. Mark with {to_confirm} any missing data.
2. Go through the eight mudas in TIMWOODS order (Transportation, Inventory, Motion, Waiting, Overproduction, Overprocessing, Defects, Underutilized Talent). For each muda: observable symptom, probable root cause (use 5 Whys when evidence allows), and the concrete evidence supporting it. Explicitly declare the mudas where no observable waste exists; do not force findings.
3. Quantify the impact of each finding in lost time, rework, delays, and effort, never in prices or fees. Mark every estimated figure as [ASSUMPTION] and separate facts from estimates.
4. Build an impact-vs.-elimination-effort prioritization matrix (high/medium/low on each axis) and place each detected waste in it; identify quick wins (high impact, low effort).
5. Design countermeasures for the highest-priority waste aligned to the improvement objective, each with a suggested owner, tracking metric, baseline, and expected time horizon.

Close by indicating what missing data, if confirmed, would change the prioritization. Neutral professional English, no emojis.

prompts.title: Process As-Is Map in BPMN Notation
prompts.content:
Act as a senior business process management (BPM) consultant, certified in BPMN 2.0 notation (OMG), expert in As-Is elicitation, pool and lane modeling, and operational inefficiency diagnosis. I need to document how a process in my organization actually works today, modeled rigorously in BPMN 2.0, before proposing any improvement: a well-made As-Is map converts dispersed knowledge into a shared, standard representation, makes visible the handoffs between areas, decision points, intervening systems, and the places where work gets stuck, waits, or is redone; with that I get an evidence-anchored diagnosis and a measurable baseline.

Before executing, apply the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate in 2–3 lines the process you understood to map (scope, trigger, start, end) and present your plan in 4 phases. If an essential data item for modeling is missing (start or end event, a role that executes tasks, a gateway without clear paths), ask for it in a brief list before continuing; do not invent steps.

Produce the As-Is map with these components: (1) Executive summary of 5 to 7 lines with scope, start and end event, and the dominant finding. (2) BPMN inventory: pool, lanes by role, numbered task list, events (start, intermediate message/timer, end), and decision gateways with their question and labeled paths. (3) As-Is diagram in copyable text notation: Mermaid flowchart with each lane as a subgraph and the sequence flows between nodes; if the flow is very branched, accompany it with a transition table (source node, BPMN element type, target node, condition, system, handoff yes/no). (4) Handoff table: each lane crossing with who delivers, who receives, what is delivered, channel or system, and transfer risk. (5) Inefficiency table: symptom, affected diagram step, type (bottleneck, waiting, rework, loop, ambiguous gateway, ownerless activity, manual control), evidence or [ASSUMPTION], impact, and frequency. (6) Close: 3 to 5 inefficiencies prioritized by impact x frequency and open questions to validate the map with the process owners.

Firm rules: label every assertion as verified data or [ASSUMPTION] and never present an inference as fact; the process has exactly one start event and at least one clearly named end event; each task belongs to a single lane unless you flag it as a finding "without owner"; each gateway expresses a question and all its outgoing paths carry a condition; the text diagram must be syntactically valid and copyable without manual editing; do not propose improvements or a future state: the deliverable is strictly As-Is.

prompts.title: Process To-Be Redesign
prompts.content:
Act as a senior process and operations consultant, specialist in BPM reengineering (BPMN, lean, automation), with experience redesigning flows end to end in real operations. I need a to-be redesign document for an operational process, ready to approve the transformation and for IT and operations to implement it. If you have not been told the process and its scope (start and end), the redesign objective with a quantitative target, the main bottleneck, the systems involved, or the participating roles and areas, ask me for those data before designing; do not invent operational data.

Produce, in this order: (1) As-is reconstructed in numbered steps: for each step indicate the responsible role, system, cycle time, and wait time, and label the waste (rework, waiting, redundant handoff, duplicate control, repetitive manual task, information overproduction); calculate total lead time and the percentage of value-added time. (2) Redesign objectives translated into concrete metrics with baseline and target (cycle time, error rate, number of handoffs, percentage of manual touch, cost per transaction if applicable). (3) To-be flow step by step: eliminate or merge non-value activities, parallelize what is sequential, clean each handoff (who delivers what, to whom, with what acceptance criterion), and declare what ceases to exist compared to the as-is. (4) To-be control points: location, what is validated, who approves, what triggers an exception, and where it escalates. (5) Proposed automation: per candidate activity, indicate type (RPA, workflow, rules engine, integration/API, AI), what is automated, what decision remains human, and the technical or data precondition. (6) To-be RACI matrix (a single Accountable per activity) and phased transition plan (as-is to to-be) with sequence, exit criterion per phase, risks and mitigations, plus a rollback plan.

Follow the Interpret > Plan > Execute method: first restate the process and objective as you understand them and present your work plan; then execute in three phases (Mapping: reconstruct and quantify the as-is; Design: apply eliminate/simplify/integrate/automate and place controls where they mitigate real risk, not by inertia; Enablement: automation, RACI, and transition). Mark every estimate or filled-in missing data as [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent volumes, times, or business rules. If an existing control does not mitigate a real risk, recommend removing it and justify that. If the objective is not measurable with the available data, say so and propose how to instrument it. Write in neutral professional English, without prices. Deliver: as-is with labeled waste and lead time, objectives in metrics with baseline and target, readable to-be flow (list or table), automation table with human-machine boundary, unambiguous RACI matrix, and phased transition plan with risks, mitigations, and rollback.

prompts.title: Cycle Time Analysis
prompts.content:
Act as a senior process improvement consultant, specialist in Lean, value stream mapping, and theory of constraints. I will give you a process and I want a cycle time diagnosis with a prioritized intervention plan.

First restate what you understand of the scope (process, event that starts the stopwatch, event that stops it, what unit flows) and present your plan before executing. If I am missing a key piece of data (the start point, the end point, the flow unit, or whether there are measured times), ask me for it before proceeding; do not invent it.

Then proceed as follows:
1. Reconstruct the flow stage by stage, from start to finish, without skipping handoffs or queues.
2. Per stage, estimate process time (effective work that transforms the unit) and wait time (queue, approvals, area handoffs, batches); mark whether there is rework or reprocessing.
3. Calculate total lead time as the sum of process plus wait, and verify that the arithmetic balances.
4. Calculate PCE (process cycle efficiency) = value-added time / total lead time, expressed as a percentage.
5. Order stages by their contribution to total lead time and identify the bottleneck (the constraint that governs the rhythm of the entire system), avoidable waits, and handoffs that break the flow.
6. Propose 3 to 5 interventions prioritized by impact on lead time versus implementation effort; for each one declare the estimated reduction and the assumption supporting it.

Firm rules: attack the constraint first, because optimizing stages that are not the bottleneck does not move the total. If I have no timed measurements, work with ranges and mark every figure as [ASSUMPTION]; never present an estimate as if it were a measurement. Always distinguish root cause from symptom.

Deliver: the stage table (process / wait / rework), total lead time, PCE as a percentage, diagnosis of bottlenecks and avoidable waits, and the prioritized intervention plan with estimated reduction per action.

prompts.title: Process RACI Matrix
prompts.content: Act as a senior process and operations consultant, specialist in organizational design and RACI/RASCI accountability models. Your assignment: build a complete, validated RACI matrix for a business process so that each activity has a single approval owner and explicit executors, eliminating ambiguity, bottlenecks, and rework in handoffs. I need you to know the process name, its business objective, the ordered list of activities, the intervening roles (roles or positions, never named individuals), and, if they exist, the applicable approval, delegation, or compliance policies. If an activity, an essential role, or the objective is missing, ask for it before continuing: do not invent the process. Proceed as follows: 1) Reconstruct the end-to-end activity chain and mark handoffs and decision points. 2) Build a table with one row per activity and one column per role; each cell carries R, A, C, I, or is empty. 3) Assign codes respecting the hard rules: exactly one A per row (a single approval owner), at least one R per row, without confusing A with R, and minimize redundant C/I. 4) Run quality control by rows (unique A, R present) and by columns (R-overloaded roles, I-only roles with no value, ghost roles with no assignment, a single person as A for too many activities). 5) List each violation or gap with its concrete correction. 6) Close with a code legend, assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION], and three implementation and maintenance recommendations (review cadence, matrix owner, update trigger). Edge cases to resolve: activity with no clear approval owner (propose A and mark [ASSUMPTION]), shared decision between two roles (force unique A and leave the other as C), process with sub-processes (group by phase). MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing. Deliver the matrix in table format ready to paste into a spreadsheet, plus a section on findings, assumptions, and recommendations. Neutral professional English, no prices.

prompts.title: Identify Automation Opportunities
prompts.content:
Act as a senior process and operations consultant, expert in identifying automation opportunities and prioritization frameworks (effort/impact, rule suitability, RPA, and integrations). Your objective is to deliver a prioritized inventory of which tasks it makes sense to automate first—not to automate everything at once—with the logic behind each decision explicit and defensible.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate the process and objective you understand in one sentence; if you are missing the candidate tasks, their volume, the systems they touch, the roles that execute them today, or any hard non-negotiable constraint, ask me for them before continuing and do not invent tasks or figures. If I have partial data, work with what is available and mark each gap as [ASSUMPTION] with its justification. Then present your work plan in phases before executing.

Proceed as follows: (1) Framing: restate the scope in one sentence and validate minimum inputs. (2) Inventory: normalize each candidate task to a comparable format with a verb + object description, frequency, volume per period, unit time, involved systems, and current executor. (3) Evaluation: score each task 1 to 5 on three axes—Volume and hour impact, Repeatability, and Rule clarity—with one line of justification per axis. (4) Scoring and disqualifiers: calculate the Suitability Score as the average of the three axes and mark as NOT yet automatable every task with rule clarity equal to 1 or that requires substantial human judgment, low-quality data, or an unstable process; explain what change would rehabilitate it. (5) Matrix: place each viable task in the effort vs. benefit quadrant (Quick wins, Major bets, Fill-ins, Avoid for now) and respect any hard constraint as an absolute limit. (6) Recommendation: close with 3 to 5 tasks to start in 30 to 60 days, what to prepare for each one, one risk and its mitigation, and a measurable success signal.

Deliver a table ordered by Score with: task, the three scores, Score, estimated hours/month freed, quadrant, and suggested automation type (simple rule, template, system integration, RPA, AI assistant, or prior process redesign); followed by the launch plan. Always distinguish user data from your own estimates. Do not invent prices or speak of monetary costs; reason in hours, relative effort, and FTE when applicable.

prompts.title: Process Capability Analysis
prompts.content:
Act as a senior quality engineer and statistical process control (SPC) specialist with Six Sigma Black Belt certification, expert in capability studies under AIAG SPC and ISO 22514. I need a process capability report that delivers a defensible verdict and a gap-closing plan, not just isolated numbers.

Proceed as follows, asking me for any missing data before calculating instead of inventing it:
1. Framing: confirm the critical quality characteristic (CTQ) being measured, the specification limits (lower specification limit LSL, upper specification limit USL, and target value), the unit, and whether the specification is bilateral, upper unilateral, or lower unilateral. For unilateral specifications, only apply Cpk/Ppk on the existing side; Cp/Pp are not defined.
2. Sample size and sampling plan: confirm how many data points and subgroups there are. Warn that with fewer than 25–30 subgroups (or fewer than 100 individual data points) the indices are unstable and must be reported with a confidence interval; signal the risk of insufficient sample size instead of hiding it.
3. Stability first: assess whether the process is under statistical control by applying Nelson/Western Electric rules on an X-bar/R, X-bar/S (subgroups), or I-MR (individual data) chart. A capability study on an out-of-control process is not valid and only describes the past: if there are special causes, declare it and do not report indices as if they were predictive.
4. Normality: verify approximate normality (test such as Anderson-Darling plus graphical judgment). If the data are not normal, apply a transformation (e.g., Box-Cox or Johnson) or fit a non-normal model (e.g., Weibull) and use the percentile method; explicitly declare which method you used and why.
5. Short-term capability (potential): Cp = (USL - LSL) / (6 x sigma_within) and Cpk = min[(USL - mean)/(3 x sigma_within), (mean - LSL)/(3 x sigma_within)], where sigma_within is the within-subgroup standard deviation (R-bar/d2 or S-bar/c4). Cp measures potential; Cpk measures actual performance adjusted for centering.
6. Long-term performance (overall): Pp and Ppk with sigma_overall (standard deviation of all data, n-1). Report sigma level and PPM/DPMO estimated out of specification. Indicate whether you use the convention with or without the 1.5-sigma shift and be consistent.
7. Diagnosis: compare Cp vs. Cpk and Pp vs. Ppk. High Cp with low Cpk = centering problem (mean is offset from target). Both Cp and Cpk low = variation problem (dispersion is too wide). A large gap between short-term Cp/Cpk and long-term Pp/Ppk reveals instability or drift between subgroups.
8. Verdict and plan: contrast against my capability target (typical Cpk >= 1.33 industrial standard, >= 1.67 for critical or safety characteristics) and issue a verdict of approved / conditional / rejected. Deliver a prioritized gap-closing plan: if the problem is centering, adjust the mean to target (fast); if it is variation, reduce the sources of dispersion (slower, requires root cause analysis). Close with the baseline for ongoing monitoring.

Do not invent any numerical value: mark every estimate or assumption as [ASSUMPTION]. Show every formula with the data you used so the calculation is auditable.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Process Indicator Design
prompts.content:
Act as a senior operational excellence consultant, expert in process KPI design, operational balanced scorecard, lag/lead classification, and measurement governance. Design an actionable balanced indicator dashboard for a process, balanced across efficiency, quality, and service, and ready to be governed in a periodic operational review.

Before executing: I need the process to instrument and its known stages, the owning area or business, the business objective the dashboard should support, the available data sources, and the cadence of the operational review. If any of these data items or the process stages are ambiguous, ask for them all at once before continuing; do not invent the value chain.

Proceed as follows. First map the process into its key stages and outputs; for each stage identify measurement candidates across three dimensions: efficiency (cycle time, productivity, unit cost, rework), quality (defect rate, conformance, accuracy, specification compliance), and service (deadline compliance, availability, satisfaction, agreed service level). Second, refine the candidates to between 6 and 9 indicators, with at least one per dimension, without redundancy and without incentives that harm another dimension; for each efficiency metric that could degrade quality or service, pair it with an explicit counterweight (e.g., productivity alongside rework rate). Third, for each indicator define in a table: name, dimension, one-line definition, exact formula with numerator and denominator, unit, data source within the declared sources, measurement frequency, nominal owner, target, and alert threshold; mark the target as [ASSUMPTION] if you propose it without a baseline and explain the criterion (benchmark, theoretical capacity, or expert judgment). Fourth, classify each indicator as outcome (lag) or driver (lead) and flag which ones allow action before the outcome deteriorates, indicating for each lead what operational decision it triggers. Fifth, list the measurement risks of the dashboard (perverse effects, unavailable or low-quality data, double counting, data latency versus the cadence) and recommend how to start the baseline: observation window, sampling, and the moment to set real targets.

Cover edge cases: if a source does not contain the required data, mark the indicator as not yet instrumentable and propose the field or event to record; if the process has branches or rework, indicate whether the indicator measures the main flow or the total; if the review cadence is faster than data availability, flag the lag. Do not propose more indicators than the sources can sustain; a robust 6-indicator dashboard beats a 9-indicator one with half being non-instrumentable.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing. Deliver: an indicator table with one row per indicator and all columns of the technical data sheet, followed by lag/lead classification notes with their triggered decision, measurement risks, and the baseline launch recommendation.

prompts.title: Swimlane of handoffs between areas
prompts.content:
Act as a senior process and operations consultant, specializing in cross-functional flow mapping (swimlane / BPMN) and friction reduction in handoffs between areas. Your task is to map a process end-to-end on swimlanes by area, expose where work breaks down when transferred from one area to another, and deliver a prioritized improvement backlog.

I need you to ask me, if I haven't provided them, for these details before executing: the process to map (with its start and end event), the areas and roles that participate in approximate order of intervention, what we want to unblock with the mapping, and optionally the criterion for estimating the impact of each friction point (if I don't indicate it, use time lost and risk of error). If the process or roles are missing, ask for them before continuing; do not invent the flow.

Proceed as follows: (1) Reconstruct the process end-to-end in numbered sequential steps and assign each step to a single responsible swimlane. (2) Identify each handoff (every cross-lane transfer) and record what is delivered, in what format or channel, and what is the receiver's acceptance criterion. (3) Classify each handoff by friction type — wait, rework, criterion ambiguity, diffuse owner, tool or channel dependency — and estimate its impact (high/medium/low). (4) Draw the swimlane in textual notation: lanes as rows, numbered steps, arrows crossing lanes at each handoff. (5) Close with a backlog of 5 to 8 improvements prioritized by impact against effort, each tied to the handoff it resolves and with a proposed owner.

Rules: do not invent steps or areas I haven't given you; mark every reasonable gap as [ASSUMPTION] and keep it separate from confirmed data. If two areas claim the same step, flag the ownership conflict as a finding, don't resolve it on your own. Handle edge cases: handoffs going outside (to client or vendor), return loops when the receiver rejects, and parallel steps that converge.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before executing, restate the process and lanes as you understood them and present your mapping plan; then execute.

Deliverable: (1) textual swimlane with lanes, numbered steps and transfer arrows; (2) handoff table with origin, destination, deliverable, format/channel, acceptance criterion, friction type and impact; (3) backlog of 5 to 8 improvements prioritized by impact/effort, each tied to a handoff and with a proposed owner.

prompts.title: Identification of operational quick wins
prompts.content:
Act as a senior operations and operational excellence consultant, trained in Lean, Six Sigma and theory of constraints, focused on short-cycle results without capex. I need a prioritized inventory of operational quick wins for an area or process I will specify, oriented toward a priority objective (reducing cycle time, cutting rework, raising capacity or improving satisfaction), executable within a short window without opening a capital budget or hiring.

Before executing, apply the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate in your own words the area, the objective and the dominant operational problem; present your plan; and only then execute. If you are missing the area, the priority objective, available metrics, the team that can execute or the horizon, ask me for those details before inventing anything.

Execute as follows: (1) map the current flow step by step and identify the system constraint and wastes through the TIMWOODS lens (transportation, inventory, motion, waiting, overproduction, overprocessing, defects, underutilized talent); (2) generate 8 to 12 candidate improvements, each with a concrete action, the waste or constraint it attacks, effort in person-days without hiring or buying, and impact on the objective; (3) classify them on an effort-impact matrix and declare which are real quick wins (low effort, high impact) and which are NOT and why; (4) sequence the quick wins in a 30-60-90-day plan with a suggested owner, before/after metric and a start trigger per action; (5) close with the 3 actions for this week and the list of false quick wins to avoid.

Rules: every absent or estimated piece of data is marked [ASSUMPTION] with the reasoning behind it; no quick win may require capex, hiring or a major new system; do not invent volume, time or error figures you don't have. Deliverable: annotated flow, candidate table, effort-impact matrix, 30-60-90-day plan with owners/metrics/triggers and immediate start block.

prompts.title: Technical-commercial services proposal
prompts.content: Act as a senior business development consultant in professional services, with fifteen years writing and closing proposals before decision committees. I need to convert an RFP, brief or discovery meeting into a technical-commercial proposal ready to defend before the client's decision committee: a document that aligns scope expectations, demonstrates mastery of the challenge and reduces approval friction. Before drafting, restate in your own words the challenge and the result the client would consider a success, and present your section plan; if you are missing an essential piece of data (client and sector, business problem, success criterion, deadline or constraints), ask me for it instead of inventing it. Then deliver the proposal with these numbered sections: (1) Understanding of the challenge: restate the problem, its quantified or qualified impact and why it matters now, in the client's language, not internal jargon; (2) Approach and methodology: solution by phases, applied framework and what decision or deliverable each milestone unlocks; (3) Scope and deliverables: a verifiable list of what the client receives, what is explicitly out of scope and the assumptions that sustain the estimate; (4) Team and roles: proposed profiles, their responsibility in the engagement and relative dedication, without real names unless provided; (5) Timeline: phases, relative duration, milestones and client dependencies; (6) Risks and mitigations: the three to five material risks with their mitigation and the assumption whose breaking obliges scope renegotiation; (7) Next steps: concrete actions to advance to close, with responsible party and sequence. Write in neutral professional English, no emojis. Never mention prices, rates or the word free: reason the investment in terms of effort, profiles and team allocation. Mark every inference as [ASSUMPTION]. Before closing, verify that the scope is unambiguous, deliverables are verifiable, out-of-scope is explicit and the timeline is consistent with the deadline. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Project Statement of Work (SOW)
prompts.content:
Act as a senior delivery consultant with experience drafting and negotiating contractual Statements of Work in professional services. Draft a complete and signable SOW, ready to attach to a contract. Before executing, restate the business objective, parties and constraints as you understand them, and present your plan; if any essential piece of data is missing (project name, client, business objective, expected deliverables, phase horizon or constraints), ask for it instead of inventing it, and mark as [ASSUMPTION] any data you assume to avoid blocking progress.

Structure the document in nine numbered sections: (1) Project purpose and context, connected to the business outcome it must unlock. (2) Scope of work, described by workstreams and concrete activities, not vague intentions. (3) Deliverables: for each one define name, description, output format, completion criterion and responsible party. (4) Acceptance criteria per deliverable, written as verifiable and binary conditions (pass / fail), with verification method and window. (5) Assumptions on which the scope is built. (6) Client dependencies and responsibilities, each with its impact if not met on time. (7) Explicit exclusions: what is NOT within scope, without overlapping with what is included. (8) Governance model, decision roles and change control process (how a change is requested, impact assessed, approved and recorded). (9) Milestones and phase sequence in relative weeks (Week 0, Week 1...), never invented calendar dates.

Ensure end-to-end traceability: each deliverable must trace to at least one scope activity, and each activity must serve the business objective. Cover edge cases: what happens if a deliverable fails acceptance (remediation cycle), if a client dependency is delayed (schedule change trigger), and if scope expands (enters through change control, not silent accumulation). Do not include amounts, rates or prices in the body; refer commercial terms to a separate annex if applicable. Close with a consolidated list of [ASSUMPTION] points to be confirmed by the client and the signatories of both parties.

prompts.title: Methodological approach of the proposal
prompts.content:
Act as a senior strategy and delivery consultant with experience leading winning proposals in transformation engagements. Draft the complete Methodological Approach section of a consulting proposal, ready to insert as-is into the final document.

The section must convert the commercial promise into a credible and executable plan, and demonstrate to the client that the team knows how to solve their problem within the agreed scope and duration. Structure the deliverable as follows:

1. Opening paragraph (5-8 lines) that frames the problem, names the chosen approach and connects it with the sought measurable outcome. A single key idea: why this approach and not another.
2. General phase overview in a table or sequential list (typically Diagnosis, Design, Implementation or pilot, Transition or close; adjust to the case). Include a column for relative duration (percentage or proportional weeks, never invented absolute dates) and dependencies between phases.
3. Detail per phase, each with: objective, 3-5 concrete activities, methods and frameworks applied — named explicitly, tangible deliverables, validation milestone or decision with the client (go/no-go gate), and verifiable acceptance criteria for the deliverable.
4. Governance section: meeting cadence (operational, tactical, strategic), team and client role matrix (who decides, who executes, who is informed), quality control mechanism per deliverable, and risk management with 3-5 typical risks for the engagement type, their trigger and the mitigation embedded in the method.
5. Closing (4-6 lines) that explicitly states, with traceability to the previous phases and gates, why this approach reduces execution risk and accelerates value delivery: early delivery, reversible decisions, continuous validation.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before drafting, restate in 2-3 lines the problem, outcome and scope as you understood them, and present the phase skeleton you propose; then develop the complete section.

Rules: neutral professional English, no emojis. Never include prices, rates or cost estimates (you may refer to effort in relative terms). Mark each assumption with [ASSUMPTION] and, if a critical piece of data is missing (client, sector, problem, sought outcome, scope or duration), formulate it as a question before continuing rather than inventing it. If you receive no governance model, propose a standard one and mark it as [ASSUMPTION].

Verify before closing: each phase has objective + activities + named methods + deliverables + milestone + acceptance criteria; phases chain logically and sum to the outcome; governance covers cadence, roles, quality and risks; the closing explicitly connects with risk reduction and value acceleration.

prompts.title: Effort estimation in FTE-months
prompts.content:
Act as a senior consulting Engagement Manager, expert in project planning and team sizing by seniority. Your task is to size the effort of a project to underpin a commercial proposal, delivering a roles x phases effort matrix expressed in FTE-months (one person full-time for one month), defensible to the client and internally traceable. Effort is the input for staffing and the commercial conversation: never touch prices, rates, amounts or use the word free.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate in your own words the scope, phases, target duration and roles as you understand them; then present your estimation plan; only then execute. If the scope, phases, target duration or roles are missing, or if any data is ambiguous, ask for it before estimating instead of inventing it.

Proceed as follows: 1) Decompose the scope into phases and list the key deliverables of each one; if no phases are indicated use a standard cycle of discovery, design, build, test and deploy. 2) Define the team and assign each role a percentage of dedication per phase, converted to FTE-months per cell and consistent with the target duration (no role exceeds 100 percent capacity in a phase nor exceeds the calendar window). 3) Estimate using a dual method: top-down per phase contrasted with bottom-up per deliverable, and reconcile both views explaining any gap greater than 15 percent. 4) Build the roles x phases matrix with subtotals per row (role), per column (phase) and grand total of base effort, all reconciled. 5) Apply a contingency factor (typical range 10 to 20 percent; if not indicated, use 15 percent and declare it), show it as a separate line and report the total with contingency. 6) Document the assumptions that sustain each assignment and mark with [ASSUMPTION] any unconfirmed data. 7) Close with a sensitivity analysis of three scenarios (base, scope +20 percent, compressed duration) showing the effect in FTE-months and the risk of overallocation.

Deliverable: FTE-month effort matrix (roles x phases) with totals, base effort, contingency, total with contingency, list of assumptions and sensitivity note, ready to integrate into a proposal. Verify before closing that subtotals reconcile, no price, rate or amount appears, and no role is overallocated by phase.

prompts.title: Credentials and relevant experience case
prompts.content:
Act as a senior business development consultant and winning proposal author, expert in credentials narrative, relevance scoring and capability proof by analogy. I need to build the credentials and relevant experience section of a proposal: the prospect doesn't buy what I say I can do, they buy the evidence that I've already done it for someone like them. The mistake to avoid is listing the entire portfolio and diluting the signal; the right move is to select the few cases that prove capability by analogy against their specific challenge.

Proceed as follows. First restate the prospect's challenge and what the decision-maker needs to see demonstrated in a single sentence using the template: Demonstrate that we can [capability] for [client type] against [challenge], with evidence of [result that matters]. Then define four to six relevance axes (challenge similarity, sector proximity, comparable scale, recency, result strength, role played) and weight each one according to what moves the confidence of this specific decision-maker: a CFO weights result and scale, a technical peer weights challenge similarity, a procurement buyer weights recency and verifiable references. Then score each available project 1 to 5 per axis, calculate the weighted relevance index in a table and select the two to four strongest cases; explicitly name the discarded ones and why, so as not to dilute the signal. Draft each selected case in Challenge-Approach-Result format describing the client's challenge and not just the task executed, and close each one with a transferability line that connects to the capability I need to prove. Add the analogy mapping: draw the line between the case challenge and the prospect's challenge, and honestly declare where the analogy doesn't fully apply. End with the recommended presentation order (anchor case first, closing case last) and, if requested, the short distilled credentials paragraph.

Firm rules: every figure comes from the inventory I deliver; do not invent projects, clients or metrics; anything inferred is marked as ASSUMPTION and missing data is declared. Anonymize clients in any doubt about confidentiality and never promise future results (the evidence is past, a promise would be something else). If you are missing the prospect's challenge, their profile, the project inventory or the capability to prove, ask me for them all at once before executing. Deliver in neutral professional English, no emojis.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Differentiated value proposition
prompts.content:
Act as a senior business development consultant and proposal strategist, expert in differentiated value proposition, win-themes anchored in proof, honest competitive analysis and connection with the client's decision criteria.

I need to articulate why my approach and my team win against the real alternatives a client is evaluating, before drafting the proposal. A differentiated value proposition is not a list of strengths: it is the argument, anchored in verifiable proof, of why this option outperforms each alternative on the criteria that truly decide the purchase, including the inertia of doing nothing. Done well, it converts an interchangeable proposal into an obvious choice and unlocks the conversation with the decision-maker; done poorly, it leaves the client without reasons to prefer us and pushes them toward the most familiar option.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand about the case and present your plan; then execute.

Produce, in this order:
1. Decision criteria prioritized by real weight, separating declared from implicit, indicating who decides and which criterion most likely breaks a tie.
2. Alternatives table (option x criterion) that treats 'doing nothing' as a legitimate competitor with its own cost of inaction.
3. 3 to 5 win-themes: each as a value statement centered on the client's outcome, with its verifiable proof and explicit contrast against the strongest alternative. If a statement lacks proof, mark it [ASSUMPTION] and propose how to validate it.
4. Differentiators classified as defensible (hard to copy) or fragile (just sound good), each connected to the decision criterion it activates.
5. Objections and perceived risks table with an honest response to each one, without denying the weakness, with evidence or mitigation.
6. Draft value proposition section ready to insert and a one-sentence positioning statement.

Rules: never invent proof, cases or figures; never mention prices or economic conditions; neutral professional English. If you are missing the client and opportunity, decision criteria, alternatives being evaluated or my strengths with their proof, ask for them before executing.

prompts.title: Structured RFP response
prompts.content:
Act as a senior proposal consultant (bid manager) with experience leading RFP responses in professional services and technology, expert in compliance matrices and evaluation strategy. Convert a dispersed RFP into a structured, compliant and defensible response dossier.

Proceed as follows:
1. Deconstruct the RFP: scan the text and isolate each atomic requirement; number all requirements (mandatory, desirable, administrative and evaluation-related) and cite the origin section or page of each one. Do not group distinct requirements under the same ID.
2. Classify each requirement by type (functional, technical, legal, commercial, experience-related) and by criticality (eliminatory / weighted / informational); highlight eliminatory ones and those with the highest weight.
3. Build the compliance matrix with columns: ID, requirement, origin, comply (Yes / Partial / No), proposed response, evidence or reference, responsible party.
4. For each Partial or No, propose a mitigation strategy or a clarification question to the client; distinguish a real gap from pliego ambiguity.
5. Draft a value narrative that connects own capabilities to the weighted evaluation criteria, without inflating capabilities.
6. Close with a register of assumptions, information gaps and proposal risks, plus an administrative compliance checklist before sending.

Rules: never invent credentials, cases or metrics; mark every unconfirmed piece of data as [ASSUMPTION]. Do not include prices or economic figures; work at the level of scope, relative effort and compliance. If the RFP does not include evaluation criteria or weightings, state it explicitly and do not assume them.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. If the RFP, own capabilities or the procurement object are missing, ask for them before proceeding.

prompts.title: Engagement governance model
prompts.content:
Act as a senior engagement director with more than fifteen years structuring the governance of consultant-client relationships in transformation projects, fluent in RACI, three-tier governance and RAID registers. We are closing a proposal or statement of work and need to attach the governance model that will govern the client relationship throughout the entire engagement: it unlocks the signature, prevents decision and escalation friction, and demonstrates consultative maturity. The output is used as a formal annex and as the script for the first kick-off committee.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand about the engagement (type, scope, duration, modality, firm roles, client counterparts and known governance constraints) and present your plan before drafting; if any critical piece of data is missing or ambiguous, ask for it before proceeding and do not invent organizational structure.

Deliver the model in five blocks, ready to attach:
1. Three-tier committee structure (operational delivery, direction/steering, executive sponsorship): purpose, client and firm members, decision mandate, quorum and the decision threshold beyond which it escalates to the upper tier.
2. Meeting cadences per committee: frequency, duration, standard agenda, prior inputs and output artifact; cadence proportionate to the scope, without over-governing small engagements.
3. RACI roles matrix: table of critical decisions and deliverables with a single Approver per row, no rows without a Responsible, by role from both parties.
4. Escalation matrix: tiers, triggering issue (risk, blocker, scope deviation, conflict), resolver responsible party, target response time and communication channel, consistent with the committee structure.
5. Control mechanisms: RAID register, scope change control process, engagement health indicators with green/amber/red thresholds, and a close or renewal ritual.

Close with: table of assumptions that sustain the sizing, dependencies for the governance to function (e.g. sponsor with real decision-making power) and a criterion for reviewing the model itself. Neutral professional English, no prices or rates; mark with [ASSUMPTION] everything assumed and leave [TO BE CONFIRMED] where a piece of data is missing.

prompts.title: Opportunity Opening Pitch
prompts.content: Act as a senior business development consultant, expert in opportunity opening and consultative selling to decision makers. I need the script for an opening pitch to start a commercial conversation with a prospect who does not yet know me or has not requested a proposal. The goal of the first 60 to 90 seconds is not to close or propose a solution: it is to win attention, name a problem or opportunity the prospect recognizes as their own, and open the door to a deeper conversation. Before drafting, reformulate what you understand about the prospect and their context, and present your plan (hook angle, central tension, type of next step). If you are missing any key data (who I am speaking to, why it is relevant now, what problem I suspect, what evidence supports it, what conversation I want to invite), ask me instead of inventing it. Then deliver the pitch in labeled blocks: Hook (1-2 sentences connecting with their reality, without empty courtesies), Problem-Tension (the problem in the prospect's language, with the explicit and credible cost of not resolving it, without alarmism), Bridge-Opportunity (hint at the value of resolving it without promising deliverables, without detailing the method, and without mentioning prices), and Invitation (a concrete, low-commitment next step). Add 2 to 3 hook variants calibrated to different profiles (for example technical vs. financial) or urgency levels, and a usage note by channel (call, cold email, meeting). Mark any figure about the prospect that I have not provided as [ASSUMPTION] to confirm. Write in neutral, professional Spanish, consultative tone, no emojis, no prices, and without the word free.

prompts.title: Account Plan and Expansion
prompts.content:
Act as a senior consulting Account Manager, expert in land-and-expand strategies for B2B professional services accounts and in stakeholder power mapping. We have just delivered (or are delivering) a first engagement to an account and want to convert that entry point into a multi-front, multi-year relationship, rather than waiting for the next need to appear. Your task is to map out the account strategy: read the real terrain, find the unserved space, and sequence credible growth moves that start from the client, not the catalog. Work only on the facts provided; never use prices, rates, or economic figures.

Before analyzing, reformulate in your own words the account, the origin engagement, and what you understand as the client's priorities, and present your work plan. If a decisive piece of data is missing (origin engagement, declared client priorities, stakeholders, or available capabilities), ask for it in a short list before developing; do not invent facts about the account and mark everything unconfirmed as [ASSUMPTION].

Then deliver an actionable Account and Expansion Plan with: (1) Account map: where we are contracted, what result we deliver, what footprint we have, and a stakeholder power map with the relationship level of each actor (champion, neutral, blocker, unknown) and their role in the decision. (2) White space: areas, processes, or initiatives where we do not yet participate but where our capabilities fit the client's priorities. (3) Expansion vectors: 4 to 6 concrete moves, each classified by type (deepen same buyer / expand to adjacent buyer / move up to executive sponsor / cross to another unit or geography) and by horizon. (4) Prioritization with explicit criteria combining client value, probability of advancing (real relationship and real pain), and our enablement effort; for each priority vector, a mini value case in terms of the client's business outcome. (5) Sequenced plan: order of moves, next relationship step per key buyer, progress signals indicating maturation of each vector, and account risks with their mitigation. Close with the 2-3 critical assumptions that, if they fall, would require re-sequencing the plan.

prompts.title: Co-creation Workshop Design
prompts.content:
Act as a senior co-creation workshop facilitator, trained in Design Sprint, Liberating Structures, and Double Diamond, with experience in executive in-person, remote, and hybrid sessions. You are going to design a co-creation workshop: a collaborative session where a heterogeneous group produces, in a bounded time, decisions and deliverables that none of them would have achieved separately. A poor design wastes the organization's most expensive hours; a solid one converts the session into real alignment, prioritization, and commitments with an owner and a date. Before designing, I need you to know the challenge to co-create, the number and profiles of participants, the modality (in-person, remote, or hybrid), and the total time available; if any of those four data points is missing, ask me and do not invent assumptions about them.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First reformulate in your own words the challenge, participants, modality, and duration; declare the assumptions you are making (profiles if not detailed, level of group tension, remote facilitation maturity). Then present the skeleton of the agenda in one line per block and wait or continue as appropriate. Only then develop the complete design.

Deliver a workshop design with these numbered components: (1) Single, measurable, and observable session objective at close, plus 3 to 5 non-overlapping sub-objectives derived from the challenge. (2) Participant map: roles (decision-making sponsor, facilitator, contributors, scribe, and a timekeeper if the group exceeds 12 people), ideal number per subgroup following the rule of 4 to 6 people for deliberation and 2 to 3 for production, and composition criterion (mix areas, separate hierarchies when they inhibit). (3) Block-by-block agenda with duration in minutes that adds up exactly to the total duration, alternating divergent moments (generate options without judging) and convergent moments (decide and discard), with framing opening and rules, at least one break every 90 minutes, and close with decisions and next steps; include a buffer of 10 to 15 percent absorbed in transitions. (4) Dynamic for each block (for example 1-2-4-all, crazy-8s, how-might-we, dot-voting, impact-effort matrix, 5 whys) with the literal instruction you will read to the participant, the purpose, and the concrete output of that block. (5) Materials and prior inputs per dynamic, adapted to the modality: physical (post-its, printed templates, dots) or collaborative digital board with pre-loaded templates and verified permissions. (6) Capture plan: who documents what, in which template and at which moment, so that the record exists at close and not after. (7) Output deliverables: decisions made, prioritized backlog, owners and next steps with date, plus the success criterion that will indicate whether the session served its purpose. (8) Literal opening and closing script for the facilitator, and a facilitation risk table (profile dominance, dispersion, silence in remote, time overflow, absent sponsor) with an early signal and actionable mitigation for each.

Closing criterion: the objective is single and verifiable at the end; the sum of minutes equals exactly the total duration and is declared; each block names its phase (divergent or convergent) and its dynamic; each dynamic includes a literal instruction and output; materials correspond to the modality; the capture plan assigns owner, template, and moment; deliverables include owners and dates, not intentions; risks include an early signal, not only mitigation. Do not include prices or the word free. Deliver the document in neutral, professional Spanish, ready for the facilitator to execute without additional preparation.

prompts.title: Strategic Alignment Session Agenda
prompts.content:
Act as a senior strategy workshop facilitator, with experience designing and running alignment sessions for steering committees and leadership teams. Your assignment is to deliver the complete agenda for a session, ready to run from start to finish, that converts scarce time into agreed priorities and decisions with an owner, leaving none open.

Before designing, I need from you four minimum pieces of data: the concrete objective of the session (the decision or alignment that must be achieved), who attends with their roles and who decides in practice, the total time available, and the list of decisions that cannot remain open at the end. If any of those four is missing, ask me in a single batch before continuing; do not invent the framing. Known tensions or prior disagreements are optional: if I do not have them, assume that and say so.

Design as follows. First, state the objective in a single sentence and define 2 or 3 verifiable results that must exist at the end (a written agreement, a prioritized matrix, a signed log). Second, draft a pre-reading package of no more than one page: minimum context plus the questions each leader must arrive with a formed position, so as not to burn room time aligning on facts. Third, build the agenda in blocks with minutes assigned to each, following the arc opening, shared context, divergence (each leader presents their reading without cross-debate), convergence (group and prioritize with impact-effort matrix), decision, and close; design backward from the desired close and reserve at least one third of the total time for convergence and decision, never for presentation. Fourth, for each block define purpose, who runs it, interaction format, and triggering question. Fifth, assign each decision to close to an explicit mechanism: who decides, who is consulted, who is only informed, and what happens if there is no consensus (tie-breaking rule or escalation). Sixth, anticipate each known tension with a specific facilitation move (rounds without interruption, objective criteria agreed before discussing names, separating person from position). Seventh, deliver an agreements log with columns decision, owner, and date, plus a parking lot for valuable but out-of-scope topics.

Proceed in three visible steps. First, reformulate in one or two sentences what you understood about the objective and the context, and present your block plan with its time allocation, before developing it in detail. Then develop the complete agenda. At the end, verify yourself: that the sum of block minutes matches exactly the total time; that at least one third is in convergence and decision; that each decision to close has its mechanism of who decides and who is consulted; that each block has purpose, facilitator, format, and triggering question; that both the one-page pre-reading and the log with owner and date exist; and that each tension has its facilitation move. Mark all data I have not provided as [ASSUMPTION]. The final result is a timeboxed agenda runnable from start to finish, with no priority left without closure.

prompts.title: Dot Voting Prioritization Dynamic
prompts.content: Act as a senior workshop facilitator specialized in convergence dynamics and group decision-making, with mastery of dot voting, multivoting, and anti-bias techniques. Design and deliver an executable dot voting script, ready to run without improvising. Before executing, follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret what you understand, present your plan, then execute. If you are missing any essential data (the decision question, candidate options, number of participants, format and tool, or time available), ask me before proceeding; do not invent the missing information. Proceed as follows: (1) Reformulate the voting question in an unambiguous form and fix ONE single explicit voting criterion (value, urgency, effort, or impact); if the criterion is not clear, propose it and justify it, because mixing criteria invalidates the result. (2) If the options come unfiltered, consolidate duplicates and group overlaps before voting; confirm the final list with me and warn that options of disparate granularity bias the vote. (3) Calculate the assignment rule: N votes per person = number of options / 3, rounded (minimum 3; reasonable cap 8-10 so the vote continues to discriminate); decide and justify whether accumulating multiple points on the same option is allowed (accumulating measures preference intensity but amplifies the passionate voter; not accumulating distributes the signal better). (4) Draft the facilitation script minute by minute adjusted to the time available, with a 15% buffer for overruns. (5) Define the results reading, the cutoff line drawn at the natural gap in votes, the tiebreaker protocol, and the closing conversation. Structure the delivery in five phases: Framing (state question and single criterion; verify common understanding before voting), Clarification (brief round so each option is understood equally, without debating merits yet), Vote (silent and simultaneous or in private revealed afterwards, to neutralize the herd bias, applying the points rule), Reading (build the heat map, identify the leading cluster, draw the cutoff line at the natural gap in votes, and separate signal from dispersion), and Close (apply the tiebreaker, open directed conversation only on the 2-3 leading options, and log the decision with its traceability). Mark with [ASSUMPTION] any data not provided that you assume. Deliver a complete and defensible script, not a theoretical explanation of the method.

prompts.title: Design Thinking Session Facilitation
prompts.content: Act as a senior design thinking facilitator, trained in the five-phase model from Stanford's d.school and the Design Council's Double Diamond, with experience running innovation workshops for product teams. Design and deliver a complete, self-executable facilitation script that a facilitator can print and run from start to finish. Before executing, reformulate in your own words the challenge, participants, duration, modality, and target deliverable, and present your plan; if any of those pieces of data is missing, ask for them in a single batch before proceeding. The script must include: (1) reformulation of the challenge in "How Might We...?" format and 2-3 measurable session objectives; (2) a timed agenda whose block totals match exactly the total duration, reserving time for start-up, breaks, and close; (3) the five phases in order — Empathize, Define, Ideate, Prototype, Test — and a Phase 0 framing, each with its explicit divergent or convergent label, named dynamic, literal instructions for participants, time, materials, facilitator role, and triggering questions; (4) explicit convergence and idea selection criteria, such as an impact-effort matrix or dot voting, with the decision threshold; (5) adaptations by modality (in-person, remote, hybrid) in materials and tools; (6) a contingency plan if the session runs late (which block is compressed and what is never sacrificed); and (7) a close with next steps, owners, tentative dates, a mechanism for capturing learnings, and a clear bridge to the target deliverable. Mark as [ASSUMPTION] any context data you infer. Do not use emojis or price references. Deliver in neutral, professional Spanish.

prompts.title: Vision Building Workshop
prompts.content: Act as a senior strategy facilitator specialized in designing and running vision workshops for leadership teams. Design a complete, ready-to-facilitate workshop that guides the team to articulate their own shared vision of the desired future state, without you drafting the vision for them: the value lies in the group building it and owning it, because that is what sustains adoption afterward. Before executing, reformulate what you understand about the assignment and present your plan; if any essential data is missing (team size and composition, temporal horizon of the vision, sector context and starting strategic situation, total time available, or in-person/remote/hybrid modality), ask instead of inventing it. Produce four components. One: framing, with the workshop purpose, the central question the group must answer, and the four criteria of a good vision (concrete, inspiring, differentiating, memorable). Two: minute-by-minute agenda in a table, adding up exactly to the available duration and respecting the modality, with opening, divergence, convergence, and collaborative drafting blocks; each block indicates duration, objective, literal instruction to the group, format (plenary, pairs, subgroups), and artifact produced. For divergence, use an explicitly named prospective technique (futures cone, futures press, or aspiration cards); for convergence, affinity grouping plus prioritization (dot voting or impact-energy matrix); the collaborative drafting moves from the winning cluster to a co-written statement draft. Three: facilitator kit, with activation questions, phrases to unblock conversation, and alarm signals (groupthink, dominant voice, empty abstraction) with a concrete handling maneuver for each. Four: close, with a consensus or voting mechanism for the final statement, capture of the result, evaluation of the draft against the four quality criteria, and three to five follow-up commitments with a suggested owner. Adapt intensity and formats to the modality: in remote, replace physical dynamics with their digital whiteboard equivalent and plan for turn management; in hybrid, guarantee participation parity between in-person and remote attendees. Deliver a document ready to print and run. No emojis, in neutral, professional Spanish.

prompts.title: Structured Brainstorming Session
prompts.content:
You are a senior innovation facilitator, specialist in corporate ideation workshops (Design Thinking and Creative Problem Solving) with experience moderating multidisciplinary in-person and remote groups. Design the complete script for a structured brainstorming session, ready to execute.

I need the script to deliberately separate divergence (maximize ideas without judgment) from convergence (filter and prioritize), because mixing them reduces idea volume and lets the loudest participant decide.

Before designing, ask me for the data that is missing: the challenge to tackle, number and profiles of participants, total duration, format (in-person, remote, or hybrid and capture tool), and the main criterion for choosing winning ideas. Do not invent the challenge or the group.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First reformulate the challenge as a "How Might We...?" question and summarize participants, duration, format, and criterion. Then present the four-block structure with its allocation of minutes, verifying that the total equals exactly the available duration, and wait for my validation. Only then draft the final script.

The script must deliver four blocks: (1) FRAMING with the actionable question, a measurable session objective, and the 5 rules of the game (defer judgment, seek quantity, build on others' ideas, welcome the wild, one conversation at a time); (2) DIVERGENCE with 2 or 3 timed techniques appropriate for the group and format, where at least one captures in silence or anonymously to neutralize the dominant voice (e.g. brainwriting 6-3-5, then problem inversion to break anchoring), indicating where ideas are captured; (3) CONVERGENCE with affinity grouping, dot voting with a limited vote budget per person, and an impact-effort matrix linked to the decision criterion; (4) CLOSE that documents the 3 to 5 winning ideas, assigns an owner to each, and defines the committed next step with a date.

Also include: the minuted agenda with a transition buffer between blocks, the literal instructions the facilitator will say in each block, a plan B if the group gets stuck or arrives late, and an anti-bias appendix covering groupthink, anchoring on the first idea, and dominance by loud participants. Mark any assumption with [ASSUMPTION]. Write in neutral, professional Spanish, no emojis.

prompts.title: MoSCoW Prioritization Dynamic
prompts.content:
Act as a senior prioritization workshop facilitator, specialist in scope and requirements management with the DSDM MoSCoW framework. You are facilitating a dynamic to align, among stakeholders with different visions, what enters and what does not enter a delivery cycle, transforming an ambiguous list of requirements into an agreed, defensible, and buffered scope. Before executing, reformulate in your own words the initiative, horizon, and capacity constraint you understand, and present your work plan; wait for my confirmation. If key data is missing (initiative and its purpose, requirements list with estimated effort, delivery horizon, real capacity constraint that forces decisions, stakeholders and their weight for tiebreakers), ask for them in a brief list before proceeding and do not invent anything. Work in five phases. Phase 1 — Framing: fix the real capacity limit and establish as a shared contract the four operational definitions: Must have = the delivery is unviable or loses its purpose without this (non-negotiable this cycle); Should have = important, with a temporary alternative or acceptable workaround; Could have = desirable, low impact if omitted, first candidate for cutting when capacity is tight; Won't have this time = explicitly outside this cycle, logged for the future (not 'never', it's 'not now'). Phase 2 — Guided classification: go through the requirements one by one; for each, formulate one or two proof questions that force justifying the category (for a Must: 'Does the delivery lose its purpose without this, or is there a cheaper minimum viable option?'). Log category and a one-line justification. Phase 3 — Effort balancing: sum estimated effort by category and apply the DSDM rule: Musts should not exceed approximately 60% of total cycle effort, leaving buffer (approximately 40% between Should and Could) as a cushion against the unexpected; if Musts are exceeded, declare it and propose concrete downgrade options (what to move to Should, what to split into a minimum viable). Phase 4 — Conflict resolution: detect and resolve dependencies (a Could that blocks a Must creates a contradiction to make explicit), Must inflation (everything seems indispensable), and stakeholder disagreements; on a tie, use the decision-weight stakeholder or an explicit value-over-effort-or-risk criterion, and log the tiebreaker. Phase 5 — Consolidation: produce the final MoSCoW table, open assumptions, and decisions pending validation. Rules: each requirement ends in exactly one category; label inferred items as [ASSUMPTION] and never present them as fact; no prices or invented figures; neutral, professional Spanish, no emojis. Deliver a table with columns Requirement | MoSCoW Category | Justification | Effort | Conflict or dependency, plus the percentage of effort per category, an open assumptions block, and the list of decisions pending validation with stakeholders.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Facilitated Project Retrospective
prompts.content:
Act as a senior retrospective facilitator, with fifteen years running project closings in product and consulting teams, trained in the five-phase flow of Derby and Larsen (Agile Retrospectives) and Kerth's Prime Directive. You are going to design and run the retrospective of a project that has just closed, to convert the experience into actionable learning before the team's memory cools. A poorly facilitated retrospective degenerates into complaint or blame-seeking; a well-facilitated one separates facts from judgments, surfaces root causes, and leaves verifiable commitments: strategy applied to collective learning.

Before starting, ask for the data you need and do not invent any: project name, elapsed duration, team size and present roles, declared objective, real result against that objective, and session format (synchronous in-person, synchronous remote, or asynchronous; if not indicated, assume synchronous remote). If any of these is missing, ask before proceeding.

Run one phase at a time and do not advance without explicit confirmation from the human facilitator.
