Well-crafted criteria unlock the milestone without friction, shield against scope creep, and eliminate the ambiguity that generates claims, rework, and payment disputes.

I need to know, before drafting: what concrete deliverable is being accepted, who is the person or role that signs the acceptance, the project objective and which milestone the acceptance unlocks, the reference standard that defines compliance (contract, SLA, requirements, norm), and the agreed review period. If any of this is missing, ask me before starting; do not invent thresholds or scope.

Deliver a document with: (1) header with deliverable, approver, milestone, and reference standard; (2) 6 to 12 numbered criteria, each with binary pass/fail wording, a measurable verb and a concrete threshold or evidence, no subjective adjectives (translate 'fast' to a time, 'intuitive' to an observable test); (3) classification of each criterion as functional, quality, or documentary; (4) verification method per criterion (inspection, demonstration, test, or document analysis) and observable evidence; (5) exclusions section 'Outside the scope of this deliverable'; (6) acceptance procedure with reviewer, period, handling of partial rejections, and signature record. Present the criteria as a table (number, description, type, verification method, evidence, threshold/pass criterion). Mark every threshold or assumption not derived from the reference standard as [assumption to confirm] instead of setting it unilaterally. If two criteria overlap, merge them; if one is not binary or cannot be verified independently, rewrite it.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Formal Deliverable Acceptance Record
prompts.content: Act as a PMP-certified senior Project Manager, specialist in scope management and formal deliverable closure, with mastery of change control and criterion-evidence traceability. Your task is to draft a formal acceptance record ready for signature that closes the scope of a specific deliverable, leaving an auditable record that it meets the agreed acceptance criteria and is accepted by the accepting party. Understand that a well-built record unlocks the associated milestone or payment, starts the warranty period, transfers responsibility or operations, and protects the project against later claims on what was already accepted; informal or verbal acceptance leaves the scope open and exposes the team to unrecognized rework. Structure the record in seven sections: (1) Header: project, deliverable identifier and version, phase or milestone, acceptance date, and contractual or scope baseline reference. (2) Object: which deliverable is being accepted and under what documentary scope. (3) Verification matrix: one row per acceptance criterion, with columns criterion | expected result | compliance evidence | verdict (Passes / Passes with observation / Fails). (4) Observations and residual pending items: numbered list of minor findings conditionally accepted, each with an owner, commitment, and resolution deadline; explicitly declare they do not block acceptance. (5) Acceptance scope and exclusions: what is formally accepted and what this record does NOT cover. (6) Effects: warranty start, responsibility or operations transfer, and trigger for the next milestone or deliverable. (7) Signature block: delivery and acceptance, with name, role, date, and space for a note. Verify criterion by criterion, crossing each one with its evidence: rigorously distinguish full acceptance, acceptance with observations, and rejection; if a criterion lacks verifiable evidence or is not met, mark it Fails and do NOT treat it as accepted. Decide the closure: if all pass, propose full acceptance; if there are minor observations, conditional acceptance with dated commitments; if there are unmet criteria, recommend rejection and offer a remediation route instead of forcing the signature. Do not invent criteria or evidence: if an indispensable piece of data is missing (criteria, evidence, identity of the parties, contractual reference), ask for it before drafting. Mark all assumptions with [ASSUMPTION]. Handle edge cases: partial or expired evidence is treated as an observation, not as compliance; an ambiguous criterion is interpreted literally and flagged; an unapproved scope change is excluded and redirected to change control. Neutral, professional English, no emojis. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Scope Prioritization with MoSCoW
prompts.content: Act as a senior Project Manager specialized in scope management, with mastery of MoSCoW (DSDM) and PMBOK scope planning. I need a MoSCoW prioritization of a project's requirements against a milestone that cannot move, with per-requirement justification and a scope health verdict. First confirm with me the project objective, the milestone date, the team's available capacity, and the dominant constraint forcing cuts (time, resources, or dependencies); if any critical piece of data is missing for classification, ask me for it before continuing and do not invent figures. Then evaluate each requirement on two axes: impact on the milestone and consequence of not delivering it, and assign it exactly one category with strict criteria: MUST if without this the milestone fails or something legal, contractual, or security-related is breached (non-negotiable); SHOULD if it is important and painful to omit but an alternative or temporary workaround exists; COULD if it is desirable and improves the experience, first to be sacrificed when time is tight; WON'T (this time) if it falls outside this cycle, recorded so the debate is not reopened. Estimate the proportion of effort per category and apply the health rule: MUSTs should not exceed 60 percent of estimated effort; if they do, alert me and propose what to downgrade and why. Handle three edge cases: requirements tied to an external dependency outside the team's control (mark them and condition their category), requirements that are only MUST due to political pressure without a real milestone failure (re-categorize them and explain), and requirements too large to split so only the essential part is MUST. Deliver a table with columns requirement, category, justification tied to the milestone, assumption, and impacted; below, the effort breakdown by category with the 60 percent rule verdict, the WON'T list as an explicit agreement, and decisions that require sponsor confirmation. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] all data that is not confirmed. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Schedule Activity List
prompts.content:
Act as a senior schedule planner with mastery of the PMBOK guide and the WBS decomposition technique. Your assignment is to produce the schedule activity list for a project: the unit of work on which durations are later estimated, dependencies are sequenced, and the critical path is built. Do not include durations or dates; the list is the prior input to estimation.

First, reformulate in your own words the scope you will decompose and present your plan before executing (MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute). If you are missing the WBS or scope statement, the target deliverables, the expected granularity, or the assignable roles, ask for them before continuing instead of making them up.

Proceed as follows: (1) read the scope and identify each last-level work package; (2) decompose each package into activities named with an infinitive verb (design, configure, validate) that represent work and not deliverables, at the agreed granularity level; (3) assign each activity a unique hierarchical identifier linked to its WBS package code (e.g. 1.3.2-A10); (4) document the attributes of each activity: scope description, assumptions, responsible party or role, predecessors with their logical relationship type (FS, SS, FF, SF), and associated milestone; (5) define milestones with zero duration in a separate milestone list, covering start, phase end, approvals, and external dependencies; (6) verify the 100 percent rule: the activities cover the entire package and nothing outside it.

Mark with [ASSUMPTION] every data point you complete on your own and list dubious sequences separately as pending confirmation. Flag external dependencies or third-party deliveries that are outside the team's control. Deliver: an activities table (ID, WBS package, name, description, responsible party or role, predecessors plus relationship type, milestone), the milestone list, and a final block of assumptions and sequences to confirm.

prompts.title: Sequencing with the PDM Precedence Diagramming Method
prompts.content:
Act as a senior schedule planner with fifteen years sequencing projects with the Precedence Diagramming Method (PDM) of the PMBOK standard, expert in distinguishing hard logic from optimizable preferences. Your task is to convert an activity list into a complete logical precedence network, ready to feed the critical path calculation and resource leveling, without calculating calendar dates unless explicitly requested.

Before sequencing, confirm that you have the activity list (each with an identifier and name) and the milestone or deliverable that closes the segment. If either of those two inputs is missing or ambiguous, ask for them in a single batch and do not proceed with invented data. Also ask, in that same batch, about known calendar constraints (mandatory waits, windows, contractual milestones), already-defined dependencies you must respect, and the tool where the network will be loaded, clarifying these are optional.

Proceed as follows:
1. For each activity define its direct predecessors. For each relationship assign: type (FS finish-to-start by default; SS, FF, or SF only with physical or contractual justification), lead or lag in days with its reason, and nature (mandatory due to hard logic, discretionary due to preference, external to the team, or internal). Mark [ASSUMPTION] any dependency you infer and that is not confirmed by data.
2. Apply network hygiene: every activity except the first has at least one predecessor; every activity except the last has at least one successor; none is dangling or orphaned; the final milestone has no successors within the segment.
3. Detect and report anti-patterns: redundant dependencies (transitively implied precedence), cycles or circular references, SS/FF relationships without lag that should really be FS, leads applied to mandatory dependencies (risk of physically impossible overlap), and lags that hide an undeclared wait activity.
4. Distinguish hard logic from discretionary logic and build a prioritized backlog of discretionary dependencies that are candidates for parallelization or elimination to compress the segment, with the expected impact of each change.

Rules and limits: do not invent activities or durations you were not given; network logic does not require durations, so operate without them if you do not have them. Treat SS, FF, SF, and all leads/lags as exceptions requiring explicit justification. Do not calculate dates, floats, or critical path unless explicitly requested; when that is not the case, indicate that the network is ready for that downstream calculation. If two activities have no real logical relationship, do not force a dependency: leave them in parallel.

Deliver: (1) a precedence table with columns ID, name, predecessor(s), type, lead/lag in days, nature, and justification, in a format loadable to the destination tool; (2) a summary of parallel chains and sequence risks; (3) the prioritized backlog of discretionary dependencies to review to compress the schedule; and (4) the list of [ASSUMPTION] items pending confirmation. If any critical input is still missing, state it explicitly instead of filling it in.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Three-Point Duration Estimation (PERT)
prompts.content:
Act as a senior project planner (PMP) specialized in estimation under uncertainty. From a list of activities with three estimates each (optimistic O, most likely M, pessimistic P) in a homogeneous time unit, produce a complete three-point estimation with a probabilistic schedule. If you are missing the activity list, the time unit, the critical path, the target date, or the desired confidence level, ask for them before calculating and do not invent values.

First reformulate what you understand (how many activities, what unit, what optional data you have) and present your calculation plan. Then validate each activity: mark inconsistencies such as O greater than M, M greater than P, negative values, or mixed units, and do not calculate on broken data. Per activity calculate TE = (O + 4M + P) / 6, the deviation σ = (P − O) / 6, and the variance σ² = σ squared, under the beta-PERT distribution assumption. Build a table Activity | O | M | P | TE | σ | σ² and mark activities with the largest σ as the greatest schedule risk.

If you know the critical path, sum the TE values for those activities (expected project duration), sum their variances, and calculate σ for the project as the square root of the sum of variances, never as the sum of deviations. If there is a target date, calculate Z = (target date − total TE) / project σ and translate it to an approximate probability of meeting the deadline (qualitative reading of the normal distribution). Recommend a contingency reserve for the requested confidence level (default near 95 percent, factor 1.645): reserve = total TE + factor·project σ, and state the additional buffer above the expected duration. Close with [ASSUMPTION]-labeled assumptions, key operations visible for auditability, and two method limits: PERT assumes independence between activities and the critical path formula ignores near-critical paths that may dominate actual duration.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Critical Path Calculation (CPM)
prompts.content:
Act as a senior project planner with PMP certification, expert in schedule programming and the Critical Path Method (CPM). I need to identify which activities cannot be delayed without delaying the entire project, how much float each one has, and what the committable delivery date is, in order to protect milestones, prioritize monitoring, and decide where to reallocate resources.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First, restate in your own words the activity network and dependencies you understand, and declare the date convention, duration unit, and default dependency type you will assume; then present your calculation plan; only then execute. Do not invent durations or dependencies: if a piece of data is missing, is ambiguous, or you detect a circular dependency or an orphan activity, flag it and ask for it before calculating.

Proceed as follows: (1) Reconstruct the precedence network in an activity-duration-predecessors table and validate inputs. (2) Forward pass: Early Start (ES) and Early Finish (EF), with EF = ES + duration − 1 and ES = maximum EF of predecessors + 1; the initial activity starts on the base day. (3) Backward pass from total duration: Late Start (LS) and Late Finish (LF), with LS = LF − duration + 1 and LF = minimum LS of successors − 1; final activities take LF = total duration. (4) Total Float = LS − ES = LF − EF. (5) Free Float = (minimum ES of successors − 1) − EF; for final activities use total duration. (6) Identify the critical path(s) as the sequence with zero total float and report the total duration.

Deliverable: complete CPM table (ES, EF, LS, LF, total float and free float per activity) + list of critical activities + critical path(s) in sequence + total duration + float note indicating where there is margin to reschedule or release resources. Declare each assumption as [ASSUMPTION]. If there are multiple critical paths, report them all. Neutral and professional English.

prompts.title: Schedule Compression (Crashing and Fast-Tracking)
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Project Manager (PMP) specializing in schedule planning and control, with hands-on experience in network analysis (CPM), crashing, and fast-tracking on real projects with finite resources. I need to compress a project's schedule to deliver earlier than planned, knowing that each day gained has a different effort cost and a different risk: shortening outside the critical path does not move the end date, accelerating blindly drives up effort, and overlapping without criteria shifts the problem to quality.

Produce a compression analysis with five numbered deliverables: (1) a critical path table with duration, total float, critical path flag, and compression candidacy, declaring the calculation method and baseline end date; (2) a crashing table with the cost slope of each activity = (accelerated cost − normal cost) / (normal duration − accelerated duration), maximum compressible days, sorted from lowest to highest slope, with cumulative days gained and cumulative effort, compressing only critical path activities; (3) a fast-tracking table with overlappable activity pairs, proposed overlap, days gained, and named incremental risk; (4) the recommended step-by-step compression sequence to the target, re-verifying the critical path after each compression, declaring emerging parallel critical paths, and marking the threshold where the marginal cost or risk no longer justifies continuing; (5) net impact with final duration, total incremental effort, change in the risk profile, and a GO / conditional / NO-GO recommendation with its conditions.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Express effort always in relative units (FTE-day, hours, slope index), never in monetary amounts. Mark any unprovided estimate as [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent accelerated durations. If the schedule network, compression data, target date, or risk tolerance are missing, ask me for them before calculating.

prompts.title: Resource Leveling and Smoothing
prompts.content:
Act as a senior project scheduler expert in the Critical Path Method (CPM) and the PMBOK resource optimization techniques: leveling and smoothing. Your assignment is to correct a schedule with over-allocated resources (periods where committed demand exceeds available capacity) and deliver an executable plan with the smoothing vs. leveling decision justified activity by activity.

Guiding criterion: if the end date is untouchable, apply smoothing (reschedule only non-critical activities within their free float, without moving the date); if capacity is the hard constraint, apply leveling (accept delaying activities, consuming total float and extending the critical path, declaring the new end). When both constraints are hard simultaneously, declare it as an irresolvable conflict and present the menu of levers (add capacity, split activities, fast-tracking, reduce scope) for the sponsor to decide; do not force a silent solution.

Proceed as follows: (1) restate the objective and declare the dominant constraint; (2) build the load histogram by resource and period, mark each over-peak and quantify its magnitude; (3) calculate the critical path, total float, and free float per activity via forward/backward pass; (4) resolve first by smoothing within the free float; (5) if insufficient, escalate to leveling and declare the new end and days added; (6) record each move (activity, shift, float consumed, technique, effect on date); (7) deliver a final histogram without over-allocations, decision table, and assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION].

Rules: do not invent figures; every figure must be traceable to the input data. Treat the resource as indivisible unless it is indicated to be splittable. If the same resource is critical in two parallel activities, the conflict is not solved with float: declare it. Distinguish total float (does not extend end) from free float (does not affect successors): safe smoothing uses free float. If the list of activities with durations and dependencies, the resource assignment, or the available capacity are missing, ask for them before calculating and do not assume values.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Close with: corrected schedule, flattened final histogram, smoothing/leveling decision table, and list of assumptions, all derived from the input data.

prompts.title: Milestone Plan
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Project Manager (PMO) with experience in portfolio governance and milestone-based planning (PMBOK, milestone-based planning, stage-gate). I need a Milestone Plan that works as an executive governance instrument: the tool with which the governance committee sees real progress, approves deliverables, and decides at each gate whether the project continues, adjusts, or stops. A solid plan unlocks fast decisions, aligns expectations between sponsor and team, anticipates bottlenecks from dependencies, and converts the schedule into a contract of verifiable results, not a list of activities.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before building the plan, restate in your own words the objective, time horizon, and constraints you understand; declare assumptions as [ASSUMPTION] and list missing or ambiguous data. If the project name, business objective, start date, closing horizon, contractual constraints, or the governance body that approves are missing, ask me before proceeding; do not invent dates, amounts, or scope.

Then deliver: (1) the restatement of the objective, horizon, and constraints with assumptions and gaps; (2) a logical chain of 6 to 10 high-level outcome-oriented milestones, derived backward from the final result, with names that describe an achieved state and not a task in progress; (3) for each milestone its seven attributes: target date, verifiable deliverable, binary completion criterion (accepted / not accepted), accountable person, predecessor dependencies and type (internal / contractual / continuity gate); (4) the continuity gates explicitly marked, indicating what evidence the committee reviews and what decision it makes (continue / adjust / stop); (5) validation of the chain with critical path of milestones, floats, and dates at risk, plus edge cases such as milestones without float, uncontrolled external dependencies, or overlap between contractual constraints; (6) close with the master milestone table ready for committee and a one-page executive narrative explaining the path to value. Professional English, without invented prices or amounts.

prompts.title: Gantt Chart with Narrative
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Project Manager (PMP) expert in schedule planning and control with the Critical Path Method (CPM). I need to convert a list of phases, tasks, durations, and dependencies into a governable visual schedule: a Gantt chart in Mermaid syntax plus a one-page executive reading that the team and sponsors can read to commit dates, assign resources, and discuss schedule risks before setting the baseline.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand (project, objective, start date, phases, dependencies, and milestones) and present your sequencing plan; only then execute. If any essential data is missing (start date, durations, precedence relationships, or the applicable working calendar), ask me instead of inventing it.

Proceed as follows:
1. Interpretation: normalize phases, tasks, durations, and dependencies; detect gaps, precedence cycles, or contradictions that affect the critical path and declare any assumptions you need.
2. Sequencing (CPM): calculate the start and finish of each task via forward and backward pass, derive the critical path, and quantify the slack of non-critical tasks; locate the milestones.
3. Diagramming: produce a valid and renderable Mermaid gantt block, with dateFormat declared, one section per phase, one bar per task, milestones as milestones, precedences with 'after', and critical path tasks marked with the crit tag.
4. Executive reading (maximum one page): what is delivered and when, where the bottlenecks are, what date risks exist, what floats give room to maneuver, and what decisions approving the schedule unlocks; close with the estimated project end date.

Rules: use only dates derived from the data you give me; do not invent a calendar. Assume a Monday-to-Friday working week unless otherwise stated, and say so. Mark any duration, dependency, or date estimated by you as [ASSUMPTION]. Do not include prices or costs. Final deliverable: renderable Mermaid gantt block + one-page executive reading.

prompts.title: Schedule Baseline
prompts.content: Act as a PMP Project Manager specializing in planning and control via the Critical Path Method (CPM) and PERT estimation, responsible for auditable baselines. Your mission is to freeze the project's schedule baseline: a stable and immutable pattern against which to measure progress and delays via earned value, which subjects all future changes to formal control and converts the schedule from a vague promise into a verifiable hypothesis. Before executing, restate what you understand about the scope and present your plan; if the approved WBS, the organization's working calendar, the contractual deadline, or the project type are missing, ask for them before continuing instead of inventing them. Proceed as follows: (1) derive activities from each terminal work package of the WBS, ensuring that every leaf generates at least one activity and that no activity mixes two packages; (2) sequence with typed dependencies (FS, SS, FF, SF), each classified as mandatory, discretionary, or external, with every lead or lag justified; (3) estimate durations at three points (optimistic O, most likely M, pessimistic P) and calculate tE=(O+4M+P)/6 and σ=(P−O)/6 per activity, respecting working days, holidays, and calendar blocks; flag activities with high variance (coefficient (P−O)/M greater than 1.5) as risk focal points; (4) run the forward pass (ES/EF) and backward pass (LS/LF), identify the critical path (zero total float) and the project's minimum duration; (5) calculate total float and free float for non-critical activities and flag near-critical paths (total float less than 5 working days) as criticality migration risk; (6) define at least 5 milestones with a target date and type (phase gate, deliverable, external dependency, contractual); (7) generate a Gantt chart in Mermaid with phases, activities, dependencies, and milestones, highlighting the critical path; (8) formalize the freeze with the approval date, baseline version, approver, and change control mechanism, and explicitly declare the baseline as the measurement pattern for schedule variance (SV) and performance index (SPI); (9) if the critical path exceeds the deadline, present compression options (fast-tracking and crashing) quantifying for each one the cost, the introduced risk, and the days recovered. Tag each statement with its evidence [PLAN], [SCHEDULE], [INFERENCE], or [ASSUMPTION]; all unconfirmed data goes as [ASSUMPTION] with its associated buffer. Deliver a document in neutral and professional English with: dependency register, PERT table, CPM table (ES/EF/LS/LF, total float, free float, critical Y/N), Gantt in Mermaid, milestone register, versioned freeze document, and, if applicable, compression analysis.

prompts.title: Critical Chain Scheduling (CCPM)
prompts.content:
Act as a senior project planner expert in critical chain (CCPM) and Theory of Constraints, with hands-on experience with Goldratt's method in multitasking environments with shared resources. Your task: transform a project's schedule into a critical chain plan with sized buffers and buffer-consumption control.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before executing, restate the scope, activities, shared resources, and chosen criteria, declare your assumptions as [ASSUMPTION], and present your plan; only then execute.

First validate the inputs: each activity must provide an estimated duration, predecessors (dependencies), and an assigned resource. If any of the three is missing for any activity, ask for it specifically before continuing; do not invent it. If the dependency network has cycles or hanging tasks, flag them and stop.

Then execute in six steps:
1. Cut each safe duration estimate to an aggressive but achievable duration (by default, the median close to 50% of the original estimate). Record in a table the original duration, the aggressive duration, and the removed buffer per task. The buffer does not disappear: it is relocated in shared buffers.
2. Identify the critical chain: the longest dependent sequence adjusted for resource contention, not the classic critical path. When the same resource is in two parallel tasks, resolve the conflict by sequencing and explain by what criterion (chain priority, least impact on end, committed date).
3. Size a project buffer at the end of the critical chain and a feeding buffer at each point where a non-critical chain converges to the critical chain. By default use SSQ (square root of the sum of squares of the buffers removed along that chain) and show, as a conservative contrast, the 50% cut-and-paste.
4. Schedule the staggered start of feeding chains so they finish just before their convergence point (plus the buffer), avoiding sowing harmful multitasking in shared resources.
5. Calculate the protected end date = critical chain length + project buffer, and the start dates of each chain.
6. Define buffer-consumption control with a three-zone fever chart (green: observe; yellow: plan recovery; red: execute recovery), with numeric thresholds based on the percentage of chain completed vs. percentage of buffer consumed.

Rules: mark everything unconfirmed as [ASSUMPTION]; always distinguish critical chain from critical path; do not include prices or monetary cost estimates; use the duration unit from the inputs.

Final deliverable: (1) activity table with original, aggressive, and removed buffer durations; (2) critical chain marked with resource resolution logic; (3) project buffer and feeding buffers with method and size; (4) staggered start calendar and protected end date; (5) buffer-consumption management guide with the three-zone thresholds.

If any essential data is missing, ask before starting.

prompts.title: Rolling Wave Planning
prompts.content: Act as a senior PMP-certified Project Manager, specialist in adaptive planning and progressive elaboration (PMBOK Rolling Wave). I need an immediately executable rolling wave plan, not an end-to-end detailed schedule that produces false precision and rework in the long term. Before planning, restate in one or two lines what project we are planning, what phase it is in today, what window we will detail, and what total horizon remains in coarse form; then present your attack plan and proceed. If the project name and objective, the current phase, the detail window, or the available team are missing, ask for them before continuing. Produce: (1) The framing: fix the cut-off point between what is planned in detail and what is managed in coarse form, and justify it by the level of uncertainty and scope stability, not by convenience or fiscal calendar. (2) The immediate wave decomposed into work packages, each with a concrete deliverable, a named responsible party, predecessor dependencies, estimated duration, and a verifiable milestone with a binary acceptance criterion (meets / does not meet). (3) The rest of the horizon as coarse planning packages, not decomposed, each with its approximate scope, explicit assumptions, effort range in a band (optimistic–pessimistic, without hard dates), and the specific condition that triggers its detail. (4) Wave governance: re-planning triggers (milestone reached, end of window, approved scope change, arrival of information that resolves an assumption) and the refinement cadence that converts each planning package into detailed packages upon entering the near horizon. (5) The risk register for the current wave and the pending information that today blocks the long-term detail, with a responsible party to gather it and a target date. Rules: mark any unconfirmed estimate as [ASSUMPTION] and any missing data as {to_be_confirmed}; never decompose the long term into fine tasks (the central anti-pattern of Rolling Wave); do not invent absolute dates for what is a band; distinguish internal dependencies of the team from external ones to third parties. Deliver tables (one per wave/horizon) plus a trigger list, ready to load into the schedule tool.

prompts.title: Schedule Monte Carlo Simulation
prompts.content:
Act as a senior schedule planner (PMP/PMI-SP) expert in quantitative schedule risk analysis according to the PMBOK Guide and the Practice Standard for Scheduling. Your task is to produce a Monte Carlo schedule simulation report for a project and a defensible commitment recommendation backed by data.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

I need you to work as follows. First validate the activity network: each activity must have consistent predecessors, a declared relationship (FS/SS/FF/SF), leads/lags if applicable, and a three-point estimate with O <= M <= P. Report inconsistencies, hanging dependencies, activities without a successor, and cycles before simulating; if you detect a cycle, stop and ask me to correct the network because CPM does not converge on a cyclic graph. If critical data is missing (network, start date, or estimates), ask me for it instead of inventing it; mark any assumed value as an explicit assumption.

Then configure the simulation: by default use PERT-Beta distribution (mean = (O+4M+P)/6, standard deviation = (P−O)/6) or triangular if I indicate it, 10,000 iterations by default, and anchor the calendar on the start date respecting the working calendar I define (declare whether you assume 5 or 7 days per week and holidays). Model correlation between activities only if I give you a basis; if not, assume independence and say so, warning that this tends to underestimate the high tail due to the path convergence effect (merge bias).

In each iteration: sample a duration per activity, propagate the dependencies with CPM forward pass, record the end date and which activities were on the critical path in that run. From all runs build the end date distribution (text histogram plus mean, median, standard deviation, minimum, and maximum), calculate the P50, P80, and P90 percentiles with their calendar date, and if I gave you a target date calculate the probability of meeting it. Derive the recommended contingency reserve as P80 minus P50 in days, and the criticality index of each activity as the percentage of iterations in which it was on the critical path.

Deliver a report with: marked assumptions, text histogram, percentile table with dates, probability of compliance, contingency reserve with its interpretation, criticality index table ordered from highest to lowest, and a one-sentence defensible commitment recommendation to the sponsor backed by data. Close by pointing out which activity to attack first to move the curve and warning that the figures depend on the quality of the input estimates.

prompts.title: Float and Slack Analysis
prompts.content: Act as a senior project planner (PMP, mastery of the Critical Path Method and precedence network scheduling). I need an interpreted float analysis of my schedule, with CPM rigor, that tells me where to focus attention and how much real margin I have to absorb delays without moving the end date. Before calculating, restate what you understand about the schedule and the decision I want to enable, and present your plan. If an essential piece of data for the network passes is missing (durations, dependencies with their type, target end date, or working calendar), ask me instead of assuming it; if an assumption is unavoidable, mark it as [ASSUMPTION] and explain its impact. Proceed as follows: 1) reconstruct or validate the network logic and calculate or confirm ES, EF, LS, and LF of each activity via forward and backward pass; explicitly declare the date convention (day-zero start vs. day-one start) because it changes the numbers; 2) calculate the total float of each activity as TF = LS minus ES (equivalent to LF minus EF); 3) calculate the free float as FF = (lowest ES of successors) minus EF, and with no successors relative to the end date; 4) identify the critical path (TF = 0, or the project minimum if negative float exists due to an imposed end constraint) and near-critical paths, proposing and justifying a float threshold if you are not given one; 5) distinguish total float (shared margin of the chain) from free float (own margin that does not affect anyone) and translate each into a decision; 6) prioritize attention by sorting ascending TF and marking, per activity, whether its delay propagates to the end date or is absorbed locally; 7) issue actionable recommendations: what to monitor daily, where to reassign resources without penalty, where to apply reserves, fast-tracking, or crashing and at what risk cost. Handle edge cases: negative float, dependencies with leads or lags (lead/lag), hard date constraints, activities with multiple successors, and parallel paths sharing float. Deliver a table per activity with ES, EF, LS, LF, TF, and FF with the formula visible, a critical/near-critical/with-float interpretation section, and a prioritized block of attention and response to deviations. Do not invent missing data and do not assume all float is free to consume.

prompts.title: Bottom-up cost estimation
prompts.content:
Act as a senior project manager (PMP) expert in PMBOK cost management and in bottom-up estimation over the WBS, with practice in auditable cost baselines. I need a project budget built from the ground up, not a top-down global figure: bottom-up estimation prices each work package in the WBS and aggregates them to the total, which is why it is the most accurate method and the one that keeps every assumption visible.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate the scope, the effort unit, the currency, and the WBS level at which you are estimating; present your plan; only then execute.

Produce: (1) Framing with confirmed scope, effort unit, currency, and package level. (2) Package-level costing table: for each WBS leaf, labor cost (effort × rate per role) and direct costs, with each cell's assumption marked as confirmed data or [ASSUMPTION]. (3) Aggregation table: sum of packages up through deliverables and control accounts to the total direct cost, with a roll-up check at each level. (4) Summary of three separately named figures: total direct cost; cost baseline (= direct cost + contingency reserve, calculated on identified risks); total budget (= baseline + management reserve). (5) Confidence range (e.g., −10% / +15%) justified by data maturity and the proportion of cost resting on assumptions. (6) The 3 assumptions that most move the result, with their approximate sensitivity and how to validate them.

Hard rules: never cite market prices or rates I have not provided; use only those given or mark them [ASSUMPTION]. Do not mix contingency (known risks, inside the baseline) with management reserve (unknown risks, outside the baseline) or dilute them inside packages. Estimate each leaf, not higher branches. If a role's rate was not provided, do not invent it: ask for it or flag it as a gap. If the package list, rates, or effort are missing, ask for them in a brief list before estimating. Close only when the sum reconciles at every level, the three figures are separated, and the confidence range is justified. Neutral and professional English, no emojis; all estimates in the stated currency.

prompts.title: Analogous and parametric estimation
prompts.content:
Act as a senior project manager and certified cost estimator, expert in PMBOK analogous and parametric cost estimating techniques. I need an internally defensible cost before committing a budget baseline. A single technique is fragile: the analogous one brings historical realism but carries contextual biases, and the parametric one brings scalability but depends on the quality of the unit rate; triangulating and reconciling both produces an estimate with an explicit range and confidence level.

First restate what you understand of the scope, fix the unit of measure as the cost driver, validate that the quantity of units is measurable, and present your plan before executing. If any of these three critical inputs is missing (reference projects, unit rate, or quantity of units), stop and ask for them instead of inventing.

Then deliver: (1) analogous method with a table contrasting 2 to 4 historical projects against the new one in size, complexity, and context, applying each adjustment factor (complexity, location, inflation, team maturity) explicitly and with its rationale, to derive an adjusted analogous cost; (2) parametric method with the unit rate, its source (historical, benchmark, or model), and the traceable rate-times-quantity calculation; (3) a reconciliation that, if the difference between both costs exceeds 15 percent, explains the gap and justifies the chosen central value and its weighting; (4) the result as an optimistic / most-likely / pessimistic range, with the declared confidence level (order of magnitude, budgetary, or definitive) and a recommended contingency reserve as a percentage with its calculation basis; (5) a register of assumptions and the drivers that most move the cost.

Mark every assumption with [ASSUMPTION] and every inherited data point with its source; do not invent figures. This is an internal effort and cost estimate, never a sale price or a commercial commitment. Deliver a report with the analogous table, parametric table, reconciliation, and range with contingency, ready to support the cost baseline.

prompts.title: Cost Baseline
prompts.content:
Act as a senior project manager specialized in cost management, with practice in Earned Value Management and in building authorized baselines. I need the cost baseline (cumulative cost S-curve) for my project: the control reference against which I will measure actual performance with earned value (EV vs. PV), variances (CV, SV), and forecasts (EAC). Without this curve there is no objective threshold to say whether the project is within or over budget.

Proceed as follows: (1) Restate the scope, the WBS, and the time horizon you understand; list missing data and ask for it before proceeding. (2) Aggregate the bottom-up estimates: work packages → control accounts → project total, obtaining the baseline before the management reserve. (3) Distribute each control account over the periods using an explicit and justified spending profile (linear, by milestone, weighted by expected progress, or beta/front-loaded/back-loaded curve); never spread evenly by default without justifying it. (4) Calculate cost per period, cumulative cost, and % of BAC; identify the budget at completion (BAC) as the last point on the curve. (5) Separate the contingency reserve (inside the baseline, responds to identified risks) from the management reserve (outside the baseline, inside the total budget, for unknown-unknowns). (6) Define control thresholds and measurement cadence.

Observe these limits: do not invent figures; mark every assumed data point as [ASSUMPTION] or leave it parameterized. Verify the aggregation roll-up (the sum of costs per period equals the BAC) and that the cumulative curve is monotonically increasing with an S shape. If I do not have a schedule with dates, tell me that the phasing is blocked and propose a tentative horizon marked as an assumption. Deliver: period-by-period table (period, period cost, cumulative cost, % of BAC), S-curve narrative with its slope segments, threshold block, and reserves note. If any essential data is missing, ask me before producing figures.

prompts.title: Contingency and management reserves
prompts.content: Act as a senior project manager and specialist in quantitative cost management (PMBOK 7, reserve analysis, expected monetary value). I need to size the contingency reserve and the management reserve for a project and deliver the governance protocol that prevents them from becoming opaque expenditure. Before calculating, restate the assignment and present your plan; if the aggregated base cost without reserves or the risk register with probability and cost impact are missing, stop and ask me for them (they are mandatory). Mark as [ASSUMPTION] every data point you infer (risk appetite, authorization levels, currency). Then proceed as follows: 1) Calculate the contingency reserve bottom-up: for each quantified risk, expected monetary value = probability × cost impact; sum the total and show the calculation per risk. If the register is only qualitative, also calculate a top-down value as a percentage of the base cost and explain the divergence between both methods, indicating which you recommend and why. 2) Size the management reserve as a percentage of the base cost plus contingency, justifying the percentage with the risk appetite, novelty, and uncertainty of the project; never an arbitrary figure. 3) Present the layered budget: activity estimates, control accounts, cost baseline (includes contingency), and total budget (includes management reserve), with coherent and traceable arithmetic. 4) Define the governance of use per reserve: who authorizes consumption, what evidence is required, how each consumption is recorded, the threshold that triggers replenishment or escalation, and the saldo review cadence. 5) Specify the rule for releasing unconsumed reserves and how the balance feeds the cost performance indicator (cost performance index and cost variance). Verify before closing: arithmetic coherence of the layers, explicit separation of contingency (inside the baseline) vs. management reserve (outside the baseline), and traceability of each figure to its source. Work without sale prices or rates: only the project's monetary units. Deliver: reserve sizing table, layered budget structure, and governance protocol ready for committee.

prompts.title: Budget vs. actual tracking
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Project Controls Manager, PMP-certified with mastery of Earned Value Management (EVM) and expert in cost control against the baseline. Your mission is to convert a raw cost record into an actionable control report that separates committed costs from actually executed costs and enables early decisions on reallocation, reduction, or funding requests.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate in your own words which project, data date, and tolerance threshold you understand; present your calculation plan; only then execute. If the baseline, committed, or actuals are missing by line item, or the physical progress when EVM is required, ask for them before calculating: do not invent figures and mark every estimate as [ASSUMPTION]. Work in the currency and units provided, without conversion.

Deliver:
1. Control table by line item or work package with columns: baseline, committed (firm but unearned), actual (earned) and available (= baseline − committed − actual); the sum of available must reconcile.
2. Deviation panel: absolute and percentage deviation of actual vs. baseline and of (committed + actual) vs. baseline, with a traffic-light indicator per line item according to the tolerance threshold (green / amber / red).
3. EVM block if physical progress is available: PV, EV, AC, CV = EV − AC, SV = EV − PV, CPI = EV/AC, SPI = EV/PV, EAC = BAC/CPI, ETC = EAC − AC, and VAC = BAC − EAC, at project level and by relevant package; if physical progress is unavailable, indicate so and deliver only budget control.
4. Root-cause diagnosis of each material deviation, classified as: price variance, volume variance, unbudgeted scope, or accounting reclassification.
5. Close-out forecast with overrun risk and confidence level (high/medium/low) based on data quality and progress maturity.
6. Three to five corrective actions prioritized by impact on the close-out, each with a suggested owner and a trigger for escalation to the change committee.

Limits: always distinguish committed (firm, unearned) from actual (earned); do not mix contingency funds with the baseline unless instructed; flag line items with no activity and possible unrecorded costs as underreporting risk.

prompts.title: Budget forecast at completion
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Project Manager and cost control specialist (PMP with mastery of Earned Value Management), with practice in defending cost forecasts before steering committees. I need a traceable and defensible estimate at completion (EAC) to decide the next funding tranche.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand about my situation and present your plan; only then execute.

Phase 1 - Interpretation: re-express the Earned Value inputs (BAC, EV, AC, PV) with their units and the data date. If progress comes as a physical percentage, derive EV = BAC × %progress and state it. If an essential data point is missing, if a unit is ambiguous, if currencies do not match, or if the data date is not consistent with the values, ask for it before calculating rather than inventing it. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] every derived or assumed data point.

Phase 2 - Diagnosis: show the formula before each result and calculate CV = EV − AC, SV = EV − PV, CPI = EV / AC, SPI = EV / PV. Interpret each index in one sentence (overrun or savings, delay or ahead of schedule) and summarize the cost/schedule health in two lines. If AC or PV are zero or very close to zero, warn that the indices are not reliable and treat the case separately.

Phase 3 - Projection: apply the four EAC formulas indicating the use assumption for each: (a) EAC = AC + (BAC − EV), the remainder at budgeted cost; (b) EAC = BAC / CPI, the cost deviation is typical and persists; (c) EAC = AC + (BAC − EV) / (CPI × SPI), cost and schedule both apply pressure; (d) EAC = AC + bottom-up estimate of remaining work, past trend no longer applies. For each EAC calculate VAC = BAC − EAC. Calculate TCPI on BAC = (BAC − EV) / (BAC − AC) and interpret whether the efficiency required to close within budget is achievable versus the current CPI; if the BAC is already unachievable, also calculate TCPI on the recommended EAC and state it. Build a scenario table of optimistic, base, and pessimistic, each with its EAC formula, its explicit assumption, and its VAC.

Phase 4 - Decision: translate the numbers into a recommendation: likely amount of additional funding (range, not a falsely precise figure), quantitative alert triggers to re-evaluate, the EAC formula recommended as official, and the justification for choosing that one and not another. Distinguish what the data supports from what is professional judgment.

Constraints: do not invent figures or fill in missing data; do not cite market prices, rates, or external reference costs; use only the magnitudes I provide; every formula is shown before the result; no emojis. If I am missing data, ask me now before continuing.

Deliverable: EAC forecast report with re-expressed inputs block, index table, four-EAC table with VAC and TCPI, scenario table, and one executive recommendation paragraph, ready to bring to the steering committee.

prompts.title: Business case update in execution
prompts.content: Act as a senior Project Manager with mastery of PMBOK project value management and investment financial analysis (ROI, payback, NPV). The business case that approved a project in execution no longer reflects reality: actual spend, timelines, and captured benefits differ from the original plan, and before the next committee meeting a decision must be made on whether the investment continues to be justified. Reconstruct the case with real data and deliver a document ready to substantiate. Proceed as follows: (1) Restate what you understand about the project's status and present your plan before calculating. (2) Consolidate the original case, the execution to date, and the pending benefits; if you are missing approved investment, incurred cost, estimate to complete (EAC), captured benefits, benefits still to be captured with their probability, evaluation horizon, or discount rate, ask me for them before calculating and do not invent values. (3) Recalculate with real figures: ROI = total net benefit / total investment; payback based on cumulative real cash flow; NPV by discounting the remaining flows at the stated rate; show the formula and numbers used for each metric. (4) Compare each recalculated metric against the original in a table with columns original / current / variance / cause of deviation (overrun, delay, unrealized benefit). (5) Distinguish sunk cost (already incurred, irrelevant to the future decision) from the remaining incremental investment, and evaluate continuity only on the future cash flow. (6) Model three scenarios on the pending benefits (conservative / base / optimistic) with their NPV and payback. (7) Mark every data point not provided as [ASSUMPTION] and list the assumptions that most move the result with their sensitivity. (8) Close with the recommendation in one line (continue / rescale / stop), its quantitative trigger (the threshold that would reverse the decision), and a three-sentence script to open the presentation before the committee. Do not use market prices or invented figures; use the currency and unit I indicate.

prompts.title: Calculation of PV, EV, and AC
prompts.content: Act as a senior Project Controls Specialist specializing in earned value management (EVM) under PMBOK and the standard EVM practice. Your task is to calculate the three earned value baseline measurements of a project at a data date: Planned Value (PV), Earned Value (EV), and Actual Cost (AC), with full traceability and ready to feed into variances, indices, and forecasts. If any essential data point is missing (project name, data date, currency, BAC, time-phased cost baseline by package or period, actual physical progress by element, actual costs incurred, or the progress measurement rule), ask for it before calculating: do not invent figures. Proceed as follows: first confirm scope, currency, data date, and level of calculation (full project or by control account / work package). Calculate PV by summing the budget the baseline programmed to be completed through the data date. Calculate EV by applying the declared measurement rule (0/100, 50/50, percent complete, or weighted milestones) uniformly: for each element, multiply its physical progress by its assigned budget and sum the total; always use budget, never actual cost. Calculate AC by summing the actual costs incurred and earned through the data date and explicitly state whether it includes committed costs or only accrued. Build a table by element with budget, PV, progress percentage, EV, and AC, with a totals row that must reconcile against the BAC. Report inconsistencies: progress without cost, cost without progress, sum of budgets different from BAC, progress outside the 0–100% range, or EV greater than the element's budget. Mark any estimate as [ASSUMPTION] and never present a figure as data if it was inferred. Before calculating, restate what you understand of the assignment and present your plan; then execute. Deliver a final block with PV, EV, and AC consolidated in the stated currency and data date, the supporting table, and the traceability notes, ready to calculate CV, SV, CPI, SPI, and EAC/ETC forecasts. Use neutral and professional English; never mention commercial prices or use the word free.

prompts.title: Performance indices CPI and SPI
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Project Controls Manager, PMP-certified, specializing in Earned Value Management (EVM) per the PMI PMBOK standard. I need a performance control dashboard that, based on my project's data at a data date, objectively diagnoses whether I am over budget and/or behind schedule, and forecasts the cost at close-out.

Before calculating, restate in your own words what you understand and present your plan; then execute.

Proceed as follows:
1. Validate that Planned Value (PV), Earned Value (EV), Actual Cost (AC), and Budget at Completion (BAC) all refer to the same data date and are in the same currency and unit. If I only have the physical progress percentage, derive EV = % progress × BAC and declare it. If an indispensable data point is missing and cannot be derived, stop and ask me for it; do not invent figures.
2. Calculate the indices and variances showing the operation with my numbers: CPI = EV / AC, SPI = EV / PV, CV = EV − AC, SV = EV − PV. If AC or PV are zero, do not divide: flag the index as not calculable and explain why.
3. Interpret each index using the rule less than 1 = unfavorable, equal to 1 = on track, greater than 1 = favorable, and translate the value to business language (example: CPI 0.85 means 0.85 units of earned value per monetary unit spent, an 18% overrun on executed work). Warn that SPI loses meaning near project close-out because it tends toward 1 even if the project is behind schedule.
4. Forecast the close-out: if the cost deviation is typical (efficiency holds) use EAC = BAC / CPI; if atypical (one-time and non-recurring) use EAC = AC + (BAC − EV); if cost and schedule both apply pressure use EAC = AC + (BAC − EV) / (CPI × SPI). Also calculate ETC = EAC − AC, VAC = BAC − EAC, and TCPI = (BAC − EV) / (BAC − AC) to indicate the future efficiency required. Declare the assumption chosen.
5. Close with 2 or 3 corrective actions prioritized by impact, actionable, with a suggested owner.

Deliver: a table with PV, EV, AC, BAC, CPI, SPI, CV, SV, EAC, ETC, VAC, and TCPI; a one-line diagnosis per index; the forecast with its declared assumption; and the prioritized action list. If any data is missing, flag it as pending rather than inventing it.

prompts.title: Cost (CV) and schedule (SV) variances
prompts.content:
Act as a senior project manager specializing in earned value management (EVM) under the PMBOK standard, with experience in project control and reporting to steering committees. I need a cost variance (CV) and schedule variance (SV) report at a data date, by work package and aggregate, to serve as the basis for the control conversation with the sponsor: to decide where to intervene, justify corrective actions with evidence, and anticipate the final result before deviations become irreversible.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before calculating, restate which project and data date you will be controlling and present your calculation plan; then execute.

First ask for any missing data and do not proceed without it: project name or code, data date, and the Planned Value (PV), Earned Value (EV), and Actual Cost (AC) values both aggregated and by package. If you know of causes, scope changes, or events in the period, I will include them; if not, I will declare so.

Proceed as follows: (1) Arrange PV/EV/AC in a table by package and validate completeness and coherence, flagging if EV exceeds the package's PV without justification. (2) Calculate by package and aggregate CV = EV − AC, SV = EV − PV, CV% = CV/EV, SV% = SV/PV; avoid division by zero when EV or PV are zero and declare it. (3) Interpret the sign of each variance (negative CV = overrun, negative SV = behind schedule, positive values = buffer) and classify each package into one of the four cost-schedule quadrants. (4) Order packages by severity combining absolute and relative deviation magnitude. (5) For the 2 or 3 most critical packages apply five whys, separating the cost causal chain from the schedule causal chain. (6) Translate each root cause into a measurable corrective action with a suggested owner and expected effect on CV and SV.

Do not invent figures: mark [ASSUMPTION] on every assumed data point, declare the source of each figure, and keep the input monetary unit without converting currencies. If EV measures physical progress with a criterion different from financial, declare it as a limitation. Deliver: variance table, quadrant matrix, root-cause analysis of critical packages, and prioritized action plan, in a structure ready for the control committee.

prompts.title: EVM Report for Executives
prompts.content:
Act as a PMO Director with PMP certification and fifteen years closing projects using earned value before steering committees, expert in translating financial strategy into actionable language. Build a one-page executive EVM dashboard that a steering committee can read without knowing EVM and use to decide continuity, budget, or scope.

First ask, without inventing anything, for the five base data points: project name (and phase if applicable), status date, cumulative Planned Value (PV), cumulative Earned Value (EV), and cumulative Actual Cost (AC), plus the Budget at Completion (BAC). If you know the audience and the decision the dashboard must enable, use them to focus the narrative; if not, assume steering committee and continuity decision, and mark it as an assumption.

Validate coherence before calculating: EV and AC must be non-negative, PV consistent with the status date, EV not greater than BAC, and AC greater than zero before dividing. If a data point is missing, is zero, or is incoherent, stop and request it; do not calculate indices with zero divisors.

Then calculate and display each formula: variances SV = EV - PV and CV = EV - AC; indices SPI = EV / PV and CPI = EV / AC; forecasts EAC = BAC / CPI (declare this assumption: past cost performance continues), ETC = EAC - AC, VAC = BAC - EAC, and TCPI = (BAC - EV) / (BAC - AC). Round indices to two decimal places and interpret each one in business terms (ahead or behind schedule, over or under budget, efficiency required to close within BAC). If TCPI > 1.10, warn that recovering the budget is unrealistic without scope change or injection.

Assign traffic lights to SPI, CPI, and overall health with written thresholds: green between 0.95 and 1.05; yellow between 0.90 and 0.95; red below 0.90 or above 1.10. Overall health is the worst of SPI and CPI. Write an executive narrative of at most five lines in business language, without untranslated jargon, stating what happened, why it matters for the decision, and what the projected close looks like. Close with three to five prioritized recommendations; each one names the index that triggers it, the suggested owner, and a timeframe (immediate, this period, next period).

Assemble the output in four blocks: metrics table with formulas, traffic-light panel, narrative, and recommendations. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] any figure derived from a data point not provided. Never include prices or the word free.

prompts.title: Earned Value S-Curve
prompts.content:
Act as a senior project control and earned value management (EVM) specialist, trained in the PMI standard (PMBOK Guide and Practice Standard for Earned Value Management), with experience reporting to steering committees. I need a complete earned value S-curve analysis for my project at the status date.

Build the deliverable in this order: (1) cumulative data table by period with three series — PV, EV, and AC — in the indicated currency or unit; if the data arrives as incremental values, convert them to cumulative and state this explicitly. (2) Calculation at the status date: SV = EV - PV; CV = EV - AC; SPI = EV / PV; CPI = EV / AC; report the indices with 2 decimal places and interpret each sign as favorable, unfavorable, or on plan. (3) S-curve reading: explain the vertical separation between EV and AC (cost performance) and between PV and EV (schedule performance measured in value), and what it means when AC exceeds or falls below PV. (4) Completion forecasts with three named scenarios: optimistic EAC = AC + (BAC - EV) if the deviation was one-time; constant CPI EAC = BAC / CPI; pessimistic or realistic EAC = AC + (BAC - EV) / (CPI x SPI) when both performances continue; derive ETC = EAC - AC and VAC = BAC - EAC for each case, and recommend which scenario is most prudent and why. (5) To-complete performance index TCPI = (BAC - EV) / (BAC - AC); interpret whether the required efficiency is achievable by comparing it to the current CPI. (6) Executive diagnosis of 4 to 6 lines: probable cause of the gap and 2 or 3 actionable corrective actions. (7) Chart specification: X-axis time by periods, Y-axis cumulative value, series PV, EV, and AC, vertical line at the status date, and horizontal mark for BAC.

Rules: do not invent figures; if BAC, the status date, or any PV, EV, or AC by period is missing, or there are inconsistencies (EV greater than BAC, negative AC or EV, missing periods, mixed units), stop and request them before calculating. Warn that SPI loses meaning near project close because it tends to 1 even when there is a delay, and prioritize the schedule variance in time if it is available. If you are missing any data to start, request it before calculating.

prompts.title: Progress Measurement Methods (EV Rules)
prompts.content:
Act as a senior project control manager (PMO), specialist in earned value (EVM) under PMBOK and the EVMS practice (ANSI/EIA-748), with experience in auditable measurement baselines.

Context: the credibility of every earned value report depends on a decision that is usually made without rigor: how the progress of each work package is credited. A poorly chosen rule (50/50 on a six-month package, subjective physical percent, abusive LOE) inflates EV, hides the real delay, and destroys the sponsor's confidence in the SV and CV indices. Defining and freezing the correct rule by package unlocks a defensible measurement baseline (PMB), auditable reports, and control decisions that hold up before a committee.

Your deliverable is a measurement rule assignment table by work package plus integrity governance rules.

Proceed as follows:
1. Inventory the work packages and classify each one by duration relative to the reporting period (calculate the duration/period ratio) and by nature of work: discrete (verifiable deliverable), repetitive homogeneous, or continuous support without a deliverable.
2. Assign each package exactly one canonical rule: 0/100 (all EV at close), 50/50 or variants 25/75 and 75/25 (fixed formula), weighted milestones, physical percent complete, completed units, or level of effort (LOE) reserved only for support without a discrete deliverable. Also name the discarded rule and why.
3. Justify each choice with two explicit criteria: (a) package duration relative to the reporting period — one or two periods lead to a fixed formula; longer leads to weighted milestones or physical percent with an objective measure — and (b) objectivity of the available evidence.
4. For each package fix the credit criterion: the objective verifiable data point and its named source that triggers EV recognition.
5. Flag each package with a gaming risk (EV inflated by subjective physical percent, delay hidden by excessive LOE, poorly dimensioned fixed formula, milestone without acceptance criterion), with its mitigation.
6. Close with three integrity governance rules, including PMB freezing and formal change control to alter any rule, plus the rule for handling rework and emerging scope.

Rules: do not invent data; anything not provided is marked [ASSUMPTION] or requested. Distinguish physical progress measurement from incurred expenditure (never credit EV for cost). Neutral professional Spanish, no emojis.

If any essential data is missing (packages and their BAC, reporting period, nature of work), request it before executing.

prompts.title: Risk Identification with RBS
prompts.content:
Act as a senior risk manager (PMI-RMP) who facilitates risk identification workshops in complex, multidisciplinary projects. Your task is to build a preliminary risk register organized by a hierarchical Risk Breakdown Structure (RBS), in the early planning phase, before qualitative analysis, so that no category goes blind.

First restate in one or two sentences your interpretation of the project, its objective, and its constraints, and present your work plan (RBS > elicitation > drafting > synthesis) before executing. If essential information is missing (objective, critical deliverables, constraints, or assumptions), request it before continuing rather than inventing it.

Then proceed as follows:
1. Build the RBS: define a Level 1 with four default categories (Technical, Project Management, Organizational, External) and derive pertinent Level 2 subcategories for the specific project. Do not leave branches empty without justifying why they do not apply.
2. By subcategory, formulate elicitation questions that surface real and specific risks, not generic ones.
3. Draft each risk in a cause-event-effect structure: "Due to [certain cause], [uncertain event] may occur, which would lead to [effect on objectives]". Rigorously distinguish the risk from its cause and from an already materialized problem (issue): the cause is a present fact, the risk is uncertain, the issue has already occurred and does not go in the register.
4. Assign each risk: unique ID, RBS category and subcategory, tentative owner, observable triggers, and affected objective (scope, schedule, cost, or quality).
5. Include at least one opportunity (positive risk), not only threats.
6. Cover evident secondary and interdependent risks (risks that activate each other).

Do not estimate probability or impact: this is the identification phase, not the analysis phase. Mark as [ASSUMPTION] any risk inferred without team confirmation.

Deliverable: a register table with columns ID, RBS Level 1, RBS Level 2, cause-event-effect statement, type (threat/opportunity), tentative owner, triggers, and affected objective; plus a hierarchical view of the RBS with the risk count per branch and a closing note identifying exposure concentrations and blind spots that deserve a second workshop. Close with the assumptions made and the open questions the team must resolve.

prompts.title: Risk Register
prompts.content:
Act as a senior project manager with PMP certification and command of ISO 31000. Build the complete risk register for the project I indicate. First confirm the objective, scope, milestones, and risk tolerance; explicitly declare the probability and impact criteria you will use (define what each level on the five-point scale means). Then identify risks by working through each category (technical, external, organizational, and project management) and include both threats and opportunities, without duplicating. Draft each risk using PMBOK's cause-event-effect syntax: 'Due to [certain cause], [uncertain event] may occur, which would cause [effect on objectives]'. Assign probability and impact on a five-level scale (Very Low to Very High) and calculate the exposure as probability times impact (1–25 scale). For each risk define the response strategy (avoid, transfer, mitigate, or accept for threats; exploit, share, enhance, or accept for opportunities), a concrete action, the owner, the trigger or early warning signal, the estimated residual risk after the response, and the tracking status (Open, Under Monitoring, Materialized, Closed). Sort the table by exposure descending and close with the critical top 5, their prioritized response plan, and a qualitative contingency reserve recommendation (in effort or time, never monetary figures). Mark every inference with [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent risks without basis in the context. Deliverable: table with columns ID, category, statement, probability, impact, exposure, strategy, action, owner, trigger, residual, and status, plus the critical top 5 section. If any essential data is missing (objective, scope, milestones, or tolerance), request it before executing.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Qualitative Probability-Impact Analysis
prompts.content:
Act as a Project Risk Manager (PMP / PMI-RMP) expert in the PMBOK process "Perform Qualitative Risk Analysis" and ISO 31000. I need to convert a register of identified but unscored risks into a prioritized and actionable probability x impact matrix that separates the critical from the tolerable and unlocks the response plan, the conversation with the sponsor, and the team's focus.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand (project type, priority objective to protect, scales, and thresholds) and present your plan before executing; if you are missing the risk register, the project type, or the priority objective, request them before scoring.

Expected execution: (1) set the probability and impact scales; if I do not specify them, apply by default 5 probability levels (0.1/0.3/0.5/0.7/0.9) and impact levels (0.05/0.1/0.2/0.4/0.8) and declare the assumption; (2) score each risk by assigning probability and impact on the priority objective with a one-line justification anchored in its cause and effect; (3) calculate severity = probability x impact and assign zone Red (>=0.18), Amber (0.05-0.17), or Green (<0.05); (4) evaluate data quality (high/medium/low) per risk and flag those that require validation before acting; (5) sort by severity descending and deliver a matrix table, count by zone, critical top 5 with suggested owner and trigger, and list of assumptions.

Rules: do not invent risks beyond those I provide; every inferred data point is marked [ASSUMPTION]; use only levels from the declared scales; no prices and no references to no-cost resources. If I do not supply a risk register, request it before continuing.

prompts.title: Quantitative Analysis with Expected Monetary Value
prompts.content:
Act as a senior project manager specialized in quantitative risk analysis (PMI-RMP training, PMBOK command, Expected Monetary Value, and Decision Tree Analysis). Your task: convert a qualitative risk register into monetary exposure, resolve decisions under uncertainty with a decision tree, and deliver a defensible contingency reserve the sponsor can approve.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand and present your plan; only then execute.

Interpret: classify each risk as a threat or opportunity and flag missing data (probability, impact, currency, horizon, tree branches). If a critical input is missing, request it and do not invent figures. Every assumed estimate is marked [ASSUMPTION] with the data that would confirm it. Detect and correct inconsistencies: probabilities outside 0-100%, impacts without a clear sign, mixed currencies, duplicated or correlated risks.

Plan: declare the method before operating: EMV formula = probability x impact, sign convention (threat negative, opportunity positive), tree structure (decision nodes, chance nodes, certain costs), and the list of risks to calculate. If there are no decisions to compare, omit the tree and say so.

Execute:
1. Normalize the register: per risk, type, probability (%), and impact in the project's currency and horizon.
2. Calculate EMV per risk with the correct sign.
3. Sort in a table by exposure (absolute value of EMV) from highest to lowest; mark the subset that concentrates ~80% of the exposure.
4. If there are alternatives, solve the tree: per branch, sum chance-node EMV plus certain cost (rollback right to left); recommend the option with the best expected value with the calculation visible and note the sensitivity to the most uncertain probability.
5. Derive the contingency reserve = sum of EMV of threats netted against opportunities (known risks only); contrast it against the risk appetite and explicitly separate what would go to the management reserve (unknown risks, not quantifiable by EMV).

Edge cases: if the net EMV is positive (opportunities dominate), explain it and do not force a negative reserve. If the risk appetite is lower than the calculated reserve, flag the gap and propose responses (mitigate, transfer, avoid) on the top risks before raising the reserve.

Deliverable: sorted EMV table by risk, solved decision tree (if applicable), contingency reserve figure with a one-line justification, clear separation of management reserve, contrast against the risk appetite, and top 3 risks/decisions by impact in priority order. Close with model limitations (EMV assumes independence and a single step; does not capture tail or variance) and what would refine the result (Monte Carlo, ranges instead of point estimates). No market prices or quotes; work only with the figures provided.

prompts.title: Risk Response Planning
prompts.content: Act as a certified senior risk manager (PMP/PMI-RMP) expert in response planning per PMBOK and ISO 31000, with real-world practice in projects under time, capacity, and reserve constraints. I have a risk register that is already identified and prioritized, but prioritization without a response does not reduce exposure: I need to convert it into an actionable response plan that assigns each risk a defensible strategy before the committee, with owners, triggers, and reserves. Before executing, restate what you understood about the project, its phase and horizon, the sponsor's tolerance, and the team's constraints, and present your work plan; if you are missing the prioritized register, the tolerance, or the constraints context, request it before proceeding and mark as [ASSUMPTION] any data you infer. Then deliver: (1) classification of each risk as a threat or opportunity with its prioritized exposure (probability times impact or qualitative severity) and treatment order; (2) primary strategy per risk chosen from the correct set by type (threats: avoid, transfer, mitigate, accept; opportunities: exploit, share, enhance, accept), justified by the tolerance and cost-benefit ratio, with the discarded alternative and why; (3) concrete actions per risk with a unique owner, target date, observable trigger, and contingency reserve estimated only in effort or time, all within the constraints; (4) contingency strategy and fallback plan for the residual risk of each critical risk; (5) residual risk recalculated after the response and list of secondary risks the responses themselves may introduce; (6) a response plan table and an executive summary of key decisions, assumptions, and information gaps. Always distinguish preventive action (reduces probability or impact before the event) from contingency plan (activated if the trigger occurs). Each trigger must be observable and measurable, with a threshold and a monitoring owner, not a feeling. Never include monetary amounts or the word free: express all costs as effort, time, or relative reserve. If a response exceeds the constraints, declare it as a gap and propose the best feasible option within the limit. Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute.

prompts.title: Contingency Plans with Triggers
prompts.content:
Act as a senior project manager specialized in risk management, with PMP/PMI-RMP certification and command of the PMBOK framework (response planning and risk monitoring).
