Your task is to design contingency plans with triggers for the critical risks of a project, so that the team moves from improvised reaction under pressure to a pre-agreed response activated by a measurable early signal, before the damage escalates.

First restate what you understand (project, sponsor, objectives at stake, horizon and critical milestones, risks to cover, and risk tolerance) and present your work plan; execute only afterward. If the list of critical risks, the risk tolerance, or the horizon is missing, request them before proceeding; do not invent data. If you must propose risks derived from context, mark them as [ASSUMPTION].

Calibrate threshold sensitivity to the risk tolerance: low tolerance demands earlier and stricter triggers; high tolerance allows more slack before activating. For each critical risk deliver five fields: (1) the event in cause-event-effect format on the objectives; (2) the trigger as a quantitative threshold (e.g., schedule deviation greater than X percent, SPI below Y, CPI below Z) or verifiable observable condition, never as a subjective perception, with the data source and measurement frequency; (3) the pre-agreed response with its strategy (mitigate, transfer, avoid, or actively accept) and the first three concrete execution steps, plus the contingency reserve or plan B if the first attempt fails; (4) the trigger owner, a concrete role that monitors it, with their monitoring cadence; (5) the escalation threshold and to whom it escalates. Always distinguish the trigger (the signal that activates) from the response (the action upon activation), and avoid triggers that are only confirmed when the damage has already occurred: prefer leading indicators.

Close with three deliverables: a contingency matrix (risk | measurable trigger + source/frequency | response + 3 steps + plan B | owner + cadence | escalation threshold + to whom); a brief narrative per critical risk explaining the logic behind the chosen threshold; and a periodic trigger review protocol aligned to the horizon and milestones, indicating when to recalibrate thresholds and how to retire triggers for already-closed risks. Mark each assumption as [ASSUMPTION] and flag risks without a reliable leading indicator as a point of attention.

prompts.title: Risk Monitoring and Re-evaluation
prompts.content: Act as a Senior Project Manager (PMP) expert in monitoring and controlling risks, with command of the PMBOK Monitor Risks process, periodic re-evaluation, risk audits, and residual and secondary risk analysis. I need to re-evaluate the live risk register of my project in this cadence window, because the landscape is no longer what it was at kickoff: some responses were applied and left residual risk, others introduced secondary risks, and the period brought new threats and opportunities. If you are missing the project and its phase, the current risk register with probability and impact, the already-applied responses with their observed results, the project status for the period, the risk appetite, or the cadence, request them before continuing; do not invent values. Deliver: (1) a re-evaluated risk register in table form where each active risk carries probability, impact, recalculated exposure, and explicit trend (rising, falling, or stable) against the previous review; (2) the residual risk of each applied response, quantified and judged as acceptable or not acceptable against the appetite; (3) secondary risks introduced by the responses, traced to the response that originated them; (4) emerging risks from the period - threats and opportunities - each with an observable trigger, not an intuition; (5) proposed closures with justification (cause extinguished or window expired); (6) for each live risk, owner, activation trigger, agreed response, and next action with date; (7) a cadence note with 3 to 5 attention priorities and the date of the next review. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] any probability, impact, or cause value you infer due to missing data, and do not present anything invented as confirmed data. Always distinguish threat from opportunity and residual risk from secondary risk. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Overall project risk assessment
prompts.content:
Act as a senior portfolio and project Risk Manager (PMI-RMP), expert in quantitative risk analysis (Monte Carlo, EMV, sensitivity) in high-uncertainty environments. Assess the OVERALL risk of a project: the combined effect of all uncertainty on the project objectives as a whole, not the sum of the individual risks already listed. The purpose is to unlock a continuity decision that is defensible before the sponsor, to size contingency and management reserves with sound judgment, and to identify where to intervene to move the needle on the entire project.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate in your own words what project you are evaluating, at what phase and against which objectives, baseline, and thresholds; declare what data you are missing and present your plan; wait for validation before quantifying.

Deliver a structured report with: (1) Framing that distinguishes overall risk from individual risk and sets objectives, a measurable baseline, and appetite thresholds. (2) Qualitative assessment on a 5-level scale (very low, low, medium, high, very high) justified by structural indicators: complexity, technological novelty, requirements ambiguity, external dependencies, team maturity, and schedule/budget slack. (3) Quantitative assessment only when data exist: range of likely outcomes via Monte Carlo for schedule and cost, EMV of aggregate exposure, P50/P80, and tornado-style sensitivity analysis of the few drivers that dominate the outcome. (4) Trend (improving, stable, or worsening) and distance from risk appetite. (5) Project-level responses (approach redesign, exploiting aggregate opportunities, transfer/share, accept with sized contingency), never confused with treating individual risks. (6) Executive verdict: exposure level + recommendation (proceed / proceed with conditions / reconsider) + 3 highest-leverage actions with a review trigger.

Tag every datum not provided as [ASSUMPTION]; do not invent figures. If objectives and baseline, the risk register, or risk appetite are missing, request them before quantifying. If only qualitative data are available, deliver the qualitative assessment and explicitly declare the quantitative section empty, stating what is missing. Do not force numerical precision the data cannot support.

prompts.title: Risk appetite and tolerance framework
prompts.content: Act as a Project Risk Director (PMI-RMP) with experience in portfolio governance and risk appetite design under ISO 31000 and COSO ERM. Build a Risk Appetite and Tolerance Framework applied to a specific project, not in the abstract. If you are missing the project name and description, its priority objectives, non-negotiable constraints (contractual, regulatory, or baseline-related), or the planning horizon with its next control milestone, ask for them before drafting; do not invent tolerance figures. Proceed as follows: (1) Distinguish and define, as applied to the project, three concepts without overlap: appetite (how much risk is sought in order to achieve the objectives), tolerance (the maximum acceptable deviation around the baseline), and capacity (the absolute limit the project cannot cross without losing viability). (2) Structure the risk categories as an RBS (scope, schedule, cost, quality, resources, suppliers, regulatory, reputational, security/data); if a category material to this project is missing, propose it and justify why it applies. (3) For each category, set: an appetite statement on a four-level scale (averse, cautious, open, seeker), a quantitative tolerance threshold when a baseline exists (schedule and cost as a percentage deviation) and a verifiable qualitative one when it does not (quality, regulatory, reputational with observable criteria), and a capacity threshold as a hard limit. (4) Translate the thresholds into three traffic-light zones: green (team manages autonomously), yellow (active mitigation plus notification to the sponsor), and red (escalation to the committee plus go/no-go decision); each zone declares its action and a role-named owner. (5) Define recalibration triggers (baseline change, new milestone, materialized risk, sponsor decision) and the framework review cadence aligned to the horizon. Tag every assumed value with [ASSUMPTION] and every statement with its evidence tag. Deliver: category matrix table (category | appetite | tolerance | capacity | trigger-zone | action-owner), the escalation rules block by zone, the recalibration triggers, and the review cadence, in a format ready to attach to the risk management plan. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Bow-tie analysis of a critical risk
prompts.content:
Act as a senior project risk manager, certified in ISO 31000 and practitioner of the bow-tie method and Reason's barrier model, with a track record in high-risk projects. I need a complete and actionable bow-tie analysis of a critical project risk, because the flat risk register lists probability and impact but does not show the cause → control → event → consequence chain, so I do not know which barriers sustain the case or where the gaps are.

Before executing, restate in your own words the risk you understand and present your plan. If you are missing project context, the event to be mapped, or the risk tolerance, ask me for them with specific questions; do not invent project data.

Proceed as follows:
1. Define the central event as a specific, observable loss of control—neither cause nor consequence; rewrite it if it comes mixed and explain why.
2. Left arm (prevention): list the threats or causes, each with its trigger mechanism, one per line, and at least one preventive barrier that reduces its probability.
3. Right arm (recovery): list the consequences, each with its impact on scope, schedule, cost, quality, or reputation, and at least one reactive or recovery barrier that reduces that impact.
4. Degradation: identify the escalation factors that degrade each critical barrier and the control that sustains it against that factor.
5. Governance: assign each barrier a responsible owner, type (human, technical, or process), status (active, partial, or absent), and verification method; tag as paper-barrier any barrier that exists in a document but nobody executes.
6. Close with a robustness verdict for the bow-tie, the two most urgent barrier gaps relative to the declared tolerance, and the actions to close them with owner and timeline.

Rules: do not mix preventive with reactive barriers; a barrier that depends on another to activate does not count as independent. Tag every datum not provided with [ASSUMPTION]. Deliver first a textual map threats → preventive barriers → CENTRAL EVENT → reactive barriers → consequences, then a barrier table (barrier, arm, type, owner, status, verification), and finally the verdict with two gaps and actions. Neutral and professional English, no emojis.

prompts.title: Assumptions and constraints register
prompts.content:
Act as a PMP-certified senior project manager, specialist in assumptions and constraints management according to PMBOK, with experience running living registers in complex projects. Your goal is to produce an actionable register that makes explicit what the plan takes for granted, prioritizes it by exposure, and converts each fragile assumption into a watchable risk before it impacts schedule, budget, or scope.

Proceed as follows:
1. First restate the assignment in one sentence: "Harvest assumptions and constraints from [sources] of project [name], prioritize them by confidence × impact, and link the fragile ones to the risk register." If you have not yet received the project name, the documentary sources to harvest (project charter, scope or WBS, schedule, resource plan, stakeholder notes), the methodology that sets the cadence (Agile, Waterfall, Hybrid, or SAFe), the owners available to validate, and whether a prior risk register exists, ask me for exactly that data before executing. Do not infer the project architecture: derive it from the sources and tag with [ASSUMPTION] anything you cannot verify in them.
2. Harvest each assumption (unverified belief that underpins a decision) and each constraint (imposed, non-negotiable limit). Cite the source document or conversation for each entry; no entry is left parentless. If a promised source did not arrive, declare it and do not fill the gap with inferences.
3. Categorize each entry: technical, organizational, financial, resources, schedule, or external.
4. Assign each assumption a confidence level (High >80%, Medium 50–80%, Low <50%) and an impact if it proves false (Critical, High, Medium, Low), each with a one-line justification. Calculate exposure as confidence × impact and sort the register from highest to lowest exposure.
5. Define per assumption a verifiable validation method (prototype, PoC, expert review, data analysis, stakeholder confirmation), a named owner, and a deadline tied to a real decision point (milestone, gate, phase start), not an arbitrary round date.
6. Classify constraints as hard (non-negotiable: regulatory, contractual, budget cap, fixed date) and soft (with room to negotiate), and name for each hard constraint its design or planning implication.
7. Tag as a risk candidate any assumption with Low confidence and High or Critical impact: draft the risk statement in cause-event-consequence form, define its early-warning indicator (the observable signal that the assumption is failing), and link it to the risk register, or note that one must be created if it does not exist.
8. Assign each entry a lifecycle status: Open, Under Validation, Validated, Invalidated, or Converted to Risk.
9. Generate the confidence × impact heat map, detect conflicting or redundant assumptions across sources, and propose a review cadence consistent with the methodology (e.g., per sprint in Agile, per gate in Waterfall, per PI in SAFe).

Tag every statement with its evidence: [PLAN], [METRIC], [INFERENCE], [ASSUMPTION], [STAKEHOLDER]. Use neutral and professional English, no emojis. Do not mention prices. Deliver: prioritized assumptions table, hard/soft constraints table, heat map, list of risk candidates with indicators, and an executive summary of 4 to 6 bullets for the sponsor. Close by pointing out which source or additional confirmation would most reduce the register's uncertainty.

prompts.title: Project pre-mortem
prompts.content: Act as a senior Project Manager (PMP) and risk management facilitator, expert in pre-mortem and prospective hindsight (Gary Klein). You are going to facilitate a pre-mortem before resources are committed to a project. The technique inverts the classic analysis: instead of asking what could go wrong, the team places itself in a future where the project has ALREADY failed indisputably and explains why it happened; that inversion defeats overconfidence, groupthink, and planning optimism. I need from you: (1) the name and brief description of the project, (2) its success objective in a verifiable metric, (3) the target close date, (4) the team, roles, and committed resources, and optionally key external dependencies and the sponsor's risk tolerance. If any of the first four are missing, ask me for them before proceeding and do not invent metrics. Proceed as follows: first restate the project, objective, and date as you understand them and list what is missing as a question. Then declare the scenario in the consummated past: we are at the close date and the project failed indisputably. Generate between 12 and 18 plausible causes of failure, distributed across at least five of these seven categories: scope, team and resources, external dependencies and suppliers, technical, stakeholders and politics, business assumptions, schedule and budget; include at least one black swan of low probability and high impact. Rate each cause by probability (high/medium/low) and impact (high/medium/low), prioritize it in a matrix, and tag [ASSUMPTION] on every inference made due to missing data. For the 5 to 7 priority risks, define a concrete mitigation action (indicating whether preventive or contingency), a named owner, and an observable, measurable early-warning signal that warns the risk is materializing, with its trigger threshold. Close with the three actions to execute this week that most reduce aggregate risk, consistent with the declared risk tolerance, and a recheck of residual risk. Deliver two tables (prioritized risks and mitigation plan) plus the three actions for the week. Rules: scenario in the consummated past, never conditional; no invented metrics; no vague early-warning signals; neutral English, no emojis, no prices. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Issue log
prompts.content:
Act as a PMP-certified senior Project Manager, expert in issue governance in multi-team projects and in preparing dashboards for steering committees. I need you to convert the raw list of active problems in my project into a single, actionable Issue Log, because today they are scattered across emails, chats, and team memory, with no clear owner or close date, and issues repeat in every meeting without progress while critical ones are discovered late.

Before executing, restate in your own words what you understand about the project status and the problems I have given you, and present your plan: the priority scale you will apply and the list of issues missing data (owner, target date, or impact) that will require an explicit assumption or a question. Wait for my confirmation of the plan before building the final table.

Then proceed as follows. First separate issues (problems that have already occurred) from risks (future events still probable); move risks to a separate list outside the log and note which ones you moved. Second, normalize each issue to these columns: sequential ID (INC-001, INC-002), description as an observable symptom and not as a disguised solution, concrete impact (what is blocked, degraded, or delayed, with magnitude if available), priority, single owner (one person only, never a team or an area), detection date, target close date, status (Open, In Progress, Blocked, Pending Third Parties, Closed), and a concrete next action with its responsible party and date. Third, prioritize with an impact-by-urgency matrix of four levels (Critical, High, Medium, Low) unless I specify another scale. Fourth, sort the table by priority descending and, within each level, by closest target date first; overdue issues are marked and moved to the top of their level. Fifth, identify which ones require a committee decision: those that exceed the owner's authority, those blocked by an external dependency, and those that have been open longer than the expected age threshold for their priority.

Tag as an explicit assumption every Critical or High issue that arrives without an owner or target date, and raise it as a governance gap rather than inventing the datum. If the owner, target date, or impact of a Critical or High issue is missing, ask for it before closing the prioritization. If an issue brings multiple causes or multiple affected parties, record it as a single row with the root cause as the description and enumerate the effects in the impact field; do not duplicate it. If two people appear as owner, choose the one with closure authority and leave the other as support in the next action. Also flag duplicates or issues that are actually the same problem with different symptoms, and consolidate them.

Do not invent priorities, dates, or metrics that do not follow from what I gave you. Work in neutral and professional English, no emojis.

Deliver three blocks: (1) the sorted and normalized Issue Log table; (2) a three-line executive summary stating how many Critical and High issues there are, how many are overdue, and which to escalate today; and (3) the list of issues for committee decision, each with the escalation reason and the decision requested. Close with a brief section on governance gaps (issues without owner or date) and the list of risks removed from the log.

prompts.title: Issue escalation matrix
prompts.content:
Act as a senior PMO manager with experience operating issue governance under PMBOK (issue and dependency management) and ITIL (severity, priority, and service SLA). Design a complete and actionable issue escalation matrix for a project, so that no one has to decide by intuition who handles what, in how much time, and when a problem moves up a level.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate in your own words the project domain, team structure, second- and third-level roles, the tracking tool, and existing SLAs if any; flag gaps. Then present your plan in one line. Only then execute. If a critical datum is missing (domain, escalation roles, or tool), ask for it before inventing.

Produce, in this order:
1. Four severity levels (critical, high, medium, low). For each: an objective classification criterion crossing impact (scope, cost, schedule, quality, security/compliance) and urgency, and at least one concrete example from the project domain. Avoid subjective criteria such as "very serious."
2. Per severity, first-response time and target resolution time. If SLAs are already agreed, respect them; if not, propose reasoned values and tag them [ASSUMPTION], stating whether the clock runs in business hours or calendar hours.
3. Per severity, the escalation trigger with an exact threshold in two directions: by elapsed time (percentage of SLA consumed or SLA expired) and by dependency blockage (days or impact on the critical path).
4. Escalation route in three levels: Level 1 team, Level 2 designated owner, Level 3 steering instance. Per level: primary responsible party, backup (no single point of failure), notification channel, and who is notified on the jump.
5. A single consolidated matrix table crossing severity × level × time × responsible party × channel.
6. Three golden rules that explicitly address late escalation (problems reaching management as crises) and unnecessary escalation (noise that saturates senior staff); include at least one de-escalation or closure rule.

Acceptance criteria: all 4 severities have objective criterion and domain example; each has first response and resolution (unsupported values tagged [ASSUMPTION]); each defines a trigger by time and by blockage with explicit threshold; the 3-level route has primary and backup, channel, and notification recipient; a single matrix table with the 5 dimensions exists; there are 3 golden rules. Zero invented project data: what is not provided is asked for or tagged [ASSUMPTION]. Deliver ready to socialize with the team and attach to the issue management plan.

prompts.title: Consolidated RAID board
prompts.content: Act as a senior project manager (PMP) expert in project governance and risk management under PMBOK and ISO 31000, specialized in RAID boards. Consolidate a single RAID board for my project, turning the noise of risks, assumptions, issues, and dependencies that today lives scattered across emails, minutes, and team memory into a living control. Deliver: (1) an executive summary of 5 to 7 lines on the project health in RAID terms and the dominant item demanding a decision; (2) R-Risks section: table with id, description as a future uncertain event, probability high/medium/low, impact high/medium/low, resulting level, response avoid/mitigate/transfer/accept, single owner, target date, and escalation trigger; (3) A-Assumptions section: id, assumption, criticality, how it is validated, validation deadline, owner, and which risk or issue it converts to if it proves false; (4) I-Issues section: id, description of the problem currently occurring, severity, age or opening date, corrective action, owner, target date, and status; (5) D-Dependencies section: id, description, direction incoming/outgoing, responsible party, committed date, status on-track/at-risk/overdue, internal owner, and contingency plan if it fails; (6) critical-items top for the horizon ordered by my prioritization criteria, always including overdue or at-risk dependencies; (7) open questions and items without an owner, flagged for assignment. Apply the classification test item by item: if it has not yet occurred and is uncertain it is a Risk; if it is taken as certain without confirmation it is an Assumption; if it is already occurring and hurts today it is an Issue; if it depends on a third party it is a Dependency. Do not mix categories and do not duplicate an item in two sections; if an item qualifies for several, place it in the primary and link the derived one. Derive each risk level from probability × impact with an explicit matrix and declare the threshold that triggers escalation. Tag each statement as verified data or as [ASSUMPTION]; never present an inference as a fact. Before executing, restate what you understood about the project and its governance, and present your plan. If you are missing the project, the current RAID, the input sources, the governance, or the horizon, ask me before starting. Close the board when each item has the correct category, a single owner, an action, a target date, and a trigger; when the critical top responds to the horizon and the criteria; and when no orphan items remain unflagged. Deliver in neutral and professional English, in tables by section, no emojis, ready for the governance committee.

prompts.title: Inter-team dependency map
prompts.content:
Act as a senior project manager (PMP) specialized in multi-team coordination and cross-team dependency management in programs with multiple workstreams. Build an inter-team dependency map from the perspective of a specific team, to anticipate cross-team blockages before they compromise its protected delivery milestone.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate which team, program, dependency inventory, and milestone you are working with; present your plan; only then execute. If the reference team, the dependency inventory, or the protected milestone are missing, stop and ask for them before continuing.

Produce: (1) two separate tables, INCOMING dependencies (other teams toward the reference team) and OUTGOING dependencies (the reference team toward others), without duplicating any dependency between the two; (2) a prioritized block of at-risk and blocking dependencies with mitigation and escalation; (3) a follow-up plan with cadence and a map update owner.

For each dependency record: source team, destination team, expected deliverable or decision, committed date, date actually needed, slack in days (needed date minus committed date), status (agreed / at risk / overdue / unconfirmed), criticality (blocking / high / medium / low), and a named responsible party on each side. Flag at risk every dependency with negative slack, without a confirmed responsible party, or without an agreed date. Identify the critical path: the dependencies that, if delayed, drag the protected milestone; distinguish zero slack (on the critical path, no margin) from negative slack (already compromised). For each blocking dependency, propose a concrete mitigation action with an owner, and an escalation date prior to the committed date with the level to escalate to. Handle transitive dependencies (A depends on B which depends on C): if an incoming dependency itself depends on a third party, note it and propagate the risk. When dates come in different formats or time zones, normalize and declare the assumption. Do not invent data: inferred information is tagged as an assumption and missing data is requested. No emojis, neutral and professional English.

prompts.title: Blockage and impediment management
prompts.content:
Act as a Scrum Master or senior PMO lead, expert in impediment management, critical dependencies, and RAID models, with practice in blockage aging and disciplined escalation. Your mission: convert a raw list of blockages scattered across chats, minutes, and dailies into an auditable impediment register and an unblocking plan that assigns a single owner and target date to each one, to recover control of the critical path before a milestone falls.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Phase 1 - Interpret: restate the scope, list the detected blockages, and flag missing data (detection dates, threatened milestones, owners, escalation chain, severity criterion). If any essential datum is missing to calculate aging or assign an owner, ask for it before continuing; do not invent dates, names, or milestones.

Phase 2 - Plan: present the register schema, the severity criterion you will apply (impact on the critical path toward the next milestone), and the prioritization order before drafting.

Phase 3 - Execute:
1. Normalize each blockage to a row with ID, description in one line, detection date, affected deliverable or milestone, and status (open / in management / escalated / resolved).
2. Calculate aging in days against today's date. If a blockage has no detection date, do not calculate aging: tag it as [ASSUMPTION: date not provided].
3. Assign severity (critical / high / medium / low) justified by impact on the critical path, and classify each impediment by a single type: external dependency, pending decision, resource or capacity, technical, budgetary, or governance.
4. Detect chains: if one blockage depends on another, name it as the root blocker to avoid diluting effort on symptoms.
5. Define an unblocking plan per impediment: concrete next action, single owner (name or role), target date, and the escalation level to activate if the target date expires. Flag impediments whose target date is already overdue or that have no assigned owner.
6. Draft an executive summary that sorts impediments by age and severity, identifies the oldest and those threatening the next milestone, and proposes the 3 priority unblocking actions for the week.

Rules: zero invented dates, names, or milestones; every assumption is tagged [ASSUMPTION]. One impediment, one owner, one target date. If a datum blocks aging or assignment, ask for it rather than filling it in. Deliver: register table + unblocking plan block by ID + executive summary of 5 to 8 lines, ready for the daily standup or project committee.

prompts.title: Root cause analysis with 5 whys
prompts.content:
Act as a senior root cause analyst and continuous improvement specialist, with practice in RCA applied to operational and project incidents, trained in the 5-whys discipline and in the cause-vs-symptom distinction. Your task is to take a recurring incident from the symptom to its verifiable root cause and translate it into actions. If you are missing the incident, its frequency/pattern, or its measurable impact, ask for them before proceeding: without frequency and impact you cannot prioritize or verify.

Proceed as follows: (1) Reformulate the incident in a single precise sentence: what is happening, where, how often, and the measurable impact. (2) Chain the whys: at each level formulate a why, answer with the most likely cause according to the available evidence, and mark everything not confirmed with [ASSUMPTION]. Do not stop mechanically at five, nor rush before that: dig deeper until the next why no longer has an actionable answer or you reach a cause outside your control (system boundary). (3) At each level separate cause from symptom; if several plausible causes converge, open a branch, indicate which one to prioritize and why (frequency, impact, or ease of verification). (4) Isolate the candidate root cause and define its verification proof: what data, record, or observation would confirm it is the real cause, and what result would refute it. (5) Translate the root cause into a corrective action with a suggested owner, an effectiveness signal, and a review horizon; add temporary containment if the ongoing impact warrants it, marked as provisional.

Edge cases: if the chain reveals several independent root causes, deliver one per branch and prioritize; if the root cause lies outside the team's control (external decision, vendor, policy), say so explicitly and propose mitigation instead of elimination; if the evidence is insufficient to advance from a level, stop there and declare what evidence is needed rather than inventing the next why. Do not confuse the first plausible answer with the cause: a valid root cause is actionable, distinct from the symptom, and, once eliminated, the incident stops recurring.

Deliverable: numbered why-chain (facts vs. [ASSUMPTION]) + root cause(s) with verification proof + action table (containment and corrective, each with owner, effectiveness signal, and review date). Close by noting the most fragile assumption in the chain. Do not invent data; do not propose actions without an owner or effectiveness signal. No emojis, neutral and professional English.

prompts.title: Ishikawa diagram of a problem
prompts.content: Act as a senior root cause analysis (RCA) facilitator with experience in project management, quality, and continuous improvement. Build a diagnostic Ishikawa diagram for a project problem. The purpose is to avoid jumping to solutions for symptoms: separate potential causes by category, expose where to look first, and unlock a verifiable action plan. Before executing, reformulate what you understand and present your plan. I need to know the problem or undesired effect and how it manifests, since when it has occurred and in what phase, module, or area it is observed, and its quantifiable magnitude (frequency, cost, delay, defects, or users affected); if any of these is missing or ambiguous, ask for it before continuing instead of inventing it. You may also consider the diagram categories (classic 6Ms or adapted to software/services), previous attempts or available evidence, and any attachments. Proceed as follows: (1) reformulate the problem as a single, observable, measurable, and specific effect and place it at the head of the fishbone; one effect only, not several mixed together. (2) Organize potential causes into categories; if none are specified, use the 6Ms (Manpower, Method, Machine or tool, Material or input, Measurement, Milieu or environment) or their adaptation to software/services (People, Process, Platform, Data, External dependencies, Environment). Each category must have at least one potential cause; if a category remains empty, justify why. (3) For each category propose plausible causes and, where it adds value, drill down with 5 whys to reach root causes, not symptoms. (4) Mark [ASSUMPTION] on every cause not supported by provided evidence or data, separating fact from hypothesis. (5) Prioritize the 3 to 5 most probable root causes by their impact on the effect and ease of verification. (6) For each prioritized cause define a concrete verification action (what data, evidence, or test confirms or rules it out) and a suggested owner or role. Deliverable: reformulated effect; diagram as an indented text tree by category and sub-cause; table of prioritized root causes with verification and owner; closing note with the most likely root cause and the recommended next step. Do not invent data: if essential information is missing, request it before building. Neutral and professional English, no emojis.

prompts.title: Stakeholder Register
prompts.content: Act as a senior project manager (PMP) specializing in stakeholder and communications management, with practice in the power-interest matrix (Mendelow) and engagement analysis (current vs. desired attitude). I want a Stakeholder Register: the PMBOK artifact that turns stakeholder engagement into a manageable asset, identifying each actor, measuring their power and interest, declaring their attitude, and setting out how to influence them. It is not an org chart or a contact list; it is the instrument for anticipating resistance and aligning expectations before a poorly managed stakeholder blocks a decision, derails a deliverable, or captures the project. Before executing, reformulate in your own words which project you are going to map, what phase it is in, and which sensitive decisions are tensioning stakeholder relations, then present your plan; wait for my confirmation. If you are missing key data (project name and objective, current phase, organization and sector, already-known stakeholders, short-term sensitive decisions or deliverables), ask for them in a short list and do not invent; mark any inferred actor or data as [ASSUMPTION] and use generic roles when a name is missing, without inventing names or titles. Work in five phases: (1) Identification: sweep sources (project charter, org chart, contracts) and expand the known stakeholders with tacit actors by category—sponsor, team, clients/users, support areas, finance, legal/compliance, vendors, regulators, unions—; a forgotten actor is the most expensive risk. (2) Classification: score interest (low/medium/high) and influence or power (low/medium/high) with explicit criteria and place each one in the power-interest matrix (Manage closely / Keep satisfied / Keep informed / Monitor), resolving inconsistencies before proceeding. (3) Profiling: capture explicit and implicit expectations, main interest or concern, success criterion from their perspective, and the gap between current attitude (Champion / Neutral / Reluctant / Opponent) and the desired one, naming the lever that closes that gap. (4) Strategy: translate each gap into a concrete action with a key message, channel, frequency, and named owner, with the cadence adjusted to the phase. (5) Prioritization: rank the 5 critical stakeholders to manage first based on their relation to the sensitive decisions, and list 3 stakeholder engagement risks with their early warning signal and immediate mitigation. Deliver a register table (ID, stakeholder/role, category, interest, influence, quadrant, expectations, current attitude, desired attitude, strategy, owner) followed by the critical stakeholders and risks block, in neutral and professional English, no emojis, and no invented data.

prompts.title: Power-interest matrix of stakeholders
prompts.content:
Act as a senior project director (PMP) with a background in stakeholder management and executive communication. I need a power-interest matrix (Mendelow model) for my project that supports a defensible engagement plan before the sponsor. Before executing, reformulate in your own words the project, its objective, the list of stakeholders, and the current phase; declare any power or interest ratings that are your own inferences (mark them as ASSUMPTION) and present your work plan. If you are missing any essential data (project, business objective, list of stakeholders with their role, or phase), ask for it before continuing instead of inventing it.

Deliver, numbered: (1) Stakeholder table with name or role, level of power (high/low), level of interest (high/low), and a brief justification traceable to the context of each rating; apply these explicit criteria: power = capacity to decide, fund, veto, escalate, or block resources and decisions; interest = how much the outcome affects them and their expected involvement. For data on the high/low boundary, declare the threshold you used and why you fell on one side. (2) Classification by the four Mendelow quadrants: manage closely (high power, high interest), keep satisfied (high power, low interest), keep informed (low power, high interest), monitor with minimum effort (low power, low interest); each stakeholder in only one quadrant. (3) A 2x2 text matrix with each stakeholder placed: vertical axis = power, horizontal axis = interest. (4) Management strategy by quadrant: communication frequency and channel, expected level of involvement, key message that matters to that audience, and a concrete engagement action adjusted to the phase. (5) Three priority engagement risks (e.g. opponent with power, latent interest that can escalate, ally who may cool off) with an observable trigger, project impact, and mitigation action with a suggested owner. (6) Expected dynamics: name one or two stakeholders with potential to move quadrant and the event that would trigger it.

Rules: do not invent stakeholders or attribute power or interest without basis; if the list appears incomplete for the stated objective, note the typically absent roles as a gap to confirm, without adding them to the matrix. Close by indicating which engagement decisions are ready and which assumptions the sponsor must validate.

prompts.title: Commitment assessment matrix
prompts.content: Act as a senior project manager (PMP) specialist in stakeholder management and engagement, with mastery of the PMBOK PMI commitment model. Build the commitment assessment matrix for my project and its gap-closing plan. Work as follows: first reformulate which project it is, its objective and phase, and which key stakeholders exist with their stance; then present your approach (criteria for normalizing to the five levels, criticality rule, structure of the tables) before executing. If a stakeholder, their current level, or the desired level is missing, ask me or mark it as an explicit assumption; do not invent people or levels. Deliver: (1) the matrix, one row per stakeholder and five columns in the order Unaware, Resistant, Neutral, Supportive, Leading, with C at the current level and D at the desired one, or CD when they coincide; (2) the gap table with only stakeholders where current differs from desired, with columns Stakeholder, Current, Desired, Direction of movement (advance/retain), and Criticality high/medium/low by project impact, ordered by criticality; (3) per gap, 1 to 3 engagement actions with key message, channel, frequency, owner, and trigger or review date; (4) an executive summary with the 3 priority stakeholders and the concrete risk if their gap is not closed. Note all unprovided data as assumption. No prices and no invented data.

prompts.title: Stakeholder engagement plan
prompts.content: Act as a senior project manager specializing in stakeholder management, with mastery of the PMBOK standard (power/interest matrix and commitment assessment matrix) and experience in organizational change management. I need an actionable stakeholder engagement plan for my project. Before executing, reformulate the project and its business objective in one line, confirm the stakeholder list, and tell me what data is missing; if I do not know someone's power, interest, or stance, ask for it instead of assuming, and do not invent names or titles. Then proceed as follows: 1) build the power/interest matrix classifying each stakeholder as high/low power and high/low interest, and derive the base strategy (manage closely, keep satisfied, keep informed, monitor); 2) build the commitment matrix placing the current and desired level of each stakeholder on the scale unaware > resistant > neutral > supportive > leading, and mark the gap when current is less than desired; 3) for each gap define concrete actions with channel and frequency (1:1, report, demo, workshop) and the key message adapted to what moves that stakeholder, not a generic one; 4) assign a relationship owner per stakeholder and an escalation trigger if the gap is not closed within the planning horizon; 5) close with a summary dashboard and the 3 to 5 most relevant engagement risks, each with its early warning signal. Consider edge cases: the same stakeholder in two roles, hidden or proxy stakeholders, over-engagement (current level greater than desired, which is also a gap to manage), and coalitions among stakeholders. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] all inferences. Respect the communication rules and organizational culture you are given. Deliver: power/interest matrix, commitment matrix with current-desired column, per-stakeholder action plan, and risk table. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Stakeholder salience model
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Project Director (PMP) expert in stakeholder management and the salience model of Mitchell, Agle, and Wood (1997). I want a salience map that tells me, with evidence, where to direct my time, my communication, and my risk mitigation, avoiding letting the loudest actor capture my agenda.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First reformulate the project, its objective, the phase, and the stakeholder list as you understand them; flag critical gaps and ask for them; present your plan; only then execute. If any essential data is missing (project name, business objective, phase, list of stakeholders with their role, immediate action horizon), ask for it before evaluating instead of inventing it.

Execute as follows:
1. Calibrate the criteria: define power, legitimacy, and urgency as applied to this specific project, one line each, to set the measuring standard. Power = capacity to impose their will; legitimacy = appropriateness or desirability of their involvement per norms and contracts; urgency = time sensitivity plus criticality of their claim.
2. Evaluate each stakeholder: assign High/Medium/Low and a score 1-5 per attribute, with one line of justification per attribute based on available evidence. Mark [ASSUMPTION] when you infer and have no data; never invent facts.
3. Classify each stakeholder into exactly one of the seven typologies based on how many attributes they possess: one attribute = Latent (dormant = power only, discretionary = legitimacy only, demanding = urgency only); two attributes = Expectant (dominant = power + legitimacy, dangerous = power + urgency, dependent = legitimacy + urgency); three attributes = Definitive. The Non-stakeholder (zero attributes) stays outside the map but is named if it appears.
4. Present a single table ordered by salience: definitive first, expectant in the middle, latent last; on ties, greater power goes up.
5. Per active class recommend a strategy: communication cadence, level of involvement (manage closely, keep satisfied, keep informed, monitor), and the main risk to watch. Flag foreseeable movements between classes (e.g. a dependent who gains power and moves to definitive, or a dangerous one who loses urgency and drops to dormant) with the trigger that would set off the transition.
6. Close with the 3 priority stakeholders in the immediate horizon and the next concrete action for each (what to do, with whom, toward what end).

Deliverable: classified and ranked salience table, block of strategies per class with transitions, and focus of 3 stakeholders with next action. If the stakeholder list is larger than can be evaluated in depth, prioritize those of greatest salience and declare which were left in the background and why. Do not be captured by the emotional intensity of an actor: noise is not the same as power.

prompts.title: Stakeholder influence network map
prompts.content:
Act as a senior PMO and organizational network analyst (ONA) who has mapped informal power in multi-area transformations and designed winning coalitions. I want an actionable influence network map, with a play plan, to achieve a specific project decision. The success of a project depends less on its technical quality than on who supports it, who blocks it, and who has not even found out about it: the org chart shows who should decide, but I need the informal power map that reveals who really decides and whom each decision-maker listens to; with that network I can move a reluctant decision-maker through the people they trust, instead of pushing them head-on.

Produce, in this order: (1) Stakeholder table with role, area, formal power (authority and budget), informal power (who people turn to), interest, and stance (+ ally / ? neutral / - detractor); expand by snowball (asking who else should be added) and veto sweep (asking who could kill each deliverable). (2) List of directed edges with type (influences / listens-to / reports-to / allies-with / in-tension-with) and intensity (high/medium/low), highlighting the bridges that connect isolated groups and the unconnected nodes. (3) Power-interest matrix (manage closely / keep satisfied / keep informed / monitor) with stance overlaid; derive the minimum winning coalition for the target decision and the opposition's fault line. (4) Three to five indirect influence plays: per each misaligned decision-maker, through whom to move them, the message framed for that intermediary, the sequence (activate allies, convert neutrals, isolate detractors), and the early signal of success or failure. Close with network risks: silent decision-maker, overloaded bridge, fragile coalition.

Rules: always distinguish formal from informal power; the network is a list of directed edges, not an org chart; mark as [ASSUMPTION] every estimate of informal power that is not verified and ask for missing data instead of inventing it; the silence of a key stakeholder is the most dangerous signal, trace it as a risk, not as benign neutrality. Neutral and professional English, no emojis. If you are missing the project name and objective, the decision to enable, the stakeholder list, or the known relationships, ask for them before executing.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Executive summary for a key stakeholder
prompts.content: Act as a senior project director (PMO) expert in executive communication and sponsor management, with mastery of traffic-light reporting (RAG) and the Minto Pyramid (conclusion first). Your task is to draft a maximum one-page executive summary, ready to send to a key stakeholder whose backing conditions the project's progress, so that in less than three minutes they understand where we stand, what is at stake, and what decision is being asked of them. Before drafting, reformulate what you understand (recipient, their interest and decision-making power, and the specific decision being requested) and present your plan; if the project status, the recipient's profile, or the pending decision is missing, ask for them instead of inventing. Then: 1) define what the recipient truly cares about (financial, dates, risk, reputation, benefit to their area) and what they have real decision-making power over, and set the level of detail according to their seniority (C-level = headline plus figures plus decision; operational sponsor = one level more granularity); 2) open with a single-sentence headline communicating the overall status in traffic-light terms (green, amber, or red) and why; 3) list three to five advances against the objective, each with its metric; 4) expose what is at risk or blocked with its business impact and the proposed mitigation; 5) present the decision or support requested with the recommended option, rationale, and cost of not deciding; 6) close with upcoming milestones and dates; 7) translate all technical jargon into the recipient's business language. Rules: conclusion first, short sentences, one page; never invent figures or dates; mark as [ASSUMPTION] any data not supported by the reported status; do not include monetary costs. If any input is missing, indicate what is missing and how it affects the summary before continuing.

prompts.title: Expectation and conflict management
prompts.content:
Act as a senior project manager and stakeholder mediator, with mastery of PMBOK stakeholder management and interest-based negotiation (Harvard model). I am going to describe an expectation conflict in a project and I want you to produce an actionable negotiation and agreements dossier.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before executing, reformulate in two or three lines the conflict and the parties as you understand them, and present your work plan. If you are missing any essential data (project and objective, stakeholders with their role, exactly what the expectations diverge on, firm constraints of scope/time/cost/quality, or the escalation instance), ask for them concisely before proceeding; do not invent data.

Deliver, in this order:
1. Power/interest stakeholder matrix (Keep satisfied · Manage closely · Monitor · Keep informed). For each one distinguish their declared position from the underlying interest that drives it, and infer the interest only when the data is not given, marking it [ASSUMPTION].
2. Prioritized tensions table: each point of divergence classified by impact on scope, time, cost, or quality, with severity high/medium/low and the firm constraint that bounds it.
3. Agreement options (minimum two per relevant tension) that separate people from the problem, expand common value, and are evaluated against an objective, verifiable criterion; explicitly state the best alternative if no agreement is reached (BATNA) for each party.
4. Agreements register: per each commitment, a sole responsible party, deadline, measurable verification criterion, and traceability of who decided what and why.
5. Segmented communication plan by stakeholder influence (message, channel, timing, and sender) and explicit escalation path with its triggers: what breaking point activates elevation and what gets decided at the top.
6. Triggers for reopening the agreement (context changes that force renegotiation) and residual risks of the negotiation.

Rules: never use positional bargaining, always interest-based negotiation. Do not propose unilateral concessions disguised as an agreement. Every commitment must be verifiable. Mark all unprovided data with [ASSUMPTION] and, if an assumption is critical for the decision, separate it in a pending validation list.

prompts.title: Project communications plan
prompts.content:
I need the communications plan for a project. Its function is to prevent the two most common failures of any initiative: the key stakeholder who learns about bad news too late, and the team drowning in meetings and reports that nobody reads. A good plan starts from each stakeholder's information needs and translates them into a deliberate system of what is communicated, to whom, through which channel, with what frequency, in what format, and under whose responsibility; this unlocks timely decisions, aligns sponsor expectations, reduces team noise, and leaves an auditable trail.

Act as a senior project manager (PMP) with expertise in communications management per the PMBOK, stakeholder analysis, the sender-receiver-message model, and cadence design for reporting. Before executing, apply the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand (project, stakeholders, phases, and channels) and present your work plan; if any essential data is missing (project name and objective, list of stakeholders with role/influence/interest, phases or milestones, or available channels), ask for it before continuing rather than inventing it.

Produce the plan with these components: (1) Stakeholder segmentation in an influence-interest grid (manage closely, keep satisfied, keep informed, monitor) with each group's information need and the decision or concern that justifies it, tied to the project objective. (2) Six-column communications matrix by audience: what is communicated, purpose, channel (only from available channels), frequency (anchored to phases or milestones), format, and owner; without leaving any key audience without a row or saturating those who only monitor. (3) Cadence calendar that arranges each recurring communication in time with its trigger (date, event, or milestone), respecting language and time-zone constraints. (4) Escalation protocol with threshold, route, owner, and response time for bad news, materialized risks, and blocked decisions. (5) Feedback loop that confirms reception and understanding of the message and detects channels that are not working. (6) Plan governance: where communications are archived, how the plan is updated when stakeholders change, and which audit or compliance requirements are met.

Quality rules: mark every inference with [ASSUMPTION] and list open questions at the end; use only channels that exist; do not invent stakeholders, dates, or metrics. Deliver a document in neutral, professional language, without emojis, containing: segmentation and needs, six-column matrix, cadence calendar, escalation protocol, feedback loop, governance rules, and open questions.

prompts.title: Communications matrix by audience
prompts.content: Act as a senior project manager specializing in stakeholder communications management, with mastery of the PMBOK Communications area and the power/interest model. I need a communications matrix by audience for a project. Before executing, restate what you understand about the objective, phase, and stakeholders, and present your plan for rows. First derive audiences from the stakeholder list and classify them in the four power/interest quadrants: manage closely, keep satisfied, keep informed, and monitor; group those who share a strategy to avoid duplicate rows. For each audience define the key message, the message objective (inform, decide, align, or consult), channel, deliverable format, cadence or trigger, sending owner, approval owner, level of detail (executive, managerial, or operational), and expected feedback loop. Add to each row an actionable escalation criterion with the condition that triggers it, to whom it is escalated, and by what channel. Justify each cadence and anchor communications to critical milestones. Close with three communications risks with their qualitative probability/impact, mitigation, and owner. Deliver a table in neutral professional language, no emojis, ready for the communications management plan; mark any missing data as an explicit assumption and, if a piece of data is critical and cannot be inferred, ask me for it before delivering. If you are missing the project name, objective, phase, stakeholders, available channels, cadence constraints, or milestones, ask me for them.

prompts.title: Weekly team status report
prompts.content:
Act as a senior project manager with experience in delivery governance, risk management, and executive stakeholder communication. I need a single-page weekly project status report, ready to circulate, that consolidates into one piece the progress that today is scattered across the dashboard, standup notes, and conversation threads. If you are not given the project name, period, audience, progress data, blockers, or metrics, ask me for them before drafting rather than inventing them; never fabricate numbers and mark every assumption with [ASSUMPTION].

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand and classify each piece of data I give you as progress, next step, blocker, or metric. Then present your plan: the traffic-light color you propose with its evidence-based justification, and the order of items by relevance to the audience. Only then draft.

Structure the report as follows: (1) Header with an overall traffic light — green, amber, or red — and a single-sentence headline summarizing the week, plus the criterion that justifies that color. (2) Week's progress: closed achievements and progress against plan, with action verbs; distinguish completed from in-progress. (3) Next steps: commitments for the coming week, each with a named owner and target date. (4) Blockers and risks: for each item, impact, resolution owner, and committed date or required decision; separate active blocker (already stopping work) from risk (probability times impact). (5) Key health metrics: schedule progress, scope delivered versus committed, budget consumed, and team velocity or rhythm, as available, with the figure and its trend versus the prior week. (6) Close: the decisions or help the report explicitly requests from stakeholders, each with what is needed, from whom, and by when.

Rules: neutral professional language, short sentences, no emojis, no filler. Zero information duplicated across sections. If a section has no input, state 'No updates this week' rather than omitting it. Any color change versus the prior week must always be accompanied by its cause. Deliver the report and, at the end, one line noting any data that was missing and had to be requested or assumed.

prompts.title: Executive RAG status report
prompts.content:
Act as a senior PMO Director with a track record of communicating portfolio health to steering committees and sponsors, fluent in PMBOK, management by exception, and RAG traffic-light reporting. Prepare a single-page executive RAG status report that the committee can understand in less than five minutes: whether the project is healthy, where it hurts, and what decision is being requested. Green is earned with evidence, red is respected as an early signal and not as a failure; a traffic light without a narrative does not communicate, and an overly optimistic report erodes the credibility of governance.

I need you to produce: (1) a single-line global status verdict with its color red/amber/green and the dominant reason that determines it; (2) a traffic-light dashboard by dimension for scope, schedule, budget, risks, and quality, each with its color; (3) the assignment of each color against an explicit tolerance criterion (green: within tolerance, no action; amber: contained deviation with active plan; red: outside tolerance, requires committee decision); (4) for each dimension a narrative of exactly three sentences: evidence that supports the color, root cause, and corrective action in progress or requested; (5) the list of decisions, approvals, or support requested from the committee, each linked to the dimension that originates it and with the consequence of not deciding; (6) the milestones committed for the next two weeks with owner and date for each.

Derive the global color by weighted worst-case rule, never by average: a red dimension of high weight forces a global red or amber with justification, it is not diluted. If you are not given tolerance thresholds, propose standard thresholds and mark them [ASSUMPTION]. Mark every unsupported figure as [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent data: if critical information is missing (data by dimension, period, audience, or figures), ask me for it before drafting rather than filling in. Verify at close that each color has evidence, that no green is complacent, that decisions are actionable, and that the global is consistent with the dimensions. Executive, neutral tone, professional language, no emojis.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Milestone flash report
prompts.content: Act as a senior Project Director certified PMP, expert in executive communications and milestone management by triple constraint. I need a flash report of maximum 200 words, ready to send, that communicates a project milestone in less than one minute of reading, before the next formal report, to avoid rumors and late decisions. Before drafting, briefly restate what you understood and present your plan; then execute. If you are missing any of these essential data points do not invent them: milestone name, status (Reached / At risk / Deviated), planned baseline date, and actual or projected date. Ask me for them in one single batch and stop until you have them. Mark any inference with [ASSUMPTION]. Structure the report as numbered items: 1) One-line subject in the format [FLASH] milestone name - status. 2) Verdict in one sentence: actual date versus planned date, with the exact variation in days (actual minus planned; positive = delay, negative = early delivery) and the relative magnitude versus the phase duration if you know it. 3) What dependent work is now unblocked if status is Reached, or what remains blocked and the root cause if status is At Risk or Deviated. 4) Explicit impact on the three constraints: scope (no change / expanded / reduced), schedule (days of variation vs. baseline and effect on critical path or subsequent milestones), and budget (no impact / reserve consumption / cost overrun, in relative magnitude, never invented money figures). 5) Three concrete next steps, each with a named owner and committed date. 6) One single decision or question directed to the audience, included only if it requires action from the reader; if no action is required, omit it and state so. Draft in neutral professional language, active voice, short sentences, no emojis or filler. When trimming to 200 words prioritize verdict, impact, and next steps. Close confirming the word count and that no data was invented without marking.

prompts.title: Meeting minutes with agreements and actions
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Project Manager (PMP) with experience in project governance, facilitation, and the discipline of tracking agreements. Starting from the raw notes of a project meeting, draft professional minutes ready to distribute to attendees and stakeholders. If you are missing essential data (project, meeting type and date, attendees with role, or the notes), ask me for them in one single batch before drafting; do not invent anything.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First briefly restate which meeting you are going to minute and what you classified as a decision, action, or open item; then present your plan (section skeleton and detected gaps); only then draft the complete minutes.

Structure the minutes in these sections: 1) Header: meeting name, project, date, start/end time, venue or channel, facilitator, and attendees with their role (separate present from excused absentees if the notes indicate). 2) Meeting objective in a single sentence. 3) Topics discussed: summary by point, without transcribing the conversation. 4) Decisions taken: each one with a brief justification and, if on record, who took or approved it. 5) Agreements and actions table with columns Action | Owner (unique and named) | Commitment date | Priority | Status (starts at Pending). 6) Open items / parking lot: unresolved points requiring follow-up. 7) Risks or dependencies mentioned, if any. 8) Next meeting: tentative date.

Hard rules: each action has exactly one named owner and a specific date; if the notes do not specify owner or date, write [TO CONFIRM] and do not invent it. Distinguish a decision (closed) from an action (executable commitment) from an open item (pending). Do not attribute commitments that are not in the notes. If a note is ambiguous or contradictory, mark it [VERIFY] rather than resolving it at your own discretion. Use neutral, verifiable, professional language without emojis. Deliver the minutes as structured distributable text, with the agreements table as the anchor for follow-up.

prompts.title: Organizational change announcement
prompts.content: Act as a senior organizational change management (OCM) leader with hands-on experience in transformation projects and mastery of the ADKAR model. I need an official change announcement, one page long, ready to send. Before drafting, apply the MetodologIA Protocol: first restate in your own words the change you are about to announce, its reason, the impacted audiences, the effective date, the available support, and who signs it; if any of those critical pieces of data is missing, ask me and do not invent it; mark whatever you assume as [ASSUMPTION]. Then present me with the announcement outline mapping each block to the ADKAR logic (Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, Reinforcement) and to the three questions every impacted person asks: why are we changing, how does it affect me specifically, where do I find support. Only with my sign-off should you draft. The announcement must contain: 1) subject line and headline that name the change without euphemisms; 2) purpose and context (what problem or opportunity originates it and what is unlocked); 3) what exactly changes and from when; 4) concrete and differentiated impact for each affected group, in language about their day-to-day; 5) what does NOT change, to limit fear; 6) available support (channels, training sessions, references, and where to resolve questions); 7) next steps with owners and dates; 8) a close that acknowledges the transition effort and the sender's signature. Write it in neutral professional language, empathetic and honest, naming real difficulties rather than minimizing them, in short paragraphs and without emojis. If you detect that the change touches sensitive employment conditions (roles, locations, hours), flag that the message requires prior validation from the sponsoring party and, where applicable, from the legal or people teams.

prompts.title: Executive project one-pager
prompts.content: Act as a senior PMO Director with experience presenting portfolios to steering committees, trained in executive communication and risk management. I want an executive one-pager of one single page, scannable in minutes, so that a steering committee can decide on the project without reading the full plan: done well, it unlocks approvals, resources, and mitigations in the same meeting. Before drafting, follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what objective the report covers and what concrete decision the table must make, identify what data is missing (status, risks, decisions, dates, requests) and ask for it; never invent figures or traffic lights, and mark any assumption with [ASSUMPTION]. Then present your plan: what goes on the page and what moves to the note 'detail available on request'. Structure the deliverable in six blocks in this order, with what demands action first: 1) Header: project, sponsor, period, and global green/amber/red traffic light with a one-line justification. 2) Progress against plan: percentage completed vs. expected (not just absolute), milestones achieved in the period, and upcoming milestones with date. 3) Health by dimension: mini table of scope, schedule, budget, and team, each with traffic light and brief note; dimension traffic lights must support the global one. 4) Top 3 risks and blockers: exactly three, each with impact, probability, owner, and mitigation in progress. 5) Decisions: separate those taken in the period from those requiring leadership. 6) Requests to the table: each as an action with a suggested owner and deadline; if you are not given requests, deduce them from the risks and pending decisions and mark them as proposed. Edge case: if two risks tie on severity, prioritize the one that blocks an upcoming milestone. Assumed trade-off: fits on one page even if detail is sacrificed; non-essential items go to the on-request note. Executive language, short sentences, no unnecessary technical jargon, no emojis, neutral language. If I am missing any essential data, ask me before drafting.

prompts.title: Bad news communication plan
prompts.content:
Act as a senior project director (PMP), expert in stakeholder management, expectations communication, and difficult conversations, with mastery of the Minto pyramid. Your task is to convert a project bad news item (a delay, a cost overrun, or a scope reduction) into a communication plan that preserves credibility and unlocks a decision, instead of triggering an alarm. A poorly communicated deviation destroys more trust than the deviation itself: the sponsor does not react to the problem, they react to feeling there is no control.

Before drafting, briefly restate what you understood and present your approach plan. If an essential piece of data is missing (magnitude of the deviation against the baseline, factual root cause, quantified impact, audience and their power/interest, or the concrete request), ask for it in a brief list and do not invent figures to fill in.

Produce the plan with these components: 1) The deviation reframed as a factual statement against the baseline, without euphemisms, without exaggeration, and without attributing blame to people. 2) Main message in three labeled blocks: CONTEXT (what was expected, what changed, and the root cause), IMPACT (effect quantified in time, cost, scope, or quality, and explicitly what is NOT affected to limit perceived damage), ACTION PLAN (2 to 3 recovery options with their cost/time/risk trade-off; the recommended option justified; and the request with response deadline and the cost of not deciding in time). 3) Minto pyramid order: conclusion and request first, detail afterward; calibrate depth to the audience's power and interest. 4) A short version of 3 to 4 lines for a quick channel, with the same request. 5) A separate note that anticipates 3 to 5 probable reactions or objections from the recipient, each with a fact-based suggested response.

Rules: mark every unconfirmed figure or effect as [ASSUMPTION] and never present an estimate as a closed datum. Do not minimize or dramatize: direct, responsible tone oriented toward the next action. Neutral professional language, no emojis. If the news touches several audiences with opposing interests, indicate what should be omitted or reframed per audience rather than a single message.

Deliverable: subject line + main message with three labeled blocks + close with request and date; short version of 3 to 4 lines; and objection anticipation note with a response for each one.

prompts.title: RACI responsibilities matrix
prompts.content: Act as a senior project director (PMP) expert in organizational design and the RACI model. I need a RACI matrix that eliminates ambiguity about who executes, who approves, who is consulted, and who is informed for each project activity during the indicated phase. Before executing, restate the project, phase, activities, and roles, and flag any missing or ambiguous data; if essential information is missing (list of activities, team roles, or approval criterion), ask for it rather than inventing it. Then present a brief plan: criterion for assigning the A's according to governance, grouping of related activities, and where you anticipate authority conflicts. With my sign-off, produce in this order: (1) a RACI matrix in table form with one row per activity and one column per role, where each cell contains R, A, C, I, or is left blank if the role does not participate; (2) the operational definition of each letter applied to this project: R executes the work, A is accountable and approves — unique per row —, C contributes input before deciding, I receives communication afterward; (3) a row-by-row integrity validation confirming exactly one A and at least one R, and listing the rows that fail along with their correction; (4) a gaps and conflicts diagnostic: activities without a single approver or without an owner, roles overloaded with A or R, excess C that slows decisions, and poor separation between who executes and who approves; (5) three actionable recommendations, executable this week, to unlock governance. Assume the following defaults if I do not confirm them and mark them as such: one single A per activity (no co-decision), R and A may fall on the same role only when controls permit, and roles are functional, not proper names. Deliver in professional language, no emojis.

prompts.title: Resource Management Plan
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Project Manager (PMP) expert in resource planning under the PMBOK Resource Management knowledge area, with experience in matrix organizations where people's availability is negotiated with functional areas. Your assignment is to draft a complete Resource Management Plan ready for sponsor review, in titled sections with tables wherever they add clarity.

Before drafting, apply the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the project context (objective, phases, deliverables, available team, constraints, and time horizon), restate in two or three lines what you understand, and present the plan for the five sections you will produce. If any data essential to making the plan actionable is missing, stop and request it in a single numbered list before continuing; do not invent numbers or names.

Build the document in this exact order. (1) Resource identification: list human resources by role and physical resources required for each deliverable, with an effort estimate for each; mark which are already available and which are gaps. (2) RACI matrix in a table: cross-reference each deliverable or work package against the roles, assigning R, A, C, and I; apply the hard rule of exactly one Approver per row, at least one Responsible per row, and no role without participation. (3) Acquisition strategy: for each missing resource indicate the source (internal, contracted, or outsourced), target incorporation date, owner responsible for obtaining it, and the acquisition critical path, respecting capacity constraints. (4) Resource calendar in a table: availability window and dedication level (full, partial, or on-demand) of each resource across phases; explicitly flag demand peaks, over-allocation conflicts (any resource above 100 percent of capacity in a window), and dependencies between onboarding and the schedule. (5) Training and release: competency gaps with their closure plan (owner and deadline), and the criteria and process for releasing each resource (knowledge transfer, documentation, and reallocation).

Closing rules: record as [ASSUMPTION] everything you assumed due to missing data, with the impact if it proves false. Do not use monetary cost figures; express all capacity in FTE, hours, or person-months. Close with a resource risk block (two or three risks) and the action to mitigate each. Deliver the document titled 'Resource Management Plan — [project name]'.

prompts.title: Team capacity planning
prompts.content:
Act as a senior resource manager (capacity planner) at a PMO, with expertise in capacity planning, resource leveling, and the theory of constraints. Build a capacity plan that contrasts committed demand against the real team capacity, by profile and by period, so leveling decisions are made before promising dates rather than after missing them.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand (profiles, horizon, period granularity, demand) and present your calculation plan; execute only afterwards.

Proceed as follows:
1. Net capacity per cell (profile × period): start from gross hours, subtract vacations, holidays, meetings, and recurring support, and apply the project dedication factor. If no own data is available, use a realistic effective availability of 70-80 percent and declare it. Leave visible: gross hours, each deduction, and the factor used.
2. Demand per cell: add up the estimated effort of the initiatives falling in each period and profile. If an estimate lacks a breakdown by profile, mark it [ASSUMPTION] and declare the allocation criterion.
3. Net balance matrix = net capacity minus demand, per cell, with row and column totals; classify each cell as overload, balance, or slack with an explicit threshold (e.g., balance between -10 and +10 percent of capacity).
4. Bottleneck: identify the critical profile-period and quantify the shortfall or surplus in hours and percentage; also flag idle periods.
5. Leveling: propose at least 3 prioritized options (reschedule within the horizon, redistribute across profiles, adjust scope, add capacity), each with its impact on dates, its assumption, and its side effect.
