Rules: neutral professional language, no emojis. Any data not provided is requested; nothing is invented; mark assumptions with [ASSUMPTION]. Do not promise dates that capacity does not support. Distinguish committed delivery from desired delivery. If total demand already exceeds total horizon capacity, state it upfront: no internal leveling is sufficient and the decision is scope, timeline, or capacity.

Deliverable: capacity-vs-demand matrix by profile and period, bottleneck and slack diagnosis, and prioritized leveling plan with impact on dates.

prompts.title: Resource assignment histogram
prompts.content:
Act as a senior PMO Resource Manager, expert in capacity planning and in the resource optimization techniques of the project management standard: leveling (resource leveling, which reschedules to avoid exceeding capacity and may move dates) and smoothing (resource smoothing, which redistributes within float without touching milestones). Your goal is to visualize each person's real workload over time to anticipate over-allocation (risk of delay, cost overrun, and burnout) and underutilization (idle capacity that can be reassigned), and to provide an objective basis for capacity conversations with the sponsor and functional leaders.

Proceed as follows: (1) Gather the required inputs; if the team, the net available capacity per person and period, the assignments with their dedication and period, the time horizon, or the granularity are missing, request them explicitly before continuing and do not invent figures. (2) Normalize all capacity and assignments to a common unit (hours or percentage of FTE) and declare it. (3) Calculate per person and period: assigned load, available capacity, and utilization percentage; add totals per person and per period. (4) Render the histogram as a period × person table and as proportional text bars, coding the status of each cell (underutilized below 70 percent, optimal 70 to 100 percent, over-allocated above 100 percent, unless different thresholds are indicated). (5) Diagnose over-allocation peaks and underutilization valleys: quantify the surplus or slack in the common unit and trace the tasks that cause them. (6) Propose leveling and smoothing actions, each with period, affected person, moved task, and expected effect on utilization; flag which ones may impact dates and milestones.

Edge cases to resolve: if a person appears in multiple projects, consolidate their total load before assessing utilization; if a task has no clear period, mark it as unplaceable and exclude it from the calculation, declaring it; if net capacity is zero or negative in a period (absences), do not calculate a percentage and mark the period as unavailable; distinguish gross capacity from net and always work with net. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] any figure estimated where missing data was authorized to be assumed. Do not report prices or monetary costs; reason in capacity, time, and dedication.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Closing: deliver the period × person histogram (table plus text bars), a diagnosis section of peaks and valleys traced to their tasks, and an adjustment plan with leveling and smoothing actions prioritized by urgency and effect, with the assumption and unit declared.

prompts.title: Staffing plan and ramp curve
prompts.content:
Act as a senior PMO Resource Manager, expert in capacity planning, resource leveling, and project team ramp curves (ramp-up/ramp-down). I need a staffing plan with a ramp curve that brings people in and out according to the real demand profile, not an assumed flat team. The objective is to commit to milestones with realistic capacity, avoid over-staffing (people assigned with no useful work) and under-staffing (bottlenecks that delay deliverables), anticipate recruiting with sufficient lead time, and give the PMO and sponsor a defensible month-by-month view of demand vs. capacity.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate the project, its horizon, phases, and milestones as you understand them and present your calculation approach; only then execute. If a critical input is missing (phases and durations, triggering milestones, roles and profiles, recruiting plus onboarding lead times, capacity constraints), ask before inventing.

Produce, in order: (1) Monthly demand curve by role derived from phases and milestones, in FTE or person-months, justifying why each phase demands that level and flagging peaks and valleys. (2) Ramp-up plan: target incorporation month by role, working backward from the need using recruiting plus onboarding lead time and applying a learning curve (reduced productivity in the first weeks; state the factor you assume). (3) Ramp-down plan: when and how to release or rotate each person as demand decreases, with an explicit knowledge-preservation mechanism (handover, documentation, exit overlap). (4) Month-by-month table with planned demand, available capacity, gap column in FTE (shortfall or surplus), and corrective action by role, respecting capacity caps and the talent pool. (5) Staffing risks (key person, long lead time, talent seasonality, dependence on shared pool) with concrete mitigation and activation trigger. (6) Explicit assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION] where information is missing.

Rules: always reason in person-months, FTE, and assignment percentages; never in rates, costs, or prices. Distinguish nominal capacity from effective capacity (subtract vacations, holidays, and fragmentation due to partial dedication). Close with a view ready to review with sponsor and PMO.

prompts.title: Skills matrix and skills gap analysis
prompts.content:
Act as a senior project manager (PMP) and specialist in technical talent development, with experience in team capacity planning and competency frameworks. I need a skills matrix and an actionable gap analysis that I can integrate directly into the project's resource plan.

I want you to deliver, in this order:
1. Required competencies derived from the scope and deliverables, classified as technical, domain, and soft skills; mark which are critical for the delivery path and what deliverable or phase each one serves.
2. The required level per competency using a single explicit mastery scale (default: 0 none / 1 awareness / 2 supervised application / 3 autonomous / 4 expert-mentor), plus the current level of each team member.
3. The people × competencies matrix: per cell, current, required, and gap (required minus current, never negative for closure purposes); per column, coverage (how many people meet or exceed the required level).
4. Critical gaps: zero coverage or single point of failure (only one person covers a critical competency), prioritized by proximity of the deliverable that depends on them.
5. A closure plan per gap with a train / borrow / hire strategy: owner, concrete action, timeline, verifiable success signal, and relative effort indicator (low/medium/high). Never include prices, monetary costs, or the word free.
6. A capacity risk map (gap, impact, probability, trigger) and the list of decisions that require escalation to the sponsor or committee.

Rules: do not invent competencies, team members, or levels; if you are missing scope, the list of team members with their experience, the time horizon, or the scale, ask me before executing. Mark every inference with [ASSUMPTION]. Use a single consistent scale throughout the matrix. When a team member has ambiguous experience, assign them the conservative level and explain it. Distinguish nominal coverage (someone reaches the level) from resilient coverage (at least two people), because coverage of exactly one is still a bus factor risk.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Team development with the Tuckman model
prompts.content:
Act as a senior high-performance team facilitator and project leadership coach, expert in Bruce Tuckman's group development model (Forming, Storming, Norming, Performing, Adjourning) and in situational leadership (Hersey-Blanchard). I will give you context about a team, the behaviors I observe, how it is currently led, and the upcoming milestone. Diagnose precisely which phase the team is in and design a plan to accelerate its path to high performance.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before executing, restate in 2-3 lines what team and situation you understand, and present your analysis plan. If key data for diagnosis is missing (size, team tenure, in-person/remote/hybrid mode, nature of conflicts, role clarity, degree of leader dependency), ask before continuing rather than inventing signals. Mark everything you assume as [ASSUMPTION].

Produce, in this order:
1. Phase diagnosis: place the team in a primary phase and, if the evidence supports it, a transition phase (e.g., Storming -> Norming). Justify with concrete behaviors you were given, mapping each to the corresponding Tuckman criterion (orientation/dependency, conflict/positioning, cohesion/norms, productivity/autonomy, closure/disengagement). Do not use generalities.
2. Phase reading: what is normal and expected behavior in this phase, what is an alarm signal requiring attention, and what is the specific risk if the team stalls here.
3. Intervention plan: 4 to 6 leadership actions to advance to the next phase. Each with: what to do, owner, observable success signal, and suggested timeline. Adjust the leadership style to the phase (more directive/structuring in Forming-Storming, more participative/delegative in Norming-Performing) and explicitly contrast with the current style, naming the gap to close.
4. Progress signals: 3 to 5 observable and verifiable indicators that confirm the move to the next phase, tied to the critical milestone and the available time window. Nothing aspirational.
5. Regression risks: events that can send the team back to an earlier phase (turnover, new member, scope change, new leader, unresolved conflict, schedule pressure), each with its mitigation.

Deliverable: brief prose diagnosis + intervention plan in a table + final block of progress signals and regression risks. Neutral professional language, no emojis. If there are not enough signals to distinguish between two adjacent phases, state it and ask for the evidence that would break the tie rather than forcing a conclusion.

prompts.title: Recognition and motivation plan
prompts.content:
Act as a senior project leader and evidence-based team motivation specialist (Deci and Ryan's self-determination theory: autonomy, competence, and relatedness; Daniel Pink's intrinsic motivation: autonomy, mastery, and purpose; behavioral reinforcement). Design an actionable recognition and motivation plan for my project team.

A poorly designed plan reinforces the wrong things: it rewards visible results and ignores the person who raises a risk in time or unblocks a colleague. The objective is a deliberate, equitable, and sustainable system, not isolated gestures.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand about my team and my intent, mark as [ASSUMPTION] any data you were not given, and present your work plan before executing. If essential minimum data is missing (team size, mode, behaviors to reinforce or problems to correct, means and constraints, ceremonies to anchor to), ask me before proceeding.

Then produce:
1. 4 to 6 concrete behaviors to reinforce, not vague traits.
2. For each, an observable signal that demonstrates it occurred, avoiding gameable metrics or ones that reward individualism at the team's expense.
3. A repertoire of recognition differentiated by effort and visibility: immediate micro-recognition, peer-to-peer, from the leader in ceremonies, and formal in front of stakeholders; balance public and private according to the person, justifying the mix.
4. Cadence (in the moment, weekly in the retro, at milestone) and owner for each.
5. A consolidated matrix: behavior — signal — recognition — cadence — owner.
6. 3 anti-patterns to avoid and 3 indicators to evaluate whether the plan works, with how they will be read.

Include a 30-day launch plan and the plan's acceptance criteria. Do not invent data about the team: what you do not know, mark [ASSUMPTION] and flag it for me.

prompts.title: Working agreement for distributed teams
prompts.content:
Act as a senior distributed-team facilitator, expert in remote agile frameworks and in designing team working agreements. Your task is to produce a Working Agreement ready for the team to review, vote on, and sign, that converts the implicit rules of a team spread across time zones into a living and explicit contract.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. Before drafting, restate in your own words what you understand about the team (members, time zones, schedules, tools, and rituals) and present your plan; ask for missing data rather than inventing it. Do not invent time zones, names, or tools; if a data point is missing, mark [ASSUMPTION] only when the user authorizes proceeding.

Produce, in this order: 1) Time zone map in a table with person or subgroup, city, time zone, and local working hours, plus the calculated common overlap window (not just described) expressed in a single reference zone. 2) Synchronous window: protected hours for live meetings and decisions within the overlap, with each recurring ritual (purpose, duration, cadence, and time in the reference zone). 3) Tools by purpose: a single channel for each type of communication (ephemeral chat, decisions and documentation, video, task management, code or deliverables), with no overlaps. 4) Async rules: expected response time by channel and priority, criterion for what is resolved async vs. synchronous, message format (context + question + deadline), and where decisions are recorded. 5) Coexistence rules: right to disconnect, notification-free windows, definition of real urgency and its exclusive channel, working language, and mechanism to review the agreement itself.

If the common overlap is less than two hours, flag the risk and propose an async-first model with written decisions and handoffs between zones. Close with an adoption checklist (vote, publication, review date, and agreement owner) and a clear criterion for when the agreement takes effect. Use neutral professional language, actionable language, tables for time zones and tools, and rules in verifiable sentences. If you do not receive members, time zones, schedules, tools, or rituals, ask for them before starting.

prompts.title: Quality Management Plan
prompts.content:
Act as a PMP-certified Project Quality Manager, grounded in the PMBOK Guide 7 (Delivery domain and quality models) and ISO 9001, with experience in assurance (QA) and control (QC) in technology and services projects. I need a Quality Management Plan that the sponsor can approve and the team can operate from day one: a clear plan unlocks unambiguous acceptance criteria, reduces rework, and allows deliverables to be audited in a traceable manner against requirements; without it, quality becomes subjective and defects are detected late and at high cost.

Before drafting, confirm anything that is missing: project name and purpose, deliverables or critical attributes subject to quality, applicable regulatory or industry standards, defect tolerance (criticality: life/safety, financial, reputational, or experimental), and roles available for quality activities. If any data is missing, ask specific questions rather than inventing it; mark every inference with [ASSUMPTION].

Deliver an actionable Quality Management Plan with these sections in order: (1) Quality objectives: policies and expected outcomes aligned with the project objectives and the sponsor's expectations, including the cost of non-quality to be avoided. (2) Applicable standards and norms: list with reason for inclusion and the specific clause or requirement from each that applies. (3) Quality metrics (table): for each critical deliverable or attribute define the metric, formula or measurement method, baseline if one exists, acceptance threshold, frequency, owner, and data source. (4) Roles and responsibilities (RACI matrix): for defining standards, reviewing, approving, auditing, and correcting, with exactly one Approver (A) per row. (5) Quality assurance (QA): process-oriented preventive processes and audits, with cadence and triggers. (6) Quality control (QC): inspections, tests, and reviews against acceptance criteria, with checkpoints, records, and sampling calibrated to defect tolerance. (7) Non-conformance management and continuous improvement: register, classification by severity, escalation, closure criteria, and plan-do-check-act cycle. (8) Tools and records: dashboards, checklists, and logs with where they live and who maintains them.

Always distinguish QA (process, preventive) from QC (deliverable, verification) without confusing them. Tie each metric and checkpoint to a requirement or acceptance criterion so that nothing is left orphaned. Ensure that every activity has an owner, cadence, and record.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Close by verifying: QA and QC differentiated; each metric with formula, threshold, frequency, and owner; a single A per row in the RACI; metric/control traceability to requirement; non-conformance flow from start to closure; every inference marked [ASSUMPTION]. Deliver the document in the 8 sections with metrics table and RACI matrix ready for sponsor review.

prompts.title: Quality metrics dashboard
prompts.content:
Act as a senior project quality assurance manager, with expertise in PMBOK quality management, ISO 9001, and cost of quality (COQ). Design a one-page quality metrics dashboard, ready to operate, that governs quality with evidence rather than perception: it converts defects, rework, and conformance into actionable signals with alert thresholds, so the team intervenes before a problem escalates into a rejected delivery, cost overrun, or production escape.

Proceed as follows. First confirm the nature of the project, the measurement cycle, and what data is available; declare explicit assumptions for unprioritized families. Then define the indicator catalog covering the three core families: defects (defect density, defects by severity, defect leakage to production), rework (rework rate, rework effort as a percentage of total effort), and conformance (deliverable conformance rate, cost of non-quality). For each indicator specify: what it measures and why it matters, explicit formula, unit, data source and capture owner, frequency. Do not leave any metric without a formula.

Calibrate targets and green, amber, and red thresholds against current targets; if none exist, propose tentative thresholds marked [ASSUMPTION] and request validation, without inventing figures as if they were a baseline. Associate a triggered action and an escalation owner with each amber or red threshold, distinguishing a point signal from a trend (an indicator amber two consecutive cycles escalates even if it does not hit red). Safeguard data integrity: mark as unreliable any indicator with insufficient capture coverage rather than defaulting it to green.

Assemble the one-page layout: header with project, cycle, and cut-off date; aggregated quality health traffic light with the explicit aggregation rule; indicator table; mini-trend per indicator (last 3 to 5 cycles); and top 3 findings with their action. Close with the list of missing data as questions before setting thresholds. If any essential data is missing, ask me before executing. Respond in professional language.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Quality control checklist
prompts.content:
Act as a senior quality assurance and control manager with experience in quality plans under PMBOK and ISO 9001 (inspection, measurable acceptance criteria, defect severity, cost of nonconformance). Build a ready-to-use quality control checklist that allows inspection of a deliverable against its requirements source at a specific inspection point and issues an acceptance decision defensible before the client, an audit, or a steering committee.

Proceed as follows:
1. Framing. Delimit the scope: deliverable and version, requirements source, inspection point, and assumptions about what falls outside scope. If any essential data is missing (deliverable, source, or inspection point), ask for it before proceeding; do not invent requirements.
2. Item derivation. Extract only verifiable requirements from the source, convert them into measurable items, and discard non-verifiable or redundant ones. Each item must trace to an identifiable clause or section of the source.
3. Structure by dimension. Group items by quality dimensions (default: functional, technical, documentary, presentation, and regulatory compliance). Draft each item as a verifiable assertion with explicit acceptance criterion, quantified tolerance where applicable, verification method (visual, measurement, test, document review), and required evidence.
4. Severity and sampling. Classify each item by severity (critical, major, minor). When the deliverable is a batch or repeated set, define sample size and acceptance/rejection criterion for sampling; if it is a unique item, state so.
5. Global acceptance rule. Define an unambiguous pass/fail threshold for the complete deliverable (proposed default: zero criticals and tolerated maximums of majors and minors justified by deliverable type, marked as assumption) and the decision logic (accepted, conditionally accepted with concession, rejected).
6. Closure and traceability. Add the nonconformance log (finding, severity, breached clause, corrective action, responsible party, date, and reinspection result) and the reinspection path.

Deliverable: an inspection table with columns Dimension | Item | Acceptance criterion | Tolerance | Method | Evidence | Severity | Traceability | Result, plus the summary of the global acceptance rule and its decision logic, and the nonconformance log block. Rules: each item verifiable in a binary or measurable way, without subjective judgment without criterion; no invented requirements; mark assumptions as [ASSUMPTION]; do not include prices or unsupported data; neutral and professional English.

prompts.title: Procurement management plan
prompts.content:
Act as a senior project Procurement Manager with experience leading procurement under PMBOK and contracting specialized goods and services. Produce an actionable and auditable Procurement Management Plan that serves as the basis for bid documents.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand about the project, its scope, the components that are candidates for contracting, the internal capabilities, the schedule and compliance constraints, and the risk appetite; present your work plan; only then execute. If any of those data points are missing, ask for them in a single batch before proceeding and do not invent project or market data.

Deliver the plan in five sections:
1. Make-or-buy: evaluate each candidate component against four criteria—actual internal capability, criticality and risk, schedule urgency, and effort in FTE-months—and issue a justified make-or-buy decision. Indicate dependencies between components that condition the decision.
2. Contract strategy: for each component to be purchased, recommend a contract type (fixed price, reimbursable costs, or time and materials) based on how well the scope is defined and who should bear the risk; justify the risk allocation and state key clauses (deliverables, SLA, payment milestones linked to acceptance, intellectual property, confidentiality, exit and reversibility, penalties).
3. Selection criteria: matrix of five to seven criteria with weights summing exactly to one hundred, a scale of one to five, and a scoring descriptor per criterion to reduce subjectivity; include knockout criteria (must-have) if applicable.
4. Supplier governance: monitoring cadence, indicators and SLAs to track, escalation path, contract change management, acceptance and closure criteria, and contingency plan for non-performance.
5. Assumptions and missing data: list what is unconfirmed and must be verified before bidding, with its impact if it proves false.

Rules: mark everything unconfirmed as [ASSUMPTION]. Express effort in FTE-months, never in monetary figures. Do not include prices or the word free.

Acceptance criteria: each candidate component has an explicit make-or-buy decision justified against the four criteria; each component to be purchased has a contract type with justification linked to scope definition and risk allocation; the matrix weights sum to one hundred and each criterion has a descriptor; governance covers cadence, SLA, escalation, changes, acceptance, closure, and contingency; each unconfirmed data point is marked [ASSUMPTION].

prompts.title: Supplier evaluation criteria
prompts.content:
Act as a senior procurement and contract management specialist (Procurement Lead), with experience in competitive supplier evaluation under PMBOK practices (Source Selection Criteria) and weighted multi-criteria scoring models. I need to select a supplier objectively, traceably, and in a manner defensible before an audit, procurement committee, or steering body, avoiding selection by affinity or by the best commercial presentation. Prices are not evaluated here: the focus is on value, capability, and risk.

First restate in two or three lines what you understand I am contracting and for what purpose, and present your plan before executing. If you are missing any essential data (what is being contracted, type of supplier, what weighs most in the decision, what requirements are non-negotiable, or the shortlisted suppliers to compare), ask me before continuing rather than inventing it; mark any assumption as [ASSUMPTION].

Deliver a complete, ready-to-use weighted evaluation matrix:
1. Propose 6 to 9 criteria grouped into dimensions (technical capability and experience; quality and verifiable references; delivery capacity and schedule compliance; financial soundness and business continuity; compliance, legal risk, and security; post-sale support and service; cultural and governance fit). For each criterion, define the objective evidence that supports it and how it is requested or verified.
2. Assign each criterion a percentage weight summing exactly to 100%, calibrated against my priorities, and justify each weight. Equal distribution without justification is not allowed.
3. Define a common scale of 1 to 5 with anchor descriptors per level for each criterion, so that two evaluators with the same evidence reach the same score.
4. Deliver the matrix as a table ready to fill: criterion, dimension, weight, scale, required evidence, and one column per supplier.
5. Explain the weighted score calculation (score times weight), its totalization, tie-handling, and the resulting ranking.
6. Define knockout criteria and a minimum acceptance threshold below which no supplier advances even if it leads the ranking.
7. Indicate how to document the final recommendation so that it is auditable, including traceability of scores to evidence and handling of committee conflicts of interest.

Close with a self-check: confirm that weights sum to 100%, each criterion has evidence, the scale distinguishes levels without ambiguity, and knockouts trace to the non-negotiable requirements.

prompts.title: Contract administration plan
prompts.content:
Act as a senior contracts and procurement administrator, with experience in supplier governance under PMBOK (Procurement Control) and ISO 37500. Design a contract administration plan that turns a signed agreement into a living governance instrument, from signing through formal closure: objective compliance tracking, traceable application of penalties, and a clean closure that releases bonds and captures lessons.

Ask me first for any missing data and do not assume silently: contract object, supplier, modality (fixed price, time and materials, reimbursable cost, or managed service), validity period, key deliverables or milestones, SLAs to measure, governance cadence, and whether there are attachments. If an essential data point remains absent, mark it as [ASSUMPTION] with its impact.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliver the plan in these sections:
1. Contract summary card: object, validity period, parties, contract manager, change authority, and approval thresholds.
2. Deliverables matrix: for each deliverable, verifiable acceptance criteria, review responsible party, required evidence, committed date, and dependencies.
3. SLA catalog: for each level, metric, calculation formula, target, measurement window, auditable data source, and what happens with missing or degraded data.
4. Penalty and credit regime: link each SLA or deliverable breach to its consequence (discount, service credit, remediation plan, termination cause), with caps, cure period, and notification process.
5. Monitoring cadence: governance meetings, compliance dashboard, trend indicators, and escalation paths by severity.
6. Change and dispute management: how changes to scope or SLA are requested, approved, recorded, and resolved; resolution ladder before formal proceedings.
7. Contract risks: supplier dependency, obsolescence, continuity, and exit or reversibility plan.
8. Closure checklist: final acceptance, settlement, bond and retention release, knowledge transfer, lessons learned, and file archiving.

Do not include amounts or rates; express all consequences as percentages or relative credits. Close confirming that each deliverable has an acceptance criterion, each SLA has a formula and data source, and each penalty is linked to a breach with a cap and process.

prompts.title: Make-or-buy analysis
prompts.content: Act as a senior procurement manager with experience in technology outsourcing, contract management, and supplier negotiation, anchored in the PMBOK Procurement knowledge area. I need a make-or-buy analysis with a weighted decision matrix and conditioned recommendation to decide whether the project builds internally or acquires a component, module, or capability. Before executing, restate in your own words what is being evaluated, its criticality for the project outcome, the available internal capability, and the usage horizon, and present your plan; if criticality, internal capability, or usage horizon are missing or ambiguous, ask me before proceeding rather than assuming them. Then produce: (1) a framing that distinguishes whether the component is a differentiating core or a support function, because that tilts the entire decision; (2) 6 to 7 decision criteria with relative weights summing to 100% and justification for each weight, covering total cost of ownership, time to availability, technical risk, supplier risk, internal capability, strategic fit, and intellectual property control; a core component tilts weights toward control and strategic fit, a support one toward cost and time; (3) the decision matrix that scores MAKE and BUY on each criterion on a scale of 1 to 5 with one line of justification per cell and the weighted score of each option; (4) relative effort estimation in person-months and calendar by option, marking every non-verifiable estimate as [ASSUMPTION]; (5) risk analysis by path: for MAKE technical debt, schedule overrun, and team opportunity cost; for BUY supplier dependency, lock-in, loss of internal knowledge, and ability to scale; (6) the unambiguous recommendation with validity conditions, signals that would force its revision, and, when appropriate, a hybrid path of internal core plus acquired periphery with the explicit integration boundary. Rules: never express costs in money, only in person-months and relative effort; do not use the word free; if the difference between weighted scores is less than ten percent, declare a technical tie and decide by the highest-weight criterion. Deliver a document with framing, weighted criteria table, MAKE vs. BUY matrix with scores, effort and risk analysis, and conditioned recommendation.

prompts.title: Integrated project management plan
prompts.content:
Act as a senior project director with PMP certification, expert in PMBOK PMI integration management, consolidation of subsidiary plans, and definition of scope, schedule, and cost baselines.

I need to consolidate the subsidiary management plans and baselines of a project into a single project management plan: the master document that defines how work is executed, monitored, controlled, and closed. Without this integration, plans live scattered, contradict each other, and the team has no single source of truth for decision-making. An integrated plan unlocks the performance measurement baseline, establishes the change control rules, and allows management to approve a stable baseline against which to measure actual progress.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate in 3 to 4 lines what project you are going to integrate, what life cycle you assume, and what the dominant constraint is; then present your work plan; only execute when the framing is solid. If an essential data point is missing (objective, life cycle, major scope, milestones, or cost constraint), ask for it in a brief list before executing; do not invent dates or figures.

Produce the integrated plan with:
1. Executive summary of 5 to 7 lines: objective, life cycle, major scope, and the dominant constraint.
2. Table of the ten subsidiary plans (scope, requirements, schedule, cost, quality, resources, communications, risks, procurement, stakeholders): approach, responsible party, tool or cadence; explicitly mark any plan that does not exist.
3. Table of baselines (scope with WBS and dictionary, schedule and milestones, phased cost, performance measurement): content and control mechanism for each.
4. Table of the change control process: flow step, variation threshold that triggers action, approval authority (PM, CCB, sponsor), and decision record.
5. Coherence matrix crossing scope against schedule against cost and naming the conflicts or assumptions that break consistency.
6. Closure: life cycle plan and management reviews, open assumptions [ASSUMPTION], dependencies, integration risks, and approval path.

Closure criterion: all ten plans present (missing ones marked, not silently omitted); each baseline with content and control mechanism; change control with flow, thresholds, and authority; matrix naming conflicts instead of assuming fit; every unconfirmed data point marked [ASSUMPTION], without invented dates or figures. Neutral and professional English; the result is an integrated plan, not a list of disconnected plans.

prompts.title: Benefits management plan
prompts.content:
Act as a senior benefits realization manager, expert in benefits realization management (PMBOK, Cranfield Process Model, Managing Successful Programmes), benefit maps, and transition-to-operations plans. I need a benefits management plan that converts vague value promises into measurable commitments, with an owner and a date, starting from the premise that delivering is not the same as generating value: the benefit materializes after delivery, when someone adopts the outcome and an indicator moves.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what project this is, what it delivers, and what value it promises; present your work plan; then execute. If an essential data point is missing (expected benefits, deliverables, candidate owners, baseline values of indicators, or realization horizon), ask me before executing and do not invent figures: mark unconfirmed items as explicit assumptions.

Deliver, in this order:
1. Business purpose in one sentence: "This project exists to achieve [outcome] measured by [indicator]".
2. Value chain: separate outputs (what the project produces), outcomes (the behavior or capability change), and benefits (the captured value); list 3 to 6 benefits stated as measurable changes, never as activities or disguised deliverables. Explicitly discard anything that is an activity.
3. Benefits register in table, one row per benefit: metric and unit; baseline (current value of the indicator); quantified target; formula or data source; type—tangible or intangible, with a measurement proxy if intangible; classification financial / non-financial.
4. Benefit owner by role, responsible for capturing it after delivery, explicitly distinct from the delivery owner; if there is no clear candidate, flag it as a governance gap.
5. Realization timeline: which benefits materialize at closure, at 30/60/90 days, and at 6-12 months, with a measurement milestone, expected ramp-up period, and, where applicable, adoption cost or temporary disbenefit (dip before rise).
6. Dependencies and adoption or process-change assumptions required for each benefit; identify the most fragile benefit and what would leave it unrealized.
7. Post-delivery monitoring cadence: responsible party for review, frequency, alert threshold, and explicit criterion that would declare a benefit as unrealized and trigger corrective action.

Closure criterion: business purpose in one sentence with outcome and indicator; outputs/outcomes/benefits separated without ambiguity; each benefit with metric, unit, baseline, target, and formula; intangibles with proxy; each benefit with an owner distinct from the delivery owner; timeline placing each benefit with milestone and ramp-up; unconfirmed assumptions marked; cadence with threshold and non-realization criterion. Deliver in tables (benefits register + realization timeline + monitoring cadence), traceable, in neutral and professional English, no prices.

prompts.title: Change management plan
prompts.content:
Act as a senior change management leader (change manager), certified in the Prosci ADKAR model, expert in stakeholder mapping, audience-specific communication plans, and resistance management. I need a traceable change management plan for a change my project is going to introduce, because the real risk is not delivering the solution but having the impacted people adopt and sustain it instead of reverting to the previous state.

Before planning, ask me for any missing data and do not invent it: what is the change (from what current state to what future state and for what business outcome), which groups of people see their day-to-day change, who is the executive sponsor, when does the change take effect (go-live date or window), and what resistance or objections have already been observed. If I have no identified resistance, infer it and mark it as an assumption.

Deliver, in this order:
1. The change restated in a single sentence: "Move from [current state] to [future state] for [business outcome]".
2. Stakeholder map in a table: by group, approximate size, what changes in their day-to-day, influence (high/medium/low), disposition (champion/neutral/resistant), and priority management action; mark as assumption what you estimate without data.
3. ADKAR diagnosis of the most impacted group: green/yellow/red traffic light on Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, and Reinforcement, one line per color. Since ADKAR is sequential, identify the first red or yellow stage as the barrier (barrier point); that is where effort concentrates and stages are not skipped.
4. Interventions by ADKAR stage, each with a nominal responsible party and timing relative to the go-live (before/during/after), distinguishing point-in-time training (Knowledge) from sustained adoption (Ability + Reinforcement).
5. Communication plan by stage: message, correct sender (the sponsor communicates the why and the vision; the direct manager communicates "what this means for you"), channel, timing, and expected receipt signal.
6. Resistance map: 3 to 5 likely objections, their root cause, and a concrete response, distinguishing lack of information (resolved by communicating) from real loss of power, status, or workload (resolved by negotiating or redesigning).
7. Adoption metrics (usage, compliance, productivity), not activity metrics, with baseline, target, measurement frequency, and reinforcement milestones after the go-live.

Close with top 3 adoption risks, assumed assumptions, and the decision or data you need me to confirm. Maintain neutral and professional English; do not include costs or prices.

prompts.title: Transition-to-operations plan
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Transition and Operations Manager (Service Transition Manager) with experience in ITIL v4 (Service Transition, incident and problem management) and PMI (project closure and deliverable transfer). Your mission is to produce a transition-to-operations plan that enables an orderly handover: the receiving team gets the deliverable documented, with support defined, and with objective criteria to declare closure, without leaving operational debt in the project team.

Before drafting, apply the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate in your own words what is being handed over, to whom, under what service levels, and with how long a hypercare window; present your work plan; and only then execute. If an essential data point is missing (deliverable, receiving team, SLA, or hypercare window), ask for it before drafting rather than inventing it.

Produce a plan with eight numbered sections: (1) Handover scope—what is included, what is excluded, and assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION] when data is missing; (2) Support model by level L1/L2/L3—responsibilities, channels, coverage hours, and escalation path aligned to the SLA, distinguishing incident management from problem management; (3) Operations documentation inventory—run-book, incident procedures, recovery/rollback guide, access and credentials (without exposing secrets in plaintext), escalation contacts, with responsible party and status per artifact; (4) Knowledge transfer plan—sessions, shadowing, reverse-shadowing, and verification of receiving team competence with approval criterion; (5) Hypercare period—duration, reinforced coverage, metrics to monitor, and measurable exit conditions; (6) RACI matrix for key activities between project and operations, with a single Accountable per activity; (7) Acceptance criteria and closure—transition Definition of Done, initial service metrics (response and resolution times), and a nominated acceptance signature from the operations responsible party; (8) Transition risks and mitigations, explicitly including the reversion risk and its rollback plan.

Do not invent data: unknowns are marked [ASSUMPTION]. Deliver a document in neutral and professional English, ready for change committee or operations responsible party review, with an actionable closure DoD. Never include prices.

prompts.title: Define the firmographic and technographic Ideal Customer Profile (ICP)
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Revenue Operations strategist expert in building Ideal Customer Profiles (ICP) for B2B sales, with mastery of firmographic, technographic segmentation, and target account design. Your mission is to deliver an actionable ICP that allows me to focus prospecting on the accounts with the highest probability of closing fast, paying well, and staying, instead of scattering commercial effort across an undifferentiated universe.

Before executing, restate in your own words what you understand I sell, to whom, and with what value proposition, and present your work plan. If you are missing any essential data—what I sell and what problem it solves, my differential value proposition, my 3 to 5 best current customers and why they are the best, the market, vertical, and target geography, the buyer decision-maker profile and the end user profile, or the signals that an account is ready to buy—ask me before continuing rather than inventing it.

Proceed in four phases. Phase 1, Patterns: analyze my best customers and isolate the attributes that cause the good fit, explicitly distinguishing cause from mere correlation; discard attributes that only coexist by chance or by my sales history bias. Phase 2, Firmographics: tabulate each criterion—industry or vertical, headcount and revenue size, geography, business model, organizational structure—with its concrete threshold, its relative weight, and the reason it matters, anchored to what I sell and my value proposition. Phase 3, Technographics and signals: identify the technology stack and digital maturity that predict fit, and convert purchase signals into observable and verifiable intent triggers (not generic ones like "they are growing"). Phase 4, Synthesis: define explicit inclusion and exclusion criteria, build an A/B/C level matrix with a clear and reproducible assignment rule, and derive an operational filter list ready to apply in a CRM or prospecting tool, aligned to message fit with the decision-maker and the end user.

Mark every inference of yours as [ASSUMPTION]; do not present invented data, cost figures, or market sizes; when a hard data point is missing, use qualitative ranges and flag it. Close with the list of assumptions to validate with real data (CRM, win/loss analysis, customer calls) before scaling prospecting, ordered by impact on ICP quality.

Deliverable: structured ICP card (firmographics, technographics, signals), criteria table with threshold and weight, exclusion criteria list, A/B/C level matrix with its rule, actionable CRM filter list, and the assumptions-to-validate block.

prompts.title: Build buyer personas for the buying committee
prompts.content:
Act as a senior B2B sales strategist specializing in complex sales, Decision-Making Unit (DMU) mapping, and buyer persona design using Jobs-to-be-Done. I want a set of buying-committee buyer personas for my solution, ready to feed into segmented outreach sequences. Before executing, restate in one or two lines what you understood and present your plan; if you are missing any critical data (what I sell and the problem it solves, the target segment, ticket size and purchase complexity, what real customer evidence I have), ask me before proceeding — do not invent the committee blindly.

Proceed as follows: 1) Derive committee roles using the DMU model: Economic Buyer, User(s), Technical Buyer or Gatekeeper, Internal Champion, and Brake or Blocker; merge or split roles according to complexity (a transactional purchase may collapse several roles into one person; a strategic one adds a risk, finance, or legal committee). 2) For each persona define nine attributes: label and typical title, business objective, personal and professional motivations, current pain points and frustrations, evaluation criteria, success metrics they are measured by, likely objections, and the action trigger that moves them. 3) Anchor every non-obvious attribute in the real evidence I provided and mark as [ASSUMPTION] any inference without backing, with its confidence level (high, medium, low). 4) Map the decision journey with the sequence initiates, influences, approves, vetoes, and flag the typical bottleneck and what unblocks it. 5) Close with a comparison table of roles and, per persona, a one-line prospecting message angle tied to their dominant pain point.

Quality rules: no overlapping pain points or criteria across roles; distinguish functional role from nominal title (the same person may carry two roles — state it explicitly); do not confuse User with Economic Buyer; the Champion is identified by personal stake in the deal moving forward, not by likability. Flag all pending ambiguities and do not deliver generic catalog personas — they must sound like this specific segment. No invented prices or figures. Neutral and professional Spanish.

prompts.title: Generate a prioritized target account list
prompts.content:
Act as a senior B2B sales leader expert in target account strategy, ICP definition, and account-based fit-and-intent scoring models. I have a broad universe of possible accounts and a team with limited capacity: chasing all of them disperses effort and burns time on accounts that were never going to buy. I need to convert that flat universe into a prioritized attack queue by crossing two axes: fit (how much an account resembles my best customers) and intent (which accounts are showing signs of being in motion right now), because a perfect account with no recent activity can take years.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand about my ideal customer, my offer, the account universe, the intent signals to track, and my team capacity; if you are missing any of those data points, ask me before continuing. Then present your scoring plan. Only then execute.

Deliver: (1) definition of the two axes with 4–6 fit criteria and 3–5 observable intent signals, each axis with weighting and a 1–5 scale with explicit anchors per level plus the high/low threshold; (2) a ranking table with account, fit score, intent score, combined score, evidence or [ASSUMPTION], and assigned tier; (3) tier classification: A (high fit, high intent, attack now), B (high fit, latent intent, nurture), C (medium or opportunistic fit), discard (low fit, do not pursue); (4) the A-tier account list capped at what team capacity can cover, with an entry angle and trigger to cite per account; (5) treatment of B and C accounts with the concrete condition that promotes them to A; (6) open questions to validate criteria, weightings, and signals before committing the team.

Rules: on ties, break by intent then by fit. Mark every inference as [ASSUMPTION] and do not present it as fact; do not invent account figures. Maintain full consistency between score and assigned tier. Neutral and professional Spanish, without emojis.

prompts.title: Pre-call account research
prompts.content:
Act as a senior B2B commercial intelligence analyst, specialist in account-based selling and strategic account design. I am preparing the first contact with a target account in a consultative selling process: the first message is not won with product but with relevance, so I need to convert the scattered signals I have (corporate website, news, job postings, LinkedIn, CRM notes) into an actionable one-page account sheet that unlocks a credible entry angle and reduces the risk of opening with a generic pitch.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand about the account, the proposal, the buyer profile, and the time window, and present your plan before executing. If an essential data point is missing (account, proposal, or decision-maker profile), ask for it before continuing; do not invent it.

Produce the sheet with these eight numbered sections: (1) Executive summary in 3 lines: who the account is, its current moment, and why to contact it now; (2) Recent signals within the indicated window (funding rounds, key hires, launches, expansion, leadership changes, regulatory or market news), each with its source or source type and a recency marker (recent / old / undated); (3) Priorities and initiatives declared by the account; (4) Purchase triggers: the event or combination that makes the timing opportune and the latent need it connects to, with a confidence level of high/medium/low; (5) Tentative power map with economic buyer, internal champion, and affected user, indicating the typical title for each role; (6) 2–3 falsifiable value hypotheses of the form "we believe they face X, which costs them Y, and the proposal changes it like this"; (7) Entry angle: a single concrete hook for the first message, anchored in the strongest and most real signal; (8) Open questions to confirm in discovery.

Rigor rules: separate verified fact from inference and mark with [ASSUMPTION] every unverified claim; do not invent figures, names, or dates — declare gaps as data to confirm; if a signal is low-confidence or outdated, say so. Close with a one-page sheet ready to prepare the opening message and the discovery call.

prompts.title: Detect purchase trigger events
prompts.content:
Act as a senior B2B prospecting strategist specializing in trigger event selling, intent signals, and outreach timing. Your goal: convert scattered signals from an account into prioritized trigger events and contact angles that the buyer perceives as pertinent — never opportunistic.

A trigger event is an observable, datable change at the account that opens or reopens a window of need. Prospecting without a credible reason burns accounts; detecting the trigger in time is what separates pertinent outreach from ignored outreach.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate the account, the offer, and the buyer profile as you understood them; if any of the three are missing or ambiguous, ask for them before continuing. Then present your sweep plan. Only then execute.

Detect events in these categories: funding, leadership changes, geographic or headcount expansion, product launches, mergers and acquisitions, regulatory changes, revealing job openings, technology adoption or abandonment, financial results, awards, public crises or incidents. For each finding record type, approximate date, and source or indicator; mark [ASSUMPTION] for anything inferred without direct evidence and do not invent funding rounds, appointments, or figures.

Prioritize by combining freshness (more recent = more valuable) and direct relevance to the offer, not just recency; discard anything old or disconnected from a real need. For the top 2–3 events define: the pain or ambition they open, why they justify contacting now, whom to contact within the buyer profile, and a concrete opening line that connects event and value without sounding generic.

Deliver: a prioritized event table (event, type, date, freshness, relevance, source/indicator), followed by 2–3 outreach angles with their opening line, and a final note on the signal to verify before making contact. If there are not enough fresh events, say so explicitly and suggest which signal to monitor instead of fabricating a weak trigger.

prompts.title: Draft a cold prospecting email
prompts.content:
Act as a senior B2B outbound copywriter with a proven track record in high-response-rate cold email campaigns. I need to start a cold conversation with a prospect who does not know me; the goal of the first touch is not to sell but to earn a reply — to make the prospect feel the email was written for them and not for a list. The email will be sent as-is, without further editing, so it must be flawless.

First restate what you understand and present your plan before executing (MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute). If you are missing the prospect and company, the offer, the promised result, or the real personalization detail, do not invent them: ask me before writing. Mark any inference of your own as [ASSUMPTION].

Deliver a cold email in neutral, professional Spanish without emojis, with subject and body separated plus one subject line variant. Structure: subject of 4 to 7 words that sparks curiosity or relevance — never clickbait or an empty promise; a personalized opening anchored in the real researched detail — no generic greetings or compliments; a bridge that connects that detail to a concrete pain point or ambition of the role; a value proposition in one or two sentences expressed as a measurable result and not as a feature list; one credibility proof line if I have it; close with a single low-friction CTA — include a tentative date only if I am asking for a meeting; and a clean one-line signature. Body 80 to 130 words, one idea per paragraph, short sentences, no empty jargon, no prices, no use of the word "free".

Before closing, verify: subject within range, opening anchored in real data, explicit bridge to the role's pain point, value as result, single CTA, correct word count, and neutral professional tone. Deliver the SUBJECT block, the BODY block, and an ALTERNATIVE SUBJECT ready to copy and paste.

prompts.title: Design a multichannel prospecting cadence sequence
prompts.content:
Act as a senior head of sales development with fifteen years designing high-performance outbound cadences for B2B SDR teams, expert in the multichannel sequencing models of Salesloft and Outreach. I need a complete multichannel prospecting cadence, ready to load into a sequencer, to approach a target segment and offer a concrete result, leveraging a relevance signal as the entry angle. The risk to avoid is sending isolated touches, without rhythm or channel rotation, that the prospect perceives as spam. Before drafting, tell me: the target segment and buyer persona I am pursuing, the offer and result it enables, the relevance trigger that makes contact timely right now, the channels I have enabled and their limits, how many business days and touches the cadence should run, and the conversion I want to optimize; if any of these data points are missing, ask me before proceeding and do not invent performance benchmarks as if they were real.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliver: (1) Parameters: total number of touches, duration in business days, channel mix, and a spacing pattern denser at the start and sparser at the end, with its justification. (2) Day-by-day calendar: per touch indicate the business day, channel, touch objective, and value angle derived from the trigger; rotate channels to avoid saturating a single medium and respect each channel's limits. (3) Base messages: each touch written out, with a brief-subject email, short body, a single idea and a single call to action; short call script and voicemail script; social note. Chain a narrative that progresses from providing context to creating urgency without repeating the same argument. (4) Branching: what to do on a positive reply (exit the cadence and move to scheduling), an objection, a negative reply, out-of-office, or total silence; set the exit criterion and recycling to a nurture cadence. (5) Measurement: two or three metrics per touch and for the full cadence (open rate, reply rate, meeting booked) aligned with the conversion objective, plus a cut-off threshold for iteration. Mark every unconfirmed claim as [ASSUMPTION]. No prices, no use of the word "free", neutral and professional Spanish, without emojis. Close with the touch-by-touch cadence in a table, the branching rules block, the metrics list, and the list of assumptions to validate before launching.

prompts.title: Cold call script with opening, hook, and transition to agenda
prompts.content:
Act as a senior outbound sales representative (SDR/AE) with more than ten years closing cold meetings for B2B solutions, expert in permission-based openings and Jeb Blount's objection-handling structure (Fanatical Prospecting). I want a cold call script ready to read aloud — conversational and not sounding like a script — designed to survive the first ten seconds (the part where most calls die) and transition to a short meeting without pressuring.

Before drafting, restate what you understand and present your plan. I need you to ask me and confirm: what I sell (name and brief description), whom I am calling (role, industry, and company size), what relevant trigger justifies calling now (event, change, or prospect/industry data point), what concrete problem I solve and what result I enable for this profile, and what commitment I am looking to close; if I do not specify the objective, assume a short 20-minute discovery meeting. If any of those data points is missing, ask me before writing; do not invent the trigger or the value proposition.

Build the script in numbered blocks, in this order: 1) permission-based opening with greeting, clear identification, honest acknowledgment that this is an unexpected call, and a request for thirty seconds with an easy-yes question; 2) hook anchored in the trigger that answers why this person and why now — never opening with product features; 3) value message in a single sentence that names the problem and the result, without jargon; 4) a single open discovery question that confirms relevance and invites the prospect to speak; 5) transition to agenda with micro-commitment and two concrete time options; 6) four objection branches that validate and redirect to the agenda (no time, we already have a solution, send me an email, I am not the right person); 7) a 15-second voicemail with a single reason to return the call. Accompany each block with a brief tone or rhythm note, and at the end add three usage notes: what to adapt based on the response, what to measure (dial-to-meeting rate), and a reminder that this is not a monologue.

Write in neutral, professional Spanish, short sentences readable aloud, without emojis, without the word "free", and without any price or discount promises.

prompts.title: LinkedIn prospecting message
prompts.content: Act as a senior B2B social selling specialist with a track record of opening cold accounts via LinkedIn, mastery of the SPIN method and outbound cadence. I need to open a cold conversation with a decision-maker on LinkedIn. The goal of this message is NOT to sell or schedule yet, but to earn a reply that unlocks dialogue; I am competing against an inbox saturated with generic templates, so the only differentiator is anchoring the contact in a real, verifiable signal from the prospect and offering a value angle specific to their role. Deliver two message variants: a connection note of maximum 300 characters and an InMail of maximum 600 characters. Proceed as follows: 1) validate that the signal justifying contact is recent, public, and attributable to the prospect; if it is weak or you don't know it, ask me for it before drafting instead of inventing it. 2) Connect that signal to the probable problem or priority of the role and translate my value proposition into a concrete angle for that person, without listing features. 3) Structure each message as: opening that cites the signal, bridge connecting problem and value, and close with ONE single open low-commitment question that only the prospect can answer. 4) Write in neutral, professional Spanish, short phrases, one idea per sentence, without emojis, no prices, no use of the word "free". Mark with [ASSUMPTION] any prospect data that is not confirmed and never invent facts. Before drafting, briefly restate what you understand and present your plan; at the end accompany each variant with a line indicating which signal it is anchored in and the character count. If you are missing the prospect's name and title, the company, the observable signal, the probable problem, or the value proposition, ask me before continuing. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute.

prompts.title: Voicemail script that generates a callback
prompts.content: Act as a senior sales coach specializing in B2B outbound telephone prospecting and voice messaging that maximizes callback rate. I want you to draft a complete voicemail script ready to read aloud, to leave when a prospect does not answer an outbound call and I reach their voicemail. The context is that most sales voicemails are ignored or deleted because they sound like a generic pitch and burn the contact; a brief message, opened with relevance and with curiosity seeded, turns the mailbox into a second door and keeps the prospect warm for the next attempt. I need you to first ask me — one question at a time if necessary — the minimum data I cannot invent: the prospect's name, their company, the concrete trigger that makes the call relevant, my name, my role and company, and the number to call back; do not invent any of these. Before writing, restate in one sentence the relevance angle you understood and show me your plan for opening, curiosity, and close. Then deliver: (1) the main script of 55–75 words (20–30 spoken seconds) that opens with the prospect's name plus the relevance trigger, seeds curiosity by hinting at the value without fully revealing it, and closes by saying the callback number twice in a slow, deliberate manner, with pauses and suggested tone marked in brackets; (2) an alternate version of ~15 seconds (30–40 words) for mailboxes that cut off quickly, which sacrifices curiosity before the number; (3) three delivery notes: rhythm and breathing, speed and digit grouping when dictating the number, and what to avoid (pressure, jargon, sounding like a read script). Hard rules: never mention prices or the word "free"; never leave more than one message without a new reason; neutral, professional, warm Spanish, without emojis. If the relevance trigger is weak or absent, tell me and suggest how to strengthen it before writing, because without genuine relevance the voicemail does not generate a callback.

prompts.title: Personalized prospecting video script
prompts.content:
Act as a senior 1:1 video prospecting strategist, expert in social selling and the video prospecting discipline: message centered on the prospect, single call to action. I need a script for a short 1:1 video of 30 to 90 seconds that breaks the ice with a cold or follow-up prospect. The personalized video outperforms plain text because it demonstrates real effort and humanizes the first contact, but it only works if the hook names the prospect and the trigger in the first 8 seconds and asks for a single low-friction micro-commitment.

Before writing, ask me in a brief list the data you need and do not invent any: who it is addressed to (name and title), company and sector, the trigger or recent signal that justifies contact, the problem I solve and my value proposition in one sentence, the sending channel (email, LinkedIn, or WhatsApp), and the closing micro-commitment. If I do not provide the trigger, do not fabricate it: ask for it, because without a real signal the video loses its reason for being. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliver five blocks with time markers: Hook (0 to 8 s, names the prospect and the trigger, without introducing yourself), Insight (8 to 25 s, relevant observation from their context), Bridge to problem (25 to 50 s, connects to the value proposition framed as a question), Brief proof (50 to 70 s, data point or case; if I have no verified figure, mark it as [ASSUMPTION] with a typical range and a note to confirm), Close (70 to 90 s, the micro-commitment as the single yes-or-no question). For each block provide the literal spoken text, a camera direction or gesture note in parentheses, and the estimated duration. Also add the message subject adapted to the channel, two lines of accompanying copy, the text for a thumbnail with the prospect's name written by hand, and three hook variants for A/B testing with the hypothesis each one validates.

Rules: center the message on the prospect and not on the sender; the full text must be readable aloud in 90 seconds or less respecting the time markers; a single call to action; no result claim without backing or without [ASSUMPTION] mark; zero price mentions and zero use of the word "free"; professional, close, and direct tone, neutral Spanish, without empty jargon or exaggerated promises.

prompts.title: Request referrals from existing clients
prompts.content: Act as a senior account executive with a background in B2B consultative sales and expertise in asking for referrals without applying pressure. We have just delivered a concrete, verifiable result to a satisfied client, and I want to leverage that moment of maximum perceived value to request a qualified referral without sounding transactional or eroding trust. I need you to draft a referral request message ready to send, plus three alternative subject lines and a timing note on when to send it. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol Interpret > Plan > Execute: first restate what you understand and present your plan; if key data is missing (client, contact and their role, milestone delivered, supporting metric, ideal-client profile we are seeking, channel) ask for it before drafting instead of inventing. Structure the message in five moves: 1) open by acknowledging the specific, recent achievement, citing the verifiable metric as proof of value, not a generic compliment; 2) connect that success to the request by leveraging reciprocity and social proof, without sounding like you are calling in a favor; 3) make a single concrete, low-friction ask anchored in the ideal-client profile (role, sector, challenge) so that thinking of someone is easy; 4) offer at least two comfortable ways to facilitate the introduction (email intro, brief call, or a forwardable message the contact can copy); 5) close by expressing gratitude and making it explicit that there is no obligation whatsoever. Write in neutral, professional, warm Spanish, no emojis. Never mention prices or use the word free. Adjust length to the channel: brief for email, even shorter for LinkedIn, telegraphic for WhatsApp. Deliverable: message ready to send + 3 alternative subject lines + 1 timing note.

prompts.title: Reactivate cold or lost leads
prompts.content: Act as a senior B2B sales executive specialized in reactivating dormant opportunities, with mastery of consultative closing (SPIN, Challenger) and Blair Enns's break-up email technique. I want to reopen a conversation with a prospect who showed interest, moved forward, and then stopped responding; chasing them with reminders erodes the relationship and abandoning them leaves value on the table. This is a reactivation strategy. I need you to first ask for the essentials if you do not have them: who the prospect is and their role, what was offered or discussed in the last exchange, how long ago that contact was and why it went cold, the sending channel (email, LinkedIn, or WhatsApp), the new and legitimate reason to reconnect now, and the goal of the message. Then deliver two ready-to-send variants. Variant A win-back: reconnects with the original pain or goal, introduces the new reason as a legitimate motive to resume now (not a simple reminder), and closes with a single, low-commitment call to action. Variant B break-up: elegantly assumes the moment is not right, releases the prospect from the pressure of responding, and leaves a single minimal-friction door open. For each variant include a subject line only if the channel is email, a body of 4 to 7 lines, a single concrete CTA, and a short note on when to use it. Before drafting, restate what you understand about the context, the probable reason for going cold, and the goal, and flag as [ASSUMPTION] everything you have not confirmed; do not invent prospect data or history. Write in neutral, professional Spanish, no emojis, no prices or discounts, no word free; adjust email to a more formal tone and LinkedIn or WhatsApp to a shorter, more informal one.

prompts.title: Break through gatekeeper barriers
prompts.content:
Act as a senior B2B consultative salesperson with expertise in cold prospecting and the psychology of decision-maker access, trained in reference-based opening, permission, and help-request techniques (Sandler style). Your mission: design opening lines that allow me to reach the decision-maker I am looking for by getting past the gatekeeper who filters, always treating them as an informed ally who knows the organization and can open the right door, never as an adversary to deceive. Here, a strategy converts the gatekeeper from a wall into a bridge.

First restate in a single sentence who I want to reach, who filters, through which channel, and for what purpose. If you are missing an essential piece of data (decision-maker, value offer, type of gatekeeper, or channel), ask for it in a single batch before drafting; do not invent names, titles, or company data.

Then diagnose the gatekeeper's probable behavior (strict blocker who protects the agenda, neutral filter who routes, or potential ally who helps when given a legitimate reason) and adjust the register and length to the channel (a cold call demands concision and a human voice; an email or LinkedIn allows a subject line and a brief body; in-person reception requires presence and courteous brevity).

Next design between 5 and 7 distinct opening lines. Each with: (a) the exact text to say or write, ready to use; (b) the tactic applied; (c) why it works with that type of gatekeeper. Valid tactics: respect and explicit request for help, purpose clarity in one sentence, legitimate reference only if real, routing question (who is the right person), genuine reciprocity, and respectful assumption of continuity. Non-negotiable ethical filter: no line lies, pressures, pretends to be a client or colleague, invents a non-existent relationship, or manipulates; if a tactic only works by deceiving, discard it and say so.

For each line, anticipate the gatekeeper's most likely objection (what is it about, send me an email, they are not in, we do not receive vendors, we already work with someone) and deliver the bridge counter-response that respects the no and reopens with value. Close with a mini two-branch decision tree: if the gatekeeper cooperates (request routing, appointment, or transfer) and if they block (obtain the decision-maker's name, their email, the best retry time, or the preferred channel), each branch with one concrete next step.

Flag with [ASSUMPTION] every claim without supporting data. Deliver in neutral Spanish, professional and human tone, no emojis. Close by reminding me of the single highest-impact action for my next attempt.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Generate high open-rate subject lines
prompts.content:
Act as a senior cold email copywriting specialist and open-rate optimizer, with experience in B2B prospecting sequences, deliverability, and subject-line A/B test design. In cold prospecting, the entire email rides on the subject line: if it is not opened, the best body in the world does not exist. The recipient receives dozens of unsolicited emails a day and decides in less than a second by reading only the subject and sender in the mobile preview. Your job is to produce a set of testable subject lines, not a hunch, that speak to the recipient's real pain or value and maximize opens without clickbait or spam filters.

First ask, in a single batch, for any missing data: who is being written to (title, sector, company size), the specific pain or result they value, the action sought upon opening, the desired tone, and whether there is a real personalization hook. Do not invent title, pain, or hook; if there is no personalization signal, work without it rather than fabricating one.

Deliver in this order: (1) a sentence restating who is being written to and what open is sought; (2) a table of 10 to 12 subject lines with columns number, line, psychological angle, and character count, covering at least once each angle: direct question to the pain, specific non-clickbait curiosity, reference to a peer or sector competitor, concrete data or figure, tangible benefit, and personalized mention; (3) the recommended variants for the first A/B test (2 or 3), each from a contrasting angle with its open hypothesis; (4) the suggested preheader that best accompanies the winners; (5) the subject-line error to avoid with this specific recipient.

Hard rules for each line: 4 to 9 words and an approximate maximum of 50 characters; no greeting or sender name inside the subject; no all-caps, no repeated punctuation marks, no spam triggers (free, offer, urgent, guaranteed, easy money) and no promises that cannot be supported by the data provided. Count the characters of each line before presenting it and discard or correct any line that violates a rule. Flag with [ASSUMPTION] any line whose hook depends on data not provided, so the user can complete or discard it; never promise a result the user did not supply. The lines should sound like one real person writing to another, not like a mass campaign, and should respect the requested tone (default executive, sober). Respond in neutral, professional Spanish.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Personalization at scale with tokens
prompts.content:
Act as a senior outbound prospecting strategist with experience running high-volume multichannel sequences and designing token systems in sales engagement platforms. I need a scale personalization system based on dynamic variables, ready to load into a sequence, that lets me send to hundreds of prospects while maintaining individual perceived relevance without falling into the template effect that triggers discard.

Produce, in this order:
1. Dynamic variable map in three layers: identity (name, title, company), context (sector, size, observable signal or trigger), and relevance (hook that connects the trigger to the proposition). For each variable indicate: token name, data field that feeds it, and data source.
2. Fill rule per variable and a safe fallback value for when the data is missing, so the message never shows a gap, a broken greeting, or an unreplaced literal token.
3. Message template for the chosen channel with the variables in position, marking what is fixed text and what is personalized text, and closing with a concrete call to action.
4. Granularity criterion: what is personalized at the individual level, what at the segment level, and what remains constant throughout the campaign, justifying where personalization moves the needle and where it only adds cost.
5. Pre-send quality checklist: unreplaced tokens, fallbacks activated excessively (threshold that reveals a low-quality list), phrases that reveal automation, and spam signals affecting deliverability.
6. Measurement plan: what metric to observe per layer (open rate for identity, reply rate for relevance) to iterate the system.

Rules: distinguish the relevance layer, which must explicitly connect the trigger to the proposition, from decorative layers. Flag any assumption as [ASSUMPTION] and, if a critical field does not exist in the data, propose how to capture it before scaling rather than inventing it. Neutral, professional Spanish, without sounding mass-produced, no emojis.

If you are missing any essential data (target segment, channel, trigger, call to action, available data fields, or tone), ask for it before executing.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Value proposition by segment
prompts.content:
Act as a senior B2B commercial strategist, expert in positioning, segmentation, and value proposition design using the Strategyzer canvas (Value Proposition Canvas). Your task is to build a segmented value proposition and derive 3 ready-to-use prospecting messages.

Before executing, restate in your own words the offer, the target segment, and the dominant pain you understood, and present your plan in one line. If you are missing any of these pieces of data to do the job well (offer and its key capabilities, segment or buyer profile, dominant pain, current alternative the buyer uses today, differentiator), ask for them in a single batch of questions before continuing; do not invent data.

Proceed in three phases:
