Phase 1 - Problem fit. Map the customer profile separately from the value map. In the profile: jobs to be done (functional, social, emotional), pains, and expected gains. Prioritize pains by intensity and frequency, do not list them flat. Flag any data not provided as [ASSUMPTION].

Phase 2 - Solution fit. Inventory the offer's capabilities and build the value map (pain relievers and gain creators). Connect each relevant capability to a specific pain or gain and discard what does not fit; if a capability has no anchor, exclude it rather than inflate it.

Phase 3 - Articulation. Draft the value proposition statement with this structure: for [segment] who [job or pain], our [offer] delivers [differential benefit], unlike [current alternative]. Then derive 3 prospecting messages anchored to the dominant pain, in the segment's language and without interchangeable jargon: (1) brief cold email with subject line and a single call to action; (2) LinkedIn connection or first-contact message; (3) 2-to-3-sentence call opening hook. Each message must open with the buyer's pain, not your product, and propose a low-friction next step.

Do not mention prices or use the word free. Deliver: (a) summarized canvas profile + map with prioritized pains, (b) one-paragraph value statement, (c) the 3 editable messages. Close with 2 key assumptions to validate with the real segment before launching.

prompts.title: Qualify lead with BANT
prompts.content:
Act as a senior B2B sales executive expert in opportunity qualification with the BANT framework (Budget, Authority, Need, Timing). I need to decide with clear criteria whether an opportunity deserves to advance to proposal, stay in nurturing, or be discarded, rather than investing sales time in leads that are not going to close. I have fragmented discovery notes and want to convert them into an actionable verdict without overvaluing weak signals.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate the opportunity, the solution, and the pipeline stage as you understand them and list the missing data; if evidence for any critical BANT dimension is missing for the verdict, ask for it before qualifying. Then present your plan and execute.

Evaluate the four dimensions, each supported only by evidence from the notes: Budget (investment capacity or funds, who controls the budget, in which cycle), Authority (economic buyer, influencers, blockers, internal champion), Need (business pain, urgency, impact quantification, solution fit), and Timing (event forcing the decision, cost of inaction, estimated buying cycle). Assign each dimension a level: Strong, Partial, Weak, or No evidence, with a justification citing the specific signal. Flag every inference with [ASSUMPTION] and never invent budget figures.

Calculate a global score out of 100 by weighting the four dimensions (Strong=25, Partial=15, Weak=5, No evidence=0 per dimension) and make the sum transparent. Emit a single verdict: Advance to proposal (>=75 with no dimension at No evidence), Nurture and re-qualify (40-74 or any recoverable No-evidence dimension), or Discard (<40 or Need at Weak/No evidence with no path to recovery). Indicate the weakest dimension to unlock first and draft 3 to 5 open discovery questions ready to use, aimed at that gap.

Deliver a report with a table of the four dimensions (level + justification cited), global score out of 100 with its logic, actionable verdict, and follow-up questions. Professional, consultative tone; no prices, discounts, or word free; budget capacity described only in qualitative terms. If I am missing any data to start, ask for it.

prompts.title: Qualify opportunity with MEDDIC
prompts.content: Act as a senior B2B Sales Engineer with operational mastery of the MEDDIC framework in complex sales cycles. I need an actionable MEDDIC qualification sheet for a specific opportunity to decide with rigor whether it deserves sales time and what I must close before the next step. Before executing, restate the opportunity you understand (account, solution, stage, level of available information) and present your plan; if an essential piece of data for qualifying is missing, ask for it rather than inventing. Then qualify the six components in order of decision leverage: Metrics, Economic Buyer, Decision Criteria, Decision Process, Identify Pain, and Champion. In each component, separate what is confirmed (with a verbatim quote or reference to the evidence) from what is assumed or unknown, flag each gap as an explicit assumption or discovery question, and formulate the specific question that closes that gap. Treat the Economic Buyer as the person who signs and controls the budget, never the end user, and if they are not identified, that lowers the traffic light. Assign each component a green, yellow, or red traffic light with a one-line justification anchored in the evidence. Calculate a global health score from 0 to 100 weighting Economic Buyer, Identify Pain, and Champion more, explain the calculation logic, and emit an explicit verdict: advance, nurture, or disqualify. Close with the three main risks (with their trigger) and the three actionable next steps, each with a suggested owner and time horizon. Do not invent client data. Properly applied, this framework is your strategy for not carrying into the pipeline what is not going to close. Deliver the sheet in six blocks plus an executive summary ready to enter in the CRM or present in a pipeline review.

prompts.title: Qualify with expanded MEDDPICC
prompts.content:
Act as a senior B2B Sales Director, expert in enterprise qualification and pipeline coaching with MEDDPICC. I need a rigorous diagnosis of an opportunity before investing more team time: the goal is to expose the gaps that kill deals at late stages (no clear Economic Buyer, no mapped buying process, no real Champion, competitor or status quo underestimated) and decide with evidence whether to advance, nurture, or disqualify.

Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before diagnosing, restate the opportunity as you understand it and present your evaluation plan; if you are missing the client, the deal name, the pipeline stage, the target close date, or the known context (contacts, pains, relative budget, competitors, meeting notes), ask for it in a single batch before concluding.

Proceed as follows:
1. Map the received context against the eight elements: Metrics (sought quantifiable impact and baseline), Economic Buyer (who signs and controls the budget, already contacted or not), Decision Criteria (formal and informal, technical and business criteria), Decision Process (steps, committee, and dates until decision), Paper Process (procurement, legal, security, privacy, signing, and timelines), Implicate the Pain (quantified business pain and cost of inaction), Champion (internal ally with power, access, and self-interest, proven or assumed), and Competition (named rivals, incumbent, and the option of not deciding).
2. For each element deliver: what we know today, the textual or source evidence that supports it, a risk color (solid green / partial yellow / absent or unknown red), and the most powerful discovery question to close the gap.
3. Calculate a health score from 0 to 100 weighting the eight elements; declare the weighting used and that a single red in Economic Buyer or Champion caps the score at 'high risk' even if everything else is green.
4. Emit a single verdict (advance / nurture / disqualify) consistent with the detected reds, with justification in one sentence.
5. List the three risks that most threaten the close, their early warning signal, and the actionable next steps with suggested owner and date, executable this week.

Rules: flag every inference with [ASSUMPTION] and never present an inference as fact; if evidence is an unconfirmed verbal note, say so; do not invent contacts, figures, or dates. If context is too thin to score an element, mark it red for unknown rather than guessing. Deliver a MEDDPICC table of eight rows plus a synthesis block (score, verdict, three risks, next steps) ready to paste into the CRM or review in a 1:1 pipeline meeting. Neutral, professional Spanish, no prices.

prompts.title: Qualify with CHAMP
prompts.content: Act as a senior B2B consultative sales leader, expert in CHAMP, MEDDIC, and pain-based discovery. I need to qualify an opportunity from my pipeline with CHAMP (Challenges, Authority, Money, Prioritization) to decide with a clear head whether to invest sales cycles in it. Before executing, restate what you understand about the opportunity and present your plan; if you are missing an essential piece of data (account, contact, conversation context), ask for it in a single batch and do not invent client data. Deliver in this order: (1) the opportunity restated in one sentence centered on the challenge to resolve; (2) the qualification of the four dimensions starting from pain and not from budget: Challenges as prioritized challenges by impact, each linked to a concrete consequence of cost, risk, lost revenue, or time, distinguishing real pain from symptom; Authority as a decision map with who decides, influences, signs, and vetoes plus the internal champion and map gaps; Money as the economic value of resolving the challenge and capacity/willingness to invest, reasoned without asking for or declaring prices or rates; Prioritization as why now, triggering event, what the initiative competes against, and realistic decision date; (3) a status Strong, Medium, Weak, or Unknown per dimension, each with one line of evidence, marking inferred items as ASSUMPTION; (4) the Advance, Nurture, or Discard verdict with the logic that supports it and the single signal that would reverse it; (5) the pending discovery questions that close the gaps, prioritizing those marked Unknown, plus the next steps with suggested owner and time trigger. If evidence is contradictory, prioritize the most recent and direct source and record the tension. Never mention prices or rate figures. Respond in neutral Spanish, professional tone, no emojis.

prompts.title: Qualify with GPCTBA/CI
prompts.content:
Act as a senior consultative sales manager with hands-on mastery of HubSpot's GPCTBA/CI framework and value-based selling. I need to qualify an opportunity with evidence, not intuition, and decide whether to invest more time in it. Build a qualification scorecard that separates what is verifiable from what is still a gap, and leaves me with the exact questions for the next conversation.

Proceed as follows: (1) Map the eight framework dimensions from my discovery notes: Goals, Plans, Challenges, Timeline, Budget, Authority, Negative Consequences, and Positive Implications. (2) For each dimension deliver a table with available textual evidence, pending gap, level (Strong / Partial / Empty), and a ready-to-use discovery question. (3) Issue a single verdict (ADVANCE / NURTURE / DISQUALIFY) with the primary reason anchored in the critical dimensions, not in the average. (4) List the two major risks of the opportunity and the specific recommended next step with its owner and trigger.

Rules: extract only what is verifiable; anything not present in the inputs is marked Empty with its question and is never filled with assumptions. Budget is evaluated as capacity and allocation process, never as a requested or invented figure. Treat Authority and Timeline as disqualification dimensions: if both are Empty, the verdict cannot be ADVANCE. Never mention prices, cost ranges, or the word free. If I am missing any essential data (discovery inputs, offer, or pipeline stage), ask for it before executing.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Qualify with SPICED
prompts.content:
Act as a senior B2B consultative sales leader expert in the SPICED framework (Situation, Pain, Impact, Critical Event, Decision). Your task is to qualify a real pipeline opportunity to decide, with evidence, whether it deserves commercial investment, and to enter the next conversation knowing exactly what still needs to be discovered and from whom.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate the opportunity and the offer in your own words and confirm key assumptions; then present your plan for the five dimensions you will evaluate and where you anticipate gaps; only then execute the qualification. Do not invent prospect data: anything unverified is marked as inferred or as a gap.

Work through SPICED in order and mark each dimension as Strong, Weak, or Empty with its reason: Situation (context, sector, size, what they already have, what gets unlocked); Pain (real pain, distinguishing symptom from root cause and verbalized from inferred); Impact (quantified or qualified consequence and who it affects); Critical Event (external date or milestone that forces a decision, or its explicit absence); Decision (decision-maker, influencers, selection criteria, process, and budget signals—without mentioning money amounts). Treat weak or absent Pain, Impact without magnitude, and absent Critical Event as flags that limit the verdict.

For each Weak or Empty dimension write the exact discovery question and whom to ask it to in the next conversation. Issue a verdict of Advance, Nurture, or Discard supported only by available evidence, never by optimism, and state the confidence level. Close with three specific next steps. If you lack information to qualify a dimension, ask for it before proceeding. Deliver a table of the five dimensions with status and reason, a prioritized block of discovery questions, the verdict with confidence level, and the three next steps. Neutral and professional Spanish, no emojis.

prompts.title: SPIN discovery questions
prompts.content:
Act as a senior B2B consultative seller, expert in Neil Rackham's SPIN methodology and in designing discovery meetings that qualify the account and create value without presenting the product too early. I need a question script for a discovery meeting. The trap I want to avoid is talking about my solution too soon: the prospect does not buy until they articulate their problem and measure how much it costs them. A good SPIN script reverses the order, leading the prospect to describe their context, recognize their pain, feel the magnitude of the consequences, and declare aloud the value of resolving it.

Before drafting, restate what I sell, to whom, at what stage I am, and the pains I suspect; mark every inference as [ASSUMPTION] and ask only for the essentials that are missing (what I sell and the problem it solves, buyer profile, hypothesized pains, sales stage). Do not proceed with critical gaps unconfirmed.

Produce the script with four blocks in order: SITUATION (3 to 5 factual questions to map context, processes, and current metrics, without re-asking what is already on record); PROBLEM (questions that surface dissatisfactions, difficulties, and risks for each pain hypothesis); IMPLICATION (questions that connect each problem with consequences in cost, time, risk, team morale, and missed opportunity, quantifying the magnitude); and NEED-PAYOFF (questions that cause the prospect to declare the value and benefits of resolving it, without yet presenting the solution). For each pain hypothesis chain a problem question, one to three implication questions, and at least one need-payoff question. For each question indicate what it seeks to reveal and one follow-up question.

Close with the recommended meeting sequence, the transition signals between blocks, a control question to confirm priority and budget without asking for figures, and three typical errors to avoid. Never mention prices; if the topic arises, indicate that the quotation is defined after the discovery. Deliver an actionable script ready to use in the meeting.

prompts.title: Deep pain diagnosis
prompts.content:
Act as a senior B2B consultative sales consultant, expert in high-value discovery and impact quantification, trained in implication and need-payoff questions (SPIN style) and in cost-of-inaction analysis. I am in the discovery phase of a consultative sale: the prospect has already expressed a superficial pain, but a vague complaint does not move budgets or persuade a committee. Your job is to transform that complaint into a quantified case for change, connected to the metric that matters to leadership, that the prospect themselves can defend internally.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate in your own words the prospect's profile, their industry, the declared pain, and the business metric; if any of those four data points is missing or ambiguous, ask before drafting. Then present your funnel plan in one line. Only then execute.

Deliver a deep pain diagnosis script with five question blocks and a closing:
1. Root cause: 3 to 5 funnel questions that start from the declared pain and drill down to the structural origin (the process, data, incentive, or capability that generates it), not the symptom.
2. Quantified impact: 3 to 5 questions asking for figures or ranges in at least four of these dimensions: time, money, risk, quality, and opportunity cost. If the prospect does not have the figure, ask for their best estimate and how they would calculate it.
3. Cost of inaction: 3 to 5 questions about what happens if nothing changes at 6, 12, and 18 months, including cumulative deterioration and the decision window.
4. Organizational scope: 3 to 5 questions to map who the problem affects, who bears the consequences, and who decides and signs off on the change.
5. Strategic connection: 3 to 5 questions that link the pain to the business metric and the current leadership agenda.
6. Synthesis: the case for change in a single sentence (problem-impact-consequence) and three observable signals that the pain is urgent enough to advance.

Rules: each question open, non-leading, in neutral Spanish and ready to read aloud; order from general to specific within each block; never mention solution, product, or provider; accompany each block with a brief note on what to listen for in the response (signals of real pain vs. cosmetic complaint). Never mention prices or offer anything at no cost. Mark every inference you make as [ASSUMPTION].

prompts.title: Quantify the cost of inaction
prompts.content:
Act as a senior B2B consultative sales strategist with 15 years building quantitative business cases for buying committees. I am in discovery with a prospect who acknowledges a problem but does not feel urgency; I want to quantify how much it costs them to sustain the status quo so that urgency arises from their own data, not from commercial pressure.

First, restate the problem, the sector, the prospect's size, and the baseline metrics you were given, and explicitly note what data is missing. If the metrics or problem definition are insufficient to calculate, stop and ask for the specific data you need before proceeding; do not invent the prospect's figures.

Then model the cost of inaction in three layers, avoiding double-counting between them: (1) Direct cost, the measurable leak already occurring today (person-hours, rework, fines, churn, overruns); (2) Opportunity cost, the value not captured by not acting (deferred revenue, efficiency, or competitive advantage), counted separately from the direct cost; (3) Compound cost, how it accumulates month by month over the analysis horizon, indicating whether it grows linearly or worsens. For each layer declare the driver, calculation assumption, formula, and a conservative range (floor-ceiling), and mark as assumption any unconfirmed data. Anchor each figure to a real prospect data point or an explicit benchmark; never inflate.

Close with: the total consolidated over the horizon with its confidence level (high/medium/low based on how many unconfirmed assumptions sustain it); a single urgency statement translated into the metric that matters to the decision-maker; and exactly three actionable validation questions to confirm the key assumptions in the next conversation. Never mention your solution's prices or use the word free: the focus is the cost of the status quo, not your offer. Before executing, restate what you understood and present your plan.

prompts.title: Commercial discovery meeting agenda
prompts.content:
Act as a senior consultative sales consultant with fifteen years closing complex B2B sales, expert in diagnostic discovery (Neil Rackham's SPIN method and the problem-impact-desired state approach of Keenan's Gap Selling). I need to run a first discovery meeting with a prospect and I want to arrive with a clear agenda and clear objectives, not improvise. In discovery you learn and diagnose, you do not present a product: the risk is jumping to sell the solution, not understanding the real problem or its impact, and leaving without a committed next step. I want a minute-by-minute runnable script, not a generic list of questions.

Deliverable: discovery meeting script by blocks. Design it as follows:
1. Opening and framing: brief rapport, confirm time available, declare the meeting objective, and propose a shared agenda that the prospect can adjust.
2. Current state and problem diagnosis: situation questions to map context and problem questions to surface difficulties, dissatisfactions, and risks.
3. Implication and impact: questions that quantify the cost of the problem (time, money, risk, effort) and its effect on metrics and people; here the prospect feels urgency and the cost of the status quo.
4. Desired state and need-payoff: questions that cause the prospect to describe what resolving the problem looks like and the value of achieving it, in their own words.
5. Qualification: probe for decision-makers and influencers, process and selection criteria, alternatives being evaluated, and timeline, without turning it into an interrogation.
6. Close and next step: summarize what was learned using the prospect's words, confirm problem and impact, and agree on a specific next step with owner and date; offer to draft a mutual action plan.

Design rules: assume 30–45 min if I did not indicate duration; distribute time giving weight to problem and impact (together close to half), a light opening (around 10%), and a firm, protected slot for the close (around 15%). For each block deliver the objective, time assigned, 3 to 6 drafted and runnable example questions, and the advance signal indicating the block is complete. Draft the blocks in sequence because each one feeds the next: situation before problem, problem before impact, impact before desired state, diagnosis before qualification, all before the next step. Close with a list of errors to avoid and a notes sheet with the fields to capture during the meeting. If I am missing any data you need (prospect, solution, problem hypothesis, attendees, duration, or objective), ask me before executing.

Never present the solution before diagnosing; if the prospect reveals no difficulty, do not invent the pain: add alternative problem questions and an advance signal that admits 'no pain confirmed'. Mark as assumption any inference about the prospect, their industry, or the problem, and do not invent client data. Neutral and professional Spanish, no prices, no word free.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Map the buying decision process
prompts.content:
Act as a senior B2B sales strategist specialized in complex sales and buying committee discovery. Your task is to reconstruct the REAL buying decision process of an account—not the one declared on the surface—so that the next contact advances to the full committee and not to a single interlocutor. Selling to the only available contact is the number-one cause of deals that die without a clear no: you unlock it by mapping who decides, with what criteria, in what signing order, and where it can stall.

First, before building anything, confirm with me the account, the type of solution being sold, and the contacts and roles already identified with their current stance. If any is missing or ambiguous, ask me: do not invent people, areas, or amounts.

Then deliver, in this order:
1. Committee map. For each relevant role (champion, economic approver, technical or operational users, legal, procurement, security or compliance if applicable) define: primary interest, perceived fear or risk, blocking power (high/medium/low), and whether they are today a mobilizer, neutral, or blocker. Note if the account is single-threaded (one contact sustains the deal) and why that is a risk.
2. Decision stages. Order the phases from problem recognition to signing; per stage indicate who enters, what evidence or deliverable is required, and what triggers advancement vs. what stalls it.
3. Criteria and signing route. Separate explicit from implicit criteria (political, career, comfort, change-aversion) without mixing them, and reconstruct the recommends > approves > vetoes sequence in real order.
4. Advance plan. Per stage: one pending discovery question, the observable signal confirming it has been cleared, and the main stall risk.

Rigor rules: mark with [ASSUMPTION] every phase, criterion, role, or signing step not confirmed by the client, and with [CONFIRMED] what has been validated, so that traceability is auditable. Consider the procurement-led purchase, regulated buyer, founder-dependent decision, and tied committee with no deciding vote cases: name the pattern if it applies. Never estimate prices or discounts. Close with prioritized discovery questions and the three most likely stall risks with their early warning signal.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Stakeholder and buying committee map
prompts.content: Act as a senior complex B2B sales strategist, expert in buying committee mapping, MEDDICC, and multi-stakeholder selling (Challenger and The JOLT Effect). I want a stakeholder map of the buying committee for a deal I am working on. Before executing, restate in one or two lines what deal you understand we are mapping and present your plan; if you are missing any essential data (account and opportunity, what I sell and what business pain it resolves, stage and next milestone, known contacts with title and the signals I have on each one), ask me for it concretely rather than inventing it. Work as follows: first fix the context, meaning what the client is deciding, what business outcome they are pursuing, and what their likely buying process is. Then classify each contact by their decision role (Economic Buyer, Champion, Influencer or Technical Buyer, User Buyer, Coach, Blocker or Detractor, Legal or Procurement) and explicitly declare any critical role without an owner as a gap, especially Economic Buyer and Champion. For each actor estimate influence (High, Medium, Low), stance (Promoter, Neutral, Detractor), their personal decision criterion or metric, and the risk they represent; label each reading as verified data or as an assumption to validate, and never invent people, titles, or intentions. Place each actor on a power-vs.-stance map (four quadrants: allies to leverage, power to convert, noise to contain, blockers to neutralize) and define the coverage play per person. Close by identifying single-threading or fragile relationship risks, and a numbered action plan with next step, owner, and date per stakeholder. Do not include prices (that goes in the quotation after discovery) or the word free; write in neutral and professional Spanish, no emojis. Deliver: executive summary of 5 to 7 lines; committee table (name or title, decision role, influence, stance, personal criterion, evidence or assumption); power-vs.-stance map with each actor's quadrant; coverage gap and relationship risk list; numbered action plan per stakeholder; and 3 to 5 pending discovery questions to complete the map.

prompts.title: Identify and develop an internal champion
prompts.content:
Act as a senior complex B2B sales strategist with fifteen years closing long-cycle enterprise deals, expert in MEDDIC and in the Mobilizer profile of the Challenger Customer (CEB / Dixon and Adamson). My problem: in this account the decision is made by a committee and I am not in the room when it is made. I need a real champion—someone with power and influence who wants me to win and will sell internally—not a friendly contact who gives me information but does not risk political capital. Confusing a coach with a champion is the silent cause of deals that go cold.

Give me a champion dossier with: (1) a committee role map, classifying each known contact as champion, coach, economic buyer, blocker or detractor, and user or technical influencer; separate observed data from inferences and mark each inference as [ASSUMPTION]. (2) Qualification of the candidate against the four hard champion tests: real power and influence, own pain that my solution resolves, visible personal gain, and access to the economic buyer; if they do not pass, declare them a coach—explicitly—and say what they lack to become a champion. (3) Strength scorecard scoring from 1 to 5 internal credibility, access to power, willingness to act, and alignment with my solution, with an overall reading and the weakest link to reinforce. (4) Empowerment plan: a one-page messaging framework the champion can defend alone before their peers, a business case with the two or three metrics that matter in the account, predictable internal objections with their response, and the order in which they should convince each role. (5) Next move and champion test: what I ask of them, what I deliver so they can act, and a verifiable signal confirming they are selling internally.

Do not invent names, titles, or intentions: if I do not have the data, mark it [ASSUMPTION] or ask. Neutral and professional Spanish, no emojis, no prices. If you are missing account, solution, candidate, or what you know about their motivation, ask me before executing.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Access the economic buyer
prompts.content: Act as a senior complex B2B sales strategist, expert in MEDDIC/MEDDPICC and multi-level selling to buying committees. My opportunity is stalled because I only speak with users or influencers and never align with the person who controls the budget: the economic buyer, the person who approves the investment and says yes—not just recommends it. I need an economic buyer access strategy plus three ready-to-send assets. First restate what you understood and present your plan before executing. Then: 1) Build a power map that distinguishes the economic buyer from the user, influencer, and champion: who signs, who they report to, and what decision criterion they use (return, risk, strategic priority). If I do not know who the economic buyer is, do NOT invent one: give me 4 to 6 qualification questions to discover them and mark anything unconfirmed as [ASSUMPTION]. 2) Translate my solution into the economic buyer's metric: business outcome, cost of not acting, and impact horizon, in executive language, not features; quantify with ranges and mark assumptions. 3) Design a multi-thread access route: primary thread of upward presentation via the champion, the context trigger that detonates the conversation, and a plan B of direct contact if the champion blocks, goes cold, or disappears. 4) Draft three assets: (a) an upward presentation message my champion can forward without editing; (b) a direct contact email of 5 to 7 lines centered on business outcome; (c) a 20-to-25-minute agenda for the first executive meeting, with an explicit request to validate priority and budget. Cover edge cases: what happens if the champion feels bypassed, if a gatekeeper appears, or if the budget is decided by a committee and not one person. Close each asset with a specific advancement request. No prices; neutral and professional Spanish. If you are missing any key data (account, solution, current contact's role, or sought business outcome), ask me before drafting the assets.

prompts.title: Capture customer decision criteria
prompts.content:
Act as a senior B2B sales consultant specialized in consultative discovery and opportunity qualification, with mastery of decision-criteria frameworks (MEDDICC-style: decision criteria, decision process, champion). Your goal is to convert what was discussed in discovery into a weighted decision-criteria matrix plus a validation plan, to focus the proposal on what truly moves the decision, anticipate objections, and expose weaknesses before it is too late.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First, restate the opportunity as you understand it and declare your open assumptions; then present your extraction and weighting plan; only then execute. If the client, solution offered, contact and their role, or opportunity stage is missing, ask for it before continuing; do not invent data.

Proceed as follows: (1) Synthesize the opportunity: the client's core need, cycle stage, and competitors or alternatives in play, including the status quo or no-decision. (2) Identify decision criteria across three families: technical/functional; economic/value-based (return, implementation effort, total cost of ownership in qualitative terms, without figures or amounts); and relationship/risk (trust, support, references, cultural fit, change risk). No family may be left empty without justifying why it does not apply. (3) For each criterion define: name, why it matters to the client, champion on the committee (role or area, not a proper name), relative weight as a percentage (exact sum of 100%), and your current positioning (strong / parity / weak). (4) Label each criterion as [CONFIRMED] by the client or [ASSUMED] by inference; a criterion is only [CONFIRMED] if the client expressed it in a verifiable way. (5) Write one concrete, open, non-leading validation question for each [ASSUMED] criterion. (6) Flag the three greatest risks: high-weight criteria where your position is weak, where the champion is unknown, or where a decisive criterion remains [ASSUMED]; for each one propose a next action.

Rules: zero price figures, amounts, or savings percentages; zero guaranteed-return promises; weightings are qualitative and relative. Always distinguish what the client said from what you infer. Neutral professional Spanish, no emojis.

Deliverable: weighted criteria matrix in a table by family (criterion, client's reason, champion, weight, position, label), list of validation questions for assumed criteria, and a block of three prioritized risks with their action. Close with the most decisive question or action for the next interaction.

prompts.title: Establish the critical buying event
prompts.content:
Act as a senior B2B sales strategist and qualification coach, expert in MEDDICC (Compelling Event component) and consultative selling with SPIN-style implication questions. Your goal is to transform a diffuse interest into a decision with a clock: identify, validate, and document the critical buying event (compelling event) — that is, the business milestone or date with real consequences that forces the prospect to act within a concrete window. Without a critical event, the deal competes against doing nothing, which almost always wins.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First, restate what you understand about the deal and list the critical missing data; ask for only those before moving forward. Then present your plan in five phases and execute it.

Phase 1 Framing: reconstruct the deal situation and explicitly flag which data is missing. Phase 2 Urgency diagnosis: classify whether what exists is a soft desire (no date, owner, or consequence) or a real critical event (milestone with date, owner, and cost of inaction); name the consequence of not acting. Phase 3 Discovery: deliver five to seven open, implication-style questions ordered from context to consequence that uncover the event: what happens if the pain is not resolved before a certain moment; what external or internal milestone sets the clock (regulation, contract expiry or renewal, fiscal close, launch, public commitment to a board or client, end of support, end of budget year); who inside the account suffers the consequence. Phase 4 Validation: apply three tests to the event candidate: verifiable date, owner accountable for that date, tangible and measurable consequence of non-compliance; mark as pending confirmation every assumption without evidence and never invent dates or figures. If the candidate does not pass the tests, co-create a legitimate event anchored to a strategic initiative or real business priority, never manufacture artificial pressure. Phase 5 Timeline and close: build the countdown from the event date to today, placing the buying-process milestones (decision, approval, contracting, implementation, time-to-value) and indicate whether the window is realistic or already at risk.

Assumptions and limits: assume consultative B2B selling with a multi-week or multi-month cycle and multiple stakeholders; if the cycle is transactional, say so and simplify. Distinguish critical event (consequence if NOT acted upon) from a mere internal deadline of the seller. Edge case: if the prospect declares a date but with no consequence or owner, treat it as a soft desire, not as an event. Edge case: if there are several candidate events, prioritize the one with the most tangible consequence and nearest date, and name the others as reinforcement.

Deliver a critical event card with: (1) event plus date plus owner, (2) consequence of inaction in business language (cost, risk, lost opportunity), not product language, (3) countdown timeline with buying-process milestones and a viability verdict for the window, (4) event maturity classification (confirmed / probable / pending confirmation) with what is needed to move up a level, and (5) two or three confirmation questions ready to take to the prospect. Professional Spanish, no emojis. If you are missing a critical data point to start, ask for it before continuing.

prompts.title: Formulate initial value hypothesis
prompts.content: Act as a senior B2B consultative sales strategist, with mastery of Jobs-to-be-Done, Customer Development value hypothesis, and MEDDIC qualification. I have an upcoming first discovery meeting with a prospect and I want to enter with a verifiable thesis about the value I could bring, not with a generic pitch. I need a ready-to-use preparation card. To produce it I need: the target company and its sector; the person and role I will be meeting; recent facts and signals from the prospect (job openings, press, announcements, regulation, competitive moves); the capability or solution I offer; and, optionally, the metric or business outcome I aim to move. If any of these data points is missing, ask me for it before continuing instead of inventing it. With that, give me: (1) context synthesis in 3–5 facts, each tagged [DATA] when it comes from research or [ASSUMED] when inferred, with the reason for the inference; (2) the likely job-to-be-done (JTBD) and business pain for the role, tied to a metric that role truly cares about; (3) the central value hypothesis in a single sentence with this structure: "We believe that [segment/role] faces [costly problem] that today they solve with [current alternative]; my offer would allow them to achieve [measurable outcome], and we will know if [observable evidence]"; (4) 2–3 alternative hypotheses in case the central one does not hold; (5) 4–6 discovery questions designed to confirm or refute the hypothesis, not to sell; (6) one confirmation signal and one invalidation signal observable in the meeting. Rules: no invented data; every claim about the prospect tagged [DATA] or [ASSUMED]; the central hypothesis must be falsifiable (problem, alternative, measurable outcome, and evidence); no prices or commercial terms; neutral professional Spanish. Before drafting the card, briefly restate what you understood and present your plan. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute.

prompts.title: Actionable post-discovery summary
prompts.content:
I just closed a B2B commercial discovery meeting and my notes are raw. Act as a senior consultative sales consultant with mastery of opportunity qualification and meeting synthesis, and convert them into a dual-use actionable post-discovery summary: internal review by the sales team and, in polished form, delivery to the prospect as a demonstration of active listening.

Structure the summary in seven sections: 1) Account context (company, sector, stakeholders with role and influence level, and declared meeting objective); 2) Key findings (4 to 6 points, separating verified facts from assumptions to confirm); 3) Prioritized pains (problems or needs ordered by impact for the prospect; for each one, who it affects and what evidence from the notes supports it, and if possible the cost of not resolving it); 4) Decision criteria (what the prospect values to move forward, approval process or budget constraint mentioned without inventing figures, alternatives or competitors in play, and timelines); 5) Qualification signals (classify the opportunity by need, authority, urgency, and fit, and indicate maturity level with brief justification); 6) Next steps (numbered actions, each with an owner and tentative date, distinguishing the team's actions from the prospect's); 7) Open questions (what was not asked or remained unanswered for the next contact).

Rules: mark every inference with [ASSUMED]; never invent figures, names, or commitments; no unvalidated commercial promises; professional and neutral tone in Spanish, no emojis. If a section lacks sufficient data, do not fill it in: convert the gap into an open question. If essential data for starting is missing (notes, meeting objective), ask for it before drafting.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Demo preparation plan
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Enterprise Sales Director with fifteen years leading long-cycle, multi-stakeholder B2B software demonstrations. A demo without focus burns the opportunity: the team shows the whole product, the prospect does not see their problem solved, and the deal does not advance. Your work is to convert the demo into a guided conversation toward an agreed progress commitment, aligning objective, audience, messages, and script before presenting, so that the prospect recognizes the demo as theirs and ends with a firm next step. Accelerate the prospect's strategy, not the product catalog.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First, restate what you understand about the product, the prospect, the audience, the cycle stage, the detected pains, and the target outcome, marking with [ASSUMED] everything you infer and naming material gaps; if a datum is missing that would change the plan, ask for it before executing and do not invent prospect data. Then present your attack plan in one line. Only then produce the deliverable.

Deliver a demo preparation plan with these sections, in order: 1) Single objective as a verifiable progress commitment consistent with the cycle stage: what the prospect decides, agrees on, or authorizes when done, not which functions are shown; include the observable success criterion and the signal that would indicate a no-go or postponement. 2) Audience map: for each attendee, role, what matters to them, their implicit question, the lever that moves them, and the risk if they are ignored; mark economic decision-maker, user, internal champion, and potential blocker; if the decision org chart is missing, flag it. 3) Three to five key messages, each tied to an explicit pain and stated as capability-plus-business-outcome, with the metric or evidence supporting it, not as a technical feature. 4) Scene-by-scene script: opening that restates the pain in the prospect's words, walkthrough with two or three high-impact demo moments in the customer's story order, and close that asks for the next step; include estimated time per scene, the data or environment that must be ready, and a plan B if the live demo fails. 5) The five most probable objections by industry and role, each with its bridge response and, where applicable, the proof or reference supporting it; include how to handle the price objection without quoting in the demo. 6) Closing advance question and proposed next step with owner, date, and the follow-up email or summary to be sent. Close with three buying signals to watch during the session and how to capitalize on each.

Use neutral professional Spanish, no emojis. Avoid the all-of-it demo, internal jargon, promising what the solution does not do, and mentioning prices or discounts. Every claim about the prospect is supported by a given datum or marked [ASSUMED].

prompts.title: Value-based demo, not feature-based
prompts.content:
Act as a senior pre-sales engineer (Sales Engineer) expert in B2B consultative selling and value-selling methodology, skilled at translating technical capabilities into business impact. I need a live value-based demo script, not a features script: a session where everything shown has a business reason and advances the opportunity toward the next step. Before drafting, confirm with me: the prospect and their sector, the product or solution to demonstrate and its real available capabilities, the 2 to 3 pains prioritized by impact (ideally in the prospect's own words), the business outcome pursued (metric or observable change), the profile of the decision-maker who will see the demo (technical, financial, or executive), and the target duration in minutes. If any of those data points is missing, ask me for it before moving forward and do not invent it.

Structure the script as follows: (1) Opening reframe that states the prioritized pains and the outcome to attack before showing anything from the product. (2) Pain-capability map: associate each pain with ONE single capability that resolves it, order the blocks from highest to lowest pain, and explicitly discard any capability that does not connect to a declared pain. (3) Mini-script per block with the pain in the prospect's words, the transition (let me show you how this changes), the exact clicks or steps to show, and the value phrase that closes by connecting to the outcome. (4) One validation question at the end of each block to confirm the pain is resolved and sustain the dialogue. (5) Close with a summary of demonstrated outcomes and one concrete, actionable next step (date, owner, progress criterion).

Adjust language to the decision-maker's profile (technical: architecture and mechanics; financial: avoided cost, efficiency, risk; executive: strategic outcome and time-to-value) and depth to the duration (if short, fewer blocks and more closed demos). Anticipate a plan B per block (what to show if a feature fails or the environment does not load) and, if you detect a pain with no capability to resolve it, say so openly rather than improvising. Do not invent product capabilities or prospect metrics; mark any unprovided datum as assumed. Before delivering, restate what you understood and present your plan; then execute.

prompts.title: Narrative demo script with tell-show-tell structure
prompts.content: Act as a senior pre-sales engineer and demo storyteller with fifteen years designing B2B demonstrations that close, expert in the tell-show-tell structure and Peter Cohan's Great Demo! method. Design the complete, executable narrative script for a demo that closes, not a screen tour: a story that starts at the moment of greatest impact, anchors in the prospect's pain and business outcome, and ends in a concrete progress commitment. To do it I need you to ask me, if I have not given it: the product or service to demonstrate (name and brief description); the prospect (role of who will see the demo, industry, size); the main pain or friction they live today; the business outcome they pursue, with a metric if available; the 3 to 5 capabilities or flows available to show; the probable objections; the minutes available; and the meeting format (live, recorded, one-on-one, or before a committee). Do not invent capabilities that do not exist or promise results without support. Build in this order, without skipping steps. 1. Anchor the demo in one line that joins prospect, pain, and desired outcome; the entire script serves that outcome, never a feature tour. 2. Vision Generation opening: open with the screen or final result the prospect most wants to see (the key moment), never login or setup, and connect it to their pain in one or two sentences. 3. Design 3 to 5 scenes from the key capabilities, ordered from highest to lowest impact for this prospect; each scene is illustrate-prove with the complete tell-show-tell block: opening TELL (what they will see and why it matters, in their language) then SHOW (click-by-click actions with the data or flow that proves the value) then closing TELL (business benefit reaffirmed, tied to their metric). 4. Write the narrative transitions between scenes so it is a continuous story. 5. Insert at least two discovery points: open questions to confirm resonance and adapt the rest of the walkthrough; define what you will do if the answer is lukewarm or negative. 6. Anticipate the probable objections: indicate in which scene and with which bridge phrase you neutralize them by showing live evidence, and separate what you can prove on screen from what you can only assert. 7. Close: recap the results seen and propose a concrete progress commitment (next meeting, scoped trial, access to stakeholders), with one alternative in case the first does not proceed. 8. Add time guards per scene and a 5-minute compressed version that keeps the impact opening, the highest-value scene, and the close. Write the presenter's text in quotes, mark screen actions and minutes per scene, and flag which scenes are cuttable under time pressure. Mark as [ASSUMED] any datum you complete without it having been provided. MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Do not include prices.

prompts.title: Structure a demo with the tell-show-tell pattern
prompts.content:
Act as a senior pre-sales engineer with fifteen years running B2B software demos that close, expert in value-based demos and the tell-show-tell pattern. I need to convert a list of features into a demo script that makes the buyer feel the product resolves their pain, not that they watched a screen tour. Before executing, restate what you understand and present your plan.

Proceed as follows:
1. Curation. From the candidate use cases, choose only the three to five that directly touch the main pain; discard the rest and justify in one line why each discarded one is excluded (hard rule: if it does not touch the pain, it does not go in the demo). Mark every claim about the product as a confirmed datum or [ASSUMED]; never invent capabilities.
2. Narrative arc. Order the chosen blocks so the first touches the most acute pain (earns early attention) and the last delivers the resolution that enables the commercial objective; each block prepares the next. Explain the ordering logic in one line.
3. Tell-show-tell blocks. For each block write the three movements. Opening tell: one context sentence that connects to the pain and leaves an open question. Show: the live action step by step, with the exact click or gesture and the observable result on screen. Closing tell: the business benefit that is unlocked, in the language of the decision-maker, closing the loop opened by the opening tell.
4. Transitions. Draft the bridge phrase from each block to the next so the demo flows as a story, not a menu tour.
5. Anti-script per block. Indicate what NOT to say or show to avoid diluting the message (out-of-focus features, jargon, dead ends, comparisons that invite objections).
6. Close. One global tell that summarizes the accumulated value and proposes a concrete next step aligned with the commercial objective.
7. Contingency plan. Anticipate two or three probable audience questions or interruptions and how to redirect without losing the arc.

Deliverable: justified selection section (included and discarded), three to five blocks in tell-show-tell format, transitions, anti-script per block, close with next step, interruption handling, and list of assumptions to confirm before the demo. If you are missing the product, audience, pain, candidate cases, or objective, ask me for it before starting. Neutral professional Spanish, no prices.

prompts.title: Customize demo to the use case
prompts.content:
Act as a senior B2B pre-sales engineer with a track record of adapting demos to the operational reality of each prospect. Your task is to convert an out-of-the-box demo with sample data into a personalized, screen-by-screen script that makes the room see themselves operating the product on their own data and priorities; the objective is to move the conversation from 'what the product does' to 'how it resolves my problem' and unlock the advancement of the opportunity.

Before drafting I need you to confirm you have: the prospect's company, sector, and size; the product to show; the pain, priority, or objective declared in discovery; the roles that will be in the room; and the total time available. If any of these data points is missing, ask me for it before moving forward; do not invent the use case.

Follow the MetodologIA Protocol in three phases. Phase 1 Interpret: restate the prospect's use case in your own words and build a map of 3 to 5 prospect priorities against the product's capabilities, discarding what does not apply. Phase 2 Plan: propose the screen order (open with the heaviest pain, close with the business outcome that unlocks the decision) and the adjustment to the available time, reserving a margin for questions; show me this plan before drafting. Phase 3 Execute: draft the final script.

For each screen deliver: what is shown, the personalized data used (realistic equivalents of the prospect's environment, never out-of-the-box sample data), a transition phrase connecting to the pain, a validation question to the prospect, and the estimated minute. Mark [ASSUMED] every value you invent and gather all assumptions in a list at the end for the prospect to confirm. Add a plan B for when something does not load or the time is cut (which screens are essential and which are sacrificable), and 3 probable objections from the audience with a one-line response each. Close with a single business-outcome message and the suggested next step for the opportunity.

Do not use prices or cost figures; if the close requires them, use markers like [VALUE_TO_CONFIRM]. Distinguish verified data from assumptions. Language: neutral professional Spanish, no emojis.

prompts.title: Iterative discovery demo
prompts.content: Act as a senior B2B pre-sales engineer with mastery of consultative selling (SPIN, Sandler) and value-based demos (discovery-led / value-based demo). Design a conductible kit for an iterative discovery demo: a session that alternates short question blocks with short demonstration blocks, where a capability is shown only after the prospect connects it to their own pain, and each block closes with a value confirmation in their words. Before starting, restate what you understand about the product, the prospect's profile, the pain to validate, and the session objective; present your plan and then execute. If you are missing the product and its real capabilities, the prospect's profile, the main pain, or the demo objective, ask for them before producing the kit. Deliver in this order: (1) a 60–90-second opening script that reframes the session as a conversation, asks permission to ask questions, and invites interruptions; (2) a battery of live discovery questions in 4 layers (current situation, pain and quantifiable impact, consequence of not acting, vision of desired state), indicating for each question which product capability its answer unlocks; (3) an anchor-demonstrate map for each probable pain and adjacent ones, with a 2–4-minute demo segment that resolves it, a bridge phrase connecting what the prospect said to what will be shown, and a value confirmation question at the block's close; (4) a table of real-time buying signals and friction signals, each with its micro-action (deepen, accelerate, or return to discovery); (5) close with a summary of validated pains, value confirmed by the prospect in their words, and a next-step proposal. Add a degradation plan for when the demo does not flow: pain that does not appear, capability that fails live, passive prospect, or multi-stakeholder with conflicting priorities. Rules: never show a capability without a declared pain that justifies it; never invent features or metrics (mark unconfirmed content as assumed and convert it into a question); no prices; neutral professional Spanish.

prompts.title: Handling objections during the demo
prompts.content:
Act as a senior presales engineer with more than ten years demonstrating B2B software to technical and business committees, trained in consultative selling. I am in the middle of a live demo and an objection has surfaced that threatens to break the rhythm and undermine credibility. I need to answer it in the moment, without becoming defensive, without opening a debate that consumes the session, and without losing the narrative thread I was building. A well-handled objection advances the deal; a poorly handled one freezes it.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First rephrase the objection as you understand it and present your handling plan; then execute.

Give me a response script in six blocks: (1) Classification: technical (capability, integration, security, performance, scalability) or value-related (perceived price, priority, ROI, change risk, timing), naming the real doubt behind the stated doubt and its intensity (curiosity / blocker / dealbreaker). (2) Rephrasing in a single sentence to confirm understanding. (3) Response ready to speak aloud in 20 to 40 seconds, without defensiveness, with an explicit bridge that returns to what you were showing. (4) Closing micro-question that resumes the demo and keeps the prospect moving forward. (5) Plan B: if it is not resolved live, how to park it elegantly with an owner and a follow-up date, without halting the session. (6) Reading signal: one observable cue to know whether the objection was truly resolved or merely silenced.

Rules: zero invented capabilities or figures; if you lack a piece of data (profile of who is objecting, citable evidence), ask for it before drafting or mark it [ASSUMPTION] to be confirmed. Never mention prices. Neutral, professional Spanish, no emojis.

prompts.title: Demo close and next steps
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Account Executive in B2B consultative sales, expert in closing demonstrations and building mutual action plans. I have just finished a demo and the immediate risk is closing with a "we'll review it internally" that cools the opportunity and dilutes momentum. Design the last 5 to 8 minutes of the demo so the prospect verbalizes the value they perceived and commits to next steps with owners and dates, leaving the following meeting scheduled live and not as a vague email promise.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First rephrase the demo situation as you understand it (solution shown, interlocutor and their role, business priority they declared as relevant) and present your plan; if you lack any critical data such as who decides or the tentative date, ask for it or record it as [ASSUMPTION] before drafting. Then execute.

Deliverable: a five-block demo closing script, ready to read and adapt live, sequenced from lowest to highest commitment. 1) Open-ended value-confirmation question that forces the prospect to name the problem they saw solved and the expected impact. 2) Executive summary of 2 to 3 lines reconnecting what was demonstrated with the business priority. 3) Next-steps proposal: each action with a named owner and a date, drafted for verbal agreement, not for delegation to email. 4) Close that schedules the next meeting before hanging up, with tentative participants according to the decision process. 5) Handling of the most likely postponement objection ("I need to check with the team") that converts it into a concrete date commitment. Add a micro-variant of block 5 if the interlocutor is not the final decision-maker (path to the real decision-maker) and an exit line if the prospect asks to send everything by email (anchor to a short review call). Neutral, professional Spanish, no prices, no the word free, no unsustainable promises, no emojis; mark all inferences [ASSUMPTION].

prompts.title: Proof-of-concept (PoC) plan
prompts.content:
Act as a senior presales engineer (Sales Engineer) with experience in B2B proofs of concept and evidence-based closes. Your mandate is to design a Proof-of-Concept Plan ready to agree with the prospect, one that transforms interest into measurable value evidence and protects both parties from scope creep and the never-ending PoC.

Before drafting, ask me for and rephrase: what prospect and sector it is, what business problem or result they want to validate, what the key metric that defines success is, what time window is available, what commercial step is unlocked if the PoC goes well, and what data, access, security, or environment constraints exist. If the problem to validate, the key metric, or the duration is missing, ask for it before proceeding; do not invent context.

Then build the plan with these components: (1) Business objective of the PoC, expressed as an outcome, not as a feature list. (2) Falsifiable value hypothesis of the form 'if we use the solution for X, then we will achieve measurable Y', tied to the key metric. (3) Scope with an explicit in-scope / out-of-scope table to shield against scope creep. (4) Three to five success criteria, each with a metric, current baseline, target threshold, and measurement method; mark [ASSUMPTION] on every baseline not provided. (5) Data, access, and environment plan with a named owner per dependency, respecting the constraints. (6) Phased schedule (kickoff, configuration, execution, evaluation, decision) adjusted to the window, with a deliverable and date per phase and one midpoint checkpoint. (7) RACI matrix with champion, economic sponsor, technical evaluator, and support team. (8) GO / NO-GO decision criterion, including the partial-result case, with a decision date and the commercial step that is unlocked.

Non-negotiable rule: no PoC starts without success thresholds and a decision date agreed by the sponsor; if those are not defined, deliver the plan marked as an unconfirmed draft. Do not include prices or the word free; assumptions are tagged [ASSUMPTION]. The final deliverable is a one-to-two-page PoC Plan, ready to send to the champion, with a success-criteria table and a phased schedule.

prompts.title: Mutual success criteria for a PoC
prompts.content:
Act as a senior presales architect in B2B technology sales, expert in closing PoCs with verifiable acceptance criteria and buying-committee management. Your task is to produce a signable mutual success-criteria agreement: the short contract both parties agree to before starting the trial, one that converts it into a purchase decision with an explicit conversion rule, not an open demo the prospect enjoys but never buys.

Before drafting, rephrase what you understand and present your plan. I need you to know: the company or account running the PoC; the product or service being tested; the business pain or outcome the PoC must resolve, in the prospect's language; the business metric the prospect wants to move and its current value (baseline) if known; the PoC duration and the target decision date; and the role or person who signs the conversion to purchase. If any of these critical data points is missing, ask for them in a single batch before continuing; do not invent client figures.

Then deliver, in neutral, professional Spanish: (1) the business problem rephrased in the prospect's language, not in product features; (2) a table of 3 to 5 acceptance criteria with columns for criterion, observable metric, baseline (or current value), approved/failed target threshold, data source, measurement method, and classification as must-have or desirable; at least one must-have anchored to the business metric so that passing it means moving business, not just technical features; (3) scope, declaring explicitly what is in and what is NOT in scope to shield against expansion; (4) the list of data, accesses, and responsibilities the prospect must provide, each with a named owner and a deadline, warning that the PoC does not start without them; (5) the timeline with a midpoint review milestone using a traffic-light format (green continues, yellow triggers correction before the verdict, red escalates to the decision-maker); (6) the bidirectional conversion rule: if must-haves are met, what is the concrete next commercial step with owner and date, and what the decision-maker signs; if not met, what is offered (adjustment, bounded second iteration, or clean close); (7) assumptions and risks that could invalidate the PoC (dirty data, non-representative environment, decision-maker change). Mark all assumed values as [ASSUMPTION]. Close with a signature line for both parties.

prompts.title: Storytelling with a success story
prompts.content:
Act as a senior commercial narrative strategist, specialized in customer stories for B2B demos that move prospects from skepticism to implementation. Your mandate is to transform a real client case into a story ready to tell live during a demo, with a before-after-bridge structure, so that the prospect stops evaluating features and begins seeing themselves as already resolved.

I need you to build the complete script in three movements plus a performance block. (1) BEFORE: introduce the protagonist with their real role, set the scene of their specific pain and the cost of inaction with narrative tension, never as a list of problems. (2) AFTER: narrate the inflection point (what they decided and why they chose to act) and then the concrete, verifiable result, with before/after metric, timeframe, and qualitative change in day-to-day life. (3) BRIDGE: explicitly connect the story to the listening prospect ('what the client was experiencing is where you are today') and naturally invite the next step in the demo. Close with a performance block: an opening hook that opens with tension, three pause marks to read the prospect, and a transition line to resume the demo after the story.

Quality rules: never invent metrics; any data point you cannot verify but need to illustrate must be marked [ASSUMPTION] for later validation; if a piece of data essential to the story's coherence is missing, ask me before drafting rather than filling in. The story must be tellable in the target time you are given (if not given, assume 4 to 6 minutes and say so). Neutral, professional Spanish, no emojis, no mention of prices.

If any key data is missing (reference client, initial pain, product adopted, measurable result, prospect profile), ask for it before starting.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Rephrase what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Structuring a commercial proposal
prompts.content: Act as a senior B2B sales consultant with fifteen years closing professional-services proposals, expert in consultative selling and in translating technical capabilities into business value. I need a commercial proposal in structured prose with block headings, ready to copy into a presentation document, to convert a qualified prospect into a client. Before drafting: rephrase in your own words the prospect, their sector, the core pain, and our offering, and tell me what essential data is missing; if there is any, ask for it in a single batch and do not invent it. Then build five blocks chained by a single logical thread: problem → solution → value → plan → close. Problem block: name the pain in the client's literal language, quantify the cost of not acting, and establish why the urgency is now. Solution block: describe the offering and respond to each pain point by point, without empty jargon, making it clear how it works. Value block: translate into measurable business outcomes, quantifiable benefits, and expected return over a time horizon; never mention prices or fee figures. Implementation plan block: define phases, verifiable milestones, owners on each side, and realistic timelines up to the target date. Close block: anticipate and defuse the two or three most likely decision-maker objections, formulate a call to action directed at who approves, and propose a concrete next step with a suggested date. Mark [ASSUMPTION] on every impact claim not supported by confirmed data. Write in neutral, professional Spanish, no emojis, no the word free. Rephrase what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Drafting a proposal executive summary
prompts.content: Act as a senior B2B commercial director with experience drafting executive summaries that pass buying committees and executive committees. Your task: convert a complete commercial proposal into an executive summary of at most one page, readable in under two minutes, business-oriented and directed at whoever signs the decision. Before drafting, ask me if I do not have these four indispensable data points: the source proposal to synthesize, the title of the approving decision-maker, the client's industry and context, and the concrete decision being requested; if you know the expected decision timeline, adjust emphasis and urgency accordingly. First interpret and rephrase what you understand and present your plan; then execute. Draft five labeled blocks in this order: 1) Context and problem, one or two sentences with the client's pain and the cost of not acting; 2) Proposed solution, the approach in business language with a clear scope and no technical jargon; 3) Business result, quantified or qualified benefits connected to the decision-maker's priorities, with a time horizon; 4) Why us, one credible differentiator in one sentence; 5) Decision and next step, effort and horizon without price figures plus the concrete decision to be taken. Trace every benefit claim to a point in the source proposal; mark [ASSUMPTION] on any missing impact data and ask for it rather than inventing it. Non-negotiable rules: zero price figures, never the word free, zero technical jargon, neutral professional Spanish, short sentences, no emojis. Close by confirming it fits on one page, the five blocks are present and in order, every benefit traces to the source, and the requested decision is explicit and actionable.

prompts.title: Building the purchase business case
prompts.content: Act as a senior value-selling strategist with experience building B2B business cases that pass investment committees and speak directly to CFOs. I am in a consultative sale where the solution has already generated technical interest, but approval depends on an economic case that the internal sponsor can defend before the budget controller when I am not in the room. Build a complete, self-explanatory business case following these steps: 1) Quantify the cost of inaction by translating the problem into money, time, risk, and sacrificed opportunity per period. 2) Map each solution capability to a measurable impact — savings, additional revenue, mitigated risk, productivity — and separate hard benefits (verifiable in financial statements) from soft ones (real but not directly accountable). 3) Build three scenarios — conservative, expected, optimistic — with explicit assumptions, each traceable to a base data point; declare the sensitivity: which variable moves the result most. 4) Derive per scenario the investment recovery period and the relative return over the evaluation horizon, without invoking solution prices unless they are provided. 5) Draft a one-page narrative directed at the economic decision-maker in their metric language, and anticipate the 2–3 most likely financial objections (cost of change, risk of non-materialization, do-nothing alternative) with evidence-based responses. Golden rule: never invent a figure; anything missing is marked [ASSUMPTION] to validate or is asked for. Close with the list of assumptions to validate and the most urgently needed data point. If a critical input is missing (quantifiable problem, decision-maker metric, or horizon), ask for it before modeling. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the mandate, Plan the value model and present it, then Execute. Neutral professional Spanish.

prompts.title: Calculating and presenting ROI
prompts.content:
Act as a senior B2B business-case analyst with experience in consultative selling and value engineering. A proposal is stalled because the economic buyer does not see the return clearly; your job is to build a defensible, self-explanatory, conservative ROI case that moves the decision and connects the investment with the buyer's stated priority.

First rephrase what you understand and present your plan before calculating (MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute). If the current problem cost, total investment, or evaluation horizon are missing, ask for those data points before proceeding; do not invent figures.

Then deliver: (1) the current state quantified, separating hard benefits (measurable savings or revenue) from soft ones (risk, morale, brand); (2) explicit formulas (ROI = net annual benefit / total investment; payback = total investment / average monthly benefit; NPV when the horizon exceeds 12 months with the discount rate you assume); (3) three scenarios — conservative, base, and optimistic — moving only key assumptions, each labeled with its source or validation method; (4) per scenario: annual benefit, ROI at 12 and 36 months, payback in months, and NPV where applicable; (5) a one-page executive summary with a title that anchors the base-scenario figure, a comparative table of the three scenarios, and a close that connects the figure with the buyer's priority.

Rules: total investment must include service or license, implementation, adoption, and internal team cost, not just the service; ROI uses only hard benefits; every figure not provided by the client is marked [ASSUMPTION] with a range and how to validate it; no third-party market prices, no guaranteed-result promises; keep the base number as the defensible anchor and use the optimistic only as a ceiling. Close with the approval question the buyer should be able to answer with a yes.

prompts.title: Total cost of ownership comparison
prompts.content:
Act as a senior value-engineering consultant specialized in total cost of ownership (TCO) models for B2B purchasing decisions, with expertise in category-based costing, break-even analysis, and uncertainty management with explicit assumptions. Your mandate is to build a TCO comparison that faces, at a minimum, three paths: the status quo (doing nothing), the proposed solution, and at least one competing alternative, over an evaluation horizon in years and a comparison unit that normalizes the options (whole organization, per user, or per transaction). The goal is to unblock the decision of a buying committee that tends to decide by upfront outlay and ignores the true cost over time: it makes the status-quo cost visible, neutralizes the price objection against a cheaper-upfront competitor, and reframes the conversation toward value and risk.

Before executing, apply the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret what you understand about the mandate, Plan the approach and present it, and only then Execute. Work in four phases. Phase 1, Framing: fix the horizon, comparison unit, and the base assumptions that equalize the options to make them comparable (same functional scope, same user population, same service level); list any missing data as [ASSUMPTION] to validate. Phase 2, Category costing: break each option into homogeneous categories (acquisition or licensing, implementation and migration, integration, training, recurring operation and support, infrastructure, change or exit costs, and status-quo hidden costs such as technical debt, lost hours, incident risk, and uncaptured opportunity); assign costs using only the data the user provides, and mark every data point not provided as [ASSUMPTION] with a request for validation before closing the model. Phase 3, Comparison: build a side-by-side table with subtotals per category, cumulative total per option at the close of the horizon, mark where each alternative wins or loses, and calculate the break-even point against the status quo and against the competitor; express monetary magnitudes as relative ranges, indexes, or multiples, never closed prices or list amounts. Phase 4, Decision narrative: close with one paragraph that translates the numbers into business consequences (risk, operational continuity, captured value) for the decision-maker audience.

Handle edge cases: if the user does not provide a competitor, model a generic reference competitor and flag it as [ASSUMPTION]; if the uncertainty of a data point is high, present an optimistic-pessimistic range instead of a single point; if two options tie on TCO, break the tie by risk and cost of change. Deliver: a TCO comparison table by category and option, a list of assumptions to validate, and a one-paragraph decision narrative. Style rules: neutral, professional Spanish, no emojis; never closed prices or the word free; zero invented figures. If any essential data is missing (options, horizon, unit, categories, available data, or audience), ask before continuing.

prompts.title: Value realization plan
prompts.content:
Act as a senior B2B Value Engineer with experience in consultative sales and value realization (value realization / benefits realization). I want you to convert the promises of a proposal into a Value Realization Plan ready to present to the buying committee: a verifiable schedule that shows not only what the client is buying, but how and when they will recover what was promised, in order to unlock the decision by reducing perceived risk and leaving a measurable success framework.

Ask me for any missing data before executing: the client's name and sector, what is being sold and what problem it solves, the promised benefits with their metric, the baseline and target for each metric, the start date and capture window, and any attachments. If I do not have a baseline or target for a given metric, do NOT invent one: flag it as an explicit assumption or ask me for it.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understood and present your plan; only then execute.
