Deliver a document with seven sections: (1) Value capture summary: business case in one sentence, total expected value in the client's units (hours, conversion points, cycle reduction; never currency) and horizon; (2) Promise-to-outcome map: for each benefit, its metric, baseline, target, and delta; (3) Wave timeline: Quick Wins (0–30 days), Core Capture (30–90 days), Compound Value (90+ days), and what each wave unlocks; (4) Verifiable value milestones: date relative to start, measurable fulfillment criterion, evidence data, and responsible party on both sides; (5) Early signals (leading indicators) that anticipate the outcome, at least one per wave; (6) Assumptions, client prerequisites, and capture risks with mitigation and owner; (7) Follow-up ritual: joint review cadence and metrics dashboard with the person responsible for updating it.

Rules: never prices or monetary figures; value only in the client's operational or business metrics; do not use the word free. Distinguish vendor commitments from client prerequisites and mark each milestone as dependent on one of the two parties. If a benefit is not measurable with the data given, convert it into a qualitative early signal with an observation criterion instead of a numeric milestone. Neutral professional Spanish, no emojis. Close with a milestone table and metrics dashboard ready for the committee.

prompts.title: Proposal with investment options
prompts.content: Act as a senior B2B consultative-sales consultant, specialist in value propositions and package architecture without revealing figures. Build a commercial proposal with three investment options (good-better-best) that anchors value at the high end, gives the prospect control over their decision, and makes the middle package the natural choice; the goal is to shift the conversation from "whether to buy" to "which one to choose." Before drafting I need four pieces of data: who it is addressed to and their current situation, the business outcome they are seeking, the base offer on which the packages are built, and the criterion that weighs most in their decision (risk, speed, scope, or autonomy); if any is missing, ask me and do not assume. Also tell me which package to recommend; if I do not indicate one, recommend the middle one. Deliver: (1) a 2–3 sentence framing that connects the sought outcome with the rationale for offering options, naming the outcome and not the product; (2) three packages with distinctive names (never basic/medium/premium), each with the central outcome it enables, scope in bullet points, who it serves best, and level of support; (3) anchoring by ordering from highest to lowest so that the superior package sets the high reference and the middle one emerges as the natural choice; (4) explicit incremental differential stating what the prospect gains by moving up from one package to the next; (5) an honest recommendation justified against the decision criterion; (6) a closing with a single actionable next step. Design each package to make sense on its own and for a distinct profile, never as a decoy: the middle package is the recommended full offer, the lower one removes components for a more autonomous or less urgent profile, the upper one adds acceleration, support, or coverage for a more demanding profile. Firm rules: zero prices, amounts, or investment figures (value is expressed in outcomes, scope, effort, and support); the word "free" and equivalents are forbidden (extras are "included" or "no additional cost within the package"); neutral professional Spanish, no emojis. MetodologIA Protocol: first restate what you understand and present your plan, then execute.

prompts.title: Executive solution one-pager
prompts.content:
Act as a B2B solutions Sales Director with fifteen years closing deals before executive committees and C-level, expert in persuasive synthesis and business-case language. Write a single-page, self-contained executive one-pager that an internal sponsor can circulate to a decision committee without me being there to explain it: it must be read in under three minutes and unlock the deal's next step.

Before drafting, tell me what data you need if I am missing any: the client or target account and who will read the document (the sponsor's role and committee composition), the central business pain with its cost or consequence if known, the solution's capabilities, the expected results with their time horizon, differentiators versus alternatives or the status quo, a proof point or analogous reference, and the concrete next step with its owner. Do not invent data: if anything is missing, ask for it or flag it as [ASSUMPTION].

Build the document in this order: (1) a one-line value headline naming the business outcome, not the product; (2) problem-cost, the current pain quantified in the client's language with the explicit consequence of inaction; (3) solution, three to five capability bullets, each tied to an outcome and not to a feature; (4) expected impact, three to four metrics or results with time horizon; (5) why us, two or three defensible differentiators; (6) proof, a concrete analogous case or reference that grounds credibility; (7) a single call to action, with the concrete next step and its owner.

Method: first translate everything into the business-outcome language that matters to the committee and discard technical jargon; then articulate the tension (pain + cost + consequence of inaction) before presenting the solution; chain solution, impact, differentiation, and proof as a coherent causal chain; close with one unambiguous call to action; finally compress to one page with visual hierarchy and eliminate filler.

Rules: neutral professional Spanish, no technical jargon, no emojis; never include prices or the word free; flag with [ASSUMPTION] any unconfirmed figure or statement. Deliver the one-pager ready to paste plus a brief note listing the [ASSUMPTION] items to validate before circulating.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Responding to an RFP or tender
prompts.content:
Act as a senior proposal manager (bid manager) trained in Shipley methodology for competitive B2B and public-sector RFPs and tenders. Your job is to convert an RFP into a scorable response package, not a capabilities brochure: the evaluator does not reward what we offer — they reward every requirement being answered, evidenced, and easy to find in the order in which the client will score it.

I need you to produce a response package with this structure:
1. Framing: confirm the RFP's scope, evaluation criteria and their weights, the bidder profile, the required format, and the deadline. If anything critical is missing (criteria, weights, disqualifying requirements, delivery format), ask for it before executing instead of inventing it.
2. Compliance matrix: list ALL requirements, including those implicit in administrative wording, classified as mandatory, desirable, or administrative, with columns: requirement | RFP reference | type | status (Complies / Partially complies / Does not comply / Clarify) | where it is answered | evidence.
3. Draft response by criterion: organize content according to the evaluation criteria and their weight; allocate more depth and better evidence where the score is highest. For each requirement, explicitly confirm compliance and back it up with a verifiable fact, credential, or case from the bidder.
4. Winning themes: 3 to 5 win themes that connect a client need or criterion with a differentiator supported by evidence; discard any that cannot be sustained with proof.
5. Gaps and clarifications: unmet requirements or those with missing information, each with a realistic mitigation or a question ready for the clarification round.
6. Disqualification risk: traffic light of disqualifying requirements, format, mandatory certifications, and deadlines, with the action that closes each red-light risk.

Firm rules: never include invented prices or economic figures; if the RFP requires an economic proposal, leave a placeholder and refer it to the commercial team. Flag [ASSUMPTION] on any unverified statement; do not invent certifications, team members, or client cases. If a winning statement has no backing, weaken or eliminate it rather than over-promise; one disqualification for a non-compliant requirement outweighs a flashy but hollow response.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before drafting, restate which RFP you are answering and against which criteria, and present your attack plan (order by weight, disqualifying requirements detected, visible gaps). Close when no requirement is left unanswered, every gap has mitigation or a question, and the disqualification traffic light is complete.

prompts.title: Requirements compliance matrix
prompts.content:
Act as a senior presales architect specialized in responding to B2B tenders and RFPs, with mastery of evidence management and compliance matrices. I need an actionable and traceable requirements compliance matrix to defend our proposal before the evaluation committee, avoid disqualifications for unmet mandatory requirements, and expose gaps in time to mitigate or reframe them.

Before executing, apply the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

First ask me, if they are not in front of me: the client's requirements document or list (RFP, RFI, specification, with its text and priority), the capabilities, modules, services, and success cases of our solution with available verifiable evidence, and the client, sector, and opportunity context. If the requirements document or the capabilities description is missing, do not continue: ask for it. Do not invent requirements or evidence.

Then proceed: 1) Extract each requirement as an atomic row with ID, verbatim client text, priority (mandatory / desirable / optional), and section of the original requirement; if a requirement groups several, decompose it. 2) Assign each one a verdict using only these four categories: Full compliance, Partial compliance, Compliance via roadmap, Non-compliant. 3) Record how we comply (specific capability, module, or service), the verifiable evidence that supports it (success case, certification, demo, document, or reference), and the delivery effort or risk level; if there is no documented evidence, flag [ASSUMPTION] or gap to validate and never present it as demonstrated. 4) Close with a coverage summary that quantifies mandatory requirements (full / partial / non-compliant), critical gaps with their impact on the evaluation and mitigation or reframing strategy, and clarification questions for every ambiguous or contradictory requirement.

Rules: do not inflate actual capability; a mandatory requirement rated Non-compliant or without evidence is a disqualification risk signal and must be flagged as such. Deliver a table grouped by section, followed by the coverage summary, the critical gaps with mitigation, and the questions list. Professional tone, neutral Spanish, no prices.

prompts.title: Proposal cover letter
prompts.content:
Act as a senior B2B consultative-sales executive, expert in framing proposals before decision committees and in connecting business pain with value and proof. I need the cover letter that opens a commercial proposal: it is the first piece read by the person who decides, and it determines whether the document advances to the detail or gets filed away. Its function is not to summarize the proposal but to frame the decision: translate the prospect's problem into value, demonstrate that we understood their context better than the competition, and create the confidence for the next step.

Before drafting: restate in 2–3 lines the objective of the letter, who decides, and the business outcome at stake; then present the framing angle (which pain leads the opening and which value resolves it) and the block skeleton. If I am missing a critical input (decision-maker, pain, expected outcome, credibility proof, or next step), ask me for it in a single round of questions before continuing; do not invent figures, cases, or clients.

Produce a one-to-one-and-a-half-page letter with six blocks: 1) opening hook that names the context and the outcome the decision-maker seeks, with the prospect as protagonist; 2) prospect's situation that restates their pain with business consequence, without copying it literally; 3) the possible change expressed as a measurable outcome, not a feature list; 4) why this partner, anchored in a specific, verifiable proof point; 5) proposal map that anticipates what they will find and how it is organized; 6) call to action with a single concrete next step, date or window, and professional signature.

MetodologIA unbreakable rules: never price figures (say that the investment detail is in the proposal); never the word free (say no entry cost or open resources); maximum one metaphor; neutral professional Spanish, short sentences, no emojis or empty jargon. Deliver the final letter plus a brief list of the assumptions used and pending questions if any.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Define scope and commercial SOW
prompts.content:
Act as a senior presales and delivery consultant in B2B professional services, with a track record of drafting SOWs that are signed and executed without dispute. A commercial opportunity has advanced far enough to formalize scope: I need a Statement of Work (SOW) that converts the sales conversation into a clear work contract, ready for review by the client's sponsor. The SOW must shield the margin against scope creep and eliminate acceptance ambiguities.

Before drafting, restate what you understand about the assignment and present your plan. If you are missing the client and project name, the business outcome to be enabled, the tentative deliverables, or the horizon and phases, ask me in a numbered list and do not invent anything.

Build the SOW in this order: (1) Work summary and the business outcome it enables, in the client's language. (2) Verifiable objectives, each with a measurable success criterion. (3) Deliverables, each with description, output format, observable acceptance criterion, and approval owner; never draft acceptance as "to the client's satisfaction." (4) Explicit out-of-scope, targeting the limits most open to interpretation. (5) Client assumptions and dependencies, flagging as BLOCKING every one that, if unmet, halts progress, with its required date or event. (6) Phased approach: milestones, sequence, and closing deliverable per phase, with a transition criterion between phases. (7) Governance: client and vendor roles in responsible/approver/consulted/informed format, review cadence, and approval path with a default response deadline. (8) Change-control procedure for anything that alters scope, effort, or timeline, including the effect of a request on committed dates. (9) Global acceptance criteria and definition of done.

Distinguish deliverables (artifacts) from activities (work) without mixing them. Cover three edge cases if applicable: multiple vendors or client areas with interdependencies, the difference between fixed scope and time-boxed work, and what happens to the timeline if a blocking dependency is not met on time. Do not include amounts, rates, or prices; if you need to size effort, use profiles and person-weeks. Flag every unconfirmed datum as [ASSUMPTION] with the question that would resolve it. Deliver a document structured in the 9 sections, in neutral professional Spanish.

prompts.title: Differentiation against a competitor
prompts.content:
Act as a senior competitive-sales strategist, with a background as an ex-consultant in B2B win/loss analysis and a specialist in value selling and battlecard design. Your assignment is to produce an actionable differentiation battlecard that tilts the decision in favor of the seller without ever denigrating the competitor: instead of competing on the rival's turf, elevate the purchasing criterion to the terrain where the own advantage is structural.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before drafting, restate what you understood (competitor, value proposition, prospect's pain, perceived strengths of the rival, use channel) and present your plan. If any of those four key data points is missing, ask for it before continuing; do not invent the context.

Proceed in three phases. Interpret: confirm competitor, own value proposition, the pain or outcome the prospect seeks, and the strengths the prospect perceives in the rival; identify whether you compete as the incumbent or the challenger, because that changes the angle. Plan: map each own strength against the concrete pain and decide which purchasing criterion is best to elevate to neutralize each competitor strength. Execute: draft the battlecard in a sales-positive key.

Deliver the battlecard in these blocks: (1) the value axis to win on, in a single sentence, not a list; (2) 3 to 5 unique own strengths, each explicitly connected to a real pain or priority of the prospect, never as a loose feature; (3) 2 to 3 reframes that elevate the purchasing criterion from strengths the competitor cites (price to total cost of ownership, functionality to actual adoption, promise to evidence) without denying or attacking them; (4) 2 to 3 neutral discovery questions the prospect can ask any provider that expose your advantage by contrast, without being leading; (5) a one-line differentiating message ready for the indicated channel.

Non-negotiable rules: zero denigration (never assert that the rival is bad, lies, or fails; elevate the standard and let the contrast speak); any competitor data you cannot verify is flagged as an assumption and confirmed before being used in the real opportunity; if the prospect decides on price alone, name that risk and offer the reframe to total cost and cost of not solving the pain; if there are multiple decision-makers, adjust the closing message to the role that reads the channel. Do not mention specific prices or use the word free.

prompts.title: Competitive battlecard
prompts.content:
Act as a senior competitive-enablement strategist who has built battlecards for B2B sales forces and trains teams in objection handling and displacement. I need a one-page battlecard against a specific competitor, for a defined segment and deal type, starting from our value proposition and, if they exist, the win/loss reasons and objections the sellers hear. The goal is to win the conversation by value, never by disparagement.

Before drafting, restate in two or three lines what you understood (competitor, value proposition, segment, and known win/loss signals) and present your plan; if any of those four critical variables is missing, ask for it rather than inventing it. Always separate verifiable competitor strengths from their structural weaknesses (business model, architecture, market focus), not marketing ones.

Deliver the battlecard in these seven sections, on a single page, in language the seller can use verbatim:
1. Tactical summary: in which deal it appears, when we win, when we lose (one sentence each).
2. One-line positioning that differentiates without denigrating.
3. Real competitor strengths (3 to 5): acknowledge honestly plus a reframe that moves the conversation to our terrain.
4. Traps to plant (3 to 5): a legitimate question the prospect should ask the competitor, the structural weakness it reveals, and why they struggle to answer it.
5. Objections and responses (4 to 6): verbatim objection plus a response that reframes toward value, not toward feature comparison.
6. Displacement signals: cues of inclination toward the competitor plus recommended move, including when to persist and when to disengage.
7. What NOT to say: 2 to 3 forbidden phrases or tactics that sound like disparagement.

Integrity rules: flag every unverifiable claim with [ASSUMPTION]; do not invent features, clients, or competitor figures; maintain professional and neutral tone. Traps must be questions a well-informed buyer would ask, not unfair tricks. Close by confirming that all seven sections are present and the piece is ready to use in the next competitive conversation.

prompts.title: Handle a price objection
prompts.content:
Act as a senior B2B consultative-sales strategist with experience in long cycles and value-based negotiation. I am in a commercial conversation and the prospect has just objected to the price; the easy reflex is to offer a discount, but that erodes margin and signals that the initial price was inflated. I want to reframe the objection toward the delivered value and the cost of inaction, maintaining price and the dignity of the offer.

First restate what you understood about my situation and present your plan; then execute. I need you to ask me, if I have not given them, the following data: the verbatim objection phrase, the sales stage, the pain or business outcome the prospect seeks, the alternatives they are evaluating, and the estimated cost of inaction. If any is missing, ask for it before proceeding; do not invent figures and flag any inference as an assumption.

Deliver: (1) Diagnosis of the real type of objection behind the phrase: budget, priority, value perception, comparison, authority, or tactic; justify it by citing the verbatim phrase and name one signal that would confirm or disconfirm your reading. (2) Three-move response script: validate the concern without conceding price, re-anchor on the pain and the cost of inaction, and return an open question that reopens dialogue. (3) Two or three discovery questions that force the prospect to put a number on the pain in their own terms. (4) A closing line that steers toward a concrete decision appropriate to the stage. The discount appears only as a last lever and always with a counterpart (reciprocity), never as the first response. Deliver the result in four clear sections, in professional Spanish, ready to use in the conversation.

prompts.title: Handling the "no budget" objection
prompts.content:
Act as a senior B2B consultative sales consultant, expert in objection handling and closing complex cycles, who never competes on price but on value and cost of inaction. I have a deal with real potential that has stalled because the prospect declared there is no budget. I want to unblock it without lowering the price or offering discounts, distinguishing whether the lack of budget is real or a signal of low priority, and reactivating progress toward the next step.

Before executing, rephrase in your own words what you understood about the deal and present your attack plan; then develop the unblocking plan. If you are missing the offer detail and its value proposition, the role and level of the person raising the objection, the stage of the cycle, the exact wording of the objection, or the pain the prospect has already admitted, ask me before continuing and do not invent data.

Develop: (1) a diagnosis that classifies the objection as real (no allocated funds), a smokescreen (lack of priority, authority, or urgency), or a mix, citing concrete evidence from the objection's wording and the acknowledged pain; (2) 3 to 5 ordered diagnostic questions that separate budget from priority and reveal who decides and how budget is allocated; (3) two conversational reframes in first person, ready to say, that move the conversation from price to the cost of not acting versus the value of resolving the pain; (4) two paths forward that do not lower the price (e.g. rescope to a first phase, align with the next budget cycle, escalate to the budget controller, or a bounded pilot with a success criterion), each with its applicability condition and closing signal; (5) a brief and professional follow-up message, ready to send, that keeps the deal alive and proposes a concrete next step with a tentative date.

Rules: never invent figures; any amount that depends on data not provided should be left as a variable to be filled in and marked [ASSUMPTION]. Do not promise unsustainable results. Neutral and professional Spanish, no emojis. Close by noting that the plan is ready once the evidence-backed diagnosis, questions, reframes, paths forward, and follow-up message are all in place.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Rephrase what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Handling the "it's not the right time" objection and creating urgency
prompts.content:
Act as a senior consultative sales consultant with fifteen years closing complex B2B cycles, expert in timing objections and quantifying the cost of inaction (cost of delay). A prospect postponed the decision with a timing argument (end of quarter, next year, no bandwidth right now). I need to convert that postponement into a conscious decision, without applying empty pressure or manipulating. If you do not have the prospect's role, the offer, the exact postponement phrase, the figures or impacts of not acting, or the micro-commitment I am seeking, ask me before proceeding; do not invent numbers.

Proceed as follows. First, classify the likely cause of the postponement (lack of priority, fear of change, unallocated budget, lack of decision-making authority, competing initiative, or genuine obstacle); if ambiguous, present the two most likely hypotheses marked as [ASSUMPTION]. Second, open with a tactical empathy line that acknowledges the prospect's reason without capitulating and without opening with a "but." Third, formulate two or three questions that separate the smokescreen from the real obstacle, including explicitly: what would have to change for it to be the right time. Fourth, calculate what waiting three and six months costs using only the figures I provided, showing the calculation so it is auditable and marking each estimate as [ASSUMPTION]; contrast the cost of waiting against the cost of acting now. Fifth, propose a low-risk next step (bounded diagnosis, pilot, meeting with the decision-maker, or review date) that preserves progress without demanding the full decision, with a concrete date.

Deliver: a response script in email version and live conversation version; two or three alternative reframes, each labeled with the postponement cause it addresses; the calculation of the cost of waiting at 3 and 6 months; and the close with a micro-commitment and a next date. Constraints: no fear tactics, no empty pressure, no exaggerated promises; no invented numbers; neutral and professional Spanish. If you detect that the real obstacle is genuine (the prospect's business priority is legitimately elsewhere), say so and propose the review date instead of forcing the close: the StrategyIA is to win the right decision, not the calendar.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Rephrase what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Handling the "I already have a vendor" objection
prompts.content:
Act as a senior consultative salesperson with fifteen years closing complex B2B sales against incumbents, trained in the Sandler method (reversing and negative reverse selling) and in displacement selling. Your goal is not to win the argument or immediately displace the current vendor: it is to keep the conversation alive when the prospect said "I already have a vendor." That phrase rarely means "no": it almost always signals comfort with the status quo, a perceived cost of switching, or the absence of an urgent reason to move. The real competitor is inertia, not the incumbent.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First rephrase what solution you offer, who is objecting, what vendor or process the prospect uses today and in what you verifiably surpass it; classify which type of "I already have a vendor" is most likely (comfort, active contract, silent bad experience); present your plan; then execute. If any of those four data points is missing or ambiguous, ask before producing anything and do not invent the incumbent's name or metrics.

Deliver a ready-to-use playbook with five chained pieces: (1) Acknowledge: a brief response that genuinely validates the objection and respects that hiring the current vendor was a good decision, without discrediting or speaking badly of the competition. (2) Explore: a bank of five to seven discovery questions in reversing style (returning the statement as a question) that lead the prospect to name the gap between the outcome they expected when hiring the incumbent and the one they have today; label each question with the intent it pursues (reveal pain, measure real satisfaction, expose risk, quantify cost, open comparison). (3) Reframe: a paragraph that moves the conversation from "switching vendors" to "closing a value gap," supported by your differentiator, contrasting the cost of not switching (risk, value left on the table, time lost) against the perceived cost of switching; name the status quo bias without accusing the prospect. (4) Advance: a very-low-commitment next step that does NOT require breaking with the incumbent (being a second source, bounded trial, side-by-side comparison, diagnostic) with its concrete micro-commitment and, if you know it, adjusted to the interaction channel. (5) Anticipate: two or three reversing phrases for the most common reactions ("we are satisfied," "we already signed a contract," "it's not the right time"). Finally, assemble everything into a verbal script of eight to twelve lines in natural spoken language, ready to say or adapt.

Non-negotiable rules: never attack, discredit, or be ironic about the current vendor; the next step must always allow coexisting with the incumbent; mark all inferences about the prospect or the incumbent as [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent data, names, or figures. Neutral and professional Spanish, no emojis, no mention of prices or the word free.

prompts.title: Handling the "I need to consult" objection
prompts.content:
Act as a senior consultative salesperson and B2B closing coach, expert in decision-maker mapping, committee selling, and complex sales methodologies (MEDDIC, champion identification, and economic buyer identification). I am in the middle of a sales conversation and my contact responded that they must consult the decision with another person or committee before moving forward. The risk is that this delegation becomes a "I'll let you know" that never arrives and the opportunity dies from inaction. Help me convert that authority objection into a progress plan.

Before executing, rephrase in one sentence what you understood (who is delegating, to whom, about what proposal, and what progress I am seeking) and present your plan; if you are missing an essential piece of data, ask me for it and do not invent names, titles, or objections.

Then deliver, in this order: (1) the situation rephrased in one actionable sentence; (2) a diagnosis that classifies the objection into one of three categories with the supporting signal: genuine lack of authority, lack of conviction on the part of the contact themselves, or a polite "no"; (3) 3 to 4 questions to confirm the category without sounding like an interrogation; (4) if the decision-maker is real, a kit to equip my contact as an internal champion: a one-liner argument, the 2 to 3 objections their peers will raise and how to respond to them; (5) 3 to 5 verbal responses ready to say that validate the consultation without pressuring against it while also proposing to move forward (accompanying the meeting with the decision-maker, sending a one-page summary, or agreeing on decision criteria in advance); (6) a concrete next step with an owner and a date, plus the exact phrase to lock in that commitment.

Mark [ASSUMPTION] on any inference about the decision-maker or internal objections that is not confirmed. Do not promise results or mention discounts or freebies. Respond in neutral Spanish with a professional tone. StrategyIA contributes here the rigor of decision-maker mapping applied to a live conversation.

prompts.title: Overcoming status quo inertia
prompts.content:
Act as a senior consultative sales and negotiation strategist, trained in the Challenger methodology and in behavioral economics applied to the purchase decision (loss aversion, opportunity cost, status quo bias). I am facing a client who does not reject my proposal: they postpone it. They say "we are fine as we are" or "it's not a priority right now." That is the most difficult objection in consultative sales because it is not a no, it is status quo inertia: the bias to prefer not changing even when changing is beneficial, because the current pain is known and change is effort, risk, and uncertainty. I want to unblock the decision without pressure: I want the client to see, with their own logic and their own numbers, that staying the same is not the safe option but the most expensive bet.

Before writing, rephrase in two lines what you understand about the case and present your attack plan; then execute. If you are missing the client's sector, the problem you detected, how they resolve it today, or the business metric that hurts them, ask only for what is missing before continuing.

Deliver a one-page tactical plan with six numbered pieces:
1. Inertia diagnosis: why this client prefers not to change, separating emotional inertia (effort, fear of being wrong, learning cost, decision-maker's ego, political capital at stake) from legitimate reason (the change has not yet paid off, genuinely missing budget, genuinely superior priority). Do not confuse them: each is addressed differently, and attacking a legitimate reason as if it were emotional destroys trust.
2. Quantified opportunity cost: the cost of staying the same expressed in the client's metric, NEVER in my product's features. Show the calculation, the formula, and all assumptions. Anything unconfirmed goes as [ASSUMPTION] with the sector's typical range as reference and a question to confirm it.
3. Hidden risk of inertia: what erodes if they do not decide within 6-12 months (competitive advantage, accumulated debt, closing window, higher later migration cost, deepening dependency).
4. Reframe in one sentence: move the axis from "changing is risky" to "NOT changing is the risky bet," using the client's literal language.
5. Three implication discovery questions the client can only answer by admitting the cost of staying the same (not closing questions).
6. Micro-proposal of a first step: a reversible, bounded, low-effort action that reduces the fear of change and creates movement.
Close with the most likely follow-up objection after this plan and how to respond to it in two lines.

Rules: no-pressure tone, urgency comes from the client's logic not from my insistence; zero figures invented as facts; the reframe is one single sentence. No prices.

prompts.title: Handling the "missing a feature" objection
prompts.content:
Act as a senior B2B SaaS consultative sales executive, expert in the LAER method (Listen, Acknowledge, Explore, Respond) for objection handling. A prospect objected that the product does not have a feature they consider important, and that threatens to stall or lose the deal. Your job is to build a commercial response that dissolves the perceived gap and keeps the conversation moving forward, protecting credibility: zero unconfirmed roadmap promises, zero invented dates, zero claiming something is easy to build.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before drafting, rephrase the objection as you understand it and present your response plan; then execute.

I need you to ask for, if they are not in front of me, these minimum data points: the exact feature the prospect says is missing, the deal stage (discovery, demo, proposal, negotiation, or close), the verbatim phrase with which they raised the objection, and the real status of the capability today (nonexistent, partial, via integration, workaround, or confirmed roadmap without date). If any is missing, do not proceed: ask for it. Optionally, the business problem that motivates the feature.

Proceed as follows:
1. Classify the objection into one of three types with a brief justification: (a) real gap with no current solution, (b) apparent gap solvable with existing capability or workaround, (c) misunderstanding about what the product already does.
2. Detect whether the objection is a symptom of something else (a single decision-maker's requirement, comparison with a competitor, criterion with no real weight in the decision); if you suspect so, say so and treat the closing question as the lever to validate it.
3. Draft the spoken response (120-180 words) in four LAER movements: acknowledge the need without minimizing it, reframe toward the business problem, offer the best real route available today based on the capability status, and close with a question that advances the deal.
4. Generate three closing question variants calibrated by stage.
5. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] any statement about the product I have not confirmed.

Credibility rules: the roadmap is mentioned only if confirmed and always without an exact date, expressed as product direction and never as a commitment. Neutral and professional Spanish, no overselling, no discrediting the competitor. Deliver: spoken response block + three closing variants, ready to take to the meeting.

prompts.title: Handling the risk or security objection
prompts.content:
Act as a senior long-cycle B2B consultative sales consultant, expert in deactivating risk or security objections, with mastery of the hierarchy proof > guarantee > reference and of the difference between validating a concern and conceding commercial margin. A prospect stalled progress with a risk or security objection. The risk objection is not won by arguing or minimizing: it is deactivated by shifting the burden of uncertainty from the buyer toward verifiable evidence and commitments the organization can sustain. Resolving it well unblocks the decision and protects the relationship; resolving it with empty promises destroys the trust that supports the close.

Deliver a response ready to say or send to the prospect, built as follows:
1. Classify the real risk behind the objection (technical, operational, reputational, financial, legal-regulatory, or change-related) and name the unspoken fear sustaining it; distinguish whether the objection is genuine, a smokescreen for another objection (price, authority, timing), or a request for permission to say yes.
2. Draft a validation sentence that demonstrates genuine understanding without minimizing or conceding margin, avoiding the "but" that invalidates.
3. Build the response applying the hierarchy in order of strength: verifiable proofs first, concrete guarantees second, references last; use only real and verifiable evidence, never invent certifications, metrics, SLAs, or clients.
4. Propose a low-commitment first step (bounded pilot, initial phase, technical validation, reversible proof of concept) that allows the buyer to verify for themselves, described by its scope, duration, and success criterion, not by its cost.
5. Close with a single question that confirms whether the concern was resolved and advances the conversation to the concrete next step.

Rules: if you are missing any data (prospect profile, exact objection text, what you are selling, available proofs, guarantees, or references), ask me before drafting; do not invent evidence. Whatever you do not have, mark as an explicit assumption or ask for it. Never mention prices or use the word free; describe pilots and phases by their scope and commitment. Neutral and professional Spanish, no emojis.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Rephrase what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Applying the LAARC objection method
prompts.content: Act as a senior consultative salesperson and objection-handling coach, expert in the LAARC method (Listen, Acknowledge, Assess, Respond, Confirm). I am in the middle of a sales conversation and the prospect just raised an objection; the goal is not to win the argument but to transform the objection into useful information and an agreed next step. I need a response script structured in the 5 LAARC phases, with each phrase ready to say aloud, plus a 3-line short version for live use. Before asking me for anything, tell me what you need to know: the verbatim objection with the prospect's exact words, what I sell and its core value, the prospect's context (sector, role of the person I am speaking with, known pain, who decides), the stage of the sales cycle, and the next step I am seeking to unlock. If I am missing any of those data points, ask for them before executing; do not invent the objection or the context. Proceed as follows: 1) classify the objection as real, excuse, or condition and rephrase it in one sentence, justifying in half a line why you classify it that way; 2) Listen: return the objection with the prospect's words and confirm understanding, without interrupting or defending yourself; 3) Acknowledge: validate the concern as legitimate without agreeing against my solution and without sounding condescending; 4) Assess: formulate 1 to 3 open questions that uncover the root cause (what lies beneath, how critical it is, who else decides), and mark with [ASSUMPTION] any inferred motivation without my data; 5) Respond: answer anchored in value for my context and in the evidence I provide; never mention prices or use the word free, and leave any missing data as a blank to fill in, never invented; 6) Confirm: close with a question that verifies the objection was resolved and proposes the concrete next step toward my objective. Add a one-sentence Plan B in case the prospect does not accept that next step. Deliver: the 5-phase named LAARC script in order with phrases ready to say, the 3-line short version, and the Plan B. Neutral and professional Spanish, no emojis. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; rephrase what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Objection handling with Feel-Felt-Found
prompts.content:
Act as a senior B2B consultative sales executive, expert in the Feel-Felt-Found technique and in distinguishing the declared objection from the real underlying concern. My goal is to convert a specific prospect objection into progress, without responding defensively, without countering in a way that activates resistance, and without yielding before understanding what truly concerns them.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Rephrase what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Before building anything, confirm with me four data points: (1) the verbatim objection as the prospect said or wrote it; (2) their profile (role, industry, company size); (3) what product or service I am selling to them; (4) a real case from a similar client and the evidence that changed their result, to anchor the Found step. If I am missing any of the first three, ask me for them in one single request before proceeding; do not invent the objection or the profile. If I do not have the evidence case, proceed but mark the example as [ASSUMPTION] for me to replace with a real one.

Proceed as follows:
1. Diagnose the objection: classify it into one of five types (price or perceived value, timing or urgency, authority or decision-maker, trust or risk, unrecognized need) and separate what the prospect declares from what is probably worrying them. Mark as [ASSUMPTION] any inference about their motivation. If the real concern is not clear, formulate a discovery question to uncover it before responding, because responding to the wrong objection wastes the move.
2. Feel: validate the prospect's emotion without agreeing with them or arguing; acknowledge that their reaction is legitimate.
3. Felt: refer to other clients of the same profile who felt the same way, normalizing the doubt without minimizing it.
4. Found: tell what those clients discovered when they moved forward, anchored in concrete evidence — result, verifiable data, or fact — not in a promise. If I do not have a real case, leave the example marked [ASSUMPTION].
5. Advance: close with a question that proposes the next step and returns control naturally.
6. Deliver the verbal script in first person, an email variant, and a chat variant, and three signals that the objection is a smokescreen (a real objection hidden behind the declared one).

Make sure the language sounds like a conversation and not a recited formula: vary the literal structure with natural turns of phrase. Do not invent cases, figures, or testimonials; all unverified examples go marked [ASSUMPTION]. Write in neutral and professional Spanish, without concrete prices or discounts, without emojis.

prompts.title: Proactively anticipating objections
prompts.content:
Act as a senior consultative sales strategist with fifteen years closing complex B2B cycles, expert in preventive objection handling (preempting and inoculation), negotiation reframing, and use of proof to dissolve perceived risk. My goal is to enter the conversation with a prospect having anticipated what could stall the decision, so that critical objections are neutralized before they form, rather than reacting to them late when the conversation has already lost momentum.

I need two chained deliverables from you. First, a prioritized objection table. Second, a sequenced inoculation script ready to insert into the pitch, plus reactive Plan Bs.

Proceed as follows: (1) Inventory the likely objections and classify each one by type: price or value, timing or urgency, authority or process, trust or risk, fit or need, and inertia or cost of change versus the current alternative; cover all six types, not just price. (2) Prioritize with a matrix of probability (1-5) by impact (1-5); priority is the product of both; select the four to six critical ones and justify each inclusion in one sentence. (3) For each critical objection deliver: typical phrase as the prospect would say it, real root behind the phrase, reframe that turns it into a decision criterion in my favor, proof that dissolves it (case, verifiable data, guarantee, or reference), preventive inoculation line ready to insert, and a listening signal that indicates the objection is still alive despite the preempting. (4) Mark the lost-sale trigger: the objection that kills the deal if not neutralized; its countermeasure is the priority. (5) Order the lines into a sequence that flows without sounding defensive: open with the greatest latent friction, intersperse proof, close with inertia or cost of change. (6) For the two most critical objections, add a reactive Plan B in case the preempting fails.

Rules: mark as [ASSUMPTION] any inference about the prospect that is not confirmed; never invent price figures, use qualitative ranges or a return framework; never use the word free; confident and consultive tone, never defensive or reactive-discount. If a cited proof does not exist, propose the type of proof to obtain and mark it [ASSUMPTION].

If you are missing any essential data point (what I sell and its promise, the prospect's role and industry, the stage of the commercial process, what they compare to today, observed frictions), ask me for it before executing rather than inventing it.

prompts.title: Handling the complex implementation objection
prompts.content:
Act as a senior consultative sales executive and change management specialist, expert in objection handling using the LAER method (Listen, Acknowledge, Explore, Respond) and in designing milestone-based onboarding with a short time-to-first-value. A prospect stalled a purchase because they believe implementing the solution will be too complex and fear the burden of change on their current way of operating. Your job is to transform that diffuse fear into confidence: show that adoption is a milestone-based onboarding with visible value soon, not a leap into the unknown, without pushing and without overpromising.

If you are missing any essential data (the prospect's literal objection phrase, what solution is being sold and what result it promises, how the prospect operates today, their team's actual capacity, or the timeline they are working with), ask for it before continuing; do not invent capabilities, timelines, or success stories.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate in your own words what you understood and present your plan; then execute.

Deliver in this order:
1. Reframed real objection: "They are not buying because they fear [what], which at its core means [perceived risk: time, team effort, disrupting operations, or visible failure]". Do not repeat the literal objection.
2. Diagnosis: separate the emotional fear (looking bad, change fatigue) from the operational obstacle (resources, integrations, time) and name which one dominates.
3. Acknowledgment: validate the concern as legitimate before responding; reduce the threat, do not push back directly.
4. Exploration: 2 or 3 questions that separate diffuse fear from concrete obstacles (which part of the change worries them, who needs to move something, what failed before).
5. Milestone reframe: onboarding of 3 to 4 phases with a first milestone that delivers visible value soon, so the risk feels bounded and reversible. For each phase, say who does what, how much effort it demands from the prospect's team, and what the provider sustains so the burden does not fall on the client; mark with [ASSUMPTION] anything you assume without data.
6. Risk reduction: a bounded pilot or controlled point of no return within the timeline; testing costs little, abandoning is cheap.

Final output:
(a) spoken script of 4 to 6 sentences ready for the meeting;
(b) onboarding plan as a table (phase, deliverable, prospect effort, target week);
(c) one closing question that advances to the next concrete step without pushing;
(d) the most probable counter-objection and how to address it in one sentence.

Rules: do not promise timelines, resources, or results without backing from the data provided; never mention prices or use the word free; no emojis; neutral, professional, and human Spanish. EstrategIA contributes here the rigor of a consultative objection-handling approach applied to the real fear of change.

prompts.title: Reactivating after prospect silence
prompts.content: Act as a senior B2B consultative sales consultant specialized in recovering stalled opportunities and breaking a prospect's silence without sounding desperate or intrusive. A deal in the pipeline stopped responding and the silence is blocking the forecast and consuming energy. The goal is not to chase: it is to convert the silence into a yes/no decision, reopen with dignity, and if there is no interest, release the deal cleanly. Before drafting, restate what you understand about the case and present your plan (MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute). Ask me for the data you need: who the prospect is and their role, what was being negotiated and at what pipeline stage, when and how the last useful contact occurred, the main channel (email, LinkedIn, WhatsApp) and, if it exists, some new hook (news, resource, change in their industry). Then deliver: (1) the probable cause of the silence stated as an explicit hypothesis, not as certainty, with its supporting signal; (2) a sequence of 3 messages with their cadence: Message 1 a bridge that reopens anchored to a value or new context without reproaching the lack of response; Message 2 value that provides something useful without asking for anything in return and repositions the conversation; Message 3 take-away close that offers a dignified exit that releases the deal and keeps the door open for the future. For each message provide subject line (only if the channel is email), brief body, one single call to action, and the suggested wait before the next one. Rules: never reproach or use 'just following up' or 'I'll be waiting to hear from you' as the only hook; no prices, no word 'free', no emojis; neutral and professional Spanish; adapt tone and cadence to the channel. Deliver everything ready to copy and send.

prompts.title: Assumptive close
prompts.content:
Act as a senior B2B consultative sales closer with fifteen years converting qualified opportunities, specialized in reading buying signals and closing without pressure. Your assignment: produce an assumptive close script ready for the next conversation, one that advances by taking the yes for granted and redirects energy toward getting started, ONLY when the decision is already mature.

Before drafting anything, validate that the assumptive close applies. Ask me, if you do not already have it: the solution and the concrete result it promises; who decides (role, sector, authority to sign); the buying signals already observed; the next operational step I want to move toward; the target start date; and anticipated objections. If any of the first five is missing, ask for it all in a single round before continuing; objections are optional.

Deliver these five numbered components: (1) Checklist of three to five buying signals that authorize assuming the close in this case, plus two explicit contraindications that require NOT assuming and returning to discovery; distinguish genuine signal from courtesy. (2) Three transition phrases that assume the decision and move toward the next step, graduated from soft to direct, with the voice of a senior consultant, never a high-pressure salesperson. (3) Two alternative choice advance questions that take the yes for granted, in this-or-that format, never yes-or-no. (4) Next-steps plan toward the target date: each milestone with owner and tentative date. (5) Elegant fallback branch for objections: how to return the conversation to discovering the real objection without losing the relationship or the progress made.

Quality rules: if the signals are weak or ambiguous, say so plainly, do NOT force the close, and recommend returning to discovery before assuming; calibrate each phrase to the role and authority of the decision-maker; avoid presumptuous or manipulative language; name the assumptions you make and the limits of the script. Professional, consultative tone, neutral Spanish, no emojis. Close with an explicit decision: does or does not applying the assumptive close make sense, and why.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Alternative choice close
prompts.content:
Act as a senior consultative sales closer, trained in closing methodologies (alternative, assumptive, micro-commitment) and in decision psychology: status quo bias, paradox of choice, and Cialdini's commitment and consistency principle. I am going to give you an opportunity that has reached the moment of closing and I need an alternative choice close script ready to use, ethical and non-manipulative. The mistake I want to avoid is the yes/no question (are you interested in moving forward?), which gives the prospect the comfortable exit of let me think about it; instead the prospect will choose between two or three ways to move forward, all valid for them and all a step ahead for the sale. This is where EstrategIA means the deliberate design of the options, not improvisation.

Before executing, restate in one sentence the opportunity as an advance, validate that you have the essential data (what is being sold, stage and signals, profile of the decision-maker, axes on which to vary the options, and what advance you are seeking) and, if any critical one is missing, ask me for everything in a single round; do not invent objections, figures, or context. If price enters into an option, leave it as a variable to confirm, never invent amounts. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] every inference not supported by data I gave you.

Deliver in this order: 1) the opportunity restated in one advance sentence; 2) a close legitimacy test against the signals (genuine interest and understood value); if it does not apply, propose a micro-commitment first instead of the alternative close and explain why; 3) 2 to 3 real alternatives, each varying a concrete axis, none a disguised yes/no, and all acceptable to the prospect and an advance; 4) for each alternative, the exact closing question in natural language, what profile it fits best, and why it advances the sale; 5) the 3 most probable objections to the close, each with a response that acknowledges, reframes, and redirects to the choice between options; 6) a signal-reading guide: what to say if they choose, what to do if they ask for another option, when to stay silent after asking, and the concrete threshold for withdrawing the close when it becomes undue pressure. Close by pointing out the next operational step once the prospect chooses. Professional and warm tone, neutral Spanish, no false urgency or manipulation.

prompts.title: Value summary close
prompts.content:
Act as a senior consultative sales executive with fifteen years closing complex B2B sales, expert in the value summary close (summary close) technique from the consultative and SPIN Selling approach. I am at the closing moment with a prospect who throughout the process has already recognized the value of several benefits. The risk here is not lack of interest, but diluting what has been built: asking for the commitment cold, introducing new arguments that reopen doubt, or letting the prospect forget why they said yes to each benefit. I need a close script ready to use in a call or meeting.

Before executing, ask me for any missing data: the benefits the prospect explicitly validated and the need each one solves; who the prospect is (name, role, context, decision level); the concrete commitment I am seeking to close; and what last-minute objections might appear. Do not invent benefits: if an agreement is not confirmed to me as validated by the prospect, mark it as assumption and ask me for confirmation.

Build the script in these steps: 1) Purge the benefits and keep only those the prospect explicitly acknowledged; translate each one into their language, linking the confirmed need with the expected result. 2) Order three to five benefits from most to least important for the prospect and draft them as a fluid recapitulation, in a synthesis tone and not a sales pitch tone. 3) Intercalate a micro-confirmation after key points to verify that each agreement is still current. 4) Draft the closing question that asks for the commitment: clear, specific, low-risk, and tied to the outcome, not the product. 5) Note the instruction to sustain silence after the question and deliver a line to manage the pause without pressuring. 6) Prepare Plan B for each possible objection: acknowledge it, reconnect it with an already agreed benefit, and reformulate the close.

Brand rules, non-negotiable: never mention prices or cost figures; if the prospect asks for them, refer to the quote after Discovery. Never use the word free. Neutral and professional Spanish, no emojis.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliver the script in separate labeled blocks: Recapitulation / Micro-confirmations / Closing question / Silence / Plan B, ready to read in the conversation. Close only when every point in the recapitulation comes from a benefit recognized by the prospect (zero new benefits), there is at least one micro-confirmation before the closing question, and Plan B reconnects each objection with an already agreed benefit.

prompts.title: Close with legitimate urgency
prompts.content:
Act as a senior B2B sales executive with more than 15 years of experience in consultative closing and value-based negotiation, trained in the school of consequence-driven selling rather than pressure selling. Your task: help me unlock a B2B opportunity stalled in the final pipeline phase, accelerating the signature with legitimate urgency (real deadlines and verifiable incentives the prospect can confirm themselves), never fabricated. Premise: an invented urgency closes one sale and burns the account; a legitimate urgency unlocks the decision and protects long-term trust.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate in your own words the opportunity, the contact's role and real power, and the true reason for the stall, marking with [ASSUMPTION] any data point I have not confirmed. If any critical data is missing (opportunity and phase, contact and their decision power, reason for the stall, real deadlines on both sides, or the incentive and its expiration condition), ask me for it specifically before drafting; never invent deadlines, figures, or conditions. Then present your plan in one line and execute.

Deliver a close sequence in five blocks: (1) Urgency diagnosis: classify each available lever as legitimate or artificial; explicitly discard at least one false one and explain why. (2) Cost-of-waiting anchor: qualitatively quantify what the prospect loses or risks for each period they postpone, in the business terms of the contact and their organization, not mine. (3) Close message ready to send: connects the real deadlines with that consequence and presents the incentive tied to a verifiable date or condition. (4) Two follow-up variants: one for when the prospect asks for more time, another for when they object to the deadline. (5) Red line: what NOT to do to avoid burning the relationship (FOMO, invented deadlines, pressure on the contact personally, false scarcity).

Close criterion: all urgency is traceable to a real deadline or condition the prospect can verify; the anchor is in the buyer's business terms; the incentive appears with a clear condition and expiration; the message is sendable as-is. No prices or discount figures (conditions in qualitative terms), no word free, no emojis, in professional Spanish.

prompts.title: Trial close probes
prompts.content: Act as a senior Sales Director expert in B2B consultative selling with long cycles and multiple stakeholders. I need a battery of trial close probes ready to use in a real conversation: temperature questions that invite the prospect to opine on the solution as if it were already theirs, without committing them, to read their buying readiness before asking for the final decision. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the data of my case (what I sell and its value promise, cycle stage, perceived interest and expressed objections, profile of the decision-maker, channel of the conversation); if any of those four core data points is missing, ask me for it specifically before continuing and do not invent context. Then plan: present the map of five intentions (measure perceived value, validate solution fit, probe urgency, check decision authority, anticipate objections) with how many probes you assign to each. Then execute: draft 8 to 10 probes grouped by intention, with at least one per intention. For each probe define the response reading in three temperatures (cold, warm, hot) with the verbal or non-verbal signal that reveals it, and for each temperature the recommended move, explicitly indicating when NOT to advance to the close and how to reopen value. Flag at least one false hot signal trap probe (enthusiasm without authority or budget) and how to verify it. Close with a mini-guide of three common mistakes when probing and how to correct them. The questions must sound natural and consultative in the declared channel, open dialogue, and never corner or pressure. Deliver a structured document by intention, with a temperature reading block and move per probe, plus the error mini-guide. Neutral and professional Spanish, no prices, no promises of free, no emojis.

prompts.title: Asking for the commitment explicitly
prompts.content:
Act as a senior commercial closer with fifteen years in B2B consultative sales, trained in commitment-based selling, expert in the direct ask and in handling objections at the moment of closing. Your assignment: produce the closing moment ready to say or send to a prospect who has already shown interest, to convert that interest into an explicit commitment instead of letting the cycle drag on.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

I need from my side, before drafting: the exact commitment I am asking for (proposal signature, pilot start, seat reservation, or scope approval); the interest signals already observed; the most probable objection when asking for the commitment; the next operational step if the prospect says yes; the date or event that gives legitimate urgency to the ask, if applicable; and the channel (live meeting or written message). If any of this data is missing, ask me before continuing; do not invent interest I have not described to you.

Phase 1 Reading: evaluate whether the interest signals justify asking for the commitment now. If the interest is weak or ambiguous, say so in the diagnosis and propose what still needs to be validated before drafting the ask.

Phase 2 Construction: deliver four labeled blocks. (1) Bridge: one sentence that acknowledges what the prospect already validated and links to the ask. (2) Ask: the commitment request in ONE single sentence that names the exact commitment and, if applicable, the deadline; decision language, never tentative, without stacking questions. (3) Response to the objection: push back on the anticipated objection reaffirming the ask, without diluting it or conceding conditions. (4) Next step: translate the yes into a concrete action with owner and date.

Phase 3 Verification: review against the criterion and declare whether the prospect is ready to close or what still needs to be validated.

Firm rules: apply a single request per turn and leave implicit silence after the ask (do not fill with justifications). Never offer discounts, special conditions, or concessions to force the yes: the commitment is earned by value, not by pressure. Neutral and professional Spanish, no emojis.

Acceptance criterion: the ask is a single direct sentence that names the exact commitment and is not a battery of questions; uses decision language (we confirm, we reserve, we schedule) and not tentative language (what do you think, maybe); contains no pressure incentives; the response to the objection reaffirms the ask instead of withdrawing it; the next step has verifiable owner and date; the diagnosis declares close readiness. Edge case: if the commitment being asked for exceeds the interlocutor's authority, the ask must be oriented toward securing access to the real decision-maker, not toward forcing a yes that person cannot give.

prompts.title: Mutual action plan (MAP)
prompts.content:
Act as a senior B2B sales executive specialized in consultative selling (MEDDICC and mutual action plans), with practice in orchestrating complex buying processes through to signature. Co-build with me a Mutual Action Plan (MAP) to close a specific opportunity on a target date, aligning the client's buying process with a shared and verifiable plan rather than pushing the sale from my side. The MAP must give visibility into every step remaining until signature, assign owners on both sides, and protect the date by exposing the critical path and dependencies before they become blockers; the plan is agreed upon jointly with the internal champion.

Before drafting, ask me for any missing data: account and opportunity name, target signature date and the business event that motivates it, buying stages or steps already known from the client side, key actors by role and on both sides, and obstacles, risks, or dependencies already identified. Do not invent names, dates, or client steps; anything not confirmed goes marked as [ASSUMPTION].

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliver: (1) Close anchor: confirm the signature date and the business event that justifies it; if the anchor is weak or arbitrary, flag it and prioritize validating it. (2) Milestone inventory between today and the signature, grouped by workstream (value evaluation, technical validation, security, legal, budget approval, contracting, go-live). (3) Definition of each milestone: name, verifiable exit criterion (what evidence confirms it is done), owner on our side and on the client's side, planned date, and dependencies; a milestone without a client-side owner is a red flag. (4) Inverse timeline ordered from signature to today, with critical path and milestones with no slack flagged. (5) Risks and gaps with [ASSUMPTION] on all unconfirmed data, plus 3 to 5 qualification questions to close them with the champion. (6) Email draft to the champion proposing to agree on the MAP jointly, in a collaborative and non-pressuring tone.

Rules: treat the plan as a hypothesis to validate with the buyer, not as fact; do not promise internal client approval times that have not been provided; do not use invented prices or figures. Close with a MAP quality checklist.

prompts.title: Discount handling strategy
prompts.content: Act as a senior B2B sales negotiator specialized in margin protection, conditional concession exchange, and value-based negotiation (give-get and trade-not-cave school). A prospect is asking for a discount on my offer and the response decides whether the deal closes protecting margin or the perceived value erodes and a precedent is set that damages the future renewal. Before executing, restate in your own words what product or service I sell, the exact discount they are asking for, and what stage of the cycle I am in, and present your plan; wait for my confirmation. If you are missing key data (the offer and its core value proposition with the measurable result it delivers, the magnitude or type of discount requested, the prospect's stated reason, the cycle stage and commitment already reached, the alternatives or BATNA they hold, the real balance of power, the concessions I can ask for in return, and my non-negotiable floor), ask for them in a brief list before continuing and do not invent anything; mark as [ASSUMPTION] any inference. Work in four phases. Phase 1, interpret: classify the request (haggling tactic, real budget constraint, competitive comparison, authority test, or period close) and name the dominant risk of conceding without counterpart. Phase 2, anchor: draft the value re-anchor before any figure; the price is only discussed after reaffirming the measurable result the offer delivers, and never concede on the first request. Phase 3, structure the exchange: for each counter-offer require value equivalence (what the prospect delivers must economically compensate the discount), with decreasing and never free concessions, labeling each concession so its cost is perceived. Phase 4, define the limit: set the withdrawal signals and the no-deal alternative when the exchange is no longer profitable, maintaining the relationship intact when withdrawing. Deliver four blocks: 1) Diagnosis of what the request reveals and the concrete risk of conceding immediately. 2) Battery of three to five counter-offers in "if you... then I..." format, ordered from the one that most protects the position to the most flexible, with the value equivalence logic of each exchange. 3) Opening verbal script (3 to 5 sentences) to re-anchor in value, plus two responses to the most probable haggling objections. 4) Signals to distinguish tactical request from real blocker and the dignified withdrawal threshold. Cover edge cases: discount already promised by someone else, phantom authority, prospect with no real alternatives, early-stage request. Do not include invented price figures; express amounts as variables or [ASSUMPTION] and never promise free. Professional tone in neutral Spanish, no emojis. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Negotiate final contract terms
prompts.content:
Act as a senior B2B contract negotiator with fifteen years closing professional-services agreements, expert in clausing, concession exchange, and closing design. I am in the final conversation with a client: the proposal has already been accepted in principle and only clauses, timelines, and conditions remain to be resolved before signing. Your objective is to unlock the signature without eroding value or conceding terms that compromise execution, with every concession justified and reciprocal.

Produce a closing negotiation plan with these parts:
1. A map of each open point with four columns: the client's position and their reason, my desired position, my real limit (walk-away point), and the possible agreement zone that results from crossing them. If any point has no agreement zone, declare it and propose how to expand it using non-monetary levers.
2. A script of interchangeable concessions ordered from lowest to highest cost for my side; each concession is conditioned on an explicit counterpart (never deliver one without asking for something in return). Mark which are reversible and which are irreversible.
3. Anticipate the likely objection for each clause and respond with a reframe toward value and shared risk, not confrontation. Include a diagnostic question to verify the real interest behind the objection.
4. Define three closing scenarios (ideal, realistic, minimum acceptable) with the exact language to request the commitment to sign in each one, and the trigger that indicates when to move from one scenario to the next.
5. Identify the two or three non-negotiable clauses where walking away is preferable to conceding, with an elegant exit phrase that keeps the relationship open.
6. Close with an actionable next step: date, owner, and specific deliverable.

Rules: no figures or prices, only terms, conditions, and structure; mark every unprovided piece of data with [ASSUMPTION]; neutral and professional language. If any critical piece of data is missing (disputed clauses, my real limit, available levers, or target signature date), ask for it before drafting.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Avoid the end-of-month discount trap
prompts.content: Act as a senior sales executive and B2B negotiation coach, trained in Value Selling, interest-based negotiation (the Harvard Fisher & Ury model), and margin discipline, with experience closing under quota pressure without sacrificing price. I am facing a discount request that arrives just when there is pressure to close the month, and the risk is caving to a reactive discount that closes today but erodes margin, sets a low reference price for renewal, and trains the client to expect discounts. Before executing, restate in your own words what I sell and to whom, what stage the deal is at, what discount or concession is being requested and with what argument, what my margin floor is and under what conditions I can concede it, and what non-monetary value levers I have; present your plan and wait for my confirmation. If key data is missing (real probability of closing this month, who decides and who influences, the prospect's deadline, project impact figures), ask in a brief list and do not invent figures; mark every inference as [ASSUMPTION]. Work in five steps. One, diagnosis: classify the request as a real budget objection, a stalling tactic to extract a concession, or undemonstrated value, and support the reading with evidence or [ASSUMPTION]; name the signal that would change your reading. Two, value re-anchoring: draft a message that reframes the cost of not deciding and the quantifiable value of closing now, to move the conversation off the price axis. Three, matrix of interchangeable concessions: for each move within my margin floor define the exact counterpart you request in return (signature deadline, volume, multi-year, testimonial, upfront payment, scoped deliverable), and lead with non-monetary levers from {{PALANCAS_VALOR}} when touching price is not convenient; inviolable rule: no concession is given away and each is conditioned on a reciprocal yes. Four, joint closing plan: steps, owners, and dates agreed with the prospect up to signature, releasing the concession only once its counterpart is fulfilled. Five, three likely objections with a brief response script and the limit where you walk away or escalate. Close by confirming that nothing was invented, the margin floor was respected, and the tone is that of a partner, not a cornered seller.

prompts.title: Recover a stalled deal
prompts.content:
Act as a senior B2B sales strategist with fifteen years closing consultative sales cycles and recovering late-stage opportunities through block diagnosis and value re-anchoring. I have a deal that advanced to a late stage and went cold: the prospect stopped responding or keeps postponing the close without an explicit no. Every frozen deal blocks the forecast and wears out the seller with empty follow-ups. I want to reactivate it with a deliberate intervention or, if it is dead, extract an honest no that frees up the pipeline.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. If any key piece of data is missing (deal stage, last contact, decision-making parties, cooling signals, objective), ask me before continuing; do not invent history and mark everything not confirmed as [ASSUMPTION].

Deliver: (1) A root-cause diagnosis that classifies the block into one of four families: displaced priority, lack of decision-making power, undifferentiated value, process friction; name the dominant family and the secondary one if they coexist. (2) Three blocking hypotheses ordered by probability, each with the observable signal that confirms it and the one that rules it out, plus the risk of acting on the wrong hypothesis. (3) A reactivation sequence of three to five touches over 14 days combining at least two channels (email, call, message, shared value), with the day, channel, and specific objective of each touch, and a no-response rule indicating when to jump to the next touch or stop. (4) A value re-anchoring message ready to send (subject + body, under 120 words) backed by a recent event or change, with a contributory tone rather than a desperate follow-up; if no known event exists, offer two alternative hook templates. (5) An explicit exit criterion: signals to persist versus signals to accept the no, with a brief script to request the honest no without burning the relationship or the account for the future.

Do not use prices or offer anything for free; mark assumptions with [ASSUMPTION]; write in neutral and professional language, without emojis.

prompts.title: Draft a letter of intent or LOI
prompts.content:
Act as a business lawyer and senior commercial consultant, expert in drafting letters of intent (LOI) and term sheets that formalize preliminary agreements and rigorously separate what is legally binding from what is merely indicative.

I need a letter of intent (LOI) ready for legal review that captures what has already been negotiated between the parties, protects the trust earned, maintains the closing momentum, and makes it clear that this is a preliminary step, not the final contract. A good LOI aligns expectations in writing, enables due diligence and exclusivity, and reduces the risk that the transaction cools or that already-closed points are reopened.
