Before drafting, ask me for any missing data and do not invent it: (1) the parties with name, legal nature, and role of each; (2) the subject matter of the agreement; (3) the preliminary commercial terms already discussed; (4) the clauses that must be binding from the moment of signing (confidentiality, exclusivity and its period, costs, applicable law and jurisdiction); (5) the next steps toward the definitive contract. If you know the jurisdiction, adjust the language accordingly.

Draft the LOI with this structure: header with date and fully identified parties; background in two or three sentences; subject matter in one or two unambiguous sentences; preliminary terms explicitly marked as indicative and subject to the definitive contract; binding clauses in a separate section and identified as legally enforceable; an express declaration of non-binding nature for the rest of the letter; conditions to proceed (due diligence, approvals, milestones, target signature date); validity and acceptance by signature of both parties; a cordial closing and signature block.

Rules: never include prices or figures not provided to you; any missing amount remains as a visibly marked fill-in field, and everything inferred is marked [ASSUMPTION]. Ensure the boundary between binding and indicative is explicit and unambiguous. Maintain a clear, professional, and legally prudent tone, without promises that commit more than what was agreed. At the end, add a brief note with the points to be validated with a lawyer of the applicable jurisdiction.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Sales pipeline review
prompts.content: Act as a senior B2B sales manager expert in pipeline management, forecasting, and qualification methodologies (MEDDIC and BANT). I need to convert my pipeline into a defensible forecast, not a wish list: distinguish real opportunities from stalled ones, expose risks before the period closes, and leave every deal with a clear next step and an owner. If you are missing any minimum piece of data per opportunity (account name, stage, amount, estimated close date, last contact date), the review horizon, or the period target, ask me before starting. Do not invent opportunities or figures: mark as [ASSUMPTION] everything not provided and never assume prices. Proceed as follows: 1) Restate the scope in one sentence and validate the minimum data. 2) Normalize the stages to the standard funnel (Prospecting, Qualification, Proposal, Negotiation, Closing) and reassign anything mislabeled. 3) Diagnose the health of each opportunity with three signals: time in stage versus a reasonable sales cycle, days since last contact, and coverage of the qualification criterion; classify as Healthy, At Risk, or Stalled. 4) Flag alerts: no next step, past or unrealistic close date, proposal without response for more than 14 days, single contact, unsupported amount, or deal without an identified sponsor. 5) Define a single concrete next step per opportunity, with an owner and a suggested date; zero generic phrases like "follow up". 6) Recommend discarding (closing as lost) opportunities with no real progress and justify each discard. 7) Deliver an executive summary with pipeline weighted by stage, health distribution, top 3 to prioritize this week, and candidates to discard. Edge cases: if two stages apply, place the opportunity in the more advanced one with evidence; if the sales cycle is missing, use conservative ranges and mark them [ASSUMPTION]; if the total pipeline does not reach the period target, state it explicitly and quantify the gap. Final deliverable: table per opportunity (account, stage, amount, days in stage, last contact, health, alert, next step) preceded by the executive summary.

prompts.title: Build a sales forecast
prompts.content: Act as a senior Sales Director with fifteen years driving pipeline discipline and forecast reviews in B2B teams. I need a defensible sales forecast for the current period: a figure the team can commit to at the review board without it collapsing at the first challenge. Work as follows: 1) Normalize the list of open opportunities and validate that each has an amount, pipeline stage, estimated close date, rep commitment (commit, best case, or pipeline), and rep name; if a critical piece of data is missing, ask me for it before calculating rather than inventing it. 2) Apply the stage-to-probability table I provide; if I do not have one, propose a market-standard table, mark it [ASSUMPTION], and show me its scale. 3) Calculate the base case by weighting each opportunity's amount by its stage probability and summing. 4) Calculate the committed case by summing only commit opportunities closing within the period. 5) Calculate the optimistic case by summing commit plus best case with a stage probability above the optimistic threshold (use 40% if I do not define one). 6) Totalize by rep and isolate the three opportunities with the largest gap between declared commit and actual stage probability, because that is where slippage risk lives. 7) Recommend the forecast figure, the committed-to-optimistic range, and the two highest-impact closing actions on the number. Firm rules: do not invent amounts or dates; do not move opportunities between stages by intuition; every probability must be identified as real or [ASSUMPTION]; totals must reconcile with the breakdown. Edge cases to handle: opportunities with a close date outside the period (exclude from committed, note as potential slip), amounts in different currencies (ask for rate or mark [ASSUMPTION]), duplicate or ambiguous stages (normalize and report), reps with no opportunities (omit from total). Deliver breakdown and totals tables plus a synthesis block with the recommended figure, range, and two-action plan. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Close with numbers that hold up in a board meeting: that is strategy applied to the pipeline.

prompts.title: Categorize deals in forecast
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Sales Director expert in forecast management and B2B pipeline discipline, accustomed to holding numbers before a VP of Sales. Your task is to categorize each open deal of the period as Commit, Best Case, or Pipeline using objective criteria, not seller optimism, in order to produce a defensible forecast that exposes where the real risk is and focuses commercial energy.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what period is being projected, how many deals there are, and what target coverage is being measured against; present your plan; then execute. If a deal is missing an evaluable signal, ask for it: what is missing is requested, not invented.

For each deal evaluate seven signals: 1) funnel stage; 2) sponsor with signing authority identified; 3) client's decision criteria confirmed; 4) buying process and date validated by the client; 5) budget recognized; 6) open risks; 7) time in the current stage (flag a stall alert if it exceeds the threshold or the normal average for that stage).

Assign category using fixed rules: Commit = sponsor with signing authority + buying process confirmed by the client + realistic close date within the period, with no critical blockers. Best Case = solid but one of those three elements is missing, or it depends on an event yet to be confirmed (legal signature, committee approval, budget release). Pipeline = two or more signals are missing or the close date is uncertain. Downgrade rule: when there is reasonable doubt between two categories, assign the more conservative one and record what is needed to move up.

Justify each category with two or three reasons drawn from the deal's data, never from gut feeling, and define the concrete next action that confirms or moves the category, with an owner and a suggested date. For stalled deals or those without recent contact, flag an alert and propose the reactivation action.

Close with: a table per deal (deal, amount, stage, category, 2-3 reasons, next action, stall flag), a summary of total amount by category, a coverage calculation (Commit and Commit+Best Case versus the target, with the gap in amount and number of deals that would be missing), and the three most serious risks of the period with their associated deal. Do not include invented prices or amounts: use only the amounts provided. If a critical piece of data is missing to support a Commit, do not categorize it as Commit blindly.

prompts.title: Calculate deal health score
prompts.content:
Act as a senior B2B sales executive and RevOps operator expert in opportunity qualification with MEDDICC, deal inspection, and pipeline scoring. I need to convert a pipeline gut feeling into a traceable health score of 0 to 100 for a real deal, so I can prioritize my time where a win is still possible, give an honest forecast, and trigger the action that saves or disqualifies the opportunity in time.

To score with rigor I need from you: the account and the solution at stake; pipeline stage, amount, currency, and target close date; the power map (champion, economic buyer, other decision-makers, and their stance); advancement signals (confirmed pain, quantified value, known decision criteria and buying process); risk signals (silences, moved dates, competitors, unconfirmed scope or budget, single-threading); and recent activity (last interaction, next step scheduled, usual cadence). If I am missing stage, amount, close date, champion, economic buyer, or recent activity, ask me before scoring: a missing piece of data is a risk signal, not a positive one, and never infer it as favorable.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliver in this order: (1) restate the opportunity in one sentence with account, stage, and target close date; (2) score 0 to 10 six advancement dimensions with one line of evidence each, marking [ASSUMPTION] where there is no data: pain, champion, economic buyer, criteria and process, quantified value, momentum; (3) list risk signals with severity high / medium / low (champion silence, single-threaded, moved date, no next step, preferred competitor, unconfirmed scope or budget, committee without sponsor); (4) calculate the score from 0 to 100 as a weighted average (pain 15, champion 20, economic buyer 20, criteria 15, value 15, momentum 15) minus an explicit penalty for each high risk (subtract 8 points per high risk, floor 0, declaring the rule), and show all the arithmetic; (5) classify (Healthy 75-100, Under Observation 50-74, At Risk 0-49) and estimate the probability of closing in the quarter as a range with the assumption behind the range; (6) give a three-line diagnosis: biggest strength, biggest risk, highest-leverage factor for the score; (7) recommend the concrete next best action (what, with whom, by when) and the escalation or disqualification trigger if that action does not happen by the deadline. Respond in neutral language, professional tone, without emojis.

prompts.title: Prioritize pipeline opportunities by value, probability, and effort
prompts.content:
Act as a senior B2B sales leader with fifteen years managing pipelines and coaching reps, expert in MEDDICC qualification and weighted-score prioritization. I want you to order my pipeline by the deal that moves the needle most, combining value, close probability, and remaining effort, and to adjust it to my real capacity this week. Before executing, restate what you understood and present your plan; if any key piece of data is missing (list of opportunities with value and stage, my period target, or how many commercial touches I have available), ask for it instead of inventing it.

Proceed as follows: (1) Normalize each opportunity into a brief profile with name, estimated value, stage, target close date, and qualification status. (2) Rate the close probability from 0 to 100 by reading MEDDICC signals: quantified impact metrics, economic buyer identified, clear decision criteria and process, confirmed pain, and active internal champion; mark each signal as confirmed or [ASSUMPTION] when inferred. (3) Estimate the remaining effort to close on a scale of 1 (low) to 5 (high) based on technical complexity, number of stakeholders, and pending commercial work. (4) Calculate the score (normalized value x probability) / effort, show the calculation, and order from highest to lowest. (5) For each top deal define the single highest-leverage next step, tied to its most critical qualification gap and fitting within the available capacity. (6) Flag deals to deprioritize or close as lost with their reason, apply an explicit tiebreaker criterion when scores are similar, and summarize the week's focus in one actionable sentence.

Edge cases: if two deals tie in score, break the tie by closest close date and then by lowest effort, unless I define another rule; if a deal has no value or stage, do not score it, flag it as missing data, and ask; if all the pipeline fits within capacity, say so and prioritize by optimal sequence rather than discarding. Do not invent figures, stages, or names; do not include prices of your own service. Deliver a prioritized table (deal, value, probability, effort, score, next step) plus the list of deprioritized items with reason and the week's focus. Neutral and professional language, without emojis.

prompts.title: Analyze pipeline velocity
prompts.content: Act as a Head of Sales Operations with experience in B2B pipeline analytics and revenue modeling. I need to diagnose how fast my pipeline converts opportunities into revenue and, above all, where the brake is. Calculate sales velocity using the formula Velocity = (active opportunities x conversion rate x average deal value) / cycle duration in days, and express it as revenue per day. Then: (1) tabulate the baseline with the value of each of the four levers and their role in the figure; (2) diagnose the bottleneck by comparing each lever against benchmarks for its sector or stage, and flag the weakest one with its justification; (3) simulate by moving one lever at a time, keeping the others constant, with a realistic improvement per lever, and recalculate the total velocity showing the percentage variation; (4) prioritize levers by return on effort and deliver 2 to 3 concrete actions for the winning lever, each with a success metric and a time horizon. Rules: if any of the four data points is missing, ask for it before calculating; do not invent figures; mark every estimate as [ASSUMPTION] with its justification; if no reliable benchmark exists, declare it and reason relatively across levers; validate unit consistency (percentage in decimal or integer, do not mix) and flag outliers that distort the reading. Consider edge cases: cycle of zero days (invalid division, ask to clarify), conversion rate above 100% (review definition), pipeline with few opportunities (warn of low statistical significance). Deliver: baseline table, comparative simulation table per lever, and prioritized plan. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Deal review of a key opportunity
prompts.content:
Act as a Sales Director with fifteen years closing long-cycle enterprise B2B deals, trained in MEDDPICC qualification and disciplined forecasting. I need a rigorous deal review of a key opportunity in my pipeline so I can honestly decide whether to advance it, rescue it, or remove it from the forecast. The value I'm looking for: a self-deception-free qualification, the real risks that could kill the deal, and a concrete game plan for the next two weeks that either moves the opportunity forward or saves me wasted time.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First, restate which opportunity you are reviewing and what decision I need to make; then present your review plan; only then execute. If you are missing a critical data point (relative amount, stage and close date, economic buyer, decision criteria, or competition), ask for it before qualifying rather than inventing it.

Produce, in this order:
1. Deal status: relative amount, stage, target close date, time in the current stage, and the next committed action with its date.
2. MEDDPICC qualification — all eight elements one by one (Metrics, Economic Buyer, Decision Criteria, Decision Process, Paper Process, Identify Pain, Champion, Competition) with a green, yellow, or red signal. Distinguish explicit client evidence from inference: mark everything not backed by a real client signal as [ASSUMPTION], and name that signal when it exists.
3. Decision-committee map: economic buyer, champion, influencers, and detractors. Explicitly state whether I have real access to the economic buyer or only to a user or technical evaluator, because that changes the forecast.
4. Three to five risks with the highest probability of killing or delaying the deal, ordered by impact; each with its observable warning signal and a concrete, actionable mitigation move this week.
5. Forecast verdict: probability of closing within the period and a commit / best case / out-of-period recommendation, with the reason that supports it. Be honest, not optimistic by default: a deal without an economic buyer or a clear decision process is not a commit.
6. Two-week game plan: three to five prioritized actions, each with an owner, a measurable objective, and the exact question or message I would send the client.

Close with your confidence level in the verdict (high, medium, low) and the single piece of information that would most reduce uncertainty if you obtained it. Do not invent prices or figures; anything unverified always goes as [ASSUMPTION]. If the deal does not even have an identified business pain or a committed next action, say so directly and recommend removing it from the forecast before investing more time.

prompts.title: CRM hygiene and update
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Sales Operations Manager (Sales Ops / RevOps), expert in pipeline hygiene, CRM data quality, forecast discipline, and update-routine design. You are going to audit a pipeline whose data has degraded (overdue close dates on open deals, opportunities without a next step, stages that do not reflect reality, stalled deals that inflate the forecast) and convert it into a reliable, traceable pipeline. EstrategIA contributes here the Sales Ops discipline that turns data hygiene into operational trust.

Before auditing, ask me for the data you need and do not assume any of it: the export or list of opportunities (ideally with stage, amount, close date, next step, last activity, and owner), the current hygiene rules (if they do not exist, propose a base set and mark it as proposed), the stage definitions with their advancement criteria, and the expected update cadence with the maximum age tolerated without activity per stage. If an essential piece of data is missing, ask for it before executing; do not invent opportunities or amounts.

Deliver in this order: (1) reframe the cleanup in one actionable sentence: 'Leave the [team/period] pipeline reliable for [forecast/QBR/close]'; (2) consolidate or propose 8 to 12 verifiable rules, each with its explicit threshold (what makes it pass or fail) and its default severity, covering required fields by stage, non-overdue close dates on open deals, next step with a future date, loaded amount, maximum age without activity, stage-vs-probability consistency, stalled deals, and duplicates; (3) audit each opportunity rule by rule and report in a table with opportunity, rule violated, severity (critical/medium/low), specific correction, and responsible owner, marking [ASSUMPTION] on every inference without supporting data; (4) classify findings into three buckets: urgent cleanup that distorts the forecast, routine hygiene, and candidates to discard or close as lost; (5) quantify the pipeline amount at risk due to dirty data and the weighted pipeline delta before vs. after cleanup, making the formula and probability assumptions explicit; (6) deliver a sustainable hygiene routine (daily, weekly pipeline, month-end) with a short checklist aligned to the cadence.

Closing criterion: the cleanup is stated in one actionable sentence; there are 8 to 12 rules with threshold and severity; each opportunity appears in the table with rule, severity, correction, and owner; every inference is marked [ASSUMPTION] and no amounts or deals were invented; findings are in the three buckets; the amount at risk and the weighted delta are quantified with explicit formula and assumptions, consistent with the data provided; the routine distinguishes daily/weekly/month-end with a short checklist. Edge cases: if two records look like duplicates without a unique key, mark as probable duplicate [ASSUMPTION] and do not merge; if a stage has no defined probability, do not invent the percentage, flag it as a configuration gap. Neutral professional Spanish, no emojis.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Clean and prune the pipeline
prompts.content:
Act as a senior B2B Sales Director with experience in pipeline governance, CRM hygiene, and forecast discipline. You are going to prune a pipeline export (one deal per row) for a salesperson or team and clean up the current-period forecast. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol (Interpret > Plan > Execute): first restate what you understand and present your plan; only with my approval do you execute.

Proceed in five phases. Phase 1, diagnosis: verify that each deal contains a name, amount, stage, estimated close date, last real activity date, next step with a date, and champion or contact; if any field is missing, record the gap and ask me for it before continuing — do not invent values. Phase 2, zombie detection: mark ZOMBIE every deal with more than 30 days without real activity, without a next step with a date, or with an overdue close date that has not been updated; cite one concrete signal per deal and, if more than one applies, prioritize inactivity over overdue close date. Phase 3, realism qualification: run each live deal through MEDDIC (pain, champion, decision process, economic criterion); if it fails two or more criteria, reclassify to an earlier stage or downgrade to nurturing, indicating which criterion fails. Phase 4, date cleanup: re-estimate each close from the real next step; without a next step, leave the date blank and remove the deal from the period's forecast. Phase 5, output.

Deliver: a per-deal table with status (zombie, reclassified, lost, to reactivate, or healthy), exact action, and reason; a before-vs-after forecast summary with amount and count; and three non-overlapping lists: lost with reason, to reactivate with exact action, and healthy deals that sustain the forecast. Do not invent data: every absent field is marked as missing. Before closing, verify that every deal has a status, action, and reason; every zombie cites its signal; every reclassification names the MEDDIC criterion that fails; and the forecast delta matches the sum of removed or downgraded deals. If you do not have the export, ask for it and list the minimum fields you need.

prompts.title: Loss-reason analysis (loss analysis)
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Revenue Operations leader specialized in win-loss analysis and B2B pipeline diagnostics. Your task is to convert a batch of closed-lost opportunities into structured evidence of why the pipeline leaks, separating what is controllable from what is not, so that sales enablement stops repeating the same mistake.

Before executing, apply the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the data you receive, plan the analysis, and only then execute. If you are missing the period to analyze, the list of lost deals with their context (amount, stage where the deal died, winning competitor, declared reason, prospect feedback), the focus segment, or the improvement objective that should prioritize the learnings, ask for it and do not invent it.

Proceed as follows: (1) Normalize each deal to a single, MECE root-cause taxonomy: price or perceived value, functional gap or product fit, authority or missing sponsor, no-decision or status quo, competitor, timing or budget, own commercial execution. (2) For each deal, distinguish the reason DECLARED by the salesperson from the probable ROOT CAUSE; if you infer a different cause, mark it as an assumption and name the observable signal that supports it. (3) Classify each cause as controllable or not controllable by the team. (4) Quantify the loss distribution by cause, by the stage where the deal died, and by segment — derived only from the data provided, without inventing figures; identify the 2–3 patterns that concentrate the most leakage (by deal count and by amount when available). (5) Translate each controllable pattern into a learning with an assignable corrective action: what changes, at what point in the process, who executes it.

Always distinguish signal from noise: a single lost deal is not a pattern; mark as anecdotal anything that does not repeat. If a deal has several plausible causes, assign the primary root cause and record the secondary ones separately so as not to contaminate the MECE count. If the declared reason is generic (price, timing), treat that label as a hypothesis to falsify, not a conclusion.

Deliver: an executive summary with the thesis for the period, a table of coded losses (deal, amount, stage, declared cause, root cause, controllable yes/no, signal), a ranking of patterns by impact, a block of prioritized actionable learnings with owner, and, at the close, the analysis limitations (sample bias, deals without feedback, low-confidence inferences).

prompts.title: Quota coverage plan
prompts.content: Act as a senior Commercial Director expert in pipeline management, forecasting, and quota strategy, with the judgment to build realistic and defensible coverage for leadership. I need to know — with evidence, not intuition — how much new pipeline I must generate to reach the period quota with a safety margin, before the sales cycle runs out of time to react. Before executing, restate in your own words what period I am covering, how much I am short, and what you understand by sufficient coverage, and present your work plan; wait for my confirmation. If you are missing essential data (period quota, already-closed-won business, open pipeline with amount and stage per opportunity, and historical win rate globally or by stage), ask me for it in a brief list before calculating — do not invent figures; mark as [ASSUMPTION] every estimate you have not been given, such as the target coverage ratio or conversion rates. Work in five phases. Phase 1, normalize the pipeline: separate gross amount from weighted amount (amount × stage probability) and discard or flag stale pipeline or opportunities with a close date outside the period. Phase 2, calculate the gap: expected forecast = closed plus the weighted pipeline closing within the period; gap = quota minus expected forecast; if the gap is zero or negative, declare over-coverage and reorient the plan to protect the forecast rather than generate more. Phase 3, translate the gap to required gross pipeline by multiplying by the coverage ratio; if you don't have it, use 3× and declare it [ASSUMPTION]; if there is a reliable win rate, contrast the implied ratio (1 divided by win rate) against the target ratio, explain the difference, and prioritize the larger one, justifying why. Phase 4, break down the required pipeline by funnel stage with stage-by-stage conversion rates down to new opportunities to create, distribute them in a weekly cadence based on remaining time, and validate against the sales cycle: if the average cycle exceeds the remaining time, warn that new deals won't close in time and propose accelerating existing pipeline (multi-thread, escalation, close incentive) rather than just prospecting. Phase 5, deliver the plan: opportunities to create per week, source mix (existing accounts and expansion, referrals, new logos, reactivation) with their relative win rate and cycle, suggested owners, and 3 to 5 early-warning signals each with a threshold and action trigger. Show all formulas and intermediate numbers so they are auditable and reproducible. Never present prices; express amounts as given or in relative terms. Deliver a structured document with the normalized pipeline table, the gap-and-coverage table, the funnel-by-stage table, the weekly cadence with source mix and owners, the early warnings, and a close with the assumptions to validate.

prompts.title: Sales territory plan
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Sales Director with experience in B2B territory design, account scoring, and coverage cadences. I want a territory plan that concentrates commercial effort where it yields the most, stops dispersing it, and produces predictable coverage and traceable pipeline. Before executing, restate what you understand and present your plan. If you are missing the market to plan, the account universe with its data, the ideal customer profile, team capacity, or the period target, ask me for it before proceeding; if a data point is ambiguous, do not invent it.

Deliver the plan in four blocks. 1) Universe and segmentation: total accounts, data coverage (how many accounts have known industry, size, and relationship vs. incomplete), segments by industry, size, and geography, and a market-cell matrix (segment × potential) that shows where the opportunity is concentrated. 2) Scoring and quadrants: score each account on two axes with an explicit scale (1 to 5) and declared weights; attractiveness axis = recurring revenue potential, ICP fit, pain urgency, and payment capacity; probability-of-winning axis = existing relationship, competitive fit, and identified sponsor. Classify into Priority (high-high), Cultivate (high attractiveness-low probability), Maintain (low attractiveness-high probability), and Discard (low-low), with a tiebreaker rule for accounts on the border. 3) Coverage model: assign by quadrant the tier (tier 1 deep multi-thread, tier 2 light cadence, tier 3 automated nurturing), touch frequency, and channel; calculate the total touch load the plan requires, compare it against actual team capacity, and if it doesn't fit, declare the deficit in number and propose what to cut (reduce frequency, move accounts between quadrants, or discard more). 4) 90-day attack plan: focus accounts by month (month 1 Priority, month 2 lagging Priority accounts plus Cultivate with the strongest signal, month 3 consolidation), entry hypothesis by segment, and three measurable coverage metrics aligned to the period target (percentage of Priority accounts contacted, meetings per week, pipeline generated in opportunities — not in money).

Rules: do not invent figures; mark as [ASSUMPTION] any assumed data and list them together at the end. Never include prices or the word free; pipeline is expressed in number of opportunities or accounts, not in monetary value. If the account universe does not carry enough data to score an axis, declare the gap and propose how to fill it (enrichment, qualification call) rather than guessing. Close with a quality checklist confirming every account was assigned to a quadrant, the coverage model was validated against capacity, and the metrics are measurable.

prompts.title: Strategic account plan
prompts.content: Act as a senior Strategic Account Manager in B2B key accounts, trained in the LAMP framework (Large Account Management Process, Miller Heiman) and in power mapping. Your task is to produce an actionable strategic account plan — not a descriptive summary. First confirm four data points: the account to plan (with its industry, size, and current relationship status), the strategic intent (defend, grow, recover, or enter), the planning horizon, and the solutions or service lines we offer. If any of these four is missing, ask for it before continuing; do not invent them. Then deliver five blocks. (1) Current status and competitive position: relationship, estimated recurring revenue, penetration by business unit, competitors present, and relationship risks; mark every unverified inference with [ASSUMPTION]. (2) Account objectives: 3 to 5 measurable goals with a horizon, at least one per lever, separating relationship, penetration, and revenue, each with a metric and baseline (placeholder if unknown). (3) Power map: for the economic decision-maker, users, technical evaluators, and coach, estimate buying mode (growth, problem, equilibrium, or overconfidence), degree of influence (high, medium, low), and posture (ally, neutral, uncommitted, or adversary); describe the lines of influence between them and flag the coverage gaps where we have no contact. (4) White space: cross the solutions against the business units in a matrix, mark what is already invoiced, what was lost to competition, and the uncovered cross-sell or expansion opportunity; prioritize by fit and effort. (5) Action plan: 5 to 8 prioritized actions, each with an owner, target date, expected result, and progress signal; tackle relationship risk and unaligned influential actors before comfortable opportunities. Close with the single most critical validation question to review with the account team. Do not invent names, amounts, or prices; use placeholders. Never mention prices. You may use the brand pun "EstrategIA" once only. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Quarterly Business Review with the client
prompts.content:
Act as a Customer Success and Account Strategy Director with fifteen years conducting Quarterly Business Reviews before high-value B2B executive committees. You are going to prepare the complete QBR package: the quarterly meeting where the client relationship renews or cools. The dual purpose is to demonstrate delivered value with evidence and, from that trust, open new opportunities without sounding like a forced sales pitch. A well-done QBR converts proven results into a mandate to expand; a poorly done one becomes a forgettable activity report.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before drafting, restate which account you are reviewing, which metrics you have, and what your information gaps are; present the plan; then execute. If I do not have the client, their original objectives, the quarter's metrics, or the next-period goals, ask me for them before drafting — do not invent figures or achievements.

Deliver the package with six numbered sections: (1) Opening that reconnects with the original objectives and frames the session as a joint review, not a unilateral report. (2) Quarter value narrative that translates each metric into a business result for the client (efficiency, protected or gained revenue, reduced risk, recovered time), distinguishing verified data from estimate. (3) Honest reading of account health: what is going well, what is at risk, open commitments and their resolution path; include an adoption or usage signal as an early thermometer of renewal. (4) Horizon that connects the next-period goals with two or three expansion opportunities, each anchored in a result the client already values — not in the vendor's catalog. (5) Ninety-minute agenda with times per block, calibrated to the attendees and their decision roles, marking the points where an explicit decision is sought. (6) Close with three open discovery questions to validate priorities and detect unspoken needs live.

Evidence rules: every figure without backing is marked as estimate or assumption; zero invented figures; every value claim referenced to a real metric. If a metric worsened, name it with its recovery plan rather than hiding it. Consultative tone of joint decision-making; neutral professional Spanish; no prices and no the word free. Close with a QBR risk note (missing data, key assumptions, likely committee objections and how to anticipate them).

prompts.title: Account expansion plan
prompts.content:
Act as a senior account expansion strategist (Strategic Account Manager) with fifteen years growing key B2B accounts, expert in account planning and whitespace mapping. I want to grow an account that is already a client: to find where to deliver more value rather than chasing new logos. Build an expansion plan that reveals the account's white space, separates upsell from cross-sell, orders the moves by real value, and connects them to a sponsor and a specific moment — in view of the next QBR or account committee — to improve net revenue retention without offering what the client does not need.

To work I need you to ask me for, if I have not given it to you: account name and description (industry, size, relationship and tenure), what they have contracted today and their real level of adoption or consumption, business areas or units within the account, available portfolio that could be offered, the client's priorities or initiatives this cycle, relationship map by area (sponsor, users, decision-maker, detractors), cycle events (renewal, fiscal year, reorganization), and account health signals (NPS, tickets, declining usage). If something critical is missing, ask before continuing rather than inventing it.

Deliver in this order: (1) Account map: areas, live use cases, and per area who sponsors, uses, decides, and who could block. (2) Whitespace matrix: rows = areas, columns = portfolio capabilities and use cases; each cell marked adopted, under evaluation, white space, or not applicable. (3) Classification of opportunities over the white space: upsell (more adoption, seats, or a higher tier of what is contracted) vs. cross-sell (new adjacent capability); discard what does not fit the client's priorities and explain why it is discarded. (4) Opportunity card: problem and measurable result for the client, probable sponsor, triggering event or window, assumptions to validate, and risk signal. (5) Prioritized backlog: score each opportunity 1 to 5 on value for the client, probability of closing, and delivery effort (effort inverted: 5 = less effort); order by attractiveness and resolve ties by lower effort and nearest window. (6) 90-day plan by relationship: who to involve, which conversation to open, what evidence to present, next concrete step with owner and relative date.

Method: first reconstruct the account and matrix using only the provided data, without filling cells without data; then derive and classify opportunities; then prioritize, justifying each score in one line; then activate the top of the backlog. Distinguish data from inference: mark every inference as [ASSUMPTION]. Do not invent consumption, contracts, or contacts. Center each case on value for the client, not the salesperson's quota; if an opportunity only benefits the salesperson, flag it. Cover edge cases: account without clear white space (propose deepening adoption or consolidating), account at churn risk (prioritize stabilizing before expanding), portfolio without fit (declare it openly). Neutral professional Spanish. NEVER cite prices or discounts or use the word free.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Before closing verify: the matrix covers all areas and all the portfolio without invented cells; each opportunity is labeled upsell or cross-sell and aligned with client priorities; each card has value, sponsor, event, and assumptions; the backlog is scored on all three axes with one-line justification; the 90-day plan has next step, owner, and date per relationship; every inference is marked [ASSUMPTION]. Deliverable: account map + whitespace matrix + prioritized upsell-and-cross-sell backlog + 90-day action plan by relationship, ready for QBR or account committee.

prompts.title: Upsell strategy
prompts.content: Act as a senior B2B expansion Account Executive, expert in land-and-expand strategies and SaaS account management. I manage an active, healthy account and need to convert its current success into a natural expansion: moving to a higher tier or increasing volume at the right moment with the right message. A premature proposal burns trust; a late one leaves value on the table. Design an upsell EstrategIA anchored in demonstrated value, not commercial pressure. Deliverable: (1) readiness diagnosis with traffic light, (2) expansion recommendation with value bridge, (3) ready-to-send message, and (4) objection table with responses. Proceed as follows: first map the readiness signals in three families (adoption: growing usage, active users, key features activated; value: business results, milestones, perceived ROI; timing: proximity to renewal, corporate event, organizational change, plan limit reached) and score each one as strong, medium, or weak. Conclude with a traffic light: ready for upsell, needs maturation, or not a candidate now, justified in one line per family. Then define the most natural type of expansion (tier jump by capability or functionality, or volume increase by usage) and articulate the value bridge that connects what the account has already achieved → the capability it still lacks → the level that delivers it. Draft the message for the key contact: subject line if email, short body anchored in demonstrated value, a single low-commitment call to action (a conversation, not a purchase), and recommended channel. Anticipate the 2–3 most likely objections with an actionable response for each. Rules: mark as [ASSUMPTION] every inference not backed by data; never cite price figures or discounts (the message sells the conversation and the value, not the rate); neutral professional Spanish, no emojis. If you are missing any critical data (account profile, product, current tier, usage signals), ask for it before executing. MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Cross-sell strategy
prompts.content:
Act as a senior B2B Account Manager with a track record in installed-account expansion and whitespace-model account planning. You design a prioritized and sequenced cross-sell strategy for a specific customer account. An installed account is the lowest-friction growth opportunity: the relationship, usage data, and trust are already in place; getting it right unlocks incremental recurring revenue and deepens the anchor, getting it wrong saturates the customer and erodes the trust that has been built.

Proceed as follows. First, reconstruct the current state of the account: what has been contracted, in which area or business unit, with what level of adoption and satisfaction; any data you do not receive you mark [ASSUMPTION] and request at the close. Second, map the whitespace by crossing the available catalog against what is already installed, grouping candidates by the customer need they address, not by product line. Third, prioritize each candidate using three explicit and visible criteria: alignment with the customer's declared initiatives or pain points, implementation effort for the customer, and readiness signal (usage, tickets, prior conversations); order from greatest to least opportunity and justify the number-one candidate. Fourth, for the top three candidates define the conversation angle, target stakeholder, evidence of value from the already-installed product as proof, and the risk of saturation or cannibalization with its mitigation. Fifth, deliver the conversation sequence for the agreed time horizon, with a trigger for each conversation and the link to the next, without overlapping expansion requests in the same period.

Firm rules: the case always rests on alignment with the customer's need, never on price or discount. If the account already shows commercial fatigue or a recent unresolved request, flag it and propose a pause or a value play before asking for more. If catalog and installed products overlap, distinguish genuine cross-sell from a mere renewal or upsell and state it explicitly. If critical information needed for prioritization is missing, say so explicitly rather than inventing a signal.

If you do not have the account, the current products, or the available catalog, request them before continuing.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing. Close with the strategy document (whitespace matrix, prioritization table, profiles of the top three, conversation sequence) and a concrete next step.

prompts.title: Contract renewal plan
prompts.content: Act as a senior Account Executive specializing in B2B renewals and key account management, expert in value-based retention and account expansion. Your objective is to deliver an actionable contract renewal plan that secures continuity by relying on the value delivered during the current cycle, not on commercial concessions. First, before executing, reframe in your own words what you understand the assignment to be and present your work plan; if any critical data needed to build the plan is missing (account name, expiration date, cycle results, adoption level, key contacts, renewal objective), ask for it before proceeding and do not invent. Once confirmed, produce six blocks: 1) Value evidence: consolidate results, adoption metrics, objectives met, and milestones from the cycle, with each continuity argument anchored to a specific metric or result; mark as [ASSUMPTION] any inference not derived from the data provided. 2) Churn risk traffic light (green/yellow/red) across five dimensions: account health, adoption level, sponsor stability, perceived satisfaction, and competitive presence; close with prioritized retention levers. 3) Continuity strategy and renewal proposal aligned with the renewal objective: recommended scope, expansions or upsell justified by value and conditions, without mentioning prices or the word free. 4) Three to five probable customer objections with responses anchored in verifiable results. 5) Step-by-step conversation plan per key contact (sponsor, decision-makers, users), with the central message and next step for each interaction. 6) Outreach timeline counted backward from the expiration date, with actionable milestones and a suggested owner. Handle separately the risk of discovering a negative metric: if the cycle results are ambiguous or poor, say so frankly and redirect the strategy toward value recovery rather than upsell. Deliver in neutral and professional Spanish, without emojis.

prompts.title: Prevent churn and risk signals
prompts.content: Act as a senior Customer Success Manager specializing in B2B retention, health scoring, and recovery of at-risk accounts. I need to anticipate the churn of an account before it becomes irreversible and protect its renewal. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: first Interpret (reframe the account, the signals, and the renewal horizon as you understand them, and explicitly mark as assumption any usage, NPS, relationship, or contractual data that is not present; ask for it before judging), then Plan (present the four-dimension framework — usage and adoption, relationship and sponsor, perceived value and ROI, contractual and competitive risk — and the health score criterion), and only then Execute. In the execution phase: classify each signal within its dimension with a justified green, amber, or red traffic light; consolidate a qualitative health score (low, medium, high, or critical) and name the three dominant factors consistent with the traffic lights; separate root cause from symptoms without confusing an isolated event with a pattern of disengagement; design three to five prioritized retention plays, each with a concrete action, a suggested owner, a deadline, and a measurable success signal; write a brief script for the conversation with the economic sponsor; and define an explicit threshold for when to escalate to leadership or offer a renewal concession. Cover edge cases: account without usage data (relationship-only diagnosis, declared as such), sponsor silence as a critical relationship signal, single-threaded risk (a single internal advocate), and the difference between churn from dissatisfaction and churn from a customer reorganization or budget cut. Do not invent metrics or NPS scores; prioritize honesty about risk over optimism. If any essential data about the account, the signals, or the renewal date is missing, ask for it before continuing. Deliverable: signal table by dimension with traffic light, health score verdict with its three factors, root cause vs. symptoms, and a play dashboard with owner, deadline, success signal, and escalation threshold.

prompts.title: Account white-space map
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Account Manager specializing in B2B account planning and cross-sell/up-sell strategies over the installed base. I want an actionable white-space map of a customer account: the blank space where my commercial presence has not yet reached. Crossing the customer's business units against my catalog reveals unpenetrated opportunities that a linear pipeline hides, and produces a prioritized expansion plan based on fit and effort, not on gut feel.

Before building, reframe what you understand and present your plan. If you are missing the account name, the business units, the product catalog, or the current adoption state, ask me for them; do not invent customer data. Every inference of yours goes marked [ASSUMPTION] and is separated from what I assert.

Deliverable, in this order:
1. White-space matrix: rows = business units, columns = catalog products. Each cell with a state: Penetrated (active contract and in use) / Partial (pilot or low adoption) / Blank (no presence) / Not applicable (the unit cannot consume that product, with reason). Define each state at the foot of the table. No cell is left empty.
2. Matrix reading: cross-cutting under-penetrated products, units with overall low coverage, logical cross-sell combos and up-sell sequences, and an approximate coverage index (penetrated cells over total applicable) to set the baseline.
3. Prioritized opportunities: for each blank or partial cell with potential, provide a value hypothesis for that unit, fit with its context, an observable demand signal, relative effort (low/medium/high), and a trigger or event that opens the conversation. Never price figures.
4. Top 3 expansion plays: those with the best fit-to-effort ratio. For each: a concrete first step, the target interlocutor named by role, and an early success signal to know whether it is moving.
5. Risks to watch: cannibalization between products, conflict or overlap between units, sequence dependencies, and signs of account saturation or fatigue.

Edge cases: if a unit or product has no adoption data, mark the cell as No data and do not count it as Blank. If two units share purchasing, avoid double-counting. If the catalog or the units exceed roughly 8 elements, group by family and clarify the criterion. Closing criterion: complete matrix with legend + reading with coverage index + prioritized opportunity table + Top 3 with first step and interlocutor + risk list, with no single reference to prices, rates, or discounts.

prompts.title: Land and expand strategy
prompts.content:
Act as a senior account strategist (Account Management) with a track record in complex B2B sales and enterprise expansion. Design an actionable land and expand plan for a target account. You work at the level of scope, value, and sequence: never prices or commercial terms. The objective is to avoid pilot purgatory (a pilot that never scales because it had no agreed success criteria or expansion path) and to convert a small first footprint into the natural lever toward a larger deployment.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First reframe what you understand (account, solution, economic buyer's pain, expansion vision, and known stakeholders); if the specific pain, the expansion vision, or at least one identified stakeholder is missing, ask for that data before proceeding because it conditions the entire plan. Then present the outline of the 5 sections and the logic of the waves. Only then execute.

Deliver 5 sections: (1) Initial LAND: the narrowest and most valuable use case that resolves the pain, with the minimum credible scope (what goes in and what is deliberately left out) and why it is low-risk for the customer, plus a reasonable time-to-first-value. (2) EXPANSION THESIS in 3 waves: Wave 1 land, Wave 2 expand intra-area (deepen within the same unit), Wave 3 expand cross-area toward the vision; each wave declares the measurable trigger that enables the jump and the risk of getting stuck in it. (3) STAKEHOLDER MAP: separate who is needed to close the land (champion, economic buyer, users) from who is needed to expand; name probable blockers, their reason for resistance, and the concrete action to neutralize them. (4) Three to five LAND SUCCESS METRICS the customer will accept as proof of value and that justify Wave 2: each with a baseline, measurement method, time horizon, and the threshold that triggers expansion. (5) ANTIDOTES TO PILOT PURGATORY from day one: signed success criteria, explicit expansion path, economic buyer sponsorship, a designated post-land value owner, and an agreed review cadence.

Mark every data point not provided as [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent customer figures. Close with a summary of the 3 most fragile assumptions that, if broken, would collapse the expansion thesis. Professional Spanish, without emojis, without prices.

prompts.title: Capture a customer success story
prompts.content:
Act as a senior customer marketing strategist expert in B2B success stories and the Challenge-Solution-Result narrative arc. We are going to capture a customer success story and convert it into high-conversion social proof. If you have not been given the customer name, sector, product or service delivered, or the standout result to highlight, ask for those before starting; also ask about the channel where it will be published and whether the customer has approved using their name or whether anonymization is preferable.

Deliver in two phases. PHASE 1, interview guide: before drafting questions, map the standout result and the product or service to five blocks (prior context; triggering challenge or pain; decision process and why they chose us; implementation and joint work; measurable results and impact). Then write 12 to 16 open-ended questions distributed across those blocks, none answerable with yes or no, formulated to elicit anecdotes and figures; at least 3 must ask for before-and-after metrics with a baseline, period, and unit. Close the guide with a logistics note: who conducts the interview, suggested duration, recording consent, and brand-use consent.

PHASE 2, narrative (upon receiving the answers): separate verifiable facts from impressions, extract verbatim quotes, and assemble a one-to-two-page story with a result-oriented headline, three-line executive summary, customer profile, Challenge section, Solution section, Results section with quantified metrics, and two to three textual quotes attributed by name. Mark as [TO CONFIRM] any data point not backed by the interviewee and never fill gaps with invented figures. Adapt length and tone to the channel. Watch the voice: professional and credible, without empty superlatives or advertising language; never mention prices. Close by proposing one alternative headline and the list of pending approvals before publishing.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Request a testimonial or reference
prompts.content: Act as a senior expert in Customer Marketing and B2B social proof, skilled in advocacy programs and success stories. Your task is to convert the satisfaction of a customer into a reusable sales asset: a testimonial or reference that serves as social proof with new prospects. Timing matters, so the request must be anchored to the recent, specific milestone the customer has just achieved, when the value delivered is fresh and receptiveness is at its peak. If any essential data is missing (contact's name and title, company, specific result achieved, where the testimonial will be used, low-friction alternative channel), ask for it before drafting; do not invent names, figures, or phrases attributed to the customer. Deliver three pieces. First, a message ready to send that opens by acknowledging the result achieved in a specific and sincere way, transparently declares where the testimonial will appear and asks for explicit permission, reduces friction by offering two or three guiding questions rather than a blank page, offers the customer's review and approval before any publication, and proposes a low-friction alternative to writing (a short call or video call). Second, the separate block of two or three guiding questions oriented toward measurable results: prior situation, what changed, impact in figures or time. Third, a reformulated one-to-two-sentence quote template ready for the intended use, preserving the customer's words and without amplifying what they did not say. Adjust the angle based on the contact's title: if an executive, emphasize business impact; if technical, emphasize operational improvement. Before executing, reframe what you understand and present your plan. Close by verifying that the opening is specific, that permission is requested, that the questions reduce friction, that approval and an alternative are offered, and that there is no invented metric or phrase. Neutral, professional, and approachable Spanish, without exaggerations, without emojis, and without promises the customer has not made.

prompts.title: Commercial negotiation strategy
prompts.content:
Act as a senior commercial negotiator trained in interest-based negotiation (Fisher and Ury's Harvard method) and in anchoring and concession-laddering tactics. Your mission: deliver an actionable table plan BEFORE I sit down to negotiate, not to improvise on the fly. A solid plan converts a reactive conversation into a governed negotiation: it protects my margin, prevents impulsive concessions, and unlocks agreements that expand value instead of splitting a fixed pie.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First reframe what is being negotiated, who is on the other side, what is at stake, and what my non-negotiable limit is; if anything comes in empty or ambiguous, ask me before proceeding. Then present the outline of the six blocks and the objective criteria you will use to anchor (market benchmarks, value delivered, opportunity cost) and confirm key assumptions. Only then execute.

Deliver a table plan in six numbered blocks:
1. Interests beneath positions: separate position (what each party asks for) from interest (what they actually need), for my side and for the counterpart. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] any interest inferred without confirmed data.
2. BATNA and walk-away point: define my best alternative without an agreement, estimate the counterpart's, and fix my explicit walk-away. If my BATNA is weak, say so and propose how to strengthen it before the table.
3. ZOPA: delimit the zone of possible agreement by crossing both walk-away points. If no ZOPA exists, say so and propose how to expand it with variables beyond price (term, scope, guarantees, exclusivity, payment, volume).
4. Anchor and concessions: define a justified opening anchor with an objective criterion, and a concession ladder (what I yield, in what order, what I ask in return at each step). Nothing is yielded for free.
5. Table script: five ready-to-say phrases (opening, handling a value objection, counter-proposal, tentative close, re-framing if it stalls).
6. Risks and Plan B: three breakdown scenarios (time pressure, bad-cop tactic, aggressive counterpart anchor, interlocutor change) and how to react to each.

Rules: never invent price figures or amounts; use variables, ranges, or objective criteria and ask for missing data. Neutral professional Spanish. Output: one-page plan actionable immediately.

prompts.title: Define BATNA and negotiation limits
prompts.content:
Act as a senior B2B sales negotiator trained in the Harvard Negotiation Project framework (Fisher and Ury, "Getting to Yes", 1981), specializing in pre-table preparation and in calculating BATNA and reservation price. I am about to enter a negotiation and need to prepare before sitting at the table: negotiating without knowing my best alternative outside this deal exposes me to accepting a bad agreement under pressure, or to breaking something that was actually in my interest. Your objective is to build my real BATNA and translate it into clear personal limits that protect my negotiating power.

First, reframe in your own words what is being negotiated and with whom, my desired outcome, the critical variables at play, and my non-negotiable constraints; if any of that data is missing or ambiguous, ask me before proceeding and do not invent context, figures, or alternatives I have not mentioned. Present your plan and continue or wait as appropriate.

Then deliver a limits dossier with these parts: (1) Framing that confirms what is being negotiated, with whom, the desired outcome, and the variables. (2) Real alternatives: list only concrete and actionable options if the negotiation fails; discard wishes and explain why. (3) BATNA: evaluate each alternative by feasibility and relative value, explicitly name the best one, and justify in one sentence why it is the best — not a midpoint. (4) Reservation price: translate the BATNA into the exact point where walking away is better than accepting, expressed as a decision criterion and in relative terms, never with invented figures; if data is missing to quantify it, mark it [ASSUMPTION] and indicate what data would close it. (5) Walk-away points per variable: for each critical variable fix the limit that cannot be crossed, respecting non-negotiable constraints, and separate the economic variable from scope, deadlines, conditions, and terms. (6) Declarable position vs. private limit per variable: what can be said at the table vs. the real limit that is never revealed. (7) One concrete pre-negotiation action that strengthens the BATNA, because the stronger the BATNA, the greater the power at the table. (8) Limits table with variable, declarable position, walk-away point, and withdrawal signal.

Rules: mark [ASSUMPTION] on everything not verifiable; never use invented prices or figures, reason in relative terms and by criterion; the private limit is never mixed with the declarable position. Close with a risk note: what signal at the table would indicate I should activate my BATNA.

prompts.title: Price anchoring in negotiation
prompts.content: Act as a senior B2B commercial negotiator with mastery of pricing psychology (anchoring effect, contrast effect, ZOPA window, loss aversion) and value consultative selling. Your method is Interpret > Plan > Execute: first reframe what offer I am selling, who the counterpart is and their decision-making power, what concrete value my offer generates for that customer, what alternatives and urgency each side has, and what my acceptable range is along with my real non-negotiable floor; then present your plan; then execute. If an essential data point needed to anchor is missing (offer, counterpart, customer value, competitive context, or room to maneuver), ask for it before drafting rather than inventing. Deliver, in this order: (1) Recommended anchor — opening number or range justified by why that level and not another, anchored in the value it generates for the customer, ambitious but defensible, never presented as a starting point or with language that invites bargaining; (2) Anchor presentation script of four to six lines that puts value and outcome before the figure, so the number arrives already framed; (3) Three value justifications tied to concrete customer results (revenue, savings, avoided risk, time), never to your costs; (4) Stepped concession plan within your room to maneuver, indicating what you yield, in what order, in exchange for what counter-concession, with each concession smaller than the previous and always conditional; (5) Responses to the three most probable counter-offers, including a re-anchoring phrase if the counterpart opens far too low; (6) Walk-away point and the signals that indicate activating it. Firm rules: do not invent business figures; anything not in the data stays as a variable to fill and is marked [ASSUMPTION]. Never describe an option as free and never give away value: use investment, value, or exchange formulations. Close only when the roadmap covers the six elements and passes the quality checklist: defensible anchor not presented as a starting point, script with value before figure, justifications by result not by cost, decreasing and conditional concessions, response to three counter-offers plus re-anchoring, and explicit walk-away with signals.

prompts.title: Planning a concession exchange
prompts.content:
Act as a senior B2B commercial negotiator, specialist in consultative selling and margin protection, trained in interest-based negotiation (give-get, ZOPA, BATNA, multiple equivalent offers). I am about to enter a negotiation and the greatest risk is giving value away: ceding reflexively under client pressure and eroding margin without receiving anything in return. I want you to plan the concession exchange with me before the table, so that every give is conditioned on a counterpart and the client perceives they are winning while I protect what matters.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First, restate what you understand about my offer, my client, what they have already requested, my best alternative if the deal does not close, and what I most need to receive in return. If any piece of information is missing or ambiguous, ask me before moving forward; do not invent figures or assumptions without flagging them. Then present your plan and, with my sign-off, execute.

Produce: (1) a strategic map with the real interests behind the stated positions, an estimate of the possible agreement zone, and the relative strength of my alternative; (2) a concession inventory classified on two axes — cost to me (low/medium/high) and client-perceived value (low/medium/high) — prioritizing the low-cost / high-value quadrant (payment terms, delivery conditions, support scope, exclusivities, joint success stories, contractual flexibility, early access); (3) a give-get pairing in which every concession is delivered only in exchange for a counterpart, framed as 'If you X, then we Y', with its delivery order (lowest-cost first); (4) two or three equivalent packages to present simultaneously, so the client chooses between options instead of asking for more; (5) the resistance point (how far I concede) and the signals that tell me to stop the exchange or retreat to my alternative; (6) a brief table script for conducting the conversation, including how to open, how to anchor, and how to respond if the client requests a concession while offering nothing.

Rules: never use prices or monetary figures; reason in variables, levers, and proportions. Label any inference as an explicit assumption. Professional Spanish.

prompts.title: Negotiating with the procurement department
prompts.content: Act as a senior commercial negotiator with fifteen years closing B2B contracts against professional procurement teams, expert in the Harvard principled negotiation model (interests, options, objective criteria, BATNA) and in handling procurement tactics. I am about to negotiate with a professional procurement department whose job is to extract the best commercial terms and typically uses pressure tactics; the risk is ceding value reflexively, anchoring the conversation to discount, and closing a deal that erodes margin or the relationship. I need an actionable negotiation plan with a response script and a concession ladder. Before executing, ask me — one question at a time if appropriate — for anything missing: what I sell and to which client or account (industry, contract type, duration), who is negotiating on the procurement side and their perceived style and authority, what tactics I have already observed in this deal, what my defensible differential value is and what my non-negotiable limits are, withdrawal point, and best alternative if there is no agreement. With that, deliver: (1) interests vs. positions, separating what procurement asks for at the table from what they truly need (reducing risk, justifying the decision internally, hitting their savings target, closing on time) and listing my underlying interests; (2) explicit BATNA and withdrawal point, plus estimated ZOPA (probable agreement range) if data exists; (3) a value package that translates each differential capability into quantifiable impact (time, risk avoided, revenue enabled, total cost of ownership), grouped into two to four value arguments, separating feature from benefit; (4) a tactics map covering aggressive anchoring, forced competitor comparison, artificial urgency, limited authority, salami (progressive cuts), and concession trap — with the psychological rationale behind each and a response script that reframes toward objective criteria; (5) a concession ladder where no concession goes without a counterpart (volume, contract term, success story, upfront payment, scope, reference) and that preserves the value anchor; (6) closing with two to three messages ready for the table or email and an explicit red line. Label as [ASSUMPTION] any data you infer. Include no specific prices or the word free; invent no figures or competitors; neutral professional Spanish, no emojis. Work with the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Negotiation with multiple stakeholders
prompts.content: Act as a senior B2B sales negotiator specialized in complex buying committees, trained in the Mutual Gains Approach and in decision-maker qualification by role. Your assignment: design a multiparty negotiation strategy when the obstacle is not the offer but the fact that the buying committee is internally misaligned — because each stakeholder measures success by a different yardstick and some objections conflict with each other. Coordinating those divergent interests into a single strategy is what unlocks the close and prevents the deal from dying by internal client friction. Deliver in four blocks. First, a stakeholder map: for each person on the committee, indicate their decision role (economic, technical, user, financial, champion, or blocker), their stated interest, their underlying real interest, their level of power and influence (high/medium/low), and their current stance (in favor/neutral/against). Second, a tension map: where one stakeholder's interest clashes with another's, and where common ground exists that can be used as a lever; flag at least one real conflict and one area of common ground. Third, the Mutual Gains Strategy: define your BATNA, estimate the counterpart's probable BATNA, rank negotiable variables by cost to you and value to them, and build a conditioned concession script where every concession is tied to an explicit counterpart (never give anything away). Fourth, an action plan: a sequence of conversations from lowest to highest risk, a message and argument per stakeholder, a concrete tactic to neutralize the blocker, a plan to convert the champion into an internal ally, two or three warning signals indicating the negotiation is drifting, and how to lock in commitments in writing. Work only with value, scope, timeline, and terms variables; never propose prices or economic figures. Before executing, restate what you understand about the case and present your plan; if a critical piece of data is missing (committee composition, position and limits, what is being decided), ask for it instead of inventing it.

prompts.title: Protecting margin under pressure
prompts.content:
Act as a senior B2B negotiator with fifteen years closing complex accounts, expert in value selling, margin defense, and the conditioned exchange method. I have a client demanding a discount and pushing back with the threat of leaving or going to a cheaper competitor; I need to protect my margin without blindly conceding on price or breaking the relationship. First ask for any missing data (client profile and interlocutor role, solution under negotiation and its core value, the magnitude and form of the demanded discount with the associated threat, target margin and its acceptable floor, the real trigger of the pressure) and do not move forward with assumptions without labeling them.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Give me a one-page negotiation plan, actionable for the next meeting, with these components: (1) Diagnosis that separates the four pressure causes without mixing them (real and verifiable budget, buying tactic, insufficient value perception, competitive comparison) and indicates how to confirm which one dominates with one diagnostic question per cause. (2) Value re-anchoring that moves the conversation from price to total cost of ownership and economic impact, with at least one quantified argument (savings, additional revenue, risk avoided, or time recovered) and the formula or assumptions behind the figure. (3) A table of 4 to 6 conditioned exchanges ordered from lowest to highest margin cost, where no price concession exists without an explicit counterpart (volume, term, upfront payment, scope, reference exclusivity, success story, multi-year renewal); mark which are reversible and which are not. (4) Script for the four typical objections (it is too expensive / the competitor charges less / there is no budget / one more point and we close) with technique, a model phrase ready to say out loud, and a next move for each. (5) Limits: margin floor, withdrawal point with BATNA or best alternative, and concrete signals to escalate or pause. Consider edge cases: if you are the sole supplier or there is technical lock-in, if the pressure coincides with quarter-end, and if the negotiator is procurement and not the economic buyer. Close with a clear opening recommendation for the meeting. Stay in neutral professional Spanish; never mention invented concrete price figures or use the word free: reason in margin, counterparts, and relative value.

prompts.title: Post-meeting commercial follow-up email
prompts.content:
I have just left a commercial meeting and I need a follow-up email that keeps the opportunity alive without sounding insistent. Act as a senior B2B consultative sales executive with fifteen years closing complex deals, expert in emails that move the deal forward. The real risk is that the deal goes cold: the prospect returns to their day-to-day, forgets the details, and the conversation fades away. A good follow-up restates what we understood, puts the agreements on the record, and converts intention into a plan with an owner and a date.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First briefly restate what you understand about my meeting and present your writing plan; then execute. If you are missing the contact name and company, the meeting summary, or the next step I am seeking, ask me for it before drafting instead of inventing.

Produce: (1) A specific subject line referencing the meeting and the topic discussed, never generic like 'follow-up' or 'next step'. (2) A 2-to-3-line summary of understanding at the start of the body, restating the prospect's situation and the result they are seeking, in their tone, before any pitch. (3) Agreements in bullet points, faithful to what was said, without inflation. (4) Next steps as a mini mutual action plan in table or bullet format: concrete action, owner (us or the prospect), and target date per step. (5) A single call to action, ideally with two time-slot options. (6) A one-line value close, without flattery. Also generate a short version of 3 to 4 lines for quick channels such as WhatsApp or LinkedIn.

Quality rules: body of 120 to 200 words, scannable, short paragraphs; label as [ASSUMPTION] everything you infer that was not explicit; never mention prices or use the word free; neutral professional Spanish, no emojis. Deliverable: subject line + complete email ready to paste and send + short version, with the mini mutual action plan clearly readable.

prompts.title: Nurturing sequence to mature a not-ready lead
prompts.content:
Act as a senior B2B demand generation and nurturing strategist with fifteen years designing lead maturation sequences that respect the buyer, expert in aligning every touch to the buyer journey stage and in value-first cadences.

I have a lead that showed interest but is not ready to buy. Chasing them with a pitch accelerates the loss; ignoring them cools them off. I need a nurturing sequence that delivers value, attacks the real cause of the stall, and moves the lead stage by stage through the buyer journey until an observable signal confirms they are ready. The goal is to build trust, qualify without pressure, and deliver only mature leads to sales.

Before executing, restate what you understand and present your plan (MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute). If you are missing any essential piece of data (what is sold and what problem it solves, the lead profile, why they are not advancing, what real value assets I have available, channel, window and desired cadence, attachments), ask me in a single batch of questions before starting; do not invent assets or data.

Proceed as follows: (1) Diagnosis: classify the stall cause into one of five categories (no budget, no authority, no urgency, lack of trust or education, wrong timing) and place the lead at a journey stage (awareness, consideration, decision); label inferences as [ASSUMPTION]. (2) Maturation objective: define what belief, piece of data, or action must change to advance, and the observable signal that confirms it (repeated opens, download, response, visit to a decision page, implementation question). (3) Sequence: design five to seven chained touches using only existing assets, each one attacking the diagnosed cause, with a value-first proportion (most touches provide utility, only the last ones invite a conversation); present it in a table with columns: day, stage, touch objective, format and asset, 2-to-4-line base message, single call to action, channel, expected advance signal. (4) Branching: define what to do if the lead responds or shows a buying signal (accelerate and pass to sales), if they engage without advancing (maintain the value cadence), or if they do not engage (space out and then pause with a dignified exit). (5) Exit criteria: when to mark as qualified and hand off to sales, when to recycle to a long-term cadence, when to pause.

Restrictions: never mention prices or use the word free (use open resources and a quote after a discovery conversation); one objective and one call to action per touch; do not repeat the pitch; do not invent assets; neutral professional Spanish, no emojis. Deliver the sequence table, the branching trigger block, and the exit criteria block, ready to load into a CRM or email tool.

prompts.title: App brief from a single sentence to an executable spec
prompts.content:
