Act as a senior product engineer specialized in taking ideas to a functional MVP, with judgment for scoping and choosing stacks that are simple to deliver. I have an app idea condensed in a single sentence and I need to convert it into an executable spec before starting to code with a code AI. An ambiguous spec wastes iterations: the AI invents scope, chooses an incoherent stack, or produces features without validation criteria. I want a precise spec that closes scope, stack, data model, and verifiable criteria from the very first implementation prompt.

Ask me for the idea in one sentence if I have not provided it yet. If you are missing the target user, destination platform, critical constraints (time budget, team, mandatory integrations), or the data sensitivity level, ask me before assuming; label reasonable assumptions as [ASSUMPTION] and do not present anything invented as certain.

Proceed in four phases. Interpret: extract from the sentence the what (core function), the for whom (user), and the why (value). Scope: define the minimum MVP that delivers value and push everything else to an explicit, non-empty out-of-scope; a feature only enters the MVP if without it the app does not solve the pain. Design: choose the stack (frontend, backend, database, authentication, hosting), model the data, and map the screens as a coherent system; every stack choice must support an MVP feature. Verify: write Given-When-Then acceptance criteria per feature, cover obvious edge cases (empty inputs, no permissions, no connection, duplicate data), define a realistic minimum non-functional floor, and order the first three implementation steps starting with foundations (data and auth before UI).

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliver a spec document in numbered sections: (1) restated problem and target user without literally repeating the sentence; (2) MVP scope with a list of essentials and a separate list of out-of-scope items; (3) recommended stack with a one-line justification per choice; (4) data model with entities, key fields, and declared relationships; (5) main routes or screens with their purpose; (6) Given-When-Then acceptance criteria per feature, including edge cases; (7) minimum non-functional requirements (performance, security and data privacy, basic accessibility); (8) the first three implementation steps in order. Close with a short list of assumed decisions and trade-offs. The result must be pasteable as the first implementation prompt to a code AI.

prompts.title: PRD-lite for an AI-built MVP
prompts.content:
Act as a senior product manager specialized in AI-guided MVPs, with experience translating fuzzy problems into actionable contracts for code agents. Your task is to produce a PRD-lite: a one-page document that acts as a stable contract between the product vision and a code agent that will build the MVP. Without this contract the agent infers scope, over-builds, and diverts the MVP from the real problem; well delimited, the agent knows what to solve, for whom, and above all what NOT to do.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Phase 1 Interpret: restate the problem and target user in your own words, and list the jobs you detect. If the problem, user, or jobs arrive empty or ambiguous, ask for them before continuing; do not invent a domain.
Phase 2 Plan: present the section order and a traceability table where each job maps to a capability in the scope and, when applicable, to a non-goal. Wait for confirmation.
Phase 3 Execute: draft the complete PRD-lite with these numbered sections:
1. Problem: one sentence with the real pain and why it matters now, without a hidden solution.
2. Target user: who suffers it, in what context, and with what technical level; never 'everyone'.
3. Jobs-to-be-done: 3 to 5 jobs in the format 'when [situation], I want [motivation], so that [expected result]', ordered by priority.
4. MVP scope: minimum list of capabilities that cover the priority jobs; each one traces to a job, nothing orphaned.
5. Non-goals: what stays out of this version, each with its rationale, to stop the agent's scope creep.
6. Success criteria: 2 or 3 observable and measurable signals that the MVP works; no invented metrics, label as [ASSUMPTION] any unconfirmed threshold.
7. Assumptions and constraints: technical or business; label [ASSUMPTION] on everything not confirmed.
8. Interpretation risks for the agent: 2 or 3 points where the agent might over-build or misinterpret, with the decision that settles each ambiguity.

Edge cases: if jobs exceed 5, trim to the 5 of highest value and send the rest to non-goals with their rationale. If two jobs compete for priority, declare the tiebreaker criterion. If there are no known technical constraints, state it explicitly instead of omitting the section.

Close: the PRD-lite fits on one page, without filler, ready to paste as the initial context for the code agent. Do not mention prices.

prompts.title: Feature decomposition into codeable stories
prompts.content:
Act as a senior product engineer and tech lead who breaks features into backlogs executable by code agents, fluent in INVEST, Gherkin, and flow-oriented design. Your task is to transform a block-described feature into an ordered backlog of codeable user stories, ready for an AI to implement and verify each story separately.

I need from you as inputs: the feature description (what it does, for whom, why), the stack and technical constraints (language, framework, database, integrations, conventions), the target role that receives the value, and the maximum acceptable granularity per story. If any of these critical pieces of data are missing, ask me for them before continuing instead of inventing them.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Proceed as follows:
1. Framing. Restate the feature in a value sentence (as [role] I want [capability] so that [benefit]). List assumptions, each labeled [ASSUMPTION]. Declare the scope boundaries: what is in and what is explicitly out. Block if a critical piece of data is missing.
2. Cutting. Trace the end-to-end flow and derive stories from the flow steps and business rules, never from technical layers (no 'backend' vs. 'frontend' stories). Validate each story against the 6 INVEST criteria: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small (fits within the agreed granularity), Testable. Merge trivial ones; split anything that does not fit.
3. Sequencing. Order by dependencies, mark them explicitly (Hn depends on Hm), verify there are no cycles, and assign a relative size S/M.
4. Specification. For each story deliver: id, title, value narrative, acceptance criteria in Gherkin (happy path + at least one edge case or error, in Given/When/Then format), implementation notes (probable modules/files and data contracts per the stack), and a definition of ready that the AI can verify objectively. Record undefined rules as open questions, without inventing requirements.

Close with a summary table (id, title, depends-on, size S/M) and flag the first recommended story with one line justifying why to start there. If you detect a story that still does not fit within the granularity despite cutting, declare it and propose how to subdivide it.

prompts.title: Definition of Ready and Done for an AI session
prompts.content: Act as a senior software engineer expert in task specification and human-agent collaboration, with mastery of verifiable acceptance criteria. Before an AI agent writes code, rework originates in two gaps: it starts without sufficient context, or it declares done something that does not comply. Your job is to convert those two moments into verifiable contracts. Produce three deliverables: (1) a Definition of Ready (DoR) with verifiable preconditions for starting the task: objective expressed as an observable and measurable output, repo context and relevant files loaded, dependencies/permissions/credentials available, acceptance criteria agreed upon, fixtures or test data identified, and scope and out-of-scope delimited; (2) a Definition of Done (DoD) with objective closing conditions: functionality meets the acceptance criteria, tests passing, existing suite intact (no-regression), code aligned to the repo style, minimal docs and comments updated, no TODOs or loose ends, atomic changes ready for commit with a proposed message; (3) a start verdict that crosses the DoR against the real state and rules Ready to start yes or no, listing blockers and their resolution action. Rules: draft each item as an objectively verifiable statement, never an opinion-based one (not 'understand the objective' but 'objective expressed as an observable output'). Mark each item as met, pending, or blocking. Distinguish blocking (prevents starting or closing) from pending (can progress in parallel). If you are missing any essential piece of data (objective, stack, repo, criteria, or testing strategy), ask me in a single batch before drafting; do not invent preconditions. MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate the task and the state you understand and present your plan; then execute. Deliver the two separate checklists and the final verdict.

prompts.title: Justified technology stack selection
prompts.content:
Act as a senior software architect who has chosen and operated multiple stacks in production under team, timeline, and cost constraints, and who decides by evidence and context fit rather than trend. I want to choose the technology stack for my project and be able to defend each choice before my team and stakeholders, because a stack poorly fitted to the constraints is paid for in time, operational cost, and rewrites. A justified selection with a tradeoffs matrix turns an opinionated decision into a traceable one: it aligns the team on the same criteria, documents in writing which tradeoff was accepted and why, and unblocks the start of development, the foundational ADR, and effort estimation.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before executing, rephrase in your own words the project, key requirements, and constraints; derive the dominant quality attributes; and present your plan. If a piece of data is missing that would change the decision (target scale, operational budget, team skills, timeline, dependencies, or compliance), ask for it before moving forward rather than silently assuming.

Deliverable, in this order:
1. Verifiable framing: project and requirements rephrased, dominant quality attributes prioritized (the 1 to 3 that govern everything), and constraints treated as non-negotiable limits. List the missing data that blocks the decision.
2. Weighted criteria: define the decision criteria and assign each a relative weight summing to 100 percent; document each weight and, if you proposed it, mark it as an assumption.
3. For each applicable layer (language, backend framework, frontend if applicable, database and data model, messaging or queues if applicable, hosting and infrastructure, authentication, observability, CI/CD) propose 2 to 3 real candidates and build the matrix: rows equal candidates, columns equal weighted criteria, cell equals score 1 to 5 with a verifiable supporting phrase, plus the weighted sum per candidate. Consider total cost of ownership: team learning curve, ecosystem and hiring, maturity and long-term support, and exit cost or lock-in.
4. Context-prioritized recommendation per layer: primary option, backup alternative, and conservative bet if risk is high. Explain why the primary wins given the constraints and explicitly name the tradeoff being accepted.
5. Full-stack coherence: verify that the chosen layers work well together (interoperability, a single language where it makes sense, reasonable total operational complexity) and flag any friction between layers.
6. Validation plan: the minimum spike or proof of concept that confirms or refutes the riskiest choice before committing to it, with an explicit success criterion; and the objective signals (metrics, thresholds) that would force a reconsideration of the stack.
7. Close: one-line summary per layer and list of residual risks with their mitigations.

Rules: never fabricate benchmarks or figures; if you cite a data point, make it verifiable or mark it as an assumption. Do not recommend based on popularity or familiarity. Distinguish hard constraint (non-negotiable) from preference (negotiable). The deliverable must be ready to underpin a foundational ADR.

prompts.title: Routes and pages map before coding
prompts.content:
Act as a senior information architect and frontend expert, specializing in sitemap design and routing, with UX judgment for states and navigation flows. I need a navigation contract for my product before generating screens with vibe coding: a single source of truth that all subsequent prompts can cite, so that screens don't invent their own structure, routes don't collide, and error and permission states don't go uncovered.

First ask me — if I haven't provided them — for the following minimum data: product name and one-line description; framework and routing convention (e.g., Next.js App Router, React Router v6, SvelteKit, Vue Router, Remix, Astro); user roles and their access level; main features or flows; and the authentication, authorization, and redirect rules you know about. If any are missing, ask before assuming; if you decide to assume something to avoid being blocked, mark it with [ASSUMPTION] and record it as an open decision.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. First rephrase in two or three lines what you understood about the product, the roles, and the framework. Then present a lightweight plan: estimated page count and the proposed hierarchy tree (public, authenticated, administrative), and wait for validation before expanding the detail. Only then deliver the complete contract.

The complete contract must include, in this order: 1) Page inventory, each view with its purpose in one phrase and its hierarchy, derived from the features and roles. 2) Routes table, with the canonical route for each page per the exact framework convention, including dynamic routes with parameters and nested or shared-layout routes. 3) Navigation states per relevant route: loading, empty, error, no-permission, and success. 4) Guards and redirects: what happens when an unauthenticated user enters a protected route, what the default destination is after login per role, and what the 404 route and behavior are. 5) Key page transitions and deep links that must resolve with direct shareable access (which parameters travel in the URL and which don't). 6) Open decisions, listed as actionable questions.

Acceptance criteria: each feature maps to at least one page and no page lacks a purpose; every route is canonical, collision-free, and respects the framework's parameter and nesting syntax; each navigable route declares its five states; each role has a defined default destination after login and their allowed and blocked routes; a 404 route and redirect behavior for unauthorized access exist; shareable deep links are explicitly marked; assumptions carry [ASSUMPTION] and open decisions are actionable questions. Final deliverable: routes table plus hierarchical tree in plain text plus list of open decisions, ready to serve as a citable source of truth for screen-generation prompts. Do not include implementation code: this is a navigation contract, not the app.

prompts.title: Conceptual data model from requirements
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data architect specializing in conceptual modeling and domain-driven design (DDD), skilled in entity-relationship notation. I want to translate the functional description of my app into a conceptual data model before writing code or defining tables, so I don't carry misunderstood business decisions into the physical schema.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Rephrase what you understand and present your plan before executing.

First rephrase the purpose of the app and the actors, and declare the model's scope: which entities are in and which are out. Then present a preliminary list of candidate entities and relationships for me to confirm before going into detail.

When modeling: 1) extract the domain language by separating nouns as entity candidates from verbs as relationship candidates; 2) retain as real entities only those with their own identity and lifecycle, and justify every dismissal of something that is really an attribute of another entity; 3) for each entity define the key attributes and a natural identifier (not a technical one); 4) establish relationships with cardinality (1:1, 1:N, N:M) and optionality on both ends; 5) distinguish strong entities from weak or associative ones, and resolve every N:M with an intermediate entity named in domain language; 6) mark every assumption with [ASSUMPTION] and list ambiguities as business questions.

Stay at the conceptual level: no physical data types, engine, or technical keys. If I'm missing any essential data (functional description, domain, actors, business rules, or level of detail), ask me before moving forward.

Deliverable: entity catalog with attributes and natural identifier, relationship list or matrix with cardinality and optionality, textual description of the entity-relationship diagram, and a final block of assumptions and open questions.

prompts.title: API-first contract (API-first)
prompts.content:
Act as a senior API Architect, specializing in REST/OpenAPI design and contract governance, with a focus on developer experience and evolutionary compatibility. We are going to define the contract for an API BEFORE implementing anything, following the API-first approach: the contract is the artifact agreed on first and becomes the single source of truth governing code, tests, and documentation downstream. A closed contract unlocks parallel work: backend implements, frontend mocks, QA writes tests, and third parties integrate. Before executing, ask me for anything missing: the API name or domain, resources and relationships, who consumes the contract and their needs, target stack and protocol, and mandatory constraints (auth, versioning, SLAs, compliance). If any data is ambiguous, ask about it; do not invent business rules: mark any assumption as [ASSUMPTION].

Deliverable: a valid OpenAPI 3.1 file in YAML plus a human-readable Markdown guide and an approval checklist. Proceed in five phases. Phase 1 (Domain modeling): inventory resources, relationships, and operations; model resources as plural nouns; define the REST route hierarchy and naming convention (kebab-case paths, camelCase JSON fields). Phase 2 (Per-endpoint specification): for each endpoint declare method, route, path/query parameters, headers, request body schema and response schema, with types, formats, required vs. optional, and real examples for each consumer. Phase 3 (Error and status contract): catalog status codes per endpoint (success 200/201/202/204; client 400/401/403/404/409/422; rate limit 429; server 500/503) with a single error schema (code, message, details, traceId). Phase 4 (Cross-cutting policies): auth/authz, pagination, filtering and sorting, idempotency on writes (Idempotency-Key), rate limiting with headers, and versioning (URL or header) with an explicit rule for compatible vs. breaking changes. Phase 5 (Assembly and verification): syntactically valid OpenAPI 3.1 + per-endpoint examples + approval checklist signed by the parties.

Edge cases to cover: empty responses and pagination with zero results; uniqueness collisions (409); semantic validation that passes the type but violates business logic (422); safe vs. unsafe retries; partial payloads (PATCH) vs. full replacement (PUT); sensitive fields that must never travel in responses; field deprecation with Deprecation or Sunset header. Tradeoffs to justify when applicable: URL versioning (cacheability, clarity) vs. header versioning (stable URLs); offset pagination (simple, drifts with volatile data) vs. cursor pagination (stable, no jumping to page N); granular errors vs. bounded catalog. Closing criterion: every endpoint declares method, route, parameters, request, response, and at least one success code and one error code; single and consistent error schema; uniform naming; HTTP codes with correct semantics (201 on creation, 204 without body, 409 on conflict, 422 on validation); critical writes with idempotency and listings with pagination/filtering/sorting; explicit versioning; valid OpenAPI 3.1 with examples; assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION] and zero invented business rules.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Rephrase what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Non-goals and out-of-scope for the MVP
prompts.content:
Act as a senior product engineer expert at delimiting MVP scope and writing scope guards for coding agents. I am about to start vibe coding and I need a scope document that shields the MVP against scope creep BEFORE generating a single line: the real risk is not what I forget to ask for, but what the agent adds on its own (complex authentication, admin panels, optimizations, integrations, edge cases) that inflates the MVP and delays the first usable version.

First rephrase in your own words the product, the sole primary user, and the single end-to-end core action; if any are missing or ambiguous, ask before continuing — don't assume. Then present your plan in one sentence and proceed.

Deliver a markdown document with these sections: (1) MVP Objectives: 3 to 5 user-observable capabilities, each traceable to the core action. (2) Non-goals: 6 to 12 exclusions grouped into five categories (deferred functionality, premature technical perfection, premature scale and performance, external integrations, edge cases and rare states); each non-goal carries what is excluded, why it is deferred, and the concrete signal that reopens it — making it a 'not yet' and not a 'never'. (3) Agent guards: 5 to 8 imperative and verifiable rules, pasteable as-is into the system prompt (e.g.: do not add social login; do not create tables outside those listed; if a task requires touching something out of scope, stop and ask). (4) Gray areas: 3 to 5 decisions that are not clearly in or out and require my explicit confirmation before coding. (5) Scope Definition of Done: one line declaring when the document is complete and approved.

Rules: define non-goals by contrast with what IS included, never in the abstract. Do not include prices or monetary amounts. Mark any inference of yours as [ASSUMPTION]. If a guard is not checkable by the agent without interpreting, rewrite it until it is.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Rephrase what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Early technical risk inventory
prompts.content:
Act as a senior software architect specializing in early technical validation and spike design, with experience retiring architecture risks before the first structural commit. I am in the specification and planning phase of a product and have not yet committed to an architecture; I want to anticipate the highest-impact technical uncertainties before writing structural code, so I don't discover late an assumption that forces a rewrite of the foundations. I need a prioritized inventory of technical risks with a spike-based mitigation plan.

Proceed as follows: (1) Rephrase in one sentence what is being built and for whom, and which constraints you take as given. (2) Extract real technical uncertainties from the product grouped into six categories: integrations and external dependencies, data and domain model, performance and scale, security and compliance, operational costs, and stack or library maturity. (3) For each risk issue a card with id, assumption that could fail, observable signal of materialization, probability (high/medium/low), architecture impact (high/medium/low), and resulting priority. (4) Order risks in a probability x impact matrix and mark the architecture bets to validate first. (5) For each high-priority risk design a spike with the question to answer, minimum experiment, effort in time slots (hours/days, never monetary costs), and a falsifiable exit criterion defining whether the risk is retired, mitigated, or confirmed. (6) Close with the recommended validation sequence and the list of architecture decisions to defer until evidence is available, each justified by the uncertainty blocking it.

Rules: name only concrete risks from the product, not generic textbook ones; each risk must be able to fail in an observable way; no risk is left without probability and impact; exit criteria must be falsifiable; label every assumption of yours with [ASSUMPTION]. If you lack the product idea, its constraints, or the tentative stack, ask before continuing and do not invent data.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Rephrase what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Greenfield project scaffold with AI
prompts.content:
Act as a senior platform engineer specializing in bootstrapping and developer experience, with idiomatic judgment per ecosystem. I need the complete and executable scaffold of a greenfield project: the first hour sets everything else, so the repo must be clone-and-run from the first commit, pass lint, build, and test empty before the first feature, and leave a readable map for whoever arrives later.

Before generating anything, rephrase what you understood and present your plan. If you weren't given the language and framework, the project type, the package manager, or the runtime version, ask me for them: don't assume a default stack, because a wrong choice costs hours of rework.

Deliver in a single block copyable to an empty folder: (1) complete folder tree in text, with a one-line comment per folder explaining its responsibility; (2) each configuration file with real and commented content: dependency manifest pinned to exact version with runtime separated from development, linter, formatter, type configuration if the stack uses it, example environment variables file with sample keys without real secrets, and version-control ignore covering artifacts, dependencies, and environment; (3) task scripts install, dev, build, test, lint, and format with the exact package manager command; (4) minimal README with prerequisites, installation, and startup; (5) the ordered sequence of terminal commands to materialize everything from scratch.

Pin exact versions, don't include unused dependencies, justify in one line each non-obvious dependency, and mark with [ASSUMPTION] every decision you made on my behalf so I can confirm it. Add a minimal .gitignore and .editorconfig, a startup health note (which command confirms the repo compiles and tests empty), and if applicable, the runtime version pin in a file (e.g., the one read by the version manager). Close by reviewing against a quality checklist before calling it done.

prompts.title: Monorepo vs. polyrepo decision and setup
prompts.content: Act as a senior platform architect who has set up and migrated repository structures (monorepo with pnpm/Turborepo/Nx and polyrepo with published packages) in product teams. I am about to start a project and the first structural decision conditions speed, CI, ownership, and cost of change for years: monorepo (one repository with workspaces and an internal dependency graph) or polyrepo (one repository per service or package with versioning and publishing between them). Choosing wrong forces a costly migration later. First ask me for the project name and purpose, how many apps and services there will be and which ones, what code is shared between them, whether deployments are coupled or independent, the team size and maturity with its ownership model, the language and package or workspace manager, and any CI, permissions, compliance, or code ownership constraints. If any critical data is missing or ambiguous, ask before deciding; don't silently assume. Then: (1) apply a weighted criteria matrix with shared code coupling, release cadence and independence, cross-cutting change atomicity, tooling and CI overhead, governance and ownership, and scale and build times, assigning each criterion a weight and a per-option score; (2) recommend monorepo or polyrepo deriving the decision from the matrix, not from preference, and write out the tradeoffs we accept and at least one trigger condition that would invalidate the decision; (3) mark every assumption with [ASSUMPTION]; (4) generate scaffolding coherent with the decision: complete directory tree, workspace manager configuration (pnpm-workspace.yaml, turbo.json, or nx.json for monorepo; semantic versioning convention plus a published shared package and its release flow for polyrepo), an example shared types or utilities package with its manifest, root-level build, test, and lint scripts, runtime and manager version management, and an aligned CI pipeline skeleton (one pipeline with affected-only filter and build cache for monorepo; per-repo pipelines with release trigger for polyrepo); (5) deliver exact copyable commands to create everything from scratch, idempotent when possible, and a future bidirectional migration note (mono to poly and poly to mono) preserving history with git subtree or filter-repo without rewriting everything. Cover edge cases: a single service with no shared code (favors simplicity), teams with compliance requiring per-repo permission isolation, and polyglot stacks where the workspace manager doesn't cover all languages. Deliver a document with matrix and recommendation, directory tree, workspace or versioning configs plus the example shared package, root scripts and CI skeleton, copyable command block, and bidirectional migration note. Neutral and professional English, no emojis. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Rephrase what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Reproducible local environment setup
prompts.content:
Act as a senior platform engineer specializing in developer experience and reproducible environments (Docker, devcontainers, startup scripting). Your mission: ensure that anyone, without the author's context, can go from cloning the repository to the application running in minutes by following a single README. Today the project starts up with undocumented manual steps and configuration that lives only on the author's machine; that slows onboarding, breaks reproducibility, and multiplies the cost of every new joiner. This is EstrategIA applied to technical startup.

Deliverable, everything ready to commit, delivering each file with its exact path and full content:
1. Devcontainer: Dockerfile or base image with pinned runtime version and system dependencies (no 'latest'), plus .devcontainer/devcontainer.json with forwardPorts consistent with the services and minimal useful editor extensions.
2. Variables: .env.example with each variable documented (purpose, example value, required yes/no), safe placeholders without real secrets, and the .gitignore line that excludes the real .env.
3. Idempotent startup scripts (setup, dev, test) that install dependencies, validate required variables and fail with an actionable message if missing, start dependent services, and leave the app running; a second execution does not break or duplicate state.
4. Startup README with numbered steps (clone, copy .env, open in devcontainer, run startup, verify it loads) and a target first-startup time.

Close with: fallback matrix without Docker (native installation), troubleshooting table for the 3-5 most likely failures (busy port, service without healthcheck, missing variable, divergent runtime version), and a verifiable final 'app running' check.

If any stack, package manager, services, or variables data is missing, first inspect the repository; mark as [ASSUMPTION] everything you infer and ask about what you cannot verify before generating files.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Rephrase what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Agent context file (CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md)
prompts.content:
Act as a senior platform engineer specializing in coding agents and developer experience, with the ability to distill a repository into minimal operational instructions. Your mission is to produce the context file that a coding agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, or other) reads at startup to operate with judgment from the very first turn, without repeating basic questions, guessing commands, or breaking conventions.

Proceed in four phases and apply the MetodologIA Protocol before drafting: Interpret what you understand, plan and present the plan, and only then execute.

Phase 1 - Inspection: read the repository's real manifests and configuration files (package.json, pyproject.toml, requirements.txt, Cargo.toml, go.mod, Makefile, Taskfile, README, Dockerfile, and the CI configuration in .github or equivalent). Derive from these the stack, versions, and true commands. Mark each command as verified or pending based on whether you confirmed it in a manifest.

Phase 2 - Gap resolution: anything not in the repository and not inferable with evidence, ask for specifically. Never invent commands, versions, paths, or conventions. When you reasonably assume something to avoid being blocked, mark it with [ASSUMPTION] and make explicit how to confirm it.

Phase 3 - Drafting: write the file in Markdown, in the imperative, actionable and concise. Link the README rather than duplicating it. Include these sections: 1) Project purpose in a single line. 2) Stack and versions verified against manifests. 3) Essential commands (install, run, test, lint, build, typecheck if applicable), each copyable, executable, and confirmed — not assumed. 4) Relevant directory map with one line of purpose per folder. 5) Code and commit message conventions. 6) Branch and Pull Request flow, including merge gates. 7) Explicit limits and prohibitions (secrets, generated files, migrations, protected branches, frozen dependencies). 8) Definition of Done as an actionable checklist the agent reviews before closing a task.

Phase 4 - Verification: confirm that every command is copyable, prohibitions are unambiguous, there are no internal contradictions, and the file stands as the single operational context source.

Acceptance criteria: the file starts an agent with no prior context and lets it operate without asking the basics; all sensitive data is verified or marked [ASSUMPTION]; zero invented commands; the file is maintainable and doesn't duplicate the README. Edge cases to cover: monorepo (declare commands per package or workspace), no tests or lint (declare 'not configured' rather than inventing), multiple package managers (declare the canonical one), contradictory instructions between README and manifests (manifest wins and a note is left). Deliver a single context file in Markdown ready to commit in the repository root. If the filename, project, purpose, or stack are missing, ask for them before generating.

prompts.title: Initial code conventions and linters
prompts.content: Act as a senior tech lead in developer experience and code conventions for AI-assisted teams, with hands-on practice in formatters, linters, and quality automation in pre-commit and CI. I am starting a project and will work with agents that generate code at high speed; I need to lock in the style from day one so every file does not start with a different standard and linting stops being a negotiation that pollutes diffs. Deliver an initial conventions package ready to version. Before executing, restate what you understand and present your plan. First confirm with me the minimum indispensable items you cannot infer with certainty: language, runtime, and frameworks; package manager; whether existing configuration is already in place that must not be broken; the scope of rules I want (format only, format plus basic lint, or strict with quality and type rules); and the CI platform, or whether there is none yet. If I do not answer something, declare the assumption as [ASSUMPTION] and continue with the reasonable ecosystem default. Then produce, in this order: (1) a choice of one standard formatter and one standard linter for the ecosystem, each justified in one line, preferring the established community style guide for the language if I do not indicate a style; (2) complete, paste-ready configuration files (formatter config, linter config, and .editorconfig if applicable) covering indentation, quotes, line length, import order, and unused variables, explicitly separating auto-fixable rules from warn-only rules; (3) a brief naming table for files, folders, variables, functions, types, and constants, plus the expected directory structure; (4) the AGENTS.md contract (or the equivalent rules file for the tool) with the conventions as imperative and verifiable instructions, including the hard rule of not introducing code that fails the formatter or linter, and how to invoke the verification command; (5) the automation: pre-commit hooks that run the formatter and linter only on staged files, and the CI step that fails the build on non-compliance, both with the exact installation and execution commands. Close with an adoption checklist and the risks of not locking this in. Rules: do not invent plugins or versions you do not know with certainty; anything unconfirmed goes as [ASSUMPTION]; keep linter rules, formatter rules, and what is written in AGENTS.md aligned so they do not contradict each other; the local hook and the CI step must run exactly the same verification; pre-commit must operate only on staged files so it does not reformat the entire repo at once. If the project already has code, propose a gradual adoption path before a mass reformat and name the isolated commit that absorbs that noise. Neutral professional Spanish, no emojis, no prices, and without the word free.

prompts.title: Scalable feature-based folder structure
prompts.content:
Act as a senior software architect specializing in code organization, modularity, and repository scalability. I need a folder structure that holds up from the first features to dozens of domains without a structural rewrite, avoiding the typical costs of improvised organization: circular imports, orphaned shared code, and features that step on each other.

Before proposing, confirm with me the stack (language, framework, package manager), the type of application (web app, API, monorepo, library, mobile app, or other), the first 3 to 5 known features or domains, and, if applicable, team size and any framework or company conventions to respect. If a critical piece of information is missing for the layout, ask for it before moving forward; do not invent the stack.

Deliver:
1. A reasoned recommendation of feature-first layout (one self-contained folder per domain) versus layered (horizontal separation by technical responsibility), justified by app type, team size, and expected rate of change; name the trade-off you accept.
2. A concrete folder tree in a code block, with real folder names based on the features, and at least one feature shown from the inside as a replicable pattern (components/logic, model or types, data access, tests, public entry file).
3. Explicit dependency rules: allowed import direction, where shared code lives and the boundary between shared and feature-specific, how to prevent cross-feature coupling, and how to break a circular import if one appears.
4. Module boundaries and public entry points per feature (index or barrel that exposes only the contract, keeping internal detail private).
5. A checklist of 5 to 7 structural degradation warning signs with their concrete threshold and corrective action (when to split, extract, or rename).
6. A minimal migration plan for when the first warning sign appears, in safe and reversible steps.

Rules: respect the idiomatic conventions of the stack instead of imposing a foreign pattern; mark as assumption anything you cannot verify against the declared stack; prefer proven ecosystem conventions over inventions; do not introduce new dependencies or tools without justifying the cost.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. Restate what you understood and present your plan before executing. Deliver a folder architecture document with a tree, dependency rules, module boundaries, degradation checklist, and minimal migration plan, ready to apply to the repository.

prompts.title: Minimal design system bootstrap
prompts.content: Act as a senior design systems engineer, specializing in design tokens and accessible UI primitive libraries. I want the scaffold of a minimal design system to launch my vibe coding project, so that every screen I generate afterward inherits the same visual language without diverging hard-coded styles. Deliver it in three chained layers. Layer 1, tokens: first define a raw scale (numeric palette 50–900, modular typographic ramp, base-4 spacing units, radii, shadows, breakpoints) and on top of it the semantic roles (background, surface, text, muted-text, border, primary and its contrast, success, warning, danger, focus); expose everything simultaneously as CSS variables and as a typed theme object consumable by code. Layer 2, primitives: implement the base components referencing exclusively semantic roles, zero raw values, with their variants and hover, focus, active, error, and disabled states, documenting in a comment what each one covers. Layer 3, theme and startup: wire the modes by reassigning the role values (not by duplicating components) and deliver a ready-to-import entry file that leaves the system operational. Hard rule: no primitive touches a raw value, only roles. If you are missing any data (product name, stack and styling approach, starting color or palette, required primitives, modes to support) ask me before generating code; do not invent silently. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] any reasonable default you adopt and propose it as adjustable. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Close with: the three-layer code consistent with the stack, plus a brief note on how to add a new component or token without breaking coherence, and a verified accessibility checklist (AA contrast, visible focus, minimum touch areas, keyboard navigation).

prompts.title: Realistic test data seed
prompts.content: Act as a senior data engineer specializing in fixtures, rapid prototyping, and coherent synthetic data design. I need a realistic seed dataset to iterate on the interface, validate flows, and demo the application without waiting for the backend or real database. Before generating, restate what you understand of the model and present your plan. Ask me for any missing data (entities and their fields with type and relationships, volume of records per entity, desired output format and target stack); do not invent the structure. Proceed as follows: 1) Map the model: list entities, the type of each field, optional fields, and relationships with their cardinality and foreign keys. 2) Fix a generation order by dependencies (parents before children) to guarantee referential integrity, and a reproducible randomness seed. 3) Generate plausible values by type: plausible names and texts in neutral Spanish, emails and phones with valid format, dates in logical sequence (created before updated, no incoherent futures), amounts and enumerations within their domain; vary values to avoid identical rows that hide rendering bugs. 4) Connect each foreign key to an existing record so none is left orphaned. 5) Inject controlled edge cases: at least one record with empty optionals, one with long text, one with an infrequent state, and values at the edges of each range; label each case so it is traceable. 6) Serialize in the requested format and add a brief execution note (command or steps to apply the seed and how to reset it). Mark with [ASSUMPTION] any field or rule you infer when it is not explicit. Verify before delivering: zero broken foreign keys, edge cases present, dates and enumerations coherent, and volume fulfilled per entity. Do not include real PII; use synthetic data.

prompts.title: Issue and PR templates for AI workflows
prompts.content:
Act as a senior platform engineer specializing in code-agent-assisted workflows and the mechanics of issues and pull requests, with hands-on experience designing templates that minimize human-agent back-and-forth. I need a pair of reusable templates (one issue template and one pull request template) plus a usage guide, ready to version in my repository, designed so a code agent can pick up a ticket without asking and open an auditable PR.

Before generating, ask me for anything that would change the syntax of the templates or the verification commands: version control platform and its template mechanism, tech stack (languages, frameworks, package manager, test/build/lint commands), target code agent, team conventions (branches, commits, style, test policy), and what issue types to support. Do not invent test commands or file paths.

Design the issue template as a structured form with minimal fields, each with help text aimed at the human author that explains what to write and why the agent needs it: goal in one sentence; context and why now; explicit scope (what is in / what is NOT in); verifiable acceptance criteria in given-when-then format or a checkable list; suspicious files or modules as a starting point; technical constraints derived from the stack and conventions (version, style, prohibited dependencies); definition of done; and verification instructions for the agent (exact test, build, and lint commands). Mark as required the fields without which the agent cannot start: goal, scope, acceptance criteria, and verification.

Design the pull request template in Markdown that enforces traceability: reference to the issue it closes with the platform's closing keyword; change summary; decisions made and discarded alternatives; verification evidence (test output, reproduction steps, screenshots if applicable); definition-of-done checklist mirroring the issue; and a section for risks or technical debt introduced. The PR checklist must correspond one-to-one with the issue checklist.

Also deliver a brief usage guide: exact file path for each file, how the agent should read and validate the issue before coding (and what to do if a required field is missing or ambiguous), and how to fill in each PR section when finished. Consider edge cases: what happens when the issue does not apply to a field (must write 'N/A' instead of leaving it blank), how to prevent an agent from closing an issue without evidence, and how to degrade gracefully if the platform does not support native forms (Markdown fallback with sections). Mark all unconfirmed data as [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent commands or paths.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Git initialization with .gitignore and hooks
prompts.content:
Act as a senior platform engineer specializing in repository hygiene and version control with git, with hands-on practice in reproducible project initialization, pre-commit hooks, and branch protection on GitHub and GitLab.

I need to found the version control of my project from the first commit, before the pace of work scales the disorder. The goal is that no secret, build artifact, or broken code ever enters the history, and that the main branch is protected so every change goes through a pull request. If you do not have the stack, package manager, remote platform, main branch name, or the validations to enforce in pre-commit, ask me for them before continuing; do not invent paths or names.

Deliver a ready-to-run initialization guide, structured as follows:
1. Framing: confirm stack, package manager, remote platform, and name of the main branch; mark [ASSUMPTION] for every path or name you infer.
2. Initialization: exact commands for git init, setting the main branch, configuring the remote with a placeholder instead of the real URL, and creating the initial commit with a conventional message (e.g. chore: initial scaffold).
3. .gitignore: stack-specific file that excludes dependencies, build artifacts, environment files with secrets (.env and variants), caches, and editor or OS files; comment each block with its reason.
4. Pre-commit hooks: configuration of a recognized manager for the stack (pre-commit for Python, husky with lint-staged for Node, or equivalent) that runs validations only on staged files, not the entire tree; include a fallback if the tool is not installed.
5. Main branch protection: rules on the remote platform in UI steps and in CLI command where available (e.g. gh api or glab), requiring a pull request, at least one approved review, and green checks before merging.
6. First-clean-commit and protected-branch verification checklist.

Rules: .env and its variants are always excluded with an explicit warning not to version secrets; use placeholders instead of real credentials or tokens; each block carries a comment explaining its reason. If you detect that a secret was already committed, warn that rotating it and rewriting history are mandatory, not optional.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Spec optimized for Claude Code
prompts.content:
Act as a senior software engineer specializing in agentic workflows with Claude Code and in spec engineering for code agents. Your goal is to convert my informal code request into a robust spec, ready to paste into Claude Code, that maximizes the probability of solving the task on the first try without long correction cycles.

Ask first, if not already visible: the informal task request, the stack and repository structure, the startup/build/test commands, the hard constraints (untouchable modules, compatibility, allowed dependencies, conventions), and the expected behavior that defines success. If something critical is missing (stack, paths, test command), ask for it before generating the final spec. Do not invent paths, commands, or versions; mark every inference as [ASSUMPTION].

Generate the spec in this order: (1) objective in a single result-oriented sentence; (2) repository context (language, framework, package manager, build/test commands); (3) files and paths to read before editing, and if unknown, instruct Claude Code to discover and list them first; (4) task as an observable behavior change; (5) explicit hard constraints, including handling of new dependencies (prohibited unless justified); (6) numbered steps that enforce read-before-write and listing files to modify before touching them; (7) acceptance criteria as a binary checklist, each closing with an executable command.

Include edge cases: what to do if tests do not exist (create them or ask for confirmation), if a constraint conflicts with the objective (stop and report the conflict), and if the change touches public interfaces (preserve compatibility or document the breaking change). Ask the agent that, if a criterion cannot be verified by command, to declare it as manual verification with exact steps.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliver: the spec in plain text ready to paste into Claude Code, followed by the list of assumptions made and open questions pending confirmation.

prompts.title: Cursor rules (.cursorrules) per project
prompts.content:
Act as a senior platform engineer specializing in code agent tooling and Cursor configuration (.cursor/rules/*.mdc modern and .cursorrules legacy). I need a project rules file for Cursor, ready to save without additional editing, that prevents the agent from drifting: inventing APIs, ignoring conventions, rewriting entire files, or touching forbidden zones.

Before drafting, ask me for the following data if you do not have it: (1) project name, what it does, and who it serves; (2) stack with fixed versions (language, framework, package manager, runtime, database); (3) conventions (names, folder structure, allowed and prohibited patterns, error handling, typing); (4) exact lint, test, and build commands that must pass before closing a change; (5) boundaries (secrets, environment variables, applied migrations, untouchable folders or paths). If the stack, conventions, or quality commands are missing, ask me before writing and do not invent versions, commands, or paths.

Protocol: first restate in one or two lines what you understood and present your plan; then execute.

Deliver a single file with these seven numbered sections: (1) Project context in one or two lines; (2) Stack and versions, with versions explicitly fixed to prevent hallucinated APIs; (3) Code conventions: names, folder structure, allowed and prohibited patterns, error handling, typing; (4) Rules for the agent: edit only what was requested, do not rewrite entire files without permission, propose a plan before large changes, cite real file paths, do not invent dependencies or APIs, prefer minimal diffs; (5) Tests and quality: use the exact commands provided, declare minimum coverage, and require lint, test, and build to pass before considering a change done; (6) Boundaries and security: never touch secrets or environment variables, do not make network calls without being asked, do not modify applied migrations, respect forbidden folders; (7) Response format: comment language, diff granularity, when to ask instead of assume.

Each rule must be actionable, concrete, and verifiable; no generalities like 'write good code'. Deliver the content in a block ready to save in .cursor/rules/<name>.mdc with frontmatter (description and globs when applicable) and indicate how to also save it as a legacy .cursorrules in the repo root.

prompts.title: Prompt for generating UI in Vercel v0
prompts.content: Act as a senior frontend engineer specializing in design systems, React with TypeScript, and writing prompts for Vercel v0. Your task is to draft a single prose prompt block, ready to paste into v0, that describes a component or screen and produces usable code with minimal iterations. Before drafting, tell me what you understand and your plan; if you are missing essential data (what component, for whom, in what context, what states it must render), ask for it and do not invent the scope: an assumed scope is the number-one cause of useless generated code. The block you deliver must cover, in this exact order and without explanatory text around it: (1) intent line: what the component is and what it does in one sentence; (2) anatomy: visible elements from top to bottom with their hierarchy; (3) states: each state described one by one (empty, loading with skeleton, with data, error with actionable message, disabled, and applicable edge states such as long list, truncated text, or a single element); (4) interactions: hover, focus, click, submit, validations, and optimistic feedback when applicable; (5) example data: typed properties with realistic domain values, never generic placeholders like Lorem ipsum or Item 1; (6) style: reference visual tone, light and dark mode support, and shadcn/ui plus Tailwind when it fits; (7) non-negotiable technical constraints plus, by default, React with typed TypeScript, Tailwind, responsive mobile-first design, and accessibility (ARIA roles and labels, full keyboard navigation, visible focus, AA contrast); (8) acceptance criterion: one verifiable success sentence. Quality rules: do not introduce unauthorized dependencies; prefer composing small components over a monolith; mark as assumption any scope decision you make due to missing data. Close by pointing out the 2 or 3 spots where v0 will likely improvise (mobile responsive version, text copy, fine visual hierarchy) so the user reviews those first.

prompts.title: Prompt for building an app in Lovable
prompts.content:
Act as a senior full-stack product engineer specializing in Lovable, React, and Supabase, with expertise in schema design and row-level security (Row Level Security). Your output is a single structured technical brief, in numbered sections, written as direct instructions to Lovable, ready to paste and start guided construction.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate in your own words the app, its user, and the outcome it seeks; present your section plan; then execute. If an indispensable piece of data is missing (the main data entity, the role that decides permissions, or the rule of the critical flow that cannot fail), ask for it before drafting; do not invent business rules.

Produce the brief with these sections:
1. Product and scope: one product sentence, plus the explicit first-version scope separating what is in from what is out, to prevent feature creep.
2. Pages and navigation: each page or view with its purpose, key components, and navigation links; mark each route as public or protected and describe the redirect when a user without a session hits a protected route.
3. Data model: each table with columns, types, primary key, foreign keys, relationships, uniqueness constraints, and audit fields (created/updated, owner). For each table, at least one Row Level Security policy coherent with the roles; enable RLS by default and explicitly declare any public-read table.
4. Authentication and roles: access method, role definitions, and a permissions matrix per role covering the four verbs (view, create, edit, delete) per entity; specify how routes are protected on the frontend and queries on the backend.
5. States and flows: the critical flow step by step, plus empty, loading, and error states for each view with data, and form validations per field (required, format, limits).
6. Edge cases and decisions: list assumed assumptions, design decisions with their justification and trade-off, and the edge cases the first version handles versus those it explicitly defers.
7. Implementation order: sequential milestones (schema and RLS first, then auth, then pages, then state polish), with a verifiable acceptance criterion per milestone.

Closing criterion: no page without backing data, no orphaned table unused in any page, RLS active on every table with user data, the permissions matrix complete, the critical flow with its three edge states, and zero time promises. Neutral professional Spanish. Deliverable: self-contained brief in numbered sections, ready to paste into Lovable.

prompts.title: Prompt for prototyping in Bolt.new
prompts.content:
Act as a senior frontend engineer specializing in rapid prototyping with Bolt.new and in designing specs for AI code generators. I need to convert a product idea into a specification precise enough that Bolt.new generates a navigable, populated, and demonstrable prototype on the first attempt, without setting up infrastructure, so it can be validated with users or stakeholders.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before drafting, restate in your own words the idea, the target user, and the minimum navigable scope; list your assumptions tagged [ASSUMPTION] and the critical gaps; present your plan. If an essential entity, screen, or rule is missing for the prototype to hold together, ask me rather than inventing it.

Deliver the specification in six numbered sections: (1) One-line prototype summary: what it is and what it unlocks for validation. (2) Exact stack and dependencies, with versions when relevant; if no stack is provided use React + Vite + TypeScript + Tailwind, justify any extra library and prefer zero backend dependencies. (3) Data model with TypeScript types: entities, fields, types, optionality, and relationships, consistent with every screen and rule. (4) Screens: for each one its purpose, route, components, states (loading, empty, error, success), and interaction behavior — not just the layout. (5) Realistic seed data that populates the app on open, covering normal cases and at least one edge; anything invented is tagged [ASSUMPTION]. (6) Final consolidated prompt in a single block ready to paste into Bolt.new, self-contained with no external references, integrating stack, persistence, screens, business rules with their UI trigger, empty state, and seed data.

Close only when: the final prompt fits in a single pasteable block and does not depend on external context; the stack is explicit and compatible with Bolt.new; the data model covers all entities that appear on screens; every screen declares its behavior and states; persistence is defined and the prototype works without a backend when applicable; every key rule has a concrete and verifiable UI trigger; and essential gaps have been asked about, not filled blindly.

prompts.title: Prompt for Replit Agent end-to-end
prompts.content:
Act as a senior full-stack engineer experienced in delivering end-to-end applications with Replit Agent: scaffolding, database, authentication, and platform deployment. I need to convert a product idea into a functional, deployed application in a single assignment, without fragmenting the work into dozens of loose instructions, and leaving the project documented so anyone can pick it up.

Take the product from zero to deployed in five phases and, on closing each one, report what is working and how to test it:
1. Setup and schema: initialize the project with the indicated stack; if no stack is provided, propose a modern one and justify the choice in one line. Define the data model for the core features, run migrations, and leave the schema versioned.
2. Features and data: implement every core feature with a usable interface (never placeholders) and seed idempotent example data so the app does not start empty, including at least one test user per role.
3. Auth: configure login, protect the indicated routes, apply role-based access control when more than one role exists, and keep secrets off the client.
4. Value: add a summary panel, empty and error states with clear messages, form validation, and interface polish.
5. Deploy and verification: configure the destination with correct build and start commands, declare every variable in the Replit Secrets manager (nothing hardcoded), and verify that the public URL responds before closing.

Assumptions: if the stack is missing, choose a modern one and justify it; if the authentication method is missing, use email and password with a session; if no routes to protect are named, protect every route that displays or mutates user data. Declare any assumption you make. Edge cases to cover: first boot with no data, invalid credentials, unauthorized access to a protected route, and a failed migration (must be reversible or re-runnable without corrupting data).

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. Before touching code, restate in your own words what needs to be built and present your phase plan; only then, with that clear, execute. If a critical piece of information is missing (what the app does, core features, deployment target), ask before proceeding.

Closing criterion: deliver a deployed app with a live, verified URL, the seeded access credentials, a README with setup, variables, and how to run locally, and the checklist of criteria checked phase by phase. Zero hardcoded secrets and zero placeholders in core features.

prompts.title: Tool comparison for choosing the right one
prompts.content:
Act as a senior platform engineer specializing in AI-assisted development tools, with neutral technical selection criteria and no vendor bias. Your job is to help me choose, with clear criteria, which tool among v0, Lovable, Bolt, Cursor, and Claude fits best with what I am going to build, given my context, and to tell me in advance when to abandon it. The tools are not interchangeable: each one optimizes a different moment in the cycle, and choosing by trend instead of by fit generates rewrites, unmaintainable code, and wasted hours.

If you do not have enough context to classify with confidence, ask me before proceeding: what I am going to build or solve in one sentence, whether I am starting from scratch or from an existing repo, my target stack, my technical level, and how much control over the code I need.

Proceed as follows:
1. Classify the task into exactly one of five archetypes, with justification: (a) disposable UI prototype, (b) full-stack app from scratch, (c) editing an existing repo, (d) complex refactoring or debugging, (e) reasoning and architecture design without writing UI.
2. Build a comparison table of the five tools with columns: Main strength, Ideal task type, Control over the code, Curve for my level, Key limitation. Base it only on the known design of each tool; do not invent versions or features and tag [ASSUMPTION] on every unverifiable claim.
3. Issue ONE single primary recommendation, naming the tool, with three reasons explicitly tied to my task, project state, stack, technical level, and control need.
4. Define a Plan B (second-best option) and the concrete, observable signal that tells me I should migrate from the primary to the alternative.
5. List three common mistakes specific to using the recommended tool for this task archetype, each with its mitigation.

Rules: derive the decision from the archetype and the required control, never from popularity. Do not mention prices or the word free. Neutral and professional English, no emojis.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliver a block with: (1) justified archetype, (2) 5x5 comparison table, (3) recommendation + 3 reasons, (4) Plan B + migration signal, (5) three common mistakes with mitigation.

prompts.title: Code handoff between AI tools
prompts.content:
Act as a senior platform engineer specializing in porting generative AI prototypes (v0, Lovable, Bolt) to real development environments (Cursor, Windsurf, local repository), with expertise in design systems, visual parity, and dependency management across runtimes. I am going to move a prototype from the tool where it was born to a real development environment, and I need you to produce a portable, self-contained handoff document, pasteable into the destination, so the destination tool reconstructs with verifiable parity instead of improvising a 'similar but not equal' result.

Before drafting, tell me what you have available: the prototype name and function in one line, the source tool, the destination environment, the target stack at the destination if already decided, elements whose fidelity is non-negotiable, and whether I am giving you access to the exported code from the source or only to screenshots and the file tree. If a critical input for the inventory or fidelity is missing, ask for it before continuing; do not reconstruct blindly.

The document has five sections: (1) Artifact inventory: screens, components, routes, state, mock data, assets, styles, theme variables, and declared dependencies from the source. (2) Fidelity specification: per screen and component, design tokens (color, typography, spacing, radii, shadows), responsive breakpoints, states (hover, focus, active, disabled, loading, error, empty), animations/transitions, and the expected behavior of each interaction, with focus on critical elements. (3) Stack and dependency manifest: framework, package manager, exact versions, UI and icon library, fonts, environment variables, and differences between the source runtime and the destination stack that break fidelity; every proprietary component with no equivalent at the destination is flagged and a replacement is proposed with its trade-off. (4) Reconstruction instructions: numbered steps to stand up the project, file-by-file source-to-destination mapping, copyable installation commands, theme/fonts/assets configuration, and migration order (UI primitives, then components, then screens, then routes, then state/data). (5) Parity verification: checklist confirming identical render per screen, identical response per interactive state, absence of console errors and broken imports, and responsive match at the declared breakpoints.

Rules: separate facts from assumptions by tagging every inference with [ASSUMPTION]; no version is invented — all come from the source or are marked as pending confirmation; never mention prices; neutral and professional English, no emojis. MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the inputs, Plan the handoff, and only then Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before drafting the final document.

prompts.title: System prompt for a custom code agent
prompts.content: Act as a senior prompt engineer specializing in code agents, with experience operating programming assistants in production repos. I need you to design the complete system prompt that will govern a custom programming agent for my project. Without a behavioral contract, a code agent improvises: it invents APIs, rewrites things it should not, and delivers changes that are impossible to review; with a good system prompt it becomes a predictable and auditable collaborator. Build the system prompt with five explicit, numbered sections: 1) Role and identity (who the agent is, its seniority, and its mission in the project); 2) Stack and conventions (language, framework, package manager, runtime, linter/formatter, folder structure, and patterns — all mandatory); 3) Hard constraints as verifiable NEVER rules, including by default: do not invent APIs or signatures, do not delete or move files without confirming, do not add dependencies without justification, do not expose or assume secrets, do not touch CI/CD configuration or data migrations without approval; 4) Workflow in numbered steps (read the relevant code before writing, restate the task, present a plan, execute the minimum change, self-verify) bounded by the autonomy level I define; 5) Unambiguous output format and protocol for requesting data when something is ambiguous instead of assuming. Write in the imperative second person directed at the agent, with verifiable rules and no filler, and make the workflow always end in verification. If the destination tool has context limits or does not allow running commands, adapt the workflow and state that. Before drafting, restate in one line what you understand and articulate your plan; if you are missing the autonomy level, stack, or hard limits, ask first. Deliver the system prompt in a single pasteable block and, below it, a brief list of assumptions tagged [ASSUMPTION] and a mini acceptance checklist for me to validate the result.

prompts.title: Packed repo context for the agent
prompts.content:
Act as a senior context engineer specializing in code agents, with software architecture judgment and strict token-budget discipline. A code agent is only as good as the context it receives: too much and the signal is diluted and budget burned; too little and it hallucinates the architecture. Your job is to package a repository into a context document, ready to paste as the agent's initial instruction, that maximizes signal per token and lets it locate where to touch the code on the first attempt, without asking avoidable questions or breaking repo conventions.

Proceed as follows:
1. Mapping: reconstruct the real topology of the repo (folder structure, dominant language and framework, entry point, dependency manifests, configuration and conventions). Detect conventions observed in the code, not assumed; tag [ASSUMPTION] on everything unverifiable.
2. Curation by task relevance: score each file and assign it a level. CRITICAL (the agent must read it in full to avoid errors), REFERENCE (only its contract is needed: signatures, interfaces, schemas, or load-bearing fragments), and CONTEXT (one line stating its existence and purpose). The guiding rule is maximum signal per token.
3. Critical distillation: for each CRITICAL file extract the public contract, invariants, side effects, and extension points; discard dispensable internal implementation. Preserve literal text only when load-bearing (exact signatures, schemas, invariants).
4. Assembly: build the document with six sections (Repo map, Rules and conventions, Distilled CRITICAL files, REFERENCE files, CONTEXT files, Omitted with reason).
5. Budget: verify the document fits within the available token limit. If it does not fit, downgrade files from a higher level to a lower one (CRITICAL to REFERENCE, REFERENCE to CONTEXT) before cutting critical content; never sacrifice a file the agent needs to read in full to succeed.

Non-negotiable rules: zero secrets, credentials, tokens, or PII in the package (sanitize them or replace with placeholders). Do not invent files or conventions. Every CRITICAL file must be justified by the task; if it does not contribute to the task, it is not critical.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

If you do not have access to the repo file tree, the specific task the agent must execute, the token budget, or the files you already know are relevant, ask for them before packaging. If the repo is too large to inspect in full, say so and propose a task-directed sampling instead of guessing.

prompts.title: Generate UI component from description
prompts.content:
Act as a senior front-end engineer specializing in design systems and accessibility (WAI-ARIA / WCAG 2.1 AA). You will translate the functional description of an interface component into production code ready to integrate: not just the happy path, but a component that is born typed, accessible, and with all its states resolved, to unblock integration into the design system without rework from forgotten states, untyped props, or accessibility failures caught too late.

Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret – Plan – Execute.
1) Interpret: restate what component you understood, its props with type, the states to cover, the destination stack, and the source of design tokens. If the component description, props, framework, or design system are missing or ambiguous, ask the minimum necessary questions and stop; do not assume the stack or invent token names, breakpoints, or import paths.
2) Plan: list the props signature (required vs. optional, exact types, default values), the states to implement, and the accessibility strategy (semantic elements, roles, ARIA only where native semantics fall short, visible focus, tab order, keyboard navigation, screen reader support, and respect for prefers-reduced-motion).
3) Execute: deliver the component code with semantic structure, each state visually distinguishable, styles consuming exclusively design system tokens, and comments only where the intent is not obvious. At the close, include the list of covered states with how to trigger each one.

Assumptions and limits: the component must be self-contained and free of business logic or network calls unless otherwise requested; visible text and screen reader support text must be externalizable via props for i18n; do not introduce new dependencies without justifying them and offering a dependency-free alternative.

Closing criterion: all props typed with their exact type and required/optional differentiated; every state implemented and visually distinguishable; every interactive element keyboard-operable with visible focus and the correct role/ARIA and no focus traps; styles without arbitrary fixed values for color, spacing, or typography; sufficient contrast for AA; the code compiles/validates on the destination stack; nothing invented — anything ambiguous was asked about in the interpretation phase. Neutral and professional English. If any essential data is missing, ask for it before generating the code.

prompts.title: Clone UI from a screenshot
prompts.content:
Act as a senior frontend engineer specializing in translating visual designs into code, with mastery of design systems, tokens, responsive layout, and accessibility. I have a screenshot of an existing screen and I need to reproduce it as componentized code. If you are missing the screenshot, the output stack, the style system, the fidelity level, or the responsive scope, ask me before proceeding; a screenshot is a partial source (a single state, a single size, no interactions, no real data) and I do not want you to invent what is not visible.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliver in this order: (1) Screenshot reading: describe what you see (screen type, apparent purpose, breakpoint it represents) to confirm a shared interpretation. (2) Visual tree: decompose the image into a hierarchy of regions and components (header, nav, hero, cards, lists, forms, footer) with nesting and layout model per region (flex, grid, stack, absolute position). (3) Inferred design tokens: color (approximate hex), typography (family, sizes, weights, line height), spacing scale, radii, shadows, borders; values that cannot be distinguished with certainty are given as a range and tagged [ASSUMPTION]. (4) Code: the componentized interface with centralized tokens (variables, theme, or constants), semantic and accessible markup (roles, labels, contrast, focus, heading hierarchy), and example data as placeholder — no scattered magic values. (5) States and responsive: declare hover, focus, active, disabled, empty, loading, and error, plus the breakpoints NOT visible in a single image; propose reasonable behavior and mark it as a decision to validate. (6) Fidelity checklist: region-by-region table comparing what was observed against what was implemented, plus the list of gaps the image does not resolve (real text, interactions, dynamic data, brand assets, licensed fonts).

Rules: do not invent business logic, endpoints, or real data; deliver only the presentation layer. Code from the outside in (region layout, then components, then token detail). Close with minimal instructions to run or preview the result and the consolidated list of assumptions and gaps.

prompts.title: Conversion-oriented landing page
prompts.content: Act as a senior product designer and conversion copywriter, specialist in single-page landing pages, AIDA model, unique value proposition, social proof, and accessible visual hierarchy. I need to convert visits into a concrete action with a real, measurable, immediately publishable landing — not a decorative page. Before writing code, ask me for the essential data if it is missing or ambiguous: what product or service I am promoting and its central value, who I am targeting (role, sector, or profile), what is the single desired conversion action (sign up, schedule a demo, leave an email, buy), and what real social proof I have available (testimonials, logos, metrics, number of clients). Never invent testimonials, figures, or logos: if social proof is missing use visible [REPLACE: ...] markers and indicate what to substitute. Do not include prices or the word free either. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol (Interpret > Plan > Execute): first restate objective, audience, and action, list what data is missing, and tag assumptions with [ASSUMPTION]; present your plan before executing.
