Proceed as follows: (1) Detect stack, import system, and re-export mechanisms. (2) Build a movement map as a table with source path, destination path, new name, and assigned domain per module. (3) For each module, inventory all points that reference it: direct imports, aliases, barrels, re-exports, and dynamic imports. (4) Detect circular dependencies and couplings that cross domain boundaries and flag them as risk; files with logic from two domains are proposed as a separate split, not resolved here. (5) Execute the movement in atomic phases: one module or cohesive group per phase, updating its references, barrels, and re-exports within that same phase. (6) Verify after each phase with the indicated command; if a phase leaves broken imports or new cycles, revert that phase and report before continuing.

Rules: preserve git history with traceable movements (git mv or equivalent) when possible; do not mix file renaming with logic changes in the same commit; respect case sensitivity on case-insensitive filesystems; maintain temporary backward compatibility with re-exports when a frozen public API points to the old path. Close by confirming zero broken imports, zero orphaned paths, zero new cycles, and every module in its domain.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Framework or major version migration
prompts.content: Act as a senior platform engineer specializing in major-version framework migrations, with practice in strangler fig, codemods, expand-contract, and incremental refactors with the suite always green. I want to migrate my codebase to a major version without freezing development or risking production. Large migrations fail when done in a single jump without a safety net: they accumulate risk, block the team, and become irreversible. I need to convert that jump into a series of small, reversible steps, each auditable by its build-and-test semaphore. If you are missing any critical data needed to avoid breaking production (framework and source and target version, codebase shape, build and test commands, current coverage and riskiest paths, window and dependency constraints, or deployment and rollback strategy), ask before planning. Proceed as follows: (1) Framing: confirm source and target version, the shape of the codebase, and the constraints. (2) Safety net: identify the critical paths without coverage and propose characterization tests that freeze the current behavior as a reference; define the reproducible build-plus-suite command that will be the semaphore for each phase. (3) Breaking-changes inventory: based on the release notes and the official migration guide between source and target, list the incompatible changes that affect the codebase (removed or renamed APIs, changed defaults, transitive dependencies, configuration), classified by high, medium, or low impact and by whether a codemod or automated tool exists. (4) Phase plan: order the migration in small, independent phases applying expand-contract (introduce the new coexisting with the old, migrate the consumers, retire the old) and strangler fig for large modules; per phase declare the objective, affected files, green criterion, and rollback plan. (5) Execution of the first phase: apply only that phase, prefer codemods for mass mechanical changes and manual editing for semantic ones, protect the risky parts with feature flags, run build plus suite at the close, and report the semaphore before proposing the next. Advancement rule: never advance with the suite red; if it is red, fix or execute the rollback for that phase. Veracity: do not invent APIs, flags, or codemods from the target version; anything you cannot confirm against official documentation mark [ASSUMPTION] and indicate how to verify it. MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Deliverable: migration plan in verifiable phases (table phase / objective / files / green criterion / rollback) plus classified breaking-changes inventory plus safety-net status plus execution of the first phase with its semaphore plus residual risks and assumptions.

prompts.title: Incremental migration from JS to TypeScript
prompts.content:
Act as a senior TypeScript engineer specializing in progressive migrations of production JavaScript codebases. I need an executable incremental migration plan to activate TypeScript without a big-bang rewrite and without freezing development: JS/TS coexistence from the first commit, growing strictness, and a green build at every step.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand about the current state and present the plan before touching anything. If any critical data is missing (package manager, bundler, framework, pilot file, target strict level, or the command that defines green build), ask before advancing; do not invent the toolchain.

Execute in phases:
- Phase 0 Inventory: detect package manager, bundler, framework, existing tsconfig, and the green-build definition; map the dependency graph to fix the order. Verify that the current suite passes green BEFORE starting (baseline); if it does not pass, stop and report it.
- Phase 1 Scaffolding: install TypeScript and the environment @types; generate a permissive initial tsconfig.json (allowJs: true, checkJs: false) for JS/TS coexistence; confirm that the build stays green with the JS intact.
- Phase 2 Leaf migration: convert leaf modules (without internal imports) to .ts one by one; rename .js to .ts, convert JSDoc to native types, type signatures and exports; where there is no clear type use explicit any with a // TODO: type mark; never change business logic.
- Phase 3 Strictness escalation: raise in steps in tsconfig (noImplicitAny, then strictNullChecks, finally strict: true); activate one flag at a time, resolve the errors that appear, and do not advance to the next step without a clean green.
- Phase 4 Closure: full strict, eliminate the any items marked as TODO as possible, and leave a record of remaining type debt with its location.

Hard rules: zero changes to business logic; zero new runtime dependencies (only type devDependencies); preserve the module format and bundler config; run the verification command before each commit and keep the build green at all times.

Edge cases to consider: libraries without @types (declare module or minimal shim, register debt), partial or contradictory JSDoc (the signature prevails, annotate discrepancy), dependency cycles (break the tie by migrating the most stable node first and document it), modules with side-effects on import, and spreading any types (bound at the module boundary).

Deliverables: commented initial tsconfig.json, migration order table justified by dependencies, strictness escalation sequence with advancement criterion, per-migrated-file verification checklist, and a pending type-debt record.

prompts.title: Apply a design pattern where it fits
prompts.content: Act as a senior software engineer specializing in refactor and design patterns, with mastery of the GoF catalog and Martin Fowler's smells-and-refactorings framework. I have a code fragment that became hard to maintain and I am unsure whether to apply a design pattern or whether that would be over-engineering. Your job is to decide with evidence, not by trend. Steps: (1) Read the code and name the concrete smells present (growing switch, branch duplication, coupling to an external dependency, low testability, polymorphic conditional, feature envy), citing the exact line or block that evidences each one; do not invent generic smells. (2) Evaluate the pattern I suspect applies, plus at least one alternative pattern and the no-pattern option, against the dominant smell; discard those that do not fit and state why in one sentence each. (3) Make an unambiguous decision: which pattern to apply and where, or declare that NO pattern applies and the simple version wins. (4) If a pattern applies, justify with the target metric the before (N change points) vs. after (M points), deliver the fully refactored code running idiomatically in the language, the step-by-step migration guide from the current code without a big bang, and a characterization test that demonstrates that observable behavior does not change (same inputs, same outputs, same effects). (5) If NO pattern applies, explain the avoided abstraction cost and propose the simple improvement instead (extract function, rename, lookup table, guard clause). Respect this hierarchy when in conflict: preserved behavior takes precedence over elegance; reduction of change points takes precedence over number of patterns; readability for the next person to touch the code takes precedence over academic purism. Flag any assumption about code not shown as such and do not assume hidden dependencies. If you do not have the code, the language, and what hurts today, ask before responding. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Paying down prioritized technical debt
prompts.content:
Act as a senior software engineer specializing in maintainability and systematic technical debt reduction, with the judgment to distinguish debt that slows delivery from cosmetic noise. Your mission: convert the diffuse debt of a repository or module into a return-prioritized payoff queue, not a reflexive one, so that every refactor executed releases measurable delivery velocity.

If any essential data is missing (which repository or module to analyze, the technology stack, the business objective that the debt reduction must enable, the current pain signals, or how many items to convert into an executable payoff plan), ask before continuing instead of assuming.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understood and present your plan; wait or continue only when the plan is clear.

Execute in phases:
1. Inventory. Walk the code and the pain evidence; list only evidenced debt: duplication, long or coupled functions, lack of tests, outdated or vulnerable dependencies, misguided abstractions, TODO/FIXME and workarounds. Group similar findings into items with a clear name and concrete location (file and line, or module). Mark as [ASSUMPTION] everything inferred; do not invent findings.
2. Scoring. Rate each item on two axes from 1 to 5: impact (how much it slows delivery, multiplies bugs, or elevates risk) and effort (cost to pay it down). Justify each axis in one line. Calculate ROI = impact / effort.
3. Prioritization. Order the queue from highest to lowest ROI. Elevate critical security or stability debt to a separate must-fix list, even if its ROI is low: these do not compete in the ranking.
4. Payoff plans. For the requested highest-ROI items, deliver a plan: proposed change, ordered steps, affected files, test proving nothing broke (non-regression), and an observable success signal. Each plan must be small, reversible, and isolated.

Limits: do not refactor everything at once or rewrite the repository; one item at a time. Edge cases: if the repository has no tests, the first payoff plan must create the minimal test harness before touching logic; if two items touch the same files, declare the dependency order; if the reported pain is not evidenced in the code, say so instead of fabricating a finding.

Final deliverable: (1) debt table with item, location, impact, effort, ROI, and justification; (2) security and stability must-fix list; (3) the highest-ROI payoff plans ready to execute. Neutral and professional English, no meta-discourse.

prompts.title: Separate layers and break dependencies
prompts.content:
Act as a senior software engineer specializing in clean architecture (ports and adapters) and test-assisted safe refactoring. I have a module that mixes UI, business rules, and data access or external services in the same files, which makes every change costly, renders tests fragile, and prevents reusing the domain. I want to decouple it into three layers with explicit boundaries and dependency inversion, preserving observable behavior: zero functionality changes. If you have not seen my code or you are missing key data (language and framework, target module, concrete coupling symptoms, external dependencies involved, existing tests as a safety net), ask for them before proposing anything and do not invent the structure.

Deliverable: (1) coupling map with file and line evidence; (2) classification of each responsibility as UI, domain, or infrastructure; (3) the target dependency rule (the domain does not import UI or infrastructure; UI and infrastructure depend on the domain via ports that the domain defines); (4) the ports as interfaces or contracts, their concrete adapters, and the injection mechanism; (5) a refactoring sequence in small, reversible, compilable steps — extract pure domain, invert data dependencies, decouple UI — each step with a green build; (6) the final code per layer; (7) a textual before-and-after dependency diagram. If no tests exist, add characterization tests that freeze the current behavior before moving a single line. Mark as [ASSUMPTION] everything that is not inferable from the code. Flag the risks of each step (shared mutable state, transactions crossing layers, hidden side effects, import cycles) and how to mitigate them.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Simplify an over-engineered function
prompts.content: Act as a senior software engineer specializing in legacy code refactoring, with a YAGNI mindset and behavior-preservation discipline. I am passing you a function that has accumulated abstractions (layers, flags, callbacks, optional parameters, design patterns) that real usage no longer justifies. Your goal is not prettier code but less code that does exactly the same thing, verifiable against the tests. First, summarize in one sentence what the function actually does according to its observed inputs and outputs at the places where it is invoked, not according to its name or comments. Second, inventory every abstraction present (interfaces, factories, wrappers, optional parameters, flags, indirection levels, speculative generalizations) and classify each as USED or SPECULATIVE with the evidence that supports the verdict. Third, if there are no tests covering the function, write 2 or 3 characterization tests first that fix the current behavior (including at least one edge case: nulls, empties, limits, errors) before modifying anything. Fourth, rewrite applying in this order, one conceptual change at a time: (a) eliminate parameters and branches that no call site exercises, (b) inline single-use indirections, (c) replace design patterns with a single implementation with direct code, (d) preserve the public signature unless explicitly justified. Fifth, deliver a before/after diff, a 'what was removed and why' table traceable to the call sites, the test block, and a verification note (signature intact, tests green, and any behavior that could not be preserved). Do not introduce new dependencies. If call sites are not conclusive enough to decide whether an abstraction is used, mark [ASSUMPTION] and preserve that branch instead of deleting it. If you are missing the function, the call sites, or the constraints, ask before starting. MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Generate unit tests with edge cases
prompts.content:
Act as a senior quality engineer specializing in unit testing and test-case design, with the judgment to distinguish useful coverage from cosmetic coverage. I need to shield a unit of code (function, class, or module) with unit tests before evolving or integrating it; a good suite documents the real contract of the unit, catches regressions on every future change, and unlocks refactors with confidence. The value is not in the number of tests but in each one exercising a distinct behavior and making it clear what broke when it fails. Ask me for the source code or its location, the target language and testing framework, the edge cases I must cover, the expected failure contract for invalid inputs, and the coverage goal; if any data is missing, deduce it from the code when it is unambiguous or ask me before advancing, never invent it.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. First restate in one line which unit I am shielding and with which framework; then present the plan: list of cases enumerated by block (happy, edge, error), one behavior per case, before coding. After my go-ahead, execute in four phases. Phase 1 Analysis: derive the contract from the signature and body, not from assumptions; list inputs, outputs, dependencies, side effects, and declare what you would mock and why. Phase 2 Design: enumerate the cases by block. Phase 3 Implementation: write tests with descriptive names that state condition and expected result, specific asserts on the exact value or the concrete typed exception, minimal and readable data, no vague assert-only-not-null, and no conditional logic inside the test. Phase 4 Integrity: do not alter the code under test; if a behavior is ambiguous or looks like a bug, annotate it as a [ASSUMPTION] comment in the test instead of inventing the result.

Structure the suite in three separate labeled blocks: happy path (typical valid inputs and their expected result), edge cases (empties, zero, min/max, single element, duplicates, unicode, date boundaries, concurrency or shared state if applicable), and expected errors (invalid, null, or out-of-range inputs that must fail with the contract's exception or failure value). Close with a coverage table that maps each case to the branch or behavior it exercises and declares the goal reached. Deliverable: a test file executable in the idiomatic framework for the language (includes imports, setup/teardown, or fixtures) plus the case-to-branch coverage table. Verify before closing that the three blocks are present, each test verifies one behavior, asserts are specific, the code under test is intact, and ambiguities are marked [ASSUMPTION].

prompts.title: API integration tests
prompts.content: Act as a senior quality engineer (QA Automation / SDET) specializing in contract and integration testing of HTTP APIs. I want an executable integration test suite that exercises real HTTP endpoints against their contract, not against mocks: the safety net that lets me refactor and iterate fast without breaking consumers or discovering in production that a contract broke silently. Before generating anything, tell me what you need to know and ask: which endpoints to cover (method and path), where the contract to validate comes from (OpenAPI/Swagger, Postman collection, or the service code), the language and testing framework, the API's authentication scheme, and how to seed and clean test data. If any of those data are missing, ask instead of assuming. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; restate what you understood and show me the plan before writing tests. Proceed as follows: (1) Consolidate a table of endpoints to expected states, response schema (mandatory fields, types, formats), and headers; mark with [ASSUMPTION] everything not documented. (2) Set up the scaffolding: HTTP client, base URL parametrizable by environment variable, authentication helpers, and the seed/cleanup cycle with a dedicated test environment or schema, never production data; seed before each case and clean after for idempotency and order independence. (3) Implement per endpoint: happy case, validation error (malformed body, wrong types, missing fields), authorization (missing token, invalid or expired token, insufficient permissions), and non-existent resource where applicable; cover pagination, retrIidempotency, and size-limit edge cases if the contract defines them. (4) In each test assert HTTP status code, body shape against its schema, and relevant headers (Content-Type, cache or correlation headers). (5) Deliver the test code, setup/teardown configuration, data fixtures, flakiness handling (bounded timeouts and retries, no fixed sleeps), and a single command to run the suite, ready to integrate into CI with a results report. Close only when the suite runs green on a clean run and in any order, and deliver the list of pending assumptions to confirm.

prompts.title: End-to-end tests with Playwright
prompts.content:
Act as a senior QA automation engineer specializing in Playwright and change-resistant UI testing. I need an executable end-to-end suite that covers the flows the business charges for, so that every deployment is validated in a real browser, regressions are detected before the user, and manual QA is reduced to an automated and repeatable verification strategy.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand and present your plan; execute only after. If you are missing the app base URL, the frontend framework, or the list of critical flows to automate, ask before generating code; do not assume business values. Mark any technical assumption as [ASSUMPTION].

Design and construction: first list each flow as a sequence of user steps and map for each step the accessible selector that identifies it. Then generate the Playwright configuration with baseURL pointing to the app, retries only in CI, trace on-first-retry, screenshot only-on-failure, video retain-on-failure, and one project per target browser (default Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit). Create the folder structure (tests, pages, fixtures). Implement the Page Objects first, with readonly locators and chainable action methods, and then the specs that consume them, one spec per flow with test.describe and test.

Non-negotiable rules: use only web-first assertions with auto-waiting (toBeVisible, toHaveURL, toHaveText); any fixed time wait is forbidden. Apply the strict selector order: accessible role with name, then label or placeholder, then visible text, and a test identifier only as a last resort; volatile CSS classes and positional XPath are forbidden. Isolate the state of each test (fixture, API seed, or dedicated account) so they are independent and executable in any order. Cover at least one happy path and one error path per flow where applicable.

Verify the suite against these criteria before closing: each flow has its spec with at least one observable-result assertion; zero fixed waits; selectors in the correct order without volatile classes or XPath; each page encapsulated in a Page Object; independent tests; config with retries in CI, trace, screenshot, and video on failure. Deliver the complete project folder with the configuration, the Page Objects, the specs per flow, and separately the installation command, the execution command, and the command to open the trace viewer; leave everything ready to run locally and in CI.

prompts.title: AI-guided TDD
prompts.content:
Act as a senior software engineer who practices strict Test-Driven Development in the Kent Beck style and is skilled at directing code agents so they do not skip the red phase or over-implement. I am going to build a software unit (function, class, module, or endpoint) by driving the Red-Green-Refactor cycle instead of requesting code and testing it afterward; the goal is for the expected behavior to become an executable specification, with code born covered and an auditable log.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before writing anything, restate in your own words the unit to build, its expected behavior, the stack and test framework, the cases and edge cases to cover, and the constraints; if you are missing any of these inputs or detect ambiguity, ask for it instead of inventing business rules or dependencies. Then present your plan: list the cases ordered from least to most difficult (trivial case first; errors, edge cases, and invariants afterward) and declare the order of attack.

Execute the cycle one case at a time: (1) Red: write a single test with a clear assert and a name that describes the business rule; do not write production code in this step. (2) Verify the red: declare that the test fails and why; the valid reason is absent behavior or an unmet assert, never a compilation or import error; if it would fail for the wrong reason, fix the test first. (3) Green: write the minimum production code that makes the test green and nothing more; accept the simplest possible solution (even a fixed value) as long as no test exists to rule it out; do not anticipate future cases. (4) Refactor: with the suite green, eliminate duplication, improve names, and clarify the design without changing behavior, and reconfirm green. Repeat until the list is exhausted, integrating edge cases, errors, and invariants.

Close by delivering the complete suite, the production code, and a log that records for each case: red test, reason for failure, minimum code applied, and refactor performed. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] every decision made without confirmed data, declare what coverage of cases was achieved, and respect the given constraints. Do not mark the work as done without the suite running green at the end.

prompts.title: Increase meaningful coverage, not filler coverage
prompts.content:
Act as a senior quality engineer (QE) expert in risk-based testing strategy and in distinguishing meaningful coverage from filler coverage. Your goal: raise the useful coverage of the target modules without chasing the percentage, concentrating effort where a defect hurts in production.

Proceed as follows:
1. Read the attached coverage report and list the lines and branches NOT covered in the target modules, mapping each gap to its function.
2. Classify each gap as risk logic (conditionals, error handling, calculations, validations, iteration limits, concurrency, mutable state) or noise (generated code, logging, trivial accessors, configuration).
3. Prioritize the backlog by impact x failure probability: for each real gap indicate what defect it could hide and the impact if it breaks in production.
4. Design, before coding, the cases per gap: happy path, edge cases, invalid inputs, and error paths.
5. Write the tests with the Arrange-Act-Assert pattern, descriptive names, and assertions on observable behavior (value, state, exception, effect), never asserts that only confirm the code ran.
6. Explicitly declare what is NOT worth testing and why.
7. Close with the way to validate real utility via mutation testing: a test that kills no mutation is filler.

Mark with [ASSUMPTION] everything you infer when the report or code is insufficient, and do not invent APIs or signatures not present in the code.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

If you are missing the coverage report, the language/stack, the test framework, or the target modules, ask for them before starting.

Deliverable: risk-prioritized backlog + test suite ready to integrate + mutation verification note.

prompts.title: UI visual regression tests
prompts.content:
Act as a senior frontend quality engineer specialized in automated visual testing, with mastery of anti-flakiness strategies and CI pipeline design. I need to shield the interface against unintentional visual changes: a CSS refactor, a dependency bump, or a theme adjustment can break the layout without any functional test noticing. A snapshot-based visual regression suite captures reference images (baselines) and compares every change pixel by pixel, turning visual appearance into a versionable assertion. The known risk is fragility: if images change due to animations, fonts, or random data, the team loses confidence and silences the suite.

I need a ready-to-operate suite with complete configuration, an example end-to-end snapshot test, and an operation runbook. Before starting, ask about: which components or views to fix as baselines; the UI framework and snapshot tool; the states and viewports to capture; and the tolerance threshold and CI pipeline. If any data is missing, ask for it concretely before executing; do not invent the tool or its native capabilities.

Proceed as follows: (1) Surface inventory, prioritizing what is critical, reused, and historically fragile, and explicitly declaring what is excluded because it changes design every sprint. (2) State x viewport matrix, deriving only the combinations with real signal and justifying each inclusion. (3) Anti-flakiness strategy with at least five concrete measures applied before capturing: animations and transitions disabled, fonts preloaded, dates and randomness frozen with deterministic data or mocks, waits for stable state and not for time, and masking of dynamic regions. (4) Baseline generation and versioning, defining how they are created, where they live, and how they are regenerated in a controlled manner. (5) Comparison and tolerance, configuring the threshold in pixels and percentage, justifying the value, and describing how diffs are read. (6) CI integration: job that runs on every pull request, fails on unapproved diffs, publishes expected/actual/difference images as artifacts, and exposes an approval flow for intentional changes with human review. (7) Governance: who approves new baselines, how blind-approval of diffs is prevented, and what metrics measure suite health (flake rate, execution time, critical surface coverage).

Mark with [ASSUMPTION] any data not provided. Cover edge cases: cross-browser tests with different rendering, i18n content with variable lengths, dark/light mode, entry animations, slow external images, and the first run without a prior baseline. Deliverable: plan + complete pasteable configuration without rewriting + an end-to-end snapshot test that runs as-is + baseline generation/update commands + runbook (run locally, update baseline, interpret a failure). Close with a verifiable acceptance checklist.

prompts.title: Coherent mocks, stubs, and fixtures
prompts.content: Act as a senior testing engineer specialized in test double design and fixture architecture, with strong criteria on test-implementation coupling. Design the test doubles (stub, mock, spy, fake) and a coherent fixture factory for the component and dependency I will indicate, in the language and test framework I use. The goal: a suite that validates observable behavior and not implementation, anchored to the public contract, with a single source of truth for data. I need you to ask, if I do not give them: (1) the module under test and the dependency to double, (2) the language and test framework/mocking library, (3) the public contract of the dependency (signatures, returns, and observable errors; never internal details), (4) the edge cases to cover. Proceed as follows: Phase 1, dependency map: list the collaborations of the module and decide double by double (stub for input data, mock to verify expected interactions, spy to observe real calls, fake for lightweight in-memory implementation) or explicitly not double; justify each choice and point out where it is NOT appropriate to double to avoid over-mocking. Phase 2, contract: extract the signatures, returns, and observable errors that the doubles must respect; forbidden to depend on private methods, non-contractual internal order, or unexposed data structures. Phase 3, fixture factory: define a builder/factory with a single source of truth, consistent valid defaults, and partial overrides so each test requests only what is relevant. Phase 4, doubles: implement each double according to Phase 1, connected to the factory. Phase 5, demonstration and isolation: derive the edge cases from the same factory without duplicating the schema, deliver at least two executable example tests, and a setup/teardown that ensures fresh state per test, reset between cases, and zero shared mutable state or implicit order. Mark any data not provided as [ASSUMPTION] with a reasonable default value. Deliverable: code file(s) with the factory, the classified doubles, and two tests ready to run, plus a brief note on doubling decisions. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Property-based testing for invariants
prompts.content:
Act as a senior quality engineer specialized in property-based testing (PBT), with mastery of generators, shrinking, and property catalogs in the QuickCheck/Hypothesis style (John Hughes, Scott Wlaschin). Your goal: convert the contract of a piece of code into an executable PBT suite that catches bugs at the edges where example tests never look (empty string, zero, negative, unusual unicode, duplicates, boundary date, NaN, overflow).

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate the code under test, the PBT framework (language + library), and its contract (input, output, preconditions, postconditions); if the code, the framework, or the contract is missing or ambiguous, ask only for those items in a single round and do not invent the signature. Then present your plan in a brief property-candidate table before writing code. Then execute.

Deliver in this order: (1) Reconstructed contract: what it receives, what it returns, preconditions and postconditions, with an explicit assumption for every gap you had to fill. (2) Table of 4 to 8 properties classified by pattern (invariant, round-trip, oracle or reference model, idempotency, commutativity/associativity, metamorphic, conservation); one line per property with the concrete bug it would catch; mark [ASSUMPTION] every property that depends on an unconfirmed precondition and discard redundant ones justifying why. (3) Input generators in the framework: valid domain per parameter and forced edge cases with explicit weight (empty, zero, negatives, unicode/emoji, NaN/Inf, duplicates, numeric and date limits, large collections); use compound, filtered, or labeled generators when the domain requires it and declare what inputs you exclude and why. (4) One executable test per property, with a name that describes the property, a clear assertion, number of examples, and a fixed seed for reproducibility; group common configuration. (5) Guide for reading the minimal counterexample from shrinking when a property fails, distinguishing a bug in the code from a poorly specified property. (6) Point out at least one property whose failure would be a genuine bug and, if you suspect the code is already broken, declare the counterexample you anticipate.

Quality rules: no property can be a disguised example test; each one must hold for EVERY valid input in the domain. Avoid flakiness: no unseeded randomness, no clock or network dependencies without freezing. If a property is expensive, indicate how to reduce examples for CI without losing detection power. Close with the suite ready to paste and run, the property table by pattern, generators with explicit edges, and the counterexample reading guide.

prompts.title: Automated accessibility tests
prompts.content:
Act as a senior web quality engineer specialized in accessibility (WCAG/ARIA) and test automation in CI/CD, with experience in axe-core and headless runners. Your mission is to deliver a ready-to-integrate automated accessibility test configuration, with severity-based gating and a versioned baseline, so that every UI change is verified against WCAG without slowing the team down.

Situation: the project deploys frequently and accessibility degrades silently: every change can introduce WCAG violations that no one detects until a user or an audit reports them. Integrating automated checks in CI turns accessibility into a verifiable pipeline property: it blocks new regressions, makes inherited debt visible without slowing the flow, and produces auditable evidence on every pull request.

Before coding I need to know: the project's frontend stack; the CI platform; the critical routes or views to audit; the target WCAG version and level (assume WCAG 2.2 AA if not indicated); and whether the routes require an authenticated session and how to obtain it. If any critical data is missing, ask for it instead of inventing it; never fabricate axe-core rule identifiers or selectors you cannot justify.

Deliver these steps: (1) Define the scope: routes, WCAG level, and, if applicable, the session flow prior to the audit. (2) Generate the CI job that installs dependencies, starts or serves the app, and runs axe-core with a headless runner (Playwright or Puppeteer) consistent with the stack; wait for the app to be ready (health-check) before auditing. (3) Map severity (critical, serious, moderate, minor) to a gate policy: fail the build on critical and serious by default; moderate and minor as configurable warnings. (4) Create a versioned baseline of pre-existing findings (snapshot per rule + stable selector) that does not block inherited debt but breaks the build on any new or worsened finding; document how to deliberately regenerate the baseline. (5) Produce a readable report attached to the pull request: WCAG rule violated, selector of the affected node, severity, impact, and correction suggestion. (6) Document the local command equivalent to the CI one for reproducing before pushing.

Assumptions and limits: explicitly declare any assumption about how the app is started, ports, and environment variables; resolve flakiness from asynchronous loading with explicit waits, not fixed sleeps; handle routes with auth via reusable session state storage. Visibly warn that automation covers only a fraction of WCAG criteria (approximately one-third) and that a complementary manual checklist is required (keyboard, screen reader, contextual contrast, visible focus).

Acceptance criteria: the job runs on the CI platform and audits all routes; axe-core runs with a headless runner consistent with the stack and the WCAG level declared in config; the gate fails on critical and serious; a versioned baseline exists that distinguishes debt from regression; the auth flow runs before auditing when applicable; the pull request report includes rule, selector, severity, and impact; the local command replicates the CI one; the partial coverage warning is present.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Basic load and performance test
prompts.content:
Act as a senior performance and SRE engineer with experience in load testing distributed systems and diagnosing resource saturation. I want to discover where my system breaks under load before users discover it in production, turning the uncertainty of whether it will handle the peak into a defensible number and a prioritized list of bottlenecks, to decide capacity, autoscaling, and release go/no-go with evidence.

I need from you, in this order: (1) SLOs and pass/fail criteria: p95 and p99 latency, target throughput in req/s, and maximum error rate, each as a verifiable threshold. (2) Load model: target virtual users or req/s, arrival profile (constant, ramp, or spikes), weighted endpoint mix summing to 100%, and a test data strategy that avoids trivial caching through parameterization and unique data per iteration. (3) Three scenarios with duration and ramp: nominal at expected load, stress with an increasing ramp until degradation, and a sudden spike. (4) Executable script with hardcoded thresholds that abort or mark the run as failed on SLO violation, parameterized by environment and with prior warmup. (5) List of server-side metrics to instrument in parallel: CPU, memory, connections, database connection pool, queue depth, GC, and external dependency latency. (6) Reading method: how to locate the knee point on the latency-vs-throughput curve, how to isolate the limiting resource distinguishing CPU saturation, pool exhaustion, lock contention, or dependency latency, and an actionable findings checklist with severity.

Rules: never test against production without an agreed window and an abort plan; declare as [ASSUMPTION] every capacity or traffic data point you assume; mark as TODO any missing real value instead of inventing it; include a single-user baseline to separate intrinsic latency from load-induced latency; consider the coordinated omission effect and how your generator mitigates it.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. If you are missing the target system, the SLOs, or the reference traffic, ask for them: they are blockers. Deliver a document with a scenario table, a script commented with thresholds, a server instrumentation list, and an actionable findings checklist prioritized by severity.

prompts.title: Design a normalized database schema
prompts.content:
Act as a senior relational database engineer and data modeler, with experience in high-volume transactional schemas and query tuning. I need to design the persistence layer of an application: a normalized schema, correct from day one, with key, index, and denormalization decisions justified against the real query flows. A poorly modeled schema is paid for throughout the product's lifetime in update anomalies, duplicated data, costly migrations, and slow queries.

Before modeling, ask me for whatever is missing: the target relational engine and version, the application domain and purpose, the main entities with their attributes and uniqueness rules and the relationships I already intuit, the most frequent read and write flows the schema must serve quickly, and the order of magnitude of rows per table with its growth rate if I know it. Do not assume the engine or invent entities; mark any unavoidable assumption as [ASSUMPTION] with its impact if it turns out to be false.

Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. First restate the domain, entities, and business rules you detect and mark the gaps; then present your modeling plan; only then execute.

Deliver in four phases. Phase 1, Understanding: list entities, attributes, and detected business rules, with gaps marked. Phase 2, Logical modeling: functional dependencies, primary keys (prefer surrogate keys unless a natural key is clearly superior, and justify), relationships with foreign keys, many-to-many resolved with junction tables, and normalization to 3NF explaining what dependency each step resolves. Phase 3, Physical modeling: types and constraints for the engine's dialect, NOT NULL, CHECK, and UNIQUE constraints that encode business rules, ON DELETE / ON UPDATE policy for each foreign key, indexes derived one to one from the frequent flows (indexed FKs, composites for frequent filters with justified column order, unique ones for uniqueness rules), and denormalizations marked with their maintenance cost. Phase 4, Delivery: complete and executable DDL script without editing, entity-relationship diagram in Mermaid, and a table that justifies each key, index, constraint, and normalization level decision.

Detect and correct anti-patterns: lists or CSVs in a single column, volatile natural keys, absence of referential integrity, boolean columns for states that should be lookup tables, dates without time zone when it matters. For each one propose the correct alternative. Close with verifiable acceptance criteria: the DDL runs cleanly on the indicated engine, each table has a justified primary key, no FK is left unindexed, each index maps to a real flow, and every exception to 3NF is documented with its reason and cost.

prompts.title: Write safe database migrations
prompts.content:
Act as a senior database engineer specialized in zero-downtime schema changes on high-volume tables. I need a production schema migration that generates no downtime or data loss and that any engineer on the team can review, execute, and revert with confidence. If you are missing any essential data (the required schema change, the database engine and version, the table and approximate row count, the migration tool and format, or the deployment strategy), ask before assuming; mark anything not provided as [ASSUMPTION] or ask.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate the change you understand, classify it (additive, data transformation, or destructive), and present your expand-contract plan before writing code.

Proceed as follows:
1. Restate the change and classify it; list the code dependencies that touch it (reads, writes, ORM, views, triggers, FKs, jobs).
2. Design the expand-contract plan in backward-compatible phases (Expand, Backfill, Switch, Contract), indicating what code deployment accompanies each phase and why each is reversible except for the final contraction.
3. For each phase write the up and down scripts, idempotent (IF NOT EXISTS / IF EXISTS or equivalent) and transactional where the engine allows it; isolate blocking DDL from long transactions.
4. Create indexes in concurrent or non-blocking mode specific to the engine; run the backfill in batches with a row limit and pause between batches to avoid long locks.
5. Deliver a runbook with the exact execution order, integrity verification commands (counts, nulls, validated constraints, replica lag), and a rollback procedure per phase; mark each destructive step as irreversible with its prior safety window.

Final deliverable: the up/down scripts per phase plus the deployment and rollback runbook, ready for peer review. Justify the trade-offs (window duration, double-write cost, temporary columns/indexes) and warn about edge cases: NOT NULL FK on data with orphans, type change with precision loss, constraint validation locks, and backfill retries on mid-run failure.

prompts.title: Integrate a managed backend (Supabase / Firebase)
prompts.content:
Act as a senior full-stack engineer specialized in Backend as a Service integrations, with strong criteria on authentication, permission modeling, and data leak prevention. My application currently runs against mocked data or local state and needs a real backend to persist information across sessions, authenticate users, and isolate their data. Integrate a managed backend (Supabase or Firebase) securely from the first commit.

Produce, in this order: (1) justified choice between Supabase and Firebase for my stack, without mentioning costs or plans; if I already have a defined provider, justify how to use it better and declare the assumption. (2) Steps to create or reuse the project in the provider and obtain the keys, explicitly separating the public ones that travel to the client from those that must never leave the server (service role / Admin SDK), with a warning about what must NOT be versioned. (3) SDK client configuration with environment variables and an example file without real secrets, plus the .gitignore entry that protects the real file. (4) Complete authentication flow: registration, sign-in, sign-out, session persistence and refresh, initial loading state while the session resolves, and route or view protection. (5) Data model: tables or collections, key fields, types, relationships, and the owner column or field that enables isolation. (6) Concrete security rules (Row Level Security in Supabase or Security Rules in Firebase) that enforce the access rules and prevent cross-user access, with the note that the table or collection must remain denied by default. (7) Step-by-step manual test with two users that confirms the rules block reading and writing another user's data.

MetodologIA Protocol: first restate provider, stack, entities, access rules, and auth method as you understood them; if anything is missing or ambiguous ask in a single round before proceeding. Then present the plan: justified provider, list of entities, permission matrix per entity and operation (read/create/edit/delete), and the files to create or modify. Only then execute delivering applicable blocks with key placeholders marked. Close with the data isolation test and a secrets checklist confirming no sensitive key ended up in the client or in version control. Constraints: never mention prices or the word free; no real secret may appear in code, examples, or logs; the result must be runnable as-is with only placeholder replacements. If you are missing the provider, frontend stack, project state, entities, access rules, or auth method, ask before generating code.

prompts.title: Implement secure authentication
prompts.content:
Act as a senior backend security engineer, specialist in identity management and session handling per OWASP ASVS. I need to add secure authentication to my application: registration, login, session management, private-route protection, and logout. A correct implementation unlocks private functionality and trust; an incorrect one opens the door to credential theft, session hijacking, and data leaks.

Before generating code, ask me for whatever is missing so you don't assume: backend language and runtime, web or API framework, where the app runs (web, pure API, mobile), which routes or areas must be protected, which roles or profiles to support, whether there is multi-device session support, and what sensitive data is at stake. If I don't specify a session model, recommend one (server-side signed session cookie vs. short-lived access JWT plus rotating refresh) and justify the choice based on my attack surface.

Deliver a ready-to-integrate implementation with code commented on every security decision, organized by layer: 1) identity model with unique email or username and a password-hash field, never plaintext; 2) registration and login hashing with Argon2id preferred (bcrypt or scrypt acceptable, never MD5 or SHA1), with password-strength validation and identifier normalization; 3) session issuance per the chosen strategy, with short-lived access tokens (5–15 min) and a rotating revocable refresh token persisted server-side; 4) secure token storage in an HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite cookie, never in localStorage where XSS risk exists; 5) middleware that protects private routes, validates signature and expiration, and distinguishes 401 (unauthenticated) from 403 (unauthorized); 6) logout that invalidates the session or revokes the refresh token; 7) defenses: rate limiting with progressive lockout against brute force, CSRF protection when cookies are used, error responses that don't reveal whether a user exists (anti-enumeration), and a uniform response-time policy. Do not hardcode secrets: deliver the list of required environment variables.

Handle edge cases: password failing the policy, duplicate identifier on registration, expired or tampered token, already-rotated or revoked refresh token (reuse detection), and concurrent logout across multiple devices. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: first restate what you understand and present your plan (identity schema, justified session strategy, files to create or modify); only then generate code. Close with a table of environment variables and secrets, and a testing note: registration, valid and invalid login, access to a protected route with and without a token, logout, expiration, and refresh-token reuse. Flag any assumption with [ASSUMPTION].

prompts.title: Consume a third-party API with resilience
prompts.content: Act as a senior backend engineer expert in external-service integration and resilience patterns (timeouts, retries with exponential backoff and jitter, circuit breaker, idempotency, and observability). I need to consume a third-party API I don't control: it has variable latency, returns transient errors, and occasionally goes down; a naive integration propagates those failures to my users, exhausts connections, duplicates operations when retrying blindly, or takes down the service when the provider degrades. I want to turn that fragile dependency into an integration that fails in a predictable and contained manner. If you're missing any essential data (stack and HTTP client, API and operations with their read/write type, authentication method, which operations are idempotent and whether there is an idempotency key, rate limits and SLA, tolerable latency, and behavior under total failure), ask me before executing rather than assuming. Deliver: (1) an error-classification table that separates transient retryable errors (timeout, 429, 502, 503, 504, network cuts) from permanent non-retryable ones (400, 401, 403, 404, 422), with the action for each case; (2) a resilience policy with separate connection and read timeouts, bounded retries with exponential backoff and jitter only on transient errors and idempotent operations, Retry-After compliance, and a circuit breaker with an opening threshold, half-open state, and recovery time — delivering recommended values with their justification and how to derive them from the latency budget; (3) idempotency handling that uses or generates an idempotency key for writes so that a retry doesn't duplicate the effect, with criteria for persisting and reusing the key across retries; (4) a wrapper client in my stack that encapsulates authentication without leaking secrets, the above patterns, the mapping of HTTP errors to typed domain errors, and the degraded fallback, with commented code ready to run; (5) observability with structured logs without secrets, latency metrics (including p50/p95/p99 percentiles), error rate, and breaker state, with per-request correlation; (6) a test suite covering timeout, transient error with successful retry, permanent error without retry, open circuit breaker that fails fast, and idempotent retry that doesn't duplicate — using a provider double; (7) a degraded-behavior table showing what the system returns in each failure mode. Consider and resolve edge cases: thundering herd when the breaker reopens (gradual recovery or single-probe half-open), a missing or HTTP-date Retry-After, client cancellation or propagated deadline, a retry budget that must not exceed the tolerable latency, and backoff with a cap to avoid waiting indefinitely. Flag every inference about the provider with [ASSUMPTION] and don't present it as confirmed data. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: first interpret and restate what you understand, then present your plan, and only then execute. Close with a verifiable checklist: no permanent error is retried, retries are bounded and respect Retry-After, connection and read timeouts are separate and fit the latency budget, the breaker has three states, writes use a tested idempotency key, logs don't leak credentials, the client exposes typed errors and an explicit fallback, and the five failure-path tests pass. Respond in neutral professional English, no emojis.

prompts.title: Inbound and outbound webhooks
prompts.content:
Act as a senior backend engineer specialized in webhook integrations and reliable event delivery. I need a production-grade implementation of a webhook receiver and emitter, with store migrations and an executable test suite. Before coding, follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret what you understand (stack, emitting provider, signature scheme, persistence, retry policy), declare as [ASSUMPTION] any missing data (signing algorithm, header name, timestamp format, tolerance window, idempotency key), and ask me for it if it blocks correctness; Plan by presenting the endpoint contract, the table and key schema, and the delivery state machine (pending > delivered / retrying > dead-letter queue) before writing code; then Execute.

Inbound receiver: POST endpoint that reads the raw body before parsing, because the signature is calculated over the exact bytes; verify the HMAC-SHA256 signature from the signature header using constant-time comparison to prevent timing attacks; validate the timestamp window and reject out-of-range requests to stop replays; apply idempotency by persisting the event key with a uniqueness constraint at the engine level, and on duplicate do not reprocess and respond 2xx; respond 2xx quickly after queuing the real processing, 4xx for non-recoverable failures like an invalid signature, 5xx for retryable transients; never execute heavy business logic synchronously inside the request.

Outbound emitter: assemble the payload with event id, type, ISO-8601 timestamp, and data; sign the body with HMAC-SHA256 and the subscriber's secret; attach signature and timestamp headers; deliver with retries and exponential backoff plus jitter on 5xx or timeouts, never retry on 4xx, and after exhausting attempts move the event to a dead-letter queue; record every attempt (status, HTTP code, latency, attempt number) in an auditable delivery log. Handle secret rotation by supporting more than one valid secret during a transition window.

Deliver idiomatic stack code, idempotency-store and delivery-log migrations, and tests covering at minimum: valid and invalid signature, replay due to out-of-window timestamp, idempotent re-delivery of the same id without reprocessing, backoff with no-retry on 4xx, and dead-letter queue dispatch after exhausting attempts. Secrets only via environment variables, never in code. Close with instructions for configuring secrets and running the suite. If you don't have the stack, the provider, or the signature scheme, ask before assuming a nonexistent API. This is the StrategyAI that separates a prototype from an operable system.

prompts.title: Integrate a payment gateway (Stripe)
prompts.content:
Act as a senior backend engineer specialized in Stripe payment integrations and idempotent, secure transactional systems with reduced PCI scope. I want you to design and implement a functional and verifiable Stripe gateway integration, with commented code and a test guide. Before coding, ask me for any missing data: the stack (language, backend framework, and database), the billing model (one-time payment, recurring subscription, or both, with currency and trial period if applicable), the plan catalog with its mapping to Stripe Price IDs, how and where I persist the customer and subscription state (tables, status fields, relationship to stripe_customer_id), and which Stripe events the backend must react to. If I don't define events, default to checkout.session.completed, invoice.paid, invoice.payment_failed, customer.subscription.updated, and customer.subscription.deleted.

Proceed as follows: (1) Model the money flow end-to-end, declaring what happens at the client, server, and Stripe, and where the single source of truth for payment state lives; treat Stripe as the authority on billing and your database as a derived replica of its events. (2) Implement server-side the creation of the Checkout session or PaymentIntent per the billing model, keeping the secret key only on the backend and exposing only the publishable key to the frontend; delegate card capture to Stripe-hosted components so no raw card data touches your server. (3) For subscriptions, create or reference the Customer, Price, and Subscription, and map the lifecycle (active, in grace period, delinquent, canceled) to status fields in the database. (4) Implement the webhooks endpoint: verify the signature with the webhook secret using the raw request body before parsing, process each event idempotently by recording the id of the already-applied event to discard re-deliveries, and respond 2xx only once the effect has been persisted. (5) Handle errors, retries, and intermediate states without leaving the user or the database inconsistent; operate currency in its smallest integer unit and never log raw card data or secrets. (6) Deliver the list of environment variables and secrets, the Stripe CLI command for replaying webhooks to the local environment, and the pre-production verification checklist.

Cover these edge cases: webhook arriving before the session creation finishes persisting, out-of-order event (an old update that must not overwrite a newer state), payment failing after the trial period, refund or dispute, and mid-cycle plan change. Close with the checklist marked or with the outstanding items flagged and a note of the assumptions you made.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Integrate an LLM as an app feature
prompts.content: Act as a senior backend engineer specialized in integrating LLMs into production, with experience in streaming, cost control, and prompt security. I need to turn an LLM call into a production feature inside my application, not a demo: the app must receive the user's input, call the model, and return the response as a token-by-token stream, with spend bounded per user or session and the prompt protected against injection and leaks. Before executing, restate what you understand and present your plan. If you're missing any essential data (which app and feature the LLM is embedded in, backend language and framework, available provider/model/SDK, budget and cost-control unit, required guard rules, or attachments such as the endpoint schema or the current system prompt), ask me for everything in a single round before coding; don't invent those data. Design and implement the endpoint end-to-end: (1) Endpoint contract: route, method, request shape (user message, session or user identifier, optional context) and streaming response shape, including the close event and the error event, plus the correct status code and headers for SSE. (2) Token-by-token streaming with server-sent events or the stack-equivalent mechanism, flushing each fragment to the client without buffering the full response, with a heartbeat to keep the connection alive. (3) Provider client layer with a per-call timeout, retries with exponential backoff and jitter only on transient errors (rate limit, 5xx, network), idempotency to avoid duplicate charges, and request cancellation toward the model when the user closes the connection. (4) Prompt assembly separating system, retrieved context, and user message; sanitize the input and apply the required guards against instruction injection and system-prompt leaks, treating user content as data and not as instructions, with explicit delimiters. (5) Cost control: count or estimate input and output tokens, apply the per-user or per-session limit over a defined window, and cut with a clear message and a typed error event when the threshold is exceeded; decide and document whether counting is prior (estimated) or posterior (actual). (6) Provider error handling (rate limit, timeout, blocked content, network failure, empty response) translated into clear client responses without leaking internal details or keys, with a correlation id for support. (7) Structured log per call: tokens consumed, latency, model, result, cut reason, and correlation id, without logging sensitive content or keys. Respect the project's real stack and names; flag any missing data as an explicit assumption and continue without inventing. Deliver: endpoint code, model client layer, prompt assembly with guards and cost control, plus integration notes (environment variables, how to test streaming locally, where to adjust model and budget). Close with a verification checklist marked against the delivered code.

prompts.title: Build a minimum viable RAG
prompts.content:
I need a minimum viable RAG over my own data that answers with verifiable backing and not from the model's intuition. I want reliable conversational search over my corpus: every claim must trace to a source and, when there isn't enough evidence, the system must declare it instead of inventing. The index must be rebuildable from scratch with a single command and the architecture must scale without being redone.

Act as a senior RAG systems and AI backend engineer, focused on reliable retrieval and attributable responses. Give me a complete, executable, commented pipeline, with a folder structure, environment variables, an indexing command, and a query command.

Cover these stages: ingestion (load the corpus, normalize text, extract metadata such as title, source, date, and section, clean headers, footers, and OCR artifacts); chunking respecting semantic boundaries and preserving source identifier and position; embeddings and a persistent, rebuildable index; top-k similarity retrieval with context assembly that respects the generator's window; cited generation that answers only from sources and appends citations [n] mapped to source and fragment, declaring when evidence is missing; and a small evaluation set with metrics for retrieval hit rate, source fidelity, and citation coverage.

Make your assumptions and decisions explicit (embedding model, vector store, indexing idempotency, handling of documents that exceed the window). If you're missing a critical piece of data such as the stack, corpus type, available models, or where to persist the index, ask me before generating code rather than assuming. Before executing, restate what you understood and present your plan.

Close with: minimal repository with commented code, two commands (index and query), evaluation layer, execution README, and a scaling note for the corpus without redoing the architecture.

prompts.title: Cron jobs and background tasks
prompts.content:
Act as a senior backend engineer specialized in distributed systems, message queues, and reliable asynchronous processing. Design and implement a deploy-ready system of cron jobs and background tasks whose goal is to not lose work, not duplicate it, and to be observable and operable.

If any critical data is missing (app stack and runtime; specific jobs separating scheduled from async; available infrastructure such as Redis, monolith, containers, or serverless, cloud provider, and number of instances; expected reliability guarantees such as at-least-once vs. exactly-once-effect, maximum attempts, retry window, and latency SLA; schedule expressions and timezone), ask for it before coding the critical parts. Don't assume Redis or services the user doesn't have; if you propose a value due to missing data, flag it as [ASSUMPTION].

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand and separate scheduled jobs from async ones, classifying each by criticality and side effect (charges, emails, writes). Then present your plan. Only then execute.

Deliver: 1) technically justified mechanism decision (scheduler for scheduled, queue for async) with explicit trade-offs and consistent with the real infrastructure; 2) job contract (name, typed payload, priority, timeout, retries with exponential backoff plus jitter, max attempts before dead-letter queue); 3) real idempotency (idempotency key, deduplication, handlers safe on re-execution); 4) concurrency (number of workers, rate limiting toward external dependencies, leader lock or single-flight so the cron doesn't fire duplicated across instances); 5) observability (structured logs with job id, metrics for queued, completed, failed, latency, and queue depth, alerts on DLQ and stuck jobs); 6) graceful shutdown that drains the in-flight job before terminating the worker on a deploy; 7) executable code (scheduler, queue definition, example worker, one real idempotent job from your use case, and deployment configuration) plus a test demonstrating retry and deduplication.

Acceptance criteria: the mechanism is consistent with the real infrastructure; idempotency verifiable under re-execution; a single cron fire across N instances; in-flight work never lost on deploy; every decision made due to missing data is marked [ASSUMPTION]. Close when the package is deployable and the test demonstrates retry and deduplication.

prompts.title: Cache and query optimization
prompts.content: Act as a senior backend engineer specialized in database performance, index design, and caching. I have an endpoint, view, report, or job that feels slow and I want to eliminate the bottleneck without scaling hardware or changing the system's observable behavior. Work as follows: first gather the minimum evidence (database engine and version, the SQL query or ORM code, the execution plan or slow-query log, the row volume of the affected tables, and the current latency vs. the desired latency); if you're missing any of these, ask me and don't invent values. Then establish a real baseline, not an estimate: list the dominant queries by cost or frequency and classify each problem as N+1 (one query per iterated row), full scan due to a missing index, or repeated and cacheable recomputation. For each N+1, rewrite to a single query with a join or eager loading and show the before and after. For each full scan, propose the exact index with columns, order, and type (composite or partial when applicable) and deliver idempotent migration SQL, warning about its cost in writes and storage. For each expensive recomputation, define a cache layer with key, TTL, and explicit invalidation policy; never propose a cache without invalidation. Consider edge cases: data with high write cardinality where an index penalizes more than it helps, queries that already use an index but with the wrong column order, cache that may serve stale data in transactional flows, and low selectivity that makes an index useless. Explicitly discard every index or cache that doesn't pay for itself. Close with a repeatable verification plan: re-run the execution plan, compare plan and latency, and confirm that the functional result hasn't changed. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Design an MCP server for the app
prompts.content:
Act as a senior agent-integration architect, specialist in the Model Context Protocol (MCP), typed API design, and application security. I want the complete design of an MCP server for my app, ready to implement, that turns its capabilities into a stable tool contract without coupling each agent to the internal API and while preserving control of permissions and effects in the app.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate which app it is, its stack and persistence, the capabilities to expose, the current authentication model, the sensitive actions, and the intended transport; present your plan; then execute. If any of those pieces of data are missing, ask me for them before proceeding and don't invent capabilities or permissions.

Execute in six phases:
1) Inventory: list every capability with its effect type (read, reversible mutation, destructive mutation), whether it handles PII, and its expected cost or latency.
2) Classification: assign each capability to one of the three MCP surfaces and justify. Resources = read-only data addressable by URI (no effects). Tools = actions with effects and parameterized reads. Prompts = reusable interaction templates. Tiebreaker rule: if it has side effects or requires execution parameters, it goes to tool; if it's a pure, cacheable read, it goes to resource.
3) Contracts: for every tool define the name in snake_case, an agent-oriented description (what it does, when to use it, when not to), a JSON Schema input schema with types, required fields, defaults, and validations, an output schema, side effects, idempotency, and a structured error field.
4) Security: design auth and authz, declare which credential the server uses, how it delegates end-user permission, minimum scopes per tool, explicit prior confirmation for every destructive action, and PII controls (minimization, masking, don't log secrets).
5) Robustness: define agent-readable error codes, cursor-based pagination for large collections, rate limits and timeouts, and choose the transport (stdio for local, HTTP with SSE for remote), justifying the decision.
6) Verification: build the test plan with valid, invalid, and edge cases per tool, including permission denied, confirmation rejected, and malformed input.

Declare your assumptions. Flag anything you can't infer as pending confirmation rather than inventing it. Don't expose as a tool anything that depends on undocumented implicit state.

Deliverable: design document with (1) capabilities table classified with effect and PII, (2) detailed contract per tool, (3) textual diagram of the agent-server-app flow including the confirmation point, (4) list of security controls with scope per tool, and (5) test plan per tool with verifiable acceptance criteria.

prompts.title: Deploy to Vercel with correct configuration
prompts.content:
Act as a senior platform/DevOps engineer specialized in Vercel deployments and git-push pipelines. I want to leave my project deployed on Vercel cleanly and reproducibly: deterministic build, environment variables separated by environment, and an operational domain. A well-configured deploy unlocks Preview environments per branch, automatic deployments on git push, and immediate rollbacks; the antipattern to avoid is the deploy that works locally but fails on Vercel due to fragile auto-detection, missing variables, or incorrectly pointed DNS.

If you're missing any essential data (project or repo, framework and version, package manager and lockfile, environment variables with their target environment, domain and DNS provider), ask me for them before continuing rather than assuming.

Proceed in four phases. Phase 1, read-only diagnosis: check the git state, the contents of the .vercel folder (project.json/repo.json to know whether it's linked), CLI authentication, and the detected framework; report findings before changing anything. Phase 2, configuration: draft an explicit vercel.json with framework preset, buildCommand, outputDirectory, installCommand, and Node version (in the project's nodeVersion or in package.json's engines.node), to avoid depending on auto-detection; build the environment-variable matrix per environment distinguishing secrets vs. public (client prefix like NEXT_PUBLIC_/VITE_/PUBLIC_) and flag missing ones; highlight risks such as a missing lockfile, Node version mismatch, or a secret exposed with a public prefix. Phase 3, deployment: run a Preview deploy first and deliver its URL; recommend linking the repo so that git push governs the environments (non-production branch to Preview, production branch to Production); production only under explicit request, ideally by promoting an already-validated Preview. Phase 4, domain and verification: assign the domain, define DNS records per apex (A) or subdomain (CNAME), verify the domain, and run the post-deploy checklist.

Security rules: always work in Preview by default, never touch Production without explicit instruction, and never print values of secret variables (only their names and environment). Assume timezone America/Bogota and don't invent variable names or domains.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Deliver: final vercel.json block, environment-variable table per environment, DNS plan, and the numbered list of exact commands to deploy to Preview and obtain the URL.

prompts.title: Minimal CI/CD pipeline for vibe coding
prompts.content:
Act as a senior platform and DevOps engineer specialized in CI/CD workflows for teams coding with AI assistants. Design a minimal, functional and fail-safe CI/CD pipeline that runs on every push and on every pull request, with three stages chained by explicit gates: lint (style and format), test (unit tests with coverage) and deploy (automatic publication), where deploy only runs if lint and test pass green and only from the main branch.

Before generating anything, confirm with me: language and framework, CI/CD platform, package manager and install command, minimum coverage threshold that approves the gate, and environment/deploy provider. If any of these are missing, ask for them; do not assume silently.

Deliver:
1. The complete workflow file, commented and ready to commit, with the three jobs chained by explicit dependencies and the branch condition in the deploy job.
2. A gates table: for each stage, the exact package manager command, the approval threshold (test requires the agreed minimum coverage) and the blocking condition that stops the chain.
3. The dependency caching strategy with a stable key derived from the lock file, and correct invalidation when dependencies change.
4. Secrets management for the deploy referenced from the platform's secure store, with least-privilege principle and log masking; never in plain text or in the repository.
5. The branch protection rule that requires a green pipeline as a mandatory check before merging (included as configuration steps, not just described).
6. An end-to-end verification checklist: green test push, intentional failure that blocks, merge blocked by missing check, and successful deploy only from the main branch.

Rules: do not invent non-existent actions, commands or flags from the ecosystem; mark any assumption as [ASSUMPTION] with its alternative. Design the pipeline idempotent and fast (effective cache, no decorative steps), with concurrency that cancels stale runs on the same branch. Close by explaining how to read a failure based on the gate that stopped it (lint vs test vs deploy) and how to safely retry.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Secure environment variable management
prompts.content:
Act as a senior platform and applied security engineer, specialist in application configuration and secrets management. I am going to organize the environment variable management of my application so that each environment has its own values and no secret leaks to the repository or the browser bundle. The objective is to unlock reproducible deploys, secret rotation without touching code and strict separation between what lives on the server and what reaches the client. The risk to eliminate is concrete: a committed or bundle-exposed secret forces credential rotation and can compromise the database or payments.

Deliver a configuration guide ready to apply plus the concrete files:
1. File hierarchy: a versioned .env.example with all keys (server and public) with dummy values and comments, and a .env per environment NOT versioned with the real values; clarify the precedence order if the framework loads several .env files.
2. The exact .gitignore lines that ignore all .env files with real values and keep .env.example.
3. Explicit separation of server variables (never reach the client) and public ones, using the public prefix corresponding to the framework; warn that any server key without that prefix must never be imported in code that runs in the browser, and note the edge case of public variables inlined at build time that require a rebuild to change.
4. Startup validation with a central schema that fails immediately if a required variable is missing or has an invalid format, naming the variable in the message; distinguish required variables, optional with default and conditional by environment.
5. How to load real production secrets from the provider's secrets manager without writing them to disk, how to reference them by environment and how to rotate them without downtime.
6. A pre-deploy verification checklist and the adoption order.

Apply the MetodologIA Protocol: first reframe what you understand and present your plan; then execute. If the framework, hosting provider, environment list or any variable is missing, ask before generating files. Do not include any real values in versioned files; use only placeholders.

prompts.title: Preview deployments per pull request
prompts.content:
