Act as a senior platform engineer specialized in CI/CD and ephemeral environments (review apps), with experience in data isolation and cost control in preview environments. I want to enable preview deployments per pull request: so that each change can be reviewed running on a real, isolated URL before merging, not just by reading the diff. The environment should be born when the PR opens, redeploy on each push and die when it is closed or merged, without residues or dangling costs.

Deliver the complete, commit-ready configuration. Follow these steps:
1. Generate the CI pipeline that fires on PR events (opened, synchronize, reopened) and installs dependencies, builds and deploys the ephemeral environment on the target platform.
2. Define the unique and reproducible URL scheme per PR (by PR number or by branch), how it resolves on each synchronize and how to avoid collision or overwriting between concurrent PRs.
3. Add a teardown job triggered when the PR is closed or merged that destroys the environment and frees resources; cover the case of abandoned PRs with an age sweep (TTL).
4. Specify data and secrets isolation: ephemeral database or sandbox seeded with synthetic data, preview-scoped secrets with minimal permissions, zero read or write access to production. If the PR comes from a fork, restrict secrets exposure.
5. Publish an idempotent automatic comment on the PR (updates the same comment, does not accumulate) with the preview URL and the deployment status (in progress, ready, failed) plus the link to logs.

MetodologIA Protocol: first reframe what you understand and present your plan (events, URL scheme, secrets and data handling, teardown policy), marking each assumed value as [ASSUMPTION]; then execute. Deliver each configuration file in a separate block, with an explanation below of what it does and why. Explicitly point out where a poorly isolated preview can leak production data or leave dangling costs, and how to mitigate it. If any critical data is missing (repository, stack, platform, CI or data and secrets strategy), ask for it before generating configuration. Close with a verification checklist to validate the first preview end to end.

prompts.title: Basic observability in production
prompts.content: Act as a senior SRE and observability engineer with experience operating production services under on-call rotation. My application has just gone to production and the team is operating blind: we do not know if it is serving traffic, if it is throwing errors or how long it takes to respond. I want the minimum essential that reduces uncertainty the most, not a complete platform. Before coding, ask for the language and framework, the production deployment environment and the telemetry destination; if a piece of data is missing that would prevent giving executable code, ask for it instead of assuming, and mark any assumption with [ASSUMPTION]. Then order the pieces by uncertainty reduction and deliver, for each one, the concrete code, where to place it in the codebase and why there, plus a verification executable in under five minutes. Pieces: (1) Structured logs in JSON with level, UTC ISO-8601 timestamp, message and a request ID propagated end to end to correlate a complete request; take or generate the ID at the edge (incoming header or uuid) and carry it through context, not as a manual parameter. (2) Centralized error capture: global handler for unhandled exceptions with stack trace and request context (path, method, request ID, status), that logs and returns a clean 500 error without leaking internals or secrets to the client. (3) Four golden signals as minimum metrics: latency (p50 and p95 per endpoint, measured as histogram not average), traffic (requests per minute), error rate (percentage of 5xx separated from 4xx, which are client-side) and saturation (CPU, memory or queue depth). (4) Health check that distinguishes liveness (the process is alive, without touching dependencies) from readiness (critical dependencies ready, with timeout to avoid hanging the check), suitable for the indicated environment. (5) One or two initial alerts with explicit numeric threshold and evaluation window, actionable and without noise. Cardinality: never use high-cardinality identifiers (user ID, request ID, path with parameters) as a metric label; group by normalized path. Close with an acceptance checklist and point out what is missing to mature (distributed traces, formal SLOs, dashboards), without implementing it now. Reframe what you understand and present your prioritized plan before executing.

prompts.title: Feature flags and gradual rollout
prompts.content: Act as a senior release engineering and progressive delivery engineer (canary, dark launch, kill switch) expert in preventing flags from becoming technical debt. We are going to put a feature into production behind a feature flag to decouple the code deploy from its activation for users: the new code travels off, is turned on progressively and observedly, and can be turned off instantly without redeploy if something degrades. The flag is a runtime switch with an owner, lifecycle and retirement date, not a forgotten if statement. If you have not been given the feature name, target stack and language, where flags live and are edited, the stable user attribute for deterministic rollout, the desired rollout stages or the relevant attachments, ask for them before continuing. Deliver: (1) a flag evaluation service with a single source of truth and a unique function isFlagActive(name, context) with safe default OFF; (2) deterministic assignment by stable hash of the user identifier against the target percentage, so that the same user always falls on the same side and between stages a user already exposed never goes back to control (monotonic rollout); (3) a single example branching point where the new and old routes coexist behind the same flag, without duplicating logic or scattering flags through the code; (4) global kill switch that turns off the feature for everyone instantly without redeploy, fail-closed: if the flags source does not respond, times out or returns corrupt data, it evaluates to OFF, with last-good-value cache and its explicit expiration policy; (5) instrumentation with logs and metrics tagged by variant (exposed vs control) plus the reason for the decision (kill_switch, percentage, override, fallback), to compare groups and audit; (6) stages table with measurable advance and rollback criteria per stage (which metric, which threshold, which observation window), plus a flag and old code retirement plan when stabilizing at 100%. Explain assumptions, limits and trade-offs explicitly: concurrency of several flags, anonymous users without a stable identifier, override lists for internal or QA users, consistency between service instances and the cost of flag evaluation in the hot path. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret what you understand, Plan and present your plan, then Execute. Close only when the quality checklist is verified.

prompts.title: Custom domain, SSL and DNS
prompts.content:
Act as a senior platform and DNS engineer, expert in TLS/ACME certificates and zero-downtime production cutovers. I have a deployed app that responds on a temporary provider URL and I want to serve it from my own domain with valid HTTPS, without downtime if there is already traffic, with the certificate renewing itself and with a clear path back if something fails.

Before touching any record, ask and confirm what is missing: domain and subdomains (apex, www, wildcard if applicable), where the DNS zone is managed and whether it supports ALIAS/ANAME for the apex, deployment target and its pointing value (fixed IP for A/AAAA, hostname for CNAME, or ALIAS/ANAME), certificate issuance method (managed by hosting or ACME HTTP-01 / DNS-01), whether the domain is already receiving production traffic and the current TTL, and the available maintenance window. If a piece of data blocks a decision, do not assume: ask for it.

Deliver a plan executed and verified in five phases: (1) Preparation and baseline: document with dig/nslookup the current records and TTL, lower the TTL of the record to be changed (e.g. 300 s) and wait for the old TTL to expire so the cutover propagates quickly. (2) Certificate: choose HTTP-01 if the origin exposes port 80, or DNS-01 with TXT _acme-challenge if going through a CDN, is apex or needs a wildcard; issue and verify SAN, dates, issuer and complete fullchain. (3) Name topology: apex via ALIAS/ANAME or A/AAAA depending on provider support, www as CNAME; declare the canonical host and leave the 301 redirect from the non-canonical one. (4) Zero-downtime cutover: update the record to the new destination only when the certificate is already valid at the destination, verify resolution from at least two independent resolvers, validate fullchain and test HTTPS, the HTTP to HTTPS redirect and HSTS if applicable. (5) Hardening and close: raise the TTL to a stable value (e.g. 3600 s), confirm automatic renewal and record the exact rollback.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing. Edge cases to cover: apex without ALIAS/ANAME support (use canonical subdomain or provider flattening), CAA blocking the chosen CA, CA rate limits during testing (use staging), and domain behind proxy/CDN that terminates TLS on its own. A poorly planned cutover strategy produces downtime or a broken padlock; a well-planned one is invisible.

Deliverable: final DNS records table (type, name, value, TTL), verification commands with their expected output, certificate issuance and renewal method, and step-by-step rollback procedure (previous record, value, TTL and reversion order). If you need any data to start, ask me.

prompts.title: Rollback and contingency plan
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Site Reliability Engineer with experience in high-risk deployments, database migrations and production incident recovery. I need a rollback and contingency runbook executable by any on-call person, even at 3 a.m. with no prior context: the objective is to turn panic into a repeatable sequence that reverts in minutes, with data intact, without depending on whoever remembers the right command.

Before drafting, confirm with me: what the application is and what it does, the stack and deploy platform, the current release strategy (blue-green, canary, rolling or direct replacement), the database engine and how migrations are applied, and the target RTO (maximum acceptable time to be healthy again). If any data is missing or ambiguous, ask for it; do not invent infrastructure.

Deliver, numbered:
1. Trigger criteria table: measurable thresholds (error rate, p95 latency, success rate, alerts) with an explicit time window that force a revert, and who has authority to decide the rollback and who to block it (freeze).
2. Reversion mechanics for the release strategy with the exact commands or steps: traffic switch, pinned previous version, scaling, and cache/CDN invalidation if applicable.
3. Data handling: classify each migration as reversible or irreversible, apply the expand-contract pattern to avoid destructive changes, define prior backup or snapshot with restore point, and identify the point of no return (when reverting only the code is no longer enough).
4. Step-by-step reversion sequence with estimated times per step that respect the RTO; revert traffic before data when possible.
5. Post-rollback verification: smoke tests, health checks and data integrity to declare the service healthy, with an explicit criterion for when NOT to declare resolved.
6. Communication: who to notify, channel and brief incident message template (opening, update, close).
7. Edge cases: what to do if the rollback also fails (plan B), if an irreversible migration has already run, and if the prior backup does not exist or is not restorable.

Mark with [ASSUMPTION] every assumption about the environment that has not been confirmed. Close with a verification checklist ready to paste into the team's operational documentation.

prompts.title: Optimize bundle and Core Web Vitals
prompts.content:
Act as a senior web performance engineer specialized in Core Web Vitals and bundle optimization in modern applications. My application is slow and I want to turn that vague perception into a measurable plan of improvements prioritized by impact, without rewriting the product.

Before moving forward, ask me for what you need: the project stack and framework, the URL or build path to analyze, the concrete and measurable target metric, the tool with which it will be measured and the constraints to respect. If any critical data is missing or ambiguous, ask for it; do not assume.

Then proceed as follows. First, measure the baseline and separate laboratory metrics from field metrics when both exist; identify the worst metric and its probable root cause (LCP is usually a large critical resource or a slow server; INP is usually JavaScript blocking the main thread or heavy handlers; CLS is usually elements without reserved dimensions, fonts with swap or late insertions). Second, break down the bundle: heaviest modules, duplicated or oversized dependencies, unnecessary polyfills and unused code on the critical path. Third, propose interventions separating bundle gains (code splitting by route, lazy loading, tree shaking, replacement of heavy dependencies, Brotli or gzip compression, deduplication) from render gains (preload of the LCP resource, defer or async of scripts, space reservation anti-CLS, fragmentation of long tasks for INP, fetch priority); each intervention with its concrete change, the metric it improves, the risk and an effort estimate. Fourth, define how to re-measure with the same tool and conditions, and the exact threshold that confirms the goal.

Edge cases: if field and lab diverge, prioritize field and explain the gap; if a constraint prohibits a high-impact intervention, offer the best permitted alternative and declare the lost gain; if there are no field metrics, say so and work with lab marking the limitation. Do not invent figures: when a real measurement is missing, ask for it and mark the gap as [ASSUMPTION]. Every improvement must trace to an observed cause, not to a generic best practice.

Deliver: a baseline findings table per metric with value, goal and cause; a list prioritized by impact over effort, each item with the affected metric, risk and effort; and a before/after verification checklist. MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. Reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Containerize the app with Docker
prompts.content: Act as a senior platform engineer with real Docker production experience and image optimization. I want to containerize my application to eliminate the 'it works on my machine' problem, achieve a reproducible build, single-command onboarding and a deployable artifact on any orchestrator. First inspect the code and confirm language, framework, dependency manager, start command, port and external services (database, cache, queue). What you cannot infer with certainty, ask for; do not invent versions, ports or paths. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the data, reframe what you understood, present your plan and only then execute. Deliver, ready to use: 1) Multi-stage Dockerfile with build stage and minimal runtime, base image with version pinned by digest or exact tag (never latest), non-root user, layers ordered for cache (copy dependency manifest and install before copying code), build variables via ARG, EXPOSE for the port, HEALTHCHECK that validates the app responds and CMD in exec form; 2) .dockerignore that excludes version control, local dependencies, build artifacts, environment files with secrets, logs, caches and temporaries; 3) docker-compose for development with hot-reload via code volume, variables from .env, port mapping and external services with persistence volumes, healthchecks and startup dependencies by health condition; 4) production compose with built image without mounted code, restart policy, CPU and memory limits, no debug ports exposed and secrets injected by environment or orchestrator; 5) exact commands block to build, bring up dev, bring up prod and verify that the app responds, with the expected result. Declare explicit assumptions, edge cases (compiled vs interpreted apps, database migrations at startup, static files, graceful shutdown signals) and justify each trade-off decision. Do not include secrets in layers or in the final image.

prompts.title: Critical review of AI-generated code
prompts.content:
Act as a senior software engineer specialized in critical code review and application security, with practice in auditing the output of AI agents and assistants and distinguishing plausible from correct. An AI assistant produced a code fragment and, before integrating it, I need a critical review and not a complacent validation: the risk of AI-generated code almost never lies in the obvious, but in subtle bugs, false assumptions about data or environment, and shortcuts that pass the happy path but break in production. Your goal is to separate what the code claims to do from what it actually does.

Before auditing, apply the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe in your own words what the code should do, under what stack and constraints it runs, and what risk surface you prioritized; present your review plan; then execute. If you are missing the code, task context, stack or constraints to audit rigorously, ask for them instead of assuming.

Structure the audit as follows: (1) Framing: confirm the code's purpose and explicitly declare what parts of the context you do not have in view. (2) Layer 1 - Correctness: subtle bugs, boundary conditions (empty, null, indices), off-by-one, loose type comparisons, ignored return values, async without await, unclosed resources, silenced errors, concurrency. (3) Layer 2 - False assumptions: what the code takes for granted without verifying (field always present, input already validated, infallible network, stable collection order, assumed library or version behavior). (4) Layer 3 - Dangerous shortcuts: empty catch, secrets in plain text, injection by concatenation of queries or commands, missing input validation, broad permissions, invented or non-existent dependencies, happy-path-only route. (5) Layer 4 - Maintainability: unnecessary complexity, duplication, misleading names, absence of tests on critical paths. (6) Integration verdict: Ready to integrate / Integrate with corrections / Do not integrate, with the list of blockers.

For each finding give: exact location (line or block), 'what the code thinks happens' versus 'what actually happens', severity (Critical / High / Medium / Low) and concrete impact. For each Critical or High finding include a minimal code patch. Honesty rules: do not invent vulnerabilities to appear rigorous; if an area is correct, declare it; mark [ASSUMPTION] everything that depends on context you do not have in view; do not use invented data or figures. Deliver a table or list of findings prioritized by severity (by impact and probability, not by count), the minimal patches, and the final verdict with blockers.

prompts.title: Quick security audit (OWASP)
prompts.content: Act as a senior application security engineer (AppSec) with experience in code review, threat modeling, and practical remediation. Perform a fast, prioritized security audit of my application against the OWASP Top 10 (2021). Before concluding, gather context: you need to know the stack (language, framework, database, hosting), the exposure surface (public endpoints, authentication, session handling, location of secrets), and the flow of user inputs toward the database or operating system. If any of these data points or the relevant code are missing, ask for them before evaluating; do not invent vulnerabilities or assume configurations you cannot see. Walk through each of the ten categories one by one: A01 broken access control, A02 cryptographic failures, A03 injection (SQL, NoSQL, commands, XSS), A04 insecure design, A05 security misconfiguration, A06 vulnerable and outdated components, A07 identification and authentication failures, A08 software and data integrity failures, A09 security logging and monitoring failures, A10 SSRF. Explicitly declare non-applicable categories and explain why. For each finding record: concrete evidence (file, line, or pattern), attack vector, and severity (critical, high, medium, low) justified by exploitability times impact. Mark as [ASSUMPTION] any finding without visible code and indicate what data is missing to confirm it. Write the exact ready-to-apply fix (corrected code or configuration), not generic advice. Order from highest to lowest risk and build a remediation plan across three horizons: today, this week, this month. Deliver a findings table ordered by severity (OWASP category, evidence, vector, severity), a block of applicable fixes, and the prioritized plan. MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Detect and remediate leaked secrets
prompts.content:
Act as a senior application security engineer (AppSec) specializing in secrets management and credential exposure response. Your task is to audit a repository for leaked secrets and deliver an actionable remediation plan. Before executing, apply the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret what you understand, Plan your approach, and only then Execute. Restate the objective and present your plan in one or two lines before acting.

Proceed as follows: (1) Inventory: enumerate branches, age and depth of the history, and confirm whether the repository is public or private, because visibility sets the rotation clock. (2) Detection: scan the working tree AND the complete commit history, not just the latest commit, looking for API keys, access tokens, private keys, connection strings with credentials, and high-entropy strings; consolidate findings without showing any secret in plaintext. (3) Per-finding record: file and line, commit and introduction date, secret type, obfuscated fragment (first 4 characters only), and live or test status. (4) Triage: classify each finding by severity (critical, high, medium, low) by crossing the access scope with repo visibility, and separate probable false positives (placeholders, documentation examples, test values) with justification. (5) Remediation in two lanes: rotation lane (for each live credential, the provider, the revocation and re-issuance procedure, and the execution order) and history purge lane (the rewrite tool, the coordinated force-push, and the notice for the team to re-clone). (6) Prevention and verification: define a detection pre-commit hook, migration to environment variables, and exclusion file, plus the closure criterion: a clean re-scan of the tree and history after the purge.

If you are missing any data needed to execute rigorously (path or repository name, visibility, target providers, preferred purge tool, or remediation deadline), ask me before continuing rather than assuming it. Final deliverable: classified findings table, two-lane remediation plan, and list of preventive controls. Inviolable rule: no complete secret appears in plaintext anywhere in the output.

prompts.title: Input validation and sanitization against injection
prompts.content:
Act as a senior application security engineer (AppSec) specializing in injection prevention, with command of the OWASP Top 10, OWASP Cheat Sheets, and secure coding. I need to harden my application against injection from a non-negotiable principle: no external input is trustworthy (forms, query params, headers, cookies, JSON payloads, uploaded files, API calls, and outputs from language models). Injection occurs when untrusted data is interpreted as code or a command in some interpreter (SQL, NoSQL, shell, browser, LDAP, XPath, parser, template engine, model); that is why the defense is not a single filter but positive validation at the edge plus a specific barrier at each context of use.

Deliver: (1) an inventory of input surfaces with their per-field contract (type, format, length, range, required/optional, allowed characters); (2) the positive validation layer with allowlist, anchored regexes, and early rejection with the correct status code; (3) the correct barrier per destination: parameterized queries/prepared statements for SQL and typed operators for NoSQL, shell-free APIs with arguments as an array for commands, contextual output encoding plus CSP for HTML, safe escaping or parsing for LDAP/XPath and deserialization with an allowlist of types, canonicalization and path confinement against path traversal, strict separation of instructions and data against prompt injection; (4) sanitization with a maintained allowlist-based library (like DOMPurify) only where rejection is not an option; (5) an abuse case suite with real vectors (quotes, union/boolean, null bytes, ../, double encoding, script tags, NoSQL operators, instruction sequences) that demonstrates neutralization barrier by barrier.

Rules: positive validation (allowlist), never negative (blocklist); regexes always anchored with ^ and $; rejection at the edge before touching logic, with a clear message that does not leak internal details; defense in depth (validating does not excuse parameterizing); fail closed on ambiguous data; handle Unicode, normalization, and multibyte correctly; treat model output as untrusted input. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] any stack detail you infer. If the stack, the inputs to protect, or the priority threats are missing, ask before generating code.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Vulnerable dependency review
prompts.content:
Act as a senior software supply chain security engineer (SCA), specialist in OSV/GHSA advisories and semver update policies. I need to audit the dependencies of my project and obtain an actionable remediation plan. If you are missing any essential data (repository path or stack, package manager and language, minimum severity to act on, appetite for breaking changes, or the command that keeps build/tests green), ask in a single round before starting and do not invent values.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand about the repository and its risk policy, then present your audit plan, and only then execute.

Proceed as follows: (1) Detect the project manifest and lockfile and set the correct ecosystem, manager, and native audit command (npm/pnpm audit, pip-audit, govulncheck, cargo audit, osv-scanner); if there is no lockfile, declare it as a limit because transitive versions will not be exact. (2) Inventory direct and transitive dependencies with their resolved version. (3) Cross-reference each dependency against known vulnerabilities via native audit plus OSV/GHSA advisories; cite the exact CVE or GHSA and its source. Never invent identifiers or versions: anything not verifiable goes marked as [ASSUMPTION] with the concrete way to confirm it. (4) Per finding report: package, current version, minimum corrected version, CVSS severity (with vector if available), direct or transitive path, and reachability of the affected code. (5) Prioritize by severity x exploitability x reachability; act on what meets or exceeds the defined minimum severity and mark as a false positive what is not reachable, justifying why. (6) Design the plan by batches respecting tolerance to breaking changes: batch 1 semver-safe patches, batch 2 minors, batch 3 majors with isolated breaking changes; flag each item that requires code adjustment. (7) For transitive dependencies without a fix from the parent, propose an override/resolution or a bump of the parent and warn of the divergence risk. (8) Tie each batch to a green build/test verification with the indicated command. Do not execute destructive changes: only plan and leave the commands ready to apply.

Deliverables: a prioritized findings table and a batch remediation plan with commands and execution order. Close with pending assumptions to confirm.

prompts.title: Verify AI hallucinations in code
prompts.content:
Act as a senior code reviewer specializing in auditing AI agent outputs, with practice in dependency verification, supply chain security, and reading official documentation by version. An agent generated code and I need to know with evidence what part is real and what part it invented before integrating it. Models hallucinate APIs, parameters, and package names that sound plausible but do not exist; an invented package also enables slopsquatting, where an attacker registers the hallucinated name and executes malicious code when it is installed. Your goal is to produce a traceable audit that unlocks a safe merge, avoids breaking the build, and closes the supply chain vector.

Before auditing, confirm four data points with me and, if any key one is missing, ask me: the language, framework, and exact versions of the key libraries; the code or diff to audit (pasted, file, or PR); what sources of truth I can consult (official docs by version, package registry, the existing repo, terminal access to install/compile/test); and the criticality of the environment where it will run (local prototype, production service, handling money or sensitive data) to calibrate rigor. If I specify nothing, assume production and that you only have official docs and public registries.

Proceed as follows. First, inventory every verifiable claim in the code: imports, packages, modules, submodules, functions, methods, classes, attributes, parameters, enum values, configuration keys, environment variables, paths, tables, and endpoints the code takes as given; order them by risk surface, with external dependencies and API calls first. Second, for each dependency verify against the source of truth that the package exists in its official registry according to the stack (npm, PyPI, crates.io, Maven Central, Go modules, NuGet, RubyGems), that the name is not a typosquat (typo of a real package) or slopsquat (plausible but non-existent variant), and that the module or submodule exists in the declared version; treat an unknown dependency as suspicious until proven otherwise, never the other way around. Third, for each function, method, parameter, or enum confirm that it exists in the real signature of that library at that version, not in another version or a similarly-named library; mark hallucinated signatures (non-existent parameters, wrong order or types) and APIs renamed, deprecated, or removed, citing since when. Fourth, identify what the code assumes without evidence (config key present, env var set, path or table existing, endpoint shape, stable behavior between versions, error handling or pagination) and convert it into a concrete question or executable check. Fifth, classify each finding as CONFIRMED_REAL, HALLUCINATION, or NOT_VERIFIABLE_WITHOUT_EXECUTING, cite the exact source (version-specific doc URL, registry page, repo line) and the command or minimal test that demonstrates it; for each confirmed HALLUCINATION propose the corrected patch and, where it exists, the real equivalent API.

Rigor rules: never declare something real without indicating how to verify it; what you cannot check with the given sources goes as NOT_VERIFIABLE_WITHOUT_EXECUTING and marked [ASSUMPTION], never as confirmed; when in doubt between two versions, ask for the version or report both. Edge cases to cover: code that mixes two versions of the same library, APIs that exist but are deprecated, internal or private packages that will not appear in public registries (do not mark them as hallucination: mark NOT_VERIFIABLE and ask for the internal index), and correct names imported from the wrong module.

Deliver, in neutral Spanish and without emojis: (1) a findings table with columns claim, verdict, severity, source of truth, and evidence or command; (2) a patches block, one per confirmed hallucination; (3) the list of commands or tests to run to close the NOT_VERIFIABLE ones (resolve the import, compile, run the test, call the API in sandbox); and (4) a global merge verdict: ready, ready-with-corrections, or blocked, with the reason. Before executing, restate in one or two lines what you understood and present your plan.

prompts.title: Rate limiting and abuse protection
prompts.content:
Act as a senior application security engineer specializing in API defense and distributed rate limiting. Your assignment: design and implement rate limiting and anti-abuse protection ready to paste, correct across multiple instances. Before coding I need to know: what application or API is being protected and its purpose; the backend stack (language and framework); the shared store for counters across instances (Redis, Memcached, or none yet); what CDN or load balancer is in front (Cloudflare, Nginx, API Gateway, or none); what routes are sensitive (login, registration, recovery, payments, public forms); and the desired limits policy by endpoint and window if it already exists. If any of these data points are missing, ask me or propose a reasonable default and mark it [ASSUMPTION]; do not invent framework signatures or APIs that do not exist.

Proceed as follows. First, map sensitive endpoints and the rest of the traffic into sensitivity levels (for example critical, sensitive, normal, public) and assign to each level a limit, window, and identification key. Second, choose and justify the algorithm against its alternatives (token bucket for controlled bursts, sliding window log for precision at a memory cost, sliding window counter as a balance) documenting the precision versus memory trade-off; choose the key (IP, token, user, or combination) warning of the risk of NAT, shared IPs, and spoofing of headers like X-Forwarded-For, and derive the real IP according to the declared edge layer. Third, implement the limiter over the shared store with atomic operations (Lua script, or INCR with EXPIRE in a single transaction in Redis) so that it is correct across instances; never local process memory. Fourth, return correct HTTP responses: 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After and RateLimit-Limit, RateLimit-Remaining, and RateLimit-Reset headers, and suggest exponential backoff with jitter to the client. Fifth, add layered defenses to sensitive endpoints: progressive temporary blocking after repeated failures, captcha or proof of work on spikes, enumeration pattern detection, and a safe exit (fail-open vs fail-closed) if the store goes down. Sixth, define what to log and alert (429 rate, top IPs or tokens, spikes per endpoint) without storing credentials or PII.

Handle edge cases: concurrent bursts competing for the same counter, exact window reset, desynchronized clock between instances, store failure, legitimate traffic behind the same corporate NAT, and clients that retry without backoff. Deliver: the endpoint matrix by level; commented middleware or limiter code at decision points; the store configuration; 429 response examples with headers; and a test plan (concurrent burst, window reset verification, multi-instance behavior, store failure simulation).

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Consistent error handling throughout the app
prompts.content: Unify the error handling of my application so that every failure follows the same path across all layers: it is typed, logged with context, and translated into a safe response. Act as a senior software engineer specializing in reliability and observability. Deliver a common error strategy implemented and documented. Steps: (1) Inventory how errors are currently captured, logged, and presented and list inconsistencies (scattered try/catch, loose logs, raw messages, disparate codes, silenced failures), classifying each finding by risk. (2) Design a typed error hierarchy that separates expected business errors, validation errors, external dependency failures, and unexpected failures; each type with a stable code, severity, whether it is retryable, and a safe message for the user. (3) Define a single capture point per layer (global handler or middleware on backend; error boundary, interceptor, or global promise handler on frontend) that routes every error to the same pipeline and guarantees that none escapes without being logged. (4) Specify the structured log format: level, timestamp, correlation identifier propagated between layers, origin, error code, and useful context, without sensitive data (declare the list of fields to redact). (5) Define the presentation layer that translates each error into a user message and into a consistent response contract, with explicit error-code-to-status mapping and a safe default message for unmapped types. (6) Refactor current points incrementally preserving public contracts, leave an end-to-end example of a business error and another of an unexpected one, and document how to add a new error type. Explicitly resolve edge cases: errors inside the handler itself, failures before the correlation identifier exists, errors in asynchronous code or uncaught promises, external dependency timeouts, and errors that should not be exposed to the user but should be logged. If I have not told you the logging system or the error response format, ask me; if you propose one, mark it as [ASSUMPTION]. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Production-readiness checklist
prompts.content: Act as a senior site reliability engineer (SRE) with experience operating web services in production and conducting pre-launch reviews. I need a production-readiness audit before exposing my application to real users, with a substantiated Go or No-Go verdict, not a generic list. A rigorous review before the cutover unlocks a launch without surprises: it avoids secret leaks, data loss without backups, and silent outages that nobody detects. Before executing, if you do not know the app name, stack (language, framework, database), infrastructure it runs on, type of data it handles (especially if there are personal or sensitive data), or launch window, ask me: they are critical to evaluate and you must not invent them. Walk through four fronts in order. Security: secrets out of code (environment variables or secrets manager), HTTPS enforced, authentication and authorization per endpoint, input validation and injection protection, dependencies without known critical vulnerabilities, security headers and restricted CORS, rate limiting on public endpoints. Data: tested and reversible migrations, indexes on hot queries, absence of test data or seed credentials in production, retention and privacy policy appropriate to the data type. Backups: scheduled automated backup, end-to-end restore tested at least once, copies in a location separate from the production environment, RPO and RTO objectives defined. Monitoring: structured error logging, alerts to a watched channel, health metrics (latency, error rate, saturation), health check endpoint, minimum incident response plan with a named owner. Mark each control as covered, partial, or absent, and record the evidence or assumption supporting it; label every assumption as [ASSUMPTION] and do not consider a backup copy proven unless it has been restored. Consider these edge cases: app without personal data (privacy still applies to operational data), serverless or managed infrastructure where some controls are covered by the provider (declare it as provider-covered rather than marking it absent), and first launch without an incident history. Close with an unambiguous Go or No-Go verdict and order blockers by risk from highest to lowest, each with a concrete closure action and the front it belongs to. MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Basic data privacy compliance
prompts.content:
Act as a senior privacy engineer with practice in privacy-by-design, consent evaluation, and compliance reviews of software products built quickly. I just built an application with vibe coding and need to know whether its handling of personal data and consent can withstand a basic privacy review before exposing it to real users. Apps generated at high speed carry typical leaks: data collected without being needed, secrets in the repository, personal data in logs, third-party SDKs that exfiltrate information by default, and consent banners that do not actually obtain consent. I want an early review that contrasts the actual data flow against the principles of privacy by design and informed consent, to launch without privacy debt and with an orderly base for scaling or complying with a formal framework (GDPR, LGPD, or another) when the time comes.

Deliver: a prioritized risk findings report with concrete code- and product-level fixes, plus a three-wave remediation plan. Proceed as follows: (1) Data inventory: list every personal data point the app collects, derives, or stores; mark sensitive categories (health, biometrics, precise location, minors). (2) Flow map: for each data point trace input (form, cookie, SDK, API), residence (database, logs, browser storage, providers), and output to third parties. (3) Contrast against seven basic requirements: minimization, legal basis and purpose, real consent (granular, revocable, no pre-checked boxes, non-blocking), retention and deletion, data subject rights (access, rectification, erasure, portability, objection), security (encryption in transit and at rest, secrets out of code, personal data out of logs), and international transfers or to sub-processors. (4) Findings: for each gap record severity (critical/high/medium/low), evidence (file, endpoint, or behavior), violated requirement, and actionable code and product fix. (5) Prioritize and build the remediation plan: criticals now, highs this week, mediums and lows in backlog.

Rules: do not invent regulations, fines, or figures; any obligation that depends on jurisdiction or business type goes marked [ASSUMPTION] to confirm. Distinguish what is verifiable in the provided material from what is inferred. Treat every SDK or third-party service as an outgoing flow until proven otherwise. Edge cases: if there is no consent banner, record the absence as a finding, do not assume it is not needed; if a datum is derived from another (profiling, scoring), inventory it separately; if minors are in the audience, raise the bar for consent and minimization. If I am missing something essential (user regions, presence of minors, third parties, code snippets, or config), ask me before evaluating rather than assuming.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Close with: findings table prioritized by severity + three-wave remediation plan, ready to convert into issues.

prompts.title: Generate SQL query from a natural-language requirement
prompts.content: Act as a senior data engineer expert in analytical SQL and dimensional modeling, with judgment for detecting granularity traps, join fan-out, and NULLs. Translate a business question in natural language into a correct, readable, executable, and auditable SQL query against the indicated schema and engine. If the schema (tables, columns, types, keys), the engine and version, the metric definitions, or the date range are missing, ask before writing SQL, because each one changes the result. Proceed as follows: (1) Reframe the question as an explicit output model: columns, metrics, row granularity, and expected ordering; declare each gap as [ASSUMPTION]. (2) Plan the join graph: base table, direction and type of each join (INNER or LEFT with justification), and at what level the aggregation occurs to avoid duplicating rows due to fan-out; when a metric lives in a table of higher cardinality, aggregate in a subquery or CTE before joining. (3) Write the query with explicit joins and clear aliases, WHERE, complete GROUP BY, HAVING only for filters over aggregates, ORDER BY and LIMIT, using the exact engine syntax; never use implicit join by comma. (4) Declare date range limits as inclusive or exclusive (recommend the half-open pattern date >= start AND date < end+1) and respect the timezone if applicable. (5) Explain each clause in one line and list detected risks with their mitigation: NULLs that an INNER JOIN silently drops, double counting by granularity, division by zero, difference between COUNT and COUNT(DISTINCT), comparisons against NULL. Deliver: the final query in a code block, the list of assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION], and the clause-by-clause explanation, ready to execute and audit. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Optimize a slow SQL query with an execution plan
prompts.content:
Act as a senior database engineer specializing in query tuning, with mastery of execution plans, optimizer cost models, indexing strategies (B-tree, covering, partial, composite, hash, GIN/GiST) and sargable rewriting. I have a critical SQL query that runs slowly and degrades a report, an API, or a batch process, and I want to optimize it based on evidence from the engine itself, not on intuition.

Before proposing anything, follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate in one or two sentences the problem and the goal as you understand them, present your plan of attack, and only then execute. If any indispensable data is missing (engine and exact version, full query text, EXPLAIN or EXPLAIN ANALYZE output, DDL for the relevant tables and existing indexes, row volume and selectivity of key filters, or the performance target), ask for it concretely before continuing; do not assume the engine or invent the schema.

Proceed as follows:
1. Read the plan and identify the most expensive nodes by time and by rows: flag full table or sequential scans, sort/hash spills to disk, nested loops over large tables, materializations, and—above all—large divergences between estimated and actual rows (a symptom of stale statistics or a poorly estimated predicate).
2. Explain the root cause of each bottleneck and link it to its source: WHERE/JOIN predicates, implicit functions or casts that break sargability, missing useful index, stale statistics, lack of selectivity, ORDER BY/GROUP BY without a supporting index, or a suboptimal join order.
3. Propose concrete indexes (table, columns, order, covering or partial where applicable) and rewrites (remove SELECT *, make predicates sargable, reorder or conditionally apply joins, avoid correlated subqueries, decide materialized CTE vs. inline, replace OR with UNION ALL where appropriate), each with its justification and explicit trade-off.
4. Deliver the rewritten query ready to execute and the exact CREATE INDEX statements with the syntax of the declared engine.
5. Define how to validate the improvement: re-run EXPLAIN ANALYZE and compare the plan, estimated cost, and actual time before/after against the target, plus a warning about the write and storage cost of the new indexes on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE workloads.

Hard rules: every bottleneck must cite a concrete node from the plan you provided, without inventing operations; any cardinality or structure not provided is marked as [ASSUMPTION]; the rewritten query must preserve the exact semantics of the original result (same row set and order if the original guaranteed it). Close only when you have delivered the prioritized diagnosis, the final query, index scripts, and measurable verification steps.

prompts.title: Refactor nested subqueries into readable CTEs
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data engineer expert in analytical SQL and query refactoring, with mastery of CTEs, execution plans, and dialect differences between engines. I have a SQL query whose nested subqueries in SELECT, FROM, WHERE, or HAVING have made it difficult to read, debug, and maintain; I want to rewrite it in Common Table Expressions (WITH clause) that are modular and sequential—readable from top to bottom—without altering a single row of the result.

Before executing, restate in your own words what you understand about the query and present your decomposition plan. If I do not have the engine and version (PostgreSQL, BigQuery, Snowflake, MySQL 8+, SQL Server, or another), the table schema or DDL, the naming convention for CTEs, or the desired comment level, ask me before continuing instead of assuming.

Proceed as follows: (1) inventory each nested subquery with its clause, purpose, and dependencies; (2) order the CTEs topologically, leaves first and aggregations, rankings, or correlated ones after, so that each depends only on prior ones, with no forward references; (3) name each CTE in descriptive snake_case, without opaque aliases or collisions; (4) comment each CTE explaining what it produces and why it exists; (5) close with a clean final SELECT that preserves the columns, order, types, filters, joins, aggregations, NULL handling, DISTINCT, and ORDER BY of the original; (6) use only syntax valid in the declared engine, without functions from another dialect. Pay special attention to correlated subqueries (which may require LATERAL, APPLY, or a rewrite to a join), scalar expressions in SELECT, EXISTS/IN/NOT IN predicates with their NULL semantics, and tiebreakers in rankings.

Deliverables: (1) the executable refactored SQL block; (2) a CTE-by-CTE table with name, purpose, and dependencies; (3) an equivalence test script with EXCEPT/MINUS in both directions plus row counts, adapted to the engine, which must return zero differences. Mark as [ASSUMPTION] any inference about NULLs, duplicates, or tiebreak criteria; do not invent columns or tables not present in the schema or the original query. If a subquery cannot be faithfully converted to a CTE (for example, a correlated one that changes semantics), declare it and propose the safest alternative. Neutral and professional English.

prompts.title: Solve ranking and running totals with window functions
prompts.content: Act as a senior data engineer specializing in analytical SQL and dimensional modeling, with mastery of the SQL:2003 window function standard and its differences between PostgreSQL, SQL Server, BigQuery, and Snowflake. I need to turn a fact table into actionable analytical metrics without collapsing per-row detail: competitive ranking within each group, progressive running totals over time, and period-over-period comparisons. Solve this with window functions instead of correlated subqueries or self-joins, to deliver readable, performant, and reusable SQL as a team pattern. Before writing code, restate what you understand and present your plan; if you are missing the source table, the partition column, the entity to rank, the numeric metric, the time grain, or the target engine, ask for them. Build in layers: a base CTE that aggregates the metric at the correct grain (first resolving whether there are duplicates per grain key), then a window layer. Include ROW_NUMBER, RANK, and DENSE_RANK with PARTITION BY of the group and ORDER BY of the metric descending, and explain when to use each one in the presence of ties (unique row, positions with gaps, dense positions) and how to break ties deterministically with a second order column. Calculate the running total with SUM and an explicit ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW frame, warning why the default RANGE sums all ties of the order value and breaks the running total. Compare periods with LAG and LEAD declaring offset and default value, and derive absolute and percentage variation, protecting against division by zero with NULLIF when the previous period is zero or null. Mark all engine-dependent syntax (date syntax, QUALIFY in BigQuery and Snowflake versus a wrapper subquery in PostgreSQL and SQL Server, NULLS FIRST/LAST, casts) and deliver a portable variant that works in all four engines. Close with executable, commented SQL plus a validation note: control counts, verification that the last running total value per group equals the group total, and a check that ROW_NUMBER produces no duplicates.

prompts.title: Build PIVOT and UNPIVOT queries for reports
prompts.content: Act as a senior data engineer specializing in analytical SQL and reporting, expert in dialect differences between engines. I need to convert a table in long format (one row per transaction) into a cross-tab ready for an executive report, and be able to validate it against the source. Give me four executable and commented SQL blocks: (1) a main PIVOT query that groups by the row columns, converts the values of the categorical column into columns, applies the aggregation function over the metric per cell, and includes a row subtotal and a grand total; (2) a reverse UNPIVOT query that brings the cross-tab back to long format (one row per row-column pair) to reconcile against the source; (3) a portable version with aggregated CASE WHEN, valid in any engine without a native PIVOT operator; (4) technical notes on NULL handling (COALESCE to zero where applicable), distinction between null and zero, stable row and column ordering, and the limits of dynamic vs. static pivoting. Before coding, restate what you understand and present your plan (engine and version, source format, cardinality of the column to pivot, static or dynamic pivot, null policy). Mark as [ASSUMPTION] every name, type, or value not provided, and do not invent anything without a mark. Close by verifying that the UNPIVOT reconstructs the source count and total, and that the row and column totals balance. If you are missing the source table, the row columns, the column to pivot, the metric, the aggregation function, or the engine and version, ask me before continuing.

prompts.title: Detect and deduplicate records with SQL
prompts.content: Act as a senior data engineer specializing in data quality and analytical SQL, with experience deduplicating transactional and master tables. I need a commented, executable, and auditable SQL package for diagnosing and eliminating duplicate records in a table, leaving evidence before touching anything. Before generating SQL, restate what you understood and present your plan: confirm the engine and version, the table name, the columns that define identity (what must be unique), whether there are columns with writing variants to normalize for fuzzy duplicates, and the rule for choosing the surviving row (most recent, most complete, or lowest id). If any of these data points is missing or ambiguous, ask for it; do not invent. Mark as [ASSUMPTION] any identity definition you infer. Deliver four commented queries in sequence: (1) exact duplicate diagnosis with GROUP BY over the identity columns and HAVING COUNT(*) greater than 1, reporting number of duplicate groups and total surplus rows; (2) fuzzy duplicate diagnosis grouping by the normalized version (lowercase, trimmed spaces, and accent removal) without altering source data, and if it does not apply, declare it and omit it; (3) inspection for human review that lists the rows of each group side by side using ROW_NUMBER partitioned by identity and ordered by the survival rule, marking row 1 as the survivor, with NULLS LAST in the tiebreak and a final deterministic tiebreak criterion (for example ascending id) to avoid non-reproducible results; (4) cleanup with a safety net: first a SELECT that shows exactly which rows would be deleted, then the equivalent DELETE and, as a non-destructive alternative, a CREATE TABLE backup of the survivors. Recommend wrapping the cleanup in a transaction, validating the count before the COMMIT, and creating a UNIQUE constraint or unique index on the identity columns to prevent recurrence; warn if there are foreign keys pointing to the rows to be deleted (re-point before deleting). Declare any syntax differences by engine and do not use functions that do not exist in it. Close by confirming that all four queries are ready to review and execute.

prompts.title: Traverse hierarchies with a recursive CTE
prompts.content: Act as a senior data engineer expert in recursive SQL and hierarchical structure modeling (org charts, bill-of-materials BOMs, category trees). I need to traverse a parent-child relationship in SQL using a recursive CTE, without knowing in advance how many levels it has, computing for each node its level and its full path from the root. If you do not have the table, the id and parent columns, how the root is marked (parent NULL or self-reference), the starting node(s), the maximum depth, or the engine and version, ask me before writing anything, because syntax and behavior differ between engines. Give me: (1) the confirmed contract with engine, column types, and how the root is identified, marking as [ASSUMPTION] anything I have not verified; (2) the complete and executable SQL as-is, with the anchor member at level 0 and the path initialized with an explicit CAST, the recursive member joining on parent = id, incrementing the level and concatenating the path, a depth cut inside the recursive clause (not only in the outer WHERE), and cycle detection with CYCLE if the engine supports it or by comparing the id against the accumulated path; (3) the final SELECT ordered by path so it reads like a tree; (4) a clause-by-clause explanation, a performance note with the recommended index on the parent column, a warning about the engine's recursion limit, and at least one variant for a different engine (SQL Server omits RECURSIVE; Oracle offers CONNECT BY; MySQL and SQLite limit path concatenation and require length control). Do not invent table or column names, do not use pseudocode, and respond in neutral and professional English, without emojis. Before executing, restate what you understood and present your plan.

prompts.title: Translate SQL between engine dialects
prompts.content: Act as a senior data engineer specializing in cross-engine SQL portability, with deep mastery of PostgreSQL, BigQuery, Snowflake, SQL Server, and MySQL. You will receive a SQL query and I need you to translate it from its source engine to the target engine, preserving the semantics, not just the syntax: the real risk is not that the SQL fails to compile, but that it compiles and returns a subtly different result. If the source engine is not indicated, deduce it from the syntax (quoting, functions, pagination) and confirm it before translating. If the target engine or the query itself is missing, ask before continuing. Proceed as follows: (1) identify or confirm source and target, and note version incompatibilities if relevant; (2) inventory each dialect-sensitive construct and classify it by category; (3) rewrite the query to the native equivalent of the target, formatted and ready to execute; when no native equivalent exists, use real primitives and mark the rewrite as APPROXIMATION, never inventing non-existent functions; (4) audit the silent behavioral differences where the literal equivalent compiles but does NOT produce the same result: integer vs. decimal division, rounding and banker's rounding, NULL ordering (NULLS FIRST/LAST and default position), collation and case sensitivity in text comparisons, time-zone handling in timestamps (with and without tz), implicit truncation of strings and numbers, three-value semantics with NULL, and aggregation or GROUP BY differences; (5) warn about source constructs with no direct counterpart and propose the most faithful approximation. Deliver: translated SQL block ready to execute, followed by three sections (Category mapping, Behavioral differences, Warnings without direct equivalent). Mark every version or configuration assumption as ASSUMPTION and every non-native rewrite as APPROXIMATION. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Explain and document a complex legacy query
prompts.content: Act as a senior data engineer specializing in reading legacy SQL, dimensional modeling, and the logical execution order of queries. You have inherited an extensive SQL query that no one fully understands and you must document it rigorously so it can be modified, migrated, or audited without silently breaking reports. Before executing, restate what you understood and present your plan. If I do not know the exact SQL engine, the apparent purpose of the query, or if you do not share the code to explain, ask me before continuing; do not assume the dialect or invent tables. Deliver: (1) a one-sentence summary in business language of what the query answers; (2) source map: each table, CTE, and subquery with its grain (what one row represents) and each JOIN with type, keys, and fan-out or duplicate risk; (3) a walkthrough by layer in logical execution order (FROM and JOIN, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, window functions, SELECT and derived expressions, ORDER BY, LIMIT), explaining each block and why it exists; (4) inferred business rules translating filters, CASE, flags, and aggregations into plain language, with confidence level per inference; (5) traps and correctness smells specific to the engine (NULLs in JOINs, implicit type conversions, DISTINCT masking duplicates, non-sargable functions, order dependency, time zones, division by zero) without proposing changes yet; (6) the same query with inline comments (-- and blocks) plus a header block with purpose, result grain, sources, and assumptions, preserving the logic intact. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] every hypothesis not verifiable in the code or schema, and close with a list of open questions to validate with business or DBA. Do not alter any line of logic: you only add comments.

prompts.title: Build a cohort and retention query
prompts.content: Act as a senior data analyst specializing in product analytics and analytical SQL. I need an executable SQL query that produces the retention matrix by acquisition cohort, in absolute counts and percentage, from a table of user activity events. Each user must be grouped by the period in which they first appeared (their cohort) and tracked period by period for the fraction that remains active. Before writing SQL, confirm with me: the event table or view, the column that identifies the user, the column for the event date/time, the cohort grain (month or week), how many periods to follow after acquisition, what condition defines a valid activity, and the target SQL engine; if a key input is missing, ask for it and do not invent column names. Structure the query in named and commented CTEs: (1) events_base that filters valid activity and discards null users or timestamps; (2) cohorts that computes for each user their acquisition period with date_trunc over the minimum timestamp; (3) activity_periods that joins events with cohorts and computes the period index relative to the cohort (0 = acquisition) by deriving the difference from truncated dates, not subtracting raw timestamps, bounded to the requested range; (4) cohort_size with COUNT(DISTINCT user) at index 0; (5) matrix that for each pair (cohort, index) computes active = COUNT(DISTINCT user) and retention_pct = active / cohort_size forcing float division. Use COUNT(DISTINCT user) in each cell so a user with multiple events in a period counts only once. Verify that index 0 reproduces the cohort size (retention = 100%). Mark as a partial cohort every row whose index exceeds the periods elapsed from the cohort to the cutoff date, so as not to confuse low retention with periods not yet observed. Deliver two outputs, one in counts and one in percentage, with cohorts in rows ordered by date and the period index in columns; declare whether you deliver long format or a pivot. Close by declaring the target engine and the list of portability adjustments (date_trunc vs. DATE_TRUNC or TIMESTAMP_TRUNC, integer vs. float division, pivot syntax) and mark with [ASSUMPTION] every name, grain, or filter inferred.

prompts.title: Solve gaps and islands in event series
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data engineer in analytical SQL, window functions, and event series modeling. I need an executable, portable, and audited gaps-and-islands solution that detects continuous streaks (islands) and interruptions (gaps) in a temporal event series, to unlock retention metrics, sessionization, churn detection, or subscription continuity.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before writing SQL, restate the problem in your own words, declare the partition entity, temporal order, and the exact continuity definition, and present the CTE plan. If you are missing the SQL engine and its version, the source table or view, the partitioning column, the time or sequence column, the granularity of the step between adjacent events, or the business objective, ask before continuing; do not invent column names or assume the engine.

Proceed as follows:
1. Interpret: restate the problem; identify entity, temporal order, and when two rows belong to the same streak. Mark every assumption with [ASSUMPTION] (time zone, treatment of duplicates on the same step, ties in the order, whether the step is strictly uniform, out-of-calendar events, open edges at the start or end of the series).
2. Plan: present the plan of four CTEs and the signature of each window function before writing the complete SQL.
3. Execute and deliver:
   - CTE 1 normalization: order by entity and time, deduplicate repeated events on the same step, and leave one row per granularity unit.
   - CTE 2 island key: assign each row the difference between ROW_NUMBER OVER (PARTITION BY entity ORDER BY time) and the temporal index normalized to granularity; adjacent rows share that difference and form the island key. Document the alternative with LAG plus cumulative sum to mark the start of each streak and say when to prefer each technique (the sequence difference requires a uniform step; LAG tolerates variable steps and a session threshold).
   - CTE 3 islands: group by entity and island key; compute start, end, duration, and event count per streak.
   - CTE 4 gaps: with LEAD over the islands, compute the gap between the end of one island and the start of the next per entity, with its duration in the granularity unit.
   - Final commented SQL by CTE, explanation of why the sequence difference is constant within an island, assumptions about ties and granularity, and a validation query that reconstructs the total range per entity (sum of island durations plus gaps must equal the range between the first and last event).

Closing criterion: SQL executable in the declared engine without proprietary syntax from another engine; island key built and explained; each CTE commented and named by its function; duplicates and ties resolved explicitly; gaps with LEAD and duration in the correct unit; validation query included; assumptions marked with [ASSUMPTION]; zero columns invented outside the source table.

prompts.title: Review parameterized SQL against injection
prompts.content: Act as a senior data security engineer specialized in SQL injection prevention and data-access code review. I am giving you dynamic SQL queries (DAOs, repositories, data-access functions) to audit and harden against injection before exposing them. First, restate what you understand and present your plan before executing (MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute). Then: (1) Inventory every point where an external variable enters the SQL and mark whether it arrives via concatenation, interpolation, or already parameterized; distinguish direct user input from header input, from another table, or from trusted configuration. (2) For each vulnerable point, quote the exact fragment, identify the unsanitized value, and classify severity (critical/high/medium) according to input origin and query scope (read, write, DDL). (3) Rewrite the query with bound parameters using the exact syntax of the target engine and the real API of the driver or ORM, separating SQL structure from values; do not invent method names. (4) For non-parameterizable identifiers (table name, column, ORDER BY direction, dynamic LIMIT/OFFSET) apply explicit allowlist validation mapped to code constants, never direct concatenation; explain why validation complements and does not replace binding. (5) Flag the cases requiring manual attention: variable-length IN clauses, dynamic ORDER BY or LIMIT, legitimate dynamic SQL, multi-statement queries, and anything you could not verify. Rules: do not introduce new dependencies without justification; preserve the functional behavior of each query; when the engine or driver is ambiguous, declare it as an assumption and request confirmation. Close with an applicable patch (corrected code + a brief comment per change) and a findings report with a severity table and a manual-attention list. If the SQL code, the database engine, or the language/driver is missing, ask for it before executing.

prompts.title: Design a star schema with facts and dimensions
prompts.content: Act as a senior data architect specialized in Kimball dimensional modeling. Design the complete star schema for a business process so that it feeds reports and BI with a single version of the truth. Work in this inviolable order: (1) confirm the business process and the measurable events it generates; (2) declare the fact table grain in ONE unambiguous sentence, at the finest available atomic event, because the grain defines everything else; (3) derive the dimensions that hang from that grain and mark which are conformed (reusable across processes); (4) identify the numeric facts and classify each measure as additive, semi-additive (do not sum across time), or non-additive (ratios, percentages: never pre-aggregate). Then specify each dimension with surrogate key, natural business key, descriptive attributes, and SCD strategy (Type 1 overwrites, Type 2 versions with validity dates and current flag, Type 3 alternate column) justified per attribute based on whether the business needs history. Resolve the fact table: surrogate FK to each dimension, measures, degenerate keys (transaction number, invoice), table type (transactional, periodic snapshot, or accumulating snapshot), and NULL handling (use an unknown dimension member, never NULL on a FK). Apply advanced patterns when applicable: role-playing dimensions (same date dimension as order/ship/delivery), junk dimensions (low-cardinality flags and indicators), late-arriving dimensions, and early-arriving facts. Deliver a dictionary per table (column, data type, role PK/FK/attribute/measure/degenerate, SCD, description), a star diagram in text, and a list of assumptions. Validate that every measure respects the grain, that every FK points to an existing dimension, that conformed ones are consistent in key and attributes, and that every target analytical question can be answered. Mark all unprovided data with [ASSUMPTION] and never present anything invented as fact. If the business process, analytical questions, analytical engine, or expected volume are missing, ask before modeling. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Decide between star schema and snowflake schema
prompts.content: Act as a senior data warehouse architect specialized in dimensional modeling (Kimball method) and optimization for columnar/MPP engines. I need a dimensional normalization ruling that decides, dimension by dimension, between a star schema (denormalized dimension), a snowflake schema (dimension normalized into hierarchical sub-tables), or a hybrid outrigger — NOT a single global default rule. Before evaluating, restate the model and its dimensions, declare what you understood, and present your plan. If you are missing cardinality, hierarchy levels, approximate row counts, target engine, dominant query patterns, or slowly changing dimension (SCD) strategy, ask for them before deciding; do not invent figures. Proceed as follows: 1) Inventory the model's dimensions. 2) Evaluate each one on three axes: (a) cardinality and hierarchy depth; (b) maintenance cost, consistency, and impact of slowly changing changes; (c) query performance and readability according to the target engine and usage patterns, keeping in mind that columnar/MPP engines compress repeated attributes and usually favor stars, while snowflake sub-tables save storage and isolate volatile hierarchies. 3) Emit a per-dimension recommendation with an explicit decision rule, quantifying the joins the snowflake introduces and the expected behavior of the engine, plus one accepted trade-off. 4) Consolidate a summary table (dimension | critical axis | recommendation | trade-off). 5) Propose a prioritized implementation plan: which dimensions to tackle first, associated risk, and validation criteria (row counts, join tests, latency comparison). Mark every assumption as [ASSUMPTION]. Neutral professional Spanish, no emojis.

prompts.title: Model slowly changing dimensions SCD type 2
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data engineer specialized in Kimball dimensional modeling and ETL/ELT pipelines. I need to model a dimension as SCD type 2 so that the data warehouse retains the complete history of attribute changes: each change in a versioned attribute must close the current version and open a new one, so that facts are associated with the value that was current on the date of the event. This enables point-in-time analytics, change auditing, and historically accurate reports without rewriting the past.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First, restate what you understand, declare as [ASSUMPTION] all missing data (engine and SQL dialect, natural key, exact list of versioned attributes, load granularity, current-flag type, time zone, handling of source-side deletes, and treatment of non-versioned attributes), and request confirmation only for blocking items. If essential information is missing, ask for it before generating SQL.

Then deliver, in this order: (1) the DDL for the dimension with an auto-generated surrogate key as primary key, the repeatable-per-version natural business key, the business attributes, and the SCD2 control columns fecha_inicio_vigencia, fecha_fin_vigencia, flag_registro_actual, and hash_atributos, plus audit metadata fecha_carga and origen_lote; (2) the open-end-of-validity convention (recommended 9999-12-31) and the insertion of the sentinel record (surrogate key -1) for keys not found, which protects fact joins; (3) change detection by comparing a deterministic hash of the normalized versioned attributes (trim, explicit NULL handling) between the source staging and the current record; (4) the incremental load with a native MERGE or close-then-insert pattern for the dialect, covering the four cases: new insert, versioned change (closes current, opens new version), no change (no-op), and absent from source (according to delete policy: logical soft-delete or ignore); (5) the strategy for non-versioned attributes (SCD1-style in-place overwrite or ignore) propagated to the current version; (6) handling of late-arriving data (records with an effective date earlier than the current version) and idempotency guarantee for re-runs of the same batch. Close with validation queries: exactly one current version per natural key, contiguous validity periods without overlaps or gaps, sentinel referential integrity, and no consecutive hash duplicates. All SQL must be executable and commented in the target dialect; no pseudocode. Spell out the trade-offs between hash vs. column-by-column comparison and between soft-delete vs. hard-ignore.

prompts.title: Normalize a relational schema to 3NF
prompts.content: Act as a senior data engineer specialized in relational OLTP modeling, with mastery of the functional dependency algebra from Codd's model. Your task is to normalize a relational schema to Third Normal Form (3NF) and deliver the resulting model with executable DDL. Proceed as follows: (1) Reconstruct the starting schema and list each attribute with its type; if I have no schema and only describe a domain, model it from scratch. (2) Declare the set of functional dependencies from the business rules and sample data; mark with [ASSUMPTION] any dependency you infer that I have not guaranteed, and do not invent cardinalities: if a key relationship is ambiguous, ask me before continuing. (3) Calculate the attribute closure to identify candidate keys and choose the primary key of each relation. (4) Apply 1NF by eliminating repeating groups and multivalued attributes until atomicity is guaranteed. (5) Apply 2NF by eliminating partial dependencies on composite keys. (6) Apply 3NF by eliminating transitive dependencies between non-key attributes. Show the model state after each normal form. (7) For each decomposition, explicitly name the anomaly it resolves (insertion, update, or deletion). (8) Verify that the decomposition is lossless (lossless join, common-attribute-as-superkey criterion) and that it preserves dependencies; declare every dependency that is not preserved and its impact. (9) Deliver the final DDL with PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, and NOT NULL. If a 3NF partition does not preserve a dependency and it is worth protecting that rule, offer BCNF as an alternative explaining the trade-off. If I allow controlled redundancy for performance, propose the denormalization as a separate note from the normalized model, with its consistency mechanism (trigger, materialized view, or computed column). Before executing, restate in your own words the domain and dependencies you understood, and present your decomposition plan. Deliverable: document with starting schema, list of functional dependencies, step-by-step 1NF-2NF-3NF derivation, final schema with keys, executable DDL, and anomaly-resolution table. If any essential data is missing, ask for it before starting.

prompts.title: Denormalize a model for analytical workloads
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data engineer specialized in dimensional modeling (Kimball school) and OLAP analytical workload optimization, with practice in data warehousing, materialized views, and lineage governance. Your task is to produce a grounded denormalization decision for a normalized transactional model: which parts to pre-join and materialize to accelerate analytical reads, without turning the analytical copy into a second source of truth. The normalized source (3NF) remains authoritative; the materialized layer is derived and rebuildable.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before designing, restate in two or three sentences what model you are receiving and what analytical workload you are going to accelerate, and present your plan; then execute. If you do not receive the source model, the most frequent or costly critical queries, or the volumes and change frequency of the source tables, ask for them before designing: they are inputs without which the grain and what to materialize cannot be decided. Do not invent tables, queries, or volumes; mark [ASSUMPTION] on every inference due to missing data.

Proceed in four phases. (1) Profile the analytical workload: extract from the critical queries the repeated join patterns, recurring filters and aggregations, and the required level of detail; order candidates by cost × frequency.
