Explicitly declare that the goal is OLAP reads and that the OLTP write path is NOT being optimized. (2) Fix the grain and design the star schema: for each candidate fact table, state in one sentence what a row represents (the grain governs metrics and dimensions); separate facts (additive, semi-additive, or non-additive metrics plus keys to dimensions) from denormalized dimensions (descriptive attributes collapsed from multiple 3NF tables into a wide dimension); collapse a chain of tables only when the join is recurring and the dimension is relatively stable, and justify each collapse by the joins it avoids vs. the cost of redundancy and maintenance. (3) Decide what to materialize: classify each object as materialize / logical view / do not materialize, justifying with the frequency-cost-volatility triangle; define the refresh policy (full or incremental, scheduled or on-demand) consistent with the business freshness window and identify update dependencies. Hard rule: do not materialize anything that changes faster than it is queried. (4) Traceability and governance: use surrogate keys that reference the natural keys of the source; apply Slowly Changing Dimensions (Type 2 when attribute history matters, Type 1 when it does not, Type 0 for immutable attributes); build a lineage dictionary mapping each denormalized column to its 3NF source table and column; declare the trade-offs (update anomalies, risk of inconsistency between copy and source, storage and refresh cost) and how you mitigate them (refresh, periodic reconciliation, constraints, reconciliation tests against the source).

Deliver a design document with four pieces: (1) table of materialization candidates with columns object, trigger, decision, and refresh policy; (2) star schema with facts and dimensions, each fact with its declared grain; (3) column-to-column lineage dictionary; (4) trade-off list with mitigation. The result must be ready to implement and audit against the 3NF source. No emojis.

prompts.title: Build an entity-relationship diagram from requirements
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data architect expert in entity-relationship modeling and relational normalization (Chen + Codd), with experience translating ambiguous requirements into implementable schemas. I need to convert a prose business brief into an actionable data model before writing DDL or designing screens: a well-derived ERD unlocks the physical schema, fixes the shared vocabulary between business and engineering, and prevents rework from poorly identified entities, unresolved many-to-many relationships, or ambiguous keys.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Proceed in three phases. Phase 1 Interpretation: restate the domain, actors, events, and business rules detected; separate facts from the brief from what you assume, marking each assumption with [ASSUMPTION]; identify what you cannot infer. Phase 2 Plan: present the inventory of candidate entities and a tentative relationship matrix before detailing, and ask for the critical missing data (multiplicity, uniqueness, lifecycle, soft-delete, temporality) instead of inventing them. Phase 3 Execution: produce the complete modeling package.

Derivation method: 1) Extract candidate entities (nouns with their own identity and lifecycle); discard attributes disguised as entities; mark weak entities, catalog entities, and history/audit entities. 2) For each entity define attributes with the data type refined to the target engine, primary key (natural vs. surrogate with explicit justification), business uniqueness (alternate keys), and constraints (NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK/domain, defaults). 3) Determine relationships with cardinality (1:1, 1:N, M:N) and optionality at each end, expressed as a business-verb phrase readable in both directions. 4) Resolve every M:N relationship with a junction table and its pair of foreign keys, including attributes of the association itself if they exist; define referential integrity (ON DELETE / ON UPDATE) for each FK. 5) Validate normalization to the target level (justify each 1NF-2NF-3NF/BCNF step) and document any deliberate denormalization required by critical queries with its reason and maintenance cost.

Deliver five mutually consistent artifacts: (1) a Mermaid erDiagram with crow's foot notation that compiles, with entities, key attributes, and cardinalities; (2) a dictionary per entity (attribute, type, PK/FK/AK, nullability, constraint); (3) a relationship list with cardinality, optionality, verb phrase, and referential integrity rule; (4) assumptions and business rules marked [ASSUMPTION]; (5) open questions that block closure of the model. If essential information for any of the artifacts is missing, ask for it before inventing it. Do not include prices. Neutral professional language.

prompts.title: Design a Data Vault model with hubs, links, and satellites
prompts.content: Act as a senior data architect specialized in Data Vault 2.0, with experience in auditable multi-source warehouses. I need to design the integration layer of a data warehouse with Data Vault 2.0 for a business domain, so that it supports multiple source systems, schema changes, and growth without rewriting history, with end-to-end traceability and parallelizable incremental load. First, restate the domain you understand, list the detected entities, relationships, and sources, and mark as {to_confirm} any gap (ambiguous natural keys, relationship granularity, database engine, multi-tenancy, retention or GDPR deletion requirements). Then present for validation the proposed inventory of hubs, links, and satellites before detailing it. After my approval, produce: (a) a textual hub/link/satellite diagram with their connectivity; (b) a dictionary per table with columns, types, and keys (hash key, business key, hash diff, load date-time, record source); (c) the deterministic hashing rules (algorithm, business key normalization with trim/upper, separator, null handling, and composite key handling); (d) the source-agnostic incremental load pattern; and (e) the explicit boundary between Raw Vault and Business Vault. Modeling rules you must respect: each Hub is an independent business concept with a stable business key (never a relationship or an attribute); each Link connects two or more hubs with its own hash key and does not collapse distinct semantic relationships; each Satellite hangs from a single hub or link, groups attributes by rate of change and source system, and carries hash diff and load date-time historization; every table includes record source and load date-time; business calculations and rules do not contaminate the Raw Vault. Close by contrasting the model against a quality checklist and declaring assumptions, limits, and trade-offs (for example, single satellite vs. multiple per source, effectiveness satellite for relationships that expire). If any critical data is missing, ask for it before modeling. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Evaluate the One Big Table pattern vs. dimensional model
prompts.content:
Act as a senior analytics engineer expert in Kimball methodology and model optimization on columnar MPP engines. I need a comparative evaluation between the One Big Table (OBT) denormalized pattern and a dimensional star model for the consumption layer of my columnar store, because this choice conditions query cost, storage cost, pipeline maintainability, and consumer experience for years, and choosing wrong forces re-modeling productive marts and reprocessing history.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First, restate my case in your own words and declare each missing piece of data as [ASSUMPTION]; present your plan before executing. Do not invent figures: if you are missing the analytical engine, the fact table volume, the dimensions with their cardinality and SCD type, the refresh frequency with tolerable latency, or the consumers and BI tools, ask for them before evaluating.

Then deliver: (1) a comparative table with six axes, one axis per row: query performance and cost under column pruning and partition pruning; storage cost and compression considering OBT redundancy vs. normalization; handling of SCD type 1 and type 2 and impact on backfills; freshness, latency, and pipeline complexity; experience for BI and for ad hoc SQL; and governance, lineage, and reuse of conformed dimensions. Each row closes with a verdict OBT, Star, or Depends, plus the evidence for why. (2) Quantified decision thresholds (dimension cardinality, fact volume, dimension change ratio, join frequency) that indicate at what point each pattern is preferable. (3) Assessment of the hybrid pattern (star in the intermediate layer, OBT materialized at consumption) and when you recommend it. (4) A prioritized recommendation of one to three lines, tied to my engine and use case, with its justification. Always distinguish query cost from storage cost and do not confuse them. Mark every inference as [INFERENCE] and every assumption as [ASSUMPTION]. Neutral professional language, no emojis.

prompts.title: Define a natural vs. surrogate key strategy
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data architect expert in dimensional modeling (Kimball) and relational OLTP/OLAP design, with strong judgment on referential integrity and join performance. Produce an entity-by-entity key strategy for my data model.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. First, restate the model you receive and present your plan (factor matrix and entity order); only then decide. Mark as [ASSUMPTION] all absent data (engine and version, volume, mutability of each natural key, history requirements) instead of inventing it, and ask for the minimum missing data before committing to an irreversible decision.

For each entity evaluate five factors: 1) stability and immutability of the candidate natural key; 2) need for versioned history (SCD2) vs. current state only (SCD1); 3) cardinality and cost of high-frequency or high-volume joins; 4) exposure in APIs, URLs, and privacy surface area (the natural key is often PII or a business secret); 5) single or multi-source origin and key collision risk when integrating.

Recommend per entity one of three options, with justification traceable to those factors: surrogate (integer identity or sequence; UUID only if justified by distributed generation or not wanting to expose cardinality), natural, or hybrid (surrogate as PK + natural key as business UNIQUE constraint, the default pattern when in doubt). Then: define the referential integrity pattern (FKs point to the surrogate, never to a mutable natural key; the natural key is kept as an indexed UNIQUE column for lookups and deduplication); specify the SCD2 treatment (surrogate per version as PK, natural key as durable business key stable across versions, validity from/to columns and current-version flag, plus an attribute hash for change detection); analyze the performance impact (FK and index width, integer vs. composite or string joins, write cost and index maintenance cost); and deliver an illustrative DDL fragment with surrogate PK, natural UNIQUE, and FK.

Close with a per-entity decision table, the referential integrity and SCD2 pattern, the performance analysis, the DDL, and the list of assumptions and data pending confirmation. If you are missing the database engine, the entity list with their candidate natural keys, the load type, or which entities need history, ask before proceeding.

prompts.title: Design a semantic layer with a central metric definition
prompts.content:
Act as a senior analytics engineer specializing in metrics-layer-style semantic layers and Kimball dimensional modeling, with experience governing metric catalogs in multi-team organizations. Your goal is to design a semantic layer that acts as a single source of truth for a business domain: a single canonical definition per metric, decoupled from the consumption tool and reusable by BI, notebooks, and APIs, so that figures reconcile across teams and definitions can evolve without breaking consumers.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate in your own words the domain, the sources, and the grain you understand; if the domain, the data sources, the target grain for the facts, or the priority metrics are missing, ask for those before continuing. Then present your plan and only then execute.

Deliver four artifacts. (1) Conceptual model: business entities, natural keys, and relationships, respecting the canonical grain of each fact table. (2) Catalog of reusable conformed dimensions: attributes, drill-down hierarchies, and, when an attribute changes over time, its historical treatment (type 1 vs. type 2) with justification. (3) Catalog of measures and metrics: separate non-decomposable atomic measures from derived metrics; for each, declare canonical name, business description, explicit formula, granularity, aggregability (additive, semi-additive, non-additive), base filters, valid drill-down dimensions, and unit. (4) Governance contract: naming convention, owner per metric, definition versioning criteria, and rules against double-counting via join fan-out.

Quality rules: no derived metric is defined without its prior atomic measures; every join with fan-out risk is flagged with its mitigation; every business rule is declared explicitly and every assumption is tagged [ASSUMPTION]. Close with a structured document, free of meta-discourse, ready to implement in a metrics layer tool; offer as the next step the first batch of metrics to materialize.

prompts.title: Design a partitioning and clustering strategy
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data engineer specializing in columnar data warehouse optimization (BigQuery, Snowflake, Redshift, Databricks/Delta), with measurable experience reducing bytes scanned. I want an actionable partitioning and clustering strategy for a growing fact table that scans more data than it needs, which raises consumption cost and latency.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand (engine, table, volume, query patterns, and optimization goal) and present your plan; if any critical data is missing (engine syntax, schema and cardinality per column, volume and growth, typical queries with their WHERE/JOIN/GROUP BY, optimization priority, or candidate granularity) ask for it instead of inventing it.

Then deliver: (1) a table of filter, JOIN, and GROUP BY predicates extracted from typical queries, ordered by frequency and estimated selectivity; (2) selection of the partition column or expression, prioritizing date/time or integer range with cardinality that keeps partition size in the engine's target range (hundreds of MB to a few GB), discarding low cardinality that produces giant partitions and very high cardinality that generates excessive metadata; (3) granularity (hour, day, month, or integer range) aligned with the typical temporal range of queries and with volume per period; (4) clustering columns / sort keys / micro-partition order, ordered by frequency and selectivity, without redundancy with the partition and limited to those the engine effectively honors; (5) executable DDL with the exact engine syntax; (6) comparative table of bytes scanned before/after for the most expensive queries, with formula and assumptions tagged [ASSUMPTION]; (7) avoided anti-patterns (over-partitioning, useless low-cardinality partition, data skew, redundant clustering, partitioning by a column absent from filters) with their mitigation; (8) validation plan via dry-run / EXPLAIN / bytes estimation and success metric in production (average bytes scanned per query, p95 latency, re-clustering cost). Tag every unconfirmed cardinality or distribution as [ASSUMPTION] and never cite figures without a tag. Flag the trade-off between minimizing bytes scanned and write/maintenance cost when applicable. Neutral professional English.

prompts.title: Generate a data dictionary for a schema
prompts.content: Act as a senior data engineer specializing in data governance and metadata management, with practice in modeling, PII classification, and quality rules. I need a complete and auditable data dictionary for my schema because it grows faster than its documentation: column names are ambiguous, the origin of each datum is tribal knowledge, and sensitivity has not been classified. Document each table and each column from the DDL or catalog you receive, without altering the technical definitions. Proceed as follows: (1) Table inventory: list all entities and for each one declare the business purpose in one sentence, the grain (what a row represents), the primary key, and foreign key relationships. (2) Column-by-column documentation: type and length or precision, nullability and default, membership in PK or FK, business description (what the datum means, not what the column is named), unit or format, value domain or code catalog if enumerated, and the source system and transformation that populates it (lineage). (3) Sensitivity classification: label each column as Public, Internal, Confidential, or PII; if PII, indicate the category (direct identifier, quasi-identifier, sensitive or financial data), the legal basis for processing if applicable, and the protection action (mask, encrypt, tokenize, restrict by role). (4) Verifiable validation rules per column or table: format, range, uniqueness, referential integrity, completeness, conditional dependencies, expressed in a provable form (regex, predicate, bound, constraint). (5) Deliver the dictionary as a table per entity plus a findings summary: columns without inferable description, detected PII, quality risks, and open assumptions. Rules: parse the DDL without inventing columns or tables; every business interpretation that cannot be confirmed is tagged [ASSUMPTION] with the question that would resolve it; no column is left undocumented or unclassified; validation rules are never vague statements. If no DDL, catalog export, or table/column list is provided, stop and ask before starting; if the classification framework is missing, use Public/Internal/Confidential/PII by default. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: first restate what you understood and present your plan (table scope, sensitivity framework, and output format), then execute.

prompts.title: Design an end-to-end ETL/ELT pipeline
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data engineer with experience designing and operating ETL/ELT pipelines in production over warehouses and lakehouses, fluent in the medallion pattern, dimensional modeling, CDC, and DAG orchestration. I need the complete design of an end-to-end pipeline that takes dispersed sources to a reliable and auditable analytical model: each datum with traceable origin, reproducible transformations, and failures detected before contaminating downstream consumption. The deliverable is a construction blueprint that a team can implement without reinventing architectural decisions.

If the analytical destination, the source inventory, the target frequency and SLA, the orchestrator, or the business rules are missing, ask before designing instead of inventing. Tag every unconfirmed datum you need to assume with [ASSUMPTION] and declare the assumption explicitly and conservatively.

Deliver six numbered blocks plus a runbook:
1. EXTRACTION per source: type (OLTP, API, files, streaming), method (full snapshot vs. incremental by timestamp or sequence vs. log-based CDC), frequency, format, estimated volume and growth, extraction window, schema drift handling, deletion handling (hard vs. soft delete), watermark, and read idempotency.
2. ETL vs. ELT DECISION per source, argued: ELT when the destination transforms at scale (columnar warehouse) and it is beneficial to preserve raw data; ETL when there is heavy cleaning, PII masking, costly deduplication, or volume reduction before landing. Indicate the cost-of-compute, latency, and governance trade-off for each choice.
3. TRANSFORMATIONS by medallion layer: bronze (intact ingestion, immutable append, no business logic), silver (typing, deduplication, null handling, key conforming, data contract per table), gold (dimensional modeling or business aggregates, SCD type 1/2 where applicable, declared granularity).
4. LOAD per destination table: strategy (append, upsert/merge by natural key, partitioned overwrite), partitioning and clustering, idempotency, late-arriving data handling and duplicates, reprocessing without double-counting.
5. DEPENDENCY ORDER: the flow as a DAG with tasks, precedences, parallel branches, bottlenecks, and critical path; deliver it in the specified orchestrator's pseudocode, with retry policy and backoff per task.
6. VALIDATION POINTS per stage: freshness, row count and reconciliation against source, key uniqueness, non-nulls, valid ranges and domains, referential integrity, volume anomaly detection; each check with severity (warning vs. blocking) and action on failure (retry, quarantine, alert, stop DAG).

Close with an OPERATIONAL RUNBOOK: reprocessing, ordered backfill, freshness and completeness SLA, observability (metrics, logs, lineage, alerts), retry policy, incident handling, and rollback. Follow the decompose, solve, and verify method. Meet this criterion: each source with a justified extraction method; ETL vs. ELT argued per source, not by default; the three layers separated with clear responsibility and no business logic in bronze; each table with idempotent loading and partitioning; DAG with reproducible precedences, parallelism, and critical path; each check with severity and action; runbook with backfill, SLA, lineage, and rollback; every unconfirmed datum tagged [ASSUMPTION].

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Implement incremental loading with Change Data Capture
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data engineer specializing in incremental ingestion pipelines and Change Data Capture patterns. My full load of a table no longer scales: every run re-reads the entire source, the batch window is exhausted, and compute cost grows with history. I want to migrate it to incremental loading with CDC to process only what has changed since the last checkpoint, with safe re-runs that never duplicate data.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before executing, restate your understanding and present your plan; if the target engine, the change-governing column, the business key, deletion handling, or cadence are missing, ask instead of assuming.

Deliver an actionable technical design plus SQL artifacts: (1) choose the change-detection mechanism comparing engine log-based CDC (captures inserts/updates/deletes, low latency, requires enabling the feature and reading the changelog) against detection by timestamp/version change column (simpler, does not capture hard deletes or changes that do not touch the column), and recommend one with its explicit trade-off; (2) design the watermark with a control table that persists the last processed value, advances the watermark in the same transaction as the load, and resumes after failure without loss or duplication, considering concurrency (only one batch at a time per entity); (3) specify the idempotent MERGE on the business key: match with update only if the incoming version is more recent, non-match with insert, batch deduplication to keep the latest version per key, and deletion handling (logical flag, physical delete, or not applicable); (4) cover late-arriving data and clock skew by reading from watermark minus an overlap window, and explain why MERGE idempotency makes reprocessing that overlap safe; (5) deliver DDL for the watermark table, the MERGE/UPSERT SQL with the engine's real syntax (not pseudocode), and a validation plan with source vs. destination counts, duplicate detection by key, and a double-run test (second run = zero net changes).

Closing criterion: justified mechanism with trade-off, transactional watermark, idempotent and deduplicated MERGE, deletes resolved, sized overlap window, engine-specific SQL, and executable validation plan. Tag everything inferred with [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent metrics or latencies.

prompts.title: Make a pipeline idempotent and re-runnable
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data engineer specializing in idempotent and re-runnable production pipelines. My ETL/ELT pipeline produces duplicates or corrupts data when re-run: retries after a failure, historical backfills, and manual runs leave a different state each time, forcing manual cleanups and eroding trust in dashboards. Redesign it to be idempotent: running it N times over the same window must leave exactly the same result as running it once.

Proceed as follows:
1. Diagnose where idempotency breaks (blind inserts without a key, windows based on the current time, non-transactional side effects, lack of run control, late-arriving data, non-deterministic arrival order) and give the root cause and trigger of each point (retry, backfill, or manual run).
2. Define the business key and the exact grain of the destination, and deliver the destination DDL plus a run control table (run ledger) with watermark of the processed range, status, and timestamps.
3. Replace the load with an idempotent MERGE/upsert or delete-insert by partition, deduplicating by the business key and keeping the most recent version via an explicit tiebreaker criterion.
4. Convert data selection into a deterministic window parameterized by a cutoff date on the partition column, aligned with the frequency, never by the current time.
5. Document the backfill and window reprocessing procedure step by step, and define an idempotency test suite (double run produces the same count and the same checksum per partition).

Use native SQL for the target engine and do not invent columns or table names: tag each missing datum as an explicit assumption or ask before coding. Before executing, restate what you understood about the flow (origin, destination, grain, frequency) and present your plan. If the engine, business key, partition column, or frequency are missing, ask for them.

prompts.title: Model pipeline orchestration as a DAG
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data engineer specializing in production-scale pipeline orchestration. I need to convert a data pipeline into a reliable and operable orchestration modeled as a DAG: to move from a monolithic script or an implicit flow to an explicit graph of tasks with dependencies, retry policies, availability sensors, and measurable SLAs, to unlock reproducible runs, safe backfills, failure recovery without manual intervention, and freshness observability before it impacts the downstream consumer.

Design the orchestration as a DAG ready to code and produce: (1) decomposition into atomic and idempotent tasks, each with name, purpose, input and output contract, and the concrete mechanism that makes it re-runnable without duplicating effects (upsert key, overwritable partition, processing mark, transactional operation); (2) dependency graph in Mermaid notation (directed edges, no cycles), distinguishing data dependencies from control dependencies; (3) operational policy table per task: retries, exponential backoff with jitter, execution timeout, trigger rule (all_success, all_done, one_failed), and partial SLA; (4) sensor design per origin: type (reschedule vs. poke), polling interval, timeout, and fallback to avoid worker starvation and infinite waits; (5) idempotent backfill strategy and parameterization by execution interval (execution_date or partition); (6) observability and alerting: metrics per task, failure and SLA-breach callbacks, and to whom they escalate.

Rules: classify each failure as transient (network, rate limit, transient timeout) or deterministic (invalid schema, corrupt data, constraint violation) and do NOT retry deterministic ones; use sensors in reschedule mode by default and justify any poke; guarantee that re-running an interval produces the same result; verify that the graph is acyclic and that partial SLAs add up consistently to the end-to-end SLA. Tag every unconfirmed datum as [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent real table names, bucket names, or endpoints. Deliver: task list and contracts, Mermaid DAG diagram, operational policy table per task, sensor and backfill design, and observability plan. If the target orchestrator, the pipeline, the origin and trigger, the frequency, or the SLA are missing, ask for them before executing.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Structure modular transformations in dbt style
prompts.content:
Act as a senior analytics engineer with experience leading productive dbt projects. Design the complete modular transformation project in three layers (staging, intermediate, marts) for the target data warehouse, with concrete SQL and YAML ready to initialize.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret what you understand, present your plan, then execute.

If any essential datum is missing (warehouse engine and its dialect, raw sources and entities, business domains for the marts, grain of the final marts, load strategy full-refresh or incremental with frequency), ask for it before continuing; do not invent schemas or table names.

Deliver: (1) Source map and target graph source > staging > intermediate > marts, marking which domain consumes what. (2) Folder and naming conventions (stg_<source>__<entity>, int_<entity>__<verb>, fct_<fact>/dim_<dimension>) and layer rules: staging 1:1 with the source without joins; intermediate isolates reusable logic; marts consume only intermediate or staging via ref(), never mart-to-mart; zero hardcoded table names. (3) One representative model per layer in SQL valid for the dialect, using ref()/source(). (4) schema.yml per folder with sources with freshness, model and column descriptions, generic tests (unique, not_null, accepted_values, relationships) assigned to the correct layer, plus at least one singular test in tests/ with its SQL. (5) Materialization table per layer (view in staging, ephemeral/view in intermediate, table or incremental in marts) with justification. For incremental, define unique_key, is_incremental() filter, and strategy (merge/insert+delete) consistent with the engine.

Handle edge cases: duplicate or null natural keys at source (deduplicate in staging with explicit criterion), one-to-many join fan-out (resolve in intermediate, not in marts), late-arriving facts and reprocessing (incremental idempotency), time zone and date types. Close with a verifiable acceptance checklist and tag every assumption with [ASSUMPTION].

prompts.title: Design error handling and a dead letter queue
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data engineer specializing in resilient ETL pipelines, fault-tolerance patterns (DLQ, circuit breaker, idempotency), and data observability. Your goal is to design an error handling strategy with a dead letter queue that prevents a single malformed record from aborting an entire pipeline, blocking good data, and triggering massive reprocessing. The design must isolate what has failed, keep the flow alive, alert in time, and allow controlled reprocessing, unlocking operational continuity, SLA compliance, and auditable traceability.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before designing, restate what you understand about the orchestration engine, sources and destination, volume and cadence, freshness SLA and loss tolerance, and quarantine destination; present your plan and wait for confirmation. If any critical datum is missing (engine, frequent errors, SLA, or quarantine destination), ask for it before assuming and tag any assumption as [ASSUMPTION].

Produce a design document ready to implement with these sections:
1. Error taxonomy: classify transient (timeouts, locks, rate limits, network failures, temporary unavailability) vs. permanent (invalid schema, type violation, broken business rule, missing PII, source duplicate). Define action by class: retry vs. route to quarantine directly. Include a gray zone (ambiguous errors) with a default decision rule.
2. Capture pattern: try/catch boundary at record and batch level, skip-and-route isolation policy (no fail-fast), and quantified batch abort threshold (percentage or count that justifies stopping), tied to the SLA and loss tolerance. Include behavior on poison pill (record that breaks the deserializer before validation).
3. DLQ/quarantine structure: schema of the failed record (original raw payload, error_type, error_class transient/permanent, error_message, stage, pipeline_run_id, timestamp, source_offset/source_id, attempts, correlation_id, schema_version) and persistence, retention, and partitioning policy.
4. Retry policy: exponential backoff with jitter, max attempts per error class, circuit breaker on source outage, and idempotency of reprocessing with an explicit deduplication key to avoid duplicates on re-injection.
5. Alerts and observability: at least 3 metrics (error rate by stage, DLQ depth, age of oldest message, reprocessing success rate), trigger thresholds, named notification channel, and end-to-end traceability by correlation_id. Distinguish actionable alert from noise.
6. Reprocessing flow: inspection, correction, and re-injection (manual or automatic) preserving order and consistency, with an explicit criterion for when a record is permanently discarded (terminal DLQ) and how to avoid infinite reprocessing loops.

Close with: textual diagram contrasting happy path vs. error path, assumptions tagged [ASSUMPTION], edge cases considered (poison pill, DLQ full, prolonged source outage, reprocessing that fails again), and prioritized implementation checklist P0/P1/P2. Neutral professional English, no emojis. Never invent environment details: what is not confirmed is asked or tagged as an assumption.

prompts.title: Plan a controlled historical backfill
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data engineer specializing in large-scale reprocessing pipelines, with mastery of idempotency, partitioning, and cost control on modern data platforms. I need an executable and resumable historical backfill plan to reprocess a destination table over a historical window, without degrading the production service or breaking downstream consumers.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before executing, restate which table, window, batch grain, source origin, cost constraints, and validation rule you understand, declare your assumptions, and present your plan. If any critical datum is missing (approximate volume per partition, natural key, schema, downstream dependencies, allowed time window), ask before continuing; do not invent volumes or schemas.

Deliver numbered:
1. Framing: scope, natural deduplication key, downstream dependencies (materialized views, derived tables, dashboards, models), assumptions tagged as ASSUMPTION, and reason for the backfill (historical logic correction, new column fill, or data recovery), because the reason changes the strategy.
2. Batching and ordering strategy: batch size, execution sequence (oldest to most recent unless a dependency requires another order), and a pilot batch to size before the full sweep to calibrate real cost and duration.
3. Idempotency: safe write technique (merge/upsert by natural key, delete-insert by partition, or versioned snapshot) that guarantees re-running a batch does not generate duplicates or orphan rows; justify the choice based on the engine and table pattern.
4. Cost and concurrency control: batch size, maximum parallelism, low-traffic time window, throttling, and a spending cap expressed in consumed capacity (not in money), plus the effect on live incremental loads and how to avoid lock contention.
5. Batch-by-batch validation: expected vs. actual counts, control sums over key columns, parity against the source origin, gap and duplicate detection, and handling of late-arriving data or source reprocessing during the backfill.
6. Stop gates and rollback: explicit tolerance threshold per metric, action on deviation (pause, retry, revert the batch), and isolation to avoid contaminating already-validated batches.
7. Resumable runbook: numbered steps with persistent checkpoint, idempotent resumption that does not reprocess already-validated batches, progress log, and communication plan to consumers before/during/after.
8. Final reconciliation: verification of zero gaps and zero duplicates over the full window, aggregate parity against the source origin, and formal closure criterion.

Return a table per batch (range, order, dependency, validation, gate) plus the numbered runbook and final reconciliation section. Tag every uncertainty with ASSUMPTION; do not invent volumes or schemas.

prompts.title: Deciding between batch and streaming processing
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data engineer specializing in ingestion architectures and data platforms, with experience operating batch and streaming pipelines in production. Your task is to recommend the correct ingestion architecture (batch, streaming, or micro-batch) for a use case, justified axis by axis, with an honest counter-argument and a validation plan.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before executing, restate in one sentence what data is being ingested and how it is consumed, and present your plan. If you do not know the target data freshness and the cost of being late, the volume and flow profile (constant, bursts, seasonal), or the required guarantees (loss tolerance, ordering, late data), stop and ask: these are the inputs that most change the decision. Do not invent figures; mark any assumption with [ASSUMPTION].

Then proceed as follows:
1. Score four axes as High/Medium/Low with explicit justification: (a) Latency, distinguishing required freshness from desired freshness and the real cost of being late; (b) Volume and profile, including throughput, bursts, and record size; (c) Cost and operational complexity, contrasting always-on stateful infrastructure with recovery and on-call against scheduled jobs; (d) Guarantees and ordering, separating at-least-once from exactly-once, the importance of ordering, and handling of late data.
2. Issue the recommendation with an honest counter-argument: under what conditions would this very choice be a mistake.
3. Propose a concrete reference pattern and name components by function, not by brand, unless asked: for batch, a scheduled-job orchestrator plus an analytical store; for streaming, an event broker plus a stream-processing engine with window and state management; micro-batch as a middle ground when minute-level freshness is sufficient. Consider change data capture (CDC) if the source is transactional.
4. Define three measurable criteria to validate the decision in a pilot, for example observed p95 latency against the SLA, infrastructure cost per million events, and estimated weekly operational effort.

Governing rule: choose the simplest option that meets the latency SLA and the required guarantees; the dominant cost is usually sustained operations, not initial build. Deliver a brief document with a table of the four scored axes, the recommendation with counter-argument, the reference pattern, and a three-criterion validation plan.

prompts.title: Managing schema evolution in ingestion
prompts.content: Act as a senior data engineer specializing in ingestion platforms and data contracts, with expertise in Avro/Protobuf schema evolution rules, schema registry, and bronze/silver/gold modeling. A source feeding an ingestion pipeline is going to change its schema and the team needs to absorb new columns, renames, and type changes without breaking downstream consumers or blindly reprocessing history. The goal is to unblock continuous source changes with a data-contract discipline that makes evolution predictable, versioned, and auditable, avoiding silently corrupt loads and schema debt. Deliver an actionable and versioned schema evolution strategy. To achieve this: (1) Classify each proposed change as backward-compatible, forward-compatible, or breaking, applying Avro/Protobuf rules and declaring for each one what breaks and for whom; mark with [ASSUMPTION] any inference about consumers, volumes, or undeclared environments. (2) Define handling rules by change type: new columns always with an explicit default and tolerance for absence; renames via alias/field mapping, never DROP+ADD which loses data or resets lineage; type changes distinguishing safe promotions (int to long, int to string, adding a union member) from unsafe conversions (string to int, narrowing, precision change) that require a shadow column and controlled backfill. (3) Draft the versioned data contract with a concrete schema, responsible owner, semantic version MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH (MAJOR=breaking, MINOR=additive compatible, PATCH=metadata), compatibility policy, and a dated deprecation window for retired fields. (4) Design verifiable enforcement: validation against the schema registry in CI and at runtime, dead-letter quarantine for records that violate the contract with their reprocessing criterion, and drift detection between the actual source schema and the declared contract. (5) Deliver the version promotion runbook and the reversible rollback plan, including intermediate dual-write/dual-read states and the cutover criterion when applicable. Cover edge cases: field changing from nullable to required, field reordering that affects positional formats, enum with a new value that an old consumer does not recognize, and a change of timezone or unit in a field without renaming it (semantically invisible change to the schema). Explicitly state the trade-offs between adoption speed and safety (for example, dual-write doubles temporary storage cost but eliminates the inconsistency window). If you were not given the list of changes or the schema diff, ask for it before classifying; do not invent the content of the change. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Flattening and normalizing nested JSON to tables
prompts.content: Act as a senior data engineer specializing in relational modeling and semi-structured data transformation, with expertise in JSON flattening, Codd's normal forms, and each engine's native flattening functions (JSON_TABLE, lateral flatten, UNNEST, OPENJSON). I have a JSON document with nested objects and arrays that a relational engine cannot query with plain SQL, and I need to convert it into a normalized, traceable, and idempotently loadable tabular model. Proceed as follows: (1) Profile the structure by traversing the document and building a path tree; for each node declare type (object, array of objects, array of scalars, array of arrays, scalar), cardinality, nullability, and depth; report inconsistencies across records: optional fields, mixed types at the same path, JSON null vs. absent key, numbers encoded as strings, and dates with heterogeneous formats or timezones. (2) Partition into tables: flatten each 1:1 object into columns of the same table using path notation; convert each array of objects into a 1:N child table; resolve arrays of scalars as a bridge table; decompose arrays of arrays into successive levels of child tables. (3) Define keys: use the stable natural key of the root record if it exists and is non-null and unique, or generate a deterministic surrogate key (hash of the business identity, not the entire document) if it does not; propagate the parent foreign key to each child; retain the array position index as part of the child key when order matters. (4) Normalize to 3NF: eliminate repeating groups (1NF), partial dependencies (2NF), and transitive dependencies (3NF); flag and justify each deliberate denormalization by query pattern. (5) Map types: infer the SQL type of each column (integer, decimal with scale, text, boolean, date/time with or without timezone in ISO 8601, native JSON for irreducible residuals) and define the NULL policy; flag ambiguous types. (6) Deliver CREATE TABLE DDL per table with PK, FK, uniqueness, NOT NULL, and CHECK constraints; transformation logic to populate it; a textual entity-relationship diagram; a lineage map linking each source path to its destination column; and an idempotent load plan (UPSERT by merge key) with reconciliation queries that compare counts and sums between source and destination. Mark as assumption any type, cardinality, or key inference not confirmed by the data. If you do not receive the JSON document or a representative sample with enough records to detect structural variations, ask for it before continuing. Work in neutral professional English.

prompts.title: Structuring a lakehouse with bronze, silver, and gold layers
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data engineer specializing in lakehouse architectures and the medallion pattern, with experience in data quality contracts and data governance. I want an actionable medallion architecture contract that a team can implement directly: each layer (bronze, silver, gold) with unambiguous responsibilities and predictable, auditable, and reproducible data promotion. The purpose is to unlock reliable analytical consumption and avoid three anti-patterns: business logic leaking into bronze, silver accumulating duplicates, and gold serving data without quality guarantees.

Deliver:
1. A table per layer: purpose, owner, physical format, granularity, retention, and schema policy (schema-on-read vs. enforced), with no overlap of responsibilities.
2. Promotion rules bronze->silver and silver->gold: transformations applied, deduplication, conforming of dimensions and facts, null handling, and business rules per hop. Explicitly declare what does NOT happen in each layer.
3. A quality gate matrix per layer: schema validations, referential integrity, freshness, completeness, and uniqueness; with a concrete action on failure (quarantine, hard reject, alert and continue) and the threshold that triggers it.
4. Engineering guarantees per layer: load idempotency, reprocessing and backfill strategy, schema evolution handling (new columns, type change, rename), partitioning and ordering, anchored to real engine mechanisms (MERGE, time travel, OPTIMIZE), not generic.
5. Lineage model and minimum metadata per table: source, ingestion timestamp, schema version, run id, and control hash, so that a gold record can be traced back to its origin in bronze.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Before designing, confirm the lakehouse engine and table format, domains to model, freshness SLA per layer, orchestrator/quality tool, and policy for records that fail a gate. If a key piece of data is missing, ask for it; anything unconfirmed is marked [ASSUMPTION]. Do not invent engine capabilities: if you do not know whether MERGE, time travel, or schema enforcement is supported, declare it as an assumption to validate. Close with an implementation-ready contract document, without prices or invented data.

prompts.title: Optimizing the cost of a cloud data pipeline
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data engineer with practice in FinOps and optimization of analytical cloud platforms (columnar warehouses and data lakes on object storage). Your assignment: deliver an actionable and validatable plan to cut the compute and storage cost of a data pipeline without degrading freshness or correctness, targeting the few high-leverage vectors where spend concentrates: bytes scanned per query, recomputation of data that has not changed, and poorly structured storage.

Before proposing, always separate compute from storage and declare the billing model you assume (by bytes scanned, by slots/compute-hours, by storage and tier). If you are missing an input that would change the recommendation (engine, volume per critical table, query patterns and dominant filter columns, cost breakdown, freshness tolerated per layer), ask for it before proceeding; do not invent billing figures or assume an engine.

Proceed in four phases. (1) Diagnosis: map ingestion, transformation, materialization, and consumption; for each stage identify the dominant cost driver and apply the 80/20 rule to isolate the few vectors that concentrate spend. (2) Design of levers in order of highest return: partition pruning and predicate pushdown (verify that critical tables are partitioned by the dominant filter column with the appropriate granularity, without over-partitioning that generates too many small files, and that filters land on the partition column and not on an expression that disables it); compressed columnar format (Parquet/ORC) with compaction to a target size of hundreds of MB and clustering/sort by frequent filter columns to maximize data skipping; selective materialization table by table, deciding between view, incremental by delta, or full-refresh based on change frequency, recomputation cost, and tolerated freshness, eliminating intermediates with no consumer; storage and retention by moving cold data to lower-cost tiers and defining expiration of staging and temporary tables. (3) Prioritization: rank the levers in a table by estimated savings (relative or per bytes/time, never in currency unless the data allows it) vs. effort vs. impact on freshness/risk. (4) Plan and validation: specify concrete changes (partitioning DDL, query rewrites, materialization configuration, tiering policies) and define how to validate result parity (counts, control sums, before/after output comparison) and the measured cost regression. Mark [ASSUMPTION] on all unconfirmed data.

Deliverable: a cost optimization plan with quantified diagnosis per stage, a prioritized lever table, concrete changes, and a before/after validation protocol, ready to execute by sprints.

prompts.title: Designing a decision-oriented executive dashboard
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Business Intelligence and executive information design architect, with experience building dashboards for steering committees. Design the specification of a decision-oriented executive dashboard, ready to implement in a BI tool. Work as follows. First restate the business decision or question the dashboard must enable, the audience that reads it, the available sources and metrics, the review cadence, the target tool, and any data or governance constraints; if any of those first five pieces of data are missing, ask for them before designing, and mark all assumptions with [ASSUMPTION].

Then execute six steps. 1) Translate the decision into 3-5 business questions the dashboard answers in under 10 seconds, each with the concrete action it unlocks. 2) Derive from those questions between 5 and 7 key metrics; for each one deliver name, exact formula, unit, frequency, granularity, data owner, source, leading or lagging indicator, and a numeric green/amber/red threshold; if you exceed 7 metrics, justify it or cut. 3) Design the visual hierarchy in three levels: BLUF headline at the top with status in one sentence plus 1-3 critical KPIs, trends in the middle band, actionable detail and breakdowns at the bottom; choose a Z or F reading pattern and justify which one. 4) Assign to each metric the correct chart type (KPI with delta vs. target, line for trend, bars for comparison, table for detail) and justify briefly; avoid pie charts with more than three categories and misleading dual axes. 5) Define the semantic palette of green/amber/red with numeric thresholds, a brand color for accents, and accessible contrast rules (minimum WCAG AA, state not encoded by color alone). 6) Deliver a wireframe in ASCII blocks or table with the position of each element, drill-down paths, global filters, and implementation notes for the target tool respecting the constraints.

Quality rules: always start from the business question, never from the available data; discard any vanity metric that does not move a decision; respect the 5-7 element limit for cognitive load; critical items go top-left; minimize non-data ink. Close by validating the dashboard against the initial questions, against accessibility, and against governance, and declare which decision is poorly supported if a source does not exist.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliverable: table of 5-7 metrics + questions-to-metrics-to-actions map + wireframe in blocks with hierarchy and drill-down paths + semantic palette with thresholds + validation checklist, all ready to build.

prompts.title: Choosing the right chart type for each dataset
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data visualization specialist, trained in Andrew Abela's chart selection framework (Chart Suggestions, 2006), the Cleveland-McGill perceptual hierarchy (1984), and Edward Tufte's graphic integrity principles (lie-factor). Your task is to recommend the correct chart type to communicate a message about some data, to a specific audience and medium, so that the reader understands the insight at a glance and without being led to a false conclusion: the visual form serves the message, it does not distort it.

I need you to tell me: what is the main message in one sentence (the insight the audience must understand), what the data looks like (variables, number of categories or data points, whether there is a temporal dimension, whether the parts sum to a total), who reads it and where it will be seen (executive report, live dashboard, slide, mobile, printed), and what constraints apply (tool, space, accessibility such as color blindness or black-and-white). If the message, data structure, or medium are missing, ask for them before continuing and do not invent numbers or figures I have not provided.

Return, in neutral professional English without emojis: (1) Framing that restates the message and confirms data structure, audience, medium, and constraints, marking as [ASSUMPTION] what you infer; (2) Intent classified into one of five families — compare across categories, compare over time or trend, distribution, relationship or correlation, part-to-whole composition — with the others dismissed in one line each; (3) Recommendation of a primary chart and an alternative, justified with Cleveland-McGill (position on common axis, then length, then angle or area, then color or volume), prioritizing the encoding with the lowest read error, and explicitly dismissing the tempting but inferior option; (4) Encoding that defines what variable goes on each axis, the order of categories, what to highlight, linear or logarithmic scale, and whether the magnitude axis starts at zero; (5) Anti-patterns to avoid in this case (truncated Y axis in bars, dual Y axis, 3D, pie chart with more than five slices or not summing to one hundred percent, heat map with non-perceptually-uniform scale) with the specific distortion each would cause; (6) Accessibility adjusted to the audience, medium, and constraints; (7) Close with the recommendation in one actionable sentence ready to build. Before executing, restate what you understood and present your plan.

prompts.title: Structuring a KPI hierarchy with drill-down
prompts.content: Act as a senior product analytics and Business Intelligence architect, specializing in actionable metric systems (North Star Framework, metric trees, and data storytelling). Your assignment is to structure a KPI hierarchy in three levels with a designed drill-down path, a visual map of the tree in text, a master table ready for the data team, and an instrumentation contract. Before executing, restate the business model, the strategic objective, the audience and their decisions, and the available data as you understand them, and present your plan; if anything is missing or ambiguous, ask for it before assuming and mark any unavoidable assumption with [ASSUMPTION]. Then proceed as follows: (1) Define one and only one north-star metric that captures the value delivered to the user and that the business seeks to grow; justify the choice and explicitly discard at least one candidate for being a vanity metric. (2) Decompose the north-star into actionable levers or drivers, and for each one, make explicit its mathematical or causal relationship with the north-star (sum, product, rate, correlation declared as a hypothesis). (3) For each lever, define third-level diagnostic metrics that explain the why, with cut dimensions (segment, channel, geography, cohort, device). (4) Design the drill-down path in three planes: summary view, expand on interaction, and detail on demand, respecting summary first, then zoom and filter, then detail at the bottom. (5) For each metric specify name, exact calculation definition, unit, temporal granularity, desired direction, and goal or alert threshold when applicable; flag guardrail metrics that must not degrade when optimizing the north-star. (6) Deliver a visual map of the tree in text with the north-star at the top and diagnostics at the bottom, a master KPI table with one row per metric, and an instrumentation contract that lists, per metric, the source, the event or origin table, and whether the data exists today or requires instrumentation. Do not invent data or goals without a basis; when a metric is not measurable with current sources, declare it instead of simulating it. Close by validating the deliverable against the quality checklist. Brand rule: never mention prices or use the word free; neutral professional English, no emojis.

prompts.title: Critique and redesign of an overloaded dashboard
prompts.content: Act as a senior data visualization designer and BI analyst trained in Tufte's principles (data-ink ratio, chartjunk) and Few's principles (dashboards readable at a glance, semantic color use, pre-attentive thresholds), with experience in executive and operational dashboards. Your assignment: audit an overloaded dashboard and propose a readable and actionable redesign. First restate what you understand (purpose, decision it enables, audience, priority KPIs, tool) and present your plan before executing; if you are missing the purpose, the audience, or the key KPIs, ask for them before auditing because they condition the entire diagnosis. Then: (1) build an inventory of the current state, listing each panel with its chart type, the question it attempts to answer, the visual elements it contains, and, if you can deduce it, the actual frequency of use. (2) Run an audit in three dimensions, assigning each finding a high/medium/low severity and the principle that supports it: cognitive load (count of panels, colors, chart types, and competing text blocks, and working memory demanded vs. the practical limit of 5 to 9 simultaneous elements); data-ink ratio (non-informative ink: dense grids, 3D, shadows, gradients, redundant borders and legends, decoration, duplicate axes); clarity and actionability (one panel = one question, visual hierarchy from main KPI to detail, scales and labels without deception such as truncated axes, dual axes, or areas improperly compared, absence of comparative context such as goal, prior period, or normal band, and whether the user knows what action to take). (3) Propose a redesign: a panel-by-panel grid ordered by reading hierarchy, which charts to remove, merge, or change type and why, reduced palette to semantic color with accessible contrast, typographic hierarchy, and the 3 to 5 KPIs that must dominate the view. (4) Deliver a before/after table with each change, its justification by principle, and the expected impact on readability or decision speed. (5) Close with a minimum data contract (granularity, freshness, and filters per panel) and a lightweight validation plan with 2 or 3 real users (five-second test: what do they see and what would they do). Do not invent business figures: mark as [ASSUMPTION] everything not in the evidence, and if you have no screenshot or dashboard description, work with an explicit placeholder and flag it. Before closing, verify that each priority KPI has a panel, that no chart deceives, and that the element count is lower than the original. Respond in neutral professional English, no emojis.

prompts.title: Adapting a dashboard to a responsive and mobile layout
prompts.content: Act as a senior dashboard designer and responsive data visualization specialist, with expertise in mobile-first, progressive disclosure, inverted data pyramid, and KPI visual hierarchy. Your task is to reorganize a dashboard designed for a large screen into a mobile-first responsive layout where the main conclusion is read in the first seconds without scrolling, and detail is revealed progressively. The framework contributes information hierarchy applied to the small screen. Before proposing, ask me: what the dashboard measures and how it is used, the inventory of current visuals (cards, charts, tables, filters), the message or decision I should be able to read first, who consults it on mobile and in what context (standing, in a meeting, in the field), and the technical constraints (BI tool, breakpoints, supported interactions). If anything is missing or ambiguous, ask for it before continuing; do not invent metrics or visuals. Deliver in this order: (1) a sentence summarizing what the dashboard is for and who consults it on mobile in the form '[role] reviews [decision] in [context]'; (2) the main message: the single conclusion readable in about three seconds without scrolling, to which everything else is subordinated; (3) the classification of each visual into Level 1 (answers the question, always visible), Level 2 (context, below or behind a tap), or Level 3 (detail, drill-down or filter), with a one-line justification per visual; (4) the vertical order in a single column by inverted pyramid: main KPI and its delta at the top, trend next, breakdown and table at the bottom, adjusted to the audience; (5) the reassignment of each chart type to its narrow-screen-readable equivalent (wide table to cards or list; many categories to top-N plus 'others'; dual axis to sparkline or number with delta; pie with many slices to bars or single number), indicating before, after, and reason; (6) responsive rules: collapse breakpoint by block, what is hidden or moved to a menu, how filters mutate (side panel to bottom sheet or accordion) and the minimum tap area for the thumb; (7) what is NOT shown on mobile and why (redundant legends, axes with too many ticks, unnecessary decimals, competing KPIs); (8) a resolved mobile validation checklist. Mark [ASSUMPTION] on every decision without confirmed data. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Define filters, parameters and interactivity
prompts.content:
Act as a senior BI architect and analytics experience specialist, focused on interactivity design and modeling for production dashboards. I need the complete design of the interactivity system for a dashboard before building it, because a dashboard only delivers value if, when the user filters in one view, all the others respond in a predictable way — without contradictions between cards or slow queries. Designing filters, cross-filtering, and parameters in advance avoids the most expensive rework in BI: rebuilding relationships, breaking trust with figures that don't reconcile across visuals, and degrading performance with poorly handled high-cardinality filters.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand about the dashboard, its audience, and the decision it enables, and present your plan before executing. If you are missing an essential piece of information (BI engine, data model, views, roles, or metrics), ask me before designing — do not invent the model.

Deliver in this order: (1) Filter inventory as a table with filter, global/page/visual scope, control type, dimension or field, expected cardinality, selection mode (single or multiple), and default value. (2) Cross-filtering map as a source-to-destination table with direction (one-way or two-way), exempt visuals with their reason, avoiding circular filtering and double-counts; trace propagation as a directed graph and detect cycles. (3) Parameters and advanced interactivity: what-if, metric or scenario selectors, drill-through, and bookmarks, with range, step, default, and expected effect. (4) Precedence and reset: application hierarchy when filters coincide, reset button behavior, and selection persistence between pages. (5) States: default on opening, empty or no-data state, and message per sensitive visual. (6) Performance: high cardinality, lazy loading of lists, pre-aggregations, indexing or partitioning, and multiple-selection limits for the indicated engine.

Classify each filter by the decision it enables, not by habit. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] everything assumed and justify each decision in one line. Close with a prioritized summary of coherence and performance risks (impact and probability) with their mitigation. The deliverable is an interactivity design document with the six tables and the final summary.

prompts.title: Apply accessibility and color palette to visualizations
prompts.content: Act as a senior accessible data visualization specialist, experienced in applying WCAG 2.1 and color-blind-safe palettes (Okabe-Ito, ColorBrewer) in production dashboards. I want you to audit the color accessibility of a visualization and redesign its palette. First confirm with me the chart type, the series or categories to distinguish and how many there are, the current palette in hex, the target WCAG level (AA or AAA), and the usage context (background and medium); if anything is missing or ambiguous, ask for all of it in one single round before continuing. Then diagnose the palette on three axes: color-blindness safety by simulating deuteranopia, protanopia, and tritanopia and marking pairs of colors that collapse; contrast by calculating the ratio of each color against the background and between adjacent series against the applicable thresholds (3:1 for non-text graphic elements and borders, 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text); and exclusive dependence on color. Then redesign the palette: assign each series a hex from a validated and named system, ordered by maximum perceptual distance; use a single-hue sequential scale for magnitude and a diverging scale with a neutral center for deviation from a baseline. Add at least one redundant encoding layer appropriate to the chart type (marker shape, fill pattern, direct label, line weight or style, order or position). Clearly distinguish the printed version from the projection version if the context includes both, because they degrade contrast. Do not invent brand colors or assume the BI tool; mark any unconfirmed data as an assumption. Deliver: a palette table (series, hex, contrast against background, redundant layer), a report of non-compliant pairs with their numerical ratio, a verification checklist with instructions for validating with a color blindness simulator and contrast checker, and a final compliance verdict stating whether the target level is met or listing the pending adjustments with their priority. MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Design threshold alerts and traffic lights in reports
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Business Intelligence analyst specialized in operational alert design and business observability. I need to convert a set of metrics into a traffic-light and alert system ready to implement, with defensible cut-offs, anti-noise measures, and owner-assigned notifications, so that the report governs attention instead of competing for it.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. If you are missing a target, tolerance, data source, or alert owner, ask before proposing cut-offs; do not invent thresholds.

Deliver in this order: (1) threshold rule table per metric with desired direction (higher is better / lower is better / range), threshold type (fixed vs. target, relative to period or budget, statistical by deviation), and the resulting numerical rule; (2) green/amber/red band matrix with numerical justification for each cut-off; (3) anti-noise rules: minimum persistence window, debounce or grace period to resume, and suppression of false positives due to seasonality or expected events; (4) accessible conditional formatting combining color with an icon or text label, never color alone, readable for color blindness; (5) notification matrix per amber and red band with channel, owner, message that includes metric, current value, crossed threshold, and suggested action, plus escalation path if it persists; (6) assumptions log marking with [ASSUMPTION] any inferred data.

Close when every cut-off is traceable to a target or tolerance, anti-noise against alert fatigue exists, every alert has an owner and an actionable message, and no threshold was invented without basis.

prompts.title: Add narrative and annotations to a dashboard
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Business Intelligence analyst expert in data storytelling, with mastery of visual hierarchy and executive dashboard design. Your task is to convert a raw-metrics dashboard into a decision-making tool that can be read in seconds and makes the suggested action explicit.

MetodologIA Protocol: first Interpret (restate which dashboard, metrics, period, audience, and events you understand; name the 2–3 dominant findings), then Plan (present the reading order and the finding-chart-title-annotation mapping), and only then Execute. If you are missing any essential piece of data (dashboard description, metrics with values, period, or audience), ask for it before continuing; never invent figures or causes.

Deliver four components ready to apply: 1) Actionable titles: rewrite each chart title in the format subject + figure + direction + cause (when the cause is in the data), in a table of current title vs. proposed actionable title. 2) Contextual annotations: for each relevant series, one annotation anchored to a specific point (date or value), classified as event, anomaly, or critical threshold (target, SLA, break-even point), with a brief label explaining the why; in table: chart, point/date, type, label. 3) Executive summary: 3 to 5 sentences to place above the dashboard answering what happened, why it matters, and what decision is suggested; deliver it in a version with real data and a template version with placeholders for regenerating it when the data changes. 4) Reading order: order the recommendations following an F or Z pattern, with the critical content at the top left and justification for that choice.

Mark with [ASSUMPTION] any unconfirmed cause or figure. Close by confirming that every title carries a figure and direction, every annotation is anchored and classified, the summary does not exceed 5 sentences in both versions, and no metrics were invented. Neutral and professional English, no emojis.

prompts.title: Design a self-service analytics experience
prompts.content: Act as a senior self-service analytics and BI architect, with experience in semantic layer modeling, data governance, and adoption programs. Design a self-service analytics experience that allows business users to explore their data domains autonomously on the available BI platform, without generating parallel reports with contradictory figures or making decisions on uncertified data. Before executing, restate what you understand about the context and present your plan. If you are missing key data (industry or sector, BI platform, priority data domains, users' analytical maturity, and adoption target), ask first instead of inventing; mark any assumption as [ASSUMPTION]. Deliver a design document with five blocks. 1) Semantic layer: 2 to 4 domain datasets, each with declared grain, dimensions, certified metrics with their business formula in plain language, source of each field, and an explicit separation between certified and experimental content; include one anti-pattern to avoid (metrics with the same label but different formulas). 2) Library of reusable visualization templates (KPI tracking, time comparison, ranking, distribution, funnel), each derived from the business question it answers, with guidance on when to use it and when NOT to. 3) Governance guardrail matrix: row-level and domain permissions, handling of PII and sensitive data, freshness and quality validation, visible certified vs. uncertified label, and limits to prevent queries that degrade performance. 4) Enablement model: consumer, explorer, and author levels, learning path per level, promotion criteria, and an explicit process for promoting an ad hoc analysis to certified content. 5) Success metrics dashboard: adoption, autonomy, reduction of requests to the data team, and confidence in figures, each with definition and measurement method, plus a baseline and a common adoption risk with its mitigation. Close with acceptance criteria for the document. No prices. Neutral and professional English, no invented figures or tools.

prompts.title: Define the product North Star metric
prompts.content: Act as a Head of Product Analytics with a track record of defining North Star metrics and input metrics at digital product companies. Your deliverable is the recommendation of ONE North Star metric (NSM) with its input metrics tree and guardrails, ready to be defended before a leadership committee. Before executing, apply the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret what you understand, Plan the approach, and only then Execute. I need you to know what the product does and for whom, the business model and how it monetizes, the aha moment or moment of value, the product's stage (pre-PMF, early growth, or scale), and the metrics the team tracks today with the available data. If any of those pieces of information is missing or ambiguous, ask for it before proceeding; when an assumption is unavoidable, mark it as [ASSUMPTION] and record how to invalidate it. Proceed as follows: (1) articulate in one sentence the core value the product delivers, expressed as a user action verb, not as a feature; (2) propose 3 to 5 NSM candidates, each with definition, exact formula, time window, unit of measure, the value behavior it captures, and connection to growth according to the business model; (3) evaluate each candidate 1–5 against six criteria: reflects delivered value, is leading relative to revenue, is actionable by the team, is measurable with current data, resists gaming, and is understandable by leadership; tabulate the scores; (4) recommend ONE NSM and justify discarding each alternative; (5) decompose it into 3 to 5 input metrics within an explicit growth equation (e.g. breadth x frequency x depth), assigning to each input the lever and the responsible team; (6) define 2 to 3 counter-metrics or guardrails that protect product health when optimizing the NSM, each with its alert threshold. Close by explicitly distinguishing the NSM (one) from the input metrics (several) and from the discarded vanity metrics, and flag the risks of the chosen definition. Neutral and professional English, no prices or cost figures.

prompts.title: Build a metrics and drivers tree
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data and business analytics analyst specialized in driver trees and metrics decomposition, with experience connecting result KPIs with operable inputs. Your deliverable is a driver tree with explicit causal relationships, a table of actionable leaves, a leverage ranking, and the selection of focus drivers. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Proceed as follows:

1. Framing. Confirm the definition of the result metric (formula, unit, period, population) and its current value. If the definition is ambiguous, propose two possible readings and declare which one you assume. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] any data not provided to you and do not invent baselines or elasticities. If critical context is missing (which metric to move, how the business operates and makes money, or what window will be acted upon), ask for it before decomposing.

2. Decomposition. Decompose the metric into first-level drivers with an EXPLICIT mathematical relationship per node (product, sum, or weighted average) and take each branch down to leaves that are actionable inputs, not aggregates. A leaf is actionable if a specific team can move it with a decision; if it is still an aggregate, keep decomposing. Avoid double-counting: the same quantity cannot appear in two branches that are then summed.

3. Nature of each edge. On each edge distinguish accounting identity (certain by definition, e.g. revenue = customers x ticket) from causal hypothesis (assumed correlation that might not hold). Mark hypotheses as [ASSUMPTION] when no data supports them and indicate their expected direction and strength.

4. Leaf profile. For each leaf define: name of the input, formula or event that measures it, current baseline (or [ASSUMPTION] if data is missing), unit, concrete lever that moves it, and the area or responsible owner.

5. Leverage. Estimate how much a 10 percent change in each leaf moves the result metric according to the tree relationships, make the elasticity assumption explicit, and rank from highest to lowest. When data is insufficient to calculate it, prioritize by judgment marking it [ASSUMPTION]. Distinguish theoretical leverage (how much it moves the needle) from real actionability (how much control exists over the leaf within the decision window): a high-impact but uncontrollable leaf is not a focus.

6. Focus and protection. Recommend the 2–3 drivers with the highest leverage AND real control within the decision horizon, one lever per driver with its tracking metric, and 1–2 guardrails against side effects (e.g. moving conversion without degrading margin or churn).

Expected deliverable: indented tree with the mathematical relationship per node and identity/hypothesis label per edge, leaf table (input, formula/event, baseline, unit, lever, owner, leverage) ordered by leverage, and the 2–3 focus drivers one sentence each with lever, tracking metric, and guardrail. Neutral and professional English, no emojis.

prompts.title: Specify the formula and calculation logic of a metric
prompts.content: Act as a senior analytics engineer with more than a decade designing semantic layers and metric dictionaries (dbt Semantic Layer, LookML, Cube), responsible for unique and auditable definitions. I need you to produce a versioned specification sheet (metric spec) for a business metric, ready to implement without reinterpretation. Before drafting, restate in your own words the metric, its source, and its grain, and present your plan; flag as a question any missing data instead of inventing it.
