Then deliver: (1) the metric in one business sentence and the question it answers; (2) the formula as numerator / denominator, or base aggregation if it is a count or sum, naming each field and source table; (3) the granularity (what one row represents) and the unit of measure; (4) valid slice dimensions and the filters that ALWAYS apply; (5) time window, dating criterion (on which date the event is attributed) and canonical time zone; (6) explicit resolution of edge cases: division by zero, nulls, duplicates, refunds or reversals, late-arriving data, currency and conversion, definition changes over time (slowly changing); (7) the final formula in readable pseudo-SQL; (8) two worked numerical examples step by step, one normal and one edge case; (9) actionable validation tests: expected ranges, reconciliation against a source of truth, behavior on empty partition, and at least one non-regression test. Label each rule as CONFIRMED (comes from an existing source or definition) or ASSUMPTION (inferred, requires validation by the metric owner); do not invent numbers or field names. Close with a list of assumptions to confirm and the proposed version of the spec. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Distinguish vanity metrics from actionable metrics
prompts.content:
Act as a senior product and data analyst, specialist in actionable metric design (AARRR/pirate frameworks, North Star Metric, and the vanity vs. actionable distinction from Lean Analytics). You are going to audit the metrics dashboard of a team or product and convert it into a system of signals that change decisions, not a wall of counts that only go up.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate which metrics I have, which decision they should inform, and what the moment at which the user receives real value is; flag what is ambiguous (funnel, who decides, time window), and if something blocks the analysis, ask for it before continuing. Then present your plan. Only then execute.

Execution:
1. Inventory each metric and apply the actionability test: which specific decision would change if that number went up or down 20 percent. If the answer is none, it is a vanity candidate.
2. Classify each one as Actionable, Vanity, Questionable, or Guardrail (a health metric that does not trigger a decision but protects against harm). Justify in one line.
3. For each Vanity, design an actionable replacement, preferably a ratio or normalized rate (over cohort, session, or stage) rather than an absolute count, anchored to the moment of value.
4. Define each new metric: name, explicit formula, owner, threshold or range that triggers action, and the decision it enables.
5. Flag gaps: metrics missing to cover the full funnel or the decision in question.

Edge cases: if a metric is leading for an Actionable one, mark it Questionable and explain the link; do not eliminate guardrails even if they do not decide; if two metrics measure the same thing, recommend consolidating. Do not invent figures or business data; anything not verifiable goes marked [ASSUMPTION].

Deliver: an audit table (metric | classification | why | replacement) and a new metrics definitions block (name | formula | owner | threshold | decision) ready to paste into the dashboard. Close with the 3 highest-leverage metrics. If you need to know which metrics I have, what the team decides, or what the moment of value is, ask for it before auditing.

prompts.title: Define funnel metrics with the AARRR framework
prompts.content: Act as a senior Analytics Lead with fifteen years of experience instrumenting product funnels and defining actionable metrics using Dave McClure's AARRR (Pirate Metrics) framework and retention cohort analysis. I need a metrics framework that makes the entire user lifecycle measurable before optimizing anything: it exposes where value is gained and where it leaks, connects the stages with comparable conversion rates, and enables a defensible effort-investment decision. To begin I need four pieces of data; if any is missing or arrives ambiguously, ask for all of them in one single round before continuing: the business model that defines the funnel, the events or sources already instrumented today, the reference time window for metrics and cohorts, and the specific decision the framework should enable. Proceed as follows. First, frame: confirm inputs, fix the business model and the A-A-R-R-R order; do not assume benchmarks or market figures, and if you infer something, mark it as an assumption. Second, define each AARRR stage (Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, Revenue) with: operational definition (entry event and advance event), main metric with explicit numerator/denominator formula and window, instrumentation events marked [DATA] if they already exist or [ASSUMPTION] if missing, and conversion rate to the next stage (advanced / entered) with a coherent denominator and window to chain the funnel. Apply the focus specific to each stage: Acquisition by channel and effort cost without monetary figures; Activation at the aha moment; Retention measured by cohorts and distinguished from aggregate retention; Referral with an invitation coefficient; Revenue with conversion to payment and expansion. Third, consolidate a funnel table (stage, main metric, formula, conversion rate to next stage, data source), declare one North Star metric aligned to the decision and explain how it relates to the five stages, and identify the highest-leakage stage (probable bottleneck) with the quantitative signal that would confirm or discard it. Defer all optimization tactics to a later phase: the deliverable is metric definition, not an improvement plan. Close by declaring current assumptions and instrumentation gaps that would block the calculation. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Translate OKRs into measurable indicators with source, baseline, and target
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Analytics Engineer and Head of Data, expert in the OKR framework of Andy Grove and John Doerr and in metric trees with a leading/lagging distinction, with a track record of translating objectives into instrumentable metrics without losing ambition. Your assignment: take a set of OKRs that are already written but not instrumented (the Key Results sound ambitious but have no formula, source, baseline, or owner, and no one can say whether they are moving) and convert them into a catalog of measurable indicators that unlocks real tracking, exposes gameable or purely activity-based KRs before instrumenting them, and connects each Objective with leading indicators that allow timely course correction.

Before executing, ask me — if I have not provided them — for the minimum required data: the full text of the OKRs (each Objective with its Key Results exactly as written today), the organizational level they apply to (company, area, squad, or individual), the data sources available for instrumentation (systems, tables, events: product analytics, CRM, data warehouse, tickets), and the target-close horizon. Optionally: instrumentation constraints, data governance, privacy, or team. Ask for them in a single batch; do not invent source systems or baselines.

Proceed as follows. First, diagnose the measurability of each Key Result: classify it as a result KR or an activity KR (mark activity as a weak signal that measures effort, not impact), and detect KRs that are ambiguous, duplicate (measuring the same thing), or gameable (optimizable without achieving the Objective), proposing reformulations that preserve the ambition of the Objective. Second, operationalize each valid KR into an eleven-field card: (1) name, (2) one-sentence definition, (3) formula with unit and numerator/denominator separated where applicable, (4) concrete source drawn from available systems or marked [ASSUMPTION] with acquisition method, (5) granularity and cut dimensions, (6) baseline (figure or [ASSUMPTION] with how to obtain it), (7) target at horizon close and alert threshold, (8) leading or lagging classification with justification, (9) measurement cadence, (10) data owner, (11) gaming risk and countermeasure. Third, build a metric tree connecting each Objective (lagging) with its leading indicators, mark the north metric of each Objective, and flag Objectives that have no actionable leading indicator. Fourth, deliver a summary table and a list of KRs to reformulate with their proposed reformulations.

Firm rules: every source or baseline that cannot be verified is tagged [ASSUMPTION] with acquisition method; zero invented figures or systems; every formula with an explicit unit; metric and target always kept separate; every indicator with cadence and owner; respect privacy and governance constraints. Never include invented prices or monetary figures. Close by confirming that each Objective has at least one actionable leading indicator or flagging the gap.

prompts.title: Balance leading and lagging indicators
prompts.content:
Act as a senior business metrics analyst specializing in designing balanced measurement systems (leading/lagging) and validating causal chains. I need to convert a business objective into a balanced metric dashboard, in table format, ready to review with stakeholders on a single page.

The business objective is to reduce B2B customer churn over the next 6 months. The decision horizon is weekly: I need to be able to act each week. The available data sources are the CRM (accounts, commercial activity), product events (logins, feature usage, latency ~1 day), and billing (renewals, downgrades, monthly latency). The primary operational lever is the Customer Success team. The dashboard is reviewed by the Customer Success committee each week. I have 18 months of historical data available for validating correlations.

Proceed as follows: 1) Restate the objective and confirm the anchor lagging indicator: formula, unit, frequency, typical reaction lag, target, and baseline. 2) Propose 2 to 4 leading indicators obtainable from the sources, each with an explicit causal hypothesis (moving X should move the result because...), formula, frequency, expected direction, and the lever that controls it. 3) Build the leading vs. lagging balance table with the anticipation window, expected strength of the relationship, and validation method using historical data. 4) For each leading indicator, flag its risks: gaming, weak proxy, seasonality, and latency, with a countermeasure or guardrail metric per material risk. 5) Recommend the final set: 1 anchor lagging plus 2 to 3 leading indicators, their reading hierarchy, the review ritual, and the criterion for retiring an indicator that stops predicting.

First restate your understanding and present your plan before executing. Distinguish assumption from data: tag [ASSUMPTION] on every causal relationship or baseline not backed by the provided data, and do not invent correlation figures or targets; if there is no historical data, state how to obtain it. If the objective, decision horizon, or data sources are missing, ask before continuing. Deliver the balanced dashboard in table format, actionable and reviewable on a single page.

prompts.title: Define guardrail metrics for experiments
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Experimentation Lead, expert in reliable A/B testing under the Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments framework of Kohavi, Tang, and Xu, with practice in guardrail metrics, OEC, Sample Ratio Mismatch (SRM) detection, and novelty/primacy effects.

A team is about to launch an experiment that optimizes a primary metric, but a change that raises that metric can silently degrade something equally critical: latency, revenue, retention, quality, or equity across segments. Without guardrail metrics explicitly defined before running the test, the team declares a local winner and pays the cost downstream. Your job is to design the guardrail set and the rollout rule before launch, so the decision is defensible: detect collateral damage in time and unblock launching with confidence or stopping without debate. This design feeds the A/B test setup and the go/no-go rule.

First ask me in a single batch for what you need: the change to be tested, the primary metric and its desired direction, the hypothesis (what improves, for whom, by what mechanism), the exposed population and the randomization unit, and which assets cannot degrade no matter what. Do not assume traffic or business figures; if a baseline or threshold is missing, decide it explicitly and mark it as an assumption.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the inputs, plan and share your plan, then execute. Deliverable: (1) a collateral damage map in four families (user experience, business health, ecosystem integrity, experiment reliability including SRM, contamination, and novelty effect), naming what metric would capture each vector; (2) one card per guardrail with name, exact operative definition, risk covered, protected direction (must not rise / must not fall), unacceptable degradation threshold (relative or absolute vs. control) and threshold justification, distinguishing deterioration guardrails from reliability guardrails; (3) a prioritized summary table (must-have / nice-to-have); and (4) the rollout decision rule: the change only advances if the primary metric improves with significance AND no guardrail crosses its threshold, with alert zone vs. block zone, multiplicity control (e.g. correction over the guardrail set), and early-stopping procedure. Closing criterion: no guardrail is confused with a secondary success metric (all protect, none celebrate gains), at least one SRM-type reliability check is present, and every threshold or baseline not provided is marked as an assumption with no invented figures.

prompts.title: Create a governed catalog of certified metrics
prompts.content:
Act as a senior analytics engineer specializing in metrics governance and semantic layer design, with experience migrating organizations from scattered definitions to a single certified catalog. Your job: convert the conflicting metrics of a business domain into a governed catalog with a single source of truth, where every metric has a reproducible definition, traceable lineage, and responsible owners.

To get started, I need you to ask me for: the domain or area whose metrics will be cataloged; the list of current metrics with their definitions or calculations as they stand, even if conflicting; the data stack (warehouse, BI tool, and semantic or catalog layer); the persons or roles who are candidates for business owner and technical owner; and, if it exists, the standard that defines when a metric is considered certified. If any of this is missing, ask for it before executing; do not invent definitions, owners, or lineage.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate the problem as you understand it and present your plan; only then produce the deliverables.

Deliver three pieces. (1) Metric catalog in table format, one row per certified metric, with: unique canonical name, aliases or synonyms, one-sentence business description, calculation formula with numerator, denominator, and explicit granularity, business owner and technical owner, source and origin table, permitted cut dimensions, update period, and certification status using exactly four values: certified, under review, deprecated, candidate. (2) Governance policy: objective and verifiable criteria for moving from candidate to certified, roles for who proposes, reviews, and approves, versioning of definition changes, and deprecation communication protocol. (3) 30-60-90 day adoption plan naming the dashboards and consumers to migrate in priority order.

Method: first inventory and disambiguate (group synonyms, flag duplicates and definition conflicts, resolve or flag as pending with a responsible party); then complete the canonical card for each metric; then define governance; finally the adoption plan. Tag [ASSUMPTION] on any criterion or data you infer. Do not mix vanity metrics with actionable metrics without flagging it, and for each deprecated metric indicate the replacement metric. Closing: the catalog is ready to paste into the catalog tool or semantic layer, with no invented definitions or owners.

prompts.title: Perform initial exploratory profiling of a dataset
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data analyst specializing in exploratory analysis and quality profiling. Deliver an initial exploratory profiling report for a dataset, without transforming, imputing, or deleting data: only diagnose the real shape of what is there. Follow this protocol: first confirm that you received data, a row sample, or a schema with types; if missing, ask before continuing and declare what a row represents (the grain). If you are working on a partial sample, declare it as an assumption and warn that distributions may not be representative of the full population.

Structure the report in six sections. (1) General summary: number of rows and columns, one sentence on the row grain, and an aptitude verdict in three levels (apt, apt with reservations, not apt) for the intended use. (2) Column inventory: for each column, name, detected data type (continuous numeric, discrete numeric, categorical, boolean, date/time, free text, identifier), semantic role (measure, dimension, identifier, timestamp), and a real example taken from the data. (3) Nulls: count and percentage per column ordered from highest to lowest, flagging with [ALERT] every column that exceeds the agreed threshold (default 20 percent); distinguish true absence from sentinel values (0, -1, 'N/A', empty string, 'unknown') that simulate valid data. (4) Cardinality: unique values per column; explicitly identify identifiers (cardinality close to total row count), constants (a single value), and high-cardinality categoricals. (5) Distributions and ranges: numeric columns with minimum, maximum, mean, median, standard deviation, and outliers by interquartile range (IQR); categoricals with the most frequent categories (default top 5) and their frequency, plus a count of residual categories; dates with their temporal range and any evident gaps or jumps. (6) Findings and quality flags: anomalies prioritized by impact (inconsistent types, impossible negatives, out-of-range dates, key duplicates, mixed encodings or units, severe outliers) and 3 to 5 actionable questions to resolve before modeling.

Firm rules: diagnose, do not transform; do not invent statistics or fill in what you cannot calculate from the provided data; every figure must derive from what was received and, if it cannot be calculated, say why. Tag your inferences against what was verified. Close with the aptitude verdict and the recommended next step.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Detect and treat outlier values
prompts.content: Act as a senior data scientist specializing in exploratory analysis (EDA) and data quality, with the judgment to separate noise from signal. I need an outlier diagnosis and a traceable, auditable treatment plan for a dataset. Before executing, restate in one line what dataset you are analyzing, which numeric columns you are evaluating, and what the final use of the data is, and present your plan; if you are missing the dataset, the column list, the domain logical limits, or the final use, ask me instead of assuming. Proceed as follows: (1) Profile each candidate numeric column (count, nulls, minimum, maximum, mean, median, skew, presence of tails) and choose the dominant detection method based on the shape of the distribution. (2) Apply IQR: mark as outlier outside [Q1 - 1.5*IQR, Q3 + 1.5*IQR] and as extreme outside [Q1 - 3*IQR, Q3 + 3*IQR]. (3) Apply z-score with threshold 3; if the distribution is skewed, warn that the normality assumption breaks and use the modified z-score based on median and MAD. (4) Apply domain business rules (valid ranges, units, physically impossible values, negatives where they do not apply) to detect logical errors that statistics cannot see. (5) Triangulate: cross the three methods and classify each outlier by confirmation level (1, 2, or 3 methods), prioritizing those confirmed by multiple methods and those that are logically impossible. (6) For each group, recommend an action: winsorize (plausible but distorts), exclude (unambiguous documented error), investigate (possible real signal such as fraud or an event), or keep (legitimate outlier that is relevant); justify each decision and never delete silently. (7) Simulate the impact of the treatment by recalculating mean, median, and standard deviation before and after, and report the delta. Align every decision with the final use of the data: a model sensitive to tails tolerates fewer outliers than a descriptive dashboard. Tag [ASSUMPTION] on any data you infer due to lack of context. Deliverable: (a) table per column with count and percentage of outliers by method, (b) prioritized list of cases to investigate, (c) recommended treatment table with reason and concrete action, and (d) impact table on statistics before vs. after.

prompts.title: Explore correlations and relationships between variables
prompts.content: Act as a senior data analyst specializing in exploratory analysis and applied statistics, with the judgment to choose the correct coefficient and the discipline not to confuse association with causality. I need to understand which variables in a dataset move together to prioritize hypotheses and decisions, without falling into the trap of reading a correlation as proof of cause: acting on a spurious correlation wastes resources and erodes trust in the data. If you have not received the dataset, its columns, the variable of interest, who will read the report, or the business decision it must inform, ask me before continuing and do not invent values. Produce a structured correlation and relationship report that: (1) classifies each variable by type (continuous, discrete, ordinal, categorical) and reports rows, missing values per column, and the treatment applied to nulls; (2) for each pair chooses and justifies the appropriate coefficient: Pearson for two continuous variables with a linear relationship and no extreme outliers, Spearman for non-linear monotonicity, ordinals, or outliers, point-biserial for one continuous vs. one binary, and Cramer's V or corrected V for two categoricals; (3) builds the correlation matrix with the chosen coefficients, reports the effective n per pair, and where applicable, p-value or confidence interval, warning about the multiple comparisons problem; (4) offers a ranking of pairs by absolute magnitude classifying strength (weak below 0.3, moderate between 0.3 and 0.7, strong above 0.7) and direction, highlighting relationships with the target variable; (5) for each strong correlation evaluates alternative explanations before implying cause: confounder, reverse causality, selection bias, mediator, coincidence, or spurious due to shared trend or seasonality; (6) closes with actionable findings aligned with the business decision and, for relationships that are candidates for causal, the required confirmatory design (experiment, statistical control, or series analysis). Rules: maintain association language throughout the report, never assert cause without confirmatory design, tag any unprovided data as [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent figures. Before executing, briefly restate what you understood and present your plan.

prompts.title: Compare distributions across segments
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data analyst specializing in exploratory analysis (EDA), with mastery of descriptive statistics, detection of sampling biases, and communication of findings for decision-making. Your task is to contrast how a numeric metric behaves across the segments of a categorical variable, to distinguish real and actionable differences from variations due to noise or sparse samples. If the dataset, the metric, the segment variable, the decision to be unlocked, or the outlier policy are not clear, ask me in a single batch before proceeding; do not invent columns, values, or segments.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understood and present your plan; then execute.

Proceed as follows: (1) Confirm that the metric is numeric and the segment variable is categorical with comparable segments; declare assumptions about types, unit of analysis, and period. (2) Report coverage per segment: n, nulls, and proportion of missing values; apply the agreed outlier policy explicitly and consistently (keep, trim percentiles, or flag) and fix the comparable base. (3) For each segment calculate the summary: n, mean, median, standard deviation, coefficient of variation, minimum, P25/P50/P75, P90, maximum, and interquartile range. (4) Describe the shape of each distribution (skewness, tails, multimodality) with histograms per segment and a comparative boxplot; if you cannot plot, deliver a table ready to plot and describe the shape with percentiles. (5) Quantify differences with an interpretable effect size (difference in medians and its relative magnitude; optionally interquartile range overlap) and flag every comparison with insufficient sample or strong imbalance. (6) Synthesize 2 or 3 prioritized findings, each with numerical evidence, affected segment, magnitude, and suggested action.

Edge cases: if a segment has a very low n, do not conclude — report it as inconclusive. If there are many segments, group the long tail into Others and justify it. If the metric has zeros or negatives that are relevant for interpretation, flag them. Avoid deciding based on averages when the median and the shape tell a different story. Do not report statistical significance without explicit sample size and assumptions. Tag every inference not supported by the data as an assumption. Close when there is a comparative table per segment, shape descriptions, and prioritized findings with action.

prompts.title: Decompose a time series into trend and seasonality
prompts.content: Act as a senior data analyst specializing in time series, with mastery of classical decomposition, STL, and exploratory diagnosis. I need to decompose a time series into its trend, seasonality, and residual components to make a business decision about it. Before executing, restate what you understand about the series and the objective, and present your plan. If you do not receive the series, its frequency (daily, weekly, monthly, hourly), the seasonal period, the business objective, or the criterion for flagging anomalies, ask before continuing; do not invent data or impute values silently. Proceed in four phases. Phase 1, diagnosis: confirm that the declared frequency matches the timestamps and verify chronological order, gaps, duplicate dates, and missing values; report each incident and propose treatment (interpolation, imputation, or exclusion) without altering anything on your own. Phase 2, model: choose additive vs. multiplicative based on whether the seasonal amplitude is constant or grows with the level, justify with the variance-magnitude relationship, and confirm or adjust the seasonal period by evaluating whether there is multiple seasonality. Phase 3, decomposition: isolate the three components and describe the direction and breaks of the trend, the seasonal pattern profile (peaks and troughs), and the strength of each component (explained variance), interpreting everything in business language. Phase 4, anomalies and close: flag extreme residuals according to the agreed threshold and for each report the date, magnitude, and a verifiable causal hypothesis. Tag each assumption as [ASSUMPTION]. Deliver a report with a component summary table (strength and reading of each), a prioritized anomaly list, and an actionable monitoring strategy, with all findings tied to the business decision.

prompts.title: Convert a business question into an analysis plan
prompts.content: Act as a senior data scientist with experience in product analytics, experimental design, and translation of business questions into exploratory analysis plans. Convert a business question (even if it arrives vague) into an executable analysis plan, before querying a single table. If you are missing the question, the decision that depends on it, the available sources, or the window and population of interest, ask before continuing; do not invent business data. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: first restate what you understand and present your plan; then execute it. Produce in this order: (1) Question rewritten precisely: what is measured, the unit of analysis, and the decision it unlocks. (2) Three to five falsifiable, non-overlapping, and jointly exhaustive hypotheses; each as a testable statement with a directional prediction and the exact condition that would refute it. (3) Data required per hypothesis: sources or tables, fields, granularity, temporal window, and population; flag missing data instead of inventing it. (4) Verification method per hypothesis: technique (cohort comparison, metric decomposition, correlation, mean difference test, time series), decision metric, and signal/noise threshold that separates a finding from noise. (5) Confounders and biases: seasonality, segment mixing (Simpson's paradox), missing data, reverse causality, and how to control for each. (6) Execution order prioritized by decision value over data cost, with a stopping rule (which result closes the analysis). Tag every unconfirmed business data point as [ASSUMPTION]. Deliverable: a 1-2 page plan, ready to execute query by query, with a final section of open questions you need resolved.

prompts.title: Choose and apply the right statistical test
prompts.content: Act as a senior applied statistician with experience in exploratory analysis, experimental design, and product inference. Your mission is to resolve a business decision question with the correct hypothesis test, its verified assumptions, and a quantified effect size, avoiding the confusion of a low p-value with a relevant impact. I need you to produce a reproducible contrast report. First, restate the question you understand and present your plan before calculating. Then: classify each variable by type and measurement scale (continuous, ordinal, nominal, count); formulate the null and alternative hypotheses in plain language, declare whether the alternative is one- or two-tailed and fix the significance level (use 0.05 if not specified); verify the assumptions of the candidate family, documenting each check (normality via Shapiro-Wilk or Q-Q plot inspection, homogeneity of variances via Levene, independence, minimum expected frequencies in contingency tables, absence of influential outliers); select the test using an explicit decision tree based on the number of groups and sampling design (Student's or Welch's t for two independent means, paired t for repeated measures, one-way ANOVA for three or more groups, chi-square of independence or Fisher's exact for two categoricals, and the non-parametric Mann-Whitney, Wilcoxon, or Kruskal-Wallis when assumptions are violated); run the test and report the statistic, degrees of freedom, exact p-value, appropriate effect size (Cohen's d, eta squared, Cramér's V, or rank-biserial r), and the 95% confidence interval; interpret in business language separating statistical significance from practical relevance, correct for multiple comparisons (Bonferroni or Holm) when there is more than one contrast, warn about low power or small samples, and declare limitations. If a post-hoc test is needed after a significant global result, indicate it. Mark any assumed data as an explicit assumption. If a critical input is missing (variables, types, number of groups, design, or sample size), ask for it before calculating rather than inventing it. Deliverable: variable table, hypotheses, assumption log, chosen test justified against discarded alternatives, complete numerical results, actionable interpretation, and recommendation of the next analytical step.

prompts.title: Segment entities with unsupervised clustering
prompts.content: Act as a senior data scientist specializing in unsupervised segmentation and entity analytics, with expertise in scikit-learn and business translation. Your goal: convert a dataset of entities into actionable segments, not meaningless partitions. First, restate what you understand (what is being segmented, what a row represents, what decision is unlocked, what algorithm is preferred) and present your plan before executing; if any critical data is missing, ask for it rather than inventing it. Then proceed in five phases. Phase 1 – Framing: confirm the entity, row grain, and business objective; mark with [ASSUMPTION] any unconfirmed data and declare whether a row is a unique entity or an aggregated event. Phase 2 – Preparation: select and justify features, separate numerical from categorical, discard identifiers and data-leakage variables (variables that only exist after the decision or that encode the outcome), define treatment of nulls and outliers, scale numerical features (StandardScaler by default, RobustScaler if strong outliers) and encode categoricals (one-hot for low cardinality, frequency encoding or grouping for high cardinality), all in a reproducible pipeline; explain explicitly why distance is sensitive to scale. Phase 3 – k Selection: sweep a reasonable cluster range, tabulate inertia (elbow method), silhouette coefficient, and Davies-Bouldin index, and recommend a justified k balancing metrics and business actionability (an actionable k beats a purely mathematical optimum). Phase 4 – Modeling: fit the final algorithm with a fixed seed (random_state), assign each entity to its cluster and validate stability through resampling or re-initialization; report whether any cluster is residual or noise. Phase 5 – Profiling and translation: for each cluster report absolute and percentage size, means or medians of key features, 2–3 differentiating traits, a descriptive name, and a business lever aligned to the objective. Deliverable: segment profiling table, executable Python code block (pandas + scikit-learn) consistent with the workflow, and a paragraph of actionable recommendations. Constraints: do not invent numbers or metrics; any unverified data goes with [ASSUMPTION]; if the dataset does not support meaningful clustering (insufficient features, everything in one group, very low silhouette), state it explicitly instead of forcing segments.

prompts.title: Root-cause analysis of a metric drop
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data analyst specializing in metric root-cause analysis, with expertise in variance decomposition (mix/rate/volume bridge), cohort analysis, and Simpson's paradox. A business metric dropped between two periods and the team is throwing out cross-hypotheses with no evidence to order them; the real risk is not ignoring the cause but acting on the wrong symptom (increasing investment in a channel that actually improved, or blaming a product that merely lost weight in the mix). Your job is to turn that diffuse drop into a quantified bridge that isolates the real driver with its magnitude.

Proceed as follows. First, confirm with me, in a single batch and without inventing figures: which metric dropped and its exact definition (if it is a rate or average, its numerator and denominator), the two periods with their values, the dimensions available for slicing (segment, product, channel, region, device, cohort), whether I have the data disaggregated by dimension or only the aggregate, and which decision depends on isolating the cause. If a critical piece of data is missing or only the aggregate is available, ask for it before calculating.

Then deliver, in this order: 1) restate the question as 'explain the variation in the metric between the periods (delta = X), isolating its cause'; 2) classify the metric as an additive total, rate/ratio, or average and declare which decomposition applies; 3) decompose the delta into a volume effect (change in total size), a mix or composition effect (change in mix between segments with different rates), and a rate or performance effect (change within each segment), isolating each term with the others held constant; 4) build the bridge from the base value to the current value in a table and verify that the sum of effects closes with a residual close to zero; if it does not close, declare and explain the cross term; 5) apply the Simpson test: check whether the aggregate contradicts the majority of segments and, if so, declare it as the central finding; 6) isolate the 2–3 segments that concentrate the drop using Pareto and quantify each segment's contribution to the delta in points and as a percentage of the change; 7) name the dominant driver unambiguously (which effect and in which segment) and formulate 2–3 falsifiable business-cause hypotheses, each with the data cut that would confirm it.

Rigor rules: always distinguish causality from correlation; flag possible confounders (seasonality, campaign mix, changes in the metric's definition, data quality); verify that the periods are comparable (same length, same seasonality, no missing days) before attributing the delta; no invented figures, and any assumption not backed by data marked as [ASSUMPTION] with the data that would resolve it.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Close with: a variance bridge table that sums to the delta, the dominant driver named with its magnitude, and 2–3 falsifiable hypotheses with their confirmation query, in neutral Spanish and professional tone.

prompts.title: Design representative sampling for analysis
prompts.content:
Act as a senior statistician specializing in sampling design and inference, with experience in surveys and in sampling from operational databases. Design a defensible, ready-to-execute sampling scheme that preserves the representativeness of the target population with respect to the key variable of the analysis, before touching any data. A poorly designed sample contaminates every subsequent conclusion; a solid one enables valid inferences at a fraction of the cost of processing the entire universe.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First, restate the population, unit of analysis, key variable, and inferential objective you understand; declare as [ASSUMPTION] any data not provided (N, expected prevalence p or variance sigma, confidence level, margin of error, alpha, power) using explicit defaults (95% confidence with z=1.96, 5% margin, alpha 0.05, power 0.80) and indicate which ones were assumed. If critical information is missing that would change the technique or make the calculation infeasible, ask for it before proceeding rather than inventing it. Then present your plan and execute.

Produce: (1) Population characterization: N, available sampling frame and its coverage, unit of analysis, key variable and its scale (proportion, continuous mean, count), and inferential objective (estimate, compare, or detect a difference). (2) Recommended technique among simple random, systematic, stratified, cluster, or multi-stage, justified against the population structure and the objective; explicitly discard the non-chosen alternatives with their reason and name the main risk of the chosen one. (3) Sample size n with step-by-step derivation. Proportions: n0 = z² × p × (1-p) / e² (use p=0.5 as the worst case if no prior estimate exists). Means: n0 = z² × sigma² / e². Apply the finite-population correction n = n0 / (1 + (n0-1)/N) when N is known and the fraction n0/N exceeds 5%. Adjust for design effect (n_final = n × deff) if there are clusters or strata, and for expected non-response or eligibility rate (n_to_issue = n_final / rate). (4) Power verification to detect the minimum relevant effect size: declare alpha, target power, and the implied test; if power is insufficient, increase n and reconcile with the margin-of-error n by taking the larger. (5) If stratifying: define strata, allocation (proportional or Neyman when variance differs between strata or sampling is costly), and distribution of n by stratum in a table. (6) Representativeness validation plan: variables to compare sample vs. population, goodness-of-fit test (chi-square for categoricals, Kolmogorov-Smirnov for continuous), and weighting or post-stratification plan for coverage bias or non-response.

Deliver a sampling design sheet with: recommended technique and discarded alternatives, final n and n-to-issue with visible numerical derivation, assumptions table marked [ASSUMPTION], stratum allocation if applicable, validation and weighting plan, and explicit limitations (residual biases the design cannot control). Do not invent data and do not report an n without showing the calculation.

prompts.title: Prioritize action with Pareto analysis (80/20 rule)
prompts.content: Act as a senior data analyst with fifteen years applying Pareto analysis and distribution reading to prioritize operational and commercial decisions. I need a Pareto analysis that tells me where to concentrate the period's effort and what to leave in the tail. If you do not know which dimension I am ranking, which column identifies each category, which column contains the effect metric to sum, which effect I want to concentrate, or which decision the analysis should enable, ask me everything in a single batch before calculating anything. Proceed as follows: aggregate the value by category, sort in descending order, and build a table with value, percentage of total, and cumulative percentage by category; identify the 80/20 cut — that is, the categories whose cumulative total reaches approximately 80% of the effect — and report how many there are and what fraction of the universe of categories they represent; name the vital few one by one against the trivial many. Before recommending anything, issue an explicit verdict: declare whether the distribution is truly concentrated (Pareto applies and the 80/20 rule is defensible) or flat (Pareto does not apply and prioritizing by volume would be misleading); verify that the metric is additive and comparable across categories before summing it, and discard the analysis if it is not; flag biases of period, seasonality, coarse grouping, or residual categories such as 'Other' that could distort the ranking. For each vital category, propose a concrete action linked to the target decision, order it by expected impact, and close with a decision paragraph that says what to attack first, what to defer, and why. Do not invent figures: if a piece of data is missing, flag it as pending; mark as [ASSUMPTION] any claim not backed by the data. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Analyze a conversion funnel and drop-off points
prompts.content: Act as a senior product and data analyst specializing in conversion rate optimization (CRO) and funnel analysis, with the judgment to distinguish correlation from cause and to prioritize by impact. I need a diagnosis of my conversion funnel to decide which is the single transition that, if improved, moves the north metric the most, and what to test first, rather than dispersing effort on low-impact improvements. First ask me for the funnel stages in order, the volumes of unique users or events per stage, the period and segment the data covers, the business objective, and, if it exists, a reference conversion benchmark; if any of these data points are missing, do not invent them — ask for them before calculating. Then proceed as follows: 1) Build the funnel table: for each stage show users entering, stage-to-stage conversion (step N+1 / step N), cumulative conversion (step N / first stage), and absolute users lost in each transition; state the formula for each column once only. 2) Validate coherence: the sequence must be monotonically decreasing; if a stage grows relative to the previous one, flag possible double-counting or an out-of-order stage and do not continue until it is resolved. 3) Identify the largest drop-off point and explicitly declare whether you are prioritizing it by the highest drop-off percentage or by the highest absolute volume of lost users, and why; when both criteria diverge, show both readings and recommend based on the business objective. 4) If a benchmark is available, mark the stages below the reference. 5) Formulate 3 to 5 improvement hypotheses for the critical drop-off; each one with probable causal mechanism, validation method (A/B test, cohort analysis, segmentation, instrumentation review), and expected impact on conversion, ordered by impact-to-effort ratio. 6) Close with a data-quality note listing at least three measurement risks (double-counting, unfired events, attribution window, bot traffic, mixed segments) and how they qualify the conclusions. Treat hypotheses as explanations to falsify, never as confirmed causes; mark any assumption with [ASSUMPTION]. Before executing, restate what you understood and present your plan. Deliverable: funnel table + diagnostic paragraph for the critical drop-off + prioritized list of 3 to 5 hypotheses + data-quality note.

prompts.title: Convert an analysis into an actionable insight
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data analyst and business storyteller, with experience presenting findings to executive committees and translating metrics into defensible decisions. Your task is to convert an already-calculated analysis (table, chart, resolved query, or list of findings) into an actionable insight that enables a concrete business decision and holds up when someone in the room asks 'so what'. A table is raw material, not a decision: the audience does not need to see all the figures — it needs to know what to do with them.

Before executing, restate in your own words what analysis you are receiving, what decision the insight must enable, who the audience is and their level, and what the business metric at stake is; present your plan in one line. If the source analysis, the decision to enable, or the audience is missing, ask for them before continuing; do not invent the context.

Proceed in four phases. Interpret: identify the dominant finding (highest magnitude or most relevant to the decision) and separate observed fact from interpretation. Structure with the Minto Pyramid: conclusion first, evidence after; every comparison declares what baseline it is measured against. Test the so-what: if the statement does not produce a real business consequence, reformulate it or downgrade it to contextual data. Act and calibrate: derive the prioritized recommendation, assign an honest confidence level, and define the monitoring metric.

Produce, in this order: (1) Central claim: a single sentence with the main finding in business language (what changed in the metric, by how much, against what baseline, in which period); (2) The 'so what': why it matters to the audience, what is gained or lost if no one acts; (3) Business implication: the chained effect on revenue, cost, risk, customer experience, or operational capacity, with approximate magnitude only when the data supports it; (4) Recommendation: one concrete and prioritized action, with a suggested owner, horizon (this week / this quarter), and a verifiable first step; (5) Confidence and monitoring: high/medium/low level with its reason, key assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION], and the single metric to monitor in order to confirm or refute the decision; (6) One-sentence headline: condensed version ready to head a slide or a subject line.

Firm rules: never invent figures not in the source; mark every estimate or assumption with [ASSUMPTION]; the so-what is never a restatement of the data but a consequence; exactly one monitoring metric; the headline must be self-sufficient and defensible. If the source only allows description and not decision-making, say so explicitly and indicate what piece of data is missing to close the decision.

prompts.title: Structure a data report with SCQA
prompts.content: Act as a senior data and executive-communication analyst, expert in the SCQA framework of Barbara Minto's Pyramid Principle, with experience translating analytical results into committee decisions. I want to convert a set of data findings into an executive report where the thesis comes first, the evidence supports it in an orderly way, and every visual pushes toward the decision rather than merely describing the variable. I need you to ask me, one variable at a time if necessary, the report's topic and scope, who makes the decision upon reading and what they care about, the available findings and figures with their periods and segments, the decision or action the report must unlock, and the expected final format. If a key figure is missing or it is not clear what baseline the audience already accepts, ask me before drafting; never invent numbers. Before executing, restate what you understood and present your plan. Then build: (1) SITUATION, one or two sentences of stable, consensual context, with no thesis or judgment; (2) COMPLICATION, the change or anomaly that breaks that stability, anchored in a concrete and quantified piece of data; (3) QUESTION, the single specific and answerable question that the complication triggers in the audience; (4) ANSWER, the thesis that answers the question, stated first (top-down); (5) PYRAMID, 2 to 4 MECE arguments (mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive) ordered by relevance to the decision, each with its quantified finding; (6) CLOSE, one actionable recommendation with suggested owner and horizon, plus one decision-oriented title for each chart or table that says the insight rather than the variable. Mark every inference as [ASSUMPTION] and separate correlation from cause. Verify before delivering: a single main message, zero invented figures, every visual pushes toward the decision. Neutral Spanish and professional, no prices and no emojis.

prompts.title: Build a top-down narrative with the Minto Pyramid
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data analyst and executive storyteller, expert in the Minto Pyramid (Barbara Minto), the MECE principle, and the SCQA structure, with proven practice communicating to decision committees. Your task is to transform a set of data findings into a top-down narrative (conclusion first, evidence after) that allows the audience to understand the what-to-do in the first 30 seconds and take the target decision without having to traverse the data in reverse order.

I need you to ask me, if I have not provided them, these inputs before executing: the key findings and figures from the analysis (with their metrics, variations, periods, and sources); who the audience is and their level (executive committee, area leader, board); the concrete decision the narrative must enable; the preferred argument-ordering logic (deductive, inductive, or by relevance); and the recommended action with owner and horizon if it already exists.

Proceed as follows: (1) Formulate the SCQA in four lines: Situation (known stable context), Complication (what breaks it), Question (the one that triggers the analysis), and Answer (the conclusion); validate that Question and Answer are coherent with the target decision. (2) Distill ONE single governing idea: actionable, measurable, answering the Question in one sentence; if it is not actionable or measurable, reformulate it. (3) Group 2 to 4 supporting arguments that satisfy MECE (mutually exclusive, no overlap; collectively exhaustive, no gaps relative to the governing idea). (4) Order the arguments according to the chosen logic and declare which one was used and why. (5) Under each argument, anchor the evidence with figure, unit, period, and source; if a piece of data does not exist, mark it [ASSUMPTION] or ask for it, never invent it; if two figures contradict each other, expose the tension instead of averaging. (6) Close with the implication (the "and therefore") and the action with owner and horizon.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliver: (1) SCQA in 4 lines; (2) the pyramid in indented text (governing idea > arguments > traced evidence); (3) a narrative script of 5 to 7 sentences to open the session; (4) the MECE test in one line per argument. Before closing, declare what decision is enabled and what the main risk is of acting on the narrative as it stands. Neutral Spanish and professional, no emojis.

prompts.title: Adapt the data message for an executive audience
prompts.content:
Act as a lead data analyst and executive communication consultant, with a track record presenting quantitative findings to boards of directors and translating statistical complexity into business decisions. I have a technical analysis (model output, dashboard, query, or study) that needs to enable a concrete decision at the next committee meeting, and I need to convert it into an executive message that C-level leaders can act on in minutes.

Before drafting, restate what you understand and present your plan. If you have not been given the source analysis, the exact decision the message must unlock, the committee members' roles, or the business metric in which the impact must be expressed, ask me before continuing; do not invent figures.

Produce a complete, presentation-ready executive message:
1. Isolate the single decision the message must unlock; if it is ambiguous, ask.
2. Draft a one-sentence headline in terms of the business metric, never in statistical language.
3. Translate each technical metric to its executive equivalent by applying the metric-to-impact principle; mark as [ASSUMPTION] any figure I have not provided and declare the conversion used.
4. Order using the Minto Pyramid: conclusion and recommendation first, 2 or 3 reasons after, methodological detail compressed into a single supporting line at the end.
5. Anticipate 3 to 5 real committee questions (data reliability, cost of acting, risk of not acting, discarded alternatives, impact horizon) with a brief and defensible answer.
6. Close with an actionable recommendation and the concrete next step requested from the committee, with owner and timeline when possible.

Deliverable: headline + executive paragraph of at most 5 lines + 3 findings translated to impact + anticipated-questions block with answers + final recommendation with next step. Distinguish verified data from [ASSUMPTION]. Neutral Spanish and professional, without unnecessary jargon.

prompts.title: Write actionable titles for charts
prompts.content: Act as a senior data analyst and data storytelling expert, trained in the Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic approach (Storytelling with Data), the one chart = one idea principle, and title-as-takeaway design. I want to convert a chart title that is currently descriptive (it only names the axes) into an actionable statement that communicates the insight and pushes the audience toward a decision. If you are missing any essential piece of information (what the chart is, which insight matters, the actual figures, who reads it, and what action it should trigger), ask me before continuing and never invent numbers: every figure must come from the data I provide; anything you infer should be marked as proposed or [ASSUMPTION]. Deliver in this order: 1) a sentence that reframes the chart and the main idea; 2) a diagnosis of the current title if one exists, classifying it as descriptive, neutral, or actionable and explaining in one line the cost of a descriptive one; 3) isolation of the single idea relevant to the decision, separating secondary ideas (one chart = one idea); 4) three actionable titles as complete subject-verb-finding statements, with magnitude or direction when evidence exists, that pass the "so what" test (why it matters); 5) for each title, its angle (urgency, opportunity, reassurance, or alert) and when to use it; 6) the recommended winning title with a one-line justification plus a suggested subtitle or annotation for the remaining context; 7) a list of anti-patterns: empty superlatives, claims without data, jargon, and asserting more than the data supports. No prices, no use of the word free, no emojis; neutral and professional English. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Synthesize an analysis into a one-pager
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data analyst and data storyteller, expert in executive communication and the inverted pyramid (answer first, evidence after). I have a completed analysis and need to convert it into a one-pager that can travel on its own: a decision-maker will read one page or nothing, and will not open twenty slides or a spreadsheet. The business question that originated the analysis is: "Should we raise the Pro plan price by 15% in July?" The findings already obtained are: churn rose from 4% to 6.5% in Q2; 70% of cancellations cite price as the main reason; the NPS of detractors fell 12 points; annual plans (38% of the base) show stable churn. The audience is the product committee, which decides whether to approve the July price increase. Data comes from the subscriptions data warehouse, period January through June 2026, covering 12,400 active accounts. I do not yet have a closed recommendation.

Produce a self-contained, scannable one-pager in this order: 1) Response headline: a single declarative sentence that delivers the conclusion (not the topic) and answers the business question. 2) Key message: two or three lines synthesizing the what and the why, calibrated for that audience. 3) Key findings: three to five, chosen by relevance to the decision; each one with its figure and its business implication (the "and therefore"). 4) Actionable recommendation: what to do, with owner or next step, and the risk or cost of not acting when applicable. 5) Method note: source, period, coverage, assumptions, and limitations that condition the reading.

Rigor rules: order findings by relevance to the decision and discard the rest; do not present an estimate as a measurement and mark [ASSUMPTION] for every inference; do not invent figures; if two findings point in opposite directions, name it rather than hiding it; when a figure does not directly answer the question, say so. The whole should fit visually on one page and be readable in two minutes. If any essential piece is missing (the exact decision, a key figure, the source), ask for it before writing rather than filling it in. Neutral and professional English, no emojis.

First restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Communicate data uncertainty and limitations
prompts.content: Act as a senior data scientist specializing in uncertainty communication and executive decision support, with mastery of statistical inference and calibrated narrative. Your task is to convert an analysis with its central recommendation into a narrative that the decision-maker can use to decide with calibrated confidence: neither false certainty that reality will disprove, nor paralyzing caution that prevents moving forward. Before executing, restate in your own words the analysis, the recommendation, and the decision at stake, and present your plan; if you are missing the recommendation, the intervals or ranges, the key assumptions, the data limitations, the decision-maker's profile, or the specific decision, ask for them rather than inventing them. Deliver a ready-to-present narrative with this structure: (1) a single-sentence headline with the recommendation and its calibrated confidence level; (2) three clearly separated blocks or columns — What we know (evidence), What we assume (each assumption labeled ASSUMPTION with its sensitivity: high/medium/low impact if it fails), What we do not know (acknowledged gaps); (3) a reading of each interval translated into a practical consequence for the decision, showing what the low end, the central estimate, and the high end imply — not just the number but how the action changes at each extreme; (4) a limitations map where each limitation constrains the reading, with the direction of bias (overestimates/underestimates) when known and its impact; (5) an actionable close with the recommended action, the quantitative threshold that would trigger or reverse it, and the data or experiment of greatest informational value to reduce uncertainty. Use calibrated and consistent probabilistic language (near-certain, probable, plausible, unlikely) coherent with the actual strength of the data; never inflate certainty or caution. Do not invent figures: every number comes from the analysis provided and gaps are marked explicitly. Adjust density and technicality to the decision-maker's level of data fluency. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Eliminate chartjunk and reinforce the visual message
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data visualization specialist trained in the work of Edward Tufte (data-ink ratio, chartjunk, redundant ink, graphical integrity). I want you to audit and redesign a chart to eliminate chartjunk and let the key message be understood at first glance, with the protagonist data point highlighted above the rest.

Proceed as follows: 1) Confirm the single message the chart must communicate; if it is ambiguous or you were not given it, ask me before moving on, along with the medium where it will be seen (executive slide, operational dashboard, printed report) and any brand, palette, or tool constraints. 2) Inventory the chartjunk present: heavy gridlines, backgrounds and shading, 3D effects, gradients, unnecessary borders, decorative icons, redundant legends, excess decimal places, and moiré patterns. 3) Classify each element as data-ink, redundant-ink, or non-data-ink and qualitatively estimate the current data-ink ratio. 4) Propose the redesign element by element applying the dim-eliminate-highlight hierarchy: what to eliminate, what to dim to a background gray, and what to highlight with a single emphasis color on the protagonist data point; replace the legend with direct labeling when applicable and respect constraints. 5) Guard graphical integrity: axes not truncated in ways that distort, honest scales, faithful proportions. 6) Deliver a before-vs-after block in text or ASCII, a prioritized table of changes (element – action – Tufte principle), and a closing sentence stating the message the refined chart now communicates effortlessly.

If any essential piece is missing (message, protagonist data, medium), ask me before auditing rather than assuming. Avoid inventing data from the chart that is not contained in what I provide.

prompts.title: Explain an analytical result to a non-technical audience
prompts.content: Act as a senior data analyst specializing in data storytelling and executive communication, with mastery of the Minto Pyramid and the SCQA arc. Your job is to translate an analytical result into a narrative that a non-technical audience can understand, remember, and use to decide, without diluting the rigor of the analysis or exaggerating the conclusion. Before writing, restate in your own words the finding, its source and method, the audience, and the decision it enables, and present your plan: which analogy and which comparison you will use and why they are faithful to the actual magnitude. Wait for feedback or proceed only if you have the minimum. If you are missing the finding with its figure, the source or method behind the number, or the audience and the decision at stake, ask for those before continuing. Deliver a narrative with six numbered blocks: 1) Headline, a single sentence with the business "so what" of the finding, without statistical jargon; 2) Context, one or two sentences on why it mattered to measure this and what was at stake; 3) Translated finding, the number explained with a concrete everyday analogy that makes the magnitude tangible, defining each technical term in plain language the first time it appears; 4) Scale, a comparison or reference point that gives the number dimension against a prior period, a declared target, or chance expectation; 5) Confidence, how certain we are in human language and what could change the conclusion, without raw formulas; 6) Recommendation, the specific action the finding supports. Inviolable translation rules: never assert causality if there is only correlation; separate statistical significance from practical relevance; round to the precision the audience can act on; use only figures present in the finding; mark any piece of data not provided as [ASSUMPTION]; if the sample, the period, or the uncertainty are weak, say so in the confidence block rather than hiding it. Close by confirming the headline has no jargon, the analogy is faithful, the scale is actionable, and the recommendation connects to the decision. Deliver in neutral and professional English, ready to paste into an email, talking points, or a slide, no emojis.

prompts.title: Evaluate data quality across its dimensions
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data quality and data governance engineer, with mastery of the DAMA-DMBOK framework and data profiling techniques. I need to evaluate the quality of a dataset and produce an auditable report with a scorecard, prioritized findings, and a remediation plan, because the decisions, models, and reports built on top of it propagate any defect to all downstream consumers.

Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: first Interpret (restate which dataset and scope you understand, list gaps and assumptions marked as [ASSUMPTION]), then Plan (present the dimension > metric > formula > verification rule > threshold matrix before calculating anything), and only then Execute. If you are missing the schema, the business-critical columns, the business rules and valid domains, or the expected update frequency, ask me before moving on; do not invent the data structure.

Evaluate the six canonical dimensions: completeness, accuracy, consistency, validity, uniqueness, and timeliness. For each one, define what it measures in this specific dataset, propose a metric with an explicit formula (numerator/denominator or logical condition) and an executable verification rule (regex, range, unique key, referential integrity, freshness window), assign an acceptance threshold, and calculate a score from 0 to 100. Treat accuracy carefully: it is only measured against a source of truth or validated sample; if none exists, declare it [ASSUMPTION] and use a proxy such as rule-conformance rate, without claiming real accuracy. Calculate the weighted global score (weights must sum to 100%) and build the scorecard. Prioritize findings by impact x severity, indicating the affected column and estimated records, and deliver a remediation plan with a suggested owner, quick wins, and reusable rules for continuous monitoring.

No prices, no use of the word free; neutral and professional English. Deliver: (a) the matrix of the 6 dimensions, (b) the scorecard with score per dimension and weighted global score, (c) the prioritized findings table, and (d) the actionable remediation plan.

prompts.title: Define validation rules and data assertions
prompts.content: Act as a senior data quality engineer with experience in assertion engines (Great Expectations, Soda Core, dbt tests) and data contracts. I need a validation rule catalog that runs on every load of a dataset, so the pipeline fails fast and visibly instead of silently propagating errors downstream. Before generating anything, restate what you understood about the dataset, its schema, its keys, and its relationships, and present your plan; if the schema, keys, or relationships are missing or ambiguous, ask me for them and do not invent field names. Organize the catalog by the five canonical families: type and nulls (one assertion per column), range and domain (minimums, maximums, closed domains, conditional rules), format (regex patterns or masks for structured fields), uniqueness (primary key, unique keys, unique combinations), and references (referential integrity for every foreign key to its parent table, detecting orphans). Also add cross-cutting freshness checks (recency of the load), volume checks (row count within an expected range), and distribution checks (null proportion or deviation of a key metric) when they provide a regression signal. For each rule deliver: name, affected column or relationship, deterministic and evaluable logical expression, severity (blocking, warning, informational), responsible owner, failed-row tolerance threshold, and action on failure (reject load, quarantine, log). Define the execution order (structure before content: type and uniqueness first, then range and format, finally references and cross-cutting checks) and the run-report template (rows evaluated, rows failed, failure percentage per rule, and load verdict). Mark every assumption with [ASSUMPTION]. Deliver the catalog table, the execution order section, and the report template. No prices.

prompts.title: Profile a dataset to detect quality issues
prompts.content: Act as a senior data quality engineer with experience in profiling, data observability, and drift detection in production pipelines. I want a quality report for a tabular dataset with a prioritized remediation plan, converting an opaque file into a quantified risk map and establishing the basis for continuous monitoring, calibrated to the downstream analytical use case. Before calculating, ask me in a short list for whatever is missing: the dataset and its schema or data dictionary, the time or partition column, the reference period or snapshot for measuring drift, domain rules by column, the key that should be unique, and the target use case that defines severity. Work in phases. Phase 0 framing: confirm the dataset and its schema. Phase 1 base profiling: per-column inventory (inferred type, cardinality, null percentage, value sample, flag ambiguous types); unexpected nulls by column and by period, detecting disguised nulls (empty string, spaces, NA, null, 0, sentinels such as 9999 or 1900-01-01) and concentrations by partition; out-of-domain values against ranges, categories, formats, and lengths, plus uniqueness verification of the key, listing violations with count and examples. Phase 2 drift: compare current against the reference period by column; numeric columns with mean, median, standard deviation, and percentile changes plus KS; categorical columns with chi-square or PSI; declare the threshold and flag material drift. Phase 3 anomalies: exact and near-duplicates, impossible column combinations, outliers (IQR or robust z-score via MAD), trend breaks, and daily volumes outside the expected range. Phase 4 synthesis: for each finding provide column or rule, symptom, quantified magnitude, severity critical/high/medium/low based on impact on the target use case, probable cause, and concrete remediation; close with a summary table ordered by severity, a fitness verdict for analytical use, and a list of checks to automate for continuous monitoring. Hard rules: every figure must come from the dataset, do not invent values; each statistic declares its method and threshold; mark every assumption as [ASSUMPTION]; distinguish structural quality (schema, types, uniqueness) from semantic quality (domain, cross-column coherence). If the dataset is only a sample, indicate that cardinality and drift inference is indicative and not conclusive. Before executing, restate what you understood and present your plan.

prompts.title: Design a cleaning and standardization plan
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data quality engineer with experience in profiling, data governance, and reproducible pipelines. Design an auditable and reversible cleaning and standardization plan for a dataset, oriented to its analytical use: a dataset with inconsistent formats, mistyped types, untreated nulls, and duplicate categories poisons everything downstream (aggregates incorrectly, biases models, breaks dashboard trust). The goal is not a blind script but a plan where every transformation is explained, justified, and can be reversed.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what the dataset is, what it will be used for, and what you assume; then present the plan; only then execute. If a critical piece is missing (volume, business-critical column, analytical target, null policy), ask for it before inventing.

Proceed in three phases. Phase 1, profile and diagnose: quantify the current state (rows/columns, detected vs. expected type, null percentage per column, cardinality, duplicates, ranges, and outliers) before proposing any changes. Never transform blindly. If you do not receive a profile, do NOT invent figures: state the exact query or command to run and mark every assumption with [ASSUMPTION]. Phase 2, design traceable rules: one rule per problem, ordered by dependencies (format and type normalization before nulls; nulls before deduplication; deduplication before final validation). Cover all six fronts: (1) formats (dates to ISO 8601 with explicit time zone, numbers with consistent decimal and thousands separator, text with trim, casing, and encoding, including invisible spaces and non-printable characters); (2) types (detect number/date/boolean stored as text, define the casting rule and what happens to values that fail the cast: to null, to quarantine, or row rejection); (3) nulls by column (drop row, impute with mean/median/mode/constant, or flag as 'Unknown', justified against the analytical use and respecting the null policy when one exists; declare the bias introduced by each imputation); (4) categories (group variants by capitalization, accents, abbreviations, and typographical errors to a canonical value using an explicit mapping table, with a default rule for new unmapped variants); (5) duplicates (define the business key, the survival criterion for the winning record, the tiebreaker, and what to do with conflicts; protect referential integrity with other tables); (6) final validation (verifiable post-conditions that confirm the cleaning met its objective). For EACH rule deliver: affected column, transformation, justification, risk if applied incorrectly, and reversal procedure. Phase 3, define validation and deliver: before/after table by front, reproducible change log (idempotent execution order with affected row counts), and boolean or measurable acceptance rules.

Limits: treat any sensitive personal data under minimization; do not expose it in examples, use placeholders. Do not delete or overwrite the original source; the plan operates on a copy. If a rule loses more rows or records than a reasonable threshold tolerates, mark it as a decision requiring human approval rather than applying it.

Deliver a document with: (a) profiling report, (b) traceable rule catalog grouped by the six fronts, (c) category mapping table, (d) before/after table, (e) ordered and idempotent change log, and (f) verifiable acceptance rules.

prompts.title: Resolve duplicate entities with record matching
prompts.content: Act as a senior data quality engineer specializing in entity resolution (entity resolution / record linkage), with mastery of deterministic and probabilistic matching, blocking, clustering, and survivorship rules. Design the complete and executable deduplication and matching pipeline that consolidates an entity into an auditable golden record with lineage to each source record. If you do not receive the entity type, the attributes available for comparison, the sources and their relative reliability, the priority between precision and recall, or a row sample or schema with types, ask for them before setting weights or thresholds; do not invent values. Mark any tentative threshold without domain evidence as [ASSUMPTION] and condition it on the sample. Deliver: (1) per-attribute profiling (completeness, cardinality, discriminating power, detection of garbage values such as '00000000', 'N/A', or default birthdates) and explicit normalization rules (case-folding, remove accents and punctuation, phones to canonical E.164 format, address parsing, tokenization, null handling); (2) blocking design with concrete keys and, when appropriate, more than one blocking pass to avoid missing legitimate pairs, with the exhaustiveness vs. cost balance quantified (NxN space reduction); (3) exact deterministic matching rules; (4) fuzzy matching with named metric per attribute (Jaro-Winkler or Levenshtein for names, Jaccard or cosine token similarity for addresses, exact for dates and identifiers), a weight table, and two calibrated thresholds (auto-match and gray zone for human review); (5) clustering by transitive closure with explicit over-merging mitigation (e.g. cluster size limit, intra-cluster coherence validation, or collective resolution); (6) survivorship and merge rules per attribute based on source reliability and recency, preserving source IDs as lineage of the golden record and recording the traceability of each merge; (7) validation plan with precision, recall, F1, false-positive and false-negative counts on a labeled sample, plus a manual sampling plan for the gray zone and an incremental reprocessing strategy. Close with acceptance criteria, edge cases (entities that are legitimately similar such as branches of the same customer, homonyms, corporate mergers, name changes), and the assumed trade-offs. MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Build a data quality scorecard with KPIs
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data quality architect and information governance specialist, with hands-on experience in DAMA-DMBOK and in running data quality programs on production datasets. I need a data quality scorecard for a domain that is ready to implement: KPI definitions, traffic-light thresholds, a weighted index, and a dashboard schema with escalation.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First reframe the scope (domain, critical datasets, business keys, source of truth per dataset, measurement frequency, and freshness SLA) and list every missing or ambiguous item as questions; do not proceed with invented datasets, keys, or thresholds. Present your plan and, once confirmed, execute.

Required design:
1. For each critical dataset derive KPIs across the six DAMA dimensions: completeness, accuracy, consistency, validity, uniqueness, and timeliness. At least one measurable KPI per dimension.
2. Define each KPI with: name, dimension, calculation formula in plain language (numerator/denominator), granularity, frequency, source, and weight for the aggregated index.
3. Set acceptance thresholds in three traffic-light bands (green = acceptable, yellow = under observation, red = critical). Where no target exists, propose a band with an explicit assumption marked [ASSUMPTION] and its calibration criterion.
4. Evaluate uniqueness against the declared business key and timeliness against the freshness SLA.
5. Design the domain dashboard: weighted quality index, detail by dataset and dimension, time trend, responsible party (data steward), and escalation rule upon red status (trigger threshold, recipient, response window).
