Edge cases: dataset without a reliable business key (mark uniqueness as unmeasurable and propose approximate duplicate detection), dimension not applicable to a dataset (document why it is excluded), data with no defined source of truth (escalate before calculating cross-source consistency).

Deliverable: scorecard table (dataset × dimension × KPI × traffic-light threshold), definition block for each KPI, weighted index formula, and dashboard schema. Do not invent figures, datasets, or keys; missing items are asked about.

prompts.title: Define a data contract between producer and consumer
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data platform engineer specializing in data contracts, schema governance, and Data Mesh / data-as-a-product producer-consumer models. I want you to produce a complete, signable, and operable data contract that governs the interface between a dataset-producing team and the teams that consume it, so that no type change, field rename, or freshness degradation silently breaks downstream pipelines.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First reframe your understanding of the dataset, delivery medium, producer, consumers, business criticality, and target freshness; present your plan; then execute. If any of those key data points are missing or ambiguous, ask for them and do not invent them.

Structure the contract in these sections: (1) Identity and purpose: canonical name, semantic version, producer owner, consumers and their use case, business domain, and criticality classification. (2) Schema: field table with name, type, nullability, format or unit, primary key, foreign keys, and PII flag; serialization format (Avro, JSON Schema, or Protobuf) and schema registry location. (3) Semantics: business-language definition of each non-trivial field, record granularity, time zone, units, value domains, and enumerations. (4) Quality guarantees: verifiable rules by dimension (completeness, uniqueness, validity, consistency, freshness, accuracy) each with a quantitative threshold and consequence upon breach. (5) Numeric SLAs/SLOs: maximum freshness or latency, update frequency, availability window, expected volume, retention, and support commitment. (6) Change policy: semantic versioning, compatible vs. breaking change criteria, deprecation and notice window, notification channel, and approval process. (7) Breach handling: detection, alerts, responsible party, runbook, and escalation path. Close with a signature checklist for producer and consumer.

Mark every inferred value with [ASSUMPTION] and every missing producer or consumer data point with {to_be_confirmed}. Do not use real PII in examples: use placeholders. Deliver a versioned data-contract.md (or equivalent YAML) document ready for approval.

prompts.title: Design data observability with monitors
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data engineer specializing in pipeline observability and reliability (data reliability engineering), with experience operating the four observability pillars on production warehouses and lakehouses. I want to move from reactive detection (broken data is discovered by a business complaint) to proactive detection: monitors that watch my critical assets and fire alerts before bad data is consumed downstream. If you do not have the asset inventory, data engine, orchestrator, freshness SLAs, or alert channels, ask me for them before proceeding; do not invent table names, column names, or metrics and mark every assumption as [ASSUMPTION].

Deliver an observability plan in six numbered sections: (1) Asset inventory with high/medium/low criticality by downstream impact, load timestamp field, granularity, and SLA; asset-to-consumer dependency map. (2) Monitor catalog by pillar for each critical asset, tabulated: freshness (maximum tolerated delay, missing loads, calendar gaps), volume (row range, drops/spikes, empty tables), schema (expected columns, types, nullability, schema drift, renames), distribution (null percentage, cardinality, min/max, mean, key uniqueness, and duplicate rate vs. baseline). (3) Baselines and thresholds: how to derive each baseline (historical window, day/week seasonality, percentiles), static vs. dynamic threshold, and distinction between hard threshold (business rule violation) and statistical threshold (historical deviation), with cold-start handling when there is insufficient history. (4) Alert policy and P1/P2/P3 severity with recipient and channel by severity, plus anti-noise rules: grouping, deduplication, suppression during maintenance windows, upstream detection to avoid double-alerting for the same root cause, and trigger threshold (n consecutive violations). (5) Incident response flow: detection > triage > root cause > containment (circuit breaker to stop downstream consumption) > resolution > postmortem, with roles, target times (detection, response, resolution), and a brief incident log template. (6) Implementation plan in the engine and orchestrator: instrumentation (SQL queries/checks or declarative tests), rule versioning in source control, gradual rollout of noisy monitors in observation mode before alerting, and a simulated incident test to validate that the correct alert fires to the correct recipient.

Acceptance criteria: covers all four pillars with at least one concrete and measurable monitor per pillar for each critical asset; each monitor declares baseline, threshold (hard or statistical), and detection signal; the alert policy maps severity to recipient and channel and includes at least one anti-fatigue rule; the incident flow defines roles and target times; the plan is executable and includes a verifiable simulated incident; no invented names; assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION]. Deliverable: document in six sections with the monitor catalog tabulated by asset and pillar, ready to review and instrument.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe your understanding and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Investigate the root cause of a data incident
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data quality engineer expert in root cause analysis, upstream lineage tracing, and preventive control design on analytical pipelines. Bad data has reached a trusted consumer and every hour that passes erodes platform credibility: someone decides, commissions, or reports on a bad number. Silencing the symptom by reloading a table is not enough; if you do not find where the defect was injected and why, the error will reappear on the next run.

Produce a root cause investigation with: (1) incident card with the erroneous value, the expected value and its source of truth, the delta, the observation point and moment, and the formal criterion that defines why the data is wrong (business rule, valid range, or reconciliation); (2) lineage map from consumer to source, each layer in order with its owner and the transformation applied at each hop; (3) injection point: the first layer where the data enters correctly but exits incorrectly, or enters already wrong from the origin, isolated with the input-vs-output comparison that demonstrates it; (4) five-whys chain from the injection point down to an actionable root cause, distinguishing root cause from contributing causes, each link with evidence or marked [ASSUMPTION]; (5) blast radius: contaminated tables, reports, periods, and consumers with severity; (6) ordered and safe correction plan aligned to pipeline cadence; (7) prevention controls (test at the injection point, alert, automated reconciliation, or data contract with the origin), each with owner and trigger.

Never present a hypothesis as a fact: mark every unverified inference with [ASSUMPTION]. If you do not know the lineage chain, the pipeline cadence, or the downstream consumers, ask for them before executing. Close with open questions and the [ASSUMPTION]s to confirm before the backfill.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe your understanding and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Define a missing-value treatment strategy
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data scientist specializing in data quality and preparation, with mastery of missingness mechanisms (MCAR, MAR, MNAR) and of statistical, model-based, and multiple imputation techniques. I need you to design an explicit and auditable strategy for handling missing values, because this decision conditions all subsequent analysis: a poorly chosen imputation biases conclusions and naive removal destroys statistical power.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First reframe your understanding of the problem and the analytical objective, present your column-by-column plan, and only then execute. If any critical data is missing (target variable, affected columns and their missingness percentage, dataset use objective, business or technical constraints), ask specifically before making any recommendation.

Produce, in this order:
1. Column inventory: missingness percentage, data type, and role relative to the target variable (predictor, identifier, target, irrelevant).
2. Diagnosis of each column's missingness mechanism as MCAR, MAR, or MNAR. State the supporting evidence and mark as [ASSUMPTION] any inference made without data. If two mechanisms are plausible, name both and specify what data would disambiguate them.
3. Impact on the analytical objective: potential bias, loss of statistical power, and risk of information leakage (where missingness or imputation leaks the target variable).
4. Column-by-column recommendation with a concrete technique (mean or median, KNN, MICE, missingness indicator, row or column discard) and justification for why it dominates the other two options given the mechanism, the impact, and the constraints. Apply the rule: the mechanism governs. MCAR tolerates removal or simple imputation; MAR requires conditional or multiple imputation; MNAR requires explicit flagging or missingness-process modeling, never silent simple imputation.
5. Residual risks and verifiable validation plan: distribution comparison before and after, stability of key correlations, sensitivity analysis between candidate paths, and, if the use is modeling, leakage control via train/test separation before imputing.

Final deliverable: a decision matrix (one row per column with mechanism, path, technique, justification, and residual risk) plus the validation plan. Treat the order of operations as part of the recommendation: fit the imputation only on training data, never on the full dataset. Flag edge cases: columns with more than 60% missingness, missingness concentrated in a subgroup, and missing values encoded as sentinel values (0, -1, 9999, empty string) that must be detected before treatment.

prompts.title: Design a data governance framework
prompts.content:
Act as a Chief Data Officer with experience leading end-to-end data governance programs in mid-size and large organizations, fluent in operating models, data policy, change management, and compliance alignment. Design an actionable data governance framework ready to present to an executive committee, grounded in the guiding principle that data without an owner is data without quality: ownership precedes the catalog and classification determines protection.

If I have not provided the organization and its sector, the priority data domains, and the business objective driving the initiative, ask for them before starting; the applicable regulatory framework and current maturity are useful but optional — if missing, assume them explicitly and flag it.

Deliver the framework with five numbered components. First, the operating model for roles: Data Owners (domain-level accountability), Data Stewards (quality and definitions), Custodians (technical controls), and the committee's role; for each role define responsibilities, who they report to, the assignment criterion by domain, and the boundary that separates them from the others to avoid overlaps. Second, the committee and decision structure: composition, cadence, quorum, and mandate of the Data Governance Committee, escalation path, policy approval mechanism, cross-domain dispute resolution, and a RACI matrix for key decisions. Third, core policies drafted as enforceable standards (scope, rule, and control mechanism), not as aspirations: data classification (public-to-restricted taxonomy with treatment per level), quality (completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, uniqueness, and validity with threshold or measurement form), access and privacy (minimization and purpose limitation), retention and lifecycle, and metadata and business definitions. Fourth, a five-level maturity model (initial, reactive, defined, managed, optimized) with observable criteria per level; place the current state and set the objective. Fifth, a phased roadmap respecting dependencies: governance and ownership first, then catalog and classification, then quality and controls, with verifiable milestones and adoption signals tied to the business objective.

Proceed in five phases: interpret the context and declare assumptions with the [ASSUMPTION] label naming the missing critical information; design governance before any tool or catalog; draft each policy as an enforceable standard; calibrate maturity and sequence the roadmap by dependencies, not convenience; and verify against the checklist before closing. Before executing, reframe your understanding and present your plan.

This is not legal advice: any regulatory obligation is validated with the legal team. Do not include cost estimates; quantification occurs after a discovery. Deliver in neutral professional English, ready for executive committee review.

prompts.title: Define data ownership and stewardship roles
prompts.content:
Act as a Chief Data Officer with a track record leading data governance programs in regulated organizations, fluent in DAMA-DMBOK and in stewardship operating models. I need a data ownership and stewardship role model by domain, ready for my data governance committee to nominate people and start operating. Today critical data circulates without a clear responsible party: no one is accountable for its quality, access is granted by custom, and the committee cannot approve the model because the roles are confused.

Before executing, reframe your understanding and present your plan. If you are missing the organization and its sector, the data domains with their critical data, the applicable regulations, or the dispute-resolution authority, ask for everything in a single batch before proceeding; do not invent domains or regulations.

Deliver: (1) definition of the four roles without accountability overlap: Data Owner (domain accountable, approves policies and access), Data Steward (quality, business definitions, glossary, and rules), Data Custodian or technical custodian (storage, security, backups in IT), Data Consumer (use under rules); explicitly set the business vs. IT boundary and the rule of a single accountable Owner per domain. (2) Responsibility table for each role across six axes: data quality, definitions and business glossary, access and authorizations, metadata and lineage, compliance and privacy, lifecycle and retention. (3) RACI matrix per domain crossing the six axes against the four roles; validate that no row has two Accountable parties and no row is left without a Responsible party, and that every Accountable party has visibility (Informed or Consulted) on the compliance axis. (4) Seniority/profile criteria, estimated dedication (as partial or full time, never cost figures), and owner-vs.-steward conflict escalation flow toward the defined authority, with resolution SLA. (5) Nomination minutes with fields: domain, role, name, date, and signature. Mark [ASSUMPTION] on everything inferred and list at the end what needs confirming. Edge cases: a single domain with multiple source systems (one Custodian per system, one Owner per domain), data shared across domains (declare the governing domain), and vacant roles (assign an interim and record the gap).

prompts.title: Classify data by sensitivity and criticality
prompts.content: Act as a senior data governance architect with experience in information classification programs, control frameworks, and privacy by design. Your task is to produce an auditable data classification matrix with controls mapped by level and a prioritized gap summary. Before executing, reframe your understanding (scope, assets, applicable regulatory framework) and present your plan; if any essential data is missing (asset inventory, applicable standards, organization or domain, control catalog), ask before inventing. Use a four-level scheme: public, internal, confidential, and restricted, defining each level unambiguously. For each asset: 1) determine SENSITIVITY by evaluating the type of information (personal, financial, trade secret, health, regulated), damage from unauthorized disclosure, and legal obligations; 2) evaluate CRITICALITY (high/medium/low) by operational impact upon loss of availability or integrity, independently of sensitivity; 3) assign the FINAL LEVEL taking the most demanding grade between both axes, with a one-line justification; 4) map minimum controls per level covering six dimensions: access control (least privilege and need-to-know), encryption at rest and in transit, masking or anonymization, retention and deletion, access logging and monitoring, and external sharing rules. Detect gaps: assets without sufficient controls for their level and missing controls in the available catalog. Mark as [ASSUMPTION] every definition, criterion, or data point you assume; do not invent assets, regulations, or undeclared control capabilities. Deliver: legend of the four levels with their definition; matrix — asset | level | sensitivity | criticality | justification | required controls; and prioritized control gap summary by risk with remediation recommendation and suggested owner.

prompts.title: Design a PII handling and anonymization strategy
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Data Governance Lead with fifteen years designing personal data protection and anonymization strategies in regulated environments, expert in distinguishing pseudonymization from real anonymization and in balancing privacy with analytical utility. I need a PII handling and anonymization strategy for a dataset that is about to be used, shared, or analyzed, where there is still no clarity about which fields are sensitive or how to protect them without breaking their utility. Treating everything the same overprotects innocuous data and leaves critical data exposed: the strategy must be field by field, according to the real use of each data point.

Before executing, apply the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret your understanding, Plan your approach, and only then Execute. If you are missing the dataset, the fields, the intended use, the regulatory framework, or the risk level, ask for everything in a single batch before proceeding; do not invent fields, compliance figures, or regulations that do not apply, and mark every assumption as [ASSUMPTION].

Execute as follows:
1. Inventory each field and classify it in a single category: direct identifier, quasi-identifier, sensitive data or special category, or non-personal data.
2. For each field declare its real use and indicate whether that use requires the original value, a consistent but unreadable value, or only an aggregated form.
3. Assign a technique justified by use and always distinguish reversible from irreversible: masking when the value is not needed; tokenization when consistency and controlled reversal via vault are required; pseudonymization when a stable alias reversible only with a separate key is sufficient (it remains personal data); generalization or grouping of quasi-identifiers (age to range, date to month, postal code to region) to approach k-anonymity; suppression if the field does not contribute to the use; irreversible anonymization only when no return link should exist, noting that real anonymization means the data ceases to be personal and is difficult to guarantee with quasi-identifiers present.
4. Define the minimization plan under least privilege: what not to collect or to purge, where each copy lives, and who accesses which version of the data.
5. List the residual re-identification risks from quasi-identifier combinations, prioritize them, and associate a mitigation with each.

Quality rules: each field in a single category; technique justified by real use, not by custom; no data the business would need to re-link marked for irreversible anonymization; every regulatory statement marked as requires legal validation. Deliver: (1) table with columns field, classification, real use, chosen technique, reversible yes/no, justification; (2) minimization decisions list; (3) prioritized residual risks with mitigation; (4) legal validation note.

prompts.title: Map compliance requirements to data controls
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Data Governance Officer expert in privacy and data protection (GDPR, Law 1581/2012 Habeas Data, and sector regulations such as PCI-DSS or HIPAA as applicable), specializing in translating legal obligations into technical and process controls for retention, consent/legal basis, and access. Your mission is to deliver an actionable and auditable requirement-to-control mapping, not a law summary.

Proceed in four phases. Phase 1 — Inventory and classification: list the in-scope data categories with their sensitivity (personal, special category personal, financial, children's data), system and location, processing purpose, declared legal basis, approximate volume, and whether there are international transfers or processors/third parties. Phase 2 — Requirement extraction: for each regulation, derive concrete obligations in the three domains (retention, consent/legal basis, access and data subject rights including DSAR), cite article or section only if verifiable and otherwise mark [ASSUMPTION], and consolidate equivalent requirements across regulations into a single requirement to avoid duplicating controls. Phase 3 — Control mapping: for each requirement define a concrete control (retention: period and deletion or anonymization method with its trigger; consent: capture mechanism, immutable record, granularity, and revocation path, or documented alternative legal basis; access: least-privilege role matrix, segregation of duties, access log and periodic review), assign a responsible party in RACI notation, verifiable compliance evidence (policy, log, screenshot, contract), implementation system, and control frequency. Phase 4 — Gaps and remediation: compare each target control against existing controls, mark status (compliant / partial / gap / not applicable), evaluate residual risk as probability x impact including sanctioning and reputational exposure, and prioritize remediation separating quick wins from structural changes with their dependencies.

Rigor rules: never assert legal obligations, retention periods, or legal bases as definitive legal facts; mark them as [ASSUMPTION] and recommend legal team validation. Do not invent article numbers or section numbers. No orphan obligations (every requirement maps to a control) and no controls without a justifying requirement. If a data category is missing its processing purpose, legal basis, or location, record the gap as a blocking question rather than assuming. If essential information is missing to start (which regulations apply or which data assets are in scope), ask for it before executing.

Deliver: (1) inventory and classification table; (2) requirement-control-evidence-owner-status matrix; (3) gap register prioritized by residual risk; (4) appendix of assumptions and interpretations requiring legal validation.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe your understanding and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Document end-to-end data lineage
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data governance architect specialized in data lineage, column-by-column mapping, and regulatory traceability. Document the end-to-end lineage of a critical data element from its source system to its final consumers, for the stated purpose (audit, impact analysis, analytical trust, or compliance). Without explicit lineage, no figure is auditable, no source change is predictable, and no decision is defensible: EstrategIA applied — lineage stops being tribal folklore and becomes a documented asset.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First, restate what data you will trace, from where, to where, and for what purpose; declare the limits of what you know; present your plan; only then execute. If you are missing the critical data element, the source system, the consumers, or the purpose, ask before proceeding — do not invent anything.

Deliverable — an end-to-end lineage document with these components:
1. Origin-to-destination chain at three levels — system, dataset/table, and field/column — without omitting intermediate staging steps or transformations. For each hop, record: source, destination, movement type (ingestion, transformation, copy, aggregation, derivation), business rule or logic applied, data owner, update frequency, expected latency, and existing quality control.
2. Lineage diagram in Mermaid (left-to-right flowchart) with one node per stage and edges labeled by transformation type.
3. Field-level lineage table with exactly six columns: Source, Transformation, Destination, Business Rule, Owner, Quality Control.
4. Downstream impact analysis — which consumers are affected if the data element changes its definition, is delayed, or fails — naming the failure mode and observable symptom for each dashboard or report.
5. Traceability gap register (undocumented hops, opaque or black-box transformations, missing owners, absent controls, duplicate definitions) prioritized by risk with a suggested action and proposed responsible party.

Rigor rules: never invent names of systems, tables, columns, metrics, or owners; mark each inference with [ASSUMPTION] and each verified claim with its source. Distinguish business definition (what the data means) from physical implementation (where and how it is calculated). If the data element has more than one definition across consumers, register it as a critical semantic-divergence gap. Close by declaring whether the lineage is complete, partial, or has unverifiable segments. Neutral professional English, no prices or monetary amounts.

prompts.title: Structure a data and metadata catalog
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data governance architect specialized in data catalogs and metadata management, with command of DAMA-DMBOK and the DCAT metadata model. Your task is to design the structural architecture of a data catalog for an organization, so that it is ready to configure any catalog tool afterward. Before executing, restate in your own words what you understood and present a brief plan; if you are missing data about the organization, the data domains to cover, the source systems, the audiences that will consume the catalog, or the governance maturity level, ask for them instead of inventing them.

Produce a structured document with: (1) data domain taxonomy and the key entities or datasets of each domain, in a navigable hierarchy; (2) three-layer metadata model — business, technical, and operational — with the fields of each layer, including upstream and downstream lineage and freshness in the operational layer; (3) standard dataset card with mandatory and optional fields, plus the business glossary entry that supports it, clearly separating the business term from the physical object; (4) sensitivity classification scheme and asset criticality levels, applicable without ambiguity; (5) population and maintenance flow — creation, approval by business owner and data steward, periodic review, and obsolescence marking — with roles and cadences; (6) catalog health KPI dashboard — coverage, metadata freshness, percentage of datasets with an assigned owner, and percentage classified by sensitivity — each with formula and initial target.

Rules: do not invent system names, domains, or real data; use the ones provided or explicit placeholders. Mark every inference with [ASSUMPTION]. If the governance level is not indicated, assume it is nascent and declare it. Distinguish verifiable truth from design recommendations. Close with a brief list of design decisions made and their trade-offs, and note the missing data that should be confirmed before configuring a tool. Neutral professional English.

prompts.title: Design least-privilege data access control
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data governance and security architect, expert in least-privilege access control, RBAC and ABAC models, row- and column-level security, dynamic masking, and sensitivity-based data classification. I need an implementation-ready least-privilege access control model for a data domain: each person and service gets exactly what their job requires and nothing more, turning a tangle of inherited permissions into an auditable decision map.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First, restate the scope, consumers, platform, and regulatory obligations you understand and present your plan; if an essential piece of information is missing (which assets are in scope, who accesses them and for what purpose, on which platform, what sensitivity taxonomy exists, which compliance frameworks apply), ask me for it before executing instead of inventing it.

Then deliver, in this order: (1) sensitivity taxonomy applied to the scope, with each asset, table, and column labeled and columns containing personal, financial, health, or trade-secret data flagged; anything unclassifiable is treated provisionally as the highest level. (2) Subject inventory grouped by business function, starting from deny-all by default and declaring the minimum data each function needs with its use case. (3) Mechanism choice per permission set: RBAC when the function is stable and roles are few, ABAC when access depends on dynamic attributes such as region, purpose, or clearance, or hybrid; justify each choice against the platform. (4) Row-level rules (predicate defining which rows each subject sees) and column-level rules (hide, mask, or tokenize according to sensitivity), expressed in a verifiable and portable form without binding to a single engine's syntax unless requested. (5) Complete access matrix crossing roles or policies against assets and columns, with one value per cell (no access, masked, read, write) and the applicable row rule, plus a segregation-of-duties map that blocks toxic combinations (e.g., whoever creates a payment does not approve it). (6) Access lifecycle: request and approval flow, emergency access with automatic expiry, periodic recertification, and audit signals to record — with responsible parties and frequency.

Mark with [ASSUMPTION] everything assumed and refer to the data owner or to security and compliance any decision that exceeds the design. Do not include prices or costs. Close with a quality checklist confirming that nothing remained unclassified, every permission has a use case, the matrix is complete, and the review plan has responsible parties and frequency.

prompts.title: Define data retention and lifecycle policy
prompts.content: Act as a senior Data Governance Lead grounded in DAMA DMBOK and with hands-on experience in privacy compliance and regulatory retention. Your assignment is to deliver a data retention and lifecycle policy ready for legal review and approval. If you are missing any essential data (organization and sector, jurisdiction that sets minimum periods, applicable regulatory framework, data categories to cover, systems where the data resides), ask before proceeding; never invent a legal retention period under any circumstance. Deliver numbered: 1) Prioritized inventory of data categories, each with data owner, technical custodian, legal basis for processing, and sensitivity level. 2) Retention matrix per category with active period, archival period, and total period before purge; cite the specific obligation that sets the minimum and justify the maximum by minimization — never by inertia. 3) Lifecycle triggers: the event that moves data from active to archived and from archived to purge, plus the legal-hold rule that freezes purge during litigation, audit, or a legal request. 4) Secure deletion procedure for each storage medium (including backups): method, execution evidence, and handling of copies by crypto-erasure or rotation expiry. 5) Governance model: RACI, record of processing activities, review cadence, and flow for handling data-subject erasure requests, including response SLA and exception handling. 6) Phased implementation plan and conversion to policy-as-code (expiry rules, purge jobs, alerts). Mark every period that depends on country or sector as an assumption to be confirmed with legal. Present output in tables, no filler prose. Before executing, restate what you understand and present your work plan. Neutral professional English, no emojis.

prompts.title: Design federated data-mesh governance
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data governance architect with proven experience implementing data mesh in multi-domain organizations, fluent in Zhamak Dehghani's four principles (domain ownership, data as a product, self-serve platform, federated computational governance) and in data contracts.

Design an actionable, phased federated governance model in data-mesh style for an organization that suffers bottlenecks because its central data team does not scale to meet domain demand. The goal is to distribute ownership by domain without losing coherence: each domain publishes its data as a trustworthy product while a minimal core of global standards ensures interoperability, security, and compliance verifiable by automation rather than manual review.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First, restate what you understand (sector, candidate domains, data maturity, platform, regulatory requirements) and present your plan; only then execute. If you are missing any of that data, ask for it before proceeding and do not invent anything; mark with [ASSUMPTION] everything you assume.

Deliver:
1. Domain map: owning domains, their initial data products, owner teams, and responsibility boundaries; distinguish source, aggregate, and consumption-oriented domains, and flag dependencies between them.
2. Standard data product: canonical template with input/output ports, versioned data contract (schema, semantics, change policy, deprecation), quality metrics, SLOs, discovery metadata, lineage, and access policies.
3. Global standards: the minimal core that applies to all domains (interoperability and addressability, naming conventions, identity and authentication, classification and security, lineage and observability).
4. Federated computational governance: council composition (domain owners + platform + security), its cadence, the boundary between global and local decisions, and how each standard is materialized as policy-as-code embedded in the self-serve platform.
5. Operating model: RACI among domain teams, platform team, and council for data-product registration, contract changes, quality incidents, and policy exceptions — including the escalation path.
6. Health and adoption: mesh health metrics and a phased adoption plan with measurable advancement criteria and stop signals (when NOT to advance).

For each design decision, explicitly declare whether it is a GLOBAL standard (centralized, non-negotiable) or a LOCAL decision (delegated to the domain), and justify the boundary by coordination cost versus autonomy. Translate each global standard into a verifiable mechanism executable by the platform (contract validation, classification scanning, deployment gate, SLO check) — never by human review. Close with the main adoption risk and its mitigation. Neutral professional English.

prompts.title: Assess data governance and analytics maturity
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data governance assessor with experience certifying maturity under DAMA DMBOK and DCAM in regulated organizations. I want a maturity diagnosis with an evolution roadmap for an organization or unit. Before assessing, restate the scope you understand and present your plan; if you are missing the sector, the sponsor, the available evidence (policies, tool inventory, data org chart, audits, interviews), the applicable compliance framework, or the desired target level, ask me in a single batch instead of inventing it.

First declare the 5-level scale (1 Initial/ad-hoc, 2 Repeatable, 3 Defined, 4 Managed/measured, 5 Optimized) and the 8 dimensions you will assess: data strategy and sponsorship, organization and roles (owner/steward/office), policies and standards, data quality, metadata and lineage, architecture and integration, security/privacy/compliance, and analytics/value realization.

Deliver: (1) scoring table per dimension with current level 1-5 and the textual evidence that justifies it, target level at 12-18 months, and the gap; (2) heat map crossing gap criticality with regulatory or business exposure; (3) the 3 to 5 priority gaps ordered by impact-vs-effort matrix; (4) roadmap in three waves (quick wins 0-3 months, foundational 3-9 months, scaling 9-18 months), each initiative with a suggested owner and dependencies; (5) success metrics per dimension to verify progress at the next assessment.

Rules: assign each level only with explicit evidence from the inputs; where data is missing, mark [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent facts, tools, or regulatory figures. Target levels must be realistic and consistent with sector and size — not everything at level 5. Sequence the roadmap by real dependencies: do not scale analytics on top of non-existent metadata or data quality. Neutral professional English.

prompts.title: Build a business glossary of data terms
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Data Governance Lead, expert in DAMA DMBOK and DCAM, who has standardized business glossaries in organizations with multiple reporting lines that contradict each other. I need to build the canonical business glossary for the commercial domain so that sales, finance, and the data team stop arguing about what each metric means. The terms to define are: net revenue, churn, active customer, average ticket, pipeline, conversion rate, and MRR — extracted from the sales dashboard and the monthly finance report. The relevant organizational structure: commercial management (natural owner of sales metrics), FP&A in finance (owner of monetary metrics), and the data area as technical custodian. Current governance maturity is initial: no formal glossary or data committee.

Proceed as follows: 1) Group terms by business subdomain and discard duplicates that are the same concept under a different name. 2) For each term, draft a card with: canonical name, definition in ONE business sentence without technical jargon or circularity, synonyms and abbreviations to deprecate, calculation rule or explicit inclusion criterion if it is a metric (numerator, denominator, filters, time window, unit), source data or system of origin, business owner plus data custodian, sensitivity classification if applicable, and status (proposed / under review / approved). 3) Raise a conflict register: term with competing definitions across areas, the concrete impact on reports (how much the figure moves), and the proposed resolution for the data committee. 4) Deliver a synonym -> canonical term mapping table, ready to feed normalization rules in BI, with no collisions (one synonym points to one canonical). 5) Close with an adoption plan calibrated to maturity: approval ritual, review frequency, versioning criterion, and how to enforce the glossary on new reports.

Do not invent proprietary calculation rules or owners: where an internal criterion is missing, leave {to_be_confirmed} and mark assumptions with [ASSUMPTION]. If the set of terms, the owner structure, or the source of any data is unclear, ask before drafting the cards. First restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Deliver: term cards grouped by subdomain, conflict register, synonym mapping table, and governance plan — ready to bring to the data committee.

prompts.title: Design a layered data warehouse architecture
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data architect specialized in dimensional data warehousing, with hands-on mastery of Kimball, Inmon (Corporate Information Factory), Data Vault 2.0, and the medallion architecture. Design a layered data warehouse architecture that unambiguously separates where raw data lands, where it is reconciled and historized, where it is modeled for analytical consumption, and where certified metrics live. This separation (staging, integration, presentation, semantic) isolates source changes, makes loading idempotent and reprocessable, and delivers a single governed source of truth. I need to know the analytical use case, data sources (system, format, frequency, business key), the target platform, expected volume and latency, and the preferred approach for the core layer; if any of this is missing, ask me before proceeding and do not invent anything about the sources or the platform.

Deliver: (1) Framing summarizing the use case, profiling sources, and deriving the target latency and load window. (2) Staging (landing/raw): faithful landing from origin with load metadata (ingestion timestamp, batch, source system), retention and reprocessing policy, no business rules. (3) Integration (historized core): where sources are reconciled, conformed, deduplicated, and historized, resolving business keys and traceability (Data Vault 2.0 with hubs, links, and satellites, or Inmon-style 3NF core). (4) Presentation (dimensional): Kimball-style star or snowflake data marts, with declared grain per fact table, classified measures (additive, semi-additive, non-additive), conformed dimensions, and history handling with SCD1, SCD2, or SCD3 per attribute. (5) Semantic: certified metrics, hierarchies, business names, and a metrics/views layer consumed by BI and self-service, separating business logic from the physical model. (6) For each layer, a table with purpose, granularity, allowed transformations, load pattern (full load, timestamp-incremental, CDC, upsert/merge, or append-only), frequency, idempotency, and owner. (7) Close with a Mermaid flow map of the four layers, architecture decisions justified with their trade-off, and a per-layer quality test plan.

Mark everything inferred as [ASSUMPTION]. Cover edge cases: late-arriving facts, slowly changing dimensions that also delete (SCD2 + soft delete), late-arriving dimensions, natural keys colliding across sources, reprocessing an already-loaded batch without duplication, and the time zone of load timestamps. The test plan must include at minimum: key uniqueness, referential integrity, freshness, and origin-to-destination count reconciliation. Define the acceptance criterion: each layer closed, no orphan nodes in the diagram, no business rules leaked into staging.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Decide between data warehouse, data lake, and lakehouse
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data and analytics architect with experience in dimensional warehouses, data lakes on object storage, and lakehouses with open table formats, operating mixed BI and ML workloads. I need to decide the analytical storage paradigm for the analytics platform.

Context:
- Data types and sources: the data types
- Volume and growth (batch/streaming): the data volume
- Priority use cases: the use cases
- Governance requirements: the governance requirements
- Team maturity and tooling: the team maturity

If any data is empty or ambiguous, ask me before recommending; do not invent it.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Proceed as follows: (1) summarize the context and mark as [ASSUMPTION] any missing data, turning each critical gap into a concrete question; (2) compare data warehouse, data lake, and lakehouse on six axes: structure and schema approach (schema-on-write vs schema-on-read), governance, quality, and ACID transactions, structural cost profile without price figures, BI and SQL suitability, data science and ML suitability, operational complexity versus the team maturity; (3) apply medallion, Kimball, and open table formats (Delta, Iceberg, Hudi) only where they add value; (4) name triggers and anti-patterns per paradigm; (5) issue a scenario-paradigm matrix and prioritized recommendation with its invalidation condition. Always differentiate BI from ML. Close with a six-axis table, scenario-paradigm matrix, and recommendation with invalidation condition.

If any data is missing, ask before executing.

prompts.title: Choose between Kimball and Inmon modeling approaches
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data architect with genuine mastery of Ralph Kimball's methodologies (dimensional modeling, bus matrix, star schemas, conformed dimensions) and Bill Inmon's (Corporate Information Factory, warehouse in third normal form as the single source, derived data marts). The organization is going to build or redirect its data warehouse and needs to decide on a modeling approach before committing team and budget. Choosing well unlocks a warehouse that scales with new sources without rewrites, delivers value to BI in credible timelines, and withstands audit; choosing by fashion condemns the team to rework.

MetodologIA Protocol: first Interpret (restate sector, use case, sources and their quality, volume and target latency, team maturity and size, governance and compliance requirements, and horizon and time-to-value; if a critical piece of data is missing to weight criteria, ask before proceeding). Then Plan (derive between 6 and 9 decision criteria with their weights from the context and present the evaluation plan before calculating). Then Execute.

Deliver an analytical architecture decision with: (1) a well-founded contrast of Kimball vs Inmon on the dimensions that matter for deciding (starting point and direction, integration granularity, time-to-value, cost of change with new sources, enterprise governance and consistency, load and maintenance complexity, BI consumption experience), honest about the trade-offs of each and without caricatures; (2) decision matrix with weighted criteria, scoring Kimball, Inmon, and a hybrid (Inmon or Data Vault integration feeding Kimball dimensional marts for consumption) on an explicit scale, with the weighted score calculation visible and reproducible; (3) clear recommendation tied to the criteria and the explicit conditions under which it would change; (4) layered target model (sources, staging, integration, presentation, and marts) indicating the modeling technique for each layer and data flow; (5) phased adoption plan with the first business process to model, deliverables per phase, risks with mitigation, and measurable signals that would require revisiting the approach.

Treat the choice as an EstrategIA data decision, above technological fashion. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] every statement about the environment that has not been confirmed and do not invent figures from the client's data. Close with a document ready to align sponsors and the data team. If you are missing any critical data, ask before continuing.

prompts.title: Design the serving layer for BI and consumption
prompts.content:
Act as a senior analytical data architect, specialist in dimensional data warehousing (Kimball) and serving-layer optimization for BI. The core warehouse modeling is solved, but BI consumption is slow, costly, and metrics do not reconcile across reports. Design the serving layer that separates the stable physical model from the changing consumption layer, to deliver predictable performance, a single version of truth per metric, and compute cost control.

Deliverables:
1. Serving-layer map: classify each object as a semantic view (logical), a materialized data mart, or an aggregation table, with an explicit criterion for when to use each one based on volume, access pattern, and cost.
2. Dimensional design of priority marts in star schema: declare the grain of each fact table in one sentence, the conformed dimensions, surrogate keys, and SCD handling (Type 1/2) where the business requires it; distinguish transactional, periodic-snapshot, and accumulating-snapshot facts.
3. Pre-calculated aggregation strategy: which rollups to create, at which levels of granularity and temporality, and how to guarantee they sum exactly to the detail level, including the handling of non-additive measures (ratios, distinct counts) that cannot be summed.
4. Caching and materialization policy: per object, physical vs. logical, full vs. incremental refresh, trigger and window, and invalidation upon late-arriving data and reprocessing.
5. Semantic metrics contract: for each KPI, canonical name, formula, grain, valid dimensions, filters, and owner, as the single layer consumed by all reports.

Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: first reformulate the objective, reports, and SLAs and flag assumptions; then present the plan (prioritized marts and shared dimensions) before designing. Close by verifying that each metric has a grain, each aggregation rolls up to the detail level, and each SLA maps to a concrete mechanism (materialization, aggregation, or cache). If any critical data is missing (engine, volume, dimensions, reports, SLA), request it before proceeding. Do not include prices. Neutral professional English.

prompts.title: Design a real-time analytics architecture
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data architect with fifteen years designing streaming pipelines and low-latency OLAP serving layers that feed live dashboards in production. I need to design an end-to-end real-time analytics architecture before building, to make operational, fraud, logistics, or product decisions with data in seconds rather than minutes or hours.

Case context: event sources are orders and inventory movements from an e-commerce, emitted as JSON by a checkout service and a WMS, with possible late and duplicate events due to retries. Volume is 8,000 events per second on average and 25,000 at campaign peak; the target end-to-end latency is less than 5 seconds and the required freshness is less than 10 seconds. The dashboard is queried by 200 concurrent users with breakdowns by hour, region, and category over 24-hour rolling windows. The permitted cloud is AWS and the team has intermediate streaming maturity. There is a 90-day retention requirement and lineage traceability.

Proceed as follows: (1) Validate that you have sources, peak volume, target latency/freshness, and consumption patterns; if anything is missing or ambiguous, request it in a single batch before designing. (2) Decide and justify the reference pattern — Kappa (single streaming path) vs. Lambda (batch plus streaming) — based on the actual need for historical reprocessing and count accuracy, not on trend. (3) Design the four layers: event ingestion and log (Kafka- or Kinesis-type bus), stream processing (windows, watermarks, at-least-once vs. exactly-once semantics), sub-second OLAP serving (columnar engine such as Druid, ClickHouse, or Pinot), and dashboard; declare partitioning and keys. (4) Specify guarantees and operations: late and out-of-order events, deduplication and idempotency, schema evolution, backpressure, retention and reprocessing, observability (consumer lag, per-stage latency, freshness). (5) Define measurable latency and freshness SLOs with their measurement method, error budget, failure modes with mitigation, and a load-test plan at peak volume. (6) Emit a recommendation: architecture ready to implement, or requires validating a critical assumption before committing to build.

Flag every concrete technology not imposed by the client as [ASSUMPTION] and always name the discarded alternative. Do not invent volume or latency figures. Do not include costs or prices: investment sizing is deferred to the Discovery. Deliver: a text layer diagram, a technology decision table (layer, choice, justification, discarded alternative), processing guarantees, SLOs with measurement method, risks with mitigation, a validation plan, and a final recommendation.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Design a reverse ETL flow toward operational tools
prompts.content: Act as a senior data architect specialized in data activation and reverse ETL, with experience in governance, identity resolution, and operation of synchronization pipelines toward SaaS APIs. Design a reverse ETL flow that activates curated warehouse models toward the business's operational tools (CRM, marketing, support) with governed, deduplicated, and end-to-end traceable synchronization. If I do not have on hand the warehouse models, the destination tools, the identity key per destination, the PII constraints, or the target freshness, ask me for them before designing the contract; do not invent table names, keys, or fields. Deliver: 1) a text flowchart showing warehouse, source models, synchronization layer, and destinations with the data direction; 2) a data contract table per activation use case (source model and grain, stable entity key, frequency, business owner); 3) a source-to-destination field mapping table with types and transformations; 4) a brief operations runbook (alerts, failure behavior, idempotent reprocessing); 5) a wave-based implementation plan with promotion-to-production criteria. Design rules: derive 3 to 5 concrete activation use cases from the available models and business questions; each case declares destination, destination object, frequency, and owner. Define identity resolution and deduplication per destination so that duplicates are not created. Define the load pattern (full refresh, incremental by change column, or by change log), diff detection to send only what changed, the write mode (upsert/insert/update), API rate-limit handling, and idempotency with retries so that a reprocess does not duplicate records. Define pipeline metrics (rows read, sent, and failed; freshness latency), pre-send quality checks (non-null key, ranges, expected volume), failure behavior (block vs. degrade), alerts with recipients, and field-to-field lineage all the way to the destination. Order use cases in waves by value and risk, validate the first sync without contaminating production (sandbox or controlled subset), and define promotion criteria. Edge cases to cover: null keys or identity collisions, records deleted in the source that must be reflected or preserved in the destination, schema that changes in the source, reprocessing window after a partial failure, and API destination quota limit. Flag every missing datum as [ASSUMPTION] and request it if it blocks the contract. Do not include prices or invented data. MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute; reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Close with the five deliverables ready for data and business review.

prompts.title: Design a feature store for analytics and ML
prompts.content: Act as a senior data and MLOps architect who has operated feature stores in production and masters offline/online patterns and point-in-time correctness. Design a feature store that serves both analytics/BI and ML models at the same time, with the explicit objective of eliminating per-project feature reprocessing and the train/serving skew that degrades models in production. Deliver an actionable design with: (1) Definition layer: declarative schema of a feature (name, owner, entity/key, type, source, transformation, aggregation window, expected freshness, PII sensitivity, version) and the registry/catalog that versions it as a contract. (2) Compute layer: separate batch features (historical aggregations) from streaming (near-real-time) by reusing a single transformation logic to prevent skew; indicate where the compute runs and how the transformation is versioned. (3) Dual storage: offline store (historical, columnar, for training datasets with point-in-time joins that avoid data leakage) and online store (key-value, low latency, for inference); define how they are synchronized and the materialization contract. (4) Reuse and discovery: feature groups, searchable catalog, end-to-end lineage, ownership, and deprecation policy. (5) Training-inference consistency: single transformation point, offline/online parity validation, skew detection, and drift monitoring. (6) Governance and SLAs: freshness per feature, freshness/completeness/nulls monitoring, access control for PII, backfill strategy, and schema-change handling. Work in this order: frame entities, keys, and use cases (flag missing assumptions); draw components and flows in text; trace an example feature end-to-end from source to online serving and offline dataset generation with point-in-time join; define the materialization contract, the parity test plan, and skew/drift detection; build the governance matrix (owner, freshness, sensitivity, SLA) and the backfill and schema-evolution policy. Close each critical feature with its acceptance criterion. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing. If critical information is missing (entities, use cases, target latency, volume, stack, or privacy requirements), request it before designing.

prompts.title: Estimate warehouse capacity, cost, and growth
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data platform architect specialized in capacity planning and data FinOps on warehouses and lakehouses (Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks, Redshift), with practice in growth modeling and compute/storage sizing. I need a capacity, cost, and growth model for my analytical platform to anticipate how storage and compute scale, size them with a clear head, justify the platform investment, and commit to a defensible plan that avoids overprovisioning and gives early signals for resizing before service degrades.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First reformulate what you understood about my platform, my baseline, and my growth assumptions; present your modeling plan (drivers, scenarios, horizon, granularity); and only then execute. If you are missing a critical datum needed to project (current volume in TB, daily ingestion, compute engine and unit in use, or retention policy), stop and request it before inventing a projection.

Deliver:
1. Normalized baseline in a table: volume in TB, daily ingestion, number of tables/domains, peak concurrency, queries per day, and compute unit in use (warehouses, slots, clusters, or DBUs and their size). Flag [ASSUMPTION] for every inferred datum and cite its source.
2. Growth model with three separate drivers — accumulated historical data, new sources and domains, and query demand — each with its explicit compound growth formula. Project storage and compute separately: storage grows with accumulation and retention; compute grows with concurrency and query complexity, not necessarily at the same rate.
3. Three scenarios — conservative, base, aggressive — each with its rates and the business triggers that activate it (new product lines, mergers, self-service BI mandates, AI and ML workloads).
4. Translation to actionable capacity units: storage per quarter, credits, slots, or DBUs per month, sustained and peak concurrency, and tier or reservation scaling thresholds, aligned to your service goals (latency, sustained concurrency, load window, retention).
5. Efficiency levers that flatten the curve (partitioning and clustering, hot/warm/cold retention, materializations and aggregates, auto-suspend and right-sizing, workload-based load separation), each with estimated impact and the risk or trade-off it introduces.
6. Budget expressed only in consumption units (credits, DBUs, slots, TB) and in FTE-months of implementation and operations, in low, medium, and high band. Never use money, amounts, or the word free.

Close with quarterly tables, visible formulas, and an executive summary with the three triggers that require resizing and the lead time with which each is detected.

prompts.title: Build a demand forecast with time series
prompts.content:
Act as a senior data scientist specialized in demand forecasting and supply-chain planning, with mastery of classical statistical models and time-series libraries. I need to convert a historical demand series into a defensible forecast for planning decisions (inventory, purchasing, capacity, budget): not a projected curve without backing, but a model chosen on merit, validated with backtesting, and communicated with explicit uncertainty, so that the team trusts the range and not only the central figure.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before executing, reformulate what you understand (series, frequency, horizon, decision it feeds) and present your plan; if the series, its frequency, or the horizon are missing, request them before continuing.

Produce a reproducible forecast report with these phases. Phase 1 Diagnosis: characterize the series according to its frequency (usable length, trend, seasonality with period and strength, cycles, missing values, structural zeros, outliers, level shifts); evaluate stationarity and whether transformation is worthwhile (log for increasing variance, differencing for trend/seasonality). Verify data sufficiency: at a minimum two complete seasonal cycles to model seasonality; if not met, degrade to a simpler method and declare it. If demand is intermittent (many zeros), flag Croston/SBA instead of classical smoothing. Phase 2 Selection: map patterns to method (moving average or simple smoothing for short or unstructured series; ETS/Holt-Winters with stable trend and seasonality; ARIMA/SARIMA with strong autocorrelation; Prophet with multiple seasonalities, holidays, or trend breakpoints; Croston/SBA for intermittent demand). Justify the choice by observed patterns, not preference, and set a seasonal naive baseline as a mandatory reference. Phase 3 Validation: apply rolling-origin backtesting (walk-forward), never a single cut; define the training window, step, and iterations, and report error per fold and aggregate against the baseline. Prohibited: training with data after each fold's cutoff (no temporal leakage). If the model does not beat the baseline, say so and reconsider. Phase 4 Forecast and communication: deliver central values plus prediction intervals at the requested levels; explain what they represent (not a guarantee) and why they widen with the horizon. Phase 5 Close: assumptions, risks (overfitting, regime change, unmodeled events, data quality), and retraining cadence with concrete triggers.

Rules: flag every unprovided datum as ASSUMPTION; do not invent figures; report the requested error metrics with their interpretation in business units. Deliver a structured report with diagnosis, chosen method and justification, backtesting error table vs. baseline, forecast table with intervals, and an assumptions/risks/retraining section.

prompts.title: Collaborative 1:1 agenda co-built with the team member
prompts.content:
Act as a senior team leader and management coach trained in the Manager-Tools model (Auzenne and Horstman's 1:1 cadence), with experience running effective 1:1s at scale. I want you to design a reusable 1:1 agenda, ready to paste into my notes tool, that puts the person and their development at the center and prevents the meeting from degenerating into a status report.

MetodologIA Protocol: first reformulate who the 1:1 is with, their role, the cadence, the actual duration, the relationship maturity, and the development focus for the period; present the minute allocation per block and the rotating-sections calendar; only then write. If any of those data points are missing, ask for them rather than assuming.

Build the agenda as follows:
1. Distribute the duration into three blocks applying 'the team member contributes first': Block 1 — team member topics (equal or greater weight than the leader), Block 2 — leader topics, Block 3 — future/development/career. The three blocks must add up to exactly the total duration.
2. For each block define the purpose in one line, 3 to 5 opening guide questions, and the leader's expected listening posture (what to do and what to avoid).
3. List the FIXED sections that repeat every session: brief personal check-in, follow-up on previous commitments, active blockers.
4. List the ROTATING sections anchored in the development focus: development (weeks 1 and 3), two-way feedback (week 2), career vision (week 4); if the cadence is biweekly, compress the cycle into two sessions and say what is covered in each.
5. Close with a commitment capture protocol: responsible party, action, date, and review mechanism in the next session.

Also add: a note on how to calibrate rapport vs. depth based on relationship maturity (more rapport if new, more depth if consolidated); 2 to 3 anti-patterns to avoid (turning it into a status update, the leader monopolizing the time, skipping the follow-up); and a clear criterion for when to reschedule rather than cancel. Flag with [ASSUMPTION] any datum that has not been confirmed. Professional tone in neutral English, no emojis.

prompts.title: Script for the first 1:1 with a new direct report
prompts.content:
Act as a senior manager with a track record of building high-performance teams, trained in leadership practices (Michael Lopp, The Manager's Path) and psychological safety (Amy Edmondson). I need a complete script for my first 1:1 with a new direct report. This first meeting sets the tone for the entire relationship: the goal is NOT to review pending items but to build trust, learn their story, align mutual expectations, and agree on how we will work together.

Before writing, follow the MetodologIA Protocol: reformulate in one or two sentences what you understood and present your plan (minute allocation per block). If you are missing any critical datum (meeting duration, remote/in-person/hybrid mode, the report's role and seniority, the leadership style I want to project), request it before writing; do not invent the context.

Deliver the script structured in five blocks, each with a suggested time that adds up to the total duration:
1. Opening and framing: how I explain the purpose of the 1:1, that it is the person's space and not mine, and why I invest in them.
2. Story and motivations: 4–5 open questions about their trajectory, what energizes them, what drains them, and how they define success.
3. Work and communication style: how they prefer to receive feedback, how they like to be recognized, their communication rhythm, and early warning signals.
4. Mutual expectations: how I articulate what I expect from them and explicitly ask what they expect from me.
5. Cadence agreements and close: frequency, duration, who sets the agenda, notes tool, and a first concrete and verifiable commitment.

For each block include: first-person script, exact questions to ask (open, not yes/no), and a brief note on why that moment matters. Close with three common errors to avoid and a bridge phrase toward the next session. Adapt the tone to the mode and leadership style. Neutral and warm English, no corporate jargon and no emojis. If the report previously had a manager or comes from another company, adjust the opening to acknowledge that history without asking them to repeat what they already shared. Deliverable: a script readable in one continuous flow on one page, ready to take to the meeting.

prompts.title: Question bank for skip-level meetings
prompts.content:
Act as a senior executive coach specialized in manager-of-managers leadership, with applied mastery of psychological safety (Edmondson), the five team dysfunctions (Lencioni), and intrinsic motivation of autonomy, mastery, and purpose (Pink). I am going to conduct a skip-level meeting: a one-on-one conversation with a person who reports to an intermediate manager who in turn reports to me. The well-done skip-level unlocks information that does not travel up the normal chain (early risks, burnout, clarity gaps) and strengthens culture; done poorly it undermines the intermediate manager, generates triangulation, and burns trust.

Before generating anything, reformulate what you understand about the context and present your calibration plan. Ask me for the data that would change the bank if missing: role or seniority of the attendee, name or role of the intermediate manager, team size, whether it is the first skip-level or recurring, manager maturity, known prior tension, remote or in-person format, and what I want to read most in this session. If everything needed is already clear, proceed.

Deliver a ready-to-use facilitation package, in this order: (1) Opening script of 3 to 5 sentences with the real purpose, explicit confidentiality framing (aggregated synthesis, no attribution, not an evaluation of the manager), and anxiety reduction. (2) Bank of 18 to 24 open questions distributed across six dimensions: clarity and purpose; psychological safety; workload and sustainability; growth and development; quality of collaboration with the manager; process and tool friction. Every question invites a concrete story, none is yes/no, and none asks the participant to evaluate or criticize the manager: use system-level, personal-experience, and desired-future angles. (3) Per dimension, one follow-up question and one observable alarm signal to note. (4) Closing script with follow-up commitments and how you will return value without exposing the person. (5) Post-meeting protocol: how to synthesize patterns, what to bring to the manager as support (not reproach), and what to keep for your own action.

Quality rules: zero yes/no questions; zero questions asking to rate the manager; the opening frames aggregated, non-attributed confidentiality; each dimension has a follow-up and an alarm signal; the protocol separates manager support from direct action without exposing sources. Before closing, verify that no question induces evaluating the manager, that all are open, and that the protocol protects confidentiality. Professional and warm tone, neutral English, no emojis. Close with the single recommended opening question to set the tone for the whole session.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Mood and workload check-in (RAG status)
prompts.content:
Act as a senior leadership coach specialized in team health and 1:1 conversations, with practice in RAG-status check-in frameworks (red-amber-green) and early overload detection. I want to open my next 1:1 meeting with a traffic-light check-in on three dimensions (energy, workload, and blockers) BEFORE jumping to tasks and deliverables, because when you go straight to tactical matters, exhaustion and overload are detected late. Deliver a ready-to-use opening script, in spoken language, brief and human, without technical jargon and without emojis, with these components in order: (1) a table with the three dimensions and the definition in one line of red, amber, and green for each, with observable and unambiguous criteria; (2) a warm opening question that invites the person to self-classify across the three dimensions without feeling evaluated on their performance; (3) per dimension, one follow-up question per color: for red and amber focused on root cause and concrete support, for green focused on reinforcing and capturing what is working; (4) a transition step that connects the declared state to the tactical agenda, with a simple rule for deciding whether a topic is addressed, reordered, or postponed; (5) three psychological safety phrases to open with and one closing line that summarizes agreements and names the follow-up. Explicitly frame that the traffic light serves to open conversation and not to score the person, and adjust the tone to the reporting relationship and the 1:1 frequency. Treat what the person shares as confidential except in the case of risk to themselves or others. Keep a single color declared per dimension and avoid interpreting silence as green. If you do not understand something, ask before executing. If you are missing any datum (name, role and reporting relationship, recent context, or 1:1 frequency), request it before writing.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: 1:1 long-term career conversation
prompts.content:
Act as a senior people manager and career coach, trained in the practice of development 1:1s and in the career-cone metaphor (growth in breadth vs. growth in height). I am going to conduct a 1:1 dedicated entirely to the long-term career of a member of my team, over a 1-to-3-year horizon. This is not a status meeting or a project meeting: it is an aspirations conversation that rarely happens in the day-to-day. The purpose is to give the person a safe space to articulate how they see themselves growing, help them think with clarity, and unlock intentional development actions rather than leaving their trajectory to chance. What gets unlocked: retention through purpose, trust in the manager–person relationship, and a growth plan the person feels ownership over.

If you are missing any essential data to personalize (name and seniority of the person, role and time in the role, horizon, known context or signal that motivates the 1:1), ask me before producing. Do not invent data about the person; flag any assumption as [ASSUMPTION].

Deliver, in this order:
1. Opening frame (2–4 sentences) that I can say literally to establish that the space is safe, confidential, and non-evaluative, and that today the protagonist is the person's career; include a bridge sentence to explicitly separate this conversation from the performance review.
2. A bank of open questions in three blocks: (a) Their vision of success on the horizon in their own words; (b) Career-cone map, separating breadth growth (deepening and expanding impact in the current role) from height growth (advancing to the next level or role); (c) Real motivators and constraints (energy, personal life, desired learning). For each block include 1–2 probing follow-up questions and at least one question designed to surface the unspoken desire.
3. A method to help the person name 2–3 growth directions, without forcing promotion if their legitimate desire is to deepen breadth; include how to reflect the tension between aspiration and reality without closing the door.
4. A close that translates the conversation into 2–3 concrete development experiments, each with an owner, a horizon, and an observable signal of progress, plus the explicit commitment I make as manager and the date of the next review.

Conduct guide: tell me where I should listen more than I talk, paraphrase to validate, and resist the temptation to solve for the person; the resulting plan belongs to the person, not to me. Keep all material in neutral professional English. Flag conversation risks (the person saying what they think I want to hear, confusing the space with a promotion or salary negotiation) and how to mitigate them. Do not promise promotions, promotion timelines, or compensation: frame everything as exploration and development. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: 1:1 notes and commitments synthesis
prompts.content: Act as a senior manager with proven discipline in 1:1 cadences and commitment follow-up; you think in terms of clarity, accountability, and people development. From the raw notes of a 1:1 meeting, produce a structured synthesis in four blocks. First, restate what you understand about the notes and present your plan before executing. Block 1: executive summary of 3 to 5 lines covering the mood of the conversation, the central topics, and the perceived emotional state (marked as perception, not fact). Block 2: group all points by topic (development and career, workload, blockers and dependencies, feedback given or received, team relationships, personal life only if the person brought it up) without losing any relevant point. Block 3: agreements table with columns Commitment, Owner, Due Date, and Action Verb; each row starts with an action verb and has a concrete date; if a date is missing, propose one consistent with the 1:1 frequency and mark it [proposed]. Block 4: points to revisit and 2 to 3 opening questions for the next 1:1. Rules: distinguish what was said from what was inferred and mark ambiguities as [to be confirmed]; do not invent commitments absent from the notes; treat sensitive feedback and personal topics with discretion and without judgment. If the notes, the person's name, or the date are missing, ask for them before continuing. Close when all four blocks are complete, with no orphan commitments missing an owner or date, in neutral professional language, without emojis, ready to archive and reuse as input for the next meeting.

prompts.title: Reactivate stalled or cancelled 1:1s
prompts.content:
Act as a senior executive coach specializing in manager–collaborator relationships and team ritual design, with the judgment to distinguish symptom from root cause. I have a 1:1 with a direct report that has lost value: it may have turned into a status report, be chronically cancelled or rescheduled, become a manager monologue, or be a safe conversation where the real topics never surface. A stalled 1:1 is not neutral: it erodes trust, hides retention and performance risks, and teaches the collaborator that this space is not theirs. I want an actionable reactivation plan.

Before executing, restate in your own words the deterioration pattern you understand and present your plan. If you are missing a key piece of data (what is wrong with the 1:1, who it is with and their seniority, how long it has been stalling, the current cadence), ask for it before moving forward; do not invent context.

Deliver four parts:
1. Deterioration diagnosis: classify the pattern into one or more of five archetypes (status disguised as a 1:1, chronic cancellation, manager monologue, safe conversation with no real topics, 100% manager agenda) and name the probable root cause separating symptom from cause. When a pattern admits opposing readings (e.g., chronic cancellation could be the collaborator's disinterest or the manager's overload), expose both hypotheses instead of closing prematurely.
2. Signal reading: for each hypothesis list the observable signals that would confirm it and the ones that would rule it out (who schedules, who cancels, who talks more, what topics appear, what topics never appear), distinguishing what is seen from what is inferred.
3. Reset conversation: draft the script to reopen the space, acknowledge the deterioration without blame, return the agenda to the collaborator, and co-define purpose, cadence, and protection rules; include 2–3 opening questions that invite discussion of what is not said.
4. New format and follow-up: deliver the rebuilt structure (opening, collaborator's agenda first, manager's topics after, close with commitments), a concrete protection mechanism (who schedules, reschedule-never-cancel rule for calendar conflicts), and how to measure in 4–6 weeks whether it has revived.
