Adjust depth to the transition type: a start-up from scratch requires more diagnosis and context-building in horizon 1; an area in change requires stabilizing before proposing; a stable area allows earlier wins. Calibrate the ambition of wins to the role level: for junior roles prioritize mastery and bounded deliverables; for leadership roles prioritize reading the system, building trust, and team decisions.

Close with: a summary table of the three horizons; the list of conditions the leader must guarantee (access, an assigned mentor or buddy, clarity of expectations, first deliverable defined); and the explicit connection between horizon 90 and the success criterion. Flag every inference not backed by data I have provided with the tag [ASSUMPTION]. Do not invent people's names, metrics, or specific dates.

prompts.title: Preboarding sequence before day one
prompts.content:
Act as a senior people leader specialized in onboarding experience, with experience coordinating preboarding across leadership, human resources, technical teams, and systems. Design an actionable preboarding sequence, ready to execute, covering the window between offer signing and the first day — the most fragile moment of the entire onboarding: the person has already said yes, but does not yet belong, is still exposed to counter-offers and pre-start regret, and every day of silence erodes the enthusiasm with which they accepted.

Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand (role and reporting line, work modality, time available until start, team culture, and business priorities); if you are missing any critical data, ask for it in a single round of questions before proceeding and flag any assumption with [ASSUMPTION]. Then present your plan: the objectives and the skeleton of the timeline and the four workstreams, without drafting the messages yet. Only then execute the full sequence.

Deliver: (1) 4 to 6 preboarding objectives, each with an observable success signal, not a vague intention; (2) a milestone timeline that realistically fits within the available time, with action, responsible party (leader, human resources, team, or systems), and channel per milestone; (3) the four parallel workstreams with concrete actions: administrative and legal, logistics and access, social and cultural, role and expectations; (4) the three drafted messages from the hiring leader ready to send (welcome after signing, team introduction, day-one agenda); (5) 3 to 4 warning signals such as prolonged silence, unresolved doubts, or probable counter-offer, each with a concrete response action; (6) a day-before-day-one checklist confirming the person is ready across all four workstreams. Write in neutral professional English, without emojis.

prompts.title: Designing a buddy or onboarding mentor system
prompts.content:
Act as a senior team leader and onboarding program designer, with proven experience building buddy and onboarding mentor systems. Design end-to-end the buddy and mentor system for the first 90 days of a new hire. Before executing, restate in one or two lines what you understood and present your plan. If any key data is missing (the new hire's role, work modality, team size, current onboarding, or priority objective), ask before continuing; do not invent context.

Produce, in this order: 1) Role definition, separating the peer buddy (social belonging, culture, day-to-day questions without judgment) from the mentor (technical judgment, business context, development), with purpose, what each one DOES do, what is NOT their responsibility, and the ideal profile for each. 2) Matching and sustainability: match criteria, how to recruit and recognize the role without using financial incentives, a cap on how many new hires one person can accompany at a time, and how to protect their regular workload. 3) Phase-by-phase cadence with frequency, duration, format, and responsible party (peer or mentor) for day 1, week 1, days 2-30, 31-60, and 61-90. 4) Guiding topics and questions per meeting in two tracks: social-cultural and operational-technical. 5) A concrete, ready-to-use script for the first buddy–new hire conversation (opening, topics, close). 6) Observable early-warning signals of poor integration, with a trigger and an escalation path to the manager. 7) Success indicators for the manager (e.g. time to first autonomous contribution, perceived onboarding quality, 90-day retention), each with a responsible party, and explicit handoffs between buddy, mentor, and manager.

Flag with [ASSUMPTION] every piece of data you assume. Close with: design limitations, edge cases (very small team with no buddy candidate, remote modality with no time-zone overlap, several simultaneous new hires), and how to adapt. Neutral professional English, without overloading the buddy or mentor. Deliver a structured document in seven sections ready to implement from day 1 with the next hire.

prompts.title: End-of-probation check-in (90 days)
prompts.content: Act as a senior people leader expert in probationary-period evaluation, evidence-based feedback (SBI model: Situation-Behavior-Impact), and difficult performance conversations. I am closing the 90-day probationary period for someone on my team and I need to move from scattered impressions to an evidence-based evaluation and to an unambiguous continuity decision: confirm, extend, or not continue. Before executing, restate what you understand about the case and present your plan; if you are missing any essential data (role and start date, expectations agreed at the outset, evidence observed during the 90 days, feedback already delivered, my preliminary inclination, or the applicable policy framework), ask me for it rather than inventing it. Deliver: (1) the reconstructed expectation baseline, flagging as [ASSUMPTION] anything that is not documented; (2) a table of expectation vs. observed evidence with a rating of exceeds/meets/in progress/below, separating facts from interpretations; (3) two to three reinforcement messages and two to three adjustment messages in SBI format, actionable and free of personality judgments; (4) a single continuity recommendation with reasoning, verifiable criteria, and the actions requiring HR or legal validation clearly flagged before any communication; (5) the plan for the scenario (development focus if confirmed, improvement plan with goals, dates, and consequences if extended, or respectful communication points if not continuing) and the conversation script with opening, body, handling of likely reactions, next steps, and commitments. Neutral professional tone, no emojis. Do not present interpretations as facts or make judgments about the person.

prompts.title: Attraction message and team employer branding
prompts.content: Act as a senior talent leader and employer branding specialist, expert in employee value propositions (EVP), honest recruitment narratives, and messages that filter by genuine fit rather than inflating expectations. I need to articulate why it is worth joining my team with an honest narrative of mission, challenge, and growth. I understand the double risk: an inflated message attracts people who are not a fit, triggers early turnover, and burns the team's reputation; a generic message says nothing and lets the talent that would genuinely fit walk past. I want the opposite: a message that tells the attractive truth, attracts those who thrive under this challenge, and gently deters those who do not, making it a fit filter. Before drafting, restate what you understand and present your plan; if you are missing the role and ideal candidate traits, the team mission tied to a tangible outcome, the honest unvarnished challenges, the concrete growth opportunities, what the culture is really like, or where it will be published, ask me first rather than inventing anything. Produce: (1) Fit profile, declaring who the message attracts and who it deters; (2) The three pillars with evidence: Mission (why the work matters), Challenge (the hard problems without varnish) and Growth (who they will become, with concrete examples), each with its evidence or a visible [ASSUMPTION]; (3) The final attraction message adapted to the channel, with an honest hook, development of the three pillars, and a clear next step; (4) A short version of two to three sentences for direct messages or headings; (5) A honesty test that lists each promise with the evidence that supports it and the condition that would have to be met for the candidate not to feel deceived upon joining. Rules: never present an inference as a fact; the Challenge pillar must name at least one genuine hard part; do not promise prices, do not use the word free, and do not offer what the team cannot deliver; neutral professional English, no emojis, no invented data.

prompts.title: Delegating with explicit authority levels
prompts.content: Act as a senior leadership coach with 15 years developing managers, specialist in Management 3.0 and the design of distributed authority systems. I want to delegate a task or area of responsibility to a person or team without falling into micromanagement (which kills autonomy and makes me the bottleneck) or abdication (handing things off without clarity and then correcting with frustration). The real problem is rarely whether to delegate or not: it is that nobody ever makes explicit who decides what. Before executing, restate what you understand and present your plan. If you are missing any key data (the task or area to delegate, who receives it, their real maturity on the topic, the cost of an error and risk tolerance, or the desired follow-up cadence), ask for it in a single round before assigning levels. Then deliver: (1) the task decomposed into 3 to 6 concrete, mutually exclusive decision areas — never a single global one; (2) for each area, a level from 1 to 7 per Jurgen Appelo's Delegation Poker (1 Tell, 2 Sell, 3 Consult, 4 Agree, 5 Advise, 6 Inquire, 7 Delegate) with the correct label; (3) the justification for each level explicitly crossing cost of error, person's maturity, and risk appetite — no generalities; (4) for each area, an observable signal that the assigned level is correct; (5) the agreement drafted as a first-person conversational script, ready to say out loud in a 1:1, not as an abstract list; (6) the non-negotiable boundaries that are not delegated at any level; (7) the follow-up mechanism with its cadence and observable triggers for moving a level up or down; (8) an explicit edge case (what happens if the person makes a decision within their level that you disagree with). Flag as assumption any data you infer. Close with a StrategyIA: which area is worth moving up a level in 90 days and why, as a signal of the person's development. Neutral professional English, no emojis, no prices.

prompts.title: Deciding what to delegate with the urgent-important matrix
prompts.content:
Act as a senior executive coach for leaders, specialist in executive time management and effective delegation with the Eisenhower matrix (urgent x important). Your judgment distinguishes the work only the leader can do from what must be delegated, automated, or eliminated, without falling into the trap of treating everything urgent as important.

I need to classify the work on my desk to decide, piece by piece, what I do, what I delegate and to whom, what I automate, what I schedule, and what I eliminate. The underlying problem is that the urgent displaces the important: the day fills up with interruptions and avoidable meetings and there is no time left for the leadership work nobody else can do (strategy, decisions, team development). I do not want a to-do list or a schedule: I want an assignment decision on each piece of my work.

Before executing, tell me what you need to know. At minimum: my role and where I should concentrate my highest-value time; the inventory of tasks, responsibilities, and recurring meetings to classify with approximate time per week; the people I can delegate to and their maturity level by topic; the tools or automations available; and the deadlines or constraints that condition what can be moved. If any data is missing, ask for it in a single round before starting.

Produce: (1) the inventory with weekly time per item; (2) the Eisenhower matrix with each task in one quadrant (Q1 important and urgent: crises, decisions only the leader can make, immovable deadlines; Q2 important and not urgent: strategy, planning, team development, process improvement; Q3 urgent and not important: interruptions, avoidable meetings, low-value requests that press; Q4 neither urgent nor important: distractions, work that does not contribute); (3) the disposition by quadrant (Q1 do now; Q2 schedule and protect in the calendar; Q3 delegate or automate; Q4 eliminate or decline) with a one-sentence justification each; (4) a decision table with one row per task: task, quadrant, action, responsible party; (5) a delegation plan that for each delegated task indicates to whom based on maturity, what authority level they receive (consult, recommend, decide and inform, decide autonomously), the expected outcome, the control point, and the risk that is covered; (6) an impact summary with weekly hours I recover and what Q2 work I reinvest them in.

Rules: truly separate importance from urgency; between delegating and automating prefer automating what is repeatable and rule-based, and delegating what develops a person; for Q4 propose to eliminate or decline with a concrete exit, never "do it later"; flag with [ASSUMPTION] every piece of data you infer. Write in neutral professional English, no emojis.

prompts.title: Outcome-oriented delegation brief
prompts.content:
Act as a senior team leader expert in effective delegation and the seven-level autonomy model (Management 3.0 delegation levels). I am going to delegate an assignment and I want a brief that transfers genuine ownership: one that fixes the WHAT and the WHY with total clarity and leaves the HOW in the person's hands. The goal is to empower without micromanaging, reduce rework, free my supervision time, and develop the collaborator's decision-making capacity.

First restate what you understand about the assignment and present your plan; if you are missing a critical data point (finished outcome, person's profile, deadline, or non-negotiable boundaries), ask before drafting rather than inventing.

Then draft a one-page delegation brief with seven numbered sections: 1) Expected outcome: a single observable sentence describing the finished deliverable, never the activity. 2) Why it matters: concrete impact on team, customer, or business and what is unlocked by achieving it. 3) Success criteria: three to five verifiable conditions the collaborator can self-assess (standards, not tasks). 4) Restrictions and non-negotiable boundaries: distinguish the closed from the open; flag as [ASSUMPTION] any boundary you propose so I can confirm it. 5) Authority level: fix one of the seven (tell, sell, consult, agree, advise, inquire, delegate), justify it based on the person's profile, and clarify who decides and who is informed. 6) Control points: by milestone or by risk, never by arbitrary calendar; for each indicate the question it will answer. 7) Resources and who to contact.

Rules: no verb should prescribe the method; the HOW stays in the collaborator's hands. Calibrate criteria and authority to the person's real experience level (more experience, greater autonomy and outcome-focused criteria; less experience, bounded autonomy and more explicit criteria). Professional, neutral, enabling tone; no emojis. Close by noting what delegation risk to watch for (reverse delegation, ownership ambiguity, or under/over-specification of the how).

prompts.title: Preventing problems from bouncing back to the leader
prompts.content:
Act as a senior leadership coach specialized in delegation, trained in the framework Management Time: Who's Got the Monkey? by Oncken and Wass (HBR, 1974, revised 1999) and its 5-level initiative scale. I just had a conversation with a collaborator about a problem and, when it ended, the next move of the problem was on my desk instead of the person who brought it: the 'monkey' jumped to me. Help me return it without abandoning the person or giving up my supervision role.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate in one sentence who brought what problem and where the monkey is today, and declare the initiative level you observe (1 wait for instruction; 2 ask what to do; 3 propose and then act; 4 act and report immediately; 5 act and report routinely). If you are missing the key data to locate the monkey or know who owns the next step, ask me for only that data before continuing. Then present your plan: a realistic target initiative level and the check-in design (a leader-to-person check-in, not the person reporting so I can decide). Then execute and deliver a block with: (a) the monkey identified and who owns it; (b) current level to target; (c) the rewritten response ready to say, in 2 to 4 sentences that acknowledge the person, reassign the next step, set the agreed level, and schedule the check-in with when, format, and progress criterion; (d) 2 or 3 typical maneuvers by which the monkey jumps back to me, each with a brief reply to return it; (e) a memorable pocket rule for the next conversation. Returned initiative is not abandonment: I retain supervision, not execution; do not suggest delegating what is non-delegable in my role.

prompts.title: Follow-up without falling into micromanagement
prompts.content:
Act as a senior team leader with experience in effective delegation and people development, trained in situational leadership and risk management. I need a plan to supervise a delegated task without falling into micromanagement: enough control to sleep soundly, with the minimum possible intrusion so the person advances with autonomy and the relationship strengthens.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Before starting, if you do not know the delegated task and its scope, the deadline, the level of risk or impact if it goes wrong, and the person's maturity (demonstrated competence and autonomy), ask me for them: without those four data points any plan would be invented.

Then deliver:
1. Risk-maturity diagnosis: cross the situational leadership framework (direct, coach, support, delegate) with an impact x probability-of-deviation matrix. Declare the recommended supervision style and why.
2. Control rhythm: how many check-ins, at what moments in the cycle, and for how long. For each indicate focus, evidence or partial deliverable the person brings, and what decision is made. Number and depth derive from the diagnosis, never from a default daily check.
3. Explicit boundary between reporting (information flowing to you) and delegated autonomy (decisions that stay in the person's hands).
4. Early warning signals that justify increasing control and good-progress signals that justify reducing it, with concrete thresholds.
5. A 5-to-8-line script for the initial alignment conversation, in an enabling-partner tone, not an auditor's.

Rules: zero invented data; flag any assumption as [ASSUMPTION]. If the risk is high but the maturity is also high, prioritize verification points over intervention. The plan is agreed upon with the person, not imposed on them. Final deliverable: a table (moment | focus | expected evidence | decision) plus the alignment script.

prompts.title: Adjust style to maturity level (situational leadership)
prompts.content:
Act as a senior leadership and team development coach, a certified expert in the Hersey-Blanchard Situational Leadership model, with a background developing first-line managers. My problem: I apply the same leadership style to the whole team, which creates micromanagement for those who already master a task and premature abandonment of those who are just starting. I want to calibrate my style to the actual maturity of each person, task by task, so you can deliver an actionable delegation map: who to direct, coach, support, or delegate to, and how to open each conversation without holding back too much or letting go too soon.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate the team, task, and challenge as you understand them and present your plan; then execute. If you lack evidence of competence or commitment for any person, or the task is ambiguous, ask me before diagnosing; do not invent the level.

Method: 1) Diagnose the development level of each person by crossing competence and commitment for the specific task (not as a global trait): D1 enthusiastic beginner (low competence, high commitment), D2 disillusioned learner (some competence, low commitment), D3 capable but cautious (high competence, variable commitment), D4 autonomous achiever (high competence, high commitment). 2) Assign the paired style: E1 Direct (high direction, low support), E2 Coach (high direction, high support), E3 Support (low direction, high support), E4 Delegate (low direction, low support). 3) Per person deliver: Dn diagnosis with the evidence that justifies it, style En, 3 concrete and observable leader behaviors, an opening conversation phrase, and the risk of applying the wrong style (over-directing stifles a D4; under-directing abandons a D1). 4) Close with 2 or 3 progress signals that would require a style change.

Closure criterion: each person with Dn correctly paired to En, diagnosis supported by cited evidence (not intuition), level per task, concrete behaviors and opening phrase, missing data asked before diagnosing, and inferences marked as [ASSUMPTION]. Deliver a profile or table per team member and then the progression signals. Neutral, professional Spanish, no emojis.

prompts.title: Define the team's decision perimeter
prompts.content:
Act as a senior team leader and delegation coach, expert in designing decision perimeters with decision-rights maps, delegated authority levels in the style of delegation poker, the reversibility principle (one-way vs. two-way doors), and RACI matrices. My team operates without an explicit decision perimeter: it is not clear what it decides on its own, what it must consult before acting, and what it must escalate. The symptom is dual and simultaneous: trivial decisions that get stuck waiting for my approval (bottleneck, micromanagement) and sensitive decisions that someone makes alone without telling me (latent risk). I want a written agreement that delegates control of reversible decisions in order to retain control of what truly matters — that is the StrategyIA.

Before producing anything, restate in one or two sentences what team and what decisions we will define the perimeter for, and what specific problem this solves. I need three minimum data points to work: the team's scope and maturity, the list of recurring decisions to define, and my risk tolerance (what type of error concerns me most). If you are missing any of the three, ask me and stop; do not invent facts, figures, amounts, or thresholds.

With that data, deliver, in this order: (1) a five-level delegated authority scale with explicit anchors: N1 Decide and execute (act, do not inform), N2 Decide and inform (act and notify afterward), N3 Consult and decide (ask for opinion, team decides), N4 Recommend and leader decides (team proposes, leader approves), N5 Escalate (decision of the leader or a higher level); with the triggers that move a decision up a level (amount, reversibility, client impact, legal or reputational risk, number of affected areas, urgency) calibrated to my risk tolerance. (2) A decision-rights map in table format: each decision, its N1-N5 level, the single owner, whom to consult or inform, and the threshold or condition that keeps it at that level; mark [ASSUMPTION] on every inferred and unconfirmed level. (3) A reversibility adjustment: reversible and low-impact decisions defaulting to N1 or N2, reserving N4 and N5 for irreversible or high-impact ones; flag at least one decision I should delegate more to stop being a bottleneck, and one that might be over-delegated for the team's maturity level. (4) Escalation rules: trigger, minimum information the team brings when escalating, the leader's committed response time, and what happens if that time expires (no-response rule). (5) A brief script to communicate the perimeter to the team, the 3 highest-risk gray zones for misunderstanding to clarify before publishing the map, and a review trigger (when the map is recalibrated: after an incident, when the team's maturity increases, or on a fixed cadence). Keep everything in neutral, professional Spanish, no emojis, no promises of results that depend on variables you do not control.

prompts.title: Design a stretch assignment
prompts.content: Act as a senior leadership coach specializing in talent development and progressive delegation, with mastery of the zone of proximal development (Vygotsky), the competence-motivation model of situational leadership, and psychological safety (Edmondson). I want you to design a stretch assignment for a member of my team: an assignment that makes them grow without crushing them, calibrated to fall within their zone of proximal development and backed by a real safety net. Before executing, restate what you understand and present your plan; if you are missing any key data (person and role, proposed challenge, their current competence in the skills required by the challenge, their motivation and self-confidence, who observes the result and what is at stake, timeline, and support I can dedicate), ask me all at once before proceeding. Deliver a plan in six blocks: (1) Challenge calibration: situate the challenge relative to the person's competence and motivation, declare whether it is trivial, optimal, or overwhelming, and adjust the scope until it falls in the stretch zone; (2) The assignment written as you would present it to them: purpose, why you are entrusting it to them specifically, and expected result with observable success criteria; (3) Safety net: scaffolding and resources, a mentor or support peer, decisions you retain, and the acceptable risk limit named concretely; (4) Check-in points: cadence and focus of each review within the timeline, with coaching questions that avoid micromanagement; (5) Recovery plan: early signs of being stuck, how to intervene without over-rescuing, and how to separate the learning from the judgment of the person; (6) Harvest conversation: brief script to close the assignment and convert the experience into learning and the next challenge. Mark any assumption as [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent data about the person. Language that conveys confidence and rigor with care: the challenge should not feel like a trap.

prompts.title: Document the handover of a responsibility
prompts.content: Act as a senior team leader specializing in responsibility transfer and operational continuity, with experience documenting handovers that survive turnover. I need a handover document that makes a function operable from day one for the person receiving it, without depending on my memory or informal conversations: it must be the single source of truth for that responsibility. Before drafting, restate in one or two lines what function you understand is being delegated, to what role, and for how long you will accompany me, and present a brief plan; if you are missing a critical data point (scope of the function, prior experience of the recipient, contacts, systems, risks, open items, or onboarding horizon) ask everything at once before continuing. Then deliver a document with eight numbered sections: (1) Purpose of the function: what problem it solves, whom it serves, and how you measure that it is going well; (2) Activity map: recurring tasks with their daily, weekly, or monthly cadence, and event-triggered tasks with their explicit trigger; (3) Key contacts: who, for what, through which channel, and with what urgency, separating internal from external; (4) Systems and access: tools, credentials to transfer, and permissions to request, flagging which ones must be requested before day one; (5) Risks and blind spots: each risk with its early signal and how it was previously resolved; (6) Observable success criteria at 30, 60, and 90 days; (7) Open items in progress: current status, next step, and responsible party for each; (8) Onboarding plan: what is reviewed, with what cadence, and the milestone at which you let go entirely. Close with a handover completion checklist (access confirmed, contacts introduced, open items with owner, first review scheduled) and the open questions the recipient must resolve in their first week. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] everything you infer and never invent contacts, systems, or metrics: if data does not exist, declare it as a gap to close. Limit: this document does not replace the transfer of trust relationships or the in-person introduction to contacts; schedule those conversations separately. Write in neutral, professional Spanish, no emojis.

prompts.title: Recover a failed delegation
prompts.content: Act as a senior leadership coach specializing in delegation and team development, with mastery of the Situational Leadership model (competence and commitment) and delegation levels. A delegation went wrong and I need to recover it without abruptly withdrawing trust (re-absorbing the work perpetuates the bottleneck) or ignoring the failure. Before executing, restate the case as you understand it and present your plan; if you are missing key data (what was delegated and its expected result, who executed it with their role and seniority, what went wrong compared to expectations and how I found out, the observable facts, and the state of the trust relationship), ask me for all of it at once before continuing. Then deliver: (1) a diagnosis that classifies the failure across the three axes CLARITY, CAPABILITY, and AUTHORITY, with your reading per axis, the concrete signal that supports it, and marking [ASSUMPTION] for every inference not supported by facts; (2) the script for the one-on-one recalibration conversation with model phrases, not just principles: open without blaming, name the fact with data, first invite the person's self-diagnosis, close with an agreement, and preserve the trust; (3) the plan per axis attacking only the diagnosed axis or axes, not all three by default: CLARITY rewrites the assignment (result, scope, quality criteria, timeline, check-in points), CAPABILITY defines the scaffolding (accompaniment, peer, training, or breaking into steps) with a calendar for removing it, AUTHORITY specifies what decisions pass to the person and what limits are maintained; (4) the delegation level adjusted to the person's actual level, without micromanagement or abandonment; (5) the follow-up with check-in cadence, observable early signs of derailment (facts, not feelings), and an explicit criterion for returning full autonomy. Neutral, professional Spanish, no emojis. If the case does not allow separating fact from judgment, say so and list the open questions needed to close the diagnosis.

prompts.title: Diagnose the source of a team conflict
prompts.content: Act as a senior team facilitator and organizational mediator, expert in Karen Jehn's conflict taxonomy and in distinguishing symptom from root cause. I lead a team with an active conflict and I need to diagnose its real source before acting: applying the wrong intervention aggravates the conflict and erodes my credibility as a leader. Before executing, restate in two or three lines what you understand about the case and present your plan; if you are missing any essential data (who the parties are and their hierarchical relationship, the concrete behaviors observed, since when it has occurred and what triggered it), ask me for it instead of inventing it. Then give me the diagnosis as follows: 1) Classify the conflict in one of four sources: TASK (disagreement about content, ideas, criteria, the what of the work), PROCESS (the how, roles, who does what, sequence, responsibilities), RELATIONSHIP (interpersonal tension, style clash, emotional friction), or VALUES (clash of principles, ethics, non-negotiable foundational priorities). 2) For each of the four sources, cite the concrete evidence from my account that supports or rules it out; do not invent facts, mark what is not provided as [ASSUMPTION], and always separate observable fact from interpretation. 3) Declare the primary source and, if the evidence supports it, a secondary one; explicitly warn if a poorly managed task or process conflict has been contaminated into a relationship conflict, and review whether a power or hierarchy asymmetry is masking the real source. 4) A list of 2 to 4 verification questions whose answers would confirm or refute your diagnosis. 5) Recommend the intervention appropriate to the source: task, structured debate and decision criteria; process, clarify roles and working agreements; relationship, mediation and trust restoration; values, make principles explicit, seek common ground, or escalate when they are non-negotiable. 6) Define a concrete alert signal indicating that the diagnosis is incorrect and should be reopened. If the account is too sparse to support a diagnosis, say so and ask for the minimum missing data before concluding. Give me a one-page diagnosis, actionable this week, in neutral, professional Spanish, no emojis.

prompts.title: Mediate a conflict between two team members
prompts.content:
Act as a senior labor mediation facilitator with fifteen years resolving interpersonal conflicts in high-performance teams, trained in the Harvard negotiation method (Getting to Yes by Fisher and Ury). I am the leader who must mediate an active conflict between two members of my team that is draining collective energy; I want a package that allows me to conduct the session and sign an agreement that both will sustain, not a truce that reappears in weeks.

Before producing anything, perform a mediability triage: if in what you describe I detect signs of harassment, discrimination, retaliation, violence, illegal conduct, or a severe power imbalance between the parties, stop and warn me that the case likely exceeds peer mediation and must go to Human Resources, compliance, or the appropriate legal authority, explaining why. If the case is mediable, continue.

First ask me for any data you are missing: who the two people are and their roles, what happened and since when with observable facts, how it affects the team, what result I seek as leader, and what limits are non-negotiable (policies, decisions already made, deadlines). Do not invent facts: mark with [ASSUMPTION] everything you infer that is not supported by what I provided.

Then produce a mediation package in seven numbered parts: (1) Leader preparation: your best alternative if no agreement is reached, your own biases to watch, and how to maintain impartiality if you are closer to one of the parties. (2) Neutral opening framing: common purpose, conversation rules (turns, no interruptions, focus on facts not people, confidentiality and its limits) and your role as impartial facilitator. (3) Question script per person that moves the focus from declared positions to underlying interests (recognition, autonomy, fair workload, role clarity, safety). (4) Side-by-side interest map: shared, divergent, and compatible. (5) At least three mutual-gain options built on the interests, evaluated with objective criteria that do not depend on the relative power of each party. (6) Concrete working agreement: each commitment with the responsible party, date, and observable compliance signal. (7) Follow-up plan with at least one review point, what to do if the agreement breaks down, and when to escalate. Impartial tone: zero blame, zero psychoanalysis, zero judgments about the people. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Choose a handling style per Thomas-Kilmann
prompts.content:
Act as a senior conflict resolution facilitator for teams, trained in the Thomas-Kilmann model (TKI) and with experience mediating between peers and direct reports. I am going to describe a conflict I am leading and I want you to deliver me a style ruling with an approach script ready to execute in my next conversation.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate the conflict in one sentence and name the two axes at play (how much the goal matters to me vs. how much the relationship matters to me); present your plan; then execute. If you are missing any key data (what happened, who is involved and their power relationship, what result is in dispute, how important it is to preserve the bond, how much urgency there is), ask me before deciding; do not invent the context.

Proceed as follows: 1) Score from 1 to 5 how much the GOAL matters and from 1 to 5 how much the RELATIONSHIP matters, justifying each score with concrete data from my case, not generic statements. 2) Translate those two axes into the TKI model (assertiveness = defending my goal, cooperation = attending to the other's) and situate the case in the quadrant: compete (high assertiveness, low cooperation), collaborate (high-high), compromise (mid-mid), avoid (low-low), or accommodate (low assertiveness, high cooperation). 3) Recommend a primary style and, if applicable, a backup style, using urgency and power relationship as modulators: high urgency discourages collaborating and avoiding; very asymmetric power against me makes competing fragile. 4) Explain why that style fits and what concrete risk there would be in choosing the opposite. 5) Deliver an approach script of 4 to 6 steps with at least one usable literal phrase per step, consistent with the style. 6) Warn about the 2 or 3 typical pitfalls of the chosen style and close with a concrete follow-up action with a verification criterion (what I should observe and by when to confirm the conflict was resolved).

Rules: distinguish conflict from mere disagreement; do not diagnose the counterpart's personality, work only on observable behavior and the interests at stake; if you detect that the real clash is over values and not interests, say so and adjust the style. Neutral, professional Spanish, no emojis.

prompts.title: De-escalate a heated discussion in real time
prompts.content: Act as a senior conflict facilitator and executive coach, with practice in mediating technical and commercial teams, trained in tactical listening and nonviolent communication. I need a de-escalation script to use LIVE during a discussion that has just escalated, not an analysis for later. Before drafting, ask about: who the parties are and their roles, the power relationship between them, the specific topic that escalated, the emotion perceived most strongly, my role in the scene (involved party, mediating leader, or neutral third party), and what I need to have at the close (a decision, an agreement on next steps, or just to lower the tension today). If any of those data points is missing or ambiguous, ask for it; do not invent the scene or assume a villain. First restate in 2-3 lines your reading of the dynamic and the de-escalation angle you will use (how much of the script is for speaking and how much for listening, adjusted to whether I am a party or a third party). Then deliver, in this order: (1) three opening phrases to name the dominant emotion out loud without judging or labeling the person; (2) a 4-step sequence to slow things down: deliberate pause, validation of what was heard, open question that returns control, and reframe toward the common objective; (3) five bridge phrases ready to say that separate person from problem and reopen dialogue, calibrated to the power relationship; (4) three observable signals that the conversation must pause, with a formula to propose a break with dignity that does not feel like punishment or retreat; (5) a 3-line close to agree on the next step and leave the relationship intact. All phrases in first person, short, speakable out loud without sounding like a manual. Mark any assumption with [ASSUMPTION] and close with a one-line note on what NOT to do because it would re-escalate. MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute.

prompts.title: Reframe a complaint with nonviolent communication
prompts.content: Act as a senior nonviolent communication facilitator trained in Marshall Rosenberg's model, with experience mediating conflicts in work teams. I am going to give you a complaint or grievance as I would say it today, with its emotional charge, and I want you to reframe it into a ready-to-use conversation kit. Before producing anything, restate in one line what you understand is at stake (the fact buried under the judgment and the need buried under the reproach) and present your plan; mark with [ASSUMPTION] any data you infer that is not in the complaint, and do not invent facts. Then deliver: (1) a diagnosis that marks the judgments, labels, always-or-never generalizations, and covert demands in the original complaint; (2) the translation into Rosenberg's four components: Observation (verifiable fact without evaluation), Feeling (genuine emotion, not a pseudo-feeling that hides a judgment such as ignored, manipulated, or pressured), Need (universal human need, not a strategy or solution, without naming the other person), and Request (specific, present tense, positive, achievable, answerable with yes or no); (3) a 3-to-5-sentence opening script in first person, without accusatory "you", adapted to the channel; (4) two script reformulations by the temperature of the bond, one warmer and one more direct, without returning to the original complaint; (5) three likely defensive responses from the other person, each with a reply that validates them and reaffirms the need without falling back into judgment; and a close with the success signal for the conversation and an alternative if no agreement is reached in the first round. If I am missing any key data to build the observation (what exactly happened, when, with whom, what channel the conversation will be in, what I want to agree on), ask me before proceeding. Neutral, professional Spanish, no filler.

prompts.title: Create working agreements to prevent conflict
prompts.content: Act as a senior team facilitator and agile team coach, expert in team chartering (Diana Larsen, Lyssa Adkins), in Liberating Structures for co-creation, and in converting recurring irritants into actionable agreements. Your assignment: convert the recurring friction of a team (unproductive meetings, decisions that get reopened, failing handoffs, focus interruptions, feedback that never arrives) into a set of working agreements that are co-created, observable, and self-imposed by the team, before friction escalates into interpersonal conflict. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: first restate in your own words what you understand about the team and its friction, then present your plan in four phases (diagnosis, co-creation, operationalization, sustainability) and only then execute. Deliver three products. One: a friction diagnosis that groups the irritants into categories (communication, meetings, decision-making, quality and handoffs, availability and focus, feedback and conflict), names the probable cause of each without blaming individuals, and prioritizes those generating the most conflict. Two: a table of six working agreements (adjust between five and eight based on the friction), each with the agreement drafted in first-person plural and in observable behavior verifiable by a third party, the irritant it resolves, the non-compliance signal, who calls it out in the moment, and a non-punitive team-agreed consequence. Three: a facilitation guide for the sixty-to-ninety-minute ratification session, with a timed agenda, a live ratification and editing mechanic, and a retrospective review block with criteria for keeping, adjusting, or retiring each agreement. Firm rules: each agreement describes an observable behavior, never a vague good intention such as 'communicate better'; each agreement traces back to a real irritant, nothing invented; mark every information gap as an assumption and formulate the question that would close it; do not present any agreement as a rule imposed by the leader; distinguish team agreement from company policy. If the team's name and size, its working mode, the specific irritants, or the operational context are missing, ask for them before drafting the agreements. Deliver in neutral and professional Spanish, without emojis.

prompts.title: Resolve friction between teams or silos
prompts.content: Act as a senior organizational alignment facilitator, specialist in productive conflict between teams (Lencioni's trust and healthy conflict) and in interface and team interaction design (Team Topologies). I have two areas that depend on each other and are in chronic friction: slow handoffs, rework, escalations, and relationship breakdown. I want an executable alignment intervention that converts the clash into collaboration with clear interfaces. Before executing, restate the conflict in a single neutral sentence without assigning blame, and tell me what data you are missing; if you do not know the two areas, how the conflict manifests today, the handoffs that trigger it, each area's separate objectives, or who has authority to decide, ask me before moving forward. Mark every inference as [ASSUMPTION] and do not present it as fact. Deliver an intervention document with six sections: (1) Root-cause diagnosis that distinguishes task conflict (what/how to do the work) from relationship conflict (people/trust) and names the structural incentive sustaining the friction (opposing objectives, boundary ambiguity, scarce resources, information or power asymmetry); include the approximate cost of not acting. (2) Shared objective: a single measurable goal, with a horizon and unit of measure, that is only met if both areas win together (not the sum of their separate goals), with 2–3 success indicators and, if applicable, a shared indicator that neither area controls alone. (3) Interface map: for each critical handoff define expected input, committed output, single owner, agreed response time, and acceptance criterion; indicate the interaction type (temporary collaboration, stable service, or facilitation). (4) Working agreement: interaction rules, tiered escalation path with deadlines, and decision mechanism when there is disagreement (who decides, by what criterion, and in how much time). (5) Alignment session: 90-minute agenda with a concrete objective and the facilitator's role per block, plus how emotional overflow is handled. (6) 30/60/90-day follow-up plan: metrics, review cadence, follow-up owner, and at least one early relapse signal per milestone with its response. Close with an explicit verification against these criteria and a block on risks of the intervention itself. Use neutral language, without assigning blame to any individual or area. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Manage a difficult-to-work-with collaborator
prompts.content:
Act as a senior leadership coach specializing in difficult conversations and team dynamics, with mastery of the SBI (Situation-Behavior-Impact) model from the Center for Creative Leadership and the principles of Crucial Conversations. I lead a team and the way a collaborator interacts is creating friction. I want a dossier to address it well.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand about the case; if key data is missing (observed behaviors, concrete impact, frequency and duration, or the behavioral change I am seeking) ask me for it before drafting and do not invent facts. Then present the plan: the facts-vs-interpretations map and the script structure. Only then produce the full dossier.

Deliver the dossier in five sections: (1) Facts vs. interpretations, classifying each statement as a documented observable behavior or as my inference marked with [ASSUMPTION]; (2) Factual restatement of each behavior as concrete behavior + context + impact, with no adjectives about the person; (3) Script for a private 1:1 conversation using the SBI model: an opening that lowers defensiveness, factual presentation of behavior and impact, open questions to understand the collaborator's perspective, and a close oriented toward agreements; (4) Two or three verifiable behavioral agreements, each with an observable success signal and a review date; (5) Handling of three probable reactions (denial, justification, emotional counter-attack) with a calm response for each that keeps the focus on the behavior and not the person. Add an escalation note: what to document and when to escalate to Human Resources if the agreements are not met. Describe what is seen, not who the person is.

prompts.title: Blameless conversation after a shared error
prompts.content: Act as a senior facilitator of engineering culture and psychological safety, with experience conducting blameless post-mortems in SRE style and applying Just Culture (distinction between human error, risky behavior, and reckless behavior) and the principle of local rationality (people made reasonable decisions with the information they had at the time). I am going to conduct a conversation to review an incident involving a shared error among several people, and I want to prevent it from degenerating into a blame hunt. Before producing anything, restate in your own words the incident, the people involved, the impact, and the trust climate as you understand them, mark everything you infer with [ASSUMPTION], and if you are missing critical context (what happened, impact, trust status, or meeting duration) ask me in a single round. Then present the plan: the conversation structure mapped to the available time, in blocks with assigned minutes. Then execute and deliver seven pieces ready to conduct without further editing: 1) a 60-to-90-second opening frame that establishes the blameless premise; 2) a neutral two-column timeline that separates the observable from the interpreted; 3) a battery of questions that redirect from 'who failed' to 'what in the system allowed it' (contributing factors, missed signals, broken assumptions, absent defenses); 4) a script for the 2 or 3 most probable tension moments (a direct accusation, someone on the defensive, an uncomfortable silence, a second affected party who self-blames) with verbatim phrases to redirect without shaming; 5) a set of actionable countermeasures with an owner, a date, and a verification signal, separating system fixes from behavioral changes; 6) a close that rebuilds trust with an explicit group commitment; 7) a brief follow-up plan defining who verifies the countermeasures and when. Tone rules: never attribute intent or bad faith; every cause is expressed as a system hypothesis, not a judgment; distinguish error (system), risky behavior (coaching), and reckless behavior (exceptional) without accusing; avoid the 'five whys' reflex that ends at a person and redirect toward conditions. Neutral and professional Spanish, without emojis. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute.

prompts.title: Foster productive dissent in decisions
prompts.content:
Act as a senior team decision facilitator, expert in productive dissent, psychological safety (Amy Edmondson lineage), groupthink (Irving Janis), and red team and devil's advocate practices from strategic intelligence. Your mission: design a productive dissent mechanism tailored to a specific high-impact decision, ready to use from the next meeting, so that disagreement improves the decision instead of breaking the relationship.

To do this I need you to ask me, if I have not provided them, for these minimum data points: the decision at stake, the current team climate (silence, false harmony, or personal clashes), the size and roles or hierarchy of the participants, and the deadline for deciding. If I have objections or reservations already expressed or latent, I will give them to you; if not, infer the most probable ones and mark them as an assumption.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. First restate in your own words the decision, the risk you perceive, and your plan; wait for my confirmation or correct it if you detect a missing critical datum before producing the deliverable.

Deliver a structured document in five parts:
1. Framing: separate the real decision from the noise, name the participants and their hierarchy, and declare what is actually in dispute.
2. Dominant risk diagnosis: groupthink and false harmony, or already personalized conflict. Justify with observable signals from the climate.
3. Selection of ONE mechanism from: rotating devil's advocate, formal red team, mandatory dissent before approving, prior silent writing, or pre-mortem. Explain why that one and why you discard the others, considering size, hierarchy, and timeline.
4. Step-by-step operational script: who does what, in what order, with suggested time blocks, conversation rules, how the idea is separated from the person, and how it closes with a decision made and an owner assigned.
5. Playbook of literal phrases for opening the dissent, disagreeing without attacking, and closing without anyone losing face; plus traps to avoid (theatrical dissent, silent retaliation, endless debate) with a countermeasure for each.

Quality rules: the mechanism must correspond to the diagnosed risk, not be generic; the close must name the decision and the owner; the playbook must include real phrases and at least three traps with a countermeasure; neutral and professional Spanish, without prices, actionable from the next meeting. If any assumption conditions the design, make it explicit at the end.

prompts.title: Define behavioral and verifiable team values
prompts.content: Act as a team leader and senior organizational culture designer, expert in behavioral values and the Netflix culture deck approach. Your objective is to produce a behavioral and verifiable values manifesto, because values written as abstract adjectives (excellence, respect, innovation) do not change behaviors: each person interprets them differently and no one knows what to do differently on Monday. Before executing, restate in your own words the team, its purpose, and the tensions the manifesto must resolve, and present your plan; if the team's name and purpose, the draft values, recent real tensions, admired and rejected behaviors, or the team's size and maturity are missing, ask for them in a single block and do not invent them. Proceed as follows: (1) distill each value into a single-sentence definition that answers what this means in real work, eliminating every adjective that has no behavior behind it; (2) for each value draft 3 to 5 pairs of It looks like (do) / It does not look like (don't) written as actions observable by a third party, not intentions or feelings, and include at least one uncomfortable pair: a valued behavior that most teams avoid in practice; (3) for each value define an anchor question for difficult decisions and an example of a real trade-off where that value wins over another value in the same manifesto, naming the value that concedes; (4) for each value define 1 to 2 observable behavioral signals that reveal whether the value is alive or dead, plus a team retrospective question; (5) close with an executive summary with each value in one line and the 3 cultural tensions the manifesto resolves. Edge cases: if the team declares more than 6 values, cut down to the 5 or 6 most distinctive and explain what you discarded; if two values overlap, merge them or delimit the boundary; if no real tensions are provided, mark the manifesto as hypothetical and note that without lived conflicts the pairs cannot be validated. Mark any inferred data as [ASSUMPTION] and do not present intentions disguised as behaviors. Deliver a manifesto with a table per value (definition, do/don't pairs, anchor question and trade-off, alive/dead signals and retrospective question) plus the executive summary, in neutral and professional Spanish, without emojis and without motivational-poster language. Close with three calibration questions to refine the manifesto with the team.

prompts.title: Diagnose and elevate psychological safety
prompts.content:
Act as a senior organizational psychologist specializing in psychological safety and high-performance team culture, with direct mastery of Amy Edmondson's framework and scale and the safety × demand axis (comfort, apathy, anxiety, and learning zones). I lead a team and I suspect people are not speaking frankly: they go silent in meetings, hide errors until they explode, do not ask for help, and do not contradict the leader. That is costly: problems are detected late, the best ideas do not surface, and learning is slowed. I want to diagnose the team's psychological safety and raise it deliberately without lowering the standard. Deliver, in this order: 1) A 7-statement mini-diagnostic faithful to Edmondson's scale, on a scale of 1 to 7, including the reversed items about punishment of error and difficulty asking for help; indicate how to apply it anonymously, how to reverse the score of negative items, how to read the average and the dispersion (a healthy average that hides polarized subgroups is a false alarm), and interpretive thresholds. 2) A reading of 6 to 8 observable behavioral signals that betray low psychological safety, each contrasted with its healthy version. 3) An elevation plan of 5 to 8 leadership actions prioritized by impact and effort; for each one the leader's concrete behavior, the frequency or timing of use, the signal that it is working, and the Edmondson lever it activates (framing work as a learning problem, modeling one's own fallibility and curiosity, actively inviting participation). 4) Three literal, brief opening phrases for the next meeting that genuinely invite dissent and early reporting of problems. 5) Two frequent errors that confuse psychological safety with lowering the standard, with their correction. 6) A 30-day plan with three milestones and the re-measurement metric. Explicitly distinguish psychological safety from comfort and from complacency. Do not invent any data about the team: mark as [ASSUMPTION] everything not provided. If critical information for diagnosing is missing (team composition, modality and meeting cadence, specific symptoms, recent history, and how the leader behaves when someone disagrees or reports an error), ask me for it in a brief list before drafting. Neutral and professional Spanish, without emojis.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Build a team charter
prompts.content:
Act as a senior high-performance team facilitator, with mastery of the Drexler-Sibbet Team Performance Model, RACI/DACI matrices, and working agreement design. Your task is to build a team charter ready to review and sign with the team in a single session: a visible contract that replaces implicit assumptions with explicit agreements, to accelerate decisions, clarify boundaries with neighboring teams, and enable the immediate onboarding of new members. This is not an archival document: it is the team's operational strategy, living and revisable.

Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. First restate in your own words who the team is, why it exists, its organizational context, and the decisions that currently generate friction. Before drafting, ask me for any essential missing data: the team's name and function, its size and roles, the organizational context, and typical decisions. Do not invent members, metrics, or neighboring teams; mark everything not confirmed with [ASSUMPTION] and list what is missing instead of filling it in. Then present a schema of the seven blocks and the data you will use in each, and only then draft.

Deliver the charter in seven blocks: (1) Mission and purpose: why the team exists, whom it serves, and what change it produces, without hollow jargon; (2) Scope: what is inside and, above all, what is outside the scope, with explicit boundaries toward neighboring teams; (3) Objectives and metrics: 3 to 5 results, each with an observable success signal and, where it exists, a baseline; (4) Roles and responsibilities: a RACI matrix by work type covering all members, with no two Approvers for the same decision and no orphaned roles; (5) Decision model: for each recurring decision, define what is decided, who decides, with what mechanism (consensus, consultative, or delegated), and how and to whom to escalate with what deadline; (6) Norms and working agreements: meetings, channels, response times, disagreement handling, and definition of done, all verifiable and not aspirational; (7) Review cadence: how often the charter is reviewed, who is its custodian, and what triggers an early review. Close with a note on how to facilitate its adoption in the team session. Closing criterion: the charter is actionable, without unmarked gaps, ready to review and sign.

prompts.title: Design team rituals that reinforce culture
prompts.content: Act as a team leader and organizational culture designer with experience building rituals that sustain high-performance teams in in-person, remote, and hybrid environments. A team's declared values die when they live in a poster and not in the routine; your job is to convert them into observable behaviors anchored to ceremonies that repeat on a cadence. Before executing, restate what you understand and present your plan. Ask about anything you are not clear on and do not invent it: the team's name or function, the 3 to 5 values to reinforce, size and composition (roles and seniority), modality and time zones, rituals that already exist today, and the specific cultural pain point to correct. Deliver a ritual system in five parts. First, a table mapping each value to an observable behavior and to the ritual type that provokes it: kickoff, progress, learning, or recognition; ensure at least one ritual per type. Second, a card per ritual with purpose in one sentence, cadence and duration, facilitator and how the role rotates, minimum step-by-step script, opening gesture or question that anchors the value, and the signal that it is still alive vs. the signal it has become theater. Reuse or reform what already exists before creating new ceremonies; do not duplicate. Third, a one-time founding ritual to name the values with the team. Fourth, a quarterly pruning mechanism to retire dead rituals with an explicit retirement criterion. Fifth, the three most probable traps based on the declared pain point and how to prevent them: the mandatory ceremony no one wants, the recognition that only rewards heroism, and the celebration that ignores whoever was not present. Respect the modality: if remote or hybrid, design for asynchrony and time zones. Close with a consolidated adoptable calendar for next week. Mark any assumption as [ASSUMPTION] and use neutral and professional Spanish.

prompts.title: Peer-to-peer recognition system
prompts.content:
Act as a senior culture and people experience designer who has already implemented peer recognition programs in knowledge teams, fluent in behavior design and engagement metrics. I want to install in my team a peer-to-peer recognition system that is frequent, specific, and values-anchored — not an annual award or vague praise. Well-designed recognition reinforces desired behaviors at the moment they occur, distributes the sense of belonging, and makes visible the work that would otherwise go unnoticed; poorly designed, it degenerates into an empty ritual, a popularity contest, or a bias toward the most visible people.

First restate what you understand about my team, values, cultural problem, channels, and cadence, and present your plan before executing. Then deliver, in this order: (1) the design principle and how it avoids the four classic anti-patterns: vague recognition, hierarchical recognition (only top-down), sporadic recognition, and transactional recognition (tied to material reward); (2) a values-anchoring schema with, for each value or observable behavior, a pair of calibrating examples 'this yes recognizes / this no recognizes'; (3) the operational mechanism on our tools, with a four-field message template (to whom, what specific behavior, what value it embodies, what impact it had), frequency, and how to lower the friction for emitting it; (4) visibility rituals that make what is recognized public without turning it into a contest; (5) a 30-60-90-day launch plan naming who models the behavior first and how adoption is sustained; (6) health metrics including participation rate, sender distribution to detect concentration in few people, per-person coverage to avoid forgotten individuals, and perceived link to values, plus warning signals of an empty ritual; (7) anti-fragility mechanisms to sustain it when the novelty wears off.

Mark what you assume as [ASSUMPTION]. Consider edge cases: remote multi-time-zone team, founders who over-emit, introverted people who are never named, and the risk that recognition is perceived as an obligation. If you are missing the team's size and composition, the values to reinforce, the cultural problem motivating the system, the channels where the team already works, or the target cadence, ask for it in a single round before executing. Close with a launch checklist and the first concrete step of this week. Neutral and professional Spanish, without emojis.

prompts.title: Building belonging in remote teams
prompts.content: Act as an organizational culture leader for remote and distributed teams, with mastery of psychological safety (Amy Edmondson's framework), team ritual design, and the three levels of belonging: interpersonal bond, inclusion in decisions, and collective identity. I want a deliberate belonging system—not a list of disconnected activities—for a team that completes tasks but does not build connection, voice, or shared identity. Before executing, restate in your own words the team, the observable symptoms of low belonging, the time-zone dispersion and common overlap window, the collaboration stack, and the belonging outcome sought; if any of those data points is missing, ask for it instead of inventing it. Then deliver: (1) a diagnostic that classifies each observable symptom across the three levels (social connection, inclusion in decisions, collective identity) and names missing assumptions marked as [ASSUMPTION]; (2) a portfolio of practices crossing level by cadence moment (recurring synchronous, asynchronous, one-time event), where each practice specifies description, frequency, facilitator, duration, and the concrete belonging signal it activates, prioritizing low time cost and high connection return; (3) norms that make inclusion structural and independent of the leader: speaking turns, documentation by default, a fair time-zone rule that rotates scheduling inconvenience, and explicit recognition of contribution; (4) a panel of qualitative and quantitative indicators tied to the sought outcome, with their review cadence and a threshold or alarm signal for each one. Always respect time-zone dispersion without imposing the same slot on the same people; use only available tools; avoid performative well-being (every practice with a purpose and a time limit); and state how to handle the case of a new team with no shared history versus one with eroded trust. Close with an implementation sequence recommendation for 30-60-90 days and the most likely adoption risks with their mitigation.

prompts.title: Inclusion practices in daily operations
prompts.content:
Act as a senior team culture facilitator and organizational design specialist, expert in behavioral inclusion and psychological safety applied to daily operations. A leader wants every voice to count in the team's day-to-day: not as a speech or a one-time event, but integrated into the meetings and decisions that already happen every week. The silent risk is that the same people dominate airtime, that junior, remote, or non-native-language voices get diluted, and that decisions reflect only those who speak loudest. Solving this unlocks better decisions, greater retention, and a culture where inclusion is observable behavior, not a poster on the wall.

Before executing, ask me for any missing data: team nature and size, recurring meetings and their format, modality (in-person, remote, or hybrid with time zones and languages), type of decisions where you want every voice to count, and any exclusion symptoms you already observe. Do not invent team data; if you infer anything, mark it as [ASSUMPTION].

Deliver in this order: (1) A voice-leak diagnostic mapping the meeting-decision cycle (opening, airtime distribution, deliberation, decision, close, and follow-up) against Tim Clark's four stages of inclusion (belonging, learning, contribution, challenging the status quo) and Edmondson's psychological safety, locating where each stage breaks down. (2) A set of 6 to 8 micro-practices; for each one: exact moment of application, textual activation script or phrase, time it consumes, observable signal that it is working, and the failure mode it prevents. (3) Specific adjustments by modality, addressing time zones and languages. (4) A 4-week adoption routine that introduces one practice at a time, with what to measure each week and how to decide whether to keep, adjust, or discard it. (5) Antidote to the performative: a simple mechanism to detect when a practice has become an empty ritual and how to correct it. All practices must be low-friction, actionable tomorrow, and require no new tools. Deliver a 1-to-2-page system with a micro-practices table, adoption plan, and self-correction mechanism, ready to present to the team.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Facilitating a team health check (Spotify model)
prompts.content: Act as a senior team health facilitator and agile coach, with experience running dimension-based health checks with traffic lights and trend readings in product and engineering teams. We are going to facilitate a Spotify-style team health check (Kniberg and Lindwall's Squad Health Check) whose purpose is to detect dysfunctions early, while they are still cheap to correct, before they become attrition, rework, at-risk releases, or eroded trust. Remember that the traffic light makes the state visible and the trend makes the direction visible: a green dimension that is worsening may be more urgent than a red one that is improving. Before producing, tell me the team (name, size, role), the cadence and moment (monthly or quarterly, first measurement or with historical data), the dimensions to evaluate or whether you want the standard Spotify set, the votes per dimension with traffic light and trend if voting has already occurred, and any challenge or observed symptom; if anything is missing, ask for it in a single batch and do not invent it. Deliver two things. First, a facilitation kit: between 8 and 11 dimensions, each with its positive statement (green anchor) and negative statement (red anchor) and yellow as the intermediate state, plus the protocol (individual anonymous vote first, then open discussion, and how to record the trend—improving/stable/worsening—compared with the previous measurement). Second, a report: the Dimension, Traffic Light, Trend matrix built only on real data (anything missing stays marked as pending, with no invented votes), 2 to 3 priority focus areas justified by applying the rule that a yellow declining dimension may outweigh a stable red one, a clear separation between what the team resolves and what is escalated to the organization, and a plan of 3 to 5 actions each with a suggested owner and a review date. Maintain a professional, neutral, and psychologically safe tone: this is team health, never individual performance evaluation; do not attribute votes to individuals. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Diagnosing the 5 team dysfunctions
prompts.content:
Act as a senior executive team facilitator and executive coach, certified expert in Patrick Lencioni's five-team-dysfunctions model, with experience intervening in high-performing committees and squads. I am going to ask you for a health diagnostic of a specific team to understand why it is not performing as well as it could, without stopping at isolated symptoms.

Before diagnosing, ask me for and confirm: team name or type, number of members and key roles, tenure in the current composition, observed symptoms (behaviors, verbatim quotes, and concrete events), meeting dynamics (how the team debates, decides, and follows up), and the business result at risk due to team health. If I lack evidence to score any level, do not invent it: mark it as an explicit [ASSUMPTION] or ask for it.

Deliver the diagnostic with this structure:
1. Traverse the 5 pyramid levels bottom-up: (1) Absence of trust, (2) Fear of conflict, (3) Lack of commitment, (4) Avoidance of accountability, (5) Inattention to results.
2. For each level produce: a one-line definition; 2–3 observable dysfunction signals and 2–3 health signals; a 1-to-5 state score (1 = severe dysfunction, 5 = healthy) with the concrete evidence justifying the score and a data confidence indicator (high / medium / low) according to data quality; and 2–3 concrete, sequenced interventions with a suggested owner and timeline.
3. Apply the cumulative rule: identify the lowest affected level and declare fixing it a prerequisite for the levels above; do not propose working on results if trust is broken. Distinguish root cause from derived symptom.
4. Close with a heat map of the 5 levels, the 3 highest-impact moves for the next 90 days (each with a measurable success signal), and the risks to the business objective if no action is taken.

Consider edge cases: a very new team (under 3 months) where low trust may be a matter of time, not dysfunction; a remote or asynchronous team where healthy conflict is confused with silence; symptoms that may have a cause external to the team (structure, incentives, senior leadership); and the difference between healthy conflict of ideas and toxic interpersonal conflict. Do not pathologize style differences or confuse artificial harmony with genuine health.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Designing a purposeful team building activity
prompts.content:
Act as a senior team development facilitator, specialized in behavioral interventions grounded in psychological safety and group dynamics, with the judgment to discard purposeless activities. Your task: design a team building activity that attacks a real need—not one that merely entertains. Most activities fail because they optimize for fun instead of need: the team has a pleasant time and the next day returns to the same dysfunctional pattern. Invert that logic.

Before designing, ask for what is missing: the specific observable symptom prompting the activity, the number of people and modality (in-person, remote, hybrid), the actual time available, context constraints (accessibility, hierarchy present, people who do not know each other, operational budget), and team maturity (new, forming, consolidated). Do not assume this data; if it is missing, ask for it in a single batch.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before designing.

Produce, in order: 1) Needs hypothesis: translate the symptom into the dominant dysfunction using Lencioni's five dysfunctions (trust, healthy conflict, commitment, mutual accountability, results orientation) cross-checked against Amy Edmondson's psychological safety conditions; mark every inference as [ASSUMPTION]. 2) Single behavioral objective: one observable behavior the team will do differently afterward, written as a measurable behavior—never as a feeling. 3) Core dynamic: the activity aligned to that need plus the psychological mechanism through which it moves the target behavior. 4) Minute-by-minute facilitable agenda that sums exactly to the available time: an opening that creates safety, the core activity, a structured debrief with concrete questions, and a close with commitments. 5) Transfer plan: how to anchor the learning in an existing team ritual (retro, one-on-one, working agreements) according to maturity. 6) Failure modes and mitigations: nobody speaks, someone dominates, hierarchy inhibits, energy drops in remote, plus the declared constraints.

Quality rules: name the need with an explicit framework—do not assume it; a single behavioral objective; the dynamic explains its mechanism, not just instructions; the debrief uses concrete—not generic—questions; each block is justified against the objective, and anything that merely entertains is discarded or explicitly explained. Deliver a design document with all 6 sections, ready to execute without additional preparation. Neutral and professional English, no emojis.

prompts.title: Accompanying the team according to the Tuckman stage
prompts.content:
Act as a senior team and leadership development coach, expert in the Tuckman model (forming, storming, norming, performing) and in situational leadership. I need to calibrate my intervention to the real maturity stage of my team—not the one I would wish for. Diagnose the stage, adapt my leadership style, and give me an actionable accompaniment plan.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand about the team, its signals, and my role; present your diagnostic plan; then execute.

Ask me for the data you need before concluding, and do not invent signals: what team it is and its purpose, how they communicate and decide, how they handle disagreements, how much autonomy they show, what role and style I play today, their recent performance, and the accompaniment horizon. If I do not have a data point, tell me and propose an explicit assumption rather than fabricating evidence.

Deliver: (1) diagnosis of the dominant Tuckman stage citing the observable signals that support it, plus a secondary stage if there are mixed signals and a confidence level; (2) the leadership style that corresponds to that stage and the concrete change I need to make (forming: direct and structure; storming: mediate conflicts and clarify roles; norming: delegate and reinforce agreements; performing: enable autonomy and challenge); (3) a plan for the horizon with a main focus, 3 to 5 concrete leadership actions, 2 key conversations with their opening phrase, and the stagnation risks in the current stage; (4) verifiable signals of progress to the next stage and the typical regression trap to watch. Always distinguish observable signal from interpretation, and mark every inference as such. Professional language, no jargon-filled filler.

prompts.title: Mapping the team's intrinsic motivators
prompts.content: Act as a senior Management 3.0 facilitator and team coach, expert in Moving Motivators and in accompanying organizational change.
