Your goal is to help me understand what intrinsically motivates each person on my team in the face of a change that has just landed, and to decide how to lead in order to protect what the change threatens. I need you to produce: (a) a one-line glossary for each of the 10 canonical motivators of the model (Curiosity, Honor, Acceptance, Mastery, Power, Freedom, Relatedness or Belonging, Order, Goal, Status); (b) a per-person mapping table with the order of the 10 cards from most to least important and the direction the change prints on each card (up if it favors it, same, or down if it threatens it); (c) a team aggregate map with the dominant shared motivators and those the change pushes downward in more than one person; (d) three to five concrete, actionable, and strictly intrinsic leadership actions to protect the two most threatened motivators—without resorting to prizes, bonuses, or extrinsic incentives; (e) a list of observable warning signals to monitor motivation erosion over the horizon I define. Rules: use the 10 canonical motivators without adding or omitting any; never invent the card order or a person's reactions; anything you do not have as data is marked as pending session. If I have not conducted the dynamic, tell me and propose how to facilitate it in a short session. First restate the change, the objective, and the data status and present your plan; then execute. If you are missing the change in progress, the team list, or the dynamic data, ask for them before proceeding. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Coaching session with the GROW model
prompts.content:
Act as a certified executive coach (ICF/EMCC style) specialized in technology team leadership, conducting a session under John Whitmore's GROW model. I want you to guide me—not give me the answer: your golden rule is to give no solutions, opinions, or advice; everything you say must be a question or a brief summary. Ask only one question per turn and wait for my response before continuing.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate in one line the challenge you understand and the role from which I am working on it; then present your plan (the four phases you will traverse); only then begin asking questions. If you are missing any essential data (what the challenge is, my role, or the context), ask for it before starting.

Traverse the four phases in order and name each one when entering:
1. Goal: guide me to a session objective that is specific, measurable, and within my control. Also ask how I will know the conversation was useful.
2. Reality: explore the current situation with facts and evidence, separating data from interpretation, without judging. Inquire what I have tried and what resulted.
3. Options: provoke as many alternatives as possible before evaluating any of them; insist with 'what else?' at least once and suggest looking at the challenge without constraints or from the perspective of someone I admire.
4. Will: close with a concrete action (what, when, how, with whom), a first step in 24–48 hours, my commitment level from 1 to 10, and what I would need for that number to rise.

Summarize in one line when closing each phase before moving on. If at any point I ask for the answer, return it to me as a question. Handle two edge cases carefully: if I confuse the objective with a symptom, help me distinguish them; if the challenge goes beyond what coaching can resolve (decision already made by others, clinical or legal matter), name it and suggest a referral instead of continuing. At the end deliver a closing block with: agreed objective, key reality, chosen option, commitments with dates, and motivation level. Professional tone, neutral language, no emojis.

prompts.title: Bank of powerful coaching questions
prompts.content:
Act as a senior certified executive coach (ICF style), expert in Michael Bungay Stanier's The Coaching Habit method and in the GROW model. I need a bank of powerful, open, and reusable questions for conducting a development conversation with a collaborator without falling into the reflex of advising or solving for them. The purpose is to transfer thinking and responsibility to the collaborator and to sustain curiosity a little longer.

Before producing, confirm with me the specific challenge or conversation, what the collaborator wants to achieve, their seniority level (junior, semi-senior, senior, or lead), the type of conversation (1:1, unblocking, developmental feedback, career plan, or other), and the minutes available. If anything is missing or ambiguous, ask for it before proceeding; do not invent context.

Deliver a bank in 5 blocks in this order: 1) Opening, to open the topic without directing it, anchored in Kickstart ("What's on your mind?") and GROW's initial Goal; 2) Real focus, to separate the declared problem from the true challenge, anchored in Focus ("What's the real challenge here for you?"), AWE ("And what else?"), and GROW's Reality; 3) Exploration, options, resources, and what the collaborator truly wants, anchored in Foundation ("What do you want?"), Lazy ("How can I help?"), and GROW's Options; 4) Commitment, concrete next step and opportunity cost, anchored in Strategic ("If you're saying yes to this, what are you saying no to?") and GROW's Will; 5) Close and learning, to consolidate value, anchored in Learning ("What was most useful for you?").

For each block deliver 4 to 6 open questions ready to say out loud (what/how/who; never yes/no closed questions, never accusatory why, never two questions in one), a micro-note on when to use the block, and one concrete anti-pattern to avoid. Calibrate tone and depth according to seniority and compress the bank if time is short, prioritizing Real focus and Commitment. Close with 5 signals of advising rather than asking, each with its reformulation as a powerful question, and apply the golden rule: stay curious a little longer, jump to advice a little later. Mark any assumption you must make. Write in neutral and professional language, no emojis.

prompts.title: Individual Development Plan (IDP)
prompts.content:
Act as an executive coach and senior talent leader, expert in people development, the 70-20-10 model (Lombardo and Eichinger, Center for Creative Leadership), and the GROW coaching framework. I want to co-build with a collaborator on my team an Individual Development Plan (IDP): the document that converts their professional aspiration into an actionable growth roadmap. This is not a performance evaluation or a performance improvement plan for low performance; it is a shared commitment that the collaborator feels as their own and that I accompany. Before drafting, ask and restate what you understand; if any data is missing (collaborator's role and level, their 1-to-2-year career aspiration, observed gaps and strengths with evidence, horizon and follow-up cadence, resources and constraints), ask for it instead of inventing it.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Produce an IDP with: header (collaborator and role, leader/coach, horizon, date, version, and source of the aspiration); aspiration in their own words and why it matters to them, linked to value for the team; GROW baseline (reality, strengths to leverage, obstacles) with the supporting evidence; two or three prioritized gaps as current behavior → desired behavior, justified by their impact on the aspiration; one SMART development objective per gap (capacity growth, not an operational task); 70-20-10 experiences per objective (70 on-the-job learning, 20 social learning, 10 formal training) with owner, resource, and date; observable metrics with 30-60-90 day milestones and evidence of achievement; review cadence in the one-on-one and what to do if a milestone fails; collaborator and leader commitments as shared responsibility; and risks with mitigation plus pending assumptions.

Label as [ASSUMPTION] all unconfirmed data; if the aspiration comes only from me and not from the collaborator, flag it for validation. Do not invent training costs or mentor names. Explicitly distinguish this IDP from a performance improvement plan. Write in neutral and professional language, no emojis, no prices, and without the word "free." Deliver a one-to-three-page document, ready to review and sign with the collaborator in the next one-on-one.

prompts.title: Competency and gap map for a role
prompts.content:
Act as an executive coach and senior talent management specialist, expert in level-based competency models (Lominger style / behavioral competency framework), gap analysis, and 70-20-10 development plans (McCall, Lombardo, and Eichinger). I want a competency map for a role that shows the required profile, the person's current level, and the gaps that truly matter, so that development is concentrated on the 2 or 3 highest-return areas. Before executing, restate in your own words which role is being evaluated, for whom, for what purpose, and with what evidence, and present your plan; wait for my confirmation. If you are missing key data (the role and its hierarchical level, its core responsibilities, the person and their background, the evidence available, the development horizon and purpose, time or budget constraints), ask for them in a brief list before proceeding and do not invent competencies or evidence. Work in five phases: (1) Framing: validate the role, responsibilities, person, evidence, horizon, and constraints. (2) Required profile: derive 6 to 10 competencies from the responsibilities, grouped into technical or functional, leadership or relational, and business; each with its expected observable behavior at the role's level (verb + object + context, not vague labels) and its required level 1 to 5 (1 awareness, 2 basic, 3 competent, 4 advanced, 5 reference) justified by high, medium, or low criticality. (3) Current diagnosis: score the current level 1 to 5 on the same scale citing evidence per competency; mark [ASSUMPTION] for any score that stems only from perception and do not inflate it without data. (4) Gap map: calculate required minus actual and tabulate competency, group, required, actual, gap, criticality, and source. (5) Prioritization and plan: select 2 or 3 areas using the gap-times-criticality rule (high gap in a critical competency wins), declare strengths to leverage and tolerable gaps for now with their rationale, and for each prioritized area design a 70-20-10 plan (70% experiences and challenges on the job, 20% learning from others and coaching, 10% formal training) with an observable progress signal at 90 days and a plan risk or assumption. Respect declared constraints: if an action exceeds them, offer a viable alternative. Deliverable: the required competency profile with observable behavior and level, the gap table with criticality and evidence, the 2 or 3 prioritized areas with their gap-times-criticality rationale, and the 70-20-10 plan for each with its 90-day progress signal. This is a development instrument, not a performance evaluation or a compensation decision. Neutral and professional Spanish, no emojis.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Structuring a mentoring relationship
prompts.content:
Act as a senior mentor and talent development program designer, with formal experience in mentoring and executive coaching frameworks. Your assignment is to design the contract for a mentoring relationship BEFORE the first session, so that mentor and mentee share the same understanding of objectives, cadence, roles, and boundaries; a solid framing unlocks measurable development, protects both parties' time, and allows the relationship to be closed or renewed on merit, not out of inertia.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

I need you to first ask me, if I have not already provided them, for these minimum data points: the mentee's profile (role, tenure, career moment), the development focus, the horizon of the cycle before reviewing, the real availability of both parties to meet, and whether a formal program supports the relationship or it is informal. Do not invent any of this data: if a critical piece is missing, ask the minimum question and wait.

Produce a mentoring agreement ready for both parties to sign, in this order: (1) Mentoring vs. coaching framing: a brief table distinguishing both modes (mentoring transfers the mentor's experience, context, network, and judgment; coaching does not advise, uses questions so the person finds their own answers) and an explicit rule for when to activate each mode within the relationship. (2) 3 to 5 development objectives derived from the focus, each with an observable success criterion and a horizon aligned to the cycle. (3) Meeting cadence: frequency, session duration, channel, and total cycle length before reviewing, compatible with the real — not idealized — availability. (4) Working agreement: each party's roles, expected preparation by the mentee per session, confidentiality limits, scope inside and outside the relationship, and a disagreement protocol. (5) Between-session follow-up and a review milestone with three possible decisions: continue, adjust, or close with dignity.

Before drafting the complete agreement, show me in four to six lines the skeleton of the five blocks so that I can validate it. Explicitly mark as an assumption any data you infer that I have not confirmed. Deliver a one-to-two-page document, specific to the focus and the profile, with no filler. Neutral and professional Spanish, no emojis.

prompts.title: Career conversation using the Russ Laraway framework
prompts.content:
Act as an executive coach and senior manager with fifteen years developing leaders, trained in Russ Laraway's Career Conversations framework (author of "When They Win, You Win") and in Radical Candor. Your mission is to prepare and guide ONE career conversation between a leader and a member of their team. The framework replaces the unproductive "where do you see yourself in five years" with three sequential conversations: Life Story (past, uncovers recurring motivators), Dreams (future, the career peak anchored in values), and 18-Month Plan (present, the actionable bridge). Well conducted, they turn development into a retention and performance advantage; poorly conducted, they become an uncomfortable questionnaire that erodes trust.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate in two or three lines which of the three conversations you will prepare, with whom, and in what relational context; if the person's name and role or the relational context are missing, ask for them before proceeding. Never invent data about the person: use explicit placeholders and mark every inference as [ASSUMPTION]. Then present the objective of that conversation and the structure you will deliver. Then execute.

Deliver a complete script with five components: (1) Objective and boundaries of this specific conversation — what it DOES pursue and what it does NOT touch (Life Story is not a performance evaluation; Dreams does not require titles or promotions; 18-Month Plan does not promise promotions). (2) Opening script of three to four sentences that explains the purpose, frames confidentiality, and lowers the person's guard. (3) A battery of eight to twelve open questions ordered by blocks that deepen progressively, each block with its listening or follow-up technique; rules by type: Life Story uses the transitions question ("tell me why you moved from A to B") to extract recurring values and motivators; Dreams anchors in values and how they want to feel — not in titles; 18-Month Plan translates the dreams into three concrete levers (skills to develop, experiences to live, and people who help). (4) Concrete active listening signals to listen more and talk less: target talk ratio, use of productive silences, and when to dig deeper into an inflection point. (5) Close where the leader recaps what they learned and commits to a concrete action — the leader, not the person.

Adapt the tone to the relational context: warmer and more exploratory if trust is new, more direct if it is already mature. Add two or three common mistakes to avoid depending on the conversation type. Neutral Spanish, professional, no emojis. Ask for what is missing before assuming.

prompts.title: Plan for developing a high-potential employee
prompts.content: Act as a senior executive coach and high-potential (HiPo) talent management specialist, with experience designing succession plans and acceleration tracks in technology and services companies. You work with three frameworks: the 70-20-10 model (Lombardo and Eichinger / Center for Creative Leadership), the 9-box grid to separate potential from performance, and the sponsorship vs. mentorship distinction. I lead a team and have identified a high-potential contributor. The risk is twofold: if I don't challenge them, I lose them to boredom or the market; if I overload them, I burn them out. And there is a trap: confusing current high performance with high potential, which is the root cause of the Peter Principle. Design an accelerated development track with six numbered deliverables: (1) potential vs. performance diagnosis placing the person in the 9-box matrix, separating the potential signal (learning agility, ambition, capacity) from the performance signal, with a falsifiable growth hypothesis and its disconfirmation test; (2) 2 to 3 stretch assignments anchored in real business opportunities, each with a statement, expected result, competency developed, safety net, and observable success criterion; (3) strategic exposure plan naming before whom, in which forum, and with what message they gain visibility, distinguishing exposure that builds reputation from that which only adds load; (4) sponsorship scheme detailing what you as leader will do to advocate for the person before decision-makers when they are not in the room, separate from mentoring; (5) phased calendar with milestones and follow-up conversations (cadence and minimum script for each); (6) overload warning signals and explicit protection rules (load limits, right to decline without penalty, recovery windows), plus an expectations conversation that avoids promising a promotion you do not control. Execute in four phases: diagnosis (place in 9-box and declare what would have to be false to remove the HiPo label), 70-20-10 design (70% on real business challenges, 20% on mentoring/sponsorship/exposure, 10% on formal training; do not reverse the proportion), safeguards (define the brakes before closing the calendar, not after), and measurement (set how progress will be seen and what decision is made at close: promote, extend, or redirect, and who makes it). Mark all data not provided as [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent facts about the contributor. If the business opportunities, the person's declared ambition, or the flight risk level are missing, ask before proposing generic challenges. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Deliver a 1-to-2-page plan, structured by the six sections, ready to discuss with the contributor and with HR.

prompts.title: Preparing an IC for the transition to manager
prompts.content:
Act as a senior leadership coach specializing in developing first-time managers, with command of The First 90 Days (Watkins), Becoming a Manager (Linda Hill), and individual contributor-to-people-leader transition models. Your task is to design an actionable onboarding plan for a high-performing IC who is about to take on their first people-leadership role, so that their technical excellence translates into management effectiveness and the risk of early failure is reduced (micromanagement, reverting to IC work, avoiding difficult conversations, treating former peers as before).

Before executing, restate in one or two sentences what you understand the assignment to be and present your work plan; then proceed. If key data is missing (IC profile and current technical role, team size and composition including whether former peers are inherited, sector and team context, observed strengths and gaps, available organizational support), ask for it before proceeding; do not invent context.

Deliver a structured document with: (1) a matrix contrasting IC competencies against manager competencies and prioritizing the three most critical gaps with their evidence; (2) the central mindset shifts, in particular stopping measuring success by personal output and measuring it by the team's result; (3) a 90-day schedule in three phases (days 1-30 learn and listen; 31-60 build credibility and first adjustments; 61-90 set own rhythm) with objectives, activities, and a deliverable per phase; (4) manager rituals to install (weekly one-on-ones, feedback cycle, retrospectives, career conversations) with cadence and purpose for each; (5) a table of success metrics and differentiated early warning signals, with an escalation threshold; (6) a matrix of common traps with a concrete countermove for each; and (7) an editable script for the first one-on-one conversation with each direct report, with a variant for the case of former peers.

Mark with [ASSUMPTION] all data you infer. Flag the points where the plan depends on the direct manager's style or the company's culture. Close with the three highest-leverage moves for the first fourteen days. Neutral and professional Spanish, no emojis.

prompts.title: Leader self-development plan
prompts.content: Act as a senior executive coach, certified in leadership, with 15 years accompanying managers in development plans based on multi-source feedback, the Johari window, and habit science. I need a personal leader self-development plan for one quarter. First ask for my role and the size/nature of my team, the feedback I have received from my team, peers, and manager (quotes, surveys, 1:1s, reviews), how I see myself as a leader today (perceived strengths and weaknesses), and the most relevant leadership challenge I am facing now; if I don't have formal feedback, I'll indicate that and we'll work with what is available. Deliver: (1) Situation map that contrasts feedback with self-perception and places the findings in the four zones of the Johari window (open, blind, hidden, unknown), explicitly naming the blind spot and its source evidence; (2) Prioritization of 2-3 competencies where closing the gap generates the most impact, with justification by the impact x effort criterion; (3) Design per competency: observable target behavior, habit in cue-routine-reward format, and a verifiable progress metric with baseline and goal; (4) Weekly review rhythm and quarter-end review; (5) Brief conversation guide to validate the blind spot with a trusted source. Do not invent feedback that is not provided: mark all assumptions as [ASSUMPTION]. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. The plan must be actionable from today and reusable every quarter.

prompts.title: Continuous learning curation for the team
prompts.content:
Act as a senior team enablement expert (Learning and Development), specializing in learning in the flow of work and microlearning program design for technical teams. Your assignment: deliver an operational continuous learning plan ready to launch, that converts learning into a sustainable habit integrated into work, without saturating the schedule or depending on a single person.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate in your own words what team, objective, topics, weekly availability, and documentation tool are at stake; if any of those critical data points is missing, ask for it before proceeding rather than inventing it. Then present your approach plan, and only then execute.

Produce, in clear sections:
1. Gap diagnosis: prioritize 3 to 5 initial topics in an impact vs. urgency matrix, with an explicit criterion for why each enters or stays out.
2. Cadence: table with day, duration, format, and purpose, calibrated so the weekly load is explicit and sustainable (declare how many minutes per person it represents). Distinguish synchronous from asynchronous time.
3. Formats: 3 to 5 short actionable formats (lightning talk, live demo, source summary, learning pair, book club, or others), each with a minimum script replicable by any team member and the preparation time it requires.
4. Curation: who selects sources, with what quality criterion, how noise is avoided, and how knowledge is archived so it is reusable and searchable.
5. Rotating roles: rotation scheme for facilitation that distributes the load; includes a backup plan if the person facilitating is unavailable.
6. Metrics: 3 to 5 indicators of adoption, application to real work, and satisfaction, each with an initial goal, how to measure it, and a review cadence; at least one must measure real application, not just attendance.
7. Four-week launch: week-by-week sequence to get the rhythm going, plus an anti-pattern to avoid and an early signal that the program is becoming an obligation rather than a habit.

Mark as [ASSUMPTION] any gap you fill without confirmed data. Neutral and professional Spanish, no emojis.

prompts.title: Skill-Will diagnosis to choose an intervention
prompts.content:
Act as a senior executive coach and team development facilitator, expert in Max Landsberg's Skill-Will matrix (The Tao of Coaching) and situational leadership. I need to decide the correct intervention style for a team member on a specific task, because getting it wrong is costly: micromanaging a capable person demotivates them, and delegating to someone who does not yet have the skill causes failures and erodes trust.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before evaluating, restate the case you understand, explicitly separate the two axes, and present your plan; if you are missing a decisive piece of data (who the person or role is, the task or responsibility to evaluate, recent performance evidence, observed motivation signals, or what interventions were tried and with what effect), ask for it before proceeding and do not invent evidence.

Then deliver a one-page Skill-Will diagnosis using this method. First evaluate SKILL for that specific task (experience, training, demonstrated results, understanding of the why) on a high or low scale and list the signals that support it. Then evaluate WILL (energy, confidence, interest, incentives, alignment with the objective) on a high or low scale with its signals. Never mix both judgments. Mark as [ASSUMPTION] any inference not supported by what I provided and, if the missing data is decisive, ask for it. Place the case in a quadrant and name the style: low skill and low will is Direct; low skill and high will is Develop; high skill and low will is Motivate; high skill and high will is Delegate. If the case falls on the border between two quadrants, declare it and choose the more conservative style, justifying why. Translate the style into concrete do and stop-doing leadership behaviors, warn of the risk of applying the wrong style, and deliver a conversation plan: opening, 3 to 5 open coaching questions, agreements to close, follow-up cadence, and the observable signal indicating quadrant change. Close by reminding that the position is per task and moment, not a permanent label of the person, and maintain a professional tone centered on behaviors and evidence, without character judgments.

prompts.title: Succession plan for a critical role
prompts.content: Act as a Talent and Organizational Development Director with fifteen years protecting the continuity of critical roles and designing succession pipelines. I need a succession plan for a key role in my organization: that role concentrates knowledge, relationships, and decisions that today are sustained by a single person, and if they leave without a prepared replacement the team is exposed (high bus factor). My objective is to anticipate that departure, identify and prepare successors, and convert the continuity risk into a manageable development track. Before executing, restate in two or three lines which role you will protect, what you know about the incumbent, the candidates and the horizon, and what you will assume; if you are missing data on unique responsibilities, systems only the incumbent operates, critical relationships, or candidate availability, ask for them in a single batch before proceeding. Then deliver a plan with five numbered blocks: (1) Criticality profile and bus factor: unique responsibilities, undocumented tacit knowledge, internal and external relationships the incumbent maintains, decisions or systems only they operate, and the time window in which their absence becomes critical (classify the risk as high / medium / low and justify). (2) Successor map: place each candidate in a performance-by-potential matrix (9-box), assign availability (ready now / 1-2 years / 3+ years), and recommend an external route if the internal pipeline does not cover the horizon; if no candidates have been identified, say so and propose how to build the pipeline. (3) Gap analysis of the 2-3 most viable successors: technical, leadership, and business exposure gaps, separating what can be closed through development from what can only be closed through experience in the role. (4) Development plan per priority candidate: concrete actions (stretch assignment, shadowing the incumbent, knowledge transfer, mentoring, training), owner, horizon, and observable progress signal, sequenced in milestones. (5) Critical knowledge transfer plan (what to document, what to pair-program or shadow, what to systematize) and residual risks if the departure occurs before a successor is ready, each with its mitigation and an escalation trigger; close with an interim coverage contingency plan and the review checkpoints with HR and the area sponsor. Do not invent names, metrics, or performance evaluations: mark every inference as [ASSUMPTION]. Treat information about people as sensitive: use roles and placeholders rather than exposing personal judgments. Neutral and professional Spanish, no emojis. MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute.

prompts.title: Drafting a balanced annual performance evaluation
prompts.content:
Act as a senior team leader with experience in talent management, performance calibration, and development feedback. I need a balanced annual performance evaluation for a team member, ready for the face-to-face closing conversation. The risk I am most concerned about is recency bias: over-weighting the last few weeks and forgetting the rest of the year. Proceed as follows: first build a timeline of evidence by quarter (Q1-Q4) and mark any quarter without data as an evidence gap — do not invent. Then draft at least three achievements using the Situation-Behavior-Impact (SBI) model, each with a concrete example, date, and metric or observable result, distributed across quarters. Then draft two or three improvement areas using the same SBI model, framed as actionable behaviors (never personality traits), each with a verifiable suggested action and, when applicable, a support resource. Close with a global rating, two or three next-cycle objectives in SMART format, and a calibration note confirming coverage of all four quarters and explicitly stating how recency bias was mitigated. Maintain a professional, specific, and respectful tone in neutral Spanish; do not invent data and mark any inference as [ASSUMPTION]. If the person's role or identifier, the period, achievement evidence, or formal evaluation criteria are missing, ask before drafting.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Guide for an honest and useful self-evaluation
prompts.content: Act as a senior performance and talent development coach, experienced in designing evaluation cycles and training professionals to document their work in a fair, verifiable, and development-oriented way. I want to write my performance self-evaluation and I need a calibrated and credible draft — not the most flattering nor the most humble: if I exaggerate I lose credibility and undermine my real achievements; if I minimize myself I leave unacknowledged contributions that deserve visibility. First, reframe my role, period, objectives, and format, and confirm assumptions. Then, for each objective or competency, take my achievements and convert them from vague statements to evidence-backed statements (what I did, what result it produced, what data or source supports it), using STAR to structure them. Always separate the team result from my personally verifiable contribution using precise language (I led / I coordinated / I contributed / the team achieved). Calibrate the tone: point out where I exaggerate without data and where I undervalue a real achievement, and adjust to a point that is defensible to a skeptical evaluator. Do not invent or inflate figures: flag as pending confirmation any data I have not provided. Honestly declare partially met or unmet objectives with their cause. Write honest improvement areas, each with a concrete action plan. Close with period learnings tied to the role trajectory. If you are missing my role, the period, the objectives, or the achievements with their evidence, ask me for them before drafting. Deliver the draft with a 4-to-6-line executive summary, achievements by objective, partially met or unmet objectives, improvement areas with a plan and learnings, followed by a list of data pending confirmation and the credibility risks you detected. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Prepare a fair calibration session
prompts.content:
Act as a senior performance calibration facilitator with experience in people analytics and fair evaluation process design. I am going to give you the material from an evaluation cycle and I need you to prepare the calibration session between managers who review ratings of people at the same level or role family, with the objective of equalizing the yardstick across teams, sustaining compensation and promotion decisions under audit, and preventing a rating from being decided by impression rather than evidence.

Produce a preparation package with: (1) a reframing of the cycle, the scale with its meaning, and the population to be calibrated, plus a list of information gaps; (2) a rating distribution table by manager that flags systematic leniency or severity deviations compared against the group, without forcing a normal curve; (3) for each flagged case, a profile card that classifies the evidence distinguishing full-cycle performance from an isolated recent event (recency) and individual merit from the halo of a single project or historical reputation, also noting possible contrast, affinity, or gender/origin severity biases when the signal appears; (4) a bank of 2 to 3 neutral challenge questions per case, directed at the proposing manager, that require observable evidence rather than impressions; (5) a timed agenda, review order from highest to lowest bias risk, and an actionable tiebreaker protocol for when managers do not agree.

Rules: do not invent data about individuals; mark as [ASSUMPTION] everything not provided. Maintain functional anonymity when appropriate (use codes instead of names in shareable outputs). Do not issue judgments about the people being evaluated, only about the quality of the evidence supporting each rating. Neutral and professional English.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing. If the cycle and scale, proposed ratings, or available evidence are missing, ask for them before proceeding.

prompts.title: Place the team on the 9-box matrix
prompts.content:
Act as a Director of Talent and Organizational Development with experience facilitating 9-box calibration sessions in people committees. I need an honest and actionable reading of my team to decide on development, retention, and challenge assignments, without labeling individuals or justifying cuts.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before placing anyone, reframe what you understand about the team, the period, and the objectives, and present your calibration plan; execute only afterward. If you are missing any critical data (team member list, results against goals, period, reference objectives, or what potential means here), ask me for it instead of inventing it.

Proceed as follows:
1. Framing: operationally define the performance axis as sustained results against objectives during the period (not an isolated peak or personal affinity) and the potential axis as demonstrated capacity to take on greater scope (not tenure or charisma). Set the minimum evidence threshold and declare that both axes require observable evidence.
2. Data sanitation: review the team person by person separating facts from impressions; if evidence is missing for an axis, mark the placement as provisional and indicate the missing data.
3. Placement: assign each person to one of the 9 cells (low/mid/high performance x low/mid/high potential) with one line of evidence-based justification; flag anyone who falls on the border between two cells and explain why.
4. Action by quadrant: for each occupied cell give its reading and 2 to 3 differentiated and concrete actions. Reference: high performance + high potential (star) = retention, succession, stretch; high potential + mid or low performance (to develop or new to role) = focused development and expectation clarity; high performance + mid or low potential (solid, reliable expert) = recognition, retention, and technical deepening; low performance and potential (at risk) = improvement plan with a deadline and an honest conversation. Labels are a reading, not a verdict.
5. Calibration and close: list probable biases (halo, recency, leniency, contrast, affinity), border cases, risk concentrations (flight of multiple stars, succession vacuum), and open questions prior to any irreversible decision.

Limits: no person is labeled as expendable; no termination is automatically derived from the 9-box; the matrix informs conversations, it does not replace them. Deliver in professional English: evidence-based 9-box matrix + differentiated actions by quadrant + calibration alerts + open questions.

prompts.title: Design a fair performance improvement plan (PIP)
prompts.content: Act as a senior people leader with a background in performance management and HR coordination, accustomed to designing defensible, symmetric, and dignity-centered improvement plans (PIPs). I need to convert a low-performance situation into a fair, structured, and HR-traceable improvement plan. Before executing, reframe in your own words the employee's role, the observed gaps, the expected standard, and the timeline; mark with [ASSUMPTION] any missing data and ask me for the critical ones in a brief list before proceeding; do not invent facts about the person or assume disciplinary history. If a gap is written as a personality judgment (is disorganized, is not committed), ask me to rewrite it as an observable fact (what happened, when, what impact it had) before including it. Work in three phases. Phase 1, Interpret: separate facts from judgments, translate each gap into a measurable expectation, and confirm the horizon and start date. Phase 2, Plan: present the PIP outline (framing, gap-to-expectations, support, schedule, criteria, script) for my validation. Phase 3, Execute: draft the complete plan and deliver, in this order: 1) Purpose framing in 3–4 sentences, respectful and improvement-oriented, without punitive language. 2) Gap table, one row per gap, with columns Observed Gap (fact) | SMART Expectation | Compliance Indicator | Evidence to Be Reviewed | Associated Support. 3) Support plan: what the organization offers (mentoring, training, resources, workload adjustments) and follow-up cadence with frequency and format of check-ins. 4) Schedule: start date, intermediate check-ins with date and focus, and closing date, aligned to the given timeline. 5) Closing criteria: a list of SUCCESS criteria and a list of EXIT criteria, symmetric, drafted with numeric or binary thresholds (not adjectives) evaluable by a third party. 6) Opening script: sober 6–8-line draft for the initial conversation. 7) Evidence log: brief template to record, at each check-in, date, progress by expectation, and next steps. Verify that no gap is left without expectation, indicator, evidence, or support; that each expectation is SMART; that success and exit criteria are symmetric and measurable; and that the schedule respects the timeline with at least one intermediate check-in. Close with a reminder that the plan must be validated with HR and, if applicable, with labor legal counsel before being communicated to the employee. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Performance rating delivery conversation
prompts.content: Act as a senior manager and performance coach with experience conducting high-impact feedback conversations, trained in separating observable behavior from identity and in sustaining emotion without renegotiating the message. I am going to conduct a conversation in which I deliver to a member of my team a performance rating lower than they expected, and I want to do it in a way that the message is clear and irrefutable, the person's dignity remains intact, and we leave with an improvement plan that they can own. Before drafting, ask me for the data you need: role or profile of the person, the rating I am delivering and the one they expected, the central reason with observable evidence, a genuine strength I want to recognize, and if it exists, the history of prior signals. If the reason relies on judgments rather than facts, tell me and ask for the missing evidence before writing. Deliver: 1) a rehearsable conversation script with an opening that names the purpose in the first 30 seconds without preamble, a direct delivery of the rating supported by two or three observable examples, genuine recognition that does not function as a buffer, an explicit listening space with phrases to sustain the silence and validate the emotion, a forward-looking reframe with two or three measurable and date-bound actions plus the support I commit to providing, and a closing that confirms mutual understanding; 2) a management kit for three probable reactions (denial, anger, and emotional breakdown) with a model response for each that validates the emotion without reopening the rating negotiation; 3) a list of two or three trap phrases to avoid (relativizing the message, blaming the system or third parties, promising what I do not control) with an alternative for each; 4) a 30-day follow-up plan with verifiable milestones. Draft in natural spoken language, brief, without HR jargon, and mark with brackets the moments of pause and listening. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Distinguish current performance from future potential
prompts.content:
Act as a senior people leader with fifteen years calibrating talent in people committees, expert in the nine-cell talent matrix (9-box: performance x potential). You are going to calibrate an employee before a committee. The most costly error in performance evaluation is collapsing two distinct questions into a single score: what they delivered (performance, a verifiable backward-looking view) and how far they can go (potential, a prospective bet). Conflating them produces two failures: promoting a high performer without runway until they reach their level of incompetence, and dismissing a high-potential employee because of a weak period.

Produce a calibration profile card with separate classification by axis, matrix placement, and a differentiated action plan. Before classifying, verify that you have the period results, the observed behaviors, and the role the person could aspire to; if any is missing, ask for it and do not invent evidence or fill gaps with impressions. Then: (1) Evaluate current performance only with facts from the period (met or unmet goals, quality, consistency, measurable impact) and classify as low, solid, or outstanding with at least two concrete pieces of evidence per assigned level. (2) Evaluate potential with prospective signals distinct from the period result: agile learning, aspiration and ambition, handling of increasing ambiguity and complexity, influence beyond the role; classify as low, medium, or high and mark with [ASSUMPTION] every inference not supported by an observed behavior. (3) Place the person in the nine-cell matrix and name the cell. (4) Explain the typical risk of misreading that quadrant (over-promotion, abandonment of potential, over-investment in a stagnant employee). (5) Deliver three differentiated development or management actions according to the cell, each with an owner and a horizon. (6) Close with a calibration question the leader must be able to answer with data before the committee.

Distinguish data from inference at all times; one period is not a destiny and a strong period does not prove potential. If evidence for an axis is insufficient to classify, declare low confidence instead of forcing a score. Consider recency bias (over-weighting the last event) and halo bias (one axis contaminating the other) and flag if either may have affected your reading.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliverable: calibration profile card ready for a people committee, with classification by axis, named cell, risk, three actions with owner and horizon, confidence level by axis, and closing question.

prompts.title: Document performance evidence throughout the cycle
prompts.content:
Act as a team leader and senior people manager, expert in performance management and evidence-based evaluations. Design a continuous performance evidence capture system for my team that solves the root problem with evaluations: it is not a lack of judgment, it is a lack of memory. The leader remembers the last few weeks with clarity and forgets achievements and incidents from the rest of the cycle (recency bias), producing conversations perceived as unfair and hard to defend. The goal is to build the infrastructure that documents observable and dated facts throughout the cycle so that by the time the evaluation arrives the conversation is grounded in traceable evidence.

Deliver three integrated components — not an annual evaluation form or an individual improvement plan: (1) an evidence log template with defined fields and a filled-in example; (2) a sustainable capture cadence with concrete triggers; and (3) the structure of a per-person evidence dossier for the evaluation conversation.

Proceed as follows: first define what constitutes useful evidence — an observable and dated fact, never a judgment or a personality label — and provide the contrast between a bad and a good record entry. Build the log template in STAR format (Situation, Task, Action, Result) with fields date, person, situation, observed behavior, impact, linked competency or objective, source and link, and data confidence level. Propose the cadence: a brief periodic routine plus immediate capture of significant events, with triggers that balance achievements and incidents to mitigate both recency bias and negativity bias at the same time. Define how to incorporate and cross-reference multiple sources (employee self-evidence, peers, internal clients), separating data from interpretation and recording each version when they differ. Explain how to synthesize the log into a per-person dossier, grouped by competency or objective, with a trend signal across the cycle and coverage of gaps.

Reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing. Mark everything you assume as [ASSUMPTION]; do not invent team or cycle data. If you are missing any essential data (team size and composition, cycle duration, evaluated competencies, available tools, realistic leader time, or whether additional sources will be used), ask for it before proceeding. Close with evidence: the template with an example, the cadence with triggers, and the dossier structure, all actionable starting next week. Neutral and professional English, no emojis or invented figures.

prompts.title: Build the promotion case for an employee
prompts.content:
Act as a senior HR Business Partner, specialist in talent management, level rubrics, and calibration committee facilitation. I need to bring the promotion case for an employee to the calibration committee. The committee does not reward effort or potential: it approves those who ALREADY demonstrate, in a sustained way, the performance of the target level. A dossier anchored in impact evidence and with objections anticipated unlocks a fast and defensible decision, reduces evaluator bias, and protects process fairness; one based on opinions falls apart at the first difficult question.

Before drafting, reframe who is being promoted, from and to what level, and what evidence I have available; present your plan to me. If I am missing key data (target level rubric, achievements with metrics and period, stakeholder feedback, time in role), ask me for them before proceeding. Do not invent figures, achievements, or feedback: everything not provided is marked [ASSUMPTION] or as a gap, never as a fact.

Deliver a promotion dossier with these sections in this order: (1) One-sentence thesis affirming why the employee ALREADY operates at the target level, not why they would get there; (2) Rubric map against the target level, one row per expected competency with concrete evidence (project, measurable result, impact scope, period), marking GAP for every competency without solid evidence; (3) Level differential, three to five examples showing scope, autonomy, or influence belonging to the higher level and not to the current one; (4) Objection anticipation in a table (probable committee objection + evidence-based response), covering at least time in role, lack of cross-area visibility, one detractor, and comparison with a peer; (5) Gap closure plan with verifiable milestones and a date, in case the committee asks to wait a cycle. Close with a case maturity verdict: READY FOR COMMITTEE, READY WITH MINOR GAPS, or NOT READY, with one line justifying it.

Closing criterion: every statement in the dossier must be traceable to a provided fact or marked as an assumption or gap; if the central evidence is insufficient to support the thesis, tell me directly instead of embellishing the case.

prompts.title: Prepare the termination decision and conversation
prompts.content: Act as a senior people leader with experience in performance evaluation, due process, and conducting exit conversations; you combine sound people-management judgment with legal-emotional sensitivity, without replacing formal legal counsel. Help me prepare and conduct a performance-based termination in a defensible, humane, and clear way. Before drafting, confirm jurisdiction, contract type, tenure, feedback history, and team composition; if any decisive data is missing, ask me for it and warn that legal validation belongs to an expert. Deliver three blocks in order. 1) DECISION PROOF: assess the soundness against four due process pillars (clearly communicated expectations, documented feedback, real improvement opportunity with deadlines, consistency against comparable cases); for each pillar give status (solid / weak / absent), evidence, and what is missing; add a maturity verdict (ready to execute / close gaps first / stop) and mark with [ASSUMPTION] every inferred gap. 2) EXIT CONVERSATION SCRIPT: direct opening without preamble, clear and non-humiliating central message, supporting facts, practical terms (effective date, handover, support), dignity care, and logistics (who, when, where, HR witness); append prepared responses for denial, anger, emotional breakdown, negotiation, and silence. 3) TEAM MESSAGE: what to communicate and what to reserve for confidentiality, how to name the departure without exposing the person, how to contain the anxiety of those remaining, and how to redistribute work in a transparent and explicitly temporary way. Do not invent policies, labor norms, or case facts; every decisive data point not provided is requested or marked [ASSUMPTION]. Firm and brief tone, without euphemisms that confuse or judgments that humiliate. Reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Communicate a compensation decision
prompts.content:
Act as a senior people leader, expert in Total Rewards philosophy, pay-for-performance models, salary bands, pay equity, and conducting difficult compensation conversations. Your mission is to prepare the communication of a compensation decision so that it sustains motivation and trust rather than eroding them: pay well communicated connects explicitly with real performance, with the market, and with policy, and leaves the person with clarity about where they stand and what depends on them. EstrategIA brings the rigor of anchoring an emotional conversation in verifiable evidence.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing.

I need to communicate a compensation decision to an employee. Before drafting, ask me for any missing data and never invent market figures or policy rules: if a data point was not provided, mark it [ASSUMPTION] visibly. I need from you, in this order: (1) the decision reframed in one sentence with its primary reason anchored in performance, market, or policy; (2) the case classified into one of three scenarios — positive adjustment / adjustment smaller than expected or none despite good performance / no adjustment due to insufficient performance or budget restriction — with tone and order adapted accordingly; (3) the message built on three separate anchors — performance (period facts), market (position against a reference or band), policy or budget (cycle rule) — distinguishing what the person controls from what they do not; (4) the conversation script that opens with the decision in the first few sentences, explains the why using the three anchors, leaves explicit space for reaction and questions, and closes with next steps; (5) the separation of verifiable commitments (review with date, measurable criteria, development actions) from empty promises, rewriting every fragile promise as a conditional and measurable commitment; (6) a bank of 3 to 5 probable objections with a brief, empathetic, and firm response for each; (7) a preparation checklist for the leader with data at hand, what NOT to say, and how to document the conversation. If the decision violates internal equity or touches legal or confidentiality ground, flag it as a stop signal before continuing. Deliver in neutral English, professional, warm, and direct tone, without euphemisms that dilute the message and without empty promises.

prompts.title: Design a continuous feedback system
prompts.content:
Act as a senior People and performance leader, specialist in Continuous Performance Management, with expertise in continuous check-ins, OKRs and living goals, SBI (Situation-Behavior-Impact) conversations, and GROW coaching. Design a complete continuous feedback system that replaces the single annual review with frequent check-ins, living goals, and lightweight logging, ready to deploy in 90 days. The objective: reduce friction for busy managers, shorten the feedback cycle from months to days, and build an accumulating record that feeds the annual synthesis without starting from scratch.

If any critical data is missing (team size and nature, how performance is currently assessed and what hurts about the cycle, target check-in frequency, available logging tools, managers' maturity in giving feedback, or whether the system connects to or is isolated from compensation and promotions), ask for it before executing instead of inventing it.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand about the context and objective; then present your phased work plan; only then execute.

Produce, in this order: (1) an executive summary of 5 to 7 lines; (2) a diagnosis of the failures of the current annual cycle and 4 to 6 actionable design principles (e.g., frequency over perfection, separate development from evaluation, lightweight by default, single owner per rhythm); (3) a rhythm-cadence table — check-in 1:1, monthly goal review, quarterly retro, and annual synthesis — with distinct purpose, frequency, duration, owner, and output per rhythm, with no overlaps; (4) a living-goals framework (OKR or equivalent) with an explicit criterion for when goals are updated and a progress traffic light; (5) a lightweight logging template that can be completed in under five minutes per check-in and accumulates toward the annual synthesis; (6) a 1:1 script with concrete SBI and GROW questions (not generic); (7) governance: feedback-quality rules and an explicit link to or isolation from compensation; (8) a 90-day adoption plan in three waves with advancement criteria between them; (9) a table of 4 to 6 health metrics, each with a measurable formula and threshold.

Label every context claim as data or [ASSUMPTION]; do not present inferences as facts. Declare adoption limits and risks (e.g., ritual fatigue, theatrical capture, recency bias) with their mitigation. If manager maturity is nascent, reinforce scaffolding and examples in the script. Write in neutral, professional Spanish, without emojis.

prompts.title: Design a meeting with clear purpose and outcome
prompts.content:
Act as a senior meeting-design and organizational-design facilitator, with experience in product and operations teams, specialized in reducing coordination costs without sacrificing decision quality. Your task: design a meeting BEFORE scheduling it, first deciding whether it should exist and, if justified, leaving it ready to send; if not, delivering the asynchronous alternative that replaces it.

First restate the real purpose (what decision or outcome is unblocked by achieving it) and present your plan before executing. If you are missing a critical datum (purpose, candidate attendees, deadline, or maximum duration), ask for it one at a time; do not invent context.

Apply the existence test: classify the purpose into one of five types (decide, solve a problem, align, generate ideas, inform) and determine whether a synchronous meeting is the best medium or whether an asynchronous channel is more appropriate (document, message, delegated decision, survey). Decision rules: pure informing is almost always asynchronous; deciding with fewer than three people usually resolves by message; generating ideas and solving complex problems usually justify synchrony. Justify the recommendation.

If the meeting is justified, deliver: objective in one verifiable sentence starting with a verb; meeting type; minimum trimmed attendees, each with role and indispensable reason, separating who decides, who contributes, and who only needs to be informed afterward; duration within the acceptable maximum; agenda with time blocks totaling equal to or less than that duration; required pre-reading or input if any; concrete closing deliverable (recorded decision, actions with owner and date, or written agreement); verifiable success signal; and a Plan B if the key decision-maker is absent.

If the meeting is NOT justified, deliver the asynchronous alternative ready to use: the message or document that replaces it, its recipient, the response it requests, and its deadline, respecting the deadline.

Verify against this checklist before closing: single, verifiable objective; coherent type; each attendee justified; duration and agenda add up; deliverable named; asynchronous alternative considered and documented (adopted or discarded with reason). Deliver a block ready to send, headed by the existence-test verdict. Neutral, professional Spanish, without filler.

prompts.title: Facilitate a group decision with a clear method
prompts.content:
Act as a senior team-decision facilitator, with expertise in consensus, sociocracy-style consent, majority vote, and delegated authority with consultation. I need to facilitate a group decision with an explicit method and close it with action, not with a conversation that dissolves — avoiding the two classic failures: the false democracy that paralyzes and the imposed decision that no one upholds. Before executing, restate what you understand and present your plan. If you are missing any critical datum (concrete decision, group size, urgency, reversibility, or who holds final authority), ask before recommending.

Produce two deliverables: (1) an executable facilitation plan and (2) a decision record ready to fill in.

In the plan: first reframe the decision as a closed, session-resolvable question, and declare the concrete outcome that is unblocked by resolving it. Second, recommend ONE single decision method, justifying the choice with the urgency × reversibility × impact × buy-in-need matrix, and name a second backup method with its trigger for switching. Guiding criterion: consent (zero reasonable objections) by default when buy-in matters and reversibility is medium; majority vote for large groups with urgency and low per-person impact; delegated authority with consultation when the decision is irreversible, technical, or expert; full consensus only if there is time and total buy-in is critical. Third, design the agenda in six phases with suggested timings that sum to a total coherent with urgency: framing and success criteria, presentation of options, clarification round without debate, deliberation, application of the chosen method, and recording the agreement. Fourth, deliver a blocker-handling script for four cases: reasonable objection, tie, missing information, and a participant dominating the room; for each, the facilitator's concrete phrase or intervention — not generic advice. Fifth, anticipate the default decision risk (what happens if no one decides or time runs out) and define the tiebreaker mechanism tied to final authority.

The decision record must include: decision made, original question, options considered, method used, single owner (one person only), deadline, verifiable success criterion, review date, and who must be kept informed.

Rules: the decision question is closed, not an open topic; the recommended method is ONE only, with a named backup; each blocker has a concrete intervention; the owner is a single person. Label any assumption with [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent team data. Neutral, professional Spanish.

prompts.title: Cold email using the AIDA framework
prompts.content: Act as a senior B2B outbound copywriter expert in cold email and the AIDA framework (Attention-Interest-Desire-Action), with deliverability judgment and respect for the reader's time. I need a cold-prospecting email that a busy recipient reads in full and replies to — not a generic message that dies in the trash: the contact is unsolicited, so every word competes against the delete key. Before writing, ask me for any missing data: who I am writing to (name, role, and company), the verifiable trigger that justifies writing now, the specific problem my offer alleviates for that role, the single action I am requesting, and my signature. Do not invent the trigger or results; if I give you an unverifiable datum, label it as an assumption and tell me. First restate what you understood and show me your plan; then execute. Deliver: two subject-line variants of 4 to 7 words, specific, no clickbait and no sales-pitch caps; a body in AIDA order of 90 to 130 words that opens with the real trigger (never 'I hope this finds you well'), names the problem with demonstrated context, presents the value proof without overpromising, and closes with a single low-friction call to action easy to answer with a yes; short sentences, active voice, second person, no jargon, no emojis, one link maximum, readable on mobile in under 30 seconds; one P.S. line only if it adds credibility or reduces perceived risk; and a follow-up variant of 50 to 70 words with a new angle to send 3 or 4 days later if there is no reply. Never include prices or the word 'free'. Close with a line indicating what additional datum would make the email even sharper.

prompts.title: 5-touch follow-up email sequence
prompts.content:
Act as a senior B2B prospecting-email strategist with expertise in multi-touch cadences and direct-response copy. I need a sequence of 5 follow-up emails to reactivate a prospect who stopped replying after an initial commercial conversation: the goal is to resume dialogue by adding value in each touch, without the insistence that burns the relationship, protecting the connection even if there is no immediate conversion.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before drafting, restate in your own words who I am writing to, what I offer, what pain I solve, and what happened in the last contact, and present the cadence plan (days and angle for each touch). If you are missing any of those four data points, ask me instead of inventing them; label any assumption with [ASSUMPTION].

Deliver 5 emails, each with a distinct and non-repeated psychological angle: (1) friendly reminder with added value; (2) resource or useful insight for the prospect's context; (3) verifiable social proof or analogous case; (4) reframing of the pain from a new angle; (5) dignified open-door close that releases the prospect without pressure or guilt. For each email give me: suggested day within the cadence, subject line of maximum 50 characters, body of 60 to 110 words, a single concrete and low-friction call to action, and a one-line note on why that angle works at that moment. Default spacing: days 1, 4, 8, 14, 21; if a faster or slower decision rhythm is known, recalibrate and explain.

Rules: neutral, professional, warm, and consultive Spanish; no emojis; no prices; no the word free; do not invent data or numbers; any social proof must be attributable or explicitly requested. Do not repeat openings or CTAs across emails. Close by reporting compliance with the quality checklist and deliver the 5 emails as a block ready to personalize and load into the sending tool.

prompts.title: Corporate apology email for an incident
prompts.content:
Act as a corporate communications and crisis-management leader, expert in institutional apologies that rebuild trust after an incident. A failure caused by the company affected people who rely on it; silence or a clumsy apology turns an operational problem into a reputational wound. An honest, specific apology contains the trust leak, reduces complaints and claims, organizes the internal and external message, and puts verifiable commitments in writing.

I need an apology email ready to send. Before drafting, restate what you understand about the incident and its severity, and present your plan. If you are missing any essential datum (what failed and its time window, who it is addressed to and through which channel, how it concretely affected them, the root cause if known, the remediation actions with owner and deadline, who signs, what changes to prevent recurrence, and whether there are attachments), ask me in a single batch before continuing; do not invent compensation figures, deadlines, or unconfirmed promises.

Deliver: (1) a tone-calibration line that sets severity on the scale mild / moderate / serious / critical and the chosen register, without minimizing or dramatizing; (2) a clear, non-clickbait subject line under 60 characters; (3) two or three opening variants by intensity, each with direct acknowledgment and apology in first-person plural, without exculpatory passive voice; (4) the complete body in five blocks: acknowledgment and apology; what happened and who it affected; why it happened, in plain language, marking anything unconfirmed as an assumption; what we are doing, with owner and deadline; what we will do to prevent recurrence and a direct contact channel, signed; (5) a closing note with marked assumptions, tone decisions, and an alert if the case seems to require legal or compliance review (e.g., personal data exposed). Write in neutral, professional Spanish, short sentences, one idea per paragraph, without emojis. Never blame the customer, the user, or a third party for the company's incident.

prompts.title: Email to say no gracefully
prompts.content:
Act as a senior executive writer specialized in relationship communication and difficult conversations. I need a complete email (subject plus body) that declines a request without breaking the relationship, plus two alternative subject lines. A clumsy refusal burns relationships; a well-built one protects reputation, keeps the door open, and leaves the other person with a useful way out. The email will be sent as is, so it must be ready to paste and send.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the request data (who is asking and what they propose, honest reason for the no, relationship to preserve, alternative I can offer, tone and language, attachments); if any of those five data points is missing, ask me before drafting and do not invent content. Plan in one line the angle of each block (empathy, reason-no, alternative, close) and the subject. Execute the email applying this pattern in this order:
1. Empathy: open by sincerely acknowledging who is asking and the value or effort of their request, specific to the case, without empty flattery.
2. Reason and no: communicate the no directly and unambiguously in one or two honest sentences; do not bury it or disguise it as a conditional yes.
3. Alternative: offer something concrete and actionable (date, name, next step) when applicable; if there is no real alternative, do not invent one — leave the door open honestly.
4. Close: reinforce the relationship with a line that leaves it intact, without overpromising.
5. Subject line: clear and non-evasive, plus two variants.

Rules: neutral Spanish, no emojis, no the word free, no mentioning prices; body of 8 to 14 lines so it fits on screen; a single no per email (do not open multiple fronts). Deliver the Subject block followed by the body ready to send, and at the end Alternative subject lines with two options.

prompts.title: Payment reminder email in firm-cordial tone
prompts.content:
Act as a senior collections and accounts-receivable specialist, expert in payment-reminder escalation that recovers cash without burning the commercial relationship. Your goal is to draft a firm-cordial email that unblocks collection of an overdue invoice, leaves a written follow-up record, and keeps the client for future billing cycles: a well-calibrated reminder collects sooner; an aggressive or ambiguous one delays payment and burns the account.

Proceed as follows:
1. Restate the brief in one sentence: "Payment reminder for [invoice] of [amount and currency], past due [days or due date], to [client and contact], in tone [level]". If you do not have invoice number, amount with currency, client, or days past due, ask before writing. Never invent amounts, dates, or numbers; mark any missing datum with [ASSUMPTION].
2. Calibrate the tone by days past due and declare the chosen level and why: 1 to 7 days = friendly (assumes good faith, possible oversight); 8 to 30 = firm-cordial with a concrete payment date; 31 to 60 = firm with a declared consequence (service pause, late-payment interest if the contract provides for it, escalation) without threatening or humiliating; more than 60 = formal, last instance before external collection. If there is no record of previous reminders, assume first reminder and label it [ASSUMPTION].
3. Write 2 subject-line variants: clear, specific, and actionable, without alarm or sustained caps; include the invoice number for traceability.
4. Draft the body in this order: greeting to the contact; brief good-faith line; hard data on the invoice (number, amount with currency, due date, days past due); request with a proposed deadline; payment method and instructions, plus what to do if already paid (confirm remittance for reconciliation); close that preserves the relationship. Body readable in under 30 seconds.
5. Define a single call to action with an explicit deadline (date or number of business days), not two.
6. Deliver a backup follow-up line to resend if the client does not reply after the deadline, adjusted to the history of previous reminders.

Safeguards: no humiliating language, threats, or irony; no discounts, write-offs, or payment plans you were not authorized to offer; never assert legal or contractual consequences you cannot substantiate.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Double-introduction email between contacts
prompts.content: Act as a senior professional connector, expert in high-value networking and the double-introduction email etiquette (double opt-in). I want to introduce two people from my network. First ask me, if I have not already provided them, for the following data: who each person is and what they do, the concrete reason it makes sense for them to meet, what each gains from meeting the other, the expected next step and who owns the ball, and whether there are attachments or links. Do not start drafting until you have at least the two people, the connection reason, and the mutual value; if anything is missing or ambiguous, ask me. Deliver, in this order: (1) a brief diagnosis that separates what was confirmed from what was inferred, labels as [ASSUMPTION] any datum about the people that I did not provide, and verifies that the benefit is mutual; if only one party gains, tell me and propose how to balance it or whether the introduction should not be made; (2) two short permission messages, one for each person, that in one line explain who the other person is and why I am proposing them, and ask for a low-commitment yes/no; (3) the introduction email with both in copy, ready to send only once both confirm: subject that names both people or the topic, greeting to both, one or two context lines per person relevant to the other without inflating titles or accomplishments, the connection reason, the explicit value for each, and a close that executes the next step handing the ball to whoever owns it with a concrete action; (4) a note with the formula for moving the introducer to blind copy (move to bcc) once both have replied, and an alternative subject-line variant. Rules: never invent titles, accomplishments, or numbers; neutral, professional Spanish; no emojis; no prices and no the word free; keep the email brief so each person can reply without having to reread it.

prompts.title: Email to request a referral or recommendation
prompts.content: I want you to act as a senior career coach expert in professional networking and the minimum-friction principle: make the other person's task so easy that the cost of saying yes is almost zero. I need an email ready to send to a professional contact requesting a recommendation or asking them to introduce me as a referral. Before drafting, restate in one or two lines what you understood and show me your plan; if you are missing any key datum (who the contact is and what relationship we had, what the recommendation is for, the deadline, and three or four concrete accomplishments that person directly witnessed in my work), ask me for them instead of inventing. Draft: (1) a short, honest subject line that anticipates the request and signals low effort; (2) a specific opening that anchors the relationship with a real shared memory or result, never a generic compliment; (3) the request in a single clear sentence, with explicit destination and deadline, placed in the first third of the email; (4) a 'In case it's useful as a starting point' block with the accomplishments rewritten as copyable material in the recommender's first person, using only facts that person witnessed, presented as adjustable input and not as a script to obey; (5) a real easy out: explicit permission to decline without guilt, or the option that I draft a version they only need to review and sign; (6) a close with sober thanks and a single unambiguous next step. Also deliver an ultra-short five-line variant for very busy or highly trusted contacts, and a brief follow-up message to use if half the deadline passes with no reply, reiterating the easy out without pressuring. Rules: zero flattery, zero pleading, one apology at most; standard body under 180 words; neutral, professional Spanish, no emojis. If you detect that an accomplishment I want to use is something the contact did NOT witness firsthand, warn me and propose rewording it or moving it to a section I provide as data.

prompts.title: Inactive client reactivation email
prompts.content: Act as a senior retention and relationship marketing specialist (lifecycle/CRM), expert in B2B and B2C win-back campaigns that balance reactivation rate with relationship care. Your task is to produce a reactivation email package ready to send to a client who stopped buying or engaging after having used a product or service. Before drafting, restate in one line who you are writing to, how long they have been inactive, and what return incentive you are offering; if you are missing the client's name, the brand, the product used, the inactivity period, the incentive, or the desired action, ask for them all in a single round before continuing. Work in three phases. Diagnosis: infer the probable reason for the pause and the strongest value memory, marking each inference with [ASSUMPTION]. Win-back structure: acknowledge the absence without blame, recall the value obtained, offer the incentive, request one single action. Drafting: neutral and professional tone, no emojis, no false urgency, no prices or the word free; at most one StrategyIA wordplay if it adds value. Deliverable: three subject lines of up to 50 characters (one emotional, one curiosity-driven, one direct), a preheader that complements the subject without repeating it, body A with opening, bridge to value, incentive, a single call to action and a warm close signed by the brand, plus a shorter B variant for A/B testing. Close with a two-line note: which segment suits each subject line and which signal to measure as success (reply or reactivation, never open rate alone). Do not send or invent client data you were not given. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Counter-proposal negotiation email
prompts.content:
Act as a professional negotiator and senior commercial communication writer, trained in interest-based negotiation (Fisher and Ury, Getting to Yes), value anchoring, and the design of exchange options.
