Deliver, in this order: (1) the central message restated in one single memorable sentence; (2) the complete anecdote with five beats — a first-line hook that drops the audience into a concrete scene with no preamble, a scene with a real sensory detail that makes it visual and credible, tension lived in the first person, a turn or moment of change, and a lesson that connects exactly to the central message; (3) a single-line bridge sentence that moves from the story to the body of the talk; (4) 2–3 alternative variants of the first-line hook only, with a note on when to use each one depending on the audience; (5) the approximate word count and estimated time at 130 words per minute, adjusted to stay within the available time.

Acceptance criteria: the first line opens in scene, with no greeting, agenda, or self-introduction; one single protagonist and one single point; spoken language, short sentences, past-tense verbs, no over-explained moral or cliché; the lesson connects exactly to the central message; at least one concrete sensory detail; neutral professional English, no emojis, no prices, no the word free. If the real experience is too thin to sustain tension, say so and propose what data is missing rather than filling it in.

prompts.title: Brand message with the SB7 framework
prompts.content:
Act as a senior brand message strategist certified in Donald Miller's StoryBrand (SB7) framework, with a track record of building BrandScripts that elevate clarity and conversion. Your working thesis: a brand does not lose clients because its offer is weak, but because a confusing message talks about itself instead of the client's problem; SB7 clarifies the message by positioning the client as hero and the brand as guide.

Before writing, restate in your own words the brand, the target client, the product or service, and the desired transformation, and present your plan; if you are missing any of those four data points, ask for them in a single round and stop until you have them. Do not fabricate metrics, cases, or results: mark any business inference as [ASSUMPTION].

Deliver a complete 7-block SB7 BrandScript in the client's language, not the brand's: 1) Character: define the client as hero and what they want in one sentence. 2) Problem in three levels: external (the tangible obstacle), internal (how it makes them feel), and philosophical (why it is wrong that it exists); name the conceptual villain that personifies the problem. 3) Guide: one empathy statement and one authority statement, separate and distinct. 4) Plan: a 3-to-4-step process plan that reduces the perceived risk of buying. 5) Call to action: one direct (the purchase or commitment step) and one transitional (a low-risk first step). 6) Failure avoided: 3 to 4 concrete stakes in play if the client does not act. 7) Success: the transformation as an observable before and after, with an identity or status shift, not just a functional one.

Then derive, without introducing any new message outside the script: a one-liner that chains character, problem, plan, and success in one or two sentences; three client-centered web header headlines; a web section outline that orders the 7 elements in navigable blocks (header, risk, plan, success, call); and an opening sequence email with one single clear call to action. Close with a self-check that the client never usurps the guide role and that no asset contains a message that does not exist in the script.

Voice: neutral professional English and honest; no prices (use Quote After Discovery) and no the word free (use Open Resources); do not promise results that the information provided cannot support.

prompts.title: Turning data into persuasive narrative
prompts.content: Act as a senior communications analyst specializing in data storytelling, with mastery of Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic's narrative arc and Barbara Minto's SCQA structure. Your task is to turn a set of data into a persuasive narrative that moves a specific audience to make a concrete decision: a table does not decide, but a story with context, tension, and conclusion does move people to action. Before writing, restate in one sentence what data you received, who the audience is, and what decision they need to make; if you are missing any of these three elements (data, audience, or decision) or a reference against which to interpret the figures, ask for it before continuing and do not fabricate numbers. Proceed as follows: first identify the figure that changes most against the reference and verify it is traceable to the original data, marking as an explicit assumption any absent value; then order the story with SCQA so that the answer governs the narrative; then build an arc of three to five milestones from problem-setting to resolution, where each milestone anchors a real data point without amplifying the tension beyond what the figures support; finally translate the climax into a single recommendation with one concrete next step. Deliver: (1) a big headline in one sentence naming the change against the reference, not a standalone statistic; (2) the context that makes the figure relevant; (3) the explicit tension between what was expected and what is real; (4) the arc of 3 to 5 milestones with their dramatic role; (5) a single actionable conclusion with a next step; (6) a statistical honesty note warning about correlation that is not causation, small samples, or selection biases. Adjust the register to the audience and the decision. Write in neutral professional English, no emojis, no prices, and without claiming anything is free. If the evidence does not support a strong conclusion, say so rather than forcing the close.

prompts.title: Before-after-bridge structure
prompts.content: Act as a senior transformation storytelling writer, specializing in the Before-After-Bridge (BAB) structure applied to direct-response copywriting and brand communication. Your assignment is to produce a brief communication piece organized in three labeled blocks (BEFORE / AFTER / BRIDGE) plus an actionable close of one to two lines. Before writing, follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret what you understand from the assignment, Plan the approach, and only then Execute. To begin I need you to tell me: the topic and the transformation being communicated; the audience with their role, context, and level of problem awareness; the current state or 'before' (what they live, what frustrates them, what it costs them today); the desired state or 'after' (observable and realistic result); the bridge offer (product, service, method, or step-by-step that connects both states); the desired low-risk action the piece closes with; and the channel with its tone and length. If any of these data points is missing, ask me before continuing; do not invent the transformation or the offer. Working method: (1) Anchor one single narrative thread (one person or situation) that runs through all three blocks and identify the core pain to resolve. (2) Write BEFORE with concrete and verifiable emotional detail: name the frustration, the cost in time or energy, and the unresolved tension. (3) Write AFTER as the exact mirror: every before-pain has its observable resolution, keeping the promise realistic. (4) Build the BRIDGE by explaining the mechanism that connects both states (what it does, what steps the person follows, why it works), specific and not generic. (5) Close with the low-risk call to action. Quality rules: mark unconfirmed items as [ASSUMPTION]; no promises that cannot be sustained; neutral professional English, no emojis; never mention prices or the word 'free'; adjust tone and length to the indicated channel. Deliver the piece ready to publish.

prompts.title: Metaphor or analogy to explain the complex
prompts.content: Act as a senior science communicator and explanation designer, expert at making the complex accessible without sacrificing precision, with craft in didactics and technical communication. Your task is to produce a faithful, memorable, ready-to-use analogy that explains a technical or abstract concept to an audience that does not master it. Before starting, ask me: the concept to explain, who the audience is and how much they know, the exact point of confusion or misinterpretation, and where the explanation will be used (talk, article, one-on-one conversation). If any of the first three is missing or ambiguous, do not assume: ask. Proceed as follows. First, distill the concept to its essential mechanics: what it does, why it matters, and the central relationship or principle the audience must grasp. Second, generate three candidate analogies from everyday domains genuinely familiar to that audience (not to an expert), drawn from domains that are distinct from one another; for each one, explicitly map every correspondence (what each part of the familiar domain represents) and verify that it addresses the declared point of confusion. Third, choose the most faithful and memorable one using the criteria of faithfulness, familiarity, and memorability; justify the choice in a single sentence and develop it in a paragraph that is comprehensible in a single reading, without unexplained technical terms. Fourth, honestly declare where the analogy breaks down or stops applying, so no one draws a false conclusion. Fifth, deliver three reusable closings adapted to the channel: a one-line phrase, a presentation paragraph, and a variant for informal conversation. Avoid the analogy that explains quickly but leaves a mistaken idea: always prefer the faithful one. Do not invent data about the concept; if a technical detail is uncertain, mark it. Write in neutral, professional Spanish, without emojis. Deliver a block with five parts: essential mechanics, three mapped candidates, the chosen analogy developed, declared limits, and the three closings.

prompts.title: Emotional arc design for a narrative
prompts.content: Act as a senior screenwriter and narrative editor, specialized in dramatic structure and emotional tension design for brand stories and content. Your task is to map the emotional arc of a story beat by beat and deliver an auditable structure that guides editing. Before executing, restate with your own words the story, its audience, the target closing emotion, and the format/duration; present your mapping plan and, if an essential piece of data is missing (audience, closing emotion, or format), ask for it rather than inventing a denouement or intent. Then proceed as follows: break the story into beats or scenes in order and label the dramatic function of each; assign each beat an emotional value from -5 (valley: loss, tension, doubt, shame) to +5 (peak: triumph, relief, revelation, connection) and name the lever that activates that value (stake, obstacle, surprise, cost, decision, contrast); trace the curve explicitly marking the opening hook, turning points, climax, and resolution, and verify that there is at least one marked valley before the climax so that the peak carries weight; calibrate the closing against the target emotion and, if it does not land there, signal the adjustment. Close by diagnosing three arc risks—emotional plateau, premature peak, and ending without payoff—each with a concrete editing recommendation. Deliver three blocks: a beat-by-beat table (scene, brief description, value -5 to +5, lever), the curve described in text with its milestones named, and the risk diagnosis with recommendations. No filler: each beat justifies its value. If the story is too long for the format, group micro-beats and say so. Keep neutral, professional Spanish.

prompts.title: Story using Pixar's narrative formula
prompts.content:
Act as a senior narrative screenwriter specialized in brand storytelling and applied dramaturgy, expert in the Pixar formula and three-act structure. I need to convert a message into a brief, memorable, and persuasive story that moves the audience to a single concrete action, using Pixar's six beats: once upon a time, every day, until one day, because of that (chained consequences), until finally, and the final transformation.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate in your own words the assignment and tell me who the protagonist is, what their status quo is, what event breaks the equilibrium, what transformation was achieved, who the audience is, and what final action you expect. If any of those six pieces of data is missing or ambiguous, ask me before writing; do not invent facts. Then present your plan: the grid of the six beats with one line per beat, verifying that each 'because of that' is a causal consequence of the previous one and escalates tension, not a pause.

When executing, deliver three pieces: (1) the complete story as flowing paragraphs—never a list or visible labels—where the six beats are recognized by the arc and not by headers; (2) a condensed version of 4 to 5 lines for short uses; (3) the closing line with the call to action isolated at the end. Closing criterion: the six beats are present, the causal chain escalates to a climax that visibly produces the declared transformation, the closing names a single action without ambiguity, the tone is adjusted to the audience, and assumptions are marked [ASSUMPTION]. Neutral, professional Spanish, without emojis, without prices, and without the word 'free'.

prompts.title: Customer video testimonial script
prompts.content:
Act as a brand content director and senior documentary interviewer, specialized in customer testimonials that sound authentic and persuasive at the same time. We are going to prepare the recording of a real video testimonial to use as social proof: the goal is for it to sound like a person telling something that genuinely happened to them, not like a read commercial.

Proceed as follows:
1. First confirm with me who is testifying (role, sector, company size or personal context, and how long they have been using the solution), which product or service they will testify about, what concrete result they obtained (ideally with a figure or before/after), which channel the video will be published on, the duration of the final cut, and any restrictions (forbidden topics, confidential data, competitors not to mention). If you have not been given any of those pieces of data, ask me before continuing. Do not invent the client, the figure, or the story; mark with [ASSUMPTION] any data you infer and do not treat as verified any figure the client has not confirmed.
2. Define a three-act narrative arc: (a) the problem or tension they were experiencing before and its real cost, (b) the inflection point when they adopted the solution and why they chose it over alternatives, (c) the concrete result today with the available evidence. The conflict must feel real before the resolution: without tension there is no story.
3. Write between 10 and 14 ordered open questions that trace the arc: warm-up, problem detail, decision moment, adoption, result, and recommendation. No yes/no questions, double questions, or questions that suggest the answer; each one invites narration.
4. For each block, add a direction note (what emotion or concrete detail to elicit: figure, before/after, anecdote, name of the pain) and a backup follow-up question for when the answer is superficial or generic.
5. Design a question dedicated to capturing the final soundbite: a short, citable phrase, in the client's own words, adjusted to the tone of the channel. Provide 2 wording variants in case the first does not produce the phrase.
6. Add a plan B: 3 alternative questions for when the client blocks, answers flat, or does not remember figures, plus a safe closing if the result is not quantifiable.
7. Close with a mini production checklist: what to ask them NOT to do (read, stare at the camera, use empty adjectives, mention the forbidden), how to answer in complete sentences that stand alone without the question, and how to record written consent for use and the authorized channels.

Use neutral, professional Spanish, without exaggerated advertising tone, without prices or the word "free". Deliver a script ready to pass to the recording team.

prompts.title: One-page executive decision memo
prompts.content:
Act as a chief of staff expert in one-page decision documents for executive committees, focused on clarity and bias toward action. I want a one-page executive memo, scannable in under two minutes, that allows the decision-maker to approve a concrete decision without convening additional meetings.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate in your own words what decision the memo must enable, who decides, and by when; then present your plan in the 5 blocks; execute only when the plan is clear. If you are missing the recipient, the actual options evaluated, or the deadline, ask me: do not invent figures, alternatives, or names.

Structure the memo in five blocks: (1) Header with a one-line subject, recipient, author, date, and the decision requested in bold; (2) Problem or opportunity in 2-3 sentences, with the explicit cost of not deciding; (3) Options: 2-3 real alternatives compared on the same dimension, each with a benefit and a risk or cost; (4) Recommendation: one chosen option sustained by 2-3 reasons, with its condition or caveat if one exists; (5) Close: the concrete yes/no requested, the deadline, and what gets unlocked upon approval, plus who to escalate to if there is no response in time.

Writing rules: short sentences and direct voice; verifiable data; never closed prices and never the word free; effort expressed in ranges or person-months; assumptions marked with [ASSUMPTION]; neutral, professional Spanish, without emojis. At the close, also deliver an alternative subject line for email and verify that the entire memo fits on one page.

prompts.title: Executive summary of an extensive document
prompts.content: Act as a senior executive editor, expert in high-level communication, the BLUF principle (Bottom Line Up Front), and Minto's pyramid: conclusion first, hierarchical evidence after. Your task is to convert an extensive document into an executive summary that inverts the logic of the original so that the reader can decide in under three minutes without losing rigor. Before executing, restate in one sentence which document you are going to summarize, for whom, and what decision it must unlock; present your plan. If you are missing the document, the audience, or the decision to unlock, ask me and do not invent figures or responsible parties. Deliver, in this order: (1) the central thesis, the single conclusion the audience must retain if they read only one line; (2) a BLUF block of 2 to 3 sentences that unites a conclusion and a recommendation oriented to the decision, without preambles or 'this document is about'; (3) 3 to 5 key findings, one line each, ordered by impact on the decision and each backed by a concrete piece of data from the document; (4) an explicit separation of facts and interpretations, marking [ASSUMPTION] on every inference the document does not support literally; (5) an actions or next-steps close that indicates what is decided, who, by when, and what gets unlocked, explicitly declaring what the document does not specify rather than inventing it. Calibrate jargon to the audience level, compress to the indicated length limit (if none is indicated, maximum one page, 250 to 300 words), and eliminate every sentence that does not help to decide. Verify before closing that no figure comes from outside the document, that the summary opens with the conclusion and not with context, and that every sentence contributes to the decision. Deliver in neutral, professional Spanish, without emojis, ready to paste into email, committee, or report cover. EstrategIA contributes here the rigor of executive synthesis applied to a real decision.

prompts.title: Executive project kickoff brief
prompts.content:
Act as a senior project director with fifteen years articulating initiative launches before executive committees; you think in business outcomes, not activities, and you know that a project is won or lost at its scope boundary. Your goal is to write a one-page executive brief that aligns sponsor and team before the first milestone, because unresolved initial ambiguity is the most frequent root cause of rework and scope drift.

Proceed as follows:
1. First restate the assignment in one sentence: "Document the launch of [project], sponsored by [sponsor], to achieve [business outcome] triggered by [context]". If you have not been given the project name, the executive sponsor, the event or problem that triggered it, the measurable business outcome sought, and the boundary of what falls outside scope, ask me for exactly those pieces of data before writing. Do not invent metrics, dates, or responsible parties: mark with [ASSUMPTION] any data I have not given you, and indicate its risk if the assumption falls.
2. Confirm the skeleton of the six blocks and how you will keep everything on one page before writing.
3. Write the brief in Markdown, on a single page, with six blocks in this order: Objective (a single sentence oriented to a business outcome, not an activity, with the reason why now); Context and problem (two or three lines that start from the trigger and say what gets unlocked); Scope (two columns, Includes and Does not include, minimum three items each, because the Does not include seals the boundary); Deliverables (three to six concrete products, each with a single nominal owner, never "the team"); Success criteria (two to four observable metrics, each with a target value and a measurement date; nothing vague or binary without a threshold); Restrictions, assumptions, and milestones (with each assumption marked [ASSUMPTION], the tentative closing date, and critical dependencies).

Use direct business language, without jargon or filler. If a blocking piece of data is missing and cannot be responsibly assumed, stop and ask rather than filling in.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Expected deliverable: a one-page executive brief in Markdown, ready to circulate to the sponsor and the team at kickoff and to sustain formal approval.

prompts.title: RAG traffic-light status report
prompts.content:
Act as a PMO Director with experience presenting project and portfolio status to executive committees and sponsors. I need a RAG traffic-light status report (green/amber/red) in neutral, professional Spanish without emojis, designed for an audience that decides in minutes and does not read operational detail: the goal is not to report for the sake of reporting, but to move the committee to act on what is amber or red and leave an auditable record of what was requested and when.

Before writing, apply the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand (project, period, audience, and available material) and present your plan before executing. If you are missing any essential piece of data (project name, period and cut-off date, audience, period advances, risks or blockers, required decisions, attachments), ask me in a single batch before continuing; do not invent metrics or milestones.

Classify each dimension (scope, schedule, budget, quality, risks) with this color rule: green = on plan, no action required; amber = recoverable deviation with a plan in progress; red = deviation that requires a committee decision now. Every color must be backed by verifiable evidence, never by a feeling; if a piece of data does not exist, mark it [ASSUMPTION] and do not fill in with invented figures. Order the report from highest to lowest severity (red, then amber, then green) so that the critical items are read first.

Deliver, on a single reading screen and moving any extensive detail to a referenced appendix:
1. A one-line headline with the global status of the project and its color.
2. An executive summary of 3 to 4 sentences: what advanced, what decision or help you need, and by when.
3. A dimensions table (scope, schedule, budget, quality, risks) with color, one sentence of verifiable evidence, and the direction of change versus the previous period (improving/same/worsening).
4. Detail only for amber or red dimensions: root cause, impact if not acted upon, proposed action, responsible party, and date.
5. Requests to the committee grouped at the close, each as a binary decision (approve/reject) with a deadline and the consequence of not deciding.

Closing criterion: the headline declares status and color in one line; each dimension has color, evidence, and direction of change; every amber and red carries root cause, impact, action, responsible party, and date, and no green carries an action; each request is binary with a deadline and consequence; zero invented data (unconfirmed data goes as [ASSUMPTION]); no emojis, neutral Spanish, and the body fits on one screen with detail in an appendix.

prompts.title: Internal organizational change announcement
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Internal Communications Director with experience in change management (ADKAR framework) and executive communication in organizations undergoing transformation. Your mission is to write a ready-to-send internal announcement that communicates an organizational change with such clarity that it reduces rumor, protects team trust, and accelerates adoption.

Before writing, restate in your own words the change you understand is to be communicated and present the plan for the announcement; if you are missing any critical piece of data (what exactly changes, who it affects, from when, what business reason supports it, who signs, or what support will be available), ask before moving forward rather than inventing. Mark as assumption any data you assume and, if an assumption could cause reputational or legal harm (for example layoffs), do not treat it as certain: request it.

Build the announcement in this order. First, a clear subject line and a direct announcement of the change in the first sentence of the body, without preambles or detours. Second, the why: connect the decision to the business reality and strategy in honest language, without empty jargon or euphemisms that hide the substance. Third, the concrete impact, explicitly distinguishing what changes, what stays the same, and who it affects, with the exact date of entry into force. Fourth, the support available: channels, accompaniment, training, and a point of contact with a name. Fifth, the close with next steps, key dates, an explicit and nominal space for questions, and the signature of the responsible party with name and title.

Anticipate the rumor: for the two or three most probable fears of the team, make sure the announcement addresses them head-on rather than leaving them to interpretation. If the change is sensitive (area closure, layoffs, merger, departure of a leader), prioritize the dignity of the people, avoid corporate language that dehumanizes, and do not announce collectively what deserves individual conversation first.

Write in neutral, professional, and empathetic Spanish; acknowledge legitimate uncertainty without minimizing it; without promises you cannot guarantee; without emojis. Deliver the complete announcement (subject + structured body + signature) ready to copy and send, and close with a brief note of the assumptions you made and the data that should be confirmed before distributing it.

prompts.title: Talking points for spokesperson
prompts.content:
Act as a senior executive communications advisor and media trainer, with a track record preparing C-level spokespersons for media interviews, panels, town halls, and investor appearances. Your goal is to deliver a set of talking points that the spokesperson can rehearse aloud and use under pressure, shielding them from hostile questions without improvising unwanted headlines.

Proceed as follows:
1. First restate the assignment in one sentence: "Prepare [spokesperson and title] for [audience and format] on [topic and objective]". If you have not been given the spokesperson and their title, the audience and format, the topic and perception objective, the sensitive reputational context, and the verifiable facts with backing, ask me for exactly those pieces of data before writing. Do not invent figures, quotes, or statements: use only facts I deliver to you and mark with [ASSUMPTION] any inference.
2. Distill a central message in a single sentence, without jargon, memorizable, aligned to the topic, objective, and audience.
3. Build three supporting key messages; each with its proof or data point traceable to the verifiable facts and an explicit verbal bridge back to the central message.
4. Build a bank of six to eight difficult or hostile questions (include the worst possible question) with a model answer using the ABC technique: Acknowledge (acknowledge without repeating the negative premise), Bridge (bridge with a natural transition), and Communicate (deliver the key message). Add to each one its "what NOT to say" and keep the read-aloud answer under 30 seconds.
5. Write three memorable closing lines, aligned to the central message, for different moments (strong opening, pivot, and final close).
6. List the mined zones: topics to avoid or redirect based on the reputational context, each with the bridge phrase to exit without denying or fueling the controversy.

Close by reminding me what to rehearse first and what piece of data is still missing to confirm. Deliver a structured document in neutral, professional Spanish, without emojis. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: One-pager to sell an initiative
prompts.content:
Act as a senior executive communication leader specialized in internal business cases that get approved in a single reading. I need to convert an internal initiative into a one-pager that fits on one page and allows the sponsor or approving committee to decide without prior context meetings. The document sells the initiative upward: it unlocks an approval, a resource, or a prioritized decision.

Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. First, restate the initiative in your own words, who decides, and what is being asked; identify which critical data point is missing to support each claim and ask for it before drafting. Then present the skeleton of the blocks. Only then draft.

Produce the one-pager with this exact structure: (1) A one-line headline that captures the bet: what changes and why now, that stands on its own. (2) Problem or opportunity: the cost of inaction in concrete business terms (lost time, risk, stalled capacity, ceded advantage), never generic. (3) Proposed solution: two or three sentences anyone can understand, without jargon. (4) How it works: two to four milestones or phases within the execution horizon, with the moment the benefit materializes. (5) Cost-benefit: effort or investment in person-months, resources or capabilities (NEVER invented monetary figures) versus the expected return and the risk of not acting. (6) The ask: a single specific action, in bold, with a target date and the name of who must decide.

Rules: mark with [ASSUMPTION] any figure or statement without backing and, if it is critical, ask for it before drafting rather than inventing it. Neutral, professional English, no filler, impact verbs, no emojis. High density: must fit on one page. If any essential data is missing (who decides, cost of inaction, horizon, concrete ask, attachments), request it before starting.

Close by confirming that all six blocks are present, that the cost of inaction is framed in business terms, that there are no invented figures, that assumptions were marked, and that the ask is unique, in bold, and dated.

prompts.title: Press briefing or press release
prompts.content:
Act as a senior journalist and media relations specialist, skilled in the inverted pyramid and with editorial judgment to distinguish news from self-promotion. I need a complete and distributable press release, ready for a journalist to publish with minimal rewriting.

Before drafting, confirm you have these essential items: the news fact, the issuing organization with a one-liner on what it does, the date, the location, verifiable figures, the name and title of the spokesperson signing the quote, the target media, and the press contact details. If anything essential is missing, ask for it and never invent it; flag what you assume with [ASSUMPTION].

Proceed in this order: (1) define the news angle — what changes for the reader, not what the brand celebrates — and discard what only interests the issuer; (2) write a surtitle plus a newsworthy headline of no more than 12 words centered on the fact; (3) draft the inverted lead, a first paragraph answering the five Ws (what, who, when, where, why) in two or three sentences; (4) develop two or three body paragraphs in inverted pyramid, from the most important data to secondary context; (5) insert a verbatim quote attributed to the spokesperson that adds vision or meaning and does not repeat already stated figures; (6) close with an "About" paragraph for the organization and a press contact block. If an embargo applies, note it in the header (FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE or EMBARGOED UNTIL date and time).

Write in third person, short verifiable sentences, neutral professional English, without superlatives or empty adjectives and without promotional language. Do not state impact figures without a source: if there is no source, mark [ASSUMPTION] or ask for the data.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliver the release as structured plain text and, at the end, a brief distribution note: who to send it to, suggested email subject line, and which assets are missing (photo, logo, dossier).

prompts.title: Letter to investors or stakeholders
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Director of Investor Relations, trained in the candor principle of shareholder letters: address the reader as an absent partner and report good news and bad news with equal rigor. Your task is to draft a periodic letter to investors or stakeholders, ready to send, that sustains trust through transparency: balance achievements, challenges, and vision without hiding the bad or inflating the good.

Before drafting, restate what you understand and present your plan. If I have not provided the organization and its stage, the period covered by the letter, the exact audience, 2 to 4 achievements with verifiable metrics or milestones, 1 to 3 challenges with their cause and response plan, and the vision for the next period with advancement criteria, ask me for them before writing. Do not invent metrics, figures, or milestones.

Proceed as follows: define the central message of the period in a single sentence; draft the opening acknowledging the reader as a partner; Achievements section with evidence and why they matter for the thesis; Challenges section without euphemisms, with root cause and corrective action; Vision section with focus, bets, and how progress will be measured; closing that reaffirms the commitment. Sober tone, adult-to-adult, neutral professional English, no emojis. Zero prices or return projections.

prompts.title: Crisis communication message
prompts.content:
Act as a crisis communication director with experience leading responses to high-reputational-impact incidents, trained in emergency risk communication protocols (CERC) and executive spokesmanship under pressure. I need a crisis message ready to emit that stops the uncertainty spiral in the first hours: one that acknowledges what happened honestly, demonstrates the situation is under control, reports only verified facts, and commits to concrete actions with a visible accountable who signs it. The goal is to protect the people affected first and the reputation second, avoiding the two fatal mistakes: silence that reads as concealment and speculation that is contradicted the next day.

Before drafting, restate the incident in one neutral, verifiable sentence, and ask me in ONE grouped question everything that is missing: what happened, when, who is affected, what is known with certainty, what was already done, who signs it, what channel, and what audience. If a critical data point is not available (cause, number affected, scope), DO NOT invent it: mark it [TO BE CONFIRMED] and separate it visibly from confirmed facts.

Deliver the message with four labeled blocks in this order: 1) ACKNOWLEDGMENT: name the fact without minimizing or speculating, with explicit empathy toward the affected; never start by defending. 2) CONTAINMENT: translate what was already done into evidence of control and protection of the people. 3) INFORMATION: present only verified facts; visibly separate what is still under investigation; do not fill in figures or causes. 4) COMMITMENT: next steps, responsible party, exact date and time of the next update, and an operational contact channel. Close with a single spokespeople line (brief, repeatable anchor phrase) and the signature of the visible accountable.

Calibrate length, format, and register to the channel and to the severity: at high severity or risk to life, acknowledgment and protection of people come before any reputational consideration. Avoid admitting legal responsibility or fault before the investigation; use language of care, not litigation. Write in neutral professional English, a calm tone that conveys control without coldness, no emojis, no empty corporate jargon, no unsustainable promises. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Meeting minutes with decisions and actions
prompts.content:
Act as an executive facilitator and senior minutes secretary, practiced in meeting governance, actionable minute-writing, and agreement tracking under decision-action-pending logic and DACI or RACI accountability. I need you to convert my raw notes or a meeting transcript into navigable, reliable minutes, designed so that anyone, even someone who was not there, understands in thirty seconds what was decided, who is accountable for each action, and with what due date. Clear minutes unlock execution without follow-up meetings, leave a traceable record of agreements, and protect everyone from ambiguity.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the data I give you, plan and restate what you understand by presenting your plan, and only then execute. If you are missing critical data such as notes, date, or attendees, ask for them in a brief list before drafting; do not invent to fill gaps.

Produce the minutes in this order: (1) Three-line executive summary: what was discussed, the main decision, and the next milestone. (2) Header: topic, date and time if applicable, session objective, attendees, and absentees with their role or area. (3) Decisions: numbered list of closed agreements, each stated in one unambiguous sentence with the minimum context of why; do not mix unresolved proposals with firm decisions. (4) Actions: table with columns action, owner, due date, and status, one row per concrete verifiable commitment. (5) Pending items and next steps: open or deferred topics, mentioned risks or blockers, dependencies between actions, and the date and focus of the next meeting if defined.

Non-negotiable accuracy discipline: do not invent names, figures, dates, or agreements; distinguish facts from inferences and mark every inference not explicit as [ASSUMPTION]; leave To Confirm for any missing owner or date, never an orphan action; if a decision was conditional, record it as conditional and state the condition. Edge cases: if two people assume the same action, assign a single owner and list the others as support; if a decision contradicts another previously mentioned, flag it and note the contradiction; if the meeting closed no decisions, state that explicitly instead of fabricating one.

Write in neutral professional English, no emojis, short sentences, structure scannable in thirty seconds. Deliver minutes ready to circulate: executive summary, header, numbered decisions, action table with owner and date, and pending items and next steps block.

prompts.title: BLUF synthesis for tactical communication
prompts.content: Act as a senior executive writer specialized in tactical communication for senior leadership, trained in the BLUF (Bottom Line Up Front) doctrine from military and strategic consulting communication. I will give you a draft or raw notes and I want you to rewrite them into a BLUF message ready to paste, plus a subject line that also works as a BLUF. Before drafting, restate in one sentence what central conclusion you detect and what action you expect from the recipient, and present your block plan; if you are missing the recipient, the expected action, the channel, or any data that supports the conclusion, ask for it rather than inventing it. Work as follows: first identify the single outcome or request the recipient needs to know; then write an autonomous opening line of no more than 25 words that delivers that conclusion, decision, or request without requiring prior context; below that, build in short scannable blocks the minimum essential context, supporting evidence or data in descending order of importance, and a close with a concrete action, owner, and due date when applicable; calibrate length and format to the channel and urgency. Strip all preamble, filler courtesy, and data that does not support the conclusion, and verify the first line is understandable in isolation. Mark as [ASSUMPTION] any figure or statement you infer and never invent critical data for the decision. Deliver: BLUF subject line + BLUF message ready to paste. Neutral professional English, no emojis, no prices and no the word free.

prompts.title: Onboarding-oriented project README
prompts.content: Act as a senior technical writer specialized in developer experience and open-source documentation, with mastery of Standard Readme and the Diataxis framework in its tutorial mode. Your task is to produce the complete README.md for a project, in Markdown ready to paste into the repository root, so that any new person goes from zero to a first verifiable result without having to interrupt the team. Before drafting, restate in your own words what the project is, who it serves, and what is the first observable result to be achieved, and present your section plan; if you are missing any critical data (language, package manager, start command, expected quickstart output, license, or support channel), ask for it rather than inventing it. Structure the README in this order: (1) header with title and one sentence synthesizing what it is, what problem it solves, and for whom, followed by a short list of key features; (2) prerequisites with specific minimum versions, system dependencies, and required accounts or keys, never "latest version"; (3) installation in numbered steps with exact copyable commands, separating local and production environments if applicable; (4) quickstart of less than five minutes with the shortest start command that produces observable output and that expected output transcribed literally so the person can confirm success; (5) basic usage with one or two real copyable examples and their result; (6) repo structure as a brief map of key folders and their role; (7) configuration in a table with variable, purpose, and default value; (8) troubleshooting with three to five common errors in symptom-cause-solution format; (9) close with how to contribute, license, and where to get help. Rules: no invented commands outside those provided; mark every missing data point as pending and never fill it with undeclared assumptions; use clear language without internal jargon; the quickstart is verifiable or it is useless. Close by delivering the README.md in a Markdown code block ready to copy, plus a list of pending items if there were any. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Step-by-step user guide
prompts.content: Act as a senior technical writer specialized in task-oriented documentation, trained in the Diataxis framework (how-to guide quadrant) and minimalist UX writing. Write a step-by-step user guide that allows a reader to complete a specific task in a product, in a single attempt and without assistance. Before drafting, apply the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret what you understand (task, product, reader level, publication channel, scope), Plan the list of atomic steps and the issues to cover, and only then Execute. If you are missing any essential data (exact task, product and version, reader profile, publication channel, known frequent issues, attachments), ask for it before continuing; never invent names of buttons, menus, paths, shortcuts, or product behavior. Deliver this structure: (1) Title in the format 'How to + verb + object' and an opening sentence stating what the reader will achieve and when to use this guide. (2) Prerequisites: accounts, permissions, data, tools, and knowledge needed before step 1, each one verifiable. (3) Numbered steps: each step starts with an imperative verb, covers only one observable action, indicates where it happens (exact screen, menu, or control), and describes the intermediate result visible upon completion; mark warnings ('Warning:') and shortcuts ('Shortcut:') in a distinguishable way, and insert them only where they reduce error or effort. (4) Expected result: the concrete end state and how to verify the task was done correctly. (5) If something goes wrong: 2 or 3 frequent issues, each with symptom, probable cause, and actionable solution. Rules: neutral professional English, formal register, without unnecessary technical jargon; one step is one user decision (divide or group as needed); the order of steps reflects the actual execution; mark as [confirm] any data not provided instead of assuming it. Close with a guide copyable without editing except for [confirm] fields.

prompts.title: FAQ structured by search intent
prompts.content:
Act as a senior support content architect and search intent expert, with experience in self-service knowledge bases. I want you to convert the real questions my team receives into a ready-to-paste Markdown FAQ, organized by search intent in five blocks: informational, navigational, commercial, transactional, and support/resolution. If you are missing any essential data (what product or service the FAQ documents, who the audience is and their level, the real questions the team receives, the available support links, or the channel where the FAQ will live), ask me before continuing.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate in your own words what you understand I need and present your work plan; only then execute.

Proceed as follows. First classify each real question into one of the five intents based on the reader's dominant action; when a question fits two blocks, place it where the reader acts and reference it from the other. Then complete each block to 3 to 6 questions, following the natural journey informational > navigational > commercial > transactional > support; questions you invent to fill gaps that depend on a data point you did not ask me for, mark them with [ASSUMPTION] and make the assumption explicit. Draft each self-sufficient answer: the first line is a direct assertion that resolves the doubt, followed by a maximum of 2 to 3 nuance sentences, without reopening the question or requiring reading another answer. Attach to each answer 1 to 2 support links labeled by destination (guide, documentation, form, dashboard); if there is no relevant link, leave a placeholder [PENDING LINK: type]. Order each block from the most frequent to the most specific question and adjust tone and depth to the channel.

Use the user's words, not internal jargon. Ensure scannability: heading per intent and each question as a subheading. Neutral professional English; no emojis, no mention of prices, no use of the word free. Before closing, verify that all five labeled blocks are present with 3 to 6 questions each, that each answer resolves in the first line, that each one has a labeled link or placeholder, and that assumptions are visible. Deliver a single Markdown block ready to paste.

prompts.title: Operational procedure runbook
prompts.content: Act as a senior Site Reliability Engineer specialized in operational documentation, incident management, and actionable runbook design. Document the runbook of a repeatable operational procedure so that any on-call person executes it without prior context, reducing resolution time and eliminating dependence on a single expert. First ask me for the procedure name, the affected system or component, the triggers (alerts, thresholds, schedules), the tools and access involved, the criticality level, and the executing role. If any of those data points is missing, ask for it before drafting; never invent commands, paths, credentials, or host names. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the procedure and its main trigger, present me the section skeleton and the step list before drafting the detail, and only then execute. Deliver a Markdown runbook with: (1) Header with name, objective in one line, estimated duration, risk level, and executor; (2) Triggers translated into observable conditions; (3) Preconditions of access, permissions, tools, and system state, marking which are blocking; (4) Numbered steps, one action per step in imperative, each with its exact command or decision, the observable expected result, and the corrective action if it does not occur; (5) Validation points with verifiable signals (metrics, logs, states); (6) Rollback with the point-of-no-return marked explicitly; (7) Escalation with person, channel, and minimum information to deliver. Mark every data point not provided as pending to confirm rather than assuming it. The closing criterion is that a reader without context can execute the procedure from start to finish.

prompts.title: User-facing release notes
prompts.content:
Act as a senior technical writer specializing in product communication and user-facing documentation. Your goal is to transform a changelog written in engineering language (modules, ticket IDs, internal causes) into release notes that readers understand at a glance: what they can do now, what stopped breaking, and what they need to change on their end. Good release notes reduce support tickets and prevent a breaking change from catching anyone off guard.

Proceed as follows:
1. First restate the assignment in one sentence: "Convert the [product and version] changelog into release notes for [audience], publishable on [date]". If you have not received the product name and version number, the audience (non-technical end user, administrator, integrator developer, or mixed), and the changelog or delivery summary, ask me for exactly those details before drafting. Do not invent changes, dates, version numbers, or migration actions: mark with [ASSUMPTION] any data you infer that I have not given you.
2. Classify each changelog item into one of three groups: new feature (new capability), improvement or fix (something that worked poorly or in a limited way and now works better), or breaking change (requires user action, breaks compatibility, or deprecates something). Discard anything purely internal with no visible effect (refactors, technical debt): it does not belong in the notes.
3. Translate each item from technical cause to user effect. "Fixed a race condition on save" becomes "Resolved the error that duplicated records when saving twice in a row". For non-technical audiences remove jargon, module names, and ticket IDs; for technical audiences keep the necessary detail but lead with the impact.
4. Draft an opening summary of 1 to 3 sentences with the most relevant highlights of the release, headed by the name, version, and date.
5. Order the body in three sections with headings (New Features, Improvements and Fixes, Breaking Changes), from highest to lowest impact within each one. Omit a section only if it is empty.
6. In Breaking Changes, state each migration step or required action as an actionable instruction: what to do, on what, and by when if there is a deadline.

Write each item in 1 or 2 sentences, with verbs in present or present-perfect tense, in neutral professional English. No emojis, no empty superlatives, no commercial promises or price mentions. Deliver the document in publication-ready Markdown and close by noting what additional data would make the notes more precise.

prompts.title: Clear internal policy or procedure
prompts.content: Act as a senior writer of internal policies and procedures, expert in plain language, document governance, and normative technique (must / may / must not). I need to convert a vague intent — currently held in a few people's heads and interpreted differently in every case — into an internal policy that anyone in the covered audience can read once and apply without doubts. Before writing, restate in your own words what policy I am documenting, who it applies to, and what behavior it seeks to regulate; present a brief plan and wait, or continue with marked assumptions. Ask for anything missing and do not invent rules, sanctions, deadlines, or legal obligations: if I have not given you a piece of data, mark it [ASSUMPTION] and propose a reasonable value. Deliver the document with these seven fixed sections in this order: 1) Purpose, in 2 to 3 sentences, opening with an anchor phrase such as 'This policy defines how [what] for [purpose], and applies to [audience]'. 2) Scope, explicitly stating which situations, roles, and areas are included and which are excluded. 3) Definitions, only for terms that admit more than one interpretation; skip the obvious ones. 4) Rules, written with the correct normative verb (must / may / must not), one idea per sentence, observable behaviors (who does what, when, with what evidence), and no ambiguities such as 'when appropriate' or 'reasonably' without a defined criterion; respect any applicable superior rule. 5) Exceptions, each with the activating condition, who authorizes it, and how it is documented; none left open. 6) Owners, named by role (policy owner, day-to-day enforcer, and escalation contact) and Effective Date and Review (effective from when and how often it is reviewed). 7) A checklist of 5 to 8 yes/no questions that allow anyone to confirm whether a concrete situation complies with the policy or not. Before closing, test that checklist against two edge-case situations and adjust any rule that remains open to two interpretations. Write in neutral professional English, no emojis, no prices, no use of the word free; leave the document ready for review and publication. The EstrategIA here is the rigor of plain language applied to a real operational rule.

prompts.title: Guided learning tutorial
prompts.content:
Act as a senior technical writer specializing in learning documentation, trained in the Diataxis model in its tutorial mode: the goal is for the reader to learn by doing and reach a real first achievement, not to consult an exhaustive reference. Before drafting, apply the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. Restate in two or three lines what you understood (topic, tool, final achievement, reader level, and available time) and present your step plan before writing the tutorial. If any essential data is missing (what is being taught, with what tool, what the final verifiable achievement is, from what starting point the reader begins, or how much time they have), ask for it before continuing; do not invent assumptions about the environment or about tool versions.

Produce a complete guided tutorial in Markdown, ready to publish and reproducible from start to finish without external assistance. Structure it as follows: (1) Title plus a promise phrase declaring in one line what the reader will know how to do when finished and the estimated time; (2) Prerequisites: exact list of what is needed (tools, versions, access, minimum knowledge) and, for each one, how to confirm in under a minute that it is ready before starting; (3) Numbered steps, one per action, where each step includes the single action, a literal copyable command or instruction, one sentence explaining why it matters, and an observable verification describing what the reader should see on screen to know it worked; (4) Common errors: two or three of the most frequent, each with its exact symptom and its fix, located next to the step where they usually occur; (5) Close: confirmation of the achievement reached and the next natural learning step.

Decompose the path to the final achievement and discard everything that does not contribute to that first achievement. Break the path into steps of a single action and a single new concept, ordered so that each step depends only on what has already been explained. Do not use any term, command, or concept that has not been introduced before. Write in second person (you), short sentences, active voice, in neutral English. Mark any missing data as pending confirmation rather than inventing it. Close by declaring how the reader can verify for themselves that they completed the tutorial.

prompts.title: Feature reference documentation
prompts.content:
Act as a senior technical writer specializing in API documentation and developer experience, with a docs-as-code approach and OpenAPI standards. I need a reference documentation entry for a function or endpoint, aimed at its reader audience. Why it matters: a precise reference unlocks integrations without support tickets, reduces usage errors, and accelerates adoption; an ambiguous or invented-data reference causes production failures and erodes trust, so accuracy takes precedence over apparent completeness.

Produce, in this order: (1) a one-line summary stating what it does and when to use it; (2) the full signature or route with method or verb, required authentication, and content-type; (3) a parameters table with name, type, required/optional, default value, validation constraints, and description; (4) detailed behavior: flow, edge cases, idempotency, side effects, rate limits, and pagination if applicable; (5) response schema with the structure and meaning of each field, including format (JSON, XML) and success status codes; (6) at least two complete executable examples (request and response) covering a success case and a boundary case, with plausible data consistent with the parameters table; (7) an error catalog in table form with code or status, cause, message, and actionable resolution.

Accuracy rules: do not invent names, values, defaults, or codes. If a verifiable piece of data is missing (signature, type, default, error code), ask me before continuing. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] plus justification anything you infer by convention. Each parameter in the table must appear in at least one example; each error in the catalog must be triggerable by a specific input. If there is versioning or lifecycle status (deprecation, beta), declare it.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what function or endpoint you are documenting and what data is missing, present your plan for the 7 sections, and only then execute. Neutral professional English, no emojis. Deliver in Markdown ready to publish on the documentation portal.

prompts.title: Architecture Decision Record (ADR)
prompts.content:
Act as a senior software architect with experience writing Architecture Decision Records in the style of Michael Nygard and the MADR format. Your goal is to produce a complete, concise ADR ready to version alongside the code in docs/adr/, that preserves the why of a decision when the team rotates, avoids relitigating what is already closed, and makes the architecture auditable.

Proceed as follows:
1. First restate the assignment in one sentence: "Document the decision to [decision] versus [alternatives], in state [proposed/accepted/superseded/deprecated]". If you have not received the specific decision, the problem context with its forces in tension, at least two real options to compare (including the chosen one), and the ADR status, ask me for exactly those details before drafting. Do not invent technical data, performance figures, or technology names I have not given: mark with [ASSUMPTION] any claim I have not confirmed.
2. Title: a numbered line in imperative naming the decision, such as "ADR-NNN: Adopt X". If you do not know the sequence number, use ADR-NNN and let me know I should assign it based on the last ADR in the repository.
3. Status: record the status with its date in ISO format (YYYY-MM-DD). If this ADR supersedes or is superseded by another, link it explicitly ("Supersedes ADR-005", "Superseded by ADR-012").
4. Context: explain the problem and the forces in tension (performance, cost, maintainability, deadlines, available talent, risk, compliance, lock-in) in neutral prose, without blame and without anticipating the decision. The reader should be able to arrive at the decision independently from the context.
5. Considered options: list at least two alternatives, including the discarded one, each with honest and balanced advantages and disadvantages; do not present straw men to inflate the chosen option.
6. Decision: state the chosen option in active and affirmative voice ("We will use…", "We will adopt…"), with the justification explicitly tied to the forces in the context.
7. Consequences: separate into three blocks the effects that become true after adopting the decision: positive, negative, and neutral. Explicitly name the accepted technical debt, new dependencies, and actionable follow-ups (tasks, migrations, dependent future decisions).

Use neutral professional English without filler; active voice; no emojis. Deliver a single self-contained Markdown document, one to two pages, ready to save as docs/adr/ADR-NNN-<slug>.md and version. Close by noting what additional data would make the ADR more solid or auditable.

prompts.title: Changelog in Keep a Changelog format
prompts.content:
Act as a technical documentation maintainer and release manager expert in Keep a Changelog 1.1.0 and Semantic Versioning (SemVer). I will give you the version number to publish, the release date, a raw list of changes (commit messages, PRs, loose notes), the reader audience, and whether I want to keep an [Unreleased] block. If any of those details are missing, ask me before drafting and do not invent content.

Produce a changelog block in Markdown ready to paste into CHANGELOG.md following this method. First interpret and restate what you understood, and present your plan before executing. Then triage: read each item in the raw list and label it in ONE single canonical category (Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed, Security); group duplicates and isolate ambiguous ones. Then draft each item as a brief impact-oriented sentence for the audience, in a consistent verb tense, without commit hashes or internal jargon. Assemble the sections in the exact canonical order Added > Changed > Deprecated > Removed > Fixed > Security, discarding all empty sections. Fix the version heading as '## [VERSION] - DATE' with a valid SemVer and ISO 8601 date. If I want to keep the [Unreleased] block, prepend an empty '## [Unreleased]' at the top plus the Keep a Changelog and SemVer adherence line. Mark breaking changes with a bold prefix and warn about compatibility when the version is 0.y.z or a major increment.

Verify before delivering: correct section order, valid SemVer, ISO date, zero empty sections, each item in one single category. Mark as {to_confirm} anything you cannot classify with certainty and ask about it instead of inventing. Deliver the Markdown block and, separately, the list of {to_confirm} items if any.

prompts.title: Canonical terms glossary
prompts.content:
Act as a senior terminologist and information architect with experience in document governance, product ontologies, and the terminological principles of ISO standard 1087. Your goal is to build a canonical glossary that unifies the language of a team or product and serves as a single reusable source of truth, not a list of improvised definitions.

Proceed as follows:
1. First restate the assignment in one sentence: "Unify the language of [team or product] by extracting terms from [sources] for [audience who will consult it]". If you have not received the team, product, or domain to unify, the sources from which to extract terms (documents, tickets, product copy, transcripts, repos), the audience who will consult the glossary (business, engineering, support, or mixed), and who will be the default owner when the source does not indicate one, ask me for exactly those details before starting. Also ask whether there are priority terms to define first.
2. Go through the sources and list candidate terms with their frequency and variants, flagging those used inconsistently or with conflicting definitions.
3. Draft each entry with: canonical term, category or domain, definition in a single self-sufficient and non-circular sentence, expanded description only if it adds value, usage context (when it applies and when it does not), accepted synonyms, confusable or prohibited terms with redirect to the canonical, a real example of correct use, owner, and status (proposed, under review, or approved).
4. Do not invent terms or definitions: anything without support in the sources goes marked [PENDING] with the partial source that exists, never filled in. Mark with a visible note [CONFLICT] each disputed definition, citing the sources that clash, so a human can resolve it; you expose the conflict, you do not resolve it.
5. Calibrate technicality to the audience: if mixed, define in business language and add a separate technical note. Treat acronyms as an entry under the abbreviation with a redirect to the expanded term, deprecated terms with status "under review" and redirect to the current one, and polysemous terms as separate numbered entries that are disambiguated.
6. Order alphabetically and close with a version control table (version, date, change, owner) and a numbered list of pending decisions.

Before drafting the complete glossary, restate what you understand and show me your extraction and normalization plan; execute only when I confirm.

prompts.title: Textual description of a flow or process to accompany a diagram
prompts.content:
Act as a senior technical writer specializing in business process documentation, with experience translating BPMN diagrams, flowcharts, and swimlanes into navigable text that anyone can follow without seeing the image. I need the textual description that accompanies the diagram of a process, because the diagram alone is not enough: there are readers who will not see the image, accessibility requirements, audits, or an operational handover where the text is the source of truth. The risk to avoid is a document that is ambiguous, leaves decision branches without a destination, or invents steps the team does not execute.

Before drafting, restate what you understand about the process and present your plan. If you are missing any essential data (process name, steps and their sequence, triggering event, responsible roles or swimlanes, decision points with their branches and exceptions, or who reads the document and for what purpose), ask me for it in a single round before continuing; do not invent steps, systems, or owners.

Deliver the description in this order: (1) A one-paragraph summary explaining what the process does, who triggers it, and what result it delivers at the end, at the detail level appropriate for the audience. (2) Start and actors: the single explicit trigger and the list of responsible roles or swimlanes; if systems or teams participate, name them. (3) Numbered sequential steps, each with an action verb at the start, a stable identifier (P1, P2...), who executes it, what input it receives, and what it produces. (4) Decisions: for each decision point, state the exact question being evaluated and describe all possible branches indicating which step each one leads to; no output is left without a destination and conditions must be mutually exclusive and exhaustive. (5) Exceptions and errors: what happens if a step fails, is rejected, times out, or exits the happy path, and how the flow is rejoined, escalated, or terminated. (6) End: the closing condition or event; if there are multiple endings (success, rejection, cancellation), enumerate them. Close with a list of gaps and assumptions to confirm with the process owner.

Working method in three phases. Phase 1 Mapping: order the information into trigger, steps, decisions, exceptions, and end; assign owners; mark as [ASSUMPTION] any step or transition you infer to close a logical gap. Phase 2 Drafting: write the text in one-to-one correspondence with the diagram, action verb at the start of each step, stable identifiers that a reader can cross-reference with the nodes. Phase 3 Verification: walk through the text as if it were the diagram and confirm that each node has a sentence, each decision has all its branches with a destination, there are no orphan steps or broken references (P-x mentioned but non-existent), and list the open questions.

Closing criterion: summary answering what-who-what it delivers; single trigger; each step with identifier, verb, owner, and output; each decision with question and all branches with destination; exceptions with their rejoining or end; end declared and multiple endings enumerated; one-to-one correspondence with the diagram with no nodes without a sentence and no orphan steps; inferred steps or transitions marked [ASSUMPTION] and zero elements invented outside the input; detail adjusted to the audience and text navigable without the image. Neutral professional English, no emojis or prices.

prompts.title: Quick-start guide (quickstart)
prompts.content: Act as a senior technical writer specializing in developer experience and adoption documentation, with the judgment to separate the essential from the accessory in a first contact. I need a single-happy-path quick-start guide (quickstart), without branches, ready to publish, that takes a new reader to their first tangible and verifiable result before they lose momentum. Before drafting, tell me what product we are documenting, who the reader is and their starting level, exactly what the first verifiable result is, within what maximum time window it must be achieved, and what prerequisites exist; if I do not have that data, ask me. Deliver in Markdown: (1) a one-sentence promise declaring what the reader will have working and in how much time; (2) prerequisites as a checklist, each item verifiable in seconds, without long installations disguised as prerequisites; (3) between three and seven numbered steps, one single action per step, in second person and present tense with an action verb at the start, each with its exact command or instruction ready to copy and the expected output that confirms progress; (4) an unambiguous and observable final success signal; (5) a failures section with the two or three most likely real stumbling blocks and their direct solution; (6) a single next step to go deeper, not a menu. Cut any branching, advanced configuration, or alternative option to the end as a note or eliminate it. Estimate the seconds for each step and confirm that the sum fits within the target window; if it does not, cut steps or defer detail. Mark any assumption with the {to_confirm} tag. One idea per sentence, no theory or filler. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Persuasive commercial proposal
prompts.content: Act as a senior B2B commercial proposal consultant with experience in consultative selling and persuasive writing aimed at decision-makers. I need a services proposal ready to send, structured in five blocks: (1) Diagnosis that accurately reflects the prospect's situation and pain in their own terms, not generic ones; (2) Solution that describes the service approach and traceably connects each element to the diagnosed pain; (3) Scope that details deliverables, phases, and assumptions, explicitly delimiting what is inside and what is outside; (4) Value that articulates the expected impact toward the business outcome in terms of time, risk, capacity, and quality, without mentioning prices or the word free; (5) Next step, a single concrete and low-friction call to action. Before drafting, restate what you understand about the prospect, the pain, the service, and the sought outcome, and present your plan. Mark everything not confirmed with [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent data, figures, or decision-maker names. If you are missing the recipient, the main pain, the service, or the sought outcome, ask me before continuing. Deliver in neutral professional English, no emojis, with crisp sentences and impact verbs.

prompts.title: Cover letter tailored to the job posting
prompts.content:
Act as a senior career coach and expert cover-letter writer with fifteen years of helping professionals get past filters and land interviews in competitive processes. Your job is not to restate my CV in prose: it is to demonstrate, in the first seconds of reading, the concrete fit between what the company asks for and what I have already achieved. I need a cover letter ready to send plus a short variant for form fields or email bodies.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. Before writing, restate in your own words which role and company I am applying to and what evidence of mine is strongest; present your plan; execute only after.

Ask for whatever is missing before writing: the role and company, the job posting or position description, my background (CV, experience, or achievements), and optionally the tone or perceived culture of the company and my specific reason for interest. If I do not have the posting, do not invent requirements: ask me for it, or work with the signals I give you and flag them as assumptions.

Proceed as follows: (1) Requirements mirror: extract from the posting 5 to 8 real requirements or signals (key responsibilities, competencies, tools, problems to solve, tone and culture) and classify each as essential or desirable. (2) Evidence mapping: pair each essential requirement with one of my achievements in compressed STAR form (situation, task, action, result), quantified when a real figure exists. Every essential requirement without genuine evidence is a gap that you must list separately — never invent data to fill it. (3) Write the letter in AIDA structure, 4 to 5 paragraphs and 250 to 400 words: a hook that names the role and shows why this company and not another; a body that proves the fit with 2 or 3 achievements mirrored to essential requirements; a value-proposition paragraph linking my contribution to a declared company goal or problem; a professional close with a call to action and availability for interview. (4) Adjust register and vocabulary to the company's tone. (5) Produce the short variant in 3 paragraphs (hook, fit, close).

Firm rules: do not invent employers, dates, or metrics; flag every unverifiable figure or achievement as an assumption. Neutral professional English, no filler clichés (nothing like 'I am the ideal candidate' without proof). Prioritize attacking the essential requirements of the posting first. Deliver: the final letter ready to send, the 3-paragraph short variant, and the gap list for me to confirm.

prompts.title: Professional biography in three lengths
prompts.content:
Act as a senior personal-brand and executive-biography writer, skilled in synthesis and third-person voice for public profiles. I need three versions of my professional biography, derived from the same core and mutually coherent, plus a per-channel usage note.

First, restate the identity core you understand (who I am, what problem I solve, for whom, and with what proof) and declare the positioning angle and the two or three achievements you will prioritize; flag any inference as an assumption. If you are missing my name as it should appear, my current role or title, two or three verifiable achievements, or the primary audience, ask for everything in a single batch and stop until I respond.

Then write in descending order, preserving the core message and key verbs:
1. HALF PAGE (150–220 words, third person): opening with positioning, body with trajectory and achievements, close with current purpose or focus.
2. PARAGRAPH (50–80 words): preserves positioning and the strongest proof; must stand alone as a speaker profile.
3. ONE LINE (15–25 words): role plus distinctive value plus audience, with no filler; must fit in a signature or podium footer without trimming.

Hard rules: do not invent titles, figures, awards, dates, or affiliations; use only the achievements I provide. Do not mix first and third person. Neutral professional language, no emojis. Close with a usage note assigning each version to a specific channel and a warning about what to update when a data point changes. Deliver a block with the three labeled biographies and the usage note, ready to copy and paste.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: LinkedIn profile headline and summary
prompts.content:
Act as a senior LinkedIn personal-brand strategist, expert in professional positioning, conversion copywriting, and optimization for the LinkedIn internal search engine and for recruiters. Your assignment is to optimize my headline and my About summary so I appear in the right searches and so the audience I care about decides to read me and contact me.

Before writing, you need from me: my current role or the one I am aiming for, the sector and industry I compete in, the audience I want to attract (recruiters, clients, peers, or investors), three to five achievements with a verifiable metric or context, and my areas of domain and key skills. If you like, also tell me the desired tone (approachable, executive, or technical) and share my current profile or CV; if not, assume neutral executive tone and flag it. If anything is missing or ambiguous, ask me everything in a single batch and do not invent data.

Proceed as follows: first map the real language of the sector and the search intent of the audience (what terms does someone who searches for me actually type). Define the value proposition with the formula "I help [audience] achieve [result] through [differentiator]" as the core of the headline and the hook. Then draft three headlines of up to 220 characters each, where you can read for whom I work, what problem I solve, and what makes me different; mark one as recommended with one line of justification. Draft the About in 3 to 5 short paragraphs: a hook on pain or aspiration in the first line, a body that links my achievements to my specialties, and a close with a call to action without artificial urgency. Close with a prioritized keyword list to reuse in the headline, experience, skills, and job titles.

Verify before delivering: every achievement must be supported by what I gave you and be traceable; flag every inference as [ASSUMPTION]; replace sensitive data with placeholders such as {city} or {contact}. Neutral professional language, no emojis, no empty corporate jargon, no unsupported adjectives; integrate keywords organically, never as a forced list inside the text.
