Edge cases: if a receipt has low probability, project it in its realistic scenario and declare the assumption; if a payment date falls on a weekend or holiday, state the shifting criterion; if data only permits a partial projection, deliver what is possible and flag the gaps. Deliverable: a 13-week dated forecast table plus an executive liquidity summary (minimum cash, alerts, 3 levers, critical assumptions) in neutral professional English, ready for committee or a financing conversation.

prompts.title: Maintain a 12-month rolling forecast
prompts.content: Act as a Senior FP&A Analyst expert in P&L rolling forecasts, driver-based modeling, and variance analysis with bridges/walks. I maintain a continuous forecast that always looks 12 months ahead: each month that closes stops being a projection and becomes actual, I release that first cell, add a new month at the end of the horizon, and rebuild the projections with what I just learned. This avoids the cliff effect of a fixed annual budget, captures in the run-rate what the close just taught us, and separates transitory noise from permanent changes. Proceed as follows. First, roll the window: mark the just-closed month as actual, reorder the horizon to 12 contiguous periods, and declare which is the new month 12 entering. Second, calculate the closed-month variance line by line (revenue, COGS, gross margin, OPEX by block, EBITDA): actual minus projected, and decompose each deviation into price, volume, mix, timing, and one-off; classify each effect as permanent (moves the future run-rate) or transitory (does not). Third, re-project the remaining 11 months and the new month from each line's drivers, not by inertia: apply the corrected run-rate and known forward-looking events; no line without an explicit driver or assumption. Fourth, build the NTM walk (next 12 months) from the previous forecast to the new one, quantifying each movement by cause (carryover from the close, driver changes, new month entering, management decisions) so that the sum explains exactly the delta, with no residual. Fifth, close with an executive read: the new number, the forecast bias per your precision history, live risks and opportunities, and assumptions requiring validation. Do not invent figures: when a data point is missing (actual figures from the close, current forecast, line-level drivers, known events, precision history) ask for it before calculating and label every estimate as an explicit assumption. Verify that in each month revenue minus COGS equals gross margin and gross margin minus OPEX equals EBITDA. Deliverable: 12-month rolling P&L table flagging actual vs. projected, close variance table with decomposition and permanent/transitory label, NTM walk table, list of drivers and assumptions by line, and a 6-to-8-line executive close. Neutral professional Spanish, no emojis.

prompts.title: Project revenue bottom-up by pipeline
prompts.content:
Act as a Senior FP&A Analyst specializing in pipeline revenue forecasting: probability-weighted bottom-up models, revenue recognition, and scenario analysis. I need a reliable, auditable revenue forecast that supports cash, hiring, and commercial target defense decisions. The method is bottom-up: rather than extrapolating a trend, I sum opportunity by opportunity from the pipeline, weight each one by its real close probability, and assign it to the period according to its close date and payment terms.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First, restate what you understand about the pipeline, the horizon, the granularity, and the scenario criteria; present your calculation plan; then execute. If essential data is missing (amount, probability, close date, payment terms, or the horizon/granularity), ask for it before calculating: do not invent figures or dates.

Proceed as follows:
1. Normalize the pipeline: for each opportunity validate identifier, amount, close probability (0–100%), funnel stage, and expected close date. Label with [ASSUMPTION] every inferred data point and with [VERIFY] every figure the business must confirm. Detect duplicates, out-of-range probabilities, past-due dates, or stages inconsistent with the stated probability.
2. Calculate the weighted value per opportunity (amount × probability) and prorate recognition according to payment terms: single payment on the close date, monthly recurring from the close, or by milestone on their respective dates. State the rule applied when the source is ambiguous.
3. Aggregate by period according to the chosen granularity (monthly or quarterly), covering the full horizon; sum the weighted values whose recognition date falls in each period.
4. Build three scenarios from the same pipeline by changing only declared thresholds: conservative (high-probability or final-stage only), base (full probability-weighted), and optimistic (includes early-stage opportunities with a smaller discount). State the criterion for each.
5. Report a forecast table by period with the three lines, the highest-impact opportunities (top drivers), key assumptions, concentration risks (one opportunity or client dominating a period), and pipeline gap signals (periods below the implied target).

Close: deliver the forecast table, top drivers, assumptions and limits, concentration risks, and a follow-up strategy with the pipeline refresh cadence and re-forecast triggers. Verify that the sum of weighted amounts by period equals the horizon total before closing.

prompts.title: Project revenue top-down by market
prompts.content: Act as a CFO/FP&A Director with experience in B2B go-to-market models and in validating forecasts before investment committees. Build a top-down revenue projection by scenarios for the market I will specify, over the horizon and granularity we define, defensible before a committee. Before calculating, restate the assignment and present your plan; if an essential input is missing (market size, ticket, or delivery capacity), ask for it instead of inventing it. Proceed as follows: (1) Size the TAM > SAM > SOM funnel, justifying and citing the origin of each cut by geography, segment, and fit; label as [ASSUMPTION] any figure without a source. (2) Set the target share over the SAM and trace a non-linear adoption curve with a slow start — never a simple proportional ramp. (3) Apply a capture rate that discounts real funnel losses (unqualified leads, unclosed opportunities, sales-cycle effect), not the direct share. (4) Convert the captured quota to revenue via ticket or ARPA, incorporating recurrence and churn if the model is subscription-based; separate new revenue from recurring. (5) Cross the revenue against delivery capacity: if the forecast exceeds it, mark the break-even point, cap it at the deliverable level, and report the capacity gap. (6) Deliver three scenarios (conservative, base, optimistic) with their differential assumptions, isolate 3–5 highest-sensitivity levers, and declare risks and the concrete condition that would invalidate the forecast. Return the step-by-step traceable calculation, the forecast capped to what is deliverable, and a log of assumptions and risks.

prompts.title: Forecast demand with time series
prompts.content: Act as a Senior Demand Planning Analyst (S&OP) with expertise in time-series forecasting and classical decomposition. I need to project the future demand of a product or aggregate from its historical series to make a concrete inventory, capacity, or purchasing decision with a basis — not by intuition: the value is not the number, it is the decision it enables. Proceed as follows. First, ask me for the period-by-period historical series, its frequency (daily, weekly, or monthly), the projection horizon, any known events (promotions, holidays, launches, stockouts), and the decision that depends on the forecast; if anything critical is missing, ask before modeling. Second, diagnose the series: length, gaps, zeros, outliers, level shifts, and questionable data, which you will flag explicitly and treat before modeling (do not model on dirty data). Third, decompose the series into trend, seasonality, and residual; fix the seasonal period and decide whether seasonality is additive (constant amplitude) or multiplicative (amplitude that grows with the level), and justify the choice. Fourth, select the smoothing method consistent with the pattern: moving average or simple exponential smoothing if there is no trend or seasonality, Holt if there is trend, Holt-Winters if there is trend and seasonality; explain why that method and not another. Fifth, project each horizon period with low, mid, and high bands derived from the residual dispersion (not from free estimates), and translate the interval into a coverage recommendation. Sixth, validate with backtesting on a holdout of the last periods and report MAPE, MAE, and over/under-forecast bias; if the error is high, say so honestly and propose an alternative method or more data. Seventh, deliver a forecast table, numbered assumptions, model limits vs. uncaptured events, and a re-forecast plan with cadence and triggers. Truthfulness rule: every number comes from the provided series or is labeled [ASSUMPTION] with its rationale; never invent figures. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Measure and improve forecast accuracy
prompts.content: Act as a Senior FP&A Analyst specializing in forecast accuracy and demand planning, with expertise in forecast error metrics (MAPE, MPE, MAD, WAPE, tracking signal). Your objective is to produce a forecast accuracy diagnostic with an iterative improvement plan, useful for the monthly FP&A close and the projection model review. Steps: (1) Cleanse the forecast-vs-actual historical series: confirm forecast-actual pairs by period, flag periods where the actual is zero, gaps, and outliers; when the actual is zero exclude them from the MAPE and report them separately with WAPE, declaring it as an assumption. (2) Calculate by period and in aggregate: MAPE = average |actual – forecast| / |actual|; WAPE = sum|actual – forecast| / sum|actual| (robust when actuals are small); MPE = average (actual – forecast) / actual to read directional bias; MAD = average |actual – forecast|. (3) Calculate tracking signal = signed cumulative error / MAD and flag if it exceeds +/–4 (bias out of control, requiring recalibration). (4) Interpret the bias sign: positive MPE = forecast understates reality, negative = overstates. (5) Decompose the error across available dimensions (business line, region, volume vs. price) to locate where it concentrates. (6) Isolate the top 3 error sources (optimistic bias, poorly captured seasonality, unmodeled events, data lag, product mix) with explicit numerical evidence. (7) Propose model adjustments prioritized by expected error reduction, aligned to the accuracy target, each with its validation metric for the next cycle. Never invent missing data: if missing, declare it and propose how to capture it. Report amounts in the indicated currency (default COP). If any critical data (series, granularity) is missing, ask for it before executing. Deliver: error table by period + aggregate metrics block with its read + decomposition by driver + top 3 error sources + iterative improvement plan. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Project expenses by run-rate and commitments
prompts.content: Act as a Senior FP&A Analyst expert in OpEx forecasting by run-rate, contractual commitments, and headcount planning with fully-loaded cost. I need to project the expenses of a unit for a future period with a figure that is defensible before management or a committee — not a back-of-the-envelope estimate: the idea is to transform the historical expense of a recent, stable base period into a forward-looking forecast built in layers (what is already running, what is already signed, and what is about to be added). Before calculating, restate the task in one sentence naming the unit, the projected period, the base period, and the output periodicity; if the detailed base expense, signed commitments, or hiring plan is missing, ask for it and do not invent figures or contracts. Then proceed as follows: (1) calculate the base run-rate using only the recurring costs of the base period, separate and exclude one-offs declaring it so, and normalize to the target periodicity; (2) incorporate contractual commitments by adding only the portion that falls within the projected period, prorating start and end dates at mid-period and applying contractual escalations; (3) model new hires with fully-loaded cost (salary plus payroll taxes and benefits) and a ramp per start date, so that a role starting mid-period only contributes the remaining months; (4) apply known adjustments (salary increases, renewals with price changes, confirmed departures, inflation escalation) and label [ASSUMPTION] where no data was given; (5) add a contingency buffer as its own line (suggested range 3–8% of variable OpEx) justifying the percentage; (6) present the forecast in a table by category and sub-period separating base run-rate, commitment delta, hiring delta, adjustments, and contingency, with row and column totals that tie; (7) reconcile the bottom-up total against the simple annualized run-rate, decompose the delta (= commitments + hires + adjustments + contingency), and declare the three assumptions that most move the total with their approximate sensitivity. Work in the currency and periodicity I indicate, in neutral professional Spanish. Do not include selling prices or commercial rates: this is an internal expense projection. Close by flagging the main risk that the forecast comes in short or over and what data would resolve it.

prompts.title: Model headcount and labor cost forecast
prompts.content: Act as a Senior FP&A Director specializing in workforce planning and fully-loaded personnel costing. I need a month-by-month labor cost forecast model that supports the annual budget, validates the growth plan, and detects cash pressure before committing to hires — separating the inertial cost of the current headcount from the incremental cost of growth. Before calculating, confirm the horizon, start month, currency, jurisdiction, and completeness of the hiring plan, payroll taxes, and attrition rate; if an essential data point is missing, ask for it and never invent rates, benefits, or market prices. Label every estimate not provided as [ASSUMPTION] with its justification. Then: (1) normalize the hiring plan into cohorts (role, positions, base salary, start month) and consolidate payroll taxes, statutory contributions, and benefits by component; (2) calculate beginning-of-month and end-of-month active headcount and average FTE, reflecting staggered hires, mid-period proration of the start month, and departures from attrition; (3) apply a salary or productivity ramp where one exists and model attrition with its replacement, coverage lag, and recruiting cost per vacancy; (4) calculate the fully-loaded labor cost by month, quarter, and total horizon, broken down by component (base, taxes, benefits, bonuses, recruiting) and separating existing headcount from new hires; (5) run base, optimistic, and conservative scenarios by varying the hiring pace and attrition rate, quantify the cost and cash delta, and identify 3 to 5 actionable findings for the budget. Deliver a monthly cost table with breakdown, the headcount curve vs. plan, the three-scenario comparison, and the findings, in neutral professional Spanish. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Adjust forecast for seasonality
prompts.content:
Act as a Senior FP&A Analyst specializing in financial planning and seasonality modeling. Your deliverable is a seasonalized monthly forecast table reconciled exactly to the annual total. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

First ask for any missing data and do not calculate with gaps: the annual total to distribute (with currency and year), the monthly historical series covering at least one complete cycle (ideally 2 to 3 years of the same twelve months), and, if applicable, any fixed costs to treat as linear, and whether cost seasonality mirrors revenue seasonality or follows its own pattern.

First validate the quality of the historical data: month coverage, gaps, zeros, negative values, and clearly atypical years (non-recurring events such as a one-time sale or a temporary closure). Flag with [ASSUMPTION] every inferred data point and propose excluding or adjusting the atypical year, explaining the impact before continuing.

Then calculate the seasonal index for each month using the ratio-to-moving-average method: divide each month's value by the average monthly value of its same cycle and average that ratio across the available years. Normalize the indices so they average 1 (sum to 12) and correct the rounding deviation in the highest-weight month. Apply the indices to the total to obtain revenue and cost for each month; leave fixed costs as linear and seasonalize only the variable component. If costs follow their own pattern, derive a second set of indices using the same mechanics. Reconcile that the sum of the twelve months equals exactly the annual total and show the tie-out adjustment if any. Calculate the monthly margin and flag peak and trough months.

Deliver a 12-row-plus-totals table with columns month, normalized index, revenue, cost, margin; add a brief note with the method applied, assumptions, excluded years, peak and trough months, and a warning if the historical data is insufficient to sustain the pattern.

prompts.title: Define re-forecast triggers
prompts.content:
You are a Senior FP&A Director with experience in rolling forecasts, monthly closes, and variance governance, accustomed to defending thresholds before a committee and a board. Design a re-forecast trigger policy that distinguishes normal noise from structural signal and prevents the forecast from becoming a historical document rather than a decision tool for cash, costs, and investment.

Before proposing any figures, ask for what is missing: the business model and expected volatility by line item, the horizon and cadence of the current forecast, the metrics to monitor, the currency, the critical line items, any existing deviation tolerance, and the roles available to detect, validate, and approve. Do not invent historical data or volatility figures; label everything you assume as an explicit assumption.

Deliver the policy with: (1) A metrics monitoring map, each metric with its reading frequency (daily, weekly, monthly) and comparison base (vs. plan, vs. current forecast, vs. same period prior year). (2) Quantitative triggers: thresholds in percentage and absolute value, separating the point deviation for the period from the year-to-date accumulated deviation, each threshold linked to its rationale (historical volatility, materiality relative to the result, irreversibility of the associated decision) and with a persistence rule to avoid triggering on a single outlier. (3) Qualitative or event-based triggers that require a re-forecast regardless of the number: loss of an anchor client, regulatory change, FX shock, merger or acquisition, pricing change, rupture of a base assumption. (4) A three-level severity matrix — watch / partial re-forecast of the affected line / full re-forecast — each level with who detects, who validates, who approves, and by what deadline. (5) A step-by-step activation protocol, from detection to publication of the revised forecast and stakeholder communication, with an auditable log (date, metric, deviation, decision, responsible party). Close by running 2 to 3 test scenarios showing each trigger firing or not, verifying that no threshold generates trivial false positives or blindness to real breaks.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

Rules: no prices or free-of-charge promises; neutral professional Spanish; every figure not provided labeled as an assumption. Deliverable: policy document ready for committee review.

prompts.title: Calculate SaaS unit economics
prompts.content: Act as a Senior SaaS Finance Analyst specializing in unit economics, with experience in revenue quality due diligence and cohort-level CAC/LTV models. I need to know whether the unit economics of my SaaS are sustainable: whether each customer returns more value than it costs to acquire and serve, and how long it takes to recover the acquisition investment. Build a unit economics model with a health verdict following these steps. First, normalize the inputs: make the currency, the period analyzed, and — above all — churn and gross margin explicit as decimal fractions consistent with a monthly horizon; if any data point is missing, ambiguous, or inconsistent (for example, sales and marketing spend without the period, or annual churn mixed with monthly ARPA), ask for it and do not invent figures. Second, calculate CAC as sales and marketing spend divided by new customers in the same period, and clarify whether it is blended or fully-loaded CAC. Third, calculate the monthly contribution margin per customer as monthly ARPA multiplied by gross margin. Fourth, calculate LTV as monthly contribution margin divided by monthly churn, indicate the implied customer lifetime equal to one divided by churn in months, and offer the discounted LTV variant if the horizon is long. Fifth, calculate the CAC payback as CAC divided by monthly contribution margin, in months. Sixth, derive LTV:CAC and, where data exist, NDR, GRR, logo churn, Magic Number, and Rule of 40, and segment by cohort or segment. Seventh, benchmark each metric and issue an actionable verdict. Show each formula with its substituted figures before each result. Label every own estimate as [ASSUMPTION] and never invent market figures. Handle edge cases: if churn is zero or near zero, declare LTV unbounded and use an explicit cut-off horizon; if the contribution margin is negative, declare infinite payback and suspend the LTV calculation. Warn explicitly when a blended average may hide a value-destroying cohort. Deliver a table with CAC, contribution margin, LTV, payback, and LTV:CAC, the segmented calculation, the benchmark comparison, and a verdict with two or three prioritized levers by impact. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Calculate and interpret the LTV/CAC ratio
prompts.content:
Act as a senior unit economics and growth finance analyst. I need a diagnosis of the LTV/CAC ratio to decide whether to scale customer acquisition investment. I want to know whether every unit invested in acquiring customers is recovered and multiplied, or whether I am buying growth that does not pay for itself.

Before calculating, ask me for the six base inputs if I have not provided them: average ticket per customer, purchase frequency and its time horizon, gross margin as a percentage, churn or retention rate (clarifying which one), total marketing and sales spend for the period, and new customers acquired in that same period. Do not invent any data; every estimate is labeled [ASSUMPTION] with its justification.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliver in this order: (1) list of inputs received and missing; (2) LTV calculation with the chosen formula visible and explained (margin-over-churn cash-flow model, or average lifetime 1/churn times margin depending on the model), validating temporal consistency between frequency, churn, and horizon; (3) CAC calculation as acquisition spend divided by new customers; (4) LTV/CAC ratio and CAC payback in months; (5) interpretation against ranges (below 1 destroys value; 1 to 3 is a tight zone; near 3 is healthy; above 5 may indicate underinvestment) crossed with payback; (6) sustainability verdict with 3 prioritized levers (margin, retention or churn, CAC efficiency) and their expected effect on the ratio. Always show the substituted figures, not just the result.

prompts.title: Calculate the CAC payback period
prompts.content:
Act as a senior unit economics and FP&A analyst for recurring-revenue businesses, with a commercial capital efficiency mindset. Calculate how many months it takes each customer to return, via gross margin, what it cost to acquire them, and do so for every combination of segment and channel, not only at the aggregate level. CAC payback is the liquidity test of growth: it reveals how much capital remains tied up per customer and for how long, which defines where to scale investment with confidence, where to optimize before scaling, and where to stop because the customer never pays off within a reasonable horizon.

Proceed as follows: first confirm that you have the four essential data points (acquisition cost for the period, new customers in the same period, monthly revenue per customer, and gross margin percentage); if any is missing, ask for it before calculating instead of inventing it. Also confirm period, currency, cost attribution basis by channel, and whether margin is uniform or varies by segment; mark everything estimated as an explicit assumption.

For each segment-channel cell calculate: CAC (attributable acquisition cost divided by new customers in that cell and period), monthly contribution per customer (monthly revenue times gross margin), and payback. If contribution is flat, payback = CAC divided by monthly contribution. If you have a retention or variable contribution curve by cohort, do not force an average: accumulate contribution month by month and report the first month in which the cumulative equals or exceeds CAC; if it is not reached within the cash-flow horizon, flag that cell as non-recovering.

Assign a health flag to each cell: healthy up to 12 months, under observation between 13 and 18, at risk above 18 or when it does not recover within the horizon. Close with three prioritized recommendations (what to scale, what to optimize before scaling, what to stop) and the two highest-impact levers on payback among raising margin, lowering CAC, raising ticket, or improving early retention, justifying why those two move the needle most. Before executing, restate what you understood and present your plan. Deliver a table by segment-channel with columns CAC, monthly contribution, payback in months, and health flag, followed by recommendations and levers, in neutral professional Spanish, with no invented figures.

prompts.title: Calculate contribution margin by product
prompts.content:
Act as a senior financial controller specialized in unit economics and product costing, with the ability to distinguish variable from fixed costs and to translate numbers into mix decisions.

My goal is to read the true profitability of my portfolio beyond gross sales: how much each product contributes to covering fixed costs and generating profit. With that I decide what to push, what to reformulate on price or cost, and what to discontinue.

Proceed as follows:
1. First confirm that you have, per product: name or code, net unit selling price (excluding pass-through taxes), unit variable costs, volume for the period, and the analysis period. If any of these five data points is missing, ask for them in a brief list before calculating; do not invent figures or fill in with industry averages.
2. Classify each cost component as variable (scales per unit: raw materials, commissions, freight, packaging, transactional costs) or fixed (for the period: rent, base salaries, software). Justify in one line why it scales or does not scale per unit. Leave fixed costs out of the unit calculation and noted separately; if a cost is semi-variable, separate the fixed portion from the variable portion and declare the assumption.
3. Calculate per product: unit contribution margin = unit price minus unit variable cost.
4. Calculate the contribution ratio = unit margin / unit price, as a percentage.
5. Calculate the total contribution for the period = unit margin x volume.
6. Sort the portfolio from highest to lowest total contribution and flag products with a negative ratio (they destroy margin on every sale) or below the minimum acceptable threshold if you give me one.
7. If a bottleneck resource exists (machine-hours, m², person-hours), recalculate the priority by contribution per unit of that resource, not just by ratio: the most profitable product per unit of scarce resource often differs from the one with the highest ratio.
8. Issue three to five actionable mix decisions (push, reformulate price or cost, discontinue) with their estimated impact on aggregate contribution and the assumption supporting each estimate.

Mark with [ASSUMPTION] every figure or classification not supported by data I have provided. Verify that unit margin × volume reconciles with the total contribution for each row. Use neutral, professional language, without embellishments. Warn that contribution margin is not net profit: it does not include fixed costs or income taxes.

prompts.title: Calculate the operating break-even point
prompts.content: Act as a senior financial controller specialized in unit economics and cost-volume-profit analysis (CVP model). I need to know the exact operating threshold of my business: the minimum volume of units and revenue where I stop losing and start gaining, plus the distance separating me from risk. Deliver an operating break-even analysis following this order. First validate the data: if the unit variable cost is greater than or equal to the unit price, stop and warn that no break-even is possible (negative or zero contribution margin); if an essential data point is missing, ask for it before calculating. Second, calculate the unit contribution margin (price minus variable cost) and the margin ratio (unit margin over price). Third, calculate the break-even in units (fixed costs divided by unit margin, rounded up to the next whole number because fractions of a unit are not sold) and in revenue (fixed costs divided by margin ratio). Fourth, if you give me reference sales, calculate the safety margin in units, in currency, and as a percentage. Fifth, build three scenarios (pessimistic, base, optimistic) by adjusting price, variable cost, and fixed costs, recalculate the break-even in each, and identify which lever moves it the most. Show every formula with its numeric substitution step by step. Label every assumption with [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent figures: what is missing remains as a pending variable. Work in neutral currency, without assuming market prices. If you do not have the data (unit price, unit variable cost, fixed costs for the period, horizon, and optional reference sales), ask me for them first. MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Close with a three-line executive reading: required volume, distance from risk, and dominant lever.

prompts.title: Model unit economics of a marketplace
prompts.content: Act as a senior financial analyst expert in unit economics of two-sided marketplaces: effective take rate, per-transaction costing, and cross-subsidies between supply and demand. I have a marketplace with an aggregated P&L that hides the unit truth: I do not know whether each transaction gains or loses, nor how much one side finances the other to sustain liquidity. Modeling the unit economics reveals the effective take rate I actually capture after incentives, exposes which variable costs each side absorbs, and shows the direction of the subsidy between both sides, in order to activate the right levers (raise take rate, cut the incentive that does not retain, lower a variable cost) before scaling volume and multiplying burn. Produce: (1) Unit and scope: declare the transaction as the unit of analysis, name the two sides (supply and demand), and list what revenue and what cost touches each side and what is shared. (2) Take rate: gross take rate (marketplace revenue over value per transaction) and effective take rate (after incentives), broken down into supply commission, demand commission, and other revenue. (3) Cost per transaction: disaggregate each variable cost, assign it to the side that originates it or to the shared portion (with an explicit proration criterion), and total it, with no orphan costs. (4) Contribution: contribution per transaction total (effective revenue minus variable costs) and contribution per side (revenue of the side minus attributable costs and incentives of the same side), declaring how you split the shared portion. (5) Cross-subsidy: make explicit whether one side operates with a negative contribution financed by the other, quantify the subsidy per transaction, indicate its direction (who finances whom), and point to the unit break-even with the lever that closes it and the magnitude of the adjustment; sensitize with the volume mix if you have it. (6) Sensitivity: show how total contribution moves when the dominant lever is varied across a reasonable range. (7) Model risks and open questions for validating it. Mark every inference with [ASSUMPTION] and never present an estimate as a closed fact. If you are missing the value per transaction, commissions by side, variable costs, or incentives, ask me for them before modeling. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Deliver tables (unit economics with gross and effective take rate; per-transaction costs classified by side and shared; total and per-side contribution), one explicit cross-subsidy line with amount and direction, the unit break-even with its lever, a mini sensitivity, and the list of open questions. Do not mention selling prices or use the word for something unpaid; neutral, professional language, no emojis.

prompts.title: Build unit economics for an ecommerce order
prompts.content: Act as a senior unit economist specialized in ecommerce profitability and per-order contribution models. Build the true unit economics of an average order in my store: gross margin on COGS misleads me because it ignores fulfillment, returns, and the gateway, which silently erode every sale. Proceed as follows. First, before calculating, restate what you understand and present your plan; if an essential data point is missing (average ticket, product cost, fulfillment cost, return rate, or gateway commission) ask for it before continuing. Work in generic currency or percentages and never invent market prices. Step 1, net revenue: start from the average ticket, subtract effective discounts and coupons, and separate the shipping charged to the customer from the shipping subsidy the store absorbs. Step 2, variable costs, quantify four families per order: (a) COGS as a percentage of price or by SKU mix; (b) fulfillment: pick-pack, packaging, last-mile, and prorated storage; (c) expected return cost, applying the return rate to the reverse logistics cost, reconditioning, and non-recoverable product, not just the unit case; (d) gateway: percentage commission plus fixed fee per transaction. Step 3, contribution: subtract variable costs from net revenue and express the contributive margin in value and as a percentage of net revenue. Step 4, derive the sustainable CAC ceiling (remainder for CAC and fixed costs), and indicate how many orders are needed to cover a fixed-cost block if I give you a reference figure, marked as ASSUMPTION if assumed. Step 5, sensitivity table: vary return rate, product mix, and shipping subsidy, and show the point where contribution turns negative. Step 6, prioritize the 3 highest-impact levers on margin with their estimated effect and a trade-off for each. Mark every estimate without a data source as ASSUMPTION and declare it at the end. Deliverable: line-by-line order decomposition table, contributive margin in value and percentage, CAC ceiling, sensitivity table, and block of 3 prioritized levers.

prompts.title: Analyze profitability by customer
prompts.content: Act as a senior financial controller specialized in customer profitability and cost-to-serve, with expertise in activity-based costing (ABC) and contribution margin. I need to see the true profitability of each customer in my portfolio for the period I indicate, because total billing hides the fact that a minority of accounts generates the bulk of the margin while another segment destroys it through discounts, support, small orders, returns, and long payment terms. Proceed as follows. First, inventory and validate the data by customer (net revenue, direct costs, and operating volume) and the pool of costs to serve to be assigned; separate structural non-assignable costs to avoid distorting margins and list for me any gaps and inconsistencies. Second, assign each component of the cost to serve using ABC logic, declaring for each one its driver, its rate (cost per driver unit), and its basis, with no black boxes, and verify that the total assigned sums to the full pool. Third, build the cascade by customer: net revenue minus direct cost equals gross margin, minus assigned cost to serve equals contribution margin, in value and percentage. Fourth, sort customers from highest to lowest by accumulated margin to trace the whale curve, identify the maximum-margin point, and tell me what percentage of customers concentrates 100% of the margin. Fifth, classify the portfolio into four segments (Core, Gems, Cost-to-Serve, Drain) with an explicit cut-off criterion, and deliver a prioritized action plan by recoverable margin with the lever per account (renegotiate, surcharge out-of-contract services, consolidate orders, migrate to self-service, de-scale, or exit), its estimated impact, and its effort. Before recommending exiting an account, contrast its strategic or future value. Never invent figures: mark every estimate as [ASSUMPTION] and ask me for any critical missing data before calculating. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: first restate what you understood and present your plan, then execute. Neutral, professional language, no emojis, no market prices or promises of free service. Deliver a customer profitability table, whale-curve reading, four-segment matrix, and prioritized action plan, ready for committee.

prompts.title: Compare profitability by sales channel
prompts.content: Act as a senior Finance and Operations Director specialized in multichannel unit economics and go-to-market design. I need to compare the true profitability of my sales channels (direct, partner, digital, or others) to make a concrete channel mix decision for a defined period. Today I decide the mix by intuition or gross revenue, without seeing the net contribution margin each channel leaves after cost-to-serve and acquisition costs. Before calculating, restate what you understand and ask for any missing data: per channel I need revenue for the period, number of customers or transactions, and known costs; the cost structure of variable, cost-to-serve, and acquisition costs indicating which are shared; the analysis period; the decision the exercise enables; and, if available, customer lifetime value or retention by channel. Then proceed as follows: 1) attribute revenue to each channel and allocate costs in three layers (direct variable, per-channel service/fulfillment cost, per-channel acquisition/commissions); for any shared cost declare the proration basis and mark it as an assumption. 2) Calculate per channel: revenue, total variable cost, absolute and percentage contribution margin, cost of acquisition per customer, and if lifetime-value data is available, LTV/CAC ratio and payback period. 3) Build a comparative table sorted by percentage margin and describe a waterfall of each channel's contribution to total margin. 4) Identify the most profitable channel by margin, the highest-volume channel, and the most acquisition-efficient channel, and make the tensions among them explicit. 5) Recommend the go-to-market mix reallocation with quantitative rationale, its sensitivity if proration assumptions change, and two risks of the move. Rules: work only with provided figures, never invent numbers, mark every estimate as an assumption with its basis, reconcile channel margins against the total, and flag the investment break-even where a channel stops being worthwhile. Close with one actionable sentence ready for committee.

prompts.title: Analyze retention and revenue cohorts
prompts.content: Act as a senior SaaS finance and RevOps analyst specialized in unit economics and revenue cohort models. I need to understand the true quality of my customer base beyond gross growth: I want to group customers by sign-up date into cohorts, follow them over time, and separate new from retained revenue to see whether recent cohorts retain better or worse than older ones and detect revenue leaks that acquisition conceals. Proceed as follows. First, validate the data integrity: confirm that a sign-up date per customer exists, recurring revenue by period, observation period, and a clear definition of active customer; if any is missing, ask for it before calculating and never invent figures. Second, declare the conventions you will use: source currency and periodicity, revenue normalization (MRR or ARR), how you treat reactivations, upgrades, downgrades, prorations, and customers with zero revenue but an active contract. Third, build the cohort matrix (rows = sign-up cohort, columns = tenure periods 0, 1, 2, …) and calculate per cell the logo retention (active over initial) and the revenue retention (revenue for the period over initial cohort revenue); mark as immature the cells with few observed periods and do not project them as a trend. Fourth, separate gross retention (GRR: only churn and contraction, capped at 100%) from net retention (NRR: includes expansion) and make the formula and basis of each explicit. Fifth, decompose the revenue movement of each period into opening base plus expansion minus contraction minus churn (revenue bridge) and verify that it reconciles against observed revenue. Sixth, identify the period at which the logo curve stabilizes and estimate average customer lifetime with its explicit logic. Seventh, compare the NRR of recent mature cohorts against older ones and triangulate with GRR to distinguish whether health comes from low leakage or from expansion that masks growing contraction. Close with three actionable findings and a warning if NRR falls below 100% or the health threshold. Respect the data currency, mark every estimate as an assumption, do not invent results or discuss prices. Deliver readable tables and a brief narrative of the underlying retention-expansion-acquisition strategy.

prompts.title: Build a financial KPI tree
prompts.content:
Act as a senior FP&A Director who builds driver trees for executive committees. I need a KPI tree that decomposes my north-star financial metric from its accounting formula all the way down to the operational KPIs that an area can actually move, and a prioritized lever table to act within the horizon I define.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate the north-star metric and its formula, confirm which data I have and which is missing, and present the tree plan; only then execute.

Proceed as follows:
1. Confirm the north-star metric and write its exact accounting formula.
2. Level 1: arithmetic components directly derived from the north-star metric (additions/subtractions).
3. Level 2: decompose each component into its drivers (e.g., revenue = volume × price; cost = units × unit cost).
4. Levels 3–4: drill down to controllable operational metrics for the sector (conversion, shrinkage, days outstanding, occupancy, churn, average ticket).
5. For each node declare the formula, the mathematical relationship with the parent node (addend, factor, divisor), and the owning area.
6. For each leaf driver mark the direct or inverse relationship with the north-star metric and its relative elasticity (high/medium/low) with the rationale.
7. Deliver a table of 3 to 5 highest-leverage levers: KPI, owner, formula, base value, concrete action for the horizon, and warning signal with threshold.

Rigor rules:
- The tree must be arithmetically consistent: every node reconstructs exactly from its children up to the root; if a residual component does not reconcile, declare it as an 'other/reconciliation' node instead of forcing the close.
- Do not mix volume, price, and mix drivers within the same node: separate them so the lever is unambiguous.
- Do not invent figures; every estimate is marked [ASSUMPTION] with its calculation basis.
- If a node has more than one owner, name the primary owner and note the shared responsibility.

If the north-star metric, the sector and business model, the base figures, or the period are missing, ask me for them before proceeding. Deliver the hierarchical tree (root to leaves) plus the prioritized lever table.

prompts.title: Define the North Star metric and support system
prompts.content: Act as a senior management-control analyst specialized in designing metrics systems for growing companies, with mastery of the North Star Metric framework and input/output metrics trees. I need a single North Star metric that aligns all teams around the real value delivered to the customer and predicts sustainable growth, along with its support metrics tree, ready to take to a control dashboard. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, and Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. First (Interpret) confirm the business, its revenue model, its stage, what is understood by value delivered to the customer or aha moment, and the available data sources; if any data is missing, ask me for it instead of inventing it, and mark as [ASSUMPTION] everything you assume. Then (Plan) propose 2 to 3 North Star candidates and evaluate each against five criteria: reflects customer value, predicts future revenue, is actionable, is measurable with available data, and resists cosmetic manipulation; present that matrix before committing to a recommendation. Finally (Execute) deliver: (1) a single recommended North Star with an exact operational profile (one-sentence definition, numerator, denominator, time window, segment, measurement frequency, and initial threshold or target if there is a baseline); (2) a tree of 3 to 5 input metrics that a specific team can move, each with its causal relationship to the North Star, suggested owner, and action lever; (3) 2 to 3 health counter-metrics (guardrails) that prevent optimizing the North Star at the expense of quality, margin, or retention; (4) at least 3 vanity metrics named with their reason for discard. Close with a note on how to instrument this in the dashboard and what to review in each cycle. Do not mix brands, do not give prices or use the word free, write in neutral and professional Spanish without emojis.

prompts.title: Design a Balanced Scorecard
prompts.content:
Act as a senior management-control and strategy consultant, trained in the Balanced Scorecard by Robert Kaplan and David Norton (HBR, 1992; The Balanced Scorecard, 1996) and experienced in designing strategy maps and KPI systems. I need to translate the strategy of my unit into a measurement system that connects day-to-day work with the underlying objectives, avoiding a dashboard of loose, unbalanced KPIs.

Proceed as follows.
1. Framing: restate the strategy as a verifiable intent sentence, confirm the unit to measure, the horizon, and the review cadence, and inventory existing KPIs to avoid duplication. Mark every piece of undelivered data as [ASSUMPTION].
2. Build the four perspectives bottom-up in this order, to ensure the causal chain: Learning and growth (capabilities, talent, culture, systems), Internal processes (the critical processes where the organization must excel), Customer (value proposition, satisfaction, retention, share, acquisition in target segments), and Financial (economic results that materialize the strategy). Each perspective carries 2 to 4 objectives phrased as verb plus focus.
3. For each objective deliver: indicator (KPI) with formula or calculation method; type — leading or lagging; quantified target or marked [ASSUMPTION] with the explicit assumption; measurement frequency; owner or responsible role; and at least one initiative or lever. Balance leading and lagging indicators: not all KPIs can be outcome measures.
4. Trace the strategy map: cause-and-effect relationships in text from learning to financial, showing how each objective in one layer enables one in the layer above, with no orphan objectives.
5. Close with 3 to 5 measurement risks (gameable or manipulable KPIs, poorly calibrated targets, indicators without owners, cobra effect, substitution of the target for the real objective) and their mitigation.

Do not invent prices or market figures; anything unverifiable goes marked [ASSUMPTION] with its assumption. If you are missing the strategy, horizon, customer segments, or inherited KPIs, ask before building.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliver one table per perspective (objective, KPI, type, target, frequency, owner, initiative), the cause-and-effect strategy map in narrative form, and a measurement-risks block with mitigation, ready to take to a management committee.

prompts.title: Translate financial strategy to OKRs
prompts.content:
Act as a fractional CFO and financial OKR designer, with mastery of financial planning (FP&A), the distinction between outcome metrics and levers, and the OKR discipline (qualitative objective + measurable Key Results, committed vs. aspirational). Your job is to translate a strategic financial objective into an executable OKR set for a quarterly cycle, so that the financial strategy stops being a board sentence and becomes the quarter's dashboard: every area knows which number to move, from what baseline, to what target, and by when.

First restate what you understand (objective, baselines, horizon, owner, ambition, and constraints) and present your plan; execute only afterwards. If the financial objective, the baselines with unit and period, the horizon, or the owner are missing, ask for them in a single batch before continuing and do not invent figures: every number you do not receive from the user goes marked as [ASSUMPTION] with the explicit assumption.

Deliver, in this order: (1) 1 to 3 directional, memorable qualitative Objectives with no numbers, aligned to the horizon. (2) For each Objective, 2 to 4 Key Results written as 'increase from X to Y by [quarter end date]', taking X from the baselines with their unit; each KR measures a single metric and is an outcome, never a task. (3) Explicitly separate the outcome KRs (margin, days of cash, MRR, CAC, collection ratio, DSO) from the levers or initiatives that drive them, and list the levers separately as bets that support each KR. (4) Calibrate each KR as committed or aspirational according to ambition and constraints, with a line justifying why the target is ambitious but achievable from the baseline; avoid sandbagging and impossible targets. (5) Assign each KR a single owner, a named data source (system or report), and a review cadence; if a KR is not measurable with existing data, declare it as a measurement risk instead of feigning precision. (6) Review that the set is coherent and non-contradictory: detect KRs in tension (e.g., grow revenue vs. improve margin vs. protect cash) and name them. (7) Close with a coherence check (if all KRs are met, is the strategic objective achieved?) and the 2 or 3 main execution risks with their early warning signal.

Rules: maximum 4 to 6 committed KRs per owner to make focus real; every numerical target comes with unit and date; use neutral Spanish, professional tone, no emojis or filler; do not include price figures or guaranteed-return promises. Deliverable: the OKR set in clean blocks (Objective, then Key Results with baseline, target, owner, source, cadence, and label, then associated levers), a summary table of all KRs, and the coherence check with gaps and risks.

prompts.title: Define operational KPIs with SMART criteria
prompts.content:
Act as a senior operations controller expert in balanced scorecards and data governance. Your task is to design a catalog of actionable operational KPIs, validated against the SMART criteria and ready to take to a dashboard, for an area and process we will define.

I first need to know: the area or operational unit, the key process to measure, the business outcome that the indicators must move, the available data sources (systems, tables, reports), the dashboard review cadence, and, if they exist, already agreed targets or benchmarks. If you are missing the area, the process, the business objective, or the data sources, do not assume: ask for them before continuing.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Proceed as follows: (1) restate the scope and objective in your own words and confirm sources and frequency. (2) Derive the indicators backwards from the business objective, traversing the outcome > process > input chain, and discard any metric that does not change a decision. (3) Propose between 5 and 8 prioritized KPIs and, for each one, complete a profile with: name and business question it answers; definition in one sentence; explicit formula with numerator and denominator; concrete data source; measurement frequency; data owner and action owner; target and green/yellow/red thresholds; unit and direction (whether higher or lower is better). (4) Validate each profile against the five SMART attributes (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) and, where any fails, write the suggested correction. (5) Avoid the cobra effect: for each KPI name a counter-measure or balancing KPI that prevents optimizing the number at the expense of another dimension (quality, cost, risk). (6) Flag instrumentation gaps: if a datum does not exist today in the sources, say so and propose how to capture it.

Mark with [ASSUMPTION] every target, threshold, source, or frequency you estimate without confirmed data. Close with a master KPI table, the detailed profiles, and a list of assumptions pending confirmation. Professional Spanish, no prices.

prompts.title: Create a metrics dictionary
prompts.content:
Act as a Head of FP&A with experience in data governance, management control, and designing corporate data dictionaries. Your task is to build a metrics dictionary that serves as the single source of truth for the area or business we will document: when every metric has a canonical definition, an explicit formula, and an owner, data disputes end and committees return to deciding instead of arguing about who has the correct number.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate which area, which metrics, and which source systems you understand; if you are missing the list of metrics, the source from which to extract them, the systems and areas of origin, the temporal granularity, or the candidate owners, ask me for them in a single batch of specific questions before proceeding. Do not invent data.

Execute in four phases. Phase 1 Inventory: list candidate metrics, group them by domain, and flag duplicates and contradictory definitions; if the metric is not given explicitly, derive it from reports and committees. Phase 2 Definition: write one profile per metric with canonical name plus aliases; business definition in one unambiguous sentence; explicit formula with each component named and its source system; unit, granularity, and allowed slicing dimensions; inclusion and exclusion criteria (what DOES and what DOES NOT enter the numerator and denominator); edge cases (returns, discounts, refunds, currency and FX conversion, taxes, nulls, late records, duplicates); calculation window and historical restatement policy; business owner and data owner; update frequency, availability latency, and authoritative source; data confidence level; and a solved numerical example that validates the formula. Every definition must be falsifiable against real data; mark each assumption with [ASSUMPTION] and each missing item as a question, never fill it in. Phase 3 Reconciliation: for each conflict record both versions, recommend the canonical one with justification, and leave the decision pending ratification by the owner. Phase 4 Packaging: deliver a master table (metric | definition | formula | business owner | data owner | source | frequency) plus the detailed profiles and a versioned change log.

Deliver in neutral and professional Spanish, without emojis. Close by confirming that each profile meets the checklist and that no data was invented.

prompts.title: Design an executive financial dashboard
prompts.content: Act as a Chief Financial Officer (CFO) with experience in management control, FP&A, and executive reporting. Design the complete specification of a single-page financial dashboard that the committee reading it can review in less than five minutes and use to decide, not merely to be informed, ready to build in a spreadsheet or in a BI tool, plus a text mockup of the layout. Before executing, ask about any missing data: type of business and revenue model, who reads and decides with the dashboard, reporting currency and units, periodicity and cut-off date, targets or KPI thresholds, and the decisions the dashboard must enable; do not set thresholds without knowing the model, the currency, the period, and the targets. Proceed in five phases. First, select between 8 and 12 critical KPIs, derived from the decisions to enable and grouped in four blocks: Profitability (e.g., revenue, gross margin, EBITDA, net margin), Liquidity and cash (available cash, operating cash flow, runway in months, days receivable), Growth (year-on-year and sequential revenue variation, new customers or contracts), and Efficiency (acquisition cost, revenue per employee); discard any metric that does not change any decision and avoid double-counting between blocks. Second, for each KPI define the exact formula, unit in the reporting currency, data source, data owner, and update frequency; when a KPI is a ratio, explicitly declare numerator and denominator. Third, set target value, yellow alert threshold, and red critical threshold with the traffic-light rule (including whether the favorable direction is ascending or descending) and, where it adds value, a tolerance band; mark with [ASSUMPTION] every target or threshold you propose for lack of data. Fourth, design the trends block: recommended visualization per KPI (line for series, bars for comparisons, sparkline for micro-trend) and a time window consistent with the period; distinguish trend from noise and flag any expected seasonality. Fifth, specify the alerts panel: list only the deviations that cross a threshold, ordered by severity (red before yellow), each with a probable cause, an actionable suggested decision, and, when known, an action owner. Define the layout of the single page (header with period, owner, cut-off date, and currency; visual hierarchy top-to-bottom: alerts and cash first, then profitability and growth, efficiency at the bottom) and close with a text mockup. Deliverable: KPI profile table, traffic-light logic, trends block, alerts panel, and layout mockup. Do not invent real data: leave value cells as placeholders and mark every assumption. If a target is unviable or a KPI is not measurable with available sources, say so and propose an alternative. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Structure a real-time operational dashboard
prompts.content: Act as a senior operations director expert in management control, operational KPI design, command-and-control dashboards, and statistical process control (traffic-light bands and escalation rules). I need to structure a real-time operational dashboard that converts a workflow into a bounded set of metrics with alert thresholds, so the team can see at a glance whether operations are running normally or need intervention today. Before executing, tell me which operational area, daily decision, candidate metrics, cadence, reference thresholds, and data sources you assume; if you are missing an essential datum, ask for it rather than inventing it. Deliver, in this order: (1) the process restated in one sentence as 'Monitor [process] for [daily decision it enables]'; (2) 5 to 8 metrics classified as leading or lagging, each with a one-line operational definition, unit, and formula, explicitly discarding those that do not trigger an action; (3) per metric, the desired direction (more is better / less is better) and three threshold bands green/amber/red, marking [ASSUMPTION] for those with no historical basis; (4) per amber and red band, a concrete action, a named owner by role, and a deadline, plus the logic for when a sustained amber escalates to red; (5) update and reading cadence per metric and the source of each number, flagging instrumentation gaps; (6) the dashboard layout in a table, with metrics actionable today at the top and context metrics below, identifying the '10-second glance' of 3 metrics; (7) a stale-data control (what happens when a number has not refreshed for more than X time) and a note on what the dashboard does NOT measure. Respect three limits: a metric is not actionable if nobody changes behavior when they see it cross a threshold; a threshold without a historical basis is a hypothesis, not a fact; and a dashboard without an alert owner is decoration. If two metrics measure the same thing or one is a linear function of the other, consolidate and explain why. Deliver in neutral Spanish, professional tone, in a table. Protocol: first restate what you understood and present your plan; then execute.

prompts.title: Define traffic lights and alert thresholds
prompts.content: Act as a senior financial controller expert in management control and scorecard design with a RAG (Red-Amber-Green) alert system and KPIs under the SMART principle. I want to move from a dashboard that only shows numbers to a control system that alerts by itself and dictates the reaction: the color decides, the owner acts, and the escalation is triggered without debate. I need you to define an actionable traffic light for each of my indicators. Proceed as follows: (1) Normalize each indicator by confirming formula, unit, direction of improvement (whether higher is better or worse), and the reference against which it is compared (target, budget, objective band, or previous period); if an indicator has no clear reference, you cannot set a traffic light for it, so flag it and ask me for the datum. (2) Set two cut-points per indicator, green-yellow and yellow-red, expressed as deviation from the reference, consistent with the direction of improvement and with my risk tolerance; justify each cut-point and avoid arbitrary numbers. (3) Ensure the three ranges cover the entire domain with no gaps or overlaps and explicitly declare the treatment of border values (to which color the exact cut-point value belongs). (4) Define the transition rule for each state including persistence (e.g., two consecutive periods in zone) to filter false alarms, and distinguish a one-time crossing from a sustained deterioration. (5) Assign each state a predefined action, an owner, and a deadline; red must include an explicit escalation path. (6) Assemble a table with columns indicator, unit, direction, target or reference, green range, yellow range, red range, transition rule, owner, frequency, and action per state, plus a summary of the 3 to 5 indicators that would currently be in red or yellow and a governance note on when and how thresholds are recalibrated. Work according to the MetodologIA Protocol: first restate what you understood and present your plan, then execute. Do not invent figures: mark every missing datum as an explicit assumption. If you are missing information on indicators, references, direction of improvement, or risk tolerance, ask me before continuing.

prompts.title: Structure the monthly management report
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Director of Financial Planning (FP&A) who assembles and defends the monthly management report before the executive committee, with mastery of price-volume-mix variance analysis, management control, and executive narrative. Build the complete monthly management report for the business unit, ready for committee: a document that explains what happened, why it happened, and what will be done about it, not just a table of figures. A well-structured report turns the review meeting into decisions; poorly done, it triggers a number hunt with no conclusions.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. First restate which period, which unit, which comparatives, and which decision is at stake; if the baseline, the period, the materiality threshold, or the detail of a line item are missing, ask before calculating. Do not invent figures: every absent figure is marked as an explicit assumption and is not mixed with real data.

Deliver six sections: 1) Executive summary, maximum five bullets with the month's verdict on revenue, gross margin, EBITDA, net income, and cash, each with its figure and key variance. 2) Results table for the material P&L lines with columns Actual, Budget, Absolute variance, Variance %, Prior year, and Variance vs. prior year. 3) Classification of each variance as favorable or unfavorable by its effect on the result and not by its arithmetic sign, flagging those that exceed the materiality threshold. 4) Management commentary that, for the most material variances, separates root cause (price, volume, mix, unit cost, timing, or reclassification), quantified effect, and classification as recurring or one-time. 5) Corrective actions in a table with action, owner, target date, and expected recovery amount, prioritized by impact. 6) Control dashboard with each KPI, its value, target, and traffic light.

Quality rules: decompose variances into price-volume-mix where data exist; verify that the arithmetic closes (sum of line variances = total variance); if a comparative does not exist, declare it rather than assuming it. Note the difference between preliminary and final close. Close with the executive summary as a defensible synthesis figure by figure. Neutral and professional Spanish, no emojis, no service prices.

prompts.title: Analyze budget vs. actual variances
prompts.content: Act as a senior FP&A analyst with mastery of budgetary management control and price-volume-mix decomposition. I will hand you a budget and an actual close for a period for a business unit, and I want a variance analysis that converts the difference between plan and reality into actionable decisions, not a repetition of the numbers. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: first restate what you understand (period, unit, currency, whether there is or is not unit and rate detail to separate effects) and present your analysis plan; only then execute. Deliver: (1) a table by line — revenue, direct costs, operating expenses, and margin — with budget, actual, absolute variance, and percentage variance in the currency of the data, with totals that balance; (2) apply a materiality threshold to flag the variances that matter and aggregate the rest in a single row to avoid diluting focus; (3) classify each material variance as favorable or unfavorable by its impact on the result, not by its arithmetic sign — lower cost is favorable, lower revenue is unfavorable; (4) for revenue and variable costs decompose the deviation into price effect, volume effect, and mix effect, showing the formula for each effect and verifying that the three reconstruct the total variance; (5) for each material variance write a verifiable root cause against the data, not a restatement of the number; (6) close with an executive commentary of at most half a page: top 3 variances by impact, reading of whether the trend puts the annual target at risk, and the next control action for each. Analytic honesty rule: if the data do not allow separating price from volume, say so and deliver the total variance without inventing the decomposition; mark any assumption with [ASSUMPTION] and never invent figures or causes. If you are missing any essential datum — period, unit, plan and actual amounts, currency, or threshold — ask me before executing rather than assuming it.

prompts.title: Decompose variation into price, volume, and mix
prompts.content: Act as a senior FP&A financial analyst expert in price-volume-mix bridge reconciliation. I need to decompose the variation of a metric (a revenue or a cost) between two periods at the appropriate level of disaggregation (SKU, line, segment, or region), separating how much of the total variation comes from the volume effect, the mix effect, and the price effect. Before calculating, tell me what you understand, confirm whether the metric is revenue or cost, validate that you have quantity and price or unit cost per line in both periods, and identify new and discontinued lines; if any data is missing, ask me for it and do not invent figures. Use this convention so the bridge closes without overlaps: Volume Effect equals the variation in total quantity valued at the base period average unit price, keeping the base mix; Mix Effect equals the change in composition valued at base prices, keeping the current total quantity; Price Effect equals the variation in price per line valued at the current quantity. New and discontinued lines are isolated in their own column and are not forcibly allocated to other effects. Deliver, numbered: 1) a bridge table starting from the base metric and summing in order volume, mix, price, and, if applicable, line additions or removals, closing at the current metric; 2) the percentage weight of each effect over total variation and the closing residual if any; 3) the 2 or 3 lines that contribute most to each effect with their contribution; 4) an executive narrative of 3 to 5 sentences naming the dominant lever, correctly interpreting the sign according to whether it is revenue or cost, and proposing the actionable implication. Watch the sign: for a cost, an increase is unfavorable; for revenue, it is favorable. If the three effects plus the additions and removals column do not equal total variation, report the residual and explain its origin instead of forcing the reconciliation. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Implement activity-based costing
prompts.content:
Act as a senior cost controller with experience designing and implementing activity-based costing (ABC) models in manufacturing and service operations. Your objective is to reveal true profitability by product and support a concrete decision, not produce an academic exercise.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the indirect costs, activities, product data, current traditional allocation base, and objective decision; Plan the model in five phases and restate your understanding before calculating; Execute only when the plan is clear.

Phase 0 - Validation: confirm that you have the overhead amount and composition with its period, the activities and their driver candidates, the product data (volume, consumption of each driver, selling price, direct material cost, and direct labor cost), the current traditional allocation base, and the decision to support. If anything is missing, ask before calculating and do not invent figures; mark all assumptions with [ASSUMPTION].

Phase 1 - Design: group activities by cost hierarchy (unit level, batch level, product level, plant support) and assign each overhead pool to its activity so that the sum of pools reconciles with total overhead.

Phase 2 - Drivers and rates: choose one cost driver per activity under the causal resource-activity-product criterion, not mere volume correlation, and calculate the rate per driver = activity pool / total driver volume. When driver volume depends on capacity rather than usage, distinguish practical capacity from used capacity and treat idle capacity cost separately instead of diluting it across products.

Phase 3 - Assignment and costing: distribute overhead to each product according to its consumption of each driver, obtain the fully loaded unit cost (direct + ABC indirect) and the ABC margin per unit and total.

Phase 4 - Contrast: replicate traditional costing with the current single base, compare ABC margin against traditional margin by product, quantify the cross-subsidy, and identify at least one over-costed and one under-costed product under the traditional method. Distinguish material distortions from immaterial ones.

Phase 5 - Decision: translate findings into prioritized recommendations for the target decision (price adjustment, mix recomposition, minimum economic lot size, discontinuation, or renegotiation), each with estimated impact, explicit assumption, and, where applicable, a warning about costs that do not disappear when discontinuing (committed overhead that gets reabsorbed by remaining products).

Deliver an ABC costing report with a profitability table by product (price, direct cost, ABC indirect cost, total cost, ABC margin, traditional margin, delta) and the three highest-impact moves prioritized. Close by noting that it is advisable to validate external or publishable figures before deciding.

If you are missing any essential data, ask before continuing.

prompts.title: Calculate standard costs and their variances
prompts.content: Act as a senior cost controller with experience in manufacturing and standard costing, trained in management accounting under the price/rate plus efficiency/usage framework. I need a standard cost variance analysis for a product or line in a given period. If you have not been given the product, the period, the unit standards (standard material quantity and price per unit; standard labor hours and rate per unit), or the actual data for the period (units produced, material consumed and its cost, hours worked and their cost), ask me before calculating and do not invent any figure. Proceed as follows: Interpret first, restating which product, period, standards, and actuals you understand, listing missing data, and marking every numerical assumption as [ASSUMPTION]. Plan next, presenting the calculation scheme: allowed standard quantity and hours (= actual units times unit standard, never the original budget), the four base variances, the F/U sign rule, and the reconciliation verification. Execute last, showing for each variance the formula and the numerical substitution. Calculate the material price variance = (actual price minus standard price) times actual quantity, and the quantity or efficiency variance = (actual quantity minus allowed standard quantity) times standard price; the labor rate variance = (actual rate minus standard rate) times actual hours, and the efficiency variance = (actual hours minus allowed standard hours) times standard rate. Label each variance as F (favorable, lowers cost) or U (unfavorable, raises it), and verify the reconciliation: price plus quantity equals total material variance, and rate plus efficiency equals total labor variance. Reconcile the sum of all variances against the total cost variance (actual cost minus standard cost of actual production); if it does not reconcile, stop and report the discrepancy before concluding. Deliver a table with columns concept, formula, value, and F/U whose totals reconcile, and close with a management narrative that prioritizes the most significant variances in amount or percentage, assigns each a probable cause and an actionable corrective action, flags any standard that looks obsolete and should be reviewed, and makes explicit any offsetting of a favorable and an unfavorable variance that hides a problem (e.g., cheaper material of worse quality that drives up consumption). Do not sign off on external figures without verification. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Perform cost-volume-profit analysis
prompts.content:
Act as a senior financial analyst in management accounting and cost-volume-profit (CVP) modeling, with experience in pricing decisions, capacity sizing, and profit planning. I need to understand how the operating profit of a product or service line reacts to movements in volume, price, and cost structure, so I can decide with evidence where to move the levers before committing resources or setting targets. The goal is a reusable model that separates what is an assumption from what is verified data.

Before calculating, tell me what data you need and ask for it if missing: the line to analyze and its reference period, the unit price or average ticket, the unit variable cost (or its detail for consolidation), the total fixed costs for the period, the current or expected volume, and the target operating profit if it exists. If any essential data is missing, ask me before continuing; do not invent figures.

Execute as follows: (1) Framing: confirm scope, period, and unit of measurement; list available and missing data. (2) Cost structure: classify each item as fixed or variable; if an item is mixed, separate it with the high-low method, declare the assumption, and consolidate the unit variable cost. (3) Core calculations, showing formula and calculation for each: unit and percentage contribution margin, break-even in units and in revenue, units and revenue for the target profit if applicable, safety margin relative to current volume, and degree of operating leverage. (4) Pessimistic, base, and optimistic scenarios varying volume, price, and costs, plus a double-entry sensitivity table of profit at variations of -10%, -5%, +5%, and +10% in price and in volume. (5) Synthesis: prioritize the 2-3 highest-impact levers and deliver an actionable recommendation.

Mark every datum not provided as [ASSUMPTION] with assumed value and justification; flag its sensitivity when it changes the conclusion. Do not include specific selling prices or promises of free services in the conclusions: reason in variables and percentages. Declare the model's limits (linearity, constant mix, fixed capacity within the relevant range). Deliver a document with formula, calculation, and executive narrative per block, scenario table, sensitivity table, and close with the recommended cost StrategyIA.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Calculate the cost to serve by segment
prompts.content:
I need a cost-to-serve model by segment that goes beyond gross margin. The objective: discover which segments are truly profitable once I subtract what it costs to serve them, and derive defensible portfolio decisions (with whom to renegotiate conditions, whom to migrate to a different channel, whom to protect). Act as a Director of Operational Finance with experience in activity-based costing (ABC) and customer profitability.
