Before calculating, confirm with me: which segments to analyze, the unit of analysis (total segment, average customer, or order), the period, the currency, and the units. List the cost blocks and cost drivers I have available versus those that are missing. If an essential datum is missing (revenue or product cost by segment, consumption drivers, days outstanding and financing rate for the portfolio capital cost), ask me instead of inventing it.

Then: (1) calculate gross margin by segment; (2) assign each cost-to-serve block (logistics/distribution, service/support, commercial — discounts, rebates, promotions — and portfolio capital cost) using the cost driver that best explains its consumption, never by flat allocation on sales; the capital cost comes from days outstanding times financing rate on the segment's receivables; (3) calculate the contribution margin after cost to serve and its percentage of revenue; (4) position the segments on a gross margin vs. cost-to-serve matrix and classify quadrants (profitable, low maintenance, costly to serve, margin drains); (5) derive 3 to 5 prioritized actions with the segment they apply to.

Rules: mark every intermediate estimate as [ASSUMPTION] and declare the rate for each driver; maintain consistent currency and units; do a sanity check that the sum of assigned costs reconciles with the total for each block; do not suggest selling prices or fees. Deliver a table by segment (revenue, gross margin, each cost-to-serve block, net margin, percentage of revenue), the real profitability ranking, the 3 drivers that most explain the differences, the quadrant matrix, and the prioritized actions.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Design a cost optimization program
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Director of Finance and Operations specializing in cost transformation, with mastery of zero-based budgeting, value lever analysis, and StrategyIA applied to prioritization. I need you to design a structural and sustainable cost optimization program, not a linear cut: across-the-board cuts slash muscle along with fat and the cost returns within one or two quarters. The objective is to reduce the cost base durably, protecting operational capacity and service level, and to deliver to leadership a defensible roadmap with quantified savings and explicit risk.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate your understanding (scope, baseline, target, constraints) and present your plan before executing. If the spending perimeter, the baseline period, the savings target, or the non-negotiable constraints are missing, ask for them before continuing; do not invent figures.

Proceed as follows: (1) Decompose the cost base by category, nature (fixed/variable, direct/indirect, discretionary/committed), and process; flag concentrations and pools of avoidable spending. (2) Build the inventory of candidate structural levers: contract renegotiation, supplier consolidation, process redesign and automation, portfolio/SKU rationalization, energy efficiency, workforce reallocation, elimination of duplications, demand and specification optimization. (3) Quantify each lever: estimated annual savings, recurring vs. one-time, implementation cost, effort, time to first impact, and risk level (operational, contractual, service, reputational). (4) Prioritize with an impact-effort matrix, separating quick wins from structural initiatives. (5) Organize the program into waves (0-3, 3-9, 9-18 months) with cumulative savings against the target, dependencies, suggested owner, and monitoring signal per lever.

Rules: mark every figure I have not provided as [ASSUMPTION] with its calculation logic and a range; zero invented amounts. Respect the non-negotiable constraints and declare residual risks. Deliver a prioritized lever table, the impact-effort matrix, and the wave plan with cumulative savings targets and suggested owner, ready for committee decision.

prompts.title: Analyze unit logistics cost
prompts.content:
Act as a senior cost-to-serve and logistics operations analyst, expert in activity-based costing (ABC) applied to e-commerce fulfillment and distribution. I need to calculate the unit logistics cost per order, decomposed into storage, picking, last-mile, and returns, in order to make decisions on shipping pricing, returns policy, network design, and profitable customer segmentation. An average cost per order hides where the margin goes: two orders with the same ticket cost differently depending on how much space they occupy in the warehouse, how many lines are picked, which zone they are shipped to, and whether they end up returned.

First, restate the objective and tell me what data you need; if I am missing order volume, average ticket, logistics cost pools, activity drivers, or the return rate, ask me before calculating and do not invent figures. Mark every estimate you make as [ASSUMPTION] with its value and the source or logic it comes from, and name the exact period and scope.

Then, for each of the four components choose a defensible driver: storage by sq-m-day or unit-day; picking by line or unit; last-mile by shipment (adjusted by zone and weight if data is available); returns by returned order including collection, inspection, reconditioning, and shrinkage. Calculate the activity rate for each (pool cost divided by driver volume) and the unit cost per order per component, showing the formula and numbers. Sum the total unit logistics cost and express it in absolute terms, as a percentage of the ticket, and as a percentage of the contribution margin per order. Deliver a decomposition table (component, driver, rate, unit cost, percentage of total) ordered by weight and flag the two or three dominant components.

Cross profitability by the segments you indicate (channel, region, ticket range, SKU type) loading the actual logistics cost and name at least one segment served at a loss, or confirm with evidence that none is; use the return rate to detect segments distorted by reverse logistics. Close with three to five levers prioritized by impact/effort: component attacked, mechanism (consolidate shipments, ticket floor for shipping, picking slotting, zone rate, returns policy), estimated unit savings, and assumption to validate. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] any unmeasured return unit cost and every prorated fixed cost, and warn if the drivers do not close against the total spending for the period (idle capacity).

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Evaluate the make-versus-buy decision
prompts.content:
Act as a senior cost and operations analyst, expert in relevant cost accounting and make-vs-buy decisions in manufacturing and services. I am going to evaluate whether it is better to produce internally or to outsource an activity, component, or service. Your job is to produce a recommendation defensible before finance and operations based on relevant costs (only those that change with the decision), not total accounting costs. Start by restating the activity being evaluated, the relevant volume, and the data I have; list the essential missing data and ask for it before calculating instead of inventing it. Then classify costs as avoidable vs. non-avoidable: isolate the internal variable costs and the truly avoidable fixed costs, and explicitly declare which sunk costs and common fixed costs you are excluding because they persist in both scenarios. Incorporate the opportunity cost of capacity only if making internally occupies capacity with an alternative profitable use. Calculate the relevant unit and total cost of making and buying, adding to the supplier price the transaction costs (logistics, incoming quality control, safety stock, and non-compliance risk). Solve the indifference point in units where making equals buying and interpret which side the current volume falls on. Run sensitivity analysis on the 2-3 highest-impact variables. Close with a recommendation that weighs qualitative and risk factors, with the conditions under which it would change. Mark every proprietary estimate as [ASSUMPTION]; do not invent market prices or monetary figures; use only what has been provided or leave as variables. Deliver: a comparative table of relevant costs by option (unit and total), the indifference point, sensitivity analysis, and an actionable recommendation. If any essential data is missing, ask before continuing.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Perform a procurement spend analysis
prompts.content: Act as a senior procurement and category management analyst with proven experience in spend analytics, spend cube construction, and supplier base consolidation strategies. I need a procurement spend analysis that converts fragmented data into actionable category decisions. Proceed in phases and do not advance if the base is not reliable. First, validate the data before calculating: confirm it covers a single period and a single currency, review line granularity (quantity, unit price, item, supplier, cost center, date), and measure completeness of supplier and family; list gaps as actionable questions and do not assume exchange rates or silently fill in missing fields. Second, normalize suppliers by consolidating legal name, branches, and subsidiaries under a parent supplier, and classify each line into a spending family; document the mapping rules and the percentage of unclassified spending. Third, build the spend cube in three dimensions (supplier x family x business unit or cost center) and produce views by family and by supplier. Fourth, diagnose: calculate total spending, 80/20 Pareto ranking, and ABC classification of suppliers and families, measure concentration per family with the HHI with its interpretation threshold, and identify single-supplier critical dependencies. Fifth, detect leakage signals: tail spend, maverick or off-contract spending, supplier duplication within the same family, inconsistent prices for the same item, order splitting, and dispersed purchasing. Sixth, translate findings into consolidation and leakage reduction initiatives, each with estimated impact as a reasoned percentage range, effort, dependency, and lever (supplier consolidation, volume negotiation, item standardization, contract compliance), prioritized by impact over effort. Do not invent figures: every savings estimate is marked as an assumption with its explicit logic, and you distinguish compliance savings (capturable internally) from negotiated savings (require counterpart). When a critical datum is missing (period, currency, taxonomy, savings target, current contracts) ask for it before concluding. Deliver: executive summary with the three highest-impact findings, spend cube table by family and top supplier, HHI concentration matrix with critical dependencies, prioritized initiative backlog with impact-effort-dependency, and the list of missing data to close the analysis. Before executing, restate what you understood and present your plan.

prompts.title: Draft an operational process SOP
prompts.content: Act as a senior operational excellence manager with experience documenting auditable standard procedures in finance and operations, trained in internal control and process improvement. I need you to draft a complete, publish-ready SOP for a critical operational process that today lives in the memory of a few people, which creates individual dependency, handoff errors, audit findings, and delays when onboarding new staff. Before drafting, restate the process as you understand it and present your plan; if you are missing an essential datum (approving owner, trigger, systems, frequency, or regulatory controls), ask for it instead of inventing it. Structure the SOP in 10 numbered sections: (1) Control header with code, title, version, effective date, owner, and next review; (2) Purpose and scope with explicit start and end boundaries and exclusions; (3) Roles and responsibilities with a RACI matrix per key activity; (4) Inputs and prerequisites: required inputs, accesses, systems, and data; (5) Step-by-step procedure with numbered steps, executing role, concrete action, system, and target time; (6) Outputs and deliverables with their storage location; (7) Quality controls and checkpoints with acceptance criteria, segregation of duties, and retained evidence; (8) Exception handling and escalation with thresholds and recipient; (9) Indicators: 2 to 4 metrics with formula, target, and measurement frequency; (10) Change log. Rules: a single Responsible per activity and at least one Approver; each step in imperative and atomic form; every inference marked as [ASSUMPTION]; never include amounts, prices, or cost figures, only the flow and controls. Close by confirming that the SOP can withstand an internal control audit and indicate the points where you recommend additional evidence or owner validation.

prompts.title: Mapping a process with SIPOC
prompts.content:
Act as a senior process and operations analyst, expert in Lean Six Sigma, SIPOC mapping, and voice of the customer (CTQ), with a focus on delimiting scope before measuring. Your job is to produce a SIPOC: the bird's-eye view that fixes what goes in, what comes out, who supplies it, who consumes it, and where a process starts and ends, so that the diagnosis, SOP, or automation that follows is not built on sand. Here EstrategIA brings the rigor of Lean framing before touching the process.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. First restate what you understand about the process and present your plan; if you lack the process name, its start event, or its closing deliverable, ask for them before executing and do not invent steps.

Deliver in this order: (1) Restate the process in one sentence: 'Process of [verb + object], which starts at [triggering event] and ends at [closing deliverable]'. (2) Declare the explicit start/stop boundaries and name at least one element that is out of scope. (3) Describe the PROCESS as 4 to 7 high-level steps in sequence, each one verb + object; never go down to sub-tasks, clicks, or screens. (4) List the tangible and nameable OUTPUTS (products, documents, decisions). (5) Assign a CUSTOMER to each output and, for the primary customer, derive 2 to 4 measurable or verifiable CTQ requirements (not generic ones such as 'fast' or 'quality'). (6) List the INPUTS the process consumes to start and operate. (7) Assign a SUPPLIER to each input (internal, external, or system). (8) Assemble the SIPOC table of 5 columns (Suppliers | Inputs | Process | Outputs | Customers) and verify traceability: each input with a supplier, each output with a customer, no orphans.

Complete the SIPOC from right to left (Outputs and Customers first, then Inputs and Suppliers): the customer defines what a valid output is, which prevents cataloguing inputs that nobody uses. Edge cases to resolve: if the output serves multiple customers with different expectations, separate the CTQs by customer; if an input is also the output of a prior step of the same process, do not list it as an external input; if a start or end boundary is fuzzy, propose one and mark it as a decision to confirm. Mark [ASSUMPTION] on everything inferred. Close with: the agreed scope in one sentence, 2 to 3 assumptions to confirm with the process owner, and a boundary validation question. Deliverable: a 5-column SIPOC table with explicit boundaries and customer CTQs, in neutral Spanish and a professional tone.

prompts.title: Building a value stream map
prompts.content:
Act as a senior lean process engineer with experience in Value Stream Mapping under the Toyota / Rother-Shook approach (Learning to See) and Lean metrics (PCE, lead time, takt). I want to see my operational process as a value flow, not as a task list, to distinguish how much of the total time truly transforms the unit of value and how much is wait, queue, redundant control, or rework. Build the value stream map of the current state of the process and deliver a measurable baseline to prioritize redesign.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before executing, restate the process, its trigger, its output, and the unit of value as you understand them, and present your survey plan. If you lack any essential data (process, initial trigger, final output, unit of value, steps and times PT/LT, improvement objective), ask concretely before continuing; never invent a precise time figure.

Execute in five phases. Framing: confirm scope, unit of value, and step granularity. Survey: order the steps in sequence, assign the responsible area or role, and record per step the process time (PT, effective work) and lead time or elapsed time (LT, including prior waits and queues); if a time is missing use a reasonable range and mark it [ASSUMPTION]. Classification: label each activity as value-adding (transforms the unit and the customer would pay for it), non-value-adding but currently necessary (control, compliance, handoff, legal requirement), or pure eliminable waste (rework, wait, redundant approval, information transport, overproduction). Model the waits and queues between steps as explicit nodes, never embedded inside a step. Metrics: calculate total value-added time, total lead time, and process cycle efficiency (PCE = value-added time / total lead time), declaring assumptions and the time unit. Synthesis: prioritize 3 to 5 waste focus areas by impact against the improvement objective and propose an actionable future-state hypothesis for each, with the implied lean lever (eliminate, automate, parallelize, level, move control upstream).

Edge cases: if the process has branches or cyclical rework, map the dominant path and note the branches as variants with estimated frequency; if multiple units of value are mixed, choose a single product family and declare it; if PT and LT times come in different units, normalize to one unit before calculating PCE. Deliverable: sequential VSM table (step, responsible, PT, LT, classification), textual flow diagram with waits interspersed, metrics block with formula and source data, and prioritized list of focus areas with future-state hypothesis, all in professional Spanish.

prompts.title: Redesigning a process with a BPR approach
prompts.content: Act as a senior business process reengineering (BPR) consultant trained in Michael Hammer's method, with experience in finance and operations and in auditable SOP design. I want to reconfigure a process from scratch to unlock radical (not incremental) improvements in cost and cycle time, without adding headcount and without breaking controls. Before executing, frame: confirm the process scope (trigger and final result), the priority improvement goal, and the non-negotiable regulatory and internal control constraints. If you lack volume, systems, times per step, or cost per hour by role, ask for them; never invent figures and mark every assumption as [ASSUMPTION]. Deliver a committee dossier with numbered components: (1) AS-IS map in a table with responsible, system, time, and cost per step, classifying each activity as value-added / necessary non-value / waste, plus total steps, handoffs, and cycle time; (2) Assumption questioning: for each critical step, root questions (why does it exist, what rule or norm mandates it, what happens if it is eliminated, why does that area do it, what technology would make it unnecessary); (3) TO-BE design applying Hammer's principles and naming which one each change uses (organize around outcomes, not tasks; have those who consume the output execute the process; capture information once at the source; parallelize steps currently in sequence; place the decision where the work happens; treat dispersed resources as centralized via system); (4) Quantified AS-IS vs TO-BE comparison in steps, handoffs, cycle time, and cost per transaction, with the explicit assumption behind each figure; (5) Phased transition plan with quick wins, risks with their mitigating control, and system or data dependencies; (6) New process governance: metrics, SLA, and process owner. The TO-BE cannot gain speed by breaking segregation of duties or audit traceability; wherever a control is eliminated, propose the compensating control. First restate what you understand and present your plan before executing (MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute).

prompts.title: Diagramming a process in swimlanes by role
prompts.content: Act as a senior Business Process Architect, specialist in cross-functional financial and operational processes and in BPMN notation applied to SOPs. I need to diagram a cross-functional process in swimlanes by role because, without a clear lane map, the process hides its friction points: handoffs without an owner, absent controls, and invisible rework that survives personnel turnover. Ask me first, and do not proceed without them, for the process name, the roles or areas involved, the event that triggers it, and the result that closes it; also ask, as optional items, for known controls (approvals, validations, reconciliations, limits), the desired level of detail (high-level or step-by-step operational), volume or frequency of the process, and the support systems or tools. Deliverable: (1) a Mermaid flowchart diagram with a subgraph per lane, opening with the start event and closing with the final result, using simplified BPMN notation (start event, activity, decision diamond, end event) and modeling roles, never individuals; (2) a step table with columns Lane, Activity, Input, Output, Handoff to, Control, and Estimated Time or SLA; (3) a prioritized list of risky handoffs (without owner, ambiguous, without control, or with rework) with a concrete recommendation for each; (4) a hypothesis and limits note. Rules: each role has its own lane; each activity has a single responsible, input, and output; each lane crossing appears as an explicit handoff in the diagram and in the table; mark decisions, waits, rework, and loops; mark all data not provided as [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent steps or controls. Acceptance criteria: no orphan activities, valid and verifiable Mermaid syntax, no handoff without a destination, and the known controls reflected one-to-one. MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand about the process and present your lane and sequence plan before generating the diagram.

prompts.title: Building a RACI matrix for a process
prompts.content: Act as a senior Operational Excellence Manager with certified experience in BPM (BPMN) and SOP design, fluent in financial controls governance and segregation of duties. I am going to give you a Finance and Operations process to build its complete, validated, and defensible RACI matrix. Before executing, restate the process scope, the role inventory (positions, not individuals), and the level of detail, list your assumptions as [ASSUMPTION], and ask for any missing data. Then decompose the process into 8 to 20 atomic activities in sequence, each written as verb plus object, without vague subprocesses. Build an activity-by-role table and assign in each cell: R for whoever executes the work, A for whoever is accountable and decides, C for whoever is consulted beforehand with two-way dialogue, I for whoever is informed of the result in a one-directional way; leave the cell empty if the role does not participate. Apply and report the integrity rules: exactly one A per activity, at least one R per activity, no excess of C that slows the decision, no orphan rows or missing mandatory roles. Verify segregation of duties: in sensitive financial controls, the executor must not approve, the recorder must not reconcile, the custodian must not authorize. Flag conflicts: activities without a clear owner, roles overloaded with R or A, and segregation violations. Close with a socialization plan in 3 to 5 bullets: validation with the process owner, communication to the roles, and review cadence. If the process or roles are missing, ask for them before inventing. Do not invent roles or steps. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Creating an operational runbook
prompts.content:
Act as a senior operations and operational excellence engineer, expert in designing runbooks and SOPs for critical financial and operational processes, fluent in incident management (ITIL) and in accounting close and reconciliation operations. I need an operational runbook that any team member on shift can execute under time pressure, without depending on memory or the availability of the author: the flight manual that is followed line by line to run a recurring operation or recover from an incident.

Before drafting, restate in one or two sentences what operation or incident you are going to document and present a brief plan; if you lack essential data (trigger, executing role, systems, steps, or failure modes), ask concretely instead of inventing.

Deliver a one-to-three page runbook with these components: (1) Header with name, purpose in one sentence, version, date, and owner. (2) Trigger and scope: distinguish whether it is a recurring operation (frequency or event) or an incident (symptom or alert) and declare what is inside and outside scope. (3) Responsible and escalation: role or operator who executes, applicable shift, and to whom and how to escalate if blocked or if the window is exceeded. (4) Prerequisites: systems, tools, accesses, permissions, and prior validations, including an explicit point of no return if one exists. (5) Step-by-step procedure in a numbered list or table: each step is an atomic action with responsible, exact command or location (system, screen, path), and an observable verification check that acts as a gate before proceeding. (6) Success verification of the complete operation, not just of individual steps (balances reconciled, job in successful state, reconciliation without differences). (7) Failure modes and recovery in a table of symptom, probable cause, and recovery action, with the rollback path to the last known safe state. (8) Time window and service limit: target time and threshold that triggers escalation. (9) Close: verifiable success criteria, evidence or record that remains (logs, screenshots, minutes), and close communication when applicable. (10) Maintenance: runbook owner and review cadence.

Do not invent commands, paths, or figures: mark every unconfirmed datum as [ASSUMPTION] and, if missing, write 'to be gathered in process interview'. Write in neutral professional Spanish, no emojis, no prices. The deliverable must be ready to post in the operational repository and audit.

prompts.title: Drafting a policy and associated procedure
prompts.content:
Act as a Director of Internal Control and Financial Governance with experience in designing policy frameworks and SOPs under COSO 2013 and the IIA three-lines model. I need to formalize the governance of a critical financial process so that it withstands audit, reduces operational risk, and gives each person clarity on what is permitted and how it is executed. Today we mix policy, procedure, and control in hybrid documents that neither govern, nor operate, nor can be audited.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. First restate in your own words the object of the policy, the scope, the compliance framework, and the risk tolerance level you will use; mark every gap with [ASSUMPTION]. If you lack the policy object, scope, framework, or tolerance level, ask me before proceeding. Then present the index of the three artifacts, the policy's candidate principles, the procedure's planned steps, and the risks to control, and confirm with me the policy/procedure/control separation before drafting.

Once confirmed, draft three differentiated and linked artifacts:
1. POLICY (the what and the why): document control header (code, version, effective date, next review, owner, approver) + purpose + scope and exclusions + definitions + guiding principles + roles and responsibilities + risk tolerance statement + approval authority + exception regime + regulatory references. Stable, rarely changes, no operational steps.
2. PROCEDURE / SOP (the how): document control header + operational objective + trigger and preconditions + numbered step-by-step flow, each step with responsible (RACI), input, action, output, and system or record + segregation of duties points + approval thresholds + exception handling path + operational indicators. Versionable, no new principles.
3. CONTROLS MATRIX (the verification): table with risk, control, type (preventive/detective), nature (manual/automatic), frequency, responsible, expected evidence, effectiveness test, and SOP step covered. Auditable.
Close with a TRACEABILITY MATRIX that connects each policy principle to the procedure step(s) and to the control(s) that assure it, with no orphans.

Quality rules: do not invent data; every assumption goes marked [ASSUMPTION]; there must be explicit segregation of duties and at least one preventive and one detective control; each risk must have evidence and an effectiveness test; neutral professional Spanish, no emojis. Deliverable: package of three documents plus traceability matrix, ready for committee approval.

prompts.title: Designing an operational control checklist
prompts.content:
Act as a senior controller expert in operational controls design and SOPs under internal control logic (COSO: control activities, segregation of duties, evidence, and traceability). I need an executable operational control checklist for a critical finance or operations task that today is executed from memory or with scattered criteria, which produces errors, rework, and audit findings. The checklist must convert that tacit knowledge into a repeatable control: any person in the indicated role executes it the same way, leaves evidence, and exceptions are detected on time.

Before drafting, confirm with me the critical task to control, the process it belongs to with its start/end boundary, the roles available to execute/approve/reconcile (always by role, never by name), and the system or repository where the evidence is kept. If any of these four data points is missing, ask for it before proceeding; do not invent systems, figures, or regulatory deadlines.

Proceed as follows: (1) Decompose the task into four sequential phases (preparation, execution, reconciliation, close) and map where an error hurts most in economic, regulatory, or reputational impact. (2) Draft each item as a verifiable and unambiguous affirmation, with verification verbs (confirm, reconcile, cross-check, approve), not as a vague instruction. Each item carries: step number, action, responsible by role, concrete evidence in the record system, frequency or trigger, and threshold or tolerance that defines when there is an exception. (3) Flag the key controls (their failure stops the process) versus good practice controls, and for each key control name the compensating control if it cannot be executed. (4) Add an exception handling section (to whom it is escalated, response deadline, how it is documented, who closes it) and a segregation of duties section that makes explicit that the executor is not the approver or the reconciler; if the available roles are insufficient to segregate, declare it as an open risk with a compensating control. (5) Close with usage instructions and a review cadence for the checklist itself.

Deliverable: checklist table with columns step, verifiable action, responsible-role, evidence, frequency/trigger, threshold-exception, and key/good-practice; plus exception handling section, segregation of duties section, and usage instructions. Mark any assumption as [ASSUMPTION]. Neutral professional Spanish, no emojis.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Standardizing handoffs between areas
prompts.content: Act as a senior operational excellence manager specialized in SOP design and internal service level agreements. I need to convert an informal handoff between two areas into an auditable delivery contract, ready to paste into a SOP. First restate the handoff in one sentence (from whom to whom, what is handed over, when it occurs) and name the main breakdown; present your plan before executing. Then produce, in this order: (1) a reduced SIPOC of the handoff (supplier, input, receiver, expected output) flagging the exact point where it breaks today; (2) the Definition of Ready, i.e. the conditions the package must meet to be considered deliverable, concrete and not aspirational; (3) acceptance criteria as a binary yes/no list, without ambiguous adjectives, that the receiver uses to accept or return; (4) the measurable SLA with response time, delivery window, format, single channel, and the explicit consequence of non-compliance; (5) the standard package format: mandatory fields, naming template, single channel, and what NOT to include; (6) the return cycle with typed rejection reasons and response time, so that returning is a process and not a discussion; (7) a minimum RACI that distinguishes who delivers, who accepts, and who escalates; (8) a handoff health indicator with formula and initial target; and (9) the three main adoption risks with their mitigation. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] everything inferred and do not invent real metrics. If you lack any essential data (areas, deliverable, frequency, current failures, or target SLA), ask me before continuing.

prompts.title: Prioritizing automation opportunities
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Operational Excellence leader specialized in financial and operations process automation, with experience prioritizing RPA and task backlogs. I need a prioritized automation opportunity backlog for an area that accumulates manual operational work; automating everything at once disperses effort and usually starts with the wrong things, so I want to distinguish quick wins from strategic projects and separate tasks whose process must be standardized before automating.

Before scoring, ask me for: the area or team, the inventory of candidate tasks, and for each task, frequency, time per execution, exception rate, and systems involved. If any of those four data points is missing for a task, request it and do not score the task with invented assumptions; if it remains missing after asking, mark that task as Not evaluable and exclude it from the ranking. Also confirm the criteria weights (if not provided, use Volume 0.25, Repeatability 0.25, Rules 0.30, Savings 0.20), the quick win threshold (if not provided, use 70), and the implementation horizon (if not provided, use one quarter).

Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: first restate what you understand (scope, area, weights, threshold, horizon, and missing data), then present your scoring plan and confirm it, and only then execute.

For each task score 1 to 5 on four criteria: Volume (frequency per horizon), Repeatability (stability of the execution pattern), Rules Degree (determinism vs judgment and exception rate), and Expected Savings (person-time freed plus error and risk reduction). Calculate the weighted composite and normalize it to 0-100. Define implementation complexity (number of systems, integrations, data maturity, API availability) as low, medium, or high, because the bands depend on composite plus complexity. Assign band: Quick win (composite greater than or equal to threshold and low complexity), Strategic project (high composite and medium or high complexity), Filler task (low composite and low complexity), Discard or redesign first (weak rules, high exception rate, or non-standardized process). Apply a safety rule: any task with an exception rate above 20 percent or without a documented process goes to Discard or redesign first even if its composite is high.

Deliver: (1) table ordered from highest to lowest composite with task, the four 1-5 scores, composite 0-100, complexity, band, and risk or dependency note; (2) block of 3 to 5 quick wins recommended for the horizon, each with justification, critical dependency, and expected success signal in person-time or exception reduction; (3) block of tasks to standardize before automating with the specific reason; (4) list of Not evaluable tasks due to missing data. Do not use monetary figures: express benefits only in person-time and percentages.

prompts.title: Build the business case for an automation
prompts.content: Act as an Operational Excellence and Finance Manager with experience valuing automations (RPA, scripts, integrations, AI agents) and defending them before investment committees. Build the business case for automating a process in order to make a GO / NO-GO decision backed by evidence. Always work in FTE-hours and internal costs in COP; never use sale prices or commercial promises. Before calculating, restate the process you are going to automate and its trigger, and request any missing data (volume and frequency, minutes per transaction including rework, fully-loaded rate per hour of the role, implementation effort, and evaluation horizon); if any data item does not arrive, declare it [ASSUMPTION] with a value and justification instead of inventing it. Deliver: (1) an assumption table with value, source, and an [ASSUMPTION] tag where applicable; (2) a baseline with annualized volume, FTE-hours consumed today, rework rate, and annualized cost valued at the loaded rate; (3) implementation cost separating initial CapEx (development hours times rate) from recurring OpEx (annualized licenses and platform, infrastructure, maintenance, and support); (4) future state with automated minutes per transaction, percentage of volume actually automatable (rarely 100%), and residual FTE-hours for exceptions; (5) net annual benefit = gross savings valued minus OpEx, payback in months, FTE-hours per year freed, and ROI at 1 and 3 years, applying a realization discount for adoption ramp in year one and declaring it; (6) sensitivity with conservative, base, and optimistic scenarios varying volume and automatable percentage; (7) a GO / NO-GO verdict with the 3 risks that would invalidate the case and the evidence still to be confirmed. Distinguish savings from redeployed capacity (freed hours reallocated to other work) from real cash savings (effective cost reduction), because only the latter appears in the budget. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Design an automated end-to-end workflow
prompts.content:
Act as a senior automation architect for financial and operational processes: you master BPMN 2.0, event-driven and batch orchestration, system integration (API/REST, webhooks, queues, RPA), and financial controls (segregation of duties, idempotency, reconciliation, dual validation). MetodologIA contributes the rigor of modeling executable processes, not vague automation intentions.

Objective: convert a financial or operational process into an end-to-end automated workflow, executable and auditable, that starts from a trigger, traverses the systems involved under business rules, and resolves its exceptions without manual intervention except where a control requires it.

Before executing, I need you to tell me: which process is being automated and why; the event that triggers it; the systems and integrations involved; the business rules and hard controls (amount limits, mandatory approvals, deadlines, segregation of duties); the expected behavior under failures or missing data. If the process, the trigger, the systems, or the hard rules are missing, request them and do not continue: never invent systems, amounts, or rules. If optional data are missing (exceptions, volume, SLA), propose reasonable default values and mark them as [ASSUMPTION].

Deliver in this order:
1. Restate the process in one sentence: "When [trigger] occurs, the system must [outcome], complying with [control]".
2. Define the trigger: type, origin, frequency, peak volume, synchronous or asynchronous, and the event deduplication policy.
3. Map the happy path in numbered, atomic steps (input, action, responsible system, output, data that persists); mark [ASSUMPTION] on anything you assume.
4. Insert each rule as an explicit gateway (what is evaluated, threshold, true branch, false branch) and include each human approval as a node with responsible role, SLA, and behavior upon SLA expiry.
5. Specify each integration: method (API/REST, webhook, queue/event, file, RPA), data that crosses, authentication, idempotency, timeout, and handling of partial or duplicate responses.
6. Design exception handling for each step that may fail: failure type, detection, retry policy (how many, backoff), compensation or rollback, dead-letter, and human escalation with SLA.
7. Define controls and traceability: what is logged at each step, non-bypassable controls (segregation of duties, dual validation, reconciliation), and how duplicate processing of the same event is prevented (idempotency key, window, store).
8. Close with metrics to validate the workflow (success rate, cycle time, percentage of exceptions reaching a human, retry rate, P95 latency) and the acceptance criteria to proceed to implementation.

Always distinguish hard control (non-bypassable, blocks the flow) from soft control (alerts and allows continuation). For every failure point, explicitly define whether retry is safe (idempotent operation) or not (requires compensation). Mark as edge cases and resolve: duplicate event, out-of-order arrival, external system down, missing or malformed data, absent approver, and amount at the exact threshold boundary.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliverable: pseudo-BPMN diagram with nodes and gateways; step-by-step table (Step, Trigger/Condition, System, Action, Exception, SLA); integration matrix (method, auth, idempotency, timeout); list of operational risks with probability, impact, and mitigation; assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION] to confirm; and a success metrics panel with acceptance criteria.

prompts.title: Automate the monthly accounting close
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Controller specialized in financial close optimization (fast close / continuous close), with hands-on practice in close by exception and in the risk-tiered reconciliation model (auto-certification, materiality threshold, detailed review in the style of BlackLine). I want to accelerate my monthly accounting close without degrading quality or controls: moving from a reactive, manual close to one designed by exception, where predictable tasks are pulled forward or templated, reconciliations are prioritized by risk, and the team only invests time in what breaks a threshold.

Before designing, ask and wait for my answers if I have not provided: (1) the ERP or accounting software in use; (2) how many business days the close takes today and the desired target; (3) the processes or accounts that delay it most; (4) what tools and degree of automation I already have; (5) the materiality threshold or tolerance for validating and reviewing by exception. Do not advance with critical gaps.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. First restate in your own words what you understood and present your phase plan; execute only then.

Deliver a design for an automated monthly accounting close with: (1) Confirmed context framing; (2) Day-by-day calendar separating pre-close tasks (estimable accruals, reconciliations of low-movement accounts, subledger validation before month-end) from close tasks, each with an owner and explicit dependency; (3) Reconciliation inventory classified into three risk tiers (auto-certification for low movement and stable balance; reconciliation by materiality threshold; detailed review for critical accounts), indicating what is automatable and how; (4) Catalog of templated recurring journal entries (accruals, deferrals, depreciation, provisions, reclassifications), each with its calculation rule, data source, and trigger (calendar or event); (5) Automated validations (three-way ties, variances against prior month and budget with tolerance, subledger vs. ledger integrity checks, unreconciled items, bridge and transit accounts at zero); (6) Exception-based close dashboard with metrics (progress, pending reconciliations, open exceptions) and escalation rules to human review only when a threshold is breached; (7) Adoption roadmap sequencing the highest-impact improvements over the declared bottlenecks, separating quick wins from structural changes, with adoption risk and success signal per milestone.

Firm rules: do not invent balances, amounts, or account names; use those I provide or leave the field parameterized. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] every assertion not supported by a provided data point. Do not include tool or license prices; reason in terms of effort and impact. Before closing, verify internal consistency: every task with owner and dependency, every validation with threshold, every journal entry with rule-source-trigger, and no invented figures.

prompts.title: Automate account reconciliations
prompts.content: Act as a senior Controller with fifteen years automating bank and control-account reconciliations, with mastery of internal controls and accounting close. Design a reusable reconciliation engine that automates the bulk of matching between statement and ledger or subledger, leaves only real exceptions for human review, and supports a clean audit trail month after month. First restate what you understand and present your plan; then execute. If you do not know the accounts to reconcile, the close period, or the format and origin of the sources, ask before designing; do not invent the scope. Deliver: (1) Canonical data model: minimum fields both sources must have to cross-match them (unique identifier, date, signed amount, counterparty, reference or description, normalization hash) and explicit rules for normalizing dates, amounts, signs, and currencies before matching. (2) Numbered match-rule cascade from strictest to most relaxed: exact match by reference plus amount plus date; amount and date with tolerance; many-to-one and one-to-many grouping for consolidated deposits or payments; fuzzy match by description similarity when a reference is missing. For each level declare the criterion, confidence threshold, and whether it auto-reconciles or only suggests; all auto-reconciliations leave a reversible trail. (3) Unreconciled-item catalog with actionable categories (in transit, date timing difference, amount difference, duplicate, missing in ledger, missing in bank, suspected error or fraud), each with an owner, resolution SLA, and typical corrective action. (4) Controls and traceability: audit log per match with rule applied, actor, and timestamp; segregation of duties between who reconciles and who approves adjustments; and escalation of items exceeding the materiality threshold. (5) Close dashboard with auto-reconciliation rate, aging of open items, net unreconciled amount, and month-over-month trend. Close with a text flowchart and a reusable open-item log template. Consider edge cases: records without reference, transactions straddling two periods, reversals and adjustment notes, unrecorded bank fees, and multiple items with the same amount and date. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] any tolerance or default you assume, do not invent figures, and do not include prices.

prompts.title: Automate the generation of financial reports
prompts.content: Act as a senior financial controller with experience in close automation, multi-entity chart of accounts, and financial data architecture (FP&A plus data engineering). I want to convert the manual consolidation of a recurring financial report into a reproducible pipeline that extracts, transforms, validates, and publishes the numbers with minimal intervention, to free the team for analysis and make the close auditable and predictable. Before designing, restate what you understood and present your plan. If a critical data item is missing (which report, its sources and formats, periodicity and target delivery date, available tools, or who consumes the report), ask for it instead of inventing it. Deliver: (1) a textual diagram of the extract, transform, validate, and publish flow; (2) a source map where for each origin you indicate format, frequency, owner, approximate volume, and a reproducible or semi-reproducible extraction method; (3) the transformation specification with normalization rules (single chart of accounts, currency conversion with rate policy, period alignment and accounting cut-off, intercompany elimination), join keys and step-by-step consolidation logic, each figure traceable to its source; (4) a validation controls table that includes at least the balance-sheet check or assets equal to liabilities plus equity, out-of-threshold variance against prior period and budget, control totals reconciled against origin, unclassified items, duplicate records, and source completeness, each control with approval criterion, severity, and action upon failure (blocks, alerts, logs); (5) the publication definition with format, destination, access control, versioning, traceability, and audit log for the consumer; (6) a phased implementation plan prioritized by effort and manual-work reduction, with quick wins first. Consider and declare edge cases: close with open period, post-close adjustments or reopening, late-arriving or reformatted source, missing exchange rates, unmapped new accounts or cost centers, and reconciliations that do not balance to the cent. Also define a rollback strategy and manual backup operation if the pipeline fails on close day, and the acceptance criteria indicating that the automated report is trustworthy enough to replace the manual one. Mark as [ASSUMPTION] every unconfirmed data point; do not invent figures, system names, or rates. No emojis, neutral and professional Spanish. The automation strategy should start from the figure that hurts most in the close.

prompts.title: Configure spending anomaly alerts
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Controller specialized in fraud detection and spending internal controls, with experience in continuous monitoring and rule design for spend management tools. I need to configure an alert system that detects and notifies atypical or out-of-policy transactions in near real time, before they become resource leakage or audit findings.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand and present your plan; execute only after confirming.

If you are missing any critical data, ask me before proceeding: which spend categories or sources we are monitoring (cards, purchase orders, reimbursements, travel, suppliers), in which currency, the current spending policies and approval limits, whether historical data exists to compute averages, the acceptable noise appetite (low, medium, high), and who receives and acts on the alerts.

Deliver me an actionable rule matrix, ready for a spreadsheet or monitoring tool, following these steps: (1) for each category, define the normal pattern vs. the anomalous one, referencing the policies; (2) build the catalog in four layers: absolute thresholds, relative thresholds (deviation vs. historical average or budget), policy rules (unauthorized category, unapproved vendor, unusual day or time), and pattern rules (splitting to evade approval, duplicates, spikes by vendor, round or repeated transactions); (3) assign each rule a severity (informational, warning, critical), notification channel, and owner; (4) define the anti-false-positive logic with time windows, seasonality exclusions, trust lists, and sensitivity calibrated to the noise appetite; (5) deliver the escalation path from detection to resolution with response times per severity and a default action when no one responds.

Rules: mark with [ASSUMPTION] any data you infer and do not invent business figures. Deliver the matrix with columns Rule | Category | Type | Condition/Threshold | Severity | Channel | Owner | Response time, plus the calibration section and the escalation path. Neutral, professional language, no prices or promises of no charge.

prompts.title: Eliminate waste with lean principles
prompts.content:
Act as a senior lean process improvement engineer with Lean/Toyota Production System training and experience in operations, finance, and value stream mapping. Your assignment is to produce a lean waste diagnostic plus a prioritized countermeasure plan for an operational or financial process, with the aim of freeing capacity and reducing cost without sacrificing what the process customer values.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before executing, restate the process, its trigger, its output, the customer and the value they expect, the baseline lead time, and the improvement objective; present your plan in one line and wait or continue based on context. If a critical data item is missing (any of those six), request it before proceeding; if a secondary data item is missing, assume it and mark it as [ASSUMPTION].

Execute in five phases. Phase 1 Framing: fix the end-to-end scope and declare assumptions. Phase 2 Flow map: list the steps from trigger to output and classify each as value-adding, wait, or non-value-adding; flag queues, handoffs, and rework; estimate in relative terms what portion of lead time is waiting. Phase 3 Waste hunt: go through each of the seven TIMWOOD types (Transportation, Inventory, Motion, Waiting, Overproduction, Overprocessing, Defects) one by one, and for each declare detected with concrete evidence from the process or not applicable with a brief reason; omit none. Phase 4 Root cause and countermeasures: for each relevant waste apply five whys where helpful, define an actionable countermeasure, and state whether it is elimination, automation, or redesign. Phase 5 Prioritization and experiment: build an effort/impact table, order the countermeasures, and define a first experiment with hypothesis, metric, baseline, success criterion, and reading horizon.

Firm rules: express all impacts in relative terms (fewer queues, less touch, shorter lead time) and never invent monetary figures or percentages without a basis; if the customer values something that a step protects, do not propose eliminating it without noting the risk; distinguish pure waste from necessary non-value-adding work (type 2) that is reduced but not eliminated at once. Deliver in neutral, professional Spanish: classified flow map, 7-waste table, countermeasures with root cause and type, effort/impact prioritization matrix, and a measurable experiment. Close by confirming that all 7 types were reviewed and that every assertion is supported by the context or a marked assumption.

prompts.title: Measure operational productivity by process
prompts.content: Act as a senior operational excellence analyst, expert in process measurement, theory of constraints (TOC), and activity-based costing (ABC). Your assignment is to build an auditable measurement system for a specific operational process over a defined time window, so that improvement and automation decisions are made on evidence rather than intuition. Before calculating anything, restate the process, the window, the start and end boundaries, and the transaction unit; if critical data are missing (stages with times, received and completed volume, assigned FTEs with their dedication percentage), stop and request them in a single batch before proceeding. Then execute four phases. Framing: fix boundaries and the transaction unit and map the process stage by stage separating processing time (value-adding) from waiting time (queue); mark with [ASSUMPTION] every missing or estimated data point and declare its sensitivity. Baseline: calculate throughput as completed units per period and per FTE, separating received from completed volume to expose backlog; end-to-end cycle time decomposed into processing vs. waiting, reporting mean, median, and 95th percentile with its sample size; cost per transaction reasoned only in FTE-hours and percentages, never in invented monetary figures, decomposed into labor by level, systems, and rework. Declare the explicit formula, unit, and window for each metric. Diagnostic: apply theory of constraints to locate the bottleneck (stage with the longest waiting time or lowest effective throughput), validate that it is the real constraint and not a downstream symptom, and quantify the recoverable inefficiency in FTE-hours per period. Action: prioritize three to five recommendations in an effort vs. impact matrix, distinguish process improvements from automation opportunities, and for each indicate the target metric and implementation risk. Close with a tracking dashboard: metric, baseline value, target, measurement frequency, owner, and data source. Deliverable: baseline of the three core metrics with formula and assumptions, bottleneck diagnostic with quantified inefficiency, prioritized recommendations, and dashboard. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Size operational capacity by demand
prompts.content:
Act as a senior operational capacity planning manager (capacity planning and workforce management) with experience in service centers and back-office processes. I need a traceable calculation memo that determines how much capacity (FTEs) is needed to absorb the demand of an operational process, ready to support hiring, reallocation, or automation decisions based on evidence rather than intuition.

If you have not been given the process, the demand volume, the period, the standard time per task, and the available working hours per FTE, ask for them before calculating: without them the sizing is not reproducible. Effective utilization (absenteeism, vacation, training, unproductive time) and the service level or peak factor are useful; if missing, assume a reasonable market-standard value and mark it as [ASSUMPTION].

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the inputs, Plan the calculation model, and restate it before Executing.

Deliver: (1) unit homogenization to hours and to the same period; (2) total workload = volume x standard time in hours; (3) effective capacity per FTE = gross hours minus absences and unproductive time, applying utilization; (4) base FTEs = total workload / effective capacity; (5) adjusted FTEs sized against peak demand and service level, with explicit headroom; (6) nominal headcount rounded up in three scenarios (optimistic, base, conservative) with the resulting utilization of each; (7) two to three efficiency levers (automation, peak reallocation, standard-time improvement) with their estimated FTE impact; (8) model limits and re-sizing signals. Each variable with its value and explicit formula so the calculation is reproducible by hand. Neutral, professional Spanish, no prices or cost amounts; all assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION].

prompts.title: Build a direct cash flow statement
prompts.content:
Act as a senior treasurer expert in liquidity management, working capital, and short-term cash planning (13-week and monthly direct flow). I need to anticipate my cash position before a mismatch catches me off guard: the accrual income statement does not tell me how much cash I have each period because an invoiced sale is not cash until the customer pays. Build a direct-method cash flow statement, period by period, that lets me decide in time whether I need a credit line, should accelerate collections, or stagger payments, and size how much funding is needed and for which period.

Proceed as follows: (1) Confirm the initial cash balance, the horizon (number of periods and unit, e.g. 13 weeks or 6 months), and the minimum cash buffer I must maintain. (2) Model inflows by concept, converting sales into actual collections according to receivable days by customer or channel (cash vs. credit), and include contributions, credit drawdowns, and other non-operating income. (3) Model outflows by concept on their actual disbursement calendar: suppliers with payment days, payroll and employer contributions, rent and utilities, taxes, debt installments (principal plus interest), capex, and other disbursements. (4) Calculate per period the net flow (inflows minus outflows) and the cumulative balance (prior balance plus net flow). (5) Alert every period whose cumulative balance falls below the minimum buffer; report the maximum gap and the peak cash-need period. (6) Recommend funding and working-capital actions (accelerate collections, stagger or renegotiate payments, size the credit line) adjusted to the gap and with their expected effect on the balance.

Rules: use real direct method (actual cash receipts and payments, never accrual); break down by concept, never in a lump sum; chain the balance period by period without breaks; distinguish operating from non-operating flow. Mark every figure I have not confirmed as [ASSUMPTION] and list them at the end for validation, with the convention you assumed (calculation basis, collection/payment days, seasonality). If an essential input is missing (initial balance, horizon, or buffer), ask me directly before projecting; do not invent the missing data. Deliver: period-by-period direct cash flow table (inflows, outflows, net flow, cumulative balance), alerts block with maximum gap and peak period, prioritized recommendation list, and assumption list. Do not mention prices, rates, or funding costs.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Calculate and reduce the cash conversion cycle
prompts.content:
Act as a treasury and working-capital director with experience in financial close, accounts-receivable and accounts-payable analysis, and the design of cash-release levers. Every day of the cash conversion cycle is cash trapped between what you pay suppliers and what you collect from customers; quantifying it converts a treasury intuition into an actionable number and enables a working-capital Strategy that is defensible to management or a bank.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First, restate which company or unit, which period, and which reduction objective you understand; then present your calculation plan; only then execute. If any financial data is missing (accounts receivable, inventory, accounts payable, credit sales, cost of goods sold, purchases) or the period and its base days, ask for it before calculating: never invent figures.

Deliver a cash-conversion-cycle report containing: (1) a normalized-data table for the period, with missing figures explicitly flagged and the source of each balance (average or closing); (2) the calculation of DSO, DIO, DPO, and CCC with the formula visible on each line; (3) translation of the CCC into tied-up cash and cash released per day reduced, in the currency of the data; (4) an inventory of levers separated by receivables, inventory, and payables, each with estimated impact in days, effort, risk, and time-to-result; (5) a realistic CCC target and the three highest-return moves, prioritized, with any side effects warned where they exist (for example, stretching payments can damage supplier relationships or trigger costs).

Calculation rules: use average balances (opening + closing) / 2 when both are available; otherwise use the closing balance marked as approximation. DSO = (average accounts receivable / credit sales) x days in period. DIO = (average inventory / cost of goods sold) x days in period. DPO = (average accounts payable / purchases, or cost of goods sold if purchases are unavailable) x days in period. CCC = DSO + DIO − DPO. Annualize partial data before comparing. Daily cost of goods sold = cost of goods sold / days in period; approximate tied-up cash = CCC x daily cost of goods sold. Mark every estimate with [ASSUMPTION] and declare the limits of the analysis (a negative CCC is favorable; seasonality and closing-date spikes distort point-in-time balances).

prompts.title: Design accounts-receivable management
prompts.content:
Act as a senior Treasury and Credit Manager with fifteen years designing and operating order-to-cash cycles, expert in credit policy, aging, and collections. Your assignment is to design a ready-to-implement accounts-receivable management system that releases working capital trapped in the portfolio and curbs delinquency without sacrificing sales: a high DSO and an aged portfolio drain cash, raise financing costs, and increase bad-debt risk.

If any data needed to calculate DSO or portfolio cost is missing (opening and closing balances of accounts receivable, credit sales for the period, days in the period, agreed payment terms, or annual financing rate), ask for it and do not proceed with invented figures. Every estimate you introduce is marked [ASSUMPTION] with its calculation basis.

MetodologIA Protocol: first Interpret (restate the assignment and confirm the data), then Plan (present your diagnostic and design plan), then Execute. Deliver:

1. Quantitative diagnosis. Current DSO = (average accounts receivable / credit sales for the period) x days in the period, shown step by step. Best Possible DSO = (current non-overdue accounts receivable / credit sales) x days, derived from agreed payment terms. DSO gap in days and its translation into tied-up cash. Financial cost of overdue portfolio = overdue balance x (annual rate / 360) x average days past due. CEI (Collection Effectiveness Index) if payment data for the period is available.

2. Credit policy. Customer scoring (criteria and weights), credit limits by segment, payment terms, guarantee or advance requirements, approval matrix by amount, and dispatch-blocking rules for delinquency or overlimit.

3. Aging and segmentation. Accounts-receivable aging report by five buckets (current, 1–30, 31–60, 61–90, over 90 days), classification of customers by risk level, and provision percentage by bucket with justification.

4. Collection process. Contact cadence pre- and post-due date (reminder, call, formal letter, escalation), RACI of responsible parties, thresholds for referral to legal collection or accounting write-off, and tracking indicators (DSO, CEI, percentage of overdue portfolio, rolling aging, fulfilled payment promises).

5. Close. Monthly control dashboard (metrics, frequency, owner, alert threshold) and 90-day implementation plan with quick wins prioritized by cash impact and effort.

Consider edge cases: sales seasonality that distorts the simple DSO, portfolio concentration in a few customers, intercompany sales, credit notes and commercial disputes that are not real delinquency, and differences between commercial and financed portfolios. Distinguish delinquency due to inability to pay from delinquency due to administrative friction, because the lever is different. Explicit trade-off: tightening credit reduces DSO but may slow sales; recommend where to set the balance depending on the sector. Neutral and professional English, no service prices or gratuity promises.

prompts.title: Optimize accounts-payable management
prompts.content:
Act as a senior treasurer and working-capital expert, specialized in accounts-payable optimization, DPO, early-payment discounts, Kraljic-style supplier segmentation, and term negotiation. I will give you my supplier portfolio with amounts and terms, my cost of capital, my cash position, the critical suppliers where I cannot risk supply, and my DPO data. If the portfolio with terms, the cost of capital, or the cash position is missing, ask me for it before proceeding and do not invent figures or terms.

Deliver, in this order: (1) the objective restated in one sentence. (2) Supplier segmentation crossing supply criticality (strategic / leverage / bottleneck / routine) with spending materiality, flagging critical suppliers as a no-term-stretching zone. (3) Early-payment discount analysis: for each supplier that offers one, calculate the annualized cost of NOT taking it using the formula cost = [d / (100 − d)] x [360 / (net_days − discount_days)], compare it against the cost of capital, and issue a verdict (take the discount or pay at net and keep cash); show the calculation, not just the result. (4) For suppliers without a discount, recommend paying at net maturity and, where the relationship permits, renegotiating longer terms or dynamic discounting, with a brief, respectful negotiation script. (5) Current and target DPO (DPO = average accounts payable / credit purchases x days in period) and the cash released per additional day of DPO, bounded by the cash position. (6) An actionable payment calendar (what to pay, to whom, on what date, why) and a per-segment payment policy.

Firm rules: never recommend paying outside the agreed term (maximizing DPO uses the agreed deadline, it does not breach it); no critical supplier ends up with terms stretched beyond what is prudent; mark every inferred figure or term with [ASSUMPTION]; when the discount ties with the cost of capital, declare the tie and decide by liquidity and relationship, not decimals. Neutral and professional English, no emojis. Here Strategy lies in deciding, supplier by supplier, when paying is investing and when paying is wasting.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Optimize inventory levels
prompts.content: Act as a senior inventory-planning and working-capital manager, grounded in operations management and finance (Wilson's EOQ model and statistical safety stock). Your objective is to optimize the replenishment policy by SKU, balancing service level against tied-up working capital, in an auditable and reproducible way. If any required data is missing (SKU list, demand history, lead time, target service level, ordering cost, or holding cost), ask for it before calculating rather than inventing it. Proceed as follows: (1) Confirm the SKU, unit of measure, history periodicity, and data completeness; report visible gaps and outliers. (2) Estimate average demand and standard deviation per SKU from history and annualize demand D, declaring the number of periods per year used. (3) Derive the Z factor from the target cycle service level (95% ≈ 1.65; 98% ≈ 2.05; 99% ≈ 2.33) and declare the source of the value. (4) Calculate safety stock SS = Z × √(lead time in periods) × demand standard deviation per period; if lead time is also variable, warn that the full formula incorporates its variance and declare the assumption adopted. (5) Calculate reorder point ROP = (average demand per period × lead time) + SS. (6) Calculate EOQ = √(2 × D × ordering cost / holding cost) and the number of orders per year (D / EOQ). (7) Calculate average inventory (EOQ/2 + SS) and the associated working capital per SKU in monetary units, valued at the holding cost or stated unit cost and NEVER at selling price. (8) Compare against the current policy if one exists and quantify cash released or additional cash required and the change in stockout risk. Show each formula with its variables and coherent units (a single period unit between demand and lead time). Include a sensitivity analysis of at least two service levels (e.g. 95% vs. 98%) and lead-time variation, showing how SS and working capital change. Mark every missing or assumed data point as [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent figures. Deliver: a per-SKU policy table (SKU, average demand, standard deviation, lead time, Z, SS, ROP, EOQ, orders/year, average inventory, working capital) followed by a decision block with cash released, stockout risk, and 3 prioritized recommendations with the best replenishment Strategy. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Calculate runway and burn rate
prompts.content: Act as a fractional CFO with a track record in startup and SME treasury, expert in cash planning and round preparation. I need to know how many months of life my cash has at the current spending rate so I can decide — in advance and not against the clock — when to open a funding round or activate cuts. Before calculating, confirm the monetary unit, the cutoff date, and the data period; if the available cash, last month's operating expenses, or recurring revenues are missing, ask for them instead of assuming, and mark every data point not provided as [ASSUMPTION]. Then: 1) calculate gross burn (total operating expenses) and net burn (expenses minus recurring revenues), declare which you use as the base and why; 2) calculate runway in months as cash divided by average net burn, showing the formula; if net burn is zero or negative, flag the operation as self-sustaining and report the monthly headroom; 3) if I have burn history, average it to smooth spikes and indicate the trend (growing, stable, or declining) and its effect on runway; 4) determine the estimated cash-zero date and subtract a safety buffer (3 months by default) to set the funding or cut trigger date; 5) model three scenarios: base, conservative (revenues −20% or expenses +15%) and stress (no new revenues), with runway, cash-zero date, and trigger date per scenario; flag non-recurring commitments (taxes, bonuses, year-end bonuses, debt) that distort the average. Deliver a comparative table by scenario and three prioritized actionable recommendations for funding or adjusting spend. Rules: no invented numbers; every derived figure comes from a data point or is marked [ASSUMPTION]; no service prices or the word free. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Plan liquidity and funding needs
prompts.content: Act as a senior corporate treasurer expert in working capital, 13-week rolling cash flow, and short-term funding structuring. Your mission is to anticipate the cash gaps of the coming weeks and design in advance the sources that cover them at the lowest cost and friction, converting treasury from Strategy instead of reaction under pressure. MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the available data, Plan and restate what you understand by presenting your approach, and only then Execute. If any critical data is missing (horizon, opening balance, minimum buffer, portfolio rotation days or supplier payment days, funding sources), ask for it before projecting; never invent figures and mark every assumption as [ASSUMPTION]. Deliver: (1) a projected weekly cash flow using the direct method from the opening balance, with inflows (receivables timed by collection days, advances, other revenues) and outflows (payroll, suppliers timed by payment days, taxes, debt service, committed CapEx, fixed costs); (2) per week, net flow, closing balance, and cumulative balance over the horizon; (3) identification of each week where the balance falls below the minimum buffer, with the gap amount and the week it appears; (4) a funding ladder by source with estimated available amount, activation time, approximate effective annual cost, and conditions or guarantees, ordered from lowest to highest cost and friction; (5) the minimum combination of sources that closes each gap without breaching the buffer or over-leveraging; (6) a weekly dated action plan with suggested owners and three early-warning triggers (for example: a key collection that is delayed, a deviation from the projection above a threshold, a shortening activation window for a source). Consider edge cases: seasonality of collections, concentration in one customer or supplier, lumpy payments (taxes, bonuses, year-end bonuses), and the difference between a transitory gap (a valley of a few weeks) and structural deterioration (a balance that declines without recovering). Close by flagging the assumption that most moves the result and what you would do if that assumption fails. Neutral and professional English, no invented figures.

prompts.title: Define a surplus-investment policy
prompts.content:
Act as a senior corporate treasurer with experience in liquidity-portfolio management under the SLR principle (Safety, Liquidity, Return, in strict order of precedence). I need a short-term treasury surplus-investment policy, ready to submit to committee and operate the next day.

First, restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. If essential data is missing (organization nature, risk appetite, surplus amount and currency, horizon and certainty of committed cash flows, or regulatory/statutory/contractual constraints), ask for it before proceeding; do not invent absolute figures and mark as [ASSUMPTION] any data you assume.

Deliver the policy in seven numbered sections: (1) Objective and scope, separating untouchable operating working capital, contingency buffer, and investable surplus, with each block traced to the cash-flow projection. (2) Criterion precedence — Safety > Liquidity > Return — with the explicit rule that Return never justifies violating the preceding two. (3) Segmentation by tranche: operating horizon (days), reserve (weeks), and strategic (months), each with its own maturity ladder. (4) Universe of eligible and prohibited instruments, with per-instrument justification consistent with the risk appetite and regulatory framework. (5) Concentration limits: caps by counterparty, by issuer, by instrument type, and minimum required credit quality. (6) Governance: who proposes, approves, and executes; dual-signature thresholds; review frequency; exception handling. (7) Control dashboard with liquidity, risk, and return indicators, each with its alert trigger and associated action.

Close with a review and validity note (update frequency and the event that forces the policy to be reopened). Do not include prices or guaranteed-return promises; express expected returns as ranges or relative references to market rates, not as promised figures.

prompts.title: Build the business case for an investment
prompts.content:
Act as a Corporate Finance Director with a proven track record presenting investment cases to committees and boards of directors. I need a complete business case, in neutral and professional English, that allows a committee to make a defensible decision on a specific investment (approve, defer, or reject) by committing scarce capital, with no subsequent surprises.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First, restate in your own words the decision to be made, the amount, the horizon, and the unit of measure; then present your modeling plan; only then execute. If any critical data is missing (amount and nature of the disbursement, expected benefits with their source, recurring and transition costs, horizon, timing of disbursements), ask before modeling instead of inventing.

Rigor rules: first define the do-nothing case as the baseline, so that every flow is incremental against it; exclude sunk costs; every figure that does not come from the provided data is marked as an assumption with its explicit basis; never invent market prices or cite amounts without a source. If the investment has phased disbursements or irregular flows, model by period respecting the actual timing of each movement.
