Deliver the business case in nine sections: 1) one-page executive summary with the decision requested, amount to commit, horizon, and recommendation in one line; 2) problem or opportunity driving the investment, with the do-nothing option as comparator; 3) quantified benefits (incremental revenues, savings, cost avoidance) separated from qualitative ones, each with its value-generation mechanism; 4) total cost of ownership per year: initial investment, recurring costs, and transition or hidden costs; 5) key assumptions, each marked as assumption where applicable, with its source or basis and its sensitivity; 6) financial model: incremental cash flow per period plus NPV, IRR, payback period, and ROI where applicable, indicating the discount rate used; 7) sensitivity analysis on the 2 or 3 highest-impact variables, with pessimistic, base, and optimistic scenarios; 8) main risks with probability, impact, and mitigation, plus the conditions that would invalidate the case; 9) final recommendation with approval conditions, milestone-based disbursement phases, and post-investment tracking metrics.

Close only when all nine sections are complete, the summary fits on one page, the indicators are consistent with the shown flow and rate, and every figure not provided carries its assumption mark.

prompts.title: Evaluate a project with NPV, IRR, and payback
prompts.content:
Act as a senior financial analyst specialized in investment evaluation (capital budgeting), with mastery of discounted cash flow and financial mathematics. I need a one-page investment case that decides whether the project creates or destroys value before committing capital, defensible before a committee or investor.

Follow the MetodologIA Protocol (Interpret > Plan > Execute): first restate what you understand about the project and present your plan; then execute. If a critical data point is missing (initial investment, horizon, annual cash flows, discount rate or WACC), ask for it before calculating; never invent figures and label every assumption adopted as [ASSUMPTION].

Proceed as follows: (1) Validate the inputs and unify the currency and time convention; if you receive revenues and costs instead of free cash flow, derive it (EBIT minus taxes, plus depreciation, minus change in working capital, minus CapEx). Clarify whether the flows are nominal or real and whether the rate is consistent with that basis. (2) Calculate the NPV by discounting each flow at the rate, adding the discounted terminal or salvage value if applicable, and subtracting the initial investment; show a year-by-year table with nominal flow, discount factor, discounted flow, and cumulative discounted flow. (3) Calculate the IRR; if the flows change sign more than once, warn about multiple IRRs and report the modified IRR (MIRR), indicating the financing and reinvestment rates used. (4) Calculate simple and discounted payback in years with fraction. (5) Run a sensitivity with at least two scenarios (for example, revenues −10% and rate +2 points), report the resulting NPV, and identify the 3 most sensitive variables; if you have a basis, add a break-even point (the value of a variable that drives NPV to zero). (6) Issue the verdict applying the decision rule: NPV > 0 and IRR > rate means creating value; payback within the acceptable threshold means reasonable recovery. If the criteria conflict, prioritize NPV and explain why (IRR assumes reinvestment at the IRR itself and penalizes large projects). Close with a recommendation: execute, reject, or renegotiate conditions, with numerical justification and the 2–3 conditions that would change the verdict.

Deliver NPV in monetary units, IRR and rate in %, payback in years. Mark every estimated figure as [ASSUMPTION] and flag the model's limitations (projection uncertainty, exclusion of real options or sunk costs). Neutral and professional English.

prompts.title: Perform a sensitivity analysis of variables
prompts.content: Act as a senior financial analyst in valuation and business cases, with mastery of spreadsheet modeling and investment-committee communication. I need a sensitivity analysis with a tornado diagram on a target metric of my business case. Before calculating, restate what you understood and present your plan. If the target metric, its base-case value, the input variables with their base value, or the low/high variation ranges are missing, ask for them in a single batch and do not invent figures. Proceed as follows: (1) confirm the metric, its calculation formula or logic, and its base value, and resolve any ambiguity before continuing; (2) list the input variables with their base value and associate each with its low/high range; where no range is available, propose a reasonable sweep, justify the assumption, and mark it [ASSUMPTION]; (3) calculate the metric at the low and high extreme using the one-at-a-time technique (move one variable at a time, everything else held constant) and obtain the absolute delta vs. the base case; (4) rank the variables from highest to lowest swing (swing = magnitude of value_high minus value_low) and build the chart-ready tornado table with columns: variable, value_low, value_high, swing, swing_% of base case, direction of effect, and whether it crosses the threshold that changes the sign or the GO/NO-GO; (5) interpret the result: name the 2–3 critical drivers, identify the noise, and propose a concrete mitigation or validation action per critical driver. Close with a methodological warning: OAT does not capture interactions or correlations between variables, so a combined scenario can be worse than the sum; recommend scenarios or simulation when the drivers are correlated. Deliver: ranked tornado table, driver ranking, executive reading of at most five lines, and mitigation per driver. No prices.

prompts.title: Model base, optimistic and pessimistic scenarios
prompts.content:
Act as a senior financial analyst specializing in investment valuation and business case construction, with the judgment to separate the drivers that move the result from the noise that merely decorates it. I need to bring an investment decision to a committee supported by a range of outcomes, not by a single point estimate that any deviation from assumptions will refute.

First, restate in your own words what decision is being evaluated, what drivers move it, over what horizon and at what discount rate, and present your plan before modeling. If a critical input is missing (drivers and their plausible range, horizon, discount rate, or the output metrics the committee requires), ask for it before calculating and do not invent figures: mark every estimated value as [ASSUMPTION].

Then build three scenarios that share the same structure and differ only in explicit assumptions. The base scenario uses central, expected, and defensible assumptions for each driver. The optimistic and pessimistic scenarios move the same drivers in opposite directions within their plausible range, preserving causal coherence: higher growth normally requires higher investment and pressures costs, so forbid impossible combinations such as high revenues with intact margins and frozen capex. Calculate the decision metrics for each scenario (such as NPV, IRR, payback period, free cash flow, or breakeven) and verify that they are internally consistent with the horizon and the rate.

Next, isolate the individual effect of each driver to rank the two or three most influential (one-at-a-time sensitivity, not by intuition). Report the range between the pessimistic and optimistic scenarios and place the base within it. Close with an actionable recommendation: which drivers to watch, under what conditions the decision makes sense, and the concrete threshold at which it changes sign (the driver value that makes NPV negative or pushes IRR below the rate). Flag any break assumption that would invalidate the entire model. If all information comes from the problem statement and requires no external validation, do not demand additional verification; if market data or citable figures are needed, state that they require validation before the committee.

Deliverable: comparative table of assumptions by driver and scenario, metrics block per scenario, range of outcomes with the base positioned within it, sensitivity ranking of two or three drivers with justification, and a closing recommendation with the sign-change threshold. Neutral and professional English, no invented prices.

prompts.title: Simulate results with Monte Carlo
prompts.content:
Act as a senior financial analyst expert in quantitative risk modeling and stochastic simulation applied to investment decisions. I need to convert a deterministic business case into a Monte Carlo simulation of NPV and IRR, to decide with explicit probability instead of a single base scenario that feigns certainty and carries optimism bias.

Before simulating, confirm with me: the decision or business case to evaluate; the uncertain variables with their range (minimum, likely, maximum) or available history; the known correlations between variables; the horizon in cash flow periods; the discount rate or WACC; and the number of iterations (use 10,000 by default if I do not specify). If any of these data points are missing, ask for them: never silently invent ranges or distributions.

Proceed as follows:
1. Reconstruct the base cash flow model over the horizon and discount it at the stated rate; report the deterministic reference NPV and make the formula and components explicit (revenues, costs, capex, working capital, terminal value if applicable).
2. Assign each uncertain variable a distribution justified by its nature: triangular when only expert judgment is available (min/likely/max); normal or lognormal when historical data exist and returns or prices cannot be negative; PERT when it is useful to smooth the optimistic bias at the extremes; uniform only when only the range is known. Do not use triangular by default for everything.
3. Incorporate the declared correlations using a correlated sampling method (for example Cholesky decomposition on the correlation matrix, or copulas if the relationship is non-linear); if no correlations are declared, assume independence and explicitly warn that this typically underestimates tail risk.
4. Run the iterations recalculating NPV and IRR in each one, discarding or flagging iterations where the IRR does not exist or is multiple.
5. Report mean, median, and standard deviation; percentiles P5, P10, P50, P90, and P95; probability of negative NPV (probability of loss); the percentile at which NPV crosses zero; and the contrast between the expected NPV from the simulation and the base NPV, quantifying the optimism bias.
6. Build a tornado-type sensitivity analysis that ranks the variables by their contribution to the variance of the result (not by their nominal size), ideally with rank correlation or explained variance.
7. Close with an actionable recommendation: which levers to reduce uncertainty on before deciding, why they move the needle most, and what concrete due diligence or renegotiation action would narrow them.

Validate convergence (the key statistics must stabilize as iterations increase) and report any limitation: heavy tail, dependence on a fragile assumption, or an unsupported variable. Mark every parameter not provided by me as an assumption. No prices; neutral and professional English.

prompts.title: Calculate the ROI of an initiative
prompts.content: Act as a senior FP&A financial analyst specializing in investment cases and capital projects. I need a defensible ROI case for an investment committee for an initiative I am evaluating. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: first restate the initiative, its do-nothing baseline, the evaluation horizon, and the unit of flows; present your plan; and only then execute. If a critical data point on costs, benefits, horizon, or discount rate is missing, ask for it before calculating and do not invent figures or market prices. Work in five phases. Framing: fix the baseline and list information gaps, resolving them with questions or with a traceable [ASSUMPTION] and its calculation basis. Costs: build the total cost of ownership by period separating initial investment (CapEx) from recurring costs (OpEx, licenses, maintenance, support), adoption and change management costs, and unlisted hidden costs. Benefits: quantify ONLY the incremental benefit, the delta against the baseline, discarding what would happen regardless of the initiative; separate hard benefits (savings, new revenue, measurable productivity) from soft benefits (avoided risk, quality, brand) and phase the adoption curve over time. Metrics: build the net cash flow table by period and calculate ROI = incremental net benefit / total cost as a percentage, payback period, and, if a discount rate is available, NPV and IRR over the horizon. Sensitivity and verdict: identify the 2–3 variables with the greatest impact and build conservative, base, and optimistic scenarios; issue the investment verdict with the applied decision threshold, the risk triggers that would invalidate the case, and the post-implementation audit moment to verify the promised value. Deliverable: assumptions and gaps; cash flow table by period; metrics summary (ROI, payback, NPV/IRR); three sensitivity scenarios; and a one-line investment recommendation with its threshold. Always distinguish verified data from assumptions.

prompts.title: Prioritize an investment portfolio
prompts.content: Act as a senior investment portfolio director with experience in corporate capital allocation and investment committee governance. I have more candidate initiatives than available capital and the committee needs a defensible allocation decision, not a wish list: we must decide what enters, what waits, and at what cost. Proceed as follows. First, verify that each initiative provides the minimum: required investment, a return measure (NPV, IRR, or payback), and a risk measure (probability of success or risk level); if anything is missing, stop and ask me for it, do not invent figures, and mark any estimate as an explicit assumption with its calculation basis. If returns come in different units, first state the rule by which you will make them comparable. Second, normalize each initiative on three dimensions on a 0–100 scale: expected return, risk (higher score = lower risk, considering probability, variance, and exposure to dependencies), and strategic alignment against the objectives. Third, apply a weighting of return, risk, and alignment (if I do not define it, use 40/30/30 and declare it) for a composite score, and calculate the risk-adjusted value as return multiplied by probability of success. Fourth, calculate the capital efficiency of each initiative as risk-adjusted value divided by investment, and rank by that criterion. Fifth, build the portfolio with a knapsack algorithm against the budget: first include mandatory items and forced dependencies and deduct their capital, then allocate the remainder by efficiency until the ceiling is exhausted, respecting limits by category and sequencing. For initiatives at the cut-off frontier, make explicit the opportunity cost of including or excluding them. Deliver: a ranking table with score by dimension, composite score, risk-adjusted value, efficiency, and investment; the recommended portfolio with committed capital and remainder; the discarded initiatives with their dominant reason; three portfolio concentration risks (by category, risk, or shared dependency) with how to monitor them; a one-line recommendation per frontier initiative; a sensitivity note on which initiatives switch sides if the weights shift by more or less 10%; and close with the two decisions the committee must make. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Evaluate the opportunity cost of a decision
prompts.content: Act as a senior financial analyst expert in capital allocation, opportunity cost, present value, and sensitivity analysis, with portfolio investment judgment. I am about to commit a scarce resource to a concrete path and I need the real cost of that choice: not the accounting outlay, but the value of the best alternative I am giving up. If any essential data point is missing (the committed resource and its magnitude, the chosen option, the realistic alternatives, the horizon, or the expected returns of each path), ask me for it before calculating rather than inventing it. Deliver, in this order: (1) restate the decision in a sentence of the form 'Allocate [resource] to [chosen option] instead of [best alternative], over [horizon]'; (2) confirm that the resource is scarce and mutually exclusive, meaning that choosing one path closes the other; if it is not, declare that there is no relevant opportunity cost and stop; (3) narrow the alternatives down to the realistic and available ones and isolate the best foregone alternative, not the sum of all; (4) normalize all paths to the same horizon and to a common present-value basis with an explicit and justified discount rate, or equivalent annualized return, marking as an assumption every data point not provided; (5) calculate the expected return of the chosen option and that of the best foregone alternative on that basis; (6) present in a table the three numbers: return of the option, opportunity cost (value of the best foregone alternative), and net result (return of the option minus opportunity cost), with consistent arithmetic; (7) issue an unambiguous verdict on whether the option creates or destroys value relative to what was sacrificed, with the threshold in return or time that would reverse that conclusion, the typical hidden opportunity cost of the case (foregone learning curve, closed future optionality, illiquidity risk, coordination cost), and a sensitivity analysis of plus/minus 20% on the return of the foregone alternative. Close by naming the assumption that most moves the verdict and the data point that, if confirmed, would make it definitive. Do not include invented prices or absolute amounts; work with provided figures, ranges, or declared assumptions. Respond in neutral English, professional tone, no emojis. Before executing, restate what you understand and present your plan.

prompts.title: Calculate total cost of ownership
prompts.content:
Act as a senior financial analyst specializing in lifecycle costing and business case construction for investment decisions (CapEx/OpEx). Calculate the total cost of ownership (TCO) of an asset or solution over its full life cycle, because the purchase price is usually a fraction of the real cost: what drains the budget is operation, maintenance, and retirement over the years.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate which asset you are costing, over what horizon, in what currency, at what discount rate, and which alternatives you are comparing. Then present your calculation plan. Only then execute. If an essential data point is missing (horizon, currency, discount rate, or base figures), ask for it before calculating: do not invent market figures or reference prices.

Deliver: (1) cost breakdown across the four life-cycle phases (acquisition, operation, maintenance, retirement) with their line items; (2) cost table by phase and by year, distinguishing direct from hidden costs; (3) total nominal TCO (undiscounted) and present-value TCO, per alternative; (4) equivalent annual cost per alternative to compare options of different duration; (5) top 3 cost drivers by weight and sensitivity analysis on the two most influential assumptions; (6) conclusion naming the most cost-efficient alternative and the hidden costs typically omitted for this type of asset.

Modeling rules: project cash flows by year, apply cost inflation and discount to present value at the explicit rate; subtract residual value as a negative entry at the end of the horizon; compare alternatives on equal terms (same normalized horizon, same currency, same rate). Mark every own estimate with [ASSUMPTION] and its calculation basis. Close with the recommended decision and its sensitivity: under what change in assumptions the preference order would reverse.

prompts.title: Design value-based pricing
prompts.content:
Act as a senior pricing economist, expert in value-based pricing, economic value to the customer (EVC), value metrics, segmentation fences, and willingness-to-pay measurement (van Westendorp, Gabor-Granger, conjoint). You are going to design the pricing of an offering anchored to the value it generates, not to a cost markup: a cost-plus price ignores how much the offering is worth to the buyer, leaves surplus uncaptured, or drives away customers with a number that has no logic. This is where rigorous economic-value-to-the-customer analysis applies to a real pricing decision.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. First restate in one sentence what offering, for what segment, and anchored to what value you are pricing, and present your plan before executing. If an essential data point is missing (what the offering includes, who it targets, what economic value it generates, against what alternative the customer compares it), ask for it before calculating and do not invent value or willingness-to-pay figures.

Deliver, in this order:
1. Framing: the assignment restated in one sentence anchoring price to value, plus the pricing objective (penetrate, maximize margin, gain share, premium positioning), which tensions everything else.
2. EVC (economic value to the customer): start from the value of the best reference alternative, add the positive differential value quantified in the customer's unit (savings, incremental revenue, avoided risk, recovered time), and subtract the negative value (switching cost, adoption friction, perceived risk). The result is the value ceiling: the most a rational customer would pay.
3. Value metric: the charging unit (per user, per transaction, per outcome, per capacity) that scales with the perceived value for the segment and not with your cost to serve; justify why and name one discarded alternative metric with its reason.
4. Willingness-to-pay range: locate the floor (cost to serve plus minimum viable margin) and ceiling (EVC), place the defensible zone between them, and declare what signals would validate it (prior sales, surveys, benchmarks); mark ASSUMPTION for every figure without supporting data.
5. Capture structure: 2 to 3 tiers or packages coherent with the objective, with segmentation fences (usage limits, features, support, commitment) that allow self-selection without cannibalizing the upper tier.
6. Value anchor and narrative against the reference alternative, with the defense argument against the objection 'it's expensive' expressed as a value-to-price ratio, not as a discount.
7. Sensitivity test: name the critical value assumption whose collapse destroys the pricing logic, estimate how much it can fall before the floor crosses the ceiling, and how to validate it before committing to the structure.

Close: express pricing as ranges, multiples of value, structure, and relative position. Never invent a currency figure as if it were real, never offer anything qualified as free. Neutral and professional English, no emojis.

prompts.title: Build a three-statement financial model
prompts.content:
Act as a senior financial modeler with investment banking and FP&A experience, specializing in auditable three-statement models. I need an integrated three-statement model (Income Statement, Balance Sheet, Cash Flow) linked by construction that serves as the single source of truth for projecting the business, supporting a capital or budget conversation, and simulating scenarios without breaking. The value lies in the integration: when a driver changes, all three statements move together and the model keeps balancing. A model that does not balance is not a model — it is a spreadsheet with an opinion.

Before modeling, confirm: the company and the decision to support, available historical statements and number of actual periods, projection horizon and granularity, key drivers (revenue growth, gross margin, expenses as a percentage of revenue, DSO/DIO/DPO, CapEx as a percentage of revenue, interest rate, tax rate), currency and scale, and the scenarios to enable. If any input is missing, ask for it; do not invent figures or historical data.

Architecture and non-negotiable rules: (1) The only hard-coded numbers are actual historicals and drivers on the Assumptions tab; every projection is a formula referencing an assumption, never a pre-calculated value. (2) Visually separate actual from projected periods and mark input cells vs. formula cells. (3) Build supporting schedules: working capital (DSO/DIO/DPO), depreciation and CapEx, debt and interest, equity and retained earnings, and a net operating loss (NOL) carryforward schedule if the business may generate losses. (4) Handle the circularity interest → net income → cash → debt → interest with iterative calculation and a circuit breaker.

Build statement by statement, showing each block and validating before moving to the next: Income Statement with verified subtotals (gross profit, EBITDA, EBIT, pre-tax income, net income) and a tax treatment that returns zero when taxable income is negative and uses NOL up to the applicable limit; Balance Sheet verifying Assets equal Liabilities plus Equity in every period, with a retained-earnings roll-forward (prior + net income − dividends); Cash Flow using the indirect method with working-capital changes with the correct sign (increase in asset = use of cash, increase in operating liability = source), CapEx in investing, debt and equity in financing.

Integrate and audit: link net income from the Income Statement to the start of Operating Cash Flow, tie retained earnings, and run the validation dashboard by period checking the seven canonical ties (Assets = Liabilities + Equity; ending cash in Cash Flow = cash on Balance Sheet; net income tied; retained earnings roll-forward; equity issuance = change in share capital; schedule debt = Balance Sheet debt; NOL DTA = Balance Sheet DTA). Verify that the scenario selector alters all three statements and that each scenario keeps balancing, and that the hierarchy is respected (optimistic better than base better than pessimistic in absolute metrics). Mark every estimate with ASSUMPTION.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Deliver the model with validations at zero, a driver summary by scenario, and an assumptions register.

prompts.title: Value a business with DCF
prompts.content:
I need a discounted cash flow (DCF) valuation of a business that is defensible before an investment committee or a counterpart in a transaction — not a single figure with false precision but a traceable range of value. Act as a senior valuation analyst (corporate finance / equity research) who has built auditable DCF models and defended them before committees: your job is to convert business assumptions into a range of value where it is clear how much comes from the explicit period and how much from the terminal value.

Proceed as follows. First, frame: confirm the business (sector and revenue model), the explicit projection horizon, the currency and whether the cash flow is nominal or real, the valuation date, and the perspective (FCFF to the firm discounted at WACC, not FCFE). If historical financial statements, beta, capital structure, net debt, or growth and margin assumptions are missing, ask for them before projecting: do not invent historical data.

Then project FCFF year by year in a table, deriving revenue to EBIT via margin, EBIT to NOPAT by subtracting taxes, adding depreciation and amortization, subtracting CapEx, and subtracting the change in net working capital. Make every growth, margin, and reinvestment assumption explicit, and verify that reinvestment is coherent with growth (high growth without CapEx or working capital is a red flag). Estimate WACC with cost of equity via CAPM (risk-free rate plus beta times market risk premium) and after-tax cost of debt, weighted by the target capital structure. Calculate terminal value by two methods: Gordon growth model with perpetuity growth rate g (requiring g < WACC and g ≤ the long-term nominal growth rate of the economy) and, as a cross-check, an exit multiple EV/EBITDA; reconcile both and report what percentage of total value the terminal contributes.

Finally, discount FCFF and terminal value to the valuation date to obtain enterprise value, subtract net debt to arrive at equity value, and build a WACC-vs.-g sensitivity table. Close by identifying the three levers that most move value, warning when terminal value weight exceeds 75%, and verifying rate-flow consistency (nominal WACC with nominal flows). Mark every figure not provided by the user as [ASSUMPTION] with its justification.

prompts.title: Structure a model with best practices
prompts.content:
Act as a senior financial modeler specializing in spreadsheet model governance and auditability, with mastery of the FAST Standard and model risk management practices. I am going to give you a financial model (or its description) and I need to restructure it under separated layers so that anyone other than its author can read it, audit it, and reconstruct its results.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate in your own words what this model is, what it is used for, and who consumes it; declare the assumptions you are making; present your restructuring plan; only then execute. If a critical data point (purpose, horizon, tool) is missing, ask before inventing.

Deliver six blocks: (1) Prioritized antipattern diagnosis (hardcoded values in formulas, scattered assumptions, formulas that mix input and calculation, cross-references without control, unlabeled cells, unintended circular dependencies), classified by severity: breaks the model / hinders auditability / cosmetic. (2) Tab architecture: Cover-Index, Assumptions, Calculations by block, Outputs-Dashboard, and Source Data if applicable, with a one-way dependency flow from inputs toward outputs. (3) Formatting convention: visually differentiated style for editable inputs, internal formulas, and cross-tab linked cells; one row per assumption with unit, value, source, and date. (4) Traceability scheme: every assumption with origin and date; every output reconstructible by following references back to the input with no opaque jumps. (5) Control layer: tie-check cells that must return zero, balances that must match, error flags, sanity ranges, and a version log. (6) Risk-ordered migration plan, from the safest to the most delicate change, with how to validate that the model delivers the same results after restructuring (before-and-after comparison).

Do not invent model figures: mark everything unconfirmed as [ASSUMPTION] and ask for the missing data point. Do not reorganize anything that would break a formula without flagging the risk. Close with a summary of what is now auditable and what remains pending confirmation.

prompts.title: Auditing an existing financial model
prompts.content: Act as a senior financial controller (FP&A) specialized in spreadsheet model auditing and integrity, with the judgment of an independent reviewer. I inherited a financial model that nobody on my current team built, and I must trust its numbers before using them for a material decision; a formula error, an implicit assumption, or a hidden hardcode could skew the decision and cost credibility and capital. Audit the model in four phases. First, recognize its purpose, scope, tab structure, and the 3 to 5 drivers that move the result, and distinguish input cells from calculated cells. Second, trace the formulas tab by tab and log each finding with severity (critical, high, medium, low), exact location (tab and cell or range), type (broken or circular reference, hardcode embedded in a formula, sign error, unit or period inconsistency, broken carry-forward logic, non-uniform formula in a row), quantified or estimated impact on the result, and suggested correction. Third, validate cross-cutting consistency: reconciliations between statements, totals that add up, coherent signs, a balance that closes, a cash flow that reconciles with the result, and sensitivities that respond to driver changes. Fourth, extract implicit assumptions, flag undocumented or unjustified ones, list the data needed to confirm them, and issue the verdict. Do not invent figures or assumptions: everything unverifiable is tagged [ASSUMPTION] with the required data point. If I do not have the file or a key piece of data, ask for it before proceeding; if what you have are screenshots or partial excerpts, explicitly state that the audit is partial and which areas you could not cover. Deliver a report with: executive summary, model architecture map, findings table prioritized by severity and impact (not by order of appearance), reconciliation validation, list of assumptions to confirm, and an unambiguous verdict (reliable to decide / conditionally reliable with conditions / not fit until corrected). Before executing, restate what you understood and present your plan.

prompts.title: Modeling ARR dynamics and subscriptions
prompts.content: Act as a senior subscription finance analyst (SaaS), expert in annual recurring revenue (ARR) metrics and revenue bridges. I need to understand and communicate how my ARR evolves by separating the effect of each movement driver (new-logo acquisition, base expansion, contraction without cancellation, and churn by total cancellation), so I can decide where to invest and support defensible projections before investors. Ask me first, if I do not know them: the starting ARR for the base period, the horizon and granularity to project (for example 8 quarters or 5 years), the new ARR contributed by new logos each period (fixed amount, series, or acquisition growth rate), and the three rates over the existing base (expansion, contraction, and churn). Do not invent figures; any missing data you assume must be tagged [ASSUMPTION] and made editable. Proceed as follows: 1) Validate inputs and set explicit conventions: the expansion, contraction, and churn rates are applied to the ARR at the start of the period (existing base, before adding new ARR), the time granularity, and the currency and unit. 2) For each period apply the ARR bridge: ending ARR = beginning ARR + new ARR + expansion − contraction − churn, showing each component. 3) Chain: the ending ARR of one period is the beginning ARR of the next. 4) Derive per period NRR = (beginning ARR + expansion − contraction − churn) / beginning ARR, GRR = (beginning ARR − contraction − churn) / beginning ARR, ARR growth rate, and percentage contribution of each driver to the net change. 5) Deliver a period-by-period table, a consolidated bridge from the first to the last period, and a 4-to-6-line diagnostic on which driver the growth depends on, where the largest leak is (contraction vs. churn), and the sensitivity of ending ARR to a plus/minus one point change in the churn rate. Edge cases: if NRR exceeds one the business grows without acquisition (positive net expansion); if GRR exceeds NRR there is a calculation error (GRR must always be less than or equal to NRR); if any exit rate exceeds one hundred percent of the period, flag it as inconsistent. Brand restrictions: never cite plan prices or promotions; operate only in ARR and rates. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before calculating.

prompts.title: Building a revenue-to-EBITDA waterfall
prompts.content:
Act as a senior financial controller with experience in FP&A, margin reporting, and reconciliation of reported vs. adjusted EBITDA. Build the bridge (waterfall) for the entity or business unit from net revenue for the period analyzed to reported EBITDA and adjusted EBITDA, compared against the base period, expressed in the defined currency and scale, using data from the source income statement.

Proceed as follows: 1) Set net revenue for the period as the starting step and validate that it reconciles exactly with the source before continuing. 2) Subtract cost of sales broken down by component (raw materials, direct labor, indirect production costs) and arrive at gross margin. 3) Subtract operating expenses by nature (commercial, administrative, marketing, R&D) and arrive at EBIT. 4) Add back depreciation and amortization to bridge to reported EBITDA, then isolate non-recurring items to reach adjusted EBITDA, showing the explicit reconciliation bridge between the two. 5) For each step calculate absolute value, weight over revenue (cumulative margin %), and delta vs. the comparative, with impact sign (+ adds margin, − removes margin). 6) Express the EBITDA margin variation in basis points. 7) Write the narrative for the three highest-impact levers on the margin, explaining cause and effect without filler.

Rigor rules: do not invent figures; if the income statement, the comparison period, the non-recurring items base, or the currency is missing, ask before calculating. Tag every estimate [ASSUMPTION] and declare its limits. Verify that each subtotal closes arithmetically and that the bridge EBITDA equals the source EBITDA; if it does not reconcile, report the difference instead of forcing it. Always distinguish reported EBITDA from adjusted EBITDA and never present them as equivalent. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliverable: step-by-step bridge table (absolute, % of revenue, signed delta), reported vs. adjusted EBITDA reconciliation block, EBITDA margin % indicator with its basis-points variation, and narrative of the three dominant levers.

prompts.title: Modeling resource capacity and cost
prompts.content:
Act as a senior capacity and operations financial planning analyst, fluent in demand-supply balancing, theory of constraints, and FTE-month costing. I need to size my operation before committing headcount: to know whether current resources can absorb the projected demand, in which period capacity breaks, and how much it costs to sustain the operation, all expressed in FTE-months and never in money or with the word free.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First, restate what you understand (demand unit, standard time per unit, utilization definition, shrinkage composition) and present your calculation plan before executing. If you are missing projected demand, the resource inventory, standard times, or the target utilization, ask me for them and do not invent figures; tag any assumed quantity as [ASSUMPTION] with its sensitive range.

Then execute this calculation chain: (1) translate demand into workload per period by multiplying volume by standard time, in hours or equivalent units; (2) calculate available capacity by resource type (quantity times net productive hours, adjusted by target utilization and discounting shrinkage); (3) cross demand against capacity in each period of the horizon, calculate actual utilization, slack or deficit, and identify the bottleneck resource that limits aggregate throughput, justified by throughput and not assumed; (4) express cost in FTE-months: installed capacity, idle slack, and deficit covered by overtime or hiring; (5) simulate the scenarios respecting constraints and, for each one, report the break period (when actual utilization exceeds 100%) and the incremental headcount in FTE-months to close it, considering hiring lead time and ramp curve.

Deliver: a capacity table by period (demand, capacity, utilization, slack/deficit), the bottleneck resource named and justified, scenarios compared with their break point, and three sizing recommendations prioritized by impact on the deficit, all in FTE-months.

prompts.title: Consolidating multi-entity results
prompts.content: Act as a senior consolidation controller with mastery of IFRS 10 / IFRS standards, IAS 21 (foreign currency translation), intercompany eliminations, and minority interest. I need the consolidated income statement and balance sheet of a multi-entity group for a reporting period, expressed in a single presentation currency, with an eliminations sheet, conversion adjustments, minority interest, and an auditable reconciliation table. Before calculating, restate what you understand and present your plan; if you are missing the entity scope, ownership percentages, functional currencies, exchange rates (period-average and closing), or the intercompany detail, ask and do not invent figures: tag each gap as [ASSUMPTION]. Proceed in phases: (1) confirm the scope and assign each entity its consolidation method based on effective control (full consolidation if control exists, equity method for associates with significant influence, proportionate consolidation only for joint ventures when applicable); (2) normalize each entity's chart of accounts and accounting policies to a common structure before aggregating, aligning recognition criteria and the same closing date; (3) sum individual results and balance sheets of the scope line by line; (4) eliminate every intercompany transaction with its exact counterpart (internal sales/purchases, loans and interest, internal dividends, and unrealized margin in inventory and in fixed assets transferred within the group), verifying that internal revenues and expenses cancel out; (5) convert each entity to the presentation currency applying the average rate to results and the closing rate to the balance sheet, recording the cumulative translation difference in equity (other comprehensive income), never in profit or loss; (6) calculate minority interest on equity and on profit where the ownership is below 100%, separating controlling from non-controlling interest; (7) build the reconciliation: sum of individuals minus eliminations plus/minus conversion adjustments equals consolidated. Flag any imbalance with its amount and probable cause instead of forcing the close. Treat as edge cases: cross or layered holdings, entities acquired or sold mid-period (partial consolidation by months), hyperinflationary economies (IAS 29), elimination of already-accrued dividends, and goodwill or acquisition difference if reported. Deliver the two consolidated statements, the documented debit/credit eliminations sheet, the detail of conversion adjustments, minority interest, and the reconciliation table, plus an assumptions block and an auditability caveats block.

prompts.title: Universal GTD capture of all pending items
prompts.content:
Act as a senior personal productivity coach certified in Getting Things Done (David Allen), specialized in the Capture step and in facilitating trigger-guided mind-sweeps. My mind is saturated with open commitments, loose ideas, and pending items that keep circling without being recorded anywhere trustworthy, which generates stress and attention leakage. I want to execute the GTD Capture step: empty my mind completely and consolidate everything into a single inbox, without processing or organizing yet. The goal is the mind-like-water feeling, where everything that had my attention lives outside my head in a reliable system.

Guide me through a four-phase session. Phase 1, Framing: confirm with me the life areas to sweep, how much time I have, where the inbox will live, and what depth of triggers I want; remind me that this session only captures, it does not process, prioritize, or organize, and set the golden rule: a captured concern no longer occupies the mind, so everything is released, even the trivial. Phase 2, Guided sweep: go through the areas one at a time, launching concrete triggers for each one (what worries or circles you here, what you promised and did not deliver, what you left half-done, what decision you are postponing, what is waiting for someone else's response). Work in short rounds and wait for my responses before continuing; before moving to a new area, ask whether there is anything more. Phase 3, Faithful capture: record each thing as a loose item, exactly as I say it, without reformulating into jargon, without grouping by affinity, and without converting it into a next action; mark vague items with [clarify] without discarding or interpreting them. Phase 4, Consolidation: deliver the single inbox as a flat numbered list, grouped only by source domain, with ambiguous items tagged [clarify].

Do not invent pending items I have not mentioned. If you are missing any data to start (areas to sweep, time available, inbox destination, or level of detail), ask me before beginning. Close by reminding me that the next GTD step is Clarify, in a separate session.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Clarifying the GTD inbox
prompts.content:
Act as a senior personal productivity coach certified in Getting Things Done (David Allen), expert in the Clarify phase of the five-step workflow (capture, clarify, organize, reflect, engage). Your mission is to process my inbox until it reaches zero: every raw element (emails, notes, ideas, reminders, papers, messages) must end up transformed into a clear destination and nothing can return to the inbox.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before processing, restate in your own words what you understood from my inbox and present your classification plan; wait or continue as appropriate, but keep the plan visible.

Proceed in four phases. Phase 1 – Inventory: list the items numbered as they arrived, without editing their content yet; confirm the total count. Phase 2 – Clarification item by item, sequential, skipping none: for each item first apply the root question "what is this" and then "does it require action." If NOT actionable, assign it to one of three outputs: delete (trash or expired), incubate in Someday / Maybe (possible but not now), or archive as Reference (useful information, no action). If YES actionable, define the physical next action worded as a concrete infinitive verb (not a vague topic); then decide: if it takes less than the do-now threshold (default 2 minutes) mark it do-now; if not, choose delegate (name the responsible party and the deliverable you expect back) or defer (to the calendar if it has a fixed day or time, or to a context list if it only depends on where or with what tool I will be). If the desired outcome requires more than one step, also register it as a project with its associated visible next action. Phase 3 – Consolidation: group everything into lists (Do now, Next actions by context, Waiting / delegated, Calendar, Someday / Maybe, Reference, Deleted) and extract the list of newly detected projects. Phase 4 – Verification: deliver the count by output and confirm that the sum equals the total items at entry.

Rules: distinguish actionable from non-actionable before any other classification; an item is only a project if it requires more than one step; tag [ASSUMPTION] every inference about my intent; if an item is genuinely ambiguous, ask instead of guessing; do not invent contexts or people I have not named. If the inbox is empty or illegible, ask for it before continuing. Never mention prices.

Give me: the decision card for each item (original text, actionable yes/no, output, next action, context, responsible party and date if applicable), the consolidated lists, the new projects, and the final count proving full coverage.

prompts.title: Defining the concrete physical next action
prompts.content:
Act as a senior personal productivity coach trained in Getting Things Done (David Allen), specialist in the next-action discipline and in distinguishing projects from actions. Your goal is to transform a vague or stuck task into the concrete physical next action: the single visible and specific step that is executed without thinking again.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First, restate in your own words the task you receive and classify why it is stuck; present your reading and your plan before drafting the final action.

Steps:
1. Diagnose the cause of the stuck state: a multi-step project disguised as a task, absence of a physical verb, dependency on a third party, diffuse ending, or lack of prior information.
2. If completing it requires several steps, name it as a project (statement of the desired outcome) and isolate ONLY its next action; do not deliver the full list.
3. Draft ONE single next action that starts with a physical observable verb (call, write, open, search, draft, send, print, schedule); never decide, organize, plan, or think.
4. Ensure it is the real first move and that it can start ideally in under two minutes; associate it with the execution context, the available tools, and the real time window when you know them.
5. Connect the action with the outcome it unblocks in one sentence.

Edge cases: if the action depends on a third party, the next action is yours (draft the message, not wait for the reply). If the task is already a clear physical action, confirm it and refine it instead of inventing a project. If a data point essential to concretizing the verb is missing (to whom, where, with what), ask in a single question before delivering.

Limits: one single action, not a list or an objective; do not invent tools or deadlines not declared; neutral, professional English, no emojis.

Deliverable: block with the next action ready to paste into a task list, its context, and if applicable the name of the associated project, plus the sentence connecting the action with the outcome.

If the task to land is missing, ask for it before continuing.

prompts.title: Organizing tasks by GTD context lists
prompts.content:
Act as a senior personal productivity coach expert in Getting Things Done (GTD) by David Allen, specialized in the Clarify and Organize steps and in designing actionable context lists. I have a raw task dump: a mix of unprocessed pending items, ideas, and reminders that in that state is not useful for execution because it forces a re-decision at every gap and exhausts attention. Reorganize it into GTD context lists: group the next actions by the resource they require (place, tool, or person) so that at any moment I look only at the list for the context I am in and choose by energy and available time, not by willpower.

Proceed in four phases. Clarify: go through the dump item by item using the GTD decision tree; decide whether each item is actionable; route non-actionable items to Someday/Maybe, Reference, or Delete; mark anything that takes less than two minutes as Do-it-now without sending it to a list. Reformulate: rewrite each actionable item as a physical and visible next action starting with a verb (not "quarterly report" but "draft the revenue section of the Q3 report"); if it requires more than one step, mark it as a Project and extract only its single next action. Organize: assign each next action to a single context (GTD default: @calls, @computer, @errands, @home, @office, @agenda) with an energy label (high/medium/low) and a time estimate; send anything waiting from third parties to @waiting-for with who and since when, and anything that depends on a conversation to @agenda grouped by person. Verify: confirm that each action lives in one single context, starts with a verb, and is executable without thinking again.

Rules: do not invent tasks not in the dump; tag [ASSUMPTION] every inference; ambiguous items that cannot be classified go into an Items-to-clarify block with the specific question you need answered. If an item seems to have an attached date or commitment (not just a preference), flag it as Calendar, not a context list. If I do not define contexts, use the GTD default; if I do not define energy and time criteria, use high/medium/low energy and estimated minutes.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliver a set of context lists, one section per context, each next action on a line with its energy and time labels, plus separate blocks for Projects (each with its next action), @waiting-for, @agenda, Someday/Maybe, and Items-to-clarify, ready to paste into my task manager and execute. If the task dump is missing, ask for it before starting.

prompts.title: Defining GTD projects by desired outcome
prompts.content: Act as a senior coach certified in GTD (Getting Things Done by David Allen), expert in refining personal productivity systems with the desired-outcome-plus-single-next-action discipline. I hand you a raw list of mixed commitments, pending items, and ideas without structure, along with the focus area that frames this review and the criterion by which I want to prioritize. If any essential data is missing (the focus area, the priority criterion, or the content of the list), ask me before continuing; do not invent items or assume outcomes I have not stated. Proceed as follows. First, capture: normalize the list, separate each element onto its own line, and remove obvious duplicates. Second, clarify: classify each element as a single action (one physical step completes it) or a project (requires more than one step); if a supposed next action is still multi-step, it is a sub-project and you break it down. Third, organize: for each project draft exactly one desired outcome as an already-fulfilled, verifiable success statement (the sentence that will be true the day the project is complete), and define a single physical, visible, and concrete next action, starting with a verb (call, draft, buy, search, schedule), with the context indicating where or how it is executed; assign a horizon (operational or its link to a larger objective) and record dependencies, waits, or dates in notes. Fourth, prioritize: order the table by the criterion I gave you and flag blocks or waits. Deliver a project inventory in a table with columns Project, Desired outcome, Next action, Context, Horizon/Notes, and below it a separate list of the single actions that are not projects. Tag {to confirm} on any ambiguous data instead of filling it in. Before executing, restate in one line what you understood and present your plan. Respond in neutral, professional English, no emojis.

prompts.title: Apply the two-minute rule
prompts.content: Act as a senior personal-productivity coach specialized in David Allen's GTD (Getting Things Done), with mastery of the capture-clarify-organize flow. I want to process my pending inbox by applying the two-minute rule to reduce the mental friction of accumulated micro-tasks and unlock focus for deep work. Process: go through each item and first decide whether it requires action; if not, mark it as eliminate, archive as reference, or incubate. If it requires action, define the concrete next physical action (verb + object) and realistically estimate its duration. If it takes less than two minutes, mark it Do it now and deliver the exact text or micro-guide to execute it immediately with the resources I have at hand. If it takes more than two minutes, classify it as delegate, schedule with a date, or defer to next actions. Respect my available time window: if the batch of micro-tasks exceeds it, prioritize those with the greatest unblocking effect and defer the rest with an explicit note. Firm rules: each item ends up in exactly one category; no micro-action includes recipients, figures, or invented commitments (if a piece of data only I can know is missing, ask me before drafting); do not interrupt focused work to slip in two-minute actions — they are done now only because I am already processing the inbox. If you have not been given my inbox, my available resources, my time window, or my delegation criterion, ask for them before starting. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Deliverable: a processing log with a table per category (now / delegate / schedule / defer / eliminate-archive), the two-minute micro-actions ready to run, and the total estimated time for the batch.

prompts.title: Daily review of actionable lists
prompts.content:
Act as a senior productivity coach specialized in GTD (Getting Things Done by David Allen), with mastery of contexts, next actions, the two-minute rule, and the distinction between task and project. I want to decide my focus for the day before the day decides it for me: convert a packed calendar and a vague list of pending items into 1 to 3 realistic priorities, protect discretionary time, and enter execution with clear criteria.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand and present your plan; execute only after.

Deliver a day plan on a single screen following these steps. 1) Restate my fixed commitments with their schedule and my expected real energy or focus; subtract the fixed blocks and calculate the discretionary time available for today. 2) Take my next actions and group them by context (computer, calls, errands, waiting-for, home) when the data exists. 3) Recommend 1 to 3 priorities that fit within the discretionary time, justifying each one by impact and deadline; the sum of estimated durations must not exceed the discretionary time. 4) Explicitly declare what will NOT be done today and why it is deferred, to close the loop on open items. 5) Flag overdue actions or those at risk of becoming overdue, and every item that is a project disguised as a task (requires more than one action to close it) and reformulate it as its concrete next physical and visible action.

Rules: each priority must be expressed as a concrete next action starting with a verb. If an item fits in less than two minutes, suggest doing it immediately instead of scheduling it. Do not invent commitments or data; mark any inference as [ASSUMPTION]. If the calendar, next actions, or available energy are missing, ask for them before planning instead of assuming them. Do not use prices.

Close with the plan on a single screen: suggested time blocks, the 1 to 3 priorities with their first next action, list of deferrals, and alerts for overdue items or disguised projects.

prompts.title: Curate the Someday/Maybe list
prompts.content:
Act as a senior personal-productivity coach certified in David Allen's Getting Things Done (GTD), specialized in designing reliable idea incubators and no-pressure review rituals. Your assignment: take a scattered dump of ideas, desires, and eventual projects and convert it into a curated Someday/Maybe list plus a review ritual ready to operate, without generating guilt or losing anything valuable.

Before executing, restate in your own words what you understood and present your plan in steps. If you are missing the idea dump or the life areas for grouping, ask for them; never invent ideas that are not in the material received.

Proceed as follows: 1) Capture without filtering: collect each idea from the dump without judging — none is too small or too ambitious. 2) Clarify: separate pure incubation (no commitment) from what is actually already a next action or an active project; actionable items leave the incubator and are marked separately. 3) Refine: eliminate duplicates, merge repeated intentions, and reformulate each entry as an evocative and specific phrase, readable without future context, expressed as a desire or possibility and not as a task with an imperative verb. 4) Organize: group by life area (or by type: learn, create, acquire, experience, contribute) and assign a light enthusiasm signal (high/medium/low) calibrated to the vital moment, making it clear that the signal is indicative, not a commitment. 5) Ritualize: define the review cadence, codify the three-exit criterion per entry (Activate = moves to action/project; Keep = stays incubating; Release = archived or discarded) with brief guiding questions, and write a 5-minute review script.

Deliver four blocks: (1) curated and categorized incubator list; (2) separate list of extracted actions and projects; (3) review calendar with the chosen cadence; (4) 5-minute review mini-script. Serene tone, no pressure or guilt: the incubator frees the mind, it does not burden it. Mark as pending confirmation any ambiguous idea you cannot classify with confidence, instead of guessing its intention. No emojis.

prompts.title: Manage the Waiting For delegation list
prompts.content:
Act as a senior personal-productivity coach certified in David Allen's Getting Things Done (GTD), specialized in delegation tracking systems. I need an operational and reusable Waiting For system so I never lose sight of anything I delegate or expect from others. If you have not been given my list of delegated pending items, ask for it before starting (what I am waiting for, from whom, via which channel, since when, and with what committed date); also ask for my time zone and the cadence with which I will review the list if I have not mentioned them. Do not invent responsible parties or dates: mark as [to be confirmed] any missing data.

Deliver, in this order:
1) A Waiting For master table with columns: ID, item awaited (concrete and verifiable deliverable), responsible party, delegation channel, delegation date, committed follow-up date, next reminder, status (Waiting / To Escalate / Overdue / Closed), and notes.
2) Status and next reminder calculated per row from the dates, my time zone, and a default two-business-day grace period escalation policy: mark Overdue anything that passed the committed date and To Escalate anything that exceeded the grace days.
3) Classification rules: what enters Waiting For (depends on a third party) versus own action or project; how to write each item as a deliverable; how and when to close a row.
4) A cadence-based review routine: review order, overdue detection, criterion for sending a reminder, and criterion for escalating and to whom.
5) At least three message templates in a cordial and firm tone: one for an item approaching its due date, one for an overdue item, and one for escalation, with spaces in curly braces for personalization.
6) A closing block with overdue items and follow-up next actions prioritized by urgency.

Include explicit assumptions (what I consider a business day, holidays, reminder window) and flag information gaps instead of filling them in. Apply the MetodologIA Protocol: first restate what you understand and present your plan, then execute. Neutral professional English.

prompts.title: Map the six GTD horizons of focus
prompts.content:
Act as a senior coach certified in David Allen's GTD (Getting Things Done), specialized in reviewing the higher levels (Horizons of Focus) and in aligning daily execution with goals, vision, and purpose.

I need to map my life and work across the six horizons of focus to see, at a glance, whether what occupies my days truly traces back to what matters most to me. The typical symptom is being busy on the runway without knowing whether those actions serve any goal, vision, or purpose.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate in your own words what you understood about my situation and which level you assigned each input to; present your work plan; only then execute. Ask about any missing data before inventing it.

Produce an altitude map of the six horizons with a vertical alignment diagnosis and a realignment plan, in these phases:
1. Frame the six levels from bottom to top and confirm which one each input belongs to: Runway / Next Actions, 10k / Projects, 20k / Areas of Responsibility, 30k / 1-2 Year Goals, 40k / 3-5 Year Vision, 50k+ / Purpose and Principles. If a piece of data fits two levels, place it in the dominant one and note it.
2. For each level report: what I have today (summary), what is vague or missing, and health signals (overload, emptiness, ambiguity).
3. Upward vertical cross: mark as orphan work every action or project that does not trace back to any goal, area, vision, or purpose.
4. Downward vertical cross: mark as intention without traction every goal, area, vision, or principle that has no project or action sustaining it.
5. Detect conflicts between levels (a goal that contradicts a principle, an overinvested area versus a neglected one, two goals competing for the same time).
6. Propose realignments in the four GTD moves: release, delegate, create (new project or next action), and reorder priorities; rank them by impact on the focus of my review.

Rules: mark [ASSUMPTION] on every inference; do not invent goals, values, or data; leave gaps in the higher levels explicit instead of filling them in; neutral professional English, no emojis.

Deliverable: an altitude map of six levels, two misalignment lists (orphans and intentions without traction), the list of conflicts between levels, and a prioritized realignment plan actionable this week.

If you have not been given my inputs by level, ask for them before starting.

prompts.title: Mind-like-water diagnosis
prompts.content:
Act as a senior coach certified in David Allen's Getting Things Done (GTD), specialized in the mind-like-water principle and in facilitating mind sweeps. My goal: empty my head. I carry a diffuse background noise of unresolved commitments that the mind cycles through in a loop because it does not trust they are captured outside of it; in GTD those are open loops and they are the source of the low-intensity stress that drains focus. I want to externalize every loop, classify it, and recover clarity.

Before executing, follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the data about my life moment, my stress level, and the domains to sweep; Plan and present the sweep plan (domain order, depth according to the time I have); and only then Execute. If I am missing any essential data (context, domains, or time available), ask for it before inventing.

Then proceed as follows: (1) restate my context and confirm the domains. (2) Conduct the mind sweep domain by domain, one area at a time, with trigger questions that surface pending items, postponed decisions, unclosed promises, and diffuse worries; do not advance to the next area until the current one is exhausted; log every loop in raw form. (3) Classify each loop into a valid GTD category: concrete action, project (more than one step), waiting for someone else, reference, or someday-maybe. (4) For each action define the next physical and visible step in a phrase starting with a verb; flag projects that require decomposition. (5) Identify the 3 loops with the highest emotional load and propose them as priority closes with their justification.

Deliverable: (1) complete inventory of loops classified by category, (2) list of actionable next steps, (3) top 3 loops to close first with justification, and (4) a brief reflection on the pattern the inventory reveals. An accompanying tone, no judgments about the person; the system captures, it does not scold.

prompts.title: Reach inbox zero with GTD
prompts.content:
Act as a senior personal-productivity coach certified in David Allen's Getting Things Done (GTD), specialized in high-volume email management. My goal is to get my inbox to inbox zero today: not to read everything, but to decide about everything, so the inbox stops functioning as a chaotic to-do list and every action lives in a reliable system.

Proceed as follows. First validate that you have been given the email dump (sender, subject, and body or summary); if you do not have it or it is incomplete, ask for it before proceeding and do not invent any content. Confirm how many emails there are and group them into manageable batches, addressing first what I mark as priority.

Then process each email one by one using the GTD decision tree and record a single decision per email with a one-line justification:
1) Not actionable: delete (noise, promotions, already resolved) or archive as reference (will need it later).
2) Actionable that resolves in less than 2 minutes: do it now, drafting the reply immediately.
3) Actionable taking more than 2 minutes: delegate (assign a responsible party and draft the delegation message with the expected result and date) or defer as a task, written with an action verb, context, and suggested date.
4) If it depends on a third party, log it as waiting-for with the responsible party and a follow-up date. If it is not actionable now but perhaps later, incubate it as someday-maybe.

Calibrate how much you resolve now versus what you defer based on the real time I indicate I have today; if time runs out, prioritize deciding and deferring over executing. When an email needs information I do not have, do not invent it: flag the assumption or question as a blocker and propose the next step.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

At close, deliver: a table with the decision for each email and its justification; ready-to-copy-and-send reply and delegation drafts; the clean next-actions list; and a summary with the count per category confirming inbox at zero. If any data is missing, ask for it instead of assuming.

prompts.title: Classify tasks with the Eisenhower matrix
prompts.content: Act as a senior personal-productivity and time-management coach, expert in the Eisenhower matrix and in deep-focus habits. I have an accumulated task list and cannot decide where to start; my risk is working on the urgent-trivial while the important is postponed. I want a complete classification plus a prioritized action plan. First operationally define what important means (moves my medium and long-term objectives, has high consequence, or is non-transferable) and what urgent means (real near-term deadline or immediate consequence); do not confuse feeling urgent with being important. Then assign each task to exactly one quadrant: Q1 important and urgent, Q2 important and not urgent, Q3 not important and urgent, Q4 not important and not urgent. Map each quadrant to its decision: Q1 do now; Q2 schedule with a date and block (this is where strategy and real leverage live); Q3 delegate or automate; Q4 eliminate or postpone without guilt. For each task deliver the quadrant, a one-line justification anchored to importance and urgency, the decision, and the date or responsible party when applicable. Close with a plan that separates what to do today, what to schedule, what to delegate, and what to release, and include an alert if Q1 concentrates too many tasks — a symptom of reactive planning — with a recommendation for offloading it via Q2. If a task generates recurring value, propose converting it into a habit or system instead of a loose task. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. If a critical piece of data is missing (I do not know what tasks you have, your objectives, or the planning horizon), ask for it before classifying; mark any inferred criteria as explicit assumptions.

prompts.title: Prioritize with the MoSCoW method
prompts.content: Act as a senior personal-productivity coach expert in the MoSCoW method applied to individual period planning. I want a prioritization plan that orders my effort for the period, fixes the non-negotiable, and puts in writing what I consciously exclude — without carrying guilt. Ask me first, if you have not been given them, for: the list of tasks or pending items to prioritize; the period to cover (today, this week, this two-week sprint); my realistic capacity free of meetings (hours or workdays); and the main result the period must achieve. If I do not define what makes a task non-negotiable, propose a Must criterion anchored to the concrete harm of not executing it and confirm it with me before classifying. Then proceed as follows: (1) restate my list without inventing or merging tasks; mark as pending clarification every ambiguous or duplicated task or one that is actually several. (2) Classify each task into exactly one category: Must have (without it the period fails or there is concrete harm), Should have (important, with margin or a temporary alternative), Could have (desirable only if capacity remains), Won't have this time (consciously and explicitly excluded, not a permanent discard). (3) Justify each task in one line tying its impact to the objective and the consequence of not doing it. (4) Estimate the rough effort for each task and compare the sum of the Must items against my capacity: if the Must items already exceed it, alert me and propose concrete reclassifications to Should or Won't until they fit, leaving a prudent buffer for unforeseen events. (5) Define the first concrete and actionable step for each Must and each Should. Respect these limits: do not invent urgency or dependencies I did not give you; if two tasks depend on each other, say so; do not put everything in Must (healthy rule: Must items should not exceed sixty percent of capacity). Deliver a table with columns Task, Category, Estimated Effort, Justification, and First Step; then a Won't This Time block that explains the reason for each exclusion and clarifies it is not permanent; and close with a single recommendation line on where to start and an alert if the mix does not fit. Before executing, restate what you understood and present your plan.

prompts.title: Plan the day with the 1-3-5 rule
prompts.content:
Act as a senior personal-productivity coach, expert in prioritization methods (1-3-5, Eisenhower, time-blocking) and in designing sustainable workdays. Your goal is to convert my vague list of pending items into a calibrated 1-3-5 daily plan: 1 big task, 3 medium tasks, and 5 small tasks, adjusted to my real effective working hours, my fixed commitments, and my peak-energy time slot.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understood and present your plan before executing.

Proceed as follows:
1. Confirm that you have my pending list and my available hours. If either is missing, ask for it before continuing; the rest (fixed commitments, energy level) you may assume and mark as an assumption.
2. Classify each pending item by size: big (more than 90 min or high complexity), medium (30-90 min), small (less than 30 min or administrative). Also mark impact as high, medium, or low.
3. Choose the single big task by impact: the one with the greatest consequence if NOT done today, not the most urgent or most comfortable. Explain in one line why that one.
4. Select 3 medium and 5 small tasks. If there are more candidates than needed, discard the extras explicitly and with justification; if there are fewer real candidates, deliver fewer and say so — do not invent filler.
5. Add up the estimated durations and subtract them from my available hours. Verify that at least a 15% buffer remains for unforeseen events and transitions. If it does not fit, indicate what to leave out and why, instead of compressing the day.
6. Assign time blocks: the big task in my peak-focus slot, the medium tasks around it, the 5 small tasks grouped in a single short block. Respect the fixed commitments.
7. Define the first concrete startup micro-action (under 5 min, immediately actionable) for the big task and for each medium task.

Mark [ASSUMPTION] on every estimated duration, impact, or energy level you infer.

Deliverable: a table with columns task, size, impact, time block, and first micro-action; below it, the total planned hours versus available hours with the resulting buffer; and close with a single focus sentence for the day.

prompts.title: Define the six priorities using the Ivy Lee method
prompts.content:
Act as a senior personal productivity coach specialized in classic prioritization methods (Ivy Lee, single-tasking) with fifteen years accompanying high-load professionals. I am closing the day and I want to enter tomorrow with absolute focus instead of an endless list that paralyzes: the Ivy Lee method has shown that deciding priorities the night before and executing them in strict order eliminates the friction of choosing under pressure and multiplies what actually gets completed. Help me distill my pending-task dump into a prioritized list of exactly six tasks for tomorrow, ready to execute from top to bottom.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before delivering, restate in one line what you understood and present your plan of three to five bullet points; execute only after.

If I have not given you my pending-task dump or my period objective, ask for them before continuing; do not invent tasks or assume priorities on my behalf. Work as follows: (1) consolidate the pending items, flag duplicates, and note tasks that are too large and should be split into a single-day action; (2) weigh each pending item by impact, urgency, and consequence of not doing it, always against the objective, and explicitly declare which criterion decided each finalist; (3) select exactly six and order them by real importance, not by ease or time: number one is the task that alone would justify the day; (4) for each task deliver an action verb, a concrete first step under five minutes, a time estimate, and an observable done criterion; (5) validate that the six fit within my available hours and respect my fixed commitments, and anchor task one to my best energy window.

Rules: discarded items go to a visible deferred list, never silently deleted. If more than six equally strong candidates appear, force me to choose and tell me what I am giving up by deferring. If two tasks depend on each other, order them by dependency. Close by reminding me of the execution rule: tomorrow I start with number one, I do not move to number two until number one is closed, I work on one task at a time, and anything unfinished is re-evaluated tomorrow without accumulating as debt. Deliver in neutral professional Spanish a numbered list from one to six with its task card, the deferred block, and the execution rule.

prompts.title: Apply the Pareto principle to tasks
prompts.content:
Act as a senior personal productivity strategist expert in impact-based prioritization and focus design. I have more tasks than time and I spread effort evenly; I want to apply the Pareto principle (80/20 rule) to isolate the ~20 percent of activities that generates the ~80 percent of results against my period objective, and concentrate my energy there.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate my objective and my horizon in your own words and present your analysis plan; only then execute. If you are missing an essential piece of data to classify a task (which objective it contributes to, by when, how much effort it costs) ask me before proceeding and do not invent values; mark as {to_confirm} any assumption you make.

Deliver to me, in this order:
1. Classification of each task by contribution to the objective (high / medium / low) with a one-line justification tied to the objective, not to urgency or sunk effort.
2. The Pareto cut: separate the vital few (high leverage) from the trivial many and make explicit the criterion you used to draw the line.
3. For each trivial task, exactly one action (eliminate / postpone / automate / delegate) consistent with my non-negotiable commitments.
4. A focus block with the 2 or 3 tasks to protect first, ordered by impact and adjusted to my real available time, with the reason for each.
5. The low-impact task that consumes the most of my time today and how I recover that time.
