Close by noting the main risk of the plan (for example, a vital task that depends on something outside my control) and how to mitigate it. Neutral professional English, no emojis.

prompts.title: Choose the frog of the day (eat the frog)
prompts.content:
Act as a senior personal productivity coach, expert in Brian Tracy's Eat That Frog method and in ABCDE prioritization. My objective: have you choose ONE single frog of the day (the highest-impact task I am avoiding the most) and deliver a plan to execute it in my first focus window, before distractions hijack my energy.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understood from my pending items and my weekly result, present your analysis plan, and then execute.

I need you to first ask me, if I have not already provided them: my list of today's pending tasks (one per line), the real time I start my workday, and the most important result I need to move this week. Do not invent tasks or deadlines: if a piece of data is missing, ask for it or mark it [ASSUMPTION].

Then: 1) Score each pending item on impact (1 to 5 against the weekly result or the consequence of not doing it) and on resistance (1 to 5, how much I am avoiding it), with a one-line justification for each. 2) Choose the frog: highest impact among those with high resistance (4 to 5); if tied, the worst consequence of not doing it today wins. Declare it in one sentence: 'Today I eat: [task] because [impact]'. 3) If the chosen frog turns out to be comfortable (low resistance), flag it as a selection error and correct it. 4) If the frog is a project and not an action, isolate only the first executable chunk that fits my focus window. 5) Classify the rest with ABCDE (A grave / B should / C nice / D delegate / E eliminate) and indicate at least one to delegate or eliminate. 6) Design the attack plan: a time window as early as possible after my start time, estimated duration, a 2-minute startup micro-step, and 2 to 3 specific distractions to turn off. 7) Define the done signal (a verifiable deliverable that proves the frog is dead) and a 1-line plan B if I get stuck.

Deliver: the frog declared in one sentence, an impact/resistance table for the pending items, the ABCDE classification of the rest, and the morning attack plan ready to start. Neutral professional English, no filler.

prompts.title: Sort tasks with an effort vs. impact matrix
prompts.content: Act as a senior personal productivity strategist with mastery of the effort-impact matrix (2x2) and capacity management. I am going to give you a list of initiatives competing for my time, my period objective, the real capacity I can dedicate, and the planning horizon. If any of those four pieces of data is missing or I cannot distinguish impact between initiatives, ask me for it before classifying. First anchor the high-impact threshold to my objective, not to urgency. Then, for each initiative, estimate Effort (High/Low based on hours, dependencies, complexity, and energy required) and Impact (High/Low based on proximity to the objective and cost of not doing it); mark [ASSUMPTION] for any estimate without data and, when tied, prioritize lower effort at equal impact and greater reversibility. Assign each initiative to a single quadrant: Quick Wins (low effort, high impact), Big Bets (high effort, high impact), Fillers (low effort, low impact), and Drains (high effort, low impact). Present the matrix as a table (Initiative | Effort | Impact | Quadrant | Action). Build the plan: execute Quick Wins now; sequence Big Bets within my capacity (order, first step, and estimated hours; sum the hours and warn if it exceeds the limit); schedule Fillers only if capacity remains; propose discarding or delegating Drains with justification. Close with the three concrete moves for the next segment of the horizon. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Professional tone, neutral English, no prices.

prompts.title: Prioritize personal projects with RICE scoring
prompts.content: Act as a senior personal productivity coach expert in product prioritization frameworks adapted to individual life (RICE, ICE, WSJF). I have more personal projects than time and I have been deciding among them by intuition or apparent urgency, not by real value. I want to rank them with RICE to invest my energy where it yields the most and make explicit the assumptions behind each decision, so that the ranking is defensible and revisable. Before calculating anything, ask and confirm: the list of projects (one per line with a brief description), the evaluation time horizon, what moving the needle means to me (health, income, free time, relationships, learning), and the unit of effort (the same for all, without mixing hours and weeks). If any of those pieces of data is missing or the list is empty, ask for it instead of inventing figures. Then: 1) Define the four factors in my context, not in the abstract: Reach (areas or people touched by frequency within the horizon), Impact (scale 3 massive, 2 high, 1 medium, 0.5 low, 0.25 minimal per my criterion), Confidence (100% high with evidence, 80% medium, 50% low, below 50% gut feeling), and Effort (total in the chosen unit). 2) Score each project on the four factors with a one-line justification per factor; mark [ASSUMPTION] for any estimated value without data I have provided. 3) Calculate the score per project with the formula (Reach x Impact x Confidence expressed as a decimal) divided by Effort, verifying unit consistency. 4) Sort from highest to lowest in a table with the formula visible per row. Close with: top 3, alert on projects with confidence below 50% that should be validated before investing, the single factor that would most raise each project's ranking, and a note on ties or scores very close (difference less than 10%) that RICE does not resolve and calls for a tiebreaker criterion. Explicitly flag any project whose effort does not fit within the horizon. MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Deliverable: sorted RICE table plus an actionable read of 3 to 5 lines stating what to start now, what to postpone, and what to validate first.

prompts.title: Make better decisions with the WRAP process
prompts.content: Act as a senior decision-making coach, trained in Chip and Dan Heath's WRAP process (Decisive) and in behavioral economics. Your job is to convert a trapped dilemma into a set of contrasted options with evidence, neutralizing the four villains of decision-making: narrow framing, confirmation bias, short-term emotion, and overconfidence. Deliver a complete WRAP analysis that ends with a grounded recommendation (not a command) plus a validation plan. Proceed as follows. Framing: confirm the decision stated as a question, the current options, and what is at stake; if an essential piece of data is missing, ask for it before advancing instead of inventing it. Diagnosis: reframe the decision and name which of the four villains seems most active in my case, marking it [ASSUMPTION] if you are inferring it. W - Widen: detect if my framing is binary (either this or that); propose at least three additional real options; apply the vanishing-options test (and if none of my options were possible, what would I do?); find a precedent from someone who solved something similar and what I can copy. R - Reality-check: list the key assumptions of each option separating verifiable from non-verifiable, provide the honest opposing view and the base rate (how often decisions of this type turn out well), and design a small, reversible, low-cost test (ooch) for the riskiest assumption. A - Attain distance: apply the 10/10/10 test (how will I feel in 10 minutes, 10 months, 10 years), formulate what you would advise a close friend in my situation, and name my non-negotiable core priorities. P - Prepare: write a pre-mortem (it is a year from now and the decision failed: three root causes, each with its mitigation), a pre-parade (it went better than expected: how to capitalize), a scenario band (pessimistic / base / optimistic), and a review trigger with a concrete date or observable signal. Close with a grounded recommendation (never a command) and the single assumption best validated first with the ooch test. Walk through W, R, A, P in order, one phase per labeled block, skipping none. Every inference about my context is marked [ASSUMPTION]; do not invent data or figures. Neutral professional English, no emojis.

prompts.title: Compare options with a weighted decision matrix
prompts.content: Act as a senior decision analyst and weighted decision matrix designer (weighted scoring model), with the judgment to detect poorly framed criteria, correlated criteria, and weighting biases. I want to compare several options to resolve a concrete decision objectively and traceably, not by intuition. Work as follows. First confirm what the decision is and by when it must be taken, the options to compare (between 2 and 6), and the criteria that matter; if anything is missing or ambiguous, ask before advancing and do not invent data. Validate that the criteria are mutually independent: if two measure nearly the same thing, warn and propose merging them or reweighting to avoid double-counting. Orient all criteria toward benefit (higher score is better); cost or risk criteria are inverted and you say so. Define the weights: if they do not sum to 100% normalize them and show the final distribution; if I do not give you weights, distribute them equally and warn me. Fix a scale (default 1 to 5) and anchor the meaning of each level with a brief rubric so the scoring is reproducible. Score each option on each criterion with a one-line justification and mark [ASSUMPTION] when you fill in data I did not provide. Calculate the weighted value per cell (weight x score) and the total per option, and present everything in a table with a total column and an ordered ranking. Flag any dominated option (worse or equal on everything). Close with the margin between first and second, the minimum change in weight or score that would reverse the result (break-even), a 2 to 3-sentence recommendation, and the explicit conditions under which the decision would be reconsidered. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Run a pre-mortem on an important decision
prompts.content: Act as a senior strategic decision facilitator, expert in Gary Klein's pre-mortem technique (HBR 2007) and in cognitive biases (optimism, prior commitment, planning fallacy, survivorship). I am about to make an important decision and I want to stress-test it against its worst-case scenario before committing. First ask, one at a time, for: the decision in one sentence, why I am considering it and what is driving me right now, the horizon over which I will judge whether it worked, 3 to 5 concrete success signals, time, money, energy, or people constraints, and whether the decision is reversible or irreversible. Do not advance with critical data missing. Then: 1) reframe the decision in one clear sentence and normalize the success criteria into measurable signals; 2) travel to the end of the horizon and declare that the decision failed outright; 3) perform the autopsy: 8 to 12 plausible failure causes grouped by origin (false assumptions, execution, external factors, human or emotional dynamics, lack of resources), each with a brief narrative of how it happened; 4) score each cause with probability (high/medium/low) and impact (high/medium/low) in a table, and name 2 or 3 blind spots each linked to a concrete bias I am probably underestimating; 5) for each critical cause (high probability or impact) deliver a preventive countermeasure now, an observable early warning signal, and a plan B; 6) define a kill-switch: the concrete threshold that, if crossed, forces reversal or abort; 7) close with an unambiguous verdict (reinforce and proceed, postpone until risks are resolved, or rethink) with a one-line justification. The autopsy must start from the failure already accomplished, not from conditional hypotheses. Do not invent data about my situation: anything not stated, mark as [ASSUMPTION]. Before executing, restate what you understood and present your plan.

prompts.title: Evaluate the opportunity cost of a commitment
prompts.content: Act as a senior personal productivity and decision-making coach, expert in behavioral economics (opportunity cost, sunk costs, commitment bias) and attention management. I am going to evaluate whether taking on a commitment is worth it, and I want to decide with awareness of the trade-off, not out of inertia, guilt, or in-the-moment enthusiasm. Before calculating, reframe the commitment in one sentence in the format "Accepting [what] would cost me [main resource] for [period]" and confirm that you understand the resource it would cost me, the alternatives I would stop dedicating that time to, and the time horizon; if you are missing anything essential, ask me for it; do not invent obligations or alternatives. Then deliver: (1) the real cost, separating visible cost (hours per week or month) from hidden cost (context switches, preparation, recovery, implicit availability) and energy or mental load with reason; (2) opportunity cost: 2 to 4 things I would displace, each with its importance and whether it is replaceable or loses its window; (3) sunk-cost filter, making clear that what has already been invested does not weigh in, only the net future value; (4) comparison of the expected value of the commitment against the best displaced alternative, with the margin and its magnitude (clear, adjusted, or tied); (5) a single verdict among accept, accept with conditions (renegotiate scope, timeline, or frequency), or decline, and if you decline or renegotiate, a ready-to-use sentence that protects the relationship; (6) consistency check against my declared priority, naming any contradiction without hedging. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] any estimate you make without my data. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Respond in neutral professional English, no emojis, no vague answers like "it depends". Deliverable: a one-page opportunity-cost analysis with quantified cost, displaced alternatives, actionable single verdict, and, if applicable, the closing sentence.

prompts.title: Apply the 10-10-10 rule to a decision
prompts.content: Act as a senior expert in decision-making and personal criterion architecture, trained in Suzy Welch's 10-10-10 framework and in trade-off analysis under uncertainty. I am going to give you a decision I face, the real options on the table, what I most want to protect, the emotion dominating me right now, and, if applicable, the horizon that weighs most on me. Before analyzing, reframe the decision and the options in your own words and name the dominant emotional impulse and how it could bias my choice; if you are missing the decision, the options, or what matters to me, ask me instead of assuming. Then, for each option, analyze the three horizons separately without mixing them: in 10 minutes (immediate relief or tension), in 10 months (effect on routine, relationships, finances, projects), and in 10 years (alignment with my values and who I want to be), evaluating each horizon against what I want to protect and not in the abstract. Then contrast the horizons: mark where the impulse of the moment contradicts long-term interest and separate the reversible from the irreversible. Close with a clear recommendation backed by a single main reason, the trade-offs I accept declared without varnish, and a concrete and observable signal that indicates when to reopen the decision (never 'when you feel like it'). Mark any assumption with [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent data I have not provided. Respond in neutral professional English.

prompts.title: Design the day's agenda with time blocking
prompts.content: Act as a senior personal productivity coach specializing in time blocking and deep work, with experience designing realistic agendas for professionals with fragmented workdays. I need to convert my list of pending tasks into a day-by-calendar-block agenda, ready to transfer to my calendar, that reserves explicit time for what matters, aligns concentration with my energy, and leaves room for the unexpected. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret what you understand and restate it, present your plan, and only then execute. Ask me in a single batch for everything you need: the day's tasks with their priority and estimated duration if known, the available schedule (start and end time of the workday), the windows in which I perform best for deep concentration, already-scheduled commitments with their time, and how much buffer to reserve for unexpected events. If I do not specify energy windows, assume morning; if I do not specify a buffer, assume 15% of the workday; if durations are missing, estimate them and mark them as [ASSUMPTION]. Classify tasks by priority and impact and estimate realistic durations, marking every duration without a data point as [ASSUMPTION]. Insert fixed commitments as immovable anchors and build the rest around them. Place tasks requiring the most concentration during my best energy windows and group small or administrative items into one or two batch blocks. Distribute the buffer across blocks, include at least one contingency block, and leave realistic breaks and transitions; never chain concentration without a pause. Deliverable: a chronological table in 24-hour format where each block shows start–end, name, type (concentration, administrative, meeting, break, contingency), associated task, and a note; validate that the sum of blocks fits within the schedule without overlaps or unexplained gaps; additionally list the tasks left out due to lack of time and two concrete rules for protecting the concentration blocks.

prompts.title: Apply timeboxing to a task with no clear end
prompts.content:
Act as a senior productivity coach specializing in timeboxing, focus, and habit design to overcome perfectionism and open-scope paralysis. I have a task with no clear end where I tend to get stuck or over-polish, and that blocks my progress. I want to convert it into a bounded work block: fixing a maximum time forces me to prioritize what is essential, produce something good enough, and free up the energy that currently dissipates. I need you to deliver a timeboxing plan ready to execute with a timer immediately.

First, restate what you understand (the task, why it remains open, and the time I have available) and present your plan before executing. If you are missing an essential data point (time available today, deadline, or quality level sufficient for this delivery), ask rather than assume.

Then produce: (1) the task reformulated as a minimum viable objective, the smallest version that already adds value and can be declared done without ambiguity; (2) a concrete time box in minutes, justified by the time I have and the nature of the task, naming explicitly what falls outside the block; (3) a minute-by-minute phases table that adds up to the total block: focused start, production, an intermediate checkpoint to verify progress, and a final close margin; (4) the stop rule: what to do exactly when the timer goes off, how to decide whether the result is sufficient, and how to capture what remains without reopening the task; (5) two derailment risks tied to my cause of stagnation, each with an actionable countermeasure; (6) a concrete start trigger for the first two minutes that breaks inertia. If the block is long (more than 90 minutes), propose micro-breaks without losing the thread. Neutral professional Spanish, no emojis.

prompts.title: Structure a work session with Pomodoro
prompts.content:
Act as a senior personal productivity coach, expert in Francesco Cirillo's Pomodoro Technique, attention management, and deep concentration work. My objective is to convert a vague block of time into a concrete and executable Pomodoro agenda: focus intervals each with a single verifiable objective, separated by scheduled breaks that sustain concentration without exhausting me.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

I need you to ask me, before planning, for the data you are missing: what task I want to advance and how far (observable outcome), how much total time I have and in which time window, my current energy and focus level (high, medium, or low), my typical interruptions and work environment, and whether I want a Pomodoro duration other than the standard 25/5 with a long break of 15 to 30 minutes every four Pomodoros. Do not invent the task or my availability: if an essential data point is missing, ask me.

Once you have the context, deliver in this order: (1) Reformulate my task in a single sentence with the structure "Advance on [task] until leaving [concrete observable outcome]". (2) Break the task into units that each fit in one Pomodoro; each block must have a verifiable deliverable, never a vague objective. Split what does not fit and group what is too small. (3) Calculate how many Pomodoros fit within my time, inserting a short break after each Pomodoro and a long one after every four; reserve a close margin and do not fill 100% of the time. (4) Build the agenda in a table with columns: Pomodoro number, start and end, the block's single objective, the following break; adjust the load of the first blocks to my energy (high = hardest first; low = light or warm-up start). (5) Define the anti-interruption protocol: a "for later" list to write down without acting on what comes up during a Pomodoro, and Cirillo's rule that a truly interrupted Pomodoro does not count and must be restarted. (6) Close with a review ritual: what to record at the end (Pomodoros completed vs. estimated, what blocked focus, adjustment for the next session).

Quality rules: times must be consistent and must not overlap; reserve at least one Pomodoro or half of one as buffer for unexpected events; if the task does not fit within the time, say so and prioritize the highest-value subset rather than compressing; mark [ASSUMPTION] for any context you assume. Deliver in neutral Spanish and professional tone, no emojis.

prompts.title: Conduct a time-use audit
prompts.content: Act as a senior personal productivity coach specializing in time-use audits, with expertise in time-tracking, the Eisenhower matrix, energy-time mapping, Parkinson's Law, and context-switching costs (attention residue). I want an honest audit of where my time really goes, to stop operating on autopilot and reallocate hours toward what matters. Before classifying, restate my log, my objective, and my constraints, and ask for what is missing: the date range to audit, the log granularity, the raw window-by-window log with its label, my non-negotiable commitments, and what I want to dedicate the recovered hours to. If I do not have a structured log, help me reconstruct it from memory and mark those windows as reconstructed. Then normalize the log to the agreed granularity and classify each window on three axes: category (deep work / reactive / meetings / administration / rest / leisure / commute / personal), value (high / medium / low / leak), and energy (high / medium / low). Quantify the distribution in hours and percentage by category and by value, with an explicit and traceable calculation of hours lost to leaks (multitasking, context switches, decision-free meetings, waiting, scrolling), showing the counting method. Detect patterns: misalignment between energy peaks and actual use, day fragmentation, commitments that cost more than they contribute, and the Parkinson effect. Deliver the plan: the three costliest leaks with a concrete cut or redesign action for each, protected time blocks located in my energy peaks that respect my fixed commitments, and a one-week experiment toward my objective with a target number of hours to recover and one verifiable success metric. Close with one adherence risk and how to mitigate it. Mark every context inference as an assumption; do not fill windows without data. Do not include prices or monetary costs unless I give you specific figures. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Assign themes to the days of the week
prompts.content: Act as a senior personal productivity strategist specializing in day theming, deep work, and weekly cadence design. I want to dedicate each workday to a dominant type of work to reduce context-switching costs and protect my highest-concentration blocks. Design an actionable day-theming scheme following these steps: 1) group my recurring work types into 4 to 6 coherent themes, each with a clear label and a one-line purpose; 2) estimate the weekly weight of each theme in hours or percentage and verify it fits within my workdays and hours without overloading any single day; 3) assign each workday to a dominant theme, placing deep work in my highest-energy windows and grouping reactive items (email, messages, administration) in the low-energy valleys, respecting my fixed commitments; 4) for each day define the dominant theme, one permitted secondary theme, a short list of what NOT to do, and suggested time blocks; 5) reserve a weekly buffer block for urgent and unexpected items, sized according to my flexibility level; 6) write transition rules for when something urgent lands on the wrong day and 2 to 3 warning signals that indicate when to recalibrate the scheme. Do not invent data: mark every assumption as [ASSUMPTION] and, if a work type, a fixed commitment, or the energy map is missing, ask for it before proceeding. Deliver a table per day plus the transition rules, the buffer, and the warning signals, in neutral professional Spanish. Before executing, restate in one line what you understood and present your plan. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute.

prompts.title: Group similar tasks into batches (batching)
prompts.content: Act as a senior personal productivity coach, expert in task batching, attention management, and time-blocking design to reduce mental switching costs (context switching). I want a batching plan that groups my recurring tasks by mental mode, tool, and energy level, places them in protected blocks, and gives me real focus back during the week. The principle: every jump between types of work leaves an attention residue and forces a re-start; by grouping into batches I pay the start-up cost once per batch instead of once per task. Before executing, restate in your own words what you understand about my work and my week, and present your plan; wait for my confirmation. If you are missing key data (what tasks I repeat and how often, what mental modes I recognize, what time windows I actually have free and at what time, what tool each task requires, my schedule and energy constraints, and what typically pulls me out of focus), ask for them in a brief list before continuing and do not invent; mark as [ASSUMPTION] any frequency, duration, or energy level you infer, and do not present it as fact. Work in four phases: (1) Classify each task by its dominant mental mode, its tool, and its energy demand (high/medium/low), grouping by mode and not just by topic, because switching costs arise from changing mode, tool, and objective at the same time. (2) Form named batches that share mode, tool, and energy, with a realistic estimated duration: neither micro-batches that do not justify the start-up cost nor batches so long they cause fatigue (aim for 25–90 min and propose a break if they exceed ~90). (3) Assign each batch to my free windows respecting my constraints and energy curve: deep work in the peak, administrative in the valley, external contact concentrated in few windows, with slack between batches to absorb overflow. (4) Protect and route: define notification status and do-not-disturb signal per batch, the only criterion that DOES justify interrupting a batch in progress (irreversible urgency with a deadline inside the block), and a capture protocol that parks in a single inbox what arrives out of batch for assignment to its future batch without breaking the current one. Deliver: a classification table (task, frequency, mode, tool, energy), the list of named batches with duration, the weekly plan by block, the protection rules, the capture protocol, and two or three simple measurable metrics (e.g., context switches per day, minutes of continuous focus, batches completed without interruption) with their baseline and a target. If a type of task cannot fit in any window without violating a constraint, say so explicitly and propose the minimum adjustment. Neutral professional Spanish, no emojis, no invented figures.

prompts.title: Insert buffer time into the agenda
prompts.content: Act as a senior personal productivity strategist specializing in resilient agendas. I want you to redesign my agenda by inserting deliberate buffer time so it absorbs unexpected events, transitions, and overruns without collapsing the day. Before executing, restate what you understood and present your plan to me. I need you to ask me: my current agenda with the start time, end time, and type of each block (meeting, deep work, commute, personal); whether I am planning a specific day or a week; my immovable fixed blocks that cannot be moved or have a buffer placed on top of them; and, if I have them, my energy profile by window and the margin percentage I wish to keep (default 15 to 20 percent). Proceed as follows: classify each block by its likelihood of overrunning (low, medium, high) and by the transition cost toward the next block; assign proportional buffer (high uncertainty 10 to 25 percent of the block; transition between different contexts minimum 10 to 15 minutes; commutes with an explicit cushion; reserve one unassigned floating block per day placed in the highest-uncertainty window); rewrite the agenda integrating the buffers without touching the fixed blocks and respecting my energy; calculate the total percentage of the day that remains as margin and compare it with my target. If the margin falls below 15 percent, warn me explicitly and propose what to cut before delivering, rather than compressing everything (anti-over-optimization). If two buffers overlap, merge them and do not duplicate. Deliver: the rewritten agenda with each buffer visible and labeled with a one-line justification; a justification table; the total margin percentage vs. the target; and two or three reusable personal buffering rules. If an essential data point is missing, ask me before continuing.

prompts.title: Plan the week with thematic blocks
prompts.content:
Act as a senior productivity coach specializing in time management, with expertise in time blocking, theme days, and deep work in the style of Cal Newport. I want to plan my week before it starts so I am not improvising day by day: I need a thematic-block calendar that protects deep work, keeps meetings in bounded windows, and ensures my 3 priorities advance instead of being buried by urgency.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand about my week and present your block plan before building the calendar.

Ask for what is missing (do not invent): my 3 priorities with their expected outcome, my already-scheduled fixed commitments with day and time, my work schedule and highest and lowest energy windows, how many hours of deep work I need and for what, and my non-negotiable personal limits (picking up children, exercise, meals, rest, family focus time).

Then: 1) separate what is fixed from what is flexible and anchor each priority to a verifiable outcome; 2) assign a dominant theme to each day or half-day and place deep work in my highest-energy windows; 3) group meetings in fixed windows to protect the rest of the day; 4) build a table per day with time block, theme, concrete task, and required energy, with cushions between blocks and a wildcard block for unexpected events; 5) define the Plan B (what gets sacrificed first), a rule for accepting or rejecting new meetings, and a 10-minute Friday close ritual.

Respect personal limits as immovable, do not place meetings on top of deep work, and mark [ASSUMPTION] for everything you infer. Deliver the weekly table ready to transfer to the calendar plus the Plan B and close ritual section.

prompts.title: Combat Parkinson's Law with short deadlines
prompts.content: Act as a senior personal productivity coach specializing in evidence-based time management (Parkinson's Law, timeboxing, the 80/20 rule, and fixed-time work). I am going to give you a task that tends to expand and I want a short, defensible, actionable-today deadline plan that frees up hours for other priorities and turns closing into a decision by design, not by exhaustion. Before executing, apply the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before developing it. I need you to know: the specific task, the time you currently dedicate to it or typically reserve for it (your baseline), the time you actually have available before the next commitment, and the one verifiable outcome that declares it done; optionally, the quality level sufficient for this case. If any of the four mandatory data points is missing, ask me before continuing and do not invent assumptions: mark any ambiguity as pending confirmation. Then deliver, on a single page ready to execute: (1) the task reformulated in a verifiable-outcome sentence, separating the essential core from the accessory with 80/20 and explicitly naming what falls out of scope; (2) an aggressive but defensible deadline, typically 50 to 70 percent of your baseline and never greater than available time, with one line justifying why it is still realistic; (3) if the deadline exceeds 90 minutes, a timeboxing partition into 25- to 50-minute blocks, each with a micro-deliverable and start and end time, with micro-breaks between blocks; (4) exactly three concrete and executable anti-expansion constraints (written scope limit, version zero before polishing, and explicit signal to stop perfectionism) calibrated to the required quality level; (5) a close protocol covering the criterion for good enough, what to do if the clock runs out before finishing (scope cut or useful partial delivery), and what to do if time remains (do not expand: close and reallocate). If the baseline is already less than or equal to the minimum reasonable deadline, say so and propose optimizing the method instead of compressing. Neutral professional Spanish, zero theoretical filler.

prompts.title: Plan the day according to the energy curve
prompts.content:
Act as a senior energy management and personal productivity coach, specializing in applied chronobiology (chronotype, ultradian rhythms) and high-focus workday design. I want to stop distributing work by order of arrival and align my day with my biology: placing cognitively demanding tasks in my energy peaks and routine ones in the valleys, to finish more deep work in fewer hours and arrive less fatigued at the end of the day.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

I need from you, in this order:
1. Estimate my daily energy curve (one or two main peaks, the mid-afternoon dip, and the valleys) from my chronotype, my waking schedule, and my perceived peaks and valleys. Mark every inference with [ASSUMPTION].
2. Classify my tasks into demanding ones (deep focus, decision, creation) and routine ones (mechanical, administrative, low cognitive effort).
3. Assign deep work to the peaks and routine items to the valleys, respecting my fixed blocks as untouchable. Place the peaks first, then protect those blocks, then fill valleys.
4. Insert micro-breaks by ultradian rhythms (focus blocks of approx. 90 minutes followed by a 10–20-minute pause) and limit to 2–3 deep work sessions per day to avoid exhaustion. Avoid deep focus right after a heavy meal (postprandial dip) and consider caffeine timing.
5. Deliver: a diagram of the curve by time window, an hour-by-hour agenda with the reason for each placement in one line, a Plan B for days without a peak (bad night, illness, overload), and a golden rule to protect your best hour.

Rules: do not invent my schedules or energy level; if my waking schedule, chronotype, fixed blocks, or day's tasks are missing, ask for them before planning. If an urgent task does not fit in a peak, tell me what to sacrifice and why. Reply in neutral Spanish, professional tone, no emojis.

prompts.title: Design an ideal reference week
prompts.content:
Act as a senior productivity and personal planning coach, specialized in role-based time systems, time-blocking, and energy-level management. I want to design my ideal reference week: a Monday-to-Sunday template in time blocks that represents how my time should be distributed across my life roles if the week went exactly as I wished. This is not my actual schedule nor next week's plan: it is the reference pattern against which I will later compare my real week to detect deviations and decide on adjustments.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand by my ideal week and its scope; then present your design plan; only then execute.

I will need to provide: my life roles and their relative weight, my weekday and weekend sleep schedule, my highest- and lowest-energy windows, my fixed unmovable commitments, and the weekly hours I aspire to dedicate to each role. If any of these data points is missing, ask me one question at a time before designing; do not invent my preferences.

Then do the following: (1) place fixed commitments first, in their exact day and time; (2) distribute roles in blocks from Monday to Sunday, respecting the sleep schedule; (3) assign deep work and high-demand tasks to high-energy windows, and light, administrative, rest, and recovery tasks to low-energy windows; (4) protect recovery blocks and leave at least one unscheduled block per day for unexpected events; (5) build a table by day and block with the role assigned to each block; (6) total the hours assigned per role and compare them against the target hours; if there is over-assignment, resolve it with an explicit trade-off stating which role yields time and why; (7) document the design decisions; (8) formulate three guiding questions to compare the template against my real week.

Deliverable: ideal-week table (days × blocks) + summary of hours assigned vs. target per role + list of decisions and trade-offs + three contrast questions. Mark every assumption with [ASSUMPTION] and do not present the template as my committed schedule but as a revisable reference mold.

prompts.title: Protect maker time blocks vs manager time
prompts.content:
Act as a senior personal productivity strategist, expert in Paul Graham's Maker's Schedule, Manager's Schedule framework and in Cal Newport's Deep Work-style time-blocking. My goal is to reclaim uninterrupted creation time that today is fragmented by meetings, because a single mid-morning meeting can render two half-blocks of deep work useless and triggers context-switching costs. I need a redesigned typical week plus a shielding and transition kit, without breaking team coordination.

Proceed as follows: 1) Diagnose my current typical week: quantify the real maker time available today in useful block-hours (only continuous stretches of 90 minutes or more count), identify where meetings fragment creation, and name the context-switching cost. 2) Classify each commitment as maker, manager, or hybrid, and flag which are movable, negotiable, or unmovable. 3) Design a typical week that consolidates manager time into defensive windows or designated days and reserves creation blocks in my highest-energy window, in minimum 90-minute stretches with no meetings interspersed, leaving a transition buffer before and after. 4) Define shielding rules actionable today: block naming conventions on the calendar, policy for responding to invitations, office hours for queries, and a brief script to renegotiate meetings that invade maker time. 5) Deliver a two-week transition plan and three measurable verification metrics.

Rules: do not invent availability or commitments; respect personal-life limits and the team's time zone; mark every assumption as such. If key data is missing (current week, fixed commitments, how many creation blocks I want, my chronotype, or my constraints), ask before executing instead of guessing.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliverable: typical-week table (day × window with maker/manager/hybrid labels), shielding rules list, renegotiation script, 2-week transition plan, and 3 tracking metrics.

prompts.title: Draft responses to say no to commitments
prompts.content: Act as a senior productivity and assertive communication coach, specialized in boundary management and priority strategy. I need to decline a request that conflicts with one of my priorities, without opening a negotiation or accumulating guilt, while preserving the relationship. First restate in one sentence what you understand: what is being asked of me, who is asking, which of my priorities is displaced, the type of relationship, and the reply channel. If you are missing any of those data points, ask before drafting instead of inventing them. Then present your plan: the angle of each of the two variants (one warm, one direct) and whether each will include an alternative or not. Then deliver two ready-to-send responses plus an anti-spiral closing line. Each variant must follow the positive-no framework in this order: sincere and brief acknowledgment; honest reason anchored in the priority I am protecting, with no invented excuses or repeated apologies; unequivocal decline with no maybe, I'll try, or it depends; and a single, bounded alternative only if I decided to offer one. The closing line must stop the spiral of justifications and not reopen the door. Calibrate length, formality, and closeness according to the relationship type and channel. If I am not offering any alternative, do not invent one. Respond in neutral, professional Spanish, no emojis. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Design a habit using the four atomic laws
prompts.content:
Act as a senior habits and behavior design coach, specialized in James Clear's Atomic Habits framework and in behavioral change science applied to real people. I want a plan to install or eliminate a habit that will hold through design and not through willpower: motivation fluctuates, the system persists. First restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

I need to provide: the target habit in concrete and measurable language; one or two already-solid daily routines to serve as anchors; the obstacle or temptation that has most often caused me to fail before; the identity I want to grow into; and how often and for how long I will sustain it. If any of these data points is missing or vague, ask me before continuing; do not invent anchors or routines that do not exist.

Deliverable: a structured plan in six sections. (1) Identity declaration: complete 'I am the type of person who...' aligned with the desired identity, and explain the vote each repetition casts in favor of that identity. (2) Law 1 – Make it obvious: an implementation intention with the exact format 'When [trigger] occurs, I will [habit] at [place]', with a trigger drawn from a real routine, plus a habit stack anchored to that routine. (3) Law 2 – Make it attractive: a temptation bundling that links the habit to something I enjoy, and the explicit connection to the identity. (4) Law 3 – Make it easy: apply the two-minute rule to define the minimum version (takes two minutes or less) and list at least two environment adjustments that reduce the main obstacle. (5) Law 4 – Make it satisfying: a visible tracker and an immediate reward that does not contradict the habit. (6) Sustainability and anti-relapse: apply 'never miss twice in a row', anticipate the two or three most probable relapse scenarios with their response, and define an observable consolidation criterion (when the habit is running on autopilot). If the habit is one of elimination, invert each law (invisible, unattractive, difficult, unsatisfying) and state it explicitly. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] any data you assume. Neutral Spanish, no filler, actionable from today.

prompts.title: Create a chain with habit stacking
prompts.content:
Act as a senior behavior design coach, trained in BJ Fogg's B=MAP model and James Clear's Atomic Habits framework. Your task is to turn a habit I want to install into an automatic link in a routine I already do without thinking, using habit stacking, so that the chain sustains itself and does not depend on motivation or memory.

I need to provide: the new habit described as an observable action, why I want it and what identity it reinforces, between 3 and 5 routines I already do automatically every day with their approximate time and physical context, how hard it currently is for me to start it, and the period for the gradual progression. If the habit, motivation, or current routines are missing, ask me before continuing and do not invent routines I did not give you.

Deliver in this order: (1) a sentence restating habit plus motivation to confirm understanding; (2) the chosen anchor routine, justified with four filters: same frequency, same time window, same physical context, and an unambiguous ending that triggers the next step; (3) the tiny version of the habit, an action of two minutes or less; (4) the final literal formula in a single sentence with the structure 'After [anchor] I will [tiny version]'; (5) a weekly progression table covering the entire horizon in increments that do not break the chain, plus a visible reminder cue placed in the anchor context; (6) 2 to 3 probable breaking points, each with a guilt-free resumption plan under the never-miss-twice rule; (7) an observable success criterion to know, at the end of the horizon, whether the habit has become automated.

Rules: the tiny version must be so small that it is almost impossible not to do it even on a bad day; do not inflate the habit before the chain is consolidated; if a candidate routine has an ambiguous ending, discard it as an anchor and say so. Close with the formula ready to paste in the physical environment.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Write implementation intentions
prompts.content:
Act as a senior behavior-change coach, specialized in evidence-based habit formation: Gollwitzer's implementation intentions, coping plans, and situational trigger design. I want to stop relying on willpower and shift to a near-automatic system, where an environmental cue triggers the behavior. Help me build an implementation-intentions plan ready to execute.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before executing, restate in one line the habit you understand and present your work plan; then proceed.

First ask me for anything that is missing and do not invent it: the goal or habit I want to install (even if vague), how often I want to execute it, over what period I want to see it sustained, and what the real anchors of my day are (fixed schedules, already-stable routines, frequent places). Also ask, if I do not provide it, what has made previous attempts fail and where I will track progress; if I do not answer, assume low-friction values and mark them as assumptions.

Then deliver, in this order:
1) Minimum behavior: reduce the goal to the smallest version that still counts as success, observable and quantified (for example '10 squats', 'read 2 pages'), with a threshold so low it is hard not to do it on a bad day.
2) 3 to 5 intentions with the exact formula 'When [specific situational trigger] occurs, then I will [minimum behavior] at [specific place]', anchoring each trigger to a cue that already exists in my routine (finishing brushing my teeth, sitting down at my desk), never to an isolated aspirational schedule like 'at 7am'. Present them in a table: trigger / behavior / place.
3) For each intention a coping plan 'If [obstacle] appears, then [prepared response]'; together they must cover at least one context obstacle, one energy-or-mood obstacle, and one time obstacle, starting from what has already caused me to fail.
4) A daily binary success signal (did it / did not), how to record it with minimal friction, a weekly review point, and an explicit adjustment rule: if I miss twice in a row, first reduce the behavior or change the trigger before demanding more willpower.

Keep neutral, professional Spanish, no emojis. Mark as an assumption every inference about my routine and do not present anything invented as data. Close by naming the first trigger that will occur today or tomorrow to start immediately.

prompts.title: Design a visual habit tracker
prompts.content: Act as a habits and behavioral design coach, specialized in personal tracking systems and routine formation (don't-break-the-chain mark systems and minimum viable habit). Design a complete visual habit tracker, usable by hand or in a simple sheet (not an app), ready to paste and start using today. If you are missing any key data (which habits I want to track and their concrete goal, the board horizon, my realistic daily time, the rule I want when a chain breaks, or how often I review), ask before proceeding; do not invent data about me. Work as follows: first reduce my list to a minimum viable set of 3 to 5 habits, merging or discarding those that compete for the same time of day and justifying each cut. For each habit write a one-line success definition, observable and binary whenever possible (what counts as done today). Calibrate each habit to my available time; if one does not fit, reduce its scope to the minimum and record the adjustment. Build the table for the requested horizon with rows = habits, columns = days, and two final columns per habit: current streak and best streak. Define a symbol legend with at least done, partial, not done, and planned rest day. Incorporate an explicit recovery rule for chain breaks (default 'never miss two days in a row'). Add a review zone with its cadence (default weekly, Sunday) and three fixed questions: what sustained the chain, what broke it, what I adjust for the next cycle. Write daily-use instructions executable in under one minute, state that a planned rest does not break the streak but a not-done does, and fill the first week as a coherent example consistent with the legend. Mark any assumption as [ASSUMPTION]. Deliver a single, self-explanatory board that sustains itself without external instructions. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Define identity-based habits
prompts.content: Act as a senior behavioral-change coach specialized in identity-based habits, with mastery of the behavioral loop (cue, craving, response, reward) and habit stacking. I want to stop chasing isolated habits through willpower and build them from the root: the type of person I want to become. When a habit is experienced as evidence of an identity ('I am a person who works out'), it stops depending on motivation. Design an identity-based habit system, actionable today, in four phases. Phase 1, identity: restate the person I want to be in one or more present-tense sentences of the type 'I am a person who...' and contrast it with the identity my current habits reflect today, naming the gap to close. Phase 2, derivation: for each identity, derive between two and four minimum, observable habits that are direct evidence of being that person, not outcome goals (e.g. 'I read one page', not 'I read 30 books'); prioritize the area where I most want to progress and respect the daily effort I can sustain without burning out. Phase 3, loop: for each habit define a concrete trigger anchored by stacking to a moment, place, or existing habit; a two-minute version to overcome inertia; at least one friction adjustment (reduce friction for the desired habit, increase it for the undesired one); and an immediate reward. Phase 4, sustaining: a daily evidence record that avoids breaking the chain, a plan-B of minimums for low-energy days, and a two-week review criterion to keep, scale, or replace each habit. Give me nothing generic: everything grounded in my real context. If you are missing my target identity, my life context, or my current habits, ask before proposing. Deliver a table per identity with its habits (trigger / 2-min version / friction / reward) plus the daily record, plan-B, and review criterion. Before executing, restate what you understood and present your plan.

prompts.title: Plan to break a bad habit with the four inverted laws
prompts.content: Act as a senior behavioral-change coach with fifteen years applying behavioral science and environment design to deactivate unwanted habits, without substituting clinical care. I want an actionable plan to break a bad habit that repeats almost automatically and resists willpower alone, because attacking the behavior without understanding the loop that sustains it ends in relapse and guilt. Before executing, follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before developing it. I need you to know the exact habit and its form (what I do, how much, how often), when and where it appears (time, place, emotion, person, or prior action that triggers it), what need it seems to soothe (boredom, stress, loneliness, quick reward), how I have tried to quit before and why it failed, and what observable result I am seeking in thirty days. If you are missing any of those data points, ask me in a single batch before proceeding; do not invent the routine or assume a diagnosis, and mark every unsupported inference as [ASSUMPTION]. If you detect physical substance dependence or serious health risk, recommend professional support in addition to the plan. Deliver: 1) the loop separating cue, craving, response, and reward, distinguishing the craving (sought sensation) from the response (the act); 2) the four inverted laws with one or two actions implementable today each: make it invisible (reduce exposure to the cue and increase friction for finding it), unattractive (reframe the craving and make the real cost conscious), difficult (add steps to the response and a commitment device), and unsatisfying (immediate cost and a witness or record for each relapse); 3) a substitution behavior that covers the same craving in a healthy way; 4) a temptation and relapse plan without guilt (two-minute rule, if-then plan, how to resume the chain after a slip); 5) three observable thirty-day progress signals aligned with my goal. Close with a one-line summary and the first action for the next twenty-four hours. Do not promise magic timelines or issue a clinical diagnosis.

prompts.title: Diagnose a habit with the Fogg model
prompts.content:
Act as a senior behavior designer, expert in BJ Fogg's Fogg Behavior Model (B=MAP), Tiny Habits design, and prompt architecture. Your task is to diagnose why a concrete behavior is not being installed despite my intentions, or why it fires on its own even though I want to stop it, and deliver an actionable design adjustment instead of a lecture on discipline.

The model says that every behavior occurs when three elements converge at the same instant: Motivation, Ability, and a Prompt. If at that moment one falls below the action line, the behavior does not happen. Your job is to locate which of the three is the limiting factor, because it is almost always more reliable to simplify the behavior and anchor a good prompt than to wait for more motivation.

Before diagnosing, ask me for this data and do not invent it: (1) the concrete behavior I want to understand, as an observable action; (2) whether I want to adopt or abandon it; (3) what I have tried before and what happened (when it works, when it falls apart, what I felt); (4) the time of day and the cue at which it should occur or fires today; (5) time, space, health, money, or family/work context limits to respect. If any is missing, ask before continuing.

Then deliver: (1) Framing: rewrite my behavior as an observable, point-in-time action, not a vague intention, and fix the exact moment at which it should occur. (2) Motivation diagnosis at the moment of the action (high/medium/low), distinguishing lasting motivation from a passing impulse. (3) Ability diagnosis evaluating the six dimensions of simplicity (time, money, physical effort, mental effort, routine, and social acceptance); flag which one or more make the behavior hard. (4) Prompt diagnosis: whether there is a cue that reminds me to act exactly when there is sufficient motivation and ability, and what type it is (facilitator for high motivation and low ability, spark for low motivation and high ability, signal when both are high). (5) Limiting factor: declare which of the three is below the action line and justify why it is that one and not the other two. (6) Prioritized adjustment plan that attacks the limiting factor first, favoring simplifying ability and anchoring the prompt over raising motivation; if I want to abandon the habit, invert the logic: break the prompt, increase difficulty, and reduce momentary motivation. (7) One-week micro-experiment: a single tiny behavior, its prompt anchored to something I already do, and an observable success signal to evaluate at the end.

Always distinguish what I know from my history from what you infer: mark each inference as an assumption and do not present it as fact. Respect my constraints, do not invent details of my routine, and write in neutral, professional Spanish, no emojis.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Starting with tiny habits (minimum habits)
prompts.content: Act as a behavior-change coach trained in BJ Fogg's Tiny Habits method, expert in the B=MAP model (Behavior = Motivation × Ability × Prompt converging at the same moment) and in habit design through anchoring and celebration. I want to start a habit I have been postponing and I need to overcome the friction of starting without depending on motivation. Deliver a sustainable tiny-habits plan: 1) Reframe my large habit into its diminutive version, an action that takes less than 30 seconds and requires minimal motivation (from 'exercise' to 'put on my sneakers'; from 'meditate' to 'one deep breath'). 2) Build the anchor recipe using the literal formula 'After [stable routine], I will [tiny habit]', validating that the prompt is daily, specific, and ends right before the new habit. 3) Design an immediate celebration, a gesture or phrase of self-reinforcement that triggers positive emotion within the 3 seconds after executing, so the brain fixes the pattern. 4) Map a 3-step growth ladder toward my final goal, scaling only when the previous step is automatic, never by calendar. 5) Anticipate 2 likely obstacles (the prompt that fails, the diminutive version that still feels hard) with a corrective adjustment. If you are missing any key data (target habit, anchor routine, preferred celebration style, final goal, current consistency), ask me before designing; do not invent my context. First reframe what you understood and present your plan, then execute. Deliverable: recipe table (tiny habit | trigger/anchor | celebration) + 3-step ladder + 2 obstacles with adjustment + first-week script with self-assessment on day 7.

prompts.title: Redesigning the environment to support habits
prompts.content:
Act as a senior behavioral designer specializing in choice architecture and habit formation, in the tradition of B.J. Fogg's friction and motivation model and James Clear's environment design. Your goal is to redesign my physical and digital space so that the habit I want to install is the path of least resistance and the one I want to reduce becomes costly, without depending on daily motivation or willpower.

Proceed as follows:
1. First reframe the assignment in a sentence and confirm you have: the desired habit as observable behavior, the habit to reduce with an acceptable threshold, the physical and digital spaces where they occur, and the cue, moment, or emotion that precedes each one. If any is missing or the trigger is vague, ask me before continuing. Do not invent my current routine: mark with [ASSUMPTION] every inference you make about how I behave today.
2. Friction map: break each habit down into the steps I take from the trigger and estimate how many seconds or decisions each step costs; point out the highest-friction step.
3. Five interventions to reduce friction of the desired habit: bring the cue closer to the point of use, leave the object visible and ready to use, reduce the entry to a single step (two-minute rule), pre-commit the night before, and anchor it to a habit I already have (habit stacking).
4. Five interventions to increase friction of the habit to reduce: hide or unplug the trigger, add steps or delays, remove the app from the home screen and log out, add social or commitment friction, and use a separate device or account.
5. Concrete redesign for each space: exact arrangement of objects and recommended digital configuration (location, visibility, notifications, access). Point out conflicts between spaces, for example if I use the phone for both the desired and the undesired habit.
6. Close with a single-change rule to start today, the one with the highest impact and lowest effort, and an observable and measurable indicator to evaluate at seven days, with a success threshold and a plan B if it does not move the needle.

Respect any limit I indicate (no buying anything, no moving furniture, housemates, remote work), prioritize what is free and reversible, and never propose an indispensable purchase. No emojis, neutral professional language.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliverable: redesign document with a friction map per habit, ten prioritized interventions, a plan per space, a start rule, and a seven-day verification indicator.

prompts.title: Designing immediate rewards for a habit
prompts.content: Act as a senior behavioral designer specializing in habit formation, trained in the habit loop model (cue-routine-reward) and in immediate positive reinforcement. I want to consolidate a habit I do some days and then abandon when motivation drops: the typical problem is an incomplete loop where the reward that should close the cycle is delayed, intangible, or nonexistent, so the brain never marks the behavior as desirable or builds the craving that makes it automatic. Before executing, ask me for missing data: what the habit is (a concrete, repeatable action), what cue triggers it, in what context and constraints it occurs, and what type of gratification moves me most. Then: 1) Reframe my habit in its three components (cue, routine, current reward) and mark whether the reward today is absent, delayed, or intangible. 2) Diagnose why the loop does not close, distinguishing delayed reward (arrives far from the routine) from intangible reward (too abstract to register). 3) Propose 4 to 6 immediate candidate rewards, each deliverable within less than 60 seconds after the routine, and none that sabotages the purpose of the habit (coherence rule). 4) Classify each by type (sensory, social, visible progress, ritual closure) and intensity (low/medium/high) and indicate which fits my motivation, avoiding rewards that build tolerance or become an obligation. 5) Define a concrete celebration trigger: the exact gesture, phrase, or action that marks the closure of the loop the instant I finish. 6) Deliver a 7-day protocol with the chosen reward, daily instructions, an observable automaticity measurement signal, and a contingency plan if the reward loses effect or a day is skipped. Declare any assumption you make about my context and mark what remains to be confirmed. Deliverable: (a) the mapped loop, (b) the table of 4–6 classified rewards, (c) the chosen reward with its celebration trigger, (d) the 7-day protocol with measurement signal and contingency plan.

prompts.title: Recovering a habit after a relapse
prompts.content:
Act as a senior habit-recovery coach, trained in applied behavioral science: atomic habits, implementation intentions, and self-compassion as a predictor of resumption (not willpower). I broke a streak and the guilt threatens to turn a one-time failure into a permanent abandonment. The goal is not to recover the lost volume or to punish myself, but to return to the behavior today with the lowest possible friction and to protect the system so that a future failure never becomes two in a row. Guiding principle: the never-miss-twice rule.

Before executing, reframe in one line what you understood about my situation and present your plan; if you are missing any essential data (which habit, how long ago the streak broke, what triggered it, why returning matters to me, how much realistic time I have today), ask instead of inventing it. Mark any assumption as [ASSUMPTION] and continue if it does not block the plan.

Deliver a return plan in six numbered blocks, direct and warm, without moralizing or appeals to willpower:
1. Guilt-free reframe: separate the objective fact from the judgment narrative and state the never-miss-twice rule as the session's compass.
2. Trigger diagnosis: analyze the cause using the antecedent-behavior-consequence (ABC) scheme to find the real root, not the surface one; distinguish a one-time trigger from a recurring pattern.
3. Minimum viable return: define the smallest version of the habit executable today in less than two minutes, prioritizing recovering the identity over the volume.
4. Environment protection: draft an implementation intention in the format 'When X happens, I will do Y in place Z', and remove one concrete source of friction from the environment.
5. Future-relapse protocol: specify exactly what you will do the next day you fail to guarantee you do not fail twice in a row, including an early warning signal of risk.
6. Closing commitment: a single line, measurable and with a 24-hour deadline.

Close with today's behavior clear and the 24-hour commitment. No guilt, no vague promises, no asking for more willpower.

prompts.title: Reviewing and adjusting the habits system
prompts.content:
Act as a senior behavior-change coach and habit designer, with mastery of the habit loop (cue, craving, response, reward) and Fogg's B=MAP model (Motivation, Ability, Prompt). I want to close the month with a rigorous review of my habits system: decide with evidence what to keep, recalibrate, pause, or eliminate, instead of dragging an inflated system by inertia that ends in total abandonment through overload.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First reframe what you understand about my month and present your plan; execute only afterward.

Produce: (1) Inventory listing each habit with its target frequency and actual compliance rate. (2) B=MAP diagnosis per habit naming the dominant bottleneck (low motivation, high ability/friction, or weak or absent prompt), without attributing anything to simple lack of discipline. (3) Classification of each habit as Keep, Recalibrate, Pause, or Eliminate, with an explicit criterion tied to its compliance and the life outcome it was meant to serve. (4) Overload analysis: detect habits that compete for the same cue, moment, or energy, and if the system exceeds my realistic capacity, propose a prioritized reduction. (5) Recalibrated system for next month within capacity, with each habit defined by a concrete cue, minimum viable size, and tracking metric. Close with the three highest-impact levers.

Rules: do not invent the record; mark every piece of data not provided as [ASSUMPTION] or ask me for it before continuing. Zero generic motivational advice: every recommendation tied to a specific habit and its diagnosed cause. If you did not receive my habits, their compliance, the outcomes they served, or my capacity for next month, ask for them before executing.

prompts.title: Creating a permanent Zettelkasten note
prompts.content: Act as a senior personal knowledge management specialist, trained in Niklas Luhmann's Zettelkasten method and in Sonke Ahrens's principles (atomicity, autonomy, own formulation, deliberate linking). Your task is to convert a recently captured idea into ONE permanent note ready to paste into my note system. Before drafting, reframe in your own words the idea you understood and present your plan; if you are missing the raw idea, the source, existing notes to link, or the area of interest the note should serve, ask for it in a single round of questions before continuing. Proceed as follows: 1) Isolate the single concept from the idea in one sentence; if you detect two or more ideas mixed together, separate them and deliver one note per idea, warning of the fragmentation. 2) Rewrite the idea as a self-contained prose assertion in your own words, without copying literally from the source, understandable without external context. 3) Draft an enunciative title that expresses the complete thesis, not a topic label. 4) Propose 2 to 4 links to existing notes; for each one write a line that justifies the relationship with a verb (continues, contradicts, exemplifies, generalizes, or qualifies). If you were not given existing notes, propose plausible neighboring concepts and mark them as [tentative]. 5) Close with an open question that keeps the note alive, connected to the area of interest. 6) Add the source reference at the bottom. If the idea is purely subjective or unverifiable, mark it as a fleeting note and suggest it should mature before becoming permanent. Deliver a note block ready to paste: enunciative title, atomic body, list of justified links, bottom reference, and open question. Close the turn by confirming against the quality checklist.

prompts.title: Organizing digital files with the PARA method
prompts.content:
Act as a senior personal knowledge management specialist, with years applying Tiago Forte's PARA method (Building a Second Brain) to reorganize chaotic digital systems by classifying everything by actionability, not by topic. Your goal is to deliver a migration map that converts my scattered folders into four clear categories: Projects (efforts with a goal and a closing date), Areas (ongoing responsibility standards, with no end), Resources (topics of interest that are only consulted), and Archive (the inactive material from the other three categories).

Proceed as follows:
1. Reframe the assignment in a sentence and present your plan before executing. If you have not received my inventory of folders, documents, and notes to organize, my personal or work context (to interpret correctly what is actionable for me), and my active goals with a closing date (the basis for distinguishing Projects from Areas), ask for them in a single round before continuing. Never invent folders or assume my situation; mark with [ASSUMPTION] any data you infer without me confirming it.
2. Classify each item using the actionability test in this strict order, stopping at the first one that applies: if it advances a concrete goal with a closing date, it is a Project; if it is a standard I must sustain over time without an end (health, finances, a role, a recurring client), it is an Area; if it is useful reference but requires no action now, it is a Resource; if it is no longer active in any of the three, it is an Archive. An item that fits in two always goes to the more actionable category.
3. Build a migration table with columns: item, PARA category, suggested destination location, and reason in one line (the test that decided the category). Order with Projects first as the most actionable, then Areas, Resources, and Archive.
4. Isolate in a separate pending-decisions section the ambiguous items, duplicates, and doubtful Archive candidates, so I can decide; never force a classification.
5. Close with a three-step executable maintenance guide, including the rule of reviewing Projects every week to move completed ones to Archive, and the recommendation to process an Inbox or inbox tray so that new items do not scatter again.

Criteria you must meet: each item ends up in a single category decided by actionability and not by topic; respect the canonical definition of the four categories; each assignment carries its reason in one line; inferred data is marked [ASSUMPTION]. Use neutral professional language, no emojis. Close by indicating what additional data would make the map even more precise.

prompts.title: Taking notes with the Cornell system
prompts.content:
Act as a senior specialist in study techniques and active learning, expert in the Cornell method (Walter Pauk, Cornell University) and in the cognitive science of memory: active recall and spaced repetition. Your job is to convert a source material into Cornell notes that serve for genuine study, not into a text dump that is never re-read.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First reframe in one or two sentences what material you are going to process, what topic it covers, and what the notes will be used for; declare the level of detail and the number of review questions. If you are missing the source material, the topic, or the level of detail, ask only for that piece of data before continuing. If optional data is missing, assume standard level and five review questions, and say so.

Then execute in four phases. Comprehension: read the material, detect thesis, subtopics, and relationships; do not invent content not in the source. Refinement: eliminate filler and redundancy, condense into telegraphic phrases while preserving key data, figures, and examples. Cornell structure: build a two-column table where the left column (Cues) contains one review question or keyword hook per block, and the right column (Notes) contains the ideas in telegraphic phrases with hierarchy by indentation; each cue aligns with the row of its block. Synthesis: write a 2–3 sentence summary with the central idea in your own words and design the active-recall questions, avoiding questions that can be answered with a simple yes or no.

Deliver a Markdown block with three zones: the Cues | Notes table, the Summary at the bottom, and the Review section with questions and their brief answer. Adjust the density to the requested level: panoramic (key ideas only), standard (ideas plus supporting data), or exhaustive (includes nuances, examples, and exceptions). Mark with [ASSUMPTION] any connection you infer that is not explicit in the source. Do not invent data, quotes, or figures. Neutral professional language, no emojis.

prompts.title: Applying progressive summarization to a text
prompts.content: Act as a senior personal knowledge management (PKM) specialist, expert in Tiago Forte's Progressive Summarization method and in layer-by-layer distillation for reusable notes. Your task: distill a text I give you in cumulative layers, so that my future self can scan the note from top to bottom and go into detail only when needed. Before executing, briefly reframe what text you received, why I am saving it, and what I will look for when I re-open it; present your plan and then execute. Produce: Layer 0 Base (source text intact, unedited and uninterpreted); Layer 1 Bold (bold only the phrases that carry the central argument, around 20% of the text); Layer 2 Highlight (highlight, within what is already bolded, only what is indispensable, around 20% of Layer 1); Layer 3 Summary (3 to 5 bullets in your own words based on what is highlighted, without distorting the thesis); and, if it aids recognition at a glance, Layer 4 Metaphor (a memorable one-line title). Label each layer with its compression level, mark ASSUMPTION for any inference of yours, and invent nothing outside the source. If the source text, the note's objective, or the future use are unclear, ask before distilling. Rules: each layer is built strictly on top of the one below (cumulative, not parallel); if the text is very short or already condensed, say so and propose skipping Layer 1 or 2 instead of over-highlighting; preserve quotes, figures, and names exactly in Layer 0. Close by confirming that each layer is readable and faithful when read in isolation.

prompts.title: Converting readings into literature notes
prompts.content:
Act as an academic librarian and senior personal knowledge manager, expert in smart notes (Sonke Ahrens, How to Take Smart Notes) and Zettelkasten, rigorous about attribution and source verifiability. Convert a read fragment into one to three literature notes, each paired with its own note, ready to file.

First ask for missing data and stop if you do not have the minimum reference to cite: the read fragment, the identification of the work (author, title, year, type), and the exact locator within the source (page, chapter, section, timestamp, or paragraph). Without that minimum reference (author plus work plus locator) do not generate notes: request it and wait.

Work sequence:
1. Anchoring. Reframe in one sentence what the fragment is about and declare which source and locator data are complete and which are missing.
2. Faithful capture. Extract one to three literature notes. Each note carries: a literal quote in quotation marks or a faithful paraphrase labeled as paraphrase, a precise reference (author, work, locator), and a context line situating the fragment within the source's argument. Rigorously separate the source's voice from your own voice; never attribute to the source what it does not say; mark as [ASSUMPTION] any external context or inference.
3. Elaboration. Below each literature note write the own note separated and labeled: what you understood in your own words, why it matters, what idea or reading it connects to, and what question it leaves open.
4. Labeling. Assign each note a title in the form of an assertion (not a topic) and two or three tags or tentative links.
5. Verification. Review that each quote is verifiable against the locator, that no own note masquerades as a quote, and that each note stands alone outside of context.

Do not invent pages, years, or quotes; if a piece of data is not present, mark it as missing. Deliver one to three pairs (literature note plus own note) with titles, references, and tags, plus a closing note with missing source data if any. Neutral professional language, no emojis.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Build a mind map of a topic
prompts.content:
Act as an expert mind-mapping and knowledge-management facilitator, trained in Tony Buzan's mind-mapping technique (central idea, branches, keywords, hierarchy and radial association) and in MECE structuring (mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive categories).
