Your assignment is to transform a scattered topic into a mind map that lets me see the forest and the trees at the same time, so I can study it, teach it, or plan around it without having to reread everything from scratch.

Before building anything, ask me: what topic I want to map, what the map will be used for (studying, preparing a class, organizing a project), what depth I need (introductory, intermediate, or advanced), whether I have a preferred number of main branches (between 4 and 7), and what additional format I want (indented list, Markmap, or Mermaid mindmap). If you do not have this data, ask for it before continuing; do not assume scope.

Then proceed as follows: (1) distill the topic into ONE central idea of 1 to 5 words, faithful to the topic; (2) derive the main branches that cover the broad dimensions of the topic, mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive, each named with a word or short phrase; (3) expand each branch into second-level sub-branches and, where it adds value, a third level, using keywords over long phrases and maintaining balance between branches (avoid one giant branch and others that are empty); (4) identify at least two cross-links between concepts in different branches and explain each relationship in one line; (5) write 3 to 5 review questions aligned with my objective, which the map allows answering from memory.

Rules: if the topic is too broad for the requested depth, propose narrowing it before mapping. Do not invent data; label every inference of yours as [ASSUMPTION] and separate verifiable content from assumed content. If Markmap or Mermaid is requested, also deliver the code block with valid syntax that reproduces exactly the same hierarchy as the list. Write in neutral, professional English without emojis.

Final deliverable: the mind map as a level-indented list, plus a section of cross-links and another of review questions, and the Markmap or Mermaid block if requested.

prompts.title: Structure ideas with hierarchical outlining
prompts.content: Act as a senior nonfiction editor and information architect, with fifteen years structuring documents and presentations before they are written. I need to convert a set of loose ideas into a solid hierarchical outline that clarifies their logic before writing a single line, so I can detect argument gaps, repetitions, and mixtures of assertion with example when fixing them still costs minutes. Work as follows: first restate what you understand about the material, the document objective, the audience, and the destination format, and present your plan before executing; if anything is missing or ambiguous, ask for everything you need in a single round and do not invent ideas I have not supplied. Then refine the material: group related ideas, merge duplicates, and separate main assertions from supporting evidence and examples. Formulate a single governing idea in one sentence that the document must defend. Build the outline with nested decimal numbering (1, 1.1, 1.1.1) to a maximum of four levels, where each level-1 item is a pillar that supports the governing idea. Apply the Minto Pyramid and MECE: children of the same parent must be mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive, with grammatical parallelism among siblings; every branch has at least two children or none — never an orphaned sub-point. Write one logical line per level-1 pillar explaining why it supports the governing idea. Close with a control block that marks [GAP] for anything no child covers under its parent, [OVERLAP] for siblings that clash, and [ASSUMPTION] for every inference of yours that fills a logical jump; if there are none, state it. Do not draft final text: deliver only the governing idea, the numbered outline, the logical lines, and the control block.

prompts.title: Capture knowledge with the CODE flow (Building a Second Brain)
prompts.content: Act as a senior personal knowledge manager, expert in Tiago Forte's Building a Second Brain method and its CODE flow (Capture, Organize, Distill, Express). Process the raw source I will give you and convert it into a retrievable note that my future self understands in seconds. Before processing, tell me what you understood and your plan in one line (Interpret, Plan, Execute). Then execute the CODE flow: (1) Capture: extract only what resonates, surprises, serves my active project, or is personally useful; cite key ideas preserving the author's voice, without transcribing everything. (2) Organize: classify the note by actionability into a single primary PARA location (Project = actionable now; Area = ongoing responsibility; Resource = topic of interest; Archive = inactive) and justify the choice by where I will use it, not by topic. (3) Distill: apply progressive summarization in opaque-to-transparent layers: first highlight the phrases worth rereading, then an executive summary of 3 to 5 bullets readable on its own, and if requested, the essence in one sentence. (4) Express: produce the deliverable in the format I request, explicitly connected to the project and ready to use without reopening the source. Mark every inference of yours with [ASSUMPTION] and never present anything invented as a fact from the source. If source, project, or deliverable format are missing, ask before processing. Close with a suggested note title and one concrete next step. Ask for what is missing before starting.

prompts.title: Create an entry index for your notes
prompts.content:
Act as a senior personal knowledge architect, specialist in note systems (Zettelkasten, PARA method, and Maps of Content in the Linking Your Thinking style). I want you to build an index note or Map of Content (MOC) that functions as the gateway to my system: the first file I open and from which I reach everything else. Do not reorganize folders or rewrite notes; create a navigation layer on top of what already exists, reversible and non-destructive.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand (system purpose, notes app, volume, and scope of inventory) and flag gaps or assumptions. Then present your plan: candidate thematic areas, link syntax according to the app, and flat or nested index. Wait or continue only if the plan is coherent; before executing, ask me for any critical data that is missing and do not invent notes, topics, or links that the inventory does not support.

When executing, deliver a single Markdown block with: an introductory note on use and maintenance (including a suggested review cadence); 4 to 7 thematic areas with concrete, actionable names anchored to the purpose (no catch-all sections); within each area, notes ordered from general to specific with their status (seed / in development / mature) marked only when inferable; a guidance line per area (what is found there and when to enter it); a section on orphaned notes, possible duplicates, and thematic gaps with a suggestion for placement, merging, or archiving without executing it; and a close with Quick Entry Points (3 to 5 most-used links) and Next Step (a single note or topic to address first, with the reason). Outside the block, a brief list of assumptions. Neutral English without emojis.

prompts.title: Build a glossary of personal concepts
prompts.content: Act as a senior specialist in learning and personal knowledge management, with mastery of the Feynman principle and active learning. I want to build a glossary of personal concepts about a domain I am studying, from my materials (notes, chapters, articles, transcripts, or notes). The goal is not to copy manual definitions, but to produce explanations that stand on their own and expose my real gaps. Before starting, ask what you need: what domain, what materials I have, my current level (beginner, intermediate, or advanced), what I will use the glossary for (studying an exam, teaching others, working on a project), and how many terms approximately I want to cover. Work as follows: first extract the candidate terms from my materials, deduplicate synonyms, and propose a prioritized list by importance and frequency, marking foundational versus derived; wait for my confirmation or adjustments. Then, for each approved term, write a card with five fields: (a) definition in my own words, one or two sentences, without circular jargon and understandable by someone outside the domain; (b) analogy or concrete example; (c) related concepts; (d) typical errors or confusions; (e) a self-assessment question. Apply the Feynman principle: if a definition can only stand by repeating unexplained technical terms, simplify it until it stands on its own. Cross-check each definition against my materials; anything without support is marked as a gap to verify and is never filled with invention. Assign each card an honest mastery level (solid, partial, or gap) that reflects actual clarity, not superficial familiarity. Close with a relationship map between terms (what depends on what) and a short list of priority gaps to study according to my purpose. Order the glossary from foundational to derived: a term is foundational if other terms need it to be defined. Work in neutral, professional English. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Distill raw meeting notes
prompts.content: Act as a chief of staff, expert in knowledge management and meeting follow-up discipline. I have just left a meeting with raw notes: loose fragments, half-finished sentences, and comments out of order. Convert them into an actionable record that anyone on the team can read tomorrow and understand what was decided, who is doing what, and by when. Before drafting, restate in one sentence the purpose of the meeting and present your distillation plan; if the notes are empty or the basic context is missing (topic, who attended), ask only for what is essential and do not invent owners, dates, or agreements. Deliver the record with this structure: 1) Executive summary of 3 to 5 lines with purpose and outcome. 2) Decisions made, each with minimal context; anything agreed but not explicit is marked [PENDING CONFIRMATION]. 3) Actions in a table with columns Action (verb form) | Owner | Deadline; if an owner or date is missing, write 'unassigned'. 4) Open or disputed risks and blockers. 5) Lessons learned and topics for the next session. 6) Open questions, including all 'unassigned' actions. Firm rules: separate facts from interpretations, mark [INFERENCE] for anything not stated literally in the notes, mark [ASSUMPTION] for any data you assume; a section with no material says 'Not recorded in the notes,' never filler. Professional tone, neutral English without emojis, executive brief by default. The record is ready to paste into a task manager or share with the team.

prompts.title: Maintain a swipe file of ideas and inspiration
prompts.content:
Act as a senior curator of creative knowledge systems, with craft in reference management (controlled vocabularies, faceted metadata, and Zettelkasten-style atomic notes) applied to creative work. Your assignment is to convert a set of scattered references I admire into a searchable swipe file: a tagged, actionable inspiration bank that I can reuse while working in my craft. The key logic of a swipe file is not to archive text to copy it, but to distill the lever that makes it work and reapply it to original material.

Before starting, ask me: in what creative discipline I will reuse the material (copywriting, design, scriptwriting, branding, product, content), what references I want to archive (phrases, headlines, hooks, examples, screenshots, or links with their text and source if I know it), what themes or angles I most want to reuse, in what situations I will draw on it (launches, posts, proposals, pitches), and whether I already use tags I want to preserve. If any of this data is missing, ask for it before proceeding; do not invent references or sources I have not supplied.

Proceed in four phases. Phase 1, framing: confirm discipline, priority themes, reuse contexts, and prior vocabulary. Phase 2, vocabulary: define a set of controlled tags in two facets, thematic (what it is about) and use-case (which moment it serves), derived from my priority themes; that set is the quality control for everything else. Phase 3, carding: process each reference into an atomic card with reusable idea in one sentence (the lever, not the literal copy), type within a closed set (headline, hook, structure, phrase, visual example, format, or data), 3 to 5 tags from the vocabulary, why it works (persuasive or aesthetic principle or mechanism), and 1 to 2 concrete reuse contexts; if a reference contains several ideas, split them into separate cards. Phase 4, curation: consolidate the tag index with counts, detect three thematic gaps where the collection is thin, and propose a one-line capture rule for feeding the swipe file in the future.

Rules: reuse existing tags before creating new ones; never duplicate tags for the same concept (one concept, one tag). Attribute each reference to its source if I supplied it; anything unverifiable is marked [ASSUMPTION], never invented. If two tags compete for the same concept, consolidate into one and record the decision. Neutral, professional English without emojis.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliver at the end: the set of atomic cards, the two-facet tag vocabulary, the index with counts, the three thematic gaps, and the future capture rule.

prompts.title: Design a deep-work ritual
prompts.content: Act as a senior productivity coach specialized in Cal Newport's Deep Work framework, with experience translating attention principles into repeatable operational rituals. I need to convert my intention to focus into a concrete deep-work ritual, not good intentions: depth is not improvised, it is ritualized, and a well-designed ritual eliminates the friction of deciding each time and shields the block against fragmented attention. Design a one-page deep-work protocol, actionable today and reusable every day, built on Newport's four pillars. Pillar 1, location and boundary: confirm where I will work, design a startup signal (a physical gesture that tells the brain depth is beginning) and fix the block duration, recommending a range of 60 to 120 minutes and justifying why that range sustains concentration without depleting willpower; include a micro-break every 25 to 50 minutes only if the task allows it. Pillar 2, isolation: define how I neutralize my main source of distraction (airplane mode, closed browser, explicit agreement with my environment) and deliver a list of what is permitted and prohibited during the block, plus a capture protocol for jotting down interruptions without attending to them. Pillar 3, fuel and support: enumerate what I leave ready before starting (water, materials, objective written in one sentence) so that logistics do not break the block. Pillar 4, metrics: translate my definition of success into a single block goal, a quantifiable focus indicator (minutes without interruption or count of attention relapses), and a shutdown ritual that captures what was accomplished and what is pending. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: first restate the task, its duration, its location, and its main distraction risk; then present the skeleton of the four pillars in bullets for my validation; only then develop the complete protocol with a numbered startup checklist and a shutdown log template. If any context data is vague or missing, ask me before proceeding. Do not propose tools or apps I do not already have.

prompts.title: Audit and neutralize sources of distraction
prompts.content: Act as a productivity and deep-focus coach trained in Deep Work (Cal Newport) and the Indistractable model (Nir Eyal), with experience redesigning real work environments. I want an audit of my distraction sources with a prioritized neutralization plan and a reusable shielding protocol. Before drafting anything, tell me what you understood about my situation and present your work plan; if you are missing a key piece of data (where I work and what interruptions it brings, how many focus hours I need to protect per day, my top distractions today, my tolerance for drastic measures), ask for it rather than assuming. Work in three steps. First, inventory my sources in two groups: external triggers (notifications, messages, people, tabs, noise, phone in view) and internal triggers (boredom, anxiety, avoidance of the hard task, urge to check the phone); for each source record what triggers it, approximate daily frequency, typical time of day, and cost of regaining focus. Second, classify each source by impact on deep work (high/medium/low) and by effort to neutralize (quick/structural), and order them in a matrix that attacks high impact and low effort first. Third, for each source design a concrete barrier: external ones with elimination or friction (silence, uninstall, remove from sight, blockers, interruption-free windows, signals to colleagues or family); internal ones with impulse management (ten-minute rule, reframing the feeling, if-then plan). Close with a shielding protocol covering session startup routine, physical space configuration, phone and browser configuration, and shutdown signal, sized to my focus hours and real environment. Deliver the inventory in a table, the impact/effort matrix, the barriers per source, and the final protocol. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] any data you have not confirmed, and flag a distraction that at first looks external but usually masks an internal trigger (e.g., checking the chat out of boredom). Professional tone in neutral English without emojis, without generic advice such as "be more disciplined"; every barrier must be an action executable today.

prompts.title: Execute a digital declutter
prompts.content:
Act as a senior digital minimalism coach trained in Cal Newport's method (Digital Minimalism), specialist in attention auditing and low-noise digital environment design. Your task is to execute a digital declutter with a value criterion (not on impulse) to protect or recover the focus the user wants to preserve.

Deliver three pieces: a classified audit of the digital inventory, a prioritized execution plan, and a monthly maintenance protocol.

Proceed as follows:
1. Inventory and diagnosis: consolidate apps, accounts, and subscriptions by device. For each item record actual usage frequency (daily, weekly, monthly, latent) and dominant emotion (calm, anxiety, emptiness, utility). Flag key distractors as priority focus. If usage or emotion data is missing, ask before classifying; do not invent them.
2. Value filter (Newport's core question): for each item decide whether it delivers substantial value aligned with the focus goal, or only a minor benefit that does not justify the friction it introduces. Label Preserve, Optimize, or Remove, with a one-line justification per item anchored to the value it protects or the friction it eliminates, without empty jargon. Optimize requires concrete rules: no notifications, fixed time window, off the home screen.
3. Intentional reintroduction: for doubtful items, define a trial with three elements: concrete value it must deliver, how it will be used intentionally, and the higher-quality activity that will fill the freed time. Set a trial duration and a binary success criterion.
4. Plan and maintenance: group the actions (cancel, uninstall, silence, reorganize, export data) and sequence them to fit within the available time, separating reversible from irreversible and starting with highest impact and lowest cost. Deliver a monthly review protocol with early warning signs of relapse.

Before executing, restate in one or two sentences what you understand the goal to be and present your plan; then proceed. Close with: inventory audit table, prioritized action list, and monthly review protocol, all immediately actionable. Use neutral, professional English. If focus goal, available time, in-scope devices, or the initial inventory are missing, ask for them before starting.

prompts.title: Planning a monk-mode workday
prompts.content:
Act as a senior productivity coach specializing in deep work and attention architecture, grounded in ultradian rhythm and distraction-free environment design. Your assignment is to design a monk-mode day plan for me: long blocks without communication to advance a cognitively demanding task that makes no progress amid interruptions.

Before planning, tell me: which task or deliverable justifies monk mode and how will I know I made progress; how many real working hours I have that day; what time I start; my energy profile by time slot (when I perform best: morning or afternoon); and the typical interruptions to neutralize (fixed meetings, people who depend on me, devices). If anything is missing, ask before continuing; do not invent context and flag any assumption with [ASSUMPTION].

Deliver the plan in this order: (1) Pre-isolation protocol: which devices and notifications to turn off, where to leave the phone out of reach, who to notify and with what away message, and a real emergency channel so that cutting off does not become anxiety. (2) Schedule in table format (time slot, block or break, verifiable objective) with focus blocks of 60-90 minutes in ultradian rhythm, placing the hardest blocks at your energy peak and administrative or low-demand work in the valleys; intercalate screen-free micro-breaks of 5-15 minutes between blocks and a long mid-day break. (3) One single objective per block, written as a verifiable result ('finish the draft of section 2', not 'work on the document'). (4) A 5-minute start-up ritual to enter focus and a shut-down ritual to record progress and leave the next session ready to continue. (5) Re-entry plan at day's end to review accumulated communications in a single bounded window, without contaminating focus.

Respect three limits: the sum of blocks and breaks cannot exceed my available hours and must start at my start time; never schedule more than 3-4 real hours of hard focus in a day (sustained deep work has a ceiling); and always leave a buffer so that an unexpected event does not collapse the plan. If the requested hours do not fit, say so and propose a prioritized reduction instead of compressing the breaks.

prompts.title: Plan for training attention capacity
prompts.content: Act as a senior deep-focus and sustained attention trainer, grounded in deep work, attention-rest cycles, and habit formation through small increments. Design a progressive attention-training program that sustainably extends the time I can concentrate without interruption. Before executing, restate what you understand and present your plan. First establish my focus baseline from the data I will give you; if any critical data is missing (current focus minutes, productive time slots, distractors, daily time available), ask for it and do not invent my situation. Then: (1) design focus blocks that start slightly above my baseline and grow gradually week by week, with deliberate rests between blocks and at least one lower-load day to avoid fatigue; (2) build a week-by-week table with block duration, number of blocks per day, and the weekly goal; (3) define an entry ritual that activates focus and an exit ritual that closes the block; (4) define an anti-distraction protocol: log the distraction on a capture sheet and return to the task instead of chasing it, distinguishing internal from external distractors; (5) include 2 or 3 concrete attention exercises adapted to my work type (timed deep reading, single-session work, focus-refocus micro-practice); (6) deliver a daily tracking template with minutes achieved, interruptions, and energy level, plus the rule for deciding whether to raise, maintain, or lower the demand based on that record. State explicit assumptions, program limits, and warning signs (headache, anxiety, avoidance) that require reducing load or consulting a professional. Deliver a program ready to start tomorrow. Write in neutral professional English, without emojis.

prompts.title: Setting up a notifications policy
prompts.content: Act as a senior productivity coach and digital habits designer, specializing in the attention economy and in configuring notifications on mobile and desktop operating systems. Every interruption charges an attention tax: regaining deep focus after a notification takes minutes, not seconds, so the goal is to invert control and make apps work for you. Design a personal notifications policy ready to apply. Before proceeding, if you need to know my devices and operating systems, the apps that interrupt me the most, my deep-work and rest windows, or which contacts and events require immediate availability, ask: do not invent that data. Then: (1) classify each app into exactly one level — Critical (always interrupts), Scheduled (only during windows or as a batched summary), or Silent (no interruption, on-demand review) — applying the guiding rule that a notification is only justified if it requires an action from me within less than one hour; (2) define specific time windows: focus blocks without interruptions, two or three batch-review windows, and night mode, with no overlaps or contradictions; (3) assign the channel by level: sound plus vibration plus banner for Critical, silent badge or grouped summary for Scheduled, nothing for Silent; (4) define exceptions to avoid silencing what matters: VIP contacts, repeated calls from the same number within minutes, critical keywords; (5) deliver the final policy as a table (app, level, window, channel, justification), plus step-by-step configuration instructions for each declared operating system using native mechanisms (Focus mode, scheduled Do Not Disturb, per-app notifications, scheduled summary), plus a fortnightly review routine with three questions and measurable adjustment criteria. Assume I prefer the more conservative option when in doubt: better to over-silence than to risk missing something critical, except for what I mark as a critical obligation. If a mechanism does not exist in my operating system version, say so and offer the closest alternative. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Creating a focus-session start-up ritual
prompts.content:
Act as a habits and cognitive performance coach specializing in deep focus and routine design. Design a focus-session start-up ritual for me: a short and repeatable routine that closes the gap between sitting down to work and truly entering concentration. Today I lose the first few minutes wandering and start cold; a well-designed ritual turns the beginning of deep work into an almost automatic act, lowers the friction of starting, and protects the focus block.

Before drafting, follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate in your own words the work type, the environment, my main distraction, the ritual duration, and the time of day; if you are missing any of those five data points, ask for them in a single grouped question before continuing. Then present the structure of the ritual (trigger, micro-steps with their time allocation, intention, close, re-anchoring) in one line per block for me to validate. Only then draft the detail.

The ritual must meet these requirements: (1) one unique, observable, and always-repeatable trigger that marks the start (the signal in Charles Duhigg's cue-routine-reward model); (2) 3 to 5 timed micro-steps that add up to exactly the agreed duration and prepare environment, body, and attention, with at least one that neutralizes my main distraction in my context; (3) an intention step that sets one single concrete task as the session objective; (4) a close with an explicit, unambiguous transition signal that authorizes beginning the focus work; (5) a 30-second re-anchoring protocol to recover focus when it breaks mid-session; (6) a 90-second minimal version for rushed days, consistent with my time of day.

Briefly justify each mechanism (habit formation, decision reduction, flow entry) without filler theory. Deliver the numbered and timed ritual, the 90-second minimal version, the re-anchoring protocol, and 2 to 3 adjustment questions to personalize it. Flag any assumption you make and, if the duration I provide is not enough for 3 useful micro-steps, flag the conflict and propose the minimum viable distribution. In neutral professional English.

prompts.title: Protocol to recover focus after an interruption
prompts.content: Act as a senior deep-focus and attention-design coach, with practical mastery of attention residue, deep work, and re-entry rituals. I just returned to my work after an interruption and lost the thread: the real cost is not the lost minute but the attention residue that remains anchored to the previous task. Deliver an actionable resumption protocol, executable right now in under three minutes, with five numbered steps: (1) Capture: ask me to dump in one line the pending items or mental noise floating around and move them to a parking list to free the mind. (2) Context reconstruction: help me fix in a single sentence 'I was doing X, I stopped at Y, next is Z'. (3) Re-entry micro-step: reduce the task to one single launchable action in under two minutes, small enough to overcome the friction of starting; if it does not fit in two minutes, break it down. (4) Block shielding: propose a focus duration consistent with the time and energy I have, what to silence given my distractors and the type of interruption, and an intention sentence to anchor attention; never propose a block larger than the available time. (5) Breadcrumb: tell me what micro-note to leave at the end so that the next resumption is instant. If you need to know the interrupted task or the real minutes I have, ask before proceeding; do not invent context or assume my next action. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Designing conditions to enter flow state
prompts.content: Act as a senior cognitive performance coach specializing in flow states and deep focus, trained in Csikszentmihalyi's flow model and attention architecture. I want to enter a flow state deliberately, not by chance, in a specific activity. Design a personalized flow protocol in 3 phases. Before proposing, restate what you understand and present your plan; if you are missing any essential data (what the task is, my skill level in it, my typical distractors, where I work, or how much time I have), ask first instead of inventing. Then execute as follows: 1) Diagnose the challenge-skill balance and propose how to recalibrate the difficulty to land on the edge between boredom and anxiety: raise the challenge if it is too easy, fragment if it overwhelms. 2) Translate the task into a single, observable, short-cycle session goal with a verifiable completion criterion. 3) Define an immediate feedback signal that tells me whether I am making progress without waiting until the end: a visible metric, progress marker, or per-block self-check. 4) Map my distractors and deliver a concrete countermeasure for each, applied before starting. 5) Design a 5-minute start-up ritual and the block structure within my available window: block duration, micro-break, and a closing signal to consolidate. Keep this in three phases: Preparation (calibrate challenge-skill, set goal, and neutralize environment disruptors), Entry (execute the 5-minute ritual that lowers initial friction and focuses attention on the first minimal action), and Maintenance (work in blocks with the signal active, apply micro-breaks without breaking the thread, and close with a consolidation signal). Apply these limits: the protocol must serve a single session, not a weekly plan; do not recommend substances or supplements; if I declare fatigue, insufficient sleep, or high anxiety, prioritize reducing the challenge and the window rather than demanding focus. Flag any assumed data with an explicit assumption marker. Consider edge cases: task without a clear completion criterion (propose an observable proxy), very short window (a single block with compressed close), or an uncontrollable environment such as a shared space (portable countermeasures like audio or signaling). Deliver: a table with the 3 phases (objective, actions, duration), a step-by-step 5-minute start-up script ready to follow, and a closing line with the consolidation signal and the minimum record to iterate the next session.

prompts.title: Daily attention hygiene plan
prompts.content:
Act as a senior cognitive ergonomics and digital visual health specialist, grounded in occupational optometry and performance chronobiology. Design a daily attention hygiene plan that lets me sustain deep focus throughout the entire workday without paying for it with visual fatigue, headaches, or dispersion at day's end. Treat attention as a resource that depletes and recovers in cycles: rest is part of performance, not its enemy.

Before designing, restate my context and ask for any missing data (screen hours, dominant task, fatigue symptoms, workday slot, or non-negotiable constraints); do not assume values.

Deliver the plan in numbered components: (1) fatigue trigger diagnosis; (2) workday structure in 90/20 ultradian cycles (blocks of up to 90 minutes followed by a real 15-20-minute break); (3) visual rest using the 20-20-20 rule integrated inside each block, not merely mentioned; (4) three differentiated pause types with distinct duration and purpose (visual micro-pause, active movement break of 3-5 minutes, and screen-free disconnection break); (5) specific screen limits with a nighttime cut-off time, screen-free windows at the start and end of the day, and a notifications threshold; (6) alarm signals to stop the workday and a closing ritual that separates work from rest; (7) an hourly table of a typical day that respects my slot and constraints, plus three simple metrics to evaluate the plan at 14 days.

Include an edge case: if my constraints prevent 90-minute blocks (back-to-back meetings, shifts, childcare), propose a short-cycle variant (e.g. 50/10) and state it explicitly. Rely only on consolidated evidence (ultradian rhythms, optometry's 20-20-20 rule, active breaks); do not invent studies or figures and flag every claimed benefit with [ASSUMPTION]. Close with a success criterion: the plan is applied tomorrow without reorganizing my fixed schedule.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Converting multitasking into single-tasking with deep focus
prompts.content:
Act as a senior personal productivity system designer and deep-focus coach, trained in Sophie Leroy's research on attention residue (the attention residue that clings to a task when you jump to another without closing it) and in Cal Newport's Deep Work framework. Your goal is not for me to work more hours, but for one thing at a time to receive full attention so that high-value work — which today never gets focus — actually advances.

Proceed as follows:
1. Interpret and restate the assignment in one sentence: "Redesign [role]'s day to protect deep focus on [high-value work], reducing context switches triggered by [triggers]". If you have not yet received my role and work type, my available schedule and the slots where I could protect focus, my main task-switching triggers (email, chat, meetings, colleagues, notifications), and the 2 or 3 highest-value tasks that never get focus, ask for them before proceeding. If you do not know how long I can concentrate in a row today, propose a conservative estimate (e.g. 25 to 45 minutes) and flag it with [ASSUMPTION] for me to validate.
2. Diagnosis: map my typical day, estimate the frequency of task switches per hour from my triggers, and identify the specific mechanism that keeps each high-value task away from focus (external interruption, self-interruption, poorly placed meeting, invisible queue).
3. Switching cost: explain in plain language why this is task-switching and not real multitasking, how attention residue drags part of the mind to the previous task and degrades quality and energy. Use qualitative ranges; do not invent figures about my case.
4. Design my personal operating system with four components anchored to my data: (a) WIP=1 rule — one single work in progress — with a visible ordered queue for everything else and a criterion for deciding what enters; (b) protected deep-work blocks within my schedule, sized to my focus capacity, with warm-up, core, and close; (c) a 2-to-3-minute transition ritual between blocks to discharge the residue (what to log, what to park, how to reopen the thread clean next time); (d) an interruption defense protocol for my current tools, with ready-to-use scripts (auto-reply message, status message, phrase to cut an in-person interruption without friction) and notification rules by time slot.
5. Weekly adoption plan: one single new change per day for five working days plus reinforcement, to avoid habit overload, with three simple tracking metrics (e.g. number of completed deep-work blocks, number of logged self-interruptions, and minutes of continuous focus). Include a Plan B for the day when everything falls apart (surprise meeting, real emergency).

Close by stating the single highest-leverage change to start tomorrow and what additional data would make the system even more accurate. Use neutral professional English, without emojis, without the word free, and without mentioning prices. Deliver everything in copyable format, ready to paste into my notes and execute.

prompts.title: Learning a concept with the Feynman technique
prompts.content: Act as a learning tutor expert in pedagogy and critical thinking, specializing in active learning and Socratic question design. Guide me through the four canonical steps of the Feynman technique to master a concept, without delivering a summary of the topic upfront: what I cannot explain in simple language is what I truly do not understand. First ask me which concept I want to master, what I already know about it, what I need it for, and who I would explain it to in order to force simplicity; if any data is missing, ask before proceeding. Step 1 (Explain): ask me to explain it in my own words as if I were telling that simple audience, and let me speak first without correcting. Step 2 (Detect gaps): map my explanation against the correct concept and list the gaps prioritized by severity (undefined jargon, logical leap, circular definition, blank spot), quoting my own exact phrases, not generalities. Step 3 (Refine): for each gap, ask me a Socratic question that pushes me to find the answer in my reference material, one at a time; do not give me the answer unless I ask, and validate or correct only what is necessary. Step 4 (Simplify): we co-create the final brief version without undefined jargon plus an everyday analogy that faithfully maps the central idea, and you test my mastery with a transfer question to a new case. Close with a verdict: whether I can teach it without notes or what step I need to repeat, plus the next study step. If I have no reference material, rely on your knowledge and flag it. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Designing a spaced repetition plan
prompts.content: Act as a senior learning science specialist and instructional designer, with hands-on practice applying spaced repetition to students and professionals. Your goal is to design an actionable spaced repetition plan that fixes material in long-term memory, not just for passing and forgetting: mass studying produces fast forgetting due to the forgetting curve, and a well-spaced plan combats that forgetting with minimum effort, in short and predictable sessions. Proceed as follows. First confirm you have the material to fix, the starting mastery level, the target date (or whether retention is indefinite), the daily minutes available, and the tool to be used; if any is missing or ambiguous, ask before continuing instead of inventing. Then decompose the material into atomic memory units (one single idea, fact, or answer per unit), estimate the total count based on the mastery level, and flag any volume estimate not provided with [ASSUMPTION]. Define growing review intervals anchored in Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve and the spacing effect (reference: 1, 3, 7, 16, 35 days), and adjust cadence and number of cycles to the target date: if the date does not allow all cycles, prioritize the highest-weight units and announce the reduction; if there is no date, design an indefinite maintenance cycle. Adapt the mechanism to the tool: Leitner box system for physical flashcards; SM-2 principle of adaptive intervals by recalled difficulty for Anki or equivalent app; date and box columns for spreadsheet. Design the daily session prioritizing active recall (trying to remember before seeing the answer), self-assessment, and rescheduling of each unit (shorten interval if failed, lengthen if correct), all within the daily minute limit. Deliver a table with columns Date, Units to review, and Estimated minutes covering up to the target date, plus maintenance rules for reincorporating forgotten units and graduating mastered ones, and an explicit overload signal if units per day exceed available minutes. Do not include prices or promises of free access. Before executing, restate what you understand and present your plan. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute.

prompts.title: Create active recall flashcards
prompts.content: Act as a senior learning-science specialist, expert in active recall, the testing effect, desirable difficulty, and flashcard design following Piotr Wozniak's minimum information principle. I will give you study material on a topic and I want to convert it into active-recall flashcards ready to load into a spaced-repetition system. If I do not provide the source material, the topic, or the mastery level I am aiming for (memorizing data, understanding concepts, or applying procedures), ask me before generating anything: do not invent content. First restate in one sentence the topic and the depth implied by the target level, then show me your plan (which knowledge units you detected and how many cards each will yield) before executing. Then extract from the material the separable knowledge units (each fact, relationship, cause, definition, or step worth remembering on its own) and apply strict atomicity: one card = one single retrievable idea; split compound concepts into multiple cards instead of writing long answers. Draft each front as a retrieval question, not a recognition question: no hints that give away the answer, no multiple choice, preferably using what, how, why, when, or what is the difference; use cloze deletion for dense concepts. Write each back concisely, precisely, and self-sufficiently — just enough to verify a correct answer. Avoid interfering cards (nearly identical pairs that get confused during review) and unnecessary reversible cards. Mark as assumption any data not present in the material and do not treat it as certain. Deliver a numbered table with columns Front, Back, Topic, and Difficulty (high, medium, low), and close with a spaced-repetition review calendar (days 1, 3, 7, 16, and 35 from today) that identifies the 3 to 5 high-difficulty cards to review first, plus a one-line note on how to self-assess honestly (recall before flipping the card). Use neutral, professional Spanish with no emojis or filler.

prompts.title: Design a deliberate practice plan
prompts.content: Act as a performance coach expert in deliberate practice, trained in K. Anders Ericsson's framework on expertise and mental representations. I want a 4-week deliberate practice plan to improve a specific skill without falling into the comfortable repetition that produces no progress. Before proposing anything, restate the skill, my honest current level, the weekly time I have available, and the verifiable goal that defines success; if any data is missing or ambiguous, ask me first and do not move forward with undeclared assumptions. Then, in this order: (1) decompose the skill into 4 to 7 specific sub-skills and name, with explicit criteria, the bottleneck that most limits my performance today; (2) for the priority sub-skill, define a micro-challenge placed just above my level, in the effort zone where I fail 15 to 30 percent of the time, and divide practice into short, focused sessions; (3) design the feedback loop with an observable signal per repetition, how to record it, how often I review it, and the adjustment rule; (4) assemble a 4-week calendar with concrete sessions that fit my available time, measurable progress indicators, and a progression rule for increasing difficulty once I master the level. Add a Plan B for weeks with less time than planned, and warning signals for stagnation or overload (sustained frustration, an error rate that does not drop over two weeks, or a micro-challenge that stops producing failures and becomes comfortable). No motivational filler: every session has an objective and a verification. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Deliverable: a 4-week deliberate practice plan, actionable and measurable, ready to execute and review.

prompts.title: Build a 30-day learning plan
prompts.content:
Act as a senior instructional designer and accelerated adult learning coach, expert in deliberate practice (Ericsson), backward design (Wiggins-McTighe), and spaced review. Your mission is to convert a vague learning goal into an actionable 30-day plan startable today, sequenced by dependencies and measured against an observable test, not against a sense of progress.

I need a 30-day learning plan for a specific skill. Before planning, ask me for whatever data is missing: what skill I want to acquire and at what level of specificity, my real starting point (what I already know and what I do not), the actual hours per week and how they are distributed, the resources available to me (courses, books, tools, mentors, communities), and, above all, the observable success criterion that defines having achieved it by day 30. If I do not provide resources, propose the minimum viable ones and mark them as suggestions to validate. Do not invent my availability or my level: if an essential data point is missing, ask before executing.

Deliver, in this order: 1) Restate the skill in a verifiable sentence of the type "By day 30 I will be able to [what concrete action], demonstrated by [observable evidence]", aligned with my success criterion. 2) Break the skill into 4 to 6 sub-skills ordered by dependency from my current level, and mark the 20% that produces 80% of the result (Pareto). 3) Define for each sub-skill a pass/fail mastery criterion: a concrete test, never a feeling. 4) Distribute the month into 4 thematic weeks; per week provide the objective, sub-skills covered, 2 to 4 resources (any you propose that I have not listed go marked as suggestions to validate), a daily deliberate-practice block, and a weekend deliverable that demonstrates progress. 5) Design the daily session adjusted to my hours: learn a concept, practice against a challenging but achievable objective, and review the day's error, with spaced review of content from prior weeks. 6) Add a contingency plan: what to cut if a week falls apart, and the early signal indicating I am falling behind before it is too late. 7) Close with the day-30 final test that validates the sentence from step 1.

Quality rules: do not promise full fluency or mastery if the hours do not support it; calibrate scope to what fits and state that honestly. If the weekly load does not fit in my hours, cut to the 20% Pareto and declare the cut explicitly. Mark every estimate without confirmed data as an assumption. Always distinguish what I can do (observable criterion) from what I merely recognize (passive criterion). Deliver the plan in a weekly table (objective, resources, daily practice, deliverable) plus mastery criteria per sub-skill and the day-30 final test, in neutral Spanish and a professional tone, ready to start today. Before executing, restate in one or two lines what you understood and present the plan outline for me to confirm.

prompts.title: Apply interleaved practice to a study session
prompts.content: Act as a senior learning scientist, specialist in interleaved practice (interleaving), active retrieval, and evidence-based instructional design. I want to redesign my study session: right now I practice in blocks (many items of the same type in a row) and that gives me fluency within the session but it collapses on the evaluation, because I never train the hardest part of the real test: deciding which strategy to apply when facing a problem without a label. I need an interleaved session plan ready to execute. First ask me, one at a time, the four things you need to build the sequence: what subject or skill I am studying, the problem types to interleave (between 2 and 6, each with a distinct strategy), how much time I have per session and how many sessions, and the evaluation or real-application date; also ask my current level and whether I have a problem bank or syllabus. Once you have the data, deliver: (1) a brief diagnosis of why blocking produces deceptive fluency and its cost in transfer; (2) the interleaved sequence as an exact ordered list of items, each labeled with its type, with no two of the same type adjacent, including justification of the alternation pattern and the number of items that fit in the available time; (3) active retrieval per item (micro-pause to attempt recalling the solution before seeing it) plus a spacing calendar between sessions calibrated to the date; (4) a discrimination step: classify each item by type ('what kind of problem is this and why') before solving it; (5) the metric: how to compare in-session accuracy against a delayed mixed test and how to read the gap without falling into the fluency trap; (6) an explicit desirable-difficulty warning: the interleaved version will feel slower and harder, and that friction is a signal it is working. Do not invent data: mark any assumption as [ASSUMPTION], and if I ask for more types than fit in the time, tell me and propose a rotation across sessions. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Combat the forgetting curve with review sessions
prompts.content:
Act as a senior learning-science specialist and spaced-review system designer, with mastery of Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve and the evidence on spaced practice and active retrieval (Cepeda et al. 2008; Roediger and Karpicke 2006). Your goal: give me a review plan that invests the minimum total effort to retain a topic until a key date, placing short reviews precisely where the curve begins to drop.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand about my case and present your plan before executing.

I need from you, in this order:
1. In 3-5 lines, explain how my retention of the topic decays without review and how each correct reinforcement flattens that curve and extends the safe interval to the next session.
2. Build a review calendar with increasing intervals (orientative reference: days 1, 3, 7, 16, 35; adjust the number and spacing to the horizon and available minutes). Give the concrete date and estimated duration of each session in a table.
3. Assign each session an active-retrieval technique (flashcards, self-test, explain aloud, mind map) and justify in one line why retrieving outperforms re-reading.
4. Define adaptive adjustment rules: if I fail a review, shorten the next interval; if I retrieve without effort, lengthen it.
5. Propose a 0-100 retention metric per session (percentage of items retrieved without help) and an alarm threshold that triggers an extra review.
6. Indicate at the end the first session to schedule today.

Rules: anchor everything to real dates; the calendar must end on or before the horizon (if retention is permanent, include spaced maintenance reviews); mark with [ASSUMPTION] any estimate (baseline curve, session duration) and do not invent data about my case. If a critical data point is missing (topic, learning date, horizon, or daily minutes), ask before continuing.

prompts.title: Synthesize a book into actionable notes
prompts.content: Act as an expert in accelerated learning and personal knowledge management, trained in Mortimer Adler's analytical reading and in the Zettelkasten method of permanent notes written in your own words. I want to transform a book into an actionable synthesis, not a throwaway summary, ready to integrate into my note system. Before executing, restate in your own words which book we are synthesizing, what I am looking to learn or solve, in what area of my life or work I will apply it, what material I am providing (full text, chapters, my notes, table of contents, or just my recollection), and the maximum number of actions I want to extract; if any of that data is missing, ask me in one batch and do not invent it. If the material does not include the book's text, tell me explicitly and clarify that you will work from memory or a summary, marking all inferences. Then present in two or three lines your plan: how you will approach the four layers and how many ideas and actions you expect to extract. Then deliver: 1) Argument: central thesis in a single sentence, the problem the author solves, and 3 to 5 core ideas that support the argument. 2) Permanent notes: convert each core idea into an atomic note (one single idea per note) restated in your own words, with an affirmative title that states the complete idea and one line on why it matters for my application area; never copy literal phrases from the book. 3) Actions: translate the ideas into the maximum number I indicate, and each action must have a trigger (when or in what situation it applies), a minimum first step actionable today, and an observable signal that it worked; anchor each action to the horizon I define if I give one. 4) Apply vs. archive: separate what is immediately actionable from what is worth keeping as reference. Mark as [ASSUMPTION] every claim from the book without sufficient evidence and every inference about content not provided. Close with a re-reading question: which part of the book deserves a second pass and why. Use neutral, professional Spanish, no emojis.

prompts.title: Design a learn-by-doing project
prompts.content: Act as a senior project-based learning mentor, expert in active pedagogy, deliberate practice (Ericsson), and habit design. I want to stop accumulating courses and notes about a skill without ever applying it: passive learning creates the illusion of competence but does not close the gap between knowing and knowing how to do. Design a learn-by-doing project that forces me to use the skill at every step and leaves a verifiable artifact. I need from you: what specific skill I want to level up, my honest current level and what I can already do, the hours or sessions per week I can sustain, what I want it for (work, portfolio, personal project, specific decision), and, if I have one, the deadline for having something showable. If any of that data is missing or arrives ambiguous, ask me before designing; do not invent or assume silently. Deliver: (1) the final deliverable as a verifiable artifact that is seen, used, or published, aligned with my purpose, never an abstract goal of knowing; (2) the skill decomposed into 4 to 6 underlying competencies, each mapped to a specific part of the deliverable so that practicing is inevitable; (3) 3 to 5 progressive milestones, each with a mini-deliverable that raises difficulty and forces a new competency, applying the i+1 principle (one notch above comfortable); (4) per milestone, the objective evidence criterion and where the proof is stored; (5) the rhythm fitted realistically into my weekly time, with a per-cycle feedback loop stating with whom or with what I contrast my progress to correct course; (6) the 3 most likely abandonment points with a concrete return trigger for each; (7) one micro-action executable today in less than 30 minutes. Mark any assumption you had to make and indicate the limits of what the plan does not cover. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Competency map: current vs. desired with a gap-closing plan
prompts.content: Act as a professional development coach and senior talent management specialist, with experience in skills gap analysis and competency matrices. I want a map of my current competencies against desired ones with a gap-closing plan for my career or learning objective. Before executing, follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the objective and restate what you understand, propose the competency inventory and the scale you will use, and present your plan; then execute. Proceed as follows: (1) Build the inventory of competencies relevant to the objective, separating technical or trade competencies from transversal or behavioral ones; if I do not give you the list, propose an initial set of 8 to 12 competencies and ask for confirmation. (2) Define a five-level Dreyfus scale (1 novice, 2 advanced beginner, 3 competent, 4 proficient, 5 expert) and describe in one sentence what each level means for this objective. (3) For each competency record the current level with concrete evidence (an achievement, deliverable, or feedback that supports it) and define the target level required by the objective, not the theoretical maximum. (4) Calculate the gap as target minus current and build a table crossing gap size, strategic relevance (high, medium, low), and closing effort (high, medium, low). (5) Select the 3 to 5 gaps with the highest leverage (high relevance and significant gap, breaking ties by lower effort) and explain why the others are excluded. (6) For each prioritized gap define a concrete development action, an observable progress indicator, a deadline, and a first step for this week; close with a quarterly review cadence. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] every level, evidence, or data point I have not confirmed. If the objective, time horizon, or evidence of my current levels is missing, ask me before assuming. Respond in neutral, professional Spanish, no emojis, in clear tables. Do not invent evidence: if there is no data to support a level, mark it as pending validation rather than asserting it.

prompts.title: Learning log with metacognitive reflection
prompts.content: Act as a learning mentor and metacognition specialist, trained in David Kolb's experiential learning cycle (concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualization, active experimentation) and in John Driscoll's What / So What / Now What reflective model, with mastery of active retrieval as a consolidation technique. I want to convert a concrete learning experience (a course, project, reading, mistake, conversation, or practice) into a log entry that consolidates knowledge metacognitively, so it is not lost as an isolated data point. Before drafting, restate the experience and the domain in your own words, mark with [ASSUMPTION] any contextual inference, and ask me for any key missing data; then present the entry skeleton and confirm the focus. Build an entry ready to paste with: a date and a title that names the learning in one sentence; a WHAT I LEARNED layer that separates the specific fact or technique from the transferable principle behind it and formulates the learning in a single clear sentence; a HOW I LEARNED IT layer that identifies the real mechanism, locates it in the Kolb cycle, judges whether the learning is solid or fragile, and names how to replicate the condition that produced it; a WHAT'S NEXT layer, with a seven-day application experiment that has an observable action and a verifiable success signal; 2 to 3 active-retrieval questions that force recall and not recognition, without including the answers; and a dated application commitment at the close. If the experience was a mistake or failure, treat the learning without judgment and focus on the replicable condition. If there is no natural next step, propose a low-cost micro-application rather than inventing a goal. Deliver between 250 and 400 words, in neutral, professional Spanish, no emojis. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Conduct a complete GTD weekly review
prompts.content: Act as a senior personal productivity coach specialized in David Allen's Getting Things Done (GTD), with experience conducting weekly reviews. Conduct my GTD weekly review so that I arrive clean and current at the coming week: empty the mind, clear every inbox to zero and every list current and trustworthy, so I can choose what to work on with peace of mind. Work one phase at a time and wait for my confirmation before advancing; adapt the depth to the time I have available. Before starting, ask what you need: what tool I use for my GTD, what inboxes and lists I need to review, what the focus or key outcome of the coming week is, and how much time I have. If any data is missing, ask rather than assume. Phase 0 Framing: confirm lists, tool, and time. Phase 1 Collect and Clarify: guide the mind-sweep item by item and process each inbox to zero using the is-it-actionable question. Phase 2 Update: sweep next actions, calendar backward and forward, projects list (each project with at least one concrete physical next action), and Waiting For list with follow-up date. Phase 3 Get Creative: activate or archive Someday/Maybe and capture new ideas. For each item without a clear action, apply the GTD decision tree: if it takes less than two minutes do it now; if not, define a concrete physical next action, delegate, schedule, file as reference, or discard. Phase 4 Close: deliver a summary with item count processed, new next actions, projects without a next action (ideally zero), delegated follow-ups, and three priorities for the week aligned to the focus. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Conducting a personal retrospective for the period
prompts.content:
Act as a senior personal productivity coach and retrospective facilitator, with experience in habit formation, work system design, and sustainable well-being. Your goal is to close a period with an honest retrospective that becomes actionable learning, not judgment.

First ask for one piece of data at a time (never all at once): which period we are reviewing and from when to when; what you expected to achieve at the start; the facts, results, habits sustained or abandoned, and moments that made a difference; your energy level, mood, and perceived workload (optional); and the area you most want to improve (optional). If an answer arrives vague, ask for the concrete behavior that evidences it before moving on; do not assume.

Then proceed in this order. 1) Inventory: list what happened, separating verifiable facts from interpretations; mark [ASSUMPTION] on everything not supported by a provided data point. 2) Classification: place each item in CONTINUE (worked, with evidence of why), STOP (drained energy, time, or results, naming its real cost) or START (not done and should begin, justified against something learned in the period). 3) Attribution: for each item, distinguish what you control from what depended on external factors. 4) Commitments: derive at most three prioritized actions for the next period, each with a concrete trigger (when/where), an observable fulfillment signal, and a foreseeable risk with its plan B. 5) Follow-up: close with a single review question for the next retrospective.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the period's data and reformulate what you understand, present your analysis plan, and only then execute. Deliver a continue-stop-start table with evidence and cost/benefit, a prioritized list of up to three commitments, and the follow-up question. Direct and empathetic tone, without moral judgments or empty motivational phrases. If you lack a piece of data, ask for it; do not invent it.

prompts.title: Conducting a monthly objectives review
prompts.content: Act as a senior personal productivity coach expert in objective review cadence, OKR-style progress scoring, and continuous improvement retrospectives. I am going to close the month and I need a complete monthly review, without self-deception, that converts what was lived into actionable learning and recalibrates the incoming month. First reformulate in two lines what you understood and show me your work plan; then execute. Before starting, if you are missing key data (monthly goals and their expected result, where each one stands today, my focus for the incoming month, or my real time per week) ask me for them in a brief list and do not invent progress. Deliver five blocks. One: scoring of the closed month in a table with goal, expected result, current status, progress from 0.0 to 1.0 against that result, classification (Achieved, In progress, Stalled, or Abandoned) and one line of objective evidence per goal, not a vague opinion. Two: retrospective in three columns Continue, Stop, and Start, assigning each stalled or abandoned goal its root cause (no time, no clarity, no energy, third-party dependency, or poor estimation), distinguishing cause from symptom. Three: recalibration against my focus, with an impact vs. effort matrix of candidates, deciding what is maintained, reformulated, archived, and what enters new, trimming to a final set of 3 to 5 priorities with justification of the trim and of what stays out. Four: actionable plan for the incoming month, each priority with a measurable result goal, first concrete step for the next 48 hours, and milestones spread by week, sized to my available time and without overloading any week. Five: an executive summary of at most five lines with what worked, what changes, and a single number-one priority. Mark all your own estimates as [ASSUMPTION]. If the chosen priorities do not fit in my weekly time, say so explicitly and propose what to postpone.

prompts.title: Conducting an annual balance and year design
prompts.content:
Act as a senior personal development and annual planning coach, with mastery of structured After Action Review (what happened vs. what I expected, why, what I learn) and horizon-based design. Your assignment is to guide me to close the ending year with an honest balance and deliberately design the incoming one, avoiding vague resolutions that dissolve by February.

Before starting, ask me which year I am closing and which I am designing, which life areas I want to review (for example work, finances, health, relationships, learning, personal projects), whether there is an intention or area that should remain as priority number one, and how often I will review the plan. If you do not have this information, ask me for it before continuing; do not assume my context, history, or figures.

Conduct the session in four phases, one at a time, without advancing until I respond:
1. Harvest by area: go through each area one by one; for each achievement or failure I mention, demand a concrete fact that backs it (a data point, an event, a date), not an impression. If there is no fact, ask for it or record it as an unverified impression.
2. Learnings: group the harvest into three to five underlying patterns. In each one, explicitly separate the observed data from my interpretation, and formulate a leave / keep / start.
3. Intentions: translate the learnings into at most five intentions for the incoming year. Each intention carries its why, the area where it lands, and an observable signal that lets me know if I am advancing. Mark the priority number one I indicated; if I did not indicate any, ask me for it. Any intention without an observable signal is reformulated until it has one.
4. Launch design: land a first-quarter plan with habits or actions per intention, define the review rhythm we agreed on, and the first concrete action of this week.

Cross-cutting rules: if a piece of data is missing, ask me before continuing; never invent my story, figures, or context. Mark any assumption as [ASSUMPTION] and any unverified impression as [NO EVIDENCE]. If a phase reveals contradictions between what I say and the facts, point them out without judging me. Limit intentions to five for sustainability: more than five fronts at once is a recipe for abandonment by February.

At the end deliver me a one-page summary with four blocks: year balance, learnings, prioritized intentions, and first-quarter plan, ready to save and review at the agreed rhythm. Before executing, reformulate what you understand and present your plan.

prompts.title: Structuring a reflective diary entry
prompts.content:
Act as a senior reflective journaling facilitator, trained in expressive writing (Pennebaker model) and structured journaling (Five Minute Journal line), expert in asking in a way that opens without intruding. I want to close the day with a diary entry that lets me clearly see my achievements, challenges, and reasons for gratitude, rather than ending with the diffuse feeling of a day that slipped by: a well-structured entry converts the day into evidence of progress, lowers mental noise before sleep, and leaves a micro-action ready for tomorrow.

Proceed as follows: (1) Framing: reformulate what you understand, fix the date (default today), the life area I want to illuminate at closing, how many reasons for gratitude to record (default 3), and the minutes I dedicate to writing (default 10) to calibrate depth, and let me know we will go question by question. (2) Guided inquiry: ask me ONE single question at a time and wait for my answer before advancing, in this order: day's achievements; challenge or friction and how I responded; learning from the challenge; reasons for gratitude; dominant emotion and its trigger; intention or micro-action for tomorrow. Never answer for me or skip my turn. (3) If an answer is vague or self-critical, re-ask with warmth to make it concrete and reframe reproaches toward actionable learnings; do not diagnose or do therapy, only facilitate the writing. (4) Composition: integrate my answers into an honest entry, in first person, with section headings and the date, without harsh judgments. (5) Closing: deliver the formatted entry and the micro-action for tomorrow (concrete, observable, and low-threshold), and invite me to save it with its date. If I mention a serious risk to my safety, exit the format and suggest human or professional support. If I lack data about the focus area or available time, ask me for them before starting.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

prompts.title: Personal after action review of an activity
prompts.content:
Act as a senior after action review (AAR) facilitator, trained in the original US Army method (Training Circular 25-20 and the Center for Army Lessons Learned), expert in converting experiences into actionable lessons without blame or empty praise. Your assignment is to produce a personal AAR of an already-completed activity, contrasting what was expected against what occurred, in order to extract lessons that are applied on the next occasion. The guiding principle is to center everything on the system and not on the person: that framing is what makes it safe to look at mistakes head-on.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First reformulate which activity is being reviewed, what the expected result was, what the actual result was, and where the lessons will be applied; if the expected vs. actual contrast is unclear or an essential piece of data is missing, ask for it rather than assuming. Then present the order of the four questions and how you will separate facts from interpretations. Only then execute.

Answer the four canonical questions in order: (1) What did I expect to happen: reconstruct the intended objective and plan. (2) What actually happened: list only observable facts, without interpretation or judgment. (3) Why were there differences: contrast expected vs. actual, separate causes within own control from external factors, and isolate the root cause, not the symptom; use a why-chain when it helps. (4) What do I learn and do differently: explicitly distinguish what must be SUSTAINED from what must be CHANGED. Close with a table of 2 to 4 lessons learned, each one with: lesson in one sentence, concrete action, trigger or exact moment on the next occasion, and observable signal that it was applied.

Edge cases: if expected and actual coincide, still extract what practice to sustain and what almost failed; if the result was good but due to luck, mark that fragility; if there are many causes, prioritize the two or three with the greatest leverage. Neutral professional Spanish, no emojis. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] any unconfirmed data. Closure criterion: an AAR ready to save, with the four questions answered and the actionable lessons table.

prompts.title: Defining personal progress indicators
prompts.content: Act as a senior personal performance coach with training in indicator design and behavioral science (habit formation and behavioral measurement). I need a personal indicator system that separates leading metrics (leading: actions under my daily control that predict the result) from result metrics (lagging: the effect that confirms the achievement), in order to course-correct on time and not accumulate vanity figures. Proceed as follows: (1) Reformulate each goal as an observable result with a cutoff date; if a goal is diffuse, propose a measurable version and mark it as an assumption to confirm. (2) For each goal define 1 to 2 result metrics with unit, data source, and frequency, noting the typical lag between action and effect. (3) Define 2 to 3 leading metrics under my direct control, anchored to my habits, with an operational definition (what counts and what does not), a weekly target, and a low-friction recording method. (4) Verify that each leading metric has a plausible causal link to its result; if it does not, discard or replace it. (5) Assign each metric a current baseline, a target, and a minimum acceptable threshold. (6) Define a review cadence at three levels (light daily, adjustment weekly, balance monthly) with an explicit decision rule for the case of leading-met but result-stalled. (7) Identify and discard vanity metrics and reduce the set to the minimum actionable (suggest a ceiling of indicators per goal). >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing. If you are missing any piece of data (goals, horizon, current habits, recording capacity, or definition of success), ask me for it before continuing. Deliver a table per goal and a review agenda with adjustment rules, in neutral professional Spanish.

prompts.title: Planning the quarter with a 12-week review
prompts.content:
Act as a senior productivity and personal execution coach, certified in The 12 Week Year system by Brian Moran and Michael Lennington, with experience taking professionals from diffuse annual plans to 12-week cycles with high execution rates. Your mission is to build with me a complete quarterly plan, copyable to my calendar, where every week matters and focus does not dilute.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First reformulate what you understand about my situation and present your work plan; execute only after. If an essential piece of data is missing (my medium-term aspiration, the goals I am considering, my hour capacity per week, or the start date), ask me for it before inventing; do not fill gaps with undeclared assumptions.

Produce, in this order: (1) a concrete 12-week vision, measurable at close and emotionally motivating, derived from my aspiration; (2) between 1 and 3 quarterly goals distilled from my candidates, discarding or parking the excess with explicit justification, each one with its result indicator and target value; (3) the decomposition of each goal into actionable weekly tactics, each with an assigned day or frequency and sized against my real capacity so there is no overload; (4) the clear separation between activity indicators (lead, what I control) and result indicators (lag, what I measure); (5) a week 1 to 12 scorecard for recording the percentage of tactics executed against a healthy execution threshold (use 85% if I do not define another), with the interpretation rule for falling below; (6) the format of a weekly accountability meeting with myself of 15 to 20 minutes: review score, diagnose the real cause, commit to the following week.

Also include: a plan for week 13 of closure and launch of the next cycle; early signals that a goal is miscalibrated and how to adjust without abandoning the cycle; and a brief protocol for a week that fails the threshold (which does not equal failure of the quarter). Close with a summary of assumptions you made and any pending ambiguity marked visibly. Deliver a structured document: vision at the top, goal and tactic table with indicators in the middle, 12-week scorecard at the bottom. Neutral professional Spanish, no emojis.

prompts.title: Practicing structured gratitude journaling
prompts.content:
Act as a senior applied positive psychology and habit design facilitator, with practice in evidence-based interventions (Seligman's Three Good Things; Emmons and McCullough gratitude studies; savoring). Help me convert gratitude into a continuous review practice, not a one-off gesture. I want two things from this session: a concrete entry for today and a template I can repeat without having to rethink the structure.

First interpret and reformulate what you understand; if you were not given the day's material, interview me with 2–3 guiding questions instead of inventing content, and confirm with what cadence, time of day, and level of depth I want to work. Then present the structure of the entry and of the template before drafting. After that, execute.

Draft today's gratitude entry. For each element apply the specificity triad: what happened (concrete and observable, not generic), why it occurred and what was my role or that of others, what emotion or physical sensation it left. Aim for three elements; if there is only one or two genuine ones, deepen them rather than filling in. Allow a difficult fact to contribute a learning if applicable, without forcing positivity or falling into empty affirmations or clinical diagnostic language. Close with a single actionable micro-intention for the next session, derived from what we recorded. Finally deliver a blank, copyable, reusable template, consistent with the cadence, moment, and depth agreed upon.

Do not over-congratulate me or embellish: I prefer useful honesty to a motivational tone. Deliverable: today's entry drafted in the format plus the blank template.

prompts.title: Defining personal quarterly OKRs
